contexts: Introduction and study aim: states that statins may affect breast cancer recurrence, but their effect on breast cancer-specific mortality is unclear, and describes the population-based Finnish cohort approach.

Methods, data sources: describes the cohort of all newly diagnosed Finnish breast cancer patients 1995–2003 (31,236 cases) from the Finnish Cancer Registry, statin exposure from a national prescription database, and the Cox regression analysis with time-dependent statin use.

Results, cohort characteristics and follow-up: reports 4,151 statin users, median follow-up of 3.25 years, 6,011 deaths of which 3,619 (60.2%) were from breast cancer, and begins the adjusted analysis (age, tumor characteristics, treatment).

Main findings: post- and pre-diagnostic statin use both associated with lower breast cancer death risk (HR 0.46 and HR 0.54), and the post-diagnostic association is attributed to healthy adherer bias, since discontinuation by dying patients inflates the apparent benefit.

Interpretation: post-diagnostic effect lacks dose-dependence and appears even at low-dose/short-term use, consistent with bias; the dose- and time-dependent benefit among pre-diagnostic users suggests a possible causal effect.
Conclusion: recommends a clinical trial to test whether statins improve survival in breast cancer patients, following the observational findings.

Introduction and study background: neurotoxicity of brominated flame retardants shown in animal and in vitro work, with human evidence noted as sparse; also introduces the Flanders biomonitoring context.
Methods: the Flanders (Belgium) biomonitoring study of high school students, using the NES-3 neurobehavioral battery and blood sampling, with cross-sectional data from 515 adolescents aged 13.6-17.

Methods on statistical approach: multiple regression adjusted for confounders, linking serum biomarkers of brominated flame retardant exposure (PBDE congeners 47, 99, 100, 153, 209, HBCD, TBBPA) to cognitive performance.

Results opening: main finding that doubling of summed serum PBDEs was linked to fewer preferred-hand taps in the Finger Tapping motor test; also introduces the thyroid outcomes (FT3, FT4, TSH) examined.
Results on thyroid and motor effects: consistent PBDE congener effects on motor speed, and decreases in FT3 associated with PBDE-99 and PBDE-100 above the quantification level versus below.
Results on TSH and domain specificity: PBDE-47 above quantification linked to a 10.1% TSH increase; PBDEs showed no effects on neurobehavioral domains beyond motor function.

Results on HBCD/TBBPA and study conclusions: HBCD and TBBPA lacked consistent associations with neurobehavioral tests; authors claim this is among the largest human studies of brominated flame retardant neurobehavioral effects.
Concluding statement: the findings align with animal data, indicating PBDE exposure is associated with altered motor function and thyroid hormone levels in adolescents.

Abstract opening: background on prenatal PBDE exposure and thyroid disruption, and the pilot study's aims of relating lower- and higher-brominated PBDEs and OH-PBDEs to thyroid measures in pregnant women.

Study methods and population: serum PBDEs, OH-PBDEs, TSH, total T4 and free T4 measured in 25 second-trimester pregnant women in California (2008-2009), plus the note that lower-brominated PBDE and OH-PBDE medians were the highest reported to date in pregnant women.

Key exposure results: median BDE-47, ΣPBDE5 and ΣOH-PBDE4 concentrations in lipid or serum units, and the first thyroid finding, a positive association between the transthyretin-binder weighted sum (ΣTTR binders) and TSH.

Main thyroid association results: positive links between TSH and several PBDE and OH-PBDE measures (ΣPBDE5, ΣOH-PBDE4, BDE-47, BDE-85, 5-OH-BDE47, 4′-OH-BDE49), an inverse link with BDE-207, and weak, inconsistent findings for free and total T4.
Concluding statement: PBDE exposures are elevated among pregnant women in California and relate to thyroid function, and further research is needed to assess pregnancy risks from PBDE exposure.
Introduction/background and objective of the CHAMACOS study on prenatal and childhood PBDE flame retardant exposure and neurodevelopment in a California birth cohort.
Study population and methods: CHAMACOS birth cohort, PBDE serum measurements in mothers and children, and neurobehavioral assessments (attention, motor, cognition) at ages 5 (n=310) and 7 (n=323).

Key results for maternal prenatal PBDEs: impaired attention (continuous performance task and maternal report), poorer fine motor coordination especially nondominant hand, and lower Verbal and Full-Scale IQ at age 7.

Key results for child PBDEs at age 7: associations with teacher-reported attention problems and lower Processing Speed, Perceptual Reasoning, Verbal Comprehension, and Full-Scale IQ, robust to adjustment for birth weight, gestational age, and maternal thyroid hormones.
Conclusions that prenatal and childhood PBDE exposures relate to poorer attention, fine motor skills, and cognition in school-age children, described as the largest such study to date.
Closing statement summarizing that the findings add to growing evidence that PBDEs adversely affect child neurobehavioral development.
Introduction and background of a study on PBDE flame retardant exposure in the U.S. population, stating the research objective of linking dietary intake to serum body burdens.

Methods section describing the use of two dietary instruments (24-hour food recall and 1-year food frequency questionnaire) from the 2003–2004 NHANES, and the list of five PBDE congeners measured in serum.
Statistical methods and key results: regression models adjusted for demographics and BMI, and findings that vegetarians had lower serum ∑PBDE levels than omnivores.
Results on food groups: serum PBDEs rose with poultry fat intake (geometric mean values by intake tertile), with similar but weaker trends for red meat fat.

Null findings for dairy and fish, comparison of robustness between the two dietary instruments, and the main conclusion that poultry and red meat intake significantly contribute to U.S. PBDE body burdens.
Final fragment completing the conclusion sentence that dietary intake of contaminated poultry and red meat contributes to PBDE body burdens in the U.S.

Abstract opening of a 2008 systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs on fibre, antispasmodics, and peppermint oil for irritable bowel syndrome, stating the objective, design, and literature data sources searched up to April 2008.

Eligibility criteria for the IBS review: randomised trials of fibre, antispasmodics, or peppermint oil versus placebo or no treatment in adults, with a minimum one-week therapy duration and required outcomes of global cure/improvement or abdominal pain relief, followed by the random effects pooling method.

Review methods and start of results from the IBS meta-analysis: the random effects model and relative risk of persistent symptoms as the effect measure, then the fibre result from 12 studies in 591 patients (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.00).

Results on fibre subtype and antispasmodics: ispaghula alone showed a benefit (RR 0.78), and 22 antispasmodic placebo-controlled trials in 1778 patients gave RR 0.68, with the subsequent start of the otilonium findings.

Key subgroup results from the IBS meta-analysis: otilonium (four trials, RR 0.55) and hyoscine (three trials, RR 0.63) showed consistent antispasmodic efficacy, peppermint oil across four trials in 392 patients gave RR 0.43, and the review's overall conclusion that all three treatments beat placebo.

Final sentence of the abstract's conclusion for the IBS systematic review, summarising that fibre, antispasmodics, and peppermint oil were all more effective than placebo in treating irritable bowel syndrome.

Introduction to a review of treatment options for functional abdominal pain in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), framing the problem for primary care, gastroenterology and pain specialists and previewing coverage of non-pharmacological and pharmacological therapies.

Discussion of psychological and dietary/drug options for IBS: cognitive behavioral therapy and hypnotherapy show strong results but are limited by availability and labor intensity; for patients refractory to first-line care, TCAs (uniquely shown to improve abdominal pain) and SSRIs give symptomatic relief.

Summary of evidence on dietary and fiber treatments for IBS: a low-FODMAP diet helps some subgroups with pain, bloating and stool pattern, while evidence for fiber is limited, with only isphagula possibly beneficial.

Overview of probiotic evidence (hard to interpret due to varied strains and doses) and the first-line status of antispasmodics, including peppermint oil, for IBS abdominal pain; begins describing second-line options for diarrhea-predominant IBS.

Second-line drug therapies for diarrhea-predominant IBS: rifaximin (use restricted due to rare ischemic colitis risk) and 5HT3 antagonists alosetron and ramosetron; also introduces chloride-secretion stimulators for laxative-resistant constipation-predominant IBS.

Conclusion on constipation-predominant IBS treatment: lubiprostone and linaclotide (a guanylate cyclase C agonist with direct analgesic effects) reduce abdominal pain and improve stool pattern in laxative-resistant patients.
Introduction and methods of a US community survey on irritable bowel syndrome (IBS): aims, quota sampling and random-digit telephone screening, and diagnostic criteria used (Manning, Rome I/II).
Methods continued: in-depth follow-up interviews collected data on IBS symptoms, general health, lifestyle, and the impact of symptoms on daily life, defining the survey's measured variables.
Results opening: overall IBS prevalence of 14.1% across 5009 screening interviews, split into medically diagnosed (3.3%) and undiagnosed but criteria-meeting (10.8%) cases, plus healthy controls.

Symptom patterns: abdominal pain/discomfort was the main reason for consultation, most sufferers reported alternating constipation and diarrhoea, and previously diagnosed GI disorders were more common among IBS sufferers.

Impact and conclusions: IBS sufferers had more days off work (6.4 vs 3.0), more days in bed and reduced activities, and 76.6% of US sufferers are undiagnosed, with substantial well-being and socioeconomic consequences.
Final conclusion sentence: IBS has a substantial effect on sufferers' well-being and health, with considerable socioeconomic consequences.

Introduction and aim of a double-blind RCT testing enteric-coated peppermint oil (Mintoil) for irritable bowel syndrome, with patients who have small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, lactose intolerance, or celiac disease excluded.

Methods, continued: inclusion of 57 IBS patients by Rome II criteria, with normal lactose/lactulose breath tests and negative celiac antibody screening, defining the study population after exclusions.
Methods: intervention design (two enteric-coated peppermint oil capsules twice daily versus placebo for 4 weeks, double blind) and the assessment timepoints T(0), T(4), and T(8).

Methods: the symptoms recorded (bloating, pain, diarrhoea, constipation, incomplete evacuation, defecation pain, gas or mucus, urgency), the 0-4 intensity and frequency scoring, and how the total IBS symptom score was calculated.

Results: the proportion of patients with a greater than 50% reduction in total IBS symptom score at T(4), 75% with peppermint oil versus 38% with placebo (P<0.009), and the start of the mean-score results.
Results: mean total IBS symptom scores (T(0) 2.19, T(4) 1.07, T(8) 1.60) showing significant reduction with peppermint oil and no change with placebo, plus the study conclusion.
Conclusion: a 4-week course of peppermint oil improves abdominal symptoms in patients with irritable bowel syndrome.

Introduction and methods of a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of enteric-coated peppermint oil (Colpermin) in 90 IBS outpatients, dosed three times daily for 8 weeks with follow-up visits.

Results on the primary outcome: the number of patients free from abdominal pain or discomfort rose from 0 to 14 in the Colpermin group versus 0 to 6 in controls (P < 0.001), with significant pain reduction in the Colpermin group.

Conclusions of the peppermint oil IBS trial: Colpermin significantly improved quality of life, caused no significant adverse reactions, and is effective and safe for IBS patients with abdominal pain or discomfort.
Final fragment of the abstract's concluding sentence stating that Colpermin is effective and safe for IBS patients with abdominal pain or discomfort.

Opening of the meta-analysis abstract's Background section: motivates the study by noting antidepressant-induced sexual dysfunction is underreported unless patients are directly asked, and states the aim to quantify it using studies with direct inquiry and specific questionnaires.

Methods section of the meta-analysis on antidepressant-related sexual dysfunction: describes the MEDLINE and ISI Web of Knowledge literature search, the inclusion of studies on patients without prior SD, analysis in RevMan 4.2, and the primary (total treatment-emergent SD) and secondary (desire, arousal, orgasm) outcomes.

Results opening of the abstract: reports that several antidepressants produced significantly higher total and phase-specific sexual dysfunction versus placebo, beginning the ranked list of drugs in decreasing order of impact (sertraline first).

Results continued: lists the ranked antidepressants with significantly higher sexual dysfunction than placebo (ending with fluvoxamine), gives the 25.8% to 80.3% SD range, and names the agents showing no significant difference from placebo (agomelatine, amineptine, bupropion, moclobemide, mirtazapine, nefazodone).

Discussion section: concludes that antidepressant-induced sexual dysfunction varies widely across compounds, and notes that open-label study inclusion and heterogeneous SD scales could weaken the findings.

Closing sentence of the discussion/abstract: states that treatment-emergent sexual dysfunction is a frequent adverse effect that clinicians should weigh when choosing which antidepressant to prescribe.

Abstract opening of an RCT on open-label placebos (non-deceptive, non-concealed) for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS); introduces the background rationale and the comparison against a no-treatment control with matched provider interaction.

Methods section describing the design: a two-group randomized controlled three-week trial (Aug 2009–Apr 2010) at a single academic center, with 80 mostly female IBS patients (Rome III criteria, IBS-SSS score ≥150) and the start of the randomization description.

Methods continued: the open-label placebo intervention wording given to patients (inert sugar-pill-like placebo framed as mind-body self-healing) versus no-treatment controls, plus the primary outcome (IBS-GIS) and secondary measures.
Findings begin: open-label placebo yields significantly higher IBS-GIS global improvement scores at the 11-day midpoint compared with controls (5.2±1.0 vs. 4.0±1.1, p<.001).

Findings continued: IBS-GIS at the 21-day endpoint (5.0±1.5 vs. 3.9±1.3, p=.002), significant reductions in IBS-SSS symptom severity and IBS-AR adequate relief at both time points, and a trend in IBS-QoL quality of life (p=.08).

Conclusion stating that non-deceptive placebos may effectively treat IBS, calling for further research on physician use of placebos consistent with informed consent, followed by the ClinicalTrials.gov registration start.
Final fragment giving the trial registration identifier, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01010191, for the open-label placebo IBS study.

Introduction and methods of a systematic review/meta-analysis on enteric-coated peppermint oil versus placebo for active irritable bowel syndrome, covering the study aim, background on IBS, and eligibility criteria for randomized trials.

Methods section of the peppermint oil IBS meta-analysis describing the literature search (up to February 2013), inclusion of cross-over trials, Cochrane risk of bias assessment, and the outcomes measured: global IBS improvement, abdominal pain, and adverse events.
Analysis approach and start of the results of the peppermint oil IBS meta-analysis: nine studies with 726 patients identified, with low risk of bias overall, leading into the efficacy findings.

Key efficacy results of the peppermint oil IBS meta-analysis: significant superiority over placebo for global symptom improvement and abdominal pain relief, with pooled relative risks of 2.23 and 2.14 and their 95% confidence intervals.

Safety results and conclusions of the peppermint oil IBS meta-analysis: patients had more adverse events, mostly mild and transient, with heartburn most common, and the authors conclude peppermint oil is a safe, effective short-term IBS treatment.

Final conclusion of the peppermint oil IBS meta-analysis calling for future research on long-term efficacy and safety and on comparisons with other IBS treatments such as antidepressants and antispasmodics.

Introduces the underestimated impact of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) on functioning and quality of life, noting poorer health status and worse HRQoL than patients with GERD, diabetes, or end-stage renal disease.
Describes disease-specific QoL instruments used in IBS clinical trials and notes that few trial data are yet available on QoL changes after treatment.

Reports that symptomatic therapeutic response is linked to HRQoL improvement, that HRQoL does not differ much by IBS subtype (constipation- vs diarrhea-dominant), and that bowel symptom severity strongly affects QoL.
States that patients with worse bowel symptoms have diminished QoL, and that sex and psychological conditions also influence HRQoL in IBS.
Concludes that considering these factors can individualize therapy to optimize long-term outcomes for IBS patients.

Introduction and background of a 2014 review on medication management of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), outlining the goals of covering symptom-specific drug evidence, dosing, adverse effects, and new treatment research.

Summary of the drugs with evidence of IBS symptom improvement, listing laxatives/bulking agents, antidiarrheals, antispasmodics, antidepressants, antiepileptics, antibiotics, and somatostatin analogs, plus mention of many new agents under investigation.

Key message identifying the most reliable evidence-backed IBS medications (rifaximin, lubiprostone, linaclotide, fiber supplementation, peppermint oil) and noting that treatment efficacy onset can be as early as 6 days.

Discussion of the limitations in the evidence, namely that most medications were not assessed prospectively at predefined time points, and a call for ongoing studies to clarify the place in therapy of current and new IBS medications.
Conclusion highlighting the most promising novel IBS pharmacologic approaches, especially the dual μ-opioid agonist/δ-opioid antagonist JNJ-27018966, followed by the 2014 Karger copyright notice.

Study design and methods of a randomized trial comparing true versus sham acupuncture for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), including the 230 participants, the 3-week run-in, and the waitlist control arm.
Outcome measures of the IBS acupuncture trial: primary outcome IBS Global Improvement Scale (IBS-GIS), with secondary outcomes IBS-SSS, IBS-AR, and IBS-QOL, and the start of the results section.

Key results of the IBS acupuncture trial: no significant difference between acupuncture and sham on IBS-GIS (41% vs 32%, p=0.25), both groups beating waitlist control, and non-significant trends on IBS-AR, IBS-SSS, and IBS-QOL.

Secondary results and safety findings of the IBS acupuncture trial: sensitivity analysis excluding run-in responders, mild side effects slightly more common with acupuncture, and the start of the conclusion.
Final conclusion of the IBS acupuncture trial: no evidence that acupuncture is superior to sham acupuncture for treating irritable bowel syndrome.

Document title and summary: this is the sole chunk, stating that linaclotide (Linzess) is indicated for irritable bowel syndrome with constipation (IBS-C) and chronic idiopathic constipation (CIC). Relevant to queries on linaclotide indications, Linzess uses, IBS-C treatment, and chronic constipation drugs.

This chunk opens the document, introducing irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), its high prevalence, its diagnosis by exclusion, and the limitations of current pharmacological treatments due to side effects.

This chunk describes the effectiveness gap left by pharmacotherapy and states that complementary and alternative medicines (CAM) are associated with better symptom management and quality of life in IBS patients.

This chunk summarizes clinical evidence that peppermint oil, Iberogast, hypnotherapy, cognitive behavior therapy, acupuncture, and yoga improve IBS treatment outcomes, and begins the authors' integrative approach proposal.

This chunk states the authors' proposed integrative approach, combining pharmacotherapy with CAM therapies to achieve the best possible outcome, and notes that practitioners are beginning to adopt this practice.
This chunk concludes the document by noting that practitioners increasingly recommend CAM therapies when pharmacotherapy alone does not sufficiently relieve IBS symptoms.

Opening of the DCCT abstract (diabetic retinopathy progression under intensive vs. conventional insulin treatment): states the objective, randomized design with 3-9 years follow-up, and begins describing the 1983-1989 enrollment of 1441 IDDM patients at 29 centers.

Describes the two enrolled cohorts in the DCCT retinopathy study: the primary prevention cohort (726 patients, no retinopathy, 1-5 years diabetes duration) and the secondary intervention cohort (715 patients, very mild to moderate NPDR, 1-15 years duration), with 95% exam completion.

Methods section of the abstract defining the interventions: intensive insulin therapy (three or more daily injections or pump, dosed by self-blood glucose monitoring, aiming for normoglycemia) versus conventional therapy (one or two daily insulin injections).

Outcome measures and start of results: retinopathy change assessed by masked stereoscopic fundus photo grading on the ETDRS severity scale every 6 months, followed by the cumulative 8.5-year progression rates framing the results.

Key results on progression rates: 8.5-year cumulative rates of 3+ step ETDRS progression (54.1% conventional vs 11.5% intensive in primary prevention; 49.2% vs 17.1% in secondary intervention), plus the early transient worsening effect at 6 and 12 months.
Time-course and recovery findings: beyond 3.5 years intensive therapy reduced progression risk five-fold or more, and recovery after progression was at least twice as likely with intensive treatment.

Subgroup consistency and conclusion: treatment effects were similar across baseline retinopathy severity subgroups, and the DCCT conclusion recommends intensive insulin treatment aiming for near-nondiabetic glycemia for most IDDM patients.
Final sentence of the abstract's conclusion, stating that glycemic targets should be as close to the nondiabetic range as is safely possible.

Introduces diabetic retinopathy as a common microvascular complication of diabetes, the leading preventable blindness cause in working-age adults, and its links to stroke, coronary heart disease, and heart failure; this opening frames the document's overview of the condition.

Covers risk management and treatment: glycaemic, blood pressure, and lipid control as the foundation for preventing progression, and laser therapy that preserves sight in proliferative retinopathy and macular oedema but rarely restores lost vision.

Discusses surgical and newer treatments: vitrectomy for advanced disease, and intraocular steroid and anti-VEGF injections, which are gentler on the retina and may help patients who respond poorly to conventional therapy.
Concludes the overview with promising future directions (inhibiting other angiogenic factors, regenerative and topical therapies) and the copyright notice from the 2010 Elsevier source.

Introduction of a review on pan retinal photocoagulation (PRP) for proliferative diabetic retinopathy, stating the review's purpose of comparing the traditional argon laser with the newer pattern scan laser (PASCAL) that was designed to reduce PRP side effects.
Continues the review's introduction and the 'Recent Findings' section, noting that PASCAL achieves results comparable to conventional argon PRP and creates well-aligned lesion arrays more quickly.

Summary section stating that PASCAL is replacing argon laser for PRP in many clinics, that its comfort profile is better, and that PASCAL settings (duration, number, size of burns) may need adjustment to maintain regression of neovascularization.

Closing of the review's summary, concluding that PASCAL settings may need tuning to prevent neovascularization recurrence and that further studies are needed to establish optimal safety and efficacy parameters.
Final fragment of the document ending the review's last sentence, referring to PASCAL as the laser being discussed.

Introduction and methods of a systematic review on managing diabetic retinopathy (DR), including diabetic macular edema: states DR as leading cause of working-age blindness in the US, the review objective, and the search strategy (MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane, ARVO, NIH trials database).
Methods continued: database sources and date range for the English-language systematic search, plus manual reference-list searching of major reviews, covering DR and diabetic macular edema evidence.

Inclusion criteria and synthesis start: English-language RCTs with over 12 months follow-up and meta-analyses, Delphi consensus used to judge study quality, and 44 studies (3 meta-analyses) included; begins noting glycemic control.

Key findings on effectiveness: tight glycemic and blood pressure control reduces DR incidence and progression; pan-retinal laser cuts moderate-to-severe visual loss by about 50% in severe nonproliferative and proliferative retinopathy; focal laser reduces moderate visual loss in macular edema.

Further evidence findings: focal laser benefit range, early vitrectomy improving visual recovery with severe vitreous hemorrhage, intravitreal steroids as option after conventional treatment failure, and insufficient evidence for lipid-lowering, medical, or anti-VEGF therapies.

Conclusions: tight glycemic and blood pressure control is the cornerstone of primary DR prevention; pan-retinal and focal laser reduce visual loss in severe DR and macular edema respectively; evidence lacking for other treatments.
Final conclusion sentence: there is currently insufficient evidence to recommend routine use of treatments beyond glycemic/blood pressure control and laser photocoagulation for diabetic retinopathy.
Opening of the document introducing CMV retinitis as the leading cause of vision loss in AIDS patients, its prevalence before HAART, and how HAART changed its incidence.
Discusses the clinical approach to CMV retinitis: evaluating immune status, classifying retinal lesions, starting or improving HAART, and the list of systemic anti-CMV drugs.
Covers local treatment options such as intravitreal injections or ganciclovir reservoir implants for zone 1 retinitis, and the outcomes of combined anti-CMV therapy with HAART.
Describes complications such as immune recovery uveitis and retinal detachment, and how treatment goals shifted from short-term control to long-term vision preservation after HAART.
Addresses resource-limited settings, where shortages of clinicians and medications exist, and suggests intravitreal ganciclovir as the most cost-effective option there.

Introduces defecography: a real-time imaging exam of rectal and anal canal morphology and function using injected barium paste and evacuation, and lists its main clinical indications (chronic constipation, anorectal pain, residual sensation, suspected prolapse).

Concludes the indications list for defecography (unexplained anal/rectal pain, residual sensation after defecation, suspected prolapse) and states that the review will cover the technique and interpretation of the exam.

Study of pressure in superficial leg veins of varicose vein patients vs. normal controls, measuring the effect of raised intra-abdominal pressure; introduces the finding that controls showed no venous pressure rise while varicose patients did.
Conclusion of the varicose veins pressure study: squatting offers no advantage over sitting, so defecation posture does not explain the geographic variation in varicose vein prevalence.

This chunk is the document's abstract/summary. It states that current aetiological theories of varicose veins, deep vein thrombosis, and haemorrhoids are judged inadequate based on epidemiological evidence, and proposes that faecal arrest from a low-residue diet is the underlying cause of these disorders.

Introduction and aims of the study: tests whether faecal retention in the colon (measured by colon transit time and radiographic faecal loading) causes functional bowel disease, appendicitis, and haemorrhoids, with patient and control cohorts.

Study population and methods: patients and healthy controls, questionnaire on symptoms, and key finding that functional bowel disorder patients (mostly women) show increased colon transit time and faecal load versus controls.

Results on correlations: colon transit time correlates with segmental and total faecal load, faecal load is stable at 48 and 96 hours (permanent reservoirs), and bloating correlates with right-colon faecal load.

Symptom correlations and hidden constipation: abdominal pain relates to distal faecal load and bloating, and a subset (n=90) has high faecal load with normal transit time, described as hidden constipation.
Regional distribution of faecal load: transit time and faecal load are highest in the right colon, including among healthy controls, and correlate with left iliac fossa mass and meteorism.
Cluster analysis of symptoms: transit time and faecal load correlate positively with a bloating/proctalgia/infrequent solid defecation factor and negatively with a frequent easy defecation factor.

Characteristics of patients with heavy faecal load but normal transit: mostly repetitive daily easy defecation with changing stool consistency; flu-like episodes co-occur with abdominal pain and meteorism.

Symptom clusters linked to palpable right iliac fossa mass and tenderness, and to seldom, difficult defecation with epigastric discomfort and halitosis; patients with seldom, difficult defecation had prolonged transit and high faecal load.

Patients with seldom, difficult defecation: more abdominal pain, right iliac fossa mass with tenderness, meteorism; in normal-transit patients with high load, only those with pain showed a load-bloating correlation.

Colonic redundancy (colon length) findings: transit time and faecal load rise with number of redundancies, which also increases bloating and pain; introduces the bowel stimulation intervention (fibre, fluid, exercise, prokinetic).

Intervention outcomes: the bowel stimulation regimen reduced transit time, faecal load, bloating, and pain, and normalised defecation toward about one easy solid stool per day, supporting faecal retention as the cause.

Further intervention effects: reduced proctalgia, flu-like episodes, tender right fossa mass, and rectal constipation; the regimen did not change transit or load in normal-transit patients, though their bloating and pain improved.
Discussion of mechanism: faecal retention does not explain its cause, but constipated and irritable bowel may share one disease dimension with faecal retention as a common factor.

Clinical implication and surgical cohort: measuring transit time and faecal load can aid functional diagnosis; 35 conservatively refractory patients underwent colectomy for prolonged transit and heavy load, often with dolichocolon and prior appendectomy.
Surgical patient characteristics: operated patients had prolonged transit, heavy faecal load, redundant colon (dolichocolon) more often, and an extremely high rate of previous appendectomy.

Surgical procedures and conversions: 21 hemicolectomies, 11 subtotal colectomies with ileosigmoidal anastomosis, and 3 stomas; some segmental colectomies were later converted to subtotal colectomy for persisting symptoms.

Surgical outcomes: total colectomy leakage rate 4.9% (one death); after mean 5-year follow-up most patients were free of pain and bloating with two to four controlled daily defecations and improved quality of life.

Appendicitis background: faecaliths in the appendix cause many acute appendicitis cases, which is rare outside white populations; introduces a case-control study of 56 patients and 44 controls testing faecal retention as the faecalith source.
Appendicitis case-control results: transit time and faecal load were higher in appendicitis patients but not significantly so; power calculations indicated more patients were needed.

Faecalith findings: faecaliths were most often in gangrenous or perforated appendices and did not differ in transit or load; right-sided faecal load was still higher than left and distal load. Also introduces haemorrhoids, found in half of functional bowel disorder patients.

Stapled haemorrhoidopexy study: first Danish reports of this procedure (n = 40 and 258 patients), mostly prolapsed haemorrhoids, with up to 5 years follow-up showing durable results and a normal anus.
Haemorrhoidopexy outcomes: short operation, low post-operative pain, rapid recovery, no incontinence, and high satisfaction linked to a normal anus without prolapse.

Haemorrhoidopexy durability and prediction: re-operation risk highest in first two years; repeated procedures for persisting prolapse worked well; preoperative severity and immediate result predicted durability.
Haemorrhoidopexy complications: bleeding requiring haemostasis was most common; one serious case involved anastomotic leak from a high anastomosis with extensive gas, resolved conservatively.

Stapling technique and common cause: stapling has transformed treatment of prolapsing haemorrhoids; introduces the idea that constipation, diverticulosis, IBS, colon cancer, and haemorrhoids share a common cause.

Epidemiological links: constipation, diverticulosis and IBS raise colon cancer and adenoma risk, and these diseases are rare where appendicitis is rare; haemorrhoids are a colonic comorbidity, and functional bowel disorder patients had much higher prior appendectomy rates.
Appendectomy and transit: patients with prior appendectomy had significantly longer transit times, supporting faecal retention as the origin of faecaliths and appendicitis.

Neoplasia link: faecal reservoirs in the right and left colon, the sites with highest adenoma and cancer incidence, were found in patients and controls; familial colorectal cancer was more common in patients with higher faecal load.

Cancer risk mechanism and totals: four malignancies and 25 adenomas were found; faecal retention raises bacterial counts and chronic mucosal inflammation, a cancer risk factor, possibly progressing functional disease to organic disease.
Conclusion: a fibre-rich diet and regular physical activity are therapeutic and preventive against colorectal diseases linked to faecal retention.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the word 'retention' and the document.
Study design and methods for a comparison of straining during defecation across three toilet postures (standard sitting, lower sitting, squatting), describing the 28 volunteers and their timed task.
Continuation of the methods: the three seating positions and their heights, the subjective rating of defecation effort, and the six recorded bowel movements per position.
Key results: time to satisfactory emptying and subjective straining were sharply lower when squatting than in both sitting positions (P < 0.0001), leading to the study's conclusion.
Concluding sentence of the study: sitting defecation requires excessive expulsive effort compared with squatting, with implications for human health.

Opening of an abstract on cerebral vascular resistance in humans during the Valsalva maneuver; introduces the measurements (CSF pressure, arterial pressure, internal carotid flow) and the straining phase II results showing reduced flow with lower mean arterial pressure.

Middle of the abstract covering phase IV, where rising arterial pressure raises internal carotid flow, and the method: perfusion pressure (MAP minus CSF pressure) and carotid flow are used to compute an index of cerebral vascular resistance.

Concluding findings of the abstract: a modest but significant drop in cerebral vascular resistance during phases II and III, returning to control in phase IV, and the conclusion that these changes were too slow or small to keep cerebral perfusion constant during the Valsalva maneuver.
Final fragment of the abstract's last sentence, ending the conclusion about the Valsalva maneuver and cerebral perfusion; contains no new content beyond the closing words.
Introduces primary (simple) constipation, attributing difficulty emptying bowels in people with normal stool frequency to the obstructive recto-anal angle created by the sitting defecation posture.
Explains that squatting is the natural defecation posture, whose recto-anal alignment allows smooth elimination and avoids straining that could damage the recto-anal region, colon, and other organs.
States that habitual timing of bowel elimination does not meaningfully aid rectal emptying, and that responding to a strong defecation reflex eases emptying via the recto-anal inhibitory reflex.
Final fragment completing the sentence on the recto-anal inhibitory reflex, which facilitates bowel emptying.
Introduction of the defecation syncope study: no prior literature, and the patient cohort description (20 patients, demographics, number of episodes) from a larger prospective syncope study.
Clinical features and diagnostic findings: recumbent/sleeping status before defecation urge, identified causes (GI, cardiac, TIA, orthostatic hypotension), and cases with no identifiable cause.
Outcomes: no identifiable cause in 11 patients with new medical problems in four, two-year follow-up showing recurrence mostly unrelated to defecation, and seven deaths from chronic disease.
Conclusions: defecation syncope is not a single entity; multiple pathologic abnormalities plus sleep and defecation physiology contribute, so careful evaluation for underlying illness is recommended.
Final sentence of the conclusion recommending thorough diagnostic evaluation of patients with defecation syncope for underlying causes.

Abstract of a case report on bowel obsession syndrome (BOS), a psychosomatic disorder, describing a 32-year-old man with chronic constipation who meets BOS criteria (restricted diet, evacuation compulsions, social isolation, depressed mood).

Continuation of the abstract: cognitive behavioral therapy produced complete symptom remission sustained at 1-year follow-up, and the conclusion argues BOS is underdiagnosed and likely more prevalent than thought, so clinicians should recognize and treat it.
Final fragment of the abstract containing the closing clinical recommendation that clinicians assess, diagnose and properly treat BOS, followed by the 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.
Introduction and methods of a study using daily bowel diaries (not just questionnaires) in women from an Olmsted County, MN community survey, with and without functional bowel disorders.

Methods and results describing the 278 sampled women: questionnaire-based classification into diarrhea (26%), constipation (21%), or neither (53%), and low frequency of bowel symptoms in asymptomatic subjects.

Findings on urgency for normal-form stools (Bristol 4), more common in diarrhea and constipation groups than normals, and odds ratios for straining at start and end of defecation as predictors of constipation.

Odds ratios linking straining, stool frequency, incomplete evacuation, and rectal urgency to diarrhea, and the finding that stool frequency and form variations did not discriminate health from disease.
Conclusion that bowel symptoms are only partly explained by stool form disturbances, supporting other pathophysiological mechanisms in functional bowel disorders.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that other pathophysiological mechanisms likely contribute to functional bowel disorders.

Opening of a study on the reliability of bowel habit histories: 150 hospital outpatients recalled their bowel habits and then recorded them in diaries over two weeks, with recalled and recorded defecation frequencies compared.

Continuation of the bowel history study's findings: patients' recall of defecation frequency was often inaccurate, they predicted changes in bowel frequency poorly, and the authors question questionnaire-only population surveys and suggest diary recording could aid irritable bowel syndrome diagnosis.
Concluding sentence of the bowel history study, stating that routine diary recording of bowel actions might improve correct diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome.

Introduces evidence of increased colonic motor activity after eating, attributing it mainly to food reaching the stomach and proximal intestine, with chemoreceptor stimulation weighted above mechanoreceptor stimulation.

Discusses possible mechanisms for the eating-induced colonic response: hormonal action via polypeptides released from the proximal gut, or neural pathways through parasympathetic and sympathetic systems.
States that the precise change in colonic motility is unknown and lists candidate sites: colonic pacemakers (slow waves and migrating spike bursts), musculature excitability, or mucosal function.
Final fragment of the sentence ending the document, naming colonic mucosal function as one possible site of the motility change.

Opening chunk of a brief introductory passage on medical care and disease in ancient Egypt, stating Egypt's status as a cradle of scientific enquiry over three millennia and that its medical knowledge has been underestimated, with few surviving artefacts describing medical organization.

Closing chunk of the same introductory passage on ancient Egyptian medicine, citing papyri, tomb bas-reliefs, and ancient historians as evidence of an intense interest in science, humanities, and medicine in an educated society that had overcome the superstitions of its nomadic ancestors.

Opening of a study on dietary fiber and personality as determinants of stool output; introduces fiber's role as a mediator of the fiber-disease relationship and reports fiber (NDF) predicting stool weight but not frequency.

Middle portion of the abstract: personality measures predict stool weight and frequency independently of diet, explaining variance comparable to dietary fiber, leading to the conclusion that personality predisposes some people to low stool output.
Final sentence of the abstract, concluding that individuals with low stool output due to personality factors may particularly benefit from dietary fiber.

Introduces bowel obsession syndrome (BOS), an OCD-like functional disorder involving fear of fecal incontinence and evacuation-checking, and frames the diagnostic challenge of distinguishing ulcerative colitis flares from functional bowel disorders; also notes the scarcity of antidepressant case studies for BOS.

States the novelty of the study: the first report of successful psychotherapy in a male ulcerative colitis patient with overlapping functional bowel symptoms and marked BOS features, and argues that recognizing BOS aids differential diagnosis and appropriate treatment.
Concludes the abstract by stating that recognizing BOS can help clinicians avoid unnecessary investigations and select the most suitable treatment for patients.

Objective and background of the Popcol study: rationale for defining normal bowel habits in the general population by excluding confounders such as IBS and GI-side-effect medications, using a prospective random-sample design.

Methods of the Popcol study: 268 randomly selected adults aged 18-70 completed one-week symptom diaries and underwent gastroenterologist evaluation, colonoscopy, and laboratory tests to exclude organic disease.
Key results of the Popcol study: among 124 subjects with no organic GI abnormality, IBS, or relevant medication, 98% had stool frequency between three per day and three per week.

Stool consistency and defecatory symptom prevalence in the Popcol study (77% normal, 12% hard, 10% loose stools; urgency 36%, straining 47%, incomplete defecation 46%), plus initial sex differences in symptoms before excluding IBS.

Conclusions on sex differences and normal frequency: women reported more symptoms than men until IBS subjects were excluded, and the study confirms normal stool frequency is three per week to three per day with no gender or age differences in frequency or symptoms.

Final conclusion of the Popcol study: no gender or age differences in stool frequency, defecatory symptoms, or bloating, and some degree of urgency, straining, and incomplete evacuation should be considered normal.
Introduction to gastroenterology in ancient Egyptian medicine: specialist organ-focused care and the prominence of digestive disorders in medical papyri.
Ancient Egyptian gastroenterological knowledge: clinical understanding of gastric and anorectal conditions and the theory that feces-derived materia peccans causes disease.
Conclusion of the ancient Egyptian theory of disease: the materia peccans rationale that justified the popular practice of self-purgation with enemas.

Introduction to a review article on colonic motility in humans, noting the colon's motor activity is poorly understood and that prolonged recording techniques have revealed circadian contraction patterns and responsiveness to meals and sleep.

Continuation of the article's introduction describing high-amplitude propulsive colonic contractions tied to defecation, and stating that the review covers these physiological properties and their alterations in chronic idiopathic constipation.
Final fragment of the introduction's closing sentence stating that the article reviews normal colonic physiological properties and their changes in patients with chronic idiopathic constipation.

Opening chunk of an abstract on colon cancer etiology: it introduces the disease burden in Western populations and proposes that dietary changes altering the bowel environment, via fecal bile acids, sterols, and transit time, drive carcinogenesis.

Continues the abstract by naming two secular dietary changes thought to be etiologically important: reduced fiber intake affecting bowel physiology, and the combination of lower fiber and higher fat raising fecal bile acids, sterols, and other noxious substances.

Covers prevention in the abstract: it says recommendations to lower fat or raise fiber-containing food intake (excluding bran fiber) are unlikely to be adopted, and begins describing future research priorities on low-mortality Western groups.

Names specific low-cancer-rate populations (Seventh Day Adventists, Mormons, rural Finns) and developing populations as priorities for intensive study, and raises the need to clarify how diet and genetics affect fecal bile acids and transit time.
Final sentence of the abstract, calling for research on how diet and genetic constitution influence fecal bile acid concentrations and transit time in populations prone and not prone to colon cancer.

Introduction and methods of a study on the cephalic phase of colonic pressure response to food, describing five normal subjects, sigmoid colon manometry, simultaneous gastric acid measurement, and the basal period before stimuli.

Describes the experimental design: after a 60-minute basal period, one of five 30-minute food-related cephalic stimuli or a neutral-topic control was given in random order, followed by 120 minutes of recording, and lists the specific stimuli tested.

Outlines outcome measures (colonic study segment activity index and gastric acid output in mmol/30 min) and begins reporting results, with food discussion significantly increasing colonic pressure activity versus control and basal periods.

Reports colonic pressure results for smell of food alone and for sham feeding and sight-plus-smell stimuli, showing significant increases versus control, and notes sham feeding and sight-plus-smell effects were not significant versus basal.

Reports that sight of food without smell or taste had no significant effect on colonic activity, identifies food discussion as the strongest colonic stimulus, and begins describing gastric acid output results for food discussion and sham feeding.

Presents gastric acid output results: food discussion and sham feeding significantly raised acid output, sight-plus-smell raised it above basal, and smell alone and sight alone did not significantly raise it.

Summarizes that sham feeding was the best gastric acid stimulus unlike its colonic effect, reports a significant correlation between colonic activity and acid output after food discussion but not in control, and states the conclusion.
Concluding sentence stating the data show a cephalic phase of the colonic response to food, following the absence of correlation between colonic activity and acid output in the control study.

Historical origins of the dietary fiber concept: early US studies of wheat bran laxative action, and Walker and Trowell's work in Africa linking cereal fiber to lower rates of colon and metabolic diseases.

Continuation of the history of the fiber concept: Cleave's hypothesis that refined sugar and white flour cause metabolic disease while fiber loss causes colonic disorders, and Burkitt's evidence of rare appendicitis in rural Africa and Asia.

Trowell's 1972 physiological definition of dietary fiber as plant food residue resistant to human digestive enzymes, and the start of Southgate's proposed chemical analysis methods for fiber components.
Concludes the passage on Southgate's chemical method for analyzing dietary fiber, naming its components: cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin.

Study methods: a prospective survey of 838 men and 1059 women (72.2% of a random stratified East Bristol sample) recording three consecutive defecations and stool form on a six-point scale, with questionnaire validity noted.

Key findings on defecation frequency: once-daily was the most common habit but a minority practice; only about 40% of men and 33% of women had a regular 24-hour cycle, so most people had irregular bowels.

Constipation and sex/age differences: a third of women defecated less than daily and 1% weekly or less; women passed constipated-type stools more often than men, and women of childbearing age showed more constipation and irregularity, including three severe slow-transit cases.

Stool type and timing: age otherwise had little effect; normal stool types (least likely to cause symptoms) made up only 56% of stools in women and 61% in men, and most defecations occurred in the early morning, earlier in men.
Conclusion: conventionally normal bowel function is found in less than half the population, and younger women are particularly disadvantaged in bowel physiology.

Introductory passage arguing that bowel movements should be treated as a sixth vital sign, noting that constipation is especially problematic in older adults and that nurses should assess and treat it with the same care as pain.

Study design and methods of a randomized controlled trial of a self-experience multidisciplinary lifestyle intervention for health care providers, with 15 matched primary-care HMO clinics in Israel (Jan-Sep 2010), following 77 HCPs and 496 patients.

Results begin: HCPs in the intervention group showed improved health initiative attitudes and reduced salt intake versus control, and their patients showed overall dietary improvement, tracking the trial's outcomes for providers and patients.

Continuation of results on patient dietary changes (salt, red meat, fruit, vegetables) and clinic-level outcomes: height, lipids, HbA1c and clinical measurement rate (CMR) rose in intervention clinics, with more angiography referrals versus control.

Correlation findings within the intervention group linking HCPs' salt pattern to lipid CMR and HCPs' body weight to blood pressure and lipid CMR, plus the opening conclusion that providers' personal lifestyles correlate with their clinical performance.

Concluding statement that HCP self-experience health interventions benefit patients and clinics and may serve as an adjunct primary prevention strategy, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Opening of the abstract for a randomized controlled trial (N=915, four family medicine clinics in southeastern Missouri) testing whether physician advice primes patient responsiveness to printed materials on smoking cessation, diet, and physical activity; covers objective, design, setting, participants, and interventions.

Describes the printed educational materials for smoking cessation, low-fat eating, and physical activity, and the main outcomes measured (recall, rating, and use of materials; changes in smoking, dietary fat, and activity), followed by the start of the results section on physician advice before materials.

Results showing that patients who got physician advice before same-topic materials were more likely to remember, share, and find them personally relevant, and reported quit attempts with odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals for smoking behavior.

Reports the remaining behavioral outcomes: 24-hour smoking abstinence (OR 1.85), dietary change (OR 1.35), and physical activity change (OR 1.51) with confidence intervals, then opens the conclusions on an integrated disease prevention model.

Concluding statement that physician advice acts as a catalyst for behavior change and must be backed by a coordinated system of detailed, individualized information and activities to sustain behavioral change.

Introduces the study's background and rationale: prior research linked physicians' healthy personal habits to discussing prevention, but no study had tested whether physicians disclosing their own healthy behaviors boosts credibility and patient motivation. Also begins the Design section describing two brief diet and exercise health education videos.

Describes the study design: two brief diet and exercise videos were shown to waiting-room subjects (n1=66, n2=65) at an Emory University general medical clinic in Atlanta. The physician-disclosure video adds half a minute about her personal healthy diet and exercise habits, with a bike helmet and apple visible on her desk.

Explains the two conditions: the physician-disclosure video includes the personal habits, apple, and bike helmet, while the control video omits them. Then reports the first results: viewers rated the physician as generally healthier, somewhat more believable, and more motivating.

Reports the remaining results: viewers rated the physician as more believable and motivating specifically for exercise and diet (P <= .001). Also states the conclusion that conveying one's own healthy habits enhances physicians' ability to motivate patients.

Closes the abstract with a recommendation that educational institutions encourage health professionals-in-training to practice and demonstrate healthy personal lifestyles, based on the study's finding that physician self-disclosure of healthy habits boosts motivation.

Opening of a document on non-communicable diseases (NCDs): introduces the shift of NCD burden from developed to developing, transition countries, covering CVD, cancer and diabetes, and notes that nearly 4 in 5 NCD deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries.

Middle section explaining drivers of the NCD increase (globalization, supermarket growth, urbanization, sedentary lifestyles) and how overweight/obesity leads to risk factors such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol and elevated blood glucose.

Concluding section on prevention: a high-quality diet with functional foods or ingredients, plus physical activity and a non-smoking policy, is a promising primary and secondary prevention strategy for NCDs, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
Copyright footer of the document: Copyright 2011 Elsevier Inc., all rights reserved.

Opening OBJECTIVE statement of the abstract: it explains why the US government and the global sugar industry oppose the 2004 WHO global diet and physical activity strategy and seek to separate it from the 2003 WHO/FAO expert report that underpins it.

Continuation of the objective: it urges national representatives at the 2004 World Health Assembly to back the strategy together with the expert report, so the strategy becomes explicit and quantified as member states requested in 2002.
States the purpose of an effective global strategy against chronic diseases driven by poor diet (low fruit and vegetables, high fatty, sugary or salty energy-dense foods) and physical inactivity.

Names obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and several cancers as leading causes of morbidity and mortality, then begins the METHOD section describing a summary of the strategy and its scientific roots.

Method continued: outlines the reasons for US government and sugar industry opposition with historical context, and summarizes the strategy's trajectory since its 2003 draft along with its weaknesses, strengths and potential.
CONCLUSION: the strategy and expert report are seen by the US administration as obstacles to trade and policy, part of broader US hostility toward the UN system as a check on American power.
Closing call to policy-makers worldwide to recognize the pressures from powerful states and industries whose interests conflict with international public health initiatives.
Final sentence of the abstract, stating that such public health initiatives aim to leave a better legacy for future generations.

Opening section of a document on the global nutrition transition and obesity pandemic in developing countries; introduces the 1970s dietary shift toward processed foods, eating away from home, edible oils, sugary drinks, and reduced physical activity that began in the early 1990s in low- and middle-income countries.

Middle section of the document on the global nutrition transition; describes how the early-1990s dietary and activity changes went unrecognized until diabetes, hypertension, and obesity spread worldwide, and notes rapid rises in overweight and obesity across urban and rural areas from sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia to higher-income countries.

Closing part of the document on the obesity pandemic in developing countries; documents concurrent diet and activity shifts and notes that few countries, despite some policy efforts, are seriously prioritizing prevention of dietary challenges.

Final fragment of the document's last sentence, concluding that few countries are seriously addressing dietary prevention despite major health challenges from the obesity pandemic in developing countries.

Describes the U.S. Sugar Association's opposition to a WHO healthy-eating guideline capping sugar at 10% of diet, including its threat to cut Congressional funding to the WHO unless the guideline is withdrawn. Relevant to queries on sugar industry lobbying against WHO sugar recommendations and funding threats.

Continues the account: the Sugar Association and six other food industry groups asked the U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary to pressure the WHO into withdrawing the sugar report, and the WHO rejected the lobby's criticisms. Relevant to queries on industry pressure on HHS and WHO's response.
Abstract of a study on lipotoxic β-cell apoptosis: introduces palmitate-induced ER stress and the mitochondrial intrinsic apoptosis pathway, and the microarray discovery of DP5 and PUMA.

Abstract continuation: identifies the palmitate-triggered ER stress signature and BH3-only proteins DP5 and PUMA, showing their knockdown reduces cytochrome c release, caspase-3 activation, and apoptosis in rat and human β-cells.
Abstract mechanistic details: DP5 induction via IRE1-JNK and PERK-ATF3 promoter binding; PUMA via PERK/ATF3, TRB3-mediated AKT inhibition, and FoxO3a activation.
Abstract conclusion: DP5-knockout mice resist high-fat diet-induced glucose intolerance and have doubled β-cell mass, highlighting ER stress–mitochondrial crosstalk driving β-cell death in diabetes.

Study design and population: cross-sectional study of 215 nondiabetic men aged 32-74 with angiographically proven coronary artery disease, examining diet, obesity, and plasma insulin (Stanford Coronary Risk Intervention Project), introducing the aim of testing diet-insulin association independent of obesity.

Main correlation results: after age adjustment, saturated fatty acid and cholesterol intake correlate positively with BMI, waist-to-hip ratio, and fasting insulin, while carbohydrate intake correlates negatively with BMI, waist-to-hip ratio, and fasting insulin.

Other dietary correlates: monounsaturated fat intake is unrelated to BMI or waist-to-hip ratio but positively correlates with fasting insulin, and total caloric intake is negatively correlated with BMI.

Multivariate result and conclusion: saturated fat intake remains significantly associated with elevated fasting insulin independent of BMI, and the cross-sectional findings suggest higher saturated fat consumption is linked to higher insulin levels.

Concluding statement: increased saturated fatty acid consumption is independently associated with higher fasting insulin concentrations in nondiabetic men with coronary artery disease, based on cross-sectional data.

Introduces the rising Type 2 diabetes burden from obesity, explaining that the disease arises when pancreatic insulin secretion fails to compensate for insulin resistance, due to beta-cell dysfunction and death.

Describes how saturated-fat-rich Western diets drive obesity, insulin resistance, and elevated circulating free fatty acids (NEFAs), which contribute to beta-cell failure and apoptosis in genetically predisposed individuals.

Covers the molecular basis of NEFA-induced beta-cell damage, identifying endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress as a mechanism mediating NEFA-induced beta-cell apoptosis and linking high-fat diet to insulin resistance.

Argues that ER stress may be a common pathway underlying both major causes of Type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance and beta-cell loss, and that understanding these mechanisms could enable targeted prevention.
Concludes that clarifying the mechanisms of pancreatic beta-cell loss will enable novel, targeted approaches to preventing Type 2 diabetes.

Introduction and objective of the ARIC cohort study: examines whether plasma cholesterol ester and phospholipid fatty acid composition (a biomarker of dietary fat) prospectively relates to incident diabetes mellitus.

Study design and methods: 2909 middle-aged adults (45-64 y) from ARIC, plasma fatty acids measured by gas-liquid chromatography as percent of total fatty acids, with 252 incident diabetes cases over 9 years of follow-up.

Main adjusted results: higher proportions of total saturated fatty acids in plasma CE and PL are significantly and positively associated with diabetes incidence after adjusting for demographic, anthropometric, lifestyle, and family history covariates; begins quintile rate ratio data.

Quintile-specific rate ratios for saturated fatty acids (CE: 1.00 to 2.08, P=0.0013; PL: 1.00 to 3.37, P<0.0001) and specific fatty acids in CE linked to diabetes: palmitic, palmitoleic, and dihomo-gamma-linolenic acids positive, linoleic acid inverse.

Specific fatty acid associations in PL (palmitic 16:0 and stearic 18:0 positive) and the study conclusion that saturated fatty acid composition of plasma is positively associated with diabetes development.
Final conclusion: the biomarker findings indirectly suggest that dietary fat profile, especially saturated fat, may contribute to the etiology of diabetes.

Study design and methods for a NASH dietary-habits study: 25 NASH patients vs. 25 matched controls, 7-day food record, oral glucose tolerance test and insulin sensitivity index, plus an oral fat load test in a subset.
Dietary intake comparison in NASH versus controls, showing higher saturated fat and cholesterol intake in NASH patients, along with the start of the lower polyunsaturated fat intake finding.
Dietary deficits in NASH patients versus controls: lower polyunsaturated fat, fiber, and antioxidant vitamins C and E, followed by the start of the insulin sensitivity index result.

Key results on insulin sensitivity and postprandial lipemia: lower ISI in NASH, higher postprandial triglyceride levels and AUC measures, and the start of the correlation of saturated fat intake with metabolic outcomes.

Correlations of saturated fat intake with insulin sensitivity, metabolic syndrome features, and postprandial triglyceride rise, plus flat postprandial ApoB48 and ApoB100 responses suggesting a defect in ApoB secretion in NASH.

Conclusion that diet may promote steatohepatitis directly through hepatic triglyceride accumulation and antioxidant activity, and indirectly through insulin sensitivity and postprandial triglyceride metabolism, supporting targeted dietary interventions.
Final sentence recommending more specific dietary interventions, particularly for nonobese, nondiabetic, normolipidemic NASH patients.
Introduction and methods opening of an in vitro study comparing oleic acid and palmitic acid effects on steatosis and hepatocyte apoptosis in hepatocytic cell lines, relevant to NAFLD research.

Methods section describing the experimental design: three hepatocytic cell lines (HepG2, HuH7, WRL68), fatty acid doses of oleic and palmitic acid, and the 24 h incubation protocol for steatosis and apoptosis assessment.
Results section beginning with gene activation findings: PPARgamma and SREBP-1 activation tied to greater steatosis with oleic acid, and increased PPARalpha expression with palmitic acid.

Results on apoptosis and insulin signalling: apoptosis inversely related to steatosis, palmitic acid impairing insulin signalling, and oleic acid showing a protective effect when combined with palmitic acid.
Conclusions of the study: oleic acid is more steatogenic but less apoptotic than palmitic acid in hepatocyte cultures, with implications for diet and NAFLD pathogenesis.
Final sentence of the abstract, stating that the findings may offer a biological basis for clinical observations on dietary patterns and NAFLD models.

Introduction to the NAFLD review: links rising Western obesity to NAFLD, notes its progression from steatosis to steatohepatitis is poorly understood, and suggests saturated free fatty acids may drive lipotoxicity.

Continues the introduction by stating that saturated FFAs may be key lipotoxic mediators in NAFLD, and previews the review's focus on hepatic lipotoxicity pathways and how lipid saturation determines cell fate under elevated FFA load.

Names the cellular processes causally linked to lipoapoptosis (ER stress, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, JNK signaling) and introduces the contrasting protective role of triglyceride synthesis.

Highlights the paradox that triglyceride synthesis, a hallmark of NAFLD, is protective against lipotoxicity, and argues that a nuanced mechanistic understanding is needed for better NAFLD therapeutics.
Concludes the abstract by noting NAFLD is increasingly prevalent and currently has no proven pharmacologic treatment to prevent or reverse its progression.

Abstract opening of a human study (seven overweight/obese non-diabetic subjects) on how 24 h oral ingestion of MUFA, PUFA, SFA or control emulsions affects insulin secretion, sensitivity and clearance, with the stated hypothesis.

Study design details: each subject received the four oral treatments (MUFA, PUFA, SFA, water control) in random order 4-6 weeks apart, followed by a 2 h 20 mmol/l hyperglycaemic clamp at 24 h to measure GSIS, insulin sensitivity and clearance.
Results section: all three fat emulsions raised plasma NEFAs about 1.5- to 2-fold, reduced insulin clearance, and SFA specifically reduced insulin sensitivity.

Results continued and conclusions opening: PUFA lowered GSIS in absolute terms, SFA subjects had insulin secretion that failed to compensate for insulin resistance, and fats of differing saturation produced different effects on secretion and action.
Conclusions/interpretation: PUFA reduces absolute insulin secretion, SFA induces insulin resistance, and the failure of secretion to compensate in the SFA study points to impaired beta cell function.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the SFA study's interpretation of impaired beta cell function.
Introduction and aims of a study on human pancreatic beta cell longevity, using lipofuscin body accumulation as an age marker, motivated by beta cell turnover defects in type 2 diabetes.

Study aims and methods: lipofuscin body accumulation measured in beta cells from individuals aged 1-81 years to estimate human beta cell lifespan; sample description begins (human, non-human primate, and mouse cohorts).

Methods and early results: sample sizes for non-diabetic and type 2 diabetic humans, non-human primates and mice, 3D mathematical modelling of total lipofuscin content, and the finding that lipofuscin area correlates with age.

Results on cell-type and species comparisons: low lipofuscin in human insulinomas, alpha cells and mouse beta cells, and 3D modelling showing the proportion of aged human beta cells rising from at least 90% under 10 years to at least 97% over 20 years.
Conclusions: human beta cells, unlike those of young rodents, are long-lived; lipofuscin proportions in type 2 diabetes and obesity indicate little adaptive change in the adult beta cell population.
Concluding sentence: the adult human beta cell population is largely established by age 20 years, closing the conclusions section of the abstract.
Abstract opening (Background, Aim, Methods start) of a study on sodium palmitate-induced lipoapoptosis in human liver cells (L02, HepG2) as it relates to NAFLD.

Continuation of the Methods section describing the treatments (sodium palmitate up to 48 h, lithium chloride as GSK-3β inhibitor, GSK-3β shRNA) and the assays used (TEM, flow cytometry, caspase-3 colorimetric assay, western blot).
Start of the Results section: sodium palmitate induces lipoapoptosis and activates GSK-3β, shown by reduced Ser-9 phosphorylation.
Results showing that inhibiting GSK-3β with lithium chloride or shRNA knockdown suppresses palmitate-induced lipoapoptosis, and reduces JNK phosphorylation and Bax upregulation.

End of the Results and start of the Conclusions: GSK-3β inhibition does not affect ER stress-induced unfolded protein response, and palmitate lipoapoptosis is regulated by GSK-3β activation leading to JNK activation.
Final conclusion of the abstract: GSK-3β inhibition is proposed as a potential therapeutic target for controlling NAFLD.

Introduces the Normative Aging Study on 652 men aged 43-85, examining body mass index, abdomen-hip ratio, and diet in relation to fasting and postprandial insulin, and reports initial correlations of log fasting insulin with adiposity and fat intake.

Reports the correlation range for fasting insulin (0.14 for total fat to 0.45 for BMI) and the multivariate results identifying BMI, abdomen-hip ratio, and saturated fatty acid intake as independent predictors of insulin after adjusting for age, smoking, and physical activity.

Quantifies the effect of reducing saturated fatty acids from 14% to 8% of energy: an 18% drop in fasting insulin and a 25% drop in postprandial insulin, and begins the conclusion that adiposity and saturated fat are key insulin predictors.

Concludes the Normative Aging Study findings: overall adiposity, abdominal obesity, and high saturated fatty acid intake are independent predictors of both fasting and postprandial insulin concentrations.

Introduction to Moses Maimonides (1135-1204), a 12th-century Jewish physician and philosopher, describing his persecution-filled life and rise as a sought-after clinician while writing extensively on medicine and philosophy.

Describes Maimonides' medical works, which cover all areas of clinical medicine and reflect rational thinking about mind-body relationships, and his famous philosophical and legal writings such as The Guide for the Perplexed and his codification of Jewish law.
Concluding statement that the review of Maimonides' life and achievements offers insight into a remarkable 12th-century physician and provides lessons relevant to physicians today.
Introduction to a 1995 first U.S. nationwide food sampling study measuring dioxins, dibenzofurans, and PCBs across 110 pooled food samples from five cities, plus human milk.
Identifies sampling locations and reports the food categories with highest and lowest WHO dioxin TEQ levels, notably farm-raised freshwater fish fillet (1.7 ppt) and simulated vegan diet (0.09 ppt).
Reports TEQ concentrations for ocean fish, meats, eggs, dairy, ice cream, and human milk (0.33-0.51 ppt), plus whole milk (0.16 ppt) and butter (1.1 ppt).
Gives estimated mean daily dioxin TEQ intake by age and sex, starting with U.S. breast-fed infants (42 pg/kg body weight) and children aged 1-11 (6.2 pg/kg), and teens aged 12-19.
Provides adult TEQ intake estimates (2.4 and 2.2 pg/kg for men and women aged 20-79), notes intake declines to 1.9 pg/kg at age 80+, and males generally exceed females.
Breaks down adult dietary TEQ sources (dioxins 42%, dibenzofurans 30%, PCBs 28%) and notes DDE was also analyzed in the pooled food samples.

Introduces the topic of widespread environmental pollutant chemicals and endocrine signaling, noting evidence from lab and wildlife studies but difficulty demonstrating clear effects in humans at typically low exposures; opens the document's review of human endocrine evidence.

Describes the review of human studies linking specific chemical exposures to endocrine outcomes (age at weaning, age at puberty, sex ratio at birth) and assessing evidence strength, concluding that human endocrine disruption remains largely undemonstrated.
Concludes the abstract: despite lack of demonstrated human endocrine disruption by pollutant chemicals, the underlying science is sound and the potential for such effects is real.

Introduction and objective of a study on serum testosterone and PCB/organochlorine exposure in an adult Mohawk population, including the endocrine-disruption background, the study aims, and the start of the methods section.
Methods detail: fasting serum samples from 703 Mohawk adults (257 men, 436 women), analyzed for 101 PCB congeners, HCB, DDE, mirex, testosterone, cholesterol, and triglycerides.

Statistical methods: logistic regression of testosterone against tertiles of organochlorine levels (wet-weight and lipid-adjusted), controlling for age, BMI and other analytes, with the lowest tertile as referent and sexes analyzed separately; begins the results on male testosterone and PCBs.

Main male results: testosterone inversely correlated with total PCBs; odds ratio of 0.17 (95% CI 0.05–0.69) for highest vs. lowest wet-weight PCB tertile after adjustment for age, BMI, lipids and three pesticides.
Further male findings: lipid-adjusted total PCB odds ratio of 0.23 (95% CI 0.06–0.78), and specific PCB congeners 74, 99, 153 and 206 inversely related to testosterone while others were not.

Female and pesticide results: female testosterone is much lower and unrelated to PCBs; HCB, DDE and mirex show no association in either sex; the conclusions section begins, linking elevated PCBs to lower testosterone in men.
Final conclusion sentence: elevated serum PCB levels are associated with lower serum testosterone in Native American men.

Abstract opening of a 2011 Elsevier study on human fetal penile (corpora cavernosa) cells exposed to three PCB mixtures, introducing the mixtures grouped by mode of action: dioxin-like Mix2 and non-dioxin-like Mix1 (estrogenic) and Mix3 (persistent CYP450 inducers).

Continuation of the abstract describing methods and key toxicogenomic findings: exposure concentrations derived from human internal exposure data, and that all PCB mixtures modulated critical genitourinary development genes but with three distinct expression profiles, starting with the DL Mix2 results.

Abstract results summarizing each mixture's distinct effects on genes: Mix2 affected actin-related, cell-cell and epithelial-mesenchymal morphogenetic processes, Mix1 affected smooth muscle genes, and Mix3 affected steroid/lipid metabolism and growth genes, concluding that realistic fetal PCB exposure alters genitourinary programming.

Concluding sentences of the abstract stating that fetal exposure to environmentally relevant PCB levels modulates several genitourinary programming patterns and that non-dioxin-like congener groups may have specific modes of action, followed by the Elsevier 2011 copyright notice.

Introduction and study aim: opens the abstract by describing acrylamide as a probable human carcinogen in everyday foods, notes prior suggestive epidemiological links to cancer, and states the prospective study's aim to examine dietary acrylamide and lymphatic malignancy subtypes for the first time.

Methods, cohort description: continues the aim sentence, then describes the Netherlands Cohort Study on diet and cancer (120,852 participants followed since 1986) and how person-years at risk were estimated from a baseline random subsample of 5,000.

Methods, exposure assessment and statistical analysis: explains that acrylamide intake was estimated from a food frequency questionnaire linked to Dutch food acrylamide data, and that hazard ratios from multivariable-adjusted Cox models were computed by sex, for never-smokers, and across continuous, quintile, and tertile exposure categories.

Results, case count and first findings: reports 16.3 years of follow-up, 1,233 microscopically confirmed lymphatic malignancy cases, and begins the main findings with hazard ratios for multiple myeloma and follicular lymphoma in men per 10 µg/day acrylamide increment.

Results and conclusion: gives the remaining key estimates, including the strong hazard ratio for multiple myeloma in never-smoking men, the absence of associations in women, and the conclusion that acrylamide may increase risk of multiple myeloma and follicular lymphoma in men.
Concluding statement: states that this is the first epidemiological study of dietary acrylamide and lymphatic malignancy risk and calls for further research to confirm the observed associations.

Introductory overview of multiple myeloma, describing it as a long-intractable blood cancer and noting recent treatment advances: high-dose melphalan with autologous stem-cell transplant and novel targeted agents (immunomodulatory drugs, proteasome inhibitors).

Concluding part of the abstract: these novel agents dramatically changed MM treatment, high response rates extended overall survival, and further research and multimodality therapy are needed to cure the disease.
Final fragment of the abstract's last sentence, stating that the goal is to cure multiple myeloma, which remains the unmet need after recent therapeutic progress.
