Concluding sentence of the abstract: resistant starch reduces the buildup of potentially harmful protein fermentation byproducts in the human colon.

Study background and aims: a prospective cohort of ulcerative colitis patients in remission from two UK district general hospitals, examining which dietary factors increase relapse risk over one year.

Methods detail: patients followed for one year; relapse measured with a validated disease activity index; diet assessed by food frequency questionnaire and split into tertiles; adjusted odds ratios from multivariate logistic regression controlling for non-dietary factors.
Results part 1: 191 patients recruited, 96% completed, 52% relapsed; meat intake (OR 3.2) and red/processed meat (OR 5.19) in the top tertile raise relapse odds, as does protein intake (OR 3.00).

Results part 2: alcohol (OR 2.71) in the top tertile associated with relapse; high sulphur (OR 2.76) and sulphate (OR 2.6) intakes also linked to relapse, possibly explaining the meat and alcohol associations.

Conclusions part 1: modifiable dietary factors such as high meat and alcoholic beverage intake are associated with increased relapse likelihood in UC patients; sulphur-related explanation is proposed.
Conclusions part 2: further research is needed to test whether sulphur compounds in these foods drive relapse and whether reducing their intake lowers relapse frequency.

Introduces the 1981 survey of 118 missionaries across 75 mission stations in 24 sub-Saharan African countries, which recorded patient volumes and cases of bloody diarrhoea, typhoid and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) in rural Africa.

Reports the survey results: about 190,000 inpatients and over 1 million outpatients, 12,859 bloody diarrhoea cases (1,914 typhoid), only 22 IBD cases, and limited histological diagnostic access, lowest in West Africa (25% of hospitals).

Concludes that IBD is rarely diagnosed in sub-Saharan rural mission hospitals, that diagnosis is limited by lack of diagnostic facilities, and that reliable incidence and prevalence estimates for Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are not yet possible.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that reliable estimates of Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis incidence and prevalence in rural African populations are still lacking.

Opening of a study on high HDL cholesterol in African populations free of coronary heart disease; introduces low HDL in CHD patients and the CHD-free elderly black African group in Western Transvaal, and begins listing the age-group HDL measurements.

Reports mean HDL values (mmol/l and mg/100 ml) across birth, childhood, adolescence, and elderly age groups, with HDL as a percentage of total cholesterol, noting that HDL did not decline with age unlike in whites.
Conclusion: attributes the high HDL in rural South African blacks to a high-fibre, low-animal-fat diet and an active lifestyle, suggesting these values reflect a population free from CHD.

Abstract opening of a 2008 BMJ meta-analysis (Medline 1966-2007) of randomised trials of blood pressure lowering drugs, stating objectives and design, including the aim of quantifying drug efficacy for CHD and stroke prevention.

Study selection details: 108 'blood pressure difference' trials comparing drug with placebo or no drug, 46 'drug comparison' trials, and seven trials falling into both categories; sets up interpretation against cohort meta-analysis expectations.

Methods and participants: results are interpreted against the largest cohort meta-analysis (958,000 people), with 464,000 participants split into no vascular disease, prior CHD, or prior stroke groups; also begins the results on beta blockers in blood pressure difference trials.
Key finding on beta blockers after prior CHD: 29% risk reduction versus 15% for other drugs, indicating an effect beyond blood pressure lowering, in secondary prevention of recurrent CHD.

Beta blocker benefit limited to the few years after myocardial infarction (31% vs 13% reduction, P=0.04), and the general finding that other blood pressure difference trials show 22% CHD and 41% stroke reductions per 10/5 mm Hg, matching cohort-predicted values.

Conclusion that benefit is explained by blood pressure reduction itself: trial reductions for 10 mm Hg systolic or 5 mm Hg diastolic closely match the cohort-predicted 25% CHD and 36% stroke reductions.

Comparison of drug classes: thiazides, beta blockers, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and calcium channel blockers perform similarly for CHD and stroke, except calcium channel blockers give a modestly greater stroke reduction (RR 0.92).

Consistency across subgroups: proportional CHD and stroke reductions are similar with or without existing cardiovascular disease and across pretreatment blood pressure levels, down to 110/70 mm Hg; also begins the combined-evidence estimate for people aged 60-69.

Combined estimate using dose-response and cohort meta-analyses: for people aged 60-69 with pretreatment diastolic BP of 90 mm Hg, three half-dose drugs in combination cut CHD by about 46% and stroke by 62%, versus about half that effect for one standard-dose drug.

Heart failure outcomes: drugs other than calcium channel blockers (except non-cardioselective beta blockers) reduce heart failure by 24%, and calcium channel blockers reduce it by 19% (wider confidence interval).

Conclusions section: apart from post-myocardial infarction beta blocker benefit and the small extra stroke effect of calcium channel blockers, drug classes act similarly per unit of blood pressure reduction, implying no material pleiotropic effects.

Implications: proportional cardiovascular benefit is the same regardless of pretreatment blood pressure or existing disease, so guidelines could be simplified to offer drugs across all blood pressure levels.
Final recommendation: lowering blood pressure should be prioritised in everyone above a certain age, rather than measuring blood pressure in everyone and treating only those found high.
Final fragment of the closing sentence of the conclusions, restating that treatment should be given to people over a certain age rather than selected by blood pressure measurement.

Abstract opening of a 2012-era Lancet-style meta-analysis of individual participant data from 27 statin trials, introducing the study design, sample sizes, and LDL cholesterol differences in people at low vascular risk.

Methods section defining major vascular events (coronary events, strokes, revascularisations) and describing stratification of participants into five baseline 5-year vascular risk categories on control therapy.
Findings opening: overall rate ratio of 0.79 per 1.0 mmol/L LDL reduction for major vascular events, consistent across age, sex, baseline LDL and prior vascular disease, and for mortality.

Risk-stratified results showing rate ratios for major vascular events from lowest to highest baseline risk category, with a trend test indicating proportional benefit at least as large in the lowest-risk groups.
Detailed risk-category findings: significant reductions in major coronary events and coronary revascularisations in the two lowest-risk categories, with confidence intervals and p-values.
Stroke outcomes by risk category, showing a reduction in participants with under 10% 5-year risk similar to higher-risk groups, and start of results for participants without prior vascular disease.
Results for participants without prior vascular disease (vascular and all-cause mortality reductions, similar by baseline risk) and null findings on cancer incidence and cancer mortality.

Start of the Interpretation section, stating that in people with under 10% 5-year risk, LDL reduction yields a benefit that outweighs hazards of statins, and that cancer and non-vascular mortality showed no increase.

Interpretation claiming an absolute benefit of about 11 fewer major vascular events per 1000 over 5 years per 1 mmol/L LDL reduction in lower-risk individuals, who are typically not recommended statins under current guidelines.

Concluding interpretation calling for reconsideration of guidelines on statin eligibility for low-risk individuals, followed by the funding sources (BHF, MRC, Cancer Research UK, EU Biomed, NHMRC, National Heart Foundation Australia).
Final fragment of the funding statement, listing the National Health and Medical Research Council and National Heart Foundation of Australia as funders.

Opening of a document on preventing noncommunicable diseases (NCDs): defines the main NCDs (cancers, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease), their large global death toll, and introduces the call for policies targeting major risk factors, with the list of prevention approaches beginning.

Middle section listing specific NCD prevention strategies: tobacco and alcohol control via taxes and sales/advertising rules, reducing salt, unhealthy fats and sugars, and promoting fruits, vegetables, healthy fats and whole grains through price and availability measures.

Closing section of the NCD prevention summary: ends the list of strategies with lowering availability barriers for healthy foods and calls for a universal, equitable primary-care system that addresses cardiometabolic risk factors and NCD-precursor infections through clinical interventions.
Introduces the study design: a cross-sectional analysis of NHANES 2005–06 US adults aged 20–85, defining elevated depressive symptoms via the PHQ with a cutpoint of 10.

Describes the exposure measures (serum carotenoids, retinol, vitamin C, vitamin E), the statistical methods (logistic and zero-inflated Poisson regression accounting for survey design), and the final sample of 1,798 adults.
Reports the main finding that higher total serum carotenoids lowered odds of elevated depressive symptoms (37% overall per SD, 34% among women), introducing the quartile dose-response analysis.

Gives the quartile dose-response result (Q4 vs Q1 OR=0.41, trend p=0.035), notes no significant link for other antioxidants, and begins identifying β-carotene and lutein+zeaxanthins as specific inverse associations.

Specifies that β-carotene and lutein+zeaxanthins (women only, adjusted for dietary intake and supplement use) were independently inversely associated with depressive symptoms, and that other serum antioxidants were not significant after adjusting for total carotenoids.
Concludes that serum total carotenoids, mainly β-carotene and lutein+zeaxanthins, are associated with lower depressive symptoms in community-dwelling US adults.

Abstract opening of a Whitehall II cohort study on dietary patterns and depressive symptoms in middle-aged adults, introducing the aim, sample (n=3486), and the 'whole food' and 'processed food' dietary patterns.

Continues the methods from the Whitehall II study, defining the 'whole food' (vegetables, fruits, fish) and 'processed food' (desserts, fried food, processed meat, refined grains, high-fat dairy) patterns, and describing depression measured 5 years later with the CES-D scale.

Results section of the dietary pattern and depression study, reporting adjusted odds ratios: lower odds of CES-D depression for the highest whole food tertile (OR 0.74) and higher odds for high processed food consumption (OR 1.58).
Conclusion of the Whitehall II dietary pattern study, stating that a processed food pattern is a risk factor for later CES-D depression in middle-aged adults while a whole food pattern is protective.

Introduces the background and design of a 14-day randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of sustained-release ascorbic acid (3000 mg/day Cetebe) versus placebo in healthy young adults, covering the hypothesized mechanisms (catecholamines, stress, oxytocin, vascular function) linking vitamin C to sexual behavior and mood.

Describes the trial methods: 42 AA and 39 placebo participants with partners logged penile-vaginal intercourse, noncoital partner sex, and masturbation in daily diaries, and completed the Beck Depression Inventory before and after; the results section begins by noting the AA group's greater intercourse frequency, with no hypothesized effect on other sexual behavior.

Reports the main results: the AA group had higher penile-vaginal intercourse frequency, strongest in non-cohabiting participants and women, with no change in other sexual behavior; only the AA group showed reduced Beck Depression scores. Concludes that AA appears to increase intercourse and that the noncohabitant effect suggests a central rather than peripheral mechanism.

Final conclusion sentence: the greater benefit for non-cohabiting partners points toward a central nervous system activation or disinhibition mechanism, rather than a peripheral one, as the likely explanation for ascorbic acid's effect on intercourse frequency.
Introduction and background of a cross-sectional study on tomato/tomato product intake (a major lycopene source) and depressive symptoms in community-dwelling elderly Japanese adults.

Methods: 986 Japanese adults aged 70+ assessed with a validated self-administered diet-history questionnaire and the 30-item Geriatric Depression Scale, using cut-offs of 11 and 14 or antidepressant use.
Results begin: prevalence of mild-to-severe (34.9%) and severe (20.2%) depressive symptoms, followed by adjusted odds ratios for depressive symptoms across tomato intake levels.

Key findings: adjusted odds ratios for tomato/tomato product intake (1.00, 0.54, 0.48, p for trend <0.01), similar results for severe symptoms, no association for other vegetables, and the study's cross-sectional limitation.
Conclusions: a tomato-rich diet is independently linked to lower prevalence of depressive symptoms and may help prevent them, though this cross-sectional design cannot support clinical diagnosis.
Closing statement calling for further studies to confirm the findings, followed by the copyright notice (Elsevier B.V., 2012).

Introduction to the document: establishes oxidative stress (excess reactive oxygen species from genetic and nongenetic factors) as a pathophysiological factor in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depression.

Explains the mechanism of harm (oxidative damage to lipids, proteins, and DNA causing abnormal neural growth and differentiation) and proposes antioxidant supplementation as a long-term therapeutic strategy for neuropsychiatric disorders.

Notes promising results from antioxidant and PUFA supplementation, cautions that excessive antioxidants may interfere with protective reactive oxygen species functions, and states the article's purpose of overviewing antioxidant therapy strategies and outcomes.

Closing statement of the introduction, stating that the article will overview the potential strategies and outcomes of using antioxidants as therapeutics in psychiatric disorders; a concluding sentence of the abstract-style summary.
Background and methods of a prospective cohort study on dietary folate intake and later depression diagnosis in Finnish men, recruited 1984-1989 and followed to 2000.
Study population and results: 2,313 middle-aged eastern Finnish men (42-60 years); mean folate intake 256 mcg/day (SD 76) in the whole cohort.

Main finding: men with below-median energy-adjusted folate intake had about three times the risk of a depression discharge diagnosis (RR 3.04), remaining significant after adjusting for socioeconomic status, baseline depression score, fibre, vitamin C and total fat.
Conclusions: low dietary folate may be a risk factor for severe depression, suggesting nutrition could play a role in depression prevention.

Abstract of a systematic review and meta-analysis on whether low folate is a risk factor for depression, introducing the hypothesis, possible sources of spurious association, and the review's study design and sample.
Abstract results of the meta-analysis of 11 observational studies, reporting pooled unadjusted and confounder-adjusted odds ratios showing a significant link between low folate and depression.

Abstract conclusions: folate levels are lower in depression, evidence linking low folate to depression is accumulating but mostly from case-control and cross-sectional designs, and causal claims need cohort studies and randomised controlled trials.
Final sentence of the abstract calling for randomised controlled trials of folate to confirm or refute a causal relationship with depression.

Background and rationale from a folic acid mood-disorder prevention trial: motivates primary prevention of mood disorders in youth and cites epidemiological links between low folate and depressive symptoms.

Methods of the trial: randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled design in 14-24 year olds at familial risk of mood disorder, receiving 2.5 mg daily folic acid or identical placebo for up to 36 months; 112 participants analysed (56 per group).
Main results: mood disorder incidence was 14.3% with folic acid versus 17.9% with placebo (non-significant), with post-hoc evidence that folic acid delayed onset among those who became unwell.

Limitations and conclusions: small sample and lower-than-expected onset rate; long-term folic acid was well tolerated with high adherence but did not significantly reduce mood disorder incidence versus placebo.
Closing conclusion and copyright notice (Elsevier B.V., 2014) for the folic acid mood disorder prevention trial, restating that no reduction in incidence was shown relative to placebo.
Abstract background and rationale of an in vitro study on cholesterol crystallization as a mechanism of atherosclerotic plaque rupture and erosion leading to cardiovascular events.

Abstract statement of the study's aim (whether growing cholesterol crystals injure the plaque cap) and the hypothesis that sharp-edged crystals forcefully expand during crystallization and damage the cap.

Abstract methods describing the two in vitro experiments: melting and crystallizing cholesterol powder in graduated cylinders with volume measurements, and placing thin biological membranes in the path of growing crystals.

Abstract results reporting up to 45% rapid peak volume increase over 3 minutes, sharp-tipped crystals tearing membranes, and correlation statistics between cholesterol amount and crystal growth peak and rate.
Abstract conclusions that crystallization of supersaturated cholesterol can induce plaque cap rupture or erosion, with the correlation statistics for cholesterol amount versus growth.
Final abstract sentence concluding that the findings may inform therapeutic strategies that alter cholesterol crystallization to prevent acute cardiovascular events.
Introduction and hypothesis of a study on cholesterol crystals (CCs) as a cause of plaque disruption (PD) in coronary and carotid arteries, noting that ethanol-based tissue preparation dissolves CCs.

Study population: coronary arteries from acute coronary syndrome (n=19) and non-ACS (n=12) patients, and carotid plaques from symptomatic (n=51) and asymptomatic (n=19) patients, examined for intimal-perforating CCs by light and SEM microscopy.
Methods: CCs were examined by SEM with ethanol or vacuum dehydration and by confocal microscopy of fresh unfixed carotid plaques at 37 degrees C; SEM crystal content was scored 0 to +3.

Results: vacuum-dehydrated SEM detected significantly more crystals than ethanol dehydration (+2.5 vs +0.25, p<0.0003), SEM and confocal findings were similar suggesting in vivo perforation at 37 degrees C, and all ACS patients had perforating CCs versus none in non-ACS patients (p=0.0001).
Associations: CCs were strongly linked to plaque disruption, thrombus, symptoms, and plaque size, with crystal content an independent predictor of thrombus and symptoms.

Conclusion: avoiding ethanol preparation revealed intima-perforating CCs associated with plaque disruption and clinical events, suggesting cholesterol crystallization plays a role in acute cardiovascular events.

Introduction to the review's hypothesis: arterial wall injury drives an inflammatory response central to atherosclerosis and plaque instability, and the underlying injurious agent (cholesterol crystals) has been overlooked; the review proposes a two-stage model of plaque rupture.

Stage I of the proposed plaque rupture model: cholesterol crystal-induced cell injury and apoptosis in foam cells, creating a vicious cycle of macrophage recruitment and extracellular lipid accumulation that forms a lipid-rich necrotic core of a vulnerable plaque.

Stage II of the model: cholesterol crystal-induced arterial wall injury, where the saturated lipid core primed for crystallization triggers core expansion and intimal injury, which can present clinically as a systemic inflammatory syndrome.

Evidence that cholesterol crystallization causes volume expansion that can tear the plaque cap, supported by observations of crystals perforating the cap and intimal surface in plaques from patients who died of acute coronary syndrome.

Evidence that statins, aspirin, and ethanol dissolve cholesterol crystals, possibly explaining their immediate benefits, and that high-sensitivity C-reactive protein may mark intimal injury by crystals (shown in an atherosclerotic rabbit model) and aid statin therapy selection.

Conclusion of the review: cholesterol crystallization may partly explain both local and systemic inflammation in atherosclerosis, with hs-CRP as a possible indicator of crystal-induced intimal injury.
Copyright and publication notice from the National Lipid Association and Elsevier (2010), marking the end of the article text.

Opening of the abstract on death row last meals: introduces the study's framing (food desires under near-zero discounting of the future) and the empirical catalog of final food requests from 247 U.S. executions over five years.

Middle of the abstract summarizing the first key findings: the average last meal's high calorie count (2756 kcal), protein and fat levels about 2.5 times recommended servings, and the most frequently requested calorie-dense foods (meat, fried food, desserts, soft drinks).

Continuation of the abstract covering the share of branded food requests (39.9%) and the interpretation that results fit environmentally contingent temporal discounting and research on food as a way to cope with stress and distress.

Closing of the abstract: the implication that people warned about obesity may overeat unhealthily, suggesting further study of mortality salience in anti-obesity campaigns, followed by the Elsevier 2012 copyright notice.
Final fragment of the copyright notice from the document's end, containing only the closing words 'reserved.' of the Elsevier 2012 'All rights reserved' statement.

Abstract opening of a study on adherence to healthy lifestyle habits in US adults, defining the five habits (fruit/vegetable intake, exercise, healthy BMI, moderate alcohol, not smoking) and the NHANES survey periods compared (1988-1994 vs 2001-2006) for adults aged 40-74.

Methods continuation defining healthy BMI range and alcohol limits, and stating the comparison of NHANES 1988-1994 with NHANES 2001-2006 in adults aged 40-74, followed by the start of the Results section.

Core results on changes over 18 years: obesity rising from 28% to 36%, physical activity falling from 53% to 43%, smoking unchanged at about 26%, and fruit/vegetable intake of 5+ servings dropping from 42% to 26%.

Results on alcohol use rising from 40% to 51%, overall adherence to all five habits falling from 15% to 8%, larger declines among non-Hispanic Whites, and lower adherence among minorities; also notes that people with hypertension, diabetes, or cardiovascular disease were no more adherent.
Closing conclusions that healthy lifestyle adherence declined over the past 18 years, with decreases in 3 of 5 habits, and the study's implications for future cardiovascular disease risk in adults.
Final sentence of the conclusion stating that the findings have broad implications for the future risk of cardiovascular disease in adults.

Introduction and study aim: compares four diet quality indices (HEI-2010, AHEI-2010, aMED, DASH) as predictors of all-cause, cardiovascular, and cancer mortality in postmenopausal women in the Women's Health Initiative Observational Study.

Methods, part 1: prospective cohort of 63,805 WHI Observational Study participants (1993-2010) who completed a food frequency questionnaire at enrollment, analyzed with Cox proportional hazards models using person-years as the time metric.

Methods and results, part 1: analysis approach (Cox models, hazard ratios and 95% CIs across quintiles of index scores) and follow-up results: 12.9 years of follow-up, with 5,692 total deaths, including 1,483 CVD deaths and 2,384 cancer deaths.
Key findings: better diet quality on all four indices was linked to 18%-26% lower all-cause and CVD mortality; HEI, aMED, and DASH (not AHEI) were linked to 20%-23% lower cancer mortality.

Conclusion and publication notice: diet consistent with a priori quality indices is associated with lower chronic disease death risk; published by Oxford University Press for the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, 2014.
Copyright statement: the work was written by US Government employee(s) and is in the US public domain.

This chunk opens the study's Objectives and Methods, describing the use of 1994–2007 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data to measure four healthy lifestyle characteristics (healthy weight, not smoking, fruit/vegetable consumption, physical activity) and defining an overall healthy lifestyle as having all four.

This chunk covers the logistic regression methods and the first key results: non-smoking rose 4% and healthy weight fell 10% from 1994 to 2007, the largest temporal changes, while fruit/vegetable intake and physical activity barely changed.

This chunk reports the main findings on overall trends and regional differences: healthy lifestyle prevalence rose only minimally over time, and in 2007 the Northeast and West (6% each) had higher rates than the South and Midwest (4% each).

This chunk gives the study's conclusions: rising overweight and declining smoking produced little net change in healthy lifestyle prevalence, and overall prevalence across the US remains very low despite regional differences.
Introduction and objectives of a 2000 US study on healthy lifestyle characteristics (HLCs) and a single healthy lifestyle indicator, using BRFSS data.
Methods: data source (2000 BRFSS, random digit-dialed telephone surveys) and definition of the first HLCs, including nonsmoking and healthy body mass index (BMI) weight range.
Methods continued: BMI 18.5-25.0 criterion, 5+ daily fruit/vegetable servings, and regular physical activity definition; HLCs summed into a 0-4 index with all-4 pattern as the indicator.
Results: sample of over 153,000 adults and prevalence estimates with 95% CIs for nonsmoking (76.0%), healthy weight (40.1%), fruit/vegetable intake (23.3%), and physical activity (22.2%).
Results continued: overall prevalence of the healthy lifestyle indicator (all 4 HLCs) was only 3.0%, with little variation across subgroups (0.8%-5.7%).
Conclusion: very few US adults in 2000 followed all four healthy lifestyle characteristics, and no demographic subgroup met recommendations closely.

Introduction stating the AHA 2020 Strategic Impact Goal of a 20% relative improvement in cardiovascular health, defined by 4 behavior and 3 health factor metrics, and the study's aim to assess trends and 2020 projections.

Methods describing the study population: 35,059 cardiovascular disease-free adults aged 20+ from NHANES 1988–1994 and 2-year cycles 1999–2008, with prevalence of poor/intermediate/ideal behaviors and factors calculated.

Defines the composite Cardiovascular Health Score (0–14 points across 7 metrics) and reports results: smoking, hypercholesterolemia, and hypertension prevalence fell, while obesity and dysglycemia rose through 2008.

Results on behaviors and projections: physical activity and diet quality changed little; projected 2020 obesity and impaired fasting glucose/diabetes rates of 43%/77% in men and 42%/53% in women; population cardiovascular health projected to improve 6%.

Individual-level projected 2020 Cardiovascular Health Scores (men 7.4, women 8.8, with confidence intervals) compared against the scores needed for a 20% improvement (men 9.4, women 10.1), showing the target is unmet.
Conclusion: under current trends, the AHA 2020 goal of a 20% improvement in cardiovascular health will not be reached.

Introduction and study design of a 2001–2010 Nationwide Inpatient Sample analysis of Clostridium difficile colitis in the US, covering rising incidence, the scarcity of prior large-sample colectomy/mortality data, and the LASSO regression methods.

Methods continued: the LASSO logistic regression with 10-fold cross-validation using patient and hospital variables to model colectomy and post-colectomy mortality, plus multivariable analysis of colectomy timing versus mortality.

Results opening: about 2.77 million US CDC discharges over a decade, 19,374 colectomies (0.7%) with 30.7% mortality, and a 47% rise in CDC rate and 32% rise in colectomy rate from 2001–2005 to 2006–2010.

Results listing LASSO-identified predictors of needing colectomy (coagulopathy, weight loss, teaching hospital, fluid/electrolyte disorders, large hospital) with their odds ratios, and the start of the predictors of post-colectomy mortality.

Predictors of mortality after colectomy with odds ratios (coagulopathy, age over 60, acute renal failure, respiratory failure, sepsis, peripheral vascular disease, congestive heart failure), and the finding that surgery more than 3 days after admission carried higher mortality (OR 1.09).

Conclusions: C. difficile colitis is rising in the US with more total colectomies, post-colectomy mortality remains high, and patient and hospital factors predict progression to surgery and death, aiding risk stratification and counseling.
Closing copyright statement (2013, American College of Surgeons, Elsevier) for the article on C. difficile colitis trends, colectomy, and post-colectomy mortality in the US.

Introduction to community-acquired C. difficile infection: traditional at-risk groups (elderly, hospitalized, antibiotic users), rising community cases in young healthy people, and C. difficile carriage in mammals, birds and reptiles.

Environmental and food reservoirs of C. difficile: soil and water may be ubiquitous (weak evidence), food products like meat, fish and vegetables can carry it, with lower prevalence reported in Europe than North America.

Quantitative and transmission evidence: toxigenic C. difficile counts in environment and food are low, the infectious dose is unknown, and direct animal/food/environment-to-human transmission remains unproven despite similar PCR ribotypes.

Authors' conclusion on epidemiology: human CDI is not driven by amplification in animals or other sources, and since no community outbreaks occur, host vulnerability factors may matter more than exposure; this sets up the contrast with ribotype 078.

Ribotype 078 and zoonotic potential: emerging ribotype 078 is abundant in piglets, calves and their environment, circumstantial evidence suggests zoonotic potential without direct proof, and future emerging ribotypes should be assessed for this.
Closing copyright and publisher attribution notice (2012, Clinical Microbiology and Infection / ESCMID) ending the article's text.

Introduction to C. difficile as a foodborne concern: its recognized importance in human disease, the newer recognition of its role in animal disease, and reported food contamination prevalence in North America (4.6%-50%) versus Europe (0-3%).

Continuation of the prevalence comparison (European samples 0-3% positive) and the chapter's scope: summarizing C. difficile associations with different foods, isolation difficulties, and its potential as a food-transmitted pathogen, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.
Closing fragment of the chapter overview restating the discussion of C. difficile as a potential food-transmitted pathogen, plus the Elsevier Inc. 2010 copyright statement.

Introduction stating the problem: rising community infections from MRSA and C. difficile, both found in retail pork, but unclear whether contamination originates on the farm or during processing; this study aims to address that gap.
Longitudinal farm results: C. difficile prevalence falls from 93% of pigs at 1 day old to 1 of 26 at market age; MRSA peaks at 74 days (68% of pigs) and drops to 3 of 26 by 150 days.

Processing-facility results: C. difficile found in the holding area with one carcass positive pre-evisceration; MRSA mainly from nasal swabs, 31% of carcasses positive at postbleed rising to 54% at postscald tanks.
Carcass and environment sampling: only one MRSA-positive carcass at postbleed with no environmental recovery; C. difficile ribotype 078 dominated the longitudinal pig isolates (all 68).
Strain typing: only three slaughterhouse C. difficile isolates (ribotype 078) were found; MRSA spa type 539 (t034) predominated on-farm and at slaughter, making up 80% of isolates.
Conclusion: C. difficile and MRSA acquired on the farm persist through to processing, but there is no significant evidence of cross-contamination between carcasses or the slaughterhouse environment.

Introduction and methods of a study on Clostridium difficile transmission in Oxfordshire, UK: background on the assumption that infection spreads mainly in health care settings, and the start of whole-genome sequencing of symptomatic cases (2007-2011).

Methods continued: single-nucleotide variant (SNV) comparison between C. difficile isolates, using evolution rates estimated from 145 patients' first and last samples to define expected SNV differences for transmitted isolates.

Methods end and results begin: the 0-2 SNV threshold over 124 days based on a 95% prediction interval, epidemiologic linking via hospital admission and community data, and the sequencing success rate across 1250 cases.

Results on genetic clustering: of 957 samples from 2008-2011, 35% had 2 or fewer SNVs from an earlier case (consistent with transmission), while 45% were genetically distinct with more than 10 SNVs from all prior cases.

Interpretation of incidence trends and contact patterns: incidence fell similarly in both genetic groups, suggesting interventions affected progression from exposure to disease; among transmission-consistent cases, 38% had close hospital contact and 36% had no detected contact.

Conclusions on the persistent reservoir: distinct subtypes kept appearing throughout the study, and 45% of cases over three years were genetically unlike any earlier case, pointing to a large unrecognized source of C. difficile.

Final conclusion and funding: genetically diverse sources beyond symptomatic patients contribute substantially to C. difficile transmission, with funding acknowledgment from the U.K. Clinical Research Collaboration Translational Infection Research Initiative.

Introduction to C. difficile as a cause of infectious diarrhoea in humans and animals, noting its detection in farm animals and meat products as a possible reservoir and food-borne transmission route.
Discussion of antimicrobial exposure as the likely driver of C. difficile colonisation in animals, and of PCR ribotype 078 being the dominant ribotype in pigs and cattle.

Evidence linking animal and human C. difficile: ribotype 078 is now a leading human ribotype in Europe, human and pig strains are genetically identical there, and community-acquired CDI is rising worldwide.
Framing of the three problems to resolve (human health, animal health, and shared environmental contamination) and the link between rising community CDI and animal reservoirs.
Conclusion calling for a 'One Health' approach that brings together physicians, veterinarians and environmental scientists to address changing CDI epidemiology.

Introduction of the review on Clostridium difficile in foods and animals: it notes that CDI epidemiology is well covered for humans, but C. difficile presence in foods/animals and exposure-reduction measures are rarely addressed, and challenges the view that CDI is confined to health-care settings.

Summarizes recent molecular and genome sequencing evidence suggesting animals and foods may contribute to human CDI epidemiology and that hospital person-to-person transmission is being disproven; notes zoonotic/foodborne transmission is unconfirmed but susceptible people can still be exposed.

States that epidemic C. difficile clones found in humans occur widely in companion and food animals, raw meats, poultry, vegetables and ready-to-eat foods such as salads, and argues that understanding how the pathogen reaches food and people is key to science-based prevention.

Describes the review's scope: it contextualizes current knowledge of CDI across humans, animals and foods, and proposes a list of educational measures to reduce susceptible people's exposure to C. difficile.
Concluding statement calling for enhanced educational efforts and behavior change aimed at both medical and non-medical personnel to reduce C. difficile exposure.

Study objective and methods overview: a life-history analysis of cow milk consumption from prenatal life through adolescence, focusing on linear growth, age at menarche, and IGF-I as a mediator, using NHANES 1999-2004 data plus a literature review.

Results summary on milk and growth: literature supports milk enhancing early growth (under age 5) but less so in middle childhood; milk is linked to early menarche and adolescent growth acceleration; the NHANES analysis is introduced.

NHANES findings: milk intake is positively associated with linear growth in early childhood and adolescence but not middle childhood, a slow-growth period; IGF-I is proposed as a candidate bioactive link, with the mechanism unclear.

Conclusions: routine milk drinking is an evolutionarily novel dietary behavior that may alter human life history parameters, particularly linear growth, with possible negative long-term biological consequences.
Closing sentence of the conclusions restating the potential long-term harms of milk-driven accelerated linear growth, followed by the 2011 Wiley Periodicals copyright notice.

Study background and objective: tests whether milk and milk proteins (skim milk, whey, casein) reduce body weight, waist circumference, HOMA, insulin, and C-peptide in overweight adolescents, motivated by prior adult findings on dairy protein.

Study design and population: 203 overweight adolescents aged 12-15 y (BMI 25.4 kg/m2) randomized to 1 L/d of skim milk, whey, casein, or water for 12 weeks, all milk drinks providing 35 g protein/L; includes a pretest control subgroup of 32.

Comparison groups and outcome measures: effects compared against baseline, the water group, and a 12-week pretest control subgroup; diet and physical activity recorded; outcomes include BAZ, waist circumference, plasma insulin, HOMA, and plasma C-peptide.

Results on body weight and insulin secretion: BMI-for-age Z-scores rose at 12 weeks in skim milk, whey, and casein groups but not in water or pretest control; plasma C-peptide increased in whey and casein groups, exceeding the pretest control change (P < 0.02).

Main conclusions: high intakes of skim milk, whey, and casein increase BAZ in overweight adolescents, and whey and casein specifically increase insulin secretion, with no C-peptide change in the skim milk or water groups.
Open question and limitation: it remains unresolved whether the body weight gain from milk proteins is a primary effect or secondary to the increased insulin secretion.
Introduction and methods of an NHANES 1999–2004 study on childhood milk and total dairy intake and age at menarche, including the two samples (adult women and girls aged 9–12).
Regression results showing a weak negative association between milk consumption at ages 5–12 and age at menarche, with beta coefficients for daily and sometimes/variable intake versus rarely/never.

Cox regression findings: no increased risk of early menarche for sometimes/varied or daily milk drinkers versus never/rarely, and no effect of total dairy kcal, calcium, protein, or past-30-day milk intake among 9–12 year olds.
Tertile-based Cox results for 9–12 year old girls: middle-tertile milk intake marginally linked to lower early menarche risk, and lowest-tertile dairy fat intake linked to higher risk.

Further tertile results showing lowest calcium intake associated with lower early menarche risk, and confirmation that findings held after adjusting for overweight and height percentile, both of which increased early menarche risk.

Racial difference in early menarche (Blacks versus Whites, which disappears after controlling for overweight) and the study's overall conclusion that greater milk intake shows some evidence of association with earlier menarche.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the study's summary statement on milk intake and age at menarche.

Methods section of a case-control study on breast-feeding and later obesity: describes the study design, sample sizes (639 clinic patients and 533 high school controls aged 12-18), and the methodologic flaws it aims to correct.

Methods and early results: explains how weight status (obese, overweight, nonobese) was measured and how feeding history was blindly collected by telephone, then reports the raw-data finding of elevated relative risk of not breast-feeding and a significant trend across weight groups.

Results on duration effects: breast-feeding's protective effect appears to grow slightly with longer duration, delayed introduction of solid foods adds little benefit, and several demographic and clinical variables act as confounders.

Confounding analysis and conclusion: the protective effect of breast-feeding remains significant after adjusting for confounders, leading the authors to conclude breast-feeding protects against obesity and to attribute conflicting prior findings to weak methodology.
Closing fragment of the conclusion, ending the abstract's statement that conflicting prior results stem from insufficient attention to methodologic standards.
Opening of the abstract introducing milk as an active nutrient system for neonatal growth and the mTORC1 signaling pathway, noting the gap in knowledge about how milk up-regulates mTORC1.

Middle of the abstract describing the proposed materno-neonatal relay mechanism, in which milk amino acids raise GIP, GLP-1, insulin, GH and IGF-1 to activate mTORC1, and introducing milk exosomes containing microRNA-21 as a possible genetic transfection system.

Later part of the abstract stating that milk exosomes likely enhance mTORC1-driven metabolism, contrasting human breast milk as ideal infant food with the proposed risks of persistent cow's milk signaling in adolescents and adults.
Final sentence of the abstract concluding that continued cow's milk consumption beyond infancy may promote mTORC1-driven diseases of civilization.

Introduction to a study on how funding sources relate to outcomes of obesity-related dairy/nutrition research, describing the 2001-2005 funded project sources (dairy checkoff programs and NIH) and the start of the methods.

Methods continued: identifying Principal Investigators of funded projects, searching Ovid MEDLINE and PubMed for their publications on dairy and obesity, and noting that sponsorship and conclusions were classified by independent co-investigator groups.

Results: 79 relevant articles were analyzed (62 checkoff-sponsored, 17 NIH-sponsored), and the study found no consistent evidence that checkoff-funded research more often reported an obesity prevention benefit from dairy.
Conclusion and publication notice: the study contributes a new methodology for detecting sponsorship bias in research, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright statement.

Introduction and study objective from a longitudinal cohort study (Amsterdam Growth and Health Study) on lifetime dietary fiber intake from adolescence to adulthood and adult arterial stiffness, including background on fiber's cardiovascular benefits.

Study design details: 373 participants, dietary intake assessed at ages 13 to 36 with 2-8 repeated measures (median 5), and arterial stiffness measured by ultrasonography of three large arteries at age 36.

Main results: after adjustment for sex, height, energy intake and lifestyle, adults with stiffer carotid arteries had lower lifetime fiber intake (g/d) across the 24-year study, based on sex-specific tertile comparisons.

Quantitative effect estimates (with 95% CIs) linking lower fiber intake to carotid stiffness across distensibility, compliance (reversed) and Young's elastic modulus measures, plus associations with lower lifetime fruit, vegetable and whole grain consumption.

Interpretation of findings: stiffer carotid arteries tied to lower lifetime fruit, vegetable and whole grain intake largely explained by low fiber; conclusion that lower lifetime fiber intake in youth is associated with adult carotid stiffness.
Concluding public health implication: promoting fiber-rich foods among young people may help prevent accelerated arterial stiffening and related cardiovascular outcomes in adulthood.

Introduction and methods of a 12-year population-based study of 1647 subjects examining whether dietary fiber intake (DFI) affects stroke incidence and risk, adjusting for many cardiovascular, metabolic, and lifestyle covariables.
Methods covariables list and the start of the results: adjusted Cox models show high DFI reduces stroke risk, and quintile-based analysis of fiber intake is introduced.
Results giving the cut-offs (soluble fiber >25 g/day, insoluble fiber >47 g/day) and the multivariate hazard ratios for stroke: HR 0.31 for soluble and HR 0.35 for insoluble fiber above the cut-offs.

Remaining results (about 50% and 46% lower stroke incidence with p-values) and the conclusion that higher dietary fiber is inversely and independently associated with stroke incidence and risk in the general population, followed by the copyright notice.
Trailing fragment of the copyright notice (Elsevier Ltd and European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism, 2012) at the end of the abstract.

Background, aims, and methods of a systematic review/meta-analysis on dietary fiber intake and first stroke risk; introduces the gap that no prior meta-analysis existed and describes the database search (1990 to May 2012) for healthy-participant cohort studies.

Results section: eight cohort studies from the US, northern Europe, Australia, and Japan; pooled finding that total dietary fiber is inversely associated with hemorrhagic plus ischemic stroke (RR 0.93 per 7 g/day, 95% CI 0.88-0.98, I2=59%).

Subtype results: soluble fiber per 4 g/day showed no significant stroke risk reduction (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.88-1.01, I2=21%), and insoluble fiber or fiber from cereals, fruit, or vegetables was reported by too few studies to draw conclusions.

Conclusions: greater total dietary fiber is significantly linked to lower first-stroke risk, supporting recommendations to increase fiber intake, while sparse data on food sources limit conclusions about fiber type and stroke.
Closing research recommendation: future studies should investigate fiber type and analyze ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes separately.

Introduces the epidemiological link between dietary fiber and lower cardiovascular disease risk, noting a stronger inverse association for cereal fiber than fruit or vegetable fiber, and the protective link of whole grains.

Notes that recent US dietary guidelines endorse fiber-rich whole grains, and lists the proposed mechanisms (lipid reduction, weight regulation, glucose metabolism, blood pressure, inflammation) by which cereal fiber may improve cardiovascular health.

Lists future research directions: studying fiber sources such as whole grains, legumes, fruits, vegetables, nuts, and resistant starch in relation to CVD risk and weight control, and investigating the biological mechanisms of fiber's cardioprotective effects.
Concludes the future research agenda by calling for studies across different ethnic groups and populations with varying dietary fiber sources.

Introduces the paper's central claim that bariatric surgery reproducibly reverses type 2 diabetes metabolic abnormalities, and that quantifying insulin secretion and action after surgery reveals the sequence of events in restoring normal metabolism, starting with liver fat and hepatic insulin sensitivity.

Describes the post-surgery recovery pattern: plasma glucose normalizes alongside hepatic insulin sensitivity, muscle insulin sensitivity stays abnormal for months, and the surgical effect is attributed solely to energy restriction, setting up the proposed causal model.

Presents the proposed causal chain of type 2 diabetes: muscle insulin resistance (genetic and environmental) promotes fatty liver during positive energy balance, and prospective observations before diabetes onset support this sequence.

Explains downstream mechanisms: fatty liver causes resistance to insulin's suppression of hepatic glucose output and raises plasma triacylglycerol, while elevated fatty acids from circulating and local fat impair glucose-stimulated insulin secretion by beta cells.

States the proposed time sequence of type 2 diabetes pathogenesis: muscle insulin resistance sets the pace of fatty liver progression, and ectopic liver and islet fat drive hepatic insulin resistance and beta cell dysfunction, with beta cell suppression first reversible then permanent.

Concludes that the hepatic insulin resistance and beta cell defects can be dramatically reversed by hypoenergetic (calorie-restricted) feeding, fully in early diabetes and partially in established disease.

Opening of a 2012 Banting Memorial Lecture arguing that Type 2 diabetes is reversible, citing rapid normalisation of glucose metabolism after bariatric surgery, attributed to reduced food intake rather than surgery itself.

Describes the Counterpoint study, in which a very low calorie diet alone restored normal glucose levels and beta cell function, and introduces the magnetic resonance methods used to measure intra-organ fat.
Reports the two time courses found during reversal: liver insulin sensitivity and liver fat recover within days, while beta cell insulin secretion recovers over weeks alongside falling pancreas fat.
Introduces the twin cycle hypothesis, which holds that chronic calorie excess causes liver fat accumulation that spills into the pancreas, tracing the reversed course of the disease's onset.

Concludes that the twin liver-pancreas cycles inhibit post-meal insulin secretion and cause hyperglycaemia, framing Type 2 diabetes as a reversible condition of intra-organ fat excess with varying individual susceptibility.
Final word fragment completing the closing sentence: people differ in how susceptible they are to intra-organ fat excess in Type 2 diabetes.

Opening chunk of a review on dietary fat and glucose metabolism: introduces the long-recognized link, animal studies showing high-fat diets impair glucose tolerance and insulin-stimulated glucose metabolism, and membrane fatty acid changes as a possible mechanism.

Human evidence on fat and insulin sensitivity: high-fat diets reduce insulin sensitivity regardless of fatty acid profile, saturated fat appears more harmful than mono- or polyunsaturated fat, and omega-3 fatty acids can ameliorate some effects.

Epidemiological findings: higher fat intake is linked to greater risk of impaired glucose tolerance and type 2 diabetes, though the data are inconsistent, possibly because high fat intake (especially animal fat) clusters with obesity and inactivity.

Metabolic comparisons: higher-fat diets rich in unsaturated fat yield better glucose metabolism measures than high-carbohydrate diets, and the chunk notes that the relationship is not yet fully understood.
Concluding sentence of the review: states that the area of dietary fat and glucose metabolism remains incompletely elucidated and needs further research.

Introduction to the document's overview of recent developments in antiemetic drugs, formulations, guidelines, and controversies for postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), covering prevention and treatment in the recovery unit and after discharge.

Describes the introduction of the newer antiemetics palonosetron (second-generation 5-HT3 antagonist) and aprepitant (NK-1 antagonist), and identifies postdischarge nausea and vomiting as the next frontier for research and therapy.

Covers the clinical factors guiding antiemetic choice (efficacy, cost, safety, dosing ease) and raises safety concerns about QTc prolongation from butyrophenones and first-generation 5-HT3 antagonists.
Discusses pharmacogenetics as a determinant of antiemetic metabolism and efficacy, and notes that ethics in PONV research has been raised by a meta-analysis of PONV studies.
Concludes by noting the SAMBA PONV consensus guidelines, which were introduced and updated to help clinicians select antiemetics and manage PONV therapy.

Study introduction and methods of a randomized trial on peppermint aromatherapy plus controlled breathing versus controlled breathing alone for postoperative nausea and/or vomiting (PONV) relief, describing the rationale and single-blind design.
Methods details on group allocation (CB n=16, AR n=26), repeat treatment at 5 minutes, final assessment at 10 minutes, and rescue medication, followed by the reported PONV incidence (21.4%, 42/196).

Key findings of the PONV aromatherapy trial: gender as the only significant risk factor (P=.0024), controlled breathing being numerically more efficacious than aromatherapy (62.5% vs 57.7%, not significant), and conclusions supporting controlled breathing as an antiemetic alternative and peppermint aromatherapy as an adjunct.

Concluding statement recommending peppermint aromatherapy combined with controlled breathing for PONV relief, followed by the 2014 copyright notice from the American Society of PeriAnesthesia Nurses and Elsevier.

Introduction and study aims for a PONV risk score study: testing cross-center validity of a risk score from Oulu (Finland) and Wuerzburg (Germany), and whether logistic-regression-based scores can be simplified.

Methods: patient populations from Oulu (n=520) and Wuerzburg (n=2202) receiving inhalational anesthesia without antiemetic prophylaxis; PONV defined as nausea or vomiting within 24 h; risk scores built by logistic regression.

Methods continued: simplified scores built by counting significant risk factors, cross-validation of original and simplified scores, a combined dataset to test for center effects and derive a final score, and evaluation via ROC area under the curve.

Results on validation: scores from one center predicted PONV in the other (AUC 0.65-0.75), simplified scores kept similar discrimination (AUC 0.63-0.73), and no center effect was found in the combined data (OR 1.06).

Final simplified score with four predictors (female gender, history of motion sickness or PONV, nonsmoking, postoperative opioid use) and the observed PONV incidences by number of risk factors present (10% to 79%).

Conclusions: the score derived in one center is valid in the other, can be simplified without significant loss of discrimination, and appears broadly applicable to adults under inhalational anesthesia for various surgeries.
Clinical recommendation: patients with at least two of the four identified predictors should be considered for prophylactic antiemetic treatment.

Introduces the study's background: high-risk PONV patients typically get prophylactic IV ondansetron and postoperative IV promethazine, and the study's aim to test whether 70% isopropyl alcohol inhalation beats promethazine for breakthrough PONV.

Describes the study population and design: high-risk patients under general anesthesia who received 4 mg prophylactic IV ondansetron, then were randomized to IPA or promethazine for breakthrough PONV.

Lists the outcome measures (demographics, VNRS nausea scores, time to 50% VNRS reduction, antiemetic use, PONV incidence) and reports the analyzed sample of 85 subjects with no baseline group differences.

Summarizes the results: the IPA group had faster 50% VNRS reduction and lower overall antiemetic requirements, with similar PONV incidence, leading to the recommendation of 70% IPA inhalation as a treatment option.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the recommendation that 70% IPA inhalation is an option for treating PONV in high-risk patients given prophylactic ondansetron.

Study design and intervention groups for a trial of peppermint aromatherapy against nausea after scheduled C-section: the peppermint spirits group, the placebo sterile water group, and the standard antiemetic group (ondansetron or promethazine).

Methods of the peppermint aromatherapy nausea study in post-C-section women: random group assignment on hospital admission, and nurses on the mother-baby unit recording baseline nausea, giving the intervention, and reassessing at 2 and 5 minutes using a 6-point scale.

Findings from the peppermint aromatherapy C-section study: 35 women became nauseated after surgery, baseline nausea was similar across the three groups, and the peppermint spirits group had significantly lower nausea at 2 and 5 minutes.

Conclusions of the peppermint spirits postoperative nausea study: peppermint may be a useful adjunct for postoperative nausea, and the work should be replicated with more participants, other aromatherapies, and varied preoperative diagnoses.

Closing recommendation of the peppermint aromatherapy nausea study: future research should replicate it with a larger sample, test a variety of aromatherapies, and include participants with different preoperative diagnoses.

Opening of the document's abstract-style overview on PONV: its prevalence (over 30%, up to 70-80% in high-risk groups without prophylaxis) and the role of 5-HT3 antagonists versus newer agents like NK-1 antagonists.

Middle portion introducing newer antiemetic strategies (NK-1 antagonists, longer-acting serotonin antagonists, multimodal management) and defining postdischarge nausea and vomiting (PDNV) as an emerging concern for providers.
Explains why PONV and PDNV matter most in ambulatory surgery, which accounts for over 60% of 56.4 million US surgery visits, given the brief facility stay and need for rapid prevention and treatment.
Closing sentence stressing swift, effective prevention and treatment of PONV and PDNV in ambulatory patients, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces the aromatherapy study on postoperative nausea: 33 ambulatory surgery patients in the PACU with nausea, randomized to isopropyl alcohol, peppermint oil, or saline placebo, with the inhalation method and baseline 100-mm VAS nausea rating.

Describes the aromatherapy inhalation procedure and the main results: nausea VAS scores fell from 60.6 mm before treatment to 43.1 mm at 2 minutes and 28.0 mm at 5 minutes after aromatherapy, with statistical p-values.

Reports that nausea scores did not differ between treatment groups at any time point, that only 52% of patients needed IV antiemetic therapy in the PACU, and that overall satisfaction with nausea management was 86.9 mm regardless of group.

Concludes that aromatherapy effectively reduced perceived postoperative nausea, and that the equal effect of the saline placebo suggests the benefit may come from controlled breathing patterns rather than the aroma itself.
Final sentence of the conclusion, stating that the benefit of aromatherapy for postoperative nausea may depend more on controlled breathing patterns than on the inhaled aroma.

Introduces the randomised, double-blind trial of Mentha spicata and Mentha × piperita essential oils for preventing chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV), and describes the four-group randomisation and statistical methods.

Methods continue with the study design: treatment and placebo groups received essential oils of M. spicata, M. × piperita, or placebo, the control group kept its usual antiemetic regimen, and 50 courses per group were analysed.

Methods describe outcome measurement by patients or guardians over 20 hours of chemotherapy (emetic event counts, nausea intensity, adverse effects), leading into the results on emetic reduction in the first 24 hours.

Results and conclusion: significant reductions in emetic event number and intensity with both mint oils versus control (p < 0.05), no adverse effects, lower treatment cost, and the conclusion that the oils are safe, effective, and cost-effective antiemetics.
Final fragment of the conclusion restating that Mentha spicata or Mentha × piperita essential oils are safe, effective, and cost-effective for antiemetic treatment in patients.

Introduces a study of 100 adult day-case surgery patients surveyed anonymously on attitudes to rectal drug administration, reporting that 54 did not want rectal diclofenac sodium analgesia under anaesthesia and preferred oral dosing.
Reports that 98 patients wanted rectally administered drugs always discussed beforehand, and concludes that prescribers of rectal diclofenac should discuss it with patients pre-operatively.
Concludes that while many patients accept suppositories, some young patients are sensitive about them and prefer oral medication instead.

Introduces the design of two studies on dietary protein and plasma cholesterol in healthy young women, comparing a conventional mixed-protein diet against a plant protein diet (soy meat analogues and soy milk replacing animal protein).

Describes the matched diet composition and details the first study (73 days, six subjects), which suggested lower plasma cholesterol on the plant protein diet, and begins describing the improved second study (78 days, cross-over design, two groups of five).

Reports the key result of the improved second cross-over study: mean plasma cholesterol was significantly lower on the plant protein (soy) diet, supporting a hypocholesterolemic effect of substituting soy protein for animal protein.

Study design and setup: an 8-man, healthy normolipidemic cross-over trial (ages 18-27) comparing a plant protein diet with a diet where 55% of plant protein is replaced by beef protein, each lasting 21 days within a 42-day study.

Methods: fasting venous blood sampling at baseline and every 7 days over the 42-day study, with serum total cholesterol and triglycerides plus plasma LDL and HDL cholesterol measured as the outcome variables.

Results for cholesterol: no significant differences in total or LDL cholesterol between diets, while HDL cholesterol was significantly higher at day 21 on the animal (beef) protein diet (48 vs 42 mg/dl, p<0.05).
Results for triglycerides: at day 7, serum triglycerides were significantly higher on the plant protein diet (136 mg/dl) than on the beef protein diet (84 mg/dl), p<0.05.
Conclusion: replacing 55% of protein with beef protein did not produce a hypercholesterolemic effect in healthy, normolipidemic young men, supporting its safety for blood lipids.

Study abstract on soy vs. animal protein diets and cholesterol: describes the study population (young men with mildly elevated cholesterol), the low-cholesterol diet design, and protein source composition.

Continues the diet design: protein sources made comparable with animal fats, egg yolk added to match cholesterol, shared grain and vegetable protein, and the count of subjects whose plasma cholesterol fell (20 of 24).
Describes the responder/nonresponder classification based on mean cholesterol reduction, and the significant percentage decreases in plasma cholesterol for responders in the animal and soy groups.
Reports that responders had higher starting cholesterol, and that HDL cholesterol dropped slightly while the HDL-to-total cholesterol ratio stayed largely constant across individuals.
Concludes that hypocholesterolemic effects of animal and soy protein and fat were similar, and that all groups significantly reduced dietary cholesterol intake.

Abstract opening of a 2000 European Journal of Clinical Nutrition randomized cross-over study comparing lean meat versus tofu diets on serum lipoproteins in 42 healthy middle-aged men, describing objectives, design, and subjects.

Intervention details of the tofu vs lean meat study: 150 g/d lean meat compared with 290 g/d tofu in isocaloric, isoprotein substitution over two 1-month periods with controlled fat intake; diet records showed similar energy, macronutrients and fibre.

Key results of the meat vs tofu lipoprotein trial: tofu diet significantly lowered total cholesterol and triglycerides relative to lean meat, but also significantly lowered HDL-C, with 95% CIs and P-values reported.

Conclusion of the tofu study explaining that its HDL-C and small LDL-C findings differ from prior soy studies (which had less fat control and used textured protein or soymilk versus casein), suggesting protein-specific effects may account for the discrepancy.

Practical implication from the tofu vs meat study: replacing meat with tofu would typically reduce saturated fat and increase polyunsaturated fat, possibly amplifying modest soy protein benefits; also lists the study sponsor, Deakin University and Commonwealth Department of Veterans Affairs funding.
Closing citation and funding acknowledgment for the tofu vs lean meat lipoprotein study, published in European Journal of Clinical Nutrition 2000, volume 54, pages 14-19.

Opening of an abstract describing a randomized crossover dietary trial at Deakin University comparing lean meat with tofu, stating its objectives (lipoproteins, Lp(a), factor VII, fibrinogen, LDL oxidation) and subject population of free-living males aged 35-62.

Middle of the abstract's methods: subject count (45 healthy males, 3 non-compliant and excluded) and the intervention design, 150 g/day lean meat versus 290 g/day tofu under isocaloric, isoprotein substitution, with one-month periods.
Results section of the abstract opening: the seven-day diet records showed comparable nutrient intake between diets, and total cholesterol and triglycerides were significantly lower on the tofu diet.

Key findings of the abstract: LDL oxidation lag phase was significantly longer on tofu, while factor VII, fibrinogen and Lp(a) were unaffected, followed by the start of the conclusions on reduced CHD risk.
Final conclusion sentence of the abstract, stating that the longer LDL oxidation lag phase on the tofu diet would be expected to lower coronary heart disease risk.

Opening of the abstract: background on limiting red meat to reduce coronary heart disease risk, and the stated objective of a meta-analysis of RCTs comparing beef with poultry/fish on lipoprotein lipids.
Methods of the beef vs. poultry/fish lipid meta-analysis: RCTs from 1950-2010, inclusion criteria requiring fasting lipid changes in subjects free of chronic disease.
Results opening: 124 RCTs screened, 8 studies with 406 subjects included, and the start of the reported mean lipid changes (mg/dL) for beef versus poultry/fish relative to baseline diet.

Numerical results of the meta-analysis: beef vs. poultry/fish changes in total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triacylglycerols with standard errors and P-values (all non-significant), plus the start of the conclusion.

Conclusion of the study: no significant difference in fasting lipid profile between beef and poultry/fish, and lean beef adds food variety that may aid long-term dietary adherence for lipid management; begins copyright notice.
Closing copyright statement from the National Lipid Association and Elsevier (2012) for the beef vs. poultry/fish lipid meta-analysis abstract.

Opening of a document on protein sources and coronary heart disease (CHD): introduces meat protein's link to heart disease and weight gain, plus Nurses' Health Study findings on diet patterns and CHD risk.
Middle section of the protein and CHD document: covers low-carbohydrate diets by protein source (animal vs. vegetable) and total mortality, and AHA-assessed soy interventions on LDL cholesterol.

Final section of the protein and CHD document: discusses dairy intake's association with weight, insulin resistance, and metabolic syndrome, and notes the only 6-month dairy intervention showed no effects.
Closing fragment of the protein and CHD document, finishing the sentence on the 6-month dairy intervention finding no effects on weight, insulin resistance, or metabolic syndrome.

Introduction stating the rationale: LDL-C lowering from almonds, low-saturated-fat, viscous fiber, soy protein, and plant sterol diets, and the aim of combining them into a single 'portfolio diet' to match statin-level reductions.

Study design: 25 hyperlipidemic subjects randomized to a portfolio diet (n=13, with specified plant sterol, soy protein, viscous fiber, and almond intake per 1,000 kcal) or a low-saturated-fat control diet (n=12).

Methods and primary results: fasting measurements at weeks 0, 2, and 4; LDL-C fell 12.1% on the low-fat diet versus 35.0% on the portfolio diet, and the LDL:HDL-C ratio fell 30.0% on the portfolio diet.

Comparative results: portfolio diet produced significantly greater reductions in LDL-C and the LDL:HDL-C ratio than the control diet (both P<.001), with similar weight loss on both diets (1.0 kg vs 0.9 kg).

Null outcomes and conclusion: no between-diet differences in blood pressure, HDL-C, triglycerides, Lp(a), or homocysteine; the authors suggest a dietary portfolio may lower LDL-C similarly to statins.
Concluding statement: the dietary portfolio approach may increase the effectiveness of dietary therapy for hypercholesterolemia by approximating statin-level LDL-C reduction.
Study introduction and design: blueberries with a high-carbohydrate, low-fat breakfast, 14 participants in a 3-week crossover with high (75 g), low (35 g) and control treatments.
Methods and measurements: serum ORAC, lipoprotein oxidation, and ascorbate, urate and glucose were measured at fasting and 1, 2, 3 h; early result that ORAC was higher for 75 g vs control.
Key results: ORAC significantly higher for 75 g vs control in the first 2 h, LO lag time trend for both doses, and no significant differences in ascorbate, urate or glucose among groups.

Conclusions: blueberries' antioxidant effect is not explained by fructose or ascorbate content, and 75 g provides significant in vivo oxidative protection after a high-carbohydrate, low-fat breakfast.
Closing speculation: the protective effect is likely due to blueberry phenolic compounds, though this was not tested directly.

Introduction and background of a meta-analysis on 'catalytic' fructose doses (≤10 g/meal) and their effects on glycaemic response, describing the search strategy across MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL and the Cochrane Library for controlled feeding trials.

Methods of the meta-analysis: eligibility criteria (controlled feeding trials ≥7 days, fructose ≤36 g/day isoenergetic exchange), generic inverse variance random-effects pooling as mean differences with 95% CI, and heterogeneity assessment via Q statistic and I².

Methods on study quality (Heyland Methodological Quality Score) and results: six feeding trials (n=118) included, with catalytic fructose significantly reducing HbA1c (MD −0.40) and fasting glucose (MD −0.25).

Results showing no adverse effects of catalytic fructose on fasting insulin, body weight, TAG or uric acid, plus subgroup and sensitivity analysis findings of effect modification and limitations from few, short trials.

Conclusion of the meta-analysis: catalytic fructose doses (≤36 g/day) may improve glycaemic control without adverse effects on body weight, TAG, insulin or uric acid, with a call for larger, longer (≥6 month) trials to confirm.
Final sentence of the conclusion calling for larger, longer trials (≥6 months) of catalytic fructose to confirm the glycaemic findings.

Background and rationale of a trial on fruit intake in type 2 diabetes: guidelines recommend fruit as part of a fiber-rich diet, but some clinicians worry fruit worsens glycemic control and advise restriction, with no prior studies on this question.

Study objective and the clinical question: whether advising fruit reduction in type 2 diabetes changes HbA1c, body weight, waist circumference, and fruit intake, since no prior studies addressed fruit restriction.

Methods of the open randomized controlled trial with two parallel arms, primary outcome being HbA1c change over 12 weeks; high-fruit group advised at least two fruit pieces daily versus low-fruit group advised no more than two.

Trial procedures: all participants received two dietitian consultations, fruit intake was measured by 3-day fruit records and dietary recalls, and analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle; results begin with 63 newly diagnosed participants.

Key results: all patients completed the trial; high-fruit group increased fruit intake by 125 g while low-fruit group reduced by 51 g; HbA1c fell in both groups with no significant between-group difference (0.19%, CI -0.23 to 0.62).

Secondary results and conclusion: both groups lost weight and reduced waist circumference without between-group differences; advice to cut fruit lowered fruit intake but had no effect on HbA1c, weight, or waist circumference in overweight newly diagnosed patients.
Final recommendation and registration: the authors advise against restricting fruit intake in type 2 diabetes, and the trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov under NCT01010594.

Abstract of a study on the synergistic neurotoxicity of methylmercury and BMAA in primary cortical cultures; introduces the research question about environmental factors in neurodegeneration and reports that BMAA potentiates methylmercury toxicity.

Middle of the abstract describing results: BMAA at non-toxic concentrations potentiates methylmercury toxicity, the combined exposures deplete glutathione, and the glutathione monoethyl ester (cell-permeant glutathione) attenuates the combined toxicity.
Concluding sentences of the abstract summarizing that BMAA and methylmercury act synergistically and that the mechanism of interaction is glutathione depletion.

Introduction to the paper on BMAA, a cyanobacteria-derived non-protein amino acid, and its proposed role as an environmental trigger in ALS and related neurodegenerative diseases, beginning with the Guam ALS/PDC association.

Continuation of the introduction describing BMAA's proposed neurotoxic mechanisms: agonist action on NMDA and AMPA receptors, oxidative stress, and glutathione depletion in motor neurons, and its implication in ALS, Alzheimer's, and other neurodegenerative diseases.

Discussion of BMAA's potential to cause intraneuronal protein misfolding, the lack of an animal model for BMAA-induced ALS despite substantial supporting evidence, and the significance of an environmental ALS trigger.
Closing statement of the introduction outlining the paper's scope: the history, ecology, pharmacology, and clinical ramifications of the ubiquitous cyanobacteria-derived toxin BMAA.

Introduction/abstract opening: defines BMAA, a neurotoxin from cyanobacteria linked to Guam neurodegenerative disease, and states the hypothesis that it may occur and bioaccumulate in other ecosystems.
Abstract methods and key finding: describes the HPLC-MS/MS extraction method and 2007–2008 Baltic Sea monitoring, showing BMAA is biosynthesized by cyanobacteria that dominate surface blooms.

Abstract results on food web transfer: BMAA is higher in higher trophic organisms (zooplankton, fish, mussels, oysters), including human-consumed pelagic and benthic fish, with peak levels in muscle and brain of bottom-dwelling fish.

Abstract conclusion: regular BMAA production in a large temperate aquatic ecosystem and its bioaccumulation through food webs ending in human consumption is a public health concern requiring attention.
Final fragment of the abstract conclusion, completing the closing sentence calling for attention to BMAA in the Baltic Sea food web.
Introduction of a case study on BMAA, a cyanobacteria-produced neurotoxin, as a possible environmental risk factor for sporadic ALS, focusing on three Annapolis, Maryland patients.

Methods and findings: a questionnaire identified frequent blue crab consumption as the shared exposure among the ALS patients, and LC-MS/MS testing of crabs from a local Annapolis fish market was set up to check for BMAA.

Results and conclusion: BMAA was detected in Chesapeake Bay blue crabs, leading the authors to propose that BMAA in the bay food web and lifetime blue crab consumption is a shared risk factor for sporadic ALS in the three patients.
Closing copyright notice (Elsevier Ltd., 2013) at the end of the abstract of the BMAA and sporadic ALS study.

Introduction and background of the study: dietary BMAA cyanotoxin exposure as a suspected ALS cause, plus the study's stated objectives of finding ALS clusters in the Hérault district of Southern France and checking for a dietary BMAA source.

Continuation of the objectives and the methods section: the spatio-temporal cluster analysis of incident ALS cases from 1994 to 2009, and the serial blind-analyzed oyster and mussel sampling in the cluster area.

Methods conclusion and start of results: the cluster analysis of Hérault ALS cases, the oyster and mussel sampling, and the significant ALS cluster (p = 0.0024) found around the Thau lagoon, a major shellfish production area.
Core results: BMAA concentrations measured in mussels (1.8–6.0 µg/g) and oysters (0.6–1.6 µg/g), with peak levels in summer when picocyanobacteria abundance was highest.
Conclusion of the abstract: the study cannot prove a direct link between shellfish consumption and the ALS cluster, but adds evidence for a possible BMAA association with sporadic ALS.
Final fragment of the abstract's conclusion, ending the sentence that describes ALS as one of the most severe neurodegenerative disorders.

Introduction of the study: cyanobacterial neurotoxin BMAA linked to ALS, and the reported cluster of ALS cases among residents of Enfield, NH near a cyanobacteria-prone lake, motivating the investigation.

Methods and key finding: records were reviewed to identify New England ALS patients, finding nine cases near Lake Mascoma in Enfield, NH, with sporadic ALS incidence 10 to 25 times the expected rate of 2/100,000/year.

Interpretation and exposure routes: the authors propose chronic exposure to cyanobacterial neurotoxins such as BMAA as the cause of the high ALS incidence, via aerosolized toxins, fish consumption, or lake water ingestion.
Conclusion and future work: further study, including brain tissue analysis for cyanobacterial toxins, is needed to test whether BMAA is associated with ALS in this cluster.
Introduces the ALS cluster in Two Rivers, Wisconsin (1975-1983, six cases, p<.05) and the case-control study design, matching two controls per case on age, gender, and residence duration.

Reports the case-control findings: physical trauma, frequent consumption of freshly caught Lake Michigan fish, and family history of cancer were more common among ALS cases, supporting a trauma role and suggesting diet be explored further.
Concludes that continued surveillance and epidemiologic investigation of ALS clusters, with retrospective analysis, may help identify the cause of ALS.
Introduction of a shark fin study: sharks' threatened status, demand for shark fin soup, and toxin bioaccumulation concerns, introducing the cyanobacterial neurotoxin BMAA (cut off mid-acronym).
