Gives the corresponding relative risks for men with all five low-risk factors, and the population attributable fractions of stroke cases linked to non-adherence to the low-risk lifestyle in women.
Reports the estimated preventable proportion of stroke among men and concludes that a low-risk lifestyle may prevent stroke, especially ischemic stroke.
Final fragment of the conclusion, restating that a healthy lifestyle may help prevent stroke, particularly ischemic stroke.

Abstract opening (Background and Methods) of a Swedish Mammography Cohort study on combined low-risk diet and lifestyle behaviors and primary myocardial infarction prevention in postmenopausal women; describes the sample of 24,444 women and the factor-analysis-derived healthy dietary pattern.
Methods continuation defining the three low-risk lifestyle factors (nonsmoking, waist-hip ratio below 0.85, physical activity thresholds) and the start of the Results describing follow-up duration.

Results section reporting 6.2 years of follow-up with 308 primary MI cases, the two dietary patterns (healthy and alcohol) linked to lower MI risk, and the description of the healthy diet's food components.

Results section giving the main finding: the combined low-risk diet and lifestyle profile, including moderate alcohol intake, was associated with a 92% reduced MI risk versus women with no low-risk factors.

Final Results sentence on the combination being present in 5% of women and potentially preventing 77% of MIs, followed by the Conclusion that most MIs in women may be preventable through diet, alcohol moderation, activity, nonsmoking, and healthy weight.
Final fragment of the Conclusion, completing the statement that maintaining a healthy weight is part of the behaviors that may prevent most MIs in women.

Introduction/background of a Health Professionals Follow-up Study analysis on how healthy lifestyle factors (diet, exercise, weight, not smoking) could reduce coronary heart disease risk, especially among US men on hypertension or hypercholesterolemia medication.

Methods of the Health Professionals Follow-up Study: 42,847 men aged 40-75, disease-free in 1986, with lifestyle factors updated via self-reported questionnaires and the five low-risk lifestyle criteria defined.

Definition of the five low-risk lifestyle factors (no smoking, BMI under 25, 30+ min/day moderate-vigorous activity, moderate alcohol intake of 5-30 g/day, top 40% healthy diet score) and the 16-year follow-up yielding 2,183 CHD cases.
Main results: men with low risk on all 5 lifestyle factors had a relative risk of CHD of 0.13 (CI 0.09-0.19) versus those with none, from multivariate Cox models.

Population-attributable findings: about 62% of coronary events may have been prevented by healthy lifestyle adherence overall, and 57% among men taking hypertension or hypercholesterolemia medication.

Effect of lifestyle change during follow-up: men adopting two or more additional low-risk factors had 27% lower CHD risk; conclusion that most CHD events among US men may be preventable even with medication use.

Final sentence of the conclusion restating that a majority of CHD events may be preventable through healthy lifestyle practices, including among men on hypertension or hypercholesterolemia medications.

Introduction and background of the INTERHEART case-control study, motivating the global assessment of myocardial infarction risk factors in low- and middle-income countries where most cardiovascular burden occurs.

Methods of the INTERHEART study: a standardised case-control design of acute myocardial infarction across 52 countries with 15152 cases and 14820 controls, listing the risk factors examined, including smoking, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, diet, activity, alcohol, apolipoproteins and psychosocial factors.

Statistical methods (odds ratios with 99% CIs and population attributable risks) and the start of the Findings section, reporting smoking's odds ratio and PAR and the ApoB/ApoA1 ratio's association with MI.
Findings continued: quantitative odds ratios and population attributable risks for ApoB/ApoA1 ratio, hypertension, diabetes, and abdominal obesity as predictors of acute myocardial infarction.

Findings concluded: odds ratios and PARs for psychosocial factors, fruit and vegetable intake, alcohol, and physical activity, with significance levels for all risk factors and their consistency across groups.

Consistency of associations across sex, age, and world regions, the combined PAR of the nine risk factors (90% in men, 94% in women), and the start of the Interpretation section on abnormal lipids and other key modifiable factors.

Interpretation: the conclusion that modifiable risk factors account for most myocardial infarction risk worldwide across sexes, ages and regions, implying prevention strategies based on similar principles globally.
Final sentence of the conclusion: the modifiable risk factors suggest the potential to prevent most premature myocardial infarction cases.
Study design and methods: the cohort of 84,941 female nurses followed from 1980 to 1996, with diet and lifestyle updated periodically, defining the starting point for the diabetes risk analysis.

Definition of the low-risk group: five combined criteria (BMI under 25, a healthy diet with high cereal fiber and polyunsaturated fat, low trans fat and glycemic load, at least half an hour of daily moderate-to-vigorous exercise, no current smoking, and moderate daily alcohol intake).
Completion of the low-risk criteria and the start of results: 16 years of follow-up documented 3,300 new type 2 diabetes cases, with overweight or obesity identified as the strongest predictor.
Individual risk factors: lack of exercise, poor diet, current smoking, and alcohol abstinence each raised diabetes risk even after adjusting for BMI, and the low-risk group was small (3.4% of women).

Key quantitative findings: the low-risk group had a relative risk of 0.09 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.17), and 91% of diabetes cases (95% CI 83 to 95) were attributable to behaviors outside the low-risk pattern.
Conclusion: the authors argue that most type 2 diabetes cases in women could be prevented by adopting a healthier lifestyle, summarizing the study's main implication.

Abstract introduction of a kiwifruit (Actinidia chinensis) human intervention trial: background on why whole foods are favored over isolated antioxidant supplements, and the study's aims on antioxidant status, DNA stability, lipids, and platelet aggregation.
Study hypothesis and design: healthy volunteers added one or two golden kiwifruits daily to their normal diet in a 2 x 4 week cross-over trial, aiming to test effects on oxidative status biomarkers.
Methods for measured markers: plasma vitamin C, carotenoids, and FRAP for antioxidant status; malondialdehyde for lipid oxidation; and the enzyme-modified comet assay for DNA damage in lymphocytes.

Key results on antioxidant and DNA findings: plasma vitamin C rose and resistance to H2O2-induced DNA damage increased; purine oxidation fell after one kiwifruit daily and pyrimidine oxidation after two.

Remaining results: DNA base excision and nucleotide excision repair unaffected; malondialdehyde unchanged; plasma triglycerides and whole blood platelet aggregation decreased with kiwifruit supplementation.
Conclusion of the kiwifruit trial stating that golden kiwifruit consumption strengthens resistance to endogenous oxidative DNA damage.

Introduces the paper's core premise: platelets actively drive inflammation in atherogenesis from its earliest stages, via platelet-endothelial interactions (activated platelets binding intact endothelium, or resting platelets adhering to activated endothelium).

Frames the clinical problem: inhibiting platelet adhesion and aggregation can prevent atherothrombosis, the leading cause of cardiovascular morbidity, with antiplatelet drugs as the pharmacological route and diet as the primary-prevention route.

Presents the paper's main claim: among healthy dietary components, tomatoes (Solanum lycopersicum L.) show effects on platelet anti-aggregation and endothelial protection that may benefit cardiovascular health.

Concluding summary of the review's scope: briefly covers platelet involvement in atherogenesis and the proposed mechanisms by which tomatoes exert platelet anti-aggregation and endothelial protective effects.

Opening section of a study on tomato extract's anti-platelet effects in vitro: compares fruits' activity and shows tomato inhibits ADP- and collagen-induced platelet aggregation but not arachidonic acid-induced aggregation.

Continues the study by describing the nature of the anti-platelet components in tomatoes (small, water-soluble, heat-stable, concentrated near seeds) and the separation methods used (gel filtration and HPLC).

Describes the purification workflow: the aqueous tomato fraction is run on a Biogel P2 gel filtration column, yielding peak-3 and major peak-4, and peak-4 is then further purified by reversed-phase HPLC.

Identifies the components of peak F2 as adenosine and cytidine via NMR and mass spectrometry, and reports that adenosine deaminase treatment abolishes activity of F2 and partially reduces peak-4 activity while peak-3 is unaffected.

Concludes that tomatoes contain anti-platelet compounds beyond adenosine, notes that unlike aspirin they inhibit thrombin-induced aggregation, and argues tomatoes may help prevent and treat cardiovascular disease.
Final sentence of the abstract, summarizing that tomatoes may be beneficial as a preventive and therapeutic dietary approach for cardiovascular disease.

Introduction to the kiwifruit cardioprotection review: general cardiovascular benefits of fruit and vegetables, their antioxidant and nonantioxidant actions, and protection of lipoproteins and vascular cells.

Kiwifruit evidence: human studies show that eating two or three kiwifruit daily for 28+ days reduces platelet hyperactivity, plasma lipids, and blood pressure, supporting kiwifruit in cardiovascular disease prevention.
Conclusion of the review: kiwifruit may serve as a new dietary tool in preventive or therapeutic strategies to modify cardiovascular risk factors, with its relevance to human health discussed.
Closing sentence noting the discussion of kiwifruit's role in lowering cardiovascular risk factors for human health, followed by the 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.

Abstract-style opening of an in vitro study on aqueous herbal extracts (camomile, nettle, alfalfa, garlic, onion) and their inhibition of human platelet aggregation, introducing the screening results and ADP-induced aggregation percentages.

Continues the results: camomile and alfalfa inhibit collagen-induced platelet aggregation, nettle is the strongest inhibitor of collagen-induced whole blood aggregation, with percentages versus control.

Covers the mechanistic findings: none of the three herbs inhibit arachidonic acid or thrombin-induced aggregation, camomile and alfalfa suppress thromboxane B2 synthesis while nettle does not, and the start of the cGMP results.
Reports that alfalfa and nettle raise platelet cGMP levels versus control, and concludes that camomile, nettle and alfalfa have potent anti-platelet properties acting through different mechanisms.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence stating that the herbs' inhibitory actions are mediated via different mechanisms.

Introduction and objective of a double-blinded crossover trial on tomato extract as a dietary supplement to inhibit platelet activation, based on prior in vitro and ex vivo findings on antiplatelet effects.

Study design section: randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 90 healthy subjects with normal platelet function, measuring hemostatic changes 3 hours after extract or control supplement intake.

Results section reporting significant reductions in ex vivo platelet aggregation induced by ADP and collagen at 3 hours after high (6 tomato) and low (2 tomato) extract doses, with specific percentage changes and P values.

Results continued: no effects from control supplements, a dose response at low platelet stimulation levels, and greatest platelet inhibition in subjects with the highest homocysteine and C-reactive protein levels.
Conclusion: tomato extract as a functional food or supplement may aid primary prevention of cardiovascular disease by reducing platelet activation and thrombotic event risk.
Background and methods of a study on how industrial tomato processing affects phenolic profile and antiplatelet activity, introducing the cardiovascular rationale and the research gap.

Methods describing testing of tomato and by-product extracts against platelet aggregation induced by ADP, collagen, TRAP-6, and arachidonic acid, plus an in vivo thrombosis model and HPLC analysis of antiplatelet compounds.

Results identifying chlorogenic, caffeic, ferulic and p-coumaric acids in tomatoes and showing that red tomatoes, tomato products (sauce, ketchup, juice) and by-product extracts inhibit platelet aggregation.

Results summarizing the varying inhibition of platelet aggregation by tomato products and by-products, highlighting pomace extract's antithrombotic activity, and the conclusion that processed tomatoes may contain more health-benefiting compounds than fresh ones.
Conclusions that pomace has the strongest antiplatelet activity and that tomato products could serve as functional ingredients adding antiplatelet benefits to processed foods.
Introduction and background of a study on tomato extract's antiplatelet effects, stating the research gap on active components, mode of action, and in vivo efficacy for cardiovascular prevention.
Study objectives and design: in vitro examination of isolated tomato antiplatelet components and a 7-hour ex vivo cannulation time-course trial in 23 healthy human subjects.
Results opening: tomato extract components inhibit ADP-, collagen-, thrombin-, and arachidonate-induced platelet aggregation, linked to glycoprotein IIb/IIIa and platelet secretion inhibition.
Key quantitative findings: baseline platelet function inhibited from 2.9% (optimal ADP) to 20.0% (suboptimal ADP) 3 hours after drinking tomato extract equivalent to six tomatoes.

Duration and conclusions: antiplatelet effects lasted over 12 hours with coagulation unaffected; the authors conclude tomato components modulate platelet function, potentially explaining tomatoes' cardioprotective effects.
Final sentence of the conclusions, restating that tomato's cardioprotective effects may stem from modulation of platelet function.

Introduction to the review on diet and thrombosis: establishes that a prothrombotic state, driven by platelet activation and aggregation, is a major risk factor for heart attack, stroke, and venous thromboembolism, and notes the side effects (such as bleeding) of drugs like aspirin, heparin, and warfarin.

Continues the introduction by arguing that diet strongly shapes individual thrombosis risk, though its role matters less once thrombotic disease is under drug treatment, and introduces dietary intervention as a way to lower serum lipids linked to cardiovascular disease.

Summarizes the document's core thesis: certain dietary components reduce platelet activation through several mechanisms, so they may lower future thrombosis risk, setting up the review of nutrient effects.

Closing statement of the abstract: it announces an up-to-date review of nutrient and nonnutrient supplements' effects on platelet aggregation and thrombosis risk, with the Thieme Medical Publishers copyright notice.

Introduction to the document: diet's role in cardiovascular disease, and the nutrient profile of tomatoes (lycopene, beta-carotene, folate, potassium, vitamin C, flavonoids, vitamin E) and how processing affects their bioavailability.

Effects of processing on tomato nutrients: homogenization, heat treatment, and added oil raise lycopene bioavailability but cause loss of other nutrients; nutrient content also varies with variety and maturity.

Antioxidant mechanism: tomato nutrients may protect lipoproteins and vascular cells from oxidation, the leading theory of atherosclerosis, supported by in vitro, limited in vivo, and epidemiological evidence linking antioxidant-rich foods to lower cardiovascular risk.

Other cardioprotective effects of tomato nutrients, including reducing LDL cholesterol, homocysteine, platelet aggregation, and blood pressure, which leads into the document's conclusion about tomatoes' value in a cardioprotective diet.
Conclusion: because tomatoes contain several nutrients with theoretical or proven cardioprotective effects and are eaten year round, they are a valuable part of a cardioprotective diet.

Introduction to a study on kiwi fruit and cardiovascular health: background on how fruits and vegetables may protect against heart disease via antioxidants and by lowering plasma lipids and platelet aggregation.
Rationale for studying kiwi fruit, which is rich in vitamin C, vitamin E and polyphenols, noting little is known about its cardioprotective effects, and explaining platelets' role in atherosclerosis.
Study aim and design: a randomized cross-over trial in healthy human volunteers testing whether kiwi fruit consumption modulates platelet activity and plasma lipids.

Key results: eating two or three kiwi fruit daily for 28 days reduced platelet aggregation to collagen and ADP by 18% and lowered blood triglycerides by 15% versus control, with no cholesterol effect.
Conclusion: the findings suggest kiwi fruit consumption may be beneficial in cardiovascular disease.

Study design and methods: describes the 64 healthy adults tested repeatedly with four platelet function test systems (PRP and whole-blood aggregometry, plus ATP release) to assess sources of variability.

Results on abnormality rates: reports the percentage of drug-free specimens with at least one aggregation abnormality across test systems (CL-PRP, CL-WB, BD-PRP, MP-WB), and how adding ATP release raised these rates; also notes the prospective food and medication exposure recording.

Effects of gender and race: epinephrine aggregation and ATP release were lower in males, and ristocetin aggregation plus collagen and thrombin ATP release were lower in Black subjects; also flags the diet effect with flavonoid-rich foods.

Diet effect and conclusions: one-third of specimens after flavonoid-rich food had aberrant results versus 8.5% without; PRP tests varied less within individuals than whole-blood tests; concludes gender, race, diet, and test system all affect platelet function results, urging caution in patient interpretation.
Concluding fragment: the final words of the summary, advising caution when interpreting platelet function testing results in patients.

Introduction of an in vitro study on tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) antiplatelet activity, motivated by cardiovascular disease prevention through fruit and vegetable intake; describes testing nine fresh hybrid tomatoes, paste, and pomace.
Study methods: in vitro antiplatelet testing of fresh hybrids, paste, and pomace from industrial processing, plus ex vivo and bleeding-time assessment in rats fed 0.1 and 1.0 g/kg pomace daily.

Key results: no significant in vitro differences among fresh hybrids; industrial processing did not change paste or pomace antiplatelet activity; 1.0 g/kg pomace prolonged bleeding time and reduced ex vivo platelet aggregation in rats.

Conclusion: tomato contains one or more compounds with antiplatelet effects, suggesting regular consumption of tomato and its industrial derivatives may support a cardiovascular disease prevention regimen.

Introduction and methods opening of a systematic review on Mediterranean diet adherence, cognitive function, and dementia; it states the knowledge gap (no prior systematic review) and begins describing the search of 11 databases up to January 2012.

Methods section of the systematic review detailing the database search (11 databases including Medline, up to January 2012), supplementary searches, duplicate independent study selection and quality assessment, and inclusion criterion of a Mediterranean diet adherence score linked to cognition or dementia.

Transition from methods to results: reports that 12 eligible papers (11 observational studies and one RCT) describing seven unique cohorts were identified, noting methodological heterogeneity and limited statistical power, and that the evidence showed a reasonably consistent pattern.

Main results of the review: higher Mediterranean diet adherence linked to better cognitive function, slower cognitive decline, and reduced Alzheimer disease risk in nine of 12 studies, with inconsistent findings for mild cognitive impairment; also begins the conclusions.

Conclusions of the review: greater Mediterranean diet adherence is associated with slower cognitive decline and lower Alzheimer risk, identifies research gaps for mild cognitive impairment and vascular dementia, and calls for long-term randomized trials.

Final concluding sentence of the review, recommending long-term randomized controlled trials of Mediterranean diet promotion to determine whether improved adherence can prevent or delay Alzheimer disease and dementia onset.

Abstract opening of a study on dietary fat types and 4-year cognitive change in older women from the Women's Health Study; covers objective, sample size (6,183), exposures (SFA, MUFA, PUFA, trans fats), and start of serial cognitive testing.

Methods continued: describes the cognitive outcomes (global cognition and verbal memory composites) and the statistical approach (response profile analysis and logistic regression) used to estimate trajectory differences and risk of worst 10% cognitive change.

Results begin: higher saturated fat (SFA) intake is linked to worse global cognitive and verbal memory trajectories, with p-trend values, and the start of the odds ratio comparison of highest versus lowest SFA quintiles.

Reports adjusted odds ratios with 95% CIs for worst cognitive change comparing highest vs. lowest SFA quintiles (about 1.64-1.65), and the contrasting protective association of higher monounsaturated fat (MUFA) intake with better trajectories.

Shows the protective MUFA odds ratios for worst cognitive change (0.52 and 0.56), states that total fat, PUFA, and trans fat were not associated with trajectory, and begins the interpretation section.
Concluding interpretation: SFA is harmful and MUFA beneficial for cognitive aging, suggesting specific fat types, rather than total fat, drive cognitive outcomes in older adults.

Introduction of a study on strawberries and platelet function: sets out cardiovascular disease prevention priorities, the role of an antithrombotic diet (fruit and vegetables), and the study's aim to examine strawberries' effect on platelet activation and thrombus formation.

Methods/results portion on strawberry extract's antiplatelet effects: concentration-dependent (0.1-1 mg/ml) inhibition of platelet aggregation induced by ADP and arachidonic acid, and the accompanying decrease in inflammatory mediators sP-selectin, sCD40L, RANTES, and IL-1β.
Conclusion of the study: strawberries may protect against thromboembolic disorders by inhibiting platelet aggregation, suggesting the antithrombotic activity also has novel anti-inflammatory effects.

Introduction and background of a study on Mediterranean diet (MeDi) adherence and mortality in Alzheimer disease (AD) patients; states prior finding that MeDi relates to lower AD risk and the study's objective.

Methods: cohort of 192 community-based AD patients in New York followed prospectively every 1.5 years; MeDi adherence scale (0-9) as main predictor in Cox models adjusted for recruitment period, age, gender, ethnicity, education, APOE, calorie intake, smoking, and BMI.

Results begin: 85 of 192 AD patients (44%) died over mean 4.4 years follow-up; unadjusted analysis shows each additional MeDi point linked to lower mortality hazard (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.69-0.91, p=0.001).

Adjusted results: HR 0.76 for each MeDi point remains significant after covariate control; by tertile versus lowest adherence, middle tertile has lower mortality risk (HR 0.65, about 1.33 years longer survival).

Highest MeDi tertile shows strongest reduction in mortality risk (HR 0.27, 95% CI 0.10-0.69, about 3.91 years longer survival, p for trend=0.003); conclusion that MeDi may affect AD disease course and mortality.

Final conclusion: the gradual decline in mortality risk across increasing MeDi adherence tertiles suggests a possible dose-response relationship between Mediterranean diet adherence and survival in Alzheimer disease.

Introduction/background of an Alzheimer's disease review: global AD prevalence (33.9 million, expected to triple in 40 years) and the aim to assess seven modifiable risk factors (diabetes, mid-life hypertension, mid-life obesity, smoking, depression, low education, physical inactivity).

Describes the review's methods: calculating population attributable risks (PARs) for the seven modifiable AD risk factors and estimating preventable AD cases under 10% and 25% risk factor reductions worldwide and in the US.

Key findings: the seven risk factors together account for up to half of AD cases (17.2 million globally, 2.9 million in the US), and a 10%–25% reduction could prevent roughly 1.1–3.0 million cases worldwide and 184,000–492,000 in the US.
Brief closing fragment of the findings sentence, specifying the US as the location for the projected prevention figures (184,000–492,000 cases) in the abstract's results.
Introduction arguing that Alzheimer's disease is incurable once significant cognitive loss occurs, so research and funding should focus on prevention of AD risk factors instead.
Explains why cure is unrealistic after neuronal damage and argues that prevention of sporadic AD risk factors, starting in cognitively intact people via mass screening, is more realistic.

States that preventing modifiable AD risk factors is cost-effective, and notes that current neurocognitive and neuroimaging tests identify at-risk people only partially and cannot pinpoint causes or interventions.

Proposes carotid ultrasound with echocardiography plus ankle-brachial index (CAUSE+ABI) as mass screening tests that could detect cardio-cerebrovascular risk factors for AD and indicate an intervention.
Describes CAUSE+ABI as simple, cost-effective, non-invasive and reasonably accurate, and argues that detecting vascular abnormalities before cognitive decline improves treatment success.
Concludes that evidence-based medicine should guide clinical decisions on evaluating and treating Alzheimer's disease risk factors.

Opening of an abstract-style review on Alzheimer's disease: notes the large body of AD research with little clinical progress on sporadic AD prevention, and introduces the goal of drastically lowering AD prevalence.
Introduces the core strategy of four prevention pillars for AD vascular risk factors: early identification, early detection, evidence-based early intervention, and patient follow-up.

States that a proactive lifestyle (healthy diet plus physical and mental activity) should accompany any therapy, and presents the view that AD is multifactorial, driven by vascular risk factors causing chronic brain hypoperfusion in advanced aging.

Describes the pathobiological cascade under chronic brain hypoperfusion leading to oxidative stress and neurodegeneration, involving biofactors such as micronutrients, trace metals, lipids, and pro-oxidants, with reference to a BioFactors special issue.
Concludes that modulating these biofactors may help prevent or control incipient AD, followed by the 2012 IUBMB copyright notice for the BioFactors article.

Introduction of a review on the glycemic index: its 1981 proposal as a food classification system, the volume of literature on it, and the open debate over its clinical significance, leading to the review's stated aim.

Concluding sentence of the document's introduction stating the review's purpose: examining the physiological effects of the glycemic index and their relevance to preventing and treating obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.
Opening of the document: introduces the point/counterpoint debate on dietary sugar, sugar-sweetened drinks, and rising obesity and type 2 diabetes, previewing the Kahn and Sievenpiper rebuttal.
Methods and rebuttal preview: data sources (NHANES, USDA dietary surveys, Homescan purchases) tracking sugar and fructose consumption, plus meta-analyses and RCTs on beverage and fructose intake.

Consumption trends and meta-analytic evidence: about 75% of foods contain added sugar, soft drink consumption rose fivefold since 1950, and SSB intake is linked to diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular disease risk.

Experimental and trial evidence: two 16-oz SSBs daily for 6 months produced metabolic syndrome and fatty liver features, and RCTs in children and adults showed reduced soft drink intake lowered weight gain.

Summary of conclusions: calorie-sweetened beverages keep rising and drive obesity, metabolic syndrome, and fatty liver disease; a possible gene-SSB interaction is noted; cutting soft drinks means less weight gain.
Final sentence restating that reducing soft drink intake is associated with less weight gain, closing the review's evidence summary.

Opening of the AHA scientific statement on dietary sugars: introduces concern over high sugar intake amid obesity and cardiovascular disease, and gives US added-sugar intake figures (22.2 tsp/day, 355 kcal) and the 1970-2005 availability increase.

Explains the 76 extra daily calories from rising sugar availability, identifies soft drinks and sugar-sweetened beverages as the main source of added sugars, and notes links between excess sugar and metabolic abnormalities and nutrient shortfalls.

Summarizes evidence that soft drink intake is associated with higher energy intake, body weight, and lower essential nutrient intake (noting limited trial data), and that added sugars drive overconsumption of discretionary calories.
Cites the 2005 US Dietary Guidelines to show added sugar intake greatly exceeds discretionary calorie allowances, and states the AHA's recommendation to reduce added sugar intake.
Gives the AHA's specific recommended limit: half the discretionary calorie allowance, i.e., about 100 kcal/day of added sugar for most women and 150 kcal/day for most men.
Final fragment completing the sentence from chunk 5 about added sugars, a trailing word-level remnant of the recommendation text with no new content.

Opening of a counterpoint essay on dietary sugar, obesity, and diabetes; it responds to Bray and Popkin's preceding argument that sugar consumption should be reconsidered, and states the thesis that no clear evidence shows added sugar is uniquely harmful versus other calories.

Middle of the counterpoint essay arguing sugar is merely a palatable energy source with no unique nutritional role, so it is not essential, and that reducing sugar intake is a reasonable starting point for those cutting calories.
Closing sentence of the counterpoint essay concluding that cutting sugar, while a sensible first step for reducing energy intake, does not by itself guarantee clinical health benefits.

Opening of the review: rise in US sugar intake since the Revolution, and the share of added sugars (sugar and high-fructose corn syrup) coming from soft drinks and fruit drinks, plus the 1950-2000 soft drink intake increase.
Continues the intake trend and summarizes meta-analyses linking sugar- or HFCS-sweetened beverages to obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and related risks.

Links sweetened beverages to nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and gout in men, and explains that beverage calories are 'add-on' calories that drive obesity because they don't reduce other food intake; begins the triglyceride discussion.

Attributes the rise in plasma triglycerides from sugar-sweetened drinks to fructose rather than glucose, citing randomized trials showing sugar or fructose raises triglycerides, body weight, visceral fat, muscle fat, and liver fat.

Describes hepatic fructose metabolism: rapid ATP depletion on uptake by the liver as phosphate is transferred to fructose, producing lipid precursors, and notes fructose enhances lipogenesis and uric acid production.
Concluding statement: fructose at currently consumed amounts worsens blood lipids and contributes to obesity, diabetes, fatty liver, and gout, making it hazardous for some people.
Introduction and objectives of a phase I Japanese study of figitumumab, an anti-IGF-1R antibody, in advanced NSCLC (NCT00603538), with study design and methods beginning.

Study methods: dose-escalation design testing figitumumab 6, 10, and 20 mg/kg with carboplatin and paclitaxel in 19 chemotherapy-naive Japanese NSCLC patients, dosed on a 21-day cycle for four to six cycles.
Start of results: figitumumab with carboplatin and paclitaxel was well tolerated up to 20 mg/kg with no dose-limiting toxicities, and plasma exposure rose approximately dose-proportionally.
Pharmacokinetic and biomarker results: about 2-fold accumulation with repeated dosing supports the 21-day regimen, and serum IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 rose without a clear dose-dependent relationship.

Efficacy and conclusions: seven of 18 evaluable patients had a partial response, and figitumumab 20 mg/kg with carboplatin and paclitaxel was well tolerated, with biomarker analysis needed for further development.
Final sentence of the conclusions stating that further biomarker data analysis is necessary for the development of figitumumab therapy.
Introduction to the study: links Western diet to cancer deaths and proposes that IGF-I, which falls during dietary restriction, may mediate DR's protective effect on cancer progression.

Study rationale and hypothesis: IGF-I's roles in proliferation, apoptosis, and tumorigenesis motivate restoring IGF-I during DR to test whether its lowering is central to slowing bladder cancer progression.
Experimental design: heterozygous p53-deficient mice given the bladder carcinogen p-cresidine are randomized into ad libitum, 20% DR, and 20% DR plus IGF-I groups after preneoplasia is confirmed.
Key results on IGF-I and tumor stage: DR lowers serum IGF-I by 24%, recombinant IGF-I fully restores it, and restoring IGF-I in DR mice increases cancer stage, independent of body weight.
Mechanistic findings: DR raises apoptosis tenfold in preneoplastic lesions, while IGF-I administration boosts proliferation sixfold in hyperplastic foci.

Conclusion: DR lowers IGF-I, shifting balance toward apoptosis over proliferation and slowing tumor progression; IGF-I supplementation abrogates DR's protective effect, the first mechanistic demonstration of this.

Introduction and study objective: the hypothesis that long-term low-protein, low-calorie intake and endurance exercise are linked to low plasma growth factors and hormones associated with cancer risk.

Study design: three groups of 21 subjects each (low-protein low-calorie diet, BMI-matched endurance runners, and age- and sex-matched sedentary Western-diet controls), with diet duration and participant ages reported.

Results on body mass index and hormone differences: BMI was lower in the low-protein and runner groups than the Western diet group, and insulin, free sex hormones, leptin, and CRP were lower while SHBG was higher in those groups.
Results on IGF-I: plasma IGF-I and the IGF-I to IGFBP-3 ratio were lower in the low-protein, low-calorie diet group, with the specific mean values reported for each group.
Comparison of IGF-I values across groups: the low-protein diet group had the lowest IGF-I and IGF-I/IGFBP-3 ratio versus runners and Western-diet controls (P < 0.005), and the conclusions begin here.

Conclusions: exercise, decreased adiposity, and long-term low-protein, low-calorie diet are linked to low cancer-associated growth factors and hormones, and low protein intake lowers circulating IGF-I independent of body fat.
Introduction/summary of the study: background on insulin/IGF-1 pathway mutations, calorie restriction lowering IGF-1 in rodents, and the open question of long-term CR effects on IGF-1 in humans.

Study findings: two long-term CR studies (1 and 6 years) show severe CR without malnutrition did not change IGF-1 or IGF-1:IGFBP-3 ratio, whereas moderate protein restriction lowered total and free IGF-1; begins describing the protein-reduction intervention.

Protein-restriction experiment details: six CR volunteers cut protein from about 1.67 to 0.95 g/kg/day for 3 weeks, lowering serum IGF-1 from 194 to 152 ng/mL; concludes long-term severe CR does not lower IGF-1 in humans, unlike rodents.
Conclusions: protein intake is a key determinant of circulating IGF-1 in humans, and reduced protein intake may be an important component of anticancer and anti-aging dietary interventions.
Final fragment of the abstract's concluding sentence, ending with the suggested role of dietary interventions against cancer and aging.
Introduction of a review on obesity-driven cancer: how obesity progresses via metabolic syndrome to type 2 diabetes and increased cancer risk, framing the role of insulin and IGFs.

Continues the review's framing: epidemiological and biochemical evidence linking insulin and hyperinsulinaemia to cancer risk and progression, and IGF-1/IGF-2 secreted by adipose tissue acting in paracrine and endocrine ways.

Mechanistic summary: steroid hormone production can amplify IGF effects, and structural studies show how insulin, IGF-1 and IGF-2 bind differently to insulin receptor isoforms A/B and the type I IGF receptor, explaining diabetes-associated cancer.
Clinical implications: the findings should guide treatment of cancers in obese and type 2 diabetic patients, and novel drugs targeting insulin/IGF signalling are in trials.
Concluding statement that targeted insulin/IGF pathway drugs should be effective when combined with biomarker-based patient stratification.

Background and objectives of a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies on body-mass index (BMI) and cancer risk, including the aim to compare associations across sexes and ethnic groups.
Methods: Medline and Embase searches (1966 to November 2007) for prospective studies of 20 cancer types, using random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression of BMI risk per 5 kg/m2 increase.

Findings: 221 datasets from 141 articles with 282,137 incident cases; in men, strong BMI associations with oesophageal adenocarcinoma, thyroid, colon, and renal cancers, with relative risks and p-values.

Findings for women: strong BMI associations with endometrial, gallbladder, oesophageal adenocarcinoma, and renal cancers; weaker associations for rectal cancer and melanoma in men and several cancers in women and both sexes.

Sex and regional differences: colon cancer association stronger in men than women; associations broadly similar across North America, Europe, Australia and Asia-Pacific, except stronger Asia-Pacific associations for premenopausal and postmenopausal breast cancer.

Interpretation: increased BMI is linked to common and less common cancers, with sex- and ethnicity-specific differences for some types, informing future research into biological mechanisms linking obesity and cancer.

Concluding sentence of the interpretation: epidemiological findings on sex and ethnic differences in BMI-cancer associations should guide exploration of biological mechanisms connecting obesity with cancer.
Opening of the document: introduces the estimated 20% of cancer cases attributable to obesity and the cancer types with strongest evidence from IARC and WCRF reports.

Continues the list of obesity-linked cancers (endometrial, colorectal, breast, prostate, renal, etc.), contrasting them with less common malignancies, and introduces the aim of understanding mechanisms for prevention and treatment.

Presents the four main systems proposed as cancer drivers in obesity (insulin, IGF-I, sex steroids, adipokines) and begins listing novel candidate mechanisms such as chronic inflammation and oxidative stress.

Completes the list of novel candidate mechanisms (tumour-adipocyte crosstalk, migrating adipose stromal cells, hypoxia, shared genetics, immune dysfunction) and states the review's purpose of examining pathogenic links between obesity and cancer.
Final fragment of the abstract's closing sentence, restating that the review covers the major pathogenic links between obesity and cancer susceptibility.

Introduction and methods opening of a study on cancer prevalence in congenital IGF-I deficiency: it notes IGF-I overexpression in childhood and adult tumors, states the study aim, and begins describing the 222 deficient patients surveyed.

Continuation of the subjects description (IGF-I deficiency types and 338 relatives surveyed), followed by the key results: no cancer in deficient patients versus 9-24% malignancy history in relatives, and the conclusion that IGF-I deficiency is protective against cancer.
Final sentence fragment of the document's conclusion, stating that congenital IGF-I deficiency acts as a protective factor against cancer development.
Introduction and background of the meta-analysis: IGF-I and IGFBP-3 hypothesised roles in tumour development, with IGF-I linked to higher and IGFBP-3 to lower cancer risk.

Methods: systematic review and meta-regression of case-control and nested case-control studies on IGF-I and IGFBP-3 for prostate, colorectal, breast (pre- and postmenopausal) and lung cancer, using dose-response slopes on a percentile scale.
Findings part 1: 21 eligible studies (26 datasets) with 3609 cases and 7137 controls; odds ratio for prostate cancer with high IGF-I (75th vs 25th percentile) reported.

Findings part 2: high IGF-I linked to premenopausal breast cancer risk, and high IGFBP-3 linked to increased premenopausal breast cancer risk; associations stronger for plasma than serum and in case-control than nested designs.
Interpretation: IGF-I and IGFBP-3 concentrations are modestly associated with common cancers, varying by site, and laboratory methods need standardising.
Concluding statement of the interpretation: the epidemiological findings may have major implications for cancer risk assessment and prevention.

Opening chunk of the Million Women Study abstract (BMI and cancer, UK cohort study): states the objective, study design, and the 1.2 million participant cohort with follow-up durations for incidence and mortality.

Continues the abstract's methods: lists the main outcome measures (relative risks for all cancers and 17 specific cancer types by BMI) and the confounders adjusted for, then begins the results with total incident cancers and cancer deaths.

Results section of the Million Women Study abstract: reports the case and death counts and the strongest BMI-associated cancer incidence finding, endometrial cancer (RR 2.89 per 10 BMI units), followed by oesophageal adenocarcinoma and kidney cancer.

Middle of the results: lists further BMI–cancer incidence associations with relative risks and 95% CIs, including leukaemia, myeloma, pancreatic, lymphoma, ovarian, all-cancer combined, postmenopausal breast, and premenopausal colorectal cancer.

Summarises mortality results as similar to incidence and notes that the BMI effect differed significantly by menopausal status for colorectal cancer, malignant melanoma, breast cancer, and endometrial cancer.
Conclusions opening: BMI significantly raises risk for 10 of 17 cancer types, and about 5% of cancers in UK postmenopausal women (roughly 6000 a year) are attributable to overweight or obesity.
Final conclusion: BMI is a major modifiable risk factor for endometrial cancer and oesophageal adenocarcinoma, with about half of cases in postmenopausal women attributable to overweight or obesity.
Background on IGF-1 and growth factor overexpression in cancer, motivating the study of IGF-1 as a possible marker of childhood cancer risk.
Study aims and design: comparing serum IGF-1 in 50 children with de novo malignancies against 50 age- and gender-matched healthy controls, and examining links to cancer type, stage, and metastasis.
Methods: 100 children enrolled, cancer patients given routine local work-up, and serum IGF-1 measured in both groups by ELISA.

Results and conclusion: children with cancer had significantly higher IGF-1 than matched controls, with no association to tumor type, stage, metastasis, or other characteristics; IGF-1 proposed as a risk indicator for common childhood cancers.
Implications: IGF-1 may help identify high-risk children and guide preventive strategies, but the small sample size means larger studies are needed to confirm the findings.
Closing limitation: the need for larger-population studies to validate the study's conclusions.

Introduction and study aim: a cross-sectional study testing whether vegan diets lower circulating IGF-I versus meat-eating or lacto-ovo-vegetarian diets in 292 British women, motivated by diet's possible role in cancer rates.
Main results: serum IGF-I was 13% lower in vegans (n=92) than meat-eaters (n=99) and vegetarians (n=101), with IGFBP-1 and IGFBP-2 concentrations 20-40% higher in vegans and their P values reported.

Further findings: IGFBP-1 and IGFBP-2 differences reported with P values; no group differences in IGFBP-3, C-peptide, or sex hormone-binding globulin; protein rich in essential amino acids correlated positively with IGF-I (partial correlation).

Conclusions: higher essential-amino-acid protein intake (r=0.27, P<0.0001) explains most IGF-I differences between diet groups, suggesting plant-based diets lower total IGF-I and raise IGFBP-1 and IGFBP-2.
Final fragment completing the IGFBP-2 reference from the conclusion sentence, ending the abstract's summary of plant-based diet effects on IGFBP levels.

Opening chunk of a passage arguing that systemic IGF-I activity drives aging, citing lifespan extension in rodents via reduced IGF-I signaling (including caloric restriction) and the inverse link between body size, IGF-I levels, and lifespan.

Continues the evidence for IGF-I as an aging regulator: the inverse relation of dog breed and rat strain lifespan to mature weight and IGF-I, and evolutionary conservation shown by lifespan extension in worm and fly insulin/IGF-I pathway mutants.

Argues IGF-I's role in sexual maturation supports a broader aging role, then proposes that if lowering IGF-I slows human aging, practical measures are available, starting with a low-fat, whole-food vegan diet.

Lists practical IGF-I-lowering measures (vegan diet, exercise, soluble fiber, insulin sensitizers, appetite suppressants, flax lignans, oral estrogen, tamoxifen) and notes they would also reduce risk of common age-related diseases.

Suggests combining several IGF-I-lowering approaches could meaningfully slow aging, but warns that since IGF-I supports nitric oxide production and cerebrovascular health, stroke prevention measures are needed.
Concludes that when pursuing IGF-I down-regulation as a longevity strategy, additional stroke-prevention steps, especially salt restriction, may be advisable.

Methods section of a 1980s NCI pooled case-control study of pesticide exposure in farming and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL) risk among men in the midwestern US (n=3417), describing simultaneous modeling of 47 pesticides with variance-stabilized estimates.

Continuation of the methods (controlling for confounding by other pesticides, prespecified variance adjustment) into the Results, listing pesticides associated with increased NHL risk: organophosphates coumaphos, diazinon, fonofos; insecticides chlordane, dieldrin, copper acetoarsenite; herbicides atrazine, glyphosate, sodium chlorate.

Results tail covering the 'potentially carcinogenic' pesticide subanalysis showing a positive dose-number trend, followed by the start of the Conclusion stressing that modeling multiple exposures is important for accurate effect estimates and realistic exposure scenarios.

Final sentence of the Conclusion of the NHL pesticide study, stating that considering multiple simultaneous exposures is necessary for accurate specific effect estimates and realistic exposure evaluation.

Introduction of the study: pesticides are sold as formulations containing confidential inert adjuvants plus a declared active principle usually tested alone; the authors set up a toxicity comparison of 9 active principles versus formulations on three human cell lines (HepG2, HEK293, JEG3).

Lists the nine tested active principles (glyphosate, isoproturon, fluroxypyr, pirimicarb, imidacloprid, acetamiprid, tebuconazole, epoxiconazole, prochloraz) as representing 3 herbicides, 3 insecticides, and 3 fungicides, and describes the cytotoxicity endpoints measured: mitochondrial activity, membrane degradation, and caspase 3/7 activity.

Key results: fungicides were most toxic at concentrations 300–600 times below agricultural dilutions, then herbicides, then insecticides, with similar profiles across cell types; Roundup (glyphosate formulation) ranked among the most toxic herbicides and insecticides despite its benign reputation; the chunk begins the finding that formulations exceed active principles in toxicity.

Main conclusion: 8 of 9 formulations were up to 1,000 times more toxic than their active principles alone, which challenges the acceptable daily intake (ADI) norm since it is derived from active-principle toxicity; the chunk begins the argument that chronic tests of single ingredients may not reflect real exposure.

Final concluding sentence of the abstract: chronic pesticide testing that examines only one ingredient of a mixture may fail to reflect relevant environmental exposures, reinforcing the call to test full formulations.

Introduction to the glyphosate review: regulatory registration of glyphosate as a herbicide and the prior belief, based on rodent carcinogenicity studies, that it lacks carcinogenic potential, motivating a human epidemiologic review.

Methods overview: the authors reviewed the epidemiologic literature on whether glyphosate exposure is causally linked to human cancer risk, plus methodological and biomonitoring studies, including seven cohort and fourteen case-control studies.

Main findings: across the cohort and case-control studies, no consistent pattern of positive associations supports a causal link between glyphosate exposure and total cancer (adults or children) or any site-specific cancer.

Exposure assessment implications: biomonitoring data show that studies need to account for pesticide formulation as well as duration and frequency of use, and that generic exposure assessments cause misclassification, so exposure algorithms should be validated against biomonitoring.
Closing statement and copyright notice (Elsevier, 2012) for the glyphosate epidemiology review, marking the end of the abstract.

Background and study introduction: prior 1989-1991 findings of elevated birth defects in the Red River Valley (Minnesota) among children of male pesticide applicators, and the design of the smaller 1997-1998 cross-sectional study of 695 families and 1,532 children.

Study design and baseline results: the first-year birth defect rate of 31.3 per 1,000 births, with 83% of reported defects confirmed by medical records, from the 1997-1998 Red River Valley farm family study.

Expanded case definition and seasonality finding: including developmental disorders through age 3 raises the rate to 47.0 per 1,000, and spring conceptions show significantly more birth defects (7.6% vs. 3.7%) than other seasons.

Recurrence and familial patterns: twelve families had multiple children with birth defects (28 children), 42% of whom were conceived in spring, and the start of the kinship analysis showing a first-degree relative with a similar defect.

Inheritance and sex ratio results: three kinship families fit a Mendelian pattern while nine do not, and male predominance (1.75:1) among affected children across pesticide categories excluding fungicides.

Fungicide-related sex ratio findings: in the fungicide exposure category, normal female births exceed male births (1.25:1), and male-to-female ratio among affected children is significantly lower (0.57:1, p = 0.02).

Pesticide-specific health associations: adverse neurologic and neurobehavioral developmental effects linked to the fumigant phosphine (OR 2.48) and the herbicide glyphosate (OR 3.6) in the neurobehavioral category, with confidence intervals.

Conclusions: spring-applied herbicides may contribute to birth defects, fungicides may influence offspring sex, and the two pesticide classes appear to affect different reproductive outcomes, motivating the study's main interpretation.
Closing statement: the paper's final sentence calling for biologically based confirmatory studies to validate the observed associations between pesticide classes and reproductive outcomes.

Introduction of a review of non-cancer human health effects of glyphosate: describes its EPA and global regulatory registration as a broad-spectrum herbicide and states the review's aim of assessing causal links to non-cancer risks and reviewing biomonitoring for exposure assessment.

Methods and scope: continues the aim, noting biomonitoring studies were reviewed to address exposure assessment and misclassification, and begins listing the study designs (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) and non-cancer respiratory outcomes examined.

Endpoints and main findings: lists the non-cancer outcomes studied (respiratory, diabetes, myocardial infarction, reproductive/developmental, rheumatoid arthritis, thyroid disease, Parkinson's) and reports no consistent positive associations suggesting causality, with weak associations near null.

Conclusions and recommendations: summarizes that most associations were weak and not significantly different from 1.0, recommends developing and validating pesticide-specific exposure algorithms because accurate exposure measurement is crucial, and includes the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
Trailing copyright fragment: the end of the Elsevier Inc. 2011 'All rights reserved' copyright notice closing the glyphosate epidemiology review abstract.
Introduction of a case series reporting two suicidal glyphosate surfactant herbicide (GlySH) ingestion deaths, framing GlySH poisoning as uncommon and setting up a literature review of the cases.

Discussion of GlySH clinical toxicity: despite being traditionally considered minimally toxic, it has caused many suicide deaths, is refractory to supportive care, and the triad of pulmonary oedema, metabolic acidosis and hyperkalaemia predicts poor outcome; begins noting GlySH differs from organophosphates.
Conclusion stating GlySH lacks organophosphate toxicity despite its carbon-phosphorus moiety, and that the paper proposes a clinical severity assessment guide and discusses treatment options.

Introduction to a study on glyphosate, the active ingredient in the widely used herbicide, examining its possible endocrine-disrupting effects and its influence on estrogen receptor-mediated transcriptional activity and expression.

Results on proliferation: glyphosate promoted growth of hormone-dependent T47D breast cancer cells but not hormone-independent MDA-MB231 cells at 10^-12 to 10^-6 M under estrogen withdrawal, and increased estrogen response element (ERE) transcription activity.

Mechanism findings: glyphosate's ERE activation (5-13 fold in T47D-KBluc cells) was blocked by the antagonist ICI 182780, showing estrogenic activity is mediated via estrogen receptors, and glyphosate altered both ERα and ERβ expression.

Conclusions and soybean context: low, environmentally relevant glyphosate concentrations showed estrogenic activity, and glyphosate combined additively with the soybean phytoestrogen genistein, relevant to glyphosate-based herbicide use on soybean crops.
Closing remarks noting that the additive effects of glyphosate contamination in soybeans require further animal study, followed by the copyright notice (Elsevier, 2013).

Case report introduction: glyphosate-surfactant herbicide (GlySH) poisoning, noting that intramuscular injection has never before been reported, and introducing a 42-year-old woman who presented to the emergency department with left upper limb swelling.

Case details: the patient self-injected 6 mL of GlySH into the lateral left elbow 15 h earlier and presented 12 h after symptom onset with painful swelling of the left arm, elbow, and forearm, showing three needle punctures.

Imaging findings and discussion opening: CT showed ill-defined heterogeneous high-density areas and marked subcutaneous swelling over the posterior elbow, followed by the discussion that surfactants likely drive GlySH toxicity and that IM poisoning differs from oral intoxication.

Clinical implication: the discussion concludes that clinicians should closely monitor for rapidly developing acute rhabdomyolysis and compartment syndrome in IM GlySH injection cases, linked to the surfactant component of the formulation.

Background and study rationale on glyphosate herbicide: prior in vitro evidence of StAR and aromatase inhibition reducing testosterone and estradiol, and the lack of prior in vivo studies on prepubertal Wistar rats.

Study design and results begin: outcomes measured (puberty progression, body development, testosterone, estradiol, corticosterone, testis morphology) and the first reported finding that glyphosate altered puberty progression in a dose-dependent manner.
Seminiferous tubule morphology results: significant decrease in epithelium height and increase in luminal diameter across glyphosate dose groups, with control and treated group means and P values.
Remaining histological and hormonal findings: no change in tubular diameter, and no differences in serum corticosterone or estradiol, contrasted with lower serum testosterone in all treated groups.

Serum testosterone results with group means (control 154.5 ng/dL vs. lower treated values, P < 0.001), followed by the authors' conclusion that commercial glyphosate formulation is a potent in vivo endocrine disruptor.
Concluding sentence of the abstract: glyphosate exposure during puberty causes disturbances in reproductive development in rats.

Opening of the abstract: introduces Roundup herbicide and states the study's aim of testing its toxicity and endocrine-disruption potential on human embryonic (293), placental (JEG3), normal human placenta, and equine testis cells.

Reports toxicity results: the LD50 of Roundup in embryonic cells falls from 0.3% at 1 h in serum-free medium to 0.06% (about 1.27 mM glyphosate) at 72 h with serum, and embryonic cells are 2-4 times more sensitive than placental cells.

Compares Roundup with glyphosate alone: at agricultural concentrations of 1-2% (21-42 mM glyphosate), Roundup is more effective than glyphosate, suggesting a synergistic effect from adjuvants, and serum-free short-term cultures reveal toxic effects seen 1-2 days later in serum.
Describes aromatase disruption at sub-toxic doses: from 0.01% Roundup (210 microM glyphosate) over 24 h, Roundup acts as an aromatase disruptor, with temperature-dependent direct inhibition.

Summarizes the aromatase findings across tissues and species (placental and embryonic kidney cell lines, equine testicular cells, human placental extracts) and shows glyphosate is a direct, dose-dependent partial inactivator of microsomal aromatase, independent of acidity.

Conclusion: cytotoxic and endocrine-disrupting effects of Roundup increase over time, suggesting possible impacts on human reproduction and fetal development, and that chemical mixtures in formulations may be underestimated.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that chemical mixtures in formulations are likely underestimated for their toxic or hormonal impact.

Introduction of the glyphosate review: describes glyphosate as a herbicide targeting the plant-only shikimate pathway and notes alleged developmental and reproductive harms in humans and animals despite its relative safety.
Methods summary of the glyphosate review: a literature analysis covering epidemiological, animal, and mechanistic studies on glyphosate's developmental and reproductive effects.

Findings on glyphosate toxicity: no consistent reproductive or developmental effects and no plausible mechanism; observed toxicity in glyphosate-based formulations is attributed to surfactants rather than glyphosate itself.
Human exposure assessment: biomonitoring data from occupational use show extremely low glyphosate exposure under normal application practices.
Comparison to regulatory limits: estimated human exposures are more than 500-fold below the U.S. EPA oral reference dose of 2 mg/kg/d (1993), supporting the safety conclusion.
Conclusion of the glyphosate review: no solid evidence links glyphosate to adverse developmental or reproductive effects at environmentally realistic exposure levels.
Introduction and main findings of a study on Roundup (glyphosate-based herbicide) toxicity: acute low-dose exposure causes oxidative stress and Sertoli cell death in prepubertal rat testis.

Mechanism of Roundup-induced toxicity: calcium influx through L-type Ca(2+) channels and ER IP3/ryanodine receptors causes Ca(2+) overload, oxidative stress, and necrotic cell death; glyphosate alone also increases 45Ca(2+) uptake.

Role of antioxidants (Trolox, ascorbic acid) in preventing these effects, involvement of PKC, PI3K, and MAPK (ERK1/2, p38) signaling in Ca(2+) influx and cell death, and Roundup's depletion of GSH with increased lipid and protein oxidation markers (TBARS, protein carbonyls).
Antioxidant enzyme responses to Roundup exposure: increased activity of glutathione peroxidase, glutathione reductase, GST, GGT, catalase, SOD, and G6PD, consistent with downregulated GSH levels.

Concluding interpretation: glyphosate is described as an endocrine disruptor of male reproduction, but its molecular basis is unclear; the authors propose Ca(2+) overload, signaling misregulation, ER stress, and antioxidant depletion may disrupt Sertoli cells and spermatogenesis, affecting male fertility.
Final sentence of the conclusion linking Roundup-induced Sertoli cell disruption to impaired spermatogenesis and male fertility, followed by the 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces the study of the glyphosate-based herbicide Roundup's effect on cell cycle regulation, using sea urchin embryo first cell divisions as a model, and the initial finding that 0.8% Roundup delays first cleavage.
Describes dose-dependence of the Roundup-induced cleavage delay and shows that glyphosate at 1-10 mM combined with subthreshold 0.2% Roundup induces the delay, while glyphosate alone does not.

Reports the synergy between glyphosate and Roundup formulation products, that the effect is non-lethal, and that it delays entry into M-phase, judged cytologically, with CDK1/cyclin B named as the universal M-phase regulator.
Presents the mechanistic results: Roundup delays CDK1/cyclin B activation in vivo and inhibits global protein synthesis while cyclin B still accumulates.

Concludes that Roundup delays CDK1/cyclin B activation through glyphosate plus formulation synergy, and argues that because this regulator is conserved across species, the findings question the safety of glyphosate and Roundup for human health.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence, ending the document's statement on human health safety of glyphosate and Roundup.

Introduction of a study on glyphosate and Roundup herbicide: background on Roundup's widespread use on GM crops, food-chain and river contamination, and reported pregnancy problems in agricultural workers, with the mechanism in mammals still questioned.

Core findings on human placental JEG3 cell toxicity: glyphosate harms these cells within 18 hours at concentrations below agricultural levels, toxicity rising with dose, time, and Roundup adjuvants, and Roundup proving more toxic than glyphosate alone.

Experiments on aromatase, the estrogen-synthesizing enzyme: glyphosate and Roundup at nontoxic doses disrupt aromatase activity and mRNA levels and bind the enzyme's active site, with Roundup's formulation enhancing these effects in microsomes and cell culture.

Conclusion and interpretation: endocrine and toxic effects of the whole Roundup product, not glyphosate alone, are seen in mammals, with the authors proposing that adjuvants increase glyphosate's bioavailability and/or bioaccumulation.
Introduces the study scope: composition and pesticide/herbicide residues in 31 soybean batches from Iowa, USA, split into GM glyphosate-tolerant, conventional, and organic groups.

Summarises nutritional findings: organic soybeans had higher sugars (glucose, fructose, sucrose, maltose), more protein and zinc, less fibre, and less saturated fat and omega-6 fatty acids than conventional and GM soy.

Reports agrochemical residues: GM soy contained glyphosate (mean 3.3 mg/kg) and AMPA (mean 5.7 mg/kg), while conventional and organic batches had none; also notes 35 variables were used for characterisation.

Concludes that the 35 nutritional and elemental variables discriminated GM, conventional and organic soybeans, showing 'substantial non-equivalence' of ready-to-market soy; includes the 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.
Closing fragment of the copyright statement (Elsevier Ltd., 2013) ending the abstract.

Opening of a paper on property rights and genetic engineering. It introduces genetically engineered seeds (mostly herbicide-resistant), their claimed harms to developing nations (food shortages, unemployment, resistant weeds, extinction of native cultivars via drift), and the thesis that current patent policies must be revised.

Continues the paper's thesis and roadmap: it surveys GE technology, presents John Locke's account of property rights, argues patent policy should be revised under Lockean ethical constraints, answers a key objection, and proposes concrete implementation steps.
Final fragment of the paper's roadmap, ending with the promise of concrete suggestions for implementing its ethical conclusions on genetically engineered seed patent policy.

Introduces the 2005 Romanian field-trial comparison of Roundup Ready soybean 40-3-2 against conventional soybean, listing the grain and forage composition analytes measured (proximates, fiber, amino acids, fatty acids, anti-nutrients).

Continues the list of measured analytes and reports that mean values for all biochemical components of Roundup Ready soybean 40-3-2 were similar to the conventional control and within the published commercial soybean range.
Describes the statistical comparison to Romanian conventional varieties using a 99% tolerance interval to capture natural compositional variability in the existing marketplace soybean population.

Gives the overall conclusion that, combined with soybean's long history of safe use in feed and food, Roundup Ready soybean 40-3-2 is compositionally equivalent and as safe and nutritious as commercial conventional soybeans.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending the statement that the GM soybean is as safe and nutritious as conventional varieties grown commercially.

Introduction to a review on herbicide residues in transgenic herbicide-resistant crops, noting the growth of GM crops since the mid-1990s and the need to assess how herbicide resistance alters residue profiles and levels.

Scope of the review: the four main herbicide resistance categories (ALS inhibitors, bromoxynil, glufosinate, glyphosate) and the topics covered, including resistance mechanisms, residue nature and levels, and effects on residue definitions and Codex/national MRLs.

Key conclusions: residue nature and levels cannot be generalized and must be assessed case by case, and missing international residue definitions and MRLs for some herbicide-crop combinations call for harmonisation.
Closing recommendation that harmonisation is needed for residue definitions and MRLs, followed by the 2011 Society of Chemical Industry copyright notice for the article.

Introduces the Tuskegee Syphilis Study as a cited reason for low minority research participation, notes few studies test this, and describes the random digit dial survey of 510 African-Americans and 253 Latinos aged 18-45.

Continues the methods: the survey examines links between knowledge of the Tuskegee study and endorsement of HIV/AIDS conspiracy theories, with respondents drawn from low-income, racially segregated inner-city Los Angeles households.

Reports the main findings: African Americans were more likely than Latinos to endorse HIV/AIDS conspiracy theories and more aware of the Tuskegee study, yet most of both groups had never heard of it (72% and 94%).
Concludes that Tuskegee awareness significantly predicts conspiracy belief, but other factors may matter more for explaining low biomedical and behavioral study participation.
Final fragment of the abstract, ending the word 'Latinos' from the last sentence (the word 'states' or similar closing the participation-rates sentence fragment).

Introduces the standard view that the bloodstream is separated from the digestive tract and that large food macromolecules (proteins, DNA) are fully degraded into amino acids and nucleic acids before absorption, setting up the study's challenge to that paradigm.

Describes the study's basis (over 1000 human samples from four independent studies) and its key finding: meal-derived DNA fragments large enough to carry complete genes evade degradation and enter human circulation by an unknown mechanism.

Reports the central results: plant DNA exceeds human DNA in one blood sample, plant DNA concentration follows a precise log-normal distribution in plasma, and the non-plasma cord blood control contains no plant DNA.
Concludes the abstract by noting that the non-plasma cord blood control sample lacked plant DNA, serving as a negative control for the plasma findings.

Introduces the study's subject: pesticides associated with genetically modified foods (glyphosate, glufosinate, Bt toxin) and states the aims of measuring maternal and fetal exposure levels in Eastern Townships, Quebec.

Describes the study's methods and key measurements: GLYP/AMPA, GLUF/3-MPPA and Cry1Ab levels in blood from 30 pregnant and 39 nonpregnant women, with initial serum detection results for GLYP and GLUF.

Reports the main findings: 3-MPPA and Cry1Ab1 toxin detected in pregnant women, their fetuses and nonpregnant women, and the claim that this is the first evidence of circulating pesticides associated with GM foods in women with and without pregnancy.
Closing fragment: concludes the implications for reproductive toxicology, nutrition and utero-placental toxicity, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.

Opening of a review on myostatin: its discovery and the 'Mighty Mouse' phenotype spurred research, with myostatin-null 'double muscling' in mice, livestock, and a child, motivating interest in enhancing muscle growth clinically and agriculturally.

Continues the motivation: blocking myostatin's inhibition may treat muscle growth disorders, and comparative studies suggest these actions are partly conserved across species, implying agricultural relevance of neutralizing myostatin.

Notes the difficulty of comparing fish and mammal models because whole genome duplication left some fish species with up to four myostatin genes, and introduces the agricultural implications of neutralizing myostatin.

Comparative evidence suggests myostatin acts beyond skeletal muscle, affecting cardiac muscle, adipocytes, and brain, so clinical or farm interventions must weigh possible side effects on these tissues.
Highlights that the multiple, actively diversifying myostatin genes in most fish offer a chance to study adaptive molecular evolution and may reveal myostatin's nonmuscle functions.
Closing statement: comparative studies of myostatin's nonmuscle actions are gaining visibility in biomedical fields.

Abstract of a pilot study on commercial conspiracy theories, introducing the study's aim of examining individual and demographic predictors of beliefs about advertising and corporate tactics (banks, alcohol, drug and tobacco companies) in a British sample of 300+ people.

Abstract of a pilot study on commercial conspiracy theories: presents the four belief clusters (sneakiness, manipulative, change-the-rules, suppression/prevention), the high overall scale reliability, and the start of the regression findings on religiosity, political leaning, pessimism and wealth.

Abstract of a pilot study on commercial conspiracy theories: reports regression results linking less religiosity, left-wing politics, pessimism, lower self-rated wealth, and lower Neuroticism and Openness to Experience with stronger belief in commercial conspiracies, notes that these individual differences explain little variance, and mentions implications for conspiracy theory research.
Closing sentences of the abstract of a pilot study on commercial conspiracy theories, stating that the implications for conspiracy theory literature and the study's limitations are discussed.

Abstract opening of a 1997-era mouse genetics paper introducing GDF-8, a new TGF-beta superfamily member expressed in skeletal muscle, identified by degenerate PCR, and framing the superfamily's roles in development and tissue homeostasis.
Continuation of the abstract describing GDF-8 expression: restricted to the myotome of developing somites in early embryos, then broadly expressed across many muscles in later embryos and adult mice.

Abstract section describing the functional study: GDF-8 was knocked out by gene targeting in mice, and the null animals were larger with widespread increases in skeletal muscle mass, with individual muscles weighing 2-3 times more.

Concluding abstract passage stating that the muscle mass increase reflects both muscle cell hyperplasia and hypertrophy, and that GDF-8 acts specifically as a negative regulator of skeletal muscle growth.
Introduction to a 2012 Elsevier article on GMO governance, framing the future of genetically modified animals as dependent on multi-level regulatory and interest-group responses in the EU and USA.

Continuation of the article's abstract, naming the key themes: cultural values, new and existing interest groups, and implications for commercializing green and red GM animal biotechnology, followed by the Elsevier copyright notice.
Introduction of the LOG12 study on conspiracist ideation and rejection of science, opening with the claim that prior evidence is sparse and summarizing LOG12's findings about climate blog visitors.

Continuation of the introduction: defines LOG12 as the reference study and states the article's aim to analyze the climate blogosphere's response, tracing hypotheses that questioned LOG12's conclusions.

Summary of the method and key results: established criteria for conspiracist ideation show conspiratorial and counterfactual content in blog hypotheses, which broadened from the LOG12 authors to other actors.

Specific examples of expanded targets (university executives, a media organization, the Australian government) and the overall conclusion that the blogosphere's response suggests conspiracist ideation may play a role in rejecting science.
Final sentence of the abstract, a brief hedge that alternative scholarly interpretations of the findings may emerge later.

Introduction and study aim: this opening chunk frames the public-health concern about MRSA emission from poultry farms and states the study's goal of assessing LA-MRSA inside and outside previously MRSA-positive poultry barns in Germany.

Study design: this chunk describes the sample size (five turkey and two broiler fattening farms, sampled four and three times) and the longitudinal study sampling animals, barn environment and air, and surroundings during one fattening period.

Sampling methods continued: this chunk details the surroundings sampled (ambient air and boot swabs at varying distances from the barn) and introduces the single cross-sectional study in late fattening period across nine farms.

Key results: this chunk reports prevalence findings, including LA-MRSA in 77.8% of barn air samples, animal detection rates of 50-77% by species, and detection in ambient air and downwind ground surfaces in the longitudinal study.

Conclusion: this closing chunk notes that identical spa types were found inside and outside barns and concludes that within-farm transmission and airborne emission of MRSA from poultry farms appear possible.

Study design: a year-long longitudinal sampling of LA-MRSA contamination (pigs, barn floor, inside and outside air, soil) around six LA-MRSA-positive German commercial pig barns, sampled once per season on four days.

Results on airborne LA-MRSA: concentrations inside barns ranged 6 to 3,619 CFU/m3 (median 151). Downwind air at 50 and 150 m had low levels (11 to 14 CFU/m3), while all upwind air samples were negative.

Soil surface contamination: LA-MRSA was found on soil downwind at 50, 150, and 300 m with no significant distance differences, sporadic positives upwind, and significantly more positives in summer for air and soil, upwind and downwind.

Seasonal and typing findings: summer showed significantly more LA-MRSA-positive samples than other seasons in air and soil; spa typing confirmed strain identity inside and outside barns, supporting airborne transmission conclusions.

Conclusions: airborne LA-MRSA transmission and deposition occur regularly up to at least 300 m from positive pig barns, strongly shaped by wind direction and season, and the boot sampling method is suitable for assessing airborne contamination of the barn vicinity.

Introduction and background of the study: describes ST398 livestock-associated MRSA (LA-MRSA) emergence in Europe, its risk to farm workers, and the study's aim to assess LA-MRSA colonization and infection in Lombardy, Italy's top pig-farming region.
Study aim and methods start: defines the Lombardy (Italy) study setting with highest pig-farming density and describes collection of 879 nasal swabs at hospital admission in March-April 2010.

Methods continued: details the hospital-based sampling of nasal swabs and collection of all community-acquired infection (CAI) MRSA isolates from March 2010 to February 2011, plus the molecular typing approaches (SCCmec, spa, MLST).
Main results on nasal carriage: of 879 swabs, 9 (1%) were MRSA; 5 were ST398 LA-MRSA (spa t899, t108, t2922), 4 likely hospital-origin, and none were PVL-positive.

Results on community-acquired infections: 20 CAI MRSA isolates (mostly skin and soft-tissue), including a PVL-negative t899/ST398 LA-MRSA from otitis externa, t127/ST1 isolates, and PVL-positive CA-MRSA.
Conclusions: in this high pig-farming area LA-MRSA colonizes the population but rarely causes infection, and typical PVL-positive CA-MRSA (notably ST8) is more common than LA-MRSA among CAI.
Final conclusion fragment restating that typical CA-MRSA outnumbers LA-MRSA among community-acquired infections in the study area.

Abstract of an experimental study on fast food branding and young children's taste preferences: describes the design (blind taste comparisons of McDonald's-branded vs. unbranded identical foods) and the setting (low-income preschools).

Continues the study abstract with the participant profile (63 preschoolers aged 3.5 to 5.4 years, mean age 4.6) and the main exposure (fast food branding), then defines the outcome measure, a total taste preference score from -1 (unbranded) to +1 (McDonald's branded).
