Results section of the study: reports the mean total taste preference score of 0.37 (median 0.20), which is significantly above zero (P<.001), meaning children preferred the same food when it carried McDonald's branding.

Reports moderator analyses showing branding effects were stronger among children with more televisions at home and those who ate McDonald's food more often, then begins the conclusion that branding influences young children's taste perceptions.

Conclusion of the study: branding of foods and beverages shapes young children's taste perceptions, supporting regulation of marketing to children and suggesting branding might help improve their eating habits.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending the study abstract with the word 'behaviors' and closing the discussion of branding's effect on children's eating.

Opening of the abstract for a study on fast food restaurants in children's hospitals. It states the study's objectives and describes the first methodological step: a survey of pediatric residency programs to measure how many hospitals host fast food restaurants.

Methods section describing the second step of the study: surveys of adults with children after pediatric outpatient visits at three hospitals. Hospital M has an on-site McDonald's, hospital R has McDonald's branding but no on-site restaurant, and hospital X has neither.

Results opening: 59 of 200 hospitals with pediatric residencies had fast food restaurants, and 386 outpatient surveys were analyzed. It begins reporting fast food consumption on the survey day, which was highest at hospital M (56%), compared with hospital R (29%) and hospital X (33%).

Results on purchasing behavior. McDonald's food purchases were highest at hospital M (53%, vs. 14% at R and 22% at X). McDonald's made up 95% of fast food eaten at hospital M, and 83% of those respondents bought it at the on-site restaurant.

Key statistical findings from logistic regression: hospital M respondents were 4 times more likely to have bought McDonald's food on the survey day. Visitors at hospitals M and R were more likely than those at X to believe McDonald's financially supported the hospital. Hospital M respondents also rated McDonald's food as healthier.

Final results sentence on perceived healthiness of McDonald's food at hospital M, followed by the conclusions. Fast food is fairly common in hospitals with pediatric residencies, and an on-site McDonald's is linked to more purchases, a belief in corporate financial support, and higher healthiness ratings.

Final sentence of the conclusions: an on-site McDonald's in a children's hospital is associated with greater outpatient purchase of McDonald's food, belief that the corporation financially supports the hospital, and higher healthiness ratings of its food.

Introduces the study's background on anabolic sex steroids used in US cattle and concern about reproductive effects on men who eat beef; describes the aim to test meat intake against semen quality and reproductive hormones in 189 young men aged 18-22.

Continues the methods: semen samples from 189 men, diet measured by a validated food frequency questionnaire, and linear regression for cross-sectional associations with adjustment for confounders; the results begin by reporting an inverse link between processed red meat and sperm count.

Reports the main result: quartiles of processed meat intake show a dose-related decrease in total sperm count (adjusted differences of 0, -3, -14, and -78 million; trend P = 0.01), with the highest quartile's confidence interval excluding zero.

Describes subgroup and mechanistic findings: the association is strongest in men with abstinence under 2 days and is driven by lower ejaculate volume with processed red meat (trend P = 0.003); the conclusion states processed meat intake links to lower sperm count in this population.
Closing limitation: the authors cannot tell whether the processed meat and sperm count association reflects residual confounding by abstinence time or a true biological effect.

Introduction: motivates the review by noting rising testis, breast and prostate cancer trends and possible sex-hormone involvement, plus disrupted hormone action linked to genital abnormalities in newborn boys and precocious puberty in girls; announces a review of childhood sex steroid levels and physiology.

Main conclusions, part (i)-(ii): prepubertal children's circulating estradiol is lower than originally claimed, yet children are highly sensitive to estradiol, showing growth and breast development responses even below current detection limits.

Conclusions (iii)-(iv): no threshold has been established below which exogenous steroids or endocrine disruptors have no hormonal effect in children, and fetal/prepubertal hormone changes may have severe consequences in adulthood.

Conclusions (v) and policy implication: FDA's 1999 estimates of daily sex steroid production in children, used in risk assessment, are highly overestimated and should be revised; because no lower estrogenic threshold exists, exposure of fetuses and children should be minimized.
Closing recommendation: avoid unnecessary exposure of fetuses and children to exogenous sex steroids and endocrine disruptors, even at very low levels.

Introduces the LIFE study's motivation: the parallel decline in sperm counts and rise in obesity, proposing that hyperlipidemia may contribute to falling male fertility alongside environmental and lifestyle factors.

Describes the population-based cohort design: 501 male partners of couples trying to conceive, with serum lipid concentrations compared against semen quality, and the prospective collection of up to two semen samples per man.

Covers sample follow-up (94% gave at least one sample, 77% gave a second about a month later) and the statistical method, linear mixed effects models adjusted for age, BMI, and race, plus the first main finding on lipids.

Reports the key results: higher total cholesterol, free cholesterol, and phospholipids linked to lower percentages of acrosome-intact sperm and smaller sperm head area and perimeter, concluding that lipids may affect sperm head morphology and male fecundity.
Closing fragment of the conclusion, emphasizing the importance of cholesterol and lipid homeostasis for male fecundity.

Study background and objective: introduces the theoretical concern that HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) could impair male gonadal function, since cholesterol is a steroid hormone precursor, and states the trial's aim to compare simvastatin, pravastatin, and placebo on testosterone production and spermatogenesis.

Trial design and population: describes the randomized double-blind design with a 6-week placebo/diet run-in, 159 hypercholesterolemic men aged 21-55 with normal basal testosterone, and allocation to simvastatin 20 mg, simvastatin 40 mg, pravastatin 40 mg, or placebo once daily.

Lipid-lowering efficacy results: at 24 weeks, the active-treatment groups reduced total cholesterol by 24-27% and LDL cholesterol by 30-34% versus placebo, all with P < .001, confirming the statins were pharmacologically active.

Primary hormonal findings: at 24 weeks, no statistically significant differences from placebo in change from baseline for testosterone, hCG-stimulated testosterone, free testosterone index, FSH, LH, or SHBG.
Semen quality and safety results: no significant differences from placebo at weeks 12 or 24 in sperm concentration, ejaculate volume, or motility, and both statins were well tolerated.
Conclusion: the authors report no evidence of clinically meaningful effects of simvastatin or pravastatin on gonadal testosterone production, testosterone reserve, or semen quality parameters.

Introduces the study design: 19 hyperlipoproteinaemic men, 28 healthy controls, and 44 infertile men, with spermiogram, seminal biochemistry, hormone, and lipid measurements, and initial spermiogram findings versus controls.

Reports semen and hormone results: most patients had normal seminal biochemistry and mainly abnormal E2 levels, and lipid abnormalities and higher lipid levels were more common in azoospermic infertile men; begins the correlation findings on cholesterol (C) and triglycerides (Tg).
Gives the correlation results linking high C and/or Tg with poor semen quality and higher FSH, and the overall conclusion that high lipid levels have adverse direct effects on the testes.

Introduces the hypothesis that environmental estrogenic compounds may cause male reproductive disorders, focusing on cows' milk as a major dietary estrogen source (60-70% of animal-derived estrogens consumed come from milk and dairy).

Explains that humans drink milk from heifers in late pregnancy when cow estrogen levels are high, and that modern genetically-improved dairy cows (e.g., Holstein) produce milk very differently from milk consumed 100 years ago.

Describes modern dairy feeding practices (grass plus grain/protein concentrates and by-products) that let cows lactate late into pregnancy, up to about 220 days, and states the authors' hypothesis that milk contributes to male reproductive disorders.
Closing fragment carrying the end of the hypothesis statement and the 2001 Harcourt Publishers Ltd copyright notice, marking the document's end.

Introduces oestrogens' role in vertebrate reproduction and quantifies dietary intake of oestradiol-17beta from cattle meat, both untreated (4.3 ng TMDI) and after growth-promoting agent use (up to 20 ng).

Continues with estimated oestradiol-17beta levels in other foods: similar amounts in pork and poultry as untreated cattle, 6.4 pg/ml mean in whole milk, and up to 200 pg/g in eggs, and begins noting limits of risk evaluation.

Covers key uncertainties in assessing oestrogenic growth promoters: analytical limits, unknown oestradiol-17alpha residues and conjugates, and the need for better mass spectrometry confirmation in food.

Lists remaining knowledge gaps: relevance of oestradiol acyl esters, daily oestradiol production in prepubertal children, the role of metabolites in cancer, and the need to study receptor subtypes and non-reproductive effects.
Final sentence of the document, concluding that oestradiol effects on non-reproductive functions require further examination.

Findings from the semen analysis study: a sample of 66 unmarried medical students aged 17-21 compared against reported values, showing differences in semen parameters and diet-related variation between non-vegetarians and vegetarians.

Opening chunk of the Rochester Young Men's Study abstract: states the research question on dairy intake and semen quality, the summary finding that full-fat dairy (mainly cheese) is linked to lower sperm motility and morphology, and background on environmental estrogens in dairy.

Background section of the abstract: hypothesis that environmental estrogens in dairy may explain the secular decline in sperm counts, noting that prior studies on dairy and semen quality have been inconsistent, followed by the start of the study design description (cross-sectional, n=189, 2009-2010, University of Rochester).

Study design and methods: cross-sectional Rochester Young Men's Study of men aged 18-22, diet measured by food frequency questionnaire, and the start of the linear regression analysis of dairy intake against conventional semen parameters.

Statistical methods: linear regression of dairy intake against total sperm count, concentration, progressive motility, morphology and ejaculate volume, adjusted for covariates including age, abstinence time, race, smoking, BMI, exercise, TV watching and calories; begins the main results heading.

Main results: total dairy intake is inversely related to sperm morphology (P-trend = 0.004), mostly driven by full-fat dairy foods, with the start of the adjusted comparison of upper versus lower half of full-fat dairy intake.

Specific effect sizes: men in the upper half of full-fat dairy intake had 3.2% lower normal sperm morphology (P<0.0001), low-fat dairy showed a weaker non-significant association, and full-fat dairy was also linked to lower percent progressively motile sperm (P=0.05); also begins the limitations heading.

Limitations and implications: the cross-sectional design limits causal inference, further research is needed to confirm a causal link between full-fat dairy and poorer semen quality, and the findings could inform explanations of secular semen trends and advice for men trying to conceive.
Funding disclosure: European Union Seventh Framework Program 'DEER' grant 212844, NIH grant P30 DK046200 and NRSA T32 DK007703-16 supported the work; begins the reference to the Grant P30 entry.
Continuation of the funding statement, completing the NIH grant citations and stating that none of the authors declared conflicts of interest.
Final fragment of the document: the closing statement that none of the authors has any conflicts of interest to declare.

Introduction to a national US study measuring 21 persistent, bioaccumulative, and toxic (PBT) pollutants in milk, sampled from 45 dairy plants in 2000-2001, motivated by milk fat being a major dietary exposure source.

Study results on detection: chlorobenzene, pesticide, and other halogenated organic compounds were below detection limits in all samples; national averages were computed for 11 detected chemicals, with CDD/CDF and PCB TEQ concentrations of 14.30 and 8.64 pg/l (total 22.94 pg/l).

Comparison of dioxin/PCB TEQ levels to a 1996 study, showing about half the earlier values, and the estimated 14% decrease in adult background dioxin exposure if this decline is real and nondairy exposure is unchanged.

National average concentrations of detected contaminants in milk: six PAHs (40-777 ng/l), cadmium (150-870 ng/l, average 360 ng/l), and lead (630-1950 ng/l, average 830 ng/l, consistently higher than cadmium).

Seasonal and geographic patterns in milk contaminants, with PAHs highest in winter, north, and east, plus the start of the adult daily intake comparison of milk fat ingestion versus total exposure from all pathways.
Daily intake comparison showing milk fat contributes CDD/CDF/PCB TEQs of 8 of 55 pg/day, PAHs 0.6 of 3 µg/day, lead 0.14 of 4-6 µg/day, and cadmium 0.06 of 30 µg/day of total intake.

Study design and objectives: a Belfast fertility study measuring individual antioxidants in sperm and seminal plasma of fertile vs. infertile men, with Percoll gradient separation and phorbol ester-induced ROS screening.
Setting and patient cohort: Queen's University Belfast clinics, 59 male patients split into an IVF-fertile group (18), normozoospermic infertile men (20), and asthenozoospermic men (21).

Outcome measures and first results: ascorbate, urate, sulphydryl, tocopherol and carotenoid levels measured in sperm and seminal plasma, with initial finding on the relative contribution of ascorbate and thiols in seminal plasma.

Key results: in seminal plasma ascorbate dominates over urate and thiols, ascorbate is significantly reduced in asthenozoospermic samples with ROS activity, while in sperm thiols are the main antioxidant contributor.
Conclusions: ascorbate, urate and thiols are the major seminal plasma antioxidants, thiols dominate within sperm, and ROS-positive samples show significantly lower seminal plasma ascorbate.

Introduces the study: a retrospective analysis of French semen quality trends by region, using Fivnat data from male partners of sterile women at an assisted reproduction center, motivated by a prior national-level finding of declining sperm concentration and morphology from 1989 to 2005.

Describes the methods and sample: men whose partners had absent or blocked tubes, recruited at an ART center, analyzed with a Bayesian spatio-temporal model with parametric time trends adjusted for age, fitted separately for each region; first results report sperm concentration declines in nearly all regions.

Reports the regional results: Aquitaine had the largest concentration decrease and Midi-Pyrénées the lowest average; total motility rose slightly in most regions except a steep, significant drop in Bourgogne; morphology declined in most regions.

Summarizes the conclusion that the concentration and morphology decline seen nationally holds across most French regions, with Aquitaine and Midi-Pyrénées declining more sharply than the overall trend, and frames this as consistent with a global change in environmental exposure.

Interprets the findings through the endocrine disruptor hypothesis, citing rising population-wide chemical exposure since the 1950s, and argues the results do not support the lifestyle explanation; also notes the most severe declines and lowest values occur in two neighboring regions.

Concludes the regional discussion by noting that the steepest declines and lowest sperm values cluster in two adjacent regions that are both heavily agricultural and densely populated, pointing to possible environmental drivers.

Abstract of a systematic review on the temporal decline in human sperm counts; this opening chunk describes the search methodology (PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, BIOSIS, Cochrane; studies 1985-2013) and introduces the conclusion that evidence for a worldwide decline is insufficient.

Continues the review's abstract: states the central conclusions that there is no scientific evidence that endocrine disruptors causally drive a temporal decline in sperm production, noting that supporting claims rest on few meta-analyses and retrospective studies not confirmed by well-conducted research.

Part of the review abstract explaining why the evidence is hard to interpret: confounding factors, variability of semen, selection criteria, population comparability in secular-trend studies, laboratory counting quality, and geographic variation in semen quality.

Closing portion of the review abstract, noting that the remaining uncertainties justify continued monitoring of semen quality, reproductive hormones, and xenobiotics, and a better definition of fecundity.
Final fragment of the abstract, completing the word 'xenobiotics' and the closing phrase calling for a better definition of fecundity, the review's last recommendation.

Abstract opening of a longitudinal study on dairy food intake and semen parameters in 155 men at a Boston fertility clinic, stating the objective, design, setting, and outcome measures (sperm count, concentration, motility, morphology).

Main results of the dairy-semen study: low-fat dairy intake is linked to higher sperm concentration and progressive motility, with quantified effects comparing the highest versus lowest intake quartiles.

Results showing low-fat milk explains the low-fat dairy association (30% higher sperm concentration, 8.7 percentage points higher motility), and introducing the finding that cheese intake is linked to lower sperm concentration among ever smokers.

Quantified cheese results among ever smokers: highest tertile of cheese intake shows 53.2% lower sperm concentration than lowest tertile, followed by the start of the study's conclusions on dairy and semen quality.

Concluding statement of the dairy intake and semen quality study: low-fat dairy, especially low-fat milk, is associated with higher sperm concentration and motility, while cheese is associated with lower concentration in past or current smokers.
Introduction of the study: defines the ROS-TAC oxidative stress score and describes the cohort of 127 patients and 24 controls whose semen was measured for ROS, TAC, and ROS-TAC.

Study cohort breakdown by diagnosis (varicocele, varicocele with prostatitis, vasectomy reversal, idiopathic infertility) and results showing higher ROS levels in infertile men, especially varicocele with prostatitis and vasectomy reversal groups.

Key findings on ROS-TAC discrimination: all infertile groups had lower scores than controls, the score identified 80% of patients and outperformed ROS for varicocele and idiopathic infertility, and pregnancy-outcome comparison begins (13 pregnant partners vs. remained infertile).

Pregnancy outcome results and conclusion: patients whose partners conceived had ROS-TAC scores (47.7 +/- 13.2) similar to controls and higher than the 39 still-infertile patients (35.8 +/- 15.0; P < 0.01), and the score is superior to ROS or TAC alone.

Final conclusion: infertile men with male factor or idiopathic diagnoses had significantly lower ROS-TAC scores than controls, and men with male factor diagnoses who later achieved pregnancy had higher scores than those who failed.

Opening chunk of an abstract on human fertility decline: falling semen quality in north-western Europe alongside rising couple fertility, plus the related rise in testicular cancer that begins this chunk.
Middle section on testicular cancer's century-long rise, which points to environmental origin with a genetic component, and on the puzzle of inherited infertility given evolutionary constraints.
Links poor semen quality to testicular cancer and to zygote development, where cancer-like disruption of the genetic apparatus affects offspring health.

States that human reproduction is more impairment-prone than in other mammals (spermatogenesis, couple fertility, pregnancy loss, embryonic aneuploidy), with both female and male pathways involved, and raises whether this human specificity is evolutionary or historico-social.
Argues that the endocrine disruption hypothesis cannot explain the main descriptive epidemiology of male reproductive impairment, and introduces an alternative pathogenesis.
Closing sentence: outlines the alternative pathogenesis and considers candidate exposures that could be responsible for the observed decline.

Background and objective of a cross-sectional study on dietary fat intake and semen quality in 701 young Danish men from the general population, motivated by prior links between saturated fat and sperm concentration in infertile men.

Study design: men recruited at military service fitness exams (2008-2010) provided semen samples, underwent physical exams, and completed a quantitative food-frequency questionnaire on food and nutrient intake.

Methods and initial results: multiple linear regression with semen variables as outcomes and dietary fat intakes as exposures, adjusted for confounders, found lower sperm concentration and total sperm count with high saturated fat intake.

Key quantitative findings: a significant dose-response relationship, with the highest saturated fat quartile showing 38% lower sperm concentration and 41% lower total sperm count versus the lowest quartile; no association found for other fat types.

Conclusions: findings may matter for public health, since dietary changes over recent decades could partly explain reported rises in subnormal sperm counts, and reducing saturated fat may benefit general and reproductive health.
Final concluding sentence: reducing saturated fat intake may benefit both general and reproductive health.
Introduction of a study on antioxidant vitamin treatment for male infertility: ROS damage to sperm DNA (8-oxo-dG formation, fragmentation) and the rationale for oral antioxidant therapy.

Study methods and first key result: sperm chromatin structure assay measures DNA fragmentation and decondensation before and after 90 days of antioxidant vitamin, zinc, and selenium treatment; DNA fragmentation decreased by 19.1%.
Main findings: the expected reduction in DNA fragmentation is paired with an unexpected rise in sperm decondensation (+22.8%), a negative side effect of antioxidant treatment.

Proposed mechanism and conclusion: vitamin C and other antioxidants may open protamine interchain disulphide bridges, disrupting paternal gene activity, which may explain conflicting evidence on antioxidants for male fertility.
Final sentence of the abstract, concluding that the decondensation effect may account for the discrepancy in results about antioxidant treatments improving male fertility.

Abstract opening of a cross-sectional study on dietary antioxidant intake and semen quality in 189 young healthy university-aged men in Rochester, NY, listing the outcome measures (volume, sperm count, concentration, motility, motile count, morphology).

Results showing higher progressive sperm motility (6.5 percentage units) in the highest vs lowest quartile of β-carotene intake, similar findings for lutein, and a positive link between lycopene intake and sperm morphology.

Quantitative lycopene findings: adjusted percentages of morphologically normal sperm across increasing lycopene intake quartiles, plus a non-linear relationship between vitamin C intake and sperm concentration, peaking in the second quartile.

Conclusions of the study: carotenoid intake was associated with higher sperm motility and, for lycopene, better morphology, suggesting dietary carotenoids may positively affect semen quality in healthy young men.
Final sentence of the conclusions, summarizing that dietary carotenoids may have a positive impact on semen quality.

Abstract opening of a study on seminal oxidative stress and antioxidant activity in male infertility, describing the aims and the sample of 138 men classified by sperm count, motility, and morphology, and listing the oxidative and antioxidant markers measured.

Continuation of the methods list of oxidative and antioxidant markers (LPO, protein carbonyls, SOD, catalase, thiols, ascorbic acid), followed by the start of the results, which report positive correlations of sperm count with progressive motility and normal morphology and negative correlations with LPO and protein carbonyls.

Core results and conclusion of the study: SOD, catalase, and thiols are positively associated with higher sperm count while LPO and protein carbonyls are negatively associated, leading to the conclusion that insufficient antioxidant enzymes and increased oxidative stress may contribute to declining semen quality.

Final conclusion sentence stating that antioxidant enzymes may protect against oxidative damage to sperm, followed by the copyright and publisher statement (Canadian Society of Clinical Chemists, Elsevier, 2010).

Study design and aims: a randomized controlled trial testing whether adding 75 g/day of whole walnuts to the usual Western diet of healthy young men (ages 21-35, n=117) improves semen quality, with primary outcomes at 12 weeks.

Outcomes and groups: the primary outcome is conventional semen parameters and sperm aneuploidy; secondary endpoints are serum and sperm fatty acid profiles, sex hormones, and serum folate. Walnut group (n=59) showed gains in sperm vitality, motility, and morphology, while the tree-nut-avoiding control group (n=58) did not change.

Statistical results: between-group differences from baseline were significant for sperm vitality (P=0.003), motility (P=0.009), and normal morphology (P=0.04). Serum fatty acid profiles also rose in the walnut group, with omega-6 and omega-3 increases (P=0.0004 and P=0.0007).

Fatty acid and aneuploidy findings: plant omega-3 alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) rose significantly in the walnut group (P=0.0001). Sperm aneuploidy, especially sex chromosome nullisomy, was inversely correlated with sperm ALA (Spearman -0.41, P=0.002).

Conclusion: the study's overall takeaway is that adding walnuts to a Western-style diet improved sperm vitality, motility, and morphology, supporting dietary walnut intake as a way to improve semen quality.

Introduces the study's rationale (fertility status may predict mortality, but semen quality's effect on mortality was unstudied) and the data source: men referred to the Copenhagen Sperm Analysis Laboratory 1963-2001, linked via personal ID to Danish registers of cancer, causes of death, and number of children.

Describes the follow-up design: men tracked until December 31, 2001, death, or censoring, with total and cause-specific mortality compared against age-standardized Danish men and across semen characteristics.

Presents the main results for 43,277 non-azospermic infertility-referred men: mortality falls as sperm concentration rises to a 40 million/mL threshold, and falls in a dose-response manner with higher motility, normal morphology, and semen volume (P(trend) < 0.05).

Reports that lower mortality among men with good semen quality spans many diseases and holds for men with and without children, arguing lifestyle or social factors alone cannot explain the association.
Concludes that semen quality may serve as a fundamental biomarker of overall male health.

Opening of the abstract for a 1992-era meta-analysis of semen quality: its objective, review design (literature search of 1930-1991 publications), and the subject pool of 14,947 men across 61 papers, with outcome measures introduced.

Results section of the semen-quality meta-analysis reporting a significant fall in mean sperm density (113 to 66 x10^6/ml, 1940-1990) and seminal volume (3.40 to 2.75 ml) from weighted linear regression.

Conclusions of the study stating a genuine decline in semen quality over 50 years, interpreting the volume and density changes as a steeper drop in sperm production and a likely reduction in male fertility.

Final conclusion linking the semen decline to rising genitourinary abnormalities such as testicular cancer, cryptorchidism, and hypospadias, suggesting environmental or other factors affecting male gonadal function.
Closing fragment of the abstract's final sentence, concluding that growing factors with serious effects on male gonadal function are implicated.

Opening of the abstract: study objective, cross-sectional design, setting, and population of 80 nonsmoking men aged 22-80 without fertility problems, examining whether micronutrient intake relates to sperm DNA damage in older vs. younger men.

Methods and outcome measures: sperm DNA damage assessed by alkaline and neutral Comet assay, and results beginning with questionnaire collection of sociodemographic, occupational, medical, reproductive, and lifestyle data.

Exposure assessment via the 100-item Modified Block Food Frequency Questionnaire for micronutrients (vitamin C, E, beta-carotene, zinc, folate), and the main finding that highest vitamin C intake was associated with about 16% less alkaline Comet sperm DNA damage.

Age-stratified results: older men (>44 years) with highest vitamin C intake had about 20% less sperm DNA damage, with similar associations for vitamin E and zinc, and beta-carotene and folate effects noted as similar in the overall analysis.

Key age comparison: older men with highest micronutrient intake reached damage levels similar to younger men, whereas younger men (<44 years) showed no benefit from higher micronutrient intake; this begins the conclusion section.

Conclusion: higher dietary and supplement micronutrient intake may reduce sperm DNA damage especially in older men, raising the question of whether antioxidants and micronutrients protect somatic cells against age-related genomic damage; includes copyright line.
Final fragment of the copyright notice (2012, Published by Elsevier Inc.), containing no substantive study content.

Introduces the study's scope: dietary polyphenols split into extractable (EPP) and nonextractable (NEPP) fractions, noting most prior studies measured only EPP, and states the aim to quantify total polyphenols including NEPP in foods and whole diet.

Methods and results: HPLC-MS identified EPP in methanol-acetone extracts and NEPP in acidic hydrolyzates of extraction residues across cereals, fruits, vegetables, nuts, and legumes, with NEPP defined as hydrolyzable polyphenols plus nonextractable proanthocyanidins.

Reports quantitative findings: NEPP content ranged from 880 mg/100 g dry weight in fruits to 210 mg/100 g in cereals, far above EPP; Spanish daily intake was 942 mg NEPP versus 258 mg EPP, with fruits and vegetables the main contributors to total polyphenol intake.

Concludes that nonextractable polyphenols make up the major share of dietary polyphenols (total intake 1201 mg/day), and that understanding NEPP intake and physiology is important for assessing health effects of dietary polyphenols.

Final sentence fragment restating that the physiological and health implications of nonextractable polyphenols matter for understanding dietary polyphenol effects; closes the conclusion of the abstract.

Introduction of the document: argues the Healthy Hunger-Free Kids Act of 2010 offers a chance to improve food quality in low-income childcare and Head Start centers, and links excessive fruit juice intake and unfiltered sucrose to obesity risk.

Continuation of the health rationale: sugar without fiber (as in fruit juice) is tied to metabolic syndrome, liver injury, and obesity, especially in preschoolers. It then makes the recommendation that USDA's Child and Adult Care Food Program, which sets meal patterns, drop juice for whole fruit.
Final sentence of the policy recommendation: the USDA Child and Adult Care Food Program should phase out fruit juice in favor of whole fruit in childcare meals for children.

Background and objective of a randomized trial on an inulin-type fructan prebiotic in pubertal adolescents, examining calcium absorption and bone mineral accretion at 8 weeks and 1 year of supplementation.

Study design: pubertal adolescents randomized to 8 g/day mixed short- and long-chain inulin-type fructan versus maltodextrin placebo, with bone measurements and stable-isotope calcium absorption testing over time.
Methods and early results: calcium absorption measured with stable isotopes, Fok1 vitamin D receptor genotyping, and the significant 8-week increase in calcium absorption in the fructan group.
Results on calcium absorption at 8 weeks and 1 year, the Fok1 genotype interaction (ff genotype showing the weakest initial response), and the start of the 1-year bone mineral content findings.

Results on 1-year whole-body bone mineral content and density gains in the fructan group versus control, followed by the study conclusion that the prebiotic fructan blend increases calcium absorption and bone mineralization during puberty.
Concluding statement that effects of dietary factors on calcium absorption may be modulated by genetic factors, specifically vitamin D receptor gene polymorphisms.

Introduction and methods of a study on apple and apple-product intake in healthy volunteers: it motivates fruit consumption via cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk and the '5 a day' campaigns, then describes a 5 x 4-week crossover trial of 23 volunteers comparing whole apples, pomace, clear and cloudy juice, and no supplement.

Methods continuation describing the crossover design and the intervention arms (whole apples 550 g/day, pomace 22 g/day, clear and cloudy juice 500 ml/day, or no supplement) and the outcomes assessed, lipoproteins and blood pressure, in 23 healthy volunteers, leading into the results on serum total and LDL-cholesterol.

Results on lipids: the intervention significantly changed total and LDL-cholesterol, with trends toward lower LDL after whole apple (6.7%), pomace (7.9%) and cloudy juice (2.2%), while clear juice raised LDL-cholesterol by 6.9% relative to whole apples and pomace. It also begins listing null outcomes.

Remaining null results (no effect on HDL-cholesterol, triglycerides, weight, waist-to-hip ratio, blood pressure, hs-CRP, gut microbiota, and glucose-metabolism markers such as insulin, IGF1 and IGFBP3), followed by the conclusions on apple polyphenols and pectin and how they segregate during juice processing.

Conclusion of the study: the fibre component (pectin and cell-wall material) appears necessary for apples' cholesterol-lowering effect, since clear juice lacks these, so clear apple juice may not substitute for whole fruit in nutritional recommendations.
Final fragment of the conclusion, restating that clear apple juice may not be a suitable surrogate for whole fruit in nutritional recommendations.
Opening of the abstract: critique that most polyphenol research uses organic-solvent extraction, so nonextractable polyphenols are ignored in biological, nutritional, and epidemiological studies.

Middle of the abstract: recent evidence that nonextractable polyphenols (NEPP) are a major share of dietary polyphenols with significant biological activity, and the proposed physiological approach based on solubility in intestinal fluids.
Core aim of the paper: clarifying the NEPP concept, contrasting chemical and physiological approaches, and noting that literature and databases cover only extractable polyphenols.
Concluding statement: greater attention to NEPP is needed to close the research gap in dietary polyphenol science.

Introduction of the review: defines nonstarch polysaccharides (NSPs) in foods as dietary fiber and lists their key physicochemical properties (water dispersibility, viscosity, bulk, fermentability) and intestinal effects.

Health relevance of NSP properties: links these features to reduced risk of diet-related diseases (coronary heart disease, colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, breast cancer, mineral abnormalities, laxation disorders) in Western and emerging economies.

Specific roles by NSP type: insoluble NSPs (cellulose, hemicellulose) act as laxatives, while soluble NSPs (notably mixed-link β-glucans) lower plasma cholesterol and normalize blood glucose and insulin, supporting diets for cardiovascular disease and Type 2 diabetes.

Colonic fermentation mechanism: much of dietary NSP passes the small intestine largely intact and is fermented into short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) by colonic and cecal commensal microflora, which promotes normal laxation.

SCFA and prebiotic effects: SCFAs have multiple health-promoting effects, especially for large bowel function, and certain NSPs favor growth of beneficial colonic bacteria (prebiotic action); the review also proposes modes of therapeutic action.
Applications and remaining gaps: NSP-based films and coatings are commercially attractive for food packaging, but the physiological mechanisms and nutritional impact are not fully understood.
Open research need: appropriate dietary NSP intake recommendations for different age groups still require further study.

Study design and population: the abstract's Objective, Design, Setting, and Participants sections describing the three US health professional cohorts (Nurses' Health Study, NHS II, Health Professionals Follow-up Study) used to examine fruit intake and type 2 diabetes risk.

Participant follow-up periods and outcome measurement: the cohorts' follow-up years, the number of men and women, the self-reported and questionnaire-confirmed type 2 diabetes outcome, and the start of the Results section reporting 12,198 cases and total person-years.

Main result for total whole fruit: after adjusting for diabetes risk factors, the pooled hazard ratio of 0.98 per three servings/week of whole fruit, which is the overall, not fruit-specific, association with type 2 diabetes.

Fruit-specific hazard ratios from mutual adjustment: pooled per-three-servings/week estimates for blueberries (0.74), grapes and raisins (0.88), prunes, apples and pears (0.93), bananas, grapefruit, and the start of the peaches/plums/apricots estimate.

Remaining fruit-specific results and juice: the rest of the individual fruit hazard ratios (oranges, strawberries, cantaloupe at 1.10), the fruit juice hazard ratio of 1.08, and the finding that associations differed significantly across fruits (P<0.001).

Conclusion on heterogeneity: findings suggest fruit-type-specific associations with type 2 diabetes, with blueberries, grapes, and apples linked to lower risk, and the start of the statement contrasting juice consumption.
Final conclusion on juice: the closing clause stating that greater fruit juice consumption is associated with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes, in contrast to whole fruit.
Introduction and background of a meta-analysis on Adenovirus 36 (Ad36) infection and human obesity, stating the study's aim to confirm Ad36's influence on obesity and metabolic markers.

Methods section describing the literature search of MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library (1951 to April 2012), inclusion of English-language original observational studies, and independent data extraction by two reviewers.
Statistical methods (random-effects model, weighted mean differences, pooled odds ratios) and the study selection results: 10 cross-sectional studies (n = 2,870) out of 237 screened.
Key results: pooled BMI WMD of 3.19 for Ad36-infected vs. non-infected, adult-only sensitivity analysis, and a significant pooled odds ratio of 1.9 for obesity associated with Ad36 infection.

Null findings for metabolic markers (total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL, blood glucose, waist circumference, systolic blood pressure), with the corresponding P-values, followed by the start of the conclusion.

Conclusion that Ad36 is linked to obesity and weight gain but not to abnormal metabolic markers or waist circumference, suggesting an association with subcutaneous rather than visceral fat accumulation.
Closing recommendation that prospective, well-designed studies are needed to determine whether Ad36 plays a causal role in the etiology of human obesity.

Abstract opening of a 2011 Animal Genetics study on broiler chicken fat deposition, introducing the comparative approach of mapping 53 human obesity candidate genes to chicken orthologues and screening SNPs for allele frequency differences between broilers and layers.

Continuation of the abstract listing the six candidate genes (ADRB2, MC5R, LEPR, MKKS, MFGE8, AK1) where broiler-versus-layer SNP allele frequency differences were found, and describing the F2 and backcross extreme-phenotype populations used to test associations with abdominal fat percentage and body weight.

Abstract methods and results summary: real-time PCR gene expression assessment in extreme-phenotype birds, reporting significant association with abdominal fat weight percentage (%AFW) for ADRB2 and MFGE8.

Abstract conclusion of the chicken fatness study: ADRB2 expression is significantly higher in liver of lean versus fat chickens, the authors propose the comparative genomics approach generalizes to other quantitative trait genes, followed by the 2011 copyright notice.
Trailing copyright line from the abstract of the 2011 Animal Genetics article, attributing rights to the authors and the Stichting International Foundation for Animal Genetics.
Opening of an abstract-style review on adenovirus 36 (AD-36) and obesity; introduces genetic, endocrine, and environmental causes of childhood fat accumulation and infection-related obesity evidence.

Continues the review: notes seroconversion to certain pathogens is more frequent in obese people, that findings are inconclusive, and introduces AD-36 as the focus of the literature review on childhood obesity.
Middle of the abstract: states AD-36 is the most studied infectious agent in animals and humans for obesity, and calls for research on whether antibody presence is merely unrelated to obesity.
Explores open questions about AD-36 and obesity: whether some people are more susceptible or prone to persistent viral infection, which could lead to obesity.
Concluding sentences of the abstract: if AD-36 causes obesity, vaccines or antiviral drugs should be investigated; ends with the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.
Introduction and study aim: Ad-36 adenovirus is linked to obesity, and this in vitro study tests whether it drives adipogenesis in primary human adipose-derived stem cells (hASC).

Results on Ad-36 infection of hASC: infection is time- and dose-dependent, and infected cells show greater lipid accumulation even under osteogenic conditions, suggesting commitment to the adipocyte lineage.
Results on differentiation: without adipogenic inducers, Ad-36 upregulates adipogenic genes (C/EBP-beta, PPAR-gamma, FABP) over time and increases lipid accumulation in a viral dose-dependent manner.

Supporting adipocyte markers: Ad-36 increases lipoprotein lipase expression and extracellular LPL, and hASC from subjects with natural Ad-36 DNA in adipose tissue differentiate more readily than DNA-negative subjects.
Conclusion: Ad-36 has the potential to induce adipogenesis in human stem cells, which may contribute to virus-induced adiposity in humans.

Introduction and background: prior serum-neutralization studies linking Adv36 antibodies to obesity across populations (USA, South Korea, Italy) versus null findings in Belgium/Netherlands and US military personnel, plus known animal and human metabolic effects of Adv36.

Background continued: reported effects of Adv36 infection on blood lipids, glucose uptake in adipose and muscle tissue, and glycemic control, followed by the start of the Principal Findings describing the novel ELISA study in central Sweden.

Study population and design: a novel ELISA was used on 1946 well-characterized Swedish participants (424 children, 1522 non-diabetic adults, 89 blood donors) from the Stockholm-area population to measure Adv36 serum antibodies.

Key prevalence and association results: Adv36 seropositivity among lean individuals rose from about 7% (1992-1998) to 15-20% (2002-2009), paralleling obesity trends, and seropositivity was associated with pediatric obesity and severe obesity in females (1.5-2 fold).

Metabolic associations: Adv36 positivity was less frequent in people on antilipid medication or with high triglycerides, and obese Adv36-positive individuals showed a non-significant trend toward lower HOMA-IR (insulin sensitivity, p = 0.08).

Conclusion: the ELISA findings indicate Adv36 infection is associated with pediatric obesity, severe obesity in adult females, and lower risk of high blood lipid levels in non-diabetic Swedish individuals.
Closing fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the study summary by specifying the non-diabetic Swedish population studied.

Introduction and objective of a UK study on fat content in chickens sold to the public (2004-2008), contrasting the 1976 recommendation to eat poultry as lean meat with the rising fat content of modern broiler chickens.

Study design and setting: randomly sampled chicken from UK supermarkets, farm shops and a football club, with fat measured by emulsification and chloroform/methanol extraction, followed by the start of the results.

Key results: fat energy exceeds protein energy in chicken, n-3 fatty acids have declined, the n-6:n-3 ratio reaches 9:1 versus the recommended ~2:1, and TAG levels exceed phospholipids in meat and whole birds.

Fatty acid findings and conclusions: DPA (22:5n-3) now exceeds DHA (22:6n-3), unlike earlier analyses, and traditional poultry and eggs were a rare land-based source of long-chain n-3 fatty acids, especially DHA.

Concluding argument: given the obesity epidemic, chickens providing several times more fat energy than protein seem illogical, and current chicken husbandry should be reviewed for animal welfare and human nutrition implications.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending the call for review of chicken husbandry regarding animal welfare and human nutrition.

Introduction and abstract opening of the study on meat consumption and BMI change in older Dutch adults (Netherlands Cohort Study), covering the contradictory hypotheses, limited prospective evidence, sample of 3902 men and women aged 55-69, and FFQ-based dietary assessment.

Methods section describing BMI measurement from self-reported height (1986) and weight (1986, 1992, 2000), the sex-specific meat and fish intake categories analyzed (total fresh meat, red meat, beef, pork, minced meat, chicken, processed meat, fish), and the linear mixed effect modeling approach.

Results beginning with cross-sectional BMI differences across total meat intake quintiles, and null prospective findings for total fresh meat in men and women after 14 years of follow-up, with reported BMI change estimates and P-values.

Results on beef intake, where men with the highest intake showed a significantly smaller BMI increase after 6 and 14 years, plus the start of findings on higher intakes linked to greater BMI increase after 14 years.

Results showing BMI increases after 14 years associated with higher pork intake in women and chicken intake in both sexes, along with robustness checks: stratification by median baseline BMI and mixed age-stratified results, and the note that subtype effects differed.

Concluding findings that subtypes of meat show differential BMI change effects, while total meat intake or closely related factors were not strongly associated with weight change over the 14-year elderly cohort follow-up.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence ending the abstract, stating the findings apply to this elderly population.
Introduction of a framework on infections contributing to human obesity: WHO obesity epidemic context, limits of behavioural management, and microbes linked to obesity in animals and humans.

Argument that if infections contribute to human obesity, different prevention, treatment, and policy strategies are needed; ethical limits prevent experimental infection of humans with candidate microbes.
Proposed method: the adipogenic human adenovirus Ad36 serves as a template for examining candidate microbes' contributions to human obesity, introducing the concept of infectobesity.
Conclusion urging clinicians to recognise infectobesity (obesity of infectious origin) and its importance for effective obesity management, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces the link between human adenovirus-36 (Adv36) infection and obesity: animal studies show causation, adult human prevalence is 30%+ in obese people but correlation is inconsistent. Begins describing the pediatric studies.

Presents the key pediatric evidence: pooled data from 559 children show Adv36 prevalence of 28% in obese vs. 10% in non-obese children, and notes the unclear reason why the link is stronger in children than adults.
Concludes that animal and human data suggest Adv36 contributed to the worldwide rise in childhood obesity, and calls for more research on prevalence and consequences across age groups and regions.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence of the document, ending the call for research on Adv36 infection across populations and locations.

Introduction and objective of the Ad36 adenovirus study: animal and cross-sectional human evidence linking Ad36 infection to higher adiposity and better glycemic control, and the aim to compare longitudinal changes in BMI, body fat, fasting glucose and insulin between infected and uninfected Hispanic adults.

Methods: post hoc screening of baseline sera from 1,400 Hispanic men and women for Ad36-specific antibodies, and comparison of adiposity and glycemic indices at baseline and about 10 years later between seropositive and seronegative subjects, adjusted for age and sex.

Methods adjustments and results start: glycemic analyses additionally adjusted for baseline BMI and restricted to nondiabetic subjects; seropositive subjects (14.5%) had greater baseline adiposity than seronegative subjects.

Main longitudinal results: seropositive subjects had greater adiposity indices but lower fasting insulin over time, and subgroup findings showed better glycemic control in normal-weight seropositive individuals.

Subgroup results and caveats: seropositivity linked to greater adiposity in overweight and obese men over time, and differences between groups were modest given the many statistical tests; conclusions begin, suggesting Ad36 increases adiposity and slows glycemic deterioration.

Conclusions and implications: findings support a role for Ad36 in increasing adiposity and attenuating glycemic decline in humans, suggesting infections may modulate obesity and diabetes risk and warranting further study of these factors.
Fragment ending the document's final sentence ("s."), a trailing sentence fragment from the conclusion about metabolic disorders.

Study background and objective: introduces the protein-satiety/thermogenesis rationale and states the aim of assessing dietary protein type and amount against subsequent weight and waist circumference change in the EPIC-based Diogenes cohort.

Methods, cohort description: 89,432 men and women from five EPIC countries, followed for a mean of 6.5 years, with exposures of animal and plant protein and outcomes of weight change (g/year) and waist circumference change (cm/year).

Methods, statistical analysis: gender- and centre-specific multiple regression with adjustment for baseline diet, anthropometrics, demographics, lifestyle and follow-up time, pooled across centres via random-effects meta-analysis; results section begins.

Main results on weight: higher total and animal protein intake predicted weight gain, strongest in women, mainly from red/processed meat and poultry rather than fish or dairy; plant protein showed no overall association with weight change.

Results on waist circumference and heterogeneity: no clear overall link between any protein measure and waist change; centre-to-centre heterogeneity existed but pooling was judged justified; conclusion section starts.

Conclusions: high protein intake was not linked to less weight or waist gain; animal protein, especially meat and poultry, was positively associated with long-term weight gain, with no clear waist findings.
Concluding fragment: completes the conclusion by stating there were no clear associations between protein intake and waist changes.

Introduction and study design for a Korean pediatric study of human adenovirus-36 (Ad-36) infection and obesity: background on the viral E4orf1 mechanism, the lack of prior childhood prevalence data, and the stated objectives and sample description.

Methods and start of results for the Ad-36 childhood obesity study: blood sampling at school or clinic visits, serum neutralization assay for Ad-36 status, serum chemistry, and the overall prevalence split (30% positive, N=25; 70% negative, N=59).

Key findings and conclusions of the Ad-36 study: infected children had higher BMI z-scores (1.92 vs 1.65, p<0.01) and waist circumference (96.3 vs 90.7 cm, p=0.05), no significant difference in cardiovascular risk factors, and the conclusion that Ad-36 is common in obese children and may contribute to the obesity and type 2 diabetes epidemic.

Final concluding sentences of the Ad-36 childhood obesity study, restating that Ad-36 infection is common in obese Korean children, strongly correlates with obesity, and may have contributed to the pediatric obesity and type 2 diabetes epidemic.

Introduction and Experiment 1 design: background on Ad-36 causing adiposity with lower cholesterol/triglycerides in animals, objective of testing Ad-36 transmissibility in chickens, and setup of cage-mate inoculation.

Experiment 1 continuation and Experiment 2 design: monitoring Ad-36 DNA in blood, and intranasal inoculation of infected donors (I-D) versus control donors (C-D), with blood transferred via wing vein to recipient chickens after 36 h.

Experiment 2 procedures and early results: recipient groups (I-R, C-R), sacrifice at 5 weeks, measurements of body weight and visceral fat, and Experiment 1 finding that Ad-36 DNA appeared in cage mates' blood within 12 h and persisted up to 25 days.

Main results of Experiment 2: increased visceral and total body fat and lower cholesterol in I-D and I-R versus controls, lower triglycerides in I-D, and Ad-36 isolated from 12 of 16 donor blood samples.

Tissue distribution and conclusion on horizontal transmission: Ad-36 DNA found in blood and adipose tissue but not skeletal muscle of infected groups, and the conclusion that Ad-36 spreads horizontally between cage mates.
Conclusions of the study: blood-borne transmission of Ad-36-induced adiposity in chickens and the stated concern that this raises for possible human transmission requiring further investigation.
Final sentence of the document calling for further investigation into the possibility of transmission of adiposity in humans.
Background and rationale from a phase I trial of Theracurmin (highly bioavailable curcumin) in cancer patients; introduces curcumin's poor bioavailability and prior healthy-volunteer safety data.

Study aim and eligibility: evaluates repeated Theracurmin dosing safety in pancreatic or biliary tract cancer patients who failed standard chemotherapy; describes the rationale for dose selection from a prior PK study.

Methods and dosing: Theracurmin at 200 mg curcumin (Level 1) escalated to 400 mg (Level 2), given daily with gemcitabine-based chemotherapy; lists endpoints including safety, PK, NF-κB activity, cytokines, efficacy, and quality of life.
Results: 10 patients at Level 1 and 6 at Level 2, with median peak plasma curcumin of 324 ng/mL (Level 1) and 440 ng/mL (Level 2), including observed ranges.

Key findings and conclusion: no unexpected adverse events, three patients continued for over 9 months, and high repeated curcumin exposure did not increase adverse event incidence with gemcitabine chemotherapy.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, stating that Theracurmin-driven high repeated curcumin exposure did not raise adverse events in patients on gemcitabine-based chemotherapy.

Introduces the epidemiology of diet and pancreas cancer: few studies exist, and foods like fat, eggs, meat, coffee, and butter have been suspected risk factors, while raw fruits and vegetables are consistently protective.

Describes the study design: a prospective study of 34,000 California Seventh-day Adventists (1976-1983) that recorded 40 pancreas cancer deaths, and notes the overall reduced mortality versus US whites.

Reports standardized mortality ratios (72 men, 90 women) showing non-significant reduced pancreas cancer death in Adventists, and states that meat, egg, and coffee showed suggestive but non-significant risk links after adjusting for smoking.

Highlights protective dietary findings: vegetarian protein products, beans, lentils, peas, and dried fruit were significantly associated with lower pancreas cancer risk, and begins noting diabetes as a risk factor.

Covers medical history results: prior diabetes and peptic or duodenal ulcer surgery increased subsequent fatal pancreas cancer risk, while tonsillectomy and allergies showed slight non-significant protection.

Concludes that protease-inhibitor-rich vegetables and fruits are more protective than meat or animal products are harmful, and that prior diabetes and abdominal surgery associations are confirmed by these data.
Final sentence reaffirming that the earlier reported links between diabetes, abdominal surgery, and pancreas cancer risk are supported by this study's data.
Introduction/purpose of a phase II trial of oral curcumin (NF-kappaB inhibitor) in advanced pancreatic cancer, motivated by poor response rates of approved drugs gemcitabine and erlotinib.
Experimental design of the curcumin trial: 8 g daily oral dosing until progression, with monitoring of serum cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-1Ra) and PBMC NF-kappaB and COX-2 expression.

Results of the curcumin trial: 25 patients enrolled (21 evaluable), low steady-state circulating curcumin in glucuronide and sulfate forms indicating poor oral bioavailability, and two patients showing clinical biological activity.

Clinical outcomes of the curcumin trial: one patient with stable disease over 18 months, one with a brief 73% tumor regression alongside 4- to 35-fold rises in serum cytokines, and no observed toxicities.

Pharmacodynamic findings of the curcumin trial: reduced NF-kappaB, COX-2, and phosphorylated STAT3 in patient PBMCs, which had higher baseline levels than healthy volunteers, plus interpatient variability in plasma curcumin levels.

Pharmacokinetic results and conclusion of the curcumin trial: plasma levels peaked at 22 to 41 ng/mL and stayed stable over 4 weeks; oral curcumin is well tolerated and biologically active in some patients despite limited absorption.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence of the curcumin pancreatic cancer trial abstract, ending the statement that oral curcumin has biological activity in some patients with pancreatic cancer.

Introduces the pancreatic cancer case-control study in the San Francisco Bay Area (532 cases, 1701 controls), its aim, and the statistical methods (principal component analysis, unconditional logistic regression) used to test dietary patterns against risk.

Describes the Prudent dietary pattern (vegetables, fruit, fish, poultry, whole grains, low-fat dairy) and its protective association with pancreatic cancer risk, roughly a 50% reduction, reported separately for men and women with odds ratios and p-trend values.

Describes the Western dietary pattern (red and processed meats, potato chips, sugary drinks, sweets, high-fat dairy, eggs, refined grains) and its 2.4-fold increased risk among men, with no association found among women.

Reports the combined effect of diet patterns in men (high Western, low Prudent intake yielding 3-fold risk) and concludes that plant-based foods, whole grains, and white meat may reduce pancreatic cancer risk, consistent with recommendations for other chronic diseases.
Concluding sentence stating that a diet rich in plant-based foods, whole grains, and white meat might reduce the risk of pancreatic cancer.
Introduction to the EPIC study on meat and fish intake and pancreatic cancer risk, stating the background burden of the disease and the study's population of 477,202 participants.

Methods and sample details: 865 nonendocrine pancreatic cancer cases observed through 2008, with calibrated relative risks estimated via multivariable-adjusted Cox regression, and the start of the red meat result.
Main results for red meat and processed meat, both null, followed by the first report of a borderline positive association between poultry intake and pancreatic cancer risk.

Fish results (no association) and the authors' interpretation: findings do not support the World Cancer Research Fund's conclusion on red and processed meat, and the poultry association may be due to chance.
Concluding statement that the poultry association contradicts most prior research and is likely a chance finding, followed by the copyright notice (UICC 2012).

Abstract opening (Purpose and Methods) of an Italian case-control study on nutrient-based dietary patterns and pancreatic cancer risk: 326 cases and 652 hospital controls, with 28 nutrients analyzed via exploratory principal component factor analysis.

Methods section of the pancreatic cancer dietary pattern study: describes the case and control recruitment, dietary assessment by a validated food frequency questionnaire, and the multiple logistic regression models used to estimate odds ratios.

Results opening of the Italian pancreatic cancer study: identifies four nutrient-based dietary patterns (animal products, unsaturated fats, vitamins and fiber, starch rich) explaining 75% of nutrient intake variance.

Results of the pancreatic cancer dietary pattern study giving adjusted odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals: animal products (OR 2.03) and starch rich (OR 1.69) positively associated, vitamins and fiber pattern inversely associated (OR 0.55).

Results and conclusions of the pancreatic cancer dietary pattern study: unsaturated fats pattern shows no association (OR 1.13), and the conclusion that high meat, animal product, refined cereal and sugar diets raise pancreatic cancer risk.

Final conclusion and copyright line of the Italian pancreatic cancer dietary pattern study: a fruit and vegetable rich diet is inversely associated with pancreatic cancer risk; published by Elsevier, 2013.

Introduces the pancreatic cancer context: gemcitabine is a first-line drug limited by chemoresistance, and the study tests Turmeric Force (a supercritical hydroethanolic turmeric extract) alone and with gemcitabine in pancreatic cancer cell lines.

Reports cytotoxicity results: Turmeric Force has IC50 values of about 1.0 and 1.22 µg/ml in BxPC3 and Panc-1 cells, outperforming curcumin, while gemcitabine's IC50 is 0.03 µg/ml but 30-48% of cells remain gemcitabine-resistant even above 100 µg/ml.

Describes the combination's effect: Turmeric Force killed 96% of cells at 50 µg/ml where gemcitabine failed, and the gemcitabine plus Turmeric Force combination was synergistic, reaching IC90 at lower concentrations in both cell lines.

Presents the quantitative synergy analysis: CalcuSyn combination index values of 0.050 (BxPC3) and 0.183 (Panc-1) at IC50 indicate strong synergism of gemcitabine with Turmeric Force, and the mechanism is linked to enhanced NF-κB and STAT3 inhibition.
Concludes the mechanistic explanation: the synergy arises because the combination inhibits NF-κB activity and STAT3 expression more strongly than either agent alone.

Abstract opening (Background and Methods) of a systematic review and meta-analysis of gemcitabine plus erlotinib for advanced pancreatic cancer, describing the database search of PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane and conference abstracts.

Methods section of the meta-analysis on gemcitabine plus erlotinib in advanced pancreatic cancer, stating the study inclusion criteria: eligible trials must report response rate, disease control, survival endpoints, or adverse events.

Methods section on statistical pooling and the study sample: response, disease control, 1-year survival and adverse event rates were pooled with Meta-Analyst random-effects models, and 16 studies with 1,308 patients were included.

Results section of the gemcitabine plus erlotinib meta-analysis giving the reported ranges across studies for progression-free survival, median overall survival, 1-year survival, response rate and disease control rate.

Results section of the gemcitabine plus erlotinib meta-analysis reporting weighted pooled estimates for 1-year survival, objective response and disease control, plus overall incidences of total and severe adverse events.
Results section of the gemcitabine plus erlotinib meta-analysis listing the most common adverse events and comparing progression-free and overall survival against gemcitabine alone.

Comparative results and conclusion of the gemcitabine plus erlotinib meta-analysis: survival benefits over gemcitabine alone come with more deaths and interstitial lung disease-like syndrome, and the regimen is presented as a new option with modest additive efficacy.
Final conclusion of the gemcitabine plus erlotinib meta-analysis stating the regimen has an acceptable safety profile that requires careful management of specific adverse events.
Introduction of a systematic review on flax (food/supplement) for menopausal symptoms and breast cancer risk, outlining its lignan, ALA, and fiber components and the review's aims.
Methods and results opening: literature search of MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Library, and AMED through January 2013, and the count of 10 included studies from 1892 records.

Study composition (2 RCTs, 2 uncontrolled trials, 1 biomarker study, 5 observational studies) and findings on hot flashes and placebo-controlled effects of flax on tumor biomarkers in newly diagnosed breast cancer patients.

Biomarker results (apoptosis, HER2, Ki-67) from the placebo-controlled trial, plus uncontrolled and biomarker study findings on hot flashes, proliferation, mammographic density, and anti-angiogenic effects at specified flax and SDG doses.
Observational study results: adjusted odds ratio for primary breast cancer risk, mental health association, and hazard ratio for mortality among breast cancer patients, with confidence intervals.
Conclusions of the review: flax may be associated with lower breast cancer risk, has antiproliferative effects in at-risk breast tissue, and may reduce mortality in women with breast cancer.
Closing sentence of the review's conclusions on reduced mortality risk for breast cancer patients, followed by the copyright notice (© The Author(s) 2013).

Introduces the study's purpose and design: examining flaxseed (the richest dietary lignan source) and breast cancer risk, using a food frequency questionnaire in 2,999 cases and 3,370 controls from the Ontario Women's Diet and Health Study.
Describes the statistical methods (logistic regression, confounder assessment) and begins the results by noting that 21% of control women ate flaxseed or flax bread at least weekly.

Reports the confounding results (none of 19 variables were confounders) and the main finding: flaxseed intake was associated with reduced breast cancer risk (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.69-0.97), with flax bread showing a similar reduction.

Gives the flax bread odds ratio (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.67-0.89) and the conclusions, stating this is likely the first Canadian study on flaxseed alone and breast cancer risk, finding an association with reduced risk.
Closes the conclusions by noting that flaxseed intake is modifiable, so the finding may be important for public health and breast cancer prevention.

Background and introduction of an in vitro study on enterolactone (a flax-derived mammalian lignan) as an anti-metastatic agent, covering actin cytoskeleton, MMP2/9/11/14 roles in breast cancer invasion, and lignan metabolism to enterolactone.

Study aims and methods: enterolactone's anti-metastatic effects on adhesion, invasion and migration in MCF-7 and MDA MB 231 breast cancer cells, with migration inhibition, actin-based motility assays, and RT-PCR for MMP2, MMP9, MMP11 and MMP14.

Results section: enterolactone inhibits actin-based cell motility (confocal imaging, migration photos) and significantly down-regulates MMP2, MMP9 and MMP14 gene expression, with no significant change in MMP11.

Conclusions on the mechanism of enterolactone's anti-metastatic activity: inhibition of cell adhesion, invasion and motility, the MMP-related gene findings, and the start of the description of effects on filopodia and lamellipodia.

Proposed mechanism of enterolactone: disruption of filopodia and lamellipodia, actin filament polymerization at leading edges, and the force-generating steps of protrusion, traction, deadhesion and tail-retraction.
Final conclusion: by down-regulating MMP2, MMP9 and MMP14, enterolactone may block the cell invasion step of breast cancer metastasis.

Abstract of a GC/MS-SIM study introducing the first quantitative plasma method for lignans and isoflavonoid phytoestrogens, describing the ion-exchange separation of diphenols into biologically active and inactive fractions.

Continuation of the abstract's method description: hydrolysis, solid phase extraction and ion-exchange purification of the fractions, and correction for losses using radioactive estrogen conjugates and deuterated internal standards.

Abstract section on the analytical finish: isotope dilution GC-MS in selected ion monitoring mode, with detection limits of about 0.2 to 1.0 nmol/l, and the start of the statement about plasma results in 27 women.
Abstract findings from plasma analyses in 27 pre- and postmenopausal omnivorous and vegetarian women, reporting the free+sulfate fraction shares (genistein 3.8%, enterolactone and enterodiol 21-25%).

Abstract results on correlation between plasma and urine, wide inter-subject variation in concentrations (pmol/l to umol/l), higher values in vegetarians especially one vegan, and enterolactone exceeding 1 umol/l.
Concluding abstract statement that a highly specific assay for 3 lignans and 4 isoflavonoids in plasma was developed and will aid future studies of lignan and isoflavonoid metabolism.

Introduction and objective of a study on estradiol, tamoxifen, and flaxseed diet effects on IL-1β and IL-1Ra (IL-1 family cytokines) in normal human breast tissue, framing sex steroids and diet as breast cancer risk/prevention factors.

Study design and methods: in vivo microdialysis in healthy women under hormone exposures, tamoxifen, and diet modifications, plus breast cancer patients sampled before surgery, and cultured breast biopsies from reduction mammoplasties.
Key results: estradiol positively correlated with IL-1β and negatively with IL-1Ra in breast tissue; tamoxifen or 25 g/day flaxseed increased breast IL-1Ra levels.

Ex vivo validation of the tamoxifen and flaxseed effects on breast biopsies, and immunohistochemistry showing no change in cellular IL-1 content, implying altered secretion rather than production; also higher intratumoral IL-1β in breast cancers.
Conclusion that IL-1 may be estrogen-controlled and attenuated by antiestrogen therapy and diet, with elevated intratumoral IL-1β in breast cancer pointing to IL-1 as a possible therapeutic target.
Final sentence of the conclusion, stating that increased IL-1β in breast cancer suggests IL-1 as a potential target for breast cancer treatment and prevention.
Introduction and methods opening of a longitudinal NACC study (2005–2011) examining whether 100 common medications are associated with cognitive change in cognitively normal adults aged 50+.

Methods continued: NACC Uniform Data Set cohort of 4414 cognitively normal older adults, with composite cognitive scores built from 10 psychometric tests and change scores computed between assessments.
Statistical methods: general linear models compared mean composite cognitive change across participants who started, stopped, continued, or never took each of the 100 most frequent medications.

Results begin: average 1.2 years between assessments, and nine medications showed significant (p<0.05) group differences in cognitive change, with improvement linked to naproxen, calcium-vitamin D, ferrous sulfate, and potassium chloride.

Results and conclusion: flax and sertraline associated with improved performance; bupropion, oxybutynin, and furosemide associated with decline; overall, common medication use relates to cognition in older adults.
Concluding sentence calling for future studies to examine the mechanisms behind the observed associations between common medications and cognitive performance.
Introduction and background: omega-3 PUFAs' benefits for children's cognition, rising supplement popularity, and fish oil as a PCB contamination source. Sets up the study's motivation.

Study objectives and sample: congener-specific PCB measurements in 13 over-the-counter children's fish oil/powder supplements, and estimation of daily ingestion exposure. Also reports that all products contained PCBs.

Key results: mean PCB concentration of 9 ± 8 ng/g supplement, daily exposure range 2.5–50.3 ng/day at suggested serving sizes, and children's exposures significantly lower than adult supplement values.

Interpretation: lower child exposure is partly due to variable fish oil and PUFA content per serving. Purification method (molecular distillation) and fish trophic level do not predict PCB levels in children's supplements.

Conclusions on dietary comparison: supplements may raise or lower PCB exposure relative to fresh fish, and eating low-PCB, high-omega-3 fish may reduce exposure versus fish oil supplementation for some products.
Fragment ending 'died.' — a truncated word tail with no meaningful content; likely the end of the preceding sentence or text, with no standalone context.
Introduces the double-masked randomized trial design, comparing term infant formula supplemented with DHA alone or with DHA plus AA on visual acuity development, and the study population setup.

Describes the cohort of 108 term infants (79 formula-fed randomized, 29 breast-fed reference) and the four time-point evaluations over the first year covering blood fatty acids, growth, and two acuity measures.
Reports the main findings: DHA or DHA+AA supplementation during the first 4 months changes red blood cell lipid composition and improves sweep VEP acuity at 6, 17, and 52 weeks but not at 26 weeks.

Compares supplemented and unsupplemented infants with human milk-fed infants, finding supplemented groups resemble breastfed infants in RBC lipids and sweep VEP acuity, while unsupplemented infants differ; also notes forced choice preferential looking was too insensitive to detect group differences.

Summarizes safety and conclusion: all diet groups grew similarly and tolerated diets well, leading to the conclusion that early intake of preformed DHA and AA is necessary for optimal infant brain and eye development.
Concludes the abstract's final sentence, restating that early dietary preformed DHA and AA are necessary for optimal development of the human infant's brain and eye.
Background and objective of a Norwegian HUNT cohort study on cod liver oil intake (high vitamin A content pre-1999) and adult-onset asthma risk.

Methods of the HUNT (Nord-Trøndelag Health Study) cohort: 17,528 asthma-free adults aged 19-55 followed 1995-1997 to 2006-2008, with cod liver oil intake defined as daily use for at least one month in the prior year.
Exposure definition and outcome measurement: incident asthma as new-onset cases over 11-year follow-up, and results showing 18% (n=3,076) of participants were regular daily cod liver oil consumers.

Main result: cod liver oil intake was associated with incident asthma (OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.32-1.98) after adjusting for confounders including age, sex, smoking, BMI, and family history, with the association consistent across subgroups.

Conclusion of the study: cod liver oil with high vitamin A content was significantly associated with increased risk of adult-onset asthma, and subgroup consistency across age, sex, family history, and BMI strata.
Introduction and aims of an Australian multicenter case-control study on latitude, UV radiation, vitamin D and childhood allergy (asthma and hayfever), stating the study's objectives.
Continuation of the aims (asthma, hayfever, and both conditions) and study design: population-based controls aged 18-61 yr across four Australian study regions spanning 27°S to 43°S latitude.

Methods: data collection via self-administered questionnaire, interview, examination and biologic sampling, plus geocoding of residential latitude/longitude and linkage of climatic data by postcode, and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D analysis.

Key results on exposure measures and latitude: serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D and silicone rubber skin casts for actinic damage; an inverse latitude gradient for asthma (9% per degree) that disappeared after adjusting for average daily temperature.
Main findings: no association of UVR or vitamin D measures with asthma; greater winter sun exposure at ages 6-15 linked to higher odds of hayfever (adjusted OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.01-1.63).

Findings on cod liver oil supplementation in childhood associated with higher odds of asthma plus hayfever (OR 2.87), the authors' call for further study of early vitamin D supplementation, and the suggestion that childhood solar exposure matters for allergic sensitization.
Concluding remarks noting plausible biologic explanations for the observations, followed by the publication copyright notice (© 2010 John Wiley & Sons A/S).

Introduces the study's motivation and design: a 124-day longitudinal supplementation trial in 47 women testing manganese and iron supplements on MnSOD activity and manganese/iron status, across four treatment arms (placebo, iron, manganese, both).
Reports the main results: manganese supplementation raised lymphocyte MnSOD activity and serum manganese from baseline, with no change in urinary manganese excretion or any iron status indices.

Covers the confounder analysis and conclusion: oral contraceptive use and menstrual cycle stage did not confound MnSOD or serum manganese as markers, fat intake affected both, and the paper concludes lymphocyte MnSOD plus serum manganese can monitor manganese exposure.
