Study design and rationale: introduces the objective of testing very low vs. very high dietary manganese (Mn) with saturated vs. unsaturated fat in healthy young women, focusing on neuropsychological and metabolic effects.
Methods: crossover feeding of 0.8 or 20 mg Mn/day for 8 weeks each, fat source (15% energy as cocoa butter or corn oil), and whole-body counting of a 54Mn tracer meal after 4 weeks.
Results: low-Mn diets increased fractional 54Mn absorption but prolonged its biological half-life; Mn intake had no effect on neurological measures and minimal effect on psychological variables.

Conclusions: efficient homeostatic mechanisms maintain Mn balance across typical Western dietary intakes, supporting that 0.8-20 mg/day over 8 weeks does not cause Mn deficiency or toxicity in healthy adults.
Final conclusion sentence: dietary Mn intakes of 0.8 to 20 mg for 8 weeks are unlikely to produce deficiency or toxicity signs in healthy adults.

Study methods: ICP-OES and flame AAS measurement of metals and minerals (Al, B, Cu, Fe, Mn, Ni, P, Zn, Ca, K, Mg) in digests and infusions of six medicinal/herbal tea plants, including hibiscus, rosehip, ginkgo, lemongrass, aloe vera and ginseng.

Study aims: focus on aluminium and heavy metals as possible raw-material contaminants, their transfer into the infusion, and their likely dietary exposure from daily herbal tea consumption; Al speciation in leachates was also studied by Ion Chromatography.

Results for dry herbs and infusions: hibiscus had the highest Al, Fe, K, Mn, Ni, Zn and B, ginkgo the highest Mg and P, aloe the highest Ca, and ginseng the highest Cu. Infusion results are summarized, with hibiscus petals giving the highest levels of most elements.

Dietary significance: at intakes above 1 L per day, hibiscus decoction is identified as a potentially significant source of certain elements, and aloe and ginkgo infusions are highlighted for Ca and Mg respectively.

Specific health-relevant levels in hibiscus infusion: boron up to 5.5 mg/L as a major dietary source, magnesium up to 106 mg/L possibly helping lower blood pressure, bioavailable manganese up to 17.4 mg/L as a possible adverse effect, and total aluminium up to 1.2 mg/L.

Safety recommendation: sensitive groups (pregnant women, children under 6 months, and children with chronic renal failure) should limit or avoid hibiscus infusion, with no more than 1 L per day for sensitive adults because of its aluminium content.
Copyright footer (Elsevier Ltd, 2013) with no substantive content; it marks the end of the abstract.

Introduces the study design: ten subjects with normal renal function receiving single doses of aluminium-containing antacids (1, 4, or 8 tablets) taken with water, orange juice, or citric acid, and the first serum aluminium finding for citric acid and orange juice.

Reports serum and urinary aluminium results: marked serum rise with citric acid and orange juice, a slight rise with water only at 4 tablets, and a significant increase in 24-hour urinary aluminium excretion after all antacid doses.

Gives the estimated absorption comparison (8-fold higher with orange juice and 50-fold higher with citric acid versus water) and concludes that measurable aluminium is absorbed from single oral antacid doses.
Final conclusion: citric acid substantially enhances gastrointestinal absorption of aluminium from aluminium-containing antacids.

Study introduction and design: investigates black tea as a manganese source, measuring dietary Mn intake, fasting blood/plasma Mn, and leucocyte MnSOD and cAP-P expression in tea versus non-tea drinkers.

Study setting and population: 24 tea drinkers (at least 1 L black tea/day) and 28 non-tea drinkers recruited by email from King's College London staff and students; also reports dietary Mn intake results start.

Key results: dietary Mn intake was significantly higher in tea drinkers than non-tea drinkers (P<0.0001), depending on the assumed Mn content of black tea; blood/plasma Mn and MnSOD/cAP-P expression did not differ, and whole blood Mn correlated inversely with MnSOD expression.

Conclusions: tea is a major dietary Mn source, often exceeding adequate intake (1.8-2.3 mg/day) and occasionally the upper limit (10-11 mg/day), while dietary Mn has little influence on Mn status markers or enzyme expression.
Final recommendation: fasting whole blood Mn and leucocyte MnSOD expression are suggested as candidate markers of manganese status warranting further investigation.

Study design of a clinical trial on dietary citric acid and aluminum absorption: ten healthy men took citric acid (lemon juice), Al(OH)3 antacid, or both, for seven-day periods, with whole-blood aluminum measured as the outcome and pretreatment baseline given.

Results of the aluminum absorption study: blood Al rose modestly after citric acid (9 µg/L) or Al(OH)3 (12 µg/L) alone versus baseline of 5 µg/L, and rose markedly to 23 µg/L (p < 0.001) when both were taken together.

Conclusion of the aluminum-citric acid study: the combined Al(OH)3 and citric acid regimen produced the highest blood aluminum (23 µg/L, p < 0.001), attributed to absorption of Al-citrate complexes formed in the gut.

Introduction and study design: a randomized experimental trial of sour tea (Hibiscus sabdariffa) for essential hypertension, with 31 experimental and 23 control patients, excluding secondary hypertension and those on more than two drugs.
Methods continued: blood pressure was measured before and 15 days after intervention; the chunk also describes exclusion criteria and the sex distribution and mean age of the experimental group.

Participant demographics for both groups (sex split and mean age of experimental vs. control) and the main results: an 11.2% systolic and 10.7% diastolic reduction in the experimental group at 12 days versus day one.

Between-group comparison showing significant differences in systolic and diastolic pressures, and the post-treatment rebound: blood pressure rose after stopping treatment, with the withdrawal effect measured three days later.
Post-washout results (systolic up 7.9%, diastolic up 5.6%, significant between groups) and the conclusion that the findings support public belief and in vitro studies, with a call for larger studies.
Final sentence of the conclusion: the study calls for more extensive research on sour tea's effect on blood pressure.

Opening of a review on aluminium toxicity in over-the-counter drugs: introduces the early 1970s recognition of aluminium-linked bone and brain disorders in chronic renal failure patients, and notes that ingestion was earlier considered harmless because absorption was thought unlikely.

Describes the extensive body of epidemiological, clinical, and animal research on aluminium toxicity and lists accepted routes of exposure: contaminated dialysis fluids, parenteral nutrition, and oral pharmaceuticals such as phosphate binders and antacids.
States that over-the-counter antacids are the largest quantitative source of human aluminium exposure and that aluminium is a potent neurotoxicant, setting up the concern about OTC antacid risk.
Notes aluminium's embryonic and fetal toxicity after gestational exposure and reports that European OTC antacid patient leaflets differ substantially in their aluminium toxicity warnings.

Recommendation that all patients receive consistent aluminium toxicity information in leaflets, especially about increased absorption when taken with citrate-containing beverages and use during pregnancy.
Final fragment of the document's closing sentence, ending with the reference to antacid use during pregnancy.

Introduces the study's methods: electrothermal atomic absorption measurement of six metals (Al, Cr, Cu, Fe, Mn, Ni) in black tea, green tea, hibiscus, and mate after acid digestion, with triplicate 0.5-g subsamples.
Reports aluminum results: hibiscus and mate have much lower Al than black or green tea, and mate is suggested as a dietary source of manganese.
Gives manganese and iron/copper findings: mate's high total Mn with about 48% leached, and hibiscus infusion supplying more iron and copper (high copper leaching, 93.4%).

Summarizes the leaching results: hibiscus delivers more iron and copper than other infusions, and element leaching correlates strongly with tannin content, with lower tannins giving better leaching (nickel excepted).
Closing fragment of the tannin-leaching finding: the correlation with tannins holds except for nickel, and lower tannin levels yield better leaching.

Study design and methods: a crossover trial in 12 healthy volunteers on a controlled aluminium diet, comparing tea infusions with milk or lemon juice against mineral water, with plasma aluminium measured before and up to 24 hours after drinking.

Analytical methods and main result: plasma aluminium was measured by graphite-furnace AAS or ICP emission spectrometry. Tea containing up to 1.60 mg Al did not raise plasma Al compared with mineral water (about 0.001 mg Al).
Conclusion: the short-term findings indicate that drinking tea does not meaningfully add to the body's total aluminium burden.
Abstract opening: study design (234 parous Indian women, radioactive Fe method) and the finding that iron absorption from juices correlates with their ascorbic acid content.
Shows ascorbic acid is not the only enhancer: laboratory orange juice with added citric acid improves iron absorption over ascorbic acid alone or water with equal ascorbic acid.
Comparison data for citric acid and ascorbic acid effects: orange juice versus water with matched ascorbic acid, and the start of the lemon juice (citric acid added to orange juice) comparison.
Results for lemon juice versus orange juice, the baseline rice-meal iron absorption (0.025), and the fruits that had little or no effect on iron absorption (grape, peach, apple, avocado).
Lists fruits with mild to moderate enhancing effects on iron absorption (strawberry, plum, rhubarb, banana, mango, pear, cantaloup, pineapple), continuing from the non-enhancing fruits.
Guava and pawpaw as the strongest enhancers of iron absorption, followed by the start of the correlation analysis between iron absorption and fruit ascorbic acid content.
Correlation results for fruit citric acid content with iron absorption, and the caveat that citric acid-containing fruits also tended to contain ascorbic acid, confounding interpretation.
Closing fragment of the abstract: the correlation of citric acid with ascorbic acid content (rs 0.70) and the note that the abstract is truncated.

Introduces the in vitro study of aluminium speciation in black tea infusion, using ultrafiltration (3000, 10,000, 30,000 Da cut-offs) and the effects of gastric juice at pH 2.3 and then pH 6.5; reports the 78% Al passing the 3000-Da filter and its rise above 90% with gastric juice.

Reports the change in Al filterability after pH 6.5 adjustment (down to about 5%), and describes the in vivo test: 1H NMR analysis of ileostomy effluent looking for low molecular weight phenol breakdown products of tea polyphenols, with none found.

Concludes that only a small fraction of tea Al is potentially available for absorption along the small bowel, and argues that estimating systemic Al absorption from total urinary aluminium excretion, as done previously, may be misleading.
Closing clause of the document stating that prior estimates of systemic Al absorption from tea were based on total urinary aluminium excretion, which the study considers a misleading method.

Study background and design: a northern Italian cross-sectional case-control study comparing 64 former aluminium dust-exposed foundry workers with 32 matched unexposed controls, motivating a possible link between aluminium inhalation and pre-clinical mild cognitive disorder or Alzheimer's disease.
Methods overview: standardised occupational and medical history, plus serum measurements of aluminium, copper and zinc, as the start of the list of neurotoxic metals assessed.

Methods continued: blood metals (manganese, lead, iron) and cognitive testing via MMSE, Clock Drawing Test and P300 event-related potential, with timed MMSE and CDT measures added to detect early mild cognitive impairment.

Results part one: exposed ex-workers had significantly higher internal aluminium (serum) and iron (blood) doses, and significant differences from controls in P300 latency, MMSE and CDT scores and times.

Results part two: correlations of serum aluminium with cognitive measures, with P300 latency positively correlated with aluminium and MMSE-time, and negative links to MMSE and CDT scores and positive links to test completion times.

Confounder control (age, height, weight, blood pressure, schooling, alcohol, coffee, smoking) and the first part of the conclusions: aluminium may cause early neurotoxic effects detectable pre-clinically by P300, MMSE and CDT measures.

Conclusion specifics: the detectable tests and a 10 micrograms/l serum aluminium cut-off, applied to foundry workers with high blood iron, along with the authors' question about early detection and treatment to prevent or delay AD.
Final sentence of the document: the authors suggest pre-clinical detection and early treatment of aluminium neurotoxicity might prevent or retard Alzheimer's disease or AD-like pathology.

Opening of the abstract: introduces how the neuroanatomic pattern of Alzheimer's disease progression, shown by MRI and earlier neuropathology studies (neurofibrillary tangle spread along connections), may hint at etiology.
Middle of the abstract: twin studies showing AD has mixed environmental and genetic causes, and the decades-long prodromal phase suggesting slow accumulation of a toxic or infective agent.

Abstract section reviewing environmental candidates to find an agent that slowly builds to toxic levels in vulnerable AD brain cells, leading to the claim that chronic aluminum neurotoxicity fits best.
Abstract passage on human aluminum exposure through food additives and alum-treated water, and the mechanism by which aluminum, resembling ferric iron, enters and damages vulnerable neurons.

Abstract discussion of the genetic component: a yet-unidentified susceptibility gene may increase aluminum absorption, supported by elevated plasma and brain aluminum in AD and Down syndrome patients.
Closing statement of the abstract: states that the review presents evidence for aluminum's role in AD neuropathology and the clinical progression of sporadic AD.

Introduces the study's method (microwave-assisted acid digestion with graphite furnace AAS) for measuring aluminum in urine, and reports significant urinary Al excretion in four volunteers after tea drinking.

Compares urinary Al excretion after drinking Oolong (black) versus Long-Jin (green) tea, finding no significant difference despite their different Al contents and species, and concludes free Al in tea did not significantly change urinary excretion.

Offers explanations for the lack of effect (ligand transformation in food and the gastrointestinal tract) and cautions that absorption differences may still exist once retention and bile or fecal excretion of Al are considered.
Final sentence of the abstract: notes that retained Al and Al excreted via bile or feces must be considered before assuming no meaningful difference in absorption.

Opening of the abstract: introduces the brain's vulnerability to metabolic errors, Alzheimer's disease as the most prevalent neurodegenerative disease of the elderly, and aluminum as a widely bioavailable neurotoxic metal.

Continues the abstract's introduction of aluminum's presence in AD-susceptible neuronal foci and summarizes the three claims used to dispute Al's role in AD (limited brain entry, efficient excretion, accumulation as consequence not cause).

Presents the counter-findings to the three disputed claims: neurotoxicity at small doses reachable through diet, Al's use of transport mechanisms to cross brain barriers, and selective brain accumulation from lifetime incremental intake.

Cites the fourth line of evidence that chronic aluminum intoxication has reproduced AD neuropathology since 1911, and begins the conclusion that misconceptions about Al bioavailability may have misled researchers.
Conclusion of the abstract: argues the Al-AD hypothesis rests on solid experimental evidence and should not be dismissed, and calls for immediate steps to reduce human Al exposure.
Final sentence of the abstract: describes aluminum exposure as potentially the single most aggravating and avoidable factor related to Alzheimer's disease.

This chunk opens the document, introducing a study of aluminium migration from cans into beer and tea over the product's shelf life, with the beer and tea increases over seven months and the mention of dented cans.
This chunk concludes the document's findings: dented cans showed especially severe aluminium migration into tea, with aluminium concentration in dented canned tea rising 9.6 mg/L over seven months.
Abstract's Purpose and Methods opening for a study on erosive potential of brewed teas: bag teas of various flavors and brands, brewed 3 minutes, with pH, titratable acidity and fluoride measured.
Methods continuation: selection of one representative tea per flavor for erosion testing on six extracted human molars, with teeth window-painted and soaked 25 hours, refreshed every 5 hours.

Methods on lesion measurement and statistics: teeth sectioned by microtome, imaged under polarized light microscopy, lesion depths measured in Image Pro Plus, and analyzed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's HSD.

Statistical methods end and start of Results: Pearson correlation for lesion depths versus physicochemical properties, and results showing pH, titratable acidity and fluoride differed by tea flavor and brand.

Key erosion results: citrus tea produced the deepest lesions (83.1 µm), followed by fruity, then black, floral and green teas, with the correlation analysis beginning (pH inversely, titratable acidity positively associated with lesion depth).
Final correlation statistics concluding the abstract: Pearson r values and P values showing pH inversely and titratable acidity positively associated with lesion depth in tea erosion.

Introduction and aims of a clinical study on vegetarian diet and periodontal health: 200 participants (100 vegetarians, 100 non-vegetarians), noting prior research on this link is rare and small-scale.
Methods: full-mouth periodontal and dental examinations of 200 patients, a questionnaire on oral hygiene habits and education, and statistical testing (Mann-Whitney, chi-square; significance P<0.05).

Results part one: periodontal risk factors (age, gender, smoking) were balanced between vegetarian and non-vegetarian groups (71 females, 29 males, 10 smokers per group; mean ages 41.45 vs 41.72 years).

Results part two: vegetarians showed significantly better periodontal and hygiene measures (pocket depth, bleeding on probing, periodontal screening index, hygiene index, tooth mobility), plus fewer missing teeth but more decayed and eroded teeth.

Results part three and conclusion start: vegetarians had higher education levels but visited dentists less often, and the study concludes they had better periodontal conditions, with less inflammation, less damage and better home care.
Closing caveat of the conclusion: vegetarians' better periodontal outcomes may reflect an overall healthier lifestyle, not only the absence of meat in their diet.

Introduction to dental erosion: its multifactorial etiology, the dominant role of acidic beverages in extrinsic erosion, and the proposed preventive approaches (reducing intake, changing drinking method).
Presents the article's two case reports on erosion lesions from chronic, excessive acidic carbonated beverage intake, and frames the study around how drinking patterns affect erosion.

Key conclusion that the evidence argues against vague terms like 'cup versus straw' in favor of a more precise description of the drinking method, and notes how drinking patterns shape lesion location across the dentition.

Argues that preventive measures are the only effective management given the extensive damage from chronic carbonated beverage intake, and previews illustrative examples of long-term excessive consumption.
States the study's specific aim: to show, via clinical and radiographic evidence, how a straw placed in the labial vestibule versus a cup affects the anatomic location of erosion lesions.

Abstract of a 2013 Elsevier study using response surface methodology on cooked pork patties, introducing roselle extract and soybean oil levels and their effects on pH, color, water-holding capacity, and thickness/diameter reduction.

Continuation of the abstract's results: roselle raises water-holding capacity and a* values while lowering pH and L*/b*; soybean oil increases water-holding capacity and b*; hardness is negatively affected by the linear effect of both ingredients (p<0.01); sensory preferences depend on both additives.

Final results and optimization portion of the abstract: sensory preference for color, tenderness, juiciness, and overall quality depends on the additives, with the maximum overall quality score (5.42) at 12.5 g soybean oil and 0.7 g roselle extract, and implications for meat industry yield.
Closing sentence of the abstract about using RSM-derived optimal ingredient levels to increase product yield in patties, followed by the Elsevier copyright notice (2013).

Introduction and methods of a double-blind RCT comparing sour tea (Hibiscus sabdariffa) with black tea in 60 type II diabetic patients with mild hypertension, describing recruitment and random allocation to the two groups.

Study protocol details: twice-daily ST or BT infusion for one month, blood pressure measured at days 0, 15 and 30, and the systolic BP results showing a significant drop in the sour tea group from 134.4 to 112.7 mm Hg.

Results for the black tea group, where systolic BP rose from 118.6 to 127.3 mm Hg, no significant diastolic BP change in either group, and the pulse pressure decrease in the sour tea group from 52.2 to 34.5 mm Hg.

Pulse pressure comparison between groups (sour tea decreased from 52.2 to 34.5 mm Hg, black tea increased from 41.9 to 47.3 mm Hg), followed by the study's conclusion that sour tea positively affects blood pressure in diabetic hypertensive patients.
Closing statement of the abstract, stating that the findings agree with earlier studies showing antihypertensive effects of sour tea (Hibiscus sabdariffa).

Introduction and objectives of a 2009 systematic review on Hibiscus sabdariffa (roselle) for treating primary hypertension, covering its folk-medicine background and the review's aim to assess effectiveness and safety.

Methods section of the systematic review of Hibiscus sabdariffa for hypertension: databases and sources searched (MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Cochrane registers, Google) up to January 2009, and the inclusion criteria for randomized trials in adults with primary hypertension.

Continuation of the methods (inclusion criteria for RCTs of Hibiscus in primary hypertension, independent dual author selection, data extraction and appraisal) leading into the results, which report four trials with 390 patients.

Results of the Hibiscus sabdariffa hypertension review: four trials compared Hibiscus with black tea, captopril, and lisinopril, finding greater blood pressure reduction than tea but less than ACE inhibitors, with most studies short-term and of poor quality (Jadad score under 3).

Quality caveats and conclusion of the review: the included studies were short-term and below international standards, so the four RCTs do not provide reliable evidence to recommend Hibiscus sabdariffa for primary hypertension in adults, followed by the 2009 Elsevier copyright notice.
Final fragment of the conclusion and copyright line (Elsevier GmbH, 2009) for the systematic review on Hibiscus sabdariffa and hypertension, ending the document.

Introduction and study design of the PREMIER 18-month trial: background on the 6-month results, objective comparing two multicomponent behavioral interventions against advice only for hypertension, lifestyle, and blood pressure, plus the 2000-2002 multicenter randomized design.

Study design, setting, and participants: multicenter 3-arm randomized trial at 4 clinical centers, enrolling 810 adults with prehypertension or stage 1 hypertension defined by specific systolic and diastolic blood pressure ranges.

Interventions compared: the 'established' multicomponent behavioral program, the 'established plus DASH' program adding the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension diet, and advice only; measurements focus on lifestyle variables and blood pressure status.

Results on lifestyle changes: both behavioral interventions significantly reduced weight, fat, and sodium intake versus advice only, and the established plus DASH group also significantly increased fruit, vegetable, dairy, fiber, and mineral intake; 94% blood pressure follow-up at 18 months.

Hypertension outcomes: odds ratios for hypertension at 18 months versus advice only (0.83 for established, 0.77 for established plus DASH, with confidence intervals), and blood pressure reductions that were greater but not statistically significant.

Limitations of the study: exclusion criteria and volunteer nature of the cohort may limit generalizability, and the trial could not assess effects on clinical cardiovascular events given the limited time and sample size.

Conclusions: over 18 months, adults with prehypertension or stage 1 hypertension can sustain multiple lifestyle modifications that improve blood pressure control, with potential to reduce chronic disease risk.
Final concluding sentence of the conclusions: lifestyle modifications sustained over 18 months may reduce the risk for chronic disease in people with prehypertension or stage 1 hypertension.
Opening of the abstract for a meta-analysis on vegetarian diets and blood pressure: states the background gap and objective, and begins describing the MEDLINE and Web of Science data sources.
Search date ranges for the databases and the study inclusion criteria (adults over 20, vegetarian diet exposure, mean BP outcome, controlled trial or observational design).
Exclusion criteria (twin participants, multiple interventions, categorical-only BP data, case series/reports) and the start of data extraction and synthesis, covering the data collected.

Synthesis method (random-effects pooling), the main outcome of net systolic and diastolic BP differences, and the study screening counts: 258 identified, 7 trials and 32 observational studies included.
Results for the 7 controlled trials (311 participants, mean age 44.5): pooled reductions in systolic BP (-4.8 mm Hg) and diastolic BP (-2.2 mm Hg) with confidence intervals and low heterogeneity.

Results for the 32 observational studies (21,604 participants, mean age 46.6), including the start of the pooled systolic BP estimate (-6.9 mm Hg) with high heterogeneity, and the diastolic BP estimate (-4.7 mm Hg).

Confidence intervals and heterogeneity statistics for the observational diastolic BP result, followed by the conclusion that vegetarian diets are associated with lower BP and may be a nonpharmacologic option.
Final sentence of the conclusions: vegetarian diets could serve as a useful nonpharmacologic means of reducing blood pressure.

Opening of the review of Hibiscus sabdariffa (HS) for cardiovascular risk factors, introducing its approach of combining RCT results with ethnomedical, phytochemical, pharmacological, and safety data.
Summarizes HS's traditional use across at least 10 countries for hypertension and hyperlipidemia, reports no adverse events, and gives its low toxicity (LD50 2,000 to over 5,000 mg/kg/day).

Covers safety findings: no hepatic or renal toxicity except possible liver effects at high doses, and evidence of diuretic action without significant electrolyte changes; also begins the animal blood pressure results.

Reports that animal studies show dose-dependent blood pressure reduction and that RCTs in adults with pre- to moderate essential hypertension and type 2 diabetes found significant SBP and DBP lowering with HS tea or extract.

Compares HS tea's antihypertensive effect to captopril (comparable) and lisinopril (less effective), and summarizes animal lipid results: lower total cholesterol, LDL-C, and triglycerides, with HDL-C generally unchanged.

Summarizes human lipid evidence, noting over half of RCTs found favorable lipid changes (lower total cholesterol, LDL-C, triglycerides and higher HDL-C), and names anthocyanins as the main proposed active compounds.

Discusses the phytochemicals responsible for effects (anthocyanins, with supporting evidence for polyphenols and hibiscus acid) and introduces proposed mechanisms for the blood pressure and cholesterol effects.
States the most common mechanistic explanation, antioxidant inhibition of LDL-C oxidation that impedes atherosclerosis, and concludes HS extracts are promising for hypertension and hyperlipidemia.
Closing call for more high-quality animal and human studies reflecting real therapeutic practice before public health recommendations can be made.

Introduction and background on Hibiscus sabdariffa tea: prior in vitro and animal evidence of antioxidant, hypocholesterolemic, and antihypertensive effects, plus the study's aim to test blood pressure effects in humans.

Methods of the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial: 65 pre- and mildly hypertensive adults aged 30-70 receiving 3 servings/day of hibiscus tea or placebo for 6 weeks, with BP measured at baseline and weekly.

Main results at 6 weeks: hibiscus tea significantly reduced systolic blood pressure versus placebo (P = 0.030), with diastolic and mean arterial pressure changes reported as non-significant or borderline compared with placebo.

Secondary findings: mean arterial pressure change was borderline significant; participants with higher baseline systolic BP responded more strongly (r = -0.421); no effects by age, gender, or supplement use.
Conclusion: daily hibiscus tea, an amount easily added to the diet, lowers blood pressure in pre- and mildly hypertensive adults and may be a useful dietary measure for these conditions.
Final punctuation fragment closing the document's concluding sentence; no substantive content beyond the end of the conclusion.

Opening of the abstract on Hibiscus sabdariffa polyphenols: describes the human (metabolic syndrome, 4 weeks) and spontaneously hypertensive rat study designs and sample sizes, and introduces the reported metabolic, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and blood-pressure-lowering effects.

Middle of the abstract: states that the blood-pressure benefits of the H. sabdariffa extract in humans and rats are explained mainly by antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and endothelium-dependent mechanisms, with diuresis and ACE inhibition playing smaller roles.

Concluding part of the abstract: highlights the favorable endothelial response to polyphenols as relevant for managing metabolic cardiovascular risk, followed by the 2014 copyright line for Molecular Nutrition & Food Research (Wiley-VCH).

Study background and objectives for a randomized controlled trial comparing sour tea (Hibiscus sabdariffa) with black tea on lipid profile in type II diabetes patients, including the hypoglycemic and hypolipidemic rationale.
Trial design section: 60 diabetes patients randomly assigned to sour tea or black tea twice daily for one month, with fasting blood sampling at baseline and study end as the outcome measures.

Results begin: 53 of the enrolled patients completed the study; in the sour tea group HDL-cholesterol rose significantly (p=0.002), while apolipoprotein A1 and lipoprotein(a) changes were not significant.

Detailed lipid results: sour tea group showed significant decreases in total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, triglycerides and Apo-B100; black tea group showed only a significant HDL-cholesterol change (p=0.002) with other measures non-significant.
Conclusion of the trial stating that sour tea has a significant effect on the blood lipid profile of patients with diabetes, in contrast to black tea's limited effect.

Introduction and study background from a clinical trial of Hibiscus sabdariffa extract (HSE) in obese adults, stating the prior metabolic and liver-protective findings and the trial's participant criteria (BMI ≥27, aged 18-65).

Trial design and main results: 12-week randomized control vs HSE groups (n=17 and n=19) showing reductions in body weight, BMI, body fat, waist-to-hip ratio, serum free fatty acids, and improved liver steatosis, with HSE well tolerated.

Safety findings and proposed mechanism: no adverse effects and no change in serum α-amylase or lipase; the benefit is attributed to HSE polyphenols since branched-chain amino acids are not notably elevated.

Conclusion of the HSE clinical trial summarizing reduced obesity, abdominal fat, serum FFA and improved liver steatosis, proposing HSE as an adjuvant for preventing obesity and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

Introduction and study design: the PREMIER trial (n=810, 18-month clinical trial of lifestyle modifications) used to examine how dietary protein, especially plant versus animal protein, relates to blood pressure.

Methods and cross-sectional result setup: multivariable linear regression on cross-sectional and longitudinal PREMIER data, first reporting that plant protein is inversely associated with systolic and diastolic BP at 6 months.
Cross-sectional findings at 6 months: plant protein and fruit/vegetable intake are inversely associated with systolic and diastolic BP, with the reported P-values for each.

Longitudinal and hypertension-risk findings: plant protein shows a marginal BP reduction from baseline to 6 months, independent of weight and waist change, and plant protein plus fruit/vegetable intake is linked to lower hypertension risk at 6 but not 18 months.
Conclusions: plant protein benefits blood pressure and lowers hypertension risk at 6 months, supporting increased plant protein intake as a strategy to prevent and treat hypertension.
Final concluding sentence of the abstract: increased plant protein intake may be useful for preventing and treating hypertension.

Introduction and methods of a randomized controlled trial comparing a standardized Hibiscus sabdariffa (roselle) calyx infusion with captopril for mild-to-moderate hypertension; describes patient eligibility (ages 30-80, untreated for at least 1 month) and study design.

Intervention details: the H. sabdariffa infusion (10 g dry calyx in 0.5 L water, 9.6 mg anthocyanins) taken daily before breakfast versus captopril 25 mg twice daily for 4 weeks, plus the defined outcome variables (tolerability, therapeutic effectiveness defined as diastolic reduction of at least 10 mm Hg, and urinary electrolyte changes).

Participant flow and early results: 90 subjects enrolled, 15 withdrew for non-medical reasons, leaving 39 in the H. sabdariffa group and 36 in the captopril group; begins reporting systolic BP falling from 139.05 mm Hg.

Blood pressure and effectiveness outcomes: systolic BP fell from 139.05 to 123.73 mm Hg and diastolic from 90.81 to 79.52 mm Hg, with no significant between-group BP difference (ANOVA p > 0.25); therapeutic effectiveness rates were 0.7895 (H. sabdariffa) vs 0.8438 (captopril), chi-square p > 0.560.

Tolerability was 100% in both groups, a natriuretic effect was observed with the hibiscus treatment, and the authors conclude the extract and captopril showed no significant differences in hypotensive effect, effectiveness, or tolerability.

Final concluding sentence of the abstract: the hibiscus extract (9.6 mg total anthocyanins) and captopril showed no significant differences in hypotensive effect, antihypertensive effectiveness, or tolerability; note it cites captopril 50 mg/day, which differs from the 25 mg twice-daily dosing in the methods.

Introduction to the PREMIER trial: background on lifestyle recommendations (weight loss, sodium reduction, physical activity, limited alcohol, DASH diet) for lowering blood pressure, and the study objective of testing multicomponent behavioral interventions.

Study design and population: randomized trial at 4 clinical centers (2000-2001) of 810 adults with above-optimal BP including stage 1 hypertension, not on antihypertensive medication, with demographic details.
Intervention arms: the 'established' behavioral group, the 'established plus DASH' group, and the sample sizes for each, with the setup of the randomization into these groups.

Main outcomes and early results: both behavioral interventions reduced weight, improved fitness, and lowered sodium; the DASH arm also increased fruit, vegetable, and dairy intake; BP gradients across groups were observed.

Systolic blood pressure results: net reductions versus the advice-only group (3.7 mm Hg established, 4.3 mm Hg established plus DASH) and the non-significant 0.6 mm Hg difference between the two intervention groups.

Hypertension prevalence results: baseline 38% falling to 26% (advice only), 17% (established), and 12% (established plus DASH) at 6 months, with P-values for comparisons against advice only and each other.
Optimal blood pressure prevalence results: 19% in advice-only, 30% in established, and 35% in established plus DASH at 6 months, with comparative P-values.
Conclusion: adults with above-optimal BP, including stage 1 hypertension, can adopt multiple lifestyle changes that lower BP and reduce cardiovascular disease risk.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence stating that multiple lifestyle changes reduce cardiovascular disease risk.

Introduction and rationale of a PREMIER trial secondary analysis: prior research on macronutrient composition and body weight is inconsistent, and subcomponents like saturated fat and plant protein are understudied; the study aims to test their effects on later weight.

Study design and population: a secondary observational analysis of the 18-month PREMIER randomized clinical trial (n=810), where participants received group and individual lifestyle sessions aimed at blood pressure control.

Methods: dietary intake measured by two 24-hour recalls at baseline, 6, and 18 months; body weight and fitness monitored regularly; regression models assessed animal/plant protein and other macronutrients as predictors of subsequent weight.

Key results: after adjusting for confounders, baseline calorie-contributing nutrients were unrelated to later weight, but higher saturated fat at 6 months predicted higher weight at 18 months (P=0.002), and higher 6-month plant protein was marginally linked to lower weight (P=0.069).

Conclusions: pre-intervention macronutrient intakes did not predict weight at 6 or 18 months, whereas saturated fat intake achieved after the 6-month intervention predicted 18-month body weight, linking lower saturated fat to better weight-loss maintenance.
Final conclusion sentence: lower saturated fat intake after the 6-month intervention is associated with lower 18-month body weight and therefore better weight-loss maintenance.

Introduction to the paper's core hypothesis: ancestral plant-based diets (high fiber, vegetable protein, plant sterols, low saturated fat) shaped human cholesterol metabolism, and genetic traits that raised serum cholesterol were conserved to meet bodily needs.

Explains the mismatch between evolutionary conserved cholesterol-raising genetics and modern high-fat diets and lifestyles, which has led to recommending cholesterol-lowering medications, especially in middle age, to reduce cardiovascular disease risk.

Reports the experimental finding that a Myocene-like diet of leafy vegetables, fruit, and nuts (rich in viscous fiber, vegetable protein, and plant sterols) lowered LDL-cholesterol by over 30% in healthy volunteers, comparable to first-generation statins.

Describes a follow-up study in hyperlipidemic patients using a modern therapeutic diet (oat, barley, psyllium fiber; soy and almonds; sterol-enriched margarine) that achieved LDL reductions similar to the Myocene-like diet and normalized most subjects' blood lipids.

Summarizes the conclusion that reintroducing plant food components abundant in ancestral diets into modern eating can correct lipid abnormalities linked to contemporary diets and reduce reliance on drug treatment.
Final concluding sentence stating that restoring ancestral plant food components can correct contemporary lipid abnormalities and reduce the need for pharmacological intervention.
Introduction and background of a prospective population-based study on whole-grain intake, type 2 diabetes, prediabetes, and TCF7L2 gene polymorphisms, stating the study objectives.
Study design: 8-10 year incidence of prediabetes and T2D in relation to whole-grain intake, with baseline data from 3180 women and 2297 men aged 35-56 years.
Main results: higher whole-grain intake (>59.1 vs <30.6 g/d) associated with 34% lower risk of deteriorating glucose tolerance in women and men combined.

Adjusted and sex-specific results: association persists after covariate adjustment, significant risk reduction in men but not women, and significant associations for prediabetes alone (overall and in men).

Insulin resistance findings and genetic modification: whole-grain intake inversely correlated with HOMA-IR, and no effect was detectable in men carrying diabetogenic TCF7L2 polymorphisms; conclusions begin.
Conclusions: higher whole-grain intake linked to lower risk of worsening glucose tolerance, likely via insulin sensitivity, with support for TCF7L2 genetic effect modification.

Opening of the Institute of Medicine 'Crossing the Quality Chasm' excerpt: notes that providers have abundant research and technology yet reports doubt American health care quality, and introduces the book's urgent call for fundamental change.

Summary of the book's main purpose: recommends a sweeping redesign of the American health care system and provides overarching principles for policymakers, leaders, clinicians, regulators, and purchasers, introducing the committee's list of offerings.

Lists the committee's specific offerings: performance expectations for the 21st century health care system, 10 new rules for patient-clinician relationships, an organizing framework aligning payment and accountability incentives with quality, and steps to promote evidence-based practice and clinical information systems.

Describes the book's analytical approach: treats health care organizations as complex systems, documents causes of the quality gap, identifies practices that impede quality care, and explores how systems approaches can implement change.
Copyright notice from 2001 by the National Academy of Sciences, with all rights reserved; closes the excerpt.

Introduces the randomized crossover study of flaxseed in overweight/obese adults with pre-diabetes (n=25), stating hypotheses about glucose, insulin, inflammation markers, and adiponectin, and the 0/13/26 g ground flaxseed 12-week design.

Reports multiple ANOVA results showing significant treatment effects on glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR, and normalized ALA, and begins the paired t-test findings on glucose changes during the 13 g versus 0 g periods.
Gives paired t-test details: glucose fell with 13 g flaxseed versus 0 g, and insulin decreased with 13 g but not with 26 g or 0 g, with means, SEMs, and P values; HOMA-IR results begin.

Presents HOMA-IR results (decrease only with 13 g) and the ALA fatty acid changes across the 0, 13, and 26 g periods, with means, SEMs, and P values, and begins listing markers with no significant differences.

Lists the outcomes with no significant differences (fructosamine, hs-CRP, adiponectin, hs-IL-6) and concludes that flaxseed lowered glucose and insulin and improved insulin sensitivity in a habitual diet; includes copyright notice.
Final fragment of the abstract's text ending the conclusion sentence and the Elsevier 2013 copyright statement.

Abstract opening of a 2012 Elsevier study on dark bean (Phaseolus vulgaris cv. Tolosana) phenolic compounds, examining how boiling or germination affects antioxidant, neuroprotective, and anticancer properties.

Continuation of the abstract's methods: HPLC-PAD/HPLC-ESI/MS phenolic profiling, ORAC antioxidant assay, U-373 astrocyte neuroprotection testing, and sulforhodamine B cytotoxicity screening on TK-10, MCF-7, and UACC-62 cancer cell lines.
Results summary showing qualitative and quantitative phenolic differences between raw and processed dark beans, with germinated samples showing reduced antioxidant capacity.
Key findings: all extracts reduced reactive oxygen species and showed cytotoxicity, but raw beans, rich in phenolics especially anthocyanins, were most active neuroprotectively and antitumorally.

Conclusion linking cooking-altered phenolic composition to neuroprotective and anticancer activity, noting cooking improves intestinal digestion and absorption while preserving cellular antioxidant protection.
Closing copyright line (Elsevier Ltd., 2012) ending the dark bean phenolic composition abstract.
Background and objective of a prospective nested case-control study (CLHLS) on dietary habits and 3-year cognitive decline among illiterate Chinese elderly.
Study design and methods: part of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Study; 6,911 illiterate residents aged 65+ with baseline socio-demographic and dietary data collected.

Outcome measurement: cognitive function assessed with the Chinese revised MMSE (MMSE-r) in 2002 and 2005; cognitive decline defined as falling below 18 among those with baseline MMSE-r of 18 or more, analyzed with logistic regression odds ratios.

Results overview: 5,691 elderly analyzed; bivariate analysis linked cognitive decline to gender, marital status, financial status, smoking, alcohol, tea, and intake of fruits, vegetables, legumes, fish, meat, egg and sugar.
Key multivariate findings: always eating vegetables (AOR 0.66, 95% CI 0.58-0.75) and always consuming legumes (AOR 0.78, 95% CI 0.64-0.96) were inversely associated with cognitive decline.
Conclusion: lower vegetable and legume intake is associated with cognitive decline in illiterate elderly Chinese, suggesting dietary factors may help prevent cognitive decline.

Introduces the VA-HIT gemfibrozil trial and the study's rationale: conventional lipid changes only partly explain CHD event reductions, so LDL/HDL particle subclass measurements are examined as additional predictors.
Describes the methods: a prospective nested case-control study of 364 men with new CHD events and 697 age-matched controls, with NMR spectroscopy used to quantify lipoprotein particle subclasses.
Details NMR measurements taken at baseline and after 7 months of gemfibrozil or placebo, plus the statistical approach of adjusted logistic regression for odds ratios per 1-SD increment.
Reports key results: gemfibrozil increased LDL size, lowered LDL particle numbers (-5%), and raised HDL (10%) and small HDL (21%) particles, which independently predicted new CHD events.

Gives specific odds ratios (LDL 1.28; HDL 0.71) with confidence intervals, notes that mean particle sizes were not associated with CHD, and states the conclusion that NMR-measured changes explain benefit beyond conventional cholesterol.
Concludes that gemfibrozil's effects on NMR-measured LDL and HDL particle subclasses, which conventional cholesterol measures miss, help explain its benefit in patients with low HDL cholesterol.

Introduction and methods of an elderly dietary cholesterol study: 42 subjects (29 postmenopausal women, 13 men over 60), excluding diabetes, heart disease, and statin use, using a randomized crossover design.

Crossover protocol details: subjects ate the equivalent of 3 large eggs daily or a cholesterol-free, fat-free egg substitute for 1 month each, separated by a 3-week washout before switching treatments.

Results on plasma lipids: LDL-C and HDL-C rose significantly during the egg period in both sexes, leaving LDL-C:HDL-C and total cholesterol:HDL-C ratios unchanged; plasma cholesterol response varied between individuals.
Further findings: LDL peak diameter increased during the egg period, while LDL oxidation markers (conjugated dienes, lag time) showed no difference between egg and substitute periods.
Study conclusion: dietary cholesterol from eggs does not raise heart disease risk in healthy elderly people, based on the lipid ratio and LDL atherogenicity results.

Opening of a review on dietary cholesterol: introduces the concern that dietary cholesterol raises coronary heart disease risk, the resulting US 300 mg/day limit, and the review's aim to challenge that restriction and highlight benefits of eggs.

Recent findings begin: lists countries and regions whose dietary guidelines lack a cholesterol upper limit, and states that epidemiological data show dietary cholesterol is not correlated with CHD risk.

Discusses clinical evidence that dietary cholesterol challenges raise LDL in a sensitive subgroup (about one-quarter of people), noting that HDL also rises, which preserves the LDL/HDL ratio, a key CHD risk marker.

Summary section: concludes that epidemiological and clinical cholesterol-challenge evidence supports reconsidering recommendations that limit dietary cholesterol, with the LDL/HDL ratio point as a key link.
Final sentence of the summary, closing the document by calling for dietary cholesterol limits to be reconsidered.

Abstract opening of a prospective cohort study of about 27,673 healthy women, introducing NMR lipoprotein particle measurement and its uncertain clinical utility for predicting incident cardiovascular disease over 11 years.
Continues the abstract's results: adjusted hazard ratios for top vs bottom quintile of NMR-measured lipoprotein particle concentrations (LDL, HDL, VLDL, and LDL/HDL ratio) for incident CVD.

Presents adjusted hazard ratios for NMR-measured lipoprotein particle size (LDL, HDL, VLDL) and begins comparing NMR measures with standard lipid measures, stating they are comparable but not superior.

Lists adjusted hazard ratios for standard lipids (total cholesterol, LDL-C, HDL-C, triglycerides, non-HDL-C, total/HDL ratio) and apolipoproteins (B100, A-1, B100/A-1) for CVD risk, used as comparators to NMR measures.

Reports reclassification and discrimination results: adding LDL particle concentration or apolipoprotein B100 to a base model gave negligible NRI gains (0% and 1.9%) and no significant c-index improvement.
Concludes the abstract's results and main finding: NMR-based lipoprotein profiles are comparable but not superior to standard lipids or apolipoproteins for CVD risk prediction in healthy women.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending with the comparison to standard lipids or apolipoproteins.

Introduces advanced lipoprotein analysis (LDL/HDL particle number and size, subfractionation, apolipoproteins B and A, Lp(a)) as used to predict cardiovascular risk and individualize prevention, noting these markers have not yet met biomarker evaluation standards.

States that it is unresolved whether these lipoprotein tests add predictive value beyond traditional risk factors, and whether treatment strategies guided by or targeting them improve cardiovascular outcomes.

Reports that niacin and fenofibrate, which alter advanced lipoprotein parameters, did not further reduce cardiovascular risk in recent randomized trials of high-risk patients on statins, suggesting such strategies may not help and could add harm and cost.

Concludes that advanced lipoprotein analysis-guided approaches need further research before being used to individualize cardiovascular prevention therapy, in contrast to the strong evidence for LDL cholesterol reduction and intensified statin therapy.

Closing statement reaffirming the strong evidence base for LDL cholesterol lowering and statin intensification, followed by the copyright notice for the American College of Cardiology Foundation and Elsevier.

Introduction/background of the study: animal research links gut microbial metabolism of dietary phosphatidylcholine to coronary artery disease via the TMAO metabolite; this human study examines that relationship.

Methods, part 1: plasma and urinary TMAO, choline, and betaine are measured by LC-MS/MS after a phosphatidylcholine challenge (two eggs plus d9-labeled PC) in healthy people, before and after broad-spectrum antibiotic suppression of gut microbiota.

Methods, part 2: the challenge is described in full (antibiotic suppression of microbiota), and a cohort of 4007 elective coronary angiography patients is followed for 3 years for death, MI, or stroke as a function of fasting plasma TMAO.
Results, part 1: the PC challenge raises TMAO, its d9 isotopologue, and other choline metabolites over time; antibiotics markedly suppress plasma TMAO, which returns after antibiotics are stopped.
Results, part 2: higher plasma TMAO is linked to major adverse cardiovascular events, with the highest vs. lowest quartile hazard ratio of 2.54 (95% CI 1.96 to 3.28, P<0.001).
Results, part 3 and conclusions: TMAO predicts MACE after adjusting for traditional risk factors and in lower-risk subgroups; TMAO production from dietary PC depends on gut microbiota metabolism.
Final conclusion and funding statement: increased TMAO is associated with incident major adverse cardiovascular events, and the study was funded by the NIH and others.

Opening of the study abstract on egg consumption and lipoprotein atherogenicity: introduces the hypercholesterolemia concern and the 3-week, 2-eggs-per-day protocol with its minor effects on glucose and urea.
Lipid and apolipoprotein results from the egg-feeding trial: LDL-driven rise in total cholesterol, triglyceride decrease, unchanged apoA-I and apoB-100, and an 11% drop in HDL cholesterol.

HDL functional results and oxidation setup: a non-significant 13% fall in macrophage cholesterol efflux, plus the AAPH and copper-ion challenges used to test plasma and LDL susceptibility to lipid peroxidation.
Oxidation outcomes: plasma and LDL susceptibility to lipid peroxidation rose 42% and 34% by TBARS (p < 0.01), and copper-induced LDL oxidation lag time fell 37%.

Remaining results and conclusion start: total plasma fatty acids rose from 2.2 to 3.2 mg/ml, vitamin E and carotenoids were unchanged, and the conclusion begins on increased plasma and LDL oxidizability from egg intake.
Concluding statement of the abstract: egg-induced increases in plasma and LDL oxidizability may promote atherosclerosis progression, relevant to populations with high cholesterol intake.
Final fragment of the document, the trailing period closing the last sentence of the conclusion on atherosclerosis and cholesterol intake.

Introduction and methods of a meta-analysis on dietary cholesterol from eggs and the total-to-HDL cholesterol ratio, covering the rationale (egg effects on LDL offset by HDL) and the literature search (MEDLINE, 1974 to June 1999).

Study selection criteria for the meta-analysis of egg/dietary cholesterol trials: crossover or parallel designs with controls, diets differing only in cholesterol or egg number, at least 14 days, and reported HDL cholesterol; 222 studies screened.
Meta-analysis results: 17 studies with 556 subjects met inclusion criteria, and adding 100 mg/day dietary cholesterol raised the total-to-HDL cholesterol ratio by 0.020 units (95% CI 0.010 to 0.030).

Quantitative effects of 100 mg/day dietary cholesterol: total cholesterol up 0.056 mmol/L (2.2 mg/dL) and HDL cholesterol up only 0.008 mmol/L (0.3 mg/dL), with confidence intervals, plus the main conclusion that dietary cholesterol adversely raises the total-to-HDL ratio.

Conclusion and public health implication: because dietary cholesterol worsens the cholesterol profile, advice to limit cholesterol by reducing eggs and other cholesterol-rich foods may still be valid.

Introduces the document's central question: how early-life adversity like maltreatment affects health decades later, proposing telomere erosion from stress as a possible DNA-level mechanism, with shorter telomeres linked to aging, morbidity, and mortality.

Presents telomere erosion as a candidate mechanism linking childhood stress to later health problems, and notes the mechanistic, methodological, and basic biology questions that must be resolved before telomere measures can be used clinically for health monitoring and disease risk prediction.
Closing statement of the abstract-style overview, saying the paper reviews the current state of research on stress and telomeres and outlines directions for future work.

Introduction and aims of a Finnish population study linking work-related exhaustion (Maslach Burnout Inventory) to shorter leukocyte telomeres as a marker of accelerated biological aging from psychological stress.

Methods: the Health 2000 Study, a representative sample of 2911 Finnish working-age adults aged 30–64, with exhaustion measured by the Maslach Burnout Inventory and relative telomere length measured by qPCR.
Results: after adjusting for age and sex, severely exhausted individuals had telomeres about 0.043 relative units shorter than non-exhausted peers (p = 0.009).

Results continued: the exhaustion–telomere association stayed significant after further adjustment for marital/socioeconomic status, smoking, BMI and morbidities (difference 0.044, p = 0.008); conclusions link exhaustion to accelerated aging.
Conclusion: work exhaustion appears related to accelerated biological aging, but this needs confirmation in a prospective study tracking telomere length changes over time.
Introduction/background of a study on leisure-time physical activity and leukocyte telomere length (LTL) as a marker of human aging, in healthy twin volunteers.

Methods of the twin study: 2401 white twin volunteers (2152 women, 249 men) completed questionnaires on physical activity, smoking, and socioeconomic status; LTL measured via mean terminal restriction fragment length and adjusted for age and confounders.
Main results: LTL rose with greater leisure-time physical activity (P<.001), and the association held after adjusting for age, sex, BMI, smoking, socioeconomic status, and work activity.

Quantitative findings: most active subjects had LTL about 200 nucleotides longer than the least active (7.1 vs 6.9 kb; P=.006), replicated in discordant twin pairs (88 nucleotides longer in more active twins; P=.03).

Conclusions: sedentary lifestyle, like smoking, high BMI, and low socioeconomic status, affects LTL and may accelerate aging, supporting regular exercise as a potentially antiaging intervention clinicians could promote.
Final sentence of the conclusions, restating that promoting regular exercise may have an antiaging effect.

Introduces the study's background: shorter leukocyte telomeres (a marker of biologic aging) are linked to coronary artery calcium (CAC), and the question is whether healthy lifestyle behaviors modify this link in adults aged 40-64 without prior CHD, stroke, diabetes, or cancer.

Describes the study sample (n = 318) and the lifestyle factors examined as possible attenuators of the shorter telomere-CAC association: fruit and vegetable intake, meat intake, exercise, healthy weight, and social support.

Reports the main logistic regression finding, adjusted for age, gender, race/ethnicity, and Framingham risk score: high social support, low meat intake, and high fruit/vegetable intake attenuated the shorter telomere-CAC relation.

Explains that people with shorter telomeres who had these healthy characteristics did not differ significantly from those with longer telomeres, and begins listing odds ratios for those with shorter telomeres and less healthy lifestyles.

Gives the specific odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals for increased CAC risk among those with shorter telomeres and unhealthy behaviors (low fruit/vegetable intake, high meat intake, low social support), and notes gender differences: similar results in men, but only fruit/vegetable intake mattered in women.
Concludes that healthy lifestyle behaviors may attenuate the link between shorter telomere length and coronary atherosclerosis as measured by CAC, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.
Contains only the end of the conclusion sentence (coronary atherosclerosis identified by CAC) and the 2010 Elsevier Inc. copyright statement.

Introduces the study's rationale: telomerase activity as a marker of cellular viability, its decline with chronic distress, and Buddhist claims that meditation reduces distress; sets up the 3-month retreat investigation of telomerase, Perceived Control, and Neuroticism.

Defines the mediators under study (Perceived Control, linked to lower stress, and Neuroticism, linked to higher distress) and states the mediation-model aim of testing whether their changes explain retreat effects on telomerase, plus the added focus on Mindfulness and Purpose in Life.

Begins the Methods: describes the retreat design of about 6 hours of daily meditation for 3 months and the hypothesis that Mindfulness and Purpose in Life, developed through practice, account for changes in stress variables and telomerase.

Details the sample: 30 retreat participants versus 30 wait-list controls matched on age, sex, BMI, and prior meditation experience, plus the concentrative and benevolence-cultivating practices taught during the retreat.

Covers measurement and analysis: psychological measures taken pre- and post-retreat, peripheral blood mononuclear cells collected post-retreat for telomerase assay, use of one-tailed significance tests justified by a priori hypotheses, and the start of the Results.

Reports main results: telomerase significantly higher in retreat participants than controls (p<0.05), greater retreat-group gains in Perceived Control, Mindfulness, and Purpose in Life and reductions in Neuroticism (p<0.01), and mediation showing Perceived Control and Neuroticism carry the retreat effect on telomerase.

Explains the mediation pathways: changes in Perceived Control and Neuroticism are partially mediated by Mindfulness and Purpose in Life, Purpose in Life directly mediates the telomerase group difference while Mindfulness does not, and the Conclusions open by claiming the first study linking meditation and positive change to telomerase.

Presents the main conclusion: increases in perceived control and decreases in negative affectivity likely contributed to higher telomerase, with possible implications for telomere length and immune cell longevity, while noting baseline telomerase was not measured.

Final conclusion and copyright: Purpose in Life is shaped by meditation and affects perceived control and negative emotionality, influencing telomerase both directly and indirectly; ends with the Elsevier 2010 copyright notice.
Fragment of the copyright line that ends the document, reading 'served.' (completing 'All rights reserved'), carrying no substantive study content.

Introduction to telomerase: its role in countering chromosome shortening from the end-replication problem, its link to disease, aging, and cancer, and the gap that the full human telomerase–telomeric DNA structure is unresolved.

Continues the background on the missing structure and unknown elongation mechanism, then describes the methods used (distant homology detection, comparative modeling, molecular docking, guided by experimental data) to build the structural model.

Describes the resulting model: a partial telomerase elongation complex of three protein domains bound to single-stranded telomeric DNA in a heteroduplex with the human RNA template region (TER), which explains telomerase processivity.

Presents the main conclusions: the RNA:DNA heteroduplex is constrained by the TEN domain across repeated extension cycles, and TEN advances the template one base at a time via translation and rotation of the double helix.

Explains the reuse mechanism: the RNA region after the template pairs with newly synthesized telomeric DNA, the template returns to the active site for the next cycle, and the model offers a detailed mechanistic picture for drug design.
Concluding sentence stating that the first structural model of human telomerase is an important target for rational drug design.

Introduction to the Look AHEAD trial: explains that overweight/obesity drive type 2 diabetes and CVD, that obese diabetics face high CVD risk, and that long-term effects of intentional weight loss in this population were previously unexamined.
States the trial's primary objective: assessing long-term effects (up to 11.5 years) of a 4-year intensive weight loss program in overweight/obese adults with type 2 diabetes.

Study population and design: about 5000 adults with type 2 diabetes aged 45-74 with BMI >=25 kg/m2, randomized to an intensive lifestyle intervention designed for weight loss via reduced calories and increased physical activity.

Describes the comparison arm (diabetes support and education), the primary outcome (time to first major CVD event), and the power calculation (0.90 probability of detecting an 18% difference in event rates).
Lists secondary outcomes: CVD risk components, cost and cost-effectiveness, diabetes control and complications, hospitalizations, intervention processes, and quality of life.
Introduction and study design of a Women's Health Initiative analysis linking dietary fat intake to leukocyte telomere length (a marker of biological aging) in 4029 postmenopausal women.

Methods and definition of the key exposure: questionnaire-assessed fat intake and telomere length measured by qPCR, with short-to-medium-chain saturated fatty acids (aliphatic tails of 12 carbons or fewer) found to be inversely associated with TL.

Quartile results for SMSFA intake: highest-intake women had shorter telomeres than the lowest-intake group (4.00 kb vs 4.13 kb, P-trend = 0.046), with lauric acid being the notable exception among individual SMSFAs.

Isoenergetic substitution finding: replacing 1% of energy from SMSFAs with other energy sources linked to about 119 bp longer telomeres, plus food-level results showing nonskim milk, butter, and whole-milk cheese (major SMSFA sources) inversely associated with TL.

Null associations for long-chain saturated, monounsaturated, and polyunsaturated fatty acids, followed by the conclusion that SMSFA and SMSFA-rich food intake are associated with shorter leukocyte telomeres in postmenopausal women.
Concluding statement that the findings suggest SMSFAs may play a role in the rate of biological aging.

Opening of the review introducing telomere science and its link between stress, aging, and telomere length across the lifespan, setting up the paper's overall focus on stress-related telomere erosion.

Continues the introduction: stress may accelerate telomere erosion early in life and even affect newborn telomere length, and the review previews its focus on stress and mental illness linked to telomere erosion.

Outlines the review's structure: prenatal stress and developmental programming of telomere length, childhood trauma and mental disorders with telomere shortening, and health-risk behaviors that may buffer stress effects.

Concludes the introduction by previewing the review's final topic (health-risk behaviors and telomere shortening) and stating its broader aim of clarifying telomere mechanisms to understand stress and mental illness effects on aging.
Closing statement of the abstract: understanding telomere biology across the lifespan may clarify the etiology and long-term aging consequences of stress and mental illness in diverse populations.

Background on telomere length as a marker of accelerated aging and chronic stress, and prior research linking other-focused behaviors (volunteering, caregiving) to health and longevity; introduces the Loving-Kindness Meditation study rationale.

Describes the study design: Loving-Kindness Meditation (a Buddhist-derived practice of unselfish kindness toward all people) practitioners compared with non-meditating controls on relative telomere length.

Methods: blood collected by venipuncture, genomic DNA extracted from leukocytes, and relative telomere length measured by quantitative real-time PCR in 15 LKM practitioners and 22 controls; notes no group differences in demographics or trauma.

Results: control group had higher BMI and lower past depression rates; LKM practitioners showed a trend toward longer telomeres overall (p=.083), and women practitioners had significantly longer telomeres (p=.007), robust to BMI and depression adjustment.

Conclusion and limitations: small sample size means results are tentative, but suggest LKM practice, especially in women, may alter telomere length, a longevity-related biomarker; includes copyright notice.
Trailing copyright notice (Elsevier, 2013) ending the abstract; contains no substantive content beyond the final fragment of the copyright statement.

Opening of the document: introduces cellular senescence as an in vivo and in vitro phenomenon and states the review's goal of testing whether whole-organism aging and cell senescence share a common initiation pathway, citing high INK4A-p16 expression in aged T lymphocytes.

Describes the telomere-shortening mechanism in culture: the Arf/Ink system (p16/p14 in humans, p16/p19 in mice) switches on and activates p53, which halts cell division; also notes p53 as a key tumor suppressor whose loss permits cancer.

Explains how p53 activation alters fatty acid metabolism, down-regulating fatty acid synthase and stearoyl-CoA (delta-9) desaturase, and how this co-suppression plus increased uptake of extracellular fatty acids raises cellular palmitate.

Covers the downstream consequences: elevated palmitate triggers apoptosis or senescence, senescent cells show altered membrane fatty acid composition that disrupts organelle structure and function (especially mitochondria), and accelerated-aging animal models show repressed stearoyl-CoA desaturase.

Gives the conclusions: calorie restriction, an anti-aging intervention, stimulates stearoyl-CoA desaturase; the authors conclude cell and organism aging share a common initiation pathway, senescence protects against cancer, and longevity is enhanced by suppressing excessive cell division.
Final sentence of the abstract, restating the conclusion that healthy longevity is best promoted by factors that actively suppress excessive cell division.
Introduction and objective of the study: links estrogen to telomere maintenance in women, and states the aim to examine habitual exercise and PBMC telomere length in postmenopausal women.

Study rationale and design: explains why postmenopausal (estrogen-deficient) women were chosen, then describes the cross-sectional experimental-control study of 44 healthy, nonsmoking, nondiabetic postmenopausal women.
Methods: participant matching by age and BMI, anthropometric and biochemical measurements, and measurement of mitochondrial DNA copy number and PBMC telomere length.

Exercise definition and baseline results: habitual exercise is defined as combined aerobic and resistance training for 60+ minutes, over three times weekly, for over 12 months; reports participant age and average duration of exercise.

Results comparing groups: habitual exercisers had significantly lower triglycerides, fasting insulin, and HOMA-IR, and higher HDL, adiponectin, mtDNA copy number, and telomere length than sedentary controls.
Regression findings: stepwise multiple regression identifies habitual exercise (β = 0.522) and adiponectin (β = 0.139) as independent factors associated with PBMC telomere length.
Conclusions: habitual physical exercise is associated with greater telomere length in postmenopausal women, suggesting it may reduce telomere attrition.
Final fragment of the document, closing the conclusion sentence about reduced telomere attrition.
Introduction/purpose statement of a review on telomeres, lifestyle factors, cancer, and aging; sets up the link between lifestyle, telomere length, and health and longevity.

Continues the purpose and recent findings: telomere length, shaped by lifestyle, influences the pace of aging and onset of age-associated diseases; begins the summary on telomere shortening with age and its cellular consequences.

Summary on cellular effects of telomere shortening (senescence, apoptosis, oncogenic transformation) and associations with disease incidence and poor survival; notes lifestyle can speed or slow shortening.
Concluding summary recommending diet and activity choices to slow telomere attrition, delaying age-associated disease and extending lifespan, and stating the review's scope.
Final fragment of the document's concluding sentence stating the review covers telomeres in aging and the lifestyle factors affecting telomeres, health, and aging.

Introduction and methods of a pilot study on yogic meditation (Kirtan Kriya) versus relaxation music for family dementia caregivers with depressive symptoms, outlining the 8-week, 12-minute daily intervention and outcome measures including telomerase activity.

Methods continued: the 8-week daily intervention and assessment of depressive symptoms, mental and cognitive functioning at baseline and follow-up, and telomerase activity in peripheral blood mononuclear cells measured pre- and post-intervention.

Results section comparing the meditation and relaxation groups, reporting greater reductions in depressive symptoms and improvements in mental health and cognitive functioning in the meditation group, with Hamilton Depression Rating scale and SF-36 MCS response rates.

Specific results comparing response rates on the Hamilton Depression Rating scale and SF-36 Mental Health Composite Summary between groups, plus the telomerase activity improvement in the meditation group (43%) versus relaxation group (3.7%).

Conclusion of the pilot study: brief daily meditation by dementia caregivers improved mental and cognitive functioning and reduced depressive symptoms, with increased telomerase activity suggesting reduced stress-related cellular aging, and a call for confirmation in larger samples.
Final sentence of the conclusion stating that the results need to be confirmed in a larger sample, a limitation of the pilot study on yogic meditation for dementia caregivers.

Abstract opening of a cross-sectional study on diet and leukocyte telomere length (LTL) in elderly adults: states the background and hypotheses that fruit and vegetable intake would be positively and fat/saturated fat intake negatively associated with LTL.

Abstract methods section: LTL measured by quantitative real-time PCR in 1942 men and women aged 57-70 from the Helsinki Birth Cohort Study, with whole-diet intake assessed by a validated 128-item semiquantitative food-frequency questionnaire.

Abstract results section: few significant findings overall; in men, total fat and saturated fatty acid intake were inversely associated with LTL after adjusting for age and energy, while in women vegetable intake was positively associated with LTL.

Abstract results continued: men with highest butter intake and lowest fruit intake had shorter telomeres; no associations found between LTL and BMI, waist-hip ratio, smoking, physical activity, or education.

Abstract conclusions: diet had only a few statistically significant effects on LTL in this elderly cohort, but overall findings partly support the hypothesis that fat and vegetable intakes relate to telomere length.

Introduction-style opening of a study on Alzheimer's disease caregivers: chronic stress linked to declining immune function, and the study design comparing 41 caregivers with 41 matched controls on depression, immune cells, and telomere measures.

Results on psychological and immune changes in caregivers: higher depressive symptoms (p < 0.001), reduced T cell proliferation, and elevated TNF-α and IL-10 production in response to in vitro stimulation.
Telomere findings: caregivers showed shorter PBMC telomeres (6.2 vs 6.4 kb, p < 0.05), with similar shortening in isolated T cells and monocytes, indicating accelerated replicative aging.

Mechanistic and telomerase results: telomere attrition was not explained by more short-telomere T cell subsets, and basal telomerase activity was higher in caregivers (p < 0.0001), likely a failed compensatory response to telomere loss.
Conclusion: chronic caregiving stress is associated with altered T cell function and accelerated immune cell aging, as evidenced by excessive telomere loss.

Introduction and background: motivates the study by framing childhood stress, via telomere erosion, as a possible mechanism linking early adversity to later disease and mortality, and introduces children's violence exposure as the focal stressor.

Study rationale and aim: describes violence exposure as a major public-health problem and states the paper's novelty, a first prospective study with repeated child telomere measures, testing whether violence accelerates telomere erosion.

Methods: defines the three violence measures (maternal domestic violence, frequent bullying, physical maltreatment by an adult) and describes the sample of 236 children from the Environmental-Risk Longitudinal Twin Study birth cohort.

Methods: telomere measurement: explains that relative telomere length was assessed in baseline and follow-up DNA samples with qPCR, expressed as the T/S ratio of telomere repeat to single-copy gene copy numbers.

Results: reports the main finding that children with two or more violence exposures had significantly greater telomere shortening from age 5 to 10 after adjusting for sex, SES and BMI, with the regression coefficient and P-value.
Conclusion: interprets the results as support for a mechanism linking cumulative childhood stress to telomere maintenance seen early in life, with implications for lifelong health.

Introduction of a study on chronic stress and cellular aging: it frames stress-related poor health (cardiovascular risk, immune function) and the hypothesis that stress accelerates cellular aging, the rate of which is the focus of the investigation.

Key findings: psychological stress (perceived stress and chronicity) is associated with higher oxidative stress, lower telomerase activity, and shorter telomeres in peripheral blood mononuclear cells of healthy premenopausal women, markers tied to cell senescence and longevity.

Main quantitative result and implication: high perceived stress is linked to telomeres shorter by roughly a decade of aging compared with low-stress women, suggesting stress may hasten age-related disease onset at the cellular level.
Closing fragment of the abstract's final sentence, concluding that stress may promote earlier onset of age-related diseases.

Context: Abstract of a randomized controlled trial (439 postmenopausal women, 12-month diet, exercise, diet+exercise, and control arms) on the effect of lifestyle interventions on leukocyte telomere length; this chunk covers the objective, study population, and intervention design.

Context: Continues the methods of the telomere length RCT in postmenopausal women, describing the group-based 10% weight-loss diet program, the 45-min, 5-days/week aerobic exercise regimen, fasting blood sampling at baseline and 12 months, and qPCR telomere measurement with GEE intention-to-treat analysis.

Context: Results section of the postmenopausal women telomere study, reporting baseline correlations of telomere length with age and VO2max (but not BMI or body fat) and beginning the report of change-in-telomere correlations.
