Context: Results and conclusion of the postmenopausal women telomere RCT, reporting an inverse correlation between telomere change and baseline length, no intervention-group difference versus controls, no association of weight loss magnitude with telomere length, and the beginning of the conclusion.
Context: Final conclusion sentence of the postmenopausal women telomere RCT, stating that 12 months of dietary weight loss and exercise did not change leukocyte telomere length.

Introduction and study design: measuring telomere length (TRF analysis) in peripheral blood lymphocytes of 56 subjects with dietary data, compared against nucleoplasmic bridge (chromosomal instability) incidence in the cytokinesis-blocked micronucleus assay.
Methods continued: NPB measurement via the cytokinesis-blocked micronucleus assay, and the added step of irradiating cells in vitro to detect slight telomere dysfunction.
Methods on confounders and first main result: age, hTERT genotype and smoking were controlled for, and higher vegetable consumption is introduced as associated with longer mean telomere length.

Key results on diet: vegetable intake is linked to higher mean TL (P = 0.013), and antioxidants, especially beta-carotene, are tied to telomere maintenance (P = 0.004). The transition sentence notes diet-related shortening did not raise NPB levels.

Key results on NPBs and short telomeres: no increase in spontaneous or radiation-induced NPBs; a slight link between radiation-induced NPBs and very short TRFs (<2 kb), and very short TRFs rise with age (P = 0.008).
Conclusion: very short TRF levels are unrelated to diet, so the telomere erosion linked to low antioxidant intake was not severe enough to cause chromosome instability.

Introduction and background of a study on physical exercise, telomere erosion, aging, and vascular protection, stating the aims: examining exercise effects on vascular telomere biology and endothelial apoptosis in mice, and long-term endurance training effects on telomere biology in humans.

Methods and early results from the mouse experiment: C57/Bl6 mice given voluntary running wheels or none for 3 weeks, with exercise increasing aortic and circulating mononuclear cell telomerase activity and vascular TRF2 and Ku70 expression.
Mouse results showing exercise reduced vascular apoptosis regulators (CHK2, p16, p53) and markedly reduced LPS-induced aortic endothelial apoptosis in running-preconditioned mice.

Transgenic mouse evidence that eNOS and TERT synergize to confer endothelial stress resistance after activity, followed by the human arm: telomere biology in circulating leukocytes of young and middle-aged track and field athletes.

Human findings: endurance athletes' peripheral blood leukocytes show higher telomerase activity, telomere-stabilizing protein expression, and lower cell-cycle inhibitors than untrained people, and long-term endurance training is linked to less leukocyte telomere erosion.
Conclusion summarizing that physical activity regulates telomere-stabilizing proteins in both mice and humans, thereby protecting against stress-induced vascular apoptosis.

Introduction of a case series of three Alzheimer's disease patients with severe behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) whose symptoms improved with turmeric, a traditional Indian medicine; lists initial symptoms such as irritability, agitation, anxiety, and apathy.

Describes the intervention, turmeric powder capsules, and reports symptom recovery without adverse reactions; also notes urinary incontinence and wandering in two patients and a significant drop in Neuro-Psychiatric Inventory-brief scores after 12 weeks.

Reports outcomes: Neuro-Psychiatric Inventory-brief reduction in symptom severity and caregiver burden; one patient's MMSE rose from 12/30 to 17/30, while the other two showed no MMSE change but recognized family members within one year.
Describes long-term follow-up: patients taking turmeric for over a year without BPSD relapse, and the authors' conclusion that turmeric may significantly improve behavioral symptoms in AD with BPSD.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that turmeric may benefit individuals with Alzheimer's disease and BPSD.

Introduction to a study of oral curcumin for Alzheimer's disease: background on curcumin's antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and beta-amyloid effects, its benefits in transgenic AD models, and the study's aim of assessing tolerability and preliminary efficacy.

Methods of the 24-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled curcumin (Curcumin C3 Complex) trial with a 48-week open-label extension, describing enrollment of 36 mild-to-moderate AD patients randomized to placebo, 2 g/day, or 4 g/day.

Continuation of the methods: the dosing schedule for weeks 24-48 (curcumin groups keep their dose, placebo group re-randomized 1:1 to 2 or 4 g/day) and the primary outcomes of adverse events, lab changes, and ADAS-Cog at 24 weeks.
Remaining methods detailing the secondary outcome measures, including NPI, ADCS-ADL, plasma and CSF amyloid-beta and tau biomarkers, and F2-isoprostanes.
Final methods on plasma curcumin metabolite pharmacokinetics, followed by the start of the Results: completer demographics (mean age 73.5, mean MMSE 22.5, n=30).

Results on dropouts (1 placebo, 5 curcumin, 3 of those for gastrointestinal symptoms) and safety findings, including clinically insignificant decreases in hematocrit and increases in glucose, plus the absence of group differences in efficacy.
Results on low plasma native curcumin levels (7.32 ng/mL) and the Conclusions stating curcumin was generally well tolerated but showed no clinical or biochemical efficacy.
Final conclusion that Curcumin C3 Complex showed no demonstrated efficacy in AD, with suggestions of limited bioavailability, followed by the trial registration number NCT00099710.
Trailing fragment of the trial registration number NCT00099710, ending the ClinicalTrials.gov identifier at the end of the document.

Introduction of a study on curcuminoids and Alzheimer's disease: describes AD patients' defective macrophage phagocytosis of amyloid-beta and the rationale for treating patient macrophages with curcuminoids in vitro.

Methods and baseline results: curcuminoid-treated macrophages from six AD patients and three controls were assessed by fluorescence and confocal microscopy, showing that untreated AD macrophages had lower Abeta uptake, with surface binding only and no intracellular uptake.

Key findings after curcuminoid treatment: Abeta uptake increased significantly in three of six AD patients' macrophages, and confocal imaging showed a shift from surface binding to intracellular co-localization with phalloidin in responsive cells.
Conclusion of the abstract: the authors suggest curcuminoid-mediated immunomodulation of the innate immune system may be a safe strategy for immune clearance of amyloid in the Alzheimer's brain.

Introduces curcumin (from turmeric in curry) as an antioxidant/anti-inflammatory compound with experimental evidence against beta-amyloid, noting the lack of epidemiologic data, and states the study aim: relating curry consumption to cognition in elderly Asians.

Describes the study design: a population-based cohort of 1,010 nondemented elderly Asians aged 60-93 in 2003, comparing MMSE cognitive scores across three levels of regular curry intake while adjusting for sociodemographic, health, and behavioral confounders.

Reports the main result: occasional and often/very often curry consumers scored significantly higher on the MMSE than those who never or rarely ate curry, and the authors call this tentative evidence needing confirmation in future studies.
Closing fragment of the abstract's final sentence, restating that the curry-cognition findings are tentative and require confirmation in future research.

Study design and objectives: a 2-year prospective population-based study in rural Ballabgarh, India, measuring age-specific Alzheimer's disease incidence and comparing it with a US reference population in the Monongahela Valley, Pennsylvania.

Methods continued: repeated cognitive and functional screening of adults aged 55+, followed by standardized clinical diagnosis using DSM-IV and NINCDS-ADRDA criteria, with dementia and AD staged by the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scale.

Key results: AD incidence per 1000 person-years (CDR >= 0.5) was 3.24 for those aged 65+ and 1.74 for those aged 55+, with confidence intervals; age-standardized to the 1990 US Census, the 65+ overall rate was 4.7, far below the 17.5 in the Monongahela Valley.

Conclusion: these are the first AD incidence rates reported from the Indian subcontinent and appear among the lowest ever recorded, with the notably lower rate versus the US comparison population highlighted.
Caveats: the authors caution that the short follow-up, cultural factors, and other potential confounders limit how confidently the very low Indian incidence rates should be interpreted.

Abstract opening of a 2000 case-series report introducing curcumin (from Curcuma longa rhizomes) as a treatment for idiopathic inflammatory orbital pseudotumours, including the dosing regimen (375 mg three times daily for 6-22 months) in eight patients.

Middle of the abstract reporting outcomes: a 2-year follow-up at 3-month intervals, five of eight patients completing the study, four with complete recovery, one with complete resolution of swelling but persistent movement limitation, and no side effects or recurrences.
Concluding sentence of the abstract proposing curcumin as a safe and effective drug for idiopathic inflammatory orbital pseudotumours, followed by the 2000 John Wiley & Sons copyright notice.

Introduction of the review: lists curcumin's broad reported therapeutic properties over the past decade and introduces the question of whether it is also neuroprotective, tested in vertebrate and invertebrate models.

Rationale for curcumin as a neurodegeneration candidate: pre-clinical efficacy and low toxicity/cost make it a nutraceutical candidate, and aging as a shared risk factor motivates testing aging-targeting compounds against neurodegenerative disease.
Proposed mechanism: curcumin may explain its general health benefits by preventing aging-associated changes in cellular proteins that cause insolubility and aggregation.
Protein homeostasis link: loss of protein homeostasis underlies several age-related diseases, and curcumin was recently shown to maintain it and extend lifespan in C. elegans.
Review aim and conclusion: the authors survey evidence from multiple animal models that curcumin improves healthspan by preventing or delaying onset of neurodegenerative diseases.

Opens the review on whether very preterm birth raises adult cardiometabolic risk: modern-care survivors are in their thirties, and older pre-modern-care cohorts show higher type 2 diabetes risk; this chunk introduces emerging cardiovascular risk evidence in young adult cohorts.

Details the young-adult cardiovascular risk factors in former very small or very preterm infants (higher blood pressure, lower lean mass, impaired glucose regulation, possibly atherogenic lipids) and the lifestyle differences (less physical activity, lower fruit and milk intake).

Concludes that blood pressure and physical inactivity are key modifiable targets with large lifetime disease-burden reduction potential, and argues enough data now exist to justify an expert evaluation of cardiometabolic evidence in this population.

Closing statement that an expert evidence review is warranted for cardiometabolic disease in very small or very preterm-born individuals, with public health implications, followed by the 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.
Introduction and methods opening of a study on garlic/allium and dried fruit intake, antimicrobial and prebiotic foods, and risk of spontaneous preterm delivery (PTD) in the Norwegian MoBa cohort.
Methods describing identification of alliums and dried fruits as antimicrobial, prebiotic-fiber foods, and the MoBa cohort sample of 18,888 women with 950 spontaneous PTD cases (<37 weeks).
Main results: alliums and dried fruits each associated with decreased spontaneous PTD risk (OR 0.82), with alliums showing a stronger reduction for early PTD at weeks 28–31 (OR 0.39).
Subgroup results: garlic was the strongest allium association for early PTD (OR 0.47), and dried fruit intake was associated with lower risk of preterm prelabor rupture of membranes (PPROM, OR 0.74).

Specific PPROM findings: raisins were the strongest dried fruit association with PPROM (OR 0.71), garlic the strongest allium association with PPROM (OR 0.74), followed by the study's conclusion on antimicrobial and prebiotic foods.
Conclusion: garlic is linked to overall lower spontaneous PTD risk, and dried fruits, especially raisins, to reduced PPROM risk, suggesting dietary intake may help prevent preterm delivery.

Introduces late preterm (LP) birth (34-36 weeks gestation), its share of preterm births, and the medical risks from immature fetal development; opens the question of which risk factors are most critical.

Notes that LP birth's effects on brain development and later childhood/adolescent neuropsychological functioning have been understudied, and cites early evidence of a graded outcome: LP children fare better than very preterm but worse than term children.

Describes the subtle intellectual and neuropsychological deficits found in LP children compared with term-born peers and calls for prospective longitudinal studies to characterize their neuropsychological profile.

Argues that moderate and LP births have distinct medical and psychological outcomes, so pooling them into one research cohort should be reconsidered; introduces the idea of fetal development as a continuum.
Concludes with the principle that fetal development is a dynamic maturational continuum from conception to birth, where each additional gestational day likely improves outcome.

Introduction to a review of lifespan mental health outcomes in individuals born extremely preterm, noting continuity of risk for inattention, socio-communicative problems, and emotional difficulties from preschool through adulthood.

Summary of evidence that behavioural and neuroimaging studies support a neurodevelopmental origin for mental health disorders after extremely preterm birth, and the paper's aim to summarise contemporary evidence and methodological considerations.
Closing statement of the abstract on methodological considerations for studies of extremely preterm birth and mental health, followed by the 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.

Opening of the garlic (Allium sativum) antimicrobial review: introduces garlic's long medicinal history, its broad activities (antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal, antiprotozoal, cardiovascular and immune effects), and the renewed interest in herbal alternatives.

Closing section of the introduction: notes that medicinal plants are driving new drug discovery and states the review's aims, namely covering garlic's historical use and sulfur chemistry and laying groundwork for antimicrobial research.
Final sentence of the document's introduction, ending the statement of the review's aim to provide a basis for further research into garlic's antimicrobial properties.
Introduction and scope of a review of recent literature on behaviour problems in preterm-born infants and preschool children, covering 14 cohort studies (2000-2012) and the risk factors examined.

Review methods and findings on risk factors (perinatal, social, relational) for behaviour problems in preterm children aged 0-2 and 3-5 years, with relational factors examined in four additional papers.

Key findings: very-preterm, very-low-birthweight, and moderately-preterm children show more behaviour problems than term-born peers after controlling for confounders, with social/interactive, self-regulation, emotional, and attention problems most common.

Conclusion that infant behaviour problems predict later problems, supporting their inclusion in follow-up programmes, plus the journal copyright notice (Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology, 2013).

This chunk opens the document's abstract, stating the objective (link between maternal dietary patterns and preterm delivery), the design (prospective cohort in Norway, 2002–2008), and the participant eligibility criteria.

This chunk continues the Participants criteria and introduces the main outcome measure: hazard ratios for preterm delivery by adherence to the three dietary patterns (prudent, Western, traditional) and their food components.

This chunk presents the key results: after covariate adjustment, the highest versus lowest tertile of the prudent pattern showed reduced preterm delivery risk (HR 0.88), and the Western pattern showed no independent association.

This chunk reports further results: the prudent pattern's link to late and spontaneous preterm delivery, no independent Western pattern association, and the start of the traditional pattern's result (reduced risk).
This chunk gives the traditional pattern's hazard ratio (0.91) and the Conclusion, that prudent and traditional patterns are linked to lower preterm risk and support for dietary advice.

This chunk concludes the document with the caveat that causality cannot be established, recommendations for a balanced diet with vegetables, fruit, whole grains, fish and water, and the claim that increasing prudent foods matters more than excluding junk food.
This final chunk is a fragment of the closing sentence, ending the document's discussion on avoiding processed food, fast food, junk food, and snacks.
Introduces the FDA's termination of Mississippi ball clay as animal feed additive after finding nanogram-per-gram 2,3,7,8-TCDD, and its sampling of eggs and catfish nationwide.
Describes the QISTMS analytical method and sample counts (42 catfish, 3 tilapia, 46 chicken eggs, 6 feeds), and the number of samples exceeding 1.0 pg/g.

Reports the threshold exceedances (6 catfish composites, 20 eggs), the 0.12 pg/g mean for catfish without ball clay feed, and isomer pattern comparisons showing ball clay differs from fly ash and 1950s reference toxic fat.
Completes the comparison, noting the ball clay TCDD isomer pattern differs from the 'chick edema factor' pattern of a 1950s reference toxic fat feed ingredient.

Introduces the study of PCDD/PCDF contamination in a combined catfish feed sample from Arkansas, USA, and its eight ingredients, highlighting soybean meal as highly contaminated with toxic 2,3,7,8-substituted PCDDs and giving its concentrations and I-TEQ values.

Compares the combined catfish feed's contamination levels (about three times lower than soybean meal) and describes the unique congener pattern and sigma PCDDs/sigma PCDFs ratio of the soybean meal, with no similar environmental or technical samples known.
Concludes that the unusual PCDD profile in the soybean meal may be due to natural formation, which cannot be ruled out, closing the discussion of the catfish feed contamination findings.

Introduces the study's motivation and method: first congener-specific dioxin analyses of U.S. food (dairy, meat, fish, 18 samples from upstate New York), since food is the main human source of PCDDs/PCDFs.
Reports TCDD toxic equivalent (TEq) concentrations in U.S. dairy, meat, and fish samples on a wet-weight basis, with the observed ranges for each food category.

Describes the estimation approach combining food data with prior breast milk and infant formula analyses to estimate adult daily dioxin intake (0.3-3.0 pg/kg, 18-192 pg TEq for a 65 kg adult, using 1986 consumption rates).
Estimates infant exposure via breast milk, about 35-53 pg TEq/kg/day in the first year, and begins comparing it with regulatory safety benchmarks.
Gives the regulatory comparison: the U.S. EPA virtually safe dose (0.006 pg TCDD/kg/day, 10^-6 cancer risk) versus the 10 pg/kg/day limit used by some European agencies.

Introduces the USDA Pesticide Data Program and the 2008-2010 catfish sampling (1479 samples), with a 202-sample subset analysed for 17 toxic PCDD/Fs, the study's starting point on dioxin contamination in US catfish.
Describes the key finding that catfish show a distinctive PCDD/F pattern with almost no PCDFs but all PCDDs present, more prominent in domestic than imported (China/Taiwan) products.
Links the catfish dioxin pattern to kaolin clays used as anti-caking agents in animal feed, and states the study's aim of testing whether catfish feed is the contamination source.
Reports the archived USFDA feed data analysis: in 61 of 112 feed samples PCDDs exceeded PCDFs by 50-fold, matching the catfish pattern and south-eastern US mined clays.

Concludes that mined clays used in feed are a likely PCDD/F source, though not definitively proven, and that their wide concentration range makes them a critical control point for food-supply contamination.
Final sentence of the conclusion, stating that clays are a critical control point for PCDD/F entry into the food supply, given their wide contamination range.
Opening chunk of a study on PCDD, PCDF, and PCB contamination in farm-raised catfish from the southeastern US; introduces the sample set and reports 2,3,7,8-substituted dioxin/furan findings.
Middle chunk of the catfish contamination study covering dioxin-like PCB levels in fillets and nuggets and the TEQ ranges (pg/g lipid) for PCDD/PCDF and PCB across catfish samples.

Chunk from the catfish dioxin/PCB study discussing the percentage contribution of dioxin-like PCB to total TEQ, the feed-versus-sediment source conclusion, and elevated CYP1A protein in pond-raised fish.
Final sentence of the catfish PCDD/PCDF/PCB study, concluding that PCDD/PCDF play a greater role than PCB in CYP1A induction.

Introduces dioxins as unintended food contaminants where diet is the main exposure route, and argues that reducing intake among pregnant women, infants, and young girls lowers body burdens in future generations.
Gives practical dietary guidance for cutting dioxin exposure: choose lower-fat meats, poultry, and dairy, while still eating all foods, including fatty fish, in recommended amounts for good health.
Introduces the study's setup: PCDD/PCDF dioxin levels measured in edible chicken tissues and abdominal fat, reported on both whole-weight and lipid-adjusted bases.

Presents the key finding: whole-weight dioxin concentrations differ markedly across edible tissues, but lipid-adjusted concentrations do not differ significantly, supporting the use of abdominal fat as a proxy.
Concludes that lipid-adjusted 2,3,7,8-PCDD/PCDF levels in abdominal fat validly indicate the presence of these compounds in other chicken tissues.

Opening of a 1994 study of PCDD/PCDF dioxin contamination in 43 supermarket food samples from southern Mississippi, USA, reporting I-TEQ levels in meat and dairy relative to other industrialized countries.

Continuation comparing Mississippi dairy samples with German and European milk, noting differences in congener contributions to I-TEQ (e.g., 2,3,4,7,8-Cl5DF share of 40% in Germany vs 16% in Mississippi), and introducing the highest-level finding in farm-raised catfish.

Presents the catfish results (10.2-27.8 pg I-TEQ/g, the highest in the study) and the unusual presence of many non-2,3,7,8-substituted congeners in catfish, which conflicts with typical vertebrate selective elimination.
Concluding sentence of the abstract-style summary, stating that vertebrates normally eliminate or metabolize non-2,3,7,8-substituted PCDD/PCDF congeners, which makes the catfish finding unusual.

Abstract of a meta-analysis on dietary cholesterol's effect on serum cholesterol; introduces the methodological novelty of modeling baseline and added dietary cholesterol together, and describes the data set (27 studies, 76 data points from metabolic kitchen controlled diets).

Presents the statistical results and fitted nonlinear equation relating change in serum cholesterol to added and baseline dietary cholesterol, including fit statistics (P < 0.0005, r = 0.617) and variable definitions.

Concludes the abstract by noting the discussion topics: the hyperbolic shape of the dose-response relationship, mechanisms behind individual variation in responsiveness to dietary cholesterol, and implications for prior studies and public health.
Final sentence of the abstract, closing the summary by stating that interpretation of prior studies and public health issues are discussed.

Study design and aim: a randomized crossover trial in 10 normolipidemic subjects testing five test meals (no fat/no cholesterol control, plus 45 g fat with 0, 140, 280, or 710 mg dietary cholesterol) and measuring postprandial plasma lipids and lipoproteins over 7 h.

Methods and measured outcomes: blood sampling over 7 hours after meals, and isolation of large and small triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (TRL), LDL and HDL. Fat-enriched meals are compared against the no-fat, no-cholesterol control meal.

Results on fat effects and dose response: fat-containing meals raised postprandial plasma triglycerides, phospholipids and free cholesterol while lowering cholesteryl esters. Meals with 0 or 140 mg cholesterol gave comparable responses, while 280 or 710 mg raised plasma phospholipids and large TRL triglycerides and lowered esterified cholesterol.

Lipoprotein-specific findings: large TRL lipid composition and small TRL lipid concentrations were unchanged by cholesterol. LDL free cholesterol rose at 3 h, and LDL cholesteryl esters fell at 3 and 7 h after high-cholesterol meals.

Further lipoprotein and biomarker findings: HDL cholesteryl esters fell at 3 h and HDL phospholipids rose at 7 h after cholesterol-rich meals. Insulin, apoA-I and apoB were not altered by dietary cholesterol.
Conclusion: the study's bottom line is that ingesting more than 140 mg dietary cholesterol per meal significantly changes the postprandial lipoprotein response in healthy people.

Background and rationale: introduces livestock-associated MRSA (LA-MRSA) in swine and contamination of pig-related workers, noting the lack of data on contamination rates among workers handling raw meat, such as butchers.

Study aim and setting: describes investigating MRSA contamination in 300 pork butchers working at wet markets in Hong Kong where freshly slaughtered pigs are cut up, plus the nasal swab collection method.
Methods: laboratory procedures for isolating and characterizing S. aureus (salt-enriched broth, MRSASelect culture, mecA confirmation, SCCmec and spa typing, PFGE) and a risk-factor questionnaire.

Results on prevalence and strain types: 17 of 300 butchers (5.6%) carried MRSA, mostly SCCmec IVb; 10 were livestock-linked t899 (CC9), and 5 were healthcare-associated strains including t701 found in two subjects at one establishment.

Remaining strain types and risk factors: t359 (CC97) from buffaloes and t375 (CC5) from bovine milk; no recent hospitalization or healthcare-worker contact; some recent antibiotic use, wound infections, and long daily meat exposure.
Conclusions: MRSA carriage was higher in butchers than the community; the predominance of t899 suggests frequent cross-contamination from pork, and handwashing after handling raw pork is recommended.
Copyright notice: attribution of the article to Blackwell Verlag GmbH, 2012, closing the abstract.

Background and rationale: links antibiotic use in US livestock feed and resulting manure containing resistant bacteria and resistance genes to community MRSA risk via crop field application, introducing the study objective on swine and dairy/veal agriculture exposure.

Study design and objective: a population-based nested case-control study of Geisinger primary care patients in Pennsylvania (2005–2010) that uses electronic health records to identify incident MRSA cases and controls.

Methods for case identification and exposure: MRSA cases classified as community- or healthcare-associated, frequency-matched controls and skin/soft tissue infection patients, with exposure variables (seasonal manure application and livestock numbers) derived from nutrient management plans.

Sub-study and outcome measures: 200 bacterial isolates collected and stratified by diagnosis location and livestock proximity, with outcomes defined as community-associated MRSA, healthcare-associated MRSA, and skin/soft tissue infection versus controls.

Study population and key counts: 446,480 patients including 1,539 community-associated MRSA, 1,335 healthcare-associated MRSA, 2,895 skin/soft tissue infection cases, and 2,914 controls, with adjusted results beginning for highest swine crop field exposure quartile.

Main quantitative findings: highest quartile of swine manure field exposure linked to higher odds of community-associated MRSA (aOR 1.38), healthcare-associated MRSA (aOR 1.30), and skin/soft tissue infection (aOR 1.37), with significant dose-response trends across quartiles.

Secondary findings and molecular results: weaker associations for swine operations with community MRSA and skin/soft tissue infection; genotyping of 200 isolates found 31 spa types, none matching CC398, though some previously found in swine.

Conclusion: proximity to swine manure application on crop fields and to livestock operations is associated with MRSA and skin/soft tissue infection, adding to concerns about public health impacts of high-density livestock production.
Opening of the document introducing MRSA, specifically livestock-associated ST398, as a reservoir in pig herds and the question of how it moves along the pork production chain.

Continues the introduction: MRSA prevalence in pig primary production and in pork products, and a review of livestock-associated MRSA across pork chain steps, identifying slaughter as decisive for farm-to-fork transmission.

Describes slaughter-stage findings: superficial heat treatments (scalding, flaming) reduce MRSA on carcasses, but recontamination can occur via machinery, fecal contamination at evisceration, and human handling.
Concluding recommendations: optimizing carcass decontamination and preventing recontamination through cleaning and personal hygiene can minimize MRSA transmission from pig to pork.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence restating that transmission of MRSA from pig to pork can be minimized.

Introduces the ESBL NDP (Nordmann/Dortet/Poirel) rapid biochemical test for detecting extended-spectrum β-lactamase producers in Enterobacteriaceae, motivated by the 24–48 h turnaround of conventional ESBL detection.
Describes the test's mechanism: cefotaxime hydrolysis by ESBLs turns the red phenol pH indicator from red to yellow, and this color change is reversed by tazobactam, which defines a positive result.

Reports the diagnostic performance on cultured strains (215 ESBL producers, 40 nonproducers): 92.6% sensitivity, 100% specificity, 100% sensitivity for CTX-M producers, and misses among cefotaxime-susceptible ESBL producers (n = 16).

Summarizes further evaluation on spiked blood cultures (100% sensitivity and specificity), the test's speed (under 1 h), low cost, and suitability for any health care facility and infection control use.
Closing fragment concluding that the test is well suited to infection control purposes, ending the document's summary of the ESBL NDP test.

Introduction of a 2013 Elsevier review on antibiotic resistance: frames it as a complex, globally shared problem driven by human behaviour, compares it to climate change, and notes the lack of coordinated political action.

Continues the introduction by stressing antibiotics' indispensability to modern health systems and medical advances (surgery, transplants, preterm care, chemotherapy), which depend on effective treatment of bacterial infections.

Warns that resistance could soon cause severe medical, social, and economic setbacks unless immediate, unprecedented global coordinated action is taken; this is the urgency argument of the review's introduction.
Closing of the introduction: states the review's aims (global situation, causes, consequences, and key areas needing urgent action), followed by the 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.

Findings from a study of 40 MRSA carriers showing that hand contamination after touching commonly examined skin sites (40%) was about as likely as after touching environmental surfaces in patient rooms (45%), suggesting contaminated surfaces are an important MRSA transmission source.

Introduces the study's background on MRSA (beta-lactam resistant, low levels in retail meat) and states its aims: estimating transfer from retail pork to food contact surfaces and human exposure risk.
Describes the experimental setup: pork loin, bacon, and fresh sausage inoculated with a four-strain MRSA mix at about 4-8 log, vacuum packaged, and stored 2 weeks at 5°C.
Explains the transfer methods: primary transfer via 5-minute contact with knife blades, cutting boards, and pork skin, and secondary transfer via product-to-surface-to-surface contact.
Reports primary transfer results: 39-49% to cutting boards, 17-42% to knives, with pork skin transfer also being discussed as a human skin model.
Gives the quantitative findings: 26-36% transfer to pork skin, 2.2-5.2% secondary transfer, and statistical analysis finding no significant differences across surfaces or concentrations.
Final fragment completing the statistical conclusion that transfer amounts did not differ significantly between surfaces or cell concentrations.

Study design and sample: a Southern California study of diet pattern and attained height in 1765 Caucasian children aged 7-18 from state and Seventh-day Adventist schools, using a food frequency questionnaire.

Diet difference between groups: Adventist and state school children differed mainly in meat consumption; Adventist children were spread across three meat-frequency categories, while 92% of state school children ate meat daily.

Vegetarian group and height reference: vegetarians (meat under once a week) differed in fruit and vegetable intake, all subgroups were at or above the NCHS 50th height percentile, and age-adjusted regression began comparing Adventist vegetarian and meat-eating children's height.

Main height result: Adventist vegetarian children were taller than meat-eating peers by 2.5 cm (boys) and 2.0 cm (girls) after age adjustment, and this held after adjusting for other food groups, parental height, and socioeconomic factors in a 518-child subsample.
Conclusion: vegetarian children and adolescents on a balanced diet grow at least as tall as children who eat meat, supporting the view that vegetarian diets do not impair attained height.

Introduction and methods of a long-term cohort study (Harvard Growth Study, 1922–1935) examining whether overweight in adolescence predicts later morbidity and mortality, defining the 508 adolescent subjects and overweight/lean criteria.

Methods section defining overweight adolescents (BMI above the 75th percentile on two occasions) versus lean adolescents (BMI between the 25th and 50th percentiles), using a large national survey as the reference population.

Methods on follow-up data collection: 1988 interviews with surviving subjects on medical history, weight, and risk factors, and death certificate data for those who died; also begins the results on all-cause mortality by sex.

Results reporting that adolescent overweight raised all-cause and disease-specific mortality in men but not women, with specific relative risks for all-cause mortality (1.8) and coronary heart disease mortality (2.3) among men, with confidence intervals and P values.

Results on morbidity outcomes: increased coronary heart disease and atherosclerosis in both sexes, colorectal cancer and gout in men, arthritis in women, and the finding that adolescent overweight predicted these risks better than adult overweight.
Conclusion stating that adolescent overweight predicted a broad range of adverse health effects independent of adult weight over 55 years of follow-up.

Introduction and objective of the technical report on T2DM management in children and adolescents, supporting the accompanying clinical practice guideline, motivated by rising childhood obesity in North America.

Continuation of the objective: the report explains the procedures and rationale behind the guideline's recommendations and the studies that informed them, then begins the Methods section describing the literature search.
Methods: the primary search (T2DM treatment) and secondary search (comorbidity screening and treatment) in children and adolescents, with inclusion criteria prospectively agreed by the committee.

Methods: article inclusion criteria, including topic, publication from 1990 onward, English language, and an abstract; only primary research or reviews with primary data or opinion were eligible, and the study population had to be children/adolescents with T2DM.

Methods continued: the adult-study exception (at least 10% under age 35), review of titles and abstracts by the consulting epidemiologist, and the start of the Results on the number of articles retrieved.
Results of the primary search: 199 abstracts screened, 58 retained for systematic review, with grade distribution of A (5), B (1), C (20), and D (32) studies.
Primary search results by subcategory: treatment studies grouped into medical (32), nonmedical (9), provider behavior (8), and social issues (9) categories.

Results of the secondary comorbidity search: 336 abstracts screened, 26 retained, with a breakdown of the article types included (systematic review, expert opinions, cohort studies, ethnic-group studies).
Secondary search results continued: counts of studies on microalbuminuria and retinopathy, and on nephropathy, by study design.
Secondary search results continued: counts of studies on peripheral vascular disease, retinopathy, and hyperlipidemia, including the AHA and ADA statements.
Grade of recommendation for comorbidity studies (no grade A, 10 B, 6 C, 10 D), and the conclusion that pediatric comorbidity data are scarce and conflicting.

Handling of comorbidity recommendations: hypertension, dyslipidemia, retinopathy, microalbuminuria, and depression recommendations were summarized from expert guideline documents, not independently assessed by the committee.
Closing note: references are provided for the comorbidity evidence, and screening tools are available in the Supplemental Information.

Opening of a pediatric office-practice review covering bullying, prediabetes screening, and pediatric oral health; this chunk introduces the purpose and begins the findings on bullying prevalence in young children and its links to psychosomatic and depressive symptoms.

Continues the findings on bullying: family therapy and school-based interventions are effective for bullies and victims. Then moves to prediabetes, noting recent work on glucose and insulin metabolism and new screening models to catch prediabetes early and prevent type 2 diabetes complications.

Covers the prediabetes screening rationale and the oral health findings: persistent gaps in dental care for the most at-risk patients, and the roles of diet and sealants in preventing dental caries. It also begins the summary section.

Summary stating that office-based pediatricians play a key role in identifying children involved in bullying, at risk for type 2 diabetes, or with poor dental health, and that future research will refine primary prevention and treatment guidelines.

Final sentence of the review's summary, closing the document by stating that future research will produce refined primary prevention and treatment guidelines for bullying, prediabetes, and dental health.

Study design and methods of a 2009 NICE-SUGAR-style randomized trial in ICU adults comparing intensive glucose control (81-108 mg/dL) with conventional control (≤180 mg/dL), with 90-day all-cause mortality as the primary endpoint.

Continuation of the methods, giving the conventional and intensive glucose targets in mg/dL and mmol/L, and the primary endpoint; then the start of results: 6104 randomized patients split into 3054 intensive and 3050 conventional arms.

Results on sample sizes and baseline comparability: primary outcome data at day 90 were available for 3010 intensive and 3012 conventional patients, and 27.5% versus 24.9% of patients died in each group.

Primary mortality result: odds ratio 1.14 (95% CI 1.02-1.28, P=0.02) favoring conventional control, plus subgroup results showing no significant difference in treatment effect between surgical and medical patients (OR 1.31 vs 1.07, P=0.10).

Safety outcome: severe hypoglycemia (≤40 mg/dL) occurred in 6.8% of intensive-control patients versus 0.5% of conventional-control patients (P<0.001), and secondary outcomes (ICU/hospital stay, ventilation, renal replacement days) showed no significant differences.

Secondary outcomes showing no significant difference in ICU or hospital length of stay, mechanical ventilation, or renal-replacement therapy days, followed by the conclusion that intensive glucose control increased mortality in ICU adults.

Final conclusion of the NICE-SUGAR trial: a looser glucose target (≤180 mg/dL) gave lower mortality than tight control (81-108 mg/dL) in critically ill adults; includes the ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT00220987 and the 2009 NEJM copyright notice.

Abstract opening of a review of epidemiologic evidence on plant foods and plant-based diets for preventing childhood obesity; introduces the finding that ready-to-eat cereal is protective while noting prospective studies are still needed.

Summarizes that evidence for fruit and vegetables, non-cereal grains, high-protein plant foods (beans, legumes, soy), fiber, and plant-based dietary patterns is inconsistent or null, and lists the limitations of the studies (cross-sectional designs, poor confounder adjustment, reporting errors, growth stage, genetics).

Concludes that calls for well-designed prospective studies, argues that the lack of an observed association does not mean plant-based diets should be discouraged, and notes that Dietary Guidelines for Americans emphasize plant foods that children currently under-consume.
Argues that advising a plant-based, low-energy-dense diet is sound, but raises ethical concerns about the high cost of such diets in the United States and how they are perceived in other countries.

Closing call to action: reducing childhood obesity and health disparities globally requires policies making plant foods affordable and accessible across income levels, along with attention to sociocultural norms shaping consumption.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the point that addressing sociocultural norms affecting food consumption is needed alongside affordability and access policies.
Opening chunk of the document introducing prediabetes as a high-risk state, defining it by intermediate glycaemic values, and giving conversion rates to diabetes and projected prevalence by 2030.

Middle chunk describing the underlying pathophysiology of prediabetes (insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction preceding detectable glucose changes) and its observational associations with kidney, nerve, eye, and macrovascular complications.

Chunk covering the complication associations of prediabetes and the proposal that multifactorial risk scores using non-invasive and blood-based metabolic markers can improve diabetes risk estimation, followed by the start of the prevention discussion.
Final chunk on prevention strategies for prediabetes: lifestyle modification as the cornerstone with a 40%-70% relative risk reduction, and emerging evidence for pharmacotherapy.
Opening of a document on type 2 diabetes in children and adolescents. Covers rising global prevalence across ethnicities and introduces the ethnic subgroups most affected.

Continues the ethnic-subgroup list (African-American, Hispanic, Asian/Pacific Islander, American Indian) and notes mild or asymptomatic childhood presentation. Introduces screening for high-risk youth with obesity.

Describes high-risk screening criteria (obesity, family history, insulin resistance features such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, PCOS, acanthosis nigricans). States the treatment approach: lifestyle intervention, then metformin, and mentions new drugs in development (DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 mimetics).
Notes the pipeline of newer drugs for youth and reports high dropout from medical care among adolescents with type 2 diabetes. Suggests this points to a need for changes in care delivery.
Concluding statement that management of youth with type 2 diabetes requires restructuring current healthcare practices to address the dropout problem.

Introduction of a review on prediabetes and type 2 diabetes in youth: opens by describing the alarming rise of childhood obesity in the US, disproportionately affecting African-American and Hispanic children, and its early metabolic and cardiovascular complications linked to insulin resistance that persist into adulthood.

Recent findings section defining the stages of diabetes progression: from normal glucose tolerance through an intermediate prediabetes (impaired glucose regulation) stage, which is marked by peripheral insulin resistance.

Continuation of the recent findings: contrasts prediabetes (impaired first-phase insulin secretion) with overt type 2 diabetes (full beta-cell failure), and describes how youth progression from prediabetes to diabetes involves weight gain and worsening insulin secretion and resistance.

Summary and conclusion of the review: recommends lifestyle modification (nutrition education, behavior modification, exercise) to reverse obesity as a key step in preventing progression from prediabetes to diabetes in youth.

Introduction to childhood obesity-driven type 2 diabetes: notes the shift from type 1a predominance in youth to a rising incidence of T2DM linked to obesity, insulin resistance, and relative insulin deficiency.

Describes early-onset microvascular and macrovascular complications in children and adolescents with T2DM, including cardiovascular disease, stroke, renal failure, neuropathy, vasculopathy, and retinopathy.
Concludes with clinical guidance for health care professionals: screen at-risk children for T2DM, diagnose early, and provide rigorous management.
Final sentence of the document, restating the recommendation to diagnose T2DM early and manage it rigorously in children.

Introduction of the article: rising childhood overweight/obesity in developing urban areas, motivating a search for food patterns that prevent obesity, since weight-loss interventions often fail long term.

Stated aim of the review: examining the link between vegetarian diets and obesity, with a focus on childhood obesity, and noting epidemiologic evidence of lower BMI and obesity prevalence in vegetarians.
Meta-analysis evidence: adult vegetarians weigh about 7.6 kg less (men) and 3.3 kg less (women), a 2-point lower BMI; vegetarian children are leaner, with the BMI gap widening in adolescence.

Conclusion that plant-based diets are a sensible childhood obesity prevention strategy, explained by their low energy density and high complex carbohydrate, fiber, and water content, which may boost satiety and resting energy expenditure.
Recommendations: promote plant-based diets for health and environmental benefits, and adopt food policies and social marketing to counter cultural and economic barriers.
Final fragment of the recommendation sentence on overcoming cultural and economic forces that hinder promoting plant-based diets.

Introduction to the document on early treatment of type 2 diabetes: describes the global burden of type 2 diabetes, its micro- and macrovascular complications, and the increased risk already present in the prediabetic glucose range.

Argues for early intervention as soon as glucose homeostasis abnormalities appear, noting that early type 2 diabetes is asymptomatic and that this makes it hard to diagnose prediabetes and early overt disease.

States the article's aims: discussing diagnostic challenges, the benefits of early intervention (especially prevention trials showing progression can be delayed by treating prediabetes), and evidence-based guidelines for prediabetes and overt type 2 diabetes care.
Closing portion of the abstract summarizing the evidence-based guidelines for standards of care at prediabetes and overt type 2 diabetes stages, followed by the 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.

Opening of a clinical review on preventing type 2 diabetes: introduces diabetes as a growing public health burden, covering its major organ complications and cardiovascular risk as a coronary heart disease risk equivalent.

Continues the review's background by describing diabetic neuropathy and foot ulceration, and noting that understanding of the disease's natural history creates the opportunity to intervene before overt disease develops.

Explains the rationale for prediabetes as a formal diagnosis moving into clinical practice, and why clinicians face uncertainty due to changing guidelines, nomenclature, new drugs and evolving evidence.

States the review's aims: summarizing epidemiology, disease pathogenesis concepts, and guideline recommendations, plus lifestyle, pharmacological and surgical therapies to stop prediabetes progressing to diabetes.

Summarizes the review's conclusions on treatment: medications, newer anti-obesity drugs and bariatric procedures show some benefit, but diet and therapeutic lifestyle change remain the mainstay for improving metabolic profile.
Closing of the abstract: looks ahead to new risk stratification tools for identifying at-risk individuals and to population-level interventions as promising future directions in practice.
Introduction/background of a study projecting the 2050 US adult diabetes burden: complications, the 2007 cost of over $174 billion, and the need for accurate projections for policy planning.

Methods overview: the authors build dynamic difference-equation models using US prediabetes/diabetes prevalence, forecasted incidence, and Census mortality and migration projections to project future US adult diabetes burden.

Description of the three model structures: a three-state model (no diabetes, undiagnosed, diagnosed), a four-state model splitting no-diabetes into prediabetes and normal glucose, and a five-state model adding a high-risk prevention intervention.

Results on incidence and prevalence: diagnosed diabetes incidence is projected to rise from about 8 to about 15 cases per 1,000 between 2008 and 2050, and prevalence under low-incidence, high-mortality assumptions rises from 14% (2010) to 21% (2050).
Prevalence scenarios: under rising incidence and low mortality, prevalence reaches 33% by 2050; a middle scenario gives 25% to 28%; intervention can reduce but not eliminate the increases.

Conclusions on drivers: projected increases are attributed to population aging, growth of higher-risk minority groups, and people with diabetes living longer, so strategies are needed to moderate these factors.
Final conclusion: widespread, reasonably effective preventive interventions targeting high-risk subgroups can considerably but not fully offset future increases in diabetes prevalence.
Fragment completing the final sentence of the document's conclusion, stating that interventions reduce but do not eliminate rising diabetes prevalence.

Introduces the 2010 prevalence of prediabetes among U.S. adults (about one in three, ~79 million) and defines prediabetes and its link to type 2 diabetes, the opening of a CDC MMWR-style report on prediabetes awareness, 2005-2010.

Describes the progression risk of prediabetes (11% per year without weight loss or moderate activity over ~3 years) and states that evidence-based lifestyle programs can delay or prevent type 2 diabetes.
Explains why identifying and informing people with prediabetes matters as the first step toward lifestyle change, and notes that only about 7% of those with prediabetes were aware of it in 2005-2006.
Describes the purpose of the report: a CDC analysis of NHANES data to examine recent changes in prediabetes awareness and associated factors among adults aged 20 and older.
Reports the key findings: about 11% of people with prediabetes were aware in 2009-2010, and awareness stayed below 14% across all subgroups and health-care access levels during 2005-2010.

Gives the public health recommendation that efforts should make people with prediabetes, including those with regular health-care access, aware of their risk and of how modest lifestyle changes can reduce it, concluding that awareness must increase.
Brief sentence fragment completing the conclusion that efforts are needed to increase awareness of prediabetes.

Opening of the abstract for a diabetes prevention trial: background on rising type 2 diabetes from sedentary lifestyle and obesity, and the study design of randomizing 522 overweight adults with impaired glucose tolerance.

Continuation of the methods: participants (172 men, 350 women, mean age 55, mean BMI 31) were assigned to intervention or control, and the intervention group received individualized counseling on weight loss, fat and saturated fat reduction, more fiber, and physical activity.
Methods end and results begin: annual oral glucose-tolerance testing with confirmation by a second test, mean follow-up of 3.2 years, and the start of the weight-loss results at end of year 1.

Key quantitative results: weight loss at year 1 (4.2 kg intervention vs 0.8 kg control) and net loss at year 2 (3.5 kg vs 0.8 kg), both significant, plus the cumulative four-year diabetes incidence (11% vs 23%).

Main efficacy findings: diabetes incidence after four years was 11% in the intervention group versus 23% in controls, a 58% relative risk reduction (P<0.001), which was directly associated with lifestyle changes.
Conclusion of the abstract: lifestyle changes in high-risk individuals with impaired glucose tolerance can prevent type 2 diabetes.

Background and rationale of the Diabetes Prevention Program-style trial: type 2 diabetes prevalence in US adults (~8%), modifiable risk factors (glucose, overweight, sedentary lifestyle), and the hypothesis that lifestyle change or metformin prevents diabetes.

Methods: randomization of 3234 nondiabetic adults with elevated fasting and post-load glucose to placebo, metformin 850 mg twice daily, or a lifestyle program targeting 7% weight loss and 150 minutes/week of physical activity.
Study population characteristics: mean age 51, mean BMI 34.0, 68% women, 45% minority group members, and the definition of body-mass index used.

Primary results: diabetes incidence per 100 person-years (placebo 11.0, metformin 7.8, lifestyle 4.8) over average 2.8 years follow-up, with relative risk reductions of 58% for lifestyle and 31% for metformin versus placebo, with confidence intervals.

Comparative effectiveness and number needed to treat: lifestyle intervention significantly outperformed metformin; 6.9 participants in lifestyle and 13.9 on metformin needed to prevent one diabetes case over three years.
Conclusions: both lifestyle modification and metformin reduce diabetes incidence in high-risk people, with lifestyle intervention proving more effective than metformin.

Opening of the document's background section: diabetes incidence and prevalence rising since 1990, projected 64% increase by 2025 (53.1 million people, ~$500 billion annual costs), and the note that prevention and effective treatment are known though not a cure.

Continues the background on treatment and prevention: early treatment prevents complications and premature death, early prediabetes detection with lifestyle changes reduces diabetes cases, and large prevalence reductions require society-wide lifestyle change.

States the study's purpose: raising public awareness of regional diabetes trends through state and metro-area forecasts for 2010, 2015, and 2025, and begins describing the modeling approach using the latest national diabetes and population data.

Describes the methods and outputs: the model converts national data and projections into state and metro forecasts for the total population and subgroups, summarized in briefing papers published online for public access.

Explains the significance of the research: little existing data project future diabetes prevalence and costs at state and metro levels, so these forecasts help stakeholders make informed decisions on resource allocation.
Final fragment of the document, completing the point that the forecasts support stakeholder decisions about diabetes impact on communities and resource allocation.

Introduction to diabetic microvascular complications (retinopathy and nephropathy): their large clinical and health-system burden, and how aggressive glycemic and blood pressure control, laser photocoagulation, and microalbuminuria treatment can largely prevent them, with future targeted interventions anticipated.

Continues the discussion of future therapies targeting the pathophysiology of diabetic microvascular complications, then states the primary care and diabetologist's role: achieving excellent glycemic control and tight blood pressure control.

Describes the practical screening duties for clinicians: annual dilated fundus examinations (ideally by an ophthalmologist or retinal specialist) and regular microalbuminuria screening, and how this management reduces risk of blindness and renal failure.
Concluding clause summarizing the goal of medical management: lessening the overall burden of diabetic retinopathy and nephropathy by reducing blindness and renal failure.
Abstract of a paper introducing the helical hydrophobic moment (HM-C) method for identifying amphipathic alpha-helical peptide hormones, describing the study's aim and comparison groups.
Abstract section reporting statistical results: mean maximum 11-residue hydrophobic moment values for amphipathic helical versus control peptides, with their significance level.

Abstract section defining the HM-C method, which plots the percentage of 11-residue segments above a given hydrophobic moment, and reporting that it significantly separated the two peptide groups better than other methods.
Abstract section summarizing findings: new candidate amphipathic peptides identified, and molecular modeling of prolactin inhibitory factor showing a strongly amphipathic helix at residues 4-21.
Concluding sentence of the abstract suggesting the computer-based hydrophobic moment method could enable rapid identification of amphipathic alpha-helix peptides.

Background and objective of a meta-analysis on whether treating prediabetes (IGT/IFG) with diet, exercise, or drugs reduces all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, by preventing progression to diabetes.

Methods of the meta-analysis: searched prospective randomised controlled trials in prediabetic populations, with inclusion criteria requiring mortality reporting, about 100 patients, and at least one year of follow-up; interventions split into pharmacological and non-pharmacological.
Results overview: ten RCTs enrolling 23,152 patients, average 3.75-year follow-up, and an overall risk ratio of 0.83 showing interventions delayed or prevented diabetes compared with control.

Comparison of intervention types and key outcomes: non-drug approaches beat drug approaches for diabetes prevention, with no significant difference in all-cause mortality (RR 0.96) or cardiovascular death (RR 1.04).

Cardiovascular outcome results: a non-significant trend toward fewer myocardial infarctions (RR 0.59, CI 0.23-1.50) and a borderline reduction in stroke (RR 0.76, CI 0.58-0.99), along with the start of the conclusions.

Conclusion: although prediabetes interventions largely succeeded in delaying diabetes, they did not reduce all-cause or cardiovascular mortality or myocardial infarction, with a possible exception for stroke.

Study design and methods of a randomised crossover trial testing a pulse-based diet (beans, chickpeas, peas, lentils, about 150 g/d) versus regular diet in adults aged 50+ for CVD risk reduction, with 2-month diet phases and a 1-month washout.

Outcome measures and crossover design details: primary outcome serum LDL-cholesterol, plus secondary lipids, glucose, insulin and C-reactive protein, measured before and after each phase; also the start of the participant characteristics (sample completing the study, sex split, age and body mass).

Main results: participant demographics (87 completers, 30 male and 57 female, mean age 59.7 years) and the pulse diet's effect on total cholesterol (8.3% reduction, P<0.001) and LDL-C (7.9% reduction, P=0.01) compared with the regular diet, with the underlying mmol/l values.

Subgroup result: in participants with high baseline cholesterol (n=20), the pulse-based diet lowered cholesterol by about 6% versus regular diet (P=0.05), with the reported mmol/l values for each diet phase.
Conclusion: the pulse-based diet reduces total cholesterol and LDL-C in older adults, and the authors infer this lowers cardiovascular disease risk.

Opening chunk of a review on chickpea (Cicer arietinum) nutritional quality and health benefits, covering its protein content and amino acid profile, including the sulphur-amino-acid limitation that cereals can complement.
Covers chickpea's carbohydrate and lipid composition: starch as the main storage carbohydrate, dietary fibre and sugars, and its unsaturated fatty acids (linoleic and oleic acids).

Describes chickpea's micronutrients: sterols (β-sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol) in the oil, minerals (Ca, Mg, P, especially K), and vitamins such as riboflavin, niacin, thiamin, folate and β-carotene.

Discusses anti-nutritional factors in chickpea seeds that cooking can reduce, then introduces its potential health benefits for CVD, type 2 diabetes, digestive diseases and cancers, especially in combination with other pulses and cereals.
Concluding sentence of the review, summarizing chickpea as an important pulse crop with diverse potential nutritional and health benefits.

Introduction to the review on legumes: defines the legume types covered and their role as a key protein source in the diets of developing countries and regions where legumes are the main protein supply.

Global legume consumption and production context, including the health interest in legumes and regional intake differences, with Mediterranean European consumption (8-23 g/day) contrasted with Northern Europe (under 5 g/day).
Physiological effects of legumes vary by type, attributed to differences in carbohydrate composition (fiber and starch), protein make-up, and phytochemical content.
Phytochemicals in legumes (enzyme inhibitors, lectins, phytoestrogens, oligosaccharides, saponins, phenolics) and their metabolic roles in regular consumers of these foods.

Health benefits of dietary phytochemicals against chronic diseases such as coronary heart disease, diabetes, hypertension, and inflammation, plus the open question of how phytochemical mixtures interact.
Unresolved challenges in understanding synergistic or antagonistic phytochemical effects and their mechanisms of action, and the stated aim of the review to overview legume nutritional quality.
Concluding statement of the stated scope: the review's overview of legumes' nutritional quality and potential role in cardiometabolic risk prevention.

Introduces the cross-sectional study design, population (82 adults on Saba Island, Caribbean), and how chronic hypertension was identified from blood pressure and medication use, within an abstract on diet diversity and hypertension.

Describes the methods for measuring diet diversity (24-hour recall, food frequency interviews, ethnographic confirmation) and states the main finding that hypertension is linked to poor overall food-group balance beyond individual cations.

Reports the key bivariate result: poorly diversified diet is significantly associated with hypertension (OR 4.25, 95% CI 1.47-12.30), and sodium, potassium, and calcium intake showed no association in bivariate analyses.
Explains that adding sodium, potassium, and calcium to logistic models with diet diversity did not weaken the diet diversity-hypertension association, supporting the robustness of the finding.

Reports that multivariable models controlling for confounders (body fat, skin color, age, sex, perceived stress, alcohol, aerobic activity, socioeconomic status) left the result unchanged, and introduces the food-group finding on legumes.
Gives the specific food-group result: lack of legumes in the daily diet is associated with hypertension (OR 4.71, 95% CI 1.71-13.01).
Introduction to the gluten-free diet: its rising popularity, its established role as treatment for celiac disease, and its benefits for wheat allergy.
Continuation covering wheat allergy's dietary nuances (rye, barley, oats) and the controversial category of gluten sensitivity, including dermatitis herpetiformis and related conditions.
Lists gluten-sensitive conditions (DH, IBS, gluten-sensitive ataxia, autism) and stresses the need to distinguish them from celiac disease despite shared GFD response; notes comorbidity risks in CD.

Compares risk profiles: celiac patients face nutritional deficiencies, cancer, and autoimmune risk, while wheat allergy and gluten sensitivity are not thought to carry these risks; calls for defining biomarkers.
Conclusion calling for high-quality, large-scale randomized trials to establish the true benefits of the gluten-free diet in gluten-related conditions.

Introduction and study aim from a cross-sectional study of patients who avoid wheat/gluten (PWAWG) without celiac disease, seen at a tertiary celiac referral center and compared with CD patients and NHANES subjects.

Methods section: cross-sectional design at a celiac disease referral center, with PWAWG baseline characteristics, labs, and comorbidities compared against CD patients from the same center and NHANES enrollees.
Results section: 84 PWAWGs compared with 585 CD patients and 2,686 NHANES patients; 30% of PWAWGs received alternative diagnoses such as SIBO and fructose/lactose intolerance.
Comparative results: PWAWGs had BMI and hemoglobin similar to CD patients, but lower BMI, folate, hemoglobin, and hypertension prevalence than NHANES participants.
Conclusion: PWAWGs resemble CD patients (possibly via shared HLA haplotypes or gluten-free diet effects), alternative diagnoses are common, and PWAWGs show lower BMI and hypertension prevalence.
Final conclusion fragment restating that PWAWGs share a cardiovascular profile with CD patients, marked by lower BMI and lower hypertension prevalence.

Introduction and methods of a study on the economic burden of a gluten-free diet for coeliac disease patients, describing the market basket of wheat-based and gluten-free products compared across venues and regions.

Methods continue with the price comparison design across store types (general, upscale, health food, and internet grocers) and regions, leading into the start of the results on gluten-free product availability.

Results on availability by venue (36% regular grocery, 41% upscale, 94% health food, 100% internet) and price findings: gluten-free products cost more overall, with bread and pasta about twice the price, and shopping venue affecting cost more than region.
Study conclusions: gluten-free foods are poorly available and costlier than gluten-containing equivalents, with implications for dietary compliance and quality of life that warrant attention.
Final sentence of the conclusions, calling for research into how higher gluten-free food costs and limited availability affect quality of life.
Opening of the review on gluten-related disorders: introduces celiac disease's rise from obscurity to global awareness and the confusion this causes for health care professionals.

Explains the gap between the number of people on a gluten-free diet and celiac patients, and the growing gluten-free market (about $2.5 billion in 2010), which the emergence of other gluten-related conditions helps explain.

States the review's aim: summarizing the three main categories of gluten reactions (allergic wheat allergy, autoimmune celiac disease/dermatitis herpetiformis/gluten ataxia, and immune-mediated gluten sensitivity).
Concludes the stated scope of the review: comparing pathogenic, clinical and epidemiological differences among gluten reactions and proposing new nomenclature and classifications.

Human clinical study design: nine healthy volunteers split into a wheat gluten hydrolysate test group (n=5, 3 g/day for 6 days) and a control group (n=4), measuring NK cell activity and hematological parameters.
Study outcome for the wheat gluten hydrolysate trial: NK cell activity rose significantly in the test group (P=0.018) after intake, and no adverse effects were seen in either group.

Study abstract opening: states the aim of testing whether inconsistent serum lipid results for wheat bran stem from particle size or high gluten content, and introduces the two studies (metabolic breads with hyperlipidemic subjects).

Study design details: the metabolic study used breads with medium or ultra-fine wheat bran plus extra gluten (10% of energy) in 24 hyperlipidemic subjects, and the ad libitum study used breakfast cereals with coarse or mixed bran in 24 mostly normolipidemic subjects, each adding 19 g/d fiber.

Methods continuation: both studies used a randomized crossover design with low-fiber, no-added-gluten control periods and fasting lipid measurements at day zero and the end of each phase; results begin with null effects of bran on cholesterol.

Key results: wheat bran did not change total, LDL, or HDL cholesterol regardless of particle size or gluten level, but increased gluten in the metabolic study lowered serum triglycerides by 13% (p = 0.005), an effect absent in the normal-gluten ad libitum study.

Conclusions: wheat bran's cardiovascular protection cannot be attributed to lowering serum cholesterol; in hyperlipidemic subjects, gluten replacing carbohydrate during high-fiber phases was linked to lower triglycerides.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the abstract's statement that high-fiber phases with gluten displacing carbohydrate were associated with lower serum triglycerides.

Abstract-style Methods opening of a study on celiac disease patients with persistent symptoms despite a gluten-free diet (non-responsive CD, NRCD); describes the referral cohort over 18 months and the aim of finding the cause of continued symptoms.

Methods continued: initial clinic workup including history, examination, routine bloods and tissue transglutaminase antibody testing, plus referral to a specialist gastroenterology dietitian to detect dietary lapses and hidden gluten sources, and a repeat small intestinal biopsy compared with prior biopsies.

Methods end and start of Results: further investigations (colonoscopy, lactulose hydrogen breath test, pancreolauryl test, abdominal CT) if symptoms persisted, follow-up for at least 2 years, and the cohort result of 112 consecutive NRCD referrals.

Results on diagnostic breakdown: 12 patients did not have celiac disease, and of the 100 remaining, 45% were not adhering to a strict gluten-free diet, with 53% inadvertently ingesting gluten and 47% admitting non-compliance.

Results on other causes and outcomes: microscopic colitis in 12%, small bowel bacterial overgrowth in 9%, refractory CD in 9% (three of whom had intestinal lymphoma), and 2-year outcomes of 78 well, 8 with ongoing symptoms, and 4 deaths.
Conclusion: a remediable cause is found in about 90% of non-responsive celiac disease patients, with continued gluten ingestion the leading cause, and the authors propose an investigation algorithm.

Opening of a document on whole grains and human health: introduces epidemiological links between whole-grain intake and reduced cancer, CVD, diabetes, and obesity risk, notes that Western intake (~1 serving/day) falls well short of the recommended three servings, and begins describing whole grains' nutrient and phytochemical richness, including high fibre content.

Describes the specific bioactive components of whole grains: dietary fibre, resistant starch, oligosaccharides, antioxidants such as trace minerals and phenolic compounds linked to disease prevention, plus other protective compounds like phytate, lignans (phyto-oestrogens), plant stanols and sterols, vitamins and minerals.

Covers evidence from whole-grain feeding studies showing biomarker improvements (weight loss, blood-lipid improvement, antioxidant protection), and notes the difficulty of isolating whole grains' protective effects from fibre and other components.

Concludes that prospective epidemiological studies show whole-grain disease protection far exceeding that of isolated nutrients or phytochemicals, suggesting the benefit lies in the whole food matrix rather than individual compounds.

Opening of the review's abstract: defines celiac disease as a gluten-dependent immune disease with 0.3-1.2% prevalence and notes that only 10-20% of cases are found from clinical signs, so laboratory testing is key for silent or atypical cases.
Continuation of the abstract: states the review's scope, covering laboratory diagnosis of celiac disease and gluten intolerance, including optimal test combinations for early accurate diagnosis.

Final part of the abstract listing the review's specific topics: new antibody tests against transglutaminase-gliadin neoepitopes, non-celiac gluten sensitivity forms, and cytokine measurement in celiac disease.
Last fragment of the abstract's closing sentence, ending the phrase about cytokine measurement in celiac disease.
Opening of the abstract (objectives and methods) for a US study estimating celiac disease prevalence using NHANES 2009-2010 serology data from 7,798 participants aged 6 and older.
Methods continuation: serology testing protocol (tTG IgA, then endomysial IgA if abnormal), interview on prior diagnosis and gluten-free diet, and the operational definition of celiac disease cases.
Results opening: 35 celiac disease cases found, most (29) undiagnosed, with demographic details of the affected participants (median age 45, mostly women and non-Hispanic white).
Key prevalence figures: overall US celiac disease prevalence of 0.71% (95% CI 0.58-0.86%), 1.01% among non-Hispanic whites, and 0.63% among those reporting a gluten-free diet.

Conclusions: US celiac prevalence of 0.71% (1 in 141), comparable to European countries, with most cases undiagnosed, rarity among minorities, 1% in non-Hispanic whites, and most gluten-free dieters lacking a diagnosis.
Final fragment of the conclusions, ending the abstract's statement that 'CD' is the abbreviation for celiac disease used throughout.

Introduces the study's background on nonceliac gluten sensitivity (NCGS) as a largely self-reported diagnosis, and states the study aim and recruitment method (advertising to adults self-believing they have NCGS).
Describes the study methods (questionnaire on symptoms, diet, and celiac investigation) and the initial results: 248 respondents, 147 completers, mean age 43.5 years, 130 women.

Reports that most respondents (72%) did not meet NCGS criteria, with reasons including inadequate celiac exclusion, uncontrolled symptoms despite gluten restriction, and not following a gluten-free diet; also gives who initiated the GFD.

Covers celiac testing gaps: 15% had no celiac investigation, and among 75 with duodenal biopsies, 29% had no or inadequate gluten intake at endoscopy; also begins listing celiac investigation adequacy by GFD initiator.

Gives inadequate celiac investigation rates by GFD initiator, then reports that among 40 respondents meeting NCGS criteria, GFD knowledge and adherence were excellent and 65% identified other food intolerances; begins the conclusions.

Concludes that only about 1 in 4 self-reported NCGS respondents meet diagnostic criteria, GFD initiation without adequate celiac exclusion is common, and symptoms remain poorly controlled in about 1 in 4 despite gluten avoidance; includes copyright notice.

Introduces the three gluten-related disorder categories: wheat allergy (allergic), celiac disease (autoimmune), and nonceliac gluten sensitivity (nonallergic, nonautoimmune), setting up the review's differential diagnosis topic.

Describes nonceliac gluten sensitivity as an emerging condition diagnosed only by gluten-dependent symptoms after excluding wheat allergy and celiac disease, and states the review's aim to cover diagnostic tools for all three disorders.
Closing statement of the review's scope: the most recent insights into differentiating wheat allergy, celiac disease, and nonceliac gluten sensitivity among gluten-related gastrointestinal disorders.

Introduces the national Canadian study of gluten cross-contamination in naturally gluten-free flours and starches, describing the sample size (640) and the headline finding that results were compared against the Codex limit.

Reports the main results: 61 of 640 samples (9.5%) exceeded the 20 mg/kg Codex gluten-free threshold, with contamination ranging 5-7995 mg/kg; labelled gluten-free products showed lower contamination (3 of 268 samples above the limit).

Notes the consistency of contamination levels across two sample lots over time, then identifies high-fibre ingredients (soy 902, millet 272, buckwheat 153 mg/kg) as having the largest and most consistent mean gluten contamination.
Concludes that among unlabelled naturally gluten-free flours and starches, high-fibre ingredients carry the greatest probability of exceeding the 20 mg/kg gluten-free threshold.

Introduction to an Italian prospective multicenter survey defining non-celiac gluten sensitivity (NCGS): its aims of describing the clinical picture and estimating prevalence relative to celiac disease.

Methods of the Italian NCGS survey: 38 centers (adult gastroenterology, internal medicine, pediatrics, allergy) enrolled patients from November 2012 to October 2013 using a standardized questionnaire for clinical, biochemical, and instrumental data.
Main results of the NCGS survey: 486 suspected NCGS patients, female/male ratio 5.4:1, mean age 38 years, and a clinical picture of combined gastrointestinal and systemic symptoms.

Symptom profile in suspected NCGS patients: listed gastrointestinal and systemic manifestations (fatigue, headache, joint/muscle pain, numbness, foggy mind, skin rash, depression, anxiety, anemia), with symptoms appearing within hours to a day after gluten intake.

Associated conditions and family history in the NCGS survey: irritable bowel syndrome (47%), food intolerance (35%), IgE-mediated allergy (22%), autoimmune disease (14%), and 18% with a celiac-affected relative.

Diagnostic findings in suspected NCGS patients: no link to HLA-DQ2/DQ8, IgG anti-gliadin antibodies in 25% tested, and duodenal biopsies (given to only some) showing normal mucosa (69%) or mild intraepithelial lymphocytosis (31%).

Conclusions and prevalence estimate of the NCGS survey: NCGS strongly associated with female gender and adulthood; suspected NCGS to new celiac disease diagnosis ratio of 1.15:1, suggesting NCGS prevalence only slightly higher than celiac disease.
Closing lines of the abstract noting that only a slight excess of NCGS over celiac disease prevalence was found, with a pointer to a related article in BMC Medicine (biomedcentral 1741-7015/12/86).

Introduction to a review of Non-Celiac Gluten Sensitivity (NCGS), covering its controversial status, unclear pathogenesis, and contrast with celiac disease (gluten-driven immune condition) and wheat allergy (IgE-mediated).
