Introduces the pilot case-control study on plasma deoxycholic acid (DCA) and breast cancer, with background on DCA in breast cyst fluid and the study's aim of comparing plasma bile acid levels in women with breast cancer.

Describes the study design and subjects: 20 postmenopausal Caucasian breast cancer patients recruited at diagnosis and 20 age- and BMI-matched healthy controls, including exclusion criteria (prior breast cancer treatment, recent HRT, diabetes, liver/gallbladder disease, abnormal liver function).
Covers the measurement method (fasting plasma bile acids by gas-liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry) and begins the results, which compare plasma DCA between breast cancer patients and controls.

Reports the key finding that mean plasma DCA was 52% higher in breast cancer patients than controls (P=0.012), and concludes that the results support a possible role for DCA in breast cancer aetiology.

Introduction of the review on fecal mutagenicity, genotoxicity, and diet in colonic cancer: sets out DNA damage as central to colon carcinogenesis, gut microbial and food-derived causes, and the open questions about Ames and Comet assay relevance.

Discusses unresolved questions about which fecal water mutagens and genotoxins and which gut bacteria matter for oncogenesis, and introduces dietary intervention evidence, such as high-protein diets raising N-nitroso compounds and Comet assay DNA damage.

Covers dietary modulation of fecal genotoxicity, where non-digestible carbohydrates and probiotics may lower it, and states the need to understand genotoxin formation in the colon and the accuracy of the Ames and Comet assays to guide public recommendations.
Concluding summary of the open research needs: understanding colonic genotoxin formation, the accuracy of the Ames and Comet assays, and how diet affects genotoxicity.

Introduction to the document's argument that bile acids may be human carcinogens: historical 1939-1940 proposals, the later view of them as promoters from rodent work, and early evidence of DNA damage (1980-2003).
Mechanism of bile-acid carcinogenicity: indirect DNA damage via oxidative stress and reactive oxygen species, which raises the mutation rate in tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes.

Apoptosis and selection: high-fat-diet bile acid levels induce frequent apoptosis, and apoptosis-resistant cells survive and proliferate, which together with DNA damage supports bile acids as likely carcinogens.

Human epidemiology: high bile acid levels are associated with elevated cancer incidence in the laryngopharyngeal tract, esophagus, stomach, pancreas, small intestine near the Ampulla of Vater, and colon.
Species difference: humans have far more cell generations in colonic and other GI epithelia than rodents, allowing time for mutations leading to cancer to arise in humans but not in rodents.

Introduction to the review on metabolic effects of slow colonic transit, covering its influence on bile acid recirculation, colonic pH, and short-chain fatty acids, and the diseases (gallstones, bowel cancer, breast cancer) it may promote.

Focuses on bile acid metabolism as the best-documented effect of slow colonic transit: increased deoxycholate and higher cholesterol saturation of bile raise gallstone risk, and the review then turns to evidence linking transit to large bowel and breast cancer.
Concludes the review's framing by noting the evidence linking slow transit to large bowel and breast cancer, and that data on colonic transit in these cancers are lacking.
Closing implication: if slow colonic transit is a significant cause of these diseases, population health could benefit from dietary and lifestyle changes that speed intestinal transit.

Study design and population: this opening chunk of a nutrition study describes the 3-day diary and 24-h recall dietary methods used on 50 matched sets of Seventh-day Adventist lacto-ovo-vegetarians, nonvegetarians, and general-population nonvegetarians, plus 18 unmatched pure vegetarians.

Methods continuation: this chunk covers the rationale for the dietary assessment methods, details of each method, and the start of the nutrient analysis results for the 24-h recall and 3-day diary across the study groups.

Analysis and comparison: this chunk describes comparing the four groups' 3-day nutrient means against sex-specific Recommended Daily Allowances, with and without supplements, and discusses the contribution of nutritional supplements to intake.

Key findings on macronutrients and vitamins: this chunk reports that all groups meet or exceed calorie, protein, and fat intake, that nonvegetarians' higher calories reflect higher fat and protein, and that A, B, and C vitamin levels are adequate with and without supplements.

Key findings on minerals and conclusions: this chunk reports that calcium is well below recommendations for pure vegetarian females, iron is low for all females, heme iron does not improve intake for nonvegetarian females, and results are compared with prior Seventh-day Adventist nutrient studies.
Closing fragment: this final short chunk completes the document's last sentence, stating that the results are compared with prior reports of nutrient intake among Seventh-day Adventists.

Introduces the randomized trial design comparing ECMO with conventional medical therapy (CMT) in newborns with severe persistent pulmonary hypertension, and reports phase I results: 4 of 10 CMT babies died versus 9 of 9 ECMO babies surviving.

Describes the halting of randomization after the fourth CMT death as pre-planned, the start of phase II in which 20 babies received ECMO (19 survived), and the note that all treatment groups were comparable in illness severity and ventilator support.
Gives the overall outcome of the trial: ECMO survival of 97% (28 of 29) versus 60% (6 of 10) for CMT, a statistically significant difference (P < .05).

Abstract of a 1970s-era ECMO study on newborn respiratory failure: introduces the problem that supportive oxygen/ventilation injures the lung and motivates prolonged ECMO to let the lung rest, describing 45 moribund infants treated.

Methods and early results of the ECMO study: referral criteria (infants unresponsive to maximal therapy), cannulation via jugular vein and carotid artery, continuous heparin targeting activated clotting time of 200-300 s, and reduced airway oxygen and pressure, with 25 of 45 surviving.

Breakdown of outcomes by primary diagnosis in the ECMO newborn study (hyaline membrane disease, meconium aspiration, persistent fetal circulation with diaphragmatic hernia, sepsis) with survivor and death counts, plus the start of the normal-development finding.

Conclusions of the ECMO newborn study: 20 of 25 survivors have normal growth, development, and brain and lung function; ECMO reduced mortality and morbidity in this phase I trial, a randomized controlled study is underway, and ECMO may help older patients if used before irreversible lung damage.
Final fragment of the conclusion of the ECMO newborn study, completing the statement that ECMO may be effective in older patients if used before irreversible lung damage occurs.

This chunk is the document's core claim, from a 'reversal therapy' post. It asserts that coronary artery disease is nearly absent where diet keeps total cholesterol under 150 mg/dl, and that advanced CAD can halt progression via a plant-based diet plus cholesterol-lowering medication. The claim is medically contested and the framing is one-sided.

This chunk opens the document, a critique of evidence-based medicine, and argues that US medical students receive little nutrition training and are biased against dietary-approach studies, because EBM favors only double-blind randomized controlled trials.

This chunk concludes the document's argument that blinding is impossible in dietary interventions, so EBM's preference for double-blind RCTs biases physicians toward drug treatments over diet for managing chronic disease, followed by a 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.
Introduction to a viewpoint article linking the Western diet to acne in adolescents, framing nutrient signalling (glycaemic load, dairy protein, insulin/IGF-1) as a possible pathogenic driver.
Explains the cell's nutrient-sensing machinery: FoxO1 and mTORC1 are introduced, and increased insulin/IGF-1 signalling is described as pushing FoxO1 out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm.
Describes FoxO1's roles beyond growth control: attenuating androgen signalling, regulating sebaceous lipogenesis proteins, immunity, and oxidative stress, and acting as a rheostat of mTORC1.
Connects FoxO1 to mTORC1-driven outcomes relevant to acne, including keratinocyte hyperproliferation, sebaceous gland hyperplasia, increased lipogenesis, insulin resistance, and higher BMI.
Summarizes the convergence model: androgen, TNF-α and IGF-1 signalling from acne-risk genetic polymorphisms all activate mTORC1, which Western diet nutrient signalling further amplifies.
Concluding statement arguing that understanding FoxO1/mTORC1 nutrient signalling is critical for explaining the Western diet's role in epidemic acne and other mTORC1-linked diseases of civilization.

Introduction of a rat study on donkey's milk: background on n-3 PUFA, mitochondrial uncoupling, and reactive oxygen species, stating the hypothesis that donkey milk (low fat, higher n3:n6 ratio) affects energy balance, lipid metabolism, and prooxidant status versus cow's milk.

Study design: rats drank raw donkey's milk for 4 weeks, and its effects on energy balance, lipid metabolism, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant/detoxifying defences were compared with an iso-energetic amount of raw cow's milk.

Key results on lipid and mitochondrial effects: donkey milk produced hypolipidemia alongside increased mitochondrial activity/proton leak and higher carnitine palmitoyltransferase and uncoupling protein 2 levels.

Key results on inflammation and antioxidant status: donkey milk lowered energy efficiency and reduced TNF-α and LPS, while raising total thiols and detoxifying enzymes (GST, NQO1), suggesting Nrf2 pathway activation.
Concluding statement attributing the beneficial effects, at least partly, to Nrf2 pathway activation, followed by the 2012 Wiley-VCH copyright notice for the abstract.

Opening chunk of a short commentary on acne research: it traces the past decade's growing understanding of acne mechanisms and the link between diet and acne, citing key ethnological, epidemiological, and clinical studies, and introduces Melnik's pair of papers.

Continuation of the commentary's introduction: it describes Melnik's papers as translational research for dermatologists, listing their topics (Western diet, dairy, FoxO1 and mTORC1 signaling, agonists vs. antagonists, current and future therapies) as pieces of an emerging picture of acne.
Final fragment of the same commentary, consisting only of the trailing period from the closing sentence of the introduction about the jigsaw puzzle coming together; it carries no independent content.

Opening of the abstract: links Western diet to acne, noting acne is absent in Palaeolithic-diet populations with low glycaemic load and no milk/dairy, and introduces two RCTs showing benefits of low glycaemic load diets.

Middle of the abstract: summarizes RCT evidence for low glycaemic load diets, epidemiological evidence that milk promotes acne, and introduces mTORC1 as a nutrient-signalling mechanism linking high glycaemic load and milk-derived insulin, IGF-1 and leucine signalling to acne.

Conclusion framing: argues acne is an mTORC1-driven disease of civilization alongside obesity, type 2 diabetes and cancer caused by Western diet, and that early dietary counselling of teenage acne patients is a key opportunity for dermatology.
Final sentence of the abstract: states that dietary counselling may improve acne and reduce long-term harms of Western diet on more serious mTORC1-driven diseases of civilization.

Introduces the hypothesis that Propionibacterium acnes-mediated inflammation may contribute to prostate carcinogenesis, motivating an indirect study of acne and prostate cancer risk in the Health Professionals Follow-up Study.

Describes the study design: severe acne was proxied by tetracycline use (self-reported on the 1992 questionnaire, for at least two months, with duration recorded) in the Health Professionals Follow-up Study.

Covers outcome ascertainment and cohort size: prostate cancer diagnoses were collected on biennial questionnaires and confirmed by medical record review, yielding 2,147 cases among 34,629 men from 1992 to 2002.
Reports the main result: men using tetracycline for four or more years had a significantly higher prostate cancer risk than non-users (16 exposed cases; multivariable RR=1.70, 95% CI 1.03–2.80).
Gives caveats on the finding: few exposed cases, indirect measurement of severe acne, and acne's complex etiology beyond P. acnes, so further biologic and epidemiologic research is needed.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence, calling for more studies to clarify P. acnes' possible role in prostate carcinogenesis.

Introduction of a paper on dietary intervention in acne, framing Western diet (high calories, glycemic load, fat, meat, insulinotropic dairy) as an environmental driver of epidemic acne via endocrine signaling.
Explains that Western diet signals are sensed by mTORC1, which integrates energy, insulin/IGF-1, and leucine signals from milk proteins and meat, in the context of acne pathogenesis.
Describes the mechanistic link from mTORC1 to SREBP-driven lipogenesis, leucine conversion into sebum lipids by sebocytes, and mTORC1-androgen amplification in sebaceous follicles.
Discusses testosterone activation of mTORC1 and suggests future research on isotretinoin's possible downregulation of sebocyte mTORC1 via FoxO1.

Argues that Western diet's role in acne must consider all mTORC1 stimuli (glucose, insulin, IGF-1, leucine) and frames acne as an mTORC1-driven disease of civilization alongside obesity, diabetes, cancer, and neurodegeneration.
States the proposed dietary intervention: reduce total energy, hyperglycemic carbohydrates, insulinotropic dairy, and leucine-rich meat and dairy proteins to attenuate mTORC1 signaling.

Notes that these dietary changes conflict with industrialized and fast food in Westernized countries, and that reducing mTORC1 activity requires more vegetables and fruit, as in vegan or Paleolithic diets.
Concludes with the dermatologist's responsibility to advise young acne patients to modify diet to limit mTORC1 activation, both to treat acne and to prevent later chronic diseases.

Study aims: examines whether breast cancer risk relates to diabetes, estrogen-associated disorders (uterine fibroids, endometriosis, gallstones), and androgen-associated disorders (acne, hirsutism, polycystic ovaries), in a population-based case-control study.

Study methods: breast cancer cases aged 50-75 from state tumor registries in Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire; controls drawn from drivers' license lists or Medicare files; data collected by telephone interview, yielding 5659 cases and 5928 controls.

Main findings begin: no overall association between breast cancer risk and diabetes, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, gallstones, or cholecystectomy history; sample sizes of interviewed participants stated.

Odds ratios for androgen-related disorders: acne OR 1.4, hirsutism OR 1.2, polycystic ovaries OR 1.6 (wide CI); androgenic conditions all trend toward increased risk. Diabetes results also begin here.

Diabetes by age of onset: diagnosis before age 35 gave OR 0.52 (CI spanning 1), while later-onset diabetes showed increased risk (OR 1.2, CI 1.0-1.4); conclusion that androgen-related phenomena may be important in breast cancer etiology.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that androgen-related phenomena are likely important in the etiology of breast cancer.

Opening of a review titled 'Milk is not just food but most likely a genetic transfection system activating mTORC1 signaling for postnatal growth,' introducing milk as a nutrient system that promotes neonatal growth via the mTORC1 pathway.
Middle section of the review describing milk as a materno-neonatal relay system, where transferred amino acids raise GIP, GLP-1, insulin, GH and IGF-1 levels to activate mTORC1.

Part of the review's central claim that milk exosomes carrying microRNA-21 may act as a genetic transfection system boosting mTORC1 metabolism, and contrasting infant human breast milk with persistent cow's milk signaling in later life.
Concluding sentence of the review, proposing that continued cow's milk consumption in adolescence and adulthood may promote mTORC1-driven diseases of civilization.
Opening chunk of an abstract/review linking acne to over-activated mTORC1 signalling as a marker for Western-diet-related risk of increased body mass index and insulin resistance.

Middle chunk explaining that high glycaemic load and milk/dairy consumption aggravate mTORC1 signalling, and stating the review's aim to summarise evidence linking acne, BMI, insulin resistance and Western diet.

Concluding chunk on the review's clinical implication: a Palaeolithic-type diet with lower glycaemic load and less milk could attenuate mTORC1 signalling, potentially improving acne and delaying mTORC1-driven diseases of civilisation.
Final fragment of the abstract's last sentence, stating that dietary change may delay progression to more serious mTORC1-driven diseases of civilisation.

Introduction stating the problem: cow-milk-based infant formula's higher protein content versus human milk is a major risk factor for childhood obesity, but no clear biochemical mechanism has been established; the article aims to link leucine-mTORC1 signalling to adipogenesis.

Explains that leucine is the main signal transducer in mammalian milk, activating mTORC1, and acts as a maternal-neonatal relay supporting mTORC1-dependent neonatal beta-cell proliferation and insulin secretion.

Describes the mTORC1 target S6K1 as central to driving mesenchymal stem cells toward adipocyte differentiation and insulin resistance, and notes that infant formulas contain more leucine than human milk.

Proposes that excessive leucine-mediated mTORC1-S6K1 signalling from formula may increase adipogenesis and lifelong adipocyte numbers, and that restricting formula leucine to human-milk levels could prevent childhood obesity.

Concluding statement that attenuating formula-induced mTORC1 signalling via leucine restriction to human-milk levels is a promising strategy for preventing childhood obesity and related metabolic diseases.
Introduction to mTOR: its role as a conserved kinase in cell growth, its activation in cancers, and its two complexes (mTORC1 and mTORC2), with only mTORC1 nutrient-regulated.

Continues the introduction: contrasts nutrient control of mTORC1 with growth-factor control of both complexes, notes the detailed knowledge of mTORC1 regulation, and flags amino acid-induced activation as the least understood mechanism.
Closing statement of the abstract: the review's purpose is to summarize current knowledge of nutrient-dependent regulation of mTORC1.

Introduces the study: kidney-transplant recipients with Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) are at risk from immunosuppression; sirolimus (rapamycin) is evaluated as a possible antitumor agent, and the methods describe stopping cyclosporine and starting sirolimus in 15 patients.

Methods continued: biopsy protocol (excisional biopsy of lesion and normal skin at diagnosis, repeat biopsy at the former lesion site at six months) and the markers examined, including VEGF, Flk-1/KDR, and phosphorylated Akt and p70S6 kinase, which are sirolimus-targeted pathway enzymes.
Results on clinical response: all cutaneous KS lesions disappeared by three months of sirolimus, with histologic remission confirmed in all patients at six months.

Results on safety and biomarkers: no acute rejection or change in graft function; Flk-1/KDR and phosphorylated Akt and p70S6 kinase were elevated in KS cells, and VEGF was elevated in KS cells and more strongly in perilesional normal skin.

Conclusion and citation: sirolimus inhibits progression of dermal KS in kidney-transplant recipients while still providing effective immunosuppression; includes the 2005 Massachusetts Medical Society copyright notice.

Opening of an abstract-style passage on how cells sense amino acid insufficiency for protein synthesis to conserve mass, covering both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells; this chunk introduces the topic of nutrient-dependent growth.

Continuation of the abstract's discussion of cellular monitoring of amino acid supply, noting that responses depend on specific amino acid abundance, followed by the 2012 FEBS copyright notice that closes the document.

Introduction to the review on mTOR biology: describes TOR as an essential metazoan master regulator of cell growth and proliferation and notes the growing but confusing body of research on its complex composition and signal integration.

Background on mTOR complexes: states the prevailing view that mTOR forms two complexes, mTORC1 (defined by RAPTOR) and mTORC2 (defined by RICTOR), and that additional incompletely characterized co-factors complicate understanding of each complex.

Motivation for an alternative framework: notes tissue-of-origin differences in mTOR function and introduces the review's proposal that mTOR complex formation and signaling reflect cell type- and basal state-dependent conditions.

Conclusion of the introduction: argues that reinterpreting mTOR biology through this cell type and basal state framework could help design therapies that more effectively inhibit this central cell behavior regulator.
Introduces mTOR as a protein kinase and its best-understood complex mTORC1, noting that its regulation and functions are heavily studied yet many questions remain open.

Covers unresolved mechanisms of mTORC1 activation: hormone and growth factor signaling via the small GTPase Rheb, amino acid signaling via other GTPases, and the incompletely understood control of Rheb.
Describes gaps in knowledge about rapamycin's selective inhibition of some mTORC1 functions and about the diverse substrates of mTORC1, whose physiological roles are often poorly understood.
Notes that how mTORC1 regulates several processes is unknown, that its role in ageing lacks clear mechanisms, and that understanding it matters for cell function and human disease.
Concludes that gaining further insight into mTORC1 control and how it governs cellular functions and animal physiology is a high priority.

Opening of an abstract on mTOR in cancer therapy: introduces mTOR pathway proteins being overexpressed or mutated in tumors and rapamycin and its synthetic analogs (rapalogs) inhibiting tumor cell growth in vitro and in vivo.
Abstract passage on rapalog clinical trial results, noting they may help treat subsets of certain cancers, and that early sporadic responses relied on a general translation-inhibition hypothesis.

Abstract passage explaining that the sporadic early clinical responses to mTOR inhibitors are now understood through better knowledge of mTOR regulatory dynamics and its role in the tumor microenvironment, and previewing the review's scope.
Closing sentence of the abstract stating the review will summarize preclinical and clinical data and recent findings on mTOR's function in cancer and growth regulation.

Introduction/opening of the abstract: fisetin, a dietary flavonol, is presented as an anti-obesity agent acting via inhibition of mTORC1 signaling, which controls growth, proliferation, and lipid biosynthesis.
Methods and early results: fisetin reduces phosphorylation of S6K1 and mTORC1 in 3T3-L1 preadipocytes in a time- and concentration-dependent manner.
Mechanism findings: in TSC2-knockdown cells, fisetin's inhibition of mTORC1 is shown to be Akt-dependent, and mTORC1 is linked to adipocyte differentiation.
Adipogenesis results: fisetin inhibits adipocyte differentiation, and this effect depends on mTOR activity, reducing intracellular triglyceride accumulation.
In vivo findings: fisetin-supplemented high-fat diet mice show reduced body weight and white adipose tissue gain, with decreased phosphorylation of Akt, S6K1 and mTORC1 in adipose tissue.

Conclusion: fisetin prevents 3T3-L1 adipocyte differentiation and HFD-induced obesity via mTORC1 inhibition, proposed as a phytochemical agent for diet-induced obesity; includes 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.
Trailing fragment of the conclusion and copyright line: fisetin is suggested as a useful phytochemical for attenuating diet-induced obesity, followed by the 2013 Elsevier copyright statement.

Opening of the review on prostate cancer: introduces androgen receptor dependence, PI3K-Akt-mTORC1 pathway aberrations, mTORC1 upregulation in advanced PCa, and the link between dairy protein intake and PCa risk.

Continuation of the introduction: describes mTORC1 as a master regulator of protein synthesis, lipid synthesis, and autophagy, and states the review's thesis that cow's milk (not human milk) promotes PCa via mTORC1 stimulation.

Presents mammalian milk as an endocrine signaling system that activates mTORC1, promotes growth and proliferation, and suppresses autophagy, and notes that this milk-mediated signaling is naturally limited to the postnatal growth phase.

Explains how persistent cow's milk protein consumption in adults supplies insulinotropic BCAAs from whey, raising postprandial insulin and, via casein-derived amino acids, hepatic IGF-1, both of which activate mTORC1.
Links elevated milk protein-driven mTORC1 signaling and exposure to cow's milk estrogens to the observed association between high dairy consumption and PCa risk in Westernized societies.

Discusses prostate development: balanced mTORC1 signaling supports prostate morphogenesis and differentiation, so excessive mTORC1 activity from high cow's milk intake during critical growth phases may cause long-term harm to prostate health.

Concluding recommendation: attenuating mTORC1 through Paleolithic-style diets and restricting dairy protein, especially during mTORC1-dependent developmental phases, may protect against dairy-associated prostate cancer in Western men.
Final sentence of the abstract, closing the conclusion by naming dairy-promoted prostate cancer as the most common dairy-associated cancer in men in Western societies.
Opening of a document on rapalogs (rapamycin analogs) in cancer prevention; introduces cancer as age-related and the idea that calorie restriction reduces cancer by slowing aging via MTOR inhibition.

Middle section noting rapalogs' anti-senescence and anti-aging effects alongside their approval as cancer treatments, and posing the central question of whether cancer prevention is direct or indirect via slowed aging.
Concluding sentence of the document stating that increasing evidence supports the indirect mechanism, i.e., rapamycin prevents cancer by slowing the aging process.
Introduction and background of a Swedish retrospective cohort study on early-life caloric restriction (modeled by anorexia nervosa) and invasive breast cancer risk, with the study objective stated.

Study design, data sources (Swedish inpatient, cancer, death, and fertility registries), and participant selection: 7303 women hospitalized for anorexia nervosa before age 40 between 1965 and 1998, including the exclusion of 31 women with prior cancer.

Main outcome definition (incidence of invasive breast cancer) and the first key result: women with anorexia nervosa had a 53% lower breast cancer incidence than the general Swedish population, with its confidence interval.

Results stratified by parity: nulliparous women showed a non-significant 23% lower incidence (CI spanning higher to lower), while parous women had a 76% lower incidence; the conclusion that severe caloric restriction may protect against breast cancer begins here.
Final conclusion: low caloric intake before first birth followed by a subsequent pregnancy is associated with an even greater reduction in breast cancer risk, closing the abstract.

Introduction and study aim from a breast cancer abstract: defines mTOR, its complexes mTORC1 (Raptor) and mTORC2 (Rictor), and states the study examines mTORC1/Rictor/Raptor mRNA expression in breast cancer and its link to hTERT.

Methods and continuation of the aims: mTORC1-hTERT correlation investigated in 150 breast cancer and 31 normal tissue samples via RT-qPCR, with transcript levels correlated to clinicopathological data; also begins results on higher mTOR expression in tumours.

Results for mTOR: higher expression in breast cancer tissue, higher grade, ductal tumours, and worse overall survival; begins describing Rictor being higher in background tissue and linked to NPI and tumour grade.

Results for Rictor and Raptor: Rictor inversely related to Nottingham Prognostic Index and grade and associated with better overall and disease-free survival; Raptor mRNA higher in tumours and linked to higher grade.

Key findings and conclusions: strong positive mTOR-hTERT correlation (P<0.00001), consistent with mTORC1's anti-apoptotic role, suggesting selective mTORC1 inhibitors may be more effective in breast cancer.
Final conclusion of the abstract: findings support the hypothesis that mTORC1 is an important upregulator of telomerase in breast cancer.

Introduction and methods opening of a cross-over study on bean and rice meals and postprandial glycemic response in adults with type 2 diabetes, describing background rationale and the aim to compare bean/rice traditional meals with rice alone.

Methods detail of the randomized 4x4 crossover trial: 17 adults aged 35–70 with type 2 diabetes (on metformin or diet/exercise), testing white rice control versus pinto, black, and red kidney bean/rice meals matched for 50 g available carbohydrate after a 12-hour fast.

Methods continued: capillary blood glucose measured at baseline and every 30 minutes up to 180 minutes postprandial, analyzed with repeated-measures MANOVA and paired t tests against the rice control, leading into the results.

Results of the bean and rice glycemic study: net postprandial glucose was significantly lower for all three bean/rice meals versus rice at 90, 120 and 150 minutes, and iAUC was lower for pinto and black bean meals but not kidney beans.

Conclusions of the study stating that pinto, dark red kidney and black beans with rice attenuate glycemic response relative to rice alone, suggesting traditional foods as non-pharmaceutical diabetes management and better dietary adherence, followed by the trial registration number.
Trial registration footer of the bean and rice type 2 diabetes crossover study, giving Clinical Trials registry number NCT01241253 and ending the conclusions section.

Abstract of a 2012 study on dietary patterns and insulin resistance in 3871 healthy Korean adults (2007-2008 KNHANES); reports that the whole grains and beans dietary pattern was associated with lower odds of insulin resistance (OR 0.80 for highest quintile, P for trend 0.013).

Closing portion of the same abstract, giving the continued statistical results for the whole grains and beans pattern (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.61-1.03, P for trend 0.013) and the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction of the study: surveys the many therapeutic agents used against diabetes mellitus before insulin's discovery and the scope of its focus on pre-insulin Europe, including the count of over 100 agents considered hypoglycemic around 1900.

Continues the introduction by describing that most of the 100+ hypoglycemic agents were used only occasionally while some were widely marketed, and names the most common medicinal plants: Syzygium cumini (Eugenia jambolana), bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus), and Phaseolus beans.

Lists other frequently used pre-insulin antidiabetic agents, including opium and opium alkaloids, quinine, Belladonna alkaloids, salicylates, alkaline sodium salts, and toxic arsenic or uranium salts, and highlights Syzygium jambolanum seed powder as among the most studied plant antidiabetics.
Concluding fragment of the sentence stating that Syzygium jambolanum seed powder is one of the most intensively studied plant-derived antidiabetic agents.

Opening chunk of an abstract on Phaseolus vulgaris (bean pod) use as an antihyperglycemic remedy for diabetes, introducing the traditional use and the contradictory historical versus recent study findings.

Middle chunk of the abstract concluding that bean preparations are not a first-choice phytopharmaceutical, noting that high doses of aqueous extracts are needed, and suggesting beans may be more useful as food due to fiber content and alpha-amylase inhibition for type 2 diabetes.
Final fragment of the abstract, completing the conclusion that beans may help prevent or ameliorate type 2 diabetes as a dietary food component.

Introduction and aims of a systematic review/meta-analysis on non-oil-seed pulses (chickpeas, beans, lentils) and glycaemic control, covering their role as slowly digestible carbohydrate and low-GI food, and the study's objective.

Methods section describing the literature search (MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Cochrane Library) for randomised controlled trials of at least 7 days on pulses and glycaemic markers in people with and without diabetes.

Methods continued: dual independent data extraction by reviewers, statistical pooling with generic inverse variance and standardised mean differences, heterogeneity measured by chi-squared and I-squared, and meta-regression for predictors of effect.

Results summary: 41 trials included; pulses alone lowered fasting blood glucose and insulin, and pulses in low-GI diets lowered glycosylated proteins (HbA1c or fructosamine), with pooled effect sizes and CIs.

Results continued: pulses in high-fibre diets lowered fasting blood glucose and glycosylated proteins; heterogeneity was high and unexplained, with modifiers including diabetes status, pulse type, dose, physical form, follow-up duration, study quality, and design.
Conclusions: pooled analyses show pulses alone or within low-GI or high-fibre diets improve longer-term glycaemic control in humans, though the size of benefit varies substantially across studies.
Final conclusion sentence noting the heterogeneity in improvements and the call for further large, well-designed randomised trials on pulses and glycaemic control.

Introduction to a review on antidiabetic potential of commonly consumed legumes: describes the rising global diabetes incidence from lifestyle changes and the limitations of oral hypoglycemic agents and insulin, and introduces diet and exercise as effective management.

Continues the introduction by highlighting diet and exercise as effective diabetes management and dietary therapy as promising for prevention and treatment, then notes legumes' nutritive value and growing use in dietetic formulations.
States the review's aim: summarizing glucose- and lipid-lowering effects of common legumes from animal and human studies, and begins the conclusion that legumes vary in antidiabetic potential.
Concluding statement that legumes differ in antidiabetic potential and also help reduce cardiovascular and renal disease risk factors.

Opening chunk of an abstract on Phaseolus vulgaris beans (pinto, black, navy, kidney) and their link to lower risk of chronic disease via reduced glycaemic stress (hyperglycaemia and hyperinsulinaemia), covering diabetes, CVD and cancer.

Closing sentence of the same abstract, stating the paper's aim: examining how P. vulgaris beans affect glycaemic response and how that may influence the risk of diabetes, CVD and cancer. It completes the sentence begun in chunk 1.

Introduction and study aim: frequent pulse consumption (yellow peas, chickpeas, navy beans, lentils) vs. energy-restriction counselling for metabolic syndrome risk factors in overweight/obese adults, from an 8-week trial.

Study design and methods: two groups (19 pulse, 21 energy-restricted) of overweight/obese adults (mean BMI 32.8); measures of body weight, waist, blood pressure, fasting blood and 24 h intake at weeks 1, 4, 8; oral glucose tolerance measures of glucose, insulin, C-peptide, GLP-1 and ghrelin at weeks 1 and 8.
Main results across both groups at week 8: reductions in energy intake, waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, HbA1c, glucose AUC and HOMA-IR after the glucose load.

Diet-dependent results: HDL and fasting C-peptide changes differed by diet (pulse group rose 4.5% and 12.3%; energy-restricted group fell 0.8% and 7.6%), and insulin AUC responses differed by diet (P < 0.05).
Sex-specific insulin AUC results: on the energy-restricted diet insulin AUC fell in females (24.2%) and males (4.8%); on the pulse diet it fell 13.9% in females but rose 27.3% in males.
Conclusion: ad libitum frequent pulse consumption reduced metabolic syndrome risk factors, with effects equivalent to and sometimes stronger than counselling for energy reduction.

Study introduction and methods: design of the case-control study of legume intake and metabolic syndrome, including sample size (80 cases, 160 matched controls), measurement methods, FFQ dietary assessment, and the ATP III MetS definition.

Methods continued and start of results: describes the dietary assessment via food frequency questionnaire and the ATP III definition of metabolic syndrome, then begins reporting mean legume servings per week in cases.

Results on legume intake: mean servings per week in cases versus controls (P < 0.05), and quartile-based trends showing lower systolic blood pressure and fasting glucose and higher HDL cholesterol with greater legume intake after adjustment for confounders.

Main odds ratio findings: highest versus lowest quartile of legume intake associated with lower odds of metabolic syndrome after lifestyle and food group adjustment (OR 0.25), with the association weakening but staying significant after BMI adjustment.
Final BMI-adjusted result (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.12-0.81) and the conclusion that legume intake is inversely associated with risk of metabolic syndrome and some of its components.

Introduction and study aim: prior adult-recalled adolescent diet studies linked vegetable fat and nuts to lower benign breast disease risk; this study tests pre-adolescent and adolescent vegetable protein and fat intake in the Growing Up Today Study cohort.

Study population and methods: Growing Up Today Study cohort of 9,039 girls aged 9–15 in 1996, with food frequency questionnaires 1996–2001 and follow-up surveys through 2010; BBD diagnoses confirmed by breast biopsy were self-reported from 2005 among women aged 18–30.

Statistical approach and outcome: logistic regression of vegetable protein and fat intake against biopsy-confirmed BBD (112 cases), with analysis of the largest individual food contributors to protein and fat intake in the cohort.

Key result for early adolescence (1996–1998): vegetable fat was inversely associated with BBD risk (OR 0.72 per 10 g/day); the main sources were peanut butter, peanuts, nuts, beans, and corn, and a daily serving of any of these lowered risk (OR 0.32).

Age-specific findings: peanut butter and nuts at age 11 were inversely associated with risk, and at age 14 higher vegetable protein was linked to lower BBD risk (OR 0.64 per 10 g/day), with a daily serving of these foods also lowering risk (OR 0.34).

Subgroup and conclusion: girls with a family history of breast cancer showed significantly lower risk with these foods or vegetable fat; the authors conclude that vegetable protein, fat, peanut butter, and nuts consumed by older girls may reduce later BBD risk.
Concluding sentence: the authors suggest that older girls eating vegetable protein, vegetable fat, peanut butter, or nuts may lower their risk of benign breast disease as young women.

Introduces walnut bioactives (ALA, phytosterols) and the study's approach of testing walnut extracts, purified compounds, and postprandial serum on breast cancer cell proliferation and gene expression; first mention of walnut oil extracts and ALA/β-sitosterol reducing MCF-7 proliferation.

Covers ALA's gene expression effects in mouse TM2H breast cancer cells, affecting PPAR, LXR, and FXR target genes (suggesting multiple cellular targets), and begins describing transactivation assay results for walnut oil extracts.

Reports transactivation assay findings that walnut oil extracts activated FXR more than other nuclear receptors, that ALA and β-sitosterol were the most efficacious FXR activators, and introduces the human serum experiment on MCF-7 cells linked to body mass index.

Concludes the findings: serum from walnut-fed individuals showed a correlation between BMI and MCF-7 proliferation in vitro, and the overall summary that walnut and its constituents affect mammary epithelial cells via multiple molecular targets.

Abstract opening (Background and Methods) of a study on nut consumption and pancreatic cancer risk in women, describing the Nurses' Health Study cohort of 75,680 participants and the rationale linking nut intake to diabetes and pancreatic cancer.

Methods and early Results from the same abstract: dietary assessment of nut intake updated every 2 to 4 years, Cox proportional hazards analysis, 466 incident pancreatic cancer cases, and adjustment for age, height, smoking, physical activity, and energy intake.

Main result from the nut-cancer abstract: women eating a 1-oz (28-g) nut serving at least twice weekly had a significantly lower pancreatic cancer risk (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.47-0.92) versus those who largely avoided nuts, with the start of the BMI and diabetes sensitivity analysis.

Sensitivity analysis and subgroup findings from the nut-pancreatic cancer abstract: after adjusting for BMI and diabetes history the inverse association held (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.48-0.95), and it persisted across strata of BMI, physical activity, smoking, red meat, fruit, and vegetable intake; the conclusion begins here.
Concluding statement of the abstract: frequent nut consumption is inversely associated with pancreatic cancer risk in a large prospective cohort of women, independent of other known risk factors.

Introduces obesity as part of metabolic syndrome and its link to higher cancer frequency, specifically liver cancer, which is typically hepatocellular carcinoma arising from cirrhosis. Sets up the paper's topic of obesity-associated hepatocarcinogenesis.

Continues the background: HCC is the third leading cause of cancer death worldwide and is increasingly diagnosed in people with obesity, where metabolic conditions coexist with classic HCC risk factors and burden the chronically diseased liver.

Describes proposed molecular mechanisms of obesity-associated HCC: chronic inflammation from adipose remodeling and adipokines, ectopic lipid accumulation and lipotoxicity, altered gut microbiota, and disrupted stellate cell senescence.

Adds insulin resistance with elevated insulin and insulin-like growth factors as a mechanism, and notes these obesity-related pathways synergize with chronic liver disease from other causes to accelerate HCC before or after cirrhosis.

Explains that overlapping oncogenic pathways from obesity and chronic liver disease may account for HCC's rising incidence in developed countries, and argues that understanding this process will improve cancer prevention, prediction, and surveillance.

Final sentence fragment containing the publisher attribution (Elsevier Inc.), closing the abstract's discussion of cancer prevention, prediction, and surveillance; it carries no substantive content beyond that.
Opening of a review on coffee's health effects: introduces coffee as the top US beverage after water and main caffeine source, and notes its many bioactive compounds beyond caffeine.
Continues the overview with cardiometabolic effects: coffee may lower risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, obesity, and depression, but may worsen lipid profiles depending on preparation.

Summarizes cardiovascular evidence: habitual coffee intake is neutral to beneficial for coronary heart disease, heart failure, arrhythmias, and stroke, and is linked to lower CV and all-cause mortality.
Lists further potential benefits (neurodegenerative disease, asthma control, some GI diseases) and states that about 2 to 3 cups daily appears safe with mostly neutral to beneficial outcomes.
Caveats the evidence: findings are mostly observational with few randomized trials, association does not prove causation, and benefits must be weighed against risks.
Describes risks, mainly from caffeine (anxiety, insomnia, tremulousness, palpitations, bone loss, possible fractures), followed by the copyright notice for the source article.
Final fragment of the copyright notice (American College of Cardiology Foundation / Elsevier, all rights reserved); contains no substantive content.

Opening of the abstract for a randomized controlled trial on coffee consumption in chronic hepatitis C; introduces the background (coffee linked to lower hepatocellular carcinoma risk) and the study design (40 patients randomized to 4 cups/day for 30 days vs coffee abstinence, then crossed over).

Baseline results from the hepatitis C coffee trial: AST and ALT were lower in the higher-coffee group (Group B) than the low-coffee group (Group A), and HCV-RNA viral load was significantly higher in Group B.

Key outcome results of the coffee and hepatitis C trial: during coffee intake, oxidative damage marker 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine and collagen levels were significantly lower than during abstinence, with statistics reported.

Telomere findings and conclusion of the coffee hepatitis C trial: telomere length was higher during coffee intake and inversely correlated with 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine, and the authors conclude coffee reduces oxidative damage linked to telomere length and apoptosis, lowering collagen synthesis and possibly mediating protection against disease progression.

Concluding mechanistic statement and copyright notice for the coffee and chronic hepatitis C randomized trial abstract, including the publisher attribution (Editrice Gastroenterologica Italiana and Elsevier) and rights statement.
Final fragment of the copyright statement at the end of the coffee and chronic hepatitis C trial abstract, reading 'rights reserved.'

Introduces HCC surveillance and diagnostic workup: cirrhotic patients get semiannual ultrasound (± AFP), and positive results prompt contrast-enhanced MRI or 4-phase CT; treatment options exist for most tumor stages but must be individualized.

Covers treatment individualization based on liver dysfunction and performance status, recommends a multidisciplinary care approach, and states the review's aim: summarizing HCC diagnosis and management.
Closing fragment stating the review's aim to summarize HCC diagnosis and management, followed by the 2014 Elsevier copyright notice.
Abstract opening of a meta-analysis on coffee consumption and liver cancer risk, covering background, and the search methods (Medline, EMBASE, Web of Science, Cochrane; studies to May 2012).

Meta-analysis results: the pooled summary odds ratio for high versus no/almost never coffee drinkers (OR 0.50) with heterogeneity statistics (Q, P, I²), and the number of case–control and cohort studies included.
Subgroup results of the coffee–liver cancer meta-analysis: ORs by study design (case–control vs cohort), by sex (males vs females), and by region (Asian vs European studies).

Final results on adjustment for prior liver disease (unadjusted vs adjusted ORs), followed by the conclusion that coffee intake is inversely associated with liver cancer and that more prospective studies are needed.
Closing sentence of the conclusions, noting that the small number of included studies calls for further prospective research on coffee and liver cancer.

Abstract opening (Aims and Methods start) of a study on coffee intake, alcohol consumption, and serum GGT activity, describing the rationale and the national cross-sectional survey population of 18,899 adults.

Methods and start of Results from the same GGT-coffee-alcohol study: sample size by sex (8807 men, 10,092 women), age range, survey design, and covariates (BMI, smoking index, age) adjusted in analyses.

Results section of the coffee-GGT study giving the distribution of coffee drinkers and alcohol drinker categories, and the finding that in men coffee over 4 cups/day reduced heavy-drinking-induced GGT elevation.

Key findings and conclusion of the study: the coffee-associated reduction in heavy-drinking GGT was significant in men but only a non-significant trend in women, concluding coffee modulates ethanol's effect on GGT in a dose- and gender-dependent way.
Final sentence of the abstract's conclusion, stating the findings bear on research into coffee's possible hepatoprotective effects in people who drink alcohol.

Background and rationale of a study on coffee intake and liver disease: prior Asian prospective evidence linking coffee to lower liver cancer and chronic liver disease risk, the gap in Western populations, and the unknown effect of brewing method.

Study population and design: 27,037 Finnish male smokers aged 50–69 from the ATBC Cancer Prevention Study, with coffee consumption recorded and up to 24 years of follow-up for liver cancer or chronic liver disease mortality.

Methods for analysis: multivariate relative risks and 95% confidence intervals estimated with Cox proportional hazards models, followed by the start of the results section on coffee intake and liver outcomes.

Main results: inverse associations of coffee intake with incident liver cancer (RR 0.82 per cup/day) and chronic liver disease mortality (RR 0.55), with P-trend values, and robustness across diabetes and HBV/HCV-negative subgroups.

Subgroup robustness and conclusion: inverse associations held across age, BMI, alcohol and smoking strata and for boiled or filtered coffee, leading to the conclusion that coffee may benefit the liver regardless of preparation method.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that coffee's liver benefits apply whether it was boiled or filtered.

Introduces the meta-analysis of coffee consumption and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk, describing the background, aims, and the PubMed/MEDLINE literature search methods (1966 to September 2012, case-control and cohort studies).

Continues the methods, explaining how summary relative risks were calculated for any, low, and high coffee consumption versus none, and the cups-per-day cut-offs (3 cups in 9 studies, 1 cup in 5 studies) used to define low versus high intake.
Reports the main results: the pooled RR of 0.60 for any coffee consumption across 16 studies (3153 HCC cases), with separate estimates for case-control (0.56) and cohort (0.64) studies.

Presents dose-response findings: summary RRs of 0.72 for low and 0.44 for high consumption versus none, 0.80 per additional daily cup, and consistency of the inverse association across sex, alcohol use, and hepatitis or liver disease history.

Gives the conclusions: coffee is associated with a 40% reduced HCC risk, the association may partly reflect reduced coffee intake by patients with liver and digestive diseases, and coffee may protect via effects on liver enzymes and cirrhosis.

Concludes the abstract with the proposed protective mechanism of coffee against liver carcinogenesis through effects on cirrhosis and liver enzymes, followed by the 2013 AGA Institute copyright notice.

Introduction and methods of a 2003 NEJM cohort study on body-mass index and cancer mortality: over 900,000 U.S. adults free of cancer at 1982 enrollment, with 57,145 cancer deaths over 16 years of follow-up, analyzed using proportional-hazards models.

Methods continued: BMI in 1982 is related to death from all cancers and site-specific cancers via multivariate proportional-hazards models, and the population attributable fraction of cancer deaths due to overweight and obesity is estimated using national prevalence data.
Start of the results section defining obesity as BMI of at least 40 (kg/m^2), the heaviest group in the cohort, whose cancer death rates are compared with those of normal-weight men and women.

Key quantitative findings: heaviest men had 52% higher and heaviest women 62% higher all-cancer death rates than normal-weight peers, with relative risks of 1.52 (men) and 1.62 (women) and their 95% confidence intervals.

Site-specific results: higher BMI was significantly associated with cancer deaths of the esophagus, colon and rectum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and kidney, plus non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and multiple myeloma, in both sexes.

Sex-specific site trends: increasing risk with higher BMI for stomach and prostate cancer in men and breast, uterus, cervix, and ovary cancer in women, followed by the estimate of the cancer death fraction attributable to excess weight.

Attributable-risk estimate (14% of cancer deaths in men and 20% in women due to overweight and obesity) and the conclusion that increased body weight is linked to higher death rates for all cancers combined and many specific sites, with copyright notice.
Trailing copyright fragment of the document (Copyright 2003 Massachusetts Medical Society), containing no substantive content.

Opening chunk of a Tromsø Heart Study abstract on gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) levels in a Norwegian general population, introducing the sample sizes, age ranges, and GGT distribution medians and the low proportion with elevated GGT.

Middle section of the Tromsø Heart Study GGT abstract, linking the low GGT levels to Norway's low cirrhosis mortality and modest alcohol use, and reporting multiple regression findings on predictors such as body mass index, alcohol, coffee, triglycerides, and fasting time.

Closing sentence of the Tromsø Heart Study GGT abstract, summarizing the regression findings on serum triglycerides and time since last meal, and noting the positive association between oral contraceptive use and GGT in women.

Introduction to a 2010 Movement Disorder Society meta-analysis on worldwide essential tremor prevalence, stating the study's aims: review population-based studies, derive a precise prevalence estimate, and examine differences across studies.

Presents the core quantitative results: 28 population-based studies across 19 countries, pooled all-ages prevalence of 0.9% with very high heterogeneity (I2 = 99%), and a crude all-ages prevalence of 0.4%.

Reports age-related findings: prevalence rises sharply with age, reaching 4.6% in the meta-analysis for those 65 and older, a median crude 6.3% at age 60-65 and above, and 21.7% in one study of people aged 95 and older.

Summarizes secondary findings on ethnic and gender differences in essential tremor prevalence, most studies showing higher rates in men, and notes the interest this raises given links between essential tremor and Parkinson's disease.
Explains the importance of precise prevalence estimates for public health planning, background disease occurrence in family studies, and clues about environmental or biological mechanisms.
Closing fragment of the abstract containing the final clause about environmental or biological factors and the copyright notice (c) 2010 Movement Disorder Society.

Introduces the study's background: beta-carbolines (norharman, harman) as possible neurotoxins in Parkinson's disease, given their structural similarity to MPTP and their formation in vivo from indoleamines and aldehydes.
Describes the study design and main finding: CSF harman and norharman were measured in 14 PD patients versus 14 age- and sex-matched controls, with significantly higher levels in the PD group.
Interprets the findings: elevated beta-carbolines may play a role in the pathophysiology of PD, but the source of the increase is unclear, with possible endogenous metabolic causes discussed.
Concludes the discussion by offering the alternative explanation that exogenous sources could account for the elevated harman and norharman levels in PD.

Introduction of a study on blood harmane levels in essential tremor, establishing ET background, harmane as a tremor-producing neurotoxin, and the prior cross-sectional evidence of elevated levels in cases.

Rationale for the study: prior harmane findings were single-timepoint, so no prior work repeat-measured blood harmane in the same subjects; the study aims to test whether the case-control difference persists at a second time point.
Methods: blood harmane was measured by HPLC in 63 ET cases and 70 controls, with about 6 years between the initial and follow-up measurements.

Results: mean log blood harmane was significantly higher in cases than controls (0.30 vs 0.08 g-10/ml), median in cases was double that of controls (0.22 vs 0.11), and highest levels appeared in cases with a family history of ET.
Conclusion: elevated blood harmane in ET cases persisted at the second time point years later, suggesting a stable association between this environmental toxin and essential tremor.

Introduction and methods of a case-control study on whether caffeine (coffee and tea) intake is associated with essential tremor, using a standardized questionnaire and multivariate logistic regression.

Methods continued and results start: 179 subjects (79 essential tremor patients, 100 age-, gender-, and ethnicity-matched controls) were analyzed; univariate analysis begins showing higher caffeine consumption in patients.

Key results: patients had higher caffeine intake than controls in univariate analysis (p=0.01), but after multivariate logistic regression caffeine was no longer significant (p=0.119); caffeine was also tested against disease duration and tremor score.

Remaining results show no significant correlation between caffeine intake and disease duration or total tremor score in patients, followed by the conclusion that caffeine was not associated with ET risk.
Final sentence of the abstract's conclusion, calling for further studies on gene-environment interaction in essential tremor.
Introduction to the study: defines harmane as a neurotoxic heterocyclic amine (HCA), notes dietary exposure via cooked meat as the main exogenous source, and states the three research goals.
Study design: describes the 30 barbecued/grilled meat samples (beef steak, hamburger, chicken) and lists the four comparison HCAs analyzed alongside harmane (PhIP, MeIQx, DiMeIQx, IFP).
Key quantitative results: reports mean harmane concentration across all samples (5.63 ng/g) and shows chicken had the highest level, with beef steak the lowest.
Comparative findings: harmane exceeded the other HCAs and correlated significantly with PhIP; it also related to doneness in beef steak and hamburger, with a weaker link than PhIP.
Conclusions on abundance and doneness: harmane was detected at nanogram-per-gram levels, was more abundant than other HCAs, and showed only a modest correlation with doneness compared to PhIP.
Closing implications: the weaker-than-PhIP doneness correlation is restated, and the authors state the data can refine estimates of human dietary exposure to harmane.

Introduction to the study of norharman and harman, two beta-carboline alkaloids in foods and tobacco smoke, describing the analytical methods (solid-phase extraction, HPLC-fluorescence) used to measure their occurrence and estimate exposure.

Results on variability of beta-carboline levels: low-processed foods such as milk, yoghurt, and uncooked meat and fish had no detectable norharman or harman, while processed foods varied by processing conditions.

Specific food sources with the highest beta-carboline concentrations, including brewed coffee, sauces such as soy sauce and Tabasco, and well-done cooked meat and fish, with reported concentration ranges.

Further high-level sources: toasted bread, fermented alcoholic beverages, and cigarette mainstream smoke (207-2780 ng per cigarette), which is highlighted as a major contributor to daily beta-carboline exposure.

Overall conclusion on daily human exposure to beta-carbolines (tens to hundreds of micrograms), ranking the major contributors: cigarette smoke, coffee, seasonings, cooked foods, and alcoholic beverages, with minor contributions from other foods.
Closing statement that foods and tobacco smoke may be potential sources of the endogenous beta-carboline presence found in humans.
Introduction and background of a study on essential tremor (ET), introducing harmane as a tremor-producing neurotoxin and the hypothesis that meat intake and meat doneness are higher in ET cases.

Methods (Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory Meat Questionnaire) and initial results comparing total current meat consumption in men and women with versus without essential tremor, showing a significant difference only in men.

Adjusted logistic regression results in males linking higher total meat consumption to essential tremor (OR = 1.006 per g/day), plus the quartile analysis start showing higher odds of ET in the highest meat consumption quartile.

Remaining results on the highest-vs-lowest meat consumption quartile (adjusted OR = 21.36), finding that meat doneness did not differ between cases and controls, and the conclusion that male ET cases show a dietary difference warranting further study.
Final fragment of the document: the end of the conclusion and the copyright notice (2008 S. Karger AG, Basel) for the essential tremor dietary epidemiology study.
Introduction to the review: essential tremor's unclear etiology, the likely roles of genetic susceptibility and environmental factors, and harmane as a tremor-producing neurotoxin linked to ET.

Summary of the epidemiological evidence so far: two New York studies found higher blood harmane in ET cases than controls, with especially high levels in familial cases, and replication outside New York and brain harmane studies are still lacking.

Gaps in the field: few studies have examined biological correlates of harmane exposure in ET patients, and the mechanisms behind elevated harmane are being investigated, beginning with dietary intake.

Proposed mechanisms for elevated harmane in ET: weak evidence for greater exogenous dietary intake in male ET cases, and initial evidence for a hereditarily reduced capacity to metabolize harmane to harmine.
Concluding assessment: the harmane-ET association is intriguing, but further studies are needed to confirm whether these toxic exposures are causally and etiologically important in essential tremor.

Introduces the study's purpose and method: quantifying co-mutagenic beta-carbolines norharman and harman in six Japanese cigarette brands' smoke condensates and 13 cooked foods via blue cotton treatment and HPLC.
Reports the measured concentration ranges of norharman and harman in mainstream and sidestream cigarette smoke (per cigarette) and in cooked foods (per gram).
Concludes that beta-carboline levels greatly exceed those of mutagenic heterocyclic amines (HCAs), implying greater everyday human exposure to norharman and harman than to HCAs.

Introduces MPTP and its selective toxicity to nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons in primates and humans, noting species differences in potency and the role of metabolism to MPP+ in determining susceptibility.

Describes the role of MAO-B in converting MPTP to MPP+, contrasting its function as a barrier at rat brain microvessels with its importance in primate astrocytes for bioactivating MPTP into the toxic metabolite.

Explains how MPP+ is taken up by catecholamine transporters and concentrated in dopaminergic neurons, and summarizes proposed mechanisms of its toxicity involving mitochondrial inhibition, free radicals, and calcium release.

Concludes that the discovery of this toxin, which produces an animal model of Parkinson's disease, has spurred research into environmental causes of the disorder and new therapeutic testing approaches.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence, completing the statement that the toxin provides a means for assessing new approaches to Parkinson's disease therapy.

Introduction of an essential tremor (ET) case-control study on blood harmane, a tremor-producing neurotoxin and co-mutagen, stating the objective of comparing cancer prevalence between ET cases and controls, and the initial result that 24.7% of ET cases versus 16.6% of controls had cancer.

Results section of the ET cancer study: adjusted odds ratio of 1.52 for cancer in ET cases (p = 0.04), colon cancer more prevalent in ET cases (2.6% vs 0.6%), and log blood harmane concentrations higher in ET cases than controls and in participants with cancer than without.

Concluding part of the ET harmane study: blood harmane was highest in ET cases with cancer relative to other groups (p = 0.009), and the Discussion calls for further research into the links between ET, cancer, and high blood harmane.

Background and objective of a pilot study on essential tremor (ET): reduced cerebellar NAA/tCr on proton MRSI indicates neuronal dysfunction, and blood harmane (a dietary tremor-producing neurotoxin) is reportedly elevated in ET.

Study objective and methods: twelve ET patients underwent 1H MRSI, with the cerebellar cortex as the primary region of interest and central cerebellar white matter, vermis, thalamus, and basal ganglia as secondary regions; blood harmane and lead were measured.
Results begin: mean cerebellar NAA/tCr was 1.52 ± 0.41, and in a regression adjusted for age and gender, log blood harmane was a predictor of cerebellar NAA/tCr.

Key quantitative finding: log blood harmane predicted lower cerebellar NAA/tCr (beta = -0.41, p = 0.009; each unit increase in log harmane linked to a 0.41 unit decrease), and the association was limited to the cerebellar cortex, not secondary regions.

Specificity and conclusion: the harmane association was specific and not seen with lead, supporting an emerging link between harmane and ET, with the authors calling for further work on cerebellar harmane and pathology.
Closing sentence of the conclusion recommending postmortem studies of ET brains to test whether cerebellar harmane concentrations relate to cerebellar pathology.

Introduction to the document on beta-carboline exposure: defines norharman and harman, their links to diseases (Parkinson's, tremor, addiction, cancer), endogenous formation and dietary sources like fried meat/fish, meat extracts, alcohol and coffee.
Dietary and plant sources of norharman and harman, with tobacco smoke named as a major source, plus estimated maximum daily dietary exposure of 4 µg/kg bw norharman and 1 µg/kg bw harman.
Tobacco smoke exposure estimates per cigarette package (1.1 µg/kg bw norharman, 0.6 µg/kg bw harman) and toxicokinetics showing rapid plasma rise and high bioavailability after inhalation.
Oral versus sublingual bioavailability of beta-carbolines and endogenous formation rates (about 50-100 ng/kg bw/day norharman, about 20 ng/kg bw/day harman), which may rise with precursor intake.

Biomarker studies reporting elevated plasma norharman/harman in diseased patients, alcoholics, smokers and people eating beta-carboline-rich food, identifying cigarette smoking as the major influence.
Concluding point that cigarette smoking is the main influence on beta-carboline exposure, while dietary exposure may also contribute.

Case report on chronic parkinsonism after intravenous use of an illicit drug; the injected substance was found to be mainly MPTP with trace MPPP, a meperidine-analog synthesis byproduct, introducing the four patients and the analysis of the substance.

Concluding part of the same report: based on the severe parkinsonian features in the patients and pathology from one prior case, the authors propose that MPTP selectively damages substantia nigra cells.

Introduction of the study: background on tremor prevalence and environmental causes, describing harmane and lead as separate tremor-producing neurotoxicants and stating the study's hypothesis about combined effects.

Study objective and methods: tests whether tremor is especially severe when blood harmane and lead are both high, and describes blood measurements in 257 participants (106 essential tremor cases, 151 controls) from an environmental epidemiology study.

Key results on tremor severity: the total tremor score (0-36) spanned the full range, and blood harmane and blood lead each showed a significant correlation with total tremor score (p = 0.007 and p = 0.045).

Combined-exposure results: mean tremor scores rose across groups, from lowest with both toxicants low (8.4), to intermediate with either high (10.5), to highest with both high (13.7), with overall p = 0.01.

Conclusions: harmane and lead separately correlate with tremor scores, and co-exposure yields the highest scores, suggesting an additive effect; the authors stress that identifying environmental determinants matters for primary prevention given high tremor prevalence.

Closing sentence of the paper's conclusion: emphasizes that because tremor disorders are very common in the population, finding environmental causes is important for preventing disease before it starts.

Opening of the study abstract: objective, cohort design, follow-up definition (interview date to death or censoring on 31 Dec 2008), and the list of collected variables such as cooking frequency and nutrition knowledge.

Continuation of the methods: linkage to death records, Cox proportional-hazards analysis of cooking frequency and death 1999-2008, and the setting as the Elderly Nutrition and Health Survey in Taiwan, 1999-2000.

Study population and early results: nationally representative free-living Taiwanese adults aged 65+ (n=1888), 695 deaths over 10 years, and the demographic and lifestyle profile of people who cooked most often.

Main survival finding: highly frequent cooking (>5 times/week vs never) was associated with lower mortality, HR 0.47 unadjusted, with diet and other behavioural correlates of frequent cooks described.

Adjusted results and sex differences: HR 0.59 after adjusting for physical function, cognition and nutrition knowledge; women gained a larger mortality reduction (51% vs 24%) from frequent cooking; a 2-year lag gave similar results.
Conclusions: cooking behaviour is favourably associated with survival in elderly Taiwanese, with the protective effect of frequent cooking appearing greater for women than men.

Study design and setting: a 2010 cross-sectional study of UK television chef recipes and supermarket ready meals, compared against WHO and UK FSA nutritional guidelines (Christmas 2012 research article).

Study sample and outcomes: 100 main meal recipes from five bestselling UK TV chef cookbooks and 100 own-brand ready meals from the three leading UK supermarkets, measured for WHO compliance and FSA traffic-light classification.
Key results part 1: no meal fully met WHO recommendations; ready meals complied more often for carbohydrate energy, sugars and fibre density, with percentages and P-values given.

Key results part 2: recipes complied more often for sodium density (salt for seasoning not assessed), and traffic-light distributions differed, with red modal for recipes and green modal for ready meals.

Per-portion nutrient results: recipes contained significantly more energy, protein, fat and saturated fat and less fibre than ready meals, with specific mean values; the conclusions section begins here.
Conclusions: neither TV chef recipes nor supermarket ready meals met WHO recommendations, and recipes were less healthy than ready meals overall.
Closing conclusion fragment: recipes had more saturated fat and less fibre per portion than ready meals, ending the study's conclusion statement.

Abstract opening of the study on US children's energy intake by eating location (home vs. away-from-home), stating the research gap, objective, and the survey datasets and sample of 29,217 children aged 2–18.

Continuation of the Subjects and Methods sections: names the specific national surveys used (1977–78 NFCS, 1989–1998 CSFII, 2003–2006 NHANES) and describes the weighted nationally representative trend analysis of energy intake by eating location.

Methods details on statistical analysis (weighted percentages and means, t-tests, 1977–2006 trends, food source comparisons from 1994–2006, stratified by three age groups), followed by the start of the Results on rising child energy intake and away-from-home eating.

Key results: children's daily calorie increase of 179 kcal/d over 1977–2006 was driven by away-from-home eating (+255 kcal/d), whose share rose from 23.4% to 33.9%, plateauing after 1994 while fast food overtook school food as the leading away-from-home source.

Further results on food sources: stores became the largest source of away-from-home calories, and fast food eaten at home and store-bought away-from-home food rose significantly, followed by the start of the Conclusion.

Conclusion stating that eating location and food source significantly affect children's energy intake and that away-from-home foods (fast food and store-prepared food) drive rising calorie intake, with a caveat about needing further research.

Final sentence of the conclusion calling for alternative data sources to verify whether store-bought away-from-home foods are increasingly store-prepared, a limitation noted in the study's findings on food sourcing.

Introduction to a literature review on food, cooking skills, and health in North America; it establishes the major shift in food practices and the gaps in research on how these practices affect health inequalities, previewing the cooking and cooking-skills discussion.

Continues the overview by introducing the review's core topics: ambiguous cooking-related terminology, the links between food choice, cooking, and health, and economic factors driving health inequalities, plus the role of the wider food system.

Closing portion of the overview, stating that the wider food system matters for food choice and cooking skills, that research gaps and future directions are examined, and that cooking practices are understudied yet central to nutritional health.
Final sentence of the overview, summarizing that cooking practices are important to understanding human nutritional health across cultural, environmental, and economic factors.

Opening of the abstract for a literature review of adult cooking/home food preparation interventions: states the rationale (growing popularity, no extensive review of overall impact), the review aim, and the design, followed by the start of the main outcome measures.

Methods section of the abstract: lists the outcome measures (dietary intake, knowledge/skills, cooking attitudes, self-efficacy, health) and describes the search of OVID MEDLINE, Agricola and Web of Science for cooking-focused intervention studies from 1980 to 2011.

Methods and early results of the abstract: describes the validity coding of studies and reports that of 28 studies identified, 12 had a control group (six non-randomized, six randomized controlled trials).

Results and interpretation of the abstract: reports timing of evaluations (post-only for five, pre/post for 23, beyond post-intervention for 15), positive qualitative and quantitative findings, and limitations such as weak designs, varied populations and non-validated tools.

Conclusion of the abstract: summarizes the limitations on stronger conclusions and calls for well-designed, rigorous studies assessing long-term effects on cooking behavior, dietary intake, obesity and other health outcomes.

Abstract (Objectives and Methods) of a study on how 2008 recession-era state unemployment affected home cooking and away-from-home eating among low-income and minority US adults, using American Time Use Study data.
Abstract (Methods and early Results) describing the multinomial and log binomial regression analyses by gender and the finding that high state unemployment produced only trivial increases in cooking.

Abstract (Results and Conclusions) reporting virtually no change in away-from-home eating, no disproportionate recession impact on low-income or minority groups, and the conclusion that US adults resist food behavior change.

Closing sentence of the abstract's Conclusions calling for further research into whether food behavior reluctance stems from time limits, lack of cooking skill or knowledge, or limited access to fresh produce and raw ingredients.

Introduction and aims of a study on heat-processed orange-fleshed sweet potato (OFSP): examines how traditional heat processing affects the microstructure and in vitro beta-carotene bioaccessibility, using simulated digestion.

Methods and results on beta-carotene bioaccessibility: simulated in vitro digestion with membrane filtration to isolate the micellar fraction; processing lowers all-trans-beta-carotene, raises 13-cis isomer, and significantly increases bioaccessibility over raw OFSP.
Key findings ranking bioaccessibility by processing method (raw < baked < steamed/boiled < deep fried) and light microscopy evidence that heat processing disrupts OFSP tissue and sloughs cell walls.
Conclusion of the OFSP beta-carotene study: heat processing improves beta-carotene bioaccessibility, likely because processing disrupts the tissue microstructure.

Introduction and aim of a study on orange-fleshed sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) biofortification in Brazil, evaluating carotenoids, phenolics, and antioxidant capacity in raw and heat-processed roots.

Methods and key raw-root results: HPLC, Folin-Ciocalteu, DPPH and ABTS assays used; all cultivars high in carotenoids, mainly all-trans-β-carotene (79.1-128.5 mg/100 g DW), implying high vitamin A activity.

Cultivar comparison and heat-treatment effects: CNPH 1194 had highest carotenoids; total phenolics ranged 0.96-2.05 mg/g DW; heat treatments mostly decreased carotenoids, phenolics and antioxidant capacity.

Processing effects and conclusions: flour processing caused the greatest losses of major carotenoids and phenolics, phenolics were more stable than carotenoids, and significant correlations existed between carotenoids, phenolics and antioxidant capacity.
Concluding fragment of the abstract's final sentence, stating that carotenoids and phenolic compounds were significantly correlated with antioxidant capacity.

Abstract of a study on sweet potato protein (SPP) effects on human colorectal cancer; this opening chunk covers the aim and the methods (MTT, Hoechst staining, transwell assays on SW480 cells, plus in vivo xenograft and lung metastasis models).

Methods continuation from the abstract: describes the in vivo models, HCT-8 cells xenografted intraperitoneally in nude mice and spontaneous lung metastasis of Lewis lung carcinoma 3LL cells in C57BL/6 mice, after the in vitro SW480 methods.

Results section start of the sweet potato protein colorectal cancer abstract: SPP dose-dependently inhibits SW480 proliferation (IC50 38.732 μmol/L in MTT assay) and Hoechst staining shows reduced viability and apoptosis.
Results on migration and invasion: transwell assays show SPP significantly reduced migrated cells at 8 μmol/L and invaded cells at 0.8 μmol/L in SW480 colorectal cancer cells versus controls.

In vivo xenograft results: intraperitoneal and intragastric SPP suppressed growth of HCT-8 colorectal tumors in nude mice to 58.0% and 43.5% of controls after 9 days, and ip trypsin inhibitor made bloody ascites disappear.

In vivo metastasis results: intragastric and intraperitoneal SPP significantly reduced spontaneous pulmonary metastatic nodules of Lewis lung carcinoma 3LL cells in C57BL/6 mice after 25 days of treatment.
