Final results and conclusion of the sweet potato protein study: ip SPP reduced primary tumor weight in mice, and the conclusion states SPP has antiproliferative and antimetastatic effects on colorectal cancer cells in vitro and in vivo.

Introduction and methods overview of a study on how baking and boiling affect nutritional and antioxidant properties of three Turkish sweet potato cultivars (Beniazuma, Koganesengan, Kotobuki), covering proximate composition, phenolics, ascorbic acid, β-carotene, antiradical activity, and free sugars.

Results on proximate composition and bioactive compounds: dry matter, protein, and starch changed significantly with treatment while ash and crude fiber did not; β-carotene decreased after baking/boiling whereas total phenolics and ascorbic acid increased versus fresh samples.

Results on antioxidant activity and sugars: antiradical activity generally rose with baking and boiling; sucrose, glucose, and fructose were found in fresh sweet potatoes, while maltose appeared in treated samples.
Concluding finding that the analyzed parameters showed no explicit differences among the three sweet potato cultivars.

Introduction and background of a study on anthocyanin-enriched purple-fleshed sweet potato clone P40 and its anti-cancer potential against colorectal cancer, noting low anthocyanin content in staple foods and undefined mechanisms.

Results on P40's composition (high total phenolics, antioxidant capacity, 7.5 mg/g dry matter anthocyanins) and in vitro effects on SW480 human colon cancer cells, where P40 extracts at 0-40 μM peonidin-3-glucoside equivalent reduced cell number.
Findings that P40 extracts cause G1 cell cycle arrest (cytostatic, not cytotoxic) in SW480 cells, and that dietary P40 at 10-30% suppresses azoxymethane-induced aberrant crypt foci in CF-1 mice.

In vivo mechanistic results in mouse colon mucosa showing reduced proliferation marker PCNA and increased apoptosis marker caspase-3, followed by the conclusion that P40 may protect against colorectal cancer via cell cycle arrest, anti-proliferative, and apoptotic effects.
Final sentence of the conclusion summarizing that anthocyanin-enriched sweet potato P40 may protect against colorectal cancer through cell cycle arrest, anti-proliferative, and apoptotic mechanisms.

Introduces the study's aim: examining acrylamide precursors (reducing sugars, amino acids) in sweet potato chips and comparing four frying oils (palm olein, coconut, canola, soybean) for their effect on acrylamide formation.
Reports the main quantitative finding that chips fried in less unsaturated oils had lower acrylamide (1443 μg/kg) than those fried in more unsaturated oils (2019 μg/kg).

Gives the measured precursor levels in sweet potato roots (glucose 4.17 mg/g, fructose 5.05 mg/g, free asparagine 1.63 mg/g) and concludes that frying oil type and conditions significantly affect acrylamide formation, with lipids playing a non-negligible role.
Closing copyright line from the Institute of Food Technologists (2013) for the sweet potato chip acrylamide study.

Introduction of a case-control study on diet and gallbladder cancer, stating the rationale: gallbladder cancer is rare and fatal, with gallstones and obesity as suspected risk factors that diet influences.

Methods of the case-control study comparing 64 gallbladder cancer cases with 101 gallstone cases, using a dietary recall questionnaire tailored to local eating habits and calculating odds ratios with 95% CIs.
Results showing statistically significant protective odds ratios for specific vegetables (radish, green chilli, sweet potato) and fruits (mango, orange, melon, papaya) against gallbladder cancer.

Results describing non-significant reductions in odds for cruciferous vegetables, beans, onion and turnip, and the start of findings on items associated with increased odds (capsicum, beef, tea, red chilli, mutton), which were not statistically significant.

Remaining non-significant risk findings for capsicum, beef, tea, red chilli and mutton, followed by the study's conclusion that vegetables and fruits are protective while red meat (beef and mutton) is linked to higher gallbladder cancer risk.
Final concluding sentence of the abstract: vegetables and fruits show a protective effect, whereas red meat (beef and mutton) is associated with increased risk of gallbladder cancer.
Introduction and study aim: proposes nutrient-based affordability metrics for vegetables (USDA data), arguing that price per gram or per calorie misrepresents healthful vegetables' cost.

Methods, part 1: defines nutrient density via the Nutrient Rich Foods (NRF) index, listing nine nutrients to encourage (protein, fiber, vitamins A/C/E, calcium, iron, magnesium, potassium) and three to limit (saturated fat, added sugar, sodium).

Methods and results, part 1: cost calculation units (per 100 g, per 100 kcal, per serving, per nutrient) and ANOVA-based significance testing; results begin, naming tomato juices/soups, dark green and deep yellow vegetables as highest in NRF scores.

Results, part 2: vegetables with highest NRF per dollar (sweet potatoes, white potatoes, tomato juice/soup, carrots, broccoli) and the finding that frequently eaten tomato sauces, raw tomatoes, and potato chips are less nutrient-efficient than alternatives.

Conclusions: the NRF-per-cost measures can guide foodservice and health professionals, and processed vegetables such as soups and juices can improve diet quality and affordability; includes copyright notice.
Publication copyright and rights statement (2013 Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Elsevier), the document's closing boilerplate.

Introduction and stated objectives of a chapter on the sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) in human nutrition: its diets, composition (beta-carotene, anthocyanins), utilization as value-added products, and potential in Africa.

Historical background: sweet potato as a staple food for indigenous populations across the Americas, Ryukyu Islands, Africa, the Caribbean, Maori, Hawaiians, and Papua New Guineans, followed by a note on its high-level objectives.

Nutritional composition: protein content ranges of sweet potato leaves (4.0-27.0%) and roots (1.0-9.0%), and the framing of sweet potato as a source of health-promoting compounds like beta-carotene and anthocyanins.
Functional food and food coloring applications: sweet potato's beta-carotene and anthocyanin content and color-extract stability make it a healthier alternative to synthetic food colorants.

Economic and development value: starch and flour processing from sweet potato creating income and employment for farmers and rural households, adding nutritional value, and repositioning production for value-added uses.
Conclusion and call to action: multidisciplinary research on production, storage, postharvest and processing technologies, and quality of sweet potato and its value-added products needed globally.

Introduces the problem of constipation in hospitalized acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients and states the study's aim: developing and testing the sweet potato/footbath/acupressure (SFA) intervention to prevent constipation and improve bowel-emptying satisfaction.

Describes the design and sample: a prospective randomized controlled trial with 93 ACS patients split into an SFA group (n=44) receiving SFA plus usual care and a usual care group (n=49), and begins listing the reported group differences.

Lists the study's main statistically significant findings between groups: lower constipation incidence, reduced laxative and enema use, higher subjective satisfaction with bowel emptying, and fewer sensations of incomplete evacuation and anorectal obstruction.
Concludes that the SFA intervention was more effective, economical, and practical than usual care alone for managing constipation and improving defecation satisfaction in hospitalized ACS patients.
Opening chunk of a review on sporamin, the major sweet potato tuber storage protein, covering its early history as 'ipomoein' and the first biochemical characterization.

Continues the review's overview of sporamin research: the 1985 purification into fractions A and B, and the protein's gene family, structure, and biological functions including storage, defense, inhibition, and ROS scavenging.

Describes sporamin's classification as a Kunitz-type trypsin inhibitor and its insect-resistance testing in transgenic tobacco and cauliflower, suggesting its multiple functions evolved to support sweet potato growth.

Covers sporamin's expression pattern: constitutive in tuberous roots, absent from stems and leaves, but induced systemically by wounding and abiotic stress, indicating environmentally modulated transcriptional regulation.

Summarizes why sporamin is a useful research model for molecular evolution, regulatory mechanisms, and physiological functions in plants, and states the review's aim of covering agricultural biotechnology approaches.
Closing chunk stating the review's focus on recent approaches and future perspectives in agricultural biotechnology, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Abstract opening (Aim and Methods) of a study on sweet potato protein (SPP) effects on human colorectal cancer cells, introducing the MTT, Hoechst, and transwell assays used for proliferation, migration, and invasion of SW480 cells.

Methods continuation describing the in vivo models: HCT-8 xenografts in nude mice and spontaneous lung metastasis of Lewis lung carcinoma 3LL cells in C57 BL/6 mice, alongside the SW480 in vitro work.
Results start: SPP dose-dependently inhibits SW480 proliferation (IC50 38.732 μmol/L in MTT assay), with Hoechst staining showing reduced viability and apoptosis induction.
Transwell results: SPP significantly reduced SW480 cell migration at 8 μmol/L and invasion through ECMatrix at 0.8 μmol/L, with the reported cell counts and P values versus control.

In vivo xenograft results: intraperitoneal and intragastric SPP reduced HCT-8 tumor growth in nude mice to 58.0% and 43.5% of controls after 9 days, and trypsin inhibitor injection made bloody ascites disappear.

Metastasis results: intraperitoneal and intragastric SPP significantly reduced spontaneous pulmonary metastatic nodules in C57 BL/6 mice after 25 days, and the primary tumor weight decreased in the ip group.
Final tumor weight result and conclusion: SPP shows significant antiproliferative and antimetastatic effects on colorectal cancer cell lines both in vitro and in vivo.

Introduces the paper's core topic: sweet potato products for NASA's Advanced Life Support Program, covering the recipe development and 6–20% dry-weight sweet potato formulations for future lunar/Mars space meals.

Describes the sensory evaluation method (appearance, aroma, texture, flavor, overall acceptability) and the panel of testers at NASA/Johnson Space Center in Houston, TX assessing the vegetarian sweet potato products.
States the vegetarian nature of the products (no animal-origin ingredients except sweet potato pie), and the 9-point hedonic scale used to rate 10 products against commercial controls.
Lists the ten product types tested (pancakes through pretzels) and reports results: all were liked slightly or moderately except sweet potato vegetable patties, which were neutral.
Explains the statistical method (Student t-test for comparing sensory scores with controls) and the final recommendation of these products for a vegetarian menu plan for lunar/Mars missions.
Concludes the recommendation sentence, specifying the menu plan is designed for lunar/Mars space missions.

Abstract of a study on sweet potato trypsin inhibitor (TI) antiproliferative effects on NB4 promyelocytic leukemia cells; introduces the objective and reports dose- and time-dependent growth inhibition with an IC50 of 57.1 µg/mL at 72 h.

Results on NB4 leukemia cells treated with sweet potato trypsin inhibitor: G1 cell cycle arrest by flow cytometry, DNA laddering as evidence of apoptosis, and involvement of p53, Bcl-2, Bax, and cytochrome c, with p53 and Bax accumulating over time.

Mechanistic findings of the sweet potato trypsin inhibitor study on NB4 cells: decreased Bcl-2, cytochrome c release from mitochondria into the cytosol, and apoptosis via a mitochondria-dependent pathway linked to caspase-3 and caspase-8 activation.

Concluding sentence of the abstract on sweet potato trypsin inhibitor in NB4 leukemia cells, summarizing that it induces apoptosis by inhibiting growth and activating the caspase-3 and caspase-8 cascades.
Abstract of a 2004 study on oral bikunin (Kunitz-type protease inhibitor): background, and the mouse methods testing once-daily oral dosing against human ovarian carcinoma HRA cells in nude mice.
Mouse study methods: nude mice randomized to bikunin doses of 3, 10, or 30 µg/g/day by gavage for 7 days versus PBS vehicle control (n=9 per group), with blinded abdominal examination on Day 9.
Mouse study results: serum detection of intact oral bikunin at 3 and 6 hours, declining by 12 hours; highest dose reduced tumor load by 40%; peak tumor uptake of [125I]bikunin at 12 hours.

Mouse safety and conclusions plus the start of the Phase I human trial: no effect on food intake or body weight, first report of oral bikunin activity against ovarian carcinoma, and the Phase I trial design for cervical cancer.

Phase I human trial design: patients with locally advanced uterine cervical carcinoma after definitive treatment received escalating oral bikunin doses (3, 10, 30 mg/kg/day) for 7 days to determine maximum-tolerated dose and safety.

Phase I human trial outcomes: no dose-limiting toxicities, maximum-tolerated dose not defined, and preliminary data on urokinase-type plasminogen activator expression at the highest dose; concluding that oral bikunin was safe and showed biologic activity.
Concluding statement and copyright notice (2004 American Cancer Society) for the study on once-daily oral bikunin, stating it was safe in humans and showed signs of biologic activity.

Abstract opening of a study on how traditional cooking methods (roasting, baking, frying, boiling) affect the glycemic index of ten sweet potato cultivars eaten in Jamaica, tested on ten nondiabetic subjects.

Results from the same Jamaican sweet potato GI study: GI ranges from 41 to 93 overall, with boiled samples lowest (41-50) and baked or roasted samples highest (79-94), showing preparation method matters more than cultivar.

Conclusion of the Jamaican sweet potato GI study: preparation method strongly influences GI more than varietal differences, and boiled sweet potatoes may help blunt postprandial glucose spikes for type 2 diabetes management.

Abstract opening of a 2010 Fundamental and Clinical Pharmacology study introducing sporamin (a sweet potato Kunitz-type trypsin inhibitor) and its aims: testing effects on proliferation, apoptosis, and Akt/GSK-3 signaling in Tca8113 human tongue cancer cells.

Abstract results on sporamin's effects in Tca8113 tongue cancer cells: concentration- and time-dependent inhibition of proliferation and apoptosis induction, with Bax up-regulated, Bcl-2 down-regulated, and Akt/GSK-3 signaling suppressed.

Abstract conclusion of the sporamin/Tca8113 study: decreased phosphorylated Bad and down-regulated Akt/GSK-3 pathway suggest sporamin's antiproliferative effect is partly due to apoptosis induction, followed by the 2010 journal copyright notice.

Final fragment of the copyright line for the 2010 Fundamental and Clinical Pharmacology article on sporamin-induced apoptosis via Akt/GSK-3 down-regulation, naming the publishers Société Française de Pharmacologie et de Thérapeutique.
Opening background and aims of a systematic review on Alzheimer's disease and dementia epidemiology in China (1990-2010), stating the study's goal of improving burden estimates and informing policy.
Methods section describing the literature search of Chinese and English reports on dementia in China (1990-2010) across CNKI, Wanfang, and PubMed databases.

Methods continued: study inclusion and exclusion criteria (internationally accepted case definitions, mainland China only, numerical estimates) and the statistical approach using Poisson regression and UN demographic data to estimate prevalence, incidence, and mortality ratio.
Findings opening: search yield of 12,642 reports, 89 included studies (75 prevalence, 13 incidence, 9 mortality), and total participant counts including 6357 Alzheimer's disease cases.
Findings on participants with other dementia forms and age-specific dementia prevalence estimates for 1990 and 2010, from ages 65-69 to 95-99.
Results on the estimated total numbers of people with dementia (3.68, 5.62, 9.19 million for 1990, 2000, 2010) and Alzheimer's disease (1.93 to 5.69 million) in China.
Incidence results: dementia, Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia, and rare dementia incidence rates per 1000 person-years.
Mortality findings from follow-up of people with dementia versus healthy controls, with the median standardised mortality ratio of 1.94:1, followed by the start of the interpretation section.

Interpretation: previous dementia burden estimates may have underestimated the burden in China, which is rising faster than assumed, and calls for rapid government responses in low- and middle-income countries.
Funding sources for the study, including the Nossal Institute, Chinese national projects, NHMRC fellowship, and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.
Final copyright statement (Elsevier, 2013) closing the abstract.

Opening chunk of an abstract-style commentary on a 1999 update about diet and Alzheimer's disease. It introduces Grant (18) as the first epidemiologic paper linking diet to AD and states the main findings: dietary fat and energy in old age are risk factors, while fish and cereals are protective.

Middle chunk of the same document. It notes that recent epidemiologic studies support the findings and proposes mechanisms: diet affects AD risk via oxidative stress and inflammation, possibly involving series 2 prostaglandins.

Final chunk of the document, the concluding statement. It recommends dietary modifications and supplements that reduce free radical production and inflammation as a meaningful way to lower AD risk with aging.

Opening of the abstract for a study comparing dementia and Alzheimer disease incidence in Yoruba (Ibadan, Nigeria) and African American (Indianapolis) older adults; this chunk covers the background rationale and the study objective.

Describes the design of the Indianapolis-Ibadan Dementia Project: a longitudinal, population-based study with a baseline survey and two follow-up waves using a two-stage in-home screening and diagnostic workup design.
Setting and participants: 2459 dementia-free Yoruba residents of Ibadan and 2147 dementia-free African American residents of Indianapolis, all aged 65+, with mean follow-up of 5.1 and 4.7 years.

Main outcome measures and start of results: age-standardized annual incidence of dementia was significantly lower among Yoruba than African Americans, with the Yoruba dementia rate (1.35%) given with its confidence interval.

Reports the remaining incidence figures: dementia in African Americans (3.24%) and Alzheimer disease incidence in both groups (Yoruba 1.15%, African Americans 2.52%), with confidence intervals, followed by the start of the conclusion.

Conclusion: first report of dementia and AD incidence differences between nonindustrialized and industrialized populations using identical methods and investigators, and a call for research on modifiable environmental or genetic factors.
Final fragment of the abstract's conclusion sentence, ending the reference to Alzheimer disease (AD) incidence differences between the two populations.

Introduction and methods of a Delphi consensus study estimating global dementia prevalence: 12 international experts estimated age-specific prevalence by WHO world region using a systematic review and UN population data.

Methods continued: experts' prevalence estimates by region, sex-combined, in 5-year age bands from 60 to 85+; UN population projections used to count dementia cases in 2001, 2020, and 2040; incidence derived from prevalence, remission, and mortality.

Key findings: about 24.3 million people have dementia worldwide, with 4.6 million new cases yearly (one every 7 seconds), and sparse representative epidemiological data in many regions; the total is projected to double roughly every 20 years to 81.1 million by 2040.

Findings on geographic distribution: most dementia cases are in developing countries (60% in 2001, 71% by 2040); growth is uneven, with developed countries rising about 100% from 2001 to 2040 and India, China, and neighbouring South Asian and Western Pacific countries rising over 300%.
Concluding interpretation: the paper's detailed prevalence estimates are presented as the best available basis for policymaking, health planning, and resource allocation for dementia care.

Introduces the study design: a dementia and animal-product consumption investigation using two Adventist Health Study cohort substudies, the first a matched sample of 272 California residents across 68 age-, sex-, and zip-code-matched quartets including vegans, lacto-ovo-vegetarians, and heavy meat eaters.

Describes the second unmatched substudy of 2,984 Loma Linda, California residents and reports the main matched-cohort result: meat eaters (including poultry and fish) had roughly double the dementia risk of vegetarians (RR 2.18, p=0.065), rising to RR 2.99 (p=0.048) after adjusting for past meat intake.

Reports that the unmatched substudy showed no significant difference in dementia incidence between vegetarians and meat eaters, notes no clear explanation for the discrepancy between substudies, and points to unexpectedly limited statistical power in the unmatched sample to detect effects of heavy meat consumption.

Concludes that vegetarians in both substudies showed a trend toward delayed onset of dementia, summarizing the overall direction of the findings on vegetarian diets and dementia in the Adventist Health Study.

Introduction and stated objective of a study on the nutrition transition, diet, and Alzheimer's disease (AD) prevalence in Japan and developing countries, including background risk factors such as Western diet, obesity, alcohol, and smoking.

Methods overview: two analytic approaches testing whether dietary or other changes explain AD trends, one comparing Japan's AD trends with national dietary supply, alcohol consumption, and lung cancer mortality with 0-25 year lags.

Methods continued (second approach comparing eight developing countries' AD prevalence with dietary supply factors at 0-25 year lags) and the start of the results, which report Japan's correlations with alcohol, animal product, meat, rice supply, and lung cancer.

Results for Japan (strongest correlation at 15-25 year lag) and the eight-country study (total energy and animal fat, 15-20 year lag), plus proposed mechanisms such as obesity and increased cholesterol, saturated fat, and iron from animal products.
Mechanistic explanations for the findings and the conclusion that AD rates will keep rising in non-Western countries unless diet, obesity, and smoking risk factors are addressed.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending the sentence about addressing smoking as a major AD risk factor in non-Western countries.

Introduces the study's objective and design: a community survey in rural Ballabgarh, northern India, of 5,126 adults aged 55+ (73.3% illiterate), screened with Hindi cognitive and functional instruments.

Describes the two-stage sampling: 536 impaired subjects (10.5%) and a random sample of 270 unimpaired controls (5.3%) underwent standardized clinical dementia assessment using DSM-IV, CDR, and NINCDS-ADRDA criteria.
Covers the diagnostic criteria used (DSM-IV, CDR, NINCDS-ADRDA for probable/possible AD) and begins the Results section with the overall dementia prevalence estimate for those aged 55+.
Reports the key prevalence figures: all-cause dementia (CDR ≥0.5) at 0.84% for ages 55+ and 1.36% for ages 65+, and AD at 0.62% for ages 55+, with 95% confidence intervals.
Gives the AD prevalence for ages 65+ (1.07%) and the associations found: prevalence rises significantly with age, with no association with gender or literacy; begins the Conclusions.

States the conclusion that dementia prevalence in this population is low, age-related, and unrelated to gender or literacy, and proposes explanations such as low life expectancy, short survival, and low age-specific incidence.
Final fragment of the Conclusions, completing the comparison to populations with higher dementia prevalence.

Introduces the Honolulu-Asia Aging Study on dementia prevalence in Japanese-American men in Hawaii, covering the study's objective (comparing with Japan and elsewhere) and the Honolulu Heart Program background and 1991-1993 examination design.
Describes the study participants (3734 Japanese-American men aged 71-93, 80% of the surviving cohort, community and institutional) and the standardized cognitive assessment methods used.

Lists the main outcome measures (age-specific, age-standardized, and cohort prevalence of all-cause dementia by two diagnostic criteria and four severity levels, plus Alzheimer and vascular dementia) and begins the results with DSM-III-R dementia prevalence.

Reports key prevalence results: DSM-III-R dementia rising from 2.1% (ages 71-74) to 33.4% (ages 85-93), age-standardized prevalence of 7.6%, and cohort estimates of 9.3% all-cause dementia, 5.4% Alzheimer disease, and 4.2% vascular dementia.

Covers mixed etiology (more than one possible cause in 26% of cases), the Alzheimer disease/vascular dementia ratio of 1.5, and begins the conclusions comparing Alzheimer prevalence with Japan and European-ancestry populations.

Concludes that Alzheimer prevalence is higher than in Japan but similar to European-ancestry groups, vascular dementia is slightly lower than in Japan but higher than in European-ancestry groups, and calls for standardized cross-national research.

Introduces the 6-month study design: a prior 3-month cola study showed sex hormone changes, and this study examines oxidative status and testosterone in testes of adult male Wistar rats exposed to Coca-Cola beverages.

Describes the methods: 50 male Wistar rats split into a water-drinking control group and groups given regular, caffeine-free, Light, or Zero Coca-Cola, with testicular oxidative and carbonyl stress markers, testicular and plasma testosterone, and StAR expression measured.

Reports the main findings: no significant differences between groups in any parameter, with oxidative/carbonyl stress, testicular and plasma testosterone, and testicular StAR steroidogenesis marker unaffected by any Coca-Cola type.
Concludes the abstract with the summary that testosterone and StAR expression were comparable across groups, followed by the 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.

Opening chunk of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics position statement, defining the total diet (overall eating pattern) approach as the most important focus of healthy eating, with moderation, portion size, and physical activity.

Continues the position statement: emphasizes balancing foods and beverages within energy needs rather than single foods or meals, and lists public policies and dietary patterns supporting the total diet approach (Dietary Guidelines, DASH, MyPlate, Let's Move, Nutrition Facts labels, Healthy People 2020, DRIs).

Contrasts the total diet approach with labeling foods as good or bad, which is overly simplistic and can foster unhealthy eating; notes alternative approaches are sometimes needed and begins listing factors influencing eating practices.

Lists the many factors shaping eating practices (taste, weight concerns, physiology, time, environment, economics, media, culture, beliefs) and states that skilled practitioners use behavioral theory and evidence-based strategies to improve nutrition education.

Advises focusing on variety, moderation, and proportionality within a healthy lifestyle rather than specific nutrients or foods, to reduce consumer confusion and unnecessary supplement use, and introduces proactive, practical messaging.

Closing chunk stating that proactive, empowering, practical messages about the total diet promote positive lifestyle change, followed by the 2013 copyright notice from the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and Elsevier Inc.

Opening of the article's background: the 1954 tobacco industry 'Frank Statement' pledging public health concern, and the stated aim to highlight tobacco lessons and recommend actions for the food industry.

Continuation of the introduction stating the article's aims, followed by the Methods section describing a review of tobacco and food industry practices, messages, and strategies for influencing opinion, legislation, litigation, and science.

Findings section describing the tobacco industry's playbook: emphasizing personal responsibility, funding doubt-creating research, dismissing harm findings as 'junk' science, and making self-regulatory pledges.

Continuation of the Findings: the tobacco industry's lobbying, 'safer' product introduction, and denial of addiction and child marketing, plus the statement that the food industry's script is both similar to and different from tobacco's.

Conclusions section: food differs from tobacco in important ways, yet the two industries share significant similarities in responding to concerns that their products cause harm, with obesity as a global problem.
Final conclusion: the world cannot afford to repeat tobacco history, where industry talks about the moral high ground but does not occupy it.

Introduction of the review: prospective epidemiological evidence linking high dietary flavanol (cocoa/chocolate) intake to lower cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, and possible mechanisms including blood pressure, platelets, thrombosis, inflammation, and endothelium.

Introduces brachial artery flow-mediated dilation (FMD) as a robust measure of endothelial function and argues it is a surrogate for hard cardiovascular endpoints, justifying its widespread use in studies.
Notes the large body of FMD research and states that acute and chronic cocoa/chocolate ingestion has been shown in numerous studies to increase FMD in humans.
Describes the dose-dependence of FMD increases after cocoa/chocolate intake and proposes that the mechanism most likely involves increased nitric oxide bioavailability.
Concludes that cocoa/chocolate's positive endothelial effects may mechanistically explain reduced cardiovascular risk, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction of a study on antioxidant capacity of cocoa and chocolate products, noting that chocolate's antioxidant claims differ from natural cocoa sources due to processing, and consumers overlook antioxidant value.
Study methods: antioxidant capacity and total phenolic content measured for cocoa nibs, cocoa masses, and chocolate bars of varying cocoa percentages and origins, using DPPH and FRAP assays.
Methods and key finding that cocoa masses show higher antioxidant power than nibs, attributed to the lipid (cocoa butter) fraction remaining in nibs; Folin-Ciocalteu used for total phenolics.
Investigation of milk, whey, and soy protein effects, and results identifying 100% cocoa extra dark bar as highest in polyphenols and DPPH/FRAP antioxidant capacity.
Conclusion naming organic dark 80%, Tanzania 80%, and Trinidad 80% bars as well performing, and stating cocoa products have higher antiradical activity than many antioxidant supplement tablets.

Background on dark chocolate's antioxidant properties and the role of endothelial dysfunction, platelet activation, and oxidative stress in atherosclerosis, especially graft atherosclerosis in transplanted hearts; introduces the rationale for flavonoid-rich dark chocolate.
Study methods: a double-blind randomized trial in 22 heart transplant recipients comparing flavonoid-rich dark chocolate with cocoa-free control chocolate on coronary vascular and platelet function.

Methods detail: coronary vasomotion measured by quantitative coronary angiography and cold pressor testing before and 2 hours after ingesting 40 g of 70% dark chocolate or control; reports the significant increase in coronary artery diameter (2.36 to 2.51 mm) after dark chocolate.

Results: endothelium-dependent coronary vasomotion improved after dark chocolate (4.5% vs -4.3% for placebo, P=0.01) and platelet adhesion fell from 4.9% to 3.8% (P=0.04) in the dark chocolate group, unchanged in controls.

Conclusions: dark chocolate causes coronary vasodilation, improves coronary vascular function, and reduces platelet adhesion 2 hours after consumption, with these immediate effects accompanied by reduced serum oxidative stress.

Final conclusion linking the acute cardiovascular benefits of dark chocolate to a significant reduction in serum oxidative stress and a positive correlation with changes in serum epicatechin concentration.
Background and objective of a study on dark chocolate (cocoa flavonoids) versus white chocolate and renal tissue oxygenation in healthy humans, measured by BOLD-MRI.
Methods: ten healthy volunteers (mean age 35, 70% women, BMI 21) had BOLD-MRI before and 2 hours after ingesting 1 g/kg of 70% dark chocolate.

Methods continued: R2* maps on four coronal slices quantify renal oxygenation (low R2* means high oxygenation); eight participants repeated BOLD-MRI after 1 g/kg white chocolate at least one week later.

Results: medullary R2* fell after dark chocolate (28.2 vs 29.6 s-1, p=0.04), unchanged after white chocolate; the change correlated with circulating (epi)catechins and was independent of plasma renin activity.

Conclusion: first evidence that dark chocolate increases renal medullary oxygenation, with open questions about perfusion versus oxygen consumption mechanisms and possible renoprotective effects of cocoa.
Final sentence of the conclusion stating that the mechanism and renoprotective potential of cocoa warrant further study.

Introduces the cocoa and endothelial function study: background on cardiovascular claims for cocoa, and the methods of a randomized crossover trial with 44 overweight adults comparing sugar-free cocoa, sugar-sweetened cocoa, and placebo.
Describes the crossover protocol (6 weeks daily treatment, 4-week washout) and begins the results, reporting flow-mediated dilation (FMD) changes for cocoa versus placebo, with confidence intervals.

Presents the detailed FMD results: change and between-group differences with 95% CIs and p-values for sugar-free and sugar-sweetened cocoa versus placebo, plus the non-significant comparison favoring sugar-free cocoa.

Summarizes the findings and conclusions: other cardiac risk biomarkers and BMI were unchanged, daily cocoa improves endothelial function without weight gain, and sugar-free preparations may further enhance the effect.
Closing fragment of the conclusions noting sugar-free preparations may augment endothelial function, followed by the 2009 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction of a review on cocoa and cardiovascular health: covers the popularity of dark chocolate, the controversial health benefit, the Kuna Indian population observations, and the lack of consensus on mechanisms.

Continues the introduction by describing proposed mechanisms: flavanols and theobromine may improve endothelial function and thereby CVD contributors such as hypertension, platelet aggregation, insulin resistance, and hypercholesterolemia.
Concludes the mechanistic discussion by noting that cocoa benefits vary with growth, development, and production, and that dark chocolate may offer a pleasurable route to CVD risk reduction.

States the review's objectives: examine cocoa's associations with lower blood pressure and reduced CVD risk, describe possible mechanisms, and highlight considerations for cocoa as a dietary supplement.
Final fragment of the review's objectives, ending with the reference to using cocoa as a dietary supplement.

Introduction and methods of a systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs on chocolate, cocoa, and flavan-3-ols and cardiovascular disease risk factors, covering the database search and study selection process.

Methods and results opening: 42 acute or short-term RCTs with 1297 participants; chocolate or cocoa lowered insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) through reduced serum insulin, with the pooled effect size and confidence interval.

Key findings on flow-mediated dilatation (FMD) improvements after chronic and acute intake, sensitivity analysis robustness, and reductions in diastolic blood pressure and mean arterial pressure with their confidence intervals.

Results on blood pressure and lipids: marginal LDL and HDL cholesterol changes, plus dose-response findings where chocolate or cocoa improved FMD at any dose and doses above 50 mg epicatechin/day produced larger blood pressure effects.

GRADE quality-of-evidence assessment rating the evidence as low to moderate, with no signs of harm, and the reasons evidence strength was reduced, such as unclear allocation concealment, dropouts, missing data, and heterogeneity.
Conclusions summarizing consistent acute and chronic benefits of chocolate or cocoa on FMD and novel promising effects on insulin and HOMA-IR, the start of the conclusions section.
Final conclusion calling for larger, longer, independently funded trials to confirm cardiovascular benefits of cocoa flavan-3-ols.
Study background, objective, and methods introduction for a double-blind randomized trial of broccoli sprouts powder (BSP) on oxidative stress markers in type 2 diabetes patients.

Study design details: 81 type 2 diabetes patients randomized to 10 g/d BSP, 5 g/d BSP, or placebo for 4 weeks, with serum oxidative stress markers (TAC, TOS, OSI, MDA, oxidized LDL) measured at baseline and 4 weeks.
Results section reporting the per-group analysis sample of 63 patients and the start of findings: significant MDA decrease with BSP treatment across groups.

Main results and conclusion: BSP significantly reduced MDA, oxidized LDL, and OSI, increased TAC (all P-values for treatment effect), had no effect on TOS, and concluded favorable effects on oxidative stress in type 2 diabetes.
Final sentence of the conclusion stating that broccoli sprouts powder had favorable effects on oxidative stress status in type 2 diabetes patients.

Introduction to young broccoli sprouts as a functional food for type 2 diabetes, naming sulforaphane as the key bioactive compound and its activation of the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway under hyperglycemic, oxidative conditions.

Mechanisms of sulforaphane: induction of phase 2 enzymes, reduction of oxidative stress, inhibition of NF-κB inflammatory signaling, and induction of PPARs that regulate lipid metabolism and glucose homeostasis.

Broader pharmacological effects of sulforaphane shown in animal and in vitro studies (antihypertensive, anticancer, cardioprotective, hypocholesterolemic, anti-H. pylori), followed by the start of human evidence in type 2 diabetic patients supplemented with high-sulforaphane broccoli sprouts.

Human clinical outcomes from broccoli sprout supplementation in type 2 diabetics: improved plasma antioxidant capacity and reduced oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, triglycerides, oxidized LDL ratio, insulin, insulin resistance, and hs-CRP, plus sulforaphane's potential against diabetic nephropathy, fibrosis, and vascular complications.
Concluding statement that sulforaphane and other bioactive components of young broccoli sprouts make them a strong candidate for supplementary type 2 diabetes treatment.

Introduces the cancer-preventive research on broccoli and broccoli sprouts, focusing on sulforaphane (from the glucosinolate in broccoli) and its emerging study against cancer stem cells, which are linked to cancer initiation and recurrence.

Explains the role of cancer stem cells in initiating cancer, recurrence, and drug resistance, and summarizes how sulforaphane may target them via NF-κB, SHH, EMT, and Wnt/β-catenin signaling across cancer types.

Notes preclinical evidence that combining sulforaphane with chemotherapy is promising, and states the article's scope: sulforaphane's effects on CSCs and self-renewal pathways plus a brief review of human broccoli sprout studies.
Ending fragment of the abstract's final sentence, referring to the brief review of recent human studies using broccoli sprout preparations.
This chunk opens the broccoli germination study, covering early growth metrics (sprout/root length, fresh and dry weight) and the rise in sprout respiratory rate between 24 and 36 h.
This chunk gives HPLC results for glucoraphanin (rise to 0-12 h, drop to 3.02 mg/g at 48 h, peak 6.30 mg/g at 72 h) and begins describing the sulforaphane trend during the first day of germination.
This chunk completes the sulforaphane description: a sharp early drop, slow rise to a 3.38 mg/g peak at 48 h, then decline, ending the document's summary of germination chemistry.

Abstract opening of a randomized double-blind trial on broccoli sprout powder (sulforaphane-rich) and insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes; introduces the study aim and the 81-patient randomization into 10 g/d, 5 g/d, and placebo groups.

Continuation of the abstract's methods: the three-arm, 4-week design (10 g/d BSP, 5 g/d BSP, placebo) and the outcome measures (fasting glucose, insulin, glucose-to-insulin ratio, HOMA-IR) taken at baseline and after treatment, plus patient retention numbers.

Concluding abstract results: 10 g/d broccoli sprout powder significantly reduced serum insulin and HOMA-IR (p = 0.05), leading to the authors' conclusion that broccoli sprouts may improve insulin resistance in type 2 diabetic patients.

Introduces the study's background: broccoli's cancer-preventive potential, the untested bioavailability of mercapturic acid pathway isothiocyanate metabolites (sulforaphane and erucin) from broccoli supplements, and the cross-over trial design comparing sprouts with supplements.

Describes the cross-over study design: 12 subjects consumed 40 g fresh broccoli sprouts, then after a 1-month washout consumed 6 broccoli supplement pills, with 4 additional control subjects receiving alfalfa sprouts and placebo pills.

Reports the methods (blood and urine sampling over 48 hours per phase, LC-MS/MS analysis of sulforaphane and erucin metabolites) and the key finding that bioavailability is dramatically lower with broccoli supplements than with fresh sprouts.

Summarizes further findings: plasma and urinary peaks are delayed with supplements, GSTP1 polymorphisms do not affect metabolism or excretion, and sulforaphane and erucin interconvert in vivo consistently within subjects but variably between subjects.

States the study's conclusion that myrosinase-deficient broccoli supplements do not yield plasma isothiocyanate levels equivalent to broccoli sprouts, and raises the concern this poses for people taking the recommended single-pill serving believing they receive equivalent doses.

Concludes the abstract by stating the practical implication: consumers taking the recommended 1-pill serving of a broccoli supplement may wrongly assume they are getting isothiocyanate doses equivalent to those from broccoli.

Introduction and objectives of a case-control study on tobacco smoking, chewing, and alcohol drinking as risk factors for lung cancer in men in southern India, focusing on bidi versus cigarette smoking.

Study design and sample: case-control study in Chennai and Trivandrum with 778 lung cancer cases and 3,430 controls (1,503 cancer controls and 1,927 healthy controls), plus the alcohol exposure aims (Indian vs non-Indian beverages).
Statistical methods: unconditional multivariate logistic regression for cigarette, bidi, chewing, and alcohol effects, and GAM with loess smoothers to model the dose-response curve.

Main results: GAM dose-response shows a plateau after 35 years of smoking or 10 cigarette-equivalent pack-years; odds ratios for >30 years of cigarette-only vs bidi-only smoking and for >12 weighted cumulative consumption are reported with 95% CIs.
Cessation and chewing results: former cigarette smokers' lung cancer risk falls faster after quitting than former bidi smokers' risk, and there is no evidence that chewing affects lung cancer risk.

Alcohol and overall conclusion: no clear alcohol effect among never-smokers except a limited-power association for Indian alcohol (OR=2.67), and the conclusion that bidi smoking is more carcinogenic than cigarette smoking across all smoking measures.
Closing sentence of the abstract stating the bidi-versus-cigarette difference holds across all smoking aspects, followed by the 2003 Wiley-Liss copyright notice.

Opening of Geoffrey Rose's 1985 IJE paper 'Sick individuals and sick populations', introducing the distinction between determinants of individual cases and determinants of incidence rate in aetiology.

Explains why case/control and cohort studies fail to detect a necessary agent when exposure is homogeneous, and contrasts the high-risk strategy (protecting susceptible individuals) with the population approach (controlling causes of incidence).
Conclusion of Rose's paper: the high-risk and population approaches are not usually in competition, but controlling the causes of incidence should be the prior concern.

Background and rationale from the Vacurin curcumin cervical cream study: HPV as a leading cause of mortality, costs of screening and vaccination, and curcumin's anticancer/antiviral potential limited by poor systemic bioavailability.

Study aim and methods continuation: testing curcumin-based cervical cancer therapy using four HPV(+) cell lines and normal fibroblasts for selectivity and potency, then developing a curcumin cervical cream and testing it on apposed HPV(+) cells and vaginal epithelium side effects in healthy mice.

Results on curcumin's selectivity: it eliminates HPV(+) cervical cancer lines (HeLa, ME-180, SiHa, SW756), suppresses E6, strongly inhibits EGFR, and induces p53, setting up the Vacurin cream results.

Key findings on Vacurin, a colloidal curcumin formulation in a clinically used amphipathic vaginal cream: it eliminates apposed HeLa cells and suppresses EGFR expression, with mouse data showing daily intravaginal dosing for three weeks.

In vivo safety and conclusion: daily intravaginal Vacurin for three weeks caused no body weight change and no adverse vaginal epithelial effects, and the authors conclude the cream eradicates HPV(+) cancer cells without affecting non-cancerous tissue.
Final conclusion and copyright: the preclinical data support Vacurin as a novel approach for treating cervical HPV infection, with the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction to a review of curcumin (diferuloylmethane) delivery methods, describing its biphasic, dose-dependent interactions with many cellular targets and the rationale that effective delivery to diseased tissue is needed for preventive or therapeutic use.

Continuation of the review's introduction: explains that because diseased tissues range from topical to systemic sites, curcumin requires lesion-oriented delivery methods, which the review goes on to cover; ends with the start of the 2013 copyright notice from the International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology.

Closing fragment of the document containing the copyright statement (2013, International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Inc.) that ends the abstract of the curcumin delivery methods review.

Introduces the study of turmeric (Curcuma longa) ethanol extract and curcumin ointment as topical treatments for external cancerous lesions, reporting symptom improvements such as reduced smell and itching, with the chunk ending mid-sentence on lesion size and pain reduction.

Continues the topical turmeric/curcumin cancer study results: 70% of cases showed dry lesions, 10% showed reduced lesion size and pain, effects lasted several months in many patients, and only one of 62 patients had an adverse reaction.

Introduction and background of a study on curcumin and quercetin for regressing colorectal adenomas in familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP); covers the disease, prior NSAID/COX-2 inhibitor treatments, and their side effects.

Study aims and methods: five FAP patients with prior colectomy (four with retained rectum, one with ileal anal pouch) took curcumin 480 mg plus quercetin 20 mg orally three times daily, with polyp assessment design.

Methods continued: polyp number and size measured at baseline and after therapy, analyzed by Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with side effects and compliance evaluated; results begin with all patients showing polyp reduction after about 6 months.

Results: all five patients had reduced polyp number and size after a mean of 6 months, with mean decreases of 60.4% in number and 50.9% in size (both P < .05), minimal side effects, and no lab abnormalities; conclusions begin.

Conclusions: the curcumin and quercetin combination appears to reduce ileal and rectal adenomas in FAP without appreciable toxicity, and randomized controlled trials are needed to validate these small-study findings.

Introduces curcumin as a potential human chemopreventive agent, summarizing its known anti-tumor effects: inhibition of NF-kappaB transcription and of lipoxygenase/cyclooxygenase, and protection in rodent chemical carcinogenesis models. Ends by naming its alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone group.

Explains that the alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone electrophile drives curcumin's NF-kappaB repression and, in other compounds, p53 inactivation. States the paper's hypothesis that curcumin acts on p53 in the same way, beginning with disruption of p53 conformation needed for serine phosphorylation.

Reports the paper's main finding that curcumin impairs p53 function in colon cancer cells. Lists the affected activities: DNA binding, transactivation of p53-responsive genes, and p53-mediated cell cycle arrest.

Introduction and study design: a dose-escalation pilot of a standardized Curcuma extract (440–2200 mg/day, 36–180 mg curcumin) in 15 patients with advanced colorectal cancer refractory to chemotherapy.

Study population and biomarkers: 15 refractory colorectal cancer patients took Curcuma extract for up to 4 months; blood cell glutathione S-transferase activity and the malondialdehyde-derived DNA adduct M(1)G were measured.

Safety and pharmacokinetic findings: extract was well tolerated with no dose-limiting toxicity; curcumin and metabolites were absent from blood and urine but recovered in feces, with curcumin sulfate found in one patient's feces.

Pharmacodynamic results: 440 mg/day for 29 days reduced lymphocytic GST activity by 59%, an effect absent at higher doses; M(1)G levels were unchanged, and five patients had stable disease for 2–4 months.
Conclusions: the extract is safe up to 2.2 g/day (180 mg curcumin), curcumin has low oral bioavailability possibly due to intestinal metabolism, and larger clinical trials are warranted.
Final concluding sentence of the abstract, recommending larger clinical trials of Curcuma extract.

Opening chunk of an abstract on colorectal carcinogenesis, introducing the two genomic instability pathways: chromosomal instability (allelic losses, aneuploidy) and microsatellite instability (subtle DNA mutations, diploidy).

Middle chunk defining microsatellite instability as caused by inactivation of DNA mismatch repair genes (mainly MLH1 or MSH2), noting its prevalence (15% of colorectal cancers) and its diagnostic methods (tumor DNA analysis, loss of mismatch repair protein expression).

Chunk describing the clinical significance of microsatellite instability: distinct pathologic features and improved survival in MSI colorectal cancers, and its link to hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome) via germline mismatch repair mutations.

Final chunk concluding that identifying the microsatellite instability pathway has major implications for the clinical investigation and management of colorectal cancer patients, tying the Lynch syndrome link to clinical practice.
Introduces the study design (16 women, 4 men switching from mixed to lactovegetarian diet for 12 months) and early dietary and 3-month effects on selenium intake and zinc, magnesium status.

Describes the 3-month results: decreased plasma/hair zinc, copper, selenium; increased magnesium; lower hair mercury, lead, cadmium; reduced urinary and fecal excretion of minerals, with small changes thereafter.

Reports the 3-year follow-up, where trace element concentrations largely returned toward baseline (copper similar, magnesium slightly higher, complex zinc and selenium patterns) and concludes that a lactovegetarian diet alters trace element status.
Final concluding sentence stating that shifting to a lactovegetarian diet changes trace element status.

Opening of the document on cadmium (Cd) health risks: introduces known high-level Cd toxicity (nephropathy, osteoporosis, fractures) and recent epidemiology linking high-normal Cd levels in non-industrially exposed populations to vascular disease, cancer, diabetes, and mortality.

Argues Cd is a likely causal risk factor for vascular disorders, cancers, diabetes, osteoporosis, and nephropathy in humans, based on reverse-causation reasoning and supporting rodent studies; also begins noting ways to reduce Cd exposure such as avoiding tobacco smoke and shellfish/organ meats.

Discusses dietary sources of Cd: plant-derived foods like leafy greens, whole grains, tubers and root vegetables are the chief sources, so vegans among non-smokers have the highest Cd burden; introduces iron, calcium, magnesium, and zinc as factors that reduce Cd absorption.

Explains that adequate iron, calcium, magnesium, and zinc reduce intestinal Cd absorption by down-regulating mineral transporters and competing with Cd for them; highlights correcting iron deficiency as especially important for controlling Cd uptake.

Describes zinc supplementation as a way to counter Cd toxicity through induction of metallothionein, which sequesters Cd via sulfhydryl groups and renders it harmless, and notes zinc's general protective role.

Covers zinc's anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and immunosupportive benefits, and proposes antioxidant supplements (spirulina, lipoic acid, melatonin, N-acetylcysteine) to counter oxidative stress, the main mechanism of Cd toxicity, based on rodent evidence.

Concludes that although Cd may be a major risk factor for morbidity and mortality, practical strategies exist to limit its absorption and pathogenic effects; followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.
Final chunk containing only the 2012 Elsevier Ltd. copyright notice that closes the document on cadmium exposure and mitigation strategies.

Introduction of a study on urinary cadmium (Cd) in NHANES 1999-2008: it states the health risks of chronic low-level Cd exposure and the study aim of testing whether U.S. population urinary Cd levels declined over the decade and why.

Methods section describing the statistical approach: variable-threshold censored multiple regression of log urinary Cd, with covariates covering demographics, smoking, housing, diet, creatinine, and survey year, applied to each subpopulation.

Results summary reporting a 20-25% decline in geometric mean urinary Cd across subpopulations, with significant declines in later survey years for teens and adults, and listing the housing and smoking covariates in the models.

Results on covariates: a list of factors significantly associated with Cd (creatinine, age, BMI, race/ethnicity, education, smoking, cotinine, certain nutrient intakes, supplement use) that did not explain the decline, which the authors attribute to unidentified time-related factors.
Concluding statement that despite the observed declines in urinary Cd, millions of Americans remain potentially at risk of adverse health outcomes from low-level Cd exposure.

Introduction and study rationale: cadmium as a food-borne estrogen mimetic, noting the lack of prior prospective evidence linking dietary cadmium to breast cancer; study aims stated (1987 baseline, overall and ER-defined breast cancer).

Cohort description and follow-up results: 55,987 postmenopausal women, 12.2 years mean follow-up, 2,112 invasive breast cancer cases split into 1,626 ER(+) and 290 ER(-) tumors, and adjustment for confounders.

Main finding for overall breast cancer: highest vs. lowest tertile of dietary cadmium intake associated with increased risk (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.07-1.36, P trend 0.02), with whole grain and vegetable intake considered as confounders and cadmium sources.

Subgroup results among lean and normal weight women: significant associations for all tumors and ER(+) tumors (RR 1.27 and 1.25), with a non-significant but similar estimate for ER(-) tumors (RR 1.22, CI 0.76-1.93).

Effect modification and interaction analysis: cadmium-breast cancer association consistent across strata of whole grain/vegetable consumption and inverse grain/vegetable association across cadmium tertiles, with no significant interaction (P interaction = 0.73).
Conclusion of the study: overall findings support a role for dietary cadmium exposure in the development of postmenopausal breast cancer.

Introduces the study's aim: examining how blood cadmium concentration relates to diet, nutrient intake (Ca, Fe, Zn, vitamins C and D), smoking, age, BMI and residence in 243 adults from Sassari Province, Sardinia.

Describes the study population (243 adults in Sassari Province, Sardinia), the stated hypothesis that offal consumption raises Cd intake and blood levels, the graphite furnace AAS measurement method, and questionnaire-based data collection.

Reports key findings: smoking significantly raises blood cadmium (P < .001), nonsmokers who eat offal have higher levels (P = .04), and slight increases are seen with rice, fish, and bread consumption among nonsmokers.

Presents correlation and regression results: blood cadmium correlates positively with age and with daily offal intake in nonsmokers, Ca intake is negatively correlated in females, and regression ranks smoking, offal consumption, BMI and age as the main risk factors.
Concludes the sentence on the regression ranking of risk factors for blood cadmium and includes the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice, marking the end of the abstract.
Abstract of a human study on how meals and meal timing affect gastrointestinal lead (203Pb) uptake: fasting uptake was high, and balanced meals sharply reduced absorption.

Continues the study by testing other factors (phytate, EDTA, caffeine, alcohol, glucose, liquid meal, snack) and attributing the meal effect mainly to calcium and phosphate, with phytate further reducing and a milk factor increasing uptake.

Findings on milk: skimmed and whole milk gave the same uptake, so the milk-increasing factor is not fat; low-mineral, low-phytate foods gave intermediate reductions, possibly via digestive secretion stimulation.
Concluding remarks: fasting uptake, meal-induced reduction, gastric emptying variation, and dietary habits may explain much of the population variation in body lead burdens.

Introduction/aim of a study on dietary cadmium (Cd) exposure in the Belgian adult population, covering the goal of comparing intake to EFSA's tolerable weekly intake (TWI) and identifying major contributing food groups; the data sources are described next.

Methods section describing the data sources: the 2004 Belgian food consumption survey (two 24-hour recalls, 3083 participants) and Cd concentration data (n = 4000 food items) from the Belgian Federal Agency for the Safety of the Food Chain control program, 2006-2008, used to calculate individual intake.

Key results of the Belgian dietary cadmium study: population mean, median and 95th percentile intakes (0.98, 0.85, 2.02 µg/kg body weight per week), the share of adults (2%) exceeding EFSA's 2009 TWI of 2.5 µg/kg body weight, with the start of the food-group findings.
Concluding finding of the Belgian cadmium study: cereal products and potatoes together account for more than 60% of dietary Cd intake, identifying them as the main dietary sources of exposure.

Introduction/background of a meta-analysis on dietary cadmium intake and cancer risk, noting diet as the main cadmium source for non-smokers and the study's aim to pool prior case-control and cohort findings.

Methods section continuing the background: literature search of PubMed, EMBASE, and MEDLINE for case-control and cohort studies, pooling eight eligible studies with random-effects summary relative risks and 95% CIs.

Results opening: overall pooled analysis shows no significant link between dietary cadmium and cancer (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.99–1.22, highest vs. lowest intake), with strong heterogeneity prompting subgroup analyses by design, location, and cancer type.

Subgroup results: positive associations between dietary cadmium and cancer appear in Western populations (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.08–1.23) and in hormone-related cancers such as prostate, breast, and endometrial cancer.

Conclusion of the cadmium–cancer meta-analysis: a positive association in Western countries, especially for hormone-related cancers, with a call for further experimental and epidemiological studies to verify the findings.
Final sentence of the conclusion, calling for additional experimental and epidemiological research to verify the meta-analysis findings on dietary cadmium and cancer risk.
Introduces the study on European moss heavy-metal monitoring: links cadmium and lead moss concentrations to EMEP modelled atmospheric deposition, noting correlations vary by country and metal.

Reports results of country-level Spearman correlations between moss Cd/Pb concentrations and EMEP deposition for 1990-2005, showing significant positive correlations in most countries and weaker or negative ones where sampling was sparse.

Summarizes that correlations improved when restricted to EMEP grids with at least three moss sites, and concludes that spatial patterns and temporal trends agree reasonably well between moss metal concentrations and modelled deposition.
Closing copyright notice from Elsevier (2012) for the moss-deposition correlation article.

Introduction and background of the NHANES III cross-sectional study on low-level environmental cadmium exposure and neurotoxicity in US adults, including the aim to link neurocognitive scores with urinary cadmium.

Study design and methods: NHANES III (1988–1994) sample of adults aged 20–59 who completed a computer-based neurocognitive evaluation, and the four outcome measures described (SRTT, SDST, SDLT trials-to-criterion, SDLT total error score).
Methods continued: multivariable-adjusted models of urinary cadmium versus test scores, and the start of the results describing the 5662 participants screened for neurocognitive testing.

Results: 5572 participants (98%) had urinary cadmium data; unadjusted analyses showed worse performance with higher cadmium across all four outcomes, but most associations lost significance after adjustment, with age the most influential covariate.

Key finding: among never-smokers without known occupational cadmium exposure, urinary cadmium was significantly associated with lower SDST (attention/perception) performance, about 1.93% decrement per 1 μg/L increase (95% CI 0.05–3.81).

Conclusions: higher cumulative cadmium may subtly impair attention and perception, especially in adults exposed mainly through diet (no smoking or occupational exposure), at levels considered without adverse effects and common in US adults.

Interpretation and recommendations: further research warranted; cadmium may mediate effects of age and smoking on cognition, so adjusting for these may underestimate associations with cumulative cadmium exposure.

Closing limitation and call for research: adjusting for age and smoking may underestimate cadmium associations, and prospective studies including never-smokers and non-occupationally exposed people are needed.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence of the abstract, completing the call for prospective studies on cadmium and neurocognition.

Introduces the study's background: breast cancer prevalence and the cadmium exposure hypothesis, and states the aim to test urinary cadmium (UCd) association with breast cancer in Long Island and NHANES samples.

Describes the study populations: a Long Island case-control sample in a high-incidence region (Suffolk County rate given) and a nationally representative NHANES 1999-2008 sample, with case and control counts.
Reports the main results: significant increasing trends in breast cancer odds across UCd quartiles in both samples (NHANES p=0.039, LI p=0.023) from the multivariable logistic model.

Gives the quartile-specific odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals for Long Island and US women, then concludes that further research on environmental cadmium and molecular mechanisms is warranted.
Closing fragment completing the final word of the conclusion sentence about underlying molecular mechanisms; a continuation of the concluding statement in chunk 4.
Abstract opening of a study on cadmium exposure in older smokers vs. nonsmokers, introducing the two- to threefold higher blood cadmium in smokers and describing the study groups and sample sizes.

Methods summary of the cadmium study: machine-smoked cigarettes yielding paired inhaled cadmium and blood cadmium measurements at monthly intervals, urine cadmium comparison, and a duplicate-diet and plasma kinetic study in four smokers.
Results on blood cadmium levels: female smokers show a higher mean and wide range versus nonsmokers, with males similar, and estimates of daily inhaled cadmium compared against dietary intake.
Interpretation that inhaled cadmium from smoking is too small to explain the roughly 3.5-fold blood cadmium elevation in smokers, suggesting cadmium accumulated in the lungs as an additional source.

Concluding finding that blood cadmium tracks inhaled cadmium linearly in most smokers, while about a quarter show much higher levels, implying heterogeneity in cadmium concentrations and possible toxicity risk.

Opening chunk of a study on faecal elimination of lead and cadmium in 16 subjects switching from a mixed diet to a lactovegetarian diet; notes the significant rise in faecal weight and the large inter-individual variation in Pb and Cd excretion during the mixed-diet period.

Middle chunk giving median and range values of faecal lead (Pb) and cadmium (Cd) elimination in micrograms per day for the mixed-diet and lactovegetarian diet periods, and the observed non-significant tendency toward higher excretion on the vegetarian diet.
Final chunk concluding that the apparent tendency toward increased faecal lead and cadmium elimination after switching to the vegetarian diet was not statistically significant.
Introduces a study measuring zinc and cadmium in seven zinc dietary supplements via ICP/MS, reporting widely varying cadmium content per 15 mg Zn daily dose (0.039–1.46 µg), a 37-fold range.

Concludes that gluconate-form zinc supplements had the lowest cadmium, and argues that cadmium, a non-essential toxic element, should be minimized in supplements and possibly regulated by government standards.

Introduction and aims of a cadmium (Cd) risk assessment study: it motivates incorporating bioaccessibility into human health risk from inhalation and seafood intake, and outlines the PBPK and Hill dose-response approach.

Methods summary: a PBPK model estimates Cd in urine and blood from seafood and inhalation exposure, a Hill-based dose-response model estimates renal dysfunction and peripheral arterial disease risk, and the study begins reporting fish versus shellfish bioaccessibility results.

Key results: fish (~83.7%) show higher Cd bioaccessibility than shellfish (~73.2%); glomerular and tubular damage risk is about 18% across genders and smokers, and nonsmokers' 50% probability of peripheral arterial disease ranges from 3.28 to 8.80%.

Main conclusions: smokers have 2-3 times higher peripheral arterial disease morbidity than nonsmokers, and Cd adverse effects are worsened when high seafood consumption coincides with smoking, supporting a dose-dependent risk framework.
Closing statement of the abstract, saying the framework improves assessment of dose dependency of Cd hazard, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces the study's background on chronic dietary cadmium harm and states the aim, then describes the methods: Caco-2 cells exposed to Cd in various foods and CdCl2 after in vitro digestion, with uptake measured by atomic absorption spectrometry.

Presents the key results: Cd bioavailability was higher from animal-based foods than vegetable-based ones, raw kale inhibited Cd uptake when mixed with boiled pig kidney, and Cd in kale was absorbed more after boiling.

Gives the conclusion that Cd binding to molecular species, other food components, food combinations, and cooking methods shape dietary Cd uptake, and begins the recommendation about a food-matrix relative bioavailability factor.
Closes the abstract by stating that a relative bioavailability factor accounting for the food matrix may be needed for dietary cadmium exposure assessment and for estimating and preventing risk.

Introduces cadmium as an environmental toxin, identifying food as its main exposure route and explaining how soil cadmium accumulates in grains, seeds, fruit and vegetables that form the core of vegetarian diets.

Describes the study design comparing blood cadmium in non-smoking vegetarian (n=80) and non-vegetarian control (n=84) groups, and reports the significantly higher vegetarian blood cadmium level (1.78 vs 0.45 µg/l).

Reports risk-level findings: six vegetarians exceeded the 5 µg/l health risk threshold versus none of the controls, and blood cadmium declined from vegans (3.15 µg/l) through lacto-vegetarians (1.75) to semivegetarians (1.34) as animal food intake rose.

Explains that vegetarians at risk (above the threshold) ate significantly more whole grain products, grain sprouts and oil seeds than those not at risk, linking dietary choices to elevated cadmium intake.
Lists correlations of blood cadmium with age, whole grain intake and years of vegetarianism, and introduces oxidative stress as the mechanism behind cadmium-induced hepatic and renal toxicity.
Concludes that vegetarians have higher plasma natural antioxidants, suggesting their antioxidant protection may offset the harmful effects of greater cadmium intake from plant foods.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence, restating that antioxidant protection may inhibit harmful effects of higher cadmium intake from plant food.

Introduces the study design: control (n=8) and triathlete (n=15) volunteers given aronia-citrus juice, with 24h urine analyzed by UPLC-QqQ-MS/MS to measure flavanone metabolites (glucuronides, sulfates, sulfo-glucuronides).

Key results: flavanone urinary excretion was about fivefold higher in triathletes than controls, with a ninefold rise in homoeriodictyol, suggesting exercise-driven overactivation of microbiota metabolism.

Concludes no sex differences in bioavailability were found, and argues aronia-citrus juice may offer synergistic health benefits via higher flavanone bioavailability, as an alternative to high-dose nutritional supplements; includes the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.
Contains only the trailing 2012 Elsevier Ltd. copyright notice, the final fragment of the abstract.
Introduction and background of a systematic literature review on the gastrointestinal bleeding risk of over-the-counter (OTC) ibuprofen, stating the study's objective.
Study methods: inclusion criteria (OTC ibuprofen defined as up to 1200 mg/day or labeled 'over the counter') and MEDLINE search through 2010 for studies reporting GI bleeding event rates.
Results opening: the 20 included studies (nine observational, ten clinical trials, one meta-analysis) and the summarized data on GI bleeding-related events with OTC-specific ibuprofen doses.

Key quantitative findings: GI hospitalization frequency below 0.2% at OTC doses, incidence rates of 0 to 3.19 per 1000 patient-years, and risk factors such as age, concomitant medications, and dose-response.
Relative risk findings (1.1 to 2.4 versus non-users) for any GI bleeding event with OTC-specific ibuprofen doses, followed by the start of the conclusions on low incidence.

Conclusions on limitations: few studies specifically on OTC ibuprofen, heterogeneous methodologies and exposure/outcome definitions preventing direct comparison, and restriction to the stated search methods.
Final conclusion recommending further research on GI bleeding risk in patients using OTC-specific ibuprofen.

Study introduction: methods of measuring intestinal permeability in healthy human subjects after NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen, indomethacin) using a 51Cr-EDTA absorption test, with the effect linked to cyclooxygenase inhibition potency.

Study results: NSAIDs raise intestinal permeability systemically (similar effect for oral and rectal indomethacin); prostaglandin E2 lowers permeability but does not block the indomethacin-induced increase.
Study conclusion: NSAIDs disrupt human intestinal barrier function, likely through damage at the level of intercellular junctions.

Introduction to the review: inflammation as a major disease risk factor, contrasting acute self-limiting inflammation with chronic inflammation that drives pathology (inflammatory cell infiltration, excess cytokines, signaling dysregulation, barrier loss).

Argues that reducing chronic inflammation is a beneficial strategy against human disease, and introduces flavonoids as abundant dietary compounds from fruits and vegetables with broad health-related biological activity, including anti-inflammatory effects.
States that flavonoids act through multiple mechanisms to prevent and attenuate inflammation and may act as cardioprotective, neuroprotective, and chemopreventive agents.

States the review's aim: summarizing current knowledge and mechanisms of flavonoids' anti-inflammatory activity and their effects on chronic inflammatory diseases; includes the 2010 Royal Society of Chemistry copyright line.
Isolated page number '10' from the source document, with no substantive content; likely a page footer for retrieval purposes.

Opening of an overview of NSAID gastrointestinal safety, introducing the widespread use of NSAIDs, their potential damage across the GI tract, and how upper GI side effects are assessed in different study types.

Continues the discussion of short-term NSAID studies (under 14 days), describing dose-dependent damage linked to drug acidity, the lack of this damage with COX-2 selective inhibitors (pKa over 7.0), the absence of serious outcomes, and no role for H. pylori.

Covers long-term (3+ months) endoscopy findings with ulcer rates of 15%-35%, epidemiological links between NSAIDs and serious events, and toxicity rankings placing ibuprofen lowest and ketorolac and azapropazone highest.

Addresses risk factors for NSAID-related bleeding (age, H. pylori, prior bleeding, anticoagulants), mega-trial evidence that COX-2 selective agents halve bleeding, and the low absolute rate of NSAID-induced gastric bleeding.
Describes NSAID enteropathy affecting about 70% of patients with intestinal blood and protein loss, and the GI safety of over-the-counter ibuprofen and diclofenac, which is comparable to placebo.

Concludes with evidence that ibuprofen is well tolerated at OTC doses, recent suggestions that OTC NSAIDs be taken on an empty stomach rather than with food, and the 2012 Blackwell Publishing copyright notice.

Introduction and study aim: frames l-citrulline (abundant in watermelon) as a muscle-soreness-reducing compound and introduces the in vitro Caco-2 intestinal absorption experiment comparing unpasteurized watermelon juice, pasteurized watermelon juice, and a pure l-citrulline standard.

In vitro results and in vivo design: reports that l-citrulline bioavailability was higher in the watermelon matrix without heat treatment, then describes the cycloergometer maximum-effort test with seven athletes.

In vivo treatments and outcomes: lists the three arms (natural watermelon juice with 1.17 g l-citrulline, enriched juice with 4.83 g extra, and placebo) and concludes both watermelon juices reduced recovery heart rate and muscle soreness at 24 h.

Study design and methods: Introduction of the cherry feeding study in 10 healthy women (ages 22-40) who ate Bing cherries after fasting, with blood and urine sampling at baseline and 1.5, 3, and 5 h postdose.

Key results on urate: plasma urate fell at 5 h postdose (183 vs 214 micromol/L baseline), and urinary urate excretion peaked at 3 h postdose (350 vs 202 micromol/mmol creatinine), both statistically significant.

Inflammation and vitamin C findings: CRP and nitric oxide dropped marginally at 3 h (P < 0.1), albumin and TNF-alpha were unchanged, and rising plasma ascorbic acid showed dehydroascorbic acid from cherries is bioavailable as vitamin C.
Conclusions: the urate decrease supports cherries' reputed anti-gout effect, and the trend toward lower CRP and NO adds to in vitro evidence that cherry compounds inhibit inflammatory pathways.
Final sentence fragment completing the conclusion that cherry compounds may inhibit inflammatory pathways, supported by in vitro evidence.
Study objective, design, and methods overview: a case-crossover study of purine intake as a risk factor for recurrent gout attacks in gout patients followed online for one year.
Methods detail: data collected at each gout attack (onset date, symptoms, medications, and 2-day pre-attack purine-containing food intake) and the same exposures over 2-day control periods.

Main results: 633 participants; odds ratios for recurrent gout attacks across increasing quintiles of total 2-day purine intake relative to the lowest quintile (1.17, 1.38, 2.21, 4.76; p for trend <0.001).

Source-specific results: odds ratios by quintile for animal-source purines (1.42 to 2.41, p for trend <0.001) and plant-source purines (1.12 to 1.39, p=0.04), plus persistence of effect across subgroups such as sex, alcohol, diuretics, allopurinol, NSAIDs, and colchicine use.

Conclusions: acute purine intake nearly quintuples (almost fivefold) the risk of recurrent gout attacks, suggesting that limiting purine-rich foods, especially animal-origin ones, may reduce gout attacks.
Final sentence of the conclusion recommending reduced purine-rich food intake, especially from animal sources, to help prevent gout attacks.

Study design and methods: a prospective online case-crossover study of 633 gout patients followed for one year, recording exposures in 2-day pre-attack and control windows to assess cherry intake and recurrent gout attacks.

Methods continued: data collected at each gout attack and matched 2-day control periods covering medications and risk factors such as daily cherry and cherry extract intake, analyzed with conditional logistic regression.
Main result: among the 633 participants, cherry intake over 2 days was associated with a 35% lower odds of gout attack versus no intake (multivariate OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.50-0.85).

Secondary results: cherry extract showed a similar inverse association (OR 0.55), and the cherry effect held across subgroups including sex, obesity, purine intake, alcohol, diuretics, and anti-gout medication use.
