Combined exposure and conclusion: cherry intake plus allopurinol use gave a 75% lower attack risk (OR 0.25), leading to the conclusion that cherry intake is associated with a lower risk of gout attacks.
Introduces the study's aim: a proteomics-based investigation of how consuming sweet cherries changes plasma biomarkers of chronic inflammatory disease in healthy adults with mildly elevated CRP.
Describes the study population (18 adults aged 45-61 with modestly elevated CRP) and the intervention of 280 g/day Bing sweet cherries for 28 days, with baseline sampling at study day 7.

Reports the study timeline and overall results: of 89 biomarkers, 9 were altered by cherry consumption, 67 were unchanged, and 13 were undetectable; also notes the sampling points at day 35 and day 63.

Lists the specific plasma biomarkers that cherry consumption significantly decreased (RAGE ligand EN-RAGE, CRP, ferritin, PAI-1, endothelin-1, EGF, IL-18) and the one it increased (IL-1 receptor antagonist), with percent changes versus day 7.

Notes that ferritin kept declining after cherry supplementation stopped, remaining significantly lower on day 63 than baseline, and states that no clinical pathology endpoints were measured because participants were healthy.
Concludes that cherry consumption selectively reduced several biomarkers associated with inflammatory diseases, summarizing the study's main finding.

Study abstract on cherry anthocyanins in rat Freund's adjuvant-induced arthritis: describes the objectives and the methods of arthritis induction with CFA and oral anthocyanin dosing (40, 20, 10 mg/kg for 28 days).
Continuation of the methods in the cherry anthocyanin arthritis study: details the assays used (RIA for serum TNF-alpha and paw PGE2, and serum T-AOC, SOD, and MDA for antioxidant status).
Results section of the cherry anthocyanin arthritis study: the 40 mg/kg anthocyanin dose reduced serum TNF-alpha and paw PGE2 and improved antioxidant markers (higher T-AOC and SOD, lower serum MDA).

Final results and conclusion of the cherry anthocyanin arthritis study: the 20 and 10 mg/kg doses had weaker effects, concluding anthocyanins have potential anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in AIA.
Introduces COX-1/COX-2 and COX-2's role in gastric mucosal repair via growth factors (HGF, VEGF); the review on cyclooxygenase in gastric mucosal protection, opening section.

Covers aspirin's acetylation of COX-2 producing the anti-inflammatory 15-(R)-epi-lipoxinA4, and introduces the three PGE synthases that convert COX-2 products into PGE2, starting with inducible mPGES-1 in the gastric ulcer bed.

Describes mPGES-1 colocalizing with COX-2 in ulcer-bed fibroblasts and macrophages, and cPGES and mPGES-2 being expressed in normal gastric mucosa without change in gastritis or ulcer; previews the review's aims.
Closing statement of the review's scope: the role of these enzymes in gastric mucosal pathophysiology and the biological significance of inhibiting them.

Introduction of the study's scope: lists the cherry, berry, and other fruit species (with cultivars and botanical names) analyzed for cyclooxygenase inhibitory and antioxidant anthocyanin content in this cyanidin glycoside study.
Continues the species list (elderberries, raspberries, strawberries) and describes the methods: anthocyanins 1 and 2 (cyanidin glycosides) quantified by HPLC in the fruits.
Reports antioxidant results: cherry anthocyanins matched commercial antioxidants (TBHQ, BHT, BHA) and outperformed vitamin E at 125 µg/ml.
Reports cyclooxygenase (COX-I and COX-II) inhibition: raspberry and sweet cherry anthocyanins showed 45% and 47% inhibition at 125 µg/ml, comparable to ibuprofen and naproxen at 10 µM.
Gives quantitative yields of anthocyanins 1 and 2 per 100 g fruit: tart cherries, sweet cherries, raspberries, and blackberries/strawberries (which contain only anthocyanin 2).
Concludes that anthocyanins 1 and 2 were absent from bilberries, blueberries, cranberries, and elderberries.
Opening of an epidemiology review on NSAID use and gastrointestinal injury; introduces NSAID prevalence and age-related prescribing patterns among elderly people.
Continues prescription-prevalence data for elderly NSAID users (Alberta 27% over 6 months; Tennessee 40% annually, 6% long-term) and begins describing the range of NSAID side-effects.

Identifies the clinically important GI side-effects of NSAIDs (dyspepsia, peptic ulceration, hemorrhage, perforation, death) and notes that epigastric pain/indigestion is the most common and a frequent reason for withdrawal or co-treatment.
Presents population data showing elderly regular NSAID users are nearly twice as likely as non-users to take anti-ulcer or anti-dyspepsia agents (20-26% vs 11%).

Quantifies NSAID burden on peptic ulcer care: Alberta anti-ulcer prescriptions attributable to NSAIDs (28%), 3-5-fold increased risk of ulcer complications, and 15-35% of complications attributed to NSAIDs.
Gives US mortality and hospitalization estimates for elderly NSAID users (41,000 hospitalizations, 3,300 deaths yearly) and begins listing risk factors for serious peptic ulcer disease.
Completes the list of risk factors for serious peptic ulcer disease (older age, prior ulcer, GI hemorrhage, dyspepsia, NSAID intolerance, poor health) closing the document.

Introduction and background of a systematic review on mortality from upper GI bleeding or perforation, noting the pre-1997 estimate of 12% and the motivation to explain NSAID-related risks to patients.

Methods section describing the systematic review design: studies before 1997 and 1997-2008, inclusion of any study design reporting deaths from upper GI bleed or perforation, and separate analyses for all cases and NSAID/aspirin users.
Key results: 61,067 cases with 5,001 deaths overall, with overall mortality falling from 11.6% pre-1997 to 7.4% post-1997, and NSAID/aspirin-exposed mortality data introduced.

Results continued and conclusion start: NSAID/aspirin patient mortality rising from 14.7% pre-1997 to 20.9% since 1997, and the caveat that upper GI bleed or perforation still carries a finite death risk.
Final conclusion: limitations of interpreting effect size across studies, and the summary that overall mortality is about 1 in 13 while NSAID/aspirin-exposed mortality is about 1 in 5.

Opening of an essay on COX-2 inhibitors (coxibs) introduced in 1999: rapid direct-to-consumer promotion, strong demand from arthritis patients, and early prescription volume for celecoxib (Celebrex) and rofecoxib (Vioxx).

Continues the COX-2 inhibitor essay with sales figures for Celebrex (sixth best-selling drug, over US$4 billion) and Vioxx (US$2.6 billion in 2001), and notes the cardiovascular risks of coxibs and their high US price.

Concluding critique of the coxib makers, arguing they exploited a weak FDA and patients for profit, compares their conduct to the tobacco industry, and closes by saying safe, effective alternatives exist.
Final sentence of the COX-2 inhibitor essay stating that safe and active alternatives to coxibs are available.

Introduces the study's premise: processing of fruits affects phytochemicals, and tart cherries' promoted antioxidant and anti-inflammatory benefits may be altered by processing. Sets up the comparison of processed tart cherry products.

Describes the study design: comparing in vitro antioxidant capacity and COX anti-inflammatory activity across four processed tart cherry products (juice concentrate, IQF frozen, canned, dried), with anthocyanin and proanthocyanidin analysis.

Reports phytochemical and antioxidant results per serving: frozen cherries had highest anthocyanins, juice concentrate had highest proanthocyanidins, phenolics, ORAC and NORAC, and dried cherries had highest HORAC and SORAC.
Summarizes that tart cherry ORAC compares favorably to USDA fruit values and that juice concentrate gave the greatest COX-1 anti-inflammatory inhibition, leading into the overall conclusion.

Concludes that all processed tart cherry products show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, that processing differentially affects content and bioactivity, and that juice concentrate was superior per serving; includes the copyright line.
Final fragment of the copyright notice from the Institute of Food Technologists (© 2012), marking the end of the article text.
Introduction to gastric mucosal defence: prostaglandins, and the two cyclooxygenase isoforms COX-1 and COX-2, including the original housekeeping vs. inflammatory role concept.
Outdated view that only COX-1 maintains gastric mucosal integrity and that NSAID ulcerogenicity stems solely from COX-1 inhibition, setting up the contrasting recent findings.
Recent evidence that COX-1 and COX-2 both contribute to gastric defence: COX-1 inhibition alone causes no lesions in normal rat mucosa, but adding a COX-2 inhibitor produces severe damage.

Comparison of normal versus acid-challenged rat stomach: normal mucosa needs dual COX-1/COX-2 inhibition for damage, whereas acid challenge makes COX-1 inhibition alone injurious, worsened by COX-2 blockade or dexamethasone.
COX-2 inhibitors alone are non-damaging in normal and acid-challenged mucosa, but become damaging when nitric oxide formation is suppressed or afferent nerves are defunctionalized.
Ischemia-reperfusion of the gastric artery upregulates COX-2 (not COX-1) mRNA; COX-2 inhibitors or dexamethasone worsen the resulting gastric damage up to four-fold, reversed by 16,16-dimethyl-PGE2.

COX-2 inhibitors blunt protection from a mild irritant or intragastric peptone, while endotoxin-induced protection depends on COX-1; selective COX-1 inhibition is less effective in the ischemia model.
COX-2 promotes gastric ulcer healing: it is upregulated in chronic ulcers, and COX-2 inhibitors impair healing as much as non-selective NSAIDs.
Concluding summary that both COX isoenzymes are essential to mucosal defence, each with specific roles across physiological and pathophysiological conditions.
Introduction and study purpose: estimates current usual protein intake among Americans aged 2+ using NHANES 2003-2004 data, expressed in g/day, g/kg ideal body weight, and percent of calories.

Intake results by age group: mean usual protein intake of about 56 g/d in young children, peaking near 91 g/d in adults aged 19-30, and falling to about 66 g/d in the elderly; notes low shares of males below the estimated average requirement.

Inadequate intake findings: 7.7% of adolescent females and 7.2-8.6% of older adult women fall below the estimated average requirement; median protein intake as percent of calories ranges from 13.4% (children 4-8) to 16.0% (men 51-70).

Upper-range intake relative to acceptable macronutrient limits: even the 95th percentile stays far below the 35% AMDR upper bound, peaking at 20.8% of calories in men aged 51-70; introduces the health benefits of higher protein.

Conclusion and recommendation: given benefits for weight management, sarcopenia, and physiologic function, Americans should be encouraged to meet the recommended 17-21% of calories from protein per MyPyramid food patterns.

Introduction and study objective of a cross-sectional study of 71,751 Adventist Health Study-2 participants comparing nutrient intakes across meat- and dairy-defined vegetarian and non-vegetarian dietary patterns.

Study design details: Adventist Health Study-2 cohort, data collected 2002-2007, assessed with a validated 204-item semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire, and five dietary pattern groups (non, semi, pesco, lacto-ovo, strict vegetarian).

Statistical methods (ANCOVA adjusted for age, sex, race; chi-square and ANOVA for BMI and demographics) and the start of results noting significant variation in nutrient intakes between dietary patterns.

Key nutrient results: non-vegetarians had the lowest plant protein, fiber, beta-carotene and magnesium intakes and the highest saturated, trans, arachidonic and DHA fatty acid intakes; strict vegetarians showed possible inadequate intakes in some nutrients.
Energy intake (about 2000 kcal/d across patterns, except 1713 kcal/d in semi vegetarians) and BMI results, with highest mean BMI in non-vegetarians (28.7) and lowest in strict vegetarians (24.0).
Conclusions: nutrient profiles differ markedly by meat and dairy intake patterns, with implications for understanding the etiology of obesity and chronic diseases.

Abstract opening of a review on viscous vs. nonviscous soluble fiber supplements, covering its purpose (health benefits, symptoms with higher fiber intake, adherence to high-fiber diets), data sources, and the core conclusion that fiber benefits depend on specific fiber characteristics.

Conclusions section of the abstract stating that many fiber health benefits correlate with the viscosity (gel-forming ability when hydrated) of soluble fibers, and that reduced viscosity attenuates these benefits while nonviscous fiber shows none.

Implications for practice from the abstract: clinical evidence that viscous soluble fiber, by increasing chyme viscosity, lowers cholesterol, improves glycemic control in type 2 diabetes, and normalizes stool form in constipation and diarrhea.

Closing part of the implications section listing metabolic syndrome outcomes improved by viscous soluble fiber (glycemic control, lipoprotein profile, BMI/weight loss, blood pressure), followed by the 2012 copyright notice from the Author(s) and American Academy of Nurse Practitioners.

Final fragment of the copyright line (©2012 The Author(s), Journal compilation ©2012 American Academy of Nurse Practitioners) closing the document abstract, carrying no substantive content on fiber mechanisms or outcomes.
Introduces diverticular disease in industrialized nations (up to 70% by age 60), linking its origin to low-fiber diet and increasing affluence.

Explains why incidence is highest in prosperous countries with decreased fiber and increased refined grains/sugars, and lists the common symptoms of diverticulosis (left-lower quadrant cramping, bloating, constipation, soiling).
Describes complications when diverticula perforate: abscesses with bleeding, fistulization often to the bladder, and that treatment targets symptoms and may need hospitalization.
Gives dietary management: low-fiber bland diets during symptomatic periods, then gradually increasing fiber to 20-30 g daily or using psyllium once the acute phase resolves.
Final fragment of the psyllium mention, ending the discussion of bulk stimulant fiber supplementation as a dietary option for diverticular disease.

Introduces the Codex Alimentarius definition of dietary fiber (nondigestible carbohydrate polymers with DP of 3+ showing health benefits) and its value for international harmonization across research, composition tables, and labeling.

Notes the consequences of non-acceptance of a global fiber definition, then states that the definition requires research community agreement on physiological effects with substantial scientific support, such as laxation, gut health, lipid, glucose and insulin effects, and colonic fermentation.

Describes the need for research protocols to prove benefits of isolated and synthesized fibers, based on evidence reviews that fairly weigh epidemiological data and account for added fibers missing from food composition databases.

Specifies study design expectations: well-controlled randomized controlled trials, animal studies for mechanisms, and agreed study variables such as subject type and baseline diet suited to the research question.
Concludes that all fiber types can help close the global fiber consumption gap, since fiber-rich and fiber-fortified foods raise intake while keeping energy within allowed levels.
Final fragment completing the point that fiber-rich and fortified foods let consumers boost fiber intake without exceeding energy needs.

Introduction and study aim of a cross-sectional comparison of nutritional quality across vegan, vegetarian, semi-vegetarian, pesco-vegetarian and omnivorous diets, using an online 52-item food frequency questionnaire.

Methods: dietary intake assessed via an online FFQ; diet quality measured with HEI-2010 and Mediterranean Diet Score; sample of 1475 participants classified into the five diet groups with their sample sizes.

Results on nutrient intake: vegans had the lowest energy, better fat profile, lowest protein and highest fiber versus omnivores; vegans also had the lowest calcium intake, below national recommendations.
Diet quality index results: vegans scored highest and omnivores lowest on HEI-2010 and MDS; high fruit/vegetable, low sodium and low saturated fat intake drove scores regardless of index used.
Conclusion on prudent diets: vegetarians, semi-vegetarians and pesco-vegetarians scored variably depending on the indexing system but generally had better nutrient quality than omnivores.

Introduction and objective of a 2012 Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics study on US adult dietary fiber intake: states the recommended fiber Adequate Intake (25-38 g/day) and the aim to track progress toward national goals over the past decade.

Study design and population: cross-sectional, weighted NHANES data on noninstitutionalized US adults aged 18+, collected through the National Center for Health Statistics' nationally representative multistage probability survey.
Methods and main outcome measures: daily dietary fiber intake of the US population, analyzed in 2-year survey groupings spanning 1999-2008.

Key results on overall trends: mean daily fiber intake by period from 1999-2000 through 2007-2008 (15.5-16.1 g/day, essentially flat), plus lower intake among adults with obesity (BMI ≥30) compared with normal weight or overweight groups.

Results on ethnic differences: Mexican Americans had higher fiber intake than non-Hispanic whites in 1999-2000 (18.0 vs 16.1 g/day) without subsequent increase, and non-Hispanic blacks had lower baseline intake that rose only modestly by 2007-2008.

Conclusions: daily fiber intake has generally not progressed toward national goals over the decade, with variation by health and social factors, indicating need for clinical practice and public health strategies.
Copyright and publication notice from Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and Elsevier, marking the end of the abstract.

Study introduction: aims, sample of 100 US vegans, questionnaire-based design, and the statistical outcomes examined (diet motives, lifestyle behaviors, BMI, chronic disease, nutrient intake vs. DRIs).

Methods and key result continuation: outcomes measured, plus the finding that health was the top-reported reason for choosing a vegan diet (47%), and the start of chronic disease prevalence by motive category.

Chronic disease prevalence by motive (health 27%, animal welfare 11%, religious/other 15%) and the finding of no significant differences across motive groups except product fat content choices; begins describing health-congruent behaviors such as regular exercise.

Congruence results: health-motivated vegans showed healthy BMI (71% normal, mean 22.6), minimal alcohol/smoking, healthy food and cooking choices, and mostly adequate protective nutrient intakes, with the start of the incongruence findings.
Conclusion of incongruent findings: 0% vitamin D intake adequacy and excessive sodium use, followed by the copyright notice (Elsevier, 2013).

Opening of an article on prescribing exercise as preventive therapy; introduces the ~1000 kcal/week activity benchmark and the idea that health benefits come from accumulated physical activity, including short 10-minute bouts.

Continuation of the article's introduction, outlining its scope: evaluating cardiovascular and musculoskeletal fitness, assessing physical activity levels, exercise recommendations (intensity, type, time, frequency), and resources for patients and physicians.
Final sentence of the introduction, closing the article's scope by referring to learning resources on evaluating physical activity and fitness and prescribing exercise.

Opening chunk of a guide to exercise prescription: establishes exercise as fundamental to health, cites ACSM and 'Exercise is Medicine' guidance to treat exercise as a vital sign and prescribe physical activity at every visit, and notes that meeting activity goals reduces all-cause mortality.

Closing chunk of a short exercise prescription guide: a fragment continuing the mortality finding, concluding that physicians can improve health by prescribing exercise, followed by the 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces the Miyagi Cohort Study methods: 1990 baseline survey of 28,333 middle-aged adults in rural northern Japan and construction of a lifestyle score counting high-risk practices (smoking, heavy drinking, short daily walking, abnormal BMI).

Describes the statistical methods: Cox regression estimating mortality relative risks by lifestyle score, adjusted for age, education, marital status, disease history and diet, over 11 years of follow-up with 1,200 deaths.

Reports the main results by sex: multivariate relative risks of death rise with the number of high-risk practices, with men's RRs of 1.20 to 3.96 and women's RRs of 1.31 to 5.56, both showing significant linear trends.

Gives the years-of-aging equivalence (2.8 years for men, 4.8 years for women per added high-risk practice) and the conclusion that more high-risk practices linearly increase all-cause mortality risk in rural Japanese adults.

Final concluding sentence summarizing the prospective cohort finding that a greater number of high-risk health practices is linearly associated with higher all-cause mortality among middle-aged Japanese men and women.

Opening of an article on exercise and longevity: introduces aging as a modifiable physiological process and the goal of 'successful aging' through healthy diet, psychosocial well-being, and regular exercise.

Continues the introduction: exercise's established benefits for mortality, chronic disease prevention and control, and life expectancy/quality of life; the review summarizes longevity benefits, mechanisms, and recommendations.

Key findings: exercise partially reverses aging effects on physiology and preserves functional reserve in older adults; a minimum quantity and quality of exercise reduces death risk, certain cancers, and osteoporosis, and increases longevity.

Recommendations on training content: programs should target cardiorespiratory fitness, muscle function, flexibility and balance; benefits relate to training volume and intensity, but more elderly-specific research is needed.

Conclusion: more precise exercise recommendations for the elderly are needed, with the main goal of fostering long-term adherence to physical activity in this growing population; includes the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Opening section of a metaepidemiological study abstract (objective, design, eligibility, data sources) comparing exercise and drug interventions on mortality via meta-analyses of RCTs in Medline and Cochrane databases up to May 2013.

Continuation of the abstract's methods and early results: data sources, the outcome measure (mortality), the random effects network meta-analysis approach, and the initial count of 16 meta-analyses (four exercise, 12 drug).

Results summary giving the total evidence base of 305 RCTs with 339,274 participants, and the 14,716 participants in 57 trials of physical activity across four conditions: coronary heart disease, stroke, heart failure, and diabetes prevention.

Key findings: no statistically detectable differences between exercise and drugs for secondary prevention of coronary heart disease and prediabetes, and the start of the stroke finding that exercise outperformed drug treatment.

Specific effect estimates: exercise was more effective than anticoagulants and antiplatelets in stroke (odds ratios with credible intervals), diuretics beat exercise in heart failure, and inconsistency between direct and indirect comparisons was non-significant.

Conclusion beginning: limited but existing trial evidence suggests exercise and many drugs are often potentially similar in mortality benefit across coronary heart disease secondary prevention, post-stroke rehabilitation, heart failure, and diabetes prevention.

Final fragment of the conclusion listing the conditions (secondary prevention of coronary heart disease, rehabilitation after stroke, heart failure treatment, diabetes prevention) where exercise and drugs show similar mortality benefits.

Opening passage of the document, introducing the claim that genetic and environmental factors (diet, lifestyle) both contribute to cardiovascular disease, cancer, and other major mortality causes, with environmental factors judged most important, and cautioning about overhyped genetic research priorities.

Middle passage continuing the document's argument: warns that inflated expectations for genetic research could distort health research priorities and spending, then argues that integrating genetic data into epidemiologic studies helps clarify causal links between lifestyle, genetics, and disease risk, concluding that a balanced approach is needed.
Final sentence of the document, concluding that a balanced approach combining lifestyle and genomics research gives the best data for informed decisions on the most effective ways to prevent disease.
Opening of the EPIC-Norfolk study abstract: background on behavioural factors and health, stating the aim to quantify the combined mortality impact of four health behaviours in the general community.

Methods of the abstract: describes the prospective cohort of 20,244 UK adults aged 45–79 without prior CVD or cancer (baseline 1993–1997, follow-up to 2006) and the four-behaviour scoring rules (non-smoking, not inactive, moderate alcohol, vitamin C fruit/veg intake).
Scoring details and first results of the abstract: 0–4 point score and adjusted relative mortality risks for three, two, one, and zero behaviours versus four, after about 11 years of follow-up.
Specific numerical results from the abstract: adjusted relative risks with confidence intervals for all-cause mortality (1,987 deaths) by number of healthy behaviours, with p-value for trend.

Robustness and interpretation in the abstract: consistency across subgroups and after excluding early deaths, strongest cardiovascular trends, and the finding that four vs zero behaviours equals about 14 years of chronological age.

Abstract conclusion (4-fold total mortality difference, equivalent to 14 years of age) followed by the start of the Editors' Summary, which introduces public confusion over lifestyle advice such as diet, exercise, and alcohol.
Editors' Summary background: examples of conflicting lifestyle research on diet, physical activity (e.g., daily walking), and alcohol, illustrating why health messages are hard to communicate.

Editors' Summary continuation: the confusing evidence on alcohol (small amounts beneficial, large amounts harmful) and how this hinders public-health officials from encouraging effective behaviour change.
Editors' Summary 'Why Was This Study Done?': notes that evidence on individual behavioural factors is strong but evidence on their combined effect is scarce, and introduces the EPIC study context.
Rationale continued: argues that combining several small lifestyle differences could have a marked population health effect, making simple behaviour-change messages more persuasive.

Study design in the Editors' Summary: EPIC study, lifestyle-mortality relationship assessed with a score based on four simple behaviours (smoking, physical activity, alcohol, fruit and vegetable intake).

Editors' Summary 'What Did the Researchers Do and Find?': describes the roughly 20,000 Norfolk UK participants aged 45–79 without cancer or cardiovascular disease, recruited 1993–1997 with questionnaires, exams, and vitamin C measurement.

Method of score construction in the Editors' Summary: one point each for non-smoking, not physically inactive, and moderate alcohol intake, plus vitamin C consistent with five daily fruit/vegetable servings; defines the key scoring criteria.
Definitions in the Editors' Summary: explains physical inactivity (sedentary job with no recreational exercise), what counts as a unit of alcohol, and that deaths were tracked until 2006.

Key findings in plain language: people scoring 0 were about four times as likely to die (especially from cardiovascular disease) as those scoring 4, and those scoring 2 were twice as likely, after adjusting for factors such as age.

'What Do These Findings Mean?' section: interprets the 4-fold difference in mortality risk over about 11 years for middle-aged and older adults and notes the risk falls as healthy behaviours increase.
Interpretation continued: concludes that a score-0 person has the same death risk as a score-4 person 14 years older, and the relationship is strongest for cardiovascular death.

Limitations and implications: findings need confirmation in other populations and analysis of quality of life, but suggest modest, achievable lifestyle changes could meaningfully improve population health.

Closing of the Editors' Summary: advises public-health officials to use these findings to encourage behaviour changes for middle-aged and older people, followed by an 'Additional Information' pointer to the online version.
Final fragment of the document: the DOI reference (journal.pmed.0050012) for the online version of the Editors' Summary.

Introduction and methods opening of an EPIC-Potsdam study on how four healthy lifestyle factors relate to reduced risk of chronic diseases (diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer) in German adults aged 35-65.

Methods continuation defining the four healthy lifestyle factors (never smoking, BMI under 30, at least 3.5 h/week physical activity, healthy diet) and the chronic disease endpoints such as confirmed incident type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, stroke, and cancer.
Methods detail on scoring the lifestyle index (1 point per healthy factor, 0 to 4 total) followed by the start of results: mean 7.8-year follow-up and the number of new cases of each disease.

Results on the distribution of healthy factors among participants (few had zero, about 9% had all four) and the adjusted hazard ratios showing chronic disease risk falling as healthy factors increase.

Key results giving the risk reduction for participants with all four healthy factors (78% overall, with 93% for diabetes, 81% for myocardial infarction, 50% for stroke, 36% for cancer) compared with those having none.
Conclusion stating that adhering to four simple healthy lifestyle factors has a strong preventive effect against chronic diseases, closing the abstract of the EPIC-Potsdam study.

Introduction and methods of a study on healthy lifestyle behaviors (not smoking, healthy diet, physical activity) and all-cause mortality, using NHANES 1999-2002 data of 8375 US adults aged 20+ followed through 2006.

Results on follow-up (mean 5.7 years, 745 deaths) and risk reductions for all-cause mortality associated with nonsmoking (56%), physical activity (47%), and healthy diet (26%), with confidence intervals.
Dose-response findings: mortality risk decreases progressively with the number of healthy behaviors, with adjusted hazard ratios of 0.60, 0.45, and 0.18 for 1, 2, and 3 healthy behaviors versus none.

Conclusion of the NHANES-based study stating that not smoking, healthy diet, and sufficient physical activity substantially reduce the risk of early death among US adults; includes publisher attribution to Elsevier.

Abstract opening of a Taiwanese cohort study on food expenditure and mortality: background, hypothesis about spending on nutritious foods, and the methods setup using the 1999–2000 Elderly Nutrition and Health Survey followed to 2008.

Methods continuation describing the sample of 1781 adults aged 65+ with 24-hour dietary recall, estimation of daily expenditures for vegetable, fruit, animal-derived, and grain food categories using monthly national food prices, and linkage to the national death registry.

Start of the Results section: 625 deaths over the 10-year follow-up, and the finding that the top expenditure quintiles for vegetables and fruits had the highest survival rates across the four food categories.

Key quantitative findings: after covariate adjustment, higher (Q4) vegetable and fruit spending versus Q1 predicted lower mortality (HRs 0.55 and 0.64), with risk falling 12% and 10% per NT$15 daily increase; animal-derived and grain spending showed no predictive association.
Conclusion of the abstract: greater and more affordable vegetable and fruit spending may strengthen food security and longevity among older adults.

Introduction/background of a Taiwan study on the life expectancy gap between Aboriginal and general populations, noting persistent male disparity despite medical investment, and stating the study's aims of quantifying cause-of-death contributions and proposing bridging initiatives.
Methods section describing the study population (about 200,000 residents of 30 Aboriginal townships in Taiwan) and the approach of decomposing the life expectancy gap by major causes of death.
Results opening: Aboriginal mortality in these townships was roughly 70% higher than general populations over 30 years, with infectious disease, cirrhosis, accidents, and suicide notably elevated.
Results on life expectancy trends: the male gap widened from 8.5 years (1971-1973) to 13.5 years (1998-2000), while the female gap stayed relatively stable (8.0 and 8.4 years).
Results on decomposition: digestive diseases (mainly cirrhosis), accidents, and infectious/parasitic diseases account for half (50%) of the 13.5-year male life expectancy gap.
Conclusions section: the female gap was 41% attributable to these preventable causes, and the authors recommend primary prevention targeting infectious diseases, liver cirrhosis, and accidents.
Final clause of the conclusion, closing the recommendation to focus primary prevention on infectious and parasitic diseases, liver cirrhosis, and accidents.

Study design and objectives from a Baltimore cohort of older women (Women's Health and Aging Studies) examining fruit/vegetable intake (serum carotenoids), physical activity, and all-cause mortality using Cox proportional hazards models.

Methods section detailing model covariate adjustment (age, education, race/ethnicity), setting in Baltimore, Maryland, the study population of 713 women aged 70-79, and how carotenoids and physical activity were measured at baseline.

Results opening: 5-year follow-up with 82 deaths (11.5%), and hazard ratios showing continuous physical activity (kilocalorie expenditure) improves survival, with the most active versus least active women compared.
Results on carotenoid associations: continuous total serum carotenoids and highest vs. lowest tertile both improve survival, with hazard ratios and confidence intervals reported.

Combined model results where physical activity and carotenoids together predict survival, followed by the conclusion that low carotenoids plus low physical activity strongly predicts earlier mortality.
Final conclusion sentence stating preliminary support that higher fruit and vegetable intake and exercise improve survival in older women.
Introduction/background and objective of a Swedish prospective cohort study on fruit and vegetable intake and all-cause mortality, using dose-response methods.

Design section: the population-based cohort of 71,706 Swedish adults aged 45-83, FV intake via self-administered questionnaire, and the statistical methods (Laplace regression for survival percentile differences, Cox regression for hazard ratios).

Results opening: 13-year follow-up with 11,439 deaths, and the finding that lower FV consumption relative to 5 servings/day is progressively linked to shorter survival, beginning with the never-consumed-FV estimate.
Key quantitative results: non-consumers of FV lived about 3 years shorter with a 53% higher mortality rate, and those never eating fruit lived 19 months shorter than those eating 1 fruit/day.

Vegetable-specific result that 3 vegetables/day associated with 32 months longer survival than never eating vegetables, plus the conclusion that intake below 5 servings/day is linked to shorter survival and higher mortality, and trial registration information begins.
Trial registration details: the Swedish Mammography Cohort and Cohort of Swedish Men registered on clinicaltrials.gov as NCT01127698 and NCT01127711.

Introduction and methods opening of a randomized, double-blind trial of curcumin in Iranian veterans with chronic sulphur mustard-induced pruritic skin lesions, describing the study aims on inflammatory biomarkers, pruritus, and quality of life.

Methods continuing with trial design: 96 male veterans randomized to curcumin 1 g/day (n=46) or placebo (n=50) for four weeks, and the serum biomarkers measured (IL-6, IL-8, hs-CRP, CGRP) and the pruritus and DLQI quality-of-life instruments.

Results beginning with biomarker outcomes: IL-8 and hs-CRP fell significantly in both groups, with a larger reduction in the curcumin group (P < 0.001), and the start of the statement on pruritus and quality-of-life measures.

Results on CGRP, IL-6 and correlations: CGRP decreased only in the curcumin group, IL-6 did not change significantly, and in the curcumin group CGRP changes correlated with IL-6 changes and DLQI changes correlated with IL-8 changes.

Regression findings and conclusion: in the curcumin group IL-8 change predicted DLQI scores, while no variable predicted pruritus scores; the conclusion states curcumin mitigates inflammation in SM-induced cutaneous complications, possibly explaining pruritus relief and QoL improvement.

Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that curcumin's anti-inflammatory effect in chronic sulphur mustard-induced cutaneous complications may account for the observed pruritus alleviation and quality-of-life improvement.
Introduction to the document arguing for promiscuous drugs over selective ones; defines drug selectivity and why it is considered desirable, citing chronic myeloid leukemia as an example.
Continues the background on selectivity, explaining why a single targeted agent works well when a disease has one molecular driver, using CML and the Philadelphia chromosome as the example.
Introduces the Discussion section: the growing understanding of disease mechanisms motivates drugs that produce specific, targeted actions in selected cell populations.
Discussion on targeted therapy against distinct molecular targets and signal-transduction pathways, noting that most diseases involve multiple abnormalities rather than a single one.

Explains why single-target drugs fall short: diseases involve several out-of-balance dysfunctional proteins, drugs may hit proteins with similar domains, and pleiotropic cytokines influence multiple normal pathways.
Notes that long-term experience shows single-target drugs have unavoidable off-target functional effects, so molecular targeting is not medically flawless; begins the Summary section.

Summary thesis: an ideal drug works by rebalancing several contributing proteins or events rather than inhibiting one target, i.e., a promiscuous drug, which could minimize side effects at low concentration.

Corollaries of the argument: pursuing truly selective drugs may be imprudent given the totality of responses, and the expensive screening methods used to find them may be medically and financially inefficient.
Final fragment of the conclusion, stating that the costly screening for selective drugs is medically and financially inefficient.

Opening thesis of the article 'From exotic spice to modern drug?': rising demand for cheaper therapeutics and worries over side effects of common drugs are renewing interest in traditional Eastern medicine, especially from India and China.

Opening of the paper's introduction: defines low-molecular-weight plant phenols as semiochemicals and argues their reactivity, biocompatibility, and evolved target affinity make them promising, under-explored drug lead compounds.

Introduction continuing the rationale: frames plant phenolics as a natural product library rich in privileged scaffolds, citing endogenous phenols, aryl-hydroxyl phytochemicals, and phenolic synthetic drugs as evidence.

Introduction describing the proposed approach: applying bio-chemo-informatic tools to the phenolic library to find new drug candidates and check ADMET suitability, followed by a brief overview of the structural diversity of plant phenolics.

Scope and problem statement: the review focuses on dietary or pharmacologically well-studied phenolics, noting that despite growing supplement use, these natural products progress slowly through clinical trials toward drug registration.

Motivation and critique: argues that the lack of progress wastes renewable resources that should be turned into high-value healthcare products, calling for reform in the name of sustainability, and states the paper's aim.

Core research question: asks why well-studied phenolics such as catechins, curcumin, resveratrol, quercetin and its glycosides, genistein, and silymarin struggle to reach registered drug or even IND status despite known health benefits.

Opening section of a paper on hormesis and dietary restriction (DR) life extension: introduces evidence that DR-level food restriction in rodents boosts stress resistance and raises plasma corticosterone, suggesting DR acts as a low-intensity stressor.

Closing portion of the same paper on hormesis in dietary restriction: restates that low-intensity stress from DR likely drives its life-extending and anti-aging effects, and concludes after weighing evidence that hormesis plays an important role.

Opening of an abstract on dietary restriction and longevity: defines the intervention (10-50% reduction below ad libitum intake) and its lifespan and disease-prevention effects across species, and previews the review's aim of examining mortality trajectories under nutrient deprivation.

Abstract passage outlining the review's structure: summarizes mortality data from species on restricted diets, asks whether calorie or specific nutrient lack drives the longevity response, and introduces hormesis as a possible proximate mechanism.

Abstract conclusion on demographic evidence: dietary restriction appears to slow cumulative age-related cellular damage and improve organisms' ability to cope with irreversible injury; also begins the point that restricting essential nutrients may matter.

Abstract discussion of nutrient restriction and hormesis: restricting essential nutrients as well as calories may affect life expectancy in a species-specific way, and hormesis, an evolutionarily conserved low-stress protective response, likely contributes to dietary restriction's health benefits.
Final sentence of the abstract restating hormesis as a likely contributor to dietary restriction's health benefits, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.

Abstract-style findings from a study of Mycobacterium avium: 3H-methyl-labeled methionine is incorporated into surface lipids via transmethylation, which is inhibited by DL-ethionine and norleucine isomers, and DL-norleucine markedly alters the outer envelope layer structure.

Introduction to the xenohormesis review: dietary phytochemicals from fruits, vegetables, and spices have health-beneficial effects through modulation of cellular signal transduction pathways, and secondary plant metabolites are introduced.

Explains the core xenohormesis concept: phytoalexins are plant toxins that defend against pests, but at low dietary doses in humans and mammals they act as mild stressors that activate adaptive cellular stress-response signaling.

States the review's purpose: examining xenohormesis mechanisms behind the chemopreventive effects of certain dietary phytochemicals, with a focus on the transcription factor Nrf2 as a key mediator, with NF-E2 named in full.
Closing part of the abstract naming Nrf2 (NF-E2-related factor 2) as the key player, followed by the 2011 New York Academy of Sciences copyright notice.

Opening passage of a short article on aging research: it contrasts a decade of work on genes and signaling pathways governing aging with a recent shift toward treatments that mimic the effects of dietary restriction to slow aging.

Opening definition of hormesis from toxicology and biology: a biphasic dose response (low-dose benefit, high-dose harm) and an adaptive response to moderate, intermittent stress, with ischemic preconditioning given as the first example.

Continues the list of hormesis examples (exercise, dietary energy restriction, low-dose phytochemicals) and describes the signaling mechanisms behind hormetic responses, namely kinases, deacetylases, Nrf-2 and NF-κB.

Explains the downstream result of hormetic signaling: cells produce more cytoprotective and restorative proteins (growth factors, phase 2 and antioxidant enzymes, chaperones), and notes that mechanistic understanding is opening new prevention and treatment approaches.
Closing sentence of the document: better cellular and molecular understanding of hormesis is leading to novel approaches for preventing and treating many diseases.

Opening of the document introducing the xenohormesis hypothesis: plant molecules affect mammalian health, and heterotrophs (animals, fungi) may sense plant stress-induced chemical cues as early warnings of deteriorating conditions.

Concluding sentence of the document's thesis: these stress-signaling chemical cues let heterotrophs prepare for adversity while conditions remain favorable, completing the xenohormesis proposal begun in the preceding chunk.

Opening chunk of an abstract on plant heat stress: introduces evolved thermotolerance responses, heat stress proteins and molecular chaperones, and Arabidopsis transcriptome findings on non-classical thermotolerance factors.

Middle chunk of the abstract covering non-classical thermotolerance factors, the roles of plant hormones and reactive oxygen species in heat stress signaling, and mutants with altered thermotolerance that reveal the response's complexity.
Final fragment of the abstract, a brief closing clause on how mutants with altered thermotolerance extend understanding of the complexity of plant heat stress responses.

Opening of the document introducing that plant and animal signalling research has developed separately, and that recent work reveals similar signalling elements across kingdoms, such as wounding-response pathways.

Middle section naming specific shared mechanisms (prostaglandin/octadecanoid wounding responses, steroid signalling, pathogen recognition) and discussing whether similarities arise from convergence or common ancestry, then starting the list of ecological implications.

Continuation of the ecological and evolutionary implications list: cross-kingdom pathogens, herbivore manipulation of plant responses, shared microbial genes, plant defenses exploiting animal signals, and human medicinal plant use.
Concluding sentence arguing that comparative study of signalling across plants, animals, and microbes offers useful insights into the ecology and evolution of interactions between kingdoms.

Opening chunk of a document defining xenohormesis, the principle that stressed plants produce bioactive compounds that benefit animals that eat them; introduces the plant stress response and its link to plants' stationary lifestyle.

Middle chunk continuing the xenohormesis definition: explains that eliciting plant stress can boost yield of health-promoting compounds, and that ingested xenohormetic compounds improve animal longevity and fitness by activating cellular stress responses.
Final chunk of the xenohormesis overview, noting the practical applications of xenohormetic compounds in drug discovery, drug production, and nutritional enhancement of diet.
Introduction/background: phytochemicals' health benefits and the concern that small, simple phytochemical structures may bind proteins with low selectivity, setting up the study's premise.
Core finding: zerumbone binds many proteins non-selectively; zerumbone-modified proteins are recognized by Hsp90, activating HSF1-dependent heat shock protein induction in hepa1c1c7 cells.
In vivo and organism-level evidence: oral zerumbone raises Hsp expression in rat liver, and zerumbone pretreatment confers thermoresistance in hepa1c1c7 cells and C. elegans.

Structure-activity comparison: phytochemicals with higher hydrophobicity or electrophilicity (e.g., phenethyl isothiocyanate, curcumin) strongly induce heat shock proteins, while most tested nutrients do not.
Conclusion and interpretation: non-specific protein modification causes mild proteostress that triggers the heat shock response (xenohormesis), potentiating protein quality control.
Closing statement: heat shock response may be a fundamental mechanism underlying the diverse bioactivities of phytochemicals.

Introduction of a review on childhood urticaria: defines urticaria (wheals and/or angioedema) as common in children and stresses paediatric-specific considerations for identifying triggers and drug therapy.

Scope of the review covering spontaneous acute/chronic and physical urticarias in children, and their underlying causes (infections, food/drug hypersensitivity, autoreactivity, autoimmune conditions) with diagnostic recommendations.

Treatment section: second-generation antihistamines as the mainstay of symptom relief with paediatric dose adjustment, plus other interventions, and a closing call for paediatric research on unmet needs.
Concluding statement of the review's aim: promoting paediatric research to enable effective management of childhood urticaria.
Introduction and methods start of a study on chronic urticaria (CU) and Anisakis simplex sensitization in an area where marinated fish is commonly eaten, including the 1% CU prevalence background.

Methods continued: 919 adults at the Bari Allergy Center were screened for CU history; CU patients and 187 controls had skin-prick testing with A. simplex extract, and reactors were placed on a 6-month raw-fish-free diet with follow-up after 3 more months.

Results begin: 213 of 919 (23%) met CU criteria, 49.7% of them were A. simplex sensitized, with an age-related difference (>65 vs <65 years), and all sensitized patients were regular marinated-fish eaters; controls had 16% sensitization.

Results continued: the 6-month raw-fish-free diet resolved urticaria in 77% of sensitized patients versus 2% of non-dietary-change subjects, and all nonresponders were house-dust mite sensitized; relapse after follow-up is introduced.

Final results and conclusion: CU relapsed in 88% of those who reintroduced raw fish versus 14% who stayed on the diet, concluding that A. simplex hypersensitivity is a frequent cause of CU where raw or marinated fish is eaten; includes copyright notice.
Copyright line only (S. Karger AG, Basel, 2012) closing the abstract text.

Introduction and background of a case study on Anisakis simplex (nematode parasite) allergy, noting that 8 patients developed allergic symptoms after eating chicken meat rather than fish, possibly due to fishmeal in chicken feed.

Background continued: explains that chicken feed often contains fishmeal that may be contaminated with Anisakis simplex, and states the study's objective of determining whether parasite proteins in chicken meat cause the patients' symptoms.

Methods section describing in vivo tests (prick, bronchial challenge, double-blind placebo-controlled meat challenge) and immunoblotting of patient and control sera to detect A simplex sensitization in the 8 patients.

Methods and start of results: testing A simplex protein presence in sera from fishmeal-fed versus cereal-fed chickens, exclusion of other chicken nematode sensitization, and the finding that all 8 patients had positive prick and challenge tests to A simplex.

Results of immunoblotting: patients 3-8 recognized a 16 kd band using fishmeal-fed chicken serum as antigen, matching fish-shellfish and A simplex larva pools, with no detection from cereal-fed chicken sera.
Conclusion of the study: in vivo and in vitro evidence shows subjects highly sensitized to A simplex can detect Anisakis species allergens in chicken meat, implying contamination via fishmeal feed.

Introduces the study's origin: a patient allergic to cat dander and pork prompted screening of cat-allergic patients for pork sensitization, using sera from 10 young patients with IgE to both cat and pork to find a shared cross-reactive allergen.

Describes the methods and first key finding: immunoblotting identified serum albumin as a jointly recognized molecule in cat and pig, confirmed by anti-albumin IgE titrations and cross-inhibition experiments.

Presents the molecular and inhibition results: cat serum albumin cDNA was cloned from liver and compared with porcine and human albumin sequences, and inhibition showed cat albumin IgE reactivity fully encompassed porcine albumin reactivity, implying cat sensitization came first.

Gives the epidemiological findings: sensitization to cat albumin occurred in 14-23% of cat-allergic persons across two cohorts, porcine albumin sensitization in 3-10%, and about a third of these may have allergic symptoms from pork eating.
Concludes that sensitization to cat serum albumin is a useful marker for possible cross-sensitization to porcine serum albumin and other mammalian serum albumins.

Opening of an allergy study abstract: objective (examining milk-allergic patients for cross-reactivity between milk, beef, pork, cat/dog dander, and inhalant allergens) and methods (19 patients selected by ImmunoCAP IgE results, tested against Johnson grass, short ragweed, pet dander, and D. farina).

Results section of the study on milk, meat, and pet allergy cross-reactivity: Pearson correlations of IgE levels between beef, pork, and milk (r2 = 0.89, 0.81, 0.60), all cat-allergic patients also reacting to beef/pork or milk, and a significant pork–dog dander correlation (r2 = 0.38).

Final results and conclusion of the study: a significant pork–dog dander IgE correlation, no correlation between milk-meat-pet and grass-weed-dust allergies, and recommendations to screen pet-allergic patients for meat and milk allergy and for milk-allergic patients to avoid cow and pork meat.
Closing sentence of the study's discussion and conclusion, recommending that milk-allergic patients avoid cows (beef/dairy) and pork meat due to cross-reactivity with pet allergies.
Opening chunk of an abstract/review on fish and shellfish allergy in children, introducing rising seafood allergy reports and the need for better diagnosis and understanding of persistent allergy.

Middle-early part of the abstract covering newly identified allergens and cross-reacting allergens across fish, shellfish, arachnids, and insects, plus the diagnostic use of prick-to-prick tests with raw and cooked seafood extracts.

Abstract section on treatment and persistence: allergen-specific immunotherapy with mutated less allergenic seafood proteins, and why allergy persists given seafood proteins' resistance to cooking and extreme pH.

Abstract passage noting that IgE from persistent-allergy patients may target different epitopes than in transient allergy, and that future technology should improve diagnosis and prognosis for childhood seafood allergy.
Closing sentence of the abstract about predicting the course of childhood seafood allergy, followed by the publisher copyright notice (© 2012 John Wiley & Sons A/S, Blackwell Publishing Ltd.).
Introduces Anisakis simplex, a parasite in raw or undercooked contaminated saltwater fish, and the two clinical presentations: gastrointestinal disease and food-allergy-type adverse reactions.

Describes the allergic reaction spectrum (rhinitis, conjunctivitis, anaphylaxis) and frames the intestinal epithelium as a defense barrier that becomes an open gate for toxins and allergens when compromised.

States the study aim, sensitization to A. simplex in patients with allergy symptoms, and cites prior evidence linking altered intestinal permeability to worse food adverse reaction symptoms; mentions the skin prick testing approach.

Details methods: food skin prick testing supplemented with the Ani s1 allergen, and intestinal permeability measured in sensitized subjects at enrolment (time 0) and after 6 months on a raw fish-free diet (time 6).
Reports results: 540 screened, 170 skin-prick positive, 87 (51.2%) Ani s1 positive; increased permeability in sensitized patients with worse symptoms that resolved after eliminating raw seafood.
Concludes that eating raw fish threatens intestinal mucosal integrity, making this an under-estimated open gate for molecules that may predispose to more serious diseases.

Opening of the document's summary: history of human Anisakis simplex infection (1960s, raw/undercooked fish) and the 1990s recognition that ingesting dead worms in fish can cause hypersensitivity reactions, possibly more common than infection itself.
Continuation of the summary: introduces gastroallergic anisakiasis and notes true anaphylaxis from allergen exposure via food, airborne, or skin contact routes, and states the review's scope.

Summary sentences stating the review's scope (A. simplex pathogenesis in humans, hypersensitivity from living infection and other allergen exposure routes) and the last 20 years of research on antigen characterization and immune responses.

Summary passage on molecular characterization of Anisakis allergens and cDNA isolation as an active research area, aimed at better diagnostics and understanding of pathogenesis and controversial allergy aspects.

Final summary sentences on parasite products (allergens, proteinases, proteinase inhibitors) and activation of basophils, eosinophils, and mast cells in A. simplex hypersensitivity from living or dead parasites.
Closing fragment of the summary, completing the phrase about hypersensitivity states induced by parasite exposure whether dead or alive.

Introduction of an evidence-based review on chronic urticaria (CU) in children: prevalence (~25% lifetime urticaria), progression to chronic disease affecting quality of life, the range of proposed causes, and the frequent label of chronic idiopathic urticaria.

Continuation of the introduction: notes that the cause of pediatric CU often cannot be identified, and states the authors' aim of creating a conceptual framework from cumulative evidence to guide categorization, evaluation, and treatment of CU in children.
Closing sentence of the abstract stating the framework's purpose for categorizing, evaluating, and treating pediatric chronic urticaria, followed by the 2011 Wiley Periodicals copyright notice.

Introduction and background of a study on pediatric 'idiopathic' allergic reactions, introducing IgE antibodies to the carbohydrate galactose-α-1,3-galactose (α-Gal) as a newly identified cause of delayed urticaria and anaphylaxis after eating mammalian meat.

Explains the study's objective: testing whether IgE to α-Gal is present in children with idiopathic anaphylaxis or urticaria, linking the reactions to beef, pork, or lamb consumed 3 to 6 hours earlier.

Methods section describing the enrollment of children aged 4 to 17 at the University of Virginia and Lynchburg, VA allergy practices, and the ImmunoCAP serum testing for total IgE and specific IgE to α-Gal, meats, cat, dog, and milk allergens.
Results section reporting 45 pediatric patients with both delayed meat-related reactions and α-Gal-specific IgE, most of whom had a prior tick bite within the past year that itched and persisted.

Conclusions stating that delayed anaphylaxis and urticaria after mammalian meat is not uncommon in local children, is hard to identify, and should prompt specific testing in areas where the Lone Star tick is common.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending the statement that the Lone Star tick is common in the study area, which motivates testing for children living there.

Opening of the review on childhood urticaria and angioedema: defines scope (acute and chronic urticaria, pediatric differential diagnosis) and introduces the recent-findings section on triggers and subtypes.

Continuation of the recent findings: urticaria triggers vary, subtypes may respond differently to therapies, allergic and infectious triggers need evaluation, and idiopathic urticaria must be distinguished from anaphylaxis, systemic and autoimmune conditions.

Discussion of treatment and impact: antihistamines remain first-line, novel agents like omalizumab help some subtypes, and chronic urticaria substantially reduces quality of life; the summary section begins here.

Summary conclusions: urticaria is common, targeted therapies for distinct subtypes are growing, and careful individualized assessment is needed to exclude other etiologies before diagnosing idiopathic urticaria.
Final sentence of the summary, completing the advice that potential etiologies must be excluded before labeling a case as idiopathic urticaria.

Opening chunk of the NEISS food-allergy study abstract: introduces the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System as a nationally representative ED sample, states the objective of measuring food-allergy adverse event magnitude and severity, and begins the methods (34 EDs, Aug–Sep 2003).

Methods completion and main results: 34 participating EDs during Aug 1–Sep 30, 2003, and extrapolated national estimates of 20,821 ED visits, 2,333 anaphylaxis visits, and 520 food-allergy hospitalizations over the 2-month period.

Demographics and food-specific findings: median patient age 26, 24% of visits in children ≤5 years, shellfish most implicated in those ≥6 years, eggs/fruit/peanuts/tree nuts in younger children, and no reported deaths; begins describing medical record review.

Treatment and diagnosis gaps: only 19% of patients received epinephrine, and 57% of likely anaphylactic events lacked an ED anaphylaxis diagnosis per 2005 symposium criteria; also opens the conclusion that NEISS data are a useful assessment tool.

Final conclusion: NEISS data are useful for assessing food-allergic event magnitude and severity, and the criteria-based medical record review suggests emergency departments underdiagnose anaphylaxis.
Introduces anti-Gal, a natural human antibody, and its specific target the alpha-galactosyl epitope, which is abundant on nonprimate thyrocytes but absent in humans; sets up prior porcine findings.

States the study hypothesis: anti-Gal may contribute to Graves' disease pathogenesis by stimulating patients' thyrocytes, building on earlier work showing TSH-like effects of anti-Gal on porcine thyrocytes.

Reports results in GD primary thyrocyte cultures: anti-Gal binds GD thyrocytes and raises cAMP, iodine-125 uptake, and DNA synthesis, and depleting anti-Gal from autologous sera sharply reduces their stimulatory effect.

Gives negative controls: no binding or stimulation by anti-Gal in normal thyrocytes or in thyrotoxic patients lacking thyroid-stimulating or TBII immunoglobulins, and concludes anti-Gal may drive continuous thyrocyte stimulation in GD.
Concludes that anti-Gal may contribute to in vivo chronic thyrocyte stimulation in GD and proposes a mechanism involving aberrant alpha-galactosyl epitopes on the TSH receptor.
Final sentence of the abstract, closing the discussion of the proposed mechanism by which anti-Gal may act on the TSH receptor in GD.
Abstract background and aim of a study on whether anaphylaxis to pork or beef kidney, like delayed meat anaphylaxis, involves galactose-α-1,3-galactose (αGal)-specific IgE.

Methods section describing the 14 patients, prick and Erbitux (cetuximab) skin tests, ImmunoCAP IgE measurements for αGal and other allergens, ELISA estimation of αGal levels, and the inhibition assay for cross-reactivity.
Results section reporting clinical features: 12 of 14 patients had anaphylactic shock, reactions typically within 2 hours, and alcohol as the main cofactor in patients with risk factors.

Results on diagnostic findings: oral challenge with pork kidney caused anaphylaxis at small doses, kidney prick tests were positive in 54%, all patients had positive Erbitux tests and detectable αGal-specific IgE levels (0.4 to 294 kU/l).

Key findings and conclusions: IgE binding to αGal was inhibited by raw pork kidney extract (mean 77%), indicating high αGal content, and the authors conclude that kidney anaphylaxis is linked to αGal IgE, possibly explaining its severity.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence attributing the severity of kidney anaphylaxis to high αGal epitope content, followed by the 2012 John Wiley & Sons copyright notice.
Introduces anti-Gal, the most abundant natural human antibody (~1% of immunoglobulins), its ligand the α-gal carbohydrate epitope, and where that epitope occurs in mammals.
Describes anti-Gal's role in immunological pathogenesis, specifically IgE-mediated allergies to meat and to the monoclonal antibody cetuximab, both involving α-gal epitopes.
Covers anti-Gal's involvement in autoimmunity (Graves' disease), Chagas' disease via Trypanosoma cruzi α-gal epitopes, and xenograft rejection, then leads into its clinical exploitation.

Presents clinical uses of anti-Gal: boosting vaccine immunogenicity (e.g., influenza) by targeting α-gal-presenting antigens to antigen-presenting cells, and converting tumour lesions into autologous vaccines via intratumoral α-gal glycolipids.

Explains how anti-Gal binding targets α-gal-expressing tumour cells for antigen-presenting cell uptake, and describes accelerated wound healing from α-gal nanoparticles that activate complement and macrophages.
Concludes with the potential of α-gal nanoparticle therapy for regenerating internally injured tissues, such as ischaemic myocardium and injured nerves.

Introduces the discovery of a natural anti-alpha-galactosyl IgG antibody (anti-Gal) in high serum titer in all normal individuals, its isolation via melibiose-Sepharose affinity chromatography, and its reactivity with alpha-galactosyl residues on rabbit RBCs, with specificity tested by carbohydrate inhibition.

Describes anti-Gal binding to alpha-galactosyl residues (possibly glycolipids) on human RBCs after pronase removal of membrane proteins, and its specific binding to normal and pathologically senescent human RBCs, suggesting a role in red blood cell aging.

Discusses the ubiquitous, lifelong high-titer presence of anti-Gal implying constant antigenic stimulation, and its theoretical interest and potential immunodiagnostic significance as a marker for the study of anti-Gal reactivity.
States the key diagnostic finding that a decrease in anti-Gal antibody titer reflects humoral immunodeficiency disorders, concluding the abstract's discussion of clinical relevance.

Introduces the paper's topic: a novel IgE antibody response to the alpha-gal oligosaccharide epitope, linked to two forms of anaphylaxis, in the context of anaphylaxis risk management when the trigger is unknown.

Describes the two alpha-gal anaphylaxis presentations (immediate reaction to first intravenous cetuximab, and delayed reaction 3-6 hours after eating beef or pork) and begins the claim that tick bites are a major cause of alpha-gal IgE in the US.

States the geographic and epidemiologic findings: tick bites likely cause alpha-gal IgE in the southern, eastern and central US, cases are rising and increasingly affect children, and the response cross-reacts with cat and dog without clearly raising asthma risk.
Concludes that the alpha-gal IgE response may interfere with diagnostic testing in some situations, closing the document's discussion of clinical implications.

Introduces the 2009 discovery of delayed anaphylaxis to red meat linked to IgE against alpha-gal, noting patients previously tolerated meat, implying an adult-life sensitizing exposure; this motivates the study of causes.

States the study's aims (investigating causes of alpha-gal IgE, focused on tick bites common in the affected region) and the methods, using biotinylated proteins and extracts on a streptavidin ImmunoCAP serum assay.

Presents key results: prospective data show 20-fold or greater rises in alpha-gal IgE after tick bites in three subjects, plus a strong statistical link between tick-bite history and alpha-gal IgE and its prevalence where Amblyomma americanum is common.

Reports the correlation between alpha-gal IgE and IgE to A. americanum proteins (rs=0.75, p<0.001) and concludes tick bites are a cause, or possibly the sole cause, of alpha-gal IgE in this US region.

Closing conclusion emphasizing the striking number of sensitized subjects and high IgE titers, and noting this is the first documented case of an ectoparasite response producing an important food allergy.
Abstract opening: introduces Neu5Gc, a sialic acid humans cannot make but accumulate from red meat and dairy, and the anti-Neu5Gc heterophile antibodies found in cancer patients.

Abstract middle: explains humans' Neu5Gc deficiency and anti-Neu5Gc antibodies, then reports that human tumors accumulate Neu5Gc attached to multiple glycan classes, raising the paradox addressed by the study.

Abstract core findings: proposes that chronic inflammation from antibody-Neu5Gc interaction drives tumor progression, and reports accelerated growth of Neu5Gc-expressing murine tumors in Neu5Gc-deficient syngeneic mice with induced antibodies and inflammatory infiltration.
Abstract experimental results: serum transfer of anti-Neu5Gc antibodies enhances tumor growth, with antibody deposition, angiogenesis, and chronic inflammation observed in the tumors.
Abstract mechanism and translation: a COX-2 inhibitor suppresses these effects, and affinity-purified human anti-Neu5Gc antibodies also accelerate Neu5Gc-tumor growth in Neu5Gc-deficient mice.
Abstract conclusion: the human propensity for diet-related carcinomas is attributed to local chronic inflammation from dietary Neu5Gc interacting with circulating anti-Neu5Gc antibodies.

Introduction to a study on anti-alpha-Gal antibody titers: it sets out the aim of tracking alpha-Gal antibody levels of all isotypes over 8 weeks in healthy adults and the hypothesis that inflammatory bowel disease patients have higher anti-Gal titers.

Methods section describing the study design: weekly serum sampling for 8 weeks in 20 healthy probands, plasma from 20 Crohn's disease and 20 ulcerative colitis patients, and ELISA measurement of anti-Gal antibodies and total immunoglobulin.

Statistical methods for the anti-Gal antibody study: random intercept model confidence intervals for longitudinal titer slopes, comparing between- and within-proband variance, plus paired t-tests and Pearson correlations for group comparisons.

Results of the anti-Gal antibody study: alpha-Gal specific IgG, IgM, IgD and IgA titers stayed stable over time, most probands lacked IgE antibodies, and Crohn's disease patients had markedly higher IgA titers than controls (P<.01).

Conclusion of the anti-Gal study: apart from IgE, antibody titers stay constant in healthy people, so significant changes reflect antigen exposure; Crohn's patients show elevated anti-Gal IgA versus controls.

Final conclusion and copyright notice of the anti-Gal study: elevated IgA in Crohn's disease is interpreted as reflecting a chronically impaired mucosal gut barrier; the chunk ends with the 2011 Elsevier copyright statement.

Introduces Lyme-like illness (STARI/Masters disease), a tick-borne condition transmitted by the Lone Star tick, describes its lymphocytic dermal lesions resembling Lyme erythema migrans, and notes that causative agents (other than Borrelia lonestari) have not been cultured.

Concludes the Lyme-like illness overview: completes the note that causative agents have not been cultured, calls for more research on this newly recognized zoonosis, and urges clinicians to be aware of it as a Lyme disease mimic.

Introduces STARI (southern tick-associated rash illness), an EM-like rash linked to Lone Star tick bites, first reported in 1980s Missouri and southeastern states, as background to Lyme disease's erythema migrans rash.

Notes that the Lone Star tick occurs in Northeast Lyme-endemic areas yet STARI had rarely been reported there, and introduces a Connecticut child who visited Long Island, NY, with a rash initially thought to be erythema migrans.
Describes the case outcome: the child did not respond to Lyme disease antibiotics, prompting an investigation that established a STARI diagnosis.

Abstract opening: introduces the clinical interest in Gal alpha 1-3Gal beta 1-4GlcNAc residues, noting the natural anti-Gal antibody in about 1% of human IgG, and prior findings on their expression on red and nucleated cells across mammal groups.
Abstract continuation: states the study's aim of analyzing these carbohydrate residues on secreted mammalian glycoproteins and previews development of a radioimmunoassay to quantify them.

Abstract methods: describes the radioimmunoassay design, using biotinylated purified anti-Gal as detecting antibody and bovine thyroglobulin enriched for the Gal alpha 1-3Gal beta 1-4GlcNAc epitope as the solid-phase antigen.
Abstract findings part one: reports for the first time that the evolutionary distribution of these residues on in vivo secreted glycoproteins mirrors that on cell line membranes and red cells.

Abstract results: gives quantitative findings, with thyroglobulin, fibrinogen, and IgG from nonprimate mammals and New World monkeys carrying 0.01 to 11 residues per molecule, while human and Old World monkey glycoproteins carry none; the abstract is truncated.
Final fragment of the truncated abstract, marking the 250-word cutoff with no additional content.

Opening of the abstract: introduces the previously shown normal-serum antibody pool that binds cytokine receptors and may interfere with cytokine capture assays, and identifies it as the natural anti-gal antibody against the alpha-gal epitope, the main barrier to xenotransplantation.

Continues the abstract with findings on anti-alpha-gal isotypes: high IgD levels in most volunteers in addition to previously described IgG2, IgA and IgM. It then states the study aim: testing whether anti-gal interferes with cytokine-receptor capture assays by measuring anti-carbohydrate antibodies in an atherosclerosis cohort.

Methods and early results: the atherosclerosis patient cohort, previously used for active TGF-beta measurement via a receptor-capture assay, is assessed for anti-carbohydrate antibodies. Reports large, significant patient-versus-control differences for many isotype/carbohydrate combinations after adjusting for age, sex and blood group.

Interpretation of the initial results: the pattern parallels the earlier active TGF-beta data, so anti-gal may have contributed to that prior finding and cannot be ruled out. Begins describing adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors.

Final conclusions: after further adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors, several anti-carbohydrate antibodies still differ significantly between patients and controls. The authors suggest these antibodies may be a new class of risk factors for advanced atherosclerosis, pending larger confirmatory studies.
Closing sentence of the abstract: states that larger studies are needed to confirm whether anti-carbohydrate antibodies are associated with the presence of advanced atherosclerosis.

Introduces the study's finding that anti-Gal alpha(1,3)Gal antibodies and IB4 lectin react with mucin-gene-encoded peptides (MUC 1, 3, 4), building on prior work showing they bind the synthetic peptide DAHWESWL.

Describes the first line of evidence: mucin-derived peptides blocked anti-Gal and IB4 binding to a Gal alpha(1,3)Gal+ pig endothelial cell line, with specificity confirmed against a random peptide and other mucin peptides.

Presents two further lines of evidence: anti-Muc1 antibodies detected Gal alpha(1,3)Gal on transfected COS cells expressing pig alpha3galactosyltransferase, and IB4 and anti-Gal antibodies bound mucin 1 on human breast cancer cells.

Concludes that natural anti-Gal antibodies present in all human serum can react with self Muc1 peptides abundant on tumour cells but not normal cells, and suggests this explains earlier reports of Gal alpha(1,3)Gal expression on human cells.
States the paper's interpretation that prior reports of Gal alpha(1,3)Gal expression on human cells were artefacts caused by anti-Gal antibodies reacting with mucin peptides.
Fragment ending the sentence 'n peptides.' from the concluding statement about anti-Gal antibodies reacting with mucin peptides; a trailing tail of the abstract's final sentence.

Case report from a Medical Journal of Australia (2009) letter describing 25 patients in tick-endemic Sydney, NSW who developed red meat allergy after large local tick-bite reactions, suggesting a novel arthropod-to-food protein cross-reactivity (alpha-gal sensitization context).

Introduction to the review, defining the alpha-gal triad (alpha 1,3-galactosyl epitope, alpha 1,3-galactosyltransferase, and anti-gal antibody) and framing its oncological relevance to host-tumor interaction.

Evidence that alpha-gal epitopes, thought absent from human tissue, appear on human cancer cell lines, senescent red blood cells, and Graves' disease thyrocytes, with alpha-gal linked to increased metastasis in animal models.

Immunological context: natural anti-gal antibodies in normal sera predict recognition of alpha-gal-expressing cells, and hypotheses about metastasis-related mechanisms such as de novo expression and unmasking by desialylation.

The unresolved question of how alpha-gal is sporadically expressed in humans, given that the galactosyltransferase gene was mutated in the human genome, with pathological re-expression thought to require cellular permissive changes.
Concluding statement that elucidating these cellular alterations is necessary to understand the metastatic phenotype, and that therapeutic strategies targeting alpha-gal expression are discussed.

Introduction to the xenotransplantation study: it contrasts well-known natural xenoreactive antibodies with the unknown status of xenoreactive T cell immunity in humans, and introduces the ELISPOT method for measuring xenoreactive PBL frequency and cytokine profiles.

Methods and key rationale: because naive T cells secrete only IL-2 in short-term culture, IFN-gamma ELISPOT responses indicate memory immunity; results show many IFN-gamma producers versus about five-fold fewer IL-2 producers when human cells are stimulated with inbred swine cells.

Comparison groups: cord blood from neonates shows swine-specific IL-2 producers but few IFN-gamma producers, consistent with a naive phenotype; adults who avoid pork show fewer swine-reactive IFN-gamma producers than adults with unrestricted diets, hinting that pork consumption primes swine-specific T cell memory.

Conclusions: the findings provide the first evidence of naturally occurring xenospecific T cell immunity in humans, and the strength of the memory response suggests it will be a major obstacle to transplanting swine organs.
Final concluding sentence of the abstract: the strong detected memory T cell response predicts a formidable barrier to swine organ transplantation.

Abstract opening of a study on microparticles (MPs) from human atherosclerotic plaques: background on procoagulant MPs and the methods (tandem mass spectrometry proteomics, NMR metabolomics, antibody profiling on combinatorial antigen libraries).
