Results on plaque MP composition: leukocyte-derived surface antigens including MHC class I and II, a dose-dependent stimulatory effect on T-cell proliferation, and enrichment of taurine, a neutrophil free organic acid that scavenges myeloperoxidase-derived free radicals.
Findings that immunoglobulins are trapped inside plaque MPs, shown by fluorescent surface protein labeling and flow cytometry on permeabilized versus nonpermeabilized MPs.

Evidence of macrophage origin: over 90% of IgG-containing MPs were CD14(+). Antigen library screening showed plaque MP antibody profiles resemble plaque antibodies but differ from plasma antibodies, with strong reactivity to oligosaccharide antigens such as blood group A.

Conclusions of the abstract: first evidence that immunoglobulins reside within plaque-macrophage-derived MPs, that plaque antibody repertoires differ from circulating plasma antibodies, and the beginning of the statement that anticarbohydrate antibodies are retained in atherosclerotic lesions.

Final conclusion clause: anticarbohydrate antibodies are retained in human atherosclerotic lesions, and plaque antibodies differ from circulating plasma antibodies, closing the study's conclusions on plaque microparticles.

Background and objective of a study on IgE antibodies to galactose-α-1,3-galactose (α-gal), a carbohydrate on nonprimate mammalian proteins, and whether these antibodies cause meat-related anaphylaxis or urticaria in patients from the University of Virginia Allergy Clinic.

Methods section describing patient history collection at the University of Virginia Allergy Clinic and the allergy testing used: skin prick tests, intradermal tests, and serum IgE analysis for indoor, outdoor, and food allergens.
Results showing 24 patients with IgE antibodies to α-gal, whose delayed anaphylaxis or urticaria 3 to 6 hours after eating meat improved with avoidance diets.

Results on test findings: small skin prick wheals to mammalian meat, larger intradermal or fresh-food responses, and CAP-RAST IgE positivity for beef, pork, lamb, milk, cat, and dog but not poultry or fish, explained by anti-α-gal IgE via absorption experiments.
Conclusion identifying a novel, severe food allergy to the α-gal carbohydrate epitope, with delayed anaphylaxis, angioedema, or urticaria after eating mammalian meat.
Final concluding clause of the abstract restating that the delayed reactions are linked to eating beef, pork, or lamb in α-gal IgE-positive patients.

Opening of the document, the third installment of a thematic review series on atherosclerosis pathogenesis and the cholesterol controversy; argues that the lack of a plausible mechanistic hypothesis linking high blood cholesterol to artery wall events fueled skepticism and delayed treatment of hypercholesterolemia.

Closing of the document's summary, stating that advances in lipoprotein metabolism in the 1950s-60s and cellular biology in the 1970s set the stage for a modern consensus on the pathogenetic mechanisms of atherogenesis.
Introduction and objective of a study on egg consumption, dietary cholesterol, endothelial function, and serum lipids in hyperlipidemic adults; sets up the rationale for the trial.
Methods continued: description of the randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial's 40 hyperlipidemic participants and the acute single-dose egg versus sausage/cheese sandwich phase.
Methods continued: sustained phase design with six weeks of daily eggs or egg substitute, the four-week washout between treatments, and outcome measures (flow-mediated dilatation and lipid panel).
Results of the acute phase showing no endothelial function difference between single-dose eggs and sausage/cheese, plus the start of the sustained-phase egg substitute findings.
Sustained-phase results: egg substitute improved flow-mediated dilatation and lowered total and LDL cholesterol versus eggs, with reported p-values and change from baseline.
Conclusions: eggs were non-detrimental to endothelial function and serum lipids in hyperlipidemic adults, while egg substitute was beneficial.

Introduction and background of a randomized controlled crossover trial on egg consumption and endothelial function, motivating the study by questioning dietary cholesterol's cardiovascular risk relative to saturated fat.

Methods of the egg vs. oats crossover trial: 49 healthy adults, two eggs or oats daily for 6 weeks each with a 4-week washout, with brachial artery reactivity (flow-mediated vasodilation) measured by ultrasound at baseline and end of each phase.
Results on flow-mediated vasodilation: FMD remained stable with no significant between-treatment difference between egg (-0.96%) and oatmeal (-0.79%) groups.

Lipid results: egg consumption left total cholesterol and LDL essentially unchanged, whereas oats significantly lowered total cholesterol (to 194 mg/dl) and LDL (to 116.6 mg/dl); BMI, triglyceride, HDL and SBP showed no differences between groups.

Secondary outcomes and conclusion: no differences in BMI, triglycerides, HDL or systolic blood pressure, and the conclusion that short-term egg consumption does not harm endothelial function, suggesting dietary cholesterol may be less harmful than thought.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending the statement that dietary cholesterol may be less detrimental to cardiovascular health than previously believed.

Abstract opening of a 2013 meta-analysis on egg consumption and cardiovascular disease/diabetes risk: states the objective and MEDLINE search methods (through Dec 2012), pooling via fixed/random-effects models, subgroup and weighted linear dose-response analyses.

Results section beginning: 14 studies with 320,778 participants; pooled relative risks for highest vs lowest egg intake for CVD (1.19), CVD in diabetic patients (1.83), and diabetes (1.68), with 95% CIs.

Dose-response results: per 4 eggs/week increment, RRs for CVD (1.06), CVD in diabetics (1.40), and diabetes (1.29), plus the start of subgroup analysis by country, introducing the other-western vs USA comparison.

Subgroup finding that populations in other western countries showed higher CVD risk (RR 2.00) than USA (RR 1.13, P=0.02 for difference), followed by the conclusion of a positive dose-response association between egg intake and CVD and diabetes risk, with copyright notice.
Closing copyright line (Elsevier Ireland Ltd., 2013) ending the abstract of the egg consumption, CVD, and diabetes meta-analysis.

Introduces the study's aim: a prospective cohort of 618 healthy adults without apparent heart disease, assessing brachial artery flow-mediated dilation (endothelial function) as a predictor of long-term adverse cardiovascular events.
Describes the methods: FMD measured by high-resolution ultrasound after overnight fasting and medication washout, and the cohort split at the median FMD of 11.3% into two groups of 309 each.

Reports that the two FMD groups were comparable on risk factors and Framingham score, and defines the composite cardiovascular endpoint (death, MI, heart failure/angina hospitalization, stroke, CABG, PCI) over a mean 4.6-year follow-up.
Presents the main results: composite CV events were far more frequent in the low-FMD group (15.2% vs 1.2%), and median FMD predicted events in univariate analysis (OR 2.78).

Gives the multivariate result that median FMD was the strongest independent predictor of CV events after adjusting for traditional risk factors (OR 2.93), and states the study's conclusion that FMD adds prognostic value beyond conventional risk assessment.
Closing sentence of the conclusion restating that FMD adds to traditional risk factor assessment, followed by the 2014 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction and background of a crossover trial on alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) from walnuts and flax: states PUFA cardiovascular benefits, prior LDL and inflammation findings, and the study objective on stress responses, flow-mediated dilation, endothelin-1, and vasopressin.

Study design section of the walnut/flax ALA trial: randomized crossover design in 20 hypercholesterolemic subjects, with a subset of 12 undergoing brachial artery flow-mediated dilation testing, and the objective measures.

Diet description in the walnut/flax crossover study: the average American diet (AAD) PUFA composition (8.7% energy, mainly linoleic acid) and the start of the LA diet description with reduced saturated fat.

Diet composition and results of the walnut/flax trial: LA and ALA diet PUFA percentages of energy (16.4% and 17%), and the main finding that both diets lowered diastolic blood pressure and total peripheral resistance at rest and during stress.

Key results of the walnut/flax ALA study: flow-mediated dilation increased 34% on the higher-ALA diet, arginine-vasopressin rose 20%, endothelin-1 was unchanged, and conclusions on possible cardioprotective mechanisms.
Final conclusion of the walnut and flax ALA trial: the findings suggest novel cardioprotective mechanisms, and further research is needed to identify the responsible bioactive compounds.

Opening of the abstract: introduces metabolic syndrome as a precursor to diabetes and CVD, notes prior evidence that walnuts reduce CVD risk markers, and states the trial's aim of testing daily walnut intake on endothelial function in overweight adults with visceral adiposity.

Methods section of the walnut crossover trial: describes the 46 overweight adults (mean age 57.4, 28 women and 18 men) with elevated waist circumference and metabolic syndrome signs, randomized to two 8-week diet sequences (walnut-enriched vs. no walnuts) separated by a 4-week washout.

Outcome definitions in the walnut trial methods: the primary outcome is change in brachial artery flow-mediated vasodilation (FMD), with secondary outcomes including lipid panel, fasting glucose and insulin, HOMA-IR, blood pressure, and anthropometric measures.

Results of the walnut trial: reports that FMD improved significantly on the walnut-enriched diet versus control (1.4% ± 2.4% vs. 0.3% ± 1.5%, p = 0.019), with trends toward lower systolic blood pressure, stable anthropometrics, and no change in other measures.

Conclusion of the walnut trial: daily 56 g walnut intake improves endothelial function in overweight adults with visceral adiposity, adding walnuts does not cause weight gain, and further research on walnuts for diabetes and CVD prevention is recommended.
Final sentence of the conclusion: a call for further study of walnut intake's potential role in preventing diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

Introduction of a review on nuts, hypertension, and endothelial function: frames high blood pressure as a major cardiovascular risk factor and states the review's aim to examine nutrients, foods (especially nuts), and dietary patterns for BP control.
Data synthesis explaining why nuts may protect against hypertension: low sodium and rich in unsaturated fats, fiber, magnesium, potassium, calcium, and antioxidants.
Summary of evidence: limited prospective and trial data suggest nuts benefit BP and endothelial function, but BP was a secondary outcome in nut trials and none used ambulatory BP monitoring.

Conclusions calling for further clinical trials, ideally with ambulatory BP monitoring, to confirm nuts' protective effect on hypertension and vascular reactivity; includes the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
A lone period ending the document's abstract text; it contains no content of its own and only closes the copyright/conclusions sentence from the preceding chunk.

Introduction and methods of a systematic review on nuts and blood lipid profiles: states the motivation (inverse link between nut intake and coronary heart disease risk markers) and describes the literature search of Medline and Web of Science up to August 2004.

Study selection criteria for the nut lipid systematic review: human intervention trials measuring independent effects of nuts on lipid concentrations; 415 publications screened, 23 included, and each paper rated on its reported methodology.
Results summary of the nut systematic review: almond, peanut, pecan and walnut trials (with daily doses) and the note that no formal statistical analysis was done because study designs varied widely.

Key findings of the nut systematic review: almond, peanut, pecan and walnut intake reduced total and LDL cholesterol versus control diets by about 2-19%, macadamia results were less convincing, and the conclusion begins with recommended nut intake for heart-healthy diets.

Concluding recommendation of the nut lipid review: about 50-100 g of nuts five or more times per week within a heart-healthy diet with roughly 35% of energy from fat (mainly mono- and polyunsaturated) may significantly lower total and LDL cholesterol in normo- and hyperlipidemic people.
Introduction and objectives of a 2008 US nationwide telephone survey on self-reported peanut, tree nut, and sesame allergy prevalence, compared with prior 1997 and 2002 surveys.

Survey methods (random telephone survey using a previously used questionnaire plus sesame questions) and results on sample size (5,300 households, 13,534 subjects) and participation rates across survey years.

Overall and adult prevalence results: 1.4% of subjects reported peanut and/or tree nut allergy versus 1.2% in 2002 and 1.4% in 1997, with adult prevalence not significantly changed, while childhood (under 18) prevalence rose to 2.1%.

Childhood prevalence trends by allergy type and survey year: peanut or tree nut allergy in children rose across waves, peanut allergy in children showed non-significant change from 2002, and childhood tree nut allergy increased significantly from 0.2% (1997) to 1.1% (2008).

Conclusions with sesame allergy result (0.1%) and the key finding that peanut and/or tree nut allergy is reported by over 1% of the US population (over 3 million people), increasingly among children over the past decade.

Closing sentences of the conclusions reiterating that sesame allergy is reported much less commonly, followed by the journal copyright and publisher notice (Mosby, Inc., American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology, 2010).

Abstract opening of a review on nuts in the diet, introducing their cardiovascular benefits and stating that the lipid-profile benefits from epidemiological and trial evidence should be weighed against potential harms.
Middle section of the abstract on nuts' energy density, questioning whether adding nuts to the diet without increasing body fat, a claim lacking supporting evidence and biological plausibility.
Closing part of the abstract noting the risk of allergic reactions to nuts, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Background and methods of a 2013 study on hazelnut-enriched diets and cardiovascular risk in hypercholesterolemic adults; introduces tree nuts' known cardioprotective effects and the gap regarding hazelnuts, then describes the 21-subject sandwich-design study.

Study design details: 21 hypercholesterolemic volunteers in a single-group, three-period isoenergetic crossover (control I, 4-week hazelnut-enriched diet supplying 18-20% of daily energy, control II), all 4 weeks each.

Outcome measures listed in the methods: endothelial function via flow-mediated dilation (FMD), LDL oxidation products, and inflammatory markers (hs-CRP, soluble ICAM-1, sVCAM-1), plus lipid and lipoprotein levels monitored across the diet periods.

Key results: the hazelnut diet significantly improved FMD (56.6%) and lipids versus control I, including total cholesterol (-7.8%), triacylglycerol (-7.3%), LDL-cholesterol (-6.17%), and HDL-cholesterol (+6.07%).

Further results and conclusion setup: oxidized LDL, hs-CRP, and sVCAM-1 were lower on the hazelnut diet than on both control diets; modest correlations linked sVCAM-1 with FMD (r = -0.49) and with hs-CRP (r = 0.66).

Study conclusions: hazelnut-enriched diets appear antiatherogenic via improved endothelial function, reduced LDL oxidation and inflammation, beyond lipid-lowering; effects reversed after 4 weeks off hazelnuts.
Final conclusion and publication information: hazelnuts can be added to the daily diet without increasing total calories for sustained heart health benefit; copyright National Lipid Association 2013.
Introduction/purpose statement of a study measuring total mercury in hair of diseased (non-Minamata) people in Tokyo area, sampled 1992–1993 from 133 volunteers.

Results: hair mercury of people with common diseases (atopic dermatitis, asthma, dementia, stroke, osteoporosis, hypertension, diabetes) ranged 2.08–36.5 ppm, notably higher than healthy controls; uptake and metabolic causes unknown.
Concluding remark that the uptake routes and metabolic mechanisms behind elevated hair mercury in diseased people remain unexplained, flagging a research gap.

Study background and objective: prospective U.S. cohort study of toenail mercury (methylmercury biomarker) and incident type 2 diabetes, including the neutron activation analysis measurement in diabetes-free adults at baseline.

Methods continued: toenail mercury measured by neutron activation analysis in 9,267 diabetes-free adults across two U.S. cohorts; diabetes case identification via biennial questionnaires and a validated supplementary questionnaire; Cox proportional hazards analysis planned.

Results begin: mean follow-up of 19.7 years yielded 1,010 incident diabetes cases; toenail mercury 95th percentiles (1.32 μg/g men, 0.76 μg/g women) compared against the EPA reference dose, showing exposures roughly 3.5-fold and 2-fold higher.
Main multivariable findings: toenail mercury not associated with higher diabetes incidence in women, men, or combined cohorts, with quintile hazard ratio results starting for women.

Quantitative results and robustness checks: hazard ratios (highest vs lowest quintile) of 0.86 women, 0.69 men, 0.77 combined; similar results across deciles and stratified by fish/omega-3 intake, BMI, and age; conclusions begin.
Conclusion: findings from two large prospective cohorts do not support adverse effects of methylmercury on diabetes development in men or women at usual exposure levels.

Introduction and study setup: background on insulin resistance and pancreatic β-cell dysfunction preceding type 2 diabetes, and the cross-sectional study of 1449 non-diabetic residents near a deserted pentachlorophenol and chloralkali factory.

Methods: metabolic syndrome factors were measured, and associations were tested between serum dioxins, blood mercury, insulin resistance (HOMA-IR above the 75th percentile), and defective β-cell function (HOMA β-cell above the 75th percentile).

Key results: after adjustment for confounders, insulin resistance rose with serum dioxins (b = 0.13) and blood mercury (b = 0.01), with a significant increasing risk trend (P(trend) < 0.001) across exposure levels.

Joint exposure findings: the highest joint tertile of dioxins and mercury had 11 times the odds of elevated HOMA-IR versus the lowest joint tertile (AOR 11.00, 95% CI 4.87-26.63), leading to the hypothesis that combined exposure raises risk more than individual exposure.
Closing copyright notice (Elsevier B.V., 2010) for the article, marking the end of the abstract.

Abstract opening (Background and Objectives) of a study on persistent organic pollutants and type 2 diabetes, stating the limited prospective evidence and the aim of a Nurses' Health Study analysis plus meta-analysis.

Abstract Methods section describing plasma PCB, DDT, DDE, and HCB measurements in 1,095 diabetes-free women from two Nurses' Health Study case-control studies, with the start of the case identification description.
Abstract Methods continuing with 48 incident T2D cases through June 2008, the PubMed/EMBASE literature search and fixed-effects pooling, followed by the start of the Results on HCB and T2D.

Abstract Results reporting the adjusted pooled odds ratio of 3.59 for HCB across extreme tertiles, the null findings for other POPs, and the start of pooling with six published prospective studies (842 cases).

Abstract Results with pooled meta-analysis odds ratios for HCB (2.00) and total PCBs (1.70), including confidence intervals and heterogeneity statistics, plus the Conclusion that POP exposure is associated with T2D risk.
Final fragment of the abstract Conclusion, restating that the findings support an association between persistent organic pollutant exposure and type 2 diabetes risk.

Introduction and objectives of a 2009 Dallas, Texas study measuring persistent organic pollutants (PFCs, organochlorine pesticides, PCBs) in U.S. composite food samples, and its companion PBDE/HBCD flame retardant study.

Companion-study reference (Schecter et al. 2010 on PBDEs and HBCD in composite U.S. food) and the start of the Methods, describing the organochlorine pesticide analysis across the composite food samples.

Methods details: 32 organochlorine pesticides, 7 PCBs, and 11 PFCs measured in 31 food types (310 samples) from Dallas supermarkets in 2009, with dietary intake estimated for an average American; start of Results on varying contamination.

Results on pesticide contamination, specifically the DDT metabolite p,p'-DDE, ranging from 0.028 ng/g ww in whole milk yogurt to 2.3 ng/g ww in catfish fillets, and the PCB congeners found mainly in fish.
Key findings on PCBs in salmon (PCB-153 and PCB-138 levels) and PFOA detection in 17 of 31 samples (0.07 ng/g in potatoes to 1.80 ng/g in olive oil), plus the dietary intake ranking of contaminants.
Conclusion: POPs persist in U.S. food despite product bans, mixtures are consumed by Americans at varying levels, and food testing for chemical contaminants should be expanded.
Final fragment completing the conclusion sentence about the need to expand food testing for chemical contaminants.

Introduction and methods of a study on dioxin exposure and type 2 diabetes: background linking dioxin to diabetes, the study objective (molecular evidence in adipose tissue of Vietnam veterans), and the design using 313 adipose samples from Operation Ranch Hand veterans and comparison veterans, analyzed by qRT-PCR.

Methods and start of results: continues the description of the Ranch Hand exposed group versus unexposed Southeast Asia comparison veterans, the qRT-PCR measurement of selected marker mRNAs, and introduces the key finding that a particular mRNA ratio is the most reliable molecular indicator of dioxin-induced diabetes.

Core result: the GLUT4:NFκB mRNA ratio (glucose transporter 4 relative to the inflammation marker NFκB) correlates with serum dioxin levels and fasting glucose in the Ranch Hand group and, surprisingly, also in the low-exposure comparison group.

Subgroup findings and conclusion onset: the correlation in the comparison group is strongest among those with obesity and family history of diabetes risk factors, and the conclusions begin, stating the GLUT4:NFκB ratio is a reliable marker of dioxin's diabetogenic action.

Final conclusion: the GLUT4:NFκB ratio is a reliable marker even at very low, general-population-level dioxin exposures, implying current exposure levels need to be addressed from a public health standpoint.

Abstract opening (Objective and Methods) of a cross-sectional study of 2,016 NHANES 1999-2002 adults, introducing persistent organic pollutants and diabetes risk and the selection of POPs detectable in at least 80% of participants.

Methods continuation listing the six selected POPs (PCB-153, heptachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin, octachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin, oxychlordane, p,p'-DDT, trans-nonachlor), followed by the start of the Results section on serum concentrations versus diabetes.

Results describing strong positive associations between lipid-adjusted serum concentrations of all six POPs and diabetes prevalence after adjustment for demographics, poverty income ratio, BMI, and waist circumference, compared with non-detectable levels.

Results reporting adjusted odds ratios (1.0 to 37.7) across categories of summed POP exposure with a significant trend, plus stratified findings that the association was stronger in younger participants, Mexican Americans, and obese individuals.
Conclusions summarizing the striking dose-response relationship between the six POP serum concentrations and diabetes prevalence, and calling for further epidemiologic and toxicological research.

Opening of the document introducing the rising global and US type 2 diabetes epidemic and the traditional lifestyle-focused explanation (exercise, diet, weight loss) that the article will challenge with evidence on persistent organic pollutants.

Middle section presenting the central claim that persistent organic pollutants (POPs) may carry greater diabetes risk than established lifestyle factors, and that obesity may matter mainly when adipose tissue holds high POP levels.

Passage naming chlorinated pesticides and polychlorinated biphenyls as strongly linked to metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and T2DM, and announcing the article's plan to review this evidence and examine farmed Atlantic salmon as a POP dietary source.

Closing sentence of the abstract stating that the article will explore farmed Atlantic salmon's possible contribution to blood sugar dysregulation conditions, given its status as a significant common dietary source of POPs.

Introduction/background of the study: establishes widespread human exposure to POPs (DDE, PCBs) and notes that prior cross-sectional diabetes studies cannot establish temporality or causality, motivating a prospective design.

Study objectives and cohort setup: aims to test whether POP body burdens predict incident diabetes in Great Lakes sport fish consumers, with the cohort established in the early 1990s and followed through 2005.

Methods: serum measurement of DDE and PCB congeners, collection of diabetes diagnosis, demographic and fish consumption data, prospective analysis of non-diabetic participants from 1994-1995, and annual percent change in exposures from 1994 to 2005.

Results: DDE is associated with incident diabetes, while PCB-118, total PCBs, and years of sport fish consumption are not; annual percent change in DDE and PCB-132/153 does not differ by diabetes status.

Conclusions: the DDE-incident diabetes association and null annual-change findings argue against reverse causality explaining POP-diabetes links, and the study concludes with a call for further research.
Final conclusion: calls for additional studies to investigate the biological mechanisms through which DDE may disrupt glucose homeostasis.
Introduction to the review: the burden of type 2 diabetes and its complications, and the role of diet, specifically dietary n-3 PUFAs, in its prevention and management.

Summary of the proposed biological benefits of dietary n-3 PUFAs (anti-inflammatory, endothelial, blood pressure, triglyceride and insulin effects) and the epidemiological link between high seafood intake and lower T2DM prevalence.
Notes that evidence on fish intake, n-3 PUFAs and T2DM risk is controversial, and states the review's aim to examine epidemiological and clinical studies on n-3 PUFAs in T2DM.
Closing statement of the abstract: the review also discusses limitations of existing studies and needs for further research, followed by the 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction to the Seveso dioxin study: early effects of TCDD exposure after the 1976 Seveso, Italy accident, with chloracne as the only effect firmly linked to exposure, and the start of long-term mortality and cancer incidence investigations.

Mortality and morbidity results over the 20 years after the Seveso accident, reporting increased risk of lymphohematopoietic neoplasms, digestive cancers (rectal in men, biliary tract in women) and lung cancer in men.

Further Seveso incidence findings: suggestive increases in thyroid and pleural cancer and soft tissue sarcomas in the largest, least-exposed sub-cohort, plus cardiovascular effects and corroborated non-cancer hypotheses.

Non-cancer outcomes in the Seveso population: cardiovascular effects, diabetes in women, a lowered male/female sex ratio in offspring of exposed men, and possible gender-specific effects consistent with animal models.

Interpretation of Seveso findings despite limitations (no individual exposure markers, short latency, small cancer subgroups): prior experimental, epidemiological and mechanistic evidence supports a possible link between observed excesses and dioxin exposure.
Concluding statement that the observed excesses may be associated with dioxin exposure and that mortality and cancer incidence follow-up of the Seveso cohort is ongoing.

Introduces the study's rationale and design: a fish intake and total/cause-specific mortality analysis using a validated food frequency questionnaire in two Chinese prospective cohorts of 134,296 men and women followed 1997–2009.

Describes outcome ascertainment (annual linkage to the Shanghai Vital Statistics Registry plus biennial home visits) and the statistical method (Cox regression with hazard ratios and 95% CIs), and notes the first year of follow-up was excluded.

Reports the number of deaths analyzed (3,666 women, 2,170 men) and the main results: fish intake was inversely associated with total, ischemic stroke, and diabetes mortality, with hazard ratios for highest vs. lowest quintile.

Gives the specific hazard ratios and CIs for total (0.84), ischemic stroke (0.63), and diabetes (0.61) mortality, notes null findings for cancer and ischemic heart disease mortality, and begins the subgroup analysis on fish type and fatty acids.
Concludes that the inverse associations are mainly driven by saltwater fish and long-chain n-3 fatty acids, and that the overall findings support the health benefits of fish consumption.

Introduction and objective of a study on whether residential proximity to persistent organic pollutant (POP) hazardous waste sites increases diabetes hospitalization in New York State, covering background, aim, and start of methods.

Methods section describing the population (hospitalized patients aged 25–74 with diabetes in New York State excluding NYC, 1993–2000), the statistical approach (descriptive statistics and negative binomial regression), and the definition of the POP site exposure group.

Methods continued with definitions of the three ZIP-code exposure groups (POP sites, other hazardous waste sites, and clean sites), followed by the start of the Results comparing diabetes hospitalization rates.

Main results giving adjusted rate ratios for diabetes discharges in POP sites (1.23) and other waste sites (1.25) versus clean sites, plus the higher rate ratio (1.36) in the higher-income Hudson River POP subset.

Final results for the Hudson River subset and the Conclusions, stating that after controlling for major confounders there is a statistically significant increase in diabetes hospitalization in ZIP codes with toxic waste sites.
Final fragment of the Conclusions sentence, ending with the statement about populations residing in ZIP codes containing toxic waste sites.

Introduction to the document on environmental contaminants (persistent organic pollutants) as diabetes risk factors; opens with occupational dioxin exposure and elevated diabetes among Vietnam-era US Air Force Agent Orange sprayers.
Continues with evidence from PCB and chlorinated pesticide exposure studies showing dose-dependent diabetes risk, and introduces NHANES population data linking several POPs to diabetes.
Discusses the NHANES findings from two groups and argues that consistent associations across different studies suggest POPs may cause diabetes; begins the obesity observation.

Explains that obese people without elevated POPs are not at higher diabetes risk, implicating POPs over obesity, and notes POPs' gene-inducing effects, including genes that alter insulin action, as a possible mechanism.
Concludes by stressing the danger of rising global diabetes incidence and the need for further research on POP exposure as a contributor to diabetes etiology.

Abstract opening of a systematic review and meta-analysis on fish and marine omega-3 (LC n-3 PUFA) intake and type 2 diabetes incidence in prospective cohorts; describes the objective and the random/fixed effects meta-analysis methods with Egger's test and I2.

Results section of the fish/omega-3 and type 2 diabetes meta-analysis reporting null pooled associations for fish/seafood (RR 1.04) and marine LC n-3 PUFA (RR 1.08), with participant counts and confidence intervals.

Heterogeneity and oily fish findings from the fish/omega-3 type 2 diabetes meta-analysis: significant heterogeneity across studies, no subgroup explanation, and a significant protective association of oily fish intake (pooled RR 0.89).

Dose-response finding that each 80 g/day of oily fish intake may lower type 2 diabetes risk by about 20%, followed by the conclusion that only oily fish, not total fish/seafood or marine omega-3, significantly affects T2D risk.
A lone period at the end of the abstract, marking the close of the conclusion sentence in the fish/omega-3 type 2 diabetes meta-analysis.

Introduction/background of the article: defines persistent organic pollutants (POPs) as hazardous food-chain chemicals and introduces their newly recognized link to type 2 diabetes and obesity, setting up the paper's aims.

Continuation of the background: states the article's aims (discussing and evaluating POP legislation for metabolic disease protection) and introduces the focus on EU regulation of POPs in animal foods, especially marine food as a major exposure source.

Discussion section: argues that current POP risk assessment and regulation fail to protect against metabolic disorders and that tighter regulatory control of POPs in dietary products is a high public health priority.

Summary/conclusion: states that the general population has enough POP exposure in concentration and diversity to induce metabolic disorders, calling for urgent attention from public health and government authorities.
Final fragment of the summary sentence, closing the conclusion by urging attention from public health and governmental authorities.
Introduction and background of a meta-analysis on marine n-3 PUFA, fish intake, and type 2 diabetes risk, noting prior inconsistent cohort and tissue-composition findings.

Study aims and methods overview: the review examines fish and n-3 PUFA intake and T2D risk, plus tissue n-3 PUFA differences, and describes the literature databases searched (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, CNKI, VIP) through January 2012.

Search and extraction methodology: databases searched, reference list review, independent data extraction by two authors, random-effects pooling of summary relative risks, and the size of the included evidence base (24 studies).
Main cohort results: summary relative risks for highest vs lowest intake of total fish, marine n-3 PUFA, and alpha-linolenic acid for T2D, all with confidence intervals crossing 1.

Subgroup results by ethnicity: fish and marine n-3 PUFA are associated with lower T2D risk in Asian populations but higher risk in Western populations, plus tissue C22:6n-3 and total n-3 PUFA findings for Asians with T2D.

Tissue composition findings and conclusion: Asian subjects with T2D have lower C22:6n-3 and total n-3 PUFA levels, leading to the conclusion that marine n-3 PUFA benefit T2D prevention in Asian populations.
Final fragment of the conclusion stating that marine n-3 PUFA have a preventive effect against T2D specifically in Asian populations.

Introduction and rationale from a study of fish consumption and type 2 diabetes in the IRAS cohort, noting inconclusive prior evidence and the gap on metabolic mechanisms such as insulin sensitivity and beta-cell function.
Methods overview: cross-sectional analysis of 951 non-diabetic IRAS participants, with fish intake (<2 vs ≥2 portions/week) assessed by a validated food frequency questionnaire.
Measurement methods (SI and AIR from frequently sampled IVGTT) and main result that higher fish consumption was independently associated with lower SI-adjusted acute insulin response.
Results on proinsulin/C-peptide ratios: positive associations with fish intake that were confounded by ethnicity, plus the fish-fasting glucose association, with reported coefficients.
Remaining results: significant positive association of fish consumption with fasting blood glucose, and null associations with insulin sensitivity and fasting insulin.
Conclusions: fish consumption was not linked to insulin sensitivity in the multi-ethnic IRAS cohort, but may relate to pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction.

Introduction and methods opening of a systematic review/meta-analysis on omega-3 fatty acid intake (fish, EPA+DHA, ALA, biomarkers) and incident type 2 diabetes risk, with the literature search through June 2011.
Methods continued: duplicate data extraction of multivariate-adjusted relative risks and 95% CIs from prospective studies, plus generalized least-squares dose-response trend estimation.

Pooling methods and main study results: 16 studies (18 cohorts, 540,184 people, 25,670 incident DM cases) were included out of 288 abstracts screened, and fish/seafood consumption is introduced as not significantly associated with DM.

Key pooled risk estimates: fish/seafood, dietary EPA+DHA, and circulating EPA+DHA biomarkers show no significant association with DM, with specific RRs, CIs, and study counts reported per exposure unit.
Results for ALA: dietary and circulating ALA show non-significant trends toward lower DM risk, followed by heterogeneity statistics (I2 about 80% for fish and EPA+DHA, under 55% for ALA).

Heterogeneity and meta-regression findings: study location (Asia vs. North America/Europe), mean BMI, and follow-up duration modified the fish/EPA+DHA-DM association in unadjusted analyses, with limited power to separate their effects due to collinearity.

Conclusions: pooled evidence shows neither major harm nor benefit from fish/seafood or EPA+DHA for diabetes development, while ALA may be modestly protective; it also notes limited power to disentangle heterogeneity sources.
Final discussion sentence: the heterogeneity across studies may reflect true biological differences, publication bias, or chance, and warrants further research.

Abstract opening (Objective and Methods) of a 1998-era systematic review and meta-analysis on fish oil supplementation in type 2 diabetes, describing the literature search and inclusion criteria for randomized placebo-controlled trials.

Methods continuation of the fish oil in type 2 diabetes meta-analysis: describes study inclusion criteria, duplicate data extraction and quality scoring, and the eighteen trials (823 subjects, mean 12 weeks) included.

Results section of the fish oil type 2 diabetes meta-analysis reporting dose range (3 to 18 g/day), outcomes studied, and the pooled effects on triglycerides (lowered) and LDL cholesterol (raised) with 95% confidence intervals.

Results continuation of the fish oil diabetes meta-analysis: no significant effect on fasting glucose, HbA1c, total or HDL cholesterol; larger triglyceride and LDL effects in hypertriglyceridemic subjects and higher doses; heterogeneity explained by baseline hypertriglyceridemia.

Conclusions of the fish oil in type 2 diabetes systematic review: supplementation lowers triglycerides, raises LDL cholesterol, has no significant glycemic effect, and calls for trials with hard clinical endpoints.
Final sentence of the conclusions of the fish oil type 2 diabetes systematic review, recommending trials with hard clinical end points.
Introduction and methods overview of a meta-analysis of cohort studies on fish and n-3 fatty acid intake and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) risk, motivated by conflicting observational results.

Statistical methods: model selection (fixed vs random effects) based on homogeneity testing, and linear and non-linear dose-response assessment via random-effect meta-regression with restricted maximum likelihood.

Main pooled results for highest vs lowest intake: relative risks of T2DM for fish (1.146, CI 0.975-1.346) and n-3 fatty acids (1.076, CI 0.955-1.213), both non-significant, followed by the start of linear dose-response results.

Linear dose-response findings: each additional ~105 g/week of fish (about four times/month) and each 0.1 g/day of n-3 fatty acids is associated with a significantly higher T2DM risk (RR 1.042 and 1.057); no significant non-linear associations were found.
Conclusion: observational evidence suggests fish and n-3 fatty acid intake may be weakly positively associated with T2DM risk, and further studies are needed to confirm this.

Opening of a review of epidemiologic studies on dietary acrylamide intake and cancer risk, noting over 15 studies across major cancer sites and the approach of separating results for never-smokers or adjusting for smoking, since tobacco is a far larger acrylamide source.

Summarizes the review's central finding: no consistent or credible evidence that dietary acrylamide raises cancer risk overall or among nonsmokers, continuing the methods note on handling smoking as a confounder.

Highlights that dietary acrylamide is not linked to breast, endometrial, or ovarian cancers, which were of interest due to a conjectured hormonal mechanism, and cites smoking-cancer patterns as indirect evidence against an association.
Argues that the lack of a smoking–ovarian/endometrial cancer link makes a dietary effect unlikely, and concludes that epidemiologic studies have failed to show increased cancer risk from acrylamide.

Interprets the scattered slightly elevated and reduced risk ratios across the reviewed papers as consistent with a true null association, and argues that further epidemiologic research on acrylamide and cancer is a misguided priority.
Final sentence of the review, restating the conclusion that continued epidemiologic investigation of acrylamide and cancer risk is a misguided research priority.

Introduction and objective of a pilot study on acrylamide in potato chips, stating the research question about links to oxidative stress and inflammation, and the study design with 14 healthy volunteers.

Study design details: 14 healthy volunteers (8 women, 6 smokers) given 160 g/day of potato chips containing 157 µg acrylamide for 4 weeks, with the start of the results on acrylamide-hemoglobin adduct levels.
Results on acrylamide-hemoglobin adducts (higher in smokers than nonsmokers) and the significant rise in oxidized LDL, hs-IL-6, hs-CRP, and gamma-GT in both groups.

Results on increased reactive oxygen radical production by monocytes, lymphocytes, and granulocytes and higher CD14 expression in macrophages after chip intake, plus partial reversal 28 days after stopping.
Supporting in vitro evidence that acrylamide raises reactive oxygen species in human monocyte-macrophages and lowers glutathione, followed by the start of the conclusion.
Conclusion that chronic intake of acrylamide-containing products induces a proinflammatory state, a risk factor for atherosclerosis progression.

Introduction and methods of a prospective US cohort study of diet and postmenopausal breast cancer risk: 40,559 women, Block food-frequency questionnaire, Breast Cancer Detection Demonstration Project 1987-1998.

Methods continued (principal components factor analysis for dietary patterns, Cox regression) and the start of results: three dietary patterns identified, including vegetable-fish/poultry-fruit, beef/pork-starch, and traditional southern.

Results describing the dietary patterns: the vegetable-fish/poultry-fruit pattern linked to higher education and similar nutrient intake to the traditional southern pattern; no significant breast cancer association for the first two patterns after adjustment.
Key finding for the traditional southern dietary pattern: a nonsignificant reduced risk overall, but significant reduction for invasive breast cancer (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.65-0.95, P for trend 0.003).

Subgroup results for the traditional southern pattern: reduced risk in women without family history, in underweight or normal-weight women (BMI < 25), and in estrogen- or progesterone-receptor-positive tumors.

Specific foods linked to reduced risk in the traditional southern pattern (legumes, low mayonnaise-salad dressing, possibly cabbage) and the study conclusion that this diet is associated with reduced invasive breast cancer risk in postmenopausal women.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the study's statement about postmenopausal women.

Introduction and background of a study on deep-fried food consumption and prostate cancer (PCa) risk, covering high-heat cooking, the role of oil/fat, and potential carcinogenic mechanisms such as aldehydes and heterocyclic amines.

Methods section describing how odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals were estimated for tertiles of deep-fried food intake (French fries, fried chicken, fried fish, doughnuts, snack chips) from a food frequency questionnaire, in 1,549 cases and 1,492 controls.

Continuation of the methods, noting analysis of aggressive PCa (regional/distant stage, elevated Gleason score or PSA), followed by the start of results: French fries showing a positive association with PCa risk at intake of at least once per week.

Results reporting odds ratios for PCa risk at intake of at least once weekly: French fries, fried chicken, fried fish, and doughnuts were positively associated, snack chips were not, and estimates were slightly stronger for aggressive disease (fried fish OR=1.41).

Conclusion stating that regular consumption of select deep-fried foods is associated with increased PCa risk, and raising the open question of whether this reflects deep-frying specifically or broader high-heat cooking and Western lifestyle factors like fast food.
Final sentence of the conclusion noting that whether the observed risk is specific to deep-fried foods or reflects Western lifestyle factors such as fast food consumption remains to be determined.

Opening chunk of an acrylamide food-science review: defines acrylamide's formation from asparagine and reducing sugars via the Maillard reaction during high-temperature (above 120°C) processing of plant-based foods like potato and cereal products.

Middle chunk of the acrylamide review: summarizes epidemiological findings that acrylamide intake shows no increased cancer risk for most cancer types (a few warrant further study) and notes that mitigation efforts have had mixed success with no universal approach.

Closing chunk of the acrylamide review: states that reducing acrylamide is probably not feasible in some foods, flags an upcoming major rat and mouse toxicology study on acrylamide intake, and says the review surveys current knowledge.
Final fragment of the acrylamide review, consisting only of the closing word 'ed.' that completes the phrase 'is reviewed' from the last sentence about the status of current knowledge.

Introduction and background of the NewGeneris European mother-child study on prenatal acrylamide exposure, its placental transfer, carcinogenicity classification, and rodent developmental toxicity, plus study objectives.

Methods: cord blood hemoglobin adduct measurements of acrylamide and glycidamide (reflecting late-pregnancy exposure) in 1,101 singleton pregnancies across five European countries, 2006–2010, with diet assessed by food-frequency questionnaires.

Main results: acrylamide and glycidamide Hb adducts linked to significantly lower birth weight and head circumference, with the quartile comparison effect estimates for birth weight (-132 g) and head circumference (-0.33 cm) and their 95% CIs.

Further results: associations held in infants of nonsmoking mothers, were consistent across countries, and persisted after adjusting for other factors linked to low birth weight; fried potatoes and other acrylamide-rich foods were tied to adduct levels and lower birth weight.
Conclusions: dietary acrylamide exposure was associated with reduced birth weight and head circumference, and specific prenatal foods raised in-utero acrylamide exposure.
Final conclusion: if the findings are confirmed, dietary acrylamide intake should be reduced among pregnant women.

Introduction and methods summary of a study on acrylamide (AA) exposure from French fries: it introduces a non-linear regression model using cooking temperature and time (R²=0.83) to estimate AA concentrations.

Results of the Monte Carlo cancer risk analysis: it reports that AA concentrations above 168 ppb would push estimated excess lifetime cancer risk for Taichung City adolescents (13-18 years) above the target ELCR, based on intake survey data and eight temperature-time frying schemes.

Conclusions on risk management: it states that AA levels in French fries may need further reduction if epidemiological observations hold, and that the limited life span was considered in the risk estimate.
Closing remarks noting the model can be a basis for future ELCR studies covering other life stages, behaviors, and population groups, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.
Introduction and objective of a hospital-based case-control study of dietary patterns and breast cancer risk among Iranian women, conducted at Shohada Teaching Hospital in Tehran.
Study design, setting, and subjects: 100 breast cancer patients aged 30-65 and 174 hospital controls, with dietary intake measured by a validated 168-item semi-quantitative FFQ.
Results begin: two dietary patterns explaining 24.31% of dietary variation, and the food groups defining the 'healthy' pattern (vegetables, fruits, legumes, fish, whole grains, etc.).
Description of the 'unhealthy' dietary pattern (soft drinks, sugars, refined grains, red and processed meat, etc.) and the start of the tertile-based risk comparison.
Main risk findings: the highest tertile of the healthy pattern had reduced breast cancer odds (OR 0.25), while the highest tertile of the unhealthy pattern had markedly increased odds (OR 7.78).
Conclusion: a healthy dietary pattern may be inversely associated with breast cancer risk, while an unhealthy dietary pattern likely increases risk among Iranian women.

Introduces the study's question: whether preschool-age diet (ages 3-5) affects adult breast cancer risk, using a case-control design of 582 cases and 1,569 controls from the Nurses' Health Study cohorts.

Describes the exposure assessment: childhood diet was reported by the mothers via a 30-item food-frequency questionnaire, and reports a higher breast cancer risk linked to frequent French fry consumption at preschool age.

Gives the main quantitative results: French fry intake per additional weekly serving (adjusted OR 1.27, CI 1.12-1.44) and a slightly protective association for whole milk per daily glass (OR 0.90, CI 0.82-0.99), with no nutrient-level associations found.

Summarizes the interpretation: the findings suggest a possible link between pre-puberty diet and later breast cancer risk, while flagging differential maternal recall between cases and controls as a key limitation.
Concludes with the call for prospective studies free from recall bias to test whether the preschool diet and breast cancer association is reproducible, plus the copyright notice.

Introduces acrylamide as a probable carcinogen and its main exposure routes, then summarizes animal and human evidence linking it to endocrine-related tumors, setting up the breast cancer mortality study.

Continues the background on dietary acrylamide and estrogen-sensitive breast cancer risk, then states the study aim: testing whether pre-diagnostic AA-Hb and GA-Hb hemoglobin adduct levels predict mortality in breast cancer cases.

Describes the study population: 24,697 postmenopausal Danish women enrolled 1993-1997, with 420 breast cancer cases before 2001 and 110 deaths before 2009, and the Cox proportional hazards analysis of adduct concentrations per 25 pmol/g globin.

Reports the main results: among non-smokers, higher GA-Hb was linked to greater breast cancer-specific mortality overall (HR 1.63) and more strongly among estrogen receptor positive tumors (HR 2.23), with AA-Hb showing a similar trend.

Gives the AA-Hb result, significant only in estrogen receptor positive tumors (HR 1.31, CI 1.02-1.69), and the conclusion that pre-diagnostic acrylamide exposure may relate to breast cancer mortality, especially for the most endocrine-related subtype.
Closing sentence of the conclusion restating that the association may be concentrated in the most endocrine-related breast cancer type, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Abstract opening of a study on lipid rafts/caveolae in cancer: introduces raft roles in cell survival and states the aim of testing raft disruption effects on viability and comparing raft levels in cancer vs. normal cells.

Abstract findings on methyl-β-cyclodextrin-induced cholesterol depletion in A431 cells: anoikis-like apoptosis via reduced rafts, Bcl-xL downregulation, caspase-3 activation, and Akt inactivation, independent of EGFR activation; begins describing cholesterol repletion effects.

Abstract results showing cholesterol repletion restores rafts, Akt activation, and viability; breast and prostate cancer cell lines have more rafts and greater sensitivity to depletion-induced death than normal counterparts.
Abstract conclusion: cancer cells have elevated raft levels, suggesting raft-modulating agents could be developed as anti-cancer drugs.

Opening chunk of a women's health advocacy paper on statin use for women. It introduces the paper as a summary of a longer report and frames it within the Women's Health Movement's call for full disclosure, informed consent, evidence-based medicine, and gender-based analysis.

Middle section of the paper stating the core problem: statin evidence for women, especially primary prevention, is weak even though Canadian data show about half of statin prescriptions go to women. It adds that safety meta-analyses do not break out results for women, ignore female vulnerability to statin-related muscle problems, and under-research women-specific concerns.

Continuation of the paper's critique of research gaps: women-centred risks such as breast cancer, miscarriage, and birth defects are under-researched, and many trials have not published non-cardiac serious adverse event data. It concludes these gaps mean the standards of disclosure, consent, evidence-based prescribing, and gender analysis are unmet.

Final sentence of the paper, which concludes that women should proceed with caution when taking statins, given the unmet standards of disclosure, consent, evidence-based prescribing, and gender-based analysis.

Introduction and background to a meta-analysis of observational studies on statin use and breast cancer risk, motivated by conflicting prior evidence and the broader suggestion that statins may reduce cancer risk.

Methods section describing the literature search of PubMed and reference lists for studies up to January 2012, plus the bias/heterogeneity assessment and the random-effects (DerSimonian and Laird) pooling of relative risks.

Study scope and analytic approach: the meta-analysis included 24 studies (13 cohort, 11 case-control) with over 2.4 million participants and 76,759 breast cancer cases, plus subgroup, sensitivity, and cumulative analyses.

Key results: no publication bias or heterogeneity found, and neither statin use nor long-term use significantly altered breast cancer risk (pooled RR 0.99 and 1.03 with confidence intervals spanning 1).

Robustness and trend findings: study design did not meaningfully change estimates, sensitivity analyses confirmed stability, and cumulative analysis showed reported risk shifting from positive to negative over 1993-2011.
Conclusion: the findings do not support a protective effect of statins against breast cancer, and call for more randomized trials and observational research with biological mechanism studies.
Abstract opening of a study on beta-sitosterol (SIT) and tamoxifen (TAM) effects on cell growth and ceramide metabolism in ER-positive MCF-7 and ER-negative MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells.

Results on growth inhibition: 16 microM SIT inhibited growth in both breast cancer cell lines, 1 microM TAM only in MCF-7, and the combination of SIT and TAM further inhibited growth, most strongly in MDA-MB-231 cells.
Findings on ceramide (a proapoptotic signal) levels: SIT and TAM each raised ceramide in both cell lines, combined treatment raised it further, and the two agents acted through different mechanisms.

Mechanistic conclusion: SIT boosted de novo ceramide synthesis via serine palmitoyltransferase activation, TAM increased ceramide by inhibiting its glycosylation, suggesting the SIT plus TAM combination may benefit breast cancer patients.
Final sentence of the abstract concluding that the combined dietary SIT and TAM regimen may be beneficial for managing breast cancer patients.

Introduction and methods opening of a case-control study on long-term statin use and breast cancer risk in Seattle-Puget Sound women aged 55-74, framing statins' mechanistic chemopreventive potential against inconsistent prior epidemiologic evidence.

Methods detail: case counts of 916 invasive ductal carcinoma and 1,068 invasive lobular carcinoma cases (ages 55-74, diagnosed 2000-2008) compared with 902 control women from the Seattle-Puget Sound population-based study.

Methods on data collection via in-person interviews and structured questionnaire capturing hypercholesterolemia and lipid-lowering medication history, plus the polytomous logistic regression analysis, and the start of the main results on statin use and risk.

Main results: current statin users of 10+ years had increased risk of IDC (1.83-fold) and ILC (1.97-fold) versus never users, and among women with hypercholesterolemia the odds ratios for IDC (2.04) and ILC (2.43) were more than double.

Conclusion and impact statement: long-term statin use was associated with increased risk of both invasive ductal and lobular breast cancer in this contemporary study, which the authors call a novel finding needing further confirmation.
Closing impact sentence calling for additional studies with similarly high statin use frequencies across various durations to confirm the novel association between statins and breast cancer risk.

Introduction to the paper's core hypothesis: evolutionary plant-based diets (high fiber, vegetable protein, plant sterols; low saturated/trans fats) shaped human cholesterol metabolism, and conserved genetic polymorphisms that raise serum cholesterol now clash with modern diets.

Explains that conserved genetic variants meant to maintain cholesterol supply raise serum cholesterol in modern humans on radically different diets, leading to current recommendations for cholesterol-lowering medication, especially in middle age.

Reports the experimental result that a hypothesized Miocene-style diet (leafy vegetables, fruit, nuts, high viscous fiber, vegetable protein, plant sterols) cut LDL-cholesterol in healthy volunteers by over 30%, comparable to first-generation statins.

Describes a follow-up study in hyperlipidemic subjects using a modern therapeutic diet (oat, barley, psyllium, soy, almonds, sterol-enriched margarine) that matched the LDL reductions of the Miocene-like diet and normalized most subjects' blood lipids.

Conclusion that reintroducing plant food components abundant in evolutionary diets into modern eating can correct lipid abnormalities and reduce reliance on drugs, with the study's main takeaways summarized.
Final sentence of the conclusion restating that restoring plant-based components in modern diets can correct contemporary lipid abnormalities and reduce the need for pharmacological treatment.

Introduction and background on dietary fat, low-fat diet and ER-negative breast cancer recurrence; introduces lipid droplet observations in basal-like MDA-MB-231/436 vs luminal MCF-7 cells, motivating the study of lipid storage.

Results on lipid storage: higher triacylglycerol and cholesteryl ester (CE) levels in ER-negative cells, with CE synthesis capacity distinguishing basal-like from luminal breast cancer cells, and higher CE under baseline, oleic acid, and LDL stimulation.

Mechanistic explanation for ER-negative vs ER-positive differences: greater ACAT1 mRNA/protein and ACAT activity, higher caveolin-1, increased LDL uptake, and reduced de novo cholesterol synthesis in ER-negative cells; also notes LDL drives proliferation of MDA-MB-231 cells.

Functional evidence: LDL promotes proliferation of ER-negative MDA-MB-231 but not ER-positive MCF-7 cells, and the ACAT inhibitor CP-113,818 reduces proliferation, especially LDL-induced proliferation of ER-negative cells.

Conclusion: enhanced uptake, storage, and use of exogenous cholesterol gives basal-like ER-negative breast cancer cells a proliferative advantage, possibly explaining the differential effect of a low-fat diet on recurrence.
Final sentence fragment of the conclusion restating that lipid uptake and storage capability may partly explain the differential effect of a low-fat diet on breast cancer recurrence.

Opening of the abstract: establishes breast cancer as the leading cause of cancer deaths in women and motivates the search for less toxic natural anticancer and preventive agents, introducing phytochemicals and dietary compounds.

Continues the abstract's background: notes the historical use of phytochemicals for their safety and low toxicity, that many are in clinical trials, and that dietary phytochemical intake is linked to reduced cancer risk.

Summarizes the proposed mechanisms by which phytochemicals inhibit or reverse carcinogenesis (detoxifying/antioxidant enzyme induction, regulation of inflammatory and proliferative signaling, apoptosis) and states the review's scope.

Closing sentence of the abstract: the review covers potential natural cancer-preventive compounds, their interactions with key signal transduction pathways, and their role in suppressing breast cancer cell growth.
Abstract of a study on LDL receptor content in primary breast cancer tissue as a prognostic marker, introducing the 72-patient cohort and the inverse correlation with survival time.

Abstract of a breast cancer prognosis study reporting that multivariate analysis identified axillary metastasis, oestrogen and LDL receptor content, tumour diameter, and DNA pattern as prognostic factors for survival.
Concluding sentence of the abstract on breast cancer prognosis, stating that better survival-prediction methods could guide treatment choices for individual patients.

Introduction to a review of diet and breast cancer: states breast cancer is the most common cancer diagnosed in US women, notes extensive research exists on diet and breast cancer risk and survival but a summary with clinical inference is needed, and announces the review's methods.

Methods section describing the review's scope: epidemiological and clinical trial evidence linking diet to breast cancer incidence, recurrence, survival, and mortality, including subtype-specific risk studies and past and ongoing dietary intervention trials.

Results on specific dietary factors: low-fat and high-fiber diets weakly protective, total energy intake and alcohol positively associated, fiber possibly acting via estrogen modulation, and fruit and vegetable intake not clearly linked to risk.

Remaining results and start of conclusion: obesity is a risk factor for postmenopausal breast cancer, adult weight gain should be avoided, diet in survivors mainly affects overall mortality rather than breast cancer-specific events, and the conclusion that diet is modestly associated with risk.

Final conclusion: diet is modestly associated with breast cancer risk, effects are stronger for postmenopausal disease, and healthy choices after diagnosis and treatment likely improve longevity more than they reduce recurrence risk.

Introduction and study design: defines phytoestrogens, their estrogen-like effects, and describes the German population-based case-control study of postmenopausal breast cancer examining phytoestrogen-rich foods and dietary lignans.

Methods: describes the study population (2,884 cases, 5,509 controls), dietary assessment via a validated food-frequency questionnaire with added phytoestrogen questions, and the conditional logistic regression approach with confounder adjustment.

Methods and key results: explains polytomous logistic regression by estrogen receptor status and reports reduced breast cancer risk with soybean and sunflower/pumpkin seed consumption, with odds ratios.
Results and null findings: states associations did not differ by ER status and reports no significant links for plant lignans, fiber, or enterolignans with breast cancer risk.
Conclusion: summarizes that higher consumption of sunflower and pumpkin seeds and soybeans is associated with reduced postmenopausal breast cancer risk.

Opening of the review on plant sterols as anticancer nutrients: introduces diet as a cancer risk factor, notes plant sterols are known for cholesterol effects, and says their cancer-mitigation research is in its early stages.

Continues the review's framing: suggests plant sterols' cholesterol-lowering actions may overlap with anticancer effects, and motivates the topic by noting breast cancer is the most common malignancy in women and needs better adjuvant therapies.
Concluding sentence of the abstract stating that plant sterols may have a distinctive role in addressing the need for effective adjuvant breast cancer therapies.

Introduces the study's purpose and methods: a prospective Korean National Health Insurance cohort of about 1.19 million adults, examined for total cholesterol and cancer incidence over 14 years of follow-up.
Reports the cohort's cancer case counts and begins the results, giving the hazard ratio for high total cholesterol (≥240 mg/dL) and prostate cancer in men.
Continues the results with positive associations of high total cholesterol with colon cancer in men and breast cancer in women, then starts the inverse associations with liver cancer.
Details inverse associations of total cholesterol with liver, stomach, and male lung cancer, and notes that liver cancer results were slightly attenuated after sensitivity analyses.
Gives sensitivity analyses for liver cancer (adjusting for liver enzymes and hepatitis B status, excluding the first 10 years of follow-up) and begins the all-cancer incidence results.
Reports the inverse association of total cholesterol with all-cancer incidence and shows it weakens after excluding liver cancers, then begins the study conclusion.
Concludes that total cholesterol is linked to several cancers, with relationships differing markedly by cancer site.

Introduction and study aim: patients with atopic dermatitis are dissatisfied with topical steroid treatment, and this open trial tests whether a vegetarian diet is an effective, scientifically evaluated remedy for atopic dermatitis.

Study design and methods: an open-trial of 20 atopic dermatitis patients on a vegetarian diet for two months, with improvement measured by SCORAD index and serological/immunological parameters to identify mechanisms.

Results part 1: after two months of the vegetarian diet, dermatitis severity markedly decreased (SCORAD, LDH5 activity, peripheral eosinophil count); eosinophils and neutrophils fell before skin improvement, and PGE2 production by PBMCs was reduced.
Results part 2 and conclusion: serum IgE levels were unchanged, and the authors conclude that, as an open-trial, the diet may be useful for adult patients with severe atopic dermatitis.
Final fragment of the conclusion: the study's suggestion that the vegetarian treatment may help adults with severe atopic dermatitis, with the trial's open-label limitation.

Introduction and study design of a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of cyclosporin (5 mg/kg/day) for severe refractory adult atopic dermatitis, with 33 enrolled patients and prior failed treatments (systemic steroids, azathioprine, photochemotherapy).

Crossover allocation details (two groups of 16 and 17, eight weeks per treatment, order of placebo and cyclosporin) and the outcome measures assessed every two weeks, plus the start of efficacy results showing significant improvement in dermatitis extent and activity.

Efficacy and safety results: significant improvement in dermatitis activity and subjective measures, adverse events reported by 20 cyclosporin versus 8 placebo patients with no withdrawals, and the start of the laboratory findings on serum urea, creatinine, and bilirubin.

Laboratory safety results showing only the bilirubin rise was statistically significant (p = 0.001), and the paper's concluding claim that cyclosporin is a safe and effective short-term treatment for severe refractory atopic dermatitis.

Introduction to a review of cyclosporin A (CyA) side-effects in severe psoriasis patients, noting that renal dysfunction and hypertension are covered elsewhere, and summarising the generally mild, transient effects (paraesthesia, hypertrichosis, gingival hyperplasia, GI disorders) and the absence of infection problems.

Discussion of CyA's malignancy risk as an immunosuppressant: skin cancers (mainly squamous cell carcinoma) occurred almost only in patients previously treated with PUVA and/or methotrexate, and a few lymphoproliferative disorders regressed after stopping the drug.

Covers the unresolved link between CyA and solid tumours, and the laboratory abnormalities seen with CyA treatment besides raised serum creatinine (renal dysfunction marker): hypomagnesaemia, hyperkalaemia, raised uric acid, liver test changes, and fluctuating cholesterol and triglycerides.
Conclusion of the review: the laboratory changes with CyA were mostly not clinically relevant, but regular laboratory monitoring of psoriasis patients on CyA is essential.

Introduction of a review on dietary polyphenols for allergic diseases: defines allergic disorders (skin, food, respiratory), the Th2-biased sensitization process, and the motivation for therapeutic approaches.

Continues the introduction by describing therapeutic strategies that modulate sensitization or allergic mediators, and introduces polyphenols from foods and plants as candidate anti-allergy agents studied in models and human trials.

Describes polyphenols' mechanisms of action: anti-inflammatory effects on immune cell recruitment to skin, prevention of secondary infection after skin barrier disruption, and protein interactions that modulate allergic sensitization.

Covers further mechanisms: direct inhibition of mast cell mediator release to relieve symptoms, endogenous antioxidant protection against free-radical cell injury, and the overall conclusion that polyphenols act on multiple pathways and merit further study.

States the review's objective: summarizing key findings and progress on polyphenols as anti-allergic ingredients, with emphasis on physiological, cellular and signalling pathways underlying their mechanisms in allergic disorders.

Closing statement of the review's scope highlighting key physiological, cellular and signalling pathways of polyphenols in allergic manifestations, followed by the 2011 Blackwell Publishing copyright notice.

Introduction and background of a birth cohort study on dietary antioxidants, allergic diseases, and atopy, stating the rising prevalence of allergy and the hypothesis that reduced antioxidant intake from fewer fruits and vegetables contributes, plus the study objective of relating age-5 antioxidant intake to atopy at ages 5 and 8.

Study objective and methods: an unselected birth cohort followed from birth, with validated respiratory questionnaires, skin prick testing at ages 5 and 8, and serum IgE measured at age 5, the cohort's data collection for the atopy outcomes.

Dietary exposure assessment and sample results: antioxidant intake at age 5 measured by a semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire and nutrient analysis software (vitamins A, C, E), and the initial result that 861 children completed both the respiratory and FFQ assessments.

Key quantitative findings: beta-carotene intake linked to lower odds of allergic sensitization at ages 5 and 8 (ORs about 0.80 and 0.81), inversely associated with total IgE levels, while vitamin E intake was associated with higher sensitization risk at age 5 only (OR 1.19).

Conclusion of the study: higher beta-carotene intake is associated with reduced allergic sensitization and lower IgE in 5- and 8-year-olds, with no association of antioxidant intake with wheeze or eczema, suggesting dietary antioxidants may influence development of sensitization.
Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that dietary antioxidants may play a role in the development of allergic sensitization in childhood.

This chunk from a clinical study on apple polyphenol (Ap) for cedar pollinosis describes the double-blind trial design: 500 mg Ap taken once daily for 12 weeks, starting about 2 weeks before cedar pollen dispersion, with symptoms assessed per allergic rhinitis guidelines.

This chunk reports the study results: Ap significantly lowered sneezing scores versus placebo during early and main pollen dispersion periods, with no adverse reactions observed, in a study of apple polyphenol for cedar pollinosis.
This concluding chunk of the apple polyphenol cedar pollinosis study states that no adverse reactions occurred and concludes that Ap may alleviate cedar pollinosis symptoms.

Background and study design for a trial of tomato extract (TE) in perennial allergic rhinitis: prior animal and pollinosis findings motivate a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 33 PAR patients.

Methods and early results of the tomato extract trial: 360 mg/day TE vs placebo for 8 weeks, with a significant reduction in sneezing scores in the TE group and trends for rhinorrhea and nasal obstruction.

Results of the tomato extract trial for PAR: quality of life significantly improved in the TE group but not placebo, and total nasal symptom scores (sneezing, rhinorrhea, obstruction) significantly improved after 8 weeks.

Safety and conclusions of the tomato extract PAR trial: TE was confirmed safe by lab tests and general condition checks, and the authors conclude TE can safely improve nasal symptoms of perennial allergic rhinitis.

Introduction and methods of a cross-sectional study on Cretan children (ages 7–18) examining whether diet, particularly fruit, vegetables, and Mediterranean diet adherence, explains low wheeze and rhinitis despite high atopy.

Methods detail the questionnaires (symptoms plus 58-item food frequency), the 12-item Mediterranean diet adherence scale, and skin prick testing for 10 aeroallergens, followed by the start of the results on fruit and vegetable intake.

Results on dietary associations: frequent fruit and vegetable intake, protective effects of local fruits (grapes, oranges, apples, tomatoes) on wheezing and rhinitis but not atopy, and inverse association of nut intake with wheezing, with margarine as a risk factor.

Specific odds ratios for margarine (risk of wheeze and allergic rhinitis) and for high Mediterranean diet adherence (protective for allergic rhinitis, more modest for wheezing and atopy), followed by the start of the conclusion.

Conclusion stating that commonly consumed fruits, vegetables, nuts, and high Mediterranean diet adherence in childhood are beneficial for asthma and rhinitis symptoms, possibly explaining the low allergic symptom prevalence in rural Crete.
Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that diet may explain the relative absence of allergic symptoms in the Cretan population.

Introduction and methods of a Caerphilly, Wales prospective cohort of 2512 middle-aged men studying diet and lung function, measuring FEV1 with a McDermott spirometer and a food frequency questionnaire at baseline and five-year follow-up.

Results showing good lung function (high FEV1 for age and height) linked to vitamin C, vitamin E, beta-carotene, citrus fruit, apples and fruit juice/squash intake, with an inverse link to magnesium and no link to fatty fish.

After adjusting for confounders such as BMI, smoking, social class, exercise and energy intake, only vitamin E and apple associations remained, with FEV1 about 39 ml higher per SD of vitamin E and 138 ml higher for five or more apples weekly.

Longitudinal results: changes in apple or vitamin E intake were not significantly associated with lung function decline between phases, and the apple-slow-decline link lost significance after confounder adjustment.
Conclusion that the cross-sectional apple-lung function association is strong and suggests a protective effect of hard fruit over soft or citrus fruit.
Final statement that the longitudinal analysis did not support the recent suggestion that the protective effects of diet on lung function are reversible.

Introduction to a prospective cohort study of diet and adult-onset asthma, describing the hypothesized mechanisms (immune and antioxidant effects on airway inflammation) and the study population of 77,866 women aged 34-68 followed for 10 years.

Main finding on dietary vitamin E: women in the highest quintile of dietary (not supplemental) vitamin E intake had reduced asthma risk (RR 0.53), but this association weakened after removing nut-derived vitamin E, which may be an allergen.

Sensitivity analysis and supplement results: without nut contribution, the vitamin E association became nonsignificant (RR 0.74); positive supplement associations for vitamins C and E likely reflect reverse causation, with high-risk women starting supplements before diagnosis.

Remaining results and conclusion: no clear asthma link for carotene (weak nonsignificant inverse), linoleic acid, or omega-3 fats; the authors conclude antioxidant supplements and adult fat intake are unimportant, with only a possible modest protective effect of dietary vitamin E.
Final sentence of the abstract, concluding that dietary vitamin E may have a modest protective effect against asthma.
Study background and methods: cross-sectional school survey of 2650 children aged 8-11 in England and Wales, measuring FEV1 against fresh fruit intake and plasma vitamin C.
Methods continued and first results: FEV1 measured, exposure via parental food frequency questionnaire and plasma vitamin C in 278 children; FEV1 positively associated with fresh fruit frequency.

Key quantitative finding: after adjusting for confounders such as social class and passive smoking, children who never ate fresh fruit had FEV1 about 79 ml (4.3%) lower than those eating fruit more than daily (95% CI 22-136 ml).

Effect modification by wheeze: fruit-FEV1 association stronger in wheezers (p=0.020 for trend difference) though wheeze unrelated to fruit intake; salad and green vegetables showed weaker associations.

Vitamin C results and conclusions: plasma vitamin C unrelated to FEV1 or wheeze and weakly related to fruit intake; authors conclude fresh fruit benefits child lung function, with further work needed on wheezers and the specific nutrient.
Final sentence of the conclusions: calls for further research to confirm whether the fruit effect is limited to children who wheeze and to identify the specific nutrient responsible.
Abstract opening of a case-control study on dietary antioxidants and allergic disease/asthma in rural Grampian, Scotland: background hypothesis and study design.

Methods section of the abstract describing the rural Grampian general practice setting, the validated dietary questionnaire, and case definitions (seasonal allergic symptoms; methacholine-confirmed bronchial hyperreactivity) versus symptom-free controls.
