Results section reporting that seasonal-symptom cases differed from controls mainly in atopy and low zinc intake, and that low vitamin C and manganese intakes were linked to over fivefold higher risk of bronchial reactivity.
Results end and conclusions of the abstract: decreasing magnesium intake linked to hyperreactivity, and the conclusion that diet modulates bronchial reactivity.
Final sentence of the conclusions, proposing that falling antioxidant intake in the British diet over the past 25 years may have contributed to rising asthma prevalence.
Introduction and aims of an ISAAC-based ecological study linking national diet data to childhood wheeze, allergic rhinoconjunctivitis and atopic eczema prevalence.
Methods: ISAAC prevalence data for 6-7 and 13-14 year olds regressed against per capita food intake, adjusted for gross national product.
Dietary data source (FAO 1995, 53 of 56 ISAAC phase I countries) and key results: the 13-14 year group showed decreased symptoms associated with higher cereal, rice, starch, nut and vegetable intake.
Results across age groups: the video questionnaire (13-14 yr) and ISAAC (6-7 yr) data showed similar food patterns, and the inverse relationship with cereals, starch, and vegetables was consistent.

Conclusion: consistent inverse association between starch, cereal and vegetable intake and the three conditions, with speculation that increasing these foods could substantially reduce symptom prevalence if findings generalise.
Final sentence of the conclusion, completing the speculation that increased intake of these foods may yield an important reduction in symptom prevalence.
Introduction and objective of a randomized controlled trial on antioxidant-rich vs. low-antioxidant diets, with or without lycopene supplementation, in adults with asthma.

Study design details: 137 asthmatic adults randomized to high-antioxidant (5 vegetable and 2 fruit servings daily) or low-antioxidant (≤2 vegetable and 1 fruit serving daily) diets for 14 days, followed by a placebo-controlled supplementation trial.

Trial arms and interventions: high-antioxidant group receives placebo, low-antioxidant group receives placebo or tomato extract (45 mg lycopene/day), continuing until week 14 or exacerbation; early results at 14 days show lower FEV1 and FVC % predicted in the low-antioxidant group.

Results at 14 days and mid-trial: lower lung function (FEV1, FVC % predicted) and increased plasma C-reactive protein at week 14 in the low-antioxidant diet group; time-to-exacerbation comparison begins.

Main clinical outcome: the low-antioxidant diet group had greater exacerbation risk (HR 2.26, 95% CI 1.04-4.91, P=0.039), and lycopene tomato extract showed no effect on airway or systemic inflammation or clinical outcomes versus placebo.

Conclusions: modifying dietary carotenoid intake alters asthma outcomes, with benefits seen only with increased fruit and vegetable intake, supporting whole-food interventions; trial registration information begins.
Trial registration details: the study is registered with the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry under number ACTRN012606000286549.

Background and rationale of a randomized trial on diet and lipid peroxidation in atherosclerosis; notes that antioxidant vitamin supplements were previously studied but dietary patterns' effect was unknown.

Methods of the trial: 123 healthy adults completed a 3-week run-in on a low-fruit, low-vegetable, low-dairy control diet (37% calories from fat), then were randomized for 8 weeks to control, fruit-and-vegetable, or combination diet.

Outcome measures and design: serum oxygen radical-absorbing capacity, malondialdehyde (in vitro lipid peroxidation marker), and breath ethane (in vivo marker) were assessed at run-in end and intervention end; describes the combination diet.

Results for antioxidant capacity: mean change in oxygen radical-absorbing capacity by diet with 95% CIs and P values vs control (fruit/vegetable diet P=0.06, combination P=0.10), showing non-significant trends.

Results for lipid peroxidation: median ethane changes by diet with P values (fruit/vegetable P=0.04; combination P=0.005 vs control, with combination diet showing decrease), and no difference in malondialdehyde between diets.
Conclusion of the study: dietary modification favorably affects serum antioxidant capacity and protects against lipid peroxidation, as shown by the breath ethane findings.

Introduction and aims of an asthma study on carotenoid levels: oxidative stress background, and the two objectives (comparing circulating/airway carotenoids with diet, and testing lycopene supplementation).
Methods: study populations (asthma n=15, healthy controls n=16) with induced sputum and blood sampling, and dietary assessment via 24-hour recall using modified Foodworks software.
Methods continued: supplementation group of healthy controls (n=9) given 20 mg/day lycopene for 4 weeks, and HPLC measurement of the five carotenoids.

Results: no dietary intake difference, but whole blood carotenoids (total, lycopene, lutein, beta-cryptoxanthin, alpha- and beta-carotene) lower in asthma, with no plasma or sputum differences; sputum levels below plasma and blood.

Results on correlations: sputum carotenoids strongly correlate with plasma (r=0.798), and changes in airway lycopene track changes in plasma lycopene after supplementation (r=0.908) despite no overall rise.
Conclusions: only whole blood carotenoids are deficient in asthma, plasma levels reflect airway levels, and supplement-driven plasma improvements are mirrored in the airways.

Introduces the study's aim and methods: an in-class survey of 2290 Taipei fifth graders on asthma, respiratory symptoms, and food consumption frequency, and lists the seven respiratory symptoms examined.

Reports the main finding that sweetened beverage consumption had the strongest association with respiratory symptoms, positively linked to six of seven symptoms, and begins giving the adjusted odds ratio range.

Gives the adjusted odds ratio range (1.05 to 1.09) for sweetened beverages, notes egg consumption linked to 5 of 7 symptoms, and says seafood, soy, and fruit were each negatively associated with one symptom.

Describes asthma-specific results: seafood negatively associated with physician-diagnosed asthma, while sweetened beverages and eggs were positively associated with suspected asthma; begins the conclusion.
Concludes that diet relates to respiratory symptoms in Taipei schoolchildren, with sweetened beverages and eggs linked to higher risk and soy products and fruits linked to lower risk.
Introduction and methods of a 2012 study on children's diet quality, asthma, and airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR), describing the aims and the food frequency questionnaire used to build diet scores.

Methods continued: diet quality scores derived from an adapted Youth Healthy Eating Index, and asthma classification by pediatric allergists into allergic versus non-allergic asthma based on skin prick testing.
Methods continued: AHR measured by the Cockcroft technique, and study participants (270 boys and 206 girls) from the 1995 Manitoba Prospective Cohort Study nested case-control design.
Statistical methods (logistic and multinomial logistic regression) and the start of results: 476 children aged about 12.6 years, 56.7% boys.

Key results: asthma prevalence 26.2% and AHR 53.8%; high vegetable intake was protective against allergic asthma and moderate/severe AHR in fully adjusted models, with odds ratios and confidence intervals.
Conclusion that vegetable intake is inversely associated with allergic asthma and moderate/severe AHR, followed by the 2012 Wiley copyright notice.

Opening of the English abstract (Background and Methods) of a 2005–2006 India NFHS-3 cross-sectional study on self-reported adult asthma prevalence and risk factors, describing the sample of women and men aged 20–49 and the logistic regression approach.

English Results section giving self-reported asthma prevalence in men (1.8%) and women (1.9%), higher rural rates, geographic differences, and the adjusted finding that women are 1.2 times more likely to have asthma than men.

English Results describing protective dietary factors (milk/dairy, green leafy vegetables, fruit) and risk factors (chicken/meat, underweight and overweight BMI with odds ratios) associated with self-reported asthma in Indian adults.
Remaining English Results (tobacco smoking OR 1.30, alcohol use OR 1.21) and the English Conclusions noting wide regional variation in asthma prevalence in India and weak associations apart from BMI.
Start of the French abstract (Résumé, Contexte et Méthodes) repeating the study aims and the NFHS-3 2005–2006 sample of 99,574 women and 56,742 men aged 20–49.

French Méthodes and start of French Résultats, covering logistic regression for prevalence odds ratios and the self-reported asthma prevalence figures (1.8% men, 1.9% women) with rural/urban and geographic differences.
French Résultats on the 1.2-fold higher adjusted asthma risk in women versus men and the beginning of the French description of dietary factors associated with asthma risk.
French Résultats on the protective dietary factors and the BMI-related associations (underweight OR 2.08, overweight OR 1.67) with asthma, plus the start of the tobacco smoking association.

French Résultats with smoking (OR 1.30) and alcohol (OR 1.21) associations, followed by the French conclusion that asthma prevalence varies widely across Indian regions and most risk-factor associations are weak except for BMI.
End of the French conclusion and the start of the Spanish abstract (Resumen, Marco de referencia y métodos) describing the aim and the NFHS-3 2005–2006 sample of women and men aged 20–49.

Spanish Métodos describing the sample of 99,574 women and 56,742 men from India's third National Family Health Survey and the multifactorial logistic regression used to estimate asthma prevalence and odds ratios.
Spanish Resultados beginning with self-reported asthma prevalence in men (1.8%) and women (1.9%), with higher rural rates and marked geographic differences across India.
Spanish Resultados on women's 1.2-fold higher adjusted likelihood of asthma compared with men, and the start of the dietary factor findings.

Spanish Resultados on protective dietary factors (dairy, leafy greens, fruit) and risk associations for chicken/meat, low and high BMI (OR 2.08 and OR 1.67), with tobacco and alcohol findings beginning.
Spanish Resultados on smoking (OR 1.30) and alcohol (OR 1.21) associations, and the Spanish Conclusión on wide geographic variation in asthma prevalence in India.
Final sentence of the Spanish conclusion stating that, apart from body mass index, associations between asthma and risk factors were weak and explain only a small proportion of cases.

Introduction to a study on an anthroposophic lifestyle and gut flora in infants: it states the intestinal flora's role in immune development and describes typical anthroposophic practices (fermented vegetable diet, restricted antibiotics, antipyretics, and vaccinations), and states the study's aim.

Methods of the infant gut flora study: 69 anthroposophic-lifestyle children under 2 and 59 traditionally raised controls were clinically examined and surveyed, with fecal samples analyzed by bacterial enumeration, biochemical fingerprinting, and microflora-associated characteristics (MACs).

Key results on fecal bacterial counts: enterococci and lactic acid bacteria (CFU/g feces) were significantly higher in children never exposed to antibiotics (enterococci 5.5x10^7 vs 2.1x10^7, p<0.001; lactic acid bacteria 10x10^7 vs 4.1x10^7, p<0.01).

Further findings: enterococci counts were higher in breastfed and vegetarian infants (p<0.01), and lactobacilli diversity (Simpson's index) was greater in infants born at home than in hospital (p<0.01).

Metabolite and conclusion findings: several microflora-associated characteristics tracked lifestyle features, with anthroposophic infants showing higher stool acetic acid and lower propionic acid proportions, and the authors conclude that anthroposophic lifestyle factors shape infant gut flora composition.
Concluding interpretation: the authors suggest these gut flora differences may explain the previously observed lower rate of atopic disease in children from anthroposophic families.

Introduction to the ISAAC Phase One review: reports large worldwide (10-20 fold) variation in asthma, rhinoconjunctivitis and eczema symptom prevalence and states that ecological analyses were conducted to explore contributing population-level factors.

Study sample details for ISAAC Phase One: symptom prevalence in the past 12 months of asthma, rhinoconjunctivitis and eczema from 463,801 children aged 13-14 (155 centres, 56 countries) and 257,800 children aged 6-7 (91 centres, 38 countries), leading into the list of ecological analyses.

Lists the population-level exposures tested against symptom prevalence in the ecological analyses: GNP per capita, food intake, immunisation, tuberculosis notifications, climate, tobacco, pollen, antibiotic and paracetamol sales, and outdoor air pollution; begins reporting the main positive association with GNP.

Key findings: prevalence of all three conditions was positively associated with GNP, trans fatty acids, paracetamol and women smoking, and inversely with plant-origin food, pollen, immunisations, TB notifications, air pollution and men smoking; associations were small but directionally consistent.

Summary of mixed results and caveats: climate and antibiotic sales showed mixed associations with symptom prevalence, causality needs further investigation, and protective or absent-correlation factors may matter as much as risk factors for policy.
Concluding policy message: interventions targeting small population-level associations could still yield substantial public health benefit, closing the review of ISAAC Phase One ecological analyses.

Opening chunk of an abstract describing a 1-year vegan diet trial for bronchial asthma: 35 long-term medicated patients (20 on cortisone), medication largely withdrawn, symptom decrease, and 24 (69%) completing the treatment with early improvement rates.

Middle chunk of the asthma vegan-diet study abstract reporting improvement rates (71% at 4 months, 92% at 1 year) and significant gains in lung function (vital capacity, FEV1, physical working capacity) and blood biochemical markers (haptoglobin, IgM, IgE, cholesterol, triglycerides).

Final chunk of the asthma vegan-diet abstract, concluding that selected patients fearing medication side effects and interested in alternative care might recover and replace conventional asthma medication with the vegan regimen.

Introduction to the ISAAC Phase Three global synthesis: its scope (regional prevalence and severity of asthma, rhinoconjunctivitis, eczema) and its scale of about 1.2 million children, 233 centres and 98 countries.

Scale claim and global prevalence figures: calls ISAAC Phase Three the most comprehensive survey of these diseases, then reports global current asthma, rhinoconjunctivitis and eczema prevalence for ages 13-14 (14.1%, 14.6%, 7.3%) and begins the 6-7 age group figures.

Completes the 6-7-year prevalence figures (asthma 11.7%, rhinoconjunctivitis 8.5%, eczema 7.9%) and describes the wide variability in prevalence and severity between regions, countries, and centres within the same country or city.

Key conclusions on socioeconomic and environmental factors: prevalence can be very high in non-affluent, low-socioeconomic centres, and the large variability points to local environmental characteristics as a major driver of differences between places.

Closing significance statement: ISAAC Phase Three supplies a large body of childhood epidemiological data from contrasting environments that should help clarify the aetiology and marked global variability of these conditions, followed by the copyright notice.
Standalone copyright notice (SEICAP 2012, published by Elsevier Espana, all rights reserved) that ends the document; contains no substantive content and serves as boilerplate publication metadata.

Introduction and aims of a pilot study on egg and milk exclusion diets for asthmatic children, including study size (22 children, ages 3-14) and design (single-blind, prospective, experimental vs control groups).
Study design details: parents chose the experimental group (avoiding eggs and milk for eight weeks) or the control group (usual diet); group sizes were 13 experimental and 9 control children.

Methods: paediatrician assessments at start and end, seven-day food intake records before, during and after the intervention, and blood sampling for food-specific antibodies and peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) testing where feasible.

Results on dietary effects and immunological outcomes: experimental group had significantly lower energy intake relative to RNI, and serum anti-ovalbumin and anti-beta-lactoglobulin IgG fell significantly after eight weeks.

Comparison of antibody results: anti-ovalbumin IgG rose significantly in the control group while anti-beta-lactoglobulin IgG stayed practically unchanged in controls, contrasting with the experimental group's decline.

Remaining findings: total IgE was unchanged in both groups, PEFR significantly improved in experimental children able to perform the test but not in controls, and the study's initial conclusion begins.
Conclusion: even an eight-week egg- and milk-free diet appears to reduce atopic symptoms and improve lung function in children with asthma, based on this pilot study.

Introduction of a study on asthma/atopic disease rising with prosperity, testing childhood infections and diet as explanations, using a 1964 primary-school cohort examining family size and infectious diseases.

Findings on family size and infections: large families reduced hay fever and eczema risk but not asthma, and this was not explained by infections; more infections were linked to higher asthma likelihood, with measles offering modest protection.

Dietary findings from the first study: lowest vitamin C intake raised bronchial hyper-reactivity risk seven-fold, while lowest saturated fat intake gave ten-fold protection; also introduces the second dietary study.

Second dietary study results: lowest vitamin E intake raised adult-onset wheezy illness risk five-fold and lowest vitamin C doubled it, with plasma vitamin and triglyceride measurements supporting these findings.

Proposed explanation and future test: changes in pregnant women's diet may have predisposed offspring cohorts to atopy and asthma, and the proposed direct test is following pregnant women's diet and nutrition into their children.
Concluding statement that the proposed study of pregnant women's diet, nutritional status, and their offspring is the authors' current research.

Background and rationale from the study on intestinal microflora in allergic Estonian and Swedish 2-year-olds: rising allergy prevalence, lower rates in formerly socialist Eastern Europe, and the reduced-microbial-stimulation hypothesis for immune maturation.

Study aims stated in the allergic Estonian and Swedish 2-year-old children microflora paper: testing whether allergy is linked to gut microflora differences between a low-prevalence (Estonia) and high-prevalence (Sweden) country, with the TH1/TH2 immune balance hypothesis motivating it.

Methods section describing participants: 29 Estonian and 33 Swedish 2-year-olds from a prospective allergy study, split into 36 nonallergic and 27 allergic children, with allergy confirmed by history and positive skin prick test to egg or cow's milk.

Laboratory methods and reported measures for the intestinal microflora study: faecal samples serially diluted and grown anaerobically, with genus/species counts and relative proportions per child, leading into the results section.
Results on allergic versus nonallergic Estonian and Swedish children: fewer lactobacilli colonization in allergic children, and higher aerobic counts, especially coliforms and Staphylococcus aureus.

Further results from the allergic vs nonallergic 2-year-old comparison: higher proportions of aerobic bacteria and coliforms, lower anaerobes and Bacteroides in allergic children, all with reported p-values.

Conclusions of the microflora and childhood allergy study: indigenous gut flora differences may shape early immune development, paralleling rodent findings, with the role of microflora in infant immunity and later allergy still needing study.

Closing conclusion of the Estonian and Swedish childhood allergy microflora study: calls for further research on microflora and infant immunity, noting probiotic administration as a potential primary allergy prevention strategy.

Introduces the trial's rationale: prior probiotic research in infant atopic dermatitis is established, but its role in allergic airway disease is unclear; states the aim of testing 8 weeks of L. gasseri A5 supplementation in school children with asthma and allergic rhinitis.
Describes the study design: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in children aged 6-12 with asthma and AR, with 49 receiving L. gasseri A5 and 56 receiving placebo daily for 2 months.
Outlines outcome measures: pulmonary function tests, physician-rated clinical severity, and diary-card records of day and night peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR), asthma symptoms, and AR scores.

Covers immunological measures (total IgE and PBMC cytokine production before and after treatment) and reports the main clinical results: improved pulmonary function and PEFR and lower asthma and AR symptom scores in the probiotic group versus controls.

Reports the cytokine findings (significant reductions in PBMC TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-12, and IL-13 after probiotic treatment) and the conclusion that probiotics may benefit children with allergic airway diseases.
Final fragment of the conclusion, restating that probiotic supplementation may provide clinical benefit for school children with asthma and allergic rhinitis.

Introduces the burden of paediatric asthma: its impact on family and society, lost school days, lost academic and social opportunities, and strain on healthcare resources. Also opens the discussion of worldwide prevalence variation. Part of the opening section of a paper on childhood asthma burden, prevalence, and risk factors.

Covers the causes of geographic variation in asthma prevalence (respiratory infection, indoor/outdoor pollution, diet) and lists the risk factors that predispose children to asthma and atopic disease: wheezing, atopy, maternal smoking, and fever episodes. Closes with the paper's stated scope. Continues the introduction of a paper on paediatric asthma.
States the paper's scope: it discusses the burden, prevalence, and risk factors of paediatric asthma. Final sentence of the introductory section of a paper on childhood asthma.

Introduction of an article on food prices and blood cholesterol. It frames cardiovascular disease (CVD) costs in the US and states the study's aim: whether food price changes relate to cholesterol and whether taxes or subsidies on specific foods could lower cholesterol and CVD costs.

Key findings and conclusion of the article. It reports that prices of vegetables, processed foods, whole milk and whole grains are significantly associated with blood cholesterol, and that subsidizing vegetables and whole grains is a cost-efficient way to reduce CVD expenditures.
Closing publisher attribution line of the article (Published by Elsevier B.V.), ending the final sentence about subsidies for vegetables and whole grains reducing CVD expenditures.

This chunk is the document's summary/abstract, stating its scope: a historical account of how agricultural systems developed and how that development contributes to obesity and disease. It sets up the document's framing of agricultural policy as a public health concern.
Background and hypothesis from a study of arsenic (As) in organic brown rice syrup (OBRS) and foods containing it; introduces inorganic arsenic from rice and the study's objective.

Study objective and methods overview: measuring total arsenic and arsenic species in brown rice syrups and OBRS-containing products such as toddler formula, cereal/energy bars, and athlete high-energy foods, using ICP-MS methods.

Methods detail on ICP-MS and ion chromatography-ICP-MS for arsenic speciation, applied to products bought online or in Hanover, NH stores; begins the discussion of findings that OBRS contains high inorganic arsenic and DMA.

Key results: an organic toddler milk formula with OBRS as primary ingredient had total arsenic up to six times the EPA safe drinking water limit, and OBRS cereal bars and high-energy foods had higher arsenic than non-OBRS equivalents.

Main speciation finding that inorganic arsenic dominates most tested foods, and the conclusion that OBRS products may add significant inorganic arsenic to diets, with no current U.S. food arsenic regulations.
Closing conclusion calling for urgent regulatory limits on arsenic in food.

Introduction to the study: background on existing U.S. EPA drinking water limits for arsenic and lead and California's 2009 bottled water rules, noting that no comparable limits exist for juices and other beverages.
Study design and key findings: 20 apple juices or ciders, 15 apple-containing juices, plus one grape and one citrus juice were tested; arsenic was found in all juices and lead in over 94%.

Main results and conclusions: 32% of samples had arsenic near or above the 10 ppb drinking water limit, no juices exceeded the lead limit, and the authors call for extending limits to juices and regular testing.
Closing conclusion: regular testing of juices would help consumers understand the risks of specific juices and brands, as the article argues for expanded beverage regulation.
Introduction and objectives of a U.S. market basket study on arsenic species (inorganic arsenic) in chicken meat, motivated by arsenic-based poultry drugs and cancer risk.

Study methods: sampling of conventional, antibiotic-free, and organic chicken from grocery stores in 10 U.S. metro areas (Dec 2010–June 2011), with counts of raw and cooked samples tested for total arsenic and speciated.

Results on total arsenic in cooked chicken (geometric mean 3.0 µg/kg) and inorganic arsenic comparison by production type, with conventional chicken showing higher iAs than antibiotic-free or organic.
Roxarsone detection frequencies by chicken type (20/40 conventional, 1/13 antibiotic-free, 0/25 organic) and iAs levels in roxarsone-positive versus negative samples.

Findings that roxarsone-positive samples had significantly higher iAs, cooking raised iAs and lowered roxarsone, and an exposure estimate of an extra 0.11 µg/day iAs from conventional versus organic chicken.
Cancer risk estimate using a proposed cancer slope factor, projecting 3.7 additional lifetime bladder and lung cancer cases per 100,000 exposed persons, plus the start of the conclusions.
Conclusions: conventional chicken has higher iAs than antibiotic-free and organic chicken, and ending arsenical drug use could reduce exposure and arsenic-related disease burden.

Introduction of the review: contrasts well-documented links between developmental chemical exposure and later reproductive, metabolic, and neurodegenerative disease with the scarce data on how such exposures affect later immune function.

Explains why immune impairment matters: the immune system is the body's first line of defense against pathogens and cancer, so early-life exposures that reduce immune function have serious consequences; also previews the review's scope.

States the review's focus on pollutants such as cigarette smoke and dioxin-like compounds, which consistently show that developmental exposure critically affects the immune system, and links this to infectious disease burden.
Concluding statement: everyday environmental chemicals may be overlooked contributors to infectious diseases, which remain among the top five causes of death worldwide.

Introduction and methods opening of a California risk assessment of dietary contaminant exposure in children and adults, noting the lack of current cumulative dietary exposure data and the study's focus on children's greater vulnerability.

Methods describing the study populations (preschool children, school-age children, parents of young children, older adults) and the eleven toxic compounds assessed via self-reported food frequency data by age group.

Methods on benchmark comparison using Total Diet Study and other public food contaminant databases, followed by Results reporting that cancer benchmarks were exceeded by all children for arsenic, dieldrin, DDE, and dioxins.

Results on non-cancer benchmark exceedances (acrylamide in over 95% of preschoolers, mercury in 10%) and preschoolers' significantly higher intakes of 6 of 11 compounds versus school-age children, plus the start of the pesticide-source food list.
The list of foods contributing most to pesticide exposure (tomatoes, peaches, apples, dairy, etc.) and the Conclusions stating that reduction strategies differ by compound.
Conclusions recommending organic dairy and produce to reduce pesticides, less animal food to cut persistent organic pollutants and metals, and fewer processed carbohydrate foods to cut acrylamide.
Final sentence of the conclusions, specifying that limiting chips, cereal, crackers, and other processed carbohydrates reduces acrylamide intake.

Introduction/study design of a Norwegian MoBa sub-cohort (BraMat) study on prenatal dietary exposure to PCBs and dioxins and childhood immune-related disease, including follow-up sample sizes at ages 0-3 years.

Methods and early findings: maternal toxicant intake estimated from a validated MoBa food frequency questionnaire, blood parameters at age three, and the reported association of exposure with increased wheeze and upper respiratory tract infections.
Key results: maternal PCB/dioxin exposure linked to reduced measles vaccine antibody response, with null findings for immunophenotype, allergic sensitization, and other vaccine responses.
Conclusion and copyright notice: prenatal dietary PCB and dioxin exposure may raise the risk of wheeze and infection susceptibility in early childhood (Elsevier, 2012).

Introduction and aims of a Swedish national survey measuring persistent organic pollutant (POP) body burdens in 246 adults, linking them to diet and lifestyle; describes the POPs' harmful effects and bioaccumulation.

Methods: serum analysis of PCBs, HCB, β-HCH, chlordane and DDE via liquid-liquid extraction, silica cleanup and GC high-resolution mass spectrometry; diet assessed by 4-day food records and questionnaires.

Methods and results on fish intake (plasma fatty acids) and clustering of PCB congeners, separating low-chlorinated PCB 28/52 from high-chlorinated mono- and di-ortho PCBs, implying different exposure sources and toxicokinetics.
Results on sex and breastfeeding differences: men had 24% higher PCB 138-180 and 32% higher chlordane levels than women, partly attributed to POP elimination via breastfeeding in women.
Results on correlations between plasma very long-chain n-3 fatty acids (a fish intake marker) and POP levels, with r values for PCBs, HCB, HCH, chlordane and DDE, all p≤0.005.

Key findings on fatty Baltic fish consumption (45% higher PCB 118), residential building age linked to PCB 28, and the conclusion that the population-based survey identified personal characteristics tied to POP burdens in Sweden.
Closing sentence of the abstract and copyright notice (Elsevier Ltd, 2012) for the study on POP body burdens and lifestyle factors in Sweden.

Introduces the BraMat birth cohort (n=205, sub-cohort of Norwegian MoBa) and the study aim: whether prenatal dietary toxicant exposure affects child immune health, focusing on PCBs, dioxins, and heat-generated acrylamide.

Describes the outcome measures: first-year infections, eczema/itchiness, and wheeze (>10 days of dry cough, chest tightness or wheeze), assessed by questionnaire in 195 children, with toxicant exposure estimated from a validated MoBa food frequency questionnaire.

Reports the main findings: prenatal PCB and dioxin exposure linked to higher risk of wheeze, exanthema subitum and upper respiratory tract infections, while acrylamide showed no associations with the outcomes.
Summarizes the conclusion that prenatal dietary dioxin and PCB exposure may raise the risk of wheeze and infectious diseases in the first year of life, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
Trailing fragment of the copyright statement (Elsevier Ltd., 2011) closing the abstract; contains no substantive content beyond the rights notice.

Opening chunk of an abstract on dietary restriction (DR) and reduced growth factor signaling as shared anti-aging mechanisms, covering their effects on oxidative stress, lifespan, tumors, and cognitive decline in model organisms and rodents.

Middle chunk of the abstract summarizing evidence that DR reduces cancer, cardiovascular disease, and mortality in monkeys and metabolic disease risk in humans, and that growth hormone receptor loss-of-function mutations confer rarity of neoplasias and diabetes, suggesting conserved aging mechanisms.

Closing chunk of the abstract stating the review's aims: examining conserved anti-aging pathways in model organisms, their link to disease prevention in mammals, and potential negative side effects that could limit human healthspan interventions.

Introduction to a review on amino acid sensing by mTORC1, framing amino acids as protein building blocks and metabolic precursors and listing the cell's adaptive responses to amino acid starvation: halted protein synthesis, increased biosynthesis and transport, and autophagy.

Closing portion of the review's abstract, stating its aim to discuss how amino acid limitation is sensed and how that signal is relayed to mTORC1 to control protein synthesis and autophagy, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Opening of the document's abstract: challenges the view that dietary restriction extends lifespan via fewer calories (caloric restriction), proposing instead that the protein-to-non-protein energy ratio is the key determinant of diet-longevity relationships.

Continuation of the abstract: describes how the protein-to-non-protein balance affects lifespan, total energy intake, metabolism, immunity, and obesity risk, and introduces the TOR and AMPK signaling nexus as a possible mechanism.
Final sentence of the abstract: concludes that the crosstalk between the TOR and AMPK pathways is emerging as a central coordinator linking macronutrient balance to lifespan.

Opening of an abstract on the target of rapamycin (TOR) kinase and mTORC1 signalling, covering its roles in cell growth, proliferation, and disease, and its activation by hormones, growth factors, and amino acids.

Middle section of the abstract describing recent findings that MAP4K3 and Rag GTPases mediate amino acid activation of mTORC1, and introducing mTORC1's established role in G1/S transition and its newly reported role in G2/M progression.
Closing sentence of the abstract stating that mTORC1 controls G2/M cell-cycle progression in both yeast and mammals, but in contrasting ways.

Opening of the abstract: background on preventive medicine behaviors and life expectancy, the study objective (diet, exercise, smoking), and the start of the methods describing the cohort of 34,192 California Seventh-Day Adventists.

Methods continued: cohort follow-up from 1976 to 1988, baseline mailed questionnaire for dietary and exposure data, and mortality ascertainment via state death tapes and the National Death Index; start of results.

Results: Adventists' life expectancy at age 30 exceeds other white Californians by 7.28 years in men and 4.42 years in women, with confidence intervals, suggesting among the highest life expectancies of any described population.

Results continued: combinations of diet, exercise, BMI, past smoking, and hormone replacement therapy can explain up to 10 years of life expectancy difference; independent effects of high- versus low-risk values range from 1.06 to 2.74 years.

Results and conclusions: each variable's effect is assessed with others at medium or high risk; conclusion that choices about diet, exercise, smoking, body weight, and hormone therapy together may change life expectancy by many years.
Final sentence of the abstract: the longevity of Adventists likely reflects the beneficial effects of more optimal health behaviors.

Introduction stating that long-term caloric restriction extends lifespan and reduces age-related disease in animals, that human effects are unknown, and that Okinawan centenarians and low intake motivated the CR hypothesis in humans.

Describes the research gap: no long-term epidemiologic study had examined traditional Okinawan diet, energy balance, CR phenotypes, or mortality in the purportedly calorie-restricted cohort; sets up the study's six-decade archival analysis.

Methods overview: the study analyzed six decades of archived data on Okinawans aged 65 and older, covering diet composition, energy intake and expenditure, anthropometry, plasma DHEA, age-related disease mortality, and survival.

Summarizes key findings supporting CR: low intake and negative energy balance early in life, stable low BMI, high DHEA in older age, low age-related mortality, and survival consistent with extended lifespan.
Conclusion that the epidemiologic findings support phenotypic benefits of caloric restriction in humans and align with animal research on CR and healthy aging.

Introduction of an abstract on mTORC1 as a mediator of cancer-preventive effects of adiponectin, metformin, rapamycin, and low-protein plant-based diets, noting mTORC1 as a key regulator of protein translation.

Explains the mechanism by which mTORC1 boosts eIF4E availability to drive translation of 'weak' mRNAs encoding pro-proliferative, invasive, angiogenic, and anti-apoptotic (chemoresistance-promoting) proteins in cancer.

Argues that inhibiting eIF4E, directly or indirectly, could aid both cancer prevention and treatment, with direct eIF4E-targeting strategies (some in clinical assessment) possibly having the broadest efficacy since eIF4E is overexpressed in many cancers.

Notes that many weak mRNAs promoting malignancy and chemoresistance are transcriptionally regulated by NF-kappaB and/or Stat3, which are active in many cancers, introducing the rationale for combined targeting.

Concludes that concurrently targeting eIF4E, NF-kappaB, and Stat3 could reduce these pro-cancer proteins at both transcriptional and translational levels, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.

Opening of the review's abstract: introduces dietary restriction (DR) and its benefits for longevity, metabolic fitness and stress resistance, and argues that amino acid restriction, not just calorie restriction, mediates these effects.

Continues the abstract with evidence that amino acid restriction drives DR benefits, citing essential amino acid imbalance in fruitflies and reduced dietary protein or essential amino acids in mammals, and states the review's aim of covering amino acid-sensing pathways.

Introduces the two conserved amino acid-sensing pathways reviewed: GCN2, an eIF2α kinase that senses uncharged tRNAs when amino acids are absent, and the setting of the review's focus on these signal transducers.

Describes the TOR pathway as a master growth regulator activated by amino acids such as leucine, and explains that GCN2 and TOR respond to amino acid deprivation by inhibiting general translation while upregulating translation of specific stress-restoration mRNAs.
Concludes the abstract by stating that these amino acid-sensing pathways (GCN2 and TOR) may together regulate longevity, metabolic fitness and stress resistance.

Abstract of a 2012 Aging Cell meta-analysis on dietary restriction (DR) and lifespan across species; this opening chunk introduces the overall finding that DR extends lifespan and that effects are modulated by moderating factors.

Continuation of the abstract summarizing moderators of DR lifespan effects: smaller effects in males and non-model organisms, protein intake mattering more than calorie restriction degree, and mortality-rate reductions driving life extension in laboratory models.

Concluding part of the abstract on the mechanistic and evolutionary interpretation: DR-longevity relationships in lab model species (yeast, nematodes, fruit flies, rodents) are better explained by convergent adaptation to lab conditions than by evolutionary conservation, plus the journal copyright line.

Final fragment of the abstract containing the closing hedge about alternative explanations and the publisher copyright notice (Aging Cell, Blackwell Publishing, Anatomical Society of Great Britain and Ireland), identifying the source publication.
Introduction: Okinawa's longevity and the traditional low-calorie, nutrient-dense, antioxidant-rich diet as a likely driver of healthy aging.
Diet pattern: vegetable- and fruit-heavy, phytonutrient-rich, low in meat, refined grains, saturated fat, sugar, salt, and full-fat dairy; linked to lower chronic disease risk.
Comparison to other healthy diets: the Okinawan pattern shares features with the Mediterranean and DASH diets, and these low-saturated-fat, antioxidant-rich traits are key to the shared benefits.

Mechanisms: low saturated fat, high antioxidant intake, and low glycemic load in these diets likely reduce risk of cardiovascular disease, some cancers, and other chronic diseases, partly via reduced oxidative stress.

Nutrient profile: compared with the Mediterranean and DASH diets, the Okinawan diet is lowest in fat (especially saturated fat) and highest in carbohydrate, reflecting high intake of sweet potatoes, orange-yellow roots, and leafy greens.
Functional foods: many traditional Okinawan foods, herbs, and spices eaten regularly could be considered functional foods, and their health-promoting properties are under active study.
Introduction of the article on healthy ageing and human longevity, framing centenarians as a model of successful ageing and motivating study of the ageing phenotype.
Continues the introduction by stressing gene-environment-lifestyle interactions in healthy ageing and the importance of modifiable factors like diet and nutrition for extending health span.

States the article's purpose: extending optimal health through a better understanding of longevity, with a focus on centenarians' dietary patterns and nutrient-sensing pathways that regulate lifespan.
Closing summary of the article's scope, noting the final discussion of the Nrf2 system's role in pro-ageing signaling and its phytohormetic activation.
Introduction of a review on caloric restriction (CR) and its links to aging and cancer, establishing that reduced calorie intake extends lifespan and lowers cancer risk in animal models.
Explains the metabolic rationale for CR's anti-cancer effect (cancer cells' glycolytic dependence) and notes CR inhibits transplantable, spontaneous, radiation-, and chemically induced tumors.
Discusses evidence for CR's anti-tumor effect in humans, citing reduced breast cancer incidence in women with early-life anorexia, while noting human research is still at an early stage.
Covers proposed mechanisms, namely nutrient-sensing and IGF-1 pathways shared with CR's anti-aging action, and notes cancer cell lines mutant for IGF-1 pathway proteins failed to respond to CR.
Describes CR lowering growth factors, anabolic hormones, inflammatory cytokines, and oxidative markers deregulated in cancers, and previews the review's scope of in vitro and mouse model experiments.
Outlines the review's scope: in vitro tumor models and in vivo mouse models (radiation/chemical induction, oncogene expression, tumor suppressor deletion), plus proposed anti-tumor mechanisms.
Closing statement arguing for gene expression studies comparing cancerous and normal cells under CR, identifying a research need the review highlights.

Opening of an abstract on rapidly rising healthy lifespan and the 'longevity riddle'; introduces the hypothesis that genetic variants like hyperactive mTOR boost early survival at the cost of faster aging.

Continues the 'revealed-slow-aging' hypothesis: robustness and fast aging are linked, slow-aging people died early in the past, so mostly fast agers reached old age until modern civilization (around 60 years ago) let slow agers survive.

Concluding part of the abstract: explains why slow aging appears as postponed healthy aging, why deterioration rate is independent of aging, and previews discussion of rapamycin use across eras and future longevity.
Final fragment of the abstract, ending the sentence about the future of human longevity.

Introduces the mTOR nutrient-response pathway as a leading target for pharmacological anti-ageing interventions, noting that lifespan extension and protection from age-related diseases have been shown in model organisms; this opening sets up the document's argument that slowing ageing is a question of timing.

Continues the discussion of mTOR inhibition: notes that clinically approved inhibitors already exist and more are in development, but adverse side effects currently rule out use in healthy people, which frames the barrier to broad anti-ageing use.

Concludes the passage by projecting that mTOR-targeting drugs could eventually become widely used in humans to slow ageing and reduce age-related disease, pointing to the translational outlook for the field.

This chunk is the document's entire content, making the core claim that aging is not programmed but is a continuation of developmental growth driven by pathways like mTOR, described as a purposeless quasi-program or shadow of actual programs, with a George R.R. Martin quote on the brightest flame casting the darkest shadow.

Opening of the review on caloric restriction (CR) in humans: establishes that lifelong CR slows aging and extends lifespan in short-lived species, but its effect in long-lived primates and humans is unknown.

Summarizes human evidence so far: short-term CR/weight-loss programs and self-selected long-term CR studies show cardiovascular benefits, yet few studies examine quality of life and pitfalls of long-term CR in humans.

Argues that CR's animal effects, including reduced age-related diseases like cancer, may translate differently to human life, and that the physiological and psychological effects of CR may differ between animals and humans.

Notes that despite CR's benefits in mammals, it may carry health concerns in humans that do not apply to experimental animals, and that these potential pitfalls or 'side effects' are poorly addressed in the literature.
Closing statement of the introduction announcing that the review will focus on the potential pitfalls and side effects of caloric restriction in humans.

Opening chunk of an article reframing aging: the traditional rusting-car analogy is replaced by a speeding car without brakes that damages itself when entering a low-speed zone, introducing the document's central thesis.

Middle chunk outlining the article's topics: origin of aging, mTOR overactivation as a cause of aging, aging causing organ damage rather than the reverse, links to age-related disease, and rapamycin-based suppression of aging.
Final fragment of the article's topic list, ending with slow aging versus aging tolerance and suppression of aging with rapamycin, which closes the overview of the document's contents.

Introduction to the rapamycin paper: discovery of the Easter Island Streptomyces hygroscopicus isolate, its antifungal activity against Candida albicans, Microsporum gypseum and Trichophyton granulosum, and extraction and naming of rapamycin.

Antifungal spectrum and potency of rapamycin: MIC of 0.02 to 0.2 µg/ml against Candida albicans across ten strains, and lower apparent activity against dermatophytes due to instability in culture media during prolonged incubation.
Selectivity and safety profile of rapamycin: no activity against gram-positive or gram-negative bacteria, and low acute toxicity in mice.
Introduction and stated objective of a systematic review assessing evidence for ABO blood type diets, including GRADE appraisal of published studies.

Continuation of the objective and design: the systematic search question on whether blood-type-specific diet adherence improves health or reduces disease, and the databases searched (Cochrane, MEDLINE, Embase).
Results section reporting search yield: 1415 screened references, 16 articles identified, and only one article meeting selection criteria.
Findings on the single eligible study (MNS blood types and LDL-cholesterol response to a low-fat diet), noting it did not answer the review question and no ABO diet health-effect studies were found.
Conclusion that no evidence validates the health benefits of blood type diets, and the call for controlled studies comparing blood-type diet adherers with a standard-diet control group.
Final clause of the conclusion specifying that such comparative trials should be conducted within a particular blood type population.

Study background and objective: introduces the ‘Blood-Type’ diet (eating by ABO blood group for cardiovascular/chronic disease prevention) and states the aim to test its links to cardiometabolic biomarkers and whether ABO genotype modifies them.

Methods, part 1: study population of 1,455 Toronto Nutrigenomics and Health study participants, with diet assessed by a one-month 196-item food frequency questionnaire used to score adherence to each Blood-Type diet.

Methods, part 2: ABO blood group determined by genotyping rs8176719 and rs8176746; ANCOVA adjusted for age, sex, ethnicity, and energy intake compares cardiometabolic biomarkers across diet score tertiles.

Results, part 1: higher Type-A diet adherence linked to lower BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, cholesterol, triglycerides, insulin, HOMA-IR and HOMA-Beta; Type-AB adherence linked to lower levels of most of these except BMI and waist circumference.
Results, part 2: Type-O adherence associated with lower triglycerides (P<0.0001); matching diet to blood group did not change effect sizes; no significant association for the Type-B diet.

Conclusions: adherence to certain Blood-Type diets is favorably associated with some cardiometabolic risk factors, but these links are independent of ABO genotype, so the findings do not support the Blood-Type diet hypothesis.

Introduction to a study on medical nutrition therapy (MNT) vs. usual care for hypercholesterolemia, framing the common assumption that heart-healthy diets are difficult and hurt quality of life; describes the 90-patient randomized design.

Study design details (90 ambulatory patients, ages 28-66, randomized to dietitian-led NCEP-based MNT or physician usual care) and early findings: no difference in QOL related to taste or enjoyment of food between groups.
Key results favoring MNT: initial QOL improvements in convenience and cost of a low-fat diet, significant lasting improvements in self-care QOL, as compared with usual care.

Patient satisfaction outcomes for MNT versus usual care (visit interactions, cholesterol management knowledge, eating habits, appearance, exercise, life in general) and absence of negative diet-related impacts such as feeling restricted or meal planning difficulty.
Concluding statement that MNT for hypercholesterolemia does not reduce, and instead improves, some QOL and patient satisfaction measures, countering popular belief.

Background and aims of the From The Heart study: why LDL-C matters for CVD prevention guidelines, first-line lifestyle advice, statin use in high-risk patients, and the study's goal of examining physicians' diagnosis, treatment, and attitudes on high cholesterol.
Study methods and response rate: physicians randomly selected from 10 countries completed a confidential semi-structured questionnaire; 750 of 2790 invited physicians (27%) responded.

Physician perceptions of risk: CVD seen as the leading cause of death and cancer as the most feared illness, with smoking (71%) rated the greatest CVD risk factor while only 50% named high cholesterol.

Practice patterns and outcomes: most physicians (81%) set cholesterol goals using guidelines, mainly national guidelines (34%) or NCEP ATP III (24%); only 47% of patients reached and maintained goals, yet 61% felt enough patients achieved them.

Study conclusion on the gap between guidelines and practice: 53% were not frustrated by limited effectiveness in treating CVD, and the study concludes physicians appreciate CVD risk but do not widely endorse the importance of healthy cholesterol levels.
Final implications: the study calls for better communication about the importance of cholesterol lowering and for investigating initiatives to improve physicians' goal achievement for patients.

Introduces the Cornell China study's design: mortality data for over 50 diseases across rural mainland China counties and villages, plus blood, urine, food, and dietary sampling of adults, with the start of a comparison of rural China diet (low fat) against the US.

Compares rural Chinese and US diets and health: lower fat, higher fiber, and much less animal protein in China, plus markedly lower mean serum cholesterol and coronary artery disease mortality in Chinese counterparts (16.7-fold for men, 5.6-fold for women).

Reports the diet-disease associations for coronary artery disease in rural China: mortality is inversely linked to green vegetable intake and erythrocyte monounsaturated fatty acids, and positively linked to salt/urinary sodium and plasma apolipoprotein B.

Explains the mechanistic chain linking diet to coronary risk: apolipoprotein B rises with animal protein and meat intake and falls with plant protein, legumes, and light-colored vegetables; also notes correlations of other diseases with dietary factors.
Concludes the findings with the study's key dose-response observation: no threshold exists beyond which additional plant-based food in the diet stops providing health benefits.

Opening of the abstract for a study of 356 hypercholesterolaemic patients and French GPs' dietary prescriptions: states adherence to cholesterol-lowering diets is the key problem, and describes the aims and survey methods.

Results section of the abstract: sample sizes (234 doctor questionnaires, 356 patient surveys) and the top patient reasons for not complying with the prescribed diet, with percentages (satisfactory food habits 34.7%, unwillingness to suffer deprivation 33.3%, family life conflicts 27.8%, cholesterol drugs 22.2%).

Findings on patient understanding versus doctors' declarations, noting that patients generally understood recommendations but reported discrepancies between doctors' and patients' views, with doctors' perceptions of patient needs beginning here.

Discrepancy findings: doctors thought patients needed more explanation on how diets lower cholesterol and avoid drugs, but only 39.4% of patients said they needed such information; other differences in perceived barriers and motivators are also noted.

Findings on rule-specific adherence and physician confidence: patients remembered advice to eat more fish (82.6%) but only 51.3% did so, and both physicians and patients showed low confidence in the efficacy of lipid-lowering diets; the conclusion begins with recommendations on patient education.

Closing conclusion of the abstract recommending better patient education on risk perception and greater dietitian involvement to improve adherence, followed by the Elsevier Masson 2012 copyright notice.

Introduction and design of a 5-year dietary cholesterol-lowering study in the Family Heart Study (Portland, Oregon), describing the cohort study aim to measure changes in negative emotions relative to diet and plasma cholesterol.

Study setting and participants (149 men, 156 women from 233 families, mean age 37.7) and measurement method (Hopkins SCL-90 for depression and aggressive hostility), followed by the start of the results describing overall emotional improvement.

Key results: the entire sample improved emotionally, and the low-fat, high complex-carbohydrate diet group had significantly greater reductions in depression and aggressive hostility and in plasma cholesterol than the high-fat 'American diet' group, with P-values and point differences.

Statistical results for hostility and cholesterol comparisons, followed by the conclusions that cholesterol-lowering participation did not worsen emotional state and that dietary improvement was linked to reduced depression and hostility.
Final conclusion of the study: improvements in diet are associated with reduced depression and aggressive hostility as well as lower plasma cholesterol levels.

Introduction to a 2001 study testing a very-high-fiber fruit and vegetable diet, modeled on the original dietary fiber hypothesis and early human diets, with the three 2-week diet arms in 10 healthy volunteers.

Description of the three metabolic diets (high-vegetable/fruit/nut very-high-fiber, starch-based early agricultural, and low-fat contemporary therapeutic), all weight-maintaining at about 2,577 kcal/d, and the start of the results comparing the high-fiber diet to the others.
Main results of the vegetable diet versus the comparison diets: the largest LDL cholesterol reduction (33%) and increased fecal bile acid output, fecal bulk, and fecal short-chain fatty acid output.

Results on fecal bile acid concentration, which was lowest on the vegetable diet despite higher output, the timing of maximal lipid reduction within 1 week, and increased urinary mevalonic acid reflecting fecal steroid losses.

Conclusions that very high vegetable fiber intake may reduce cardiovascular and possibly colon cancer risk factors, with a call for further study of vegetable and fruit fibers, plus the 2001 copyright notice.

Opening of a document on the new pathophysiology of coronary artery disease: introduces how the understanding of atherosclerosis has changed, noting that non-visible soft plaque, not angiographically apparent plaque, causes most MIs.

Continues the discussion of atherosclerotic risk: diet-related changes in vascular reactivity, why total cholesterol alone is a poor predictor (most infarcts occur with normal cholesterol), and the total-to-HDL cholesterol ratio as a better risk marker.

Concludes the discussion of risk markers: the triglyceride-to-HDL ratio, practical steps for assessing patient risk, and evidence from primary prevention trials that diet and drug therapy can sharply reduce coronary disease risk.
Final fragment of the document's closing sentence, stating that primary prevention trials show coronary artery disease risk can be lowered dramatically with diet and drug therapy.
Opening of an abstract on colonic cancer epidemiology: population differences, the negative fiber-cancer correlation, and the hypothesis that high-fiber diets are protective.

Continues the abstract by reanalyzing dietary data to propose phytic acid (inositol hexaphosphate) as the protective element, describing its heat- and acid-stability and its presence in cereals, nuts, and seeds.
Describes the mechanism: phytic acid chelates metals and suppresses iron-catalyzed redox damage, which may counter oxygen radicals produced by colonic bacteria and protect intestinal epithelium.

Summarizes animal-model evidence that dietary phytic acid protects against experimentally induced colonic cancer and states that further support would make dietary phytic acid increase a simple way to reduce colon cancer risk.
Closing sentence concluding that deliberately increasing dietary phytic acid could be a simple way to lower the risk of colonic carcinogenesis.

Background on IP6 (inositol hexaphosphate) as an anti-cancer agent that inhibits cancer cell adhesion to extracellular matrix proteins, migration, and invasion, and the hypothesis that it acts by suppressing integrin receptors and signaling in MDA-MB 231 breast cancer study.

Study hypothesis that IP6 reduces cell adhesion by suppressing integrin receptors and their downstream signaling, followed by methods: flow cytometry of integrin expression and immunocytochemistry/Western blotting of focal adhesion proteins in estrogen receptor-negative MDA-MB 231 breast cancer cells.

Results begin: IP6 significantly decreases expression of integrin heterodimers alpha2beta1 (collagen receptor), alpha5beta1 (fibronectin receptor), and alphavbeta3 (vitronectin receptor) in MDA-MB 231 cells.
Subunit-level findings: flow cytometry shows the alpha5 subunit is specifically down-regulated by IP6, while alpha2, alphav, beta1, and beta3 subunit expression is unaffected.
Cell surface integrin results: IP6 causes an 82% decrease in surface alpha5beta1 (P<0.0001), with no effect from the inositol hexasulfate (IS6) analogue control.

Focal adhesion findings: IP6 disrupts paxillin clustering and makes tyrosine-phosphorylated proteins discontinuous and scattered at the cell periphery, and modestly suppresses FAK autophosphorylation at tyrosine-397.
Conclusion: IP6-induced inhibition of cancer cell adhesion, migration, and invasion may act through modulating integrin dimerization, cell surface expression, and integrin-associated signaling.
Final conclusion fragment: IP6's anti-metastatic effects are proposed to be mediated via integrin dimerization, surface expression, and the integrin-associated signaling pathway.

Abstract of a study on inositol hexaphosphate (IP6) and human neutrophils, introducing IP6's known extracellular effects and the investigation of its inflammatory cytokine effects (IL-8, TNF-alpha, IL-6) on adherent neutrophils.

Methods and key result from the IP6 neutrophil study: cytokine release (IL-8, TNF-alpha, IL-6) by neutrophils on plastic or laminin, stimulated with LPS or fMLP, with the finding that IP6 increased IL-8 secretion.

Conclusions of the IP6 neutrophil study: IP6 alone did not change morphology of laminin-attached cells but altered shape with fMLP, and IP6 triggered sustained F-actin assembly, suggesting modulation of selective neutrophil functions.
Final concluding sentence of the abstract stating that low-level IP6 exposure modulates selective neutrophil functions.

Introduces inositol hexaphosphate (IP6) and its lower forms as ubiquitous molecules in mammalian cells that regulate signal transduction, proliferation, and differentiation, and opens the discussion of IP6's anti-cancer action.

Describes the proposed mechanism of IP6's anti-cancer effect (internalization, dephosphorylation to IP(1-5), growth inhibition), the enhancing role of inositol (Ins), and IP6's effects on proliferation and differentiation.

Covers IP6-induced differentiation of malignant cells toward a normal phenotype and concludes that signal transduction, cell cycle, differentiation, oncogene, and tumor suppressor genes likely mediate IP6's anti-neoplastic action.
Final sentence concluding that the anti-neoplastic action of IP6 likely involves tumor suppressor genes, closing the document's discussion of mechanisms.

Introduces the study's scope: in vitro evaluation of antioxidant, chemopreventive, and ACE, α-glucosidase, and pancreatic lipase inhibitory properties of three Australian-grown faba bean genotypes (Nura, Rossa, TF(Ic*As)*483/13), with the opening of the HPLC post-column derivatisation finding on phenolics.

Reports that post-column derivatisation HPLC showed active phenolics in the coloured genotypes but not the white breeding line, and that roasting lowered phenolic content and reagent-based antioxidant activity (DPPH, ABTS, ORAC) by 10-40%.
Describes cellular antioxidant activity results, where coloured genotypes gained activity after roasting, and reports protection against H2O2-induced DNA damage in RAW264.7 cells.
Covers anticancer findings: extracts inhibited proliferation of several human cancer cell lines (BL13, AGS, Hep G2, HT-29) with negligible effect on non-transformed CCD-18Co cells.
Reports flow cytometry showing apoptosis induction in HL-60 leukaemia cells and enzyme inhibition by extracts, then ranks genotypes: Nura and Rossa comparable, TF(Ic*As)*483/13 weakest.
Concludes that the faba bean results support greater dietary use of faba beans for health benefits.
This chunk opens the study's Background and Patients/methods sections: a 2005-2007 randomized pilot trial of IP6 + inositol in breast cancer patients receiving adjuvant polychemotherapy.
This chunk continues Methods: 14 stage-matched invasive ductal breast cancer patients were randomized to IP6 + inositol or placebo, with the same lab parameters monitored in both groups.

This chunk covers the start of the Results: chemotherapy patients on IP6 + inositol showed no cytopenia or leukocyte/platelet drops, and red cell counts and tumor markers were unchanged, with the quality-of-life outcome introduced via QLQ-C30 and QLQ-BR23 questionnaires.

This chunk gives the key quality-of-life findings (p = 0.05 for quality of life, p = 0.0003 for functional status) and the Conclusion that IP6 + inositol helps ameliorate chemotherapy side effects and preserve quality of life.
This final chunk is the tail end of the Conclusion sentence, restating that IP6 + inositol preserves quality of life in chemotherapy-treated patients.

Opening section of a document on traditional non-Western diets; introduces the core idea that traditional cultures balanced health through lifestyle, rarely had modern diseases, and treated food and medicine as interwoven, using functional foods to prevent illness.

Middle section of the document on traditional diets; covers how the same food could serve as either food or medicine, how cultivation and cooking methods maximized community health, and how traditional cooking improved mineral and nutrient bioavailability.

Closing section of the document on traditional non-Western diets; states the article's scope: researcher observations on indigenous food traditions, disease patterns, specific foods, and environmental factors affecting people who still eat traditional foods.

Introduction of the IP(6) anti-angiogenesis study: states the hypothesis that IP(6) reduces tumor growth by inhibiting angiogenesis, and sets up the investigation of its effects on endothelial and tumor cells.

Results on endothelial cells in vitro: IP(6) inhibits proliferation and induces differentiation of bovine aortic endothelial cells (BAECs), with a dose-dependent MTT growth inhibition (IC50 = 0.74 mM).
Combination and tube formation results: IP(6) plus vasostatin synergistically inhibits growth more than either alone, and IP(6) blocks HUVEC tube formation on Matrigel and disrupts pre-formed tubes.

In vivo and gene expression results: IP(6) significantly reduces bFGF-induced vessel formation in the Matrigel plug assay (P < 0.01), and in HepG2 hepatoma cells it dose-dependently lowers VEGF mRNA at 8 h by RT-PCR.

VEGF protein and conclusion: IP(6) reduces VEGF protein in conditioned medium of HepG2 cells at 24 h in a concentration-dependent manner (P = 0.012), concluding that IP(6) inhibits induced angiogenesis.

Introduces IP(6) (inositol hexaphosphate) as a natural polyphosphorylated carbohydrate found in plant foods like cereals and legumes, and in small amounts in mammalian cells where it regulates signal transduction, proliferation, and differentiation.
Notes IP(6)'s long-recognized role as a natural antioxidant and its recent attention for cancer prevention and control of experimental tumor growth, progression, and metastasis.

Lists IP(6)'s other health benefits (immune enhancement, preventing calcification and kidney stones, lowering serum cholesterol, reducing platelet activity) and states the review's aim of showing efficacy and molecular mechanisms.

Describes the mechanism: exogenous IP(6) is taken up into cells, dephosphorylated to lower inositol phosphates that alter signal transduction and cause cell cycle arrest, with striking anticancer effects in experimental models.

Summarizes anticancer actions beyond growth inhibition (inducing differentiation of malignant cells, enhanced immunity, antioxidant effects) and preliminary human findings that IP(6) and inositol boost chemotherapy effects and control metastases.
Argues IP(6) + inositol is promising for cancer prevention and therapy because it is abundant in diet, well absorbed, and safe, and concludes the evidence justifies initiating clinical trials.
Final sentence concluding that existing evidence warrants full-scale human clinical trials of IP(6) and inositol for cancer.

Introduction to a study on inositol hexaphosphate (IP6) and its effect on matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) and TIMP expression in colon cancer cells, framing MMPs and TIMPs in tumor invasion and metastasis.

Continuation of the introduction: IP6's known anticancer effects against colon cancer and its in vitro inhibition of cancer cell adhesion and migration, leading to the study aim of testing IP6 on MMP/TIMP genes in unstimulated and IL-1β-stimulated Caco-2 cells.

Methods and start of results from the Caco-2 study: real-time QRT-PCR measuring MMP and TIMP transcription after treatment with 1 ng/ml IL-1β, 2.5 mM IP6, or both for 6, 12, and 24 h, and the initial finding that IL-1β overexpresses MMP and TIMP mRNAs.

Key results on gene expression: IP6 significantly lowered basal MMP-13, MMP-3, MMP-2, and TIMP-1 expression, and at 6 h reduced IL-1β-induced MMP-1, MMP-9, and TIMP-2 transcription; at 12 h IP6 reduced IL-1β-induced MMP-2 mRNA.
Conclusions beginning: IL-1β upregulates MMP and TIMP mRNAs in Caco-2 cells, and 2.5 mM IP6 affects constitutive MMP/TIMP expression while downregulating IL-1β-stimulated transcription of some genes.
Final conclusion: IP6 exerts anti-metastatic activity by modulating MMP and TIMP gene expression, thereby preventing colon cancer cell migration and invasion.
Opening of a case-control study of diet and colorectal cancer in Athens, Greece, describing the study setting and the patient case series recruited from two hospitals.
Continues the study design: orthopaedic control patients matched by age and sex, and the dietary history method (frequency of about 80 food items) administered by one interviewer.

Key findings: cases ate significantly fewer vegetables (beets, spinach, lettuce, cabbage) and more meat (lamb, beef), with the high-meat vs. high-vegetable diet contrast linked to a risk ratio of about 8.
Interpretation of the diet risk ratio as large enough to explain much of international colorectal cancer variation, plus null findings for alcohol and for interactions with age, sex and tumor site.
Concluding statement that no significant interactions were found between diet effects and age, sex, or anatomic site (colon vs. rectum).

Abstract opening of a paper on dietary suppression of colonic cancer; introduces variation in colon cancer incidence across populations, the proposed protective role of dietary fiber, and the gap that high-fiber diets don't always protect, implying other dietary constituents.

Continuation of the abstract introducing phytic acid (inositol hexaphosphate), a plant seed component found in many fiber-rich diets, and the authors' finding that it potently inhibits iron-mediated formation of the hydroxyl radical.

Concluding sentence of the abstract proposing that phytic acid chelates reactive iron to reduce intracolonic hydroxyl radical generation, which may explain its suppression of colonic carcinogenesis and inflammatory bowel diseases.

Introduction to the abstract: frames prostate cancer (PCA) as a slow-growing disease of elderly men suited to preventive intervention, and introduces dietary and non-dietary phytochemicals as potential preventive agents.
Describes the biology of PCA growth and progression: aberrant mitogenic and survival signaling, deregulated cell cycle, and gradual accumulation of genetic and epigenetic changes over years.

Lists implicated molecular mechanisms (overexpressed growth, survival and angiogenic factors and receptors; loss of p53, retinoblastoma, and CDK inhibitors) and concludes that phytochemicals targeting them may aid PCA prevention or therapy, leading into IP6.

Introduces inositol hexaphosphate (IP6) as a dietary compound abundant in cereals, legumes, nuts, and soybean, sold as a supplement with a good safety profile, and notes its in vitro anticancer activity across human, mouse, and rat prostate cancer cells.
Summarizes in vivo evidence: oral IP6 inhibits human PCA xenograft growth in nude mice without toxicity, and a pilot study showed preventive effects in the TRAMP transgenic mouse model.
Covers mechanistic findings: IP6 acts on mitogenic and survival signaling, cell cycle progression, and angiogenesis, with pleiotropic targets that support its use as a preventive candidate.
Concluding sentence: IP6 is proposed as a suitable candidate agent for preventing prostate cancer in humans.

Introduction and study background from the Polyp Prevention Trial (PPT) paper: prior evidence on fruit and vegetable intake and colorectal adenomas, and the PPT's low-fat, high-fiber dietary intervention design.

Describes the PPT cohort analysis methods: the trial's null result on adenoma recurrence between intervention and control arms, and the use of multiple logistic regression for advanced and nonadvanced adenoma recurrence.
Methods detail: odds ratios estimated across quartiles of baseline and 3-year change in fruit and vegetable intake, adjusted for age, energy intake, NSAID use, BMI, and gender.

Key results: no significant association of overall fruit and vegetable change with nonadvanced adenoma recurrence, but the highest quartile of dry bean intake increase was linked to a significantly reduced odds of advanced recurrence (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.18-0.69, P for trend 0.001).
Concluding findings: the highest dry bean intake quartile had a median intake 370% above baseline, and the authors conclude dry beans may be inversely associated with advanced adenoma recurrence.

Introduces the hospital-based case-control study of diet and colorectal cancer among Singapore Chinese, including sample size (203 cases, 425 controls) and the food frequency questionnaire method used to measure dietary intake.

Describes how dietary intakes were stratified by control tertiles and adjusted for age, sex, dialect group and occupation, then begins reporting the main finding that high cruciferous vegetable intake is protective for colon and rectal cancer combined.

Reports the key combined colon/rectum results: protective effect of high cruciferous vegetable intake (OR 0.50) and predisposing effect of high meat/vegetable ratio (OR 1.77), then gives the rectal-cancer-only protective findings for protein, fibre, beta-carotene and vegetables.

Lists the significant protective dietary factors for rectal cancer alone (protein, fibre, beta-carotene, cruciferous and total vegetables) and notes that multivariate, trend and quintile analyses consistently confirmed cruciferous vegetables and the meat/vegetable ratio.

Covers the coffee finding (low coffee intake associated with high risk, OR 1.59, trend p<0.05), notes lack of consistent trends for fat or fibre, and introduces non-dietary results on cholecystectomy as a risk factor.

Presents the cholecystectomy findings (OR 3.43 for both cancers combined, OR 4.39 for colon cancer alone) and begins the conclusion about Asian populations undergoing industrialization and changing cancer patterns.
Concludes that protective effects of dietary constituents such as cruciferous vegetables may matter more than the traditionally emphasized carcinogenic roles of fat and protein in colorectal cancer.

Opening chunk of a study on nonstarch polysaccharide (NSP) dietary fiber intake in 30 men aged 50-59 across two urban and two rural Scandinavian populations with differing large bowel cancer incidence, measured by duplicate food chemical analysis.

Reports the rural-urban gradient in NSP intake (Finland and Denmark, rural vs urban means and SDs) and notes that food-table estimates from 4-day weighed food records were compared with the duplicate-portion method.
Explains that food-table NSP estimates ran 2-2.5 g/day higher than chemical analysis due to outdated composition tables, and highlights considerable day-to-day variation in individual NSP intake.

Concludes that average NSP intake and some component sugar intakes were inversely related to colon cancer incidence across populations, and that individual-level prospective studies need accurate NSP assessment methods.
Closing fragment restating the conclusion that accurate NSP consumption assessment methods are required to demonstrate individual-level diet-cancer relationships in prospective studies.
Abstract opening of a study on inositol hexaphosphate (IP(6)) anticancer activity, introducing its reported effects on solid tumours and the aim to test it in leukaemia.
Methods and results overview: IP(6) dose-dependent cytotoxicity in leukaemic cell lines with G2M accumulation in two of five lines, and analysis of fresh CML progenitor cells.

Molecular findings from cDNA microarray analysis after IP(6) exposure, showing downregulated transcription and cell cycle genes, upregulated cell cycle inhibitors, and CD34+ CML progenitor CFU-GM inhibition versus normal marrow.

Reported CFU-GM result (P = 0.0062) comparing CML to normal bone marrow, the absence of differentiation effect on HL60 cells, and the start of the concluding statement on antiproliferative and antitumour activity.
Concluding sentence of the abstract: IP(6) confirms antiproliferative activity and may have a specific antitumour effect in chronic myeloid leukaemia through active gene modulation.

Study design and population: a 6-year prospective Adventist Health Study cohort of 32,051 non-Hispanic white members (California, 1976-1982) free of cancer at baseline, analyzed with proportional hazards regression for colon cancer risk.

Main results for total meat intake: a positive association with colon cancer (RR 1.85 for at least weekly vs. no meat), followed by red meat and white meat associations among subjects who favored specific meat types.

Specific meat-type and legume findings: red meat (RR 1.90) and white meat (RR 3.29) intake are positively associated with colon cancer, while legume intake shows an inverse association (RR 0.53 for >2 times/week vs. <1 time/week).

Body mass index and combined-factor findings: among men, higher BMI tertile is positively associated with colon cancer (RR 2.63), and the text introduces a complex interaction pattern of diet and body mass.

Mechanistic interpretation of the combined pattern: high red meat, low legume intake, and high body mass gave over threefold risk, plausibly reflecting insulin resistance and glycemic load, implicating hyperinsulinemia in colon carcinogenesis.
Overall conclusions: red meat and white meat are important dietary risk factors for colon cancer, and the red meat risk may reflect a more complex etiology than diet alone.
Concluding fragment of the abstract: the final clause suggesting that the risk associated with red meat intake may arise from a more complex etiology.
Introduction of the IP6 and inositol cancer review: defines IP6 as a ubiquitous natural polyphosphorylated carbohydrate and notes its striking anticancer effects and moderate inositol activity.
