States the review's aim: compiling available evidence on curcumin's efficacy from in vitro cartilage and osteoarthritis models and from studies in other diseases; closes the abstract.
Introduction to curcumin, the main active compound in turmeric, and its reported anti-inflammatory effects and role in weight loss and obesity-related disease in the article 'Curcumin and obesity'.

Explains that obesity involves chronic low-grade metabolic inflammation, motivating research on curcumin, which directly targets white adipose tissue to suppress this inflammation, in the article on curcumin and obesity.

Describes curcumin's mechanisms in adipose tissue: inhibiting macrophage infiltration and NF-κB activation, and reducing proinflammatory adipokines TNFα, MCP-1, and PAI-1, as discussed in the curcumin and obesity article.

Covers curcumin inducing adiponectin, inhibiting adipocyte differentiation, and boosting antioxidant activity, summarizing how these mechanisms reduce obesity and its health effects in the curcumin and obesity article.
Copyright notice from the International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (2013) closing the curcumin and obesity article.

Study design and methods introduction: a randomized controlled trial in Bangkok, Thailand, of Curcuma domestica (turmeric) extract versus ibuprofen for pain and function in primary knee osteoarthritis, with eligibility of patients with pain score of 5 or higher.

Methods detail: 107 knee OA patients were randomized to ibuprofen 800 mg/day or C. domestica extract 2 g/day for 6 weeks; outcomes were pain on level walking and stairs, plus timed 100-m walk and stair climbing, with adverse events recorded.

Results on enrollment and baseline: 52 patients got C. domestica extract and 55 got ibuprofen, with comparable baseline characteristics; outcome scores improved significantly from baseline at weeks 0, 2, 4, and 6 in both groups.

Comparative efficacy and safety findings: no between-group difference in outcomes except pain on stairs (p = 0.016), and no significant difference in adverse event rates (33.3% turmeric vs 44.2% ibuprofen, p = 0.36).
Conclusion: Curcuma domestica extract appears similarly efficacious and safe to ibuprofen for treating knee osteoarthritis, summarizing the trial's overall takeaway.

Introduces osteoarthritis: its causes (injury, cartilage loss, inflammatory imbalance), joint damage, weight-bearing pain, lack of a cure, and treatment goals. Opening background of the polyphenol review.

Covers the no-cure situation, since cartilage is hard to restore once destroyed, and lists treatment goals: pain relief, joint mobility, joint strength, and limiting disability. Then links dietary polyphenols to preventing osteoarthritis-related inflammation.

States the review's scope: polyphenols studied for osteoarthritis, including curcumin, EGCG/green tea, resveratrol, nobiletin/citrus, pomegranate, genistein, and soy protein, with a focus on molecular antiosteoarthritic mechanisms.
Closing fragment of the abstract that finishes the molecular-mechanisms focus and carries the 2012 Elsevier Inc. copyright notice.

Introduces osteoarthritis as the most common US arthritis and leading cause of disability, noting its epidemiologic definition (radiographic findings plus symptoms) and rising incidence/prevalence tied to aging and obesity.

Lists OA risk factors (age, sex, obesity, genetics, and joint-specific abnormal loading) and notes methodologic challenges in OA research that hamper identifying relationships; continues the sentence about obesity from chunk 1.
Final word completing the sentence 'identify pertinent relationships' from chunk 2, ending the document's brief overview of OA epidemiology.

Introduction to the review on obesity-associated osteoarthritis: establishes obesity as a risk factor for OA in weight-bearing and non-weight-bearing joints and introduces pro-inflammatory metabolic factors and infrapatellar adipose tissue as a local source of inflammatory mediators.

Describes adipose-derived inflammation in osteoarthritis: infrapatellar fat releases pro-inflammatory mediators that rise with obesity and degrade cartilage in culture models, with leptin proposed as a key adipokine acting synergistically with other cytokines.

Covers biomechanical contributions to osteoarthritis: mechanical factors can drive cellular inflammation and oxidative stress, whereas physiologic cyclic loading is protective by suppressing inflammation and cartilage degradation.

Links obesity, sedentary behavior, and inflammation in knee osteoarthritis: many obese patients with knee OA are inactive, suggesting low physical activity may heighten inflammatory susceptibility, and calls for studying how obesity changes daily joint loading.

Concluding statement of the review: a more comprehensive view of how obesity alters daily biomechanical exposure in joints may clarify the protective and damaging roles of mechanical factors in osteoarthritis inflammation.

Introduces the long-term (eight-month, 100-patient) study of Meriva, a curcumin-phosphatidylcholine complex, for osteoarthritis, following a previous three-month study of 50 OA patients that showed reduced joint pain and improved function.

Describes the outcome measures used in the eight-month Meriva osteoarthritis study: clinical endpoints (WOMAC score, Karnofsky Performance Scale, treadmill walking) plus inflammatory markers including IL-1beta, IL-6, sCD40L, sVCAM-1, and ESR.

Frames the study as the most ambitious evaluation to date of curcumin's clinical efficacy and safety as an anti-inflammatory agent, and reports significant improvements in both clinical and biochemical endpoints for Meriva versus the control group.
Concludes that Meriva's significant benefits plus excellent tolerability make it worth considering for long-term complementary management of osteoarthritis.
Introduction to the curcumin review: chemotherapy is the core of cancer treatment, but drug resistance remains a major obstacle, motivating investigation of molecular resistance mechanisms.
Lists the five mechanisms of drug resistance: drug efflux pump overexpression, enhanced drug detoxification, rapid DNA repair, apoptosis defects, and active cell survival signals.

Motivates using curcumin, the turmeric pigment with pleotropic activity, to address multidrug resistance side effects and the need for safe multi-targeted drugs; introduces the literature review methods.
Describes the PubMed/Medline literature review and the review's core claim that curcumin sensitizes cancer cells by regulating multiple multidrug resistance pathways with one drug.

Summarizes curcumin's specific actions: restoring apoptosis, modulating drug-target interactions, restraining overexpressed survival pathways, and sensitizing resistant tumours through alternate routes.
Notes the review also examines whether curcumin targets cancer stem cells, the key drivers of resistance, and concludes curcumin is a promising chemosensitizing agent.
Final concluding sentence: curcumin's unique properties may be exploited for successfully managing resistant tumours.
Opening of the review on curcumin: introduces curcumin's multi-pathway signaling effects and the body of clinical trials on its safety, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy in humans.

Continuation of the introduction listing the pro-inflammatory and other diseases (cancer, cardiovascular, arthritis, IBD, ulcers, psoriasis, etc.) in which curcumin showed promising effects in patients.
Continues the list of diseases where curcumin showed promise, from gastric ulcer through chronic bacterial prostatitis, covering diabetes, renal, hematologic, and biliary conditions.

Summarizes further conditions curcumin protected against (hepatic, arsenic exposure, alcohol intoxication), reports dose-escalation safety up to 12 g/day for 3 months, and begins describing its molecular targets.
Lists the signaling molecules and biomarkers (cytokines, NF-κB, COX-2, STAT3, CRP, AST/ALT, etc.) that curcumin modulates in human participants, explaining its pleiotropic effects.

Notes that curcumin has been tested alone or combined with other agents and in various formulations (nanoparticles, liposomes, capsules, powder), and previews the review's disease-by-disease discussion.
Closing sentence of the introduction stating that the review will discuss in detail the human diseases in which curcumin's effects have been studied.

Introduction to curcumin: the turmeric spice's yellow pigment (diferuloylmethane), its traditional Ayurvedic use for inflammation, and the broad activities revealed by research over the past half century.

Curcumin's molecular mechanisms: binding to proteins and inhibiting kinases, modulating transcription factors to regulate inflammatory enzymes, cytokines, adhesion molecules, and cell survival proteins.

Curcumin's effects on cell-cycle and tumor-suppressor regulators (cyclins D1 and E, MDM2, p21, p27, p53) and preclinical evidence for antiproliferative, anti-invasive, antiangiogenic, chemopreventive, and chemo/radioresistance-modulating activity.

Preclinical evidence of curcumin as a therapeutic in wound healing, diabetes, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, cardiovascular, pulmonary disease, and arthritis, plus pilot phase I trials showing safety at 12 g/day for 3 months.

Clinical trial evidence suggesting curcumin's therapeutic potential in gastrointestinal, metabolic, cardiovascular, dermatologic, and ocular conditions such as colitis, pancreatic and colon cancer, atherosclerosis, psoriasis, uveitis, and arthritis.
Concluding remark: curcumin has moved from the kitchen to the clinic and may prove to be a therapeutic agent, punningly called "Curecumin".

Introduction to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD: ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease), current conventional drug treatments, and their long-term side effects that motivate the search for new agents.

Motivation for novel non-toxic agents and preclinical evidence that curcumin, the active principle of turmeric (Curcuma longa), prevents or ameliorates ulcerative colitis and inflammation in animal studies.
Review of experimental IBD models showing curcumin's mechanisms: free radical scavenging, increased antioxidants, and modulation of multiple signaling pathways, especially kinases.

Specific molecular targets curcumin inhibits in IBD (myeloperoxidase, COX-1/2, LOX, TNF-α, IFN-γ, iNOS, NF-κB), plus clinical findings that curcumin co-administered with conventional drugs is safe and well-tolerated.

Clinical benefits of curcumin in IBD (maintaining remission, preventing relapse, improving clinical activity index) and the conclusion that large randomized controlled trials are needed to establish oral curcumin's therapeutic potential.
Introduction to curcumin from Curcuma longa: its traditional and dietary uses and the antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer properties linked to its preventive and therapeutic effects.
Background on decades of research into curcumin's molecular mechanisms, stating that it acts on molecular targets through altered gene expression, signaling pathways, or direct interaction.

Specific list of genes and proteins whose expression curcumin regulates: inflammatory cytokines, growth factors and receptors, enzymes, adhesion molecules, apoptosis proteins, and cell cycle proteins such as cyclin D1.

Curcumin's modulation of transcription factors (NF-κB, AP-1, STAT) and their pathways, and its potential for preventing or treating diseases such as cancers, arthritis, neurodegeneration, diabetes, and autoimmune disorders.
Closing summary stating the review's purpose of covering curcumin's modulation of gene expression, followed by the 2012 International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology copyright notice.
Final fragment of the copyright notice, naming the International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Inc. (2012) as the publisher of the document.

Introduction to curcumin: the traditional use of turmeric (Curcuma longa root) for inflammatory diseases in Ayurveda and traditional Chinese medicine, and the early identification of curcumin as its active component.

Curcumin's molecular mechanisms: modulation of transcription factors, enzymes, cell cycle proteins, cytokines, receptors, and adhesion molecules, listing specific targets such as NF-kappaB, COX2, cyclin D1, TNF, and EGFR.

Clinical applications of curcumin across many diseases (cancer, arthritis, diabetes, Crohn's, cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, Alzheimer's, psoriasis), followed by introduction of 6-gingerol as a similar analog from ginger.

6-gingerol from ginger (Zingiber officinalis) shares curcumin's biologic activity profile; the document concludes that curcuminoids' efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness justify returning to traditional roots.
Final fragment of the document: closing quotation mark and punctuation ending the concluding phrase "get back to our roots."

Introduction to curcumin, the turmeric-derived phytochemical, and the general claim that dysregulated cell signaling via altered regulatory proteins underlies cancer, with curcumin modulating these proteins; lists cancer types studied.

Continuation of the introduction: research on curcumin's protective effects across many cancer types (gastrointestinal, genitourinary, gynecological, hematological, pulmonary, thymic, brain, breast, bone) and note that its mechanisms are still under investigation.
Describes curcumin's multi-level inhibition of cell signaling and its carcinogenicity-inhibiting effect via cell cycle modulation, starting the enumeration of direct and indirect molecular targets.

Lists the specific molecular targets curcumin acts on: transcription factors (NF-kB, STAT3, β-catenin, AP-1), growth factors (EGF, PDGF, VEGF), enzymes (COX-2, iNOS, MMPs), kinases (cyclin D1, CDKs, Akt, PKC, AMPK), inflammatory cytokines (TNF, MCP, IL-1, IL-6), and pro- and anti-apoptotic proteins (Bax, Bad, Bak; Bcl-2, Bcl-xL).

Concludes the targets list with apoptosis regulation and states that animal and human studies show curcumin is safe and well tolerated even at very high doses; previews the review's aim of covering chemopreventive pathways and therapeutic value.

Closing summary of the review's focus on curcumin's chemopreventive molecular pathways and therapeutic value for treating and preventing a wide range of cancers, followed by the 2013 International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology copyright notice.
Opening of the curcumin review: introduces curcumin as a pleiotropic turmeric polyphenol and its traditional Asian use for skin conditions like acne, psoriasis, and dermatitis.

Summarizes newer mechanistic research (microRNA, cancer stem cells, autophagy pathways) and the broad range of disease areas (cancer, pulmonary, neurological, liver, metabolic) where preclinical and clinical work supports curcumin's pharmaceutical use.
Covers autoimmune, cardiovascular, and chronic diseases, then notes animal safety and efficacy studies across several species as a basis for human evaluation.
Reports the scale of human clinical work: more than 65 completed trials with over 1000 patients, up to 35 ongoing trials, and curcumin's use as a dietary supplement in multiple countries.
Closing statement of the review's purpose (presenting evidence for curcumin's pharmaceutical uses) followed by the 2013 IUBMB copyright notice.
Opening chunk of the review introducing plant polyphenols (isothiocyanates, catechins, capsaicin, resveratrol, curcumin) as anti-inflammatory compounds that may increase disease resistance.

Continuation explaining that chronic diseases are sustained by systemic inflammation, and that treatment may improve by restricting pro-inflammatory AGE/ALE molecules and increasing plant polyphenol intake.
Introduces the curcuminoid family, especially curcumin, as the best-documented polyphenols and states the review's aim of summarizing knowledge on turmeric-derived ingredients.
Summarizes curcuminoid mechanisms as antioxidants and inhibitors of COX-2, LOX, NF-kappaB and AGE, noting many experimental effects but few human clinical studies.
Proposes curcuminoids and polyphenols as complements to pharmaceutical or prebiotic treatment for therapy-resistant conditions such as Crohn's disease, ICU patients, and various chronic diseases.
Closing fragment listing further chronic conditions (liver cirrhosis, chronic renal disease, COPD, diabetes, Alzheimer's disease) where curcuminoid supplementation is suggested as a possible adjunct.

Introduces curcumin, the yellow compound from turmeric, as a remedy for inflammatory diseases and lists the conditions (obesity, diabetes, arthritis, cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, cancer) where inflammation drives progression.

Covers turmeric's Ayurvedic use for inflammatory disorders and identifies curcumin as turmeric's active ingredient, with evidence that it inhibits inflammatory cell proliferation, invasion, and angiogenesis.

Describes curcumin's mechanisms: it is safe and non-toxic and works by down-regulating inflammatory transcription factors, cytokines, redox status, protein kinases, and pro-inflammatory enzymes across multiple molecular targets.

Explains that curcumin induces apoptosis via mitochondrial and receptor-mediated pathways and caspase activation, and states the paper's aim of evaluating its anti-inflammatory effects in chronic inflammatory diseases.
Concludes that in vitro, in vivo, and clinical data support translating curcumin into clinical use for preventing inflammatory diseases, and carries the 2012 IUBMB copyright notice.
Final fragment of the copyright line naming the International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Inc., closing the document.

Opening chunk of a curcumin overview: introduces turmeric-derived polyphenol curcumin, its anti-inflammatory and anti-cancer properties, and begins listing its mechanisms of action (antioxidant activity, cell signalling inhibition, enzyme effects).

Middle section of the curcumin overview: continues the mechanisms list (cyclooxygenase and glutathione S-transferase effects, immunomodulation, angiogenesis, cell-cell adhesion) and notes gene transcription and apoptosis effects relevant to cancer chemoprevention and chemotherapy.

Later part of the curcumin overview discussing pharmacokinetics: low systemic bioavailability after oral dosing, yet biologically active levels demonstrated in the gastrointestinal tract in animals and humans, leading into the clinical recommendation.

Concluding sentence of the curcumin overview recommending phase II clinical trials of oral curcumin in patients with invasive or pre-invasive gastrointestinal tract malignancies, especially colon and rectal cancer.

Abstract opening (Objectives) of a review on curcumin's effects on articular chondrocytes in osteoarthritis, introducing its anti-catabolic, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties and the review's aims.

Continuation of the Objectives: the review's scope on benefits and drawbacks of curcumin for OA, and its exploration of AP-1/NF-kappaB gene-expression signalling in chondrocytes, osteoblasts and synovial fibroblasts.

Methods and start of Results from the abstract: a PubMed/Medline computer-aided search with a text-mining tool on the ResNet Mammalian database, and the start of findings on curcumin protecting human chondrocytes from IL-1beta catabolic effects (MMP-3, collagen II, beta1-integrin).

Results and start of Conclusions: curcumin blocks IL-1beta-induced proteoglycan degradation, AP-1/NF-kappaB signalling, chondrocyte apoptosis and caspase-3 activation, and in vitro/in vivo data suggest it may be a complementary OA treatment in humans and companion animals.

Conclusions continued: further basic research is needed to improve curcumin's solubility, absorption and bioavailability, and to clarify its safety and efficacy across species before extensive clinical trials.

Final conclusion: curcumin and related compounds may become safer nutraceutical alternatives to NSAIDs for OA once these obstacles are overcome, followed by the start of the copyright notice (2009 Osteoarthritis Research Society International).
Closing copyright line of the abstract (Osteoarthritis Research Society International, 2009; all rights reserved), ending the document.

Introduction and scope of a study on turmeric (Curcuma longa) and cancer: lower cancer incidence in turmeric-consuming regions motivates testing turmeric's effects on tumor cell proliferation and the NF-κB and STAT3 transcription factors, plus the methods overview.

Methods and key results on turmeric's effects: MTT, EMSA, Western blot, FACS, and TRAP assays show NF-κB inhibition and downregulation of survival (Bcl-2, cFLIP, XIAP, cIAP1), proliferation (cyclin D1, c-Myc), and metastasis (CXCR4) gene products.

Further results: turmeric suppresses STAT3 activation, induces death receptors DR4 and DR5, increases ROS, suppresses tumor cell growth, and sensitizes tumor cells to capecitabine and taxol chemotherapy.

Comparative and bone-related findings plus conclusion start: turmeric outperforms pure curcumin in growth inhibition, blocks RANKL-induced NF-κB activation and osteoclastogenesis, and is concluded to block tumor proliferation via NF-κB and STAT3 suppression.
Final concluding sentence of the abstract: turmeric effectively blocks tumor cell proliferation by suppressing the NF-κB and STAT3 pathways.
Introduction/purpose of a review on curcumin's antiulcer (gastroprotective) effects against ulcer causes such as H. pylori, NSAIDs, and exogenous substances.
Mechanistic background: ulcers linked to altered ROS, nitric oxide synthase, lipid peroxidation and excess gastric acid, arising from an imbalance of aggressive versus defensive factors.
Epidemiology of gastric ulcer causes (NSAIDs ~80%, H. pylori ~10%, spicy/fast food ~8-10%) and the limitations of existing antiulcer drugs and cytoprotectants.
Introduces curcumin, the yellow pigment from Curcuma longa rhizome, as a dietary compound being explored as a new antiulcer agent from natural sources.

Summarizes curcumin's suggested protective role against inflammatory disorders, attributed to anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity, and the review's conclusion that curcumin prevents GI ulcers and could be a novel treatment.
Final concluding sentence recommending curcumin as a novel drug for preventing and treating gastrointestinal-induced ulcers.
Abstract of a randomized pilot study on curcumin for active rheumatoid arthritis; introduces the 45-patient, three-arm design (curcumin 500 mg, diclofenac 50 mg, or combination).

Describes the study's endpoints: primary outcome is reduction in DAS28 disease activity, secondary outcomes are ACR criteria for joint tenderness and swelling; notes all arms showed significant DAS changes.
Reports results: curcumin alone gave the greatest improvement in DAS and ACR20/50/70 scores, significantly better than diclofenac, and the text starts describing curcumin's safety.

Concludes that curcumin was safe with no related adverse events and claims first evidence of its safety and superiority in active RA, calling for larger trials; includes the 2012 John Wiley & Sons copyright.
Closing fragment of the abstract calling for large-scale trials in RA and other arthritic conditions, followed by the 2012 John Wiley & Sons copyright notice.

Introduction to a review on curcumin (turmeric's yellow pigment), covering its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity and its potential roles in cancer therapy and Alzheimer's disease, with focus on curcumin-induced cell death.

Continuation of the review's overview: argues that because oxidative stress and inflammation drive aging, curcumin may slow aging broadly, and describes its effects as xenohormetic by triggering a stress response in mammalian cells.
Final sentence of the review's abstract summarizing the authors' claim that curcumin acts as a xenohormetic agent by activating a stress response in mammalian cells.

Opening of the document on cancer as an age-related disease, introducing plant-based treatments and the question of how active principles in traditional medicines work against cancer, setting up curcumin as the example.

Introduces curcumin as a diferuloylmethane from turmeric, used traditionally for inflammation, and begins listing the cell signaling pathways it interferes with, such as cell cycle, apoptosis, and proliferation.

Continues the list of curcumin's molecular targets: apoptosis regulators, proliferation factors (HER-2, EGFR, AP-1), the PI3K/AKT survival pathway, and invasion-related MMP-9 and adhesion molecules, with angiogenesis beginning.

Covers curcumin's effects on angiogenesis (VEGF), metastasis (CXCR-4), and inflammatory mediators (NF-kappaB, TNF, IL-6, IL-1, COX-2, 5-LOX), then lists the range of cancer types where its activity has been reported.

Concludes the document by noting curcumin's activity across many cancers reflects its multi-target action, and closes with the thesis that an old-age disease like cancer calls for an age-old treatment.
Opening chunk of an abstract/review on turmeric (Curcuma longa) listing its many reported biological activities, introducing curcumin as the most-studied component.

Continues the abstract: notes curcumin's extensive citation record and that numerous non-curcumin chemical entities in turmeric have been identified, raising the question of whether activities stem from curcumin or other compounds.

Discusses whether turmeric's activities come from curcumin alone or from other compounds acting uniquely, additively, or synergistically, and notes turmeric oil can enhance curcumin bioavailability; introduces curcumin-free turmeric (CFT).

States that curcumin-free turmeric components show anti-inflammatory, anticancer, and antidiabetic activity, notes elemene is approved in China for cancer treatment, and sets the review's focus on anticancer and anti-inflammatory effects.

Lists the individual turmeric components covered by the review (turmerin, turmerone, elemene, furanodiene, curdione, bisacurone, cyclocurcumin, calebin A, germacrone) and gives the 2013 Wiley-VCH copyright line.

Introduction and methods opening of a study on lipidated curcumin in healthy middle-aged adults: states the rationale (prior trials used high doses of poorly absorbed curcumin in sick patients) and the aim to test a low dose's effect on wellness measures.

Methods continuation describing the design: 40–60-year-old healthy adults randomized to 80 mg/day lipidated curcumin (N=19) or placebo (N=19) for 4 weeks, with blood and saliva sampled before and after.

Results opening: lists the statistically significant changes seen only in the curcumin group, including lower plasma triglycerides, lower salivary amylase, and higher salivary radical scavenging and plasma catalase.
Remaining results: continues the curcumin-only effects, covering lower beta amyloid and sICAM, higher myeloperoxidase without CRP change, higher nitric oxide, and lower ALT activity.
Conclusion: summarizes that a low-dose curcumin-lipid preparation produced a range of potentially health-promoting effects in healthy middle-aged people.

Introduction to a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial testing soy protein (SP) supplementation for osteoarthritis (OA) pain, motivated by the growing popularity of complementary therapies; describes the study aim and the start of the participant description.

Study population and design: 135 free-living adults (64 men, 71 women) with diagnosed OA or chronic knee pain not due to injury or rheumatoid arthritis, randomly assigned to 40 g daily of SP or milk-based protein (MP) for 3 months.

Outcome measures: pain, knee range of motion, and physical activity assessed monthly; serum YKL-40 (cartilage degradation marker) and IGF-I (cartilage synthesis growth factor) measured at baseline and study end.
Main results: SP improved range of motion and several pain and quality-of-life factors versus MP, but the benefits were mainly driven by effects in men rather than women.

Cartilage biomarker findings supporting SP efficacy in men: significantly higher serum IGF-I and significantly lower YKL-40 compared with MP; authors claim this is the first evidence of possible SP benefits for OA management.
Conclusion: calls for research on the long-term effects of soy protein on OA symptoms, particularly in men.

Abstract opening of a human bioavailability study on herbs and spices: states the objective (protecting lymphocytes from oxidative injury and reducing inflammatory biomarkers in THP-1 cells) and describes the methods, including the 13 supplement groups and 7-day consumption protocol.

Methods continuation: blood sampling before and 1 hour after the final capsules, antioxidant capacity measured by ORAC or DPPH on serum and herb/spice extracts, and PBMCs exposed to hydrogen peroxide to induce DNA strand breaks.

Methods details on the ex vivo assays: PBMCs in autologous serum are challenged with hydrogen peroxide, and subject serum treats activated THP-1 cells to measure TNF-α, IL-1α, and IL-6 mRNA levels; the results section begins here.

Results on oxidative protection: paprika, rosemary, ginger, heat-treated turmeric, sage, and cumin protected PBMCs from DNA strand breaks, with paprika also affecting apoptosis; TNF-α was the most sensitive cytokine in oxLDL-treated macrophages.

Results on inflammation: clove, ginger, rosemary, and turmeric reduced oxLDL-induced TNF-α expression, ginger serum lowered all three cytokines, and ginger, rosemary, and turmeric were protective by both oxidative and inflammatory measures.
Conclusion stating that DNA strand breaks and inflammatory biomarkers serve as good functional measures of a food's bioavailability.

Introduction to the paper on curcumin as an oral TNF blocker: background on TNF-α as an inflammatory mediator and the FDA-approved TNF-blocking biologics (infliximab, Humira, Enbrel) for osteoarthritis, IBD, psoriasis and ankylosis.

Describes the costs and drawbacks of approved TNF-blocking biologics: over $20 billion annual market, $15,000–20,000 per patient per year, required injection, and an FDA black box warning for adverse effects.

Introduces curcumin (diferuloylmethane), the turmeric compound, as an inexpensive, orally bioavailable, safe alternative that blocks TNF-α action and production in vitro, in animals and in humans, with evidence across the diseases treated by TNF blockers.

Summarizes the paper's scope: curcumin's activity against the diseases targeted by TNF blockers, its mechanisms for inhibiting TNF-α production and TNF-activated signalling pathways, and its potential to address health-care cost and safety concerns.
Closing metadata noting the article belongs to a themed section on Emerging Therapeutic Aspects in Oncology in the British Journal of Pharmacology, with a link to the issue's table of contents.

Introduction and background of a systematic review/meta-analysis on major congenital malformations risk in gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) versus a reference population, contrasting with the established risk in pregestational diabetes (PGDM).

Methods section describing the MEDLINE literature search (1995-2009), inclusion criteria of studies with GDM and reference groups, data extraction by two investigators, and handling of pregestational diabetes information.

Methods continued (review process, meta-analysis tools, MOOSE/PRISMA guidelines) and the start of the results: 2 case-control and 15 cohort studies selected from 3488 abstracts, with the onset of findings on malformation risk in GDM offspring.
Results giving pooled effect estimates for major congenital malformations in GDM offspring (RR 1.16 in cohort studies, OR 1.4 in case-control studies), and the start of the PGDM comparison.

Results comparing PGDM offspring (RR 2.66 in cohort studies, OR 4.7 in one case-control study) with the reference group, followed by the start of the conclusion that GDM carries a slightly higher risk.

Conclusion stating GDM is associated with a slightly elevated malformation risk, much lower than PGDM, with unresolved contributions of overt hyperglycemia and other factors; includes copyright notice (2011, John Wiley & Sons).

Introduces the study's rationale and aim: testing whether prepregnancy dietary and supplemental iron intake is linked to gestational diabetes (GDM) risk, based on iron's prooxidant effects on pancreatic β-cells in the Nurses' Health Study II GDM analysis.

Describes the study design and methods: a prospective Nurses' Health Study II cohort of 13,475 women with singleton pregnancies (1991–2001), 867 incident GDM cases, and pooled logistic regression estimating relative risks by iron intake quintile.

Reports the main result: dietary heme iron is significantly associated with GDM, with multivariable relative risks rising across quintiles of heme iron intake (reference 1.0, then 1.11, 1.31, 1.51, 1.58).

Gives the dose-response and null findings: each 0.5 mg/day increase in heme iron yields RR 1.22 (1.10–1.36), a significant linear trend, while total dietary, nonheme, and supplemental iron show no significant association with GDM.
Concludes that higher prepregnancy dietary heme iron intake is associated with increased GDM risk, indicating heme iron as a potentially modifiable dietary factor for GDM prevention.
Study background and methods: Nurses' Health Study prospective cohort of 85,031 women aged 34-59 followed 1980-2000 to examine dietary iron intake and type 2 diabetes risk.
Results overview: 4,599 incident type 2 diabetes cases over 20 years; no association found for total, dietary, supplemental, or nonheme iron, setting up the heme iron finding.
Main finding on heme iron: animal-derived heme iron is positively associated with diabetes risk, with relative risks rising across cumulative intake quintiles (P trend < 0.0001) after adjustment.
Dose-response and subgroup details: seven-category heme iron model shows RR 1.52 for highest versus lowest intake, and the association holds in both overweight and lean women.
Conclusion: the large cohort indicates higher heme iron intake is significantly associated with increased type 2 diabetes risk.

Abstract of a hospital-based cross-sectional study on the prevalence of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) among Indian pregnant women, describing the study objective and the sample of 325 women screened with a 75 g 2-hour OGTT.

Continuation of the abstract's methods and results: chi-square testing of variables associated with GDM, and the conclusion that poor obstetric history, obesity, high-calorie (especially non-vegetarian) diet, and low physical activity raise GDM risk.

Final fragment of the abstract's text, the trailing end of the word 'GDM' (gestational diabetes mellitus) from the results and conclusions sentence in the study on GDM prevalence in Indian pregnant women.

Introduction and methods opening of a systematic review/meta-analysis on type 2 diabetes risk after gestational diabetes, stating the study aim: quantifying risk, timing of onset, and modifying factors.

Methods continued: eligibility of cohort studies (1960 to 2009, Embase and Medline), 205 reports hand-searched, 20 studies selected covering 675,455 women and 10,859 type 2 diabetes events, with unadjusted relative risks pooled by random-effects model.
Methods describing the statistical approach and subgroup analyses (case numbers, ethnicity, follow-up duration, maternal age, BMI, diagnostic criteria), followed by the start of the Findings section.

Main results: women with gestational diabetes had about 7.43-fold higher risk of type 2 diabetes (95% CI 4.79-11.51) versus normoglycaemic pregnancy; the largest study showed RR 12.6, and subgroup RRs were broadly consistent.

Interpretation section arguing that awareness of the magnitude and timing of type 2 diabetes risk after gestational diabetes could enable dietary, lifestyle, and pharmacological prevention or delay, followed by the funding statement.
Final fragment of the document stating the funding source as none, ending the abstract on gestational diabetes and subsequent type 2 diabetes.

Opening of an epidemiological review on type 1 diabetes aetiology: rising incidence in the Western world (especially Scandinavia), low twin concordance showing genes are necessary but not sufficient, and HLA chromosome 6 as the strongest genetic risk region.

Continues the genetic discussion: other chromosomes carry risk genes, implying gene-environment interaction. Introduces the proposed autoimmune pathogenesis and the two roles environmental factors may play: initiating autoimmunity or accelerating existing beta-cell destruction.

Lists the accelerating environmental risk factors identified by epidemiology (cold climate, high growth rate, infections, stressful life events) and begins naming initiating factors, such as early exposure to cow's milk proteins.

Completes the initiating risk factors (nitrosamines, early foetal events like blood group incompatibility and foetal viral infections) and gives the conclusion that population-based epidemiology confirms experimental models and adds new findings on aetiology.
Final sentence of the document: epidemiological findings help reveal the complex aetiology of type 1 diabetes, with the ultimate aim of primary prevention.

Introduces the study's background: egg and cholesterol intake linked to type 2 diabetes, but unknown for gestational diabetes; describes the prospective cohort (1996–2008) and case-control (1998–2002) designs and the food frequency questionnaire method.

Describes the methods (multivariable relative risk models) and the cohort results by weekly egg consumption category, showing a rising risk of gestational diabetes with more eggs (RR 0.94 to 2.52, P for trend = 0.008).

Reports the key cohort findings: women eating 7 or more eggs weekly had 1.77-fold higher GDM risk, and the highest cholesterol quartile (≥294 mg/day) had RR 2.35 versus the lowest (<151 mg/day), with confidence intervals.

Summarizes the case-control results: odds ratio of 2.65 for ≥7 eggs/week versus <7, a dose-response trend for cholesterol intake (P = 0.021), and the overall conclusion that high egg and cholesterol intake before and during pregnancy raises GDM risk.
Final sentence of the abstract restating the conclusion that high egg and cholesterol intakes before and during pregnancy are associated with increased gestational diabetes risk.
Introduction and study design of a prospective Nurses' Health Study II analysis of prepregnancy dietary fat intake and gestational diabetes (GDM) risk, stating the rationale and objectives.
Study population and methods: 13,475 women with singleton pregnancies (1991-2001) in NHS II, 860 incident GDM cases, and pooled logistic regression estimating RRs across fat intake quintiles.
Main results for animal fat and dietary cholesterol across quintiles, with RRs, 95% CIs, and P-trend values showing increasing GDM risk with higher animal fat intake.
Continuation of results: cholesterol quintile RRs, and the substitution analysis showing that replacing 5% of energy from carbohydrates with animal fat raised GDM risk (RR 1.13).
Null findings for polyunsaturated, monounsaturated, and trans fats, followed by the conclusion that higher prepregnancy animal fat and cholesterol intakes are linked to elevated GDM risk.

Introduction and study objective: motivates the question by linking higher heme iron to type 2 diabetes, notes the research gap on gestational diabetes, and describes the prospective cohort design of 3,158 pregnant women with preconceptional and early pregnancy iron intake.

Methods summary: describes the prospective cohort of 3,158 pregnant women, assessment of maternal diet by food frequency questionnaire, and multivariable generalized linear regression to estimate relative risks. Results begin with about 5.0% of the cohort (n = 158) developing GDM.

Key results for heme iron: a significant positive trend with GDM risk (Ptrend = 0.04). The highest intake group (≥1.52 vs. <0.48 mg/day) had a 3.31-fold increased risk (95% CI 1.02–10.72) after adjusting for confounders.

Fully adjusted estimates: each 1 mg/day increase in heme iron linked to 51% higher GDM risk (RR 1.51, 95% CI 0.99–2.36). Nonheme iron showed a non-significant inverse association across quartiles (RRs 1.00, 0.83, 0.62, 0.61; Ptrend = 0.08).

Conclusions: high dietary heme iron during preconception and early pregnancy may increase GDM risk, while the evidence for nonheme iron is less clear, and the findings need confirmation in future studies.
Closing fragment of the conclusion sentence calling for future studies to confirm the findings on heme iron and gestational diabetes risk.

Opening of the study abstract: aims, hypothesis, and cohort methods for a prospective study of dietary patterns and gestational diabetes (GDM) risk in the Nurses' Health Study II, including the 1991 food frequency questionnaire.

Methods continued: describes the Nurses' Health Study II pregnancy follow-up (1992-1998) and the factor analysis that identified 'prudent' and 'Western' dietary patterns, defined by their food components.

Results begin: 758 incident GDM cases documented, and adjusted analysis of the Western dietary pattern covariates; also the food groups defining the Western pattern (red meat, processed meat, refined grains, sweets, French fries, pizza).

Key findings: relative risks of GDM for highest vs lowest quintile of the Western pattern (1.63) and lowest vs highest quintile of the prudent pattern (1.39), with confidence intervals and trend p-values, plus per-serving risks for red meat (1.61) and processed meat (1.64).

Conclusions of the abstract: per-serving red and processed meat intake associated with significantly higher GDM risk, and the interpretation that pre-pregnancy dietary patterns may influence GDM development.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence stating that a diet high in red and processed meat is associated with elevated GDM risk.

Introduces the background of gestational diabetes (GDM) diagnosis using the 2-hour 75 g OGTT, comparing WHO and IADPSG (HAPO-based) criteria, and states the systematic review's aim of assessing adverse outcomes.

Describes the review's aim and methods, listing the databases searched (MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane, LILACS, etc.) for cohort studies of GDM under WHO/IADPSG criteria and adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes.

Methods detail inclusion criteria (cohort studies, untreated women, universal 75 g OGTT) and the statistical approach: pooled relative risks with 95% CIs via random-effects models and I² > 50% defining inconsistency.

Results begin: eight studies with 44,829 women; greater adverse-outcome risk for both criteria, and WHO-criteria pooled RRs for macrosomia, large for gestational age, perinatal mortality, preeclampsia, and cesarean delivery.

Reports WHO-criteria pooled relative risks with confidence intervals for macrosomia, LGA, perinatal mortality, preeclampsia, and cesarean delivery, noting consistent associations and limited data for IADPSG criteria.

Presents IADPSG-criteria results: limited data and inconsistent associations (I² ≥ 73%) with pooled RRs for LGA, preeclampsia and cesarean delivery, plus sensitivity analysis excluding HAPO or EBDG studies.

Concludes that both WHO and IADPSG criteria identify women at small increased risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes with similar magnitudes, but IADPSG results show high inconsistency, especially after sensitivity analyses.
Final conclusion: high inconsistency for IADPSG-criteria associations, and additional studies outside the HAPO setting are needed to fully evaluate the IADPSG criteria.
Introduction to the study: RPE cell vulnerability to ageing and light (UV and visible) damage, and the aim of testing blueberry anthocyanins in in vitro senescence and light-damage models.
Methods: preparation of blueberry anthocyanin extract (BAE, 31% total anthocyanins) and induction of replicative senescence in RPE cells by serial passaging from passage 4 to 10.

Results on replicative senescence: from passage 5 RPE cells show reduced proliferation and more β-galactosidase-positive cells; BAE at 0.1 μg/ml maintains viability and lowers senescent cell percentage.
Results on light-induced damage: 12 h exposure to 2500 lx light causes premature senescence, reduced viability and elevated VEGF in untreated RPE cells compared with negative controls.
Conclusions on mechanism: BAE protects RPE cells from light damage by suppressing ageing and apoptosis and reducing over-expressed VEGF to normal levels.
Overall conclusion: blueberry anthocyanin extract is effective against both replicative senescence and light-induced damage of retinal pigment epithelial cells.
Introduction and study objective: background on egg yolk carotenoids lutein and zeaxanthin accumulating in the macular retina, and the aim to test whether eggs raise macular pigment.
Methods: design of the 12-week trial with 24 women randomized to a pill control or one of two egg groups (6 eggs/wk), with lutein and zeaxanthin content per yolk (331 vs 964 micrograms).

Methods and early results: measurement timepoints for serum cholesterol, serum carotenoids, and MPOD, plus cholesterol and triglyceride changes that rose in the PILL control group but not the egg groups.
Results: serum zeaxanthin (not lutein) and MPOD increased in both egg groups, with P values reported, and a comparison of egg carotenoid content to spinach.
Conclusion: despite modest carotenoid content per yolk, egg carotenoids appear highly bioavailable to the retina, and eating 6 eggs/wk may effectively raise macular pigment optical density.

Abstract opening of a review on ultraviolet phototoxicity, stating the scope: UVA and short-wavelength visible light effects on the retina and retinal pigment epithelium, with methods based on a literature survey.

Results section introducing the three interaction mechanisms of light with tissue (thermal, mechanical, photochemical) and noting that the anterior eye absorbs most UV, though UVA (315-400 nm) reaches the retina.

Explains that long-duration natural UV exposure, such as sunlight, causes photochemical rather than thermal or mechanical retinal damage, and introduces the Type 1 and Type 2 photochemical damage pathways.

Describes Type 2 reactions involving reactive oxygen species and states that drugs like certain antibiotics, NSAIDs, psychotherapeutic agents, and herbal medicines can act as photosensitizers that increase retinal UV damage.
Conclusions: the anterior eye is most UV-susceptible, but longer UV wavelengths that pass through the ocular media still threaten the retina.
Final conclusion sentence suggesting that dietary antioxidants and protective phytonutrients may counteract or reduce UV phototoxicity.

Introduction and purpose of a study on goji berry (Lycium barbarum) supplementation, specifically the milk-based Lacto-Wolfberry formulation, examining effects on macular characteristics and plasma zeaxanthin/antioxidant levels in elderly subjects.

Methods of the double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled trial: healthy elderly subjects aged 65-70 receiving 13.7 g/day LWB (n=75) or placebo (n=75) for 90 days, with ophthalmic exams of macular pigmentation and soft drusen plus blood draws.

Results section start: placebo group showed macular hypopigmentation and soft drusen accumulation while the LWB group remained stable, and the outcome measures of plasma zeaxanthin and antioxidant capacity are introduced.

Key results and conclusion: LWB significantly raised plasma zeaxanthin (26%) and antioxidant capacity (57%) with no change in placebo, no product-related adverse events, and the conclusion that 90 days of goji supplementation increases antioxidant levels and protects against macular changes.

Final conclusion of the goji berry trial: 90-day supplementation boosts plasma zeaxanthin and antioxidants and protects macular pigmentation and drusen in elderly, but the mechanism is unclear since changes in zeaxanthin did not correlate with macular changes.
Final fragment of the document's closing sentence, concluding the discussion of macular characteristics in the goji berry supplementation study.
Introduces the background of age-related macular degeneration and the rationale that zeaxanthin-rich foods may help, with wolfberry (Lycium barbarum, Kei Tze) named as the source.

Describes wolfberry's zeaxanthin dipalmitate content and the study design: a single-blinded, placebo-controlled, parallel human intervention trial measuring fasting plasma zeaxanthin changes from whole wolfberry supplementation.
Details the methods: 14 supplemented subjects took 15 g/d wolfberry (about 3 mg zeaxanthin) for 28 days with fasting blood drawn at baseline and day 29, while age- and sex-matched controls took none.

Reports the statistical comparison (Mann-Whitney test) and the results: plasma zeaxanthin rose from 0.038 to 0.096 micromol/l in the supplementation group (P<0.01), versus 0.038 to 0.043 in controls (P>0.05).
States the conclusion that zeaxanthin in whole wolfberries is bioavailable and that a modest daily intake markedly raises fasting plasma zeaxanthin, with the 2.5-fold increase noted.
Closes by stating that the findings will support further research into dietary strategies for maintaining macular pigment density.

Introduces AMD and cataract as leading blindness and most common surgery in developed countries, and explains lutein and zeaxanthin as retinal antioxidants whose depletion leads to lens opacification (cataract).
Argues that cataract reduces retinal oxidative stress and thus AMD risk, and that AMD and cataract share oxidative stress at the retina as a common pathway rather than being independent processes.

Concludes that cataract is a retinal self-defense response against oxidative stress, that boosting lutein and zeaxanthin intake lowers AMD and cataract risk, and that removing the opaque lens raises retinal oxidative stress and AMD rate.
Copyright notice (Elsevier Ltd., 2011) closing the document, containing no substantive content about cataract, AMD, or lutein/zeaxanthin.

Introduces the myopia public health problem and frames nearwork as an environmental factor in permanent myopia, with nearwork-induced transient myopia (NITM) as a possible contributor; this is the opening background of the abstract on the PM–NITM link.

Continues the abstract by noting that the suggested PM–NITM connection has been indirect and elusive, then announces a five-fold argument for a possible PM–NITM link based on clinical, laboratory, and modelling evidence; this is the closing statement of the abstract.

Background and methods of a study on label variability for the 10 best-selling herbal products (1998 sales), surveyed across 20 retail stores; introduces the problem that patients may not accurately report herb ingredients or doses.

Methods continue with the survey design (20 convenience-sample retail stores in a metropolitan area) and list the 10 herbs studied, ranked by 1998 sales dollars, including echinacea, St John's wort, ginkgo, garlic, ginseng, and valerian.

Results: wide variation in label ingredients and recommended daily dose across 880 products; 43% matched the benchmark in ingredients and RDD, 20% in ingredients only, and 37% were inconsistent or had insufficient label information.

Conclusions and predictors: price per label RDD significantly predicted consistency with the benchmark while store type did not; self-medicating consumers may ingest ingredients and quantities that differ substantially from benchmarks.

Final conclusion of the herbal product label study: higher price per RDD was the best predictor of benchmark consistency, and health providers and consumers should carefully check labels of seemingly identical herbal products.

Introduction and methods of a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study testing whether bilberry extract (160 mg, 25% anthocyanosides) improves night visual acuity and night contrast sensitivity in young males, beginning with group sizes and the active capsule description.
Methods continued: dosing schedule of three capsules daily for 21 days, placebo contents, and the one-month washout period designed to clear any bilberry effect on night vision before crossover.
Crossover design details: group assignment reversal in the second three-week treatment period, the three-month testing schedule for night VA and CS, and the start of the results section.

Results reporting no significant difference between active bilberry and placebo for night visual acuity or night contrast sensitivity, whether using averaged or last-measurement values across all measurement periods.

Conclusion that the study found no bilberry effect on night VA or CS at a high dose over a sustained period, casting doubt on bilberry supplements as a night vision treatment at currently available forms and recommended doses.

Final sentence of the conclusion restating that bilberry supplementation, in current forms and recommended doses, is not shown to be an effective treatment for improving night vision in this population.

Introduction and methods of a systematic review and meta-analysis on dietary lutein and zeaxanthin intake and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) risk, covering the search strategy (five databases up to April 2010) and review procedures.

Methods continued: independent dual-reviewer literature search, data extraction and quality assessment, quantitative pooling via meta-analysis, and evaluation of heterogeneity and publication bias; this chunk also introduces the yield of six longitudinal cohort studies.

Main results: the six cohort studies yielded a non-significant pooled RR of 0.96 (95% CI 0.78-1.17) for early AMD comparing highest vs lowest lutein/zeaxanthin intake, and a significant reduction in late AMD risk (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.57-0.97).

Further results: a significant inverse association between lutein/zeaxanthin intake and neovascular AMD (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.51-0.92), with subgroup analyses by participant characteristics showing essentially consistent findings.

Conclusion: dietary lutein and zeaxanthin are not significantly associated with reduced early AMD risk but may be protective against late AMD, though additional studies are needed to confirm these relationships.
Final sentence of the conclusion stating that further studies are needed to confirm the relationships between lutein/zeaxanthin intake and AMD.

Opening of a 2012 randomized, placebo-controlled, double-masked trial of oral black currant anthocyanins (BCACs, 50 mg/day vs placebo, 19 per group, 38 OAG patients) examining effects on open-angle glaucoma progression over 24 months, including the outcome measures (blood pressure, pulse, IOP, laser-speckle ocular blood flow, Humphrey visual field MD).

Continuation of the methods listing measured outcomes, followed by the RESULTS section defining the primary outcome: change in visual field mean deviation (MD) deterioration in the eye with better baseline MD over 24 months in the BCAC versus placebo groups.

Core result of the black currant anthocyanin glaucoma trial: a statistically significant between-group difference in mean MD change from baseline at 24 months (p = 0.039, unpaired t test), along with the start of the finding that BCAC increased ocular blood flow relative to placebo.

Remaining results and conclusions: ocular blood flow rose with BCAC versus placebo, while IOP and other systemic and ocular measures showed no significant change over 24 months; the authors conclude BCACs may be a safe, promising adjunct to antiglaucoma medication.

Closing sentence of the conclusions suggesting oral BCACs as a safe, promising supplement alongside antiglaucoma medication for open-angle glaucoma patients, followed by the 2012 S. Karger AG, Basel copyright notice.

Introduction and study purpose: establishes that lutein and zeaxanthin forming macular pigment may help prevent neovascular AMD, and states the aim of raising retinal MP density through dietary L and Z intake from foods, with methods beginning (psychophysical MP measurement in 13 subjects).

Methods detail: serum L, Z, and beta-carotene measured by HPLC; 11 subjects added 60 g spinach (10.8 mg L, 0.3 mg Z, 5 mg beta-carotene), 10 of them also added 150 g corn, and 2 received only corn; diet modification lasted up to 15 weeks.

Results overview for spinach/corn groups, identifying three response types: eight 'retinal responders' with rises in serum L (33%) and MP density (19%); two 'retinal nonresponders' with serum L increases but no MP gain (-11%); the response categories are defined here.

Remaining results: one 'serum and retinal nonresponder' showed no change in serum L, Z, beta-carotene or MP; for the two corn-only subjects, serum L changed little, while one subject had serum Z up 70% and MP density up 25%.

Conclusions: MP density increases appeared within 4 weeks for most but not all subjects, and elevated MP persisted for at least several months after returning to an unmodified diet; begins the statement that MP augmentation is feasible.
Final conclusion sentence: augmentation of macular pigment via diet appears feasible for many persons for both experimental and clinical investigation.

Introduces the prospective cohort study design: Nurses' Health Study and Health Professionals Follow-up Study participants over 40, followed biennially for primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) with eye exams, and the start of repeated dietary intake measurement.

Describes dietary assessment via validated food frequency questionnaires and the case definition: 474 self-reported POAG cases with visual field loss confirmed by medical chart review, plus the Cox regression and random-effects pooling methods.

Explains the statistical approach (cohort-specific Cox proportional hazards models pooled with random effects) and begins reporting pooled multivariate rate ratios for highest vs. lowest quintile of cumulative updated antioxidant intake, starting with alpha-carotene.

Lists pooled rate ratios and 95% confidence intervals for POAG by antioxidant: alpha-, beta-carotene, beta-cryptoxanthin, lycopene, lutein/zeaxanthin, vitamin C, vitamin E, and the start of vitamin A results. All intervals include 1.
Gives the final vitamin A rate ratio and the study's conclusion that no strong associations were found between antioxidant consumption and primary open-angle glaucoma risk.

Introduction and methods opening of a study on macular pigment optical density and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) risk in a northern European population, stating the two key risk factors (age and advanced disease in the fellow eye) and the psychophysical MP measurement in 46 subjects and 9 high-risk eyes.

Methods continuation describing psychophysical measurement of macular pigment optical density in healthy-macula subjects (21-81 years) and in high-risk eyes whose fellow eye had advanced AMD, with each high-risk eye matched to a control on iris color, gender, smoking, age, and lens density.

Results section reporting an age-related decline in macular pigment optical density in non-diseased volunteers (right and left eye r-squared and P values) and that healthy eyes predisposed to AMD had significantly less MP than matched controls (Wilcoxon signed rank P = 0.015).

Conclusions of the study: the two major AMD risk factors (age and fellow-eye advanced disease) are linked to lower macular pigment, supporting the hypothesis that supplemental lutein and zeaxanthin may delay, avert, or modify AMD progression.
Final sentence fragment of the conclusions, completing the hypothesis that supplemental lutein and zeaxanthin may delay, avert, or modify the course of age-related macular degeneration.

Introduction and study aim: examines whether iris color relates to macular pigment optical density (MP), noting that melanin (iris) and carotenoids (macula) may protect the retina through similar mechanisms, with 95 subjects studied.

Study design and variables measured in the 95 subjects: iris color, MP, plasma lutein/zeaxanthin and beta-carotene, dietary carotenoid intake, and total fat intake; also introduces the iris color self-assessment method.

Methods: iris color groups (I blue/gray, II green/hazel, III brown/black) by self-assessment, and MP measured psychophysically via heterochromatic flicker photometry at 460 and 550 nm; plasma carotenoids assayed by reverse-phase HPLC.

Methods and key results: dietary intake assessed with a food-frequency questionnaire; despite similar diet and blood carotenoids, MP differed significantly (P < 0.02) across iris color groups, with group-specific sample sizes and MP means introduced.

Results and interpretation: reports group sizes and MP means (I=0.25, II=0.32, III=0.38), and argues that the covariation of iris color and MP means past epidemiologic studies have not adequately isolated the independent effects of either factor.

Discussion of mechanisms: proposes two possible explanations for the iris color–MP link, a shared evolutionary tendency to accumulate melanin and carotenoids under similar environmental pressures (light, oxygen), and MP depletion from greater light transmission through light irises causing oxidative stress.
Final fragment of the discussion, completing the sentence on increased oxidative stress from light transmission through light-colored irises.

Opening of the abstract for a cross-sectional study of glaucoma and fruit/vegetable intake in 662 older African American women from the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures, describing purpose and methods (disc photos, visual fields, Block FFQ).

Methods continued: masked graders and two glaucoma specialists reviewed images, Block Food Frequency Questionnaire used, logistic regression adjusted for confounders; start of the Results on the analytic sample.
Results: 584 women included (88.2% of cohort), 77 (13%) with glaucoma in at least one eye; women eating 3+ servings/day of fruit/juice had 79% lower odds of glaucoma (OR=0.21).
Specific food findings: more than 2 servings/week of fresh oranges (OR=0.18) and peaches (OR=0.30) were linked to lower glaucoma odds; start of the vegetable results on collard greens/kale.

Vegetable results and trend p-values: collard greens/kale >1 serving/week cut odds by 57% (OR=0.43); protective trends for fruit/juice, oranges, peaches, and collard greens; borderline associations for carrots and spinach.
Nutrient-level results from food sources: protective trends for vitamin A, vitamin C, and α-carotene, and near-significant trends for β-carotene, folate, and lutein/zeaxanthin.

Conclusion: intake of fruits and vegetables high in vitamins A and C and carotenoids may be associated with lower glaucoma likelihood in older African American women; start of the call for randomized trials.
Final sentence of the conclusion calling for randomized controlled trials to test whether specific nutrient intake changes glaucoma risk.
Study purpose, design, and population: cross-sectional analysis of 3,833 NHANES 2007–2008 adults aged ≥40 examining supplemental calcium and iron intake (oxidants) in relation to glaucoma prevalence.

Methods continued: 30-day interview data on dietary supplement and antacid use, calcium and iron intake aggregated and split into quintiles, plus collection of glaucoma status, demographics, comorbidities, and behaviors.
Main results begin: calcium ≥800 mg/d or iron ≥18 mg/d supplementation linked to higher adjusted odds of diagnosed glaucoma compared with non-users, with the calcium odds ratio given.
Specific effect estimates: adjusted odds ratios with 95% CIs for calcium (2.44) and iron (3.80), and a higher combined-use odds ratio (7.24); also notes no clear quintile-based dose–response pattern.
Conclusions: findings suggest a possible threshold intake of iron and calcium above which glaucoma risk rises, and no clear dose–response across quintiles was observed.
Final conclusion: calls for prospective longitudinal studies to determine whether oxidant (calcium and iron) intake is a risk factor for glaucoma development and progression.

Introduction and objectives of a Bayesian hierarchical meta-analysis estimating the dose-response relationship between prenatal maternal mercury body burden and childhood IQ decrements, integrating three epidemiologic studies.

Methods section describing the model inputs: dose-response coefficients from the Faroe Islands, New Zealand, and Seychelles Islands studies, with the Faroe Islands coefficient derived from three IQ subtests.

Methods detail on the Faroe Islands IQ coefficient estimation and the inclusion of other cognition/achievement tests in the hierarchical model to better capture study-to-study and endpoint variability; the start of the Results giving the central IQ coefficient estimate.

Results reporting the central estimate of -0.18 IQ points per ppm of maternal hair mercury with its 95% confidence interval, comparing it to the Faroe Islands, Seychelles, and New Zealand estimates, and noting sensitivity analyses.

Sensitivity analysis range for the IQ coefficient (-0.13 to -0.25) and the Conclusions on IQ as an endpoint, its limitations for capturing attention and motor deficits, and the value of the integrated estimate.
Final concluding statement that the integrated IQ coefficient gives a more robust dose-response description of prenatal mercury exposure and cognitive functioning than any single study.

Introduction to the Seychelles Child Development Nutrition Study: framing the dual role of maternal fish consumption, providing fetal LCPUFA for brain development while exposing the fetus to methylmercury neurotoxicity.
Study aims: the SCDNS examines whether maternal serum Ω-3 and Ω-6 LCPUFA, with or without adjustment for prenatal MeHg, are associated with BSID-II child development outcomes at 9 and 30 months.

Sample and 9-month results: 229 children with complete data; PDI at 9 months is positively linked to total Ω-3 LCPUFA and negatively to the Ω-6/Ω-3 ratio, with stronger associations after adjusting for MeHg.

Secondary and 30-month findings: MeHg effect at 9 months varies by the Ω-6/Ω-3 ratio; no LCPUFA-PDI associations at 30 months, but adverse prenatal MeHg associations with 30-month PDI emerge when LCPUFA is included; MDI shows no associations.
Conclusions: prenatal Ω-3 LCPUFA from fish and dietary LCPUFA appear important for child development, and LCPUFA benefits may mask the adverse effects of prenatal MeHg in observational studies.
Final conclusion sentence: LCPUFA's beneficial effects can obscure detection of prenatal methylmercury harms in longitudinal observational research.

Introduction/background of a study on speciating ethylmercury (from thimerosal vaccines) and methylmercury (from maternal fish diet) in breastfed infants, stating the aim to evaluate a new hair-based analytical method.

Methods section describing the study population (infants under 12 months exposed to Hepatitis B and DTaP thimerosal-containing vaccines) and the analytical approach, beginning to describe isothermal gas chromatography coupled with cold-vapor atomic fluorescence spectrometry.

Methods detail on the GC–CV-AFS technique for MeHg and EtHg speciation, followed by Results reporting MeHg (10.3–668 ng/g) and EtHg (3.7–65.0 ng/g) concentrations in infant hair samples, with EtHg detected in 15 of 20.

Key findings linking hair EtHg levels to time since last vaccine dose, showing a significant inverse correlation (r=-0.5572, p=0.0384), and the conclusion that the method is sensitive enough to quantify EtHg after acute thimerosal exposure.

Concluding statement that hair mass above 10 mg allows speciation and quantification of organic mercury exposure in infants' first hair, with implications for clinical and forensic studies, followed by the copyright notice.
Trailing copyright notice (Elsevier B.V., 2011) closing the abstract of the study on ethyl- and methyl-mercury speciation in breastfed infants' hair.

Opening of the fish consumption abstract: it introduces the goals (toxicological, nutritional, ecological, economic perspectives and past advisories) and begins the methods, describing the review of literature and U.S.-focused advisories.

Methods conclusion and start of the Discussion: it states the scope of the conclusions for groups with similar consumption patterns, then opens the discussion that no fish consumption pattern optimizes all domains.
Discussion core trade-off: fish as a nutrient source versus methylmercury and toxicant exposure, plus the inadequacy of wild fish stocks for a growing world population.

Discussion on economic and guidance gaps: fish choices affect the fishing industry, most guidance ignores ecological and economic impacts, and the Conclusion notes the lack of integrated health, ecological, and economic information.
Conclusion calling for clear, simple, more comprehensive guidance covering multiple impacts of fish consumption, plus policy and fishery management interventions.
Final sentence of the abstract: policy and fishery management interventions are needed to ensure long-term availability of fish as a key source of human nutrition.

Introduction to the CPT hit reaction time (HRT) measure, explaining that its latencies reflect visual processing speed and shift in neuropsychological demands over the test's duration, from orientation to sustained attention.

Study rationale and sample: prenatal methylmercury exposure is linked to slower reaction times, so HRT at age 14 is examined across three time intervals in 878 adolescents (87% of the birth cohort) who completed the CPT.

Test procedure and main results: the 10-minute CPT used visual targets every 1000 ms, and adjusted regression coefficients show the association with prenatal methylmercury exposure differs by time interval.

Quantified effect sizes: beta coefficients per ten-fold exposure increase rise from weak in the first two minutes (3.41) to strong at 3-6 minutes (6.10) and strongest at 7-10 minutes (7.64), with the pattern holding after adjusting for simple reaction time and finger tapping.

Interpretation: postnatal exposure had no effect, and the time-dependent pattern implies sustained attention is especially vulnerable to developmental methylmercury, suggesting frontal lobe dysfunction; the authors conclude CPT results should be analyzed by time from test start rather than as overall averages.
Concluding recommendation: when CPT data are used as a neurotoxicity measure, reaction times should be analyzed by time elapsed since test initiation instead of as a single overall average.

Abstract opening of a study on PCB elimination half-lives in children, introducing the rationale (PCB exposure is never fully abolished in observational studies) and the whale-blubber-exposed breastfeeding cohort with follow-up from ages 4.5 to 14 years.

Methods and early results from the same study on PCB elimination in children: follow-up cohorts (99 and 101 subjects), use of structural equation models adjusting for body weight and blubber intake, and the note that background exposure made half-lives appear unexpectedly long across all members.

Key results from the PCB elimination study: apparent half-lives for specific congeners (CB-138, CB-105, CB-118, CB-156, CB-170, CB-187, CB-153, CB-180) among children with above-median and highest-quartile exposures, ranging from about 3 to 9 years.

Concluding interpretation from the PCB half-life study: the longest half-lives reflect parent PCB elimination only via daily fat excretion of 1-2 g, whereas shorter half-lives imply metabolic breakdown of the congeners.
Introduction and study design of a human milk study comparing macrobiotic and omnivorous mothers at different lactation stages (2-3 and 9-13 months postpartum), with sample sizes.
Results on lactation-stage effects on protein and zinc, and macrobiotic vs omnivorous differences in calcium, magnesium, saturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids in breast milk after adjustment.
Non-significant trends in protein, fat and lactose, and lower vitamin B12, hexachlorobenzene (HCB) and PCB levels in the macrobiotic group's breast milk.
Associations of diet and smoking with milk nutrient and contaminant levels: meat, fish and dairy linked to vitamin B12, dieldrin, PCBs and DDT, with smoking linked to DDT and dieldrin.

Conclusions that reducing smoking and moderating animal product intake could lower milk contamination, while avoiding meat, fish or dairy entirely risks nutritional deficiency, and calling for further quantitative research.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending the call for further research on reduced animal product consumption and smoking effects on breast-milk contamination.

Opening of the abstract: introduces methylmercury as a neurotoxicant, notes possible low-level effects on neurologic and other systems, and flags confounding by beneficial fish nutrients and limited prior synthesis.

Continuation of the background (limited synthesis of low-level MeHg literature) and the stated objective: a review of human health effects of low-level MeHg exposure to guide research, risk assessment, and remediation policy.

Methods section describing data sources: original human epidemiologic studies with direct mercury biomarkers, with exclusions of case series and high-exposure populations (fish, marine mammal, or contaminated fish consumers).

Exclusion criteria continued (Seychelles, Faroe Islands, circumpolar indigenous groups, Amazon gold-mining regions), then the start of the data synthesis: possible effects on fetal growth in susceptible subgroups.
Key findings: infant growth in the first two years, age/sex/timing-dependent neurologic effects, no clear cardiovascular disease (CVD) pattern, and inconsistent immunologic results.
End of the findings and the conclusions: calls for research on mechanisms, individual susceptibility, sexual dimorphism, and non-linear dose response to inform prevention and regulation.
Final sentence of the conclusions: states that such research would guide future prevention, policy, and regulatory efforts on MeHg exposure.
Opening of an abstract on berry fruits and cancer prevention, introducing the evidence for anticancer benefits and the phytochemicals (polyphenols, stilbenoids, lignans, triterpenoids) in berries.
Describes how berry bioactives exert anticancer effects by counteracting and repairing oxidative stress and inflammation damage, continuing the list of phytochemical classes.

Covers the molecular mechanisms of berry bioactives: regulating carcinogen-metabolizing enzymes, transcription and growth factors, cytokines, and pathways of proliferation, apoptosis, and angiogenesis, plus chemosensitization.

Mentions chemotherapy resistance and therapy toxicity protection, then states the scope: the North American berries studied (blackberries, black raspberries, blueberries, cranberries, red raspberries, strawberries).
Clarifies the review focuses on whole berries (extracts, juices, freeze-dried powders) rather than single purified bioactives, and previews discussion of phenolic mechanisms and bioavailability.
Closing statement of the abstract noting it also briefly discusses mechanisms and bioavailability of berry phenolics, knowledge gaps, and recommendations for future research.

Introduction to death receptor (apoptosis) signaling in tumors: regulation by decoy receptors, ligand aggregation state when used as anti-tumor drugs, and the role of receptor/decoy balance in tumor sensitivity.

Explains that tumor sensitivity to death receptor ligands depends on death vs. decoy receptor levels and intracellular apoptotic/antiapoptotic balance, and that in vivo tumor killing by immune effector cells depends on lymphoid cell function and tumor genetics.
Describes the double-edged nature of death receptor ligands: expressed on immune effector cells they kill tumor cells, but expressed on tumor cells they kill the attacking killer cells.
States that the in vivo outcome of death ligand activity depends on infiltrating cell number and activation, the tumor cytokine milieu, and tumor-secreted factors that inhibit cytolytic function.
Final fragment of the document's closing sentence, noting tumor-produced soluble factors that inhibit killer cell cytolytic functions.

Introduction to the berry health benefits document: opens on berries' role in preventing chronic diseases (cancer, heart disease, neurodegenerative disease) and the rising cancer burden in aging populations.

Continues the introduction: explains why consumers are turning to medicinal foods for prevention, and states that berries of all colors have strong research support for positively affecting multiple disease states.
Describes berries' nutritional and bioactive content: beyond vitamins, minerals and fiber, they contain phytochemicals (phytonutrients) spanning fat-soluble and water-soluble compounds.
Summarizes current research: global laboratories have clarified the biological effects and mechanisms of action of eating berries, introducing the set of papers that follows.
Closing context: the paper collection reflects topics from the 2009 International Berry Health Benefits Symposium and offers insight into research trends on berry and berry-product health benefits.
Final fragment of the document's closing sentence, noting that the papers evaluate health benefits from consuming berries and their derived products.

Introduces the study's rationale: traditional combined use of Lycium barbarum, lack of modern single-herb clinical evaluation, and the aims of testing immune, well-being, and safety effects of a standardized goji juice.
Describes the methods: a 30-day randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 120 mL/day GoChi L. barbarum juice versus placebo in 60 healthy older adults aged 55-72.

Reports immune results: GoChi significantly raised lymphocyte count, IL-2, and IgG versus baseline and placebo, while CD4, CD8, NK cells, IL-4, and IgA were unchanged; placebo showed no immune changes.
Reports subjective outcomes: GoChi significantly improved well-being (fatigue, sleep) and trended toward better short-term memory and focus, whereas placebo showed no meaningful positive changes.

Summarizes safety findings: no adverse reactions or abnormal changes in body weight, blood pressure, pulse, vision, urine, stool, or blood biochemistry in either group, with the study's overall conclusion that GoChi boosts immunity and well-being safely.
Final sentence concluding that daily GoChi consumption improved well-being without adverse reactions.
Introduction of the study: rationale that spice immunomodulation research is scarce, and the aim to test black pepper (Piper nigrum) and cardamom aqueous extracts on splenocyte proliferation.

Results on T cell cytokines: black pepper and cardamom differentially modulate Th1 (enhanced by black pepper, suppressed by cardamom) and Th2 (suppressed by black pepper, enhanced by cardamom) cytokine release from splenocytes, measured by ELISA.

Inflammatory and macrophage findings: black pepper and cardamom act as pro- and anti-inflammatory agents respectively, with nitric oxide production by macrophages increased by black pepper and reduced by cardamom.

Anti-cancer findings: black pepper and cardamom extracts significantly enhance natural killer cell cytotoxic activity, suggesting potential anti-cancer effects, and the overall conclusion that both spices are immunomodulatory and antitumor.

Conclusion and implications: black pepper and cardamom are natural agents that support a healthy immune system and may serve as therapeutic tools to regulate inflammation and prevent or attenuate carcinogenesis.
