Introduces human natural killer (NK) cells as innate lymphocytes, noting their discovery over 30 years ago and their distinction from T and B cells, which rearrange antigen receptor genes.

Describes the past two decades of progress in understanding how NK cells recognize targets, their role in immune surveillance, and how receptor biology discoveries have driven translational cancer treatment advances.
Concludes the introduction by noting that recent NK-cell receptor discoveries have produced notable results in treating human malignancy.

Introduction and study aim: a comparison of carotid atherosclerosis, Vitamin B12, homocysteine, and sVCAM-1 between healthy postmenopausal vegetarians and omnivores, with the cardiovascular effects of long-term vegetarianism as the motivation.

Study population (57 vegetarians vs. 61 age-matched omnivores) and results: carotid atherosclerosis by ultrasound showed no significant difference, while fasting glucose, LDL cholesterol and Vitamin B12 were lower and Hcy and sVCAM-1 were higher in vegetarians.

Regression findings: Vitamin B12 was negatively associated with homocysteine; vegetarianism and Hcy were univariately associated with sVCAM-1, but after covariate adjustment only age remained a determinant rather than vegetarianism.

Multivariable results for carotid intima-media thickness and overall conclusion: age and systolic blood pressure, not vegetarianism, determined common carotid IMT, and the study concluded there was no significant difference in carotid atherosclerosis between groups.
Final conclusion and implication: elevated homocysteine in vegetarians highlights the importance of preventing Vitamin B12 deficiency in vegetarian diets.
Introduction and methods of a study comparing arterial function (carotid and brachial) in 49 postmenopausal vegetarians versus 41 age-matched omnivores, including the measurement techniques used.

Methods continued: carotid duplex and pulse dynamics measures of brachial distensibility, compliance and resistance, plus fasting blood markers (lipids, glucose, Lp(a), hs-CRP, homocysteine, vitamin B12); begins the results on lipid and glucose differences.

Results comparing vegetarians and omnivores: lower cholesterol, LDL, HDL and glucose, lower vitamin B12 and higher homocysteine, no difference in Lp(a) or hs-CRP, and no carotid stiffness difference between groups.

Results on arterial measures: no group differences in carotid beta stiffness index, BAC or BAD after covariate adjustment, lower BAR in vegetarians, and regression showing age and pulse pressure as key determinants.

Discussion and conclusion: vegetarians are not better in arterial elasticity measures, have reduced brachial artery resistance, and the authors suggest preventing vitamin B12 deficiency may benefit cardiovascular health.
Final sentence of the conclusion stating that preventing vitamin B12 deficiency might benefit cardiovascular health in vegetarians.

Introduction to the review on CT scan radiation and cancer risk: rapid growth in CT use (over 70 million US scans in 2007) and the prominence of chest CT for pulmonary embolism and coronary artery disease.
Concern about low-dose ionizing radiation from CT: growing population exposure, and evidence from atomic bomb survivors and other low-dose-exposed groups suggesting increased lifetime cancer risk.

The cancer risk link from CT radiation is debated and not conclusive, yet it has drawn scientific and public attention, making physician understanding and patient communication about risk increasingly important.

Scope of the article: reviews the public health debate on CT and cancer risk, quantifies radiation doses for specific chest CT studies, and describes efforts to reduce population-wide radiation exposure.
Specific chest CT examinations covered: pulmonary and coronary angiography, high-resolution CT, low-dose lung cancer screening, and triple rule-out CT.

Introduction and study aim from the LILAC study: testing whether carotid intima-media thickness (IMT) predicts cardiovascular mortality in elderly community-dwelling people beyond age and MMSE, using a multivariate Cox model.

Methods and cohort description: bilateral carotid IMT and plaque ultrasonography in 298 people over 75 (120 men, 178 women, mean age 79.6), LILAC study start July 2000, annual follow-up ending November 30, 2004, mean follow-up 1152 days.

Outcomes: 30 deaths (21 men, nine women) during follow-up, of which nine were cardiovascular (myocardial infarction and stroke cases by sex), and the age- and MMSE-adjusted relative risk method for all-cause mortality.

Results: each 0.3 mm increase in left and right IMT was associated with higher relative risks for all-cause mortality (1.647 and 3.327) and cardiovascular mortality (2.351 and 2.890), with 95% confidence intervals.
Conclusion: carotid IMT measured by ultrasonography is positively associated with increased risk of all-cause and cardiovascular death in elderly community-dwelling people.

Background and aims of a five-year prospective study on how a vegan diet affects serum vitamin B-12 in healthy omnivore adults, comparing natural-products diets with B-12 fortified food as an alternative to supplements.
Study methods: 20 healthy omnivore adults switched to a strict vegan diet for five years, split into ten eating only natural products and ten eating B-12 fortified food.
Methods and results setup: serum B-12 was measured at baseline and at 6, 12, 24 and 60 months, and the first result reports a significant overall decrease in B-12 after 60 months of the vegan diet.

Results and conclusions: the B-12 decline was confined to the natural-products-only subgroup (p < 0.0001), and the authors conclude that moving from an omnivore to a vegan diet carries a risk of B-12 deficiency.
Final conclusion: B-12 fortified products may be a valuable option for vegans who refuse vitamin supplements.

Introduction and methods start of an abstract on cardiometabolic risk, comparing a low-calorie low-protein vegan diet and endurance exercise against a Western diet and sedentary lifestyle; cross-sectional study design begins.

Methods section describing the three study groups: 21 sedentary long-term low-calorie low-protein raw vegan dieters (mean 4.4 years on diet, mean age 53.1), 21 BMI-matched endurance runners on Western diets, and 21 age- and gender-matched sedentary Western-diet controls.
Results opening: BMI comparison showing the vegan diet and runner groups had lower BMI (about 21) than the sedentary Western diet group (26.5), with p < 0.005.

Results on blood markers: lipids, lipoproteins, glucose, insulin, C-reactive protein, blood pressure, and carotid intima-media thickness were lower in the vegan diet and runner groups versus Western diet controls (all p < 0.05); begins comparing systolic and diastolic BP across groups.

Detailed blood pressure results: vegan diet group had lowest systolic and diastolic BP (104/62 mmHg) versus runners (122/72) and Western controls (132/79), p < 0.001; BP linked to sodium, potassium, and fiber intake. Conclusions begin.

Final conclusion: long-term low-calorie low-protein vegan diet or regular endurance training is associated with low cardiometabolic risk, with the vegan diet's specific components suggested to give extra blood pressure benefits.
Introduction to the systematic review: explains why consistent, current U.S. SCA/SCD incidence data is needed, citing a SCATLA Think Tank of national experts and cardiology/heart rhythm stakeholders.

Methods: describes the systematic MEDLINE search strategy using MeSH and keyword terms for sudden cardiac death, sudden cardiac arrest, and related arrhythmic deaths to estimate the magnitude of the problem.
Study selection and impact assessment: includes peer-reviewed primary U.S. SCD incidence studies and uses Web of Science Cited Reference Search to measure each primary source's citation impact.

Results: U.S. annual SCD incidence estimates from 6 studies range from 180,000 to over 450,000, with variation attributed to data source age (1980-2007), definitions, case ascertainment, and estimation methods.
Conclusion on current evidence: true U.S. SCA/SCD incidence remains unclear because available estimates vary widely and are outdated, which limits risk stratification and prevention efforts.
Call to action: future research should adopt uniform SCA/SCD definitions and prospectively, precisely capture cases across the overall U.S. population.

Study design and methods section of an abstract on the Chinese lacto-vegetarian diet's effects on metabolic and cardiovascular health, describing the enrolled healthy male participants (169 lacto-vegetarians, 126 omnivores) and the outcomes measured, including carotid IMT and CVD risk.

Methods continuation and start of the Results section, describing CVD risk point and 5-10 year CVD probability calculations for men aged 24-55, then reporting that lacto-vegetarians had lower BMI, blood pressure, and lipid, glucose, and uric acid levels compared with omnivores.

Results section detailing the specific biomarkers where lacto-vegetarian men differed from omnivores (lower triglycerides, cholesterol, LDL, apolipoprotein B, GGT, creatinine, uric acid, fasting glucose, TC/HDL ratio), and the start of the beta-cell function findings.

Results and conclusion transition: vegetarians showed higher HOMA-β and insulin secretion index and thinner carotid IMT, with lower CVD risk scores and 5-10 year CVD probability, followed by the start of the conclusions on blood pressure effects.

Concluding statement of the abstract: the lacto-vegetarian diet appears protective for blood pressure, lipid profiles, metabolic parameters, and carotid IMT in healthy Chinese men, with lower CVD risk reflecting its beneficial effect.

Abstract opening of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study on vitamin B-12 supplementation and arterial health in community-dwelling vegetarians, stating the rationale: subnormal B-12 status is linked to impaired endothelial function and increased intima-media thickness.

Study design and intervention details: 50 healthy long-term vegetarians received 500 µg/day vitamin B-12 or placebo for 12 weeks, with a 10-week placebo washout, then open-label B-12 for 24 more weeks; outcomes measured were brachial artery flow-mediated dilation and carotid intima-media thickness by ultrasound.
Baseline results: mean participant age 45±9 years, 44% male, and 70% had serum B-12 below 150 pmol/l; B-12 supplementation significantly raised serum B-12 levels and lowered plasma homocysteine.
Main efficacy results after B-12 but not placebo: brachial FMD rose from 6.3% to 6.9% and carotid IMT fell from 0.69 mm to 0.67 mm, with the start of further gains during open-label treatment.

Continued results: FMD improved further to 7.4% and IMT to 0.65 mm after 24 weeks open-label B-12; blood pressure and lipids were unchanged; multivariate analysis linked changes in B-12 (not homocysteine) to changes in FMD.
Conclusion: B-12 supplementation improved arterial function in vegetarians with subnormal B-12 levels, suggesting a potential strategy for preventing atherosclerosis.

Opening of the abstract stating the study's purpose: measuring organ and effective radiation dose from adult cardiac and pulmonary 64-detector CT angiography in an anthropomorphic female phantom, and estimating lifetime breast and lung cancer risk.
Materials and methods, part one: the scan parameters for the 64-detector CT pulmonary vein and native coronary artery ECG-gated angiography protocols (collimation, kVp, mA, rotation time).

Materials and methods, part two: the pulmonary embolus CT protocol parameters, the dosimetry method using MOSFET detectors in the female phantom, and how effective dose was calculated from organ doses and dose-length product.

Results opening: effective dose range of 12.4-31.8 mSv for the adult cardiac and pulmonary CT angiography protocols, and which organs (skin, breast, esophagus, heart) received the highest absorbed doses.

Results and conclusion: relative risk estimates for breast cancer in girls and women (1.004-1.042) and lung cancer in men and women (1.005-1.076) from a single exam, and the conclusion that doses exceed prior reports with greatest risk in younger patients.
Closing sentence of the conclusion restating that breast and lung cancer induction risk from these CT studies is highest for younger patients, followed by the RSNA 2007 copyright notice.

Introduction and objective of the Antioxidant Food Table study: why plant-based diets and dietary plant antioxidants matter, and the goal of building a comprehensive total-antioxidant food database for nutrition research.

Continuation of the background describing the intended uses of the database (in vitro, animal, clinical trial, and epidemiological nutrition research) and the start of the Methods section on sample procurement.

Methods section: samples were collected from countries worldwide and assayed for total antioxidant content with a modified FRAP assay, with origin and brand information recorded to form the Antioxidant Food Table; the Results section begins.

Results: thousand-fold variation in antioxidant content across foods, with spices, herbs, and supplements being the richest sources and berries, fruits, nuts, chocolate, and vegetables as common high-antioxidant foods.

Conclusions opening: claims the database is the most comprehensive published antioxidant food database and that plant-based foods supply significantly more antioxidants than non-plant foods, with large variation between comparable samples.

Conclusion continued: the variability between similar samples underscores the need for a comprehensive database and detailed food registration in clinical and epidemiological studies, making the database an essential research tool.
Final sentence of the conclusion: the antioxidant database is positioned as a tool for elucidating the potential health effects of phytochemical antioxidants in the diet.

Study objectives and scope: defines the three aims (whether fruit/berry meals raise plasma hydrophilic or lipophilic ORAC antioxidant capacity, whether added macronutrients change postprandial AOC, and whether intake recommendations can be derived) and introduces the methods.

Study design: describes the five clinical trials (6-10 subjects each) testing single meals of various berries and fruits, and notes that blueberry and grape studies added carbohydrate, fat, and protein to control and treatment meals.

Methods and results: explains blood sampling before and after meals, then reports that dried plums and dried plum juice had no effect on H- or L-AOC AUC, while blueberry and mixed grape powder (with specific TE doses per study) increased hydrophilic AOC AUC.

Specific findings: blueberry meal with 12.5 mmol TE raised lipophilic AOC, and 280 g cherries (4.5 mmol TE) raised L-AOC but not H-AOC; also notes that control meals with macronutrients in Studies 4 and 5 showed declines from baseline AOC.

Conclusions on food effects and macronutrients: states that blueberries, mixed grape, and kiwifruit raised postprandial plasma AOC, while an antioxidant-free macronutrient meal was linked to a fall in AOC.

Caveats and intake estimates: notes that long-term clinical trials are needed before increased plasma AOC can be linked to lower chronic disease risk, and that preliminary antioxidant needs were estimated from energy intake.
Final recommendation: concludes that eating high-antioxidant foods with every meal is advised to avoid postprandial oxidative stress periods.

Abstract of a paper on atherogenesis as a postprandial phenomenon, introducing the hypothesis that chylomicrons from cholesterol-rich diets are atherogenic and that arterial cells take up chylomicron remnants and LDL.

Concluding part of the same abstract, covering the possibility of atherogenesis in the postprandial period without familial hyperlipoproteinemia, research directions for assessing chylomicron remnants as a risk factor, and the call for lipoprotein studies after fat- and cholesterol-containing test meals.

Introduces the study's premise: dietary lipid peroxides rise in plasma after meals, possibly linking postprandial hyperlipidemia to cardiovascular disease risk, and describes the new direct plasma measurement method used in a pilot study.

Reports the pilot study results: plasma lipid hydroperoxides rise after a fatty meal, peaking 2-4 hours later and returning to baseline in step with postprandial hyperlipidemia, with wine consumption markedly suppressing the rise.

Concludes that the wine-related suppression of postprandial hydroperoxides suggests these peroxides form and are absorbed during digestion, supporting a dietary origin for elevated plasma lipid peroxides.

Study introduction: background that glucose (300 kcal) raises ROS and NF-kappaB in mononuclear cells, and the hypothesis that orange juice or fructose (orange juice's other main carbohydrate) would produce a smaller response.
Study design and methods: four groups of eight normal-weight subjects drank a 300-cal glucose, fructose, orange juice, or saccharin-sweetened water (control) drink, followed by blood sampling.

Key results after glucose: significant increases in ROS generation by mononuclear and polymorphonuclear cells and in NF-kappaB binding over baseline at 2 h, with no such changes after fructose, orange juice, or water.

Comparative results and in vitro findings: ROS and NF-kappaB were significantly lower after orange juice, fructose, and water than glucose, and flavonoids hesperetin and naringenin reduced ROS in mononuclear cells while fructose and ascorbic acid did not.

Conclusions: orange juice or fructose intake induces neither oxidative nor inflammatory stress, possibly due to orange juice's flavonoid content, with the numerical in vitro flavonoid reductions as supporting evidence.
Final conclusion sentence: because orange juice and fructose do not trigger oxidative or inflammatory stress, they may be a potentially safe energy source.

Introduction of a review on postprandial metabolic events and fruit-derived phenolics, stating the rationale (postprandial state and chronic disease risk) and the two main research questions about fruit phenolics and meal-time consumption.

Continuation of the introduction: states the two review questions (role of phenolic-rich fruits in postprandial metabolic management, and whether eating these fruits with meals reduces disease risk) and begins describing the scope of the review of postprandial literature.

Scope of the review: covers human postprandial studies on fruit and fruit phenolics measuring lipaemia, glycaemia/insulinaemia, oxidative stress and inflammation, and reports that over half of the well-controlled trials used wine or wine components while the rest used berries.

Main findings: notes the need for more research, then reports that phenolic-rich fruits raise blood antioxidant capacity and may counter the pro-oxidant, pro-inflammatory effects of high-fat, high-carbohydrate meals.
Conclusion: argues that, given the fat and carbohydrate content of the Western diet, regularly eating phenolic-rich foods with meals is a prudent way to maintain oxidative balance and health.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, stating that consuming phenolic-rich foods with meals helps maintain oxidative balance and health.

Introduction and aims of a study on glucose challenge in 14 normal subjects, examining ROS generation by leucocytes, p47phox (NADPH oxidase component), and alpha-tocopherol, with background linking diabetes and obesity to oxidative stress.
Results after a 75 g oral glucose load: ROS generation by PMNL and MNC peaks at 2 h (about 244% and 233% of basal), and p47phox levels in MNC homogenates rise significantly at 2 h and 3 h.
Conclusion of the study: alpha-tocopherol falls significantly at 1, 2 and 3 h after glucose intake, and glucose stimulates ROS generation and NADPH oxidase activity, raising oxidative load.
Introduction/background of a human trial on strawberries: defines lipid risk factors (TC, LDL, TG) for cardiovascular disease, introduces oxidized LDL and polyphenol cardioprotection.

Study objectives: testing whether strawberry phenolic compounds reduce postprandial high-fat-meal effects on OxLDL and alter lipid metabolism, continuing the background on polyphenols and LDL oxidation.
Methods of the randomized, single-blind, placebo-controlled 12-week crossover trial in 24 hyperlipidemic adults (mean age 50.9), with a 10-day run-in and strawberry vs placebo beverage intervention.
Intervention details: 10 g freeze-dried strawberry beverage vs energy-matched placebo for 6 weeks, high-fat challenge meal dosing, and the blood lipid and OxLDL measurements taken.
Results on run-in period: after the high-fat meal, triglycerides and OxLDL were lower following strawberry than placebo, with reported p-values.
Results after 6 weeks of strawberry: decreased postprandial lipid levels and a sex-by-treatment interaction for OxLDL, followed by the start of the conclusion.
Conclusion: strawberry may mitigate fed-state oxidative stress that could contribute to atherogenesis, closing the abstract.
Introduction and objective of a 2001 Lithuanian case-control study examining whether egg consumption, as a modifiable dietary risk factor, is associated with risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Design and setting details: a custom questionnaire collected risk factor data, odds ratios with 95% CIs were estimated by conditional logistic regression, and the study was conducted at a Lithuanian out-patient clinic.

Study population of 234 newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes cases and 468 disease-free controls, followed by the results section listing confounders (BMI, family history, smoking, education, morning exercise, plasma TAG) retained in multivariate models.
Main results: after adjustment for confounders, consuming 3-4.9 eggs/week was associated with more than twofold increased diabetes risk (OR 2.60) relative to eating fewer than 1 egg/week.

Key quantitative findings: eating 5 or more eggs/week gave about threefold higher type 2 diabetes risk (OR 3.02, 95% CI 1.14-7.98) versus <1 egg/week, and the authors conclude the data support a possible egg-diabetes relationship.
Concluding sentence of the abstract, stating that the findings support a possible link between egg consumption and increased risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Background and methods of a 2002 Jiangsu, China study (n=2849 adults ≥20 y) on egg consumption and diabetes risk, noting sparse prior diabetes evidence in Chinese populations.

Methods detail: data from a nationally representative household survey in Jiangsu, with diet measured by a validated food frequency questionnaire, 3-day weighed food records, and fasting blood specimens.

Main results: after adjusting for age, calories, education, smoking, family diabetes history, and sedentary activity, egg intake is positively linked to diabetes, with total-sample odds ratios for <2/wk, 2-6/wk, and ≥1/d (2.28, CI 1.14-4.54; P trend 0.029).

Sex-specific findings: in women, egg consumption odds ratios are 1.00, 1.66, and 3.01 (P trend 0.022); BMI adjustment weakens but preserves the association, while men show a similar but non-significant pattern.

Secondary findings and conclusion: women eating ≥2 eggs/week had higher plasma triglycerides and total cholesterol, and the study concludes egg consumption is positively associated with diabetes risk among Chinese adults, especially women.
Closing fragment of the conclusion and copyright notice (Elsevier, 2011) for the egg consumption and diabetes study, restating the female-specific association.
Introduction and objectives of a prospective cohort study on egg consumption and incident type 2 diabetes (T2D) in older adults, from the Cardiovascular Health Study abstract.

Study design details: 3898 Cardiovascular Health Study participants (1989–2007), egg intake assessed by picture-sorted food questionnaire, annual T2D ascertainment via hypoglycemic agents and plasma glucose, and Cox proportional hazards analysis.

Key results: mean 11.3-year follow-up, 313 incident T2D cases, and crude incidence rates by egg consumption category (never to almost daily), with the almost-daily group showing the highest rate (12.20 per 1000 person-years).

Adjusted findings: multivariable models showed no association between egg intake and T2D risk in either sex or overall; dietary cholesterol was not linked to diabetes (P for trend = 0.47); eggs had no clinically meaningful effect on fasting glucose, insulin, or insulin resistance.
Conclusion of the abstract: in older adults with limited egg intake, neither egg consumption nor dietary cholesterol was associated with increased incident T2D risk.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the abstract's statement that egg consumption and dietary cholesterol were not associated with increased incident T2D.

Introduction and objective of a prospective cohort study on egg consumption and type 2 diabetes risk, noting no prior research on this link, with aims stated for the Physicians' Health Study and Women's Health Study.

Methods section describing the study design: data from 20,703 men (Physicians' Health Study I, 1982–2007) and 36,295 women (Women's Health Study, 1992–2007), egg intake assessed by questionnaire, and Cox proportional hazards models used to estimate relative risks of type 2 diabetes.

Results opening: mean follow-up of 20.0 years in men and 11.7 in women, with 1,921 men and 2,112 women developing type 2 diabetes, followed by the multivariable hazard ratios for men across egg consumption categories (<1 to ≥7 eggs/week).

Detailed results comparing men and women: the male hazard ratios by egg intake category (significant increases at 5–6 and ≥7 eggs/week) and the corresponding female hazard ratios, with trend p-values for both sexes.
Conclusions of the egg and type 2 diabetes study: high daily egg consumption is linked to increased diabetes risk in men and women, and the authors call for confirmation in other populations.

Introduction and study aims: the Malmö Diet and Cancer cohort (27,140 adults aged 45-74) is introduced to examine macronutrient, fibre and protein-source intake in relation to incident type 2 diabetes, since long-term evidence on macronutrient composition is limited.

Study population and methods: the cohort's dietary assessment (a modified diet history method including cooked meals) and the 12-year follow-up that identified 1,709 incident type 2 diabetes cases are described.

Main results on protein: high protein intake raises type 2 diabetes risk (HR 1.27, highest vs lowest quintile), and replacing 5% of energy from carbohydrates or fat with protein is associated with similarly increased risk (HR 1.20 and 1.21).
Food-source results: the highest quintiles of processed meat and eggs are associated with higher diabetes risk, while fibre-rich bread and cereals show an inverse association (HR 0.84).

Conclusion: the large prospective study links high protein intake to greater type 2 diabetes risk, suggesting that replacing protein with carbohydrates may be beneficial, particularly fibre-rich breads and cereals as the carbohydrate source.
Final sentence of the conclusion, recommending fibre-rich breads and cereals as preferred carbohydrate sources when protein is replaced.

Introduction of the study: rationale that iron accumulation in Parkinson's disease brains causes oxidative stress and dopaminergic neuron loss, and the aim to test phytic acid (IP6), a natural iron chelator, against MPP(+)-induced death in rat mesencephalic cells.

Methods: MPP(+) induces cell death under normal and iron-excess conditions in immortalized rat dopaminergic cells; cytotoxicity measured by MTT and trypan blue, apoptosis by caspase-3 activity, DNA fragmentation, and Hoechst staining.

Results part 1: at 30 micromol/L, IP6 raised cell viability 19% and cut cell death 22% versus MPP(+) alone; MPP(+) had tripled caspase-3 activity and doubled DNA fragmentation, which IP6 reduced by 55% and 52%.
Results part 2: in iron-excess conditions, IP6 at 30 and 100 micromol/L increased cell survival (18% and 42%) and reduced caspase-3 activity by 40% and 52%, showing dose-dependent protection.
Results part 3: 100 micromol/L IP6 reduced DNA fragmentation by 45% under iron excess; Hoechst staining confirmed anti-apoptotic protection, and similar effects appeared in differentiated cells.
Conclusion: the study concludes that phytate (IP6) has significant neuroprotective effects in a cell culture model of Parkinson's disease.

Abstract background on inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6) and its known effects on mineralization, contrasted with bisphosphonates, and the unknown direct effect on osteoclasts; introduces the study's motivation.

States the study aims: testing IP6 on RAW 264.7 mouse cells and human primary osteoclasts, and begins the first finding that IP6 reduces RANKL-induced osteoclastogenesis without affecting proliferation or viability.

Details the RAW 264.7 results: IP6 lowers TRAP-positive cell counts and osteoclast marker mRNA (TRAP, calcitonin receptor, cathepsin K, MMP-9) in RANKL-treated cells, while adding IP6 to mature osteoclasts increases resorption and TRAP mRNA.
Reports the human findings: 1 µM IP6 inhibits osteoclastogenesis from human PBMNC and reduces resorption activity whether applied to undifferentiated cells or mature osteoclasts.
Conclusions: IP6 inhibits osteoclastogenesis in human PBMNC and RAW264.7 cells, suggesting it may be a novel selective osteoclast inhibitor useful for osteoporosis treatment.

Introduction and methods of a study on bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (BRONJ) in oncologic patients: defines the problem, states the aim, and describes the cohort of 142 patients treated with intravenous bisphosphonates.
Methods continuation and early results of the BRONJ cohort study: descriptive analysis focused on surgical outcome, with the finding that the mandible was affected in 58% of patients.

Results of the BRONJ cohort study covering prior invasive dental procedures (all but two patients), mean bisphosphonate duration of 37.1 months, the 86% surgical treatment rate, and the soft-tissue reconstruction techniques used.

Closing results and conclusion of the BRONJ surgical study: no bony reconstruction was performed, and evidence for vascularized bone reconstruction in oncologic BRONJ patients is limited, so surgical treatment remains challenging.

Abstract of a human iron-absorption study: introduces the 199-subject trial testing how maize-bran phytate (phytate P, 10-58 mg) and the polyphenol tannic acid inhibit nonheme iron absorption from white bread.

Abstract continuation reporting dose-dependent inhibition by phytate (overcome by 30 mg ascorbic acid) and tannic acid (12-55 mg), and estimating that at least 50 mg ascorbic acid is needed to offset meals with over 100 mg tannic acid.

Concluding sentence of the abstract on ascorbic acid counteracting polyphenol and phytate inhibition of nonheme iron absorption; argues dietary iron bioavailability can be predicted by accounting for promoters and inhibitors.
Introduction motivating the study: nutrient absorption is often assumed proportional to intake, which fails for non-haem iron, so iron intake-health associations in epidemiology may be invalid.

Describes limitations of previous iron-intake adjustment algorithms, which underestimated absorption and performed poorly on independent data, and introduces the new algorithm's dietary modifiers (ascorbic acid, meat/fish/poultry, phytate, polyphenols, calcium).

Explains the new algorithm's basis in test-meal absorption data and current iron absorption understanding, claiming it is robust and universal for use in large cohorts, and states its goal is available iron rather than absorption prediction.
Defines available iron as iron accessible for absorption from the gut after enhancing or inhibiting dietary effects, and notes the algorithm's aim is to estimate this measure for epidemiological use.
Reports results: the algorithm accurately estimated average iron availability in its construction test meals and gave plausible predictions on independent dietary data, unlike other algorithms.
Concluding statement that future research is needed to determine whether the algorithm is useful for relating iron to health outcomes in epidemiological studies.

Introduces the osteoporosis study's aim: evaluating phytate (a whole-grain compound) intake as a risk factor, and describes the first cohort of 1,473 volunteers whose bone density was measured at the calcaneus by dual absorptiometry.
Describes the study's second validation cohort of 433 subjects, with bone mineral density measured at the lumbar spine and femoral neck, plus the individual risk-factor interviews.
Covers the dietary methodology: phytate intake was assessed by questionnaires given twice, 2-3 months apart, and the statistical tests (ANOVA or Student's t test) used to compare groups.
Presents the main findings: bone mineral density rose with phytate consumption, and multivariate regression identified body weight and low phytate intake as the strongest influences on bone density.
Concludes that phytate has a protective effect against osteoporosis, so low phytate consumption should be regarded as a risk factor for the disease.
Study design of a zinc metabolism experiment in male rats fed zinc-adequate diets with or without 2% sodium phytate, using 65Zn kinetics and compartmental modeling of plasma zinc.
Findings on zinc kinetics across tissues (plasma exchanges faster with liver and kidney zinc than with testes, muscle, or bone) and total body zinc content versus exchangeable zinc pool size in rats.

Effects of phytate on zinc homeostasis: higher whole-body 65Zn retention and lower endogenous fecal zinc excretion in phytate-fed rats, interpreted as a homeostatic response to reduced zinc absorption.
Quantitative absorption results (apparent and true zinc absorption percentages for phytate versus basal diets) and the dietary relevance of the 60:1 phytate:zinc molar ratio in whole grains or seeds.
Closing caveat that the effects of sodium phytate may not generalize to phytic acid naturally present in foods, which the study could not determine.

This chunk opens the study: its aim (linking urinary InsP6/phytate levels to bone mass loss and fracture risk in postmenopausal women), the 157-participant cohort, the three urinary phytate groups (low, intermediate, high), and the methods (neck densitometry at enrollment, lumbar spine and femoral neck at 12 months, and FRAX 10-year fracture risk).

This chunk gives the first results: women with low urinary InsP6 lost significantly more lumbar spine bone mass over 12 months than those with high levels (3.08% vs 0.43%), setting up the comparison between low and high phytate groups.

This chunk reports further results: a larger share of low-InsP6 women lost over 2% lumbar spine bone mass (55.6% vs 20.7%), and the low-phytate group had significantly higher 10-year hip and major osteoporotic fracture probabilities than the high-phytate group.

This chunk gives the end of the fracture comparison (hip 0.37% vs 0.18%, major osteoporotic 2.45% vs 1.83%) and begins the Discussion, which concludes that high urinary phytate is linked to less lumbar bone loss and lower fracture probability.
This chunk is the final sentence of the Discussion, which states that increased phytate consumption may help prevent osteoporosis; it is a causal claim drawn from an observational association.
Introduction to the review on phytic acid (phytate) in legume seeds, framing its antinutritional effect from strong mineral and protein chelation via its six phosphate groups.

Describes phytate breakdown into inositol and phosphates by phytase enzymes or nonenzymatic cleavage, and the wide distribution of phytase-producing organisms, within the review's discussion of phytic acid chemistry.

Explains that stepwise dephosphorylation of hexa- and penta-phosphate forms is needed to reduce phytate's mineral-binding ability, and lists processing methods (cooking, germination, fermentation) that reduce its inhibition of mineral absorption.

Concludes the review by listing soaking and autolysis as further methods reducing phytate's mineral inhibition, and notes inositol hexaphosphate's emerging benefits in cancer prevention and cholesterol lowering.

Introduces the retrospective pilot study on phytate urinary levels and bone parameters, describing the 180 postmenopausal women in a cross-sectional design and how they were grouped by urinary phytate concentration.

Describes the measurement methods: bone mineral density in the lumbar spine and femoral neck for low- and high-urinary-phytate groups, and linkage of urinary phytate to dietary phytate intake, leading to the reported group comparison.

Reports the main findings: higher BMD in the lumbar spine and femoral neck among women with high urinary phytate, i.e., a positive correlation between urinary phytate and bone mineral density in postmenopausal women.
Concludes that the findings suggest phytate could be used to treat bone-related diseases, proposing a mechanism of action similar to some bisphosphonates.

Introduction to the ASBMR task force report on bisphosphonate-associated osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ), stating why the task force was formed and the topics it covers (case definition, epidemiology, risk factors, imaging, management, research).
Introduction section explaining that growing recognition of a possible link between bisphosphonates and ONJ prompted the ASBMR leadership to commission the task force.
Materials and methods (multidisciplinary expert review of published data and FDA adverse event reports) and the start of the results, where a standard case definition for ONJ was developed.

The task force's formal case definition of ONJ (exposed maxillofacial bone not healing within 8 weeks after provider identification) and the start of its estimate of ONJ risk with oral bisphosphonates for osteoporosis.

Estimated low incidence of ONJ with oral bisphosphonates for osteoporosis (1 in 10,000 to <1 in 100,000 patient-treatment years), caveats that true incidence may be higher, and the much higher risk in cancer patients on high-dose IV bisphosphonates.

Higher ONJ risk (1-10 per 100 patients) in cancer patients receiving high-dose intravenous bisphosphonates, plus future diagnostic imaging prospects (OCT, contrast MRI) for detecting early disease and the note that management is largely supportive.
Conclusion of the report: supportive management of ONJ and the call for a research agenda to fill major knowledge gaps about the disorder.

Abstract opening of a 2013 Elsevier study: the purpose, background, and methods of an autopsy-style analysis of chicken nuggets sampled from two national U.S. fast food chains, using formalin fixation and microscopic histology.

Results and conclusion of the chicken nugget histology study: striated chicken muscle was not the main component of either nugget, fat was equal to or greater than muscle, and other tissues like bone, nerve, and connective tissue were present, leading to the conclusion that nuggets are mostly fat.
Closing fragment of the chicken nugget study abstract, containing the final words of the conclusion that nuggets are a misnomer, followed by the 2013 Elsevier Inc. copyright notice.

Introduction to the NTP toxicology/carcinogenicity study of 4-methylimidazole (4MI): its industrial uses, presence in fermented foods and tobacco smoke, and the rationale for studying it, followed by the design of the F344/N rat study.
Rat study design details: dosing groups for male and female F344/N rats over 106 weeks, and the calculated average daily doses in mg/kg body weight.
Rat study results on survival and body weight: survival was similar to controls, body weights were reduced in the high-dose groups, and feed consumption was lower in 5,000-ppm females.

Rat toxicity and neoplasia findings: neurological signs (clonic seizures, hyperactivity, impaired gait) in high-dose females and a significant increase in mononuclear cell leukemia in 5,000-ppm females.
Rat non-neoplastic liver findings (histiocytosis, chronic inflammation, fatty change, foci) plus the start of the B6C3F1 mouse study design.
Mouse study design: dosing groups for male and female B6C3F1 mice over 106 weeks, with calculated average daily doses in mg/kg body weight.
Mouse study results on survival, body weight, and feed consumption, followed by the start of the lung tumor findings (alveolar/bronchiolar adenoma and carcinoma).

Mouse neoplasia results: significantly increased alveolar/bronchiolar adenomas, carcinomas, and combined tumors in exposed groups, along with alveolar epithelial hyperplasia in high-dose females and the conclusion that 4MI is carcinogenic in mice.
Final conclusion of the study: 4MI is carcinogenic in male and female mice, and it may also induce mononuclear cell leukemia in female rats.

Introduces 4-methylimidazole (4-MEI), a food-occurring compound, and describes the NTP two-year feeding bioassay in mice and rats, including the rat results: equivocal evidence in females (leukemia) and no evidence in males.

Reports dose-related, statistically significant tumor decreases in male and female rats in the NTP bioassay, with a 25-fold drop in high-dose female mammary tumors, and notes NTP's brief remark that some decreases exceeded what body weight alone could explain.

States the paper's aim: a detailed evaluation of whether 4-MEI shows tumor preventive activity in rats based on the NTP bioassay, and begins the argument that reduced body weight only partly explains the tumor reductions.

Concludes that reduced body weight is only a partial explanation and not the primary cause of decreased tumor incidence, suggesting 4-MEI itself may have tumor-preventive ability; followed by the Elsevier copyright notice.

This chunk opens the document, which discusses the carcinogenicity of 2- and 4-methylimidazole contaminants in ammonia-catalyzed caramel colorings and the federal and California regulatory limits and policy recommendation for the FDA.

This chunk closes the document, completing the California 30 microgram-per-day warning threshold and concluding with the recommendation that the FDA bar food use of excessively contaminated caramel coloring.

Opening chunk and entire document: introduces the principle that correlated disease patterns point to a shared etiology, previewing a case study of Western-civilization diseases attributed to dietary fiber removal.

Opening chunk of the document's abstract introducing the link between common diseases in developed Western societies and modern Western dietary change, framing these diseases as a failure of adaptation to diet.

Closing sentence of the abstract, stating that dietary changes to alleviate and prevent these Western diseases are discussed and recommended; a continuation of chunk 1's text that repeats the phrase about alleviation and prevention.
Introduces the link between long-term cooked/processed red meat consumption and colorectal cancer risk, contrasted with fish and poultry, and the usual chemical-carcinogen explanation.
Presents geographic epidemiology: colorectal cancer tracks high beef consumption, with low rates in beef-absent India and lamb/goat-eating Arab countries.
Covers country-level trends: intermediate cancer rate in pork-eating China, post-war beef/pork imports in Japan and Korea, and the steep rises after 1970 (Japan) and 1990 (Korea).

Links the rise to popularity of undercooked beef dishes and proposes a beef factor, possibly thermoresistant oncogenic bovine viruses (polyoma-, papilloma-, or ssDNA viruses), causing latent colorectal infections.
Concludes that these viral infections, combined with exposure to cooking-related chemical carcinogens, may act synergistically to raise colorectal cancer risk.
Closing copyright notice (UICC, 2011) for the article.

Introduction of the 'Western disease' paper arguing that medicine's cure-focused strategy has failed and that prevention should be prioritized, with the main goal of shifting public opinion toward taking prevention seriously.

Continuation of the paper's argument: a wide-ranging public education campaign to encourage healthier lifestyles is the chief activity, and medicine must be restructured, including reform of medical education to train students accordingly.
Proposes an integrated approach involving government, industry and medical research, with government using taxation and subsidies on foods and tobacco to shift consumption toward healthier products.

Specific policy recommendations: tighter tobacco sales and advertising laws, health education, better food labelling, and making industry more responsive to population health needs through public education and government action.
Concludes that medical research should shift from studying detailed disease mechanisms ('complex research') toward examining lifestyle factors ('simple research').

Introduction of the methylmercury review: background on epilepsy as a common neurological disease, unknown causes for most cases, and the role of gene-environment interactions and environmental chemical exposure as risk factors.

Introduces methylmercury (MeHg) as a prominent environmental CNS neurotoxicant and notes that acute or chronic MeHg poisoning in patients and animals often causes seizures or increased seizure susceptibility, suggesting a link to epileptogenesis.

States the mini-review's scope: examining how MeHg exposure, especially developmental exposure, affects seizure susceptibility in humans and animals, and considering whether low-level MeHg exposure contributes to epileptogenesis.

Proposes the review's mechanistic hypothesis: MeHg preferentially affects the inhibitory GABAergic system, causing disinhibition of excitatory glutamatergic function, as a potential mechanism for MeHg-induced changes in seizure susceptibility.

Introduces the study's core tension: DHA in fish supports prenatal brain development, while methylmercury harms the developing nervous system, using child IQ as the outcome measure of in utero neurodevelopment.

Describes the quantitative method: maternal DHA intake is compared with its epidemiologically observed IQ effect, and maternal MeHg intake is converted to maternal body burden and compared with its observed IQ relationship.

Presents the findings: using MeHg and DHA content of 33 fish species, the net IQ effect is computed; MeHg harm usually outweighs DHA benefit, with long-lived predators showing IQ losses up to 10 points.
Concludes with dietary recommendations: favor high-DHA, low-MeHg fish species for fish-consumption interventions, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.

Opening of the document: introduces the 2002 estimate of $54.9 billion in annual US child costs from environmental diseases, notes the lack of federal policy changes to limit toxic chemical exposure, and states the authors' updated analysis.

Middle of the document: gives the updated finding that costs of seven conditions (lead poisoning, prenatal methylmercury exposure, childhood cancer, asthma, intellectual disability, autism, ADHD) reached $76.6 billion in 2008, and lists policy actions needed to prevent further cost increases.
Final sentence of the document: concludes the list of recommended policy actions, ending with curbing mercury emissions from coal-fired power plants.

Introduction to the review: defines methylmercury as a neurotoxicant, notes possible low-level health effects, confounding by beneficial fish nutrients, and the lack of prior synthesis on low-level MeHg exposure.

Stated objective of the review: synthesize current knowledge on human health effects of low-level MeHg exposure to guide research, risk assessment, and exposure remediation policy; begins describing the literature search methods.

Methods on inclusion criteria: original human epidemiologic studies using a direct mercury biomarker, excluding case series and high-exposure populations such as high-fish-eating, marine-mammal-eating, and gold-mining regions.

Transition from methods to results: introduces the data synthesis, beginning with evidence that low-level MeHg may affect fetal growth in susceptible subgroups and infant growth in the first two years.
Synthesized findings across outcomes: neurologic effects may vary by age, sex, and exposure timing; no consistent pattern for cardiovascular disease risk; immunologic study results are inconsistent.
Conclusions: calls for research on mechanisms, individual susceptibility, sexual dimorphism, and non-linear dose response to inform prevention, policy, and regulation of MeHg.
Final sentence of the conclusions, closing the abstract by stating that such research would guide future MeHg prevention, policy, and regulatory efforts.

Introduces the autopsy study of 32 Seychelles neonatal brains (plus 12 Rochester reference brains), describing the six sampled brain regions and the paired tissue-block sampling method used for histology and mercury analysis.

Summarizes main findings: no clear developmental abnormality, only low-grade nonspecific destructive changes, and elevated total mercury (mostly organic) in many Seychelles specimens; also notes the Rochester comparison group.

Reports that mercury levels varied widely across cases and between regions within individual brains, that mercury did not correlate with histologic changes, and that all total mercury values were below 300 ppb.

Regional statistics show higher mercury in phylogenetically older structures (deep subcortical nuclei, brainstem, cerebellum), and describes the paired-region analysis of mercury concentrations within each brain.

Reports high correlations between mercury concentrations across all region pairs, suggesting a concentration-dependent relationship between intake and brain content, and no significant grey versus white matter difference in 12 specimens.
Compares findings with prior studies: toxicity appears at total brain mercury above 1,000 ppb, so this study found no toxicity below 300 ppb.

Notes limitations (submicroscopic, subcellular, and subtle architectonic changes not excluded), calls for threshold-effect research on fetal brain, and observes that about half of mercury is in white matter glia.
Concludes that because roughly half the mercury sits in glial cells, developmental research on methylmercury should focus on glia as well as neurons.

Opening of the methylmercury study: 27 volunteers exposed via fish at the provisional tolerable weekly intake for 14 weeks, followed by a 15-week washout, to reevaluate hair-to-blood ratio and half-life.

Study methods and early results: blood sampled every 1-2 weeks, hair cut every 4 weeks, total mercury measured; T-Hg rose significantly over time, from 6.7 to 26.9 ng/g in blood and 2.3 to 8.8 µg/g in hair.

Key quantitative findings: mean hair-to-blood ratio of 344 ± 54 after time-lag adjustment, and raw half-lives of about 94 days (blood) and 102 days (hair), introducing the background-subtraction analysis.

Background-corrected half-lives (57 ± 18 days blood, 64 ± 22 days hair) and the conclusion that past methylmercury hair-to-blood ratios appear underestimated, with the crude half-life preferred over the recalculated one.
Final conclusion: the recalculated half-life may approximate the conventional value, but the crude half-life is preferred because background levels are impractical and uncertain to determine.

Introduction to methylmercury (MM) as a potent neurotoxin, covering its environmental pollution and exposure routes via poisoned fish or misused fungicide-treated grain, with the sentence cut off mid-mention of Japan's Fetal Minamata disease.

Lists major methylmercury poisoning epidemics (Japan's Fetal Minamata disease, Iraq, Pakistan, Guatemala, Ghana), sporadic cases in the US and Canada, and notes the lack of an effective antidote for MM's central nervous system effects, with hope for better acute therapy.
Concluding fragment of the document's final sentence, expressing hope that the documented findings will lead to more effective therapy for acute methylmercury poisoning cases.

Introduces the study's premise: methylmercury exposure during CNS development can cause congenital abnormalities, and maternal hair mercury reflects blood and fetal brain mercury levels. Describes the prospective study of 137 pregnant women on the coast with newborns screened by ultrasonography.

Describes the study design: 137 women with term, normal pregnancies and their newborns assessed by ultrasound, split into an exposed group (hair mercury ≥1 μg/g) and a control group (<1 μg/g), with neurosonographic examination performed on all newborns.

Details the cerebellar measurements taken in the sagittal-medial plane (maximum height and width from the roof of the fourth ventricle) and the exposure distribution: most mothers were under 1 μg/g (N=107), with mean hair mercury 0.88 μg/g (SD 1.24), range 0.02 to 8.71 μg/g.

Reports the results: no significant group difference in cerebellar width (Mann-Whitney Z=1471, p=0.141), but a significant difference in cerebellar length, with statistically significant smaller cerebellum in newborns of mothers with hair mercury above 1 μg/g (Z=2329, p=0.019).

Gives the study's conclusion that prenatal exposure to low-level methylmercury affects fetal brain development, seen as a reduced newborn cerebellar size, while noting the clinical question of low-level exposure effects on neurodevelopment remains unresolved.

Outlines future research plans: detailed neuropsychological testing of children at 18 months of age to detect subtle neurological or neuropsychological deficits that might follow prenatal low-level methylmercury exposure.
Closing chunk stating that the follow-up tests could reveal subtle deficits, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice for the article.
Abstract opening of a study on methylmercury (MeHg) toxicity in Atlantic salmon, introducing the fish oil (high n-3/n-6) vs. vegetable oil (low n-3/n-6) diet design and the 5 mg Hg/kg exposure.

Continuation of the abstract describing the exposure duration (three months), dietary effects on tissue fatty acid composition, MeHg bioaccumulation (liver accumulating about three times more than brain and white muscle after 84 days), and the start of the molecular biomarker results.

Abstract results on biomarkers: MeHg effects in liver on vitamin C, heme oxygenase, TUBA and Cpt1 transcription, and dietary lipid effects in liver on TBARS, tocopherols, and several gene transcripts (thioredoxin, PPARB1, D5D, D6D), followed by the start of brain findings.

Concluding abstract section covering brain-tissue dietary effects (MT-A, HIF1, Bcl-X, TUBA), MeHg-by-diet interaction effects across all tissues, the conclusion that dietary fats modulate MeHg toxicity, and the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
Tail fragment of the copyright statement at the end of the abstract, stating Elsevier Ltd. (2011) and all rights reserved.

Introduces the case study: two full-term newborns exposed to methylmercury in utero from contaminated bread eaten early in pregnancy, with high brain mercury levels at autopsy and an initial report of developmental disturbance.

Describes the developmental abnormalities found at autopsy: incomplete or abnormal neuronal migration to cerebral and cerebellar cortices, deranged cerebral cortical organization, and heterotopic neurons in the white matter (continues mid-sentence into the laminar cortical pattern).

Details the disrupted laminar cortical pattern in the cerebrum, shown by irregular cell groupings and misaligned cortical neurons, and introduces prominent diffuse gemistocytic astrocytosis in cerebral and cerebellar white matter with mercury grains in astrocyte cytoplasm.

Concludes that the fetal brain is highly vulnerable to methylmercury, and that the main effect is faulty development rather than focal destructive neuronal damage, which contrasts with mercury poisoning in postnatally exposed adults and children.
Final sentence of the abstract, completing the contrast between prenatal developmental injury and focal neuronal damage seen in postnatal mercury intoxication of adults and children.

Introduction and objectives of a study estimating the dose-response relationship between maternal mercury body burden and childhood IQ decrements, using a Bayesian hierarchical model across three epidemiologic cohorts.

Methods section describing the inputs to the Bayesian hierarchical model: dose-response coefficients from Faroe Islands, New Zealand, and Seychelles studies, with the Faroe Islands IQ coefficient estimated from three IQ subtests.

Methods continued: inclusion of other cognition/achievement tests in the hierarchical model to better estimate study-to-study and end point variability, followed by the start of the Results with the central IQ coefficient estimate.

Results giving the central estimate of -0.18 IQ points per ppm of maternal hair mercury (95% CI -0.378 to -0.009), comparing it to the Faroe Islands, Seychelles, and New Zealand study estimates, and noting sensitivity analyses.
Sensitivity analysis range of IQ coefficient estimates (-0.13 to -0.25) and the start of the Conclusions discussing IQ as an end point and its limits for capturing attention and motor deficits.
Final conclusion that the integrated IQ coefficient gives a more robust dose-response description for prenatal mercury and cognitive functioning than any single study.

Introduction and background of a cross-sectional study on persistent environmental chemicals (marine food pollutants) as a possible cause of type 2 diabetes in elderly Faroese, with methods beginning.

Methods section describing the clinical examination of 713 Faroese residents aged 70-74, including fasting glucose, insulin and glycosylated hemoglobin, and how lifetime contaminant exposure from pilot whale and traditional food was estimated.

Methods conclusion (exposure assessment via dietary questionnaire and PCB blood analysis) and early results: septuagenarians with diabetes or impaired fasting glycemia had higher PCBs and traditional food intake, especially in childhood and adolescence.
Key quantitative results in non-diabetic subjects: fasting insulin decreased 7% and fasting glucose rose 6% per doubling of PCB concentration, adjusted for sex and BMI at age 20.

Robustness results and main conclusion: associations persisted in subjects without impaired fasting glycemia, were attenuated by adjustment for current BMI and lipid parameters, and impaired insulin secretion is implicated in diabetes pathogenesis from lipophilic food contaminants.

Final sentence of the conclusions, completing the statement that impaired insulin secretion is an important part of type 2 diabetes pathogenesis linked to persistent lipophilic food contaminant exposure.

Abstract opening of a systematic review and meta-analysis on fish consumption, long-chain n-3 fatty acids, and type 2 diabetes risk; describes the rationale (inconsistent evidence) and the literature search methods (PubMed/EMBASE through Dec 2011).
Continues the methods section: eligibility criteria requiring prospective studies reporting RRs with 95% CIs, and the use of a dose-response random-effects model to pool study-specific estimates.

Presents the main results: 16 studies with 527,441 participants and 24,082 cases, with heterogeneity largely attributed to geographic differences, and begins the reported per-serving-per-week fish consumption findings.
Gives the pooled dose-response estimates by region for fish consumption (U.S., European, Asian/Australian) and begins the long-chain n-3 fatty acid estimates per 0.30 g/day increment.
Reports the remaining long-chain n-3 pooled estimates by region and the conclusions, noting geographic differences in associations and calling for further investigation of the heterogeneous results.
Final conclusion: calls for further research on the heterogeneous relationship but states that current public health recommendations on fish consumption should remain unchanged.

Opening of the abstract on fish consumption choices: it introduces the background and objectives (toxicological, nutritional, ecological, economic viewpoints; review of past advisories) and the methods of reviewing literature and U.S.-focused advisories.

Continuation of the methods, noting the U.S. focus and that conclusions generalize to groups with similar consumption patterns, followed by the start of the discussion on trade-offs among fish consumption choices.

Discussion core trade-off: fish is a rich nutrient source, but methylmercury and toxicant contamination mean higher intake raises exposure, and no consumption pattern optimizes all domains; it also begins the point about wild fish stock shortfalls.

Discussion on wild fish stock inadequacy for growing world nutrient demand and the economic impact on the fishing industry, noting that most guidance ignores ecological and economic impacts, leading into the conclusion on the information gap.

Conclusion calling for clear, simple guidance that integrates health, ecological, and economic impacts, and for policy and fishery management interventions to keep fish available as a nutrition source.
Final sentence of the conclusion, stating that policy and fishery management interventions are needed to ensure long-term availability of fish as an important source of human nutrition.

Introduction of a study on mercury (Hg) in marine fish: benefits and risks of fish consumption, mercury as a neurotoxin driving fish advisories, and the open question of whether local contamination matches national/regional levels.

Study objectives: measuring Hg in six commonly consumed marine species caught off the North Carolina coast and comparing them with regional (Monterey Bay Aquarium Seafood Watch) and national (EPA and FDA) averages, action levels, and guidelines.
Key findings on significant differences in Hg among species and correlations with fish length and trophic level, plus the opening of the species-specific results compared against EPA action levels.

Species-specific results: mahi mahi and triggerfish fall below the EPA action level (0.3 ppm); wahoo and grouper exceed EPA but not FDA (1.0 ppm) levels; king mackerel has the highest Hg and exceeds both EPA and FDA action levels.

Comparison of local results with EPA/FDA database averages and Seafood Watch recommendations: local values often disagree with national averages, and Hg-based advice would conflict with Seafood Watch's sustainability-based recommendations.
Conclusion: regional and national Hg averages do not always reflect local contamination, so local data may be needed to accurately assess consumer risk from eating North Carolina marine fish.
Introduction and objectives of a study on mercury (Hg) concentrations in U.S. commercial seafood, framing Hg as a toxic exposure risk and noting uncertainty from limited data.
Methods section describing how the study built a Hg-in-seafood database from government monitoring and scientific literature, and set up comparisons with exposure estimates and consumption advice.
Methods continued: calculation of sample-size-weighted grand means per seafood item and comparison against FDA Mercury Monitoring Program and EPA human health criteria.
Results on variability: Hg means differ widely among studies (0.3–2.4 orders of magnitude), and wild seafood contains 2- to 12-fold more Hg than farmed fish.
Results on knowledge gaps and discrepancies: farmed fish, certain items, and Asian and South American imports are understudied, and database means differ greatly from FDA-MP estimates for most items.
Conclusions: high seafood Hg variability matters for public health and consumption guidelines, and smaller datasets used in exposure assessments fail to capture available evidence.

Introduction to the Seychelles Child Development Nutrition Study: the dual role of maternal fish consumption, providing fetal LCPUFA for brain development but also exposing the fetus to methyl mercury neurotoxicity.

Study aims and design: a priori models testing whether maternal serum Ω-3 and Ω-6 LCPUFA associate with BSID-II child development at 9 and 30 months, with or without adjustment for prenatal MeHg exposure.
Sample and 9-month results: 229 children analyzed; PDI positively associated with total Ω-3 LCPUFA and negatively with the Ω-6/Ω-3 ratio, with stronger associations after adjusting for MeHg.

Secondary and 30-month findings: MeHg effect at 9 months varied by Ω-6/Ω-3 ratio; no LCPUFA-PDI associations at 30 months, but adverse prenatal MeHg associations with 30-month PDI emerged when LCPUFA were included; MDI unassociated with exposures.
Conclusions on importance: prenatal Ω-3 LCPUFA from fish and overall dietary LCPUFA support child development, and LCPUFA benefits may mask adverse MeHg effects in observational studies.
Final conclusion sentence: LCPUFA beneficial effects can obscure detection of adverse prenatal MeHg effects in longitudinal observational research.

Introduction/background of a 1990s international case-control study on smoking and lung cancer in men, framing the puzzle of higher lung cancer rates in American men than Japanese men despite higher Japanese smoking prevalence.
Study design and sample: a multicentric case-control study in New York City, Washington DC, and Nagoya, Japan (1992-1998), describing the numbers of US and Japanese cases and controls enrolled.
Key results on odds ratios: the lung cancer OR for current US smokers versus nonsmokers (40.4) compared with Japanese current smokers versus hospital controls (OR 3.5), with confidence intervals.

Comparison continues: Japanese smokers versus community controls (OR 6.3, CI 3.7-10.9), and findings that years of smoking and cigarettes per day were similar between US and Japanese cases and controls.

Conclusions on the difference: American cases started smoking about 2.5 years earlier, and smoking-associated lung cancer risk was substantially higher in US than Japanese men, consistent with population statistics.

Proposed explanations for the risk difference: more toxic American cigarette formulation with higher tobacco-specific nitrosamine levels, and wider use of activated charcoal filters in Japanese cigarettes.
Concluding remarks listing other possible contributors to the difference: documented differences in genetic susceptibility and lifestyle factors apart from smoking.

Introduces the FDA's 2001 advice on mercury in fish, which named shark, swordfish, king mackerel, and tilefish as fish to avoid for at-risk women and young children, following earlier Great Lakes state advisories from the 1970s.

Describes the 2004 joint FDA and EPA reissue of the mercury fish advisory, which added canned tuna and recreationally caught fish guidance, and notes that prior studies of advisory awareness rarely used representative data.

States the study's aim: to assess changes in awareness and knowledge of mercury as a fish problem using the pooled, nationally representative 2001 and 2006 Food Safety Surveys, with the two sample sizes given.
Reports the main finding that consumer awareness of mercury as a fish problem rose from 69% in 2001 to 80% in 2006 (p<.001), and begins describing regression results on parents of young children.

Reports that parents of children under 5 were more aware and knowledgeable than other adults, while women of childbearing age (18-45) were less aware than other women in both years, with women of all ages gaining more than men.

Lists the significant predictors of awareness and knowledge about mercury in fish (race, education, income, region, fish preparation experience, recent foodborne illness, and food safety risk perceptions) and includes the copyright notice.
Final copyright line (Elsevier, 2011) closing the abstract, with no substantive content about mercury awareness or advisories.

Introduces the pilot fMRI study's objective: testing whether fMRI can visualize brain function changes linked to neurobehavioral deficits in boys with high prenatal MeHg and PCB exposure, building on known cognitive, sensory, and motor effects of these neurotoxicants.
Describes the study population: twelve adolescent boys from the Faroese birth cohort (1986–1987), selected for prenatal MeHg and PCB exposure, all scanned with fMRI during behavioral tasks at age 15.

Reports the comparison design: high versus low mixed MeHg/PCB exposure groups on fMRI photic stimulation and motor tasks, with low-exposure boys showing activation patterns typical of normal controls.

States the key finding: highly exposed boys showed activation in more brain areas with different and wider patterns than the low-exposure group, interpreted as consistent with the known neurotoxicity of MeHg and PCBs and supporting fMRI's potential for mapping exposure-related neurobehavioral dysfunction.

Concludes that the methodology may be useful for visualizing the structural neural system determinants of exposure-induced neurobehavioral dysfunction, closing the study's summary of its pilot findings.

This chunk opens the study: a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 50 mg naltrexone on eating and subjective appetite in 20 male volunteers, with appetite measured by a disguised digital balance that paused feeding for ratings.

This chunk describes the test meals (cheese or tomato pasta) and the main intake result: naltrexone reduced food consumed versus placebo and familiarisation days, and also lowered pleasantness ratings.

This chunk reports the hunger analysis: naltrexone reduced eating rate and removed the positive linear hunger component (initial appetite stimulation) while leaving the intercept and negative quadratic term unchanged.
This chunk covers the mood and interpretation: naltrexone produced mild sedation, but mood alone did not explain the appetite effects, pointing to opioids stimulating appetite via palatability.
This chunk is the final word of the abstract, completing the conclusion that opioids specifically stimulate appetite through palatability.

Document introduction and objective/method of an fMRI study on cue-induced cocaine craving: describes the hypothesis that drug cues drive craving and the design comparing cocaine users (N=17) and comparison subjects (N=14).

Study methods: subjects viewed three films (crack cocaine smoking, outdoor nature, explicit sex) during fMRI, and the criteria for identifying candidate craving sites based on activation in cocaine users watching the cocaine film.
Specificity criteria for candidate craving sites (population and content specificity) and the start of the results, noting the regions satisfying these criteria were largely left lateralized.

Results listing the brain regions meeting the specificity criteria (frontal, parietal, insula, limbic cingulate areas) and the count of 13 putative craving sites, of which three were then tested against the sex film.

Comparison of the cocaine film with the sex film in cocaine users: only anterior cingulate, right inferior parietal lobule, and caudate/lateral dorsal nucleus showed greater activation, suggesting cocaine cues recruit substrates similar to natural evocative stimuli.

Additional finding that cocaine users responded less than comparison subjects to the sex film, followed by the conclusion that craving lacks a dedicated neuroanatomical circuit and that the distinctive feature of users is drug cues producing comparable activation to nondrug stimuli.
Final concluding sentence of the abstract: learned drug-related cues in cocaine users produce brain activation comparable to nondrug evocative stimuli in healthy comparison subjects.

Introduction to a PET study of smokers vs. nonsmokers: motivates the link between nicotine addiction, the mesolimbic dopamine reward system, and the aims of comparing brain reward activation in the two groups.

Methods summary: describes the PET measurement of regional cerebral blood flow with H2(15O) in healthy smokers and nonsmokers during a pattern-recognition task, comparing nonmonetary and monetary reinforcement against a nonsense-feedback baseline.

Results for monetary reward: both groups show activation in frontal/orbitofrontal cortex, occipital cortex, cingulate, cerebellum and midbrain, but only nonsmokers show striatal (dopaminergic) activation.

Results for nonmonetary reinforcement and group contrast: nonsmokers show a similar activation pattern to monetary reward, while smokers show activation only in the cerebellum, indicating altered reward processing.

Interpretation: the differing activation patterns suggest smokers process reward differently, particularly in dopaminergic regions including the striatum, with a discussion of whether this reflects tobacco use or a pre-existing brain condition.
Conclusion: the authors attribute the differences to tobacco smoking, supported by nonimaging studies, while noting that a short-term effect of recent smoking cannot be ruled out.

Background section of the study: rationale that frequent energy-dense food intake (e.g., ice cream) may blunt striatal reward responses, citing obesity, dopamine receptor reductions, and repeated-intake dopamine decreases.

Study objective and hypothesis: testing whether frequent ice cream consumption is linked to reduced reward-region (striatal) activation to an ice cream-based milkshake, and whether body fat and food specificity matter.
Design and methods: fMRI in 151 healthy-weight adolescents during milkshake and tasteless solution receipt, with body fat, food intake, craving, and liking measured.

Key results: milkshake robustly activated striatum, but frequent ice cream consumption predicted weaker striatal response, while body fat, total energy, macronutrient, and other energy-dense food intake showed no relation.
Conclusions: frequent ice cream intake, independent of body fat, reduces reward-region responsivity, paralleling drug addiction tolerance, with the effect appearing specific to the consumed food.
Concluding interpretation: attenuated reward responsivity is specific to the particular energy-dense food, suggesting sensory eating experiences and reward learning drive this specificity.

Introduces the hypothalamus's role in food intake regulation and glucose-sensitive neurons, noting prior fMRI evidence of glucose effects on hypothalamic activity is limited and dose-dependency is unexplored.
Continues the background gap and states the study aim: fMRI measurement of how two different glucose loads affect neuronal activity in the human hypothalamus.
Describes the methods: 15 normal-weight men fasted overnight, scanned for 37 min, and after 7 min drank water or a 25 g or 75 g glucose solution.
Reports the main results: a prolonged, dose-dependent fMRI signal decrease after glucose, strongest in the upper anterior hypothalamus, similar across loads in the upper posterior hypothalamus.
Concludes with no effect in the lower hypothalamus and proposes a possible link between the hypothalamic response and changes in blood insulin concentration.
Opening of an obesity-review article introducing the parallels between drug addiction and obesity, both framed as reward-saliency disorders driven by abrupt dopamine surges.

Continues the introduction: dopamine surges in vulnerable people can override homeostatic control, and brain imaging is starting to reveal shared circuitry between addiction and obesity, sparking debate.
Summarizes imaging findings that obese and drug-addicted individuals both show dopaminergic impairments affecting reward, motivation, and overlapping brain circuits.
Describes the dopaminergic deficits extending to conditioning, self-control, stress and interoception, and notes key differences, especially peripheral homeostatic signals regulating food intake.
Closing statement of the review's scope, focusing on shared neurobiological substrates of obesity and addiction, followed by the copyright notice from the 2012 journal article.

Introduction/background of a fMRI study on fat intake and cerebral blood flow: hypothalamus as homeostatic control, glucose vs. fat effects, and the gustatory/insular cortex's role in food processing.
Continuation of background plus study objective (compare high- vs low-fat meals on hypothalamus and insular cortex) and design: 11 healthy men, single-blinded fMRI on two measurement days.

Study design details: CBF measured before and at 30 and 120 min after high- and low-fat yogurt intake, with hunger ratings and blood samples; start of the results describing a hypothalamic CBF decrease after high-fat yogurt.

Key results: high-fat yogurt reduced hypothalamic CBF, correlating with insulin change; insular activity rose after 120 min only in the low-fat condition; CBF changes in both regions correlated in the high-fat condition.

Conclusions: fat-induced hypothalamic decrease and hypothalamus-insula interaction may support energy homeostasis, making fat a modulator of homeostatic and gustatory regions; trial registration NCT01516021.
Trailing fragment of the trial registration number (clinicaltrials.gov NCT01516021) from the study's conclusion.

Introduction to a 2012 paper on whether food addiction exists, framing the debate over overeating and substance/behavioral addiction and noting DSM-5's proposed shift from 'Substance-Related Disorders' to 'Addiction and Related Disorders'.

Discusses psychiatry's historical reluctance to classify behavioral addiction and the broad overlap between chemical and behavioral addiction across phenomenological, therapeutic, genetic, and neurobiological dimensions.

Presents the leptin argument: leptin's effect on the brain's reward system suggests an indirect link between overeating and chemical addiction, so leptin-deficient individuals might meet food addiction criteria.

Outlines the paper's structure: reviewing psychological findings on substance and behavioral addiction to analyze their overlap, then assessing the diagnostic validity of food addiction as chemically and/or behaviorally based.
Copyright notice for the 2012 S. Karger GmbH publication, with no substantive content about food addiction.

Introduction framing obesity and drug addiction as parallel disorders of abnormally enhanced reward saliency, linked to dopamine-mediated reinforcement in the limbic system that can overwhelm homeostatic control.

Motivation for studying shared vulnerabilities between addiction and obesity, introducing brain imaging findings that reveal common features and overlapping circuits underlying stereotypic behavioral deficits.
Summary of brain imaging results indicating that obese and drug-addicted individuals both show impaired dopaminergic pathways governing reward, motivation, and related neural systems.

Enumerates the functions affected by dopaminergic impairment (reward sensitivity, incentive motivation, learning, impulse control, stress reactivity, interoceptive awareness) and states the review's aim of integrating PET findings.
Closing statement of the review's scope: synthesizing PET-based evidence on dopamine in addiction and obesity and proposing an updated working model to inform shared treatment strategies.

Introduces the opioid system's role in reward-driven addictive behavior (opioid, nicotine, alcohol self-administration) and its involvement in the broader neural network regulating eating via homeostatic and hedonic mechanisms, with emphasis on palatable food.
