Links opioid antagonism reducing both drug taking and palatable food appetite to the idea that craving for palatable food is a form of opioid-related addiction, then names the three opioid receptor families (µ, ĸ, δ) and notes µ-receptors are most implicated in reward.

Describes pharmacological evidence from rodent studies: µ-agonist infusion into the NAcc induces feeding even in satiated animals while µ-antagonists reduce intake, and ĸ- and δ-receptors also appear to contribute.

Reports preliminary transgenic knockout findings that mice lacking certain opioid receptors resist high-fat diet-induced obesity, followed by the 2012 S. Karger GmbH copyright notice closing the document.
Introduction of a 2012 review on brain PET imaging in obesity and food addiction, framing obesity as a health epidemic and raising the parallel between compulsive overeating and drug addiction.

Explains that the review surveys PET studies of the cerebral control of food intake and obesity, listing brain regions (prefrontal, orbitofrontal, somatosensory cortices, insula, thalamus, hypothalamus, amygdala) involved in the reward properties of food.

Summarizes the review's first two proposed concepts: somatosensory regions respond to food sight, taste and smell and may be hyperresponsive in obesity, and executive-drive areas overreact to anticipated pleasure during food cue exposure.

Gives the review's third proposed concept, that inhibitory and cognitive control regions are resistant to reward perception after food exposure in obese subjects, and notes these features together drive intake of palatable, energy-dense foods.

Caveats the food-addiction analogy: the same regions are implicated in drug and gaming addiction, but direct resemblance may be oversimplified given study heterogeneity and exclusion of sensitive groups.

Concludes that further work is needed to address the multifaceted obesity phenotype and clarify the role of food dependency in its pathophysiology, followed by the 2012 S. Karger GmbH copyright notice.

Opening of an abstract (Addiction Biology, 2011) on parallels between obesity and addictive disorders, covering phenomenological and neurobiological similarities, appetite regulation linked to reward, and the start of the neuropsychological findings on cognitive alterations.

Middle section of the abstract stating that cognitive alterations in obesity and addiction may impair control over consumption, and that the review summarizes overlapping pathways and implications for new obesity treatments.
Closing sentence of the abstract stating the review discusses treatment implications, followed by the copyright notice for Addiction Biology and the Society for the Study of Addiction (2011).
Background and aims of a human fMRI study comparing brain BOLD responses to glucose versus fructose, motivated by animal findings of opposing central effects on appetite and weight.

Methods: nine healthy normal-weight subjects received IV glucose, fructose, or saline in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design while BOLD fMRI was measured, with blood sampled for glucose, fructose, lactate and insulin.
Results begin: saline produced no significant BOLD changes, and cortical control-area BOLD signal is described as the key outcome measure for the infusion conditions.
Key findings: cortical BOLD signal increased with glucose infusion (alongside rising plasma glucose and insulin) but decreased with fructose infusion (alongside rising plasma fructose and lactate).

Conclusion and hypothalamic null result: neither sugar significantly changed hypothalamic BOLD signal, and cortical responses to glucose and fructose are opposite, suggesting a neurologic link to dietary fructose-related food intake dysregulation.
Closing sentence of the conclusion, linking differential brain responses to sugars and their metabolites with high dietary fructose intake, followed by the 2011 Blackwell Publishing copyright notice.

Introduces the CPT hit reaction time measure and the hypothesis that its neuropsychological meaning shifts over the test duration, setting up the study of methylmercury effects on attention in adolescents.

States the rationale that prenatal methylmercury exposure increases reaction times, describes the study sample of 878 adolescents at age 14, and introduces analysis across three time intervals of the CPT.

Reports the CPT procedure (10 minutes, targets every 1000 ms) and the main finding that associations between prenatal methylmercury biomarkers and HRT differ by time window, with effect estimates for the first two minutes.

Gives the effect sizes (beta and SE per ten-fold exposure increase) showing the association strengthens from the first two minutes to the 3-6 and 7-10 minute intervals, and notes robustness to covariates such as simple reaction time and finger tapping.
Summarizes that postnatal exposure had no effect and concludes that sustained attention is especially vulnerable to developmental methylmercury, suggesting frontal lobe dysfunction.
Concludes with the practical recommendation that CPT neurotoxicity analyses should consider time from test initiation rather than relying on overall average reaction times.

Abstract opening (Context, Objective) of a fMRI study on 'food addiction': introduces the addictive process in obesity and the hypothesis that food addiction scores relate to neural activation patterns similar to substance dependence.

Continuation of the abstract's Design, Participants, and Main Outcome Measure: a between-subjects fMRI study of 48 healthy adolescent females, measuring BOLD activation to receipt and anticipated receipt of chocolate milkshake.
Start of the Results section: food addiction scores (N=39) correlated with greater ACC, medial OFC, and amygdala activation during anticipation of food, with FDR-corrected statistics.
Group comparison results: higher vs. lower food addiction scorers showed greater DLPFC and caudate activation during anticipation, but less lateral OFC activation during food receipt.
Conclusions of the abstract: similar neural patterns to substance dependence, with elevated reward-circuit activation to food cues and reduced inhibitory-region activation during food intake.
Final fragment of the Conclusions sentence, restating reduced activation of inhibitory regions in response to food intake in the food addiction fMRI abstract.

Opening chunk of an abstract on phosphorus-containing food additives in best-selling grocery products in northeast Ohio; states the study objective and begins the design section describing label review of 2394 products and matching top-selling additive products to non-additive counterparts.

Continues the study design from the abstract: matched non-additive products were analyzed for phosphorus content, four days of sample meals were built from additive and additive-free foods, and daily phosphorus and price differences were computed; the setting (northeast Ohio) is introduced.

Results section of the abstract on phosphorus additive prevalence: 44% of best-selling grocery items contained phosphorus additives, with the highest rates in prepared frozen foods (72%), dry food mixes (70%), packaged meat (65%), bread and baked goods (57%), soup (54%), and yogurt (51%).

Reports quantitative findings from the phosphorus additive study: additive-containing foods averaged 67 mg phosphorus per 100 g more than matched additive-free foods (p=.03), and sample meals dominated by additive foods contained 736 mg more phosphorus per day.

Summarizes the cost comparison and conclusion of the phosphorus additive study: additive-free meals cost about $2.00 more per day, additives are common and substantially raise phosphorus content, and low-cost additive foods may lead people with chronic kidney disease to unknowingly consume more bioavailable phosphorus.

Final sentence of the conclusion of the study on phosphorus additives in popular grocery foods, stating the kidney-health concern that persons with chronic kidney disease may unknowingly increase intake of highly bioavailable phosphorus by buying low-cost additive-containing groceries.

Introduction establishing Campylobacter as a major cause of bacterial food poisoning and explaining how this oxygen-sensitive, fastidious bacterium persists in food processing to reach consumers; sets up the study of Campylobacter persistence on processed chicken.
Methods describing the collection of sterilized chicken exudates from consumer-sale products, split into 'enhanced' (marinade added during processing) and 'nonenhanced' (no additives) types.

Methods detailing the composition of enhanced exudates (polyphosphate mixture) and the experimental design: inoculating exudates with C. jejuni or C. coli and enumerating viable bacteria under varied environmental conditions, beginning with the 42°C microaerobic condition.

Results showing that at 42°C microaerobic conditions, enhanced chicken exudates increased survival of C. jejuni and C. coli versus nonenhanced exudates (by under 1 to over 4 log CFU/ml), and introducing the more relevant 4°C normal-atmosphere storage condition.

Results and conclusion that enhanced exudates also improved survival at 4°C, that polyphosphates were largely responsible for the difference, and that polyphosphate use in chicken enhancement may sustain Campylobacter numbers and raise risk of cross-contamination or undercooked-poultry illness.

Concluding sentence of the abstract stating that polyphosphates used to enhance chicken quality help sustain Campylobacter numbers, increasing the opportunity for disease via cross-contamination or improperly cooked poultry.

Introduction and methods of a study measuring aluminum levels in milk and dairy products (bulk farm milk, market milk, processed cheese, milk powder) via GFAAS, compared against provisional permissible limits, with an estimated dietary intake calculation and a cookware leaching experiment.

Continuation of the methods description (dietary intake calculation and boiling/cookware leaching experiment) and the first results: negligible aluminum in bulk farm milk, and higher aluminum in market milk with 65% of samples above the provisional limits.

Results comparing aluminum concentrations: market milk variability, and significantly higher aluminum in processed cheese wrapped in aluminum foil than in cheese packed in glass, plus the start of the milk powder finding.

Milk powder results (20% exceeding limits of 0.01 to 0.4 mg/kg) and the maximum estimated dietary intake (MEDI) percentages of the PTDI for each dairy sample type, beginning with the list of sample categories.

Completion of the MEDI percentages relative to PTDI (e.g., 428% for foil-wrapped cheese, 220% for glass-packed cheese, 166% for milk powder) and cookware leaching results showing no significant difference between control market milk and milk boiled in aluminum or stainless-steel cookware.

Practical application section stating that aluminum in milk kept in aluminum containers and dairy packed in aluminum foil exceeds permissible limits and poses a health hazard, with recommendations for milk cans and cheese packaging.

Final recommendations: stainless steel milk cans, preventing tap water contamination, glass packaging for processed cheese, and evidence that aluminum leaching increases more during storage than boiling, so milk should be refrigerated in stainless steel or glass.
Final fragment of the document's conclusion, completing the advice to refrigerate milk in stainless steel or glass containers.

Introduction to the paper on hidden dietary phosphorus sources in the American diet, opening with why elevated serum phosphorus matters for dialysis patients and why dietary restriction is central to managing hyperphosphatemia.
Covers average daily phosphorus intake figures by sex (about 1550 mg males, 1000 mg females) and notes that phosphate additives in many processed foods are changing these intake levels.
Explains how phosphate additives in processed foods can add up to about 1 g/day of phosphorus and why nutrient composition tables underestimate patients' actual phosphorus intake.
Concluding statement of the paper's aim: to describe the phosphorus content of the current American diet so nephrologists can better control hyperphosphatemia.

Introduction and methods of a study on phosphorus-containing food additives in chicken products, comparing lab-measured phosphorus content against nutrient database values; relevant to kidney disease and dialysis diet management.
Methods and results: 35 of 38 chicken products contained phosphorus additives, and actual phosphorus levels exceeded database-expected values for every additive-containing category.
Quantitative results showing the gap between measured and expected phosphorus, with breaded breast strips averaging 84 mg/100g higher and breast patties varying from 59 to 165 mg/100g.

Clinical significance and conclusion: two 100 g servings of additive-containing chicken supply about 440 mg phosphorus, roughly half the daily intake for dialysis patients, and nutrient databases fail to capture this.

Conclusions and recommendations: additives significantly raise phosphorus, database values are inaccurate and too variable for patients and dietitians to estimate intake, and dialysis patients should limit such products.
Final recommendation that phosphorus content be listed on nutrition facts labels so patients with renal disease can track intake.

Opening background section of a paper on phosphate food additives: it introduces hyperphosphatemia as a mortality predictor in advanced CKD, citing the 12% of CKD stage 5 deaths attributable to elevated serum phosphate.

Continuation of the background: high-normal serum phosphate as an independent predictor of cardiovascular events and mortality in the general population, motivating concern about phosphate additives and the Methods section that begins here.

Methods and start of Results: describes the literature review of PubMed and EU databases using the search terms 'phosphate additives' and 'hyperphosphatemia', then argues natural organic phosphate need not be restricted because it is poorly absorbed.

Results on absorption: inorganic phosphate in food additives is effectively absorbed and measurably raises serum phosphate in advanced CKD patients, unlike natural organic phosphate, and dietary restriction of natural phosphate could cause protein malnutrition.

Results on who is affected and mechanisms: foods with added phosphate are eaten mainly by lower-socioeconomic groups consuming processed and fast food, and phosphate's main pathophysiological effect is vascular damage such as endothelial dysfunction and calcification; it also notes the 1000 mg/day guideline limit for advanced renal failure patients.

Guideline limit and conclusion: patients with advanced renal failure should not exceed 1000 mg phosphate daily; notes the lack of prospective controlled trials and argues the public should be informed that added phosphate harms health given high CKD prevalence.
Final sentence of the conclusion: calls for mandatory labeling of added phosphate content in foods, closing the paper's public health recommendation.

Introduction to a survey study on hidden phosphate in processed food and drinks, motivated by phosphate toxicity and dietary guidance for chronic kidney disease (CKD) and hemodialysis patients, who rely on physicians and nurses for advice.

Survey methodology: researchers at Hirosaki University School of Medicine in Japan aimed to measure awareness of high phosphate content in commercially processed food and drinks among future medical and nursing professionals.

Survey sample and key awareness results: 190 randomly selected medical and nursing students (mean age 21.7 years) were quizzed on added phosphate ingredients, with near-universal awareness of sugar in soda but very low awareness of phosphate in soda (6.9%).
Low awareness findings: only 11.6% knew of phosphate in processed foods like hamburgers and pizza, and 67.7% were unaware of the harms of unrestricted phosphate-containing food and drink consumption.
Consumption habits and intentions: about 28% eat fast food weekly and 40% drink 1-5 cans of soda weekly, and after learning about long-term risks, 40.5% considered reducing phosphate intake.
Interest in education: 48.4% of students wanted more information on negative health effects of excess phosphate, and the authors conclude that educational initiatives are needed.
Concluding statement of the study: educational efforts are needed to raise awareness of the health risks from excessive consumption of phosphate additives.

Introduction to a study on hidden phosphorus from food additives in renal patients' diets: explains why dietary phosphorus restriction matters in kidney disease and defines the study's objective of measuring phosphorus in common protein foods with and without phosphate additives.

Continuation of the background and aims: frames phosphate additives as a 'hidden' phosphate load for renal patients and dietitians, then begins the Methods by noting the measurements taken (dry matter, nitrogen, total and soluble phosphate).

Methods and start of Results: describes the sample of 60 processed meat and poultry items (cooked ham, roast turkey and chicken breast), split equally into 30 with declared phosphate additives and 30 without, and begins reporting total phosphorus comparisons.

Results on phosphorus content: reports higher total and soluble phosphorus (mg/100 g) in products with additives versus without (P < .001), and notes no difference in dry matter between the two groups.

Remaining results and start of conclusions: reports no difference in total nitrogen, shows phosphorus per gram of protein is much higher in additive-containing foods (15.0 vs 9.3 mg/g), and states additive foods have about 70% more phosphorus.
Conclusions on clinical impact: explains the extra phosphorus is nearly fully absorbed, worsening phosphate balance control and raising the need for phosphate binders and their costs.
Closing recommendations: calls for patient education about phosphate-additive foods and for authorities to require food labels that clearly state natural and added phosphorus content.
Copyright and publication notice for the article, from the National Kidney Foundation and Elsevier (2011), ending the abstract.
Introduces the background on phosphorus intake in chronic kidney disease, noting that protein sources drive phosphorus balance and that prepared-food phosphorus content is largely unknown.

Describes the study design and setting: phosphorus content measured in 44 food products, including 30 refrigerated or frozen precooked meat, poultry, and fish items, with the outcome being measured and reported phosphorus content.
Covers the analytical methods (AOAC official methods 984.27 for phosphorus and 990.03 for protein) and the main result that phosphorus-to-protein ratios ranged from 6.1 to 21.5 mg/g.

Reports that products listing phosphorus additives had a higher mean phosphorus-to-protein ratio (14.6 mg/g) than those without (9.0 mg/g), that only one precooked product was in a major dietary database, and states study limitations.

Lists further limitations (non-generalizability, changing manufacturer formulations, incomplete direct protein measurement) and concludes that better manufacturer labeling of phosphorus could aid dietary phosphorus control without causing protein malnutrition.

Introduction to a descriptive sensory study of broiler breast fillets marinated in phosphate, salt, and acid solutions, listing the marinade treatments (2P, 2C, 2A, 1C, 1A) against the 6S NaCl control and the oven-cooking conditions.

Sensory evaluation methods: a 9-member trained panel rated 26 flavor and texture attributes on 15-point line scales for oven-cooked fillets, analyzed with SAS general linear model procedures at P <= 0.05.

Results: all sensory attributes scored in the low intensity range (1.5 to 5.0), and only brothy, vinegar, and residual particles differed significantly among marinade treatments; multivariate analysis begins here.

Conclusion: multivariate analysis found two dimensions explaining 57% of variation, and the low texture intensity values suggest possible negative effects of phosphates, salt, and acids on fully aged broiler fillets.

Introduction to Campylobacter's fastidious, oxygen-sensitive nature and its paradoxical survival in food, leading to it being the top cause of foodborne bacterial disease, which motivates the proposed polyphosphate marinade mechanism.

Proposed mechanism: polyphosphate-containing marinades used in poultry processing may aid Campylobacter survival; C. jejuni and C. coli incubated in exudate from marinade-treated birds show 1 to 4 log CFU/ml survival advantages over untreated exudate.
Polyphosphates make up much of commercial poultry marinades and account for most of the marinade effect on Campylobacter survival, setting up the focus on polyphosphates as the active component.

Comparison of six food-grade polyphosphates (pyrophosphates, triphosphate, polyphosphate, monosodium and trisodium phosphate) on Campylobacter survival in chicken exudate, finding significant differences among them.
Mechanistic finding: polyphosphates raise chicken exudate pH, with more sodiated forms raising pH more than less sodiated ones, linking polyphosphate type to the pH shift and survival differences.
Conclusion: the polyphosphate-mediated pH change is confirmed as responsible for the observed increase in Campylobacter survival in chicken exudate.
Introduces the study's aim and methods: measuring phosphorus, potassium, and protein in 36 uncooked, phosphate-enhanced meat and poultry products using AOAC official methods.
Reports the main phosphorus finding: additive-containing products had a phosphate-protein ratio about 28% higher on average than additive-free products, with some up to nearly 100% higher.
Reports potassium results: additive-free products all had under 387 mg/100 g, while five of 25 additive products had at least 692 mg/100 g (max 930 mg/100 g), and notes labeling of additives.
Covers labeling gaps (eight of 25 enhanced products did not list additives), limitations on generalizability, and that additive composition may change over time.
Concludes that enhanced uncooked meat and poultry may nearly double phosphorus and triple potassium content, a change not visible from the food label, relevant to dialysis patients.

Introduction and aim of a study on whether camel urine (virgin, lactating, pregnant) modulates cancer-activating enzyme Cyp1a1 in Hepa 1c1c7 murine hepatoma cells, motivated by traditional use of camel urine against cancer.

Materials and methods: real-time PCR for Cyp1a1 mRNA, Western blot for protein, 7-ethoxyresorufin activity assay, and EMSA plus AhR-dependent luciferase reporter assays to test the aryl hydrocarbon receptor mechanism, comparing camel versus bovine urine.
Results begin: all camel urines, unlike bovine urine, differentially inhibited TCDD-induced Cyp1a1 gene expression, with TCDD described as the most potent Cyp1a1 inducer and known carcinogen.

Results continue: virgin camel urine gave the strongest inhibition of Cyp1a1 activity (followed by lactating and pregnant urines) and significantly reduced TCDD-induced Cyp1a1 mRNA and protein levels.

Mechanistic finding: virgin camel urine's inhibition of Cyp1a1 strongly correlated with reduced AhR-dependent luciferase activity and AhR DNA binding by EMSA, implicating an AhR-dependent mechanism; followed by the start of the conclusions.

Conclusions: camel but not bovine urine inhibits TCDD-mediated toxicity by suppressing Cyp1a1 expression at transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels via AhR, the first such evidence; includes the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.
Final fragment of the copyright statement (Elsevier Ireland Ltd., 2010, all rights reserved) closing the abstract.

Opening of an abstract-style review arguing that tobacco smoking drives cardiovascular disease via activation of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR, the dioxin receptor) by tar-derived aryl hydrocarbons, and linking this to the Mediterranean diet and French paradox.

Closing of the same abstract, noting that the Mediterranean diet and French paradox are controversial epidemiological concepts reinterpreted through AhR, and introducing resveratrol as a natural AhR antagonist with potential for preventing and treating cardiovascular diseases.

Abstract of a study on dietary flavonoids (flavones and flavonols) as antagonists of dioxin-induced aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) transformation, introducing the rationale that dietary AhR inhibitors could protect against dioxin toxicity.

Results from the same study: flavones and flavonols antagonistically suppressed AhR transformation induced by 1 nM TCDD without agonistic activity, with antagonistic IC50 values of 0.14 to 10 microM, near human physiological levels.
Concluding fragment of the abstract stating that the effective IC50 concentrations are close to physiological levels in humans, supporting the dietary relevance of these flavonoids.

Background of the review on AhR: introduces halogenated and non-halogenated aromatic hydrocarbons (dioxins, PAHs) as AhR ligands that trigger receptor transformation, noting dietary exposure as the main route and food factors' regulation of AhR and drug-metabolizing enzymes.

Objective and methods of the review: aims to explain how food factors act on AhR transformation given incompletely understood mechanisms, and summarizes recent studies on the molecular mechanisms by which food factors regulate AhR and downstream drug-metabolizing enzymes.

Results/conclusion on AhR ligands: classical ligands such as dioxins are established AhR agonists, whereas food factors act as antagonists by suppressing AhR transformation through different mechanisms.
Final conclusion of the review: understanding the fate and metabolism of food factors is important for explaining their mechanisms of AhR regulation.

Opening chunk of an introductory passage on the mucosal immune system and intestinal intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs). It describes constant exposure to commensal and pathogenic microbes and the need to balance pathogen elimination, commensal tolerance, and autoimmunity prevention.

Closing chunk of the same introduction. It continues the balance theme and states that intestinal intraepithelial lymphocytes form the first line of defense at the gut barrier, so understanding their immune role is critical.

Opening of the document introducing the gut as both nutrient-absorbing organ and protective barrier, hosting commensal bacteria, and the immune challenge of distinguishing harmful from harmless microbes.

Discusses the dilemma of distinguishing nonself from self in the gut: immune responses must block pathogens without harming dietary or commensal bacteria, driving evolution of immune diversification to preserve the mucosal barrier.

Explains that immune system expansion and specialization are reflected in the adaptive intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs), covering their phylogeny, ontogeny, organization, and regulation, and introduces IELs as the topic.
Concluding statement that intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs) are key players in the unique intestinal defense mechanisms evolved in mammals.

Introduction to a review on the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) as a link between environmental agents and immune dysregulation in inflammatory bowel disease, stating the review's aim to summarize AhR's role in intestinal immune homeostasis.
Begins the 'Recent Findings' section, describing how dietary AhR ligands are needed to maintain or expand innate gut immune cells such as intraepithelial lymphocytes and IL-22-producing ILC22 cells.

Reports mouse findings: AhR-deficient mice lack IELs and have fewer ILC22 cells, making them more susceptible to infection and experimental colitis; AhR activators reduce inflammatory cytokines and attenuate colitis via IL-22.

Presents human evidence that T cells and NK cells from Crohn's disease patients express low AhR and respond to AhR ligands by suppressing inflammatory cytokines and increasing IL-22, followed by the review's summary statement.
Closing sentence of the summary, concluding that these AhR findings may explain how environmental factors regulate mucosal immune responses.

Opening of the review on intestinal intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs): introduces them as mostly T cells in the epithelium and their position between the outside antigen-rich world and the sterile body core, plus the gut's commensal bacteria.

Explains the immunological dilemma of the gut: defensive immunity protects against pathogens, but similar reactions to food antigens or harmless commensal bacteria can cause unnecessary, damaging inflammation.
States that this gut-specific dilemma led to multiple IEL subsets that share an 'activated yet resting' phenotype, while differing in phenotype, ontogeny, and function; sets up the review's aim.

Summarizes the review's aim: discussing IEL subtypes and their distinct differentiation pathways into specialized effector memory T cells that regulate protection to preserve intestinal epithelial integrity.
Closing fragment of the abstract, restating that IELs preserve the integrity and vital functions of the intestinal mucosal epithelium.

Introduction to the review on epithelial barrier biology, covering how skin and gut mucosal surfaces, aided by intraepithelial lymphocytes, defend against microbes while maintaining tolerance to commensal bacteria.

Discusses how immune cells and environmental factors such as antibiotics and diet shape microbiota composition, and how mucosal immunity balances tolerance to commensals with responses against harmful organisms.
Covers the growing recognition that gut microbiota influence systemic (not just local) immunity, and that loss of microbial homeostasis can drive inflammatory disease; sets up the review's scope.
Closing statement of the review's aim: to summarize current understanding of how immune cells and diet affect the microbiota.

Abstract-style opening of a commentary on Li et al. (2011): introduces the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) as known for mediating dioxin toxicity, and states that dietary compounds from cruciferous vegetables act through AhR to promote intestinal immunity, linking diet and immunity.
Closing sentence of the same commentary restating AhR as a critical diet-immunity link, followed by the Elsevier 2011 copyright notice; the document's end, repeating the chunk 1 conclusion.

Introduction and study scope: lists the eight AHR-active pharmaceuticals and states they were tested in aggressive Ah-responsive BT474 and MDA-MB-468 breast cancer cells, measuring AHR, CYP1A1, CYP1B1, and migration.

Methods and general findings: TCDD used as positive control; describes that AHR agonist activity depends on structure, response, and cell context, with the cell-line and endpoint measurements introduced.

Results in MDA-MB-468 vs BT474: most drugs act in BT474, while MDA-MB-468 responses vary; 4-hydroxytamoxifen, mexiletine, and tranilast fail to induce CYP1A1 there, and mexiletine, tranilast, and 4-hydroxytamoxifen show antagonist activity with TCDD.

Key agonist and antagonist results: omeprazole is a full agonist, sulindac and leflunomide partial agonists, and mexiletine a potent antagonist; these effects are concluded to show the drugs are selective AHR modulators.
Conclusion and implications: the drugs are selective AHR modulators, so any therapeutic targeting of the AHR with these drugs must be validated in the most relevant cell context.

Opening of the review's abstract introducing intestinal intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs) and their role at the gut epithelial barrier, where they must balance protective immunity against barrier integrity to maintain organismal homeostasis.

Concluding sentences of the abstract stating the review's aim: to examine how the unique development and functions of intestinal IELs enable them to strike this balance between protective immunity and epithelial barrier integrity.
Introduction to the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) as a ligand-activated transcription factor, and a report on a recent Düsseldorf meeting that begins describing its highlights.
Describes the meeting's shift in AhR research from dioxin toxicity to biological roles, including AhR-responsive retrotransposon elements contributing to genome structure.
Covers new findings on dietary plant compounds supporting gut immunity, AhR use by human brain tumours for growth, and other topics such as neurotoxicology, circadian rhythm, and immune cell types.
Concludes the meeting summary with discussion of new xenobiotic and natural AhR ligands, translational medicine applications, and AhR in cancer biology.

Opening chunk of a document on lifestyle medicine as a structured approach to managing lifestyle-related chronic disease in primary care; it introduces the gap between public and clinical health and defines lifestyle medicine as adding behavioural, motivational and environmental skills to conventional practice.

Closing chunk of a document on lifestyle medicine for chronic disease; it continues the description of adding behavioural, motivational and environmental skills and states that multidisciplinary lifestyle medicine offers cost and effectiveness benefits now beginning to be realised.
Introduces the DietCompLyf multi-centre prospective cohort study of phytoestrogens, diet, lifestyle and breast cancer recurrence/survival, including recruitment of 3159 women from 56 UK hospitals.

Describes DietCompLyf data collection (annual clinico-pathological, diet, lifestyle and quality-of-life data for 5 years, stored biological samples) and introduces the phytoestrogen exposure measure via the EPIC-Norfolk 130-item food frequency questionnaire.
Reports the analysed sample of 1797 women with complete data and begins the findings, noting higher isoflavone intake among younger patients, non-smokers, breastfeeders and supplement users.
Gives the lignan intake findings: higher among older at diagnosis, ex-smokers, breastfeeders, supplement users, lower BMI, lower age at menarche and nulliparous women.
States that no significant links were found between phytoestrogen intake and prognostic factors, and raises potential for future research on recurrence and survival to inform patient dietary advice.
Concludes the abstract with the discussion of using DietCompLyf data to guide post-diagnosis dietary and lifestyle advice, followed by the Elsevier 2013 copyright notice.

Opening chunk of a breast cancer study abstract: background on soy isoflavones as dietary anti-cancer agents, conflicting ovarian cancer evidence, and the stated aim to test whether soy intake relates to breast cancer death risk.

Methods and early results of the same abstract: a prospective study of 256 breast cancer patients recruited 2004-2006 and followed up from 2011, analyzed with univariate Cox regression, plus the start of the results listing prognostic factors (education, menopausal status, ER/PR status, TNM stage).

Results section of the abstract reporting that the highest soy isoflavone intake was associated with decreased breast cancer death risk (OR=0.25), and that higher soy protein consumption showed a trend toward reduced risk (OR=0.38 for highest vs. lowest).

Closing results and conclusion of the abstract: highest soy protein consumption significantly reduced cancer risk, and the authors conclude soy intake is linked to lower breast cancer death risk in a Chinese population, calling for larger studies.

Final sentence of the abstract's conclusion, calling for larger-sample studies to confirm the inverse association between soy consumption and breast cancer survival, specifically by menopausal status.

Introduction of a study on BRCA1 loss in sporadic (non-hereditary) breast cancer, noting prior association of BRCA1 only with hereditary cases and the unclear mechanism behind reduced BRCA1 mRNA/protein, and stating the aim to examine protein expression and promoter methylation in a North Indian cohort.
Results on BRCA1 protein expression levels in the sporadic breast cancer cohort: normal (>50% tumour cells) in 43%, reduced (20-50%) in 35%, and absent/markedly reduced (<20%) in 22.1% of cases.

Association of BRCA1 protein loss with molecular profile: BRCA1-negative tumours were more often basal marker-positive (29% vs 5%) and ER-negative (62% vs 39%), and BRCA1 promoter methylation was found in 11/45 cases (24%).

Link between BRCA1 promoter methylation and protein loss: all 11 methylated cases showed absent or reduced BRCA1 protein, supporting 'BRCAness' of sporadic breast cancer via promoter hypermethylation, similar to hereditary BRCA1-mutant cancers.

Conclusion that BRCA1 loss in sporadic breast cancer, via promoter hypermethylation, suggests PARP inhibitors and other BRCA1-pathway-targeted therapies used for hereditary cancers may also apply to sporadic breast tumours.
Final fragment of the document's conclusion, ending the sentence about using BRCA1-pathway therapeutics for sporadic breast tumours.
Abstract opening of a study on soy isoflavones (genistein, daidzein) and epigenetic DNA methylation of BRCA1/BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes in breast cancer cell lines (MCF-7, MDA-MB 231, MCF10a).

Abstract methods: cell lines studied, 5-azacytidine (demethylating) and budesonide (methylating) used as controls, methylated DNA immunoprecipitation with PCR for methylation, and Western blot, immunohistochemistry, and confocal microscopy for protein expression.

Abstract key results: 18.5 μM genistein or 78.5 μM daidzein reversed BRCA1/BRCA2 hypermethylation and restored expression; 5-azacytidine enhanced re-expression while budesonide had the opposite effect.

Abstract conclusion: findings, though needing replication, suggest epigenetic mechanisms by which genistein and daidzein regulate BRCA1/BRCA2, and call for future work on whether the demethylating effect is global or gene-specific.
Final sentence of the abstract stating that future studies are needed to determine whether genistein and daidzein's demethylating effect is global or targets select candidate genes.
Introduction and methods of a study on Canadian dietitians' counselling practices promoting legumes in low-fat, high-fibre diets, using an e-mail survey of Dietitians of Canada members.

Survey results on dietitians' personal legume use, frequency of recommending legumes, and the legume types (peanuts, kidney beans, split peas, chickpeas, lentils) preferred by dietitians and clients, plus commonly recommended products such as canned beans and tofu.

Findings on client barriers to legume use (flatulence, unfamiliarity, preparation knowledge) and dietitians' dissatisfaction with existing counselling resources, particularly among clinical counsellors.

Results on the resources dietitians most want (recipes, pamphlets, food demonstrations, Internet sites) and the conclusion calling for client-level research to test legume promotion strategies in counselling.
Final fragment of the study's conclusion, closing with the need for research on legume promotion in counselling.

Introduction and methods of a study on CpG island promoter methylation of tumor suppressor genes in periareolar fine-needle aspiration samples from 109 high-risk women, motivated by the fact that only 5% of breast cancers stem from BRCA1/2 mutations.

Methods continue with the list of methylation targets (RARB M3/M4, ESR1, INK4a/ARF, BRCA1, PRA, PRB, RASSF1A, HIN-1, CRBP1), followed by results showing overall methylation frequency rising with age but no individual event linked to age.

Results linking specific promoter methylation events (RARB M4, INK4a/ARF, HIN-1, PRA) and overall methylation frequency to abnormal Masood cytology, and the start of the BRCA1/2 analysis in 40 premenopausal women.
Results comparing 40 unaffected premenopausal women by BRCA1/2 mutation status: BRCA1/2 carriers had low methylation counts (≤4 events), while non-carriers had high counts (5-8 events).

Remaining results on BRCA1/2 carriers, with no HIN-1 methylation and rare RARB M4, INK4a/ARF, or PRB methylation, followed by the conclusion that this is the first evidence of tumor suppressor promoter methylation in non-BRCA1/2 familial breast cancer.
Final fragment of the conclusion stating the study's novelty: first evidence of CpG island methylation of tumor suppressor gene promoters in non-BRCA1/2 familial breast cancer.
Introduction and study design of a study on how habitual versus infrequent legume (bean) consumption affects colonic function, comparing two subject groups.

Results showing no group differences in fecal output, transit time, VFA excretion, or fecal pH during 23-day periods of usual diet or 100 g daily red kidney beans, but beans increased dietary fiber, fecal output, and fecal VFA concentration.
Conclusion that fecal output is driven by dietary fiber intake and VFA excretion, and that beans are a physiologically useful fiber source that favorably affects colonic function.

Introduction to a study on U.S. dietary intake: it motivates estimating the share of the population above or below dietary targets and states the study's aims, namely demonstrating NCI's usual-intake method and measuring how many Americans fail federal dietary recommendations.

Methods section describing the data source and food translation: 2001–2004 NHANES data for 16,338 persons aged 2 and older, with 24-hour recall food quantities converted into food-group amounts using the MyPyramid Equivalents Database.

Statistical modeling and main finding on food groups: usual intake distributions were modeled with covariates (sequence, weekend/weekday, sex, age, poverty income ratio, race/ethnicity), and most people fell short of recommendations for nutrient-rich food groups except total grains and meat and beans.

Results on discretionary energy: overconsumption of 'empty calories' from solid fats, added sugars, and alcohol was widespread, with over 80% of those aged 71+ and over 90% of other sex-age groups exceeding discretionary calorie allowances.
Conclusion: nearly the entire U.S. population has a diet not in line with recommendations, which the authors frame as further evidence of a nation's diet in crisis.
Introduction and background of a study on whether eating beans causes flatulence and GI discomfort, motivated by dietary guidelines promoting legumes for chronic disease prevention.

Study purpose and methods: participants in three heart-disease biomarker bean trials completed a weekly questionnaire on flatulence, stool changes, and bloating after eating ½ cup of beans daily for 8 or 12 weeks.

Design details of Studies 1 and 2, which were randomized crossover trials comparing pinto beans, black-eyed peas, baked beans, and canned carrot controls over 8-week phases, with Study 1 having 17 participants.

Design of Study 2 (29 participants, baked beans vs. carrot control) and Study 3, a 12-week parallel-arm trial of 40 pinto bean consumers versus 40 control soup consumers, with flatulence, stool, and bloating as primary outcomes analyzed by chi-square tests.

Statistical methods (chi-square tests by gender, age, BMI, and bean type) and the start of results: under 50% reported more flatulence from pinto or baked beans in week one, versus 19% for black-eyed peas.

Key results and conclusions: 3-11% reported increased flatulence even on control diets, suggesting bean-related flatulence concerns may be exaggerated, with advice for nutritionists to address GI discomfort when increasing bean fiber intake.

Final conclusion emphasizing that public health nutritionists should discuss possible gastrointestinal discomfort with clients when increasing bean fiber, and that individual responses vary by bean type.

Introduction and background of a pooled cohort study (After Breast Cancer Pooling Project) examining whether postdiagnosis soy isoflavone intake affects breast cancer outcomes, stating the rationale: antiestrogenic/anticancer versus estrogen-like concerns.

Study design and methods: 9514 invasive breast cancer survivors (1991-2006) from two US cohorts and one Chinese cohort, with soy isoflavone intake from validated food-frequency questionnaires and delayed-entry Cox regression for hazard ratios.

Main results: mean follow-up of 7.4 years, 1171 total deaths (881 breast cancer-specific), 1348 recurrences, and an inverse association between isoflavone intake and recurrence in both US and Chinese women with no heterogeneity.
Pooled hazard ratios for consumption of at least 10 mg isoflavones/day: nonsignificant reduced all-cause mortality (HR 0.87) and breast cancer-specific mortality (HR 0.83), with the CIs given.
Pooled result for recurrence: a statistically significant reduced risk at at least 10 mg isoflavones/day (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.61-0.92), followed by the start of the conclusion summarizing the findings.

Conclusion restated: soy at at least 10 mg/day gives a nonsignificant mortality reduction and a significant recurrence reduction; also notes the Women's Healthy Eating & Living Study trial registration (NCT00003787).
Trailing fragment of the clinicaltrials.gov registration reference (NCT00003787) for the Women's Healthy Eating & Living Study, one cohort within the pooling project.

Introduces the FHILL study (Food Habits in Later Life), a multi-country cohort of 785 adults aged 70+ in Japan, Sweden, Greece, and Australia, with baseline diet data collected 1988-1991 and follow-up up to seven years, aimed at finding dietary predictors of survival in the oldest adults.

Describes the statistical analysis: an alternative Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for age at enrollment, gender, and smoking, and reports that legume intake was linked to a 7-8% lower mortality hazard per 20g daily increase, with or without ethnicity adjustment (RR 0.92 and 0.93).
Concludes that, aside from legumes, no other food group consistently predicted survival across the FHILL cohorts, so legumes are the key dietary predictor identified in this study.
Study design and methods for a Taiwanese cohort on bean-free diets and mortality: the NHIS 2001 sub-sample with physical exams, followed into the TwSHHH survey in 2002.
Study setting and population: records linked to death files 2002-2008, with 2820 men and 2950 women tracked over about 6.8 years, plus initial results on person-years and 225 all-cause deaths.
Results on metabolic syndrome: generalized linear models show beans are favourable for metabolic syndrome components in men, and for waist circumference and HbA1c in women.

Key quantitative findings: cumulative logistic regression odds ratios for bean-free diet and metabolic syndrome scores (NCEP-tw) in men and women, and Cox regression hazard ratios for all-cause mortality by sex.
Conclusions: a bean-free diet may contribute to metabolic syndrome in both genders and independently predicts all-cause mortality in Taiwanese women but not men.

Abstract opening of a Chinese prospective cohort study (2004–2006) on soy isoflavone food intake and breast cancer prognosis; covers background on isoflavones and the study design with Cox regression methods.

Methods continuation describing face-to-face structured questionnaire interviews on dietary habits and confounders, and the Cox proportional hazards analysis yielding hazard ratios and 95% CIs for predictors of the endpoint (death).
Results section reporting median follow-up of 52.1 months and 79 breast cancer deaths, with an inverse association between high soy isoflavone intake (above 17.3 mg/day) and breast cancer mortality.

Results continuation giving the soy protein hazard ratio (0.71, 95% CI 0.52–0.98) for breast cancer death and ER-stratified findings showing better prognosis in ER-positive patients with high isoflavone intake (HR 0.59).
Conclusion of the abstract stating soy food intake is linked to longer survival and lower recurrence in breast cancer patients, and calling for larger, long-term cohort studies.

Background and study design of a 2-6 week olestra trial: defines olestra as a nonabsorbable fat substitute, states the objective of comparing GI symptoms in household snack consumption, and describes the 6-week double-blind randomized placebo-controlled design.

Study setting and intervention details: a general community sample of 3181 volunteers aged 2-89, with households receiving identical packages of olestra or regular (control) corn or potato chips, and the measurement approach for GI symptoms.

Primary result: overall GI symptom prevalence was 38.2% in the olestra group versus 36.9% in controls (difference 1.3 points, 95% CI -3.6 to 6.2, P=0.60), with the measurement of symptoms and their impact recorded in a daily diary.
Symptom-specific results: no significant group differences for most individual GI symptoms, except nausea, which was reported more often by controls (8.4% vs 5.7%, P=0.02).

Symptom-day results: the only difference in mean symptom-days was more frequent bowel movements in the olestra group (3.7 vs 2.8 symptom-days, P=0.04), with no group difference in the impact of symptoms on daily activities.
Conclusion of the olestra chip trial: the authors find no clinically meaningful or bothersome GI effects associated with unregulated home consumption of olestra corn and potato chips.

Introduction of the poppy seed study: states the concern over opiate alkaloids in food poppy seed, introduces the LC/MS/MS method for morphine and codeine, and gives the optimal cold methanol extraction procedure for unground seed.
Describes the method's extraction conditions and the study of morphine fate during food processing, reporting significant reductions of morphine and codeine and low morphine recovery in poppy cake.

Reports the processing results: very low morphine remaining in poppy buns at 220 degrees C, lower recovery in ground versus untreated seed, and the conclusion that processing losses matter for maximum morphine limits in poppy seed.
Final sentence of the abstract concluding that morphine elimination during food processing must be considered in the ongoing discussion of maximum permitted morphine limits in poppy seed.

Introduces the study of urinary morphine concentrations after eating poppy seeds, reporting peak levels (~18 µg/ml) measured by RIA, EMIT-ST and GC, and immunoassay positivity persisting up to 60 hours.

Covers the seed morphine content (4-200 mg/kg) and the forensic limitation that minor poppy alkaloids cannot distinguish seed eaters from opiate users, with 6-O-acetylmorphine analysis and GC/MS recommended below about 5 µg/ml total opiates.
Final sentence specifying that GC/MS is the preferred analytical method for opiate urine analysis when total opiate concentrations fall below roughly 5 µg/ml.

Introduces the study's background: opium poppy seeds are legal, widely eaten foods that can carry morphine and opiate alkaloids from harvest contamination, and states the aim of reviewing poppy seed food toxicology for effects on opiate drug tests (95 references identified).

Covers the core findings: normal poppy seed consumption is considered safe, food processing cuts morphine content by up to 90%, poppy food can cause false-positive opiate tests, and no unambiguous markers distinguish poppy ingestion from heroin or pharmaceutical morphine.

Addresses the implications for heroin-assisted maintenance programs, where patient abstinence from other drugs including illicit heroin is required, and notes the lack of forensic ingestion trials accounting for factors that affect morphine levels in biological matrices.

Discusses methodological limitations of prior studies, which failed to control for processing losses and thus overestimated initial morphine doses, and questions the continued validity of the 'poppy seed defence' given reduced morphine content in modern foods, while noting no safe consumption threshold is established.

Concludes with research recommendations: studies are needed to determine whether today's poppy foods still can influence drug tests, and future trials should account for morphine losses during processing.
Final fragment completing the conclusion sentence on future trials, which should account for processing-related morphine losses.

Introduces a study of resting metabolic rate and sympathetic nervous system activity comparing young male vegetarians and nonvegetarians, with the measurement methods used (indirect calorimetry, norepinephrine kinetics, food diary, underwater weighing).

Reports dietary differences between vegetarians and nonvegetarians: higher carbohydrate and lower fat intake among vegetarians, with no group differences in energy intake, body composition, or VO2max.
Presents the main results: vegetarians had an 11% higher absolute RMR, higher plasma norepinephrine concentration, and greater norepinephrine appearance rate than nonvegetarians.
Describes the key analysis: after adjusting for dietary carbohydrate and fat and norepinephrine levels, the RMR difference between vegetarians and nonvegetarians disappeared.
Concludes that the higher RMR in young male vegetarians is partly explained by dietary macronutrient composition and increased sympathetic nervous system activity.

Introduction of the paper on therapeutic diet acceptability: states that many conditions are treated with diets, that acceptability has been neglected in nutrition research, and that the paper proposes a working definition and reviews data on common diet regimens.

Continuation of the introduction: states the paper's goal of improving therapeutic diet success and defines 'acceptability' as the user's judgment of a diet's advantages and disadvantages (palatability, costs, eating behaviour, health) that affect adherence.

Findings on short-term studies (up to one year): very low-calorie, reduced-fat omnivorous, vegetarian/vegan, and low-carbohydrate diets were acceptable to most users, judged by attrition, adherence, and eating-behaviour questionnaires.

Findings on longer-term studies: fewer exist, but vegetarian, vegan, and reduced-fat diets appear acceptable based on sustained nutrient intake changes, while very low-calorie and low-carbohydrate diets have few long-duration studies.
Conclusion of the abstract: calls for long-term studies of adherence and acceptability of therapeutic diets, especially very low-calorie and low-carbohydrate diets.

Introduction and background: motivates the study by noting that exercise affects child health both beneficially and adversely (e.g., exercise-induced asthma), possibly via exercise-driven increases in circulating immune cells, and that the effect of brief, naturally occurring exercise bouts is poorly understood.

Study objectives: states the two aims, namely whether a 6-minute exercise bout raises circulating inflammatory cells in healthy children, and whether this effect is greater in children with a history of asthma; also begins the methods description.

Methods: describes the sample of children with mild-moderate persistent asthma and age-matched controls (n=14 per group, mean age 13.6 years), the 6-minute cycle-ergometer exercise protocol, spirometry, and blood sampling before and after exercise with flow cytometry.

Results (part 1): exercise reduced spirometry only in asthmatic children but increased most leucocyte types, including lymphocytes and eosinophils, to a similar degree in both groups, with mean cell counts reported for each group.
Results (part 2): exercise increased T helper cells and most other lymphocyte subtypes in both groups; basophils and CD4+ CD45RO+ RA+ lymphocytes rose in controls but not in children with asthma.

Conclusions (part 1): summarizes that exercise increased many circulating inflammatory cells in both asthmatic children and controls, and that asthmatic children showed increases but not greater than controls.

Conclusions (part 2): notes that basophils and CD4+ CD45RO+ RA+ memory transition T cells failed to increase in asthmatic children while rising in controls, and concludes that even brief exercise robustly mobilises circulating immune cells in children and adolescents.
Introduction and study aim from a study on baker's yeast β-glucan (Wellmune WGP) supplementation to minimise post-exercise immunosuppression in the context of strenuous aerobic exercise.

Study design and methods: recreationally active participants (n 60) in a crossover trial comparing placebo (rice flour) with 250 mg/d yeast β-glucan for 10 days before a 49-minute cycling bout in hot, humid conditions.

Methods for blood sampling timepoints (baseline, PRE, POST, 2H) and laboratory measurements: monocyte subsets by four-colour flow cytometry and plasma and LPS-stimulated cytokines by multiplex assays.
Key results: β-glucan increased total (CD14+) and pro-inflammatory (CD14+/CD16+) monocytes at POST and 2H, and boosted LPS-stimulated IL-2, IL-4, IL-5 and IFN-γ production at PRE and POST.

Further results and conclusion: plasma IL-4, IL-5 and IFN-γ were higher at 2H with β-glucan, suggesting increased leucocyte cytokine production potential and possible immune-altering effects after strenuous exercise.
Final concluding statement that β-glucan may have potential to alter immunity following a strenuous exercise session.

Study overview: a placebo-controlled, double-blind trial of Beta 1,3/1,6 glucan (Wellmune WGP) dietary supplement in 75 marathon runners, describing participant demographics and the dosing design (placebo, 250 mg, or 500 mg daily) during the 4-week post-marathon period.

Study methods: 4-week post-marathon supplementation period after the 2007 Carlsbad Marathon, with outcomes measured via the Profile of Mood States (POMS) questionnaire and a health log tracking URTI symptoms and health status at 2 and 4 weeks.

Study results: compared with placebo, the 250 mg and 500 mg beta-glucan groups reported significantly fewer upper respiratory tract infection symptoms, better overall health, and improved POMS mood scores (less confusion, fatigue, tension, anger; more vigor).
Conclusions and key points: the authors conclude that beta-glucan may help prevent URTI symptoms and improve overall health and mood after a competitive marathon.

Introduces the question of whether endurance athletes face higher upper respiratory tract infection risk during heavy training and in the 1-2 weeks after races, noting most athletes remain healthy and that regular moderate training is linked to lower URTI risk.

Explains that regular training without overreaching lowers infection risk, and that while exercise-induced immune changes should logically relate to infection risk, studies have so far failed to demonstrate this link.

Describes the mechanism behind the link: several innate and adaptive immune functions are suppressed for hours after heavy exertion, but this response is transient and its underlying mechanisms need further study before clinical use.

Covers attempts to blunt exercise-induced immune suppression and lower infection risk using drugs or nutrients such as indomethacin, glutamine, vitamin C, and carbohydrate, while stressing that such research is still needed.
Concludes that nutritional interventions have not yet been consistently shown to alter exercise immunology or URTI risk in athletes.

Introduces the study's premise: senescent T-cells accumulate with age, reducing the naive T-cell repertoire and raising infection risk, and sets up the question of whether aerobic fitness (VO2max) relates to this age-related accumulation in 102 healthy males, with flow cytometry methods.

Describes the flow cytometry panel (KLRG1, CD57, CD28, CD45RA, CD45RO on CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells) and reports the positive association of age with senescent T-cell proportions and the inverse association with naive T-cell proportions.

Reports the VO2max results: VO2max is inversely associated with senescent CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells, and age's association with senescent and naive T-cell proportions disappears after adjusting for VO2max, while VO2max's association persists after adjusting for age, BMI, and body fat.

Gives the tertile comparison based on age-adjusted VO2max, showing the highest tertile has more naive CD8+ T-cells and fewer senescent CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells than the lowest, and begins the finding that VO2max is not linked to latent CMV, EBV, or HSV-1 infection.

Concludes that the VO2max associations are not confounded by persistent viral infections and states that this is the first study to link aerobic fitness with reduced age-related accumulation of senescent T-cells, suggesting benefits of an active lifestyle for the aging immune system.
Final sentence fragment of the abstract closing the conclusion on physical activity and the aging immune system, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction: argues exercise-induced oxidative stress is beneficial, so fruit-derived antioxidants may blunt exercise benefits; summarizes human and cell findings, starting with blackcurrant supplementation suppressing plasma carbonyls after exercise.

Results continued: plasma carbonyl values (placebo vs. blackcurrant) and in vitro THP-1 data showing anthocyanin-rich blackcurrant extract reduces LPS-stimulated TNF-alpha and IL-6 secretion and NF-kappaB activation.

Results continued: postexercise plasma after blackcurrant supplementation alters the temporal LPS-stimulated inflammatory response in THP-1 cells, linking the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of blackcurrant to exercise.

Results continued: early suppression of TNF-alpha and IL-6 secretion at 24 h by postexercise plasma (placebo vs. blackcurrant), then introduces the oxidative stress cell model using hydrogen peroxide preincubation before extract exposure.

Results and conclusion lead-in: H2O2 preincubation before extract gives greater suppression of LPS-stimulated cytokine secretion at 24 h, not seen with simultaneous exposure; summary begins that blackcurrant anthocyanins alleviate oxidative stress.
Conclusion: blackcurrant anthocyanins alleviate oxidative stress and, given at appropriate amount and timing, may complement exercise's enhancement of immune responsiveness to pathogens.

Introduces vitamin C's dual role in exercise: it may reduce exercise-induced oxidative damage (muscle damage, immune dysfunction, fatigue), but reactive oxygen species may also drive beneficial training adaptations, and high doses (>1 g/day) were found to impair sport performance in the review of 12 studies.

Reports the review's specific findings on high-dose vitamin C (>1 g/day) impairing performance in four of four studies, a proposed mechanism of reduced mitochondrial biogenesis, and recommends a lower intake of about 0.2 g/day from five or more servings of fruit and vegetables as a potentially sufficient dose.

Concludes that the low dietary vitamin C intake (about 0.2 g/day from fruit and vegetables) can reduce oxidative stress and provide health benefits without impairing training adaptations, closing the document's recommendation.
Abstract of an in vitro study on dietary flavonoids inhibiting xanthine oxidase (measured by HPLC uric acid formation), introducing the enzyme's role in ischemia-reperfusion oxidative injury.

Abstract results on structure-activity relationships: planar 7-hydroxyl flavones and flavonols (chrysin, luteolin, kaempferol, quercetin, myricetin, isorhamnetin) are potent mixed-type xanthine oxidase inhibitors (IC50 0.40-5.02 microM), while nonplanar isoflavones and anthocyanidins are weaker.

Concluding sentence of the xanthine oxidase flavonoid abstract: weaker activity of nonplanar flavonoids, and the implication that certain flavonoids may reduce in vivo reactive oxygen species and urate production via xanthine oxidase inhibition.

Introduction of the study: exercise-induced muscle damage and oxidative stress from ROS in plasma and white blood cells, the dual role of exercise ROS in adaptation, and the aim to test moderate lemon verbena antioxidant supplementation in healthy males on a 90-min eccentric running protocol.

Study design and methods: healthy male volunteers, 90-minute eccentric running for 21 days, with antioxidant enzyme activities and oxidative stress markers measured in neutrophils, and inflammatory cytokines in whole blood and muscle damage in serum.

Main exercise results: 21 days of intense running increased neutrophil antioxidant enzymes catalase, glutathione peroxidase and glutathione reductase; moderate lemon verbena supplementation did not block this adaptive response.

Supplementation effects: lemon verbena extract reduced exercise-induced oxidative damage to proteins and lipids in neutrophils, decreased myeloperoxidase activity, and maintained or lowered serum transaminases, indicating muscle tissue protection.

Cytokine findings and conclusion: exercise decreased interleukin-6 and interleukin-1β after 21 days in basal conditions, unaffected by supplementation; overall conclusion that lemon verbena protects neutrophils and reduces muscle damage without blocking exercise adaptation.

Final conclusion sentence: moderate lemon verbena antioxidant supplementation protects neutrophils from oxidative damage and reduces muscle damage signs during chronic running exercise while preserving cellular adaptation.

Abstract opening: background that exercise improves longevity and insulin resistance via mitochondrial ROS, and the study question of whether antioxidant supplements (vitamins C and E) alter these exercise benefits, including the vitamin dosing.

Study design: the vitamin C and E intervention and the hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp measuring insulin sensitivity (GIR) in untrained and pretrained healthy young men over a 4-week exercise intervention, with baseline and post-intervention measurements.

Main results on insulin sensitivity: exercise raised GIR and plasma adiponectin only without antioxidants, in both untrained and pretrained men, with the P-values reported; also describes the methods of muscle biopsies, gene expression, and plasma sampling.
Mechanistic results: exercise increased ROS-sensitive transcriptional regulators PPARγ and coactivators PGC1α and PGC1β only in the absence of antioxidants, with significance levels stated.

Endogenous antioxidant defense: exercise induced SOD1, SOD2, and glutathione peroxidase, an effect blocked by antioxidant supplementation, leading to the mitohormesis interpretation that exercise-induced oxidative stress drives adaptive benefits.

Conclusion: exercise-induced oxidative stress is proposed to improve insulin resistance and boost antioxidant capacity, and the paper concludes that antioxidant supplements may prevent these health benefits of exercise in humans.

Opening chunk of a sports nutrition Q&A on whether diet can limit exercise-induced immunodepression; covers how prolonged/heavy training weakens immune function, the need for a balanced diet meeting energy, carbohydrate, protein, and micronutrient needs, and carbohydrate intake during strenuous exercise blunting stress hormone rises and immune suppression.

Middle chunk of the same nutrition and immunity document; discusses evidence that antioxidant vitamin supplementation may reduce exercise stress and leukocyte impairment, and notes that further research is needed on other antioxidants and dietary immunostimulants like probiotics and echinacea.
Final short chunk of the document, completing the sentence on research needed for probiotics and echinacea as dietary immunostimulants against exercise-induced immune impairment in athletes.

Introduction to a review on free radicals in skin and muscle, framing antioxidants traditionally as protectors against metabolism-produced free radical damage, and introducing their possible subtler role in regulating oxidant-induced gene expression.

Continues the review's argument that free radicals act as signals for cell adaptation across cell types, noting ongoing research into how they influence gene expression, and that this is especially relevant for tissues routinely under variable oxidative stress.
Concludes the introduction by naming the example tissues most affected by routine oxidative stress: skin exposed to UV light and skeletal muscle subjected to repeated exercise bouts.

Introduction and aims of a study on acute pre-exercise dark chocolate (high polyphenol) intake and its effects on antioxidant status, oxidative stress and immunoendocrine responses to prolonged exercise.

Methods and early results: 14 healthy men cycled 2.5 h at ~60% VO2max after consuming dark chocolate, control bar, or nothing; reports pre-exercise antioxidant status and F2-isoprostane (oxidative stress) findings.

Results on oxidative stress and insulin: dark chocolate raised pre-exercise antioxidant status and trended toward lower post-exercise F2-isoprostane, with plasma insulin significantly higher than the control bar trial pre- and 1 h post-exercise.

Results on glucose and immunoendocrine outcomes: dark chocolate better maintained plasma glucose during exercise, and no between-trial differences were found for HPA axis hormones, IL-6, leukocytosis, neutrophilia or neutrophil function.

Conclusion section summarising that acute dark chocolate consumption affects insulin, glucose, antioxidant and oxidative stress responses but has minimal effects on immunoendocrine responses to prolonged exercise.
Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that acute dark chocolate intake has minimal effects on immunoendocrine responses to prolonged exercise.

Introduction to a study on legume-derived polyphenols and flavonoids as xanthine oxidase inhibitors, covering XO's role in exercise-related free radicals and in diseases such as vascular disorders, cancer, and gout.

Study aims and methods: polyphenolic fractions and pure compounds from Vicia faba and Lotus edulis extracts were tested for XO inhibition, with the first fraction IC50 results reported for Vicia faba.

Key results: IC50 ranges for the Vicia faba and Lotus edulis fractions, Ki values of 13–767 µM for pure polyphenolic compounds, and the inhibition modes, with ten non-competitive inhibitors and one competitive inhibitor.

Conclusions: flavonoid isolates from legume extracts are presented as novel natural XO inhibitors, with ongoing mode-of-action research aimed at drug design for conditions involving excess XO activity.

Background and study aim of a study on calcified neurocysticercosis in primary headache: prior evidence of association and the question of whether neurocysticercosis is more common in headache patients than in other neurological disorders.

Methods: cohort design over 20 years at one institution, comparing neurocysticercosis prevalence in primary headache patients against four control groups (cerebrovascular disease, degenerative CNS disorders, head trauma, primary brain tumors).

Results: overall neurocysticercosis prevalence was 4.7% in primary headache patients (48/1017) versus 1.8% in controls (31/1687), with p<0.0001; calcified parenchymal cysticerci are highlighted as more frequent in headache patients than in the cerebrovascular, degenerative, and head trauma control groups.

Results continued: group-by-group comparisons of calcified parenchymal cysticerci showing headache patients exceeded cerebrovascular disease, degenerative CNS disorders, and head trauma controls, while no significant difference appeared versus the primary brain tumor controls (4.7% vs 3.5%).

Conclusions: a relationship exists between calcified neurocysticercosis and primary headache disorders, with a proposed mechanism that periodic remodeling of cysticercotic calcifications releases antigens into brain parenchyma, contributing to headache.

Final sentence of the conclusions, completing the proposed mechanism: antigen liberation from remodeling cysticercotic calcifications into the brain parenchyma may contribute to headache in these patients.

Abstract opening of a longitudinal study on cognitive status and quality of life in neurocysticercosis (NCC), a parasitic CNS infection; describes the aim and the Sabogal Hospital setting in Lima, Peru.
Study design and participants: a longitudinal study of new-onset NCC cases, with 14 NCC patients, 14 healthy neighborhood controls, and 7 epilepsy controls recruited at the Lima, Peru hospital.
Methods: standardized neuropsychological battery and brain MRI (NCC patients only) at baseline and 6 months, with NCC results compared to controls at both time points.

Key results: at baseline NCC patients scored lower on attention tasks than epilepsy controls (not healthy controls); after 6 months of anti-parasitic treatment, psychomotor speed improved significantly; baseline QoL was impaired in NCC and epilepsy groups.

Further findings and conclusions: QoL social function improved at 6 months in NCC patients (p=0.006); newly diagnosed NCC patients showed mild cognitive deficits and greater QoL decline than controls, with improvement after treatment.
Author summary restating the background: NCC is a common CNS parasitic infection and its cognitive effects have been frequently reported but poorly studied.

Author summary on study recruitment and procedures: new-onset NCC cases were matched with healthy and epilepsy controls in Lima, Peru, and all groups completed neuropsychological testing at baseline and 6 months.
Author summary on key takeaways: NCC patients showed mild cognitive deficits and worse baseline QoL, and both cognition and QoL improved after treatment.
Closing statement claiming this is the first longitudinal assessment of cognition and QoL in NCC patients, offering new data on an important clinical morbidity outcome.

Study on Taenia solium cysticerci: a culture method for scolex evagination is used to test how low temperatures affect parasite survival, finding refrigeration above 0 °C harmless but freezing of infested pork kills cysts.

Concludes the study with practical freezing guidelines for killing cysticerci in pork muscle (4 days at -5 °C, 3 days at -15 °C, 1 day at -24 °C) and notes these measures could prevent the most common parasitic infection of the human central nervous system.
Final phrase of the document's concluding sentence, stating the public-health target: the central nervous system parasitosis that the freezing measures aim to prevent.

Opening of a document on neurocysticercosis and oncogenesis, introducing the hypothesis that neurocysticercosis is a cancer risk factor and listing the first proposed mechanism: parasite-induced modulation of host immune surveillance.

Continues the list of proposed oncogenic mechanisms (genetic material transfer from the parasite causing DNA damage, and chronic inflammation with nitric oxide and tumor suppressor gene inhibition), then calls for further research to confirm cysticercosis's role in cancer.

Describes specific research needs: identifying cysticercotic factors that transfer genetic material and checking for tumor suppressor gene mutations in proliferating astrocytes near cysticercotic lesions, plus the start of the call to study host immune and cytokine interactions.

Concluding sentence of the document, stating that the interaction between host immune state, cytokine release, and nitric oxide-releasing inflammatory cells (causing DNA damage and impairing tumor suppression) still needs investigation.

Abstract opening (Objectives): introduces polyphenols from plant foods as compounds that fight oxidative stress and support synaptic plasticity, positioning them as broad-acting, non-traditional options for cognitive and mental health and neurodegenerative recovery.

Abstract Objectives continued: frames diet, specifically the molecular link between food intake and brain function, as a possible viable approach to treating cognitive and psychiatric disorders, and begins the Methods description.

Abstract Methods and start of Results: states the review will cover molecular pathways linking polyphenols, the gut, and the brain, plus human and animal studies on polyphenol effects on brain plasticity and cognition, and begins the Results on energy metabolism and signaling.

Abstract Results and Conclusion: explains that dietary factors affect brain plasticity via energy metabolism and signaling pathways, then concludes that polyphenol-rich diets may be a non-invasive, natural, inexpensive therapy for brain health.
Final sentence of the abstract Conclusion: restates that dietary manipulation with polyphenol-enriched diets could support a healthy brain as a non-invasive, natural, low-cost therapeutic option.
Opening of a 2009 California statewide hospital discharge study of neurocysticercosis (NCC): case count, incidence, and demographics (ethnicity, sex, average age).
Continuation of the demographics: geographic distribution of hospitalizations (Southern California, Los Angeles County) and sex differences in severity, hydrocephalus, and length of stay.
Sex differences in hospitalization costs, the six recorded deaths, total NCC-related charges and estimated costs, and the study's conclusion on economic burden in California.
Author Summary introduction: NCC as a neglected poverty-related infection, California's high burden, and under-reporting despite NCC being reportable.
Author Summary describing the study's aims (NCC hospitalization distribution, demographics, and 2009 charges) and key finding that most cases are in Southern California, mainly Los Angeles County.
Author Summary on men's longer, costlier hospitalizations with more severe disease such as hydrocephalus, which suggests extraparenchymal infection.
Author Summary on unexplained gender differences in NCC severity (not due to care-seeking delay or language barrier) and the economic burden of hospital care in California.
Final sentence of the summary, restating the considerable economic burden NCC imposes in California.

Introduction to a 2012 AWHONN case study on neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium pork tapeworm infection) in pregnancy, covering its global prevalence, its severity when the parasite invades the central nervous system, and rising US cases linked to immigration from endemic areas.

Concluding part of the introduction to a 2012 AWHONN case study of a pregnant woman at 35 weeks' gestation with neurocysticercosis, stating that the study covers an evidence-based approach to diagnosis, treatment, and eradication of this preventable infection.

Study methods on a cohort of 90 untreated neurocysticercosis (NCC) patients: baseline cognitive testing (MMSE, NCSE, IQCODE), DSM-IV dementia classification, imaging and CSF data, with cognitive measures repeated six months after albendazole and steroid treatment.

Key results: 15.5% (n=14) of NCC patients had dementia at baseline, associated with older age, lower education, and more brain parasitic lesions (frontal, temporal, parietal); cognitive measures were re-assessed six months post-treatment.
Follow-up outcomes: after six months, 21.5% of the dementia group still met DSM-IV dementia criteria while 78.5% no longer did, though some retained mild cognitive decline.
Conclusion of the NCC dementia study: dementia is common in untreated neurocysticercosis and is reversible in most cases, suggesting treatment can resolve it.
Introduces neurocysticercosis (NCC), a CNS infection caused by Taenia larval cysts, and notes factors behind its endemicity and how inflammation may be out of proportion to cyst count.

Continues on diagnostic difficulty when inflammation is disproportionate to cysts, especially in low-endemic or resource-poor regions, and classifies CNS cysticerci into isolated cysts (CC) and racemose cysts (CR) by location.
