Describes the clinical picture of NCC: two core syndromes (epilepsy and intracranial hypertension), varying severity and course (asymptomatic to fatal, acute to chronic, remission or exacerbation).
Covers CSF findings, which may be normal even with viable cysts, and the role of CT and MRI for non-invasive diagnosis, noting their risk of false negatives.
Addresses treatment: it is controversial and individualised, with praziquantel and albendazole as the common cysticidal drugs and steroids or dexchlorpheniramine as anti-inflammatory options.

Discusses hydrocephalus as a common complication, requiring ventriculoperitoneal shunting before cysticidal treatment, and notes that surgical removal of cysts can eliminate the surrounding inflammation.

Summarises variable disease progression (simple or complicated, remission with or without treatment, symptoms that may fade or persist) and lists unresolved topics: fourth ventricle syndrome, chronic brain oedema, psychiatric complaints, low CSF glucose, and re-infection.
Final sentence closing the abstract, stating that the unresolved issues (including low CSF glucose and re-infection) are discussed in the paper.

Opening of the document: introduces neurocysticercosis (NCC) as the most common parasitic brain disease, notes CT/MRI imaging defines diagnosis, and states treatment (antihelmintics, steroids, symptomatic drugs, surgery) is individualized per case.

Middle of the document: explains that treatment choice depends on number, location, and biological stage of lesions plus inflammatory response, and that epilepsy is the typical presentation of parenchymal NCC while hydrocephalus typifies meningeal NCC.

Closing of the document: restates that parenchymal NCC most often presents as epilepsy and meningeal NCC as hydrocephalus, then concludes that eradication of cysticercosis is achievable through public education and sanitation in endemic areas.

Introduction/objectives of a cross-sectional controlled study on cognitive impairment and dementia in neurocysticercosis (NCYST, a CNS parasitic infection), motivating comparison with healthy controls and cryptogenic epilepsy patients.

Methods section: 40 treatment-naive NCYST patients (mean age 39.25 years, active lesions on MRI) underwent cognitive and functional evaluation and were compared with 49 healthy controls and 28 cryptogenic epilepsy patients matched for age, education, and seizure frequency.

Results section comparing NCYST patients with healthy controls: significant deficits in executive function, verbal and nonverbal memory, constructive praxis, and verbal fluency (p < 0.05), and introduction of the dementia finding.

Results continued: 12.5% of NCYST patients met DSM-IV dementia criteria; compared with cryptogenic epilepsy patients, NCYST patients showed impairments in working/episodic verbal memory, executive function, naming, verbal fluency, praxis, and visuospatial orientation.

Conclusions and correlation findings: cognitive scores did not correlate with lesion number, location, or type on MRI; cognitive impairment was widespread in active NCYST and not explained by antiepileptic drug use or seizure frequency.
Final conclusion: dementia was present in a significant proportion of NCYST patients, broadening understanding of NCYST's clinical presentation and its public health impact.

Opening of a case report on neurocysticercosis (NCC) and cerebral aneurysm: a 49-year-old woman with subarachnoid haemorrhage from a right MCA bifurcation aneurysm, with a viable cysticercus found distal to the aneurysm at surgery and no inflammation noted.

Middle portion of the case report covering postoperative treatment with albendazole and dextrochlorpheniramine, the three-year asymptomatic follow-up with drugs for seizure and hypertension prevention, and the start of the discussion on the NCC-aneurysm relationship.
Final sentence of the abstract, stating that the paper discusses the relationship between neurocysticercosis and the presence of cerebral aneurysm.

Study design and methods for a 38-outpatient cross-sectional study of psychiatric morbidity in neurocysticercosis, describing diagnostic imaging/CSF criteria and the psychiatric and cognitive assessment instruments used.
Main results: psychiatric signs found in 65.8% and cognitive decline in 87.5% of patients, with depression the most common psychiatric diagnosis (52.6%) and 14.2% psychotic.

Risk factors and non-correlates of psychiatric morbidity: active disease and intracranial hypertension were linked to higher morbidity, prior mood disorder to current depression, while lesion number/type, neuropsychological severity, epilepsy, and steroid use showed no correlation.

Conclusions on clinical significance: depression syndromes are frequent in neurocysticercosis, and mild cognitive impairment, though rarely considered a cause of dementia, may be far more prevalent than assumed.

Discussion of mechanism: it remains unclear how far organic brain-lesion mechanisms drive the mental changes, but matching sex distribution in depressed and non-depressed patients and the observed correlations support an organic causal role.
Closing sentence of the conclusions, restating that the evidence points to organic factors contributing to these psychiatric and cognitive syndromes in neurocysticercosis.

Opening of the document's abstract: states the review's objective (estimating magnitude and disease pattern of human cysticercosis in Canada) and methods (MEDLINE and manual search of case reports/series, extracting year, citizenship, clinical manifestations, and form).

Middle of the abstract's findings: 21 articles reporting 60 Canadian cysticercosis patients, two-thirds diagnosed in the last two decades, most cases from Ontario and Quebec, and immigrants making up 96% of cases with known citizenship.

Clinical findings section of the abstract: neurocysticercosis in 55 patients versus isolated striated muscle involvement in five; seizures as primary or sole manifestation in 72%, mostly with parenchymal brain cysticerci; and Taenia egg positivity in two of seven tested patients, with no household contacts investigated for taeniasis.
Conclusion of the abstract: reports an increase in Canadian cysticercosis cases over the past two decades, suggesting rising prevalence, and notes that most cases are in immigrants.
Final sentence of the conclusions: acknowledges that at least some patients may have acquired cysticercosis domestically within Canada despite most cases being immigrants.

Introduces the study's background on multiple myeloma bone involvement and the imaging modalities used (WBSS, MR, 18F-FDG PET/CT), setting up the rationale that low FDG uptake in MM lesions motivates testing 11C-Choline.
Describes the study aim and methods: ten MM patients underwent 11C-Choline and 18F-FDG PET/CT within one week, with lesions compared by number, site, and SUVmax.
Reports the patient-level results: concordance patterns between 11C-Choline and 18F-FDG PET/CT (4 negative, 2 identical positive, 4 positive but differing lesion counts).
Presents the quantitative findings: higher mean SUVmax for Choline (5 vs 3.8, P=0.042) and total lesion detection of 37 for Choline vs 22 for FDG, a non-significant difference (P=0.8).

States the conclusion that 11C-Choline appears more sensitive than 18F-FDG for detecting myelomatous bone lesions and may be a more appropriate functional imaging complement to MRI for MM bone staging, pending larger studies.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the recommendation that 11C-Choline PET/CT paired with MRI could be used for MM bone staging.

Abstract opening of a 2010s-era clinical trial on the Beef in an Optimal Lean Diet (BOLD) study: background on lean beef and LDL cholesterol, and the study objective comparing DASH, BOLD, BOLD+ and a healthy American diet (HAD).

Study objective continued, defining the four dietary arms by daily beef amount (DASH 28 g, BOLD 113 g, BOLD+ 153 g) against the HAD comparator, followed by the start of the design section describing the randomized population of hypercholesterolemic adults.

Design section of the BOLD trial: 36 hypercholesterolemic participants randomly assigned to four 5-week diets, with macronutrient and beef-intake profiles for HAD, DASH, BOLD and BOLD+, and the start of the results on cholesterol changes.
Results section reporting reductions in total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol after the DASH, BOLD and BOLD+ diets relative to the HAD diet, with mean changes in mmol/L.

Results on apolipoproteins: decreases in apolipoprotein A-I, C-III and C-III bound to apoA1 particles after BOLD and BOLD+ versus HAD, and a greater apolipoprotein B decrease with BOLD+ than HAD (P < 0.05).

Results on baseline C-reactive protein (CRP) subgroups, showing LDL and total cholesterol reductions by CRP level for DASH, BOLD and BOLD+, followed by the start of the conclusions on low-SFA heart-healthy diets with lean beef.
Conclusions of the trial: low-SFA heart-healthy diets with lean beef produce CVD lipid and lipoprotein benefits comparable to the DASH pattern, with apolipoprotein benefits from BOLD and BOLD+.
Closing conclusion of the BOLD trial supporting lean beef in heart-healthy diets, noting BOLD+ had greater apolipoprotein benefits, and the clinicaltrials.gov registration number NCT00937898.

Introduces the study's rationale: cheese, despite high saturated fat, appears not to raise LDL cholesterol versus equal-fat butter, possibly due to its calcium boosting fecal fat excretion. Sets out the trial's objectives.

Describes the objectives (blood pressure, serum lipids, CRP, glucose, insulin, and fecal fat across cheese, butter, and habitual diets) and the randomized crossover design with a 14-day run-in and two 6-week periods.
Details the methods: 49 participants who replaced 13% of energy from dietary fat with cheese or butter, in a randomized crossover design preceded by a habitual-diet run-in period.

Reports the results: after 6 weeks cheese lowered total, LDL, and HDL cholesterol and raised glucose versus butter; cheese did not raise total or LDL cholesterol relative to the run-in; fecal fat did not differ between periods.
States the conclusions: cheese lowers LDL cholesterol versus equal-fat butter and does not raise it relative to a habitual diet, followed by the trial registration.
Trial registration identifier NCT01140165 (clinicaltrials.gov), the final fragment of the abstract's conclusion section.

Introduction to the review on fruit/vegetable-drug interactions: phytochemicals in produce can alter drug absorption and pharmacology via drug transporters and drug-metabolizing enzymes, mainly in the intestine and liver.

Mechanism section: phytochemicals at high concentrations in intestine and liver can alter cytochrome P450 and other enzyme activity, affecting drugs with extensive first-pass metabolism; transitions into the gap in nutrient-drug interaction knowledge.

Gap statement: despite many nutrient-drug interaction studies and reviews, no general conclusions exist on how nutrient-drug interactions affect drug bioavailability; unintended consequences of combined nutrient and drug use are noted, and many phytochemicals have documented pharmacokinetic interactions.

Scope of the review: limited to commonly consumed fruits and vegetables with beneficial nutritional and folk-medicine value, and it lists the specific fruits (grapefruit, orange, tangerine, grapes, cranberry, pomegranate, mango, guava, black raspberry, black mulberry) whose phytochemistry and pharmacokinetic interactions are discussed.

Remaining listed produce (apple, broccoli, cauliflower, watercress, spinach, tomato, carrot, avocado) and the conclusion that knowledge of nutrient-drug interaction risks is limited, so efforts to identify food-drug risks should be intensified.
Closing conclusion: calls for intensified efforts to elucidate food-drug interaction risks to prevent harmful clinical outcomes, followed by the 2011 Institute of Food Technologists copyright notice.

Background and rationale from a study of grapefruit intake and postmenopausal breast cancer risk: explains that grapefruit inhibits CYP3A4, which metabolizes oestrogens, so grapefruit may raise plasma oestrogen and thus breast cancer risk.

Study design and population from the Multiethnic Cohort Study (Hawaii–Los Angeles): a prospective cohort of over 50,000 postmenopausal women across five racial/ethnic groups, with 1657 incident breast cancer cases analyzed.

Key results of the grapefruit–breast cancer study: highest intake (one-quarter grapefruit or more daily) vs non-consumers was associated with increased breast cancer risk (RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.06–1.58; Ptrend=0.015).

Subgroup findings and conclusion: similar increased risk among oestrogen therapy users, oestrogen+progestin users, and never hormone users, concluding grapefruit intake may raise breast cancer risk in postmenopausal women.
Introduction/background of a 12-week randomized trial in obese adults comparing grapefruit, grapefruit juice, and water preloads (energy density and preload form for weight control).
Methods: study design, 85 obese adults (BMI 30-39.9) randomized to 127 g grapefruit, grapefruit juice, or water preload after a 2-week caloric restriction phase.

Methods continued: preloads matched for weight, calories, water content, and energy density; outcomes measured weekly and at endpoints (blood pressure, weight, anthropometry, dietary intake, resting energy expenditure, body composition, cardiometabolic biomarkers).

Results: total food grams unchanged, but dietary energy density and energy intake fell 20-29% with preloads plus caloric restriction; 7.1% overall weight loss with significant fat and waist reductions.
Results: no significant between-group differences in body composition, but HDL-cholesterol rose in grapefruit (+6.2%) and grapefruit juice (+8.2%) groups versus a decline in the water group (-3.7%).

Conclusions: low energy dense preloads with caloric restriction are an effective weight loss strategy, but preload form (solid vs liquid) did not differentially affect energy balance, weight, or body composition; grapefruit groups had better lipid profiles.
Closing conclusion on lipid benefits for grapefruit and grapefruit juice groups, followed by the ClinicalTrials.gov registration number NCT00581074.

Introduction of a study on grapefruit juice and naringenin inhibiting CYP1A2-mediated caffeine metabolism: describes the in vitro finding that naringin is a competitive inhibitor of caffeine 3-demethylation in human liver microsomes.

In vivo results of the caffeine study: grapefruit juice containing naringin reduced caffeine oral clearance by 23% and prolonged its half-life by 31% (n=12), with the conclusion that grapefruit juice and naringenin inhibit CYP1A2 in humans.

Concluding statement of the grapefruit juice and CYP1A2 caffeine study: despite the inhibition, the modest effect on caffeine clearance implies grapefruit juice likely lacks clinically significant interactions with other CYP1A2 substrate drugs.
Introduction and methods overview: comparison of bioactive compounds and antioxidant potential in red vs. blond grapefruit, and the study population of hypertriglyceridemic patients.
Study design: 57 hyperlipidemic post-coronary bypass patients aged 39-72 randomly assigned to red, blond, or control groups (19 each) over a 30-day trial, with antioxidant assays listed.
Intervention and measurements: red or blond groups received one fresh grapefruit daily for 30 days, and serum lipids and antioxidant activity were measured before and after the trial.

Results on lipid changes: reductions in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides in the red and blond groups compared with the control group after treatment, with percentage decreases given.
Control group results and conclusions: no lipid changes in controls, and red grapefruit has higher bioactive content and antioxidant potential than blond grapefruit.
Conclusions on dietary benefit: red grapefruit supplementation improves serum lipid fractions, especially triglycerides, and antioxidant activity, supporting its use in hyperlipidemic patients.
Final recommendation: adding fresh red grapefruit to accepted diets may benefit hyperlipidemic, especially hypertriglyceridemic, patients with coronary atherosclerosis.

Introduction to grapefruit-drug interactions: explains that grapefruit affects medication metabolism via intestinal CYP3A4, raising toxicity risk, and lists drug characteristics (CYP3A4 metabolism, low bioavailability, narrow therapeutic index) that make interactions likely.

Names the prominent drug classes that interact with grapefruit (statins, antiarrhythmics, immunosuppressants, calcium channel blockers) and notes that equally effective non-interacting alternatives exist and can be substituted.
Concludes the management guidance: substituting alternative drugs when a patient has or is at risk of an interaction, or avoiding grapefruit in favor of other fruits, including other citrus, instead.

Introduces the EPIC cohort study of grapefruit intake and breast cancer risk, with a rationale based on grapefruit's inhibition of CYP3A4 and possible effects on estrogen metabolism; describes the study population of 114,504 women.

Methods and results overview: median 9.5-year follow-up, 3,747 incident breast cancers, grapefruit consumption prevalence (59% eat it, 4% at least 60 g/day), and the Cox proportional hazards modeling approach with its covariate adjustments.

Main finding: no association between grapefruit intake and breast cancer risk; the highest intake group (60+ g/day) had HR 0.93 (95% CI 0.77-1.13) versus non-consumers, with no significant linear trend (p=0.5).

Subgroup analyses show no relationship between grapefruit intake and breast cancer risk in premenopausal, postmenopausal, or HRT-stratified women, and no association with estradiol or estrone levels in postmenopausal women.
Concluding statement: the EPIC study found no evidence that grapefruit intake is associated with breast cancer risk.

Study design section of a grapefruit and metabolic syndrome trial: 91 obese patients randomized to four arms (placebo capsules with apple juice, grapefruit capsules, grapefruit juice, or fresh grapefruit half before meals), with metabolic parameters measured over 12 weeks.

Weight loss results after 12 weeks of the grapefruit trial: fresh grapefruit lost 1.6 kg, grapefruit juice 1.5 kg, grapefruit capsules 1.1 kg, and placebo 0.3 kg, with fresh grapefruit significantly outperforming placebo (P < .05).

Secondary and statistical findings from the grapefruit study: in obese patients with metabolic syndrome, all three grapefruit groups lost significantly more weight than placebo (P < .02), introducing the insulin outcome.

Key conclusions on insulin and weight: grapefruit reduced 2-hour post-glucose insulin versus placebo, fresh grapefruit before meals produced significant weight loss, the effect extended to grapefruit products in metabolic syndrome patients, and insulin resistance improved with fresh grapefruit.
Closing conclusion of the grapefruit weight-loss study: the mechanism is unknown, but including grapefruit in a weight reduction diet appears reasonable based on the trial's findings.

Opening of the abstract for a review on grapefruit's metabolic and cardiovascular effects; introduces grapefruit as a nutritious fruit and begins describing its drug interactions involving CYP3A4 metabolism of prescribed drugs.

Continues the abstract by explaining the mechanism of grapefruit-drug interactions via intestinal CYP3A4, P-glycoprotein, and organic cation transporters, and notes that the clinical impact is under-documented because many cases go unreported.

Concludes the abstract by noting grapefruit's flavonoid-related benefits for diabetes and cardiovascular disorders, framing the review's dual focus on both the risks and the therapeutic potential of grapefruit.
Final fragment of the abstract, closing the sentence that says the review addresses this potentially explosive subject.
Introduces the study comparing fruit versus oat cookies added to free-living women's diets, matched for fiber and calories but differing in energy density; sets up the Rio de Janeiro clinical trial.
Describes the trial design: 49 women aged 30-50 with BMI over 25 randomized to add apples, pears, or oat cookies (with their energy densities) for 10 weeks, with similar fiber content (~6g).
Covers the statistical method (mixed models for repeated measures) and the main result that apples and pears significantly lowered energy density relative to the oat group during follow-up.
Reports energy intake and body weight outcomes: intake fell for apple and pear groups but rose slightly for oats, and apple and pear groups lost weight while the oat group's weight was unchanged.
Concludes that the energy density of fruits, independent of fiber content, can reduce energy intake and body weight over time.
Introduces a pharmacokinetic study of grapefruit juice's effect on ethinylestradiol (EE2) bioavailability, comparing it with herbal tea in 13 healthy volunteers after a single 50 microgram oral dose.
Reports the key results: grapefruit juice significantly raised EE2 Cmax to 137% and AUC0-8 to 128% relative to herbal tea, with the associated p-values and ranges.
Concludes that grapefruit juice increases bioavailable EE2, proposes inhibition of metabolic degradation as a likely mechanism, and calls for long-term studies to assess clinical importance.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending with the recommendation that clinical significance of the increased EE2 bioavailability be investigated in long-term studies.

Introduces the background and aim of a randomized controlled trial of daily grapefruit in overweight adults, covering the folklore claim about weight control and prior evidence on blood pressure and lipids.

Describes the trial design: a 3-week low-bioactive washout diet, then randomization of 74 overweight adults to a control diet or daily grapefruit (half a Rio-Red grapefruit three times daily) for 6 weeks.

Reports results: no between-group differences in weight, blood pressure, or lipids, with modest non-significant weight loss, a significant waist circumference reduction, and a significant systolic blood pressure drop versus baseline in the grapefruit group.
Reports within-group lipid changes for the grapefruit group, with total cholesterol down 11.7 mg/dL and LDL down 18.7 mg/dL compared with baseline, both statistically significant.

Gives the study's conclusion: 6 weeks of daily grapefruit did not significantly beat control on weight, lipids, or blood pressure, but the within-group improvements justify further study in obesity and cardiovascular disease prevention.
Closing fragment of the conclusion recommending further evaluation of grapefruit for obesity and cardiovascular disease prevention, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces how the average high-protein, low-produce American diet creates dietary acid load, and how the kidneys and skeleton (bone resorption) respond to buffer it, linking calciuria to net acid excretion.

Explains that food proteins differ in acid-producing potential, that acid-ash proteins drive excessive calcium loss, and begins describing how adding exogenous buffers to a high-protein diet changes the setup.

Describes the effects of adding buffers (chemical salts or fruits and vegetables) to a high-protein diet: less acid urine, lower net acid, ammonium and titratable acid excretion, decreased calciuria, halted bone resorption, and possible bone accretion, plus alkali buffers reversing acid-induced calcium loss.
Concludes that excessive protein from high renal acid load foods harms bone unless offset by alkali-rich foods or supplements.
Introduction framing the long-standing question of why dietary protein increases urinary calcium, and the historical assumption that bone is the source of this excess calcium.

Explains the acid-load hypothesis that protein-driven bone resorption would weaken the skeleton, notes that no definitive intervention trials support it, and introduces the lab's new finding that protein affects intestinal calcium absorption.

Describes the lab's short-term adult trials with low, medium, and high protein diets, reporting hypercalciuria on high protein and an unexpected secondary hyperparathyroidism within 4 days on low protein.

Details the mechanism: low protein lowered intestinal calcium absorption (measured with dual stable calcium isotopes), which drove the persistent secondary hyperparathyroidism lasting about two weeks.
Discusses the unknown long-term skeletal consequences of low-protein-induced calcium changes, citing epidemiological links between low protein intake, reduced bone density, and bone loss.
Concludes with the call for studies to determine whether low protein intake directly alters bone resorption, bone formation, or both.

Introduction and methods of a study on age-related changes in systemic acid-base balance, describing the collection of blood acid-base data from healthy adults and the variables extracted (blood [H+], plasma bicarbonate, PCO2, age) for 61 age-group means.

Methods and principal results: linear regression across eight 10-year age intervals (20 to 100 years) showing that increasing age is associated with rising blood hydrogen ion concentration and falling plasma bicarbonate, both highly significant (p < .001), suggesting a progressive low-level metabolic acidosis.

Results and interpretation: blood PCO2 declines with age (p < .05), consistent with respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis, and the acidosis is attributed partly to the normal age-related decline in renal function.
Concluding statement of the abstract: the potential role of age-related metabolic acidosis in the pathogenesis of degenerative diseases of aging is suggested as worthy of further consideration.
Background and rationale: links metabolic acidosis from a high net acid diet (protein and cereals vs. fruit and vegetables) to muscle wasting and lean mass loss in older adults, motivating the study.

Study objective and design: tests whether 24-h urinary potassium and a fruit/vegetable dietary index are associated with percent lean body mass or its change, in 384 adults aged 65+ from a 3-year calcium and vitamin D trial.

Methods: 24-h urine potassium measured at baseline; percent lean body mass (non-fat, non-bone tissue weight divided by body weight) measured by DXA at baseline and 3 years, with physical activity, height and weight also assessed.

Results: mean baseline urinary potassium was 67.0 mmol/d; higher potassium was significantly associated with baseline %LBM after adjustment but not with 3-year change, while %LBM rose 2.6% over the study.
Conclusion: higher intake of potassium-rich foods such as fruit and vegetables may help preserve muscle mass in older men and women, consistent with alkaline diets favoring lean tissue.

Background of a study on how urine pH from acidic vs. alkaline diets affects uric acid excretion, questioning the prior finding that alkaline urine promotes uric acid excretion and motivating clearance measurements.

Study rationale and transition to methods: simultaneous serum and urine creatinine and uric acid measurements to calculate clearances, identifying which excretion mechanism explains the unexpected alkaline-urine finding.

Methods describing the dietary design: acidic diets (high protein, low vegetables/fruit) versus alkaline diets (low protein, high vegetables/fruit), developed under a Japanese government health promotion program in a crossover study.

Participants and urine analysis: healthy female university students in consecutive 5-day diet tests, with whole-day urine measured for volume, pH, organic acids, creatinine, uric acid, titratable acid, and cations and anions for acid-base balance.
Blood sampling schedule (early morning fasting on days 1, 3, and 5) for serum creatinine and uric acid, and results opening: urine pH reached steady state after 3 days on the specified diets.

Acid-base findings: net acid generation linearly related to acid excretion, showing urinary H+ derives from food metabolism, and the previously reported linear relationship between uric acid and urine pH is confirmed.

Key clearance finding: among five factors used in clearance calculations, serum and urinary uric acid differed markedly between diets, with higher serum and lower urinary uric acid in the acidic group.

Interpretation: the altered serum and urinary uric acid levels in acidic conditions explain reduced uric acid clearance, suggesting renal tubular reabsorption of uric acid is more active in acidic urine.
Conclusion: the authors conclude that alkaline-prone, nutritionally well-designed diets that alkalize urine are effective for removing uric acid from the body.

Introduction and design of a short-term crossover metabolic study testing whether dietary protein acid load causes hypercalciuria (calcium excretion) linked to nephrolithiasis, using an alkali salt with a high-protein diet.

Study participants (11 healthy volunteers) and the four-phase crossover protocol: control diet (CD) versus eucaloric high-protein diet (HPD adding 60 g/d animal protein) with fixed calcium and sodium content.

Intervention details: during HPD phases, subjects took 30 mEq twice daily of potassium citrate (alkaline salt) or potassium chloride (neutral control), and results showing KCitrate neutralized HPD acid load and raised urinary citrate.

Key results on urinary calcium: HPD raised urinary calcium versus control, with no significant difference between HPD+KCl and HPD+KCitrate (182 vs 170 mg/d, P=0.28); KCitrate also abrogated HPD-induced increases in urinary saturation of calcium oxalate and uric acid.
Conclusions: acid load is not the main driver of short-term HPD-induced hypercalciuria; KCitrate's protective effect against nephrolithiasis works through correcting declines in urine pH and citrate.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that KCitrate's benefit on nephrolithiasis risk with high protein intake is via correction of urine pH and citrate declines.

Introduces the study's research question: whether high-protein diets cause hypercalciuria via bone buffering of dietary acid load, investigated in women using dual stable calcium isotopes to measure calcium kinetics.
Describes the study design: a 2-week lead-in diet followed by 10 days of either moderate (1.0 g/kg) or high (2.1 g/kg) protein diets, given to 13 healthy women in random order.
Reports the main results: intestinal calcium absorption and urinary calcium both rose significantly on the high-protein diet versus moderate, and urinary calcium of bone origin fell significantly.
Concludes that bone turnover trended lower without significant change in net bone balance, so short-term high-protein diets do not appear harmful to bone.

Introduces the abstract's core problem: the unclear net role of dietary protein in bone health, citing the known harms of dietary acid load from sulfur-containing amino acids and protein-driven urinary calcium loss, versus recent studies showing no effect or modest benefit.

Explains the proposed resolution of the contradictory findings: protein has a two-faced relationship with bone, with simultaneous positive and negative pathways, and the positive pathways counter the negative effects of dietary acid load.

Lists the specific positive pathways by which protein may benefit bone (improved calcium absorption, increased insulin-like growth factor 1, greater lean body mass and bone strength) and states the paper reviews mechanisms and literature limitations.

Concludes that considered together, positive and negative pathways suggest protein offers modest bone benefits when dietary calcium and acid-neutralizing fruits and vegetables are adequate; includes the 2011 International Life Sciences Institute copyright notice.
Fragment of the copyright line at the end of the abstract, naming the 2011 International Life Sciences Institute as the copyright holder.
Introduces the review's core finding: high-protein diets cause hypercalciuria and lower urinary pH, which were once thought to promote skeletal demineralization.

Argues that the extra calcium excreted on high-protein diets does not reflect impaired calcium balance, since protein may increase intestinal calcium absorption, and no clinical evidence shows harm to bone except when calcium intake is inadequate.

Notes that high-protein intake supports bone growth and slows bone loss, and that low-protein diets are linked to higher hip fracture risk; also raises the concern that acid and calcium excretion could favor kidney stones and renal disease.

Reports that healthy subjects show no kidney damage from high-protein diets in observational or interventional studies, with possible harm limited to people with pre-existing metabolic renal dysfunction, and concludes that high-protein diets do not cause calcium bone loss.
Closing statement that protein's effect on calcium and bone is complex and depends on other dietary factors and nutrients present in the diet.

Introduction and objective of a cross-sectional study on diet (vegan, lacto-ovo vegetarian, omnivore) and urine pH, comparing excess acid/alkaline ash (EAA) and estimated net acid excretion (NAE) as predictors.

Study design and setting: cross-sectional design with 10 vegan, 16 lacto-ovo vegetarian, and 16 omnivorous women in the Boston area, using six 3-day food records per group to compute EAA and NAE and correlate them with urine pH.
Results begin: mean urine pH by group (vegans 6.15, lacto-ovo vegetarians 5.90, omnivores 5.74; ANOVA P = .013), and EAA and NAE comparisons across the three dietary groups.

Detailed results: EAA did not differ significantly among groups, while mean estimated NAE differed significantly (17.3, 31.3, 42.6 mEq/day; P = .01), with correlations of urine pH to EAA (0.333) and to NAE (-0.768 deattenuated).

Regression result (pH = 6.33 - 0.014 NAE, P = .02, r = -0.54) and the conclusions: habitual diet and estimated NAE predict the likely ranking of urine pH and acid-base status, whereas EAA is not predictive.
Final sentence of the conclusions: EAA calculations were not predictive of urine pH, ending the abstract.

Opening of an abstract-style review of the alkaline diet's health role, describing the PubMed search topics (pH, renal acid load, bone, muscle, growth hormone, back pain, vitamin D, chemotherapy) and review of lay alkaline-diet books against medical literature.
Concluding portion of the same review abstract, stating that an alkaline diet may help reduce morbidity and mortality from chronic diseases and that further studies are warranted.
Study introduction: defines dietary acid load (DAL) and bone mineral density (BMD) concern, states objectives, and describes the NHANES 2005–2008 sample of men and women aged 60+.
Methods: explains how acid load measures NEAP and PRAL (PRALdiet vs. PRALtotal, including supplemental calcium) were computed from 24-hour dietary recalls, with BMD outcomes at hip and lumbar spine.

Methods and early results: describes trend tests across energy-adjusted NEAP/PRAL quartiles and calcium effect-modification analysis at 800 mg/d; reports mean age and that women showed a positive PRALdiet–proximal femur BMD trend.
Results: details null findings for PRALtotal and men overall, and reports a borderline PRALdiet × calcium interaction at the proximal femur in men.

Key results and conclusion: men with dietary calcium under 800 mg/d show an inverse PRALdiet–proximal femur BMD association, none at 800 mg/d or above; no interaction with PRALtotal; overall no DAL–BMD link when supplements are counted.

Discussion and conclusion: summarizes that low calcium intake in men shows an inverse acid load–femur relation, that calcium counteracts DAL's bone effects, and calls for research on very low calcium intake.
Final sentence fragment of the document: recommends further research on how DAL relates to BMD change under very low calcium intake.

Study design and objective: a randomized crossover trial in 16 postmenopausal women comparing a low-protein/low-PRAL diet with a high-protein/high-PRAL diet on calcium absorption and bone metabolism markers.

Diet protein and PRAL values, 7-week diet periods with a 1-week break, the 47Ca whole-body scintillation method, and key results: higher serum IGF-I and lower serum intact PTH on the high-protein diet.

Main calcium findings: high-protein/high-PRAL diet raised fractional 47Ca absorption and urinary calcium excretion, while the net calcium balance (absorbed minus urinary) did not differ between diets, and other bone markers were unaffected.

Summary conclusion: the high-protein, high-PRAL diet increases fractional calcium absorption, partly offsetting higher urinary calcium loss, and the study's interpretation of IGF-I/PTH changes and unchanged bone turnover markers as showing no adverse bone effects.

Final conclusion sentence: increased IGF-I and decreased PTH with no change in bone resorption or formation biomarkers are taken to indicate that a high-protein diet has no adverse effect on bone health.

Background and rationale: links metabolic acidosis from a high net acid diet (protein and cereal grains vs. fruit and vegetables) to lean tissue loss in older adults, motivating the study of potassium and muscle mass.

Study objective and design: examines whether 24-h urinary potassium and a fruit/vegetable dietary index are associated with %LBM or its change, in 384 adults aged 65+ from a 3-year calcium and vitamin D vs. placebo trial.

Methods: urinary potassium measured from 24-h collections at baseline; %LBM calculated as nonfat, nonbone tissue weight divided by total weight, measured by DXA at baseline and 3 years; physical activity, height, and weight also assessed.
Key results: mean baseline urinary potassium was 67.0 mmol/d; it was positively associated with baseline %LBM (beta 0.033, P=0.006) but not with 3-year change, while %LBM rose 2.6% over the study.
Conclusion: the authors suggest that diets rich in potassium, such as fruit and vegetables, may help preserve muscle mass in older men and women.

Introduces the study's aims: estimating the acid-base (PRAL) balance of vegetarian versus non-vegetarian diets, and whether the standard PRAL food list needs extension; describes the matched sample of 30 vegetarians and 30 non-vegetarians aged 18-30.

Describes the method (3-day food diaries scored with the PRAL method) and reports the standard-table results: vegetarians had an alkaline load of -5.4 mEq/d versus an acid load of 10.3 mEq/d for non-vegetarians.
Reports the extended-table PRAL results (vegetarians -10.9 mEq/d alkaline vs non-vegetarians 13.8 mEq/d acid, both p<0.001) and begins the conclusion that vegetarian diets are more alkaline.
Concludes that vegetarian diets produce more alkaline outcomes than non-vegetarian diets and that the standard PRAL table alone is sufficient to discriminate between the two dietary patterns.

Introduction to the document's main claim: the Western diet (low in fruits/vegetables, high in animal products) causes unrecognized diet-induced metabolic acidosis that worsens with age as kidney function declines.

Describes the kidney's compensatory responses to diet-derived metabolic acidosis (removing non-metabolizable anions, conserving citrate, increasing ammoniagenesis and ammonium excretion) and their effect of lowering urine pH.

Explains the urinary consequences of these adaptive processes (hypocitraturia, hypercalciuria, nitrogen and phosphate wasting) and their links to uric acid and calcium stone risk, plus the start of the insulin resistance point.

Covers the metabolic and cardiovascular implications of acidosis: mild acidosis causes muscle insulin resistance, and dietary acid load may predict metabolic and cardiovascular risk across several populations, including diabetes and chronic kidney disease.

Summarizes the link between high dietary acid load and diabetes/hypertension, and reports observational evidence associating insulin resistance with acidosis markers (low bicarbonate, high anion gap, hypocitraturia, low urine pH).
Copyright notice from Elsevier Ltd and the European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (2011), marking the end of the document.

Introduces the study's aim: examining whether vegetable intake affects breast cancer recurrence, with stratification by tamoxifen use and a focus on cruciferous vegetables based on phytochemical evidence.
Describes the methods: a secondary analysis of 3,080 breast cancer survivors from the WHEL Study, using vegetable intake from repeated 24-hour dietary recalls.
Covers the study population and analysis plan: participants averaged 23.5 months post-diagnosis at enrollment, and recurrence hazard was modeled overall and in tamoxifen users.

Reports the main results: baseline intake levels (about 3.1 total and 0.5 cruciferous servings/day) and hazard ratios for recurrence comparing highest vs. lowest vegetable intake tertiles, overall (HR 0.69) and in tamoxifen users (HR 0.56 total, 0.65 cruciferous).

Presents the combined-intake subgroup findings: tamoxifen users with high cruciferous intake above the median and top-tertile total vegetable intake had the lowest recurrence hazard (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.32-0.70).
Summarizes the conclusion that vegetable intake may reduce recurrence or new events, especially with tamoxifen, while noting the need for further study.
Final caveat: vegetable intake may simply be a marker for other health-promoting behaviors, a confounding possibility that cannot be ruled out.
Introduction to the UK DietCompLyf study: motivation for examining how breast cancer diagnosis changes survivors' diet, using pre- and post-diagnosis food frequency questionnaires in 1,560 patients.
Results on diet after breast cancer diagnosis: significant increases in fruit and vegetables, wholegrains and lean protein intake, measured by FFQs about one year post-diagnosis.
Results on diet decreases after diagnosis: reduced high-fat/high-sugar products, red meat, coffee, some alcohol and refined grains, plus accompanying macronutrient, vitamin and mineral changes.

Supplement use results: prevalence rose from 56.1% pre-diagnosis to 62.8% post-diagnosis, with fish oils, multivitamins/minerals and evening primrose oil most used; oestrogenic botanical supplement use more than doubled to 8.4%.
Conclusion summarizing that British breast cancer patients in the DietCompLyf study significantly changed dietary intake and supplement use after diagnosis.
Closing statement on the significance of the findings for understanding female cancer survivors' dietary behaviours and developing recommendations.

Introduction and study design: this chunk opens the abstract of a European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC) study of macronutrient intake and urothelial cell carcinoma (bladder cancer) risk among 469,339 participants, describing the Cox regression methods and covariate adjustments.

Methods and main cohort results: this chunk covers the Cox regression adjustments (sex, age, centre, smoking, BMI, total energy) and reports 11.3 years of follow-up with 1,416 incident urothelial cell carcinoma cases, then begins the key finding on animal protein.

Key findings on protein and other nutrients: this chunk reports that higher animal protein energy intake was associated with about 15% higher risk, plant protein with about 23% lower risk (with confidence intervals and trend p-values), and that fat, carbohydrate, fibre and calcium showed no association.
Conclusion: this chunk concludes that animal and/or plant protein may influence urothelial cell carcinoma risk, calls for replication in other studies, and carries the 2012 UICC copyright notice.

Opening of the abstract for a randomized pilot trial of a dietary intervention in men with recurrent prostate cancer after primary treatment; introduces the aim of testing a plant-based, fish-emphasizing diet and its effects on quality of life and PSA velocity.

Methods section of the prostate cancer diet pilot trial: 36 men and partners randomized to 11 dietary/cooking classes with mindfulness practice or a wait-list control, with assessments at baseline, 11 weeks, and 3 months post-intervention.

Results section of the prostate cancer dietary trial: intervention group reduced saturated fat and animal proteins (including dairy), increased vegetable proteins and quality of life, with PSA doubling time findings introduced.

Final results and conclusions of the prostate cancer diet pilot trial: no significant difference in PSA increase rate between groups, longer PSA doubling time in the intervention group at 3 months, and conclusion that men with rising PSA can adopt a prostate-healthy diet with improved QOL.

Conclusions of the prostate cancer diet trial: no significant difference in log PSA slope between groups, but substantially increased PSA doubling time in the intervention group versus controls, followed by a call for larger, longer future trials.

Final sentence of the abstract for the prostate cancer dietary intervention pilot trial, recommending future trials with a larger sample of men and longer follow-up to study the prostate-healthy diet.

Introduction and study design of a pilot prostate cancer dietary program: motivation for diet change in recurrent CaP, the A:V (animal:vegetable protein) ratio as the outcome measure, and the 11-week dietary/cooking classes with mindfulness training.

Study population and methods: 36 men with recurrent prostate cancer randomized to the mindfulness-integrated dietary intervention or wait-list control, with assessments at baseline, 3 and 6 months, and completion numbers (14 of 17 intervention, 17 of 19 control).

Key results: intervention group showed a significant decrease in A:V ratio at 3 months versus controls (p=.01) that was maintained at follow-up (p=0.049), and A:V ratio correlated with lycopene, fiber, saturated fat, and dietary cholesterol.

Secondary findings: changes in A:V ratio correlated with changes in fiber, saturated fat, and dietary cholesterol, and regular mindfulness practice correlated with both initiating and maintaining the dietary change.

Conclusions: pilot evidence supports the feasibility of a dietary program with mindfulness training for men with recurrent prostate cancer, and suggests mindfulness may help both start and sustain dietary change, warranting further study.
Closing fragment of the conclusion: mindfulness training may support maintenance of dietary changes over time, inviting further research.

Introduces the study rationale: prior evidence linking cruciferous vegetables, tomato sauce, and legumes to lower advanced prostate cancer incidence, plus lab/animal hints of anti-progression effects, and states the prospective aim of testing post-diagnosis intake against progression.

Describes the study population of 1,560 men with non-metastatic prostate cancer from the CaPSURE US registry and notes the secondary aims covering other vegetable subgroups, total fruit, and fruit subgroups.

Covers methods and follow-up: community-based clinic participants followed 2004–2009, intake measured by semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire, outcomes from urologist reports and medical records, and the start of the event count.

Reports the progression results: 134 events (biochemical recurrences, secondary treatments, bone metastases, prostate cancer deaths) over 3,171 person-years, and the top-quartile cruciferous vegetable finding of a 59% lower progression risk.

Gives the key statistics for the cruciferous vegetable result (HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.22–0.76, p-trend 0.003) and reports that no other vegetable or fruit group showed a significant association with progression.
Final concluding sentence: post-diagnosis cruciferous vegetable intake may lower the risk of prostate cancer progression.

Opening of the evidence report on mitoxantrone (Novantrone) in multiple sclerosis: covers its 2000 MS approval, the 2003 efficacy conclusions, and the 2005 FDA black box warning prompted by cardiac and leukemia reports.

Background and review purpose in the mitoxantrone MS evidence report: reported heart failure and leukemia signals led to the 2005 FDA black box warning, and the review re-examines efficacy and safety since 2003, with methods beginning.

Methods and results of the mitoxantrone MS evidence review: literature was graded by the AAN evidence classification scheme, and Class III and IV evidence links mitoxantrone to systolic dysfunction and therapy-related acute leukemia (TRAL).

Quantitative safety findings for mitoxantrone in MS: systolic dysfunction ~12%, congestive heart failure ~0.4%, leukemia ~0.8%, number needed to harm 8 for systolic dysfunction and 123 for TRAL, and no new efficacy evidence.

Conclusions of the mitoxantrone MS evidence report: cardiac and leukemia risks exceed prior estimates, efficacy recommendation unchanged, and postmarketing surveillance data are lacking; ends with the glossary heading.
Final fragment of the mitoxantrone MS evidence report, noting the lack of comprehensive postmarketing surveillance data and marking the start of the glossary section.

Study design and methods: a prospective cohort of symptomatic atherosclerotic patients (retinal photography and brain MRI), with blinded ophthalmologists scoring retinal arterial narrowing, crossings, sclerosis, and tortuosity, and observers rating white matter lesions and lacunar infarcts on MRI.
Methods continued: lesion-rating agreement rules (abnormal only if both raters agree) and the operational definition of cerebral small-vessel disease as presence of WML or lacunar infarcts.

Main results in 179 patients: retinal vascular abnormality was far more common in those with MRI small-vessel disease (92% vs 77%, p<0.01), with only retinal arterial narrowing and sclerosis differing significantly between groups.

Normotensive subgroup (109 patients) results: any retinal vascular change correlated with small-vessel disease (p=0.01), and the study's conclusion that retinal arterial changes parallel small cerebral artery changes in both hypertensive and normotensive patients.
Concluding statement: retinal arterial pathology parallels damage to small cerebral arteries causing white matter lesions and lacunes, in both hypertensive and normotensive patients.

Opening of a study on a low-saturated-fat (≤20 g fat/day) diet in multiple sclerosis patients, introducing the 34-year trial of 144 patients and comparing outcomes for adherent versus non-adherent groups across disability levels.

Concluding part of the multiple sclerosis low-fat diet study, reporting that the greatest benefit occurred in patients with minimal disability at trial start, where 95% of those not dying from non-MS causes survived and stayed physically active.

Introduces the study's aim: testing whether a single LDL apheresis improves impaired coronary endothelium-dependent dilation in hypercholesterolemia, citing prior evidence that LDL-lowering drugs improve coronary endothelial function over months.

Describes the methods: coronary artery diameter and blood flow were measured by Doppler wire and quantitative angiography before and after one LDL apheresis in 15 patients with familial hypercholesterolemia.

Details the study protocol: acetylcholine infusions (1, 10, 50 microg/min) tested endothelium-dependent vasodilation, nitroglycerin-like isosorbide dinitrate or papaverine tested endothelium-independent vasodilation, and a 3-hour apheresis lowered LDL cholesterol.

Reports the key results: LDL fell by about 86.6%, and acetylcholine (50 microg/min) responses improved significantly, with diameter change going from -19.7% to -2.9% and blood flow change from 80.7% to 155.3%.

Summarizes the specificity of the findings: endothelium-independent responses to isosorbide dinitrate or papaverine were unchanged, and the authors conclude that epicardial and microvascular endothelial function improved after one apheresis session.
Concludes the abstract with the main takeaway that a single LDL apheresis markedly lowering LDL improves coronary endothelial function, followed by the 2004 Wiley-Liss copyright notice.
Introduction and study objective of a retrospective British Columbia cohort study on whether interferon beta slows disability progression (EDSS 6) in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.

Study population and design details: 868 interferon beta-treated RRMS patients compared with untreated contemporary (n=829) and historical (n=959) cohorts, with the primary outcome defined as time to sustained EDSS 6.

Definition of the main outcome: time from treatment eligibility to a confirmed, sustained EDSS score of 6 (needing a cane to walk 100 m), with EDSS described as a 0-10 disability scale, plus the statistical approach of a Cox model with time-varying treatment.

Statistical methods and follow-up results: time-varying Cox regression and propensity score adjustment for confounding by indication, together with the start of the median active follow-up times for each cohort.
Median follow-up durations (about 5.1, 4.0, and 10.8 years across the treated, contemporary, and historical cohorts) and the observed rates of reaching sustained EDSS 6 (10.8%, 5.3%, 23.1%).

Adjusted hazard results: after controlling for sex, age, disease duration, and baseline EDSS, interferon beta was not significantly associated with reaching EDSS 6 versus the contemporary cohort (HR 1.30, 95% CI 0.92-1.83, P=.14).

Historical cohort comparison and robustness checks: HR 0.77 (95% CI 0.58-1.02, P=.07) versus the historical cohort, with further adjustment for comorbidities and socioeconomic status and propensity scoring not changing the conclusions.
Conclusion: interferon beta was not associated with a reduction in disability progression among patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.
Abstract of a narrative review on nutritional intervention in multiple sclerosis (MS), introducing nutrition as a possible environmental factor and the lack of diet integration into MS therapy.

Abstract of a 2011 narrative review on MS nutrition: states the need to assess bioactive dietary molecules and their targets to overcome skepticism about dietary control and encourage nutritional interventions.

Abstract of an MS nutrition review stating its aim: to give a molecular-level rationale for nutritional intervention by examining how dietary molecules affect inflammatory and autoimmune processes, and noting their pleiotropic effects.

Abstract of an MS nutrition review summarizing findings that dietary molecules shift cell metabolism toward catabolism and reduce inflammation via enzymes, nuclear receptors, and transcription factors, plus proposed dietary strategies.

Closing abstract text of a 2011 MS nutrition review proposing gut dysbiosis control, low-fat hypocaloric diets with vitamins, fish oil, and polyphenols to slow MS progression, followed by the Elsevier copyright notice.

Opening of the abstract: background on atherosclerosis beginning in childhood, and the prior Pathobiological Determinants of Atherosclerosis in Youth risk scores for predicting advanced lesions in ages 15-34 using traditional CHD risk factors.

Continues the study's stated aim of relating these risk scores (gender, age, lipoproteins, smoking, hypertension, obesity, hyperglycemia) to early atherosclerotic lesions, and begins the Methods describing lesion measurement in the LAD, RCA, and abdominal aorta.

Methods detail: persons aged 15-34 who died from external causes and were autopsied in forensic labs. Results begin, reporting that modifiable-risk-factor scores link to microscopic AHA grade 1 lesions in the LAD and to fatty streak extent in the RCA and aorta.

Results continue: modifiable-risk-factor scores are associated with higher-severity microscopic lesions (intermediate and advanced) in the LAD and with more extensive intermediate and raised gross lesions in the RCA and abdominal aorta.

Results conclude and the Conclusions open: risk scores from traditional CHD risk factors identify young people with high probability of advanced lesions and also track with earlier lesions, including the earliest gross lesion.

Conclusions continue: the scores are linked to the earliest anatomically demonstrable lesion, supporting youth lifestyle modification to prevent initial lesions and progression to advanced lesions and later coronary heart disease.
Final sentence of the conclusions: lifestyle modification in youth is supported to prevent or delay coronary heart disease by stopping initial lesions and their progression to advanced lesions.

Abstract of a Bogalusa Heart Study paper on serum lipoprotein and systolic blood pressure risk factors versus early atherosclerosis (aortic and coronary fatty streaks) in 35 young decedents; this chunk covers the study population, the higher aortic fatty streak prevalence in blacks versus whites, and the link between fatty streaks and total and LDL cholesterol.

Continues the abstract's findings: aortic fatty streaks correlate with total and LDL cholesterol independent of race, sex, and age, and inversely with the HDL to LDL plus VLDL cholesterol ratio; this chunk also begins the report on coronary-artery fatty streaks and VLDL cholesterol.

Reports coronary-artery findings in the Bogalusa Heart Study abstract: coronary fatty streaks correlate with VLDL cholesterol, and systolic blood pressure tends to be higher in subjects with coronary fibrous plaques (112 vs 104 mm Hg, P = 0.09).

Concluding section of the Bogalusa Heart Study abstract, stating that risk-factor levels matter for early aortic and coronary changes, that progression from fatty streaks to fibrous plaques is uncertain, and that cardiovascular disease prevention should begin early in life.
Final fragment of the Bogalusa Heart Study abstract, ending the concluding sentence that prevention of cardiovascular disease should begin early in life.

Study design and population: the Special Turku Coronary Risk Factor Intervention Project (STRIP) randomizes 7-month-old infants to a low-saturated-fat diet or an unrestricted control diet, setting up the 11-year endothelial function outcome.

Measurement methods: at age 11, brachial artery flow-mediated (endothelium-dependent) and nitrate-mediated (endothelium-independent) dilation are measured by high-resolution ultrasound in 179 intervention and 190 control children, with the boys' result reported as significant.

Results by sex: the intervention effect on endothelial function is significant in boys (P=0.0034) but not girls (P=0.69), with maximum flow-mediated dilation values (mean±SD) for each group; nitrate-mediated dilation was unaffected.

Cholesterol adjustment analysis: in boys the intervention difference stays significant after adjusting for current serum total or LDL cholesterol but loses significance after adjusting for mean cholesterol under age 3 (adjusted means 9.46% vs 8.54%, P=0.11), suggesting early cholesterol mediates the effect.

Conclusions: an infancy-onset low-saturated-fat diet maintained through childhood is associated with enhanced endothelial function in boys, and this effect is partly explained by the diet-induced lowering of serum cholesterol.
Final fragment: a truncated word ending the abstract's conclusion sentence about the diet-induced reduction in serum cholesterol explaining the endothelial effect.

Introduces the study's motivation: aging is conserved across species, protein oxidation may link oxygen radicals to aging, and long-lived animals should show lower oxidative protein damage markers than short-lived ones.

States that this comparison had not been tested and describes the study design: heart levels of oxidation, glyco/lipoxidation, lipoxidation markers and amino acid composition measured across mammalian species.

Reports the cross-species results: oxidation markers correlate directly with maximum life span (MLSP), glyco/lipoxidation markers do not, and the lipoxidation marker MDA-lysine correlates inversely with MLSP.
Reports that methionine is the only amino acid strongly and negatively correlated with MLSP (r2=0.93), suggesting lower steady-state levels of oxidized methionine residues in long-lived species.

Concludes that high longevity in homeothermic vertebrates is partly achieved by reducing the sensitivity of tissue proteins and lipids to oxidative damage through selection of less oxidizable structural components.
Final sentence of the conclusion: longevity is supported by selecting protein and lipid structural components less susceptible to oxidative modification.

Introduction to the document: argues that metastatic prostate, lung, and GI tumors respond poorly to chemotherapy and presents dietary methionine restriction as a promising novel strategy, alone or combined with chemotherapy.
Preclinical evidence: in vitro and animal studies show methionine restriction inhibits growth and kills cancer cells while normal host tissues are relatively resistant, motivating a clinical trial.
Clinical trial findings: a phase I trial of dietary methionine restriction in adults with advanced cancer found it safe and feasible, with preliminary signs of antitumor activity.

Specific clinical responses: a hormone-independent prostate cancer patient had a 25% PSA reduction after 12 weeks, a renal cell cancer patient had an objective radiographic response, and synergy with chemotherapy is being explored.
Conclusion: the findings to date justify further investigation of dietary methionine restriction as a novel treatment strategy for advanced cancer.
Introduction/objective of a canine scent detection study for colorectal cancer (CRC) screening, motivating a non-invasive, economical alternative to FOBT.
Study design: exhaled breath and watery stool samples from CRC patients and healthy controls collected before colonoscopy, with five samples per test group placed in boxes.
Test procedure: a specially trained Labrador retriever and handler identify the cancer-positive sample among five boxes by sitting in front of the station where cancer scent is detected.
Results: 33 breath and 37 stool sample groups tested, with sensitivity 0.91 for breath (specificity 0.99) and 0.97 for stool (specificity 0.99) versus colonoscopy diagnosis.
Key findings: high accuracy even for early-stage cancer, and no confounding from current smoking, benign colorectal disease, or inflammatory disease.

Conclusions: a specific cancer scent exists, cancer-specific compounds may circulate in the body, and odour materials may be useful CRC screening tools, pointing to future VOC identification research.
Final sentence of the conclusion, emphasizing that identifying cancer-specific volatile organic compounds will be important for developing new early CRC detection methods.

Introduces the rodent evidence that methionine restriction extends lifespan and mimics caloric restriction, setting up the idea that moderate methionine restriction may be practical for humans via vegan diets.

Explains why plant-based diets are low in methionine (legume and nut proteins are poorer sources), and notes that vegan diets have lower total protein per calorie, making moderate methionine restriction more feasible than caloric restriction.

Describes whole-food vegan diet composition that keeps methionine low (moderating beans and soy, emphasizing fruit and wine or beer), while noting lower plant protein bioavailability and the need for B12 supplementation.
Argues that low-fat vegan diets with exercise lower insulin and free IGF-I to promote longevity, with methionine restriction potentially amplifying the IGF-I reduction.
Expresses uncertainty about whether IGF-I down-regulation alone explains the rodent longevity effects of low-methionine diets, leaving other mechanisms open.

Study objective and design: a proof-of-principle experiment in which six dogs are trained to detect bladder cancer from urine odour, then tested by picking the cancer sample out of six options (chance 1 in 7).
Participant details: 36 bladder cancer patients (27 used for training, 9 for testing) and 108 diseased or healthy controls (54 for training, 54 for testing), with age ranges given for each group.
Outcome measure and start of results: success is the mean proportion of correct selections per dog versus the 14% chance expectation, with the group-level count framing the first result.

Main results: dogs correctly identified bladder cancer urine on 22 of 54 trials, a 41% success rate with confidence intervals (normality and bootstrap), well above the 14% chance level; multivariate analysis indicates the odour signal is independent of standard urinalysis chemistry.

Conclusions: dogs can detect bladder cancer by urine odour above chance, implying tumour-related volatile compounds form a distinct odour signature, separate from secondary effects such as bleeding, inflammation and infection.
Final conclusion sentence: the distinct cancer odour signature is attributed to tumour-derived volatiles rather than bleeding, inflammation or infection, which are secondary effects of the tumour.

This chunk is the entire abstract of a short historical experimental study on cell culture. It reports that substituting homocystine for methionine in a folic acid and cyanocobalamin-rich medium lets normal adult mammalian cells survive while three highly malignant cell types from different species, including human, die.

Introduces methionine as an essential amino acid and its roles in protein synthesis, DNA methylation and polyamine synthesis, and begins the review's argument that methionine restriction may control cancer growth, especially in methionine-dependent tumors, which may arise from defects in methionine de novo and salvage pathways.

Explains the mechanisms behind methionine dependence in cancer: deletions, polymorphisms or altered expression of genes in the methionine de novo and salvage pathways leave cancer cells unable to regenerate methionine, with folate metabolism defects possibly contributing.

Summarizes supporting evidence: methionine-deficient culture media selectively killed methionine-dependent cancer cells co-cultured with normal cells, and methionine-restricted diets in animal studies inhibited cancer growth and extended healthy life-span.
Covers translational strategies: low-methionine vegan diets may be useful for cancer growth control in humans, and methioninase, which depletes circulating methionine, is another proposed approach.
Concludes that combining nutritional methionine restriction and methioninase with chemotherapy is the current focus of clinical studies, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces methionine dependence, a metabolic defect in many human tumor cell lines (not normal cell strains), where replacing methionine with homocysteine (MET-HCY+ medium) causes late S/G2 cell cycle arrest; raises the open question of whether this occurs in fresh patient tumors.
States the study's aim to test whether methionine dependence occurs in fresh patient tumors as in cell lines, using sponge-gel-supported histoculture to grow tumors directly from surgery.

Describes methods: nuclear DNA content measured by image analysis to determine cell cycle position in MET-HCY+ versus MET+HCY- medium across 21 patient tumors, with cell-line controls identified by cell count.

Explains the validation logic: methionine-dependent cell lines show reduced G1 fraction in MET-HCY+ medium relative to MET+HCY-, so late cell cycle arrest serves as the marker of methionine dependence in histocultured tumors.
Reports results: 5 of 21 patient tumors (colon, breast, ovary, prostate, melanoma) were methionine dependent, suggesting the dependence may be common in cancer patients and relevant to therapy.
Final sentence noting that implications for potential therapy based on methionine dependence are discussed.

Introduces the lung cancer burden and the lack of a screening test, then the proposed use of electronic nose sensors to detect cancer-specific breath VOCs; this opening chunk sets up the background for the sniffer dog research approach.

Continues the discussion of electronic noses as breath-based screening tools, notes that three decades of research produced no clinically applicable device, and begins stating the paper's new approach of using trained sniffer dogs.

States the paper's core proposal: using specially trained sniffer dogs in research strategies to exploit their ability to identify lung cancer from patients' breath samples, as an alternative to electronic noses.

Introduction to the document on chitin synthesis and degradation as pesticide targets: it defines chitin as an extracellular aminosugar biopolymer in fungi and arthropods and frames pesticides as disrupting biochemical targets in pests.

Explains chitin's structural roles in fungal cell walls, insect cuticle, and nematode eggshells, making it a selective pesticide target, and notes that only the membrane-associated polymerization steps are currently open to chemical interference.
Covers commercial pesticides acting on chitin synthesis: polyoxins and nikkomycins are competitive chitin synthase inhibitors, and benzoylaryl ureas are insecticides already on the market.

Discusses the unclear mode of action of benzoylaryl ureas, which likely act after polymerization such as chitin chain translocation, and introduces chitin hydrolytic degradation as essential for fungal hyphal growth, septation, and arthropod molting.
Describes allosamidin, an actinomycete-derived metabolite that specifically suppresses insect chitinases, and the role of induced chitinases in plant defense against pathogens.

Covers chitin, chitosan, and their oligomers as elicitors that boost plant chitinase levels, and N-acetylglucosamine-binding lectins that interfere with fungal and insect chitin synthases, with plant lectins possibly mediating plant-pathogen interactions.

Concluding sentence on the proposed role of plant lectins in suppressing fungal invasion during plant-pathogen interactions, closing the discussion of chitin-targeting defense and pesticide mechanisms.

Opening of the review on methionine dependency as a cancer treatment target: motivates exploiting tumor metabolic abnormalities because chemotherapy has limits, and notes many tumors require methionine while normal cells are resistant to its restriction.
Continues the review's background: the biochemical basis of methionine dependence is still unclear, and investigators have tried to exploit it in vivo by lowering plasma and tumour methionine.

Describes methods used to deplete methionine in vivo, including methionine-free diets, methionine-deprived parenteral nutrition, and the enzyme methioninase, which causes tumour regression or growth inhibition in animal models.

Explains that prolonged dietary or methioninase-based methionine restriction is impractical clinically due to toxicity and quality-of-life concerns, so its use alongside chemotherapy is proposed as a better application.

Summarizes preclinical evidence of synergy between methionine restriction and cytotoxic chemotherapy, concluding that it may become an additional cancer therapy, especially combined with chemotherapy.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence of the review, restating that methionine restriction is a potential additional cancer therapeutic strategy in association with chemotherapy.

Opening of the review's introduction: defines amino acid auxotrophy as a cancer vulnerability, cites early clinical results for asparagine- and arginine-depleting drugs, and introduces methionine auxotrophy as an emerging therapeutic target.

Continuation of the introduction and the 'Areas covered' statement: outlines the review's scope, covering the discovery of methionine auxotrophy and in vitro, in vivo, and patient data on methionine depletion, and previews the discussion of pegylation, bioengineering, and red blood cell encapsulation.

Closing of the 'Areas covered' section and the start of the expert opinion: notes the review's aim to support future pharmacology, toxicology, and cytotoxicity studies of methionine depletion, and begins the expert opinion on methionine auxotrophy as a viable target.

Expert opinion section: calls for research on normal versus cancer cell toxicity, further study of the molecular mechanisms of methionine depletion therapy, and new methods to reduce the immunogenicity of methionine-depleting drugs.
Final sentence of the expert opinion: identifies reducing immunogenicity as a current challenge for protein therapeutics, specifically for methionine-depleting drugs.

Introduction/background of an abstract on a hypothesized chemical reaction in tumours: glucose and methionine react non-enzymatically, possibly producing carcinogenic and gaseous sulfur compounds that may drive cancer growth.

Continuation of the background stating the speculation about gaseous sulfur-containing compounds in tumour tissue, followed by the study aims and the methods overview (in vitro gas chromatography of glucose-methionine reaction products).

Methods section describing the sampling approach: near-edge x-ray fine adsorption structure spectroscopy on flatus from colon cancer patients and exhaled air from lung cancer patients versus healthy controls, plus the start of the HT29 mouse xenograft design.

Mouse xenograft comparison in the methods (HT29 colon cancer cells, with and without sodium hyaluronate gel to block gas diffusion), leading into the results on gaseous sulfur products such as methanethiol and hydrogen sulfide from glucose reacting with methionine, homocysteine, or cysteine.
Results reporting that sulfur-containing gas concentrations were significantly higher in flatus from colon cancer patients and exhaled air from lung cancer patients than in healthy individuals.
Results on animal experiments showing a pronounced antitumour effect from blocking diffusion of sulfur compounds, and the start of the conclusions that these gases are the main tumour products.
Final conclusion: preventing diffusion of gaseous sulfur-containing compounds reduces tumour proliferation, suggesting a new cancer treatment approach.

Introduces the link between long-lived mammals' low mitochondrial ROS and oxidative damage, and notes that dietary restriction in rodents reduces mtROS and oxidative damage to mtDNA and proteins; protein restriction is singled out as having the same effect.

Explains that protein restriction lowers mtROS and oxidative stress in rat liver while carbohydrate and lipid restriction do not, and contrasts protein restriction's longevity benefit and practicality for humans with the lack of longevity effect from carbohydrate or lipid restriction.

Presents evidence that isocaloric methionine restriction reduces mtROS generation and oxidative stress in rodent tissues and extends maximum longevity in rats and mice, pointing to methionine as the key amino acid.

Concludes that reduced dietary methionine may be responsible for the lower mitochondrial ROS and oxidative damage seen under DR and for part of its longevity gain, and notes excess dietary methionine raises mtROS in rat liver.

Argues that Western mean protein (and methionine) intake exceeds needs, so lowering it to recommended levels could reduce tissue oxidative stress and extend healthy lifespan in humans without the drawbacks of DR diets.
Closing statement that reducing protein intake to recommended levels offers a way to lower oxidative stress and improve human healthspan while avoiding the undesirable effects of dietary restriction.

Opening of the document: a 2007 Minnesota Department of Health report of 11 cases of an unexplained neurological illness at a Austin, MN pork plant, with sensory-predominant polyradiculoneuropathy symptoms.

Describes the clinical picture (sensory more than motor, nerve root irritation) and the epidemiological finding that the only shared exposure was a pork brain extraction procedure using compressed air.
Reasoning about etiology: negative cultures and asymptomatic relatives suggest a non-infectious cause; the syndrome resembles CIDP, and lab tests show peripheral nerve and nerve root inflammation.
Shows the syndrome differed from CIDP and had a novel IgG immunostaining pattern, suggesting an unidentified antigen causing the inflammation.

Names the syndrome progressive inflammatory neuropathy, theorized as an autoimmune reaction to aerosolized porcine neural tissue, and gives total case counts across Minnesota, Indiana, and Nebraska plants.
Outcomes and control measures: plants stopped using compressed air to remove pork brains, all cases stabilized or improved, and some needed immunosuppressive and analgesic treatment.
Concluding remarks: the investigation is ongoing, highlights the value of epidemiology in outbreak response, and includes the journal citation (Mt Sinai J Med 2009) and copyright.
Trailing citation fragment of the Mt Sinai J Med 2009 article (volume 76, pages 442-447) with the Mount Sinai School of Medicine copyright notice.

Opening chunk of a review on phosphate (P) as a vascular toxin: introduces elevated P in advanced renal failure within CKD-MBD and the evidence linking increased P to vascular calcification and mortality.

Summarizes mechanistic and clinical evidence that high phosphate causes vascular damage: apoptosis and bone-like conversion of vessels in vitro, and increased vessel wall thickness, arterial stiffness and coronary calcification in dialysed children.

Describes epidemiological evidence that raised phosphate independently predicts mortality in adult dialysis patients, cardiovascular changes in pre-dialysis CKD and in people with normal renal function, and that phosphate binders lower serum P.

Covers the FGF-23 response to raised phosphate: it protects early CKD by increasing P excretion but rises thousands-fold in dialysis, possibly acting as an independent cardiovascular risk factor, with FGF-23 and Klotho possibly acting directly on vessels.

Concludes that FGF-23-Klotho disturbances and raised P are linked to premature aging, and that high P has adverse vascular effects, suggesting that keeping serum P in the normal range should reduce cardiovascular risk and mortality.
Final sentence of the document: the overall conclusion that maintaining serum phosphate in the normal range reduces cardiovascular risk and mortality.

Introduces human APOBEC3G as an innate antiviral factor and the study's main experiment: long-term co-culture showing reduced PERV transmission from pig to human cells when APOBEC3G is expressed in pig kidney cells.
Describes the mechanism of PERV inhibition by APOBEC3G: it is deamination-independent and acts after particle production but before integration into human genomic DNA.

Reports that PERV inhibition does not need APOBEC3G's cytosine deaminase activity (no hypermutations), contrasts it with the pig's endogenous APOBEC3 which did not significantly block transmission, and states the proof-of-principle conclusion.

Concludes that APOBEC3 proteins can strengthen cellular antiviral defenses against zoonotic endogenous retroviruses, and suggests human APOBEC3G-transgenic pigs as safer xenotransplantation sources and broader cross-species restriction strategies.
Final sentence extending the implications: cross-species APOBEC3-dependent restriction may help against other endogenous and exogenous retroviral infections.
