Notes that the interventions also lower blood pressure or prevent hypertension, and that certain angiotensin II receptor blockers improve erectile function and reduce oxidative stress. Introduces ED as a warning sign in men under 60 and in men with diabetes or hypertension.

Highlights ED as a critical warning sign for existing or impending cardiovascular disease and death risk, and the antiarrhythmic role of omega-3s for men at highest sudden-death risk. Begins the conclusion on physicians using these factors to help patients.

Concludes that understanding these factors lets physicians prevent vascular disease and improve erectile function, motivating men to change lifestyle habits. Ends with the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.

Study objectives and methods: a cohort of 300 consecutive patients with acute chest pain and angiographically confirmed coronary artery disease, assessed by semi-structured interview and the International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF) to examine erectile dysfunction (ED) prevalence, onset timing, and risk factors.

Study population results: mean patient age 62.5±8 years (range 33-86), mean prior duration of myocardial ischaemia symptoms 49 months, and angiographic findings of 1-, 2- and 3-vessel coronary disease in 32.6%, 29.3% and 38% of patients.
ED prevalence and severity: 49% of the 300 patients (147/300) had erectile dysfunction, graded as mild, mild-to-moderate, moderate and severe in 14%, 21%, 14% and 51% of those affected, respectively.

Comparison of groups and timing: patients with and without ED showed no significant difference in clinical or angiographic characteristics; in 99 of 147 patients (67%) with both conditions, ED appeared before coronary artery disease symptoms.

Onset interval and subgroup findings: ED preceded CAD by a mean of 38.8 months (range 1-168), with no differences in risk factors or clinical/angiographic features between early and late ED onset; all type I diabetic patients with ED developed sexual dysfunction before CAD (p<0.001).

Conclusions: a substantial share of patients with angiographically proven CAD have ED, which often precedes angina in nearly 70% of cases; the authors note that a control group with normal erectile function is needed to determine whether ED is a true predictor of ischaemic heart disease.

Closing recommendation: the final sentence calls for future studies with a CAD control group lacking ED to verify whether erectile dysfunction can be considered a genuine predictor of ischemic heart disease.

Introduction to a review on lifestyle and dietary recommendations for erectile dysfunction (ED) and female sexual dysfunction; notes that evidence linking lifestyle factors to ED is suggestive but limited, and that evidence for female sexual dysfunction is sparse.

Conclusion of the review: healthy behaviors cannot yet be shown to affect female sexual dysfunction, and adopting these lifestyle measures benefits overall health and well-being, which may reduce the broader burden of sexual dysfunction in men and women.
Closing copyright notice (Elsevier Inc., 2011) for the lifestyle and sexual dysfunction review; the final sentence of the well-being and burden paragraph.

Background and objective of a systematic review/meta-analysis of RCTs on lifestyle modification and CV risk-factor pharmacotherapy effects on erectile dysfunction severity, citing shared risk factors with coronary artery disease.

Methods: comprehensive multi-database search through August 2010, inclusion criteria of RCTs with at least 6 weeks follow-up of lifestyle or pharmacotherapy interventions for CV risk factor reduction, dual independent study selection.
Methods continued: primary outcome is weighted mean difference in IIEF-5 erectile function scores with 95% CIs using a random-effects model; results section begins describing the included trials.

Results: 740 participants from 6 trials in 4 countries; pooled weighted mean difference of 2.66 (95% CI 1.86-3.47) in IIEF-5 for lifestyle and pharmacotherapy, plus sensitivity analysis excluding statin trials (n=143).

Results continued: excluding statin trials, the 4 lifestyle-modification trials (n=597) show significant IIEF-5 improvement, weighted mean difference 2.40 (95% CI 1.19-3.61); the conclusion statement begins.
Conclusion: findings strengthen evidence that lifestyle modification and CV risk-factor pharmacotherapy effectively improve sexual function in men with erectile dysfunction.

Study design and methods for a population-based longitudinal cohort of erectile dysfunction (ED) and future coronary artery disease (CAD), 1996-2005, screening 1402 community-dwelling men with regular sexual partners, with age-stratified incidence and Cox models.
Prevalence of erectile dysfunction by age group in the cohort: about 2% at ages 40-49, 6% at 50-59, 17% at 60-69, and 39% at 70 and older, and the start of the CAD incidence density results.

CAD incidence densities per 1000 person-years by age group, comparing men without ED (0.94, 5.09, 10.72, 23.30) with men with ED (48.52, 27.15, 23.97, 29.63) across the 40-49, 50-59, 60-69, and 70+ age bands.

Conclusion of the ED and CAD study: ED and CAD may share a common vascular pathology; ED in younger men marks a sharply higher future cardiac risk, while ED in older men has little prognostic value, so young men with ED are candidates for cardiovascular risk screening.
Final concluding sentence of the ED and CAD study recommending that young men with erectile dysfunction be prioritized for cardiovascular risk factor screening and medical intervention.

Introduction and study design: establishes that men with metabolic syndrome have higher erectile dysfunction rates, and describes selection of 65 ED patients from a lifestyle-trial database for a Mediterranean diet study.

Inclusion criteria and group allocation: details eligibility (ED plus metabolic syndrome, full follow-up, diet-focused intervention) and the split of 35 men to the Mediterranean-style diet versus 30 to the control diet.

Results on diet and biomarkers: after 2 years the Mediterranean group ate more fruits, vegetables, nuts, whole grains and olive oil, and their endothelial function and C-reactive protein improved while the control group stayed stable.

Main outcome and conclusion: 13 intervention men versus 2 control men reached an IIEF score of 22 or higher (P=0.015), leading to the conclusion that a Mediterranean-style diet may reduce ED prevalence in metabolic syndrome.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the abstract's statement that the Mediterranean diet may reduce erectile dysfunction prevalence in men with metabolic syndrome.

Introduction and objectives of a 2011 meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies on erectile dysfunction (ED) as a risk factor for cardiovascular disease, background on the unresolved question of whether ED independently predicts CVD.

Methods section describing the PubMed literature search through January 2011, reference list review, independent data extraction by two authors, and use of fixed- or random-effects models to pool risk estimates.
Results opening: twelve prospective cohort studies with 36,744 participants were included, and the pooled analysis of men with ED is about to be reported.

Pooled relative risks for men with ED versus reference: CVD 1.48, coronary heart disease 1.46, stroke 1.35, and all-cause mortality 1.19, with 95% confidence intervals, plus the start of the sensitivity analysis description.

Sensitivity analysis adjusting for conventional cardiovascular risk factors gave similar results, no publication bias was found, and the conclusions state ED significantly raises CVD, CHD, stroke, and all-cause mortality risk, probably independent of standard risk factors.
Closing copyright and publisher notice (American College of Cardiology Foundation, Elsevier Inc., 2011) ending the abstract of the ED and cardiovascular risk meta-analysis.

Introduction and methods of a systematic review on dietary factors, the Mediterranean diet, and erectile dysfunction (ED); this chunk states the rationale and begins describing the literature search across MEDLINE, EMBASE, and SCOPUS.

Methods and outcome measures of the review: the systematic search terms (erectile dysfunction, diet, dietary patterns, Mediterranean diet, lifestyle) and the aim of examining the relationship between diet and ED and the effect of dietary treatment; the results section begins with the note that few studies addressed diet and ED.

Results on dietary patterns: a pattern high in fruit, vegetables, nuts, whole grains, and fish but low in red/processed meat and refined grains is more common among men without ED, and the Mediterranean diet is introduced as a healthy pattern linked to better survival.

Results on Mediterranean diet evidence for ED: among type 2 diabetic men, the highest adherence was associated with the lowest ED prevalence and greater sexual activity, and the Mediterranean diet outperformed a control diet in clinical trials.

Final results and conclusion: in clinical trials, the Mediterranean diet improved or restored erectile function in people with obesity or metabolic syndrome, leading to the conclusion that adopting this diet may improve ED.

Introduction and aim of a Taiwan nationwide cohort study on erectile dysfunction (ED) as a risk factor for subsequent stroke, using Longitudinal Health Insurance Database data and a 5-year follow-up design.

Methods continuation: the study cohort of ED patients (first ambulatory visit 1997-2001) is compared against a randomly selected comparison group drawn from the Longitudinal Health Insurance Database in Taiwan, with stroke tracked over 5 years.

Methods detail: the combined sample of 9,006 subjects (1,501 ED patients and 7,505 comparisons) is followed for five years from the index visit, and the main outcome is measured with stratified Cox proportional hazards regression comparing stroke-free survival.
Results beginning: stroke incidence over 5 years was 12.5% (188 of 1,501) in the ED cohort versus 9.7% (730 of 7,505) in the comparison cohort, overall 918 (10.2%) strokes.

Results continuation: log-rank test shows significantly lower 5-year stroke-free survival in ED patients (P < 0.001), and the adjusted analysis covers income, location, and comorbidities including hypertension, diabetes, and peripheral vascular disease.

Key finding: after adjusting for confounders including coronary heart disease, atrial fibrillation, and hyperlipidemia, ED patients had a hazard ratio of 1.29 (95% CI 1.08-1.54, P < 0.01) for stroke, with the conclusion beginning.
Conclusion: the study concludes that erectile dysfunction serves as a surrogate marker for future stroke in men, published with a 2010 International Society for Sexual Medicine copyright notice.

Introduction of the paper: ED as an early marker of systemic atherosclerosis and predictor of coronary artery disease and cardiac events, and the paper's goal of guiding urologists and non-cardiologists in basic cardiovascular evaluation.

Outline of the paper's approach: reviews the evidence and pathophysiology linking ED to cardiovascular disease, then describes how to perform a basic cardiovascular evaluation (history, physical exam, objective data).

Summary of findings and recommendations: lifestyle modification and medical therapy improve mortality, cardiovascular outcomes and ED; guidance on when to refer to an internist or cardiologist; treating CV risk factors may save the patient's life.
Concluding sentence restating that treating cardiovascular risk factors may benefit ED and potentially save the patient's life.

Introduction and methods opening of a study on penile color Doppler ultrasound (PCDU) peak systolic velocity (PSV) in flaccid state for erectile dysfunction (ED) patients, describing the cohort of 1,346 men.

Methods and main outcome measures: flaccid vs. dynamic (prostaglandin E1) PCDU in all patients, plus a 20-subject type 2 diabetes subset undergoing adenosine stress SPECT for silent coronary heart disease with penile flow measured before and after adenosine.
Results beginning: flaccid PSV correlates significantly with dynamic PSV (r = 0.513), and ROC analysis begins for predicting dynamic PSV thresholds.

Results on ROC accuracy: a 13 cm/s flaccid PSV threshold predicts dynamic PSV below 25 and 35 cm/s with 89% and 82% accuracy, and impaired coronary flow reserve occurred in 9 of 20 diabetic subjects (45%).

Results on coronary and psychological associations: flaccid PSV predicted impaired coronary flow reserve with 80% accuracy (AUC 0.798), while anxiety correlated with dynamic but not flaccid PSV after adjustment.
Conclusions: flaccid-state PCDU can be routinely used to evaluate cavernosal arterial flow and identify pathological dynamic PSV with over 80% accuracy.
Final conclusion sentence: preliminary data suggest the same flaccid PCDU examination may identify diabetic subjects with impaired coronary flow reserve with 80% accuracy.

Introduces erectile dysfunction as a vascular disorder, listing its shared atherosclerotic risk factors and the vascular syndromes (CAD, hypertension, stroke-related disease, PAD, diabetes) it commonly accompanies.

Continues the list of associated vascular syndromes and notes shared early endothelial dysfunction and late obstructive vascular changes in ED and other vascular diseases, then introduces the artery size hypothesis linking ED and CAD.

Explains the artery size hypothesis: atherosclerosis is systemic, yet symptoms appear at different times across vascular beds, which is attributed to differing arterial diameters tolerating the same plaque burden.
Applies the artery size hypothesis to penile versus coronary arteries, predicting that ED patients rarely show CAD symptoms while CAD patients often report ED.
Concludes the artery size hypothesis by stating that available clinical evidence appears to support the predicted pattern linking ED to CAD.

Opening chunk of an abstract on erectile dysfunction (ED) as a vascular condition linked to coronary disease: gives prevalence (40% of men over 40, 1 in 3 over 70), notes ED often precedes cardiovascular events by 3-5 years, and links it to acute coronary syndromes and mortality.

Middle chunk of the same ED and coronary disease abstract: argues early ED identification creates a window for cardiovascular risk reduction, describes its relationship impact and the success of treatment for quality of life, and recommends routinely querying ED in clinical care.
Final chunk of the ED and coronary disease abstract: concludes that early ED detection may prevent early death, followed by the 2012 Elsevier Ireland Ltd copyright notice.
Introduction and methods of a 2011 study on cardiovascular mortality in men with erectile dysfunction, using linked death registration and hospital morbidity data against a reference male population.
Main outcome measures (CV death proportions, age-specific rates, MRR, SMRR, adjusted HR) and the first results: overall CV mortality of 4.0% and the elevated SMRR of 2.2 for CV death in men with ED.

Results showing higher CV mortality risk in men with ED, specifically those with prior CV disease (adjusted HR 1.7) or prior CV hospital admissions (adjusted HR 2.2), plus the significantly increased MRR in the 40-69 age group.
Timing results: median 10-year interval between ED onset and CV death, and the finding that a larger share of oncological than CV deaths occurred within 5 years of ED onset (25.0% vs. 10.8%).

Conclusions of the ED mortality study: CV mortality risk is higher in men with ED, yet nearly as many die of cancer as of CV causes, with cancer deaths occurring sooner after ED onset. Copyright 2011 International Society for Sexual Medicine.
Closing copyright line of the 2011 International Society for Sexual Medicine article on cardiovascular mortality in men with erectile dysfunction.
Introduction to the chapter on marine edible algae (seaweeds) as disease preventers, framing rising noncommunicable diseases and growing consumer interest in natural, healthy foods.

Describes seaweeds' historical use as food in China, Japan, Egypt, and India, their potential as functional foods, and introduces metabolic syndrome as the basis for linking seaweeds to high blood pressure and cancer prevention.
Closing sentence of the abstract naming the two target illnesses (high blood pressure and cancer), followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
Introduction and methods of a case-control study on Korean seaweed intake (gim and miyeok) and breast cancer risk, describing 362 cases and matched hospital controls.
Methods continued: dietary assessment via a 121-item quantitative FFQ, conditional logistic regression for odds ratios, and initial result that gim intake was lower among cases.
Main results: higher daily gim intake was inversely associated with breast cancer risk (5th vs 1st quintile OR 0.48), with stratified menopausal-status analysis beginning.
Stratified results by menopausal status showing similar inverse gim associations in premenopausal and postmenopausal women, and no significant association for miyeok consumption.
Conclusion of the study: high gim intake may reduce breast cancer risk, while miyeok showed no significant association.

Introduction and trial design: a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled study of dietary seaweed (Undaria pinnatifida) in 27 adults with metabolic syndrome symptoms, recruited in Quito, Ecuador.

Methods: the crossover design assigns Group 1 to placebo then 4 g/d seaweed, and Group 2 to 4 g/d then 6 g/d seaweed, with blood pressure, weight, waist circumference, inflammation markers and lipids measured monthly and analyzed by repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey's tests.

Results on blood pressure and waist circumference: systolic pressure fell 10.5 mmHg in Group 2 on 6 g/d seaweed, mainly in those with high-normal baseline values, and waist circumference changed only in women, with a decrease after placebo in Group 1.

Detailed waist circumference results for women: Group 1 lost 2.4 cm on placebo, Group 2 lost 2.1 cm on 4 g/d and a further 1.8 cm on 6 g/d seaweed, with confidence intervals and p-values; no other outcomes changed.
Conclusion: the authors suggest that 4 to 6 g/d seaweed, a typical intake in Japan, may be linked to the low prevalence of metabolic syndrome there.

Introduction of the Bay Area Thyroid Cancer Study: motivation, limited and inconclusive prior research on iodine and thyroid cancer, use of fish/shellfish as proxy, and this study's added dietary and toenail-biomarker iodine measures.

Study design: a multiethnic Bay Area population of women aged 20-74 diagnosed 1995-1998 (1992-1998 for Asian women), compared against random-digit-dial general population controls, with a wide range of thyroid cancer incidence and iodine exposure.

Study sample and established risk factors: interviews in six languages with 608 cases and 558 controls, and odds ratios for head/neck radiation, goiter/nodule history, and family history of proliferative thyroid disease.
Main finding: contrary to the hypothesis, higher dietary iodine, likely from multivitamin use, was linked to reduced papillary thyroid cancer risk.

Stratified results: the protective association appeared in low-risk women (no established risk factors, OR 0.53) but not high-risk women (slight, nonsignificant elevation, OR 1.4), and the biomarker showed no association in either group.
Conclusions: the biomarker showed no association, no ethnic differences were found, and the authors conclude iodine exposure has at most a weak effect on papillary thyroid cancer risk.

Opening of the Hawaii thyroid cancer case-control study: its aim to test dietary iodine and goitrogenic vegetable hypotheses, plus the case and control sample sizes, begins with seafood and harm ha intake.

Dietary findings among women: seafood, shellfish, harm ha fermented fish sauce, and iodine raise thyroid cancer risk, while cruciferous goitrogenic vegetables lower it; begins listing non-dietary risk factors.

Non-dietary risk factors (miscarriage, fertility drugs, family history, obesity, farm labor) and odds ratios for combined high iodine intake with first-pregnancy miscarriage (4.8) and with fertility drug use (7.3).
Male risk factors (obesity, farm labor, benign thyroid history) and the study's conclusion that these factors fail to explain the high thyroid cancer rates among Filipino women in Hawaii.
Final fragment of the conclusion noting the study could not fully explain the exceptionally high thyroid cancer incidence among Filipino women in Hawaii.

Introduces the study's background: Japanese postmenopausal women's lower breast cancer rates linked to seaweed/soy diets and estrogen metabolism, and describes the design of a double-blind seaweed-supplementation trial with 15 participants.
Describes the trial protocol: randomization to 7 weeks of 5 g/day Alaria seaweed or maltodextrin placebo, a soy protein isolate challenge in week 7, and a crossover after a 3-week washout.

Reports the key finding that seaweed dose was inversely correlated with serum estradiol (E2), with the regression equation, correlation coefficient and P value, plus soy's effects on urinary isoflavone and lignan excretion.
Presents urinary estrogen metabolite results: soy and SeaSoy raised 2-hydroxyestrogen and the 2-OHE:16αOHE1 ratio, and soy increased equol excretion in the five equol excretors.

Summarizes the equol-producer results (58% further equol increase and 315% rise in the 2:16 ratio with SeaSoy) and concludes that seaweed favorably alters estrogen and phytoestrogen metabolism, likely via colonic bacteria.
Fragment ending the document's abstract text; contains only the trailing fragment 'a.' with no substantive content.

Introduction to a study on seaweed and breast cancer chemoprevention: prior work found wakame suppressed DMBA-induced rat mammary tumor proliferation, possibly via apoptosis, motivating the current investigation of mekabu.

Methods and key findings: mekabu seaweed was soaked in distilled water and filtered; the solution strongly suppressed rat mammary carcinogenesis in drinking water without toxicity and induced apoptosis in three human breast cancer cell lines.

Comparative and safety results: mekabu solution induced apoptosis more strongly than a standard breast cancer chemotherapy agent, spared normal human mammary cells, and is a safe, inexpensive food widely eaten in Japan.
Conclusion: the findings suggest mekabu has potential as a chemopreventive agent for human breast cancer.

Introduces the study's rationale (iodine as a suspected thyroid cancer risk factor, seaweed as the main iodine source in Japan) and the cohort design: Japanese women aged 40-69 in the JPHC study, followed ~14.5 years, with 134 thyroid cancer cases.

Describes the methods: seaweed intake measured by food-frequency questionnaire in three categories (≤2 days/week as reference, 3-4 days/week, almost daily), and the Cox proportional hazards model used to estimate HRs and 95% CIs.

Reports the main result: seaweed consumption was associated with higher papillary carcinoma risk, with almost-daily intake giving HR 1.71 (95% CI 1.01-2.90, trend P=0.04) versus the reference category.

Gives the menopausal-status stratified results: a strong increased papillary carcinoma risk in postmenopausal women (HR 3.81, 95% CI 1.67-8.68) but no association in premenopausal women (HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.44-1.91).
Concludes that seaweed consumption is positively associated with thyroid cancer risk, especially papillary carcinoma, in postmenopausal Japanese women.

Introduction to a 2011 study on watercress (Cruciferae) aqueous leaf extract: background on its dietary role, oxidative DNA damage in aging-related and carcinogenic disease, and the stated aim of testing antigenotoxic effects via comet assay on peripheral blood cells.

Methods of the watercress study: preparation of an aqueous leaf extract (juice processing, centrifugation, filtration, storage at -20 °C) and testing of two concentrations, 13.2 and 26.4 mg/mL, in the in vitro comet assay model.

Results of the watercress comet assay: no change in cell viability versus controls, and significant antigenotoxic effects at both concentrations measured by damage index (p = 0.005 at 30 min; p < 0.001 at 60 and 90 min), with similar 67.1-75.2% damage reductions.
Conclusion of the watercress antigenotoxicity study: the authors argue dietary watercress consumption may help health and quality of life, followed by the 2011 John Wiley & Sons copyright notice.

Opening chunk of an abstract/review on exercise-induced oxidative stress: it states that exercise raises free radical generation and measurable oxidative modifications despite assay flaws, but the underlying mechanisms are unclear, and it begins critiquing the assumption that mitochondrial oxygen consumption drives ROS production.

Middle section of the abstract on exercise-induced oxidative stress: it rejects the idea that higher mitochondrial O2 consumption directly increases ROS, notes that other sources (xanthine oxidase, inflammation, haem protein auto-oxidation) are poorly characterised, and introduces ROS's role in muscle fatigue.

Part of the abstract on exercise-induced oxidative stress discussing ROS and fatigue: ROS can contribute to muscle fatigue in situ, but direct in vivo human evidence that ROS impair performance is lacking, and the significance of oxidative modifications (harmless, damaging, or redox regulation) remains unresolved.

Concluding sentences of the exercise-induced oxidative stress abstract: ROS have established physiological roles at rest, but their specific functions during exercise are still not well understood and need further investigation.

Introduces oxidative stress as an imbalance between free radical production and antioxidant defences, noting both beneficial and harmful effects of free radicals, in a review on whether vegetarian diets reduce exercise-induced oxidative stress.

Continues the background: free radicals' harmful role in apoptosis regulation, cancer and cardiovascular disease; defines antioxidants; and notes regular exercise is healthy but increases oxidative stress, setting up the vegetarian-antioxidant link.

Argues that typical vegetarian diets are rich in antioxidant foods, so they may enhance antioxidant capacity and reduce exercise-induced oxidative stress, and mentions vegetarian diets' link to lower cardiovascular and cancer risk.
Concludes the introduction of the review by stating its aim: to examine current evidence connecting exercise, vegetarian diets, antioxidants, and oxidative stress.

Introduction to the review on antioxidant defences: the traditional view of vitamins as deficiency-preventing nutrients, and the newer concept (championed by Linus Pauling for vitamin C) of high-dose vitamin functions beyond preventing deficiency.

Continues the introduction: Pauling's high-dose vitamin concept, with vitamins C and E (antioxidants) regarded as healthy at high intakes, possibly beneficial in special cases such as preventing Alzheimer's disease progression.

Presents the counter-evidence: recent epidemiological studies do not support antioxidant vitamins improving well-being or lifespan, and supplementation may even be harmful. It also introduces the authors' new concept that nutrients up-regulate endogenous antioxidant defences.

Describes the proposed mechanism, using phytoestrogens as the example: they bind oestrogen receptors and up-regulate antioxidant gene expression. It also states the review's aim of weighing the pros and cons of antioxidant vitamin supplementation.

Closing statement of the introduction: the review considers whether ingesting certain nutrients can boost antioxidant defences by up-regulating the activity of antioxidant enzymes already present in cells.
Introduction and study design of a human study on whether vitamin C and NAC act as pro-oxidants after an eccentric-exercise-induced muscle injury that triggers an acute inflammatory response.
Description of the intervention (placebo vs. vitamin C 12.5 mg/kg and NAC 10 mg/kg for 7 days post-injury) and the rise in serum bleomycin-detectable iron, which was higher in the supplemented group.
Results on muscle damage markers: LDH, CK, and myoglobin elevated 2-4 days post-injury, returning to baseline by day 7, with greater LDH and CK elevation in the vitamin C and NAC group.

Results on oxidative stress: lipid hydroperoxides and 8-iso-PGF2alpha and antioxidant enzyme activities rose after injury, with higher lipid hydroperoxides and 8-iso-PGF2alpha in the vitamin C and NAC group at day 2.
Conclusion that post-injury vitamin C and NAC supplementation transiently increases tissue damage and oxidative stress in this acute human inflammatory model.

Introduces the study design: a 6-week antioxidant (vitamin C and vitamin E) vs. placebo supplementation trial in 21 runners, examining exercise-induced DNA damage measured by the comet assay during a 50 km ultramarathon.

Describes the sampling timepoints for leukocyte DNA damage (pre-race, mid-race, 2 h postrace, and daily for 6 days), race performance and energy expenditure by sex, and the key finding that DNA damage rose at midrace but returned to baseline by 2 h postrace.
Reports the statistical results: a significant gender x treatment x time interaction, and that women taking antioxidants had 62% less DNA damage than placebo-taking women one day after the race.
Concludes that men showed no significant treatment differences at any time point, so the study finds endurance exercise causes DNA damage and antioxidants appear to aid recovery in women but not men.

Introduction and study aim of a human exercise study on whether high-intensity exercise generates free radicals capable of causing DNA damage, including the participant description (12 healthy young males with VO2max measured).

Study methods: 12 healthy males perform three incremental 5-minute aerobic exercise stages (40, 70, 100% VO2max) with 15-minute rests, and blood is drawn after each bout for measuring free radicals, DNA damage, protein carbonyls, lipid hydroperoxides, and lipid-soluble antioxidants.

Results on free radicals: lipid-derived oxygen-centered free radicals, identified by ESR hyperfine coupling constants, rise with moderate and high-intensity exercise, and DNA damage also increases significantly.

Further results: lipid hydroperoxide (LOOH) and lipid-soluble antioxidant levels change significantly during exercise, while protein carbonyl concentration stays unchanged, leading to the conclusion that lipid-derived radicals may contribute to mononuclear cell DNA damage.

Conclusions: lipid-derived free radicals are proposed as contributors to peripheral mononuclear cell DNA damage during exercise, occurring with lipid oxidation but without protein oxidation, with implications for immune function, aging, and carcinogenesis.
Closing clause of the conclusions on immune function, aging, and carcinogenesis, followed by the copyright notice (Wiley-Liss, 2010) for the article.

Introduction and rationale: limitations of high-dose pharmacological antioxidant vitamins for exercise-induced oxidative stress, and the proposed protective role of watercress nutrients (β-carotene, α-tocopherol) in a study on watercress supplementation and exercise oxidative damage.

Study hypothesis and design: a randomised controlled trial testing whether acute (2 h pre-exercise) and chronic (8-week) watercress supplementation attenuate exercise-induced oxidative stress, with the participant description (ten healthy young males).

Methods: participant characteristics (age, stature, body mass) and the crossover protocol, in which subjects completed an 8-week chronic watercress period plus control, then the single-dose acute phase with control.

Methods and sampling: blood collected at baseline, pre-exercise rest and post-exercise, and subjects performed incremental exercise to exhaustion after chronic, acute, or control conditions; begins the reported main findings on DNA damage and lipid peroxidation.

Results: exercise increased DNA damage and lipid peroxidation under control conditions, whereas acute and chronic watercress attenuated these markers and reduced H2O2 accumulation after exhaustive exercise, with P-values versus control.

Results and conclusion: watercress markedly increased lipid-soluble antioxidants (α-tocopherol, γ-tocopherol, xanthophyll) in both phases, leading to the conclusion that short- and long-term watercress intake has potential antioxidant benefits against exercise-induced DNA damage and lipid peroxidation.
Final conclusion fragment: concluding phrase stating that watercress ingestion may protect against exercise-induced DNA damage and lipid peroxidation.

Abstract of a study on oxidative DNA damage in human peripheral leukocytes after a 42 km marathon, introducing the hypothesis that exercise-generated reactive oxygen species reach cell nuclei and cause unrepaired DNA base oxidation, measured alongside urinary 8-OHdG.

Results from the marathon study: single cell gel electrophoresis with lesion-specific endonucleases shows oxidized pyrimidines (endonuclease III-sensitive sites) account for most postexercise nucleotide oxidation in leukocytes.

Concluding findings of the marathon study: oxidative DNA damage correlates with plasma creatine kinase and lipid peroxidation markers, persists for over a week after the race, and may contribute to exercise-induced immune dysfunction.

Introduces the comet assay (SCG) as a method for detecting DNA strand breaks in individual cells, and describes the study design: peripheral blood cells from three volunteers, measured during treadmill running with cardiovascular and metabolic monitoring.
Continues the methods: blood sampling before, during, and after exercise, plus the two running protocols, an incremental test to exhaustion and a 45-minute run at a fixed aerobic speed.

Reports the main finding from the incremental exercise test: increased DNA migration in white blood cells, peaking 24 h after exercise, returning to control levels by 72 h, and reflecting a broad effect across most cells.

Describes the cell-level distribution of DNA migration showing that most white blood cells were affected, and introduces the parallel sister chromatid exchange (SCE) cultures set up from the same blood samples as another genotoxicity marker.

Reports that SCE frequency showed no significant increase in any culture, and that the DNA migration effect did not appear in the second, aerobic-metabolism exercise. The abstract is truncated at 250 words.

Abstract of a randomized controlled trial on whole-body vibration training (WBVT) as a pre-exercise intervention to prevent delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), stating the study's background, rationale, and objective.

Study design and participants: 32 healthy untrained volunteers randomized to a WBVT group (n=15) or control group (n=17), with the eccentric exercise intervention protocol introduced in the DOMS WBVT trial.

Intervention details: the eccentric exercise protocol (6 sets of 10 maximal isokinetic knee extensor contractions) and the WBVT parameters (35 Hz, 5 mm peak-to-peak, 100° knee flexion, 60 seconds) applied before exercise, versus no vibration for controls.

Outcome measures and timing schedule: muscle soreness, thigh circumference, pressure pain threshold, and maximal voluntary isometric and isokinetic knee extensor strength assessed at multiple postexercise time points in the WBVT DOMS study.

Results summary: the WBVT group showed less strength loss, lower serum creatine kinase, less pressure pain threshold change, and less muscle soreness compared with controls (P < .05), describing the protective effect against DOMS.

Conclusions of the WBVT DOMS trial: WBVT applied before eccentric exercise may reduce DOMS via improved muscle function, though no effect on thigh circumference was found, and no effect on thigh circumference was evident in the study.
Final conclusion sentence of the abstract recommending further research on whether WBVT effectively attenuates DOMS in athletes.

Introduction and study design: background on massage therapy for muscle rehabilitation, the unknown cellular mechanisms, and the setup of 11 young males with exercise-induced muscle damage receiving massage or no treatment.

Methods and first findings: quadriceps (vastus lateralis) biopsy timepoints (baseline, after 10 min massage, after 2.5 h recovery), and the start of results describing massage activating the mechanotransduction pathway FAK.
Signaling results: massage activating FAK and ERK1/2, boosting PGC-1α mitochondrial biogenesis signaling, and reducing the exercise-induced rise in NF-κB (p65) nuclear accumulation.
Metabolic and inflammatory results: massage did not change glycogen or lactate, but reduced TNF-α and IL-6 production and HSP27 phosphorylation, lessening cellular stress from myofiber injury.
Conclusion: summarizes that massage given to acutely damaged muscle appears clinically beneficial by reducing inflammation and promoting mitochondrial biogenesis.
Introduces DOMS as the soreness that follows unaccustomed eccentric exercise causing tissue disruption, and notes the late-1970s hypothesis linking it to acute inflammation.
Explains that the inflammation hypothesis was not supported by later research, and states the paper's thesis that much DOMS research reflects acute inflammatory events.

Lists the specific parallels between DOMS and acute inflammation (pain, swelling, lost function, macrophage infiltration, lysosomal and acute phase protein markers, early histological changes) and previews the paper's final section.
Closing fragment stating that the final section proposes a theoretical sequence of DOMS events based on acute inflammation research.
Introduction to muscle soreness from a review article on immediate soreness vs. delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), covering how they differ in timing and the multiple underlying mechanisms.
Describes the DOMS pathophysiology sequence: microtrauma to muscle and connective tissue, followed by inflammation, fluid and electrolyte shifts, and possible muscle spasms that worsen symptoms.
Summarizes management of immediate soreness and DOMS, noting varied outcomes across modalities and that judicious NSAID use and continued exercise are the most reliable, recommended methods.

Concluding caveat that the review and cited studies are only one part of clinical decision-making, and that assessing temporary soreness-related deficits and medical management remain the clinician's responsibility.

Study design: healthy adults (n=18) given 280 g/day Bing sweet cherries for 28 days, with fasting blood sampling at baseline, mid-study, end, and a post-washout follow-up; objective is effects on plasma lipids and inflammation markers.

Main results during supplementation: CRP, RANTES, and NO concentrations fell by 25%, 21%, and 18% respectively (significance reported for CRP and RANTES, NO borderline at P=0.07) after 28 days of cherry consumption.
Post-discontinuation follow-up: RANTES kept declining at day 64 (P=0.001), while CRP and NO returned to levels not different from pre-cherry (d 7) or end-of-supplementation (d 35) values.

Null findings: IL-6, soluble IL-6 receptor, ICAM-1, and TIMP-2 were unchanged; cherries had no effect on total, HDL, LDL, VLDL cholesterol, triglycerides, lipoprotein subfractions, particle sizes, or numbers.

Other null outcomes and conclusion: fasting glucose, insulin, and other chemical and hematological variables were unaffected; authors conclude sweet cherries selectively modulate CRP, NO, and RANTES, suggesting anti-inflammatory benefit for inflammatory disease management and prevention.
Concluding sentence fragment of the abstract stating that the anti-inflammatory effects of sweet cherries may benefit management and prevention of inflammatory diseases.

Introduction to a study on blueberry intake and exercise: describes anthocyanin antioxidants and strenuous running as an acute oxidative stress/inflammation model, and states the aim of testing 250 g/day for 6 weeks plus a 375 g dose 1 h before 2.5 h running.

Study design and participants: 25 well-trained subjects randomized to blueberry (BB, n=13) or control (CON, n=12) groups, with blood, muscle, and urine sampling pre-exercise, immediately post-exercise, and 1 h post-exercise.

Blood measurements used as outcomes: F2-isoprostanes for oxidative stress, cortisol, cytokines, homocysteine, leukocytes, T-cell function, NK and lymphocyte counts for inflammation/immune activation, and plasma ferric reducing ability for antioxidant capacity.

Muscle and urine outcomes and statistics: muscle biopsies for glycogen and NFkB expression, urinary 8-OHdG (DNA) and 5-OHMU (RNA) as nucleic acid oxidation markers, analyzed with a 2 (treatment) x 3 (time) repeated measures ANOVA.

Results: F2-isoprostanes and urinary 5-OHMU rose significantly less in the blueberry group, plasma IL-10 and NK cell counts were significantly higher in BB than CON, and all other markers showed no group difference.
Conclusion: daily blueberry intake for 6 weeks increased NK cell counts, and acute pre-exercise ingestion reduced oxidative stress and increased anti-inflammatory cytokines.

Abstract-style opening of a 2009 study on tart cherry juice vs. placebo for marathon recovery: describes the design (20 recreational marathon runners, 5 days pre-race through 48 h post-race) and the outcome markers for muscle damage, inflammation, and oxidative stress.

Methods and measured markers: lists the muscle damage indices (creatine kinase, LDH, soreness, isometric strength), inflammation markers (IL-6, CRP, uric acid), antioxidant status (TAS), and oxidative stress markers (TBARS, protein carbonyls) assessed before and after the marathon.

Key results: isometric strength recovered faster in the cherry juice group (P=0.024), other damage indices showed no difference, inflammation was reduced (IL-6, CRP, uric acid), and total antioxidant status was about 10% higher with cherry juice.

Remaining results and conclusion: protein carbonyls did not differ, TBARS was lower with cherry juice at 48 h, and the authors conclude cherry juice aids recovery by boosting antioxidant capacity and reducing inflammation and lipid peroxidation.
Publication copyright line: a 2009 John Wiley & Sons A/S notice closing the abstract of the tart cherry juice marathon recovery study.

Study introduction: antioxidant supplements (vitamin E, beta-carotene, later vitamin C) tested on blood lactate and aerobic/anaerobic thresholds in 15 amateur male athletes randomized to placebo or supplement groups.
Study design continues: the 90-day supplementation regimen (vitamin C added in the last 15 days) and pre/post maximal cycle ergometer testing with blood lactate and physiological measurements.
Results: VO2max, maximal blood lactate, and maximal workload rose significantly in both groups after 3 months of training, with lower maximal lactate in the supplemented group.

Results on thresholds: the anaerobic threshold as a percentage of VO2max rose in both groups, ending higher in the supplemented group, leading to the conclusion that supplements reduce lactate increases.
Conclusion: antioxidant supplements produced smaller rises in blood lactate after maximal exercise and may improve the efficiency of aerobic energy production.

Study overview: aim, population (18 adults with NIDDM), and design comparing unsweetened fruit juice vs. regular decaffeinated soda as liquids in mixed meals, within the diabetic exchange meal-planning framework.

Methods: three test breakfasts identical except the fruit exchange, using carbohydrate-equivalent fresh orange slices (breakfast 1), unsweetened orange juice (breakfast 2), and regular decaffeinated Coke (breakfast 3), with serum glucose measured at fasting and 1, 2, and 3 hours.

Results and conclusion: no difference in postprandial serum glucose between Coke and orange juice in the breakfast, which questions using unsweetened fruit juices in routine meal planning for people with NIDDM.
Concluding fragment: final words of the conclusion stating that the findings question the use of unsweetened fruit juices in routine meal planning for individuals with NIDDM.

Abstract opening of a study on orange juice and blood lipids: background on orange juice's hypocholesterolemic effects in animals, the objective, and the design sample of 16 men and 9 hypercholesterolemic women.

Study design continuation: participants sequentially added 1, 2, or 3 cups (250 mL each) of orange juice to their diets for 4 weeks per dose, followed by a 5-week washout, with lipid, folate, homocysteine, and vitamin C (compliance marker) measured at each stage.

Results section: 750 mL/day of orange juice, but not 250 or 500 mL, raised HDL-cholesterol by 21%, triacylglycerol by 30%, and folate by 18%, while the LDL-HDL ratio fell 16% and homocysteine was unchanged.

Remaining results and conclusion start: homocysteine unaffected, plasma vitamin C rising 2.1 to 3.8 times across dietary periods, and the conclusion that 750 mL/day orange juice improved lipid profiles in hypercholesterolemic subjects.
Final conclusion: 750 mL/day of orange juice improved blood lipid profiles in hypercholesterolemic subjects, supporting recommendations to eat 5-10 daily servings of fruit and vegetables.
Abstract opening of the study: objective and methods of a trial on orange juice plus aerobic training in 26 overweight middle-aged women (13 per group, 3 months).
Results section comparing weight and fat mass loss between the control group (aerobic training only) and the orange juice group after 3 months.
Results on dietary intake changes from orange juice (vitamin C, folate) and the effects on serum LDL-C and HDL-C lipid profile in the experimental group.
Results on anaerobic threshold and blood lactate changes in both groups, followed by the start of the conclusions about cardiovascular risk and muscle fatigue.

Conclusions summarizing that orange juice with aerobic training reduced cardiovascular disease risk via LDL-C and HDL-C changes, and improved blood lactate and anaerobic threshold, ending with the copyright notice.
Copyright notice (Elsevier Ireland Ltd, 2010) closing the abstract of the orange juice and aerobic training study.

Opening of the abstract for a prospective cohort study on fruit and vegetable intake and ischemic stroke risk; introduces the background, objective, and the Nurses' Health Study (women) and Health Professionals' Follow-up Study (men) populations and follow-up periods.

Continues the study design and methods: confirms participants were free of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and diabetes at baseline, names the main outcome (ischemic stroke incidence by fruit/vegetable intake quintile), and begins the results with case counts.

Core results: stroke case totals (366 women, 204 men) and the top-versus-bottom quintile comparison of fruit and vegetable intake, with median servings per day and an adjusted relative risk of 0.69 for the highest quintile.

Dose-response findings: each additional daily serving of fruit or vegetables linked to 6% lower ischemic stroke risk (RR 0.94, test for trend P=.01), and subtype results showing cruciferous and green leafy vegetables as protective.

Specific food contributors: citrus fruit, including juice and citrus juice alone, contribute most to the protective effect; legumes and potatoes showed no association; also gives the pooled total stroke RR per 2 servings per day.

Conclusion of the abstract: states that fruit and vegetable consumption, especially cruciferous and green leafy vegetables and citrus fruit and juice, supports a protective relationship against ischemic stroke.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, restating the protective link between citrus fruit and juice and ischemic stroke risk.
Abstract opening of a study on flavonoid glycosides in lettuce and endive: sample varieties and total flavonoid content ranges (aglycon units, µg/g fresh weight).
Identifies the specific quercetin, luteolin, and cyanidin conjugates measured in green-leafed lettuce and red-leafed lettuce varieties, plus kaempferol conjugates in endive.

Reports the three kaempferol conjugates in endive, notes first-time identification of kaempferol 3-O-(6-O-malonyl)glucoside in endive, and begins describing the effect of shredding and light exposure on lettuce.

Gives percentage losses of the flavonoid moiety after shredding and light exposure across lettuce cultivars (e.g., green oak leaf 94%, iceberg 36%) and notes cos and green salad bowl showed no loss; also starts endive shredding losses.
Covers endive shredding losses (escarole, frisee types), demalonation of quercetin and cyanidin glucosides in lettuce and the kaempferol analogue in endive, and begins describing storage conditions.

Describes storage of whole lettuce and endive heads in the dark at 1 °C and 98% humidity for 7 days, with 7-46% losses of flavonol glycosides, and concludes on the importance of sugar and substitution identification for bioavailability and bioactivity of salad flavonoids.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence stressing the relevance of flavonoid profiles in salads to biological activities.

Introduction and rationale: fruit/vegetable intake and postprandial oxidation, plus the hypothesis that an orange flavonoid mixture would outperform single flavonoids or sugar/ascorbic acid but trail orange juice, in a crossover trial.
Study design: placebo-controlled crossover trial with 16 participants, 4 treatments, and 4 visits, describing the placebo and the hesperidin treatment arms.

Methods: the four treatments (placebo, placebo plus hesperidin, placebo plus the hesperidin/luteolin/naringenin mixture, and orange juice as positive control) and the outcome measures (serum ORAC, total plasma phenolics, lipoprotein oxidation) at baseline and 1-3 hours.
Results: the placebo-plus-mixture and orange juice groups significantly increased ORAC and LO lag time, while total plasma phenolics results were inconsistent with these measures.

Conclusion: orange phenolics directly contribute to postprandial serum antioxidant protection, contrary to prior work crediting fructose and ascorbate, despite inconsistent TP changes; includes the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
Introduction and objectives of a randomized crossover trial on orange juice, its flavonoid hesperidin, microvascular reactivity, blood pressure, and cardiovascular biomarkers in healthy volunteers.

Study design: 24 healthy overweight men aged 50-65 in a crossover trial with three 4-week periods comparing orange juice, control drink plus hesperidin (CDH), and control drink plus placebo (CDP), plus a postprandial study at the start of each period.

Methods detail on fasting measurements and blood collections before and after each 4-week period, and timing of the postprandial study, followed by the start of the results reporting diastolic blood pressure.

Results: diastolic blood pressure was lower after 4 weeks of orange juice or CDH versus CDP, while fasting microvascular endothelial reactivity was unchanged, but postprandial reactivity improved with orange juice and CDH at peak hesperetin levels.

Conclusions: regular orange juice lowers diastolic blood pressure and postprandially improves endothelium-dependent microvascular reactivity in middle-aged overweight men, with the postprandial results emphasized alongside the chronic effect.
Final conclusion that hesperidin may causally mediate orange juice's vascular benefits, followed by the clinical trial registration number NCT00983086 on clinicaltrials.gov.

Introduces the study of hesperetin (HN) and its analogue (HA) for apoptosis induction in HT-29 colon cancer cells, and reports MTT assay results showing dose- and time-dependent reduction in cell growth.

Gives the 24-hour IC50-type result (70 μM HN, 32 μM HA giving 50% growth reduction) and reports acridine orange/ethidium bromide staining showing apoptotic morphology and Rhodamine 123 staining showing mitochondrial membrane potential loss.

Reports DNA damage confirmed by comet assay, elevated lipid peroxidation (TBARS) and protein oxidation (PCC) markers, and slightly reduced antioxidant enzyme activities (SOD, CAT, GPx) versus untreated HT-29 controls.

Presents Western blot findings of increased cytochrome C, Bax and cleaved caspase-3 with decreased Bcl-2, and begins the conclusion that HN and HA induce apoptosis via a pathway involving oxidant/antioxidant imbalance.
Concludes that HN and HA trigger apoptosis in HT-29 cells through a Bax-dependent mitochondrial pathway linked to oxidant/antioxidant imbalance, followed by the copyright notice (Elsevier, 2011).

Abstract opening of a 2012 Royal Society of Chemistry study on micronized water-dispersible hesperetin, introducing its citrus-flavonoid background, vasodilatation expectation, and the study's aims (bioavailability, endothelial cell and human volunteer testing).
Continuation of the abstract describing the pharmacokinetic result: rapid absorption, Cmax of 10.2 ± 1.2 μM, and Cmax reached within 1 h after oral administration of 150 mg in humans.
Abstract passage identifying the plasma metabolites at Cmax (Hp7GA, Hp3'GA, hesperetin sulfate) by LC-MS, and reporting that Hp7GA enhances nitric oxide release, similar to hesperetin.

Mechanistic and clinical findings: Hp7GA inhibits NADPH oxidase to boost NO release in human umbilical vein endothelial cells, and a single-dose volunteer study in women with cold sensitivity showed peripheral vasodilatation.

Conclusion linking rapid accumulation and higher plasma concentration of hesperetin metabolites to endothelial vasodilatation, suggesting water-dispersible hesperetin may improve the health effects of dietary hesperetin.
Closing fragment of the abstract ending the conclusion about dietary health benefits, followed by the Royal Society of Chemistry 2012 copyright notice.

Introduces the cohort study question: whether plant food intake (fruits/berries, vegetables, cereals) predicts lower cerebrovascular disease incidence in a Finnish population with low fruit/vegetable and high wholegrain intake, motivated by prior contradictory findings.

Describes the study population and design: 3932 men and women from the Finnish Mobile Clinic Health Examination Survey (1968-72), aged 40-74 and free of cardiovascular disease at baseline, with plant food intake assessed by a 1-year dietary history interview.

Reports the main outcome and key finding: 625 cerebrovascular disease cases over 24-year follow-up (hospitalisation or death), with an inverse association between fruit consumption and cerebrovascular disease, ischaemic stroke, and intracerebral haemorrhage.

Gives the adjusted relative risks comparing highest vs lowest fruit intake quartiles for total cerebrovascular disease (0.75), ischaemic stroke (0.73), and intracerebral haemorrhage (0.47), and notes the associations were mainly from citrus fruit and seen only in men.

States that total vegetable and cereal intake showed no association with cerebrovascular disease, while cruciferous vegetables predicted reduced risk of cerebrovascular disease (RR 0.79), ischaemic stroke (RR 0.67), and intracerebral haemorrhage (RR 0.49).
Concludes that fruit consumption, especially citrus, and cruciferous vegetables may protect against cerebrovascular diseases.

Introduction to the review on natural pancreatic lipase inhibitors: states the rising obesity prevalence, the scarcity of approved antiobesity drugs, and the rationale for targeting lipid-metabolism enzymes.

Explains the therapeutic strategy of blocking dietary triglyceride absorption by inhibiting pancreatic lipase, the main source of excess calories, and notes natural products as a rich pool of candidate inhibitors.

Concludes the abstract by stating the review's scope: plant- and microbe-derived extracts and secondary metabolites with pancreatic lipase inhibitory activity, identified as candidates for drug development.
Background and objective of a human crossover study on orange juice, hesperidin, and leukocyte gene expression, introducing prior findings on blood pressure and endothelial reactivity.
Study design: randomized controlled crossover trial with three 4-week periods comparing orange juice, control drink plus hesperidin, and control drink plus placebo.
Methods and sampling: daily intake regimens, blood samples taken from 10 overnight-fasted subjects after treatment, and whole-genome cDNA microarray gene expression profiling.
Key results: orange juice and hesperidin both significantly altered leukocyte gene expression, with counts of regulated genes (3,422 and 1,819) and 1,582 genes shared between the two groups.

Interpretation of findings: shared regulated genes involved in chemotaxis, adhesion, infiltration, and lipid transport, suggesting reduced leukocyte recruitment to vessel walls and less lipid accumulation.

Conclusions and trial registration: chronic orange juice intake shifts leukocytes toward an anti-inflammatory, anti-atherogenic profile with hesperidin playing a relevant role; registered as ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00983086.

Introduction of the citrus flavonoid review: links dietary factors and oxidative stress to neurodegeneration, and notes flavonoids' cardioprotective, chemopreventive, and neuroprotective effects via antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and signaling activity.

Argues that understanding whether flavonoids act as antioxidants or signaling molecules is key to using them against neurodegeneration and as brain foods, and that citrus flavonoids show little adverse effect and low or no cytotoxicity to healthy cells.

States that the main citrus flavonoids cross the blood-brain barrier, making them promising for neurodegeneration intervention, and outlines the review's scope: bioactivity, neuroprotective mechanisms, and antioxidant and signaling properties.

Previews the review's later topics: receptor-mediated neuroprotection, parallel signaling pathways, and induction of cellular defense proteins against oxidative stress and neurotoxicity by hesperetin, a widespread citrus flavonoid.
Concludes that citrus fruits, rich in hesperetin and other flavonoids, are promising sources for food-based neuroprotection and brain foods.

Introduction and objective of a review on flavonoids and cancer prevention, covering flavonoid subclasses and the epidemiological evidence linking flavonoid intake to reduced risk of breast, colon, lung, prostate, and pancreatic tumors.

Discusses mixed epidemiological findings on flavonoids and cancer (some inconclusive or harmful), and methodological limits of the evidence, namely reliance on case-control studies and retrospective intake assessment.

Covers sources of heterogeneity in flavonoid intake across US, European, and Asian populations (agriculture, sociodemographics, lifestyle), and notes that dose and timing of exposure may shape the anticancer effect of flavonoid-rich diets.

Summarizes the limited intervention trial evidence, the proposed anticancer mechanisms (inhibiting proliferation, inflammation, invasion, metastasis; activating apoptosis), and calls for prospective studies and biomarker development.
Concluding research needs: mechanistic studies to determine how flavonoid-rich diets regulate gene expression for cancer prevention.
Background and objective of a US study on phytonutrient intake from fruits and vegetables, using NHANES data to estimate usual intakes of nine phytonutrients.

Study objective continued: comparing phytonutrient intakes of Americans meeting vs. not meeting fruit and vegetable recommendations, and identifying food sources; notes these phytonutrients are mainly found in fruits and vegetables.
Design methods: NHANES 2003-2006 food consumption data combined with USDA and literature phytonutrient concentration data to estimate energy-adjusted usual intakes, compared with Student's t tests.

Results begin: energy-adjusted phytonutrient intakes were considerably higher in men and women meeting fruit and vegetable recommendations than in those not meeting them, with ellagic acid as the exception.

Results detail: ellagic acid intake was higher only in women meeting recommendations; for five of nine phytonutrients (α-carotene, β-cryptoxanthin, lycopene, hesperetin, ellagic acid) a single food supplied 64% or more of intake.
Conclusions: carotenoid and flavonoid intakes are higher among those following fruit and vegetable guidance, and a limited number of foods supply most of these phytonutrients.
Final conclusion: the findings offer useful reference information on phytonutrient contributions of a diet rich in fruits and vegetables.

Introduces the USP Dietary Supplements Information Expert Committee (DSI-EC) and its role in reviewing dietary supplement safety for USP-NF quality monographs, plus FDA's misbranding enforcement authority tied to USP conformance claims. Part of a document on the USP safety evaluation of spirulina.

Explains FDA enforcement authority over supplements falsely claiming USP conformance, then states that DSI-EC recently conducted a safety evaluation of spirulina, a widely used dietary ingredient. Part of the USP spirulina safety evaluation document.

Describes the evidence DSI-EC reviewed for spirulina (human clinical trials, animal studies, regulatory and pharmacopeial sources, and 31 adverse event reports) and the outcome: a Class A safety rating for Spirulina maxima and S. platensis, enabling USP-NF quality monographs.

Notes that DSI-EC continually monitors safety reports for supplement ingredients with USP monographs and that it may revisit spirulina's Class A safety classification as new information emerges. Part of the USP spirulina safety evaluation document.

Closing sentence stating that the spirulina safety classification may be revisited when new information on the ingredient becomes available. Concludes the USP DSI-EC spirulina safety evaluation document.

Introduces the concern that weight loss supplements contain potent pharmacoactive ingredients that may cause harm, and that safety/efficacy trials are often small, short, and lack financial conflict of interest disclosures, misleading consumers when advertising cites such research.

Names specific weight loss products (Metabolife-356, Hydroxycut, Xenadrine, LeptiCore) backed by conflicted or low-quality research, and continues the point that advertising falsely implies science has proven safety and effectiveness.
Concludes with calls for better conflict of interest disclosure in weight loss supplement research and for regulators to scrutinize how research findings are used in marketing claims.

Introduction of a case report on aloe-induced toxic hepatitis: background on aloe's use in phytomedicine, its reported anti-inflammatory and anti-aging properties, and the poorly understood hepatotoxicity that motivates reporting three cases.

Case presentation from the aloe-induced toxic hepatitis report: three women (aged 55, 57, and 62) admitted with acute hepatitis after months of oral aloe preparation use, whose findings met RUCAM criteria for toxic hepatitis.
Conclusion of the aloe-induced toxic hepatitis case report: liver enzymes normalized after stopping oral aloe preparations, supporting aloe as a causative agent of hepatotoxicity.

Introduction and study design of an 8-week randomized, double-blind placebo-controlled trial of a Ma Huang/Guarana herbal weight-loss supplement (72 mg/day ephedrine alkaloids, 240 mg/day caffeine) in overweight adults with BMI 29-35, stating the objective and primary outcome (body weight change).

Study population and enrollment: overweight men and women randomized to placebo (n=32) or active Ma Huang/Guarana (n=35), with 24 completers per group; outcome measures listed as primary body weight change and secondary anthropometric, metabolic and cardiovascular changes.

Main efficacy results: active Ma Huang/Guarana produced significantly greater weight loss (-4.0 kg vs -0.8 kg placebo, P<0.006) and fat loss (-2.1% vs +0.2%) over 8 weeks, plus greater reductions in hip circumference and serum triglycerides.

Safety and tolerability results: 23% of active-treatment subjects (8 of 35) withdrew due to potential treatment-related effects versus none on placebo; dry mouth, insomnia and headache were the most frequently reported adverse symptoms in the herbal group.
Conclusions of the trial: the Ma Huang and Guarana herbal mixture effectively promoted short-term weight and fat loss, but long-term safety requires further investigation.

Introduction to the report on mangosteen and other botanical liquid dietary supplements: their growing market, juice-like appearance, unknown health and safety effects, and manufacturers' reliance on low-quality research for promotion.

Purpose and scope of the report: it examines science-based marketing claims for two widely consumed mangosteen liquid supplements and compares those claims against the findings of the research they cite.

The reviewer's key findings: the marketing claims overstate the significance of the research and omit severe methodological weaknesses, with a warned public health risk if similar products follow the same pattern.
Concluding clause of the report's warning that consumers may wrongly believe product safety and effectiveness are supported by rigorous scientific evidence.

Introduction of the Hydroxycut case series: background on the Muscletech Hydroxycut weight loss supplement, its May 2009 recall for hepatotoxicity, and the study objectives of characterizing liver injury and assessing causality.

Study design and methods for the Hydroxycut hepatotoxicity case series: case series design, academic tertiary care and FDA database settings, and DILIN methodology for causality assessment and injury severity grading.

Results of the Hydroxycut liver injury study: eight hospitalized patients (3 requiring liver transplant) from multiple medical centers, plus nine FDA MedWatch cases including one fatal acute liver failure.

Clinical findings and causality adjudication for Hydroxycut-associated liver injury: common symptoms (jaundice, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain), predominantly hepatocellular injury pattern, and causality ratings of definite, highly likely, probable, and possible cases.

Conclusions of the Hydroxycut case series: Hydroxycut is clearly linked to severe liver injury, acute liver failure and death, and weight loss supplements should be considered capable of severe hepatic toxicity when other causes are excluded.

Abstract's AIM section stating the study goal: evaluating weight-loss effects of HCA-SX alone and combined with niacin-bound chromium and Gymnema sylvestre extract in moderately obese subjects, using body weight, BMI, appetite, lipids, leptin, and urinary fat metabolites as outcomes.

Abstract background on the ingredients: HCA-SX reduces appetite and fat synthesis without CNS stimulation, niacin-bound chromium supports healthy insulin levels, and Gymnema sylvestre extract aids weight and blood sugar regulation.

Abstract METHODS describing the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled 8-week trial in 60 moderately obese adults (ages 21-50, BMI >26) in India, with three groups receiving HCA-SX alone, HCA-SX combined with NBC and GSE, or placebo.

Abstract RESULTS part one: all subjects were on a 2000 kcal diet with supervised walking, and at 8 weeks body weight and BMI fell 5-6% in the HCA-SX and combination groups, with reduced food intake, cholesterol, LDL, triglycerides, and leptin.
Abstract RESULTS part two: HDL and urinary fat metabolite excretion rose in both active groups, while the placebo group showed marginal or non-significant effects across all parameters.

Abstract CONCLUSION stating that optimal-dose HCA-SX, and more so the HCA-SX, NBC and GSE combination, is an effective and safe weight-loss formula that reduces body weight, BMI, and supports healthy blood lipids.

Case report opening the abstract of a paper on acute liver injury (hepatotoxicity) in a 14-year-old boy after drinking noni (Morinda citrifolia) berry juice, and calling for greater clinical awareness as noni consumption grows.
Introduction on reducing fat in ground beef: health motivation, how fat replacers alter meat flavor/aroma, and the need to add water and water-binding agents when fat is removed.

Continuation on water replacement and water-binding compounds to prevent cook loss and patty shrinkage, followed by the classification of fat replacers into protein-based, lipid-based (emulsifiers like soy lecithin), and carbohydrate-based types.

Lists specific carbohydrate-based replacers (flours, starches, gums) and states that replicating fat's characteristics typically requires combining replacers to balance juiciness and firmness without harming flavor.
Concluding sentence on the need for replacer combinations to maintain juiciness and firmness without flavor loss, followed by the publisher copyright line (Elsevier Ltd) ending the document.

Introduces carrageenan (lambda, kappa, iota forms) as a sulfated galactose food additive and its structural resemblance to endogenous sulfated galactose/GalNAc glycosaminoglycans (chondroitin sulfate, dermatan sulfate, keratan sulfate), noting differing glycosidic bonds.

Explains the glycosidic bond difference (alpha-1,3 in carrageenan vs. beta-1,3/beta-1,4 in GAGs) and the rationale that carrageenan's high sulfation may inhibit sulfatase activity, motivating the study.

Reports the main finding that carrageenan exposure in human intestinal and mammary epithelial cells significantly reduced activity of multiple sulfatases (e.g., GALNS, GALNS-6, IDS, STS, ARSA, SULF-1/2, heparan sulfamidase).

Describes downstream consequences: GAG content rose after carrageenan exposure, with altered chondroitin sulfate disaccharide profiles (increased CSD 2S6S and CS-E 4S6S; decreased CS-A 4S and CS-C 6S).
Details heparin-heparan sulfate disaccharide changes (increased 6S, NS, and 2S6S) and concludes that sulfatase inhibition redistributes cellular GAG composition toward more di-sulfated CS.
Concludes that the redistribution of cellular GAG composition toward di-sulfated CS may have potential consequences for cell structure and function.

Introduces the study's background: food additive carrageenan (CGN) causes intestinal inflammation and colitis-like effects in animals, and the study examines CGN's effects on NF-κB and EGR-1 transcription factors regarding human intestinal epithelial barrier integrity.

Describes results: CGN elevates both NF-κB and EGR-1, but only NF-κB drives pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-8 induction; also notes the in vitro epithelial monolayer's integrity under CGN exposure is being assessed.

Presents key findings: NF-κB and EGR-1 both help maintain monolayer integrity under CGN; suppressing either worsens CGN-induced barrier disruption, linked to reduced zonula occludens 1 (tight junction) expression and irregular localization.
Closing portion of the abstract containing the end of the zonula occludens 1 localization finding and the copyright notice (Elsevier Ireland Ltd., 2012).
Introduction to a Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee report on food additive safety, covering ADI recommendations, identity/purity specifications, and tolerable intake evaluation for food contaminants.
Describes the report's structure: a general section on toxicological evaluation and dietary exposure assessment principles for food additives and contaminants, followed by a summary of evaluations.

Lists the specific food additives evaluated by the Committee (e.g., aluminium-containing additives, Ponceau 4R, pullulan, Quinoline Yellow, Sunset Yellow FCF, rosin glycerol esters, polydimethyl siloxane) and the two contaminants: cyanogenic glycosides and fumonisins.

Notes the food additives and contaminants evaluated, then states that specifications for several additives were revised, starting with aluminium lakes of colouring matters and carotenoid-related substances.

Continues the list of additives with revised specifications (beta-carotene synthetic, hydroxypropyl methyl cellulose, magnesium silicate, modified starches, nitrous oxide, sodium carboxymethyl cellulose, sucrose monoesters) and introduces the annexed summary tables.
Closing statement that annexed tables summarize the Committee's dietary exposure recommendations and toxicological evaluations for all additives and contaminants covered in the report.

Opening chunk of an abstract from the second French Total Diet Study on dietary acrylamide exposure; introduces acrylamide as a heat-induced carcinogen and reports highest mean concentrations in potato chips, fries, and salted biscuits.

Middle section of the abstract, continuing the food-level acrylamide concentrations and describing how exposure for adults and children was estimated by combining analytical results with national consumption data.
Reports the estimated mean daily acrylamide exposure for adults and children (μg/kg bw/day) and the margins of exposure, which are very low especially for young children, indicating a health concern.
Concluding part of the abstract recommending continued efforts to reduce dietary acrylamide exposure, followed by the publisher copyright notice.

Introduction to carrageenans: definition as sulfated seaweed polysaccharides and their use in food and meat industries, including reduced-fat meat products, plus the basic composition of meat as a complex system.

Role of carrageenans in meat systems: interactions among muscle, connective tissue, fat, and water determine functional properties, and carrageenans aid gel formation and water retention, which is especially relevant to low-fat meat products.

Benefits of carrageenans in low-fat meat: fat reduction causes tough textures, and carrageenan addition reduces toughness and increases juiciness; also notes that carrageenan-milk protein interactions are well studied while carrageenan-meat interactions are not.
Research gap: the mechanism by which carrageenans interact with meat proteins and other meat components remains poorly understood, despite extensive study of carrageenan-milk protein interactions.

Introduces the study's motivation: prior animal studies link food additive carrageenan to intestinal inflammation and neoplasia, and this is the first in-vitro test of very low doses (1-10 mg/L) of undegraded high-molecular-weight CGN on human intestinal epithelial cells.

States the exposure relevance and the main findings in NCM460 cells and primary human colonic epithelial cells: CGN at 1-8 days caused cell death, reduced proliferation, and cell cycle arrest, with these doses below estimated Western diet exposure.
Details the cell cycle results after 6-8 days of CGN exposure (fewer cells re-entering G0-G1, more in S and G2-M) and the molecular evidence of arrest, namely increased activated p53, p21, and p15.
Reports the cell death mechanism assays (DNA ladder, PARP Western blot, nuclear DNA staining, caspase 3/7 activity), which showed no apoptosis and instead pointed to CGN-induced necrotic cell death.
Concludes that low-dose CGN markedly harms survival of normal human intestinal epithelial cells, a first-of-its-kind finding suggesting CGN exposure may contribute to human intestinal pathology.

Introduces carrageenan, a sulfated polygalactan food additive, and its known inflammatory effects in rheumatological and colitis models; sets up the study of its direct effects on human intestinal cells, including NCM460 and primary cells.

Describes the study methods: cell types tested (primary human colonic epithelial cells, NCM460 line, rat ileal cells), the treatment of lambda-carrageenan at 1 μg/ml for 1-96 h, and the readouts measured (IL-8, NF-kappaB, IkappaBalpha, Bcl10).

Reports the main results: carrageenan increased Bcl10, nuclear and cytoplasmic NF-kappaB, IL-8 promoter activation and IL-8 secretion, and Bcl10 siRNA knockdown reduced the IL-8 increase in NCM460 cells.

States the conclusion that carrageenan triggers a distinct Bcl10-dependent NF-kappaB/IL-8 inflammatory pathway in intestinal epithelial cells, and notes Bcl10's caspase-recruitment domain as a possible link to NOD2/CARD15 and Crohn's disease.

Discusses the broader implications: a possible link between genetic (NOD2/CARD15-like) and environmental causes of inflammatory bowel disease, with the findings relevant given carrageenan's widespread dietary use as a food additive.
Concludes that the widespread dietary use of carrageenan means the findings may have clinical significance.

Introduction of a review on carrageenan's harmful gastrointestinal effects: links carrageenan exposure to colonic ulcers and GI neoplasms in animal models, and notes IARC's 1982 finding on degraded carrageenan's carcinogenicity despite its continued use as a food additive.

Describes the review's scope and methods: examining experimental data on carrageenan-associated ulcerations and neoplasms, and the widespread use of carrageenan as a thickener, stabilizer, and texturizer in Western processed foods.

Summarizes the review's methods (established sources on degraded carrageenan production and intake) and key finding that both undegraded and degraded carrageenan are associated with intestinal ulcerations and neoplasms.
Proposed mechanisms for the observed carrageenan-associated intestinal harm: low-molecular-weight contamination, acid hydrolysis during digestion, and interactions with intestinal bacteria.

Regulatory history: the 1972 FDA consideration of restricting carrageenan to average molecular weight above 100,000, which was never adopted, and the lack of subsequent restrictions despite known carcinogenic and cancer-promoting effects.

Concluding recommendation that the widespread dietary use of carrageenan in the Western diet should be reconsidered given its carcinogenic and cancer-promoting effects in animal and experimental models.
Background section of the Cochrane review on NSAIDs for primary dysmenorrhoea, defining dysmenorrhoea and explaining the prostaglandin mechanism that NSAIDs target.
Continuation of the background explaining NSAID mechanism of blocking prostaglandin production, followed by the review's objectives and the start of the search strategy description.
Search strategy section of the review, listing the databases and trial registers searched (Cochrane Menstrual Disorders group, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE) and additional sources checked.

Continuation of the search strategy (other sources such as citation lists and conference abstracts), then the selection criteria specifying randomised controlled comparisons of NSAIDs against placebo, other NSAIDs, or paracetamol.
Data collection and analysis methods: two reviewers independently assessed quality and extracted data, using odds ratios and weighted mean differences; start of the main results section.

Main results: NSAIDs were significantly more effective than placebo for pain relief but produced more adverse effects, with the odds ratios and confidence intervals reported; also notes comparisons with other NSAIDs or paracetamol.
Main results continued: little evidence that any single NSAID is superior in efficacy or safety, due to low statistical power from few small trials; start of reviewer's conclusions.
Reviewer's conclusions: NSAIDs are effective for dysmenorrhoea but carry significant adverse-effect risk, and evidence is insufficient to identify the single safest and most effective NSAID.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending the sentence about treating dysmenorrhoea with the most safe and effective individual NSAID.
