Opening of a systematic review on surgical pelvic nerve interruption (uterosacral nerve ablation, presacral neurectomy) for dysmenorrhea; describes the objectives and the databases and registers searched.

Continues the search strategy description (registers, citation lists, author contact) and states the review's inclusion criteria: RCTs of uterosacral nerve ablation or presacral neurectomy, open or laparoscopic, with pain relief and adverse effects as outcomes.
Covers review methods (two independent reviewers extracting data) and the start of results: nine RCTs included, two open presacral neurectomy trials, the rest laparoscopic.
Reports primary dysmenorrhea findings: laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation beat control/no treatment at 12 months (OR 6.12), and begins the comparison against presacral neurectomy.

Gives the head-to-head result that presacral neurectomy was more effective than uterosacral nerve ablation for primary dysmenorrhea at 12 months (OR 0.10), and reports secondary dysmenorrhea results where uterosacral ablation added nothing to endometriosis surgery (OR 0.77).

Reports that presacral neurectomy improved pain in secondary dysmenorrhea (OR 3.14), that adverse events were far more frequent with presacral neurectomy (OR 14.6), and gives the conclusion that evidence is limited.
Final conclusion calling for methodologically sound, adequately powered randomized controlled trials on nerve interruption for dysmenorrhea.

Introduces the study on rectal pain threshold in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) vs. functional abdominal pain syndrome (FAPS) and healthy controls, testing repetitive rectal painful distention (RRD) as a conditioning method and whether rectal hypersensitivity reliably marks IBS.

Methods section describing barostat-based rectal sensory testing: a baseline ramp distention at 40 ml/min measuring pain threshold and maximum tolerable pressure, followed by the RRD conditioning protocol (60-s phasic distentions with 30-s intervals).

Continues the methods: RRD is repeated with a tracking method until six pain reports, then the ramp distention is repeated to re-measure the same parameters, with normal values defined from control 95% confidence intervals.

Results: most IBS patients had reduced baseline rectal pain threshold or maximum tolerable pressure, and all IBS patients showed reduced thresholds after RRD, unlike FAPS patients who showed no reduction.

Results and conclusions: RRD significantly lowered both thresholds only in the IBS group (P < 0.05), with no effect in controls or FAPS, leading to the conclusion that RRD-induced rectal hypersensitivity may be a reliable IBS marker and conditioning-induced visceral hypersensitivity may be pathophysiologically relevant.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that conditioning-induced visceral hypersensitivity may play a pathophysiologic role in IBS.

Introduces postinfectious IBS (PI-IBS) as a functional GI disorder: new IBS symptoms appearing right after an acute illness meeting defined criteria (fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or positive stool culture), in someone not previously meeting Rome IBS criteria.

Explains the believed pathophysiology of PI-IBS: unknown exact mechanisms, but transient inflammation during the acute infection is thought to cause subtle, lasting structural and functional changes in the digestive system that produce symptoms.

States the review's scope: recent evidence on how inflammatory mediators drive hypersensitivity, and the mediators and mechanisms behind abdominal pain and discomfort after acute inflammation resolves, including mast cell-nerve fiber anatomic changes.

Notes that mast cell-nerve fiber anatomic changes are necessary but not sufficient for symptoms, and begins listing risk factors for PI-FGID (prolonged initial illness, bacterial strain toxicity, smoking, mucosal inflammation markers, female sex) used to estimate risk.
Completes the risk factor list for developing PI-FGID: depression, hypochondriasis, and adverse life events in the preceding 3 months.

Introduction to postinfectious irritable bowel syndrome (PI-IBS): defines PI-FGDs as functional GI disorders that begin after an acute infectious diarrhea episode, noting about 10% of affected patients have this origin, and frames the review's purpose around pathogenesis and natural history.

Recent findings on PI-IBS: describes cohorts of patients with acute diarrhea or dysentery being followed prospectively for PI-IBS development, and identifies persistent mucosal inflammation, gut air trapping, and altered motility as contributors to symptoms in genetically susceptible individuals.

Prognosis and summary of the review: notes PI-IBS has a more favorable outlook than idiopathic IBS, and argues that characterizing postdiarrheal FGDs can clarify early disease mechanisms and inform understanding of common idiopathic forms.

Concluding implication: predicts that identifying specific gut pathophysiological alterations in postinfectious FGDs will allow reclassifying them from a vaguely defined functional group into distinct, specific gastrointestinal disorders.
Fragment ending the document's final sentence, consisting only of the trailing period of the closing statement about reclassifying postinfectious FGDs as specific gastrointestinal disorders.

Editorial introduction on postinfectious functional gastrointestinal disorders (PI-FGID), noting bacterial PI-FGID is well documented and that risk extends to protozoan and helminth infections; sets up the norovirus finding.
Concluding sentence of the editorial: highlights Zanini et al.'s finding that norovirus gastroenteritis also leads to post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome in a substantial proportion of patients.

Introduction to cisapride: its mechanism as a benzamide prokinetic (acetylcholine release from enteric nerves) and the GI conditions it treats orally, including GERD, functional dyspepsia, gastroparesis, pseudo-obstruction and chronic constipation.

Cisapride's efficacy in gastro-oesophageal reflux disease in adults and children: symptom relief, mucosal healing, and prevention of oesophagitis relapse with long-term use, plus improved gastric emptying in gastroparesis.

Cisapride's effects on gastroparesis and functional dyspepsia: sustained gastric emptying with long-term use (unlike domperidone and metoclopramide), symptom improvement, and comparisons with other agents in dyspepsia trials.

Comparative efficacy of cisapride against metoclopramide, domperidone, clebopride, ranitidine and cimetidine in dyspepsia, and its use in constipation: more stool frequency, less laxative use in idiopathic constipation, with poor response in severe slow-transit cases.

Investigational uses of cisapride in chronic pseudo-obstruction, postoperative ileus, peptic ulcer and irritable bowel syndrome, noting further trials are needed, along with adult dosing ranges (5 mg three times daily to 20 mg twice daily).

Safety and paediatric dosing of cisapride: generally well tolerated in short and long-term adult treatment, and well tolerated in children at 0.2 to 0.3 mg/kg three to four times daily; the abstract is cut off at 250 words.
Study aim and methods of a trial on red pepper (capsaicin) for functional dyspepsia: 30 patients, exclusion of GERD and IBS, 2-week washout, then randomized double-blind design.
Methods continued: patients received 2.5 g/day red pepper powder or placebo before meals for 5 weeks, recording daily symptom diary scores averaged weekly and overall.

Results of the red pepper dyspepsia trial: symptom scores (overall, epigastric pain, fullness, nausea) significantly lower than placebo from week 3, with about 60% reduction versus under 30% for placebo.

Conclusions of the red pepper functional dyspepsia study: red pepper outperformed placebo, likely via capsaicin desensitizing gastric nociceptive C-fibres, suggesting potential therapy for functional dyspepsia.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence stating red pepper could be a potential therapy for functional dyspepsia.

Introduction and background of a preliminary study on red pepper (capsaicin) for irritable bowel syndrome, stating the rationale that capsaicin desensitizes TRPV1 fibres to reduce visceral hypersensitivity causing abdominal pain.

Methods of the red pepper IBS trial: 50 Rome II-diagnosed patients, a 2-week washout, then randomized double-blind dosing of 150 mg enteric-coated red pepper powder pills (4/day for 6 weeks) versus placebo.

Outcome measures in the red pepper IBS study: daily diary scoring of abdominal pain and bloating on a 5-point Likert scale, with weekly mean scores and final subjective effectiveness ratings analyzed statistically between and within groups.

Results on adherence and dropouts in the red pepper IBS trial: 8 patients withdrew (6 red pepper, 2 placebo, mostly for abdominal pain), and 8 patients had their dose reduced to 2 pills/day due to early abdominal pain.

Key efficacy results of the red pepper IBS study: within the red pepper group, abdominal pain and bloating significantly improved in the final weeks versus baseline (unlike placebo), and patients rated red pepper significantly more effective than placebo.

Conclusions of the preliminary red pepper IBS study: chronic enteric-coated red pepper powder was significantly more effective than placebo at reducing abdominal pain and bloating, and patients judged it more effective.
Final closing clause of the conclusions, restating that patients considered red pepper more effective than placebo for reducing abdominal pain and bloating in IBS.

Introduction and background of a study on functional abdominal pain syndrome (FAPS) versus irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), noting rectal hypersensitivity in IBS and the lack of prior visceral sensory evaluation in FAPS.

Study aim and hypothesis: testing whether FAPS shows altered visceral sensation versus healthy controls or IBS, measuring rectal perceptual thresholds, VAS sensation intensity, and rectal compliance during barostat balloon distention.
Methods part 1: barostat protocol with ramp distention at 40 ml/min to measure discomfort, pain, and maximum tolerance thresholds, followed by randomized phasic distentions of 10, 15, and 20 mmHg.

Methods part 2: subjects rate sensation intensity on a VAS after each phasic distention; rectal compliance is derived from the slope of the pressure-volume curve during ramp distention using simple regression.

Results: IBS shows reduced rectal thresholds, increased VAS ratings at phasic distention near controls' discomfort threshold, and reduced compliance, whereas FAPS shows decreased VAS ratings and no threshold or compliance change.
Conclusion: the paper concludes that inconsistent visceral sensitivity between low and high pressure distention may be a key feature in the pathogenesis of FAPS.

Introduction and methods opening of an IBS study on rectal visceral perception as a biological marker: states the aim of measuring prevalence of altered rectal perception in IBS and its link to symptoms.

Methods and early results: describes anorectal manometry and balloon-distention rectal perception testing in 100 IBS patients vs 15 controls, questionnaire symptom assessment, a 3-month reassessment of 15 patients, and begins reporting that 94% showed altered perception.

Results detailing the nature of altered perception: lowered discomfort thresholds, increased sensation intensity, or altered viscerosomatic referral, with hypersensitivity specific to rapid phasic distention while stool and slow ramp thresholds were normal.

Results on subgroups and longitudinal findings plus the start of the conclusions: cluster analysis yields three IBS subgroups, and changes in perception thresholds correlate with symptom severity over time.
Final conclusion of the abstract: because altered rectal perception is near-universal in IBS and tracks symptom change, it is proposed as a reliable biological marker for the disorder.

Introduces cluster headache as a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia and outlines its three-step treatment framework (acute, transitional, preventive), noting greater occipital nerve block as a bridge therapy alternative to oral steroids.
Concludes the discussion of cluster headache treatment by describing botulinum toxin type A as a recently studied preventive option for chronic cluster headache, with limited success.

Opening chunk of a human study on capsaicin applied to the nasal mucosa: it covers burning sensation, sneezing, dose-dependent nasal secretion, and comparison with histamine, substance P, CGRP, and methacholine.

Middle section of the nasal capsaicin study reporting pharmacological pretreatments (ipratropium, dexchlorpheniramine, indomethacin, lidocaine) and their effects on pain and rhinorrhea, plus desensitization and recovery time course.

Later section of the capsaicin nasal study covering desensitization after repeated applications, full recovery over 30-40 days, and the start of the authors' proposed mechanism involving primary afferent neurones.

Concluding sentence of the capsaicin nasal mucosa study, stating the proposed mechanism: primary afferent neurone excitation producing burning pain, a sneezing reflex, and nasal secretion via peripheral transmitter release.

Introduces the study on repeated nasal capsaicin for cluster headache prevention, stating its aim to compare efficacy depending on whether the treatment is applied to the attack side (ipsilateral) or the opposite side, and begins describing the 52 episodic patients divided into two groups.

Describes study design: episodic patients split into ipsilateral versus contralateral treatment groups, 18 chronic patients alternating both treatments, and the key result that 70% of ipsilaterally treated episodic patients improved markedly while contralaterally treated patients did not improve.

Reports that ipsilateral efficacy was also seen in chronic patients, but their maximum amelioration lasted no more than 40 days, and that the difference between ipsilateral and contralateral treatment effects was statistically significant.

Concludes that the significant ipsilateral-versus-contralateral difference holds in both episodic and chronic patients, and states the results agree with prior reports of capsaicin's therapeutic effect in other pain syndromes such as postherpetic neuralgia, diabetic neuropathy and trigeminal neuralgia.
Final conclusion that the findings support using nasal capsaicin to produce selective analgesia in cluster headache, closing the abstract.
Opening of the document: introduces the lower chronic-degenerative disease incidence in Mediterranean populations and attributes it to plant phytochemicals, specifically melatonin, in the diet.

Middle of the document: argues that melatonin in edible plants may improve human health through its biological activity and good bioavailability, and may support nutritional therapy against cancer, cardiovascular, and neurodegenerative diseases.

Closing argument: links the presence of melatonin in Mediterranean foods and beverages to the hypothesized health benefits of the Mediterranean diet, while noting the evidence is still preliminary and incomplete.
Final sentence fragment: states that the available data supporting the Mediterranean diet's melatonin-related health benefits are preliminary and incomplete.

Study background and aims: tart Montmorency cherries as a dietary source of melatonin; trial objective to test whether tart cherry juice concentrate raises urinary melatonin and improves sleep in healthy adults.

Study design and measures: randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial with 20 volunteers taking placebo or tart cherry juice for 7 days; sleep assessed by actigraphy and questionnaires, plus 48-hour urine sampling for 6-sulfatoxymelatonin.

Analytical methods: cosinor analysis of melatonin circadian rhythm (mesor, acrophase, amplitude), total urinary melatonin quantification over the sampling period, and repeated measures ANOVA for trial comparisons.

Key results: total urinary melatonin significantly higher with cherry juice versus no difference between baseline and placebo; significant gains in time in bed, total sleep time and sleep efficiency with cherry juice (P < 0.05).

Circadian findings and conclusions: melatonin rhythm timing unchanged, with only a trend toward higher mesor and amplitude; authors conclude tart cherry juice concentrate boosts exogenous melatonin and may improve sleep duration and quality and help manage disturbed sleep.
Concluding statement restating that tart cherry juice concentrate may benefit sleep duration and quality in healthy men and women and could be useful for managing disturbed sleep.

Introduction and study aim: background on melatonin's physiological roles and its suspected peripheral vasodilatory effects, stating that its effect on cerebral blood flow is unknown and describing the design of testing a single melatonin pulse against peripheral blood flow as a positive control.

Methods: study population of ten healthy young male volunteers in a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled cross-over design, comparing a 10 microgram intravenous melatonin infusion with a saline placebo.

Methods and results on measurements: cerebral blood flow measured by phase contrast MRI, peripheral blood flow from skin temperature gradient and finger pulse volume, and serum melatonin concentrations rising from baseline to peak values at 5 and 10 minutes after administration.

Results and conclusions: no significant difference in cerebral blood flow or cerebrovascular resistance over time, while melatonin significantly increased peripheral blood flow versus placebo, leading to the finding that melatonin has no acute regulatory effect on cerebral blood flow.
Concluding statement: the final sentence summarizing the study's finding that melatonin does not acutely regulate cerebral blood flow in humans.

Introduction and study scope: comparative evaluation of phenolics and neuronal protective effects in four sweet and four sour fresh cherry cultivars, beginning the abstract's description of methods and total phenolic results.
Quantitative results: total phenolic and total anthocyanin ranges (mg GAE and mg C3G equivalents per 100 g) for sweet versus sour cherries, followed by the start of the HPLC analysis description.

Phytochemical composition from HPLC: anthocyanins (cyanidin, peonidin derivatives), hydroxycinnamic acids (neochlorogenic, chlorogenic, p-coumaric), and flavonol glycosides (quercetin, kaempferol, isorhamnetin), plus comparison showing sour cherries contain higher total phenolics.

Method validation and comparison: a strong linear correlation (r2 = 0.985) between HPLC summed anthocyanins and pH differential method anthocyanin values, supporting agreement between the two quantification approaches.
Bioactivity findings: cherry phenolics protect PC12 neuronal cells from oxidative stress in a dose-dependent manner, mainly attributed to anthocyanins, with the conclusion beginning.
Conclusion: cherries are rich in phenolics, especially anthocyanins, with strong antineurodegenerative activity, making them a good dietary source of biofunctional phytochemicals.

Introduction to non-vertebrate melatonin: its broad detection across bacteria, unicells, algae, plants, fungi and invertebrates, noting that roles are often unknown and circadian timing is not guaranteed.

Continues the discussion of non-vertebrate melatonin, covering nocturnal maxima, the biosynthetic pathway matching vertebrates, and photoperiod and temperature responses studied mainly in dinoflagellates.

Covers melatonin's proposed roles in plant photoperiodism (unconfirmed, no flowering stimulation shown) and its possible antioxidative function in aerobic non-vertebrates, where physiological evidence is lacking.

Describes melatonin's protective effects against oxidotoxic stress and lifespan extension in diverse organisms (Lingulodinium, Paramecium, Philodina, Drosophila), and introduces dietary uptake of melatonin.
Concludes the discussion of dietary melatonin uptake, its implications for ecophysiology, human nutrition, and pharmacology given high levels in medicinal plants.
Introduction and study design: background on melatonin in vegetables and the Japanese trial of 94 healthy women recruited via a public health center, setting up the intervention.

Intervention protocol: the intervention group was asked to eat about 350 g/day of six selected vegetables for 65 days, while controls avoided them; first-void morning urine was collected at baseline and endpoint.

Results part 1: measured creatinine-adjusted 6-sulfatoxymelatonin levels and the daily melatonin intake from vegetables (1288.0 ng intervention vs 5.3 ng control), plus intervention group urinary concentrations with 95% CIs.
Results part 2: control group urinary 6-sulfatoxymelatonin concentrations before and after the intervention period, with 95% confidence intervals, for comparison with the intervention group.
Statistical comparison and conclusion: between-group difference in change of 6-sulfatoxymelatonin (P = 0.03) and the authors' conclusion that increased vegetable intake raises circulating melatonin.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that increased vegetable consumption raises circulatory melatonin concentrations.

Opening of a narrative review on diet and sleep: introduces sleep as essential, notes that prior studies link short sleep to poorer dietary choices (energy-dense foods, fewer vegetables, irregular meals), and sets up the question of whether food affects sleep.
Continues the review's framing: states the paper's reversed question (can food affect sleep?) and its aim to assess whether the nutrients and foods eaten before bedtime matter for sleep.
Describes the review's scope: examines traditional sleep-promoting foods such as milk and herbal products using mostly healthy-subject clinical trial data, and plans to discuss underlying mechanisms.

Summarizes the review's conclusion: evidence supports a diet-sleep link, with foods that affect tryptophan availability and serotonin and melatonin synthesis likely being most useful for promoting sleep.
Closing caveat and copyright notice: physiological connections are clear, but clinical relevance needs further study; includes the 2012 Elsevier copyright line.
Introduction and study aim: melatonin's role in the circadian timing system, and the goal of collecting normative 24-h melatonin excretion data in healthy adults in a natural environment.
Methods: urine collection from 75 healthy subjects (ages 20-84) across five time periods, and measurement of 6-sulfatoxymelatonin (aMT6s) by competitive ELISA at IBL Hamburg.
Results on age association: 24-h, nighttime, morning, and evening aMT6s excretion were negatively correlated with age, while daytime excretion showed no significant association.
Results on variability: night-day ratios differed between young and older subjects, and total and nighttime aMT6s excretion varied about 20-fold between individuals.
Conclusions: an age-related decline in melatonin excretion was observed, and high inter-individual variability may explain why normative data are of limited use for replacement strategies.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence about normative data being of no use in replacement strategies.

Introduction of a study on Jerte Valley cherries: tryptophan, serotonin, and melatonin content and the evaluation design (seven cultivars, middle-aged and elderly volunteers, sleep-wake cycle, 6-sulfatoxymelatonin, urinary antioxidant capacity).

Methods and early results: actigraphic monitoring of nocturnal activity and rest, ELISA measurement of 6-sulfatoxymelatonin, colorimetric assay of total antioxidant capacity, and the start of the reported sleep-related outcomes.

Results: each cherry cultivar improved actual sleep time, total nocturnal activity, assumed sleep, and immobility, and significantly raised urinary 6-sulfatoxymelatonin and total antioxidant capacity.
Conclusion: Jerte Valley cherry intake positively affects sleep and may serve as a nutraceutical tool to counteract oxidation.
Background and objectives of the Cochrane review on melatonin for jet-lag: causes of jet-lag, melatonin's role in circadian rhythms, and the aim to assess oral melatonin dosing regimens.

Continues the objectives and describes the search strategy: electronic databases (Cochrane, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsychLit, Science Citation Index), hand-searched journals, citation tracking, and contact with authors for unpublished trials.

Search strategy for adverse events: hand-searched journals and systematic searches of drug side-effect sources (SED, Reactions Weekly, MEDLINE, WHO UMC, FDA databases) for melatonin reports outside randomised trials.

Selection criteria: randomised trials of oral melatonin versus placebo or other medication in airline passengers, airline staff, or military personnel, along with the search sources for adverse event reports.

Eligible outcome measures for jet-lag (subjective ratings, wellbeing, daytime tiredness, sleep onset and quality, psychological functioning, recovery time, circadian indicators), and the start of data analysis: ten trials met inclusion criteria.

Data analysis details: all ten trials compared melatonin with placebo (one also with zolpidem); nine were adequate quality and one had a design fault and was excluded; adverse event sources identified.

Main results: melatonin taken near destination bedtime (10pm–midnight) reduced jet-lag for flights crossing five or more time zones in nine of ten trials; daily doses of 0.5–5mg are similarly effective.
Dose findings: 5mg improves sleep onset and quality over 0.5mg, doses above 5mg are no more effective, slow-release 2mg is less effective, and the number needed to treat is 2.

Factors affecting benefit and safety: benefit increases with more time zones crossed and is smaller for westward flights; wrong timing (early in day) causes sleepiness and delays adaptation; other side effects are rare; epilepsy and warfarin cases noted.
Reviewer's conclusions begin: melatonin is remarkably effective against jet-lag and occasional short-term use appears safe.

Recommendations: melatonin should be advised for adult travellers crossing five or more time zones, especially eastward and with prior jet-lag; 2–4 zones optional; calls for study of pharmacology, toxicology, and product quality control.
Final research needs: the effects of melatonin in people with epilepsy and its possible interaction with warfarin require further investigation.

Introduces melatonin as an antioxidant found in edible plants and seeds, and describes the study's method: detecting and quantifying melatonin in fresh-frozen Balaton and Montmorency tart cherries (Prunus cerasus) via HPLC.

Reports the main quantitative result: Montmorency tart cherries contain about 6 times more melatonin (13.46 ng/g) than Balaton cherries (2.06 ng/g), and both cherry types have high melatonin levels relative to mammalian blood.
States that neither orchard of origin nor harvest time affected melatonin levels, and argues that cherries may be an important dietary melatonin source since it is readily absorbed orally.
Concludes that melatonin is both endogenously produced and present in the diet, based on previously published data and the present results.

Abstract opening of a paper describing an HPLC-MS/ESI method for simultaneously quantifying serotonin, melatonin, piceid, and resveratrol isomers, introducing the chromatography setup (cut off mid-sentence at the mobile phase description).

Continues the method description: the acetonitrile/water with 0.1% formic acid gradient mobile phase, the SRM mass spectrometry optimization, and the comparison of methanol extraction against ethyl acetate extraction.

Covers the extraction comparison and states the study's application: quantifying the four compounds across 24 commonly consumed fruits, with the first results on plantain (highest serotonin) beginning at the end.

Reports key findings: plantain had the highest serotonin, orange bell peppers the highest melatonin, and grapes the highest piceid and resveratrol levels, concluding the method enables rapid, accurate fruit quantification.
Final sentence of the conclusion restating that HPLC-MS with simple sample preparation enables rapid, accurate fruit analysis, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.

This chunk opens the abstract of a study on tart cherry anthocyanins (1-3) and their aglycon cyanidin, reporting in vitro lipid peroxidation inhibition percentages at 2 mM compared with commercial antioxidants.

This chunk continues the abstract, comparing the antioxidant activity of anthocyanins 1-3 and cyanidin to tert-butylhydroquinone, butylated hydroxytoluene, and vitamin E, then giving cyanidin's antiinflammatory IC50 values against COX-1 and COX-2 (prostaglandin H endoperoxide synthase enzymes).
This final fragment completes the COX-2 (prostaglandin H endoperoxide synthase-2) reference in the abstract's cyanidin antiinflammatory IC50 result.
Introduces melatonin and serotonin as indoleamines, their biological roles, and their reported presence in edible plants, motivating the review of their analysis by LC and LC-MS.

Continues the background: limited analytical literature for melatonin and serotonin in edible plants, with prior use of liquid chromatography (LC) for their quantification, and introduces LC-MS as a method.
States the advantages of LC-MS (selectivity, sensitivity, precision, simultaneous determination) and the review's scope: LC/LC-MS methods and reported melatonin and serotonin levels in edible plants.
Closing fragment of the abstract containing the copyright notice (© 2011 Crown Copyright).

Introduces the pilot study of CherryPharm tart cherry juice vs. placebo for insomnia in older adults, describing the randomized double-blind crossover design with 2-week treatment and washout periods.

Describes the outcome measures: sleep continuity variables (onset, WASO, total sleep time, efficiency) from 2-week sleep diary means and Insomnia Severity Index scores, in a cohort of 15 otherwise healthy older adults with chronic insomnia.

Reports results: significant pre-post improvements on all sleep variables with the tart cherry beverage, and a significant reduction in wake after sleep onset versus placebo, with no placebo-relative gains in other measures.
Summarizes the moderate-to-negligible effect sizes and concludes that CherryPharm has modest sleep benefits, with effect sizes comparable to valerian and some melatonin studies.
Concludes that the tart cherry juice's effects are considerably smaller than those of evidence-based insomnia treatments, namely hypnotic medications and cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia.
Closing fragment finishing the sentence on cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia as the stronger evidence-based comparator.

Study background and objective: introduces tart cherry antioxidant/anti-inflammatory properties and describes the randomized, placebo-controlled crossover methods (14 male students, cherry juice vs placebo, 8 days of twice-daily dosing) for testing exercise-induced muscle damage prevention.

Methods detail: the eccentric elbow flexion exercise bout on day 4 of supplementation, and the outcome measures (isometric strength, pain, tenderness, relaxed elbow angle) recorded before and for four days after exercise.

Crossover design and key results: the protocol was repeated two weeks later with arms and treatment order swapped to avoid the repeated bout effect, and the study reports that strength loss and pain were significantly lower with cherry juice (time by treatment p<0.0001 and p=0.017).

Results and conclusions: relaxed elbow angle and muscle tenderness showed no treatment difference (p=0.85 and p=0.81), and the authors conclude the cherry juice reduces some symptoms of exercise-induced muscle damage.
Key quantitative finding: averaged over four days post-exercise, strength loss was 22% with placebo versus 4% with cherry juice, the study's most notable result.

Introduction to the cherry health review: describes the nutritional composition of sweet cherries (anthocyanins, quercetin, vitamin C, potassium, etc.) and factors such as ripeness, storage, and processing that alter these levels.

Covers the potential preventive health benefits of cherry intake (cancer, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, inflammation, Alzheimer's) and the mechanisms behind them, including antioxidant activity, low glycemic response, and COX-1/2 inhibition.
Concludes the review by noting that the anti-carcinogenic effects are shown in vitro and in animals, and that well-designed human cherry feeding studies are still needed to confirm health benefits.

Introduction to the epidemiology of insomnia: summarizes the 50+ community-sample studies and the four prevalence definitions (symptoms, symptoms with daytime consequences, sleep dissatisfaction, diagnoses).
Prevalence by definition: about one-third of the general population has at least one DSM-IV insomnia symptom; with daytime consequences, prevalence is 9-15%; sleep dissatisfaction affects 8-18%.

Diagnosis-based prevalence and sex/age patterns: 6% meet DSM-IV insomnia diagnosis criteria; all four definitions are more common in women, and symptom prevalence rises with age while dissatisfaction and diagnosis rates vary little.
Risk factors for insomnia: mental disorders and organic diseases are the most studied factors, and insomnia is consistently linked to major depressive episodes.
Insomnia and depression over time: longitudinal studies show persistent insomnia predicts new depressive episodes; future research should examine the natural course of insomnia.
Research gaps: the closing statement that the genetic epidemiology of insomnia remains unstudied, pointing to needed future work.

Opening of the abstract for a 2011 SLEEP journal cross-sectional study of 28,670 older Chinese adults in Guangzhou, stating the aim (sleep factors and memory impairment), design, setting, and sample characteristics.

Methods summary from the Guangzhou Biobank Cohort Study abstract: face-to-face interviews collected sleep and cognitive data, and confounders (smoking, alcohol, physical activity, blood pressure, glucose, lipids, etc.) were adjusted for.

Key result from the Guangzhou Biobank sleep study: an inverted U-shaped link between habitual sleep duration and delayed word recall test (DWRT) memory scores, peaking at 7 to 8 hours, with trend P-values reported.

Quantitative findings from the abstract: adjusted odds ratios for memory impairment at short (3-4 h) and long (≥10 h) sleep versus 7 h, plus lower DWRT scores linked to daytime napping, morning tiredness, and insomnia.

Study conclusion from the Guangzhou Biobank sleep and memory abstract: short or long sleep is an independent risk marker for memory impairment and possible cognitive decline in older adults, followed by the start of the citation.
Full bibliographic citation for the Xu et al. 2011 SLEEP paper (Guangzhou Biobank Cohort Study on sleep duration and memory impairment in older Chinese), including journal, volume, issue, and pages.

Abstract opening of a sleep study (Van Dongen et al.-style chronic sleep restriction experiment) stating the objective: comparing chronic sleep restriction against total sleep deprivation to assess whether reduced human sleep has consequences, and describing the design of 4h/6h/8h time-in-bed conditions and the 3-night total deprivation condition.

Study design details: the chronic restriction arms (4 h, 6 h, 8 h time in bed for 14 days) and the total sleep deprivation arm (3 nights, 0 h), each with 3 baseline and 3 recovery days, conducted under standardized laboratory monitoring in the sleep research abstract.

Setting, participants, and interventions of the sleep restriction study: standardized lab conditions with continuous monitoring, 48 healthy adults aged 21-38, and the restriction protocol limiting nocturnal sleep to 8, 6, or 4 hours per day for 14 days versus 0 hours for 3 days, with all other sleep prohibited.

Results on cognitive and subjective outcomes: chronic restriction to 4 or 6 h per night caused cumulative, dose-dependent cognitive performance deficits on all tasks, while subjective sleepiness rose acutely and then plateaued, failing to distinguish the 6 h and 4 h groups.

Physiological results: polysomnography and non-REM delta power (a marker of sleep homeostasis) responded acutely to restriction and showed negligible further change over the 14 restricted nights, contrasting with the cumulative cognitive decline.

Comparison with total sleep deprivation: total deprivation produced disproportionately large waking neurobehavioral and delta power responses relative to sleep lost; a statistical model linked behavioral lapses near-linearly to cumulative wakefulness beyond about 15.84 hours, regardless of deprivation mode.

Key conclusion: chronic restriction to 6 h or less nightly produced cognitive deficits equal to up to two nights of total sleep deprivation, indicating even moderate sleep restriction seriously impairs waking neurobehavioral function, with the 15.84 h wakefulness threshold quantified (s.e. 0.73 h).

Interpretation of the findings: sleepiness ratings suggest subjects were largely unaware of their growing cognitive deficits, which may explain why the cognitive impact of chronic sleep restriction is commonly assumed to be benign.

Synthesis: physiological sleep responses did not mirror waking neurobehavioral responses, yet cumulative wakefulness beyond 15.84 h predicted performance lapses across all four experimental conditions, supporting a model of sleep debt as additional wakefulness.
Concluding statement of the abstract: sleep debt is best understood as additional wakefulness carrying an accumulating neurobiological 'cost' over time, framing the theoretical takeaway of the study.

Introduction and study aim: kiwifruit's antioxidant and serotonin content as potential sleep-disorder treatment; the study evaluates kiwifruit's effects on sleep onset, duration, and quality using a free-living, self-controlled diet design.

Methods: 24 adults (2 male, 22 female, aged 20-55) ate two kiwifruits one hour before bed nightly for 4 weeks; sleep was measured with the Chinese Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (CPSQI), a 3-day sleep diary, and Actigraph watches.

Outcome measures: the subjective and objective sleep parameters assessed before and after the intervention, including bedtime, sleep onset, wake after sleep onset, getting-up time, total sleep time, sleep onset latency, and sleep efficiency.

Results: after 4 weeks of kiwifruit, CPSQI score, wake after sleep onset, and sleep onset latency significantly decreased (42.4%, 28.9%, 35.4%), while total sleep time and sleep efficiency significantly increased (13.4%, 5.41%).
Conclusion: kiwifruit may improve sleep onset, duration, and efficiency in adults with self-reported sleep disturbances, and its sleep-promoting properties merit further investigation.

Introduction to the history of antidepressant discovery: describes the 1950s introduction of iproniazid (an MAO inhibitor) and imipramine (the first tricyclic), and their social-health and research-tool contributions to psychiatry.

Continues the 1950s discussion of iproniazid and imipramine, explaining their pharmacological value as neurobiology research tools that enabled the first aetiopathogenic hypotheses of depressive disorders.

Bridges to later developments: the late-1980s introduction of fluoxetine (an SSRI) as a second major revolution in depression therapy, and the paper's stated aim to review the historical discovery process of these drugs.

Concludes the historical review's framing by noting that the paper traces how these drugs were discovered and their role in neuroscience, then argues that current antidepressants all share a monoaminergic synaptic mechanism.

Final conclusion of the document: argues that future antidepressant therapy may depend on searching for extraneuronal non-aminergic or intraneuronal biochemical mechanisms beyond monoaminergic modulation.

Study design and objective: a prospective cohort of older Taiwanese (population-based, multistage random sampling) examining how intake frequency of major food categories predicts new depression 4 years later, using logistic regression.

Setting and subjects (n=1609 adults aged 65+), and the start of results: the regression model adjusts for demographic, socio-economic, lifestyle and health variables, with fruit and vegetable associations with later depressive symptoms reported.

Key results before cognitive adjustment: fruit (OR 0.66) and vegetable (OR 0.38) intake are protective against depressive symptoms at 4 years; after adjusting for cognitive status, only vegetables remain protective (OR 0.40, P=0.039).

Remaining findings: egg consumption is borderline significant in both models (P=0.087 and 0.069), while meat/poultry, fish, seafood, dairy, legumes, grains and tea show no significant association with depression risk.

Conclusions: higher vegetable consumption appears protective against depressive symptoms in the elderly, with the caveat that confounding cannot be fully excluded; the authors call for further research on causality and mechanisms.
Closing sentence of the conclusion, calling for further studies to clarify the causal role and mechanism linking food intake to depression in older adults.

Opening chunk of a pharmacology abstract on MAO-A inhibitors as antidepressants and the 'cheese effect' (hypertensive reaction from dietary tyramine); introduces MAO-A as the predominant intestinal form in human and rat tissue.

Middle chunk of the abstract covering rat everted intestinal transport studies showing extensive intestinal tyramine metabolism, and the contrast between clorgyline (MAO-A inhibition, raising unchanged tyramine) and L-deprenyl/selegiline (MAO-B inhibition, no significant effect).
Final chunk of the abstract concluding that reversible MAO-A inhibitors only partly reduce intestinal tyramine metabolism, and only when their inhibition is competitive in nature.

Introduction and study aim: the paper asks whether dietary compounds (and smoking-related compounds) reach levels sufficient to partially inhibit monoamine oxidase, based on a literature review of dietary MAO inhibitors, food levels, pharmacokinetics, and tissue levels.

Methods: a literature search identified dietary MAO inhibitors and their food levels, absorption/distribution pharmacokinetics, and tissue levels, then compared estimated daily intake and expected tissue concentrations with measured MAO inhibition efficacies.

Results by compound: norharman, harman, and quercetin were consistent with reaching neuronal MAO levels from diet or smoking, whereas 1,2,3,4-tetrahydroisoquinoline, eugenol, 1-piperoylpiperidine, and coumarin were not.

Quercetin focus: quercetin is equipotent with norharman as an MAO-A inhibitor, its metabolite isorhamnetin also inhibits, and quercetin is the most abundant compound in the sample diet; a healthy diet may deliver enough brain quercetin to modestly reduce neurotransmitter breakdown despite variable bioavailability.
Conclusion: the final claim that dietary quercetin could produce a small decrease in neurotransmitter breakdown via MAO-A inhibition in the brain, the paper's main takeaway.

Opening chunk of an abstract on monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibition in addiction: PET imaging shows MAO activity falls in tobacco smokers and recovers after quitting, attributed to MAO-inhibiting tobacco constituents.

Middle chunk of the abstract: notes that MAO inhibition is not unique to smoking, since Type II alcoholics show a similar MAO decrease that reverses on quitting alcohol, and previews the review of MAO-inhibiting tobacco compounds and the claim that the alcoholics' decrease is likely from concomitant tobacco use.

Final chunk of the abstract: concludes the review's central argument that MAO inhibition by tobacco and tobacco smoke constituents enhances tobacco smoking addiction, and explains the alcoholics' MAO decrease as likely due to concurrent smoking.
Introduction and background of a pilot randomized controlled trial on omnivorous diets, arachidonic acid (AA), EPA/DHA intake, and mood in omnivores versus vegetarians.

Continues the background with the prior cross-sectional finding that omnivores reported worse mood than vegetarians, then describes the study aim and the design: 39 omnivores randomized to OMN, FISH, or VEG groups.

Methods section describing the three diet arms (daily meat/fish/poultry, fish 3-4 times weekly without meat, or vegetarian) and the outcome measures at baseline and two weeks: food frequency questionnaire, Profile of Mood States, and DASS.
Results summary: VEG participants lowered EPA, DHA, and AA intake and showed significant mood improvements, FISH participants increased EPA and DHA, and OMN and FISH mood scores were unchanged.
Conclusion of the trial: restricting meat, fish, and poultry improved some short-term mood domains in omnivores, and this is the first trial of this kind in omnivores.

Introduces the study's background and objective: the monoamine theory of depression, MAO-A's role in metabolizing monoamines, and the aim of testing whether brain MAO-A is elevated in untreated depression at a tertiary psychiatric hospital.

Describes the study population: 17 healthy and 17 depressed participants with major depressive disorder, all otherwise healthy and nonsmoking, with depressed individuals medication-free for at least 5 months.
Specifies the outcome measure: carbon-11-labeled harmine PET imaging with its MAO-A-selective radioligand, used to compute MAO-A specific distribution volume (DVS) across ten named brain regions.
Reports the main results: MAO-A DVS was significantly elevated in every assessed brain region (P=.001 to 3x10^-7), with an average 34% increase (2 SD) throughout the brain in major depression.

States the conclusion: the large effect and lack of alternative explanations for monoamine loss indicate that elevated MAO-A density is the primary monoamine-lowering process in major depressive episodes.
Brief closing fragment completing the final sentence of the conclusion, stating that elevated MAO-A density drives monoamine lowering during major depression.

Introduces monoamine theories of depression (low brain monoamine levels), their mid-1960s popularity, and the article's aim to review their historical development and impact on biomedical research, including a bibliometric look at alleged West European vs. US divisions.

Continues the abstract: describes the bibliometric examination of West European versus US researcher divisions, then previews the coverage of monoamine theories in the NIMH Collaborative Program on the Psychobiology of Depression.

Concludes the abstract with the article's central argument: the impact of monoamine theories is best explained by researchers, government agencies, and pharmaceutical companies invoking them to advance their projects and agendas.
Opening of a review on flavonoids as anti-metastatic dietary phenolics: defines cancer metastasis and introduces flavonoids as a large, food-abundant phenolic subclass with preventive potential.
Continues the introduction: notes growing literature on flavonoids as natural inhibitors of invasion and metastasis, then begins listing the most-studied catechin derivatives (EGCG, EGC, ECG, EC).

Names other well-investigated flavonoids for anti-invasion/metastasis effects (genistein/genistin, silibinin, quercetin, anthocyanin) and begins listing dietary vegetable flavonoids with anti-metastatic activity.

Completes the list of dietary flavonoids (luteolin through naringenin) and explains that an effective anti-metastatic compound must block the full metastatic cascade: attachment, barrier degradation, migration, invasion, adhesion, and angiogenesis.
States the review's scope: flavonoid effects on the metastatic cascade and related proteins, in vitro anti-invasive activity, and antiangiogenic and in vivo anti-metastatic models.
Concluding summary of the introduction: the evidence shows flavonoids, a ubiquitous dietary phenolic subclass, have extensive in vitro anti-invasive and in vivo anti-metastatic activity.
Abstract opening of a study on fisetin's antiangiogenic activity; introduces fisetin's known antitumor effects and sets up the investigation in HUVECs.
Abstract results on fisetin's dose- and time-dependent inhibition of HUVEC growth and survival (VEGF and serum induced), plus cell cycle arrest at G1/G2-M with changes in cyclin D1 and p53.
Abstract results on fisetin-induced HUVEC apoptosis (survivin decrease, caspase-3/-7 and PARP cleavage, Bax/Bcl-2 ratio) and inhibition of Matrigel tube formation and migration.
Abstract results linking reduced tube formation and migration to lower eNOS and VEGF in HUVECs, and reduced eNOS, VEGF, iNOS, MMP-2 and MMP-9 in A549 and DU145 cancer cells.
Abstract in vivo findings from the Matrigel plug assay in mice (smaller plugs, less vascularization and hemoglobin content with fisetin) and the study's overall conclusion.
Concluding sentence of the abstract: fisetin's antiangiogenic effects may underlie its antitumor activity, supporting further study of its angiopreventive potential for cancer control.

Introduction to the paper's motivation: projected doubling of annual new cancer cases from 2000 to 2050 and rising treatment costs, framing the need for efficacious cancer prevention strategies and Folkman's original proposal of antiangiogenesis for preventing dormant microtumors.

Discussion of antiangiogenic drug use: these agents are approved for many advanced malignancies (colorectal, lung, breast, kidney, liver, brain, thyroid, neuroendocrine, multiple myeloma, MDS), but cost and toxicity limit their use for prevention, setting up the case for dietary alternatives.

Core proposal: potent antiangiogenic molecules found in dietary sources suggest a rationally designed antiangiogenic diet could be a safe, widely available, novel cancer prevention strategy, and the paper's scope of scientific, epidemiologic, and clinical evidence is outlined.
Concluding statement of the paper's aim: it reviews scientific, epidemiologic, and clinical evidence supporting an antiangiogenic diet as a cancer prevention approach.

Introduction to the review on dietary phytoconstituents and breast cancer: establishes breast cancer's burden as the leading cause of cancer deaths in women and the link between diet and breast cancer risk/progression, motivating dietary agents for prevention and treatment.

Introduces angiogenesis as the proposed target: dietary compounds can interfere with angiogenic pathways, and angiogenesis (formation of new capillaries from existing vessels) is described as a key process whose disruption offers a therapeutic avenue against breast cancer.

Summarizes the evidence base and rationale: dietary phytochemicals kill breast cancer cells in vitro and suppress progression in preclinical animal models, and the review's stated aim is to examine dietary phytoconstituents' value through modulation of angiogenesis.

States the review's scope: examines dietary phytoconstituents in breast cancer prevention and treatment via angiogenesis modulation, and addresses benefits, challenges, and future research directions for anti-angiogenic dietary phytochemicals.
Closing bibliographic detail of the abstract: the end of the abstract with its copyright notice (© 2012 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim), identifying the publication source.

Introduces the study on purple rice bran extract (PRE) and its anthocyanidin constituents cyanidin and peonidin, examining their protective effects against VEGF-induced angiogenesis via tube formation and 14-day HUVEC/fibroblast co-culture assays.

Describes the antiangiogenic mechanism methods: VEGF-induced proliferation and migration of HUVECs and/or HRMECs, and phosphorylation of ERK and p38, and begins summarizing that PRE significantly suppressed tube formation, proliferation and migration.

Summarizes key results: PRE suppressed VEGF-induced tube formation, proliferation, migration, and ERK/p38 phosphorylation in HUVECs and HRMECs, and cyanidin and peonidin also suppressed VEGF-induced proliferation and migration.

Concludes that PRE and anthocyanidins inhibit VEGF-induced angiogenesis by blocking proliferation and migration, implicating inhibition of phosphorylated ERK and p38 as the likely mechanism, followed by the 2011 copyright notice.
Introduction to the study: epidemiological link between plant-food and polyphenol intake and reduced cancer risk, via effects on tumor growth, survival, and angiogenesis.
Background on lifestyle risk factors (high body mass, physical inactivity) that drive chronic low-grade inflammation, a key driver of tumor progression, motivating the study's focus.

Study objectives: test how diet-derived polyphenols inhibit IL-6-triggered angiogenesis and probe the underlying mechanisms; introduces the key finding that apigenin and luteolin are the most potent inhibitors.
Mechanistic results: apigenin and luteolin act via the IL-6/STAT3 pathway and ERK1/2 signaling, reducing endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and morphogenic differentiation.
Additional molecular effects: polyphenols modulate IL-6 receptor (IL-6Rα) expression, MMP-2 secretion, and SOCS3 expression, with the conclusion that diet may aid cancer prevention.
Concluding statement on the significance of the findings for diet's role in cancer prevention, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction to the paper's proposal of a 'multifocal angiostatic therapy' (MAT): it contrasts new anti-angiogenic drugs for inoperable cancer with the idea that combined nutritional measures can slow tumor angiogenesis.
Explains the MAT rationale of combining complementary anti-angiogenic measures and begins listing the candidate measures, starting with a low-fat, low-glycemic vegan diet.
Describes the first candidate measures: a vegan diet reducing IGF-I activity, and omega-3 fish oil inhibiting endothelial Flk-1 (VEGF receptor) and pro-angiogenic eicosanoids.

Covers high-dose selenium (reducing tumor VEGF), green tea polyphenols (suppressing endothelial response to VEGF and FGF), and high-dose glycine (possible inhibition of endothelial mitosis via glycine-gated chloride channels).
Introduces copper depletion as an angiostatic strategy, since tumor angiogenesis requires copper, and names tetrathiomolybdate as the most efficient chelator.

Offers high-dose zinc as a practical alternative or maintenance option for copper depletion, and states the provisional nutritional MAT protocol (vegan diet plus fish oil, selenium, green tea polyphenols, glycine, zinc).
Concludes with the suggestion that COX-2-specific NSAIDs may be an adjunct, citing COX-2 overexpression in cancers and cAMP's role in boosting angiogenic and autogenous growth factors.
Final fragment of the COX-2-specific NSAID adjunct recommendation, ending the document's discussion of the MAT protocol.

Introduction to a review of epidemiological studies on phytochemicals and cancer risk, noting that phytoestrogens and carotenoids are the most-studied classes and that no prior systematic review covered all phytochemicals.

Describes the systematic review of 96 epidemiological studies, the finding that most studies reported null associations between individual phytochemicals and cancer risk, and the summary of the review's scope and results.

Summarizes the inconsistency and modest magnitude of past findings, then lists the most consistent protective associations: β-carotene and renal cell cancer, β-cryptoxanthin and lung cancer, and isothiocyanates and lung cancer.

Completes the list of consistent protective associations (isothiocyanates and gastrointestinal cancer, lignans and postmenopausal breast cancer, flavonoids and lung cancer) and explains why elevated risks cannot be concluded due to limited or inconsistent evidence.

Concludes that single-study associations need further confirmation and calls for research on the cumulative and interactive effects of multiple phytochemicals and phytochemical-rich foods on cancer risk.
Final sentence of the review's conclusion, emphasizing the need for research on cumulative and interactive effects of numerous phytochemicals and phytochemical-rich foods on cancer risk.
Introduction and study objective: background on HPV as the most common STI, and the aim of measuring baseline US female HPV prevalence from NHANES 2003-2004 before widespread HPV vaccine use.
Methods: NHANES sampling of females aged 14-59, home interview followed by mobile exam center self-collected vaginal swabs tested for HPV DNA by L1 consensus PCR and type-specific hybridization.
Methods and start of results: outcome measure (PCR-based HPV prevalence), collection of demographic and sexual behavior data, and the overall prevalence of 26.8% with its confidence interval.
Results by age group: HPV prevalence among females aged 14-59, with the peak of 44.8% in women aged 20-24 and lower rates in the 14-19, 25-29, 30-39, 40-49, and 50-59 groups.
Age trend results: prevalence rises significantly with each year of age from 14 to 24, then declines gradually through age 59, with the associated P values.
Vaccine-type results: prevalence of HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18 (vaccine types, low- and high-risk) at 3.4% overall, with type-specific rates and confidence intervals.

Risk factors and conclusions: age, marital status, and numbers of lifetime and recent sex partners were independent predictors; HPV is common, burden exceeds previous estimates, and peaks at ages 20-24.
Final conclusion: the prevalence of HPV vaccine types was relatively low, closing the summary of the study's findings.
Introduction and methods opening of a study on vegetarian diets and cancer incidence in the Adventist Health Study-2; defines dietary patterns examined and the cohort of 69,120 participants.

Methods continued: describes dietary pattern categories (non-vegetarian, lacto, pesco, vegan, semi-vegetarian), cancer case identification via registry matching, and Cox proportional hazards analysis using attained age.

Results opening: reports 2,939 incident cancer cases and the multivariate hazard ratio for overall cancer among vegetarians vs non-vegetarians (HR=0.92), plus a significant gastrointestinal cancer association.

Results on specific diets: vegan diet shows significant overall cancer protection (HR=0.84) and female-specific cancer protection (HR=0.66), with gastrointestinal cancer hazard ratio (HR=0.76) for vegetarians.

Results conclusion and summary: lacto-ovo-vegetarians show lower gastrointestinal cancer risk (HR=0.75); the study concludes vegetarian diets protect against cancer and begins the Impact statement on vegan diets.
Impact statement closing the abstract: vegan diet linked to lower overall and female-specific cancer risk, and lacto-ovo-vegetarian diets linked to protection from gastrointestinal tract cancers.
Background on oncogenic HPV as the main cause of cervical neoplasia and the proposed role of nutritional cofactors and micronutrients in protection, introducing the study's rationale.
Study aim and methods: examines vitamin A and carotenoids in HPV persistence (intermittent vs. persistent infection), with Hybrid Capture II HPV testing at baseline, ~3 and ~9 months.

Statistical methods (multivariate logistic regression by micronutrient tertile) and main result that higher vegetable consumption was associated with reduced HPV persistence risk (aOR 0.46, 95% CI 0.21-0.97).
Key finding on plasma cis-lycopene: highest versus lowest concentration tertile linked to a 56% lower risk of HPV persistence (aOR 0.44, 95% CI 0.19-1.01).
Concluding statement that vegetable consumption and circulating cis-lycopene may protect against persistent HPV infection.
Introduction of the study: PDTC antioxidant treatment of HPV-16-immortalized keratinocytes, showing increased AP-1 binding to the viral regulatory region alongside suppressed viral gene expression.

Results on AP-1 composition: despite increased AP-1 binding needed for HPV-16 transcription, viral transcription initiation is suppressed, and supershift assays reveal that the Jun-homodimer-dominant AP-1 complex is altered after PDTC.

Mechanistic details of the altered AP-1 complex: c-jun is phosphorylated and heterodimerizes mainly with fra-1 (also induced by PDTC), with increased c-jun/junB complexes, despite enhanced c-fos expression.

Conclusion linking the AP-1 reorganization to the transcriptional block: fra-1 and junB interfere with c-jun/c-fos trans-activation, so the viral suppression is attributed to antioxidant-induced reconstitution of AP-1, with a note on differentiation-regulated c-jun/c-fos expression.

Closing implication: the reorganization of the central viral transcription factor AP-1 may be a novel mechanism controlling pathogenic HPV transcription during keratinocyte differentiation and progression to cervical cancer.

Introduces the core premise that persistent high-risk HPV infection is a necessary cause of cervical cancer, noting that most infections are transient and that progression to carcinoma takes 12-15 years via CIN stages, implying a multi-step process.
Continues the multi-step argument and states the review's approach: merging in vitro hrHPV transformation studies with clinical specimen data into a single cervical cancer progression model.

Describes the model's early stage, where individual host susceptibility to specific HPV types, shaped by immune surveillance genetics, determines outcome, and the later step where altered regulation of E6/E7 oncogenes drives genomic instability once a CIN lesion forms.
Explains how additional (epi)genetic alterations accumulating in high-grade CIN lesions push progression toward overt malignancy, distinguishing transformation from productive viral infection.

Details the late-stage changes, namely immortality and reduced sensitivity to cytokine and adhesion-mediated growth control, and previews the review's clinical relevance for hrHPV testing, biomarkers, screening, and CIN management.

Concludes the abstract by noting the discussion of clinical implications for cervical screening and CIN management, followed by the 2006 copyright and publisher notice (Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland; John Wiley & Sons).

Opening of the abstract: introduces the accepted view that cervical neoplasia is a sexually transmitted disease caused by some HPV types, and notes recent studies failing to link sexual activity with HPV infection or cancer risk.
Continues the abstract's framing of the incoherent findings, stating the paper's aim to analyze them through etiologic models and the role of HPV misclassification in interpreting assumed relations.

Describes the paper's core claim that small HPV misclassification levels can substantially distort estimated HPV prevalence, the sexual activity–HPV association, and the adjusted cancer relation, with field-survey DNA assay overestimation noted.

Covers practical consequences: DNA assays like filter in situ hybridization may grossly overestimate true viral prevalence, and moderately misclassified test results can seriously bias effect estimation and covariate adjustment.

Concluding statement of the abstract: the apparent incoherence in recent epidemiology should not be taken as evidence against HPV's etiologic role in cervical cancer or against the sexually transmitted disease model.

Introduction to invasive cervical cancer: its ranking as a gynecologic malignancy, prognostic factors (stage, tumor size, grade, nodal status), and why staging matters for choosing surgery versus radiation, including the limits of the FIGO clinical staging system.

Role of CT in cervical cancer: explains the FIGO staging error rates in advanced disease that led to unofficial extended staging with cross-sectional imaging, and CT's use in staging advanced disease and monitoring for recurrence.

CT imaging appearance of cervical cancer: the primary tumor's hypoattenuating, heterogeneous look on contrast-enhanced scans, and the most reliable CT signs of parametrial extension (periureteral fat plane obliteration, soft-tissue mass) and pelvic side wall invasion (under 3 mm separation, vascular encasement).

Patterns of spread in cervical cancer on CT: lymphatic routes along the external and internal iliac chains and presacral route to paraaortic nodes, and distant metastases to liver, lung, and bone in primary or recurrent disease.
Final fragment of the document's discussion of distant metastasis sites in cervical cancer, specifying bone as a site of spread to the liver and lung.

Introduction of an Indian study on HPV prevalence in asymptomatic women from eastern Uttar Pradesh, stating the background and the study's aim of assessing HPV prevalence and socio-demographic associations.

Methods summary: 2424 cervical scrape samples from asymptomatic women were screened using L1 consensus primers, positives were genotyped by sequencing, and univariate binary logistic regression assessed socio-demographic factors.
Key results on overall HPV infection rate (9.9%) across 26 genotypes and the proportion of single versus multiple infections among HPV-positive women.
Genotype distribution results showing HPV-16 as the dominant type (63.7%) followed by HPV-31, HPV-6, HPV-81, and HPV-33, plus significant associations with non-vegetarian diet and rural residence.

Conclusion emphasizing the high HPV-16 prevalence in asymptomatic women, comparable to invasive cervical cancer, and the resulting need for a therapeutic HPV vaccine targeting HPV-16 and other high-risk types.
Introduction of a CDC report on nonfatal bathroom injuries in the US in 2008 among persons aged 15 and older, establishing the overall injury burden and the assumption that bathrooms are hazardous.

Describes the study method: CDC analysis of a nationally representative emergency department sample (NEISS-AIP) to measure incidence and circumstances of bathroom injuries among people aged 15 and older.
Key findings: an estimated 234,094 bathroom injuries treated in US EDs based on 3,339 cases, injury rates rising with age, and falls causing 81.1% of injuries.
Conclusion and recommendations: older adults and everyone should be aware of high-risk bathroom activities and consider environmental modifications to reduce injury risk.

Opening of the document: challenges the 93% HPV-positivity figure for invasive cervical cancer as a possible underestimate, due to PCR target (L1 gene) problems and sample inadequacy, prompting reanalysis of HPV-negative cases.

Describes the reanalysis methods: HPV serology (HPV 16 VLP, E6, E7 antibodies) on subsets of HPV-negative and HPV-positive cases, and a sandwich procedure applying three HPV PCR assays targeting different ORFs to the inner sections of the HPV-negative biopsies.
Reports the serology result: no significant difference in HPV 16 protein antibodies between cases originally PCR-negative and PCR-positive for HPV.
Reports type-specific E7 PCR results: HPV DNA found in 69% of originally negative amplifiable specimens, across 8 named high-risk HPV types, plus 4% more detected only by E1/L1 consensus PCR.

Links HPV-negative results to specimen quality: inadequate samples were far more often HPV-negative on all PCR tests (13 of 21) than adequate ones (2 of 34), p<0.001; also gives the combined worldwide prevalence of 99.7% after excluding inadequate specimens.

Concludes that HPV is present in virtually all cervical cancers, the highest attributable fraction reported for a specific cause of a major human cancer, and argues for HPV testing in cervical screening, possibly instead of cytology.
Closing sentence restating the rationale for HPV testing in cervical screening, followed by the 1999 copyright notice from John Wiley & Sons.

Abstract of a paper on ancestral antibiotic resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis: introduction stating that intrinsic resistance, aided by the low-permeability cell envelope, limits TB drug options, and introducing a whiB7-based system that resists drugs reaching cytoplasmic targets.

Abstract continuation describing the whiB7 gene, which pathogenic mycobacteria share with the antibiotic-producing genus Streptomyces, and its role in tolerating diverse antibiotic classes that inhibit cytoplasmic targets; begins the M. tuberculosis induction findings.

Abstract results describing whiB7 induction in M. tuberculosis by subinhibitory erythromycin, tetracycline, and streptomycin, hypersusceptibility of whiB7 null mutants in Streptomyces and Mycobacterium, antibiotic sensitivity in a monocyte model, and induction by fatty acids.

Abstract findings on fatty acid induction of whiB7 relevant to host infection, and gene expression profiling showing whiB7 transcription controls a regulon of ribosomal protection and antibiotic efflux genes that determines drug resistance.
Abstract conclusion proposing components of the whiB7 system as drug targets for inhibitors that would make M. tuberculosis, including multidrug-resistant strains, more antibiotic-sensitive.

Introduction and purpose of the 1995-1996 CDC report on older adults (65+): frames the expected growth in older-adult population and the resulting rise in persons at risk for costly chronic disease and injury, and names the data reporting period.

Data sources section: identifies the NCHS datasets used, namely National Vital Statistics System causes of death (1996), National Hospital Discharge Survey (1996) for hospitalization causes, and National Health Interview Survey (1995) for chronic conditions.

Methods description of the data systems: explains that the National Vital Statistics System covers all US death certificates, NHDS is a probability sample of short-stay nonfederal hospital discharges, and NHIS is an annual household survey of the civilian noninstitutionalized population; also notes HCFA expenditure sources.

Results begin with mortality: leading causes of death among adults 65+ are heart disease, malignant neoplasms, and cerebrovascular disease, with age-adjusted-style rates per 100,000 population given for each.

Racial differences in leading causes of death among older adults: Alzheimer's disease is more frequent among whites, while diabetes, kidney disease, septicemia, and hypertension are more frequent among blacks; also notes hospitalization rates and stay length rise with age.

Hospitalization findings: heart disease accounts for the largest share of discharges among older adults (23%), and discharge rates for cancer, stroke, and pneumonia are similar across ages 65+ and are higher for men than women.

Morbidity and chronic conditions: women have higher fracture hospitalization rates than men, and arthritis, hypertension, and heart disease are the most prevalent chronic conditions in adults 65+. Also begins the expenditure findings, with 1995 health spending figures.

Health-care spending: in 1995, adults 65+ were 13% of the population but accounted for 35% ($310 billion) of personal health care dollars, with per capita real spending growing 5.8% annually over 1985-1995; also notes projections of substantial future increases after 2000.

Focus on three example conditions: hip fracture, dementia, and urinary incontinence are highlighted as prevalent, costly older-adult conditions that differ in preventability, and were selected for that reason.
Interpretation and recommendations: the high burden of serious, costly conditions among adults 65+ underscores the need for preventive health measures in this population.
Public health actions: the morbidity, mortality, and expenditure data serve as benchmarks for evaluating public health efforts to reduce modifiable risk factors among older adults.

Study on the second-meal effect: how the glycemic index of the previous evening's dinner (low vs. high GI, single foods or mixed meals) affects the blood glucose response to a standard breakfast the next morning.

Results: breakfast glycemic responses were significantly lower after low-GI dinners than high-GI dinners, with dinner differences predicted by GI; fiber content at equal GI had no effect on postbreakfast glycemia.
Conclusion: GI predicts glycemic response differences for mixed dinner meals, and eating low-GI foods the previous evening improves breakfast carbohydrate tolerance.

Introduction and background of a study on the second-meal effect (SME), where LGI foods in a first meal are usually thought to explain reduced glycemia at a later meal, while noting LGI foods also ferment in the colon.

Study objective and design start: the aim is to test whether greater colonic fermentation of HGI and LGI carbohydrates in a previous meal produces the second-meal effect; ten volunteers receive breakfast test meals.

Experimental design details: the three breakfast test meals (HGI with nonfermentable starch and cellulose, HGI-Lac with fermentable lactulose, and LGI with amylose and partly fermentable starch), followed five hours later by a standard lunch of 93 g available carbohydrate.

Methods and measurements: blood glucose, insulin, and NEFA sampling, breath hydrogen as a marker of colonic fermentation, and postlunch gastric emptying by ultrasonography; the start of the results describes glucose tolerance improvement.

Key results and conclusion: both HGI-Lac and LGI meals improved lunch glucose tolerance, with HGI-Lac linked to low NEFA levels and delayed gastric emptying, and the conclusion begins on fermentable carbohydrates regulating second-meal responses.

Final conclusion: fermentable carbohydrates regulate second-meal responses mainly by reducing NEFA competition with glucose disposal and, to a minor extent, by slowing intestinal motility, independent of glycemic index.

Introduces the study design: lentil vs. wholemeal bread breakfasts with identical carbohydrate in seven volunteers, reporting lentils' 71% lower blood glucose area and flatter insulin and GIP responses.

Reports that a lentil breakfast flattened the glucose response to a bread lunch 4 hours later (38% lower), and that slowly fed bread breakfast mimicked this pattern, while a low-carbohydrate bread breakfast impaired lunch glucose tolerance.

Describes the low-carbohydrate bread control (168% of control lunch glucose response) and breath hydrogen studies in four volunteers, concluding the lentil effect is not due to carbohydrate malabsorption.
Concludes that slow-release 'lente' carbohydrate foods like lentils may benefit diets for people with impaired carbohydrate tolerance.

Study design and objective: tests whether pulses (chickpea, lentil, yellow split pea) consumed as a fixed 250 kcal meal affect appetite and blood glucose before and after a later ad libitum pizza test meal in 25 young males, versus a macaroni and cheese control.

Methods: participants randomly consumed four isocaloric meals (three canned pulse types with macaroni and tomato sauce, or macaroni and cheese control), and food intake was measured at a pizza meal 260 min later.

Results on appetite and intake: lentil and yellow pea (not chickpea) lowered appetite ratings during the 260 min pre-pizza period and reduced food intake at the pizza meal compared with macaroni and cheese; blood glucose measurement period spans 0 to 340 min.

Results on blood glucose: all pulses lowered glucose at 20 min, with no overall pre-pizza glucose AUC effect; after pizza, chickpea and lentil lowered glucose immediately and across the post-pizza AUC more than yellow pea.

Conclusion: the appetite-suppressing, food-intake, and glycemic benefits of a pulse meal on a later meal depend on pulse type, with post-pizza glucose AUC lower for chickpea and lentil than yellow pea.

Introduces the study's background and objective: examining how white rice and beans intake relate to metabolic syndrome and its components in Costa Rican adults without diabetes, given the rice-and-beans staple diet.

Describes the study design: multivariate-adjusted component means by daily servings of rice and beans and by bean-to-rice ratio, plus odds ratios for metabolic syndrome from substituting beans for rice.

Reports main results on cardiometabolic markers: more white rice servings track with higher systolic BP, triglycerides, and fasting glucose and lower HDL, while more beans track with lower diastolic BP.
Details ratio-based findings: favorable trends in HDL, BP, and triglycerides at bean-to-rice ratios of 1:3 through 2:1, and a 35% lower metabolic syndrome risk when substituting beans for white rice.
Concludes that raising the bean-to-white-rice ratio or substituting beans for rice may lower cardiometabolic risk factors.

Abstract of a study on the spermicidal effects of Coca-Cola and Pepsi-Cola: tests Old Coke, New Coke variants, Diet Coke and Pepsi on sperm motility, finds none reduce motility below 70% of control in an hour, and disputes an earlier claim of varying potency across Coke formulations.

Concluding part of the same study on cola and sperm motility: states that any spermicidal effect of cola is relatively weak compared with well-known spermicidal agents, and restates that the earlier claim of marked differences between Coca-Cola formulations was not confirmed.

Study abstract opening: states the aim (dietary fats vs. semen quality), the sample of 99 men, and that fatty acids in sperm/seminal plasma were measured by gas chromatography in a 23-man subgroup, analyzed with linear regression.

Results section start: describes the cohort demographics (mostly Caucasian, mean age 36.4, majority overweight/obese, two-thirds never smokers) and the initial finding that higher total fat intake is negatively associated with sperm count and concentration.

Quantified results: men in the top third of total fat intake had roughly 43% lower sperm count and 38% lower concentration versus the bottom third (Ptrend = 0.01), an effect attributed to saturated fat; also reports a negative correlation between sperm saturated fatty acid levels and concentration, with no link to saturated fat intake.

Omega-3 and morphology results: higher omega-3 intake is linked to better sperm morphology, with top-third men showing about 1.9% higher normal morphology (Ptrend = 0.02); the results section then transitions into the conclusions.

Conclusions: as a preliminary cross-sectional study, high saturated fat intake is linked to lower sperm concentration while omega-3 intake is linked to better sperm morphology, with larger studies needed to confirm.
Final sentence of the conclusions, calling for larger samples to confirm the findings of this preliminary cross-sectional study on dietary fat and semen quality.
Introduction: Carlsen et al.'s 1992 finding of global sperm density decline (1938-1990) and the authors' 1997 reanalysis of those studies.
Findings of the 1997 reanalysis: significant sperm density declines in the US and Europe/Australia after controlling for abstinence, age, fertility, and collection method.
Comparison of decline rates (US ~1.5%/yr, Europe/Australia ~3%/yr vs. Carlsen ~1%/yr) and lack of decline in non-Western countries; introduces the current expanded study.
Current study adds 47 English-language studies (1934-1996); overall average decline slope essentially unchanged from Carlsen et al. (-0.94 vs. -0.93) and geographic slopes similar to earlier results.
