Secondary results on HAM-A somatic (subscore I) and psychic (subscore II) anxiety, which decreased similarly in both groups during active treatment, plus mention of other secondary measures.
Secondary outcome measures (SAS, PSWQ-PW, SF-36, CGI items, sleep diary) showing comparable positive effects for both drugs, and the study's conclusion that silexan is as effective as lorazepam.

Conclusions on safety and tolerability: silexan showed no sedative effects or abuse potential, positioning it as an alternative to benzodiazepines for generalized anxiety, followed by the copyright notice.
Copyright notice (Elsevier GmbH, 2009) closing the abstract, with no substantive content about the study.

Introduces the study's aim: examining how academic stress affects salivary cortisol and lactic acid bacteria activity, and describes the sample (23 undergraduates) and the two 1-week collection periods (semester start as low-stress baseline vs. exam week as high-stress).

Describes the questionnaire measures (perceived stress, GI symptoms, nutritional intake) and reports the key finding that faecal lactic acid bacteria levels were lower under high stress, with perceived stress rising during exams.
Concludes that perceived stress was higher during exams than at baseline, and states the study's contribution: further insight into the link between stress and gut flora activity in humans.

Opening of the Dahlem Conference document on psycho-neuroimmunology and the intestinal microbiota; introduces the slow clinical application of neural-immune knowledge and the goal of linking brain-microbiota interactions to clinical relevance, previewing the gut–brain axis discussion.

Middle of the Dahlem Conference introduction: outlines the document's structure, covering established gut–brain axis facts and gut bacteria's role, emerging data toward a new microbiota–gut–brain axis framework, and future directions of the field.
Fragment ending the document's opening paragraph on the rapidly emerging field of psycho-neuroimmunology and the intestinal microbiota.
Introduction to chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) and its frequent gut dysfunction, including higher rates of prior irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) diagnosis and IBS-like symptoms.
Interactions among intestinal microbiota, mucosal barrier function, and the immune system proposed as contributors to CFS pathogenesis, with a note on microbial microecology studies of the GI tract.
Evidence linking CFS to altered gut microbiota, mucosal barrier dysfunction with bacterial translocation, and an altered mucosal immune system.

The article's aim: examining how microbiota, barrier, and immune changes in CFS may cause GI dysfunction by modulating the enteric nervous system, and proposing gut-targeted therapy as a possible way to affect disease course.

Therapeutic proposal that modifying gut microbiota, e.g. with probiotics, could improve barrier function, reduce pro-inflammatory cytokines, and positively influence mood in CFS patients with elevated emotional and inflammatory symptoms.
Concluding point that probiotics may improve gut motility, which is dysfunctional in many CFS patients.
Fragment ending the document's final sentence, noting that gut motility is dysfunctional in many CFS patients.

Opening of the document: introduces the gut–brain connection as a bidirectional communication system tied to digestion, mood, motivation, and intuitive decision making, setting up the overview of the gut–brain axis topic.

Middle section: describes the gut–brain system's roles in maintaining gastrointestinal homeostasis and digestion and its likely effects on affect, motivation, and higher cognition, and begins noting that its disturbances are linked to disease.
Closing sentence: lists the disorders implicated when the gut–brain system is disrupted, namely functional and inflammatory GI disorders, obesity, and eating disorders, concluding the abstract.

Introduction to a pilot study on a probiotic (Lactobacillus casei Shirota) for emotional symptoms in chronic fatigue syndrome, covering CFS background, anxiety as the most common emotional symptom, gut microbiota alterations, and the gut-mood link.
Study design of the pilot trial: 39 CFS patients randomized to daily Lactobacillus casei strain Shirota (24 billion CFU) or placebo for two months, with the outcome measures introduced.

Results of the trial: increased Lactobacillus and Bifidobacteria in the probiotic group, and a significant reduction in anxiety versus controls (p = 0.01) on the Beck Depression and Anxiety Inventories.
Conclusion of the study, interpreting the findings as supporting a gut-brain interface possibly mediated by intestinal microbes.

Background and rationale for the study: a prior clinical trial showed a probiotic formulation (L. helveticus R0052 + B. longum R0175) reduced stress-induced GI discomfort, motivating the hypothesis that probiotics may improve mood and psychological distress via the gut-brain axis.

Study aims and design overview: investigates the anxiolytic-like effects of the probiotic formulation in rats and its effects on anxiety, depression, stress and coping in healthy human volunteers, with the preclinical part using 2 weeks of daily dosing before behavioural testing.

Methods: rats were tested in the conditioned defensive burying anxiety screening model after PF dosing, and a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised human trial gave PF for 30 days, measured with HSCL-90, HADS, Perceived Stress Scale, Coping Checklist and urinary free cortisol.

Results summary: daily PF reduced anxiety-like behaviour in rats and alleviated psychological distress in volunteers, notably on HSCL-90 subscales (global severity, somatisation, depression, anger-hostility), HADS global score and anxiety, CCL problem solving, and urinary free cortisol, with statistical significance values reported.

Detailed statistical findings: lists specific P-values for HSCL-90 global severity index, somatisation, depression and anger-hostility, HADS global and anxiety (P<0.06), the CCL problem-solving subscale, and UFC levels, showing which psychological and cortisol outcomes improved with the probiotic formulation.

Conclusion: the combined strain formulation of L. helveticus R0052 and B. longum R0175 shows anxiolytic-like activity in rats and beneficial psychological effects in healthy adults, supporting probiotics as a possible approach to mood and stress.

Introduction/thesis of the paper: hypothesizes that probiotics' ability to synthesize neuroactive compounds offers a unifying microbial endocrinology mechanism explaining how commensal microbiota affect gut and psychological health, with probiotics interacting across microbiological, immunological, and neurophysiological components.

Continues the framework: microbial endocrinology as a trans-disciplinary lens that reveals candidate mechanisms only if they are shared across microbial, immune, and neurophysiological components, and begins describing the neurochemicals probiotics produce.

Core argument: probiotics produce neurochemicals whose receptor targets on intestinal and extra-intestinal immune and neuronal cells are well characterized, so probiotics can be viewed as delivery vehicles for neuroactive compounds.

Conclusion: the microbial endocrinology hypothesis may guide selection and design of clinical probiotics and highlights the underappreciated role of neuroscience in understanding microbial influences on health; includes the 2011 Wiley copyright notice.

Introduction to the review on gut microbiota: evidence that gut microbes influence neural development and function, both in the enteric nervous system and the brain, framing the gut bacteria as a virtual inner organ relevant to host health.

Describes the scale and diversity of the intestinal microbiome (100 times the human body's cellular genetic material, with about 60% of microbes never cultured), noting that characterizing this population is only beginning.

Explains that gut microbes normally live in symbiosis with their host, but a disordered microbial balance is linked to chronic conditions like obesity and inflammatory bowel disease, and that psychiatric evidence is still limited but growing.

States the review's focus: emerging evidence that changes in gut microbe composition may be associated with altered nervous system function, and the proposal that this link merits further study for mood disorders.
Concluding statement of the introduction: the gut-microbiota concept could help understand mood disorders and may reveal missing links to co-morbid medical diseases.

Introduction of a study on probiotic survival during digestion, establishing the confusion over whether probiotics should be taken before, during, after, or without meals, and the study's aims about meal timing and food buffering capacity.
Methods portion describing the in vitro IViDiS upper gastrointestinal model and the commercial multi-strain probiotic ProtecFlor® being tested.

Description of the ProtecFlor® capsule's four microbial strains (two lactobacilli, one Bifidobacterium, and S. cerevisiae boulardii) and the main finding that survival was best when taken with or 30 minutes before a meal of oatmeal with milk.

Results comparing survival across conditions: poor survival when taken 30 minutes after a meal, better survival in milk with fat and oatmeal-milk gruel than in apple juice or spring water, and S. boulardii being unaffected by meal timing or buffering, with protein content judged less important than fat.
Conclusion that protein is less important than fat for bacterial survival, and the recommendation that non-enteric coated probiotics be taken with or just before a fat-containing meal.
Background and objectives of a Cochrane review on probiotics for preventing acute upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs), stating the lack of prior evidence on benefits and adverse effects.
Continuation of the objectives and search strategy, listing the databases searched (CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, Chinese databases) with date ranges up to May 2011.

Search strategy detail continued: remaining databases searched, including Web of Science, Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, Chinese Medicine Popular Science Literature Database, and a Beijing Union Medical College dissertation database.

Selection criteria (randomised controlled trials comparing probiotics with placebo for preventing acute URTIs) and data collection methods (two authors independently assessing eligibility, quality, and extracting data).
Main results opening: 14 RCTs included, with 10 trials (3451 participants) meta-analysed, and the finding that probiotics beat placebo in number of participants with at least one URTI episode.
Specific quantitative results: odds ratios and rate ratios for URTI episodes (at least one, at least three, rate of episodes) and reduced antibiotic prescriptions, with 95% confidence intervals.
Results for duration of episodes and adverse events, which showed no difference from placebo, noting minor side effects mainly gastrointestinal, plus heterogeneity in some subgroups.
Authors' conclusions: probiotics outperform placebo in reducing URTI episodes and antibiotic use, suggesting they may be more beneficial for preventing acute URTIs.
Closing caveats of the review: limitations of the results and the absence of data for older people.

Study design and setting for a trial of Lactobacillus rhamnosus HN001 in low-fat milk, introducing the objective, three-stage pre-post design over nine weeks at Taipei Medical College Hospital, and the 52 healthy middle-aged and elderly subjects.

Participant demographics and intervention protocol: the 52 volunteers' sex and age details, then the three stages (run-in LFM diet, HN001 in LFM or lactose-hydrolyzed LFM at 10^9 CFU/g, and LFM wash-out), each lasting three weeks.

Outcome measures and early results: in vitro phagocytic capacity of PMN leukocytes and NK cell tumoricidal activity, with the finding that the LFM run-in diet alone had no effect on immune responses and the start of the reported increase in phagocytic PMN cells.

Main quantitative results: HN001 consumption in either LFM or LFM-LH raised phagocytic PMN cells by 19% and 15% and NK cell tumor killing by 71% and 147%; levels mostly declined after cessation but stayed above baseline.

Conclusion of the study stating that dietary L. rhamnosus HN001 in low-fat or lactose-hydrolyzed low-fat milk appears to enhance systemic cellular immunity and may serve as a dietary supplement to boost natural immunity.

Background and rationale from a Danish cohort study on maternal vaginal microflora during pregnancy and childhood wheezing/asthma; introduces the idea that infants acquire microbes at birth from the maternal vaginal flora, which may shape infant flora and allergic disease risk.

Objective and methods of the study: a population-based Danish cohort in which vaginal bacterial samples were collected during pregnancy from 2927 women (3003 live infants), with wheezing defined as asthma hospitalization by age 3 and asthma as 3+ antiasthma medication packages at ages 4-5.

Methods continued with study population and outcome definitions, and the start of results describing maternal vaginal colonization as the exposure of interest in relation to infant wheezing and asthma.

Key results: maternal Ureaplasma urealyticum colonization linked to infant wheezing (OR 2.0) but not asthma at age 5; maternal staphylococci colonization (OR 2.2) and antibiotic use in pregnancy (OR 1.7) linked to asthma in the fifth year of life.
Results conclusion and overall takeaway: the composition of the maternal vaginal microflora may be associated with wheezing and asthma in offspring up to 5 years of age.

Opening of the abstract: aims and methods of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial testing Lactobacillus plantarum HEAL 9 and Lactobacillus paracasei 8700:2 probiotics against naturally acquired common cold infections.

Methods continued: the study outcomes (cold episodes, symptom days, symptom frequency/severity, cellular immune response) and enrollment of 272 healthy subjects randomised to daily probiotics (10^9 cfu, n=135) or control (n=137) for 12 weeks.
Results begin: cold incidence fell from 67% in controls to 55% with probiotics (p<0.05), and symptom days dropped from 8.6 to 6.2 days over the 12-week period.

Further results: total symptom score decreased (mean 44.4 control vs 33.6 probiotic), pharyngeal symptom reduction was significant, and B lymphocyte proliferation was significantly counteracted in the probiotic group.
Conclusion: the authors conclude that the probiotic strains L. plantarum HEAL 9 (DSM 15312) and L. paracasei 8700:2 (DSM 13434) reduce the risk of acquiring common cold infections.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the abstract's statement on reducing common cold infection risk.
Introduction and objective of a meta-analysis on caesarean section delivery and offspring allergic disease risk, including the literature search method (MEDLINE, 1966 to May 2007).
Methods section: the systematic MEDLINE search and the six allergic outcomes examined (food allergy, inhalant atopy, eczema, allergic rhinitis, asthma, asthma hospitalization).
Methods continued: the summary odds ratio meta-analysis approach accounting for heterogeneity, and the funnel plot assessment of publication bias; start of the results summary identifying 26 studies.
Results: pooled odds ratios for c-section and food allergy, allergic rhinitis, asthma, and asthma hospitalization, all showing increased risk.
Results continued: null associations for inhalant atopy and eczema/atopic dermatitis, funnel plot concerns about food allergy interpretation, and attributable fraction of cases (1-4%).
Conclusion start: c-section linked to moderate risk increases for rhinitis, asthma, asthma hospitalization, and possibly food allergy, but not inhalant atopy or atopic dermatitis.
Final conclusion: the rising c-section rate likely contributed little to the allergy epidemic of recent decades.

Introduction and objective of a study on whether the probiotic Bifidobacterium lactis HN019 can enhance cellular immunity in elderly people, including the trial's design summary (30 healthy elderly volunteers).

Study design section describing the 3-stage, 9-week dietary supplementation trial in elderly volunteers, starting with a 3-week low-fat milk run-in (base-diet control) and the start of the intervention stage with B. lactis HN019-supplemented milk.

Study design continuation detailing the two B. lactis HN019 doses (typical 5 x 10^10 and low 5 x 10^9 organisms/day) during the 3-week intervention, the 3-week low-fat milk washout stage, and the longitudinal blood-sample assays of leukocyte subsets, phagocytosis, and tumor-cell killing.

Results section reporting increases in total, CD4+ helper, and CD25+ activated T lymphocytes and natural killer cell proportions in blood after B. lactis HN019 consumption, and the start of the phagocytosis findings.

Remaining results and conclusion: elevated ex vivo phagocytic capacity and NK tumoricidal activity, greatest immune changes in subjects with poor pretreatment responses, similar effectiveness of both doses, and the conclusion that HN019 may be an effective probiotic supplement for cellular immunity in the elderly.
Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that B. lactis HN019 could be an effective probiotic dietary supplement for enhancing some aspects of cellular immunity in the elderly.

Abstract opening of a 2012 study on probiotic potential of autochthonous lactic acid bacteria from fruits and vegetables; covers gut survival under simulated gastric/intestinal conditions (35% of strains, mainly L. plantarum) and lack of effect on Caco-2 immune-mediation.

Continuation of the abstract on immunomodulation: all strains stimulated all 27 immune mediators in PBMCs, with significant increases in most cytokines and growth factors and only a few chemokines stimulated.

Abstract results on specific immune mediators: pro-inflammatory IL-17, EOTAXIN and IFN-γ were strongly stimulated by all strains, IL-12/IL-2/IL-7 were strain-dependent, few increased anti-inflammatory cytokines, and six L. plantarum strains were selected for further testing.

Abstract results on the six selected L. plantarum strains: adhesion to Caco-2 cells (four strongly adhesive, two adhesive), growth and acidification on fructo-oligosaccharides (FOS) as sole carbon source, and FOS fermentation end-products.

Abstract conclusion: all strains inhibited enterohemorrhagic E. coli K12 and Bacillus megaterium F6 of human origin, concluding that some lactic acid bacteria from raw produce are novel probiotic candidates; includes 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.
Final fragment of the abstract containing the closing phrase on novel probiotic candidates and the 2012 Elsevier copyright statement.

Study design and objectives: introduction to a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial of a probiotic for preventing antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) and C. difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) in hospitalized adults, including enrollment of 255 patients into three arms.

Arm allocation and intervention details: the three groups (Pro-2, Pro-1, placebo) with sample sizes, and the composition of each probiotic capsule (50 billion CFU of L. acidophilus CL1285 and L. casei LBC80R Bio-K+ CL1285).

Dosing timeline and primary AAD results: prophylaxis start within 36 h of antibiotics, continuation 5 days after the last dose, 21-day follow-up, and AAD incidence of 15.5% (Pro-2), 28.2% (Pro-1), and 44.1% (placebo).

Secondary outcomes: symptom duration in patients with AAD (Pro-2 2.8 days, Pro-1 4.1 days, placebo 6.4 days), CDAD incidence (Pro-2 1.2%, Pro-1 9.4%, placebo 23.8%), and lower gastrointestinal symptom frequency in treatment groups.

Conclusions: the proprietary probiotic blend was well tolerated and reduced AAD and especially CDAD risk, with a dose-ranging effect where 100 billion CFU outperformed 50 billion CFU and produced fewer GI events.
Trial registration: the ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT00958308 is cited as the registry number for this study.

Introduction/objectives of a study on standardized frozen fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) for recurrent Clostridium difficile infection, noting FMT's efficacy but limited use due to practical barriers such as donor screening costs and aesthetic concerns.

Study objective and methods: a University of Minnesota clinical FMT program reviewing 43 consecutive recurrent CDI patients, describing the shift from patient-identified donors to standard volunteer donors to simplify donor screening.
Methods continued: material preparation moved from the endoscopy suite to a standardized laboratory process and then to banking frozen, processed fecal material ready for use when needed.

Results: standardizing donor material preparation simplified FMT practice without apparent loss of efficacy against recurrent CDI; about 30% of patients had inflammatory bowel disease and responded equally well.
Conclusion: key steps in standardizing donor material preparation significantly simplified clinical FMT for recurrent CDI in patients who failed antibiotic therapy.

Opening chunk of a review on probiotics for diarrhea prevention and treatment in children and adults; it summarizes RCT and meta-analysis findings on primary and secondary prevention of gastroenteritis and notes modest benefit of selected Lactobacillus strains in primary prevention.

Middle section of the review covering strain-specific evidence: Saccharomyces boulardii for antibiotic-associated and C. difficile diarrhea and possible prevention in day-care centers, plus Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG reducing duration and severity of diarrhea, especially childhood rotavirus diarrhea.

Continuation of the findings on S. boulardii and L. rhamnosus GG, noting both are in pediatric gastroenteritis guidelines, other Lactobacillus data are preliminary, and efficacy depends on cause, early administration, and bacterial load, with proposed immune or intestinal mechanisms.
Start of the summary section, stating probiotics are an adjunct to rehydration for infantile gastroenteritis, with efficacy less convincing in adults but promising for antibiotic-associated diarrhea.
Final conclusion of the review: evidence of efficacy is limited to a few probiotic strains, which tempers the overall recommendation for probiotic use in diarrhea.

Background and objective of a systematic review on probiotics and prebiotics in formula-fed preterm infants, contrasting with earlier reviews focused on NEC, sepsis, and diarrhea, plus the Cochrane RCT methods introduction.

Methods detail: eligible RCTs comparing preterm formula with probiotics or prebiotics against conventional preterm formula, and the statistical reporting approach (mean difference for continuous outcomes, risk ratio for dichotomous outcomes, with 95% CIs).

Heterogeneity assessment methods (forest plot inspection, chi-square test, I² with substantial heterogeneity defined as >50%), and the included study counts: four probiotic studies (N=212) and four prebiotic studies (N=126), with start of probiotic results on weight gain.

Probiotic results: no significant difference in weight gain or maximal enteral feed, and a significant increase in stools per day in the probiotic group from a single study; prebiotic (GOS/FOS) results begin.
Prebiotic GOS/FOS results for weight gain and length gain, plus head growth and age at full enteral feed, showing no significant differences across studies.
Prebiotic outcomes on stool frequency (significant increase) and bifidobacteria counts for GOS/FOS and FOS (higher in prebiotic groups).
Conclusion: insufficient evidence that probiotic or prebiotic supplementation improves growth and clinical outcomes in exclusively formula-fed preterm infants.

Opening chunk of an abstract-style review on human gut microbiota: defines probiotics and notes over 700 randomized controlled human trials supporting their use for GI disorders and metabolic syndrome.
Middle chunk stating the review is based on AGA, ISAPP, and ILSI North America webinar presentations on gut microbiota, probiotics, and prebiotics for gastroenterologists and researchers.

Closing portion describing the webinar content: gut microbiota's influence on health and disease, clinical intervention strategies, and practical probiotic/prebiotic guidelines, with a 2011 ILSI copyright notice.
Final fragment of the document containing the end of the webinar-content description and the 2011 International Life Sciences Institute copyright line.

Introduction and study aim of a 2009 microbiological evaluation of commercial probiotic products sold in the USA, covering the lack of regulation and prior non-conformity findings, and stating the goal of checking label accuracy for viable bacteria counts, species identity, and cross contamination.
Key results of the 2009 USA probiotic label study: only 4 of 13 products (31%) matched their label claims, which is the main finding that highlights mislabeling problems in the market.

Concluding recommendations of the probiotic label study: calls for stronger control of probiotic manufacturing and periodic screening by competent authorities to monitor how storage affects product quality.

Introduction and study design: a retrospective case series of 18 patients with recurrent C. difficile colitis who received donor stool via nasogastric tube over a 9-year single-institution period, framed against C. difficile complications from systemic antimicrobial use.

Antimicrobial exposure and outcomes: patients received a median of 3 antimicrobial courses (range 2-7, total 64) before stool treatment; over 90 days post-treatment, 2 patients died of unrelated causes and 1 of 16 survivors had a single C. difficile recurrence.

Safety and conclusion: no adverse effects were attributed to donor stool treatment, and the authors conclude that nasogastric delivery of healthy-donor stool may benefit patients with recurrent C. difficile colitis.

Opening of the Cochrane-style review on probiotics for preventing pediatric antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD): background rationale (gut microbiota disruption by antibiotics) and the review's efficacy and adverse-event objectives.

Continuation of the objectives, followed by the search strategy: electronic databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE, CENTRAL, CINAHL, AMED, Web of Science) searched to August 2006, plus specialized registers and trial registries.

Search methods continued: specialized registers (Cochrane IBD/FBD group, CISCOM, Chalmers PedCAM), trial registry searches to 2005, outreach to trial authors and companies, and hand searching of conference proceedings, dissertations and reference lists.
Selection criteria: randomized, parallel, controlled trials comparing co-administered probiotics with antibiotics against antibiotic-associated diarrhea in children aged 0 to 18 years.

Data collection and analysis methods: independent quality assessment and extraction by two authors, with pooled relative risks for dichotomous outcomes and weighted mean differences for continuous outcomes, including 95% CIs.
Analysis plan: adverse events summarized as risk differences; prespecified sensitivity analyses (per protocol vs intention to treat, random vs fixed effects, quality criteria) for diarrhea incidence.

Main results begin: ten studies met inclusion criteria, testing Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Streptococcus, or Saccharomyces boulardii alone or combined; subgroup analyses by strain, dose, AAD definition, and antibiotic.
Study characteristics and key efficacy finding: six single-strain and four multi-strain studies; per protocol analysis of diarrhea incidence favored probiotics (pooled RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.74).

Intention-to-treat result was non-significant (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.63); five of ten trials monitored adverse events (n=647) with no serious adverse events reported; start of authors' conclusions.

Authors' conclusions: probiotics are promising, per protocol estimates are significant and clinically meaningful (including high-quality studies), but the intention-to-treat estimate was not significant.

Recommendations for future research: test strains and doses with the best evidence (L. GG, L. sporogenes, S. boulardii 5-40 billion CFU/day); the review cannot determine effects of age or antibiotic duration.

Final recommendations: develop a validated, sensitive primary outcome for AAD meaningful to clinicians, parents and children; conclusion that evidence is promising but insufficient to routinely recommend probiotics for pediatric AAD.
Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that it is premature to routinely recommend probiotics for preventing pediatric antibiotic-associated diarrhea.

Introduces the Women's Health Study (US, 1992-2004) examining moderate alcohol intake and breast cancer risk, reporting case counts (1,484 total; 1,190 invasive, 294 in situ) among 38,454 cancer- and CVD-free women with ~10 years of follow-up.

Reports the main finding that higher alcohol intake modestly raises breast cancer risk, with relative risks for >=30 g/day vs. none of 1.32 for total breast cancer (CI 0.96-1.82) and 1.43 for invasive breast cancer (CI 1.02-2.02).
Describes that the increased risk is confined to ER+PR+ tumors, giving per-10 g/day relative risks by tumor subtype: ER+PR+ 1.11 (804 cases), ER+PR- 1.00 (125 cases), and ER-PR- 0.99 (167 cases).

Notes that the alcohol-related association appeared strongest in current postmenopausal hormone users, though the interaction test was not significant, and begins the prospective study's overall conclusion.
Concludes that the prospective study findings indicate moderate alcohol consumption increases breast cancer risk.

Opening chunk of a abstract on a healthy lifestyle index and breast cancer risk: introduces the study aim, a 2004-2007 Mexican population-based case-control design, and matching of cases and controls.

Continues the methods of the Mexican breast cancer case-control study: 1,000 cases and 1,074 controls, and construction of the healthy lifestyle index via principal components from diet, physical activity, alcohol, and smoking, analyzed with conditional logistic regression.

Results section defining the healthy lifestyle index (physical activity, low fat, processed foods, refined cereals, complex sugars, no smoking or alcohol) and beginning the odds ratio findings for premenopausal women.

Reports the key odds ratios comparing highest versus lowest index quintiles: protective effects in pre- (OR 0.50) and postmenopausal women (OR 0.20), plus the conclusion that healthy lifestyle reduces breast cancer odds and should be promoted for primary prevention.

Closing conclusion and impact statement: calls for integrated primary prevention and strategies to engage women in healthy lifestyles, noting this is the first study to assess a healthy lifestyle index against breast cancer risk (AACR 2011 copyright).

Opening of the abstract describing a prospective study of 1,490 early-stage breast cancer survivors (diagnosed 1991-2000, enrolled about 2 years post-diagnosis) examining how physical activity, diet, and obesity interact in relation to survival.

Results section beginning: only seven women were lost to follow-up through 2005; univariate analyses show weak associations of survival with vegetable-fruit intake, physical activity, and healthy BMI, and the multivariate Cox model introduces the combined diet-activity finding.

Key finding: the combination of five or more daily vegetable-fruit servings plus 540+ MET-min/week (about 30 minutes of walking 6 days a week) gave a significant survival advantage (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.31-0.98).

Findings that the roughly 50% risk reduction from the healthy lifestyle held in both obese and nonobese women, that fewer obese women adhered to it (16% vs 30%), that obesity had no apparent effect among adherents, and that the effect was stronger in hormone receptor-positive cancers.

Conclusion: only a minority of survivors follow the healthy diet-plus-moderate-activity pattern, and the strong protective effect justifies further study of combined diet and physical activity on breast cancer survival.
Final sentence of the conclusion calling for further investigation of the combined influence of diet and physical activity on breast cancer survival.

Introduction to the study: background on the 2007 WCRF/AICR cancer prevention recommendations (diet, physical activity, weight management) and the objective of testing their link to cancer risk in the EPIC cohort.

Study design: the EPIC cohort of 386,355 participants from 9 European countries, with dietary, anthropometric, and lifestyle data collected at recruitment, and the construction of a concordance score based on WCRF/AICR recommendations.

Score methodology: the components of the WCRF/AICR concordance score (weight management, physical activity, weight-gain foods/drinks, plant and animal foods, alcohol, breastfeeding), its 0-6 (men) and 0-7 (women) range, and the use of multivariable Cox regression to estimate cancer risk.

Main results part 1: higher concordance is linked to lower cancer risk, with a 1-point score increase associated with 5% lower total cancer risk, and 12% lower colorectal cancer risk, with confidence intervals.

Main results part 2: a 16% risk reduction for stomach cancer per score point, significant associations for several other cancers (breast, endometrium, lung, kidney, upper aerodigestive tract, liver, esophagus), and no significant association for prostate, ovarian, pancreatic, or bladder cancer.
Conclusion: adherence to WCRF/AICR cancer prevention recommendations may lower the risk of most types of cancer.
Introduction and methods opening of a pilot study on red vs. white wine as a nutritional aromatase inhibitor in premenopausal women, covering breast cancer risk background and the crossover design.

Methods continued: crossover assignment of 36 premenopausal women to 1 month of red or white wine, and the hormones measured from twice-per-cycle blood samples (E2, E1, androstenedione, testosterone, SHBG, LH, FSH).
Results on hormone changes: red wine raised free testosterone and lowered SHBG relative to white wine, with estradiol lower but not statistically significant.

Results and conclusion: LH was significantly higher with red wine while FSH was unchanged, and the conclusion states red wine is associated with higher free T, lower SHBG, and higher LH in healthy premenopausal women.
Final conclusion sentence: the data suggest red wine acts as a nutritional aromatase inhibitor, which may explain why it does not appear to increase breast cancer risk.
Introduction on aromatase in breast cancer: in situ estrogen synthesis as a chemoprevention target, with the abstract's study of red wine as a source of aromatase inhibitors.
Rationale that fruit/vegetable phytochemicals inhibit aromatase; prior work found grapes and wine contain potent aromatase inhibitors, and red wine is compared against white wine.
Comparison of red and white wine: red wine suppresses aromatase more effectively, white wine shows a weak alcohol-driven induction, and red wine's anti-aromatase compounds outweigh that effect.
Methods overview: whole red wine is fractionated by liquid-liquid extraction, silica gel chromatography, SPE columns, and HPLC to isolate active aromatase inhibitors.
Key results: an active Pinot Noir SPE C18 fraction outperforms whole wine in aromatase assays, and the extract is tested in a mammary aromatase-overexpressing transgenic mouse model.

In vivo findings and conclusion: gavaged red wine extract fully prevents aromatase-induced mammary hyperplasia and neoplasia, suggesting a chemopreventive supplement for high-risk postmenopausal women.
Closing statement on ongoing work to purify and characterize the specific red wine compounds that inhibit aromatase.

Introduction and study aims from the allergy epidemic paper: describes the rise of allergic disease in western societies and the objective of comparing atopic sensitization across birth cohorts more than 60 years apart.

Methods section: four cohorts of 100 subjects each (ages 7, 27, 47, 67; born 1990, 1963-66, 1943-46, 1923-26), with serum total and specific IgE testing for aeroallergens and dietary allergens and a symptom questionnaire.

Results on sensitization: aeroallergen-specific IgE positivity rose steadily from the oldest to youngest cohorts (chi2 trend 56.809, P<0.0001), with no similar trend for dietary allergen sensitization.

Results on asthma and cohort differences: diagnosed asthma varied significantly across cohorts (chi2=13.45, P=0.004), and the 1943-46 cohort, born during or after WWII, had the lowest asthma and dietary sensitization rates.

Conclusions: airborne allergen sensitization increased long term unlike dietary sensitization, supporting early-life programming of immunity by external factors and cautioning against short-term studies of the allergy epidemic.
Final sentence of the conclusion: short-term studies may be insufficient for judging the pace and causes of the allergy epidemic.

Opening of an abstract on allergies and cancer: states the review's objective, describes the literature search sources (MEDLINE, EBSCO), and begins the study selection criteria (asthma, hay fever, allergy-related diseases).

Continues the study selection criteria, then reports the main finding that people with allergies have a decreased risk for many cancers, such as glioma, colorectal, laryngeal, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, esophageal, oral, pancreatic, stomach, and uterine body cancers.
Lists cancers with increased risk in allergy patients (bladder, lymphoma, myeloma, prostate) and cancers showing no association or conflicting results (breast, leukemia, lung, melanoma, thyroid).
Notes cancers where evidence is insufficient (Kaposi sarcoma, liver, ovarian) and begins the conclusion that the allergy-cancer association is site specific.
Final conclusion sentence calling for further research to verify the findings and explain why these site-specific associations exist.

Background on the clinical problem: chronic P. aeruginosa infection and inflammation drive lung morbidity and mortality in cystic fibrosis, motivating new anti-inflammatory treatments. Introduces the study context for Emblica officinalis and Pyrogallol research.

Motivation for medicinal plant research: traditional Asian medicine plants are gaining interest for efficacy and safety, and identifying the effect of individual active compounds in plant extracts is needed for selective, reproducible applications.

Methods and key results: Emblica officinalis extract tested in IB3-1 CF bronchial epithelial cells exposed to P. aeruginosa PAO1, where it strongly suppressed expression of IL-8, GRO-alpha, GRO-gamma, ICAM-1, and IL-6.
Compound-level findings: Pyrogallol from EO reproduces the anti-inflammatory gene suppression of the whole extract, while the purified compound 5-hydroxy-isoquinoline shows no effect.

Conclusion and next steps: Pyrogallol is identified as the active anti-inflammatory compound of EO, and the authors recommend in vivo airway animal model studies to assess its efficacy and safety for CF chronic lung inflammation.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence ending the abstract, referring to testing the molecule in chronic lung inflammatory disease in cystic fibrosis.

Opening of the document's introduction: frames inflammation's link to modern diseases (obesity, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, cancer) as an unsolved problem and describes inflammation as a protective response with a cost to tissue function.

Middle of the introduction: explains that the cost-benefit tradeoff of inflammation was optimized over evolutionary time, and that rapid environmental change from niche construction outpaces natural selection, creating a mismatch with modern conditions.

Introduction's transition to the paper's aim: argues that the mismatch leaves physiological tradeoffs unoptimized for modern life, raising disease susceptibility, and states the paper will examine inflammation from an evolutionary perspective.
Closing sentence of the introduction: says the paper will discuss unique aspects of inflammation and its evolutionary history to explain its association with modern human diseases.

Introduces the review's core premise: autoimmune diseases arise from gene-environment interactions, and serum autoantibodies can be detected months to years before clinical onset, opening the door to prediction.

Covers predictive markers beyond antibodies (genetic susceptibility), notes type 1 diabetes as the most accurate current example using first-degree relatives and autoantibody tests, and looks ahead to multi-marker models.

Concludes that combining antibody tests with genetics, epigenetics, and immunological markers may enable precise prediction, which could allow preventive interventions to avoid or delay disease; includes the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
Contains only the tail of the copyright statement (Elsevier B.V., all rights reserved) from the document's end, with no substantive content.
Introduction and objective of a human study on Agaricus bisporus white button mushroom (WBM) dietary intake and salivary secretory IgA (SIgA) mucosal immunity.
Methods: design of the randomized trial with 24 healthy volunteers (control vs. 100 g/day blanched WBM for 1 week), with participant ages and group sizes.
Methods: saliva collection schedule over 3 weeks and measured variables (flow rate, sIgA concentration, osmolality, sIgA:osmolality ratio, sIgA secretion rate).
Results: control group showed no pre/post change; WBM group's sIgA secretion rate rose significantly by 53% at week 1 and 56% at week 2 versus week 0 (P < 0.0005).

Results: WBM group's sIgA secretion returned to baseline by week 3, changes exceeded controls; osmolality and salivary IgG were unchanged in both groups, while the sIgA:osmolality ratio increased significantly.
Conclusion: WBM intake significantly accelerates salivary sIgA secretion, suggesting benefits for mucosal immunity; includes the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.
Elsevier copyright and rights statement (Crown Copyright 2012) closing the abstract of the WBM salivary sIgA study.

Opening of an abstract on the global asthma epidemic: it describes asthma's multifactorial heterogeneity, its burden (300 million sufferers, 250,000+ deaths yearly), and rising prevalence in low- and middle-income countries and in previously low-prevalence ethnic groups.

Middle portion of the abstract on causes of the asthma increase: spatio-temporal prevalence differences tied to environmental exposure, evidence for host susceptibility and stress, and a call for research into mechanisms behind asthma's rise or stagnation.
Closing sentence of the abstract calling for further mechanistic investigation of asthma increase or stagnation, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Opening chunk of an abstract on gut immunology: it introduces the gut immune system's dual task of defending against pathogens while tolerating food antigens and commensal bacteria, and notes that chronic gut inflammation is common in developed countries without overt infection.

Middle chunk of the abstract stating that mutations in genes governing innate immune recognition, adaptive immunity, and epithelial permeability are linked to gut inflammation in both mice and humans, concluding that disrupted homeostasis between gut antigens and host immunity drives inflammation and allergy.
Final fragment of the abstract's concluding sentence, identifying the disruption of gut antigen-immunity homeostasis as a critical factor in the development of gut inflammation and allergy.

Abstract opening of the study introducing the two-step method for quantifying the infection rate of Zoophthora anhuiensis on Myzus persicae, including the first step's time-dose-mortality model from bioassay 1.
Describes bioassay 2 design: six nymphal aphid colonies (4 days old or younger) exposed to conidial showers at four dosages, followed by chlorothalonil immersion to remove surviving conidia.
Details the chlorothalonil disinfection step (0.1% solution, 0.5 min) applied 1-12 h post-exposure at 15 and 20 °C, and defines the infection rate as observed mortality divided by expected mortality.
Summarizes the main finding that Z. anhuiensis infection of M. persicae is very rapid, with negligible difference between aphids held at 15 and 20 °C before fungicide immersion.
Reports that the first 6 hours post-exposure are critical for infection, that infection rate depends strongly on conidial dose, and gives specific times to reach 50% and 90% infection at high doses.
Final fragment giving the quantitative threshold: over 90% of aphids infected within about 1 hour at doses above 50 conidia/mm2.

Abstract opening of a paper on immuno-inflammatory disease: rising autoimmune, allergic and inflammatory disease incidence in Western countries, proposed to be driven by gut microbiome changes acting through regulatory T cells (Tregs), which set the peripheral antigen-recognition threshold.

Explains the proposed mechanism: Tregs tonically suppress dendritic cell costimulation and maintain DC tolerogenicity. Small Treg deficits lower the activation threshold, letting low-affinity self-reactive CD4 T cells that escaped thymic negative selection expand and differentiate.

Concluding part of the hypothesis: if DCs exposed to commensal microbes and allergens fail to keep a tolerogenic state, this can trigger pathogenic allergic and inflammatory responses at epithelial surfaces.

Introduces the study's scope: comparison of chemical composition and nutritional value of five widely consumed cultivated mushroom species (Agaricus bisporus white/brown, Pleurotus ostreatus, Pleurotus eryngii, Lentinula edodes/Shiitake, Flammulina velutipes), beginning with the macronutrient findings for Shiitake.

Reports the comparative results: Shiitake has the highest sugars, tocopherols, PUFA and lowest SFA; white and brown A. bisporus share similar macronutrient, sugar, MUFA, PUFA and tocopherol values; oyster and king oyster mushrooms have the highest MUFA.

Summarizes further findings: oyster and king oyster mushrooms show similar fatty acid profiles (PUFA, MUFA, SFA) and similar moisture, ash, carbohydrate and energy values; the study aims to build nutritional databases of popular fungi for comparison, and notes cultivated and wild samples of the same species differ in composition.
Concluding sentence on cultivated versus wild samples differing in sugars, fatty acids and tocopherol profiles, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.

Background and rationale: introduces Th17 cells and IL-17 in allergic disease, and the reported link between CD161 expression and IL-17-producing T cells, motivating the study of CD161(+) T cells in allergic rhinitis.

Study aims and methods: describes the comparison of peripheral CD161(+) T cell frequency between allergic rhinitis patients and healthy controls, the cohort sizes (44 AR patients, 29 controls), and the immunofluorescence/FACS approach with Visual Analogue Scale symptom scoring.

Results: reports that AR patients had significantly higher frequencies of CD3(+), CD4(+) and CD8(+) CD161(+) cells than non-allergic controls (p < 0.0001), and that CD161 expression correlated with clinical severity.
Conclusions and citation: summarizes that higher peripheral CD161(+) T cell frequency is found in allergic rhinitis patients, and gives the 2012 S. Karger AG, Basel copyright notice.

Study overview: introduces the aim of comparing antioxidant levels in fresh, frozen, freeze-dried strawberries and strawberry jam, and the ABTS/H₂O₂/HRP method used to measure HAA, LAA and total antioxidant activity (TAA).

Statistical methods and first key result: describes one-way ANOVA with Dunnett's T3 comparisons, then reports that freeze-dried strawberries had significantly higher as-consumed TAA than fresh, frozen and jam, with 95% CIs.

Dry-weight results and conclusion: reports that fresh strawberries had significantly higher dry-weight TAA than freeze-dried, frozen and jam (with CIs), and begins the concluding statement that results agree with prior work on strawberries as an antioxidant source.
Concluding sentence: states that the findings agree with previous studies showing strawberries are a valuable dietary source of antioxidants for consumers.

Opening of a 2012 International Society for Sexual Medicine review on whether oral sex (fellatio, cunnilingus) is linked to rising oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) and HPV; introduces the epidemiological shift in head and neck cancers.

Continues the introduction: OSCCs are linked to HPV, and some researchers attribute the shift in head and neck cancer epidemiology to changing sexual practices, a claim the review treats as possibly premature.
States the review's stated aim, to clarify contradictory evidence on oral sex and head and neck cancer so sexual medicine professionals can give accurate, up-to-date patient information.

Methods and results of the review: a PubMed search on HPV, oral sex, oral cancer, and OSCC, with counts of relevant articles found (196 on HPV, 63 on oral sex, 55 on oral cancer, 5 on OSCC). It has no outcome data.
Conclusions: HPV infections are common and usually clear within 18 months, so they are not a concern for monogamous couples with a closed sexual system and no immune compromise.

Final conclusions: HPV becomes a concern only with immune compromise and persistent infection; the article reviews factors behind immune compromise, HPV persistence, and oncogenesis. Includes the 2012 ISSM copyright line.
Copyright footer of the 2012 International Society for Sexual Medicine article, the tail end of the document's conclusions.

Study purpose and background: topical 10% freeze-dried black raspberry gel aimed at oral intraepithelial neoplasia (IEN), measuring histology and loss of heterozygosity (LOH) markers linked to progression to oral squamous cell carcinoma.

Background on LOH/microsatellite risk, prior phase I evidence that black raspberry preparations are well tolerated with antioxidant, apoptotic, and differentiation-inducing effects, and the start of the experimental design where each participant serves as their own control.
Methods detail: pre-treatment photography and biopsy for baseline diagnosis and molecular variables, plus the gel dosing regimen (0.5 g four times daily for 6 weeks) starting one week after biopsy.

Molecular methods: DNA extracted from laser-captured basilar and suprabasilar epithelial cells, PCR with primers for INK4a/ARF, p53, and FHIT loci, and allelic imbalance assessed by sequencing against normal tissue marker patterns.

Results summary: none of 27 participants had gel-related toxicity (confirming phase I), with histologic regression in some patients and statistically significant LOH reduction at tumor suppressor loci.
Conclusion: the preliminary findings justify further evaluation of berry gels for chemoprevention of oral IEN.

This chunk is the document's sole summary paragraph, introducing the link between unprotected oral sex and head and neck cancers in younger patients, and noting rising incidence that may partly reflect improved HPV detection methods.

Introduces the American Cancer Society's Nutrition and Physical Activity Guidelines, their purpose, and that they are updated every 5 years by an expert panel reflecting current evidence on diet, activity, and cancer risk.
Explains that individual dietary and physical activity choices are shaped by the surrounding community context, which can either support or hinder healthy behavior.

States that community efforts are needed to build a social environment promoting healthy food and physical activity, introducing a community-action recommendation that complements four individual-choice recommendations for reducing cancer risk.

Argues that a supportive social environment is essential so people at all levels of society can genuinely choose healthy behaviors, and notes the ACS Guidelines align with heart and diabetes prevention guidance.

States that the ACS Guidelines are consistent with American Heart Association and American Diabetes Association recommendations and with the HHS 2005 Dietary Guidelines for Americans on general health promotion.
Abstract opening (Purpose): aim of formulating PLGA/PLA injectable millicylindrical implants loaded with black raspberry extract to sustain delivery of chemopreventive anthocyanins CS, CG, and CR.

Abstract Methods (continued): identification/quantitation of anthocyanins by MS and HPLC, and preparation/characterization of the RE:TA-β-CD inclusion complex via kneading, XRD, NMR, and UV-vis spectroscopy.

Abstract Methods (continued): implant preparation by solvent extrusion, and in vitro (PBS-Tween-80, pH 7.4, 37°C) and in vivo (subcutaneous, male Sprague-Dawley rats) release study design, with HPLC quantitation at 520 nm.

Abstract Results: anthocyanin content in the extract (CS 0.2, CG 1.5, CR 3.5 wt%) and pH-dependent solution stability, with degradation increasing from pH 2.4 to 7.4; start of results on 5 or 10 wt% RE implants.

Abstract Results (continued): unmodified RE/PLGA/PLA implants show high initial burst and short release (35–52% and 80–100% CG+CR at 1 and 14 days), attributed to water uptake and porosity from osmolytic non-anthocyanin components.

Abstract Results (continued): spectroscopy shows non-anthocyanin RE molecules complex with TA-β-CD, reducing hydrophilicity; the hydrophobic inclusion complex improves sustained release of anthocyanins in vitro and in vivo.

Abstract Results and Conclusion: 20 wt% RE:TA-β-CD IC/PLA implants release 16–24% and 97–99% CG+CR at 1 and 28 days, owing to reduced water uptake and porosity; concludes these are optimal for one-month delivery.
Abstract Conclusion (final sentence): PLA millicylindrical implants with RE:TA-β-CD complex are optimal dosage forms for one-month continuous delivery of chemopreventive FBR anthocyanins.

Introduction of a study on black raspberry chemoprevention: background on freeze-dried black raspberries inhibiting oral, esophageal, and colon cancer in rodents, and on extracts blocking benzo(a)pyrene-induced transformation, with the mechanisms and active components still unknown.

Identifies the study's key components: ferulic acid, beta-sitosterol, and the RO-ET ethanol-eluted silica column fraction from freeze-dried black raspberry extract, which inhibit growth of premalignant and malignant but not normal human oral epithelial cells.

Results on growth inhibition: the DM:ET fraction and ellagic acid inhibit normal as well as premalignant and malignant human oral cell lines, contrasting with the selective effects of ferulic acid, beta-sitosterol, and RO-ET.

Methods and cell cycle findings: flow cytometry and Western blotting of cell cycle regulatory proteins were used to probe how ferulic acid, beta-sitosterol, and RO-ET selectively inhibit premalignant and malignant oral cells; RO-ET caused no discernible cell cycle distribution change.

Cell cycle distribution effects by compound: ferulic acid drives premalignant and malignant cells into G2/M, beta-sitosterol causes G0/G1 accumulation in premalignant and G2/M in malignant cells, and RO-ET lowers cyclin A and cdc2 in premalignant cells.

Protein-level changes: RO-ET reduces cyclin B1, cyclin D1, and cdc2 in malignant lines and raises p21waf1/cip1 there; ferulic acid increases cyclin B1 and cdc2 and induces p21 in malignant cells; beta-sitosterol alters cyclin B1, cdc2, and p21 levels.

Conclusion: beta-sitosterol lowers cyclin B1 and cdc2 while raising p21waf1/cip1 in both cell lines; the authors conclude that the growth-inhibitory effects of black raspberries may reside in specific components targeting aberrant cell cycle signaling.

Final sentence of the conclusion, stating that specific black raspberry components may act on aberrant signaling pathways that regulate cell cycle progression in premalignant and malignant human oral cells.

Introduces the study's background: reduced proapoptotic and differentiation gene expression alongside elevated COX-2 and iNOS is linked to malignant progression of oral intraepithelial neoplasia, motivating a black raspberry gel intervention.

States the study aims (effects of 10% freeze-dried black raspberry gel on IEN histopathology, gene expression, COX-2/iNOS proteins, and microvessel density) and the prior finding that black raspberries have antioxidant, pro-apoptotic, and differentiation-inducing effects.

Describes the study design: baseline biopsy hemisected for diagnosis and baseline measures, then gel applied four times daily for 6 weeks starting one week after biopsy, with RNA isolated from snap-frozen lesions for microarray analysis.

Covers the methods for molecular and protein analysis: microarray with qRT-PCR validation, gene-specific epithelial qRT-PCR, and image-analysis-quantified immunohistochemistry for surface epithelial COX-2, iNOS, and microvascular density.

Reports key results: berry gel uniformly suppressed genes for RNA processing, growth factor recycling, and apoptosis inhibition; most participants had lower iNOS and COX-2 after treatment, but only COX-2 decreases were statistically significant.

Concludes that berry gel modulated oral IEN gene expression and reduced epithelial COX-2 protein, and that in a patient subset it lowered superficial connective tissue vascular density and induced keratinocyte terminal differentiation genes.
Final sentence of the abstract, summarizing the subset finding that berry gel induced genes associated with keratinocyte terminal differentiation in patients with oral IEN.
Introduction and methods of an Italian case-control study on dietary patterns and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma risk, describing 304 cases, 743 controls, and food frequency questionnaire data.
Methods continue with principal component factor analysis of 28 nutrients to derive dietary patterns, and logistic regression on factor-score quartiles adjusted for confounders; results begin.
Results identify five dietary patterns and report the positive association of the 'animal products and related components' pattern with esophageal cancer risk (OR 1.64).

Results report inverse associations of the 'vitamins and fiber' and 'other polyunsaturated fatty acids and vitamin D' patterns with esophageal cancer (ORs about 0.5), no significant association for other patterns, and the start of the conclusion.
Conclusion: a diet high in animal-origin foods and low in vitamin- and fiber-rich foods is suggested to increase esophageal cancer risk.
Introduction and study design of a population-based case-control study of dietary patterns and oesophageal cancer, describing the OAC, OGJAC, OSCC case and control sample sizes.

Methods: data collection via self-administered questionnaires and principal component analysis deriving three dietary patterns (meat and fat, pasta and pizza, fruit and vegetable), with unconditional logistic regression used to estimate risks by pattern score quartiles.

Results for the meat-and-fat dietary pattern, showing multivariable-adjusted odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals for increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma (OAC), oesophagogastric junction adenocarcinoma (OGJAC) and oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).

Results for the pasta-and-pizza and fruit-and-vegetable dietary patterns, including the inverse association of pasta-and-pizza with OSCC and the borderline and significant protective associations of fruit-and-vegetable with OGJAC and OSCC.
Conclusion highlighting that high-fat dairy foods drove the meat-and-fat pattern's association with OAC and OGJAC, and calling for prospective studies to confirm the findings.
Final sentence of the abstract stating that prospective studies are needed to confirm the findings of this dietary pattern study on oesophageal cancer.

Abstract opening of a study on cisplatin combined with curcumin and EGCG in ovarian cancer, stating the aim of testing sequenced drug administration effects on synergism in A2780 and cisplatin-resistant cell lines.

Study design from the abstract: binary cisplatin combinations with curcumin and EGCG tested across five administration sequences, with combination index criteria defining synergism, additivity, and antagonism.

Methods and key result from the abstract: platinum accumulation and platinum-DNA binding measured by graphite furnace AAS, and the finding that cisplatin given 4 h before curcumin and EGCG (0/4 h) was most synergistic.
Mechanistic explanation and results from the abstract: the 0/4 h sequence increased cellular platinum and platinum-DNA binding relative to cisplatin alone, which accounts for the observed synergy.
Concluding statement from the abstract: lower concentrations and shorter time gaps between the two drug additions appear to yield greater cytotoxicity in both ovarian cancer cell lines.
Opening of the review's introduction: establishes cancer as a leading cause of death and motivates chemoprevention, specifically using low-cost, safe nutraceuticals from fruits and vegetables.

Continues the introduction: summarizes supporting evidence from human, animal, and cell studies for nutraceutical chemopreventive effects, and notes that single-agent approaches have failed in clinical trials, motivating combinations.

States the rationale for nutraceutical combinations that mimic real-life conditions and target multiple pathways with minimal toxicity, then announces the review's aim: summarizing combinatorial chemopreventive studies.

Concludes the abstract by describing the review's scope: studies of combined nutraceuticals and their combinations with anticancer drugs, followed by the 2011 New York Academy of Sciences copyright notice.

Opening of a 2012 AACR editorial on a phase II strawberry powder trial for esophageal cancer prevention in China, introducing the preclinical rationale for berries and grapes and the trial's two dosing arms (60 g/d vs 30 g/d).

Summarizes the trial results (60 g/d reduced dysplasia grade and localized biomarkers; 30 g/d ineffective) and lists open questions about strawberry powder formulation, active components, and mechanism that need standardized preparations.
Concluding remarks calling the strawberry powder trial a proof-of-principle for dietary and natural-product approaches to cancer prevention, with the AACR copyright notice.
Introduces oxidative stress and ROS as links between environmental toxicity and carcinogenesis, describing the endogenous antioxidant defense system and how imbalance causes oxidative stress.

Explains that chronic oxidative stress damages DNA, lipids, and proteins, notes that many chemotherapy drugs act by generating ROS/free radicals, and introduces radiotherapy's tumor-killing mechanism via ionizing radiation.

Describes how radiotherapy damages DNA directly, notes that oncology-generated free radicals cause serious side effects, and states the review's aim: to examine antioxidants' effects, events, and efficacy during cancer treatment.
Discusses the debate over whether antioxidant supplementation alters chemotherapy efficacy, and notes limited evidence suggesting some supplements may reduce adverse reactions and toxicities.

Argues that reducing toxicity can prevent dose-limiting effects so more patients complete chemotherapy, potentially improving tumor response and survival, followed by the 2013 Elsevier copyright notice.
Final fragment of the Elsevier copyright notice (2013) closing the abstract.
Introduces the background for a randomized phase II trial of freeze-dried strawberries in esophageal dysplasia patients in China, motivated by prior rat esophageal SCC studies.
Describes trial enrollment: 75 endoscopically identified patients with dysplastic esophageal premalignant lesions randomized to 30 g/d or 60 g/d of freeze-dried strawberry powder for six months.
Reports the primary endpoint (blinded histologic grade change): the 30 g/d dose had no significant effect, while 60 g/d reduced lesion grade in most evaluated patients.
States the 60 g/d histologic result (29 of 36 patients, 80.6%, P<0.0001) and the powder's safety, with no toxic effects or serious adverse events, plus the start of the biomarker results.
Gives biomarker findings for the 60 g/d group: reductions in iNOS (79.5%), COX-2 (62.9%), pNFκB-p65 (62.6%), pS6 (73.2%), and Ki-67 labeling index (37.9%, P=0.023).
Concludes that freeze-dried strawberry powder shows potential for preventing human esophageal cancer and warrants further clinical testing; includes the AACR copyright notice.
Opening of an esophageal cancer review: rising US incidence and mortality, and the note that squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma differ in histology and distribution.

Middle section of the esophageal cancer review: shared risk factors (dietary deficiencies, tobacco) and shared carcinogenesis mechanisms across both subtypes, plus precursor lesions (squamous dysplasia, Barrett's esophagus).
Closing sentence of the esophageal cancer review: precursor lesion identification and risk factor research have enabled chemoprevention studies, some with promising results.

Introduction/background on endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) versus EMR for large superficial GI neoplasms, covering its advantages (en bloc resection, complete resection, lower recurrence) and drawbacks (time, difficulty, complications) in a rectal LST case report.

Continuation of the background: ESD's drawbacks and efforts to reduce complications, noting that en bloc ESD of huge lesions still carries increased complication risk, setting up the rationale for a combined approach in rectal LSTs.

Case presentation describing the combined ESD/EMR technique used on huge rectal laterally spreading tumors: circumferential ESD of about two-thirds of the lesion followed by piecemeal EMR of the central part in 2-3 pieces.

Outcomes and conclusions for the three treated patients: complete polyp dissection and histological evaluation, no complications or recurrence at 6-month follow-up, and the proposal that combined ESD/EMR may be a suitable alternative to surgery in selected rectal LSTs.

Closing conclusion stating that combined ESD/EMR is a suitable option for selected rectal LSTs where either technique alone is unreliable or unsafe, and that larger trials with longer follow-up and technical improvements are needed.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence about needing improvements in techniques and technical devices to confirm the combined ESD/EMR results.

Introduction and study aim for a trial comparing glycemic responses to sweetened dried cranberries, raw cranberries, and white bread in adults with type 2 diabetes (n=13), with the first treatments (WB, RC, SDC, SDC-LS) listed.

Trial treatment details (portion size, calories, fiber, polydextrose in SDC-LS) and the plasma glucose results: peak times and mmol/L values for WB, RC, SDC, and SDC-LS, with WB remaining elevated at 120 min.
Plasma insulin results: peak timing and pmol/mL values for each treatment, with SDC-LS showing significantly lower insulin at 60 min than WB or SDC.
Insulin AUC comparison showing RC and SDC-LS lower than WB and SDC, and the methods for phenolic analysis of SDC and SDC-LS (80% acetone extraction, HPLC, ESI-MS).

Phenolic findings (caffeoylquinic acid, quercetin glycosides, epicatechin dimer) and the conclusion that SDC-LS gave a favorable glycemic and insulinemic response, plus the start of the practical application statement.

Practical application section: comparison of phenolic content and glycemic responses across cranberry products, aim to expand palatable portable food options for type 2 diabetes, and the novel polydextrose bulking agent for calorie and glycemic reduction.
Closing sentence of the practical application, stating that polydextrose's role in reducing calories and potential glycemic response is characterized in the study.

Introduces cranberry products and juice's use for urinary tract infections, and reports Folin-assay measurements of free and total phenolic antioxidants, ranking cranberry foods by polyphenol content per fresh weight.

Continues the polyphenol ranking, giving the per-serving order of cranberry products, then introduces high fructose corn syrup (HFCS) as a major U.S. sugar source containing glucose and fructose, potential mediators of oxidative stress.

Describes the human study design: 10 normal overnight-fasted individuals consumed HFCS with ascorbate, with or without cranberry juice (control), and plasma antioxidant capacity, glucose, triglycerides, and ascorbate were measured over 7 hours after a 240 mL serving.

Reports results: control HFCS slightly decreased plasma antioxidant capacity, indicating oxidative stress despite ascorbate, while cranberry juice significantly increased antioxidant capacity compared with control at all time points.

Concludes that postprandial triglycerides, arising from fructose in the beverages, were mainly responsible for the oxidative stress and correlated with antioxidant capacity, and that cranberries are a high-quality antioxidant source warranting human supplementation studies.
Final sentence of the abstract, recommending that cranberries, as an excellent source of high-quality antioxidants, be examined in human supplementation studies.
Introduction of the cranberry flavonoid study: health benefits linked to anthocyanins and proanthocyanidins, and how pressing, canning, concentrating, and drying can degrade them.
Study design: fresh cranberries, freeze-dried berries, and skin/flesh tissues were compared across juices, commercial and homemade sauces, and sweetened dried cranberries.

Key findings on freeze-drying (no flavonoid loss) and tissue localization: anthocyanins concentrated in skin, proanthocyanidins higher in skin except procyanidin A-2 dimer in flesh; juice comparison begins.
Juice results: not-from-concentrate juice has higher anthocyanin (8.3 vs 4.2 mg/100 mL) and proanthocyanidin (23.0 vs 8.9 mg/100 mL) content than reconstituted juice from concentrate.

Sauce and dried-product results: homemade sauce has the highest anthocyanins and proanthocyanidins, exceeding whole-berry canned and jelled sauces; sweetened dried cranberries are low in anthocyanins but retain considerable proanthocyanidins.
Conclusions on processing: commercial products have significantly lower polyphenols than fresh and home-processed versions, and anthocyanins degrade more readily than proanthocyanidins.
Practical application: because cranberry products are consumed for benefits such as UTI prophylaxis, processing effects on bioactive anthocyanins and proanthocyanidins matter.
Closing copyright notice (2012 Institute of Food Technologists) ending the abstract.

Opening of the abstract: background, objective, and study design of a prospective cohort examining habitual dietary flavonoid intake and incident hypertension, including the NHS I, NHS II, and HPFS participant counts.

Study design continued: cohort sizes for NHS II women, NHS I women, and HPFS men, plus how flavonoid and subclass intakes were estimated from semiquantitative food-frequency questionnaires using an updated USDA database.

Results opening: 14-year follow-up yielded 29,018 hypertension cases in women and 5,629 in men, and pooled analyses show the highest anthocyanin quintile (mainly from blueberries and strawberries) linked to lower hypertension risk.

Anthocyanin findings by age: overall 8% risk reduction (RR 0.92), 12% reduction in participants aged 60 or younger (RR 0.88), no significant reduction over 60 (RR 0.96), with a significant age interaction P-value of 0.02.
Other flavonoid results: other subclasses showed no association with hypertension, but the flavone apigenin showed a 5% risk reduction for highest versus lowest intake quintile.

Flavan-3-ol result and conclusions: catechin showed a 6% risk reduction in participants aged 60 or younger, and the authors conclude anthocyanins and some flavones and flavan-3-ols may help prevent hypertension.
Final conclusion sentence: proposes that the vasodilatory effects of these compounds may stem from structural features such as B-ring hydroxylation and methoxylation patterns.

Introduces the study of anthocyanin pigments in male bracts of 10 wild banana species (Musa and Ensete) from Thailand, and lists the six major anthocyanins identified by HPLC, MS, and MS/MS with their m/z values, starting with delphinidin-3-rutinoside.

Continues the list of the six identified anthocyanins (cyanidin, petunidin, pelargonidin, peonidin, malvidin-3-rutinoside with m/z values) and states that wild bananas are classified into 5 groups by pigment type, introducing the first group (M. itinerans, Musa sp. one and two, M. acuminata).

Describes the first group's pigment profile (nearly all anthocyanins except pelargonidin-3-rutinoside, nonmethylated and methylated) and the second group, M. acuminata subsp. truncata, which contains only malvidin-3-rutinoside, and begins the third group, M. coccinea.

Details the third group (M. coccinea with cyanidin- and pelargonidin-3-rutinoside), the fourth group with no detectable anthocyanin (M. acuminata yellow bract, E. glaucum), and the fifth group (M. balbisiana, M. velutina, M. laterita, E. superbum) with only nonmethylated anthocyanins; begins the total content result.

Reports total anthocyanin content in bracts (0-119.70 mg/100 g fresh weight) and concludes that the variation in anthocyanin type and amount shows biochemical diversity among wild bananas, useful for group identification and studying flavonoid metabolism evolution.
Final sentence concluding that the biochemical diversity of wild bananas may help clarify the evolution of flavonoid metabolism within each banana group.

Introduction of a study on antioxidant and antiproliferative activities of common fruits, motivating why bound phenolics must be measured, since their omission has underestimated phenolic content and antioxidant activity.

Study aim and methods: profiling total phenolics (soluble free and bound forms) in common fruits using solvent extraction, base digestion, and solid-phase extraction, with the first reported ranking of phenolic content (cranberry highest).
Results on total phenolic content ranking and antioxidant capacity measured by the TOSC assay, where cranberry again leads (177.0 micromol vitamin C equiv/g) and a full fruit ranking is given.
Antiproliferative results against HepG2 human liver-cancer cells, where cranberry shows the strongest inhibition (EC50 14.5 mg/mL) and a ranking of the other fruits is listed.
Conclusion proposing a bioactivity index (BI) as a new alternative biomarker for dietary cancer prevention and for future epidemiological and health promotion studies.

Introduction to the cranberry extract study: describes cranberry phytochemicals (flavonol glycosides, anthocyanins, proanthocyanidins, phenolic acids) and the chromatographic methods used to fractionate the total cranberry extract (TCE).

Fractionation results and methods: TCE is separated into sugar, organic acid, total polyphenol, proanthocyanidin, and anthocyanin fractions (39.4, 30.0, 10.6, 5.5, 1.2%), and the luminescent ATP viability assay at 200 µg/mL is introduced for testing against oral, colon, and prostate cancer cell lines.

Antiproliferative results for oral and colon cancer cells: the total polyphenol fraction is the most active, inhibiting KB (96.1%) and CAL27 (95%) oral cancer cells, and its colon cancer activity is described, starting with the comparison across colon cell lines.

Colon and prostate cancer results: total polyphenol activity is highest against HCT116 (92.1%) versus lower inhibition in HT-29, SW480, and SW620, and TCE and fractions reach at least 50% inhibition in prostate lines (RWPE-1, RWPE-2, 22Rv1), with polyphenols most active; cranberry sugars are introduced.

Negative control and mechanistic conclusion: cranberry sugars (78.8 µg/mL) show no inhibition of any cancer line, and the greater activity of total polyphenols over TCE and individual compounds is taken to suggest synergistic or additive interactions among anthocyanins, proanthocyanidins, and flavonol glycosides.

Concluding sentence of the study: the synergy or additive effects of anthocyanins, proanthocyanidins, and flavonol glycosides within the cranberry extract, the final point of the discussion of antiproliferative activity.
Study background and design: introduces the lack of human pharmacokinetic data on berry anthocyanins and describes the trial of 15 participants with coronary artery disease.
Study protocol and dose: blood and urine collected over 0-4 h after 480 mL cranberry juice (94.47 mg anthocyanins), with marked inter-individual variation in plasma kinetics and peak timing at 1-3 h.
Key pharmacokinetic findings: cranberry anthocyanins are bioavailable with differences in Cmax and AUC(0-4h) between individuals; plasma and urine glucoside patterns mirror the juice composition.
Quantitative results: plasma individual anthocyanin levels of 0.56-4.64 nmol/L and urinary recovery of 0.79% of the dose, supporting poor absorption and rapid plasma clearance.
Conclusion and interpretation: plasma anthocyanin levels are too low to change radical load or redox potential but may influence cell signaling and gene expression.
Introduces prostate cancer prevalence and motivates research into whole crop extracts, specifically American cranberry, as possible cancer-related agents in the DU145 in vitro study.
Describes the study design: whole cranberry extract (WCE) treatment of DU145 human prostate cancer cells at 10, 25, and 50 μg/ml for 6 h, and the significant reduction in cell viability.
Reports cell cycle effects of WCE: decreased G2-M phase and increased G1 phase proportions at 25 and 50 μg/ml after 6 h, linking the alterations to cell cycle regulation.
Details molecular findings: WCE reduced CDK4, cyclins A, B1, D1 and E, and increased p27 expression, while noting the non-significant changes in p16(INK4a) and pRBp107.

Concludes that American cranberry phytochemical extracts affect prostate cancer cell behaviour in vitro, with the p16(INK4a) and pRBp107 changes flagged as not statistically significant, supporting cranberry's health benefits.
Final sentence of the abstract restating that cranberry extracts support potential health benefits in relation to cranberries.

Introduction to the article on cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon) as a functional food, noting its growing production and consumption and its in vitro anti-tumor activity from extracts and isolated constituents.

Summary of supporting evidence: animal studies reinforce cranberry's anticancer reputation, and likely mechanisms against prostate and other cancers include apoptosis induction and inhibition of cellular invasion and migration.
Closing statement of the article's scope: it reviews cranberry's potential chemopreventive properties, open research questions, and factors to consider for future work, with a 2011 copyright notice.
Fragment completing the copyright line ("Society of Chemical Industry") at the end of the article's text.
Introduction of a Canadian survey study on placebo use, framing the controversy over placebo conceptualization and noting physicians still prescribe placebos in clinical practice.

Study aims and design: the authors compare placebo use and attitudes between academic psychiatrists and physicians of other specialties at Canadian medical schools, introducing the web-based survey method.
