Survey methodology and sample: an anonymous 21-question online survey sent to all 17 Canadian medical schools, emphasizing psychiatry departments, yielding 606 respondents including 257 psychiatrists.

Key results on prescribing: psychiatrists gave significantly more subtherapeutic medication doses than other physicians, and about 20% of both groups regularly prescribed placebos in routine practice.

Key results on beliefs: only 2% of psychiatrists versus 6% of nonpsychiatrists considered placebos of no clinical benefit, and over 60% of psychiatrists versus under 45% of others believed placebos have therapeutic effects.
Conclusion: psychiatrists appear to better value placebos' mind and body effects and hold more favourable attitudes toward placebo phenomena than other physicians in this pan-Canadian survey.
Introduction and aims of a systematic review evaluating the evidence for medicinal claims made for Bach flower remedies, covering the search methods and the seven randomised trials identified.

Results and conclusion of the systematic review of Bach flower remedies: of seven randomised trials, the placebo-controlled ones showed no efficacy, so the most reliable trials find no difference between flower remedies and placebos.
Introduction and study design of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of megestrol acetate (800 mg/day) for cancer-associated anorexia and cachexia, with 133 patients enrolled.
Results on appetite and food intake improvement with megestrol acetate versus placebo, plus weight-gain outcomes (15 lb or more in 16% vs. 2%), in the megestrol acetate cancer cachexia trial.
Comparative results on weight gain, nausea, and emesis for megestrol acetate versus placebo, and the safety finding that toxicity was minimal apart from mild edema.
Concluding statement that the trial demonstrated megestrol acetate's ability to stimulate appetite and food intake, producing significant weight gain in some patients with cancer anorexia-cachexia.

Study design and setting: a retrospective questionnaire survey of placebo use in Jerusalem-area hospitals and community clinics, describing the participant groups (physicians, head nurses, family physicians) and the stated objectives and outcome measures.

Participant counts and key results: of 89 respondents, 60% (53) reported using placebos, with a 95% confidence interval of 49% to 70%, and the results begin reporting how often users prescribed placebos.

Detailed survey findings among placebo users: frequency of prescribing (62% at least monthly), disclosure to patients (68% told patients they were receiving actual medication), belief in placebos as a diagnostic tool (28%), and perceived effectiveness (94%).

Conclusion of the study: most surveyed practitioners continue to use placebos, placebos may have a legitimate therapeutic role if used wisely, and wider recognition and debate about the practice are needed.
Background and study design of a meta-research analysis on placebo composition reporting: purpose, journals searched, and the screening scope (randomized placebo-controlled trials, 2008-2009).

Data extraction methods for the placebo reporting study: independent reviewers abstracted introduction and methods sections, coding treatment type (pill, injection, other) and whether placebo composition was stated.

Key results of the placebo reporting analysis: most trials did not disclose placebo composition, with pills disclosing it less often than injections/other treatments (8.2% vs. 26.7%, P = 0.002), plus the stated limitation about journal representativeness.

Limitation and conclusion of the placebo composition study: high-impact journals may not be representative, placebos for pills/capsules were seldom described, and placebo formulation should be disclosed because it can influence trial outcomes.
Final fragment closing the conclusion of the placebo reporting study, ending the sentence about placebo-controlled trials.

Introduction of a retrospective hospital study on placebo use: it describes the sample (230 nurses, 70 physicians) and the study's focus on placebo effects, prescribing patterns, and staff attitudes, and notes that medical practice ignores decades of experimental placebo research.
Findings on staff placebo use and knowledge: 80% of staff had used placebos, their understanding of placebo effects was deficient, and 89% of placebo use aimed at relieving pain.

Conclusion and recommendations: the authors urge educating staff to view pain in emotional, social, and physiological terms rather than purely physical ones, and to address staff disagreements over the ethics of placebo use.

Introduces Daniel K. Sokol's argument that benignly deceiving patients can occasionally be morally acceptable, and his decision checklist to guide doctors in such ethical dilemmas (medical ethics, patient deception, clinical decision-making).

Abstract of a study surveying Dunedin general practitioners on their willingness to use placebo treatments, their understanding of the placebo effect, and how they perceive their own placebo use compared with colleagues; this chunk introduces the study aims and the main finding that nearly all GPs would use placebos in some circumstances.

Continuation of the abstract's findings: GPs tended to understate their placebo use relative to colleagues, and many viewed placebos as more appropriate for 'imaginary illnesses'; this chunk also begins the note that results are compared with overseas studies.

Closing sentence of the abstract stating that the results are compared with overseas studies and discussed for their implications for medical training, concluding the summary of this New Zealand general practice placebo survey.
Opening of the paper: introduces the dominant view that prescribing placebos deceptively is unethical and notes the AMA policy that effectively bars doctors from using placebos in clinical practice.

Thesis and argument setup: the author contends that deceptive placebo use lacks the moral objections of other clinical deception, since the usual grounds of limited autonomy and broken trust do not apply to ethically bounded placebo prescribing.

Core conclusion: placebos prescribed within ethical limits do not undermine autonomy or trust, patients have reason to want responsible placebo prescribing, and so the AMA should endorse and promote deceptive placebo use.
Final sentence of the abstract restating the conclusion that the AMA is obligated to endorse and promote responsible deceptive placebo use in clinical practice.

Introduction and methods of a systematic review of systematic reviews on homeopathy's effectiveness: describes the database search and the 17 included articles, 6 of which re-analyse one landmark meta-analysis.

Results on the re-analyses and independent reviews: the re-analyses undermine the landmark meta-analysis's positive finding, and the 11 independent reviews found no strong evidence favouring homeopathy over placebo for any condition.

Key findings: no condition responds convincingly better to homeopathy than placebo or other controls, and no homeopathic remedy shows clinical effects clearly distinct from placebo; this leads into the paper's conclusion.
Final conclusion of the review: the best available clinical evidence does not justify positive recommendations for using homeopathy in clinical practice.

Introduces the study's objective, definition of placebo treatments, and design (cross-sectional mailed survey of 1200 US internists and rheumatologists), setting out the methods and participant pool for the placebo prescribing survey.

Continues the methods section, listing the main outcome measures: self-reported placebo use and attitudes, ethical judgments, recommended placebo treatments, and communication practices with patients.
Begins the results: 679 physicians (57%) responded, about half reported regularly prescribing placebos, and most (62%) considered the practice ethically permissible.
Details which treatments physicians reported using as placebos in the past year: saline and sugar pills were rare, while over-the-counter analgesics (41%) and vitamins (38%) were common.

Reports less common placebo choices (antibiotics and sedatives, 13% each) and how physicians describe placebos to patients, mostly as a potentially beneficial treatment (68%) and rarely as placebos (5%).

Summarizes the conclusions: placebo prescribing is common and viewed as ethically permissible, vitamins and OTC analgesics are the most used, and physicians may not be fully transparent with patients.
Final conclusion sentence stating that physicians may lack transparency about placebo use and may have mixed motivations for recommending these treatments.

Opening of the study: describes the Danish clinician questionnaire design (772 randomly selected clinicians, 65% response) and reports GP placebo use rates over the past year, with confidence intervals.

Middle of the study: reports that hospital-based doctors and private specialists used placebos less often (p < .001), gives the main motive (avoiding confrontation with patients), and cites antibiotics for viral infections as a typical placebo.
Concluding findings: reports clinicians' beliefs in placebo effects on objective outcomes (about 30%) and the share finding clinical placebo use ethically acceptable (about 46%).

Study design: a randomized trial of 200 general practice patients with symptoms but no abnormal physical signs or definite diagnosis, assigned to positive or negative consultation manner, with or without treatment.

Results at two weeks: patient satisfaction differed significantly by consultation manner (positive vs negative) but not by treatment, and 64% vs 39% improved after positive vs negative consultations (p = 0.001).
Treatment effect on recovery: 53% of treated patients improved versus 50% of untreated patients (p = 0.5), a non-significant difference, indicating consultation style mattered more than treatment.
Opening of the abstract: background and objective on alcohol consumption and breast cancer risk in the Nurses' Health Study, noting gaps around low-level intake and drinking patterns.
Study objective and design: prospective Nurses' Health Study cohort of 105,986 women followed 1980-2008 with repeated alcohol assessments; outcome is invasive breast cancer relative risk.

Main results: 7,690 breast cancer cases over 2.4 million person-years; risk significant from 5.0-9.9 g/day (3-6 drinks/week), with RR 1.15 (95% CI 1.06-1.24) and incidence of 332 cases/100,000 person-years.

Further findings: after adjusting for cumulative intake, binge drinking (not frequency) predicted breast cancer risk, and alcohol intake earlier and later in adult life was independently associated with risk.
Conclusion: low alcohol intake yields a small breast cancer risk increase, with cumulative lifetime adult intake the most consistent measure; early and late adult intake both matter independently.
Final fragment of the abstract's conclusion, ending the sentence on alcohol and breast cancer risk.

Study design: introduction and methods describing eight volunteers sipping 5 ml of 40% ethanol (no acetaldehyde) versus 40% calvados containing 2400 μM acetaldehyde, with salivary acetaldehyde and ethanol measured by gas chromatography, repeated after ethanol ingestion.

Methods and results: the protocol repeated after ethanol ingestion (0.5 g/kg), followed by key findings that salivary acetaldehyde at 30 s was significantly higher after calvados than ethanol, with and without alcohol ingestion (215 vs 128 μmol/l; 258 vs 89 μmol/l).

Results on time course and systemic effects: after 2 min salivary acetaldehyde levels did not differ significantly between beverages, remained above the carcinogenicity threshold at 10 min, and blood-to-saliva alcohol distribution had no additional effect.

Conclusions: carcinogenic acetaldehyde concentrations form in the oral cavity from ethanol immediately after a small sip of strong alcoholic drink, exposure lasts at least 10 min, and beverage acetaldehyde contributes only a short-term effect.
Copyright notice: 2011 Elsevier Ltd. copyright statement closing the abstract of the study on oral acetaldehyde exposure from sips of strong alcoholic beverages.
Introduction and background: acetaldehyde as the genotoxic metabolite of ethanol, and the unresolved question of oral cancer risk from ethanol-containing mouthwashes.

Study design: ready-to-use alcohol-containing mouthwashes (n=13) rinsed by four healthy nonsmoking volunteers as intended by manufacturers, with salivary acetaldehyde measured by headspace gas chromatography at several time points.
Results: salivary acetaldehyde concentrations (micromolar, with means and ranges) at 0.5, 2, 5 and 10 minutes after mouthwash use, declining over time.
Exposure and risk assessment: comparison with endogenous and alcoholic-beverage levels, estimated systemic acetaldehyde exposure from twice-daily use, lifetime cancer risk, and margin of exposure.

Conclusion: systemic risk and margin of exposure suggest low public health concern, but local salivary acetaldehyde levels reach concentrations linked to DNA adducts and sister chromatid exchange in vitro, so local oral carcinogenic concern remains.
Final sentence concluding that local carcinogenic concerns for the oral cavity remain despite low systemic risk estimates.

Opening of an abstract on alcohol-related cancers: it gives the ~3.6% global cancer burden attributable to chronic drinking and introduces acetaldehyde as the leading suspected carcinogenic mechanism.

Continuation of the abstract's discussion of mechanisms: covers ethanol's effects on DNA methylation and retinoid metabolism, and notes that alcohol-related cancer risk interacts with smoking, diet, comorbidities, and genetic susceptibility.
Final fragment of the abstract's last sentence, completing the point that alcohol-related carcinogenesis depends on genetic susceptibility.

Opening of the 2012 update on alcohol and breast cancer epidemiology and pathophysiology; states the aims (updating data, emphasizing light drinking, reviewing mechanisms) and the methods (Nov 2011 literature search and meta-analysis of light drinking).

Presents the main epidemiological results: about a 4% risk increase at up to one drink/day, a 40-50% increase for heavy drinking (3+ drinks/day), and the methods section's meta-analysis findings carried into the results.

Gives the population attributable fraction estimates: up to 5% of breast cancers in northern Europe and North America and about 50,000 cases worldwide attributable to alcohol, with 1-2% attributable to light drinking alone due to its higher prevalence.

Summarizes proposed carcinogenic mechanisms: alcohol raises estrogen levels, which act via the estrogen receptor or directly, plus acetaldehyde, oxidative stress, methyl-transfer epigenetic changes, and reduced retinoic acid affecting the cell cycle.
Concludes the abstract with practical recommendations: women should not exceed one drink per day, and those at elevated breast cancer risk should avoid alcohol or drink only occasionally.
Background and rationale of a meta-analysis on light alcohol drinking (up to 1 drink/day) and cancer risk, noting existing evidence mostly comes from moderate/high intake studies.

Methods section describing the meta-analytic search of PubMed, ISI Web of Science and EMBASE (pre-December 2010) for light drinking and cancers of the colorectum, breast, larynx, liver, esophagus, oral cavity and pharynx, and the start of the results on included studies and participant numbers.
Main results giving pooled relative risks for light drinking and oropharyngeal cancer, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, and female breast cancer, with 95% confidence intervals.

Results on attributable deaths worldwide in 2004 from light drinking, the null findings for colorectal, liver and laryngeal tumors, and the start of the conclusion that light drinking increases cancer risk.
Final sentence of the conclusion summarizing that light drinking increases the risk of cancers of the oral cavity and pharynx, esophagus, and female breast.

This chunk opens the abstract of a paper reviewing alcohol's health effects, establishing that high alcohol intake raises risk for dementia, several cancers, cirrhosis, and alcohol dependency, and introducing its claimed cardiovascular benefit.

This chunk, from the abstract of an alcohol health-effects review, states that alcohol benefits some individuals by preventing heart thrombosis, and endorses the UK and Danish weekly drinking limits (21 units for men, 14 for women) as public health guidance.

This closing chunk of the abstract argues that promoting alcohol's benefits as a broader public health message is unwarranted in Western societies, where few people abstain and those who do likely have good reasons.

Study design and methods for a cross-sectional survey of 100 food items across 225 stores in 18 Lower Mississippi Delta counties (AR, LA, MS), assessing food cost, energy, and nutrient profiles using Naturally Nutrient Rich methodology.

Methods and results: food items grouped into 6 food groups, price per 100 g converted to price per serving, ANOVA used; findings show significant group differences, with fats/oils/sweets highest in energy density and lowest in price per serving, and vegetables highest in nutrient density.

Results and conclusions: meats have the highest price per serving; implications suggest nutrition education on complete diets should address food costs and recommend swapping part of meat servings for culturally acceptable, lower-cost, nutrient-dense foods.

Closing conclusion sentence recommending lower-cost nutrient-dense food substitutions for meat, followed by the copyright notice (2012, Society for Nutrition Education and Behavior, published by Elsevier) for this Lower Mississippi Delta food cost study.

Opening of the abstract: background on 1800s USDA food cost comparisons, the objective of updating food cost-energy-nutrient relations, and the start of the design section describing the FNDDS 1.0 and CNPP price databases.

Methods section: details the 1387 foods analyzed and key variables (energy density, serving size, unit price, serving price, energy cost), plus the regression and statistical tests (ANOVA, Spearman's correlations) used.
Continuation of the methods, ending the design section, and the beginning of the results, which open with the finding that grains and fats supply the lowest-cost dietary energy.

Results on energy cost by food group (vegetables higher than all but fruit), serving size relative to water content and energy density, and per-serving prices (highest for meats, poultry, fish; lowest for fats).

Remaining results on nutrient-price associations after adjusting for energy (carbohydrates, sugar, fat linked to lower price per 100 g; protein, fiber, vitamins, minerals linked to higher price), and the start of the conclusions comparing grains and sugars with vegetables and fruit.

Final conclusion: grains and sugars are cheaper per calorie and per serving than vegetables and fruit, and these price differences may explain links between low-cost, nutrient-poor, energy-dense foods and lower education and income.

Introduction and objective of a cross-sectional study on urine osmolality as a marker of cell hydration (hyperosmotic cell stress) in US schoolchildren, with the study's aim and background on suboptimal water intake.

Study design and setting: cross-sectional convenience samples of children in Los Angeles and New York City, morning urine collection at an outpatient clinic in spring 2009, and a dietary record of food and beverages consumed after waking.
Subjects and early results framing: children aged 9-11 years (LA n=337, NYC n=211) who considered themselves healthy enough for school, with the start of the results section on urine osmolality.

Key results: prevalence of elevated urine osmolality (>800 mmol/kg) in 63% of LA and 66% of NYC children, and multivariable logistic regression showing association with not reporting morning drinking water intake (odds ratios with 95% CIs).
Breakfast and water intake findings and conclusions: over 90% ate breakfast but 75% did not drink water, and the authors call for further research to confirm results and assess health implications.

Introduces the debated link between severe dehydration (from intense exercise/heat) and cognitive performance, noting early findings on short-term memory and vision that later studies did not consistently confirm.

Covers counterarguments that water loss may not explain the observed effects, the failure of fluid compensation to prevent symptoms, and limited child studies on extra water intake and cognition, leading into older adult evidence.

Concludes that evidence for mild dehydration affecting cognition is insufficient in older adults (around age 60), lacking for frail elderly and dementia patients, and undermined by methodological heterogeneity.
Final sentence of the passage stating that, given methodological heterogeneity, a relationship between mild dehydration and cognitive performance cannot be supported.

Abstract opening of a study on mild dehydration's effects on cognition and mood in young men; describes the 26-participant design with three trials (diuretic-induced dehydration, placebo dehydration, euhydration control) and the exercise protocol.

Methods continuation describing the exercise protocol (three 40-min treadmill walks in heat) and the outcome measures: computerised six-task cognitive battery, profile of mood states, and symptom questionnaire.

Statistical methods and key cognitive results: paired t-tests comparing dehydrated trials (about 1.59% body mass loss) with euhydrated control, showing increased vigilance errors and slowed visual working memory response latency.

Mood and physiological results: dehydration increased fatigue and tension/anxiety at rest and fatigue during exercise, raised plasma osmolality, and did not change resting gastrointestinal temperature.
Conclusion of the abstract: mild dehydration without hyperthermia in men adversely affects vigilance and working memory and increases tension/anxiety and fatigue.
Introduction and study design of a study on whether drinking extra water improves cognition in 58 children aged 7-9, comparing a water group to a control group.
Results of the water-drinking study: children given extra water reported lower thirst (p=0.002) and performed better on visual attention and spot-the-difference memory tasks.
Remaining p-values for the spot-the-difference memory task results in the water-drinking children study.

Opening of an abstract describing a study of school-day supplementary water intake and cognitive performance/subjective states (fatigue, vigor) in 168 children aged 9-11 in a hot climate (Sardinia, Italy), with random class assignment to intervention or control.

Methods portion of the abstract: defines dehydration as urine osmolality above 800 mOsm/kg H2O (citing Katz et al., 1965) and explains that hydration, cognitive scores, and subjective states were correlated between morning and afternoon.

Results opening: cites a prior observational study of school children's hydration in a hot country (Bar-David et al., 2005) and reports that 84% of children were in mild, voluntary dehydration at the start of the school day.
Key findings: dehydration correlated negatively with auditory number span (short-term memory benefit from supplementary water at school) and positively with verbal analogy task performance.
Closing of the abstract: discussion framing the complex neurobiological links between hydration and cognition, followed by the 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces the study's motivation and design: a small pediatric experiment (23 children aged 6-7) testing whether drinking water improves cognitive performance from baseline to test, with the main reported results on thirst/happiness ratings and visual attention and search.

Summarizes the study's findings, noting which cognitive measures improved (visual attention, visual search) and which did not (visual memory, visuomotor), and concludes that even mild dehydration unrelated to exercise, deprivation, or heat can be reversed by drinking water to improve children's cognition.
Final fragment of the abstract's conclusion, completing the statement that children's cognitive performance can be improved by drinking water.

Introduction and methods of a prospective 6-month study comparing ovulatory function in vegetarian and nonvegetarian women with normal menstrual cycles, including inclusion criteria and basal body temperature cycle classification.

Methods continued: dietary restraint assessed with the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire and food records, followed by baseline group comparisons of BMI and percentage body fat between vegetarians and nonvegetarians.
Results comparing vegetarians and nonvegetarians: restraint scores, luteal phase lengths, and a chi-square difference in cycle types, showing vegetarians had fewer anovulatory cycles.
Results on restraint within the sample: highly restrained women had fewer ovulatory cycles and shorter luteal phases than less restrained women, followed by the start of the study's conclusion.
Concluding statement that ovulatory disturbances and restrained eating are less common among vegetarians, and that dietary restraint influences ovulatory function.

Introduces the question of whether menstrual disturbances are more common in vegetarian versus nonvegetarian women, defines clinical and subclinical cycle disturbances, and notes monitoring and recruitment bias issues in study design.

Explains why monitoring cycles helps avoid recruitment bias (women with menstrual problems may be more likely to volunteer), and introduces three general mechanisms that might differ between vegetarians and nonvegetarians.

Lists the three mechanisms possibly linking diet type to menstrual disturbances: energy imbalance from body weight or exercise, psychosocial and cognitive factors, and dietary components, and states the article reviews evidence for each.

Summarizes findings: cross-sectional studies suggest clinical disturbances are more common in vegetarians, while a prospective study with many confounders controlled found subclinical disturbances less common in weight-stable healthy vegetarian women.
Concludes that the prospective study's sample may not represent all vegetarian women, so results can't be generalized, and calls for population studies before drawing definitive conclusions.
Opening of the abstract: introduces metabolomics and CVD as leading cause of death, and identifies choline, TMAO, and betaine (phosphatidylcholine metabolites) as plasma markers predicting CVD risk.

Continues the abstract with validation of the three metabolites as CVD predictors in a large clinical cohort, and mouse supplementation results showing upregulated macrophage scavenger receptors and promoted atherosclerosis with choline or TMAO.

Mechanistic findings: germ-free mice show choline and gut flora are required for TMAO production and increased macrophage cholesterol accumulation and foam cell formation; antibiotic suppression of gut microflora inhibits choline-enhanced atherosclerosis.

Genetic link and conclusion: variations in flavin monooxygenase (FMO) expression, an enzymatic TMAO source, associate with atherosclerosis in hyperlipidemic mice, and the gut flora-phosphatidylcholine-CVD relationship suggests new diagnostics and therapies.

Final sentence of the abstract stating that the discovery of gut flora-dependent phosphatidylcholine metabolism in CVD pathogenesis opens opportunities for novel diagnostic tests and treatments for atherosclerotic heart disease.

Introduction and study setup for a 1H NMR spectroscopy study of choline compounds in normal human prostate cells versus metastasis-derived tumor cells, testing whether malignant transformation raises choline levels.

Key findings on choline compound composition: metastasis-derived cells show significantly higher phosphocholine and glycerophosphocholine than normal prostate epithelial and stromal cells, explaining the clinical choline peak.

Interpretation that the clinical choline elevation in prostate cancer reflects altered phospholipid metabolism rather than cell density or doubling time, followed by androgen deprivation effects on androgen receptor-positive cell lines.
Androgen deprivation results: choline compounds rise after chronic deprivation in LNCaP cells and fall after acute deprivation in LAPC-4 cells, supporting the study's clinical conclusions.
Concluding clinical implication: proton MR spectroscopic imaging of choline may aid prostate cancer diagnosis, monitoring response to androgen ablation therapy, and detecting recurrence.

Study introduction: rationale for examining red meat, poultry, and egg intake in relation to lethal prostate cancer risk, including the motivation from prior evidence on processed meat and post-diagnostic poultry and eggs.

Study design and population: prospective cohort of 27,607 men followed 1994–2008, defining lethal prostate cancer (distant metastases or prostate cancer death), plus a case-only survival analysis of 3,127 men with non-metastatic diagnosis.
Main incidence results: 199 events over 306,715 person-years; men eating 2.5+ eggs/week had 81% higher lethal prostate cancer risk vs. <0.5/week (HR 1.81, 95% CI 1.13–2.89, p-trend 0.01).

Case-only survival results: 123 events over 19,354 person-years; suggestive but non-significant positive associations for post-diagnostic poultry (HR 1.69) and processed red meat (HR 1.45) with progression of localized cancer to lethal disease.

Survival analysis details and conclusion: confidence intervals and trend p-values for post-diagnostic poultry and processed red meat (not statistically significant), and the overall conclusion that egg consumption may increase risk of lethal prostate cancer in healthy men.
Final sentence of the conclusion: egg consumption may raise the risk of developing a lethal form of prostate cancer among healthy men.

Introduces fish odour syndrome (trimethylaminuria) as a metabolic disorder of abnormal trimethylamine excretion, and explains the normal liver pathway that converts it to odourless trimethylamine N-oxide.

Explains that impaired trimethylamine oxidation causes the fish-like body odour, notes that choline-rich foods worsen it, and stresses that recognising the condition matters because dietary changes can reduce the odour.

Covers management of fish odour syndrome: dietary adjustments to lower trimethylamine excretion, and an occasional short antibiotic and lactulose course (metronidazole, neomycin, lactulose) to suppress gut bacteria producing trimethylamine, followed by the document's keywords.
Final fragment of the keyword list at the end of the document, repeating the term trimethylaminuria as an alternate name for fish odour syndrome.

Introduction and rationale of a prospective cohort study on dietary choline/betaine intake and colorectal cancer risk in men (Health Professionals Follow-up Study), stating the one-carbon methyl-donor hypothesis and the unknown association.

Study methods: Health Professionals Follow-up Study cohort of 47,302 men, 987 incident colorectal cancer cases (1986-2004), with intake assessed every four years via a validated semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire.

Statistical methods (Cox proportional hazards model, multivariate RRs with 95% CIs, two-sided tests) and the headline finding of no statistically significant association for choline or betaine intake with colorectal cancer risk.

Quintile results: top vs bottom quintile RRs for choline (0.97) and betaine (0.94) with null trends, plus no association for choline subtypes (free choline, glycerophosphocholine, phosphocholine, phosphatidylcholine, sphingomyelin).
Conclusion: the data do not support an inverse association between choline/betaine intake and colorectal cancer risk.

Introduction and background of a prospective study on one-carbon metabolism (B vitamins and related metabolites) and prostate cancer risk, stating the rationale, mechanisms (DNA methylation, DNA repair), and the aim of a comprehensive investigation.

Study aim and methods continuation: selection of seven circulating B vitamins and metabolites (betaine, choline, cysteine, methionine, MMA, vitamin B2, vitamin B6) for analysis in the prostate cancer prospective study.

Methods detail: plasma measurements in 561 prostate cancer cases and 1,034 age- and recruitment-date-matched controls from the Northern Sweden Health and Disease Cohort, analyzed with conditional logistic regression.

Key results: positive associations of choline and vitamin B2 and an inverse association of methylmalonic acid (MMA) with prostate cancer risk, including relative risks per doubling of concentration with 95% CIs and P(trend) values.

Results continuation and conclusion: betaine, cysteine, methionine and vitamin B6 showed no association; elevated choline and vitamin B2 may increase prostate cancer risk, supporting a role for one-carbon metabolism in prostate cancer etiology.
Concluding sentence of the abstract: novel findings support a role of one-carbon metabolism in prostate cancer etiology and warrant further investigation.
Introduces the study's choline- and betaine-controlled diets served to human research subjects, noting they were built from per-food analyses and checked against whole-day combined samples.

Reports validation results: lab-measured choline and betaine in whole-diet samples matched calculated estimates, and the diets were adjusted to several choline/betaine levels and were well accepted for up to 2 months.
States the article's applications: using these diets in clinical research on methyl-group requirements and in clinical counseling for clients needing a choline-controlled diet.

Introduction and background of a study on 11C-Choline vs 18F-FDG PET/CT for bone involvement in multiple myeloma, stating the study aim of assessing added value and limitations of choline imaging over FDG due to low FDG uptake in some myeloma lesions.

Methods and start of results: ten MM patients each underwent 11C-Choline and 18F-FDG PET/CT within one week, compared by lesion number, sites and SUVmax, followed by the initial patient concordance findings.

Patient-level results comparing the two PET/CT modalities: four patients were negative on both scans, two were positive with identical lesion counts and sites, and four were positive but with discordant lesion numbers.

Quantitative results: choline showed higher mean SUVmax (5 vs 3.8, P = 0.042), and overall choline detected 37 bone lesions versus 22 for FDG, a difference that was not statistically significant (P = 0.8).

Conclusion of the study: preliminary data suggest 11C-Choline PET/CT is more sensitive than 18F-FDG PET/CT for detecting myelomatous bone lesions and may be a more appropriate functional imaging complement to MRI for MM bone staging if confirmed in larger cohorts.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the recommendation that 11C-Choline be considered alongside MRI for multiple myeloma bone staging.

Introduction to the paper: gut microbiota metabolism of choline/phosphatidylcholine to TMA and TMAO is known; the paper proposes that dietary L-carnitine, abundant in red meat, is similarly converted to TMAO and promotes atherosclerosis.

Human findings: omnivores produce more TMAO than vegans/vegetarians after L-carnitine intake via a microbiota-dependent route; fecal bacterial taxa associate with plasma TMAO and diet; plasma L-carnitine predicts CVD and major adverse cardiac events (n = 2,595) only when TMAO is also high.

Clinical cohort results and start of the mouse studies: plasma L-carnitine predicts cardiovascular outcomes only with high TMAO in cardiac evaluation patients, and chronic dietary L-carnitine in mice alters cecal microbiota and boosts TMA/TMAO synthesis.

Mouse mechanistic experiments: L-carnitine increases atherosclerosis only with intact microbiota (not after microbiota suppression), and dietary TMAO, carnitine, or choline reduce reverse cholesterol transport in vivo.
Concluding statement: the gut microbiota may explain the established association between high red meat intake and cardiovascular disease risk.

Background section of a Health Professionals Follow-Up Study abstract on dietary choline (from meat, milk, eggs) and lethal prostate cancer risk, stating the knowledge gap that no prior study examined this.

Objective and design of the study: prospective analysis of choline, choline-containing compounds, and betaine intake and lethal prostate cancer among 47,896 men in the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study.

Case-only survival design detail (4282 men with nonmetastatic diagnosis during follow-up), validated diet questionnaire administered six times over 22 years, and the start of the results on lethal cases in the incidence analysis.

Main incidence results: 695 lethal prostate cancers over 879,627 person-years, with the top choline intake quintile showing a 70% higher risk (HR 1.70), and the start of the case-only survival findings (271 lethal cases).

Case-only survival result: postdiagnostic choline intake was not statistically significantly associated with lethal prostate cancer (HR 1.69, CI 0.93–3.09, P-trend 0.20), followed by the study's overall conclusion.
Final sentence of the abstract's conclusion, stating that choline intake was associated with increased risk of lethal prostate cancer in the 47,896-man study population.

Introduction and objective of a prospective cohort study on postdiagnostic meat, fish, poultry, and egg intake and prostate cancer recurrence or progression, noting prior research focused on diet before diagnosis.
Study design: prospective cohort of 1294 men with prostate cancer, participants in the CaPSURE registry, followed for an average of 2 years, with no recurrence or progression as of 2004–2005.
Main results: 127 events over 2610 person-years; red meat, fish, total poultry, and skinless poultry intake showed no association with recurrence or progression.

Key findings: eggs and poultry with skin were associated with roughly doubled risk of recurrence or progression when comparing extreme intake quantiles, with hazard ratios and trend p-values reported.

Interaction result: men with high prognostic risk and high poultry intake had about 4-fold increased recurrence or progression risk versus low/intermediate risk with low intake (P for interaction = 0.003); conclusions begin, stating unprocessed and processed red meat, fish, and skinless poultry were not associated with risk.
Conclusion: postdiagnostic intake of red meat, fish, or skinless poultry is not linked to prostate cancer recurrence or progression, whereas eggs and poultry with skin may increase the risk.

Introduces the rationale for a very low-fat diet (about 20% of calories) to reduce breast cancer risk, and describes the feasibility intervention study enrolling postmenopausal breast cancer survivors and premenopausal women with cystic breast disease and cyclical mastalgia.

Reports the outcome of the 3-month low-fat diet intervention: both groups adopted the diet, and premenopausal women showed decreased serum estrogen levels; also notes that nutrition-education programs in institutions, restaurants, and schools promote dietary fat reduction.
Concludes the document by stating that public nutrition-education efforts in research institutions, restaurants, and schools aim to raise awareness and change behavior about reducing dietary fat.

Abstract opening of a study on serum prolactin and oestradiol in women with cyclical mastalgia (breast pain); describes the patient group (20 women with severe mastalgia) and the control group (10 normal women) and the hormone measurement design.

Middle of the abstract reporting results: prolactin is significantly higher in mastalgia patients though within normal range, oestradiol does not differ between groups, and oestradiol and prolactin are positively correlated, more strongly in patients.

Concluding sentences of the abstract: the findings suggest a prolactin secretory hypersensitivity to oestradiol in cyclical mastalgia, and prolactin is proposed as a central factor triggering the condition.

Study design and sample description from a global cross-sectional survey on women's premenstrual symptoms and daily-life impact, covering 7226 women aged 15-49 across 11 countries recruited by random sampling plus Internet panels in Japan, Korea and Australia.

Continuation of the sample description (Italy, Spain, UK, Brazil, Mexico, Hong Kong, Pakistan, Thailand, Internet-panel samples in Japan, Korea and Australia) followed by the main outcome measures: a 23-symptom questionnaire, sociodemographics and lifestyle, activities of daily life (ADL), and knowledge of premenstrual terms.

Key results on the most prevalent premenstrual symptoms (bloating, cramps/abdominal pain, irritability, mastalgia, joint/muscle/back pain) and the strong correlation (R = 0.78) between symptom severity and duration, plus the linear model linking symptom prevalence to age, parity, smoking and country.

Remaining results on impact and knowledge: physical and mental symptom domains had similar negative effects on ADL, ADL impact was modified by education and exercise, and women's knowledge of PMS and PMDD varied by symptom intensity, age, education and country.

Conclusions of the study: four of the five most prevalent premenstrual symptoms are physical, experiences are broadly similar across countries and regions, and women's knowledge of PMS terminology depends strongly on their country.
Final fragment of the conclusions, stating that women's knowledge of PMS terms is highly dependent on the country in which they live.

Study design and objective: this opening chunk of a clinical trial abstract on diet and sex-hormone binding globulin (SHBG) describes the hypothesis that a low-fat vegetarian diet reduces dysmenorrhea and premenstrual symptoms, and the crossover methods (33 women, diet phase vs. placebo supplement phase).

Methods and start of results: this chunk covers the assessed outcomes (dietary intake, SHBG, body weight, pain, premenstrual symptoms) and begins reporting the result that mean serum SHBG was higher during the diet phase (46.7 nmol/L) than the supplement phase (39.3 nmol/L).

Quantitative results: this chunk reports SHBG, body weight (lower during diet, 66.1 vs 67.9 kg), and dysmenorrhea duration (3.9 baseline to 2.7 days on diet vs 3.6 on supplement), with the associated P values.

Pain and premenstrual symptom results: this chunk reports that pain intensity fell during the diet phase on the worst three days and that premenstrual concentration, behavioral change, and water retention symptom durations were significantly reduced versus the supplement phase.

Conclusion: this chunk summarizes the study's main finding that the low-fat vegetarian diet was associated with higher SHBG and reduced body weight, dysmenorrhea duration and intensity, and premenstrual symptom duration, and states that effects may be mediated by estrogen activity.
Final conclusion sentence: this last chunk closes the abstract by proposing that the symptom benefits of the low-fat vegetarian diet might be mediated by dietary influences on estrogen activity.

Introduces mastalgia (breast pain): its prevalence, that it is usually benign, and its associations with PMS, fibrocystic breast disease, psychological causes, and rarely breast cancer or extramammary causes like Tietze syndrome.

Covers the clinical approach to mastalgia: a thorough evaluation is needed, most women are reassured, about 15% need pain-relieving therapy, and first-line options are mechanical breast support, a low-fat high-carbohydrate diet, and topical NSAIDs.

Discusses hormonal treatments for mastalgia (bromocriptine, tamoxifen, danazol), their efficacy and side-effect limits, and that danazol is the only FDA-approved hormonal option, best used cyclically.

Describes lisuride maleate as a newer, encouraging mastalgia treatment, and gives outcomes: 60% of cyclic mastalgia recurs after treatment, while noncyclic mastalgia responds poorly but often resolves spontaneously.
Concludes the sentence on noncyclic mastalgia, stating that it resolves spontaneously in up to 50% of cases.
Introduction to the study: defines lignans (enterodiol, enterolactone) and describes a randomized crossover trial of flax seed powder's effect on the menstrual cycle in 18 women.
Study design: 18 women alternated between a control low-fiber diet and a flax seed-supplemented diet over 3 cycles each, with the second and third cycles of each condition compared.
Results on cycle ovulation and luteal phase: anovulatory cycles occurred only in the control condition, and flax cycles showed longer luteal phase lengths (12.6 vs. 11.4 days, P = 0.002).
Hormone results: estradiol and estrone levels did not differ between flax and control cycles across follicular and luteal phases, while the luteal progesterone/estradiol ratio was higher with flax.

Additional hormone findings: midfollicular testosterone was slightly higher with flax, DHEA-S, PRL, and SHBG were unaffected, and the authors conclude lignans play a specific role in diet-related sex steroid action.
Concluding implication: the authors suggest lignans may influence sex steroid action and possibly the risk of breast and other hormonally dependent cancers.

Abstract opening of a double-blind crossover study of bromocriptine (a prolactin inhibitor) vs. placebo in painful benign breast disease, describing the patient groups (cyclical and non-cyclical pain) and the 5 mg daily dosing over six menstrual cycles.

Results and conclusion of the same study: bromocriptine significantly improved breast symptoms and lowered prolactin in the cyclical mastalgia group but had no effect in the non-cyclical group, supporting its use for cyclical breast pain.
Final sentence of the abstract, concluding that bromocriptine is a new and effective management option for cyclical breast pain.

Study design: the Moos Menstrual Distress Questionnaire (MMDQ) in 30 premenopausal women randomized to weight-maintaining diets with P/S fatty acid ratio 1.0 or 0.3, starting with a one-cycle baseline before the high-fat diet phase.

Diet phases: both groups eat a high-fat diet (40% energy from fat) for four menstrual cycles, then a low-fat diet (20% energy from fat), with findings that no symptom differences existed between P/S groups.
Results: low-fat diet during menses and premenstrual week significantly reduced water-retention symptoms, and symptoms in the 'arousal' group decreased during the rest of the cycle.

Introduces the WHI Dietary Modification trial and its aim: testing whether a low-fat, fruit/vegetable/grain diet intervention affects risk of benign proliferative breast disease, a precursor to invasive breast cancer.

Describes the trial design: a randomized controlled primary prevention trial at 40 US centers (1993–2005) enrolling 48,835 postmenopausal women aged 50–79 without prior breast cancer, and the dietary targets of 20% fat and increased fruit, vegetable, and grain intake.

Notes that the diet intervention produced smaller than intended but significant dietary changes, that participants had biennial mammograms and clinical breast exams, and that biopsy-confirmed benign cases were gathered for central histologic review.
Reports follow-up results: over an average of 7.7 years, 570 benign proliferative breast disease cases occurred in the intervention group versus 793 in the comparison group.

Gives the main finding: a hazard ratio of 1.09 (95% CI 0.98–1.23) for benign proliferative breast disease with the diet intervention, with risk varying by baseline vitamin D intake, and concludes the modest diet change does not alter this risk.
Concluding sentence stating that the modest reduction in fat and increase in fruit, vegetable, and grain intake does not change the risk of benign proliferative breast disease.

This chunk is the opening of a 2003-era SOGC clinical practice guideline on mastalgia (breast pain), covering its objective, treatment options for cyclical and noncyclical pain, desired outcomes, and the literature search method (English MEDLINE/Cochrane reports, 1975 to July 2003).

This chunk continues the SOGC mastalgia guideline's Evidence and Values sections: it describes the literature search period and databases, the Canadian Task Force levels-of-evidence grading, and begins listing the guideline's authors (a dietitian, surgeon oncologist, and nurse).

This chunk, from the SOGC mastalgia guideline, covers the expected benefits, harms and costs of applying the guideline (consistent practice, fewer ineffective interventions, appropriate medication use) and begins the Validation section noting comparison with other protocols.

This chunk, from the SOGC mastalgia guideline, states that no formal clinical testing or existing clinical guidelines were found for validation, identifies the SOGC as sponsor, and explains the guideline was created to meet practice needs at the Winnipeg Regional Health Authority Breast Health Centre.

This chunk gives the start of the numbered recommendations in the SOGC mastalgia guideline: education and reassurance as first-line treatment, and supportive well-fitting bras for cyclical and noncyclical breast pain, each with evidence-level and grade codes.

This chunk lists mid-range recommendations from the SOGC mastalgia guideline on hormone replacement therapy adjustment, caffeine reduction (not advised), and vitamin E (not recommended), plus the insufficient-evidence statement on evening primrose oil, with evidence grades.

This chunk, from the SOGC mastalgia guideline recommendations, covers flaxseed as first-line for cyclical mastalgia and topical diclofenac 2% gel for localized pain, with evidence grades, and begins recommendation 8.

This chunk, from the SOGC mastalgia guideline, gives the final recommendations: tamoxifen 10 mg or danazol 200 mg when first-line treatments fail, and advice against mastectomy or partial mastectomy as an effective treatment for mastalgia.

This final chunk of the SOGC mastalgia guideline contains only the end of the last recommendation, stating that mastectomy or partial mastectomy should not be considered an effective treatment for breast pain (level III, grade E).

This chunk opens the document's description of a randomized trial of diet in women with severe persistent cyclical mastopathy, introducing the study population (21 patients), the control versus low-fat, high-complex-carbohydrate intervention arms, and the 6-month follow-up design.

This chunk continues the trial methods, describing outcome measurement through food records, plasma hormone and lipid levels, daily symptom diaries, and blinded physician assessments at baseline and study end, and it introduces the main finding of significantly reduced premenstrual breast symptoms in the intervention group.

This chunk gives the trial results: the intervention group's significant reduction in premenstrual breast tenderness and swelling, and the physical examination findings showing reduced swelling, tenderness, and nodularity in 6 of 10 intervention patients versus 2 of 9 control patients.

Introduces methylchavicol (CH3-CV), a constituent of tarragon and basil, and its suspected carcinogenicity via cytochrome P450/sulfotransferase bioactivation to a genotoxic metabolite; background for the HepG2 oxidative stress study.
States the study's aim: testing whether pure methylchavicol induces oxidative stress in HepG2 hepatoma cells and alters procarcinogenic biomarkers, linking carcinogenesis to oxidative stress.
Lists the biomarkers examined (CYP2E1, iNOS, Cu/Zn-SOD, Mn-SOD) that regulate the cellular redox balance, as the methods/measurement targets of the methylchavicol HepG2 experiment.

Reports the results: methylchavicol significantly induced oxidative stress (measured by luminol-dependent chemiluminescence) and altered CYP2E1, iNOS and Mn-SOD expression, suggesting a nitric oxide-dependent toxic mechanism; herb extracts did not.

Concludes that oxidative stress is likely significant in methylchavicol-induced toxicity, and that tarragon, chervil and basil extracts, despite containing methylchavicol, did not cause toxicity, possibly due to protective compounds.

Closing sentences restating that the natural extracts (tarragon, chervil, basil) lacked this toxicity, possibly containing counteracting compounds, followed by the 2012 Elsevier Masson copyright and publisher notice.
Case report opening: background on nutmeg abuse causing ED visits, and presentation of a 13-year-old girl who ingested 15-24 g of nutmeg in gelatin capsules alongside marijuana.

Clinical symptoms of the teen's nutmeg toxicity: hallucinations (visual, auditory, tactile), bizarre behavior, nausea, gagging, temperature sensations, and progressive visual disturbances including double and triple vision.

Further clinical course: neurological findings (nystagmus, weakness, ataxia), normal vitals and labs, treatment with activated charcoal, and an uneventful 2-day admission, followed by the proposed amphetamine-like biotransformation mechanism of nutmeg's CNS effects.

Concluding mechanistic discussion: the unproven hypothesis that nutmeg's CNS effects come from conversion to amphetamine-like compounds, and the note that its constituents structurally resemble known neuromodulatory substances.

Introduction to the review of Artemisia dracunculus (tarragon), covering its traditional use, the two cultivars, and its main bioactive metabolites such as essential oils, coumarins, flavonoids, and phenolcarbonic acids.

Summary of pharmacological findings from mainly Russian rodent in vivo studies (anti-inflammatory, hepatoprotective, antihyperglycemic), and the safety discussion of estragole and methyleugenol, noting no acute toxicity or mutagenicity at dietary-relevant doses.

Safety conclusion that water extracts contain very low estragole and methyleugenol and pose limited risk, followed by the closing recommendation that future research needs more clinical studies and precise taxonomic and phytochemical characterization.
Final sentence of the review restating the need for precise taxonomic and phytochemical definition of the source material in future research on tarragon.

Introduces methylchavicol (estragole) in tarragon and its confirmed genotoxicity in rat hepatocyte UDS tests (in vitro and in vivo), contrasting it with the lower genotoxicity of deep-frozen tarragon and the negative result for desiccated tarragon.

Reports in vitro findings that both tarragon forms significantly reduce methylchavicol's genotoxicity at specified concentrations, attributing this to antimutagenic leaf properties and/or adsorption that lowers bioavailability.
Describes in vivo results: desiccated tarragon powder was non-genotoxic up to 6.25 g/kg bw (18.75 mg/kg bw methylchavicol) and showed no antimutagenic effect in vivo.

Gives the risk-assessment rationale for safety: low exposure at maximum daily tarragon intake, rapid human detoxification and excretion, and a no-genotoxic-effect level in rats, yielding a high margin of exposure.
Concludes that tarragon consumption presents no genotoxic risk to humans, followed by the Elsevier 2009 copyright notice.
Introduces the comet assay methodology used to test mutagenicity of tarragon (Artemisia dracunculus) extract on human blood cells, with sodium dichromate as positive control.
Describes the comet assay readout (DNA migration, fluorescence microscopy, mutagenicity index) and begins the in vivo mouse oral-dosing liver toxicity part of the tarragon study.
Covers the liver toxicity measures in mice: serum ALT and AST enzymes as liver function markers, plus H&E liver histology, and states the main finding of dose-related effects.

Summarizes conclusions linking tarragon dose to mutagenicity, liver enzymes and liver histopathology, attributing effects to methylchavicol and other genotoxic compounds, with implications for dietary and therapeutic risk assessment.
Closing copyright notice (Elsevier Ltd, 2012) for the tarragon toxicology and mutagenicity article.

Introduces the review's core claim: winter spices (nutmeg, cinnamon, clove, anise) contain allylbenzenes and propenylbenzenes, which Shulgin proposed 40 years earlier act as metabolic precursors of amphetamines; the biotransformation to nitrogen-containing metabolites is reviewed.

Notes that these precursor-to-metabolite reactions have not been documented in humans, questions whether spice pharmacology and toxicology (e.g., nutmeg) can be explained by allylbenzene/propenylbenzene content, and raises possible human exposure to amphetamines formed in forno during baking.

Explains in forno amphetamine formation during baking and cooking, using Lebkuchen (Christmas gingerbread) as the example, and suggests this may partly lift winter mood, while acknowledging that the spices' aromatic effects as odours evoking memories may also matter.
Concludes that it remains unresolved whether spices have a true pharmacological effect or act mainly as aromatherapy, calling for clinical and laboratory studies to settle the question.

Introduces cinnamon (Cinnamomum spp. bark) and its traditional and experimental links to blood glucose, framing the unresolved question of its effect on fasting blood glucose in type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, which motivates the meta-analysis.

States the study's purpose: a meta-analysis of clinical trials in type 2 diabetes and/or prediabetes that adds three new trials to five from earlier meta-analyses to assess cinnamon's effect on fasting blood glucose.

Describes the methods: literature search (PubMed and Biosis through May 2010) for randomized placebo-controlled trials of cinnamon or cinnamon extract and FBG, yielding eight studies analyzed in Comprehensive Meta-Analysis.

Explains the statistical approach: a random-effects model computing standardized mean differences of change in control versus cinnamon groups, divided by pooled SD of post-intervention scores, for whole cinnamon and cinnamon extract.

Reports the results: whole cinnamon or extract significantly lowered FBG (-0.49 mmol/L, n=8, P=.025), extract alone lowered it (-0.48 mmol/L, n=5, P=.008), concluding cinnamon improves FBG in type 2 diabetes or prediabetes.

Introduction and methods start of a human study on cinnamon's effects on glucose tolerance: background on spices' insulin-potentiating activity in vitro, then the aim and the participant description (seven lean healthy male volunteers).

Methods continuation: the randomized-crossover design with three oral glucose tolerance tests, comparing a 5 g placebo control against 5 g cinnamon given with the glucose load or 12 h before, followed by the start of the results.

Results: cinnamon reduced plasma glucose AUC (-13% for the immediate dose, -10% for the 12 h pre-dose, both p<0.05) and improved insulin sensitivity by Matsuda index in both cinnamon trials versus control.

Results and conclusions: insulin sensitivity improvements in both cinnamon OGTT trials compared with control, and the conclusion that cinnamon supplementation may aid glycaemic control and insulin sensitivity, with effects lasting about 12 h.
Final sentence of the conclusion: the cinnamon effects are immediate and appear sustained for 12 hours.

Abstract opening of a 2-week, crossover human study of daily cinnamon (3 g/day) vs placebo in 8 healthy male volunteers, introducing the question of cinnamon's effects on glucose and insulin sensitivity and describing participant characteristics and study design.

Study results from oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT) on days 0-20: cinnamon reduced the glucose response on day 1 (significant) and day 14 (non-significant trend), and the placebo period following the 14-day intervention is described.

Key findings of the cinnamon study: reduced insulin response and improved insulin sensitivity on day 14 compared with baseline, with these benefits lost after cinnamon was stopped, concluding that cinnamon may aid glycaemic control but effects reverse quickly.
Final sentence of the abstract concluding that the cinnamon-associated improvements in glycaemic control and insulin sensitivity are quickly reversed after supplementation stops.

Study aims, design, and population: a 24-week randomized trial comparing calorie-restricted vegetarian vs conventional diabetic diets (alone and with exercise) in Type 2 diabetes patients, with insulin resistance, visceral fat, and oxidative stress as focus outcomes.

Trial arms and intervention details: 74 Type 2 diabetes patients split into vegetarian (n=37) and conventional diabetic diet (n=37) groups, both isocaloric at -500 kcal/day with all meals provided, and aerobic exercise added in the second 12 weeks.

Measurement schedule and primary outcomes: assessments at baseline, 12 and 24 weeks; primary endpoints were insulin sensitivity (hyperinsulinaemic isoglycaemic clamp), visceral and subcutaneous fat volume (MRI), and oxidative stress (TBARS), analyzed by intention to treat.
Initial results: diabetes medication reduction (43% vs 5%, P<0.001) and greater body weight loss in the vegetarian group (-6.2 kg vs -3.2 kg), with confidence intervals and group-by-time interaction.

Insulin sensitivity and fat outcomes: insulin sensitivity rose more in the vegetarian group (30% vs 20%, P=0.04), and both visceral and subcutaneous fat reductions were larger in that group (P=0.007 and P=0.02).

Adipokine and antioxidant findings: in the vegetarian group, adiponectin increased and leptin decreased, and vitamin C, superoxide dismutase, and reduced glutathione rose, with the specific P-values reported.

Secondary findings and conclusion opening: exercise amplified between-group differences, insulin sensitivity and enzymatic antioxidant changes correlated with visceral fat change, and the vegetarian diet was concluded to better improve insulin sensitivity over 24 weeks.
Proposed mechanism and conclusion: the greater visceral fat loss and improved adipokine and oxidative stress markers with the vegetarian diet may explain the reduction in insulin resistance.
Final summary sentence: exercise training further enhanced the benefits of the vegetarian diet, closing the study's conclusions.
Introduction of the sulfo-carrabiose anti-cellulite study: defines cellulite as fat accumulation in adipose tissue pressing on skin and introduces caffeine as the standard ingredient.

Background on mechanisms: caffeine's cAMP/phosphodiesterase action, and evidence that polyamines spermine and spermidine promote fat storage and suppress fat breakdown, plus heparan sulfate's affinity for polyamines.
Study rationale and design: molecular modelling screened heparan sulfate-like structures, identifying sulfo-carrabiose as a candidate polyamine trap.
Mechanistic and in vitro results: sulfo-carrabiose dose-dependently inactivates spermine and spermidine in tubo and, in cultured adipocytes, reduces lipogenesis and increases lipolysis.
In vivo clinical results: cosmetic formula with sulfo-carrabiose improved thigh circumference over caffeine at 28 days, and combining it with caffeine outperformed caffeine alone.

Further clinical outcomes: fringe projection showed reduced thigh volume, clinical evaluation showed reduced cellulite appearance within 28 days, followed by copyright notices from BASF and the Society of Cosmetic Scientists.
Closing copyright and attribution notice for the article (BASF Beauty Care Solutions; Society of Cosmetic Scientists and Société Française de Cosmétologie, 2010).

Introduction to the study: background on polyamines (putrescine, spermidine, spermine), ODC as the rate-limiting enzyme, and the study's aim of estimating dietary polyamine exposure and linking it to colorectal adenoma outcomes.

Study objective and design: hypothesis that high polyamine intake raises colorectal adenoma risk and that ODC G>A +316 genotype modifies this, plus the pooled sample (n=1164) drawn from control arms of two adenoma prevention trials.

Design details: the two source trials (Wheat Bran Fiber low-fiber arm, n=585; Ursodeoxycholic Acid placebo arm, n=579), assessment via baseline food-frequency questionnaire, and the eligibility requirement of a prior colorectal adenoma diagnosis; begins the results on above-median polyamine intake.

Main results: above-median polyamine intake linked to 39% higher adenoma risk in the pooled sample (adjusted OR 1.39), with significantly increased odds in younger participants, women, and ODC GG genotype carriers, with their ORs and CIs.
Conclusions: the study supports a role for dietary polyamines in colorectal adenoma risk and, if corroborated, would identify a previously unrecognized modifiable dietary risk factor.
Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that corroboration would establish a modifiable dietary risk factor for colorectal adenoma.

Introduces cellulite as a multifactorial cosmetic disorder of subcutaneous fat and skin, and states the background rationale that adiponectin, a protective anti-inflammatory and vasodilatory adipokine from subcutaneous fat, may be involved in its pathogenesis.

States the study hypothesis: reduced adiponectin expression in subcutaneous adipose tissue of cellulite areas may contribute to the altered microcirculation seen in these regions, since adiponectin acts as a humoral vasodilator.

Methods: describes the study population of 15 lean women with cellulite and 15 age- and BMI-matched controls, and the measurement approaches, real-time RT-PCR for adiponectin gene expression and a commercial immunoassay for plasma adiponectin.

Key results: gluteal subcutaneous adipose tissue adiponectin mRNA is significantly lower in cellulite areas (12.6 vs 16.6 AU, P=0.006), while plasma adiponectin levels are reported as not differing between groups (20.3 vs 19.3 μg/ml).

Conclusions: adiponectin expression is significantly reduced in subcutaneous fat of cellulite-affected areas, though circulating levels are unchanged, offering new insight into cellulite and possible clues for treatment; includes the 2011 International Society of Dermatology copyright notice.
Closing fragment of the conclusions and copyright line: notes the findings may guide treatment of this cosmetic issue, attributed to The International Society of Dermatology, 2011.

Introduction and aims of a human study on adiponectin: its role in energy balance and insulin sensitivity, prior links to fasting metabolic syndrome markers, and the aim of measuring postprandial adiponectin release in relation to metabolic syndrome traits.

Study design and methods: 110 non-diabetic men given an oral glucose tolerance test and a standardised fat-containing mixed meal, with fasting and postprandial adiponectin correlated to anthropometric and metabolic parameters and genotyped for the -11388 G/A promoter SNP.

Results on the time course of adiponectin after both meals (slight overall decline, significant drops at 5-6 h after lipid load and 2 h after glucose load), and the start of comparison showing postprandial adiponectin correlates with HDL more strongly than fasting adiponectin.

Correlation coefficients comparing postprandial versus fasting adiponectin with metabolic syndrome traits: HDL, insulin (AUC and fasting), BMI, waist, and systolic and diastolic blood pressure, with postprandial values generally showing stronger correlations.

Multivariate and genetic findings: postprandial triacylglycerols were the only independent predictor of adiponectin, and no significant association was found between adiponectin, NEFA or TAG and the -11388 G/A promoter polymorphism.

Concluding statement of the abstract: postprandial adiponectin shows the strongest and independent associations with postprandial triacylglycerol metabolism, supporting its interpretation in relation to lipid handling.

Introduction and objective of a study on meal effects on IL-8, IL-18, and adiponectin in healthy versus type 2 diabetic subjects, including the design rationale about high-fat meal endothelial activation.

Study design details: 30 newly diagnosed type 2 diabetic patients and 30 matched nondiabetic controls ate three isoenergetic 780-kcal meals (high-fat, high-carbohydrate low-fiber, high-carbohydrate high-fiber with whole-wheat flour) one week apart.

Results begin: baseline comparison showing diabetic patients had higher fasting IL-8 and IL-18 and lower adiponectin than nondiabetic subjects, with measurements taken at baseline and 2 and 4 h after meals.
Post-meal results for the high-fat meal: IL-18 rose and adiponectin fell in both groups; the high-carbohydrate high-fiber meal is also introduced as the comparator where IL-18 changed.

Further results: IL-18 decreased after the high-fiber meal in both groups, adiponectin decreased after the low-fiber meal in diabetics, and IL-8 showed no significant change after any meal; conclusions begin.

Main conclusion: circulating IL-18 and adiponectin are modulated by familiar foods in humans, suggesting dietary modulation of atherogenic cytokines may be a safe strategy to reduce inflammation in diabetes.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence about reducing atherogenic inflammatory activity in diabetic patients through meal modulation.

Introduction to the polyamine database study: motivation (polyamines' role in cancer) and the lack of U.S. dietary polyamine data that justify quantifying dietary spermine, spermidine, and putrescine.
Describes the study's core work: building a polyamine database linked to the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center FFQ, with values reported per serving in nmol, and begins noting which foods were evaluated.

Food-level findings: corn (fresh and frozen) has the highest putrescine and spermidine per serving, and green pea soup the highest spermine, followed by the testing of the database and FFQ on a convenience sample of 165 people.

Intake results from the validation sample: average daily putrescine, spermidine, and spermine intakes, plus the main dietary sources, namely orange and grapefruit juices for putrescine and green peas for spermidine.
Concluding summary: ground meat is the top source of dietary spermine, and the report closes by stating the database and FFQ enable polyamine intake estimation for cancer research.
Opening of the cellulite review: notes the scarcity and conflicting findings of the literature, and the lack of consensus on the nature, origin, and histopathological classification of the disorder.

Covers the lack of a recognized name for cellulite, contrasting the scientific meaning of 'cellulitis' (a gangrenous infection) with related terms such as panniculitis, lipodystrophy, EFP, liposclerosis, and lipoedema.

Introduces the three major conflicting theories of cellulite's etiopathogenesis that emerged over recent decades, beginning with the first (oedema from excessive hydrophilia of the intercellular matrix).

Lists the three competing causal theories: intercellular matrix oedema, regional microcirculatory homeostatic alteration (EFP), and female-specific subcutaneous anatomy differing from male morphology.
Argues that all three theories need revisiting in light of current understanding of the adipose organ as an endocrine and energy-regulating organ that secretes hormones and parahormones.
Final sentence summarizing the adipose tissue's role in modulating metabolism through glandular secretion of hormones and parahormones, closing the discussion of physiopathology.

Introduces the study's rationale: prior research linked dietary lignans to lower breast cancer risk, but no earlier work had examined lignan intake and breast cancer survival. Describes the cohort of 1122 women diagnosed 1996–2001 in the WEB Study, with vital status followed through 2006.

Describes the methods: diet in the 12–24 months before diagnosis was measured with an extensive food frequency questionnaire, confounders came from an epidemiologic interview and clinical records, and lignan intake was computed from published food composition data.

Details the statistical approach: Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios and 95% CIs for all-cause and breast cancer mortality, adjusted for age, education, race, total energy, tumor stage, and BMI. Notes 160 deaths among the 1122 women with complete dietary data.

Reports the main results for postmenopausal women: highest versus lowest lignan quartile was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.49) and breast cancer mortality (HR 0.29), with the confidence intervals given.

Presents secondary findings: dried beans showed a weak, non-significant inverse association with overall mortality, while fruits, vegetables, and grains showed no such link. Concludes that higher lignan intake may be linked to better survival in postmenopausal breast cancer patients.
Concludes the abstract's final sentence, stating that higher lignan intake may be associated with improved survival among postmenopausal women with breast cancer.

Introduces phytoestrogens (plant compounds with weak oestrogenic activity) and the epidemiological observation that breast cancer incidence is lower where phytoestrogen intake is high, suggesting a possible protective role for risk and survival.

Identifies isoflavones and lignans as the most common dietary phytoestrogens and states the article's scope: human observational and intervention studies on their exposure relative to breast cancer risk and survival.
Notes the growing dietary supplement market and that breast cancer patients increasingly take supplements alongside standard treatment, hoping to prevent recurrence or relieve menopausal symptoms.

Summarises mixed evidence: observational studies suggest isoflavones (and possibly lignans, inconsistently) protect against breast cancer, while short-term intervention studies hint at a stimulatory effect on breast tissue, raising safety concerns for patients.

Concludes that the role of phytoestrogens in recurrence and survival is unclear due to few human studies, so there is insufficient evidence for clinical guidelines, and patient awareness of this uncertainty is recommended.
Final sentence reiterating the recommendation that clinicians raise patient awareness of the uncertain effects of phytoestrogens, since no firm clinical guidance exists.
Introduction to a pilot study of the plant lignan secoisolariciresinol diglycoside (SDG) and its effect on breast cancer risk biomarkers in premenopausal women, including eligibility criteria.

Study design details: eligibility criteria (regular cycles, no oral contraceptives, >3-fold 5-year risk, baseline Ki-67 ≥2% in hyperplasia via RPFNA), SDG 50 mg daily for 12 months, and the primary (Ki-67) and secondary endpoints.
Secondary endpoints measured (cytomorphology, mammographic density, estradiol, testosterone, IGF-I, IGFBP-3, plasma lignans) and study results on enrollment completion, compliance, and side effects.

Results on biomarker changes: plasma enterolactone and total lignan increases, and the decrease in Ki-67 proliferation index in 80% of evaluable women with Wilcoxon test significance, plus the start of the atypical cytology finding.

Result on the decline in atypical cytology (p=0.035) and the conclusion that favorable biomarker changes and absence of adverse events justify launching a randomized SDG vs. placebo trial in premenopausal women.

Introduces the study's rationale: prior research linked dietary lignans to lower breast cancer risk, but no earlier work had examined lignan intake and breast cancer survival. Describes the cohort of 1122 women diagnosed 1996–2001 with follow-up through 2006.

Describes methods: diet in the 12–24 months before diagnosis was measured with an extensive food frequency questionnaire, confounders came from an epidemiologic interview and clinical records, and lignan intake was estimated from published food composition data.

Covers the statistical approach: Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios for all-cause and breast cancer mortality, adjusted for age, education, race, total energy, tumor stage, and BMI. Notes 160 deaths among the 1122 women with complete dietary data.

Reports the main finding: among postmenopausal women, the highest versus lowest lignan quartile had reduced all-cause mortality (HR 0.49) and breast cancer mortality (HR 0.29), both statistically significant.

Gives secondary results: dried bean intake was weakly associated with lower overall mortality (HR 0.61, CI crossing 1), while fruit, vegetable, and grain intakes were not. Concludes that higher lignan intake may be linked to better survival in postmenopausal breast cancer patients.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence, restating that higher lignan intake may be associated with improved survival among postmenopausal women with breast cancer.

Introduction and experimental aims of a randomized placebo-controlled trial testing dietary flaxseed effects on tumor markers and urinary lignans in postmenopausal newly diagnosed breast cancer patients.

Study design details: randomization to a 25 g flaxseed muffin (n = 19) versus placebo muffin (n = 13), with tumor tissue analyzed at diagnosis and at surgery for Ki-67, apoptosis, c-erbB2, and hormone receptors.

Methods continued: outcome measures including Ki-67 (primary end point), receptor levels, 24-hour urinary lignans, 3-day diet records, and mean treatment durations of 39 days (placebo) and 32 days (flaxseed).

Main results: flaxseed group showed significant reductions in Ki-67 index (34.2%) and c-erbB2 expression (71.0%) and increased apoptosis (30.7%), with no such changes in placebo; intake of calories and macronutrients was unchanged.

Further results and conclusion: urinary lignan excretion rose 1,300% in the flaxseed group versus placebo; flaxseed intake correlated with c-erbB2 and apoptotic index changes, supporting a potential tumor-growth-reducing effect.
Concluding statement that dietary flaxseed has the potential to reduce tumor growth in patients with breast cancer, closing the abstract's results and conclusions.

Background of a breast cancer study: rising Western incidence, need to understand sex steroid mechanisms, diet as prevention, and angiogenesis regulated by extracellular pro- and anti-angiogenic factors.

States the study aims: testing whether tamoxifen affects extracellular angiogenesis regulators VEGF, angiogenin, and endostatin in normal breast tissue in vivo, and whether flaxseed diet mimics tamoxifen.
Describes the methods: microdialysis sampling of extracellular proteins in normal breast tissue before and after six weeks of tamoxifen, before and after 25 g/day flaxseed, or in control women.
Reports results: estradiol correlates with VEGF, angiogenin, and endostatin in vivo, confirmed ex vivo, and tamoxifen lowers VEGF and angiogenin levels in the breast.
Summarizes flaxseed effects: no change in VEGF or angiogenin, but endostatin rises as with tamoxifen, and concludes tamoxifen shifts the angiogenic balance toward an anti-angiogenic state.
Concludes that flaxseed has limited effects on pro-angiogenic factors while endostatin may be diet-modifiable, and calls for further diet-based breast cancer prevention studies.
Introduction of a pilot study on SDG lignan's effect on breast cancer risk biomarkers in premenopausal women, including eligibility criteria for the study population.
