Eligibility details (regular cycles, no oral contraceptives, >3-fold 5-year risk, baseline Ki-67 ≥2% from RPFNA) and study design: SDG 50 mg daily for 12 months with repeat RPFNA, primary endpoint Ki-67 change.
Listing of secondary endpoints (cytomorphology, mammographic density, hormones, IGF-I/IGFBP-3, plasma lignans) and study results on enrollment completion, compliance, and side effects.
Key results: plasma enterolactone and total lignan increases, and 80% of evaluable women showing a significant Ki-67 decrease (median 4% to 2%, p<0.001), with an atypical cytology reduction noted.

Reports the significant decrease in atypical cytology (p=0.035) and concludes that favorable biomarker changes and absence of adverse events justify a randomized SDG vs. placebo trial in premenopausal women.

Introduction and study design: defines enterolactone and enterodiol as colon-microflora-produced mammalian lignans with possible anticancer effects, and introduces the food bars (flaxseed, sesame, combined) tested in the study.
Methods and design: describes the randomized crossover trial in healthy postmenopausal women, 4-week supplementation periods with 4-week washouts, and urinary lignan excretion as the outcome measure.

Results: reports the increase in urinary mammalian lignan excretion (65.1-81.0 umol/day, P<0.0001) across treatments with no differences among them, comparison to ground flaxseed studies, and detection of an unidentified metabolite with sesame-containing bars.

Conclusions: states the first-time findings that unground flaxseed and sesame seed precursors are converted by colonic bacteria to mammalian lignans, and that sesame alone or with flaxseed yields lignan production equivalent to flaxseed alone.
Closing fragment of the conclusion sentence, stating that sesame seed in combination with flaxseed produces lignans equivalent to flaxseed alone.

Abstract opening (Purpose) of a study on lignans and breast cancer: introduces phytoestrogens and sets the aim of comparing plant lignans (secoisolariciresinol, matairesinol) with human lignans (enterodiol, enterolactone), estradiol, and tamoxifen on proliferation of breast carcinoma cells.

Methods and early Results of the lignan breast cancer study: describes BrdU proliferation assays in MCF 7 and BT 20 cells, then begins reporting that enterodiol and enterolactone inhibited cell growth more strongly than secoisolariciresinol and matairesinol.

Late Results and Conclusions of the lignan breast cancer abstract: notes inhibition was weaker in BT 20 than MCF 7 cells, and concludes that human lignans enterodiol and enterolactone are more biologically active than their precursors and may be considered key cancer-prevention agents.

Final fragment of the abstract's conclusion, ending the sentence that calls enterodiol and enterolactone the real drugs in cancer prevention, relative to the plant lignan precursors secoisolariciresinol and matairesinol.

Introduces the hypothesis that antibiotics, by reducing lignan status, may raise breast cancer risk; describes the Finnish cohort study of 9461 women that examined history of urinary tract infection treatment as a predictor of breast cancer.

Reports the study's follow-up (1973–1991, 157 breast cancer cases) and the main finding: women with past or present UTI medication had elevated breast cancer risk, with an age-adjusted relative risk of 1.34 (CI 0.98–1.83).

Gives age-stratified results: the association was concentrated in women under 50 (RR 1.74, CI 1.13–2.68), versus no elevation in older women (RR 0.97), plus the younger group's risk by follow-up duration (RR 1.47 for first 10 years).

Shows the younger-group risk for follow-up beyond 10 years (RR 1.93, CI 1.11–3.37) and concludes that premenopausal women on long-term UTI medication may have a possible elevated future breast cancer risk, though results are inconclusive.
Closing caveat that the results remain inconclusive and the hypothesis needs testing in other studies, followed by the copyright notice (© 2000 Cancer Research Campaign).

Introduction of a retrospective cohort study on serum enterolactone (a mammalian lignan) and mortality in early breast cancer patients, extending prior findings that enterolactone is linked to lower breast cancer incidence in healthy women; describes the 300-patient cohort and serum measurement method.

Methods section detailing enterolactone measurement by time-resolved fluoro-immunoassay in cryopreserved serum from 300 operated breast cancer patients, and the statistical approach: Cox proportional hazards models for prognostic factors, hazard ratios, and interaction tests with enterolactone levels.

Statistical methods continued, specifying the Fine and Gray competing risks regression model used to estimate probabilities of breast cancer-related versus unrelated mortality, followed by the cohort's median follow-up of 23 years (range 0.6-26.1).

Results: of 300 patients, 180 died (112 from breast cancer), and enterolactone levels at or above 10 nmol/l were associated with decreased risk of both all-cause and breast cancer-specific mortality, with statistically significant hazard differences.

Results and interpretation: the mortality hazard difference weakened and lost significance after 10 years, yet competing risk analysis showed breast cancer-related mortality stayed consistently lower in higher-enterolactone patients; findings align with recent literature.
Conclusion: the study concludes that mammalian lignans may play an important role in reducing all-cause and cancer-specific mortality in women operated on for breast cancer.

Abstract opening of a paper describing an HPLC method for quantifying secoisolariciresinol diglucoside (SDG) and hydroxycinnamic acid glucosides in defatted flaxseed flour, highlighting NaOH direct extraction and o-coumaric acid internal standard.

Concluding part of the abstract reporting the method's ease, speed, and repeatability, and the reported variability of (+)-SDG, (-)-SDG, p-coumaric acid glucoside, and ferulic acid glucoside contents across flaxseed samples on a dry matter basis.
A lone period character; the chunk is an empty fragment with no substantive content, marking the end of the abstract text.

Introduces the abstract's setup: two phenolic compounds found in GC-MS analysis of urinary steroid extracts from humans and animals, with TMS spectra resembling oestrogens but atypical of steroids, and ruled out as isolation artefacts.

Explains why the compounds were judged genuine urinary constituents (blank controls, varied extraction, predominance as glucuronic acid conjugates) and introduces compound 180/442, whose cyclic excretion during the vervet monkey menstrual cycle prompted further characterization.
Reports the distribution of these compounds in humans, baboons, vervet monkeys and rats, and notes that related compounds have so far been found only in vervet monkey urine.
States the paper's main finding: the two original compounds are lignans with a 2,3-dibenzylbutane skeleton, and contrasts them with plant-derived lignans as mammalian metabolites.
Specifies the distinguishing structural feature of the mammalian lignans: their phenolic hydroxy groups occur only at the meta positions of the aromatic rings.

Introduction and methods of a meta-analysis on dietary lignans/enterolignans and breast cancer risk: states the inconsistent prior evidence, the aim, and the MEDLINE search covering 1997 to August 2009.

Methods continued: lists the pooled risk estimate exposures analyzed (total lignans, dietary intake, enterolignans, enterolactone blood/urine levels, stratified by menopausal and ER status), and begins the results with the study count of 21 (11 prospective, 10 case-control).

Main results: overall lignan exposure shows no significant association with breast cancer risk (RE 0.92), with notable heterogeneity, but high lignan intake in postmenopausal women is linked to a significantly reduced risk (RE 0.86).

Subgroup results: enterolignan exposure is inversely associated with breast cancer risk (RE 0.84, 4 studies) while blood or urine enterolactone shows no association, and ER-status subgroups did not differ significantly.
Conclusions: high lignan exposure may reduce breast cancer risk in postmenopausal women, and the authors call for further research to clarify the lignan-breast cancer relationship.
Introduces lignans as fiber-associated plant phenolics and their conversion by gut microbiota into enterolignans (ENL, END), with ENL linked to lower breast cancer risk.
Describes animal evidence that lignans metabolized to ENL, or ENL itself, inhibit or delay experimental mammary cancer, and notes ENL's proposed role as an estrogen signaling modulator.

Explains interest in lignans as ingredients in breast cancer risk-reducing functional foods, stresses identifying target groups who would benefit most, and calls for validated biomarkers of lignan/ENL action.
Concludes that biomarkers indicating lignan or ENL action and breast cancer risk reduction across different disease stages are important to develop and validate.

Introduces the unidentified phenolic substance X, found in gas chromatography of female urine, and its biphasic excretion pattern in the ovulatory cycle and early pregnancy, which suggests biological significance.

Explains why X was initially thought to be a steroid, based on its excretion pattern and its chemical and chromatographic similarity to known phenolic steroids, and notes its apparent presence in the vervet monkey.
States the study's aims: detailing X's excretion pattern, isolating the pure compound from pooled pregnancy urine, and determining its chemical structure using spectroscopic methods.
Gives the final result: X is identified as trans-(+/-)-3,4-bis[(3-hydroxyphenyl)methyl]dihydro-2-(3H)-furanone (HPMF), a non-steroidal lactone, with the structure confirmed by synthesis.
Introduction to the study: lignans and isoflavonic phytoestrogens found in human urine, their weak estrogenic/antiestrogenic and anticarcinogenic biological interest.

Origin and metabolism of these compounds: plant lignans and phytoestrogens from fiber-rich foods (grain, beans) are modified by intestinal bacteria and found in urine at much higher levels than estrogens.

Proposed mechanism of action: low-affinity binding to estrogen receptors and possible induction of liver SHBG, potentially influencing sex hormone metabolism; also introduces the five measured compounds and the GC-MS methodology.
Study design: urinary measurement of five compounds (enterolactone, enterodiol, daidzein, equol, O-desmethylangolensin) in 53 women across five dietary groups in Boston and Helsinki.

Study population and sampling: dietary groups (omnivores, lactovegetarians, macrobiotics) in Boston and Helsinki, 94 72-hour urine samples, and the finding that macrobiotics had the highest enterolactone excretion while omnivores had the lowest.
Quantitative results: mean 24-hour enterolactone excretion by group (macrobiotics 17,680 nmol highest, Boston omnivores 2,050 nmol lowest), with other diphenols showing a similar pattern.

Comparison with prior work and conclusions: an earlier Boston study found the lowest enterolactone excretion (1,040 nmol/24 h) in postmenopausal breast cancer patients; further research is needed on these compounds in cancer and disease.
Overall conclusion: the evidence suggests these lignans and phytoestrogen metabolites may be dietary factors protecting against hormone-dependent cancers in vegetarians and semivegetarians.

Background and aims of a study on serum enterolactone (a dietary lignan biomarker) and survival in postmenopausal breast cancer patients, introducing lignans' anticarcinogenic properties and bioavailability.

Study population and methods: 1,140 postmenopausal breast cancer patients aged 50-74 diagnosed 2002-2005, with vital status ascertained through population registries and death certificates through 2009, and recurrence data verified by clinical records.

Statistical methods: Cox proportional hazards models stratified by age at diagnosis and adjusted for prognostic factors, assessing postdiagnostic serum enterolactone against overall survival and distant disease-free survival; also begins the results with median enterolactone levels in deceased versus living patients.

Results on survival: median enterolactone of 17.0 nmol/L in deceased vs 21.4 nmol/L in living patients, 162 confirmed deaths over a median 6.1 years follow-up, and hazard ratios for death per 10 nmol/L increment and for the highest quartile.

Quantitative findings: hazard ratios for death (0.94 per 10 nmol/L, highest quartile HR 0.58) and for distant disease (0.94 per 10 nmol/L, highest quartile HR 0.62, not significant), with confidence intervals and P values.

Subgroup results by estrogen receptor status: the highest enterolactone quartile was protective against death only in ER-negative tumors (HR 0.27), not ER-positive tumors (HR 0.91), with a heterogeneity P value of .09; concludes high enterolactone may be linked to better survival.
Final conclusion sentence: postmenopausal breast cancer patients with high serum enterolactone levels may have better survival.

Introduction to phytoestrogens: definition as plant polyphenols similar to estradiol, their protective link to hormone-related cancers, and their typical low levels in UK foods, with soya highest, from the EPIC Norfolk phytoestrogen and cancer study.
Dietary sources and intake levels: breads are the main UK source of isoflavones (about 450 microg/100 g), and phytoestrogen consumption in UK cases and controls was far below that in Asian countries.

Key findings by cancer type from the EPIC Norfolk study: no breast cancer association with phytoestrogen intake; colorectal cancer inversely linked to enterolignans in women only; prostate cancer positively linked to enterolignans before adjustment.

Conclusion on prostate findings: the enterolignan–prostate cancer association disappears after adjusting for dairy, so enterolignans may just proxy dairy or calcium intake; includes the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces the study's background on lignans (oestrogenic dietary substances) and postmenopausal breast cancer, and describes the methods: a follow-up of 2653 postmenopausal breast cancer patients diagnosed 2001–2005, with vital status verified through 2009.

Describes the statistical methods for the survival analysis: Cox proportional hazards models with hazard ratios and 95% CIs for enterolignans, lignan-rich foods, and dietary fibre in relation to overall survival and breast cancer-specific survival, stratified by age at diagnosis and adjusted for confounders.

Reports main results: median follow-up of 6.4 years and 321 deaths (235 from breast cancer), with high enterolactone and enterodiol levels linked to significantly lower overall mortality (HR≈0.60 and 0.63 in the highest quintile), and fibre intake also associated with lower mortality.

Presents secondary findings: enterolignan associations persisted only at low (not high) median fibre intake, and no effect modification by oestrogen receptor status or menopausal hormone therapy, leading into the study's conclusion.

Gives the study's concluding statement that postmenopausal breast cancer patients with high estimated enterolignans may have better survival, summarising the overall takeaway of the lignan–survival association.

Introduction of the hypothesis that antibiotic use may increase breast cancer risk, citing prior proposals, observed associations in women with long-term antibiotic-requiring conditions (acne, recurrent UTI), and the lack of verification or clear biological mechanisms.

Background on a Finnish cohort study linking antibiotic use for UTI to higher breast cancer risk, and the proposed mechanism that antibiotics alter intestinal microflora's ability to metabolise plant phytochemicals into cancer-protective compounds.

The paper's extended hypothesis: antibiotics may affect breast cancer risk via immune and inflammatory factors (cytokines, T lymphocytes, prostaglandins, matrix metalloproteinases) and via disrupted microflora-mediated metabolism of phytochemicals and oestrogen.
Conclusion of the hypothesis: different mechanisms may raise or lower breast cancer risk, with the direction depending on the class of antibiotic involved.
Introduces lignans and enterolignans (mainly enterolactone) as estrogen-like biomarkers of lignan exposure, and their early epidemiological study in relation to breast cancer risk.
Summarizes the conflicting evidence on enterolactone and breast cancer: case-control studies show reduced risk at high levels, while prospective cohort results are less clear.

States the review's aim: explaining contradictory epidemiological findings via age, enterolactone measurement error, breast cancer subtype heterogeneity, genetic factors, and differing precursor sources.

Concludes that robust evidence requires addressing methodological issues, especially reducing enterolactone measurement error and identifying effect modifiers, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.
Copyright notice (2010 Elsevier Inc.) closing the abstract.
Background and objective of a meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies on dietary fiber intake and breast cancer risk, including the PubMed search design (through January 2011).
Study design and methods continuation: inclusion criteria requiring prospective cohort studies reporting RRs with 95% CIs, and use of fixed- and random-effects models for summary estimates.
Main results: 10 prospective cohort studies (16,848 cases, 712,195 participants) yielding a combined RR of 0.89 (95% CI 0.83-0.96) for highest vs. lowest fiber intake, with little heterogeneity.

Subgroup and sensitivity findings: no significant differences in the fiber-breast cancer association by geographic region, follow-up length, or menopausal status, and robustness when any single study is omitted.

Dose-response and bias findings: each 10 g/day increase in fiber linked to a 7% lower breast cancer risk, little publication bias, and the conclusion of a significant inverse dose-response association.
Closing fragment of the conclusion sentence, restating the inverse dose-response association between dietary fiber intake and breast cancer risk.

Study overview: a Connecticut case-control study of 557 breast cancer cases and 536 matched controls, describing the aims (dietary fiber type, menopausal status, hormone receptor status) and the methods (food frequency questionnaire, unconditional logistic regression).

Methods and start of results: details on how dietary intake was collected via in-person interviews with a semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire, then the beginning of the results on soluble fiber in pre-menopausal women.

Key pre-menopausal results: highest versus lowest soluble fiber quartile linked to reduced breast cancer risk overall (OR 0.38), and a stronger protective association in pre-menopausal women with ER-negative tumors (OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.03-0.69).

Post-menopausal null findings and conclusion start: no reduced risk for soluble or insoluble fiber in post-menopausal women, by ER status; the conclusion begins by stating soluble fiber is linked to lower ER-negative breast cancer risk in pre-menopausal women.
Conclusion and limitations: soluble fiber intake is associated with reduced ER-negative breast cancer risk in pre-menopausal women, and the authors call for larger studies to confirm these findings.

Abstract of a combined analysis of 12 case-control studies on diet and breast cancer, reporting a positive association between saturated fat intake and breast cancer risk in postmenopausal women (RR 1.46, highest vs. lowest quintile).

Continuation of the abstract's findings: fruit and vegetable markers show a protective effect, with vitamin C having the strongest inverse association with breast cancer risk (RR 0.69, highest vs. lowest quintile, P < .0001).

Concluding sentence of the abstract estimating the attributable risk of breast cancer preventable through dietary modification in the North American population: 24% for postmenopausal and 16% for premenopausal women, assuming causality.

Introduction to 'sensitive skin' as a recent, self-reported complaint of heightened adverse sensory reactions to personal-care products, and its rising prevalence among women and men in industrialized countries.

Describes sensitive skin as self-diagnosed without obvious physical irritation signs, and notes that the growing number of claimants tracks the expansion of products marketed to this group, leading dermatologists to view it as a 'princess and the pea' phenomenon.

Explains that sensitive skin has largely escaped focused research, but recent evidence of measurable biophysical changes linked to its sensory symptoms has emerged, aided by better detection of subclinical irritation.

States that although the aetiology remains incompletely understood, current research supports a biophysical origin, and lists needed work: diagnostic methods, intrinsic and extrinsic contributors to neural hypersensitivity, and mechanisms of discomfort.
Concludes that prevention and treatment approaches for sensitive skin are still needed, closing the document's call for further research on diagnosis, mechanisms, prevention, and treatment.

Introduces the study's background on skin sensitivity in the Western population and the rationale for testing daily flaxseed oil and safflowerseed oil supplementation in healthy volunteers with sensitive skin.

Describes the methods: a randomized, double-blind 12-week trial with two female groups (n = 13), measuring plasma fatty acid profile, skin sensitivity, hydration, TEWL, and skin surface at day 0, week 6, and week 12.

Reports the main results for flaxseed oil: significant reductions in nicotinate-irritation sensitivity, TEWL, roughness and scaling, increased smoothness and hydration, and a decreased plasma n-6/n-3 FA ratio.

Reports the safflowerseed oil results, which showed only improved roughness and hydration, with weaker, later effects than flaxseed oil and an increased plasma n-6/n-3 ratio, followed by the conclusion that daily flaxseed oil intake modulates skin condition.
Contains the closing copyright notice (S. Karger AG, Basel, 2010) that ends the abstract, marking the document's end and source attribution.

Introduction and methods of a 2007 US phone survey on sensitive skin prevalence, describing the aim, the representative adult sample, and the data collected (demographics, environment, skin type, disorders, cosmetics, dermatologist visits).
Methods continuation (quota-sampled representative US adult cohort) followed by the start of results: 994 respondents (495 men, 499 women), with 44.6% reporting sensitive or very sensitive skin.

Results on sensitivity by sex (women 50.9% vs men 38.2%, P<0.0001), no significant differences by region, age, or ethnicity, and the skin types and characteristics of sensitive-skin subjects (dry 34.5%, mixed 35.7%, fair phototype, disorders, reactivity).

Results comparing sensitive-skin subjects with those reporting slight or no sensitivity, highlighting higher reactivity to cosmetics and environmental factors, and the dermatologist's strong influence via skin care product prescriptions.

Conclusion stating high US prevalence of sensitive skin, its association with dry skin, fair phototype, climatic/environmental and cosmetic reactivity, and the significant role of American dermatologists in its care.
Closing sentence of the conclusion on American dermatologists' involvement in managing sensitive skin, followed by the 2011 International Society of Dermatology copyright notice.

Abstract opening of a randomized crossover study on flaxseed in obese, glucose-intolerant adults: background on obesity-driven inflammation and insulin resistance, aim to test flaxseed's antioxidant activity, and the methods design (40 g ground flaxseed vs. 40 g wheat bran daily for 12 weeks, 4-week washout).

Continuation of the abstract's Methods and start of Results: outcome measures include plasma inflammatory biomarkers (CRP, TNF-α, IL-6), glucose, insulin, and TBARS; reports that flaxseed significantly lowered TBARS (p = 0.0215) and HOMA-IR (p = 0.0382), and that neither supplement changed inflammatory markers.

Core Results and Conclusions of the flaxseed crossover trial: the positive TBARS–HOMA-IR correlation (r = 0.62, p = 0.0003), and the cautious conclusion that flaxseed's reduction in insulin resistance may be secondary to its antioxidant effect.
Closing sentence of the abstract's Conclusions, calling for further study of the mechanism behind flaxseed's reduction in insulin resistance, specifically using flaxseed lignan.
Introduction and 4-week human trial design: 50 g/day raw ground high-ALA flaxseed in healthy female volunteers, providing about 12-13% of energy intake.

Results on lipids and biomarkers: flaxseed raised plasma and erythrocyte ALA and long-chain n-3 fatty acids, increased urinary thiocyanate 2.2-fold, and lowered serum total and LDL cholesterol (9% and 18%).

Bioavailability and glycaemic findings: ALA changes from ground flaxseed flour matched flaxseed oil, suggesting high bioavailability; flaxseed carbohydrate and mucilage meals reduced postprandial blood glucose by 27%.

Food safety and baking findings: muffins with flaxseed oil or flour showed malondialdehyde levels similar to wheat muffins, and cyanogenic glycosides were highest in mucilage and undetected in baked muffins.
Conclusion: up to 50 g/day of high-ALA flaxseed is palatable, safe, and potentially beneficial by raising plasma and erythrocyte n-3 fatty acids and reducing postprandial glucose responses.
Study abstract opening: objectives, design (34 randomized participants), and baseline characteristics of adults with type 2 diabetes in a flaxseed trial on glycemia, n-3 status, and adipokines.
Intervention details: the control, milled flaxseed (32 g/d), and flaxseed oil (13 g/d) groups over 12 weeks, with both flax arms receiving matched ALA (7.4 g/day).

Outcome measures section: primary outcomes are fasting glycemic markers (HbA1c, glucose, insulin) and phospholipid fatty acid composition; secondary outcomes are leptin, adiponectin, and anthropometric measures.
Start of results: both flax groups increased plasma phospholipid n-3 fatty acids (ALA, EPA, DPA but not DHA), with the flaxseed oil group showing more EPA and DPA than the milled flaxseed group.

Results on energy and weight: caloric intake was similar across groups; controls gained 4% body weight while both flax groups kept stable weight, and other measures including glycemic control were unchanged.
Conclusions: milled flaxseed and flaxseed oil do not alter glycemic control in well-controlled type 2 diabetes, and flax may help prevent weight gain, which needs further study.
Final sentence of the conclusions, calling for further investigation of flax consumption's possible role in preventing weight gain.
Introduction to the open-label flax seed (Linum usitatissimum) diabetes study: background on diabetes mellitus, metabolic complications, and the role of nutritional therapy and functional foods.

Rationale for the flax seed study: flax seed is a functional food rich in omega-3 fatty acids and antioxidants and low in carbohydrates, and recipes containing it showed a lower glycemic index, motivating the efficacy trial in type 2 diabetics (n=29).

Study design and methods: 29 type 2 diabetic subjects were allocated by participation preference to an experimental group (n=18) receiving 10 g daily flax seed powder for 1 month, or a control group (n=11) with no supplementation or placebo, with diet and medications unchanged.

Outcome assessment method: the efficacy of daily flax seed powder supplementation was measured via clinico-biochemical parameters, with the context noting that the control group received no placebo and that the experimental group's diet included 10 g of flax seed powder.

Study results: flax seed supplementation reduced fasting blood glucose by 19.7% and glycated hemoglobin by 15.6%, and improved lipid profile with reductions in total cholesterol, triglycerides, LDL cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B, plus a rise in HDL cholesterol.
Conclusion of the flax seed diabetes study: the observed glycemic and lipid improvements suggest flax seed has therapeutic potential in managing diabetes mellitus.
Introduction and methods opening of a randomized controlled trial on flaxseed and low-fat diets in prostate cancer patients awaiting prostatectomy, describing rationale and study design.

Methods continued: the trial enrolls 161 prostate cancer patients scheduled at least 21 days before surgery, randomized to control, flaxseed (30 g/day), low-fat (<20% energy), or combined flaxseed plus low-fat diet arms.
Methods continued: blood biomarkers measured at baseline and pre-surgery (PSA, hormones, IGF-1, CRP, cholesterol), and tumors assessed for Ki-67 proliferation (primary endpoint) and apoptosis.

Results: men were on protocol about 30 days on average; proliferation was significantly lower in flaxseed arms (P<0.002), with median Ki-67 ratios for each arm listed, beginning with the flaxseed-supplemented diet groups.

Results and conclusions: Ki-67 values for control and low-fat arms are compared to flaxseed arms; no differences in side effects, apoptosis, or most serologic markers, but low-fat diets significantly lowered serum cholesterol (P=0.048); flaxseed judged safe and potentially protective.
Final conclusion: flaxseed appears safe and linked to biologic changes potentially protective against prostate cancer, and low-fat diets further support managing serum cholesterol.
Abstract opening of a study on mammalian lignans (enterolactone and enterodiol) and their effects on human prostate cancer cell lines, introducing background and methods (PC-3, DU-145, LNCaP cells).

Methods and early results of the lignan prostate cancer study: cells treated with vehicle, 10-100 microM enterolactone, enterodiol, or genistein for 72 hours, with viability measured by a propidium iodide assay, followed by the start of the results on which cell lines were inhibited.

Results of the lignan prostate cancer study comparing potency: enterolactone inhibited all cell lines and was more potent than enterodiol, both weaker than genistein, with IC50 values for LNCaP cells (EL 57 microM, ED 100 microM, genistein 25 microM), leading into the conclusion.

Concluding sentence of the lignan prostate cancer abstract stating that enterodiol and enterolactone suppress prostate cancer cell growth, possibly through hormone-dependent and hormone-independent mechanisms.

Introduction and background of a study on lignans and isoflavonoid phyto-oestrogens in plasma and prostatic fluid of men, comparing prostate cancer incidence in Chinese versus European and North American men and dietary sources of these compounds.

Continues the background on lignan sources and vegetarian intake, then the Methods section describing GC-MS measurement of lignans and isoflavonoids in plasma and prostatic fluid from Portuguese, Chinese and British men on traditional diets, leading into the Results.

Results section reporting mean prostatic fluid enterolactone levels by country (Hong Kong 31, Portugal 162, Britain 20.3 ng/ml), very high enterolactone in some Portuguese men, and high equol and daidzein values in a Hong Kong sample.

Results on daidzein levels: mean prostatic fluid daidzein is highest in Hong Kong (70 ng/ml) versus Portugal (4.6) and Britain (11.3), and mean plasma daidzein is higher in Hong Kong (31.3 ng/ml) than Portugal (1.3) and Britain (8.2).

Plasma enterolactone results (similar across centres: 6.2, 3.9, 3.9 ng/ml for Hong Kong, Portugal, Britain) and the start of the Conclusions, which summarise the isoflavonoid findings in Hong Kong men.

Conclusions contrasting higher isoflavonoid (daidzein, equol) levels in Hong Kong men with much higher enterolactone in Portuguese prostatic fluid, and suggesting these compounds may explain lower prostate cancer rates in Asia and Mediterranean countries.
Final conclusion that soya isoflavonoids, abundant in the prostatic fluid of Asian men, may protect against prostate disease, closing the study's discussion of its findings.
Final sentence fragment of the conclusion stating that soya isoflavonoids may be protective against prostate disease; the last chunk of the abstract.
Background and objectives of a pilot study on a flaxseed-supplemented, low-fat diet and its effect on benign prostatic epithelium, introducing the rationale from prior prostate cancer research.
Methods of the pilot study: aim to measure epithelial proliferation plus PSA, testosterone, and cholesterol, and the enrollment of fifteen men scheduled for repeat prostate biopsy.

Intervention details: men followed a low-fat (<20% kcal) diet with 30 g/day flaxseed for 6 months, with PSA, testosterone, and cholesterol measured at baseline and follow-up, and biopsy reports compared using MIB-1 proliferation rates.
Results on biomarkers: significant drops in PSA (8.47 to 5.72 ng/mL, P=0.0002) and cholesterol (241.1 to 213.3 mg/dL, P=0.012), with no significant change in total testosterone.
Results on biopsy proliferation: among 13 men with repeat biopsy (2 skipped due to PSA normalization), benign epithelium MIB-1 proliferation fell significantly from 0.022 to 0.007 (P=0.0168).
Conclusions: the pilot data suggest the flaxseed, fat-restricted diet may alter prostate biology and biomarkers, the first step toward further study.
Final recommendation calling for a randomized controlled trial to test flaxseed, low-fat diet, or their combination for controlling overall prostatic growth.

Introduces a 2-phase trial study of 145 men with prostate cancer examining how four diet arms (control, low-fat, flaxseed, flaxseed plus low-fat) affect 50 plasma cytokines and angiogenic factors, motivated by diet's uncertain role in angiogenesis and inflammation.

Describes the design of the randomized pre-operative phase-II trial with four dietary arms and a mean intervention duration of 30–31 days, and begins reporting results comparing baseline with pre-operative follow-up.

Reports results: the low-fat arm showed the most significant cytokine/angiogenic factor changes (19 decreased, 1 increased), and six factors, including SDF-1α, G-CSF and M-CSF, were lower in the low-fat arm versus controls, with 3 and 4 changes in the flaxseed and flaxseed plus low-fat arms.

Links the low-fat diet to weight loss that correlated with VEGF decreases, and notes that all factors changed in the low-fat arm are regulated by NF-κB, pointing toward a possible mechanistic pathway.

Pathway analysis identifies NF-κB as the most likely regulatory network behind the low-fat arm changes but not the flaxseed arms, leading to the conclusion that low-fat diet without flaxseed may lower inflammatory and angiogenic factors via NF-κB.
Final concluding statement that NF-κB signaling may mediate the diet-induced changes in inflammatory cytokines and angiogenic factors in men with prostate cancer.
Introduces the USDA FSIS Pathogen Reduction HACCP program, a staged 1996-2000 effort to reduce microbial contamination in meat and poultry, as background for the broiler Salmonella study.
Notes that broiler chicken carcasses showed one of the largest contamination reductions under the FSIS program, and that its effect on U.S. salmonellosis case totals had not been assessed.
Describes the study's method: a model combining public health surveillance data and poultry slaughter industry surveys to estimate broiler-related salmonellosis cases over time.

Reports the main result: a 56% drop in contaminated broiler carcasses (1995-2000) corresponded to about 190,000 fewer broiler-attributed salmonellosis cases in 2000, with uncertainty of roughly 37,000 to 500,000.

Reports that the smaller 13% contamination reduction from 2000 to 2007 gave no statistically significant illness reduction, and mentions an analysis of how large a contamination change must be to be detectable through human surveillance.

Introduction to the study: background on Salmonella as a foodborne pathogen, ceftriaxone (an extended-spectrum cephalosporin) as treatment, and NARMS surveillance showing rising ESC resistance in Salmonella Heidelberg.

Continues the background on rising ESC resistance in Salmonella Heidelberg across food animals, retail meat, and humans, noting that US ESC resistance is usually mediated by plasmid-encoded bla(CMY) β-lactamase, and introduces the 2009 isolate collection.

Describes the 2009 study population: 47 ESC-resistant bla(CMY)-positive Heidelberg isolates from humans, slaughter animals, and retail meat, with about 90% of animal and meat isolates from chicken, and outlines the methods used.

Methods overview: screening isolates for bla(CMY), testing whether the gene is plasmid-encoded, using PFGE to assess genetic diversity, and classifying plasmids by incompatibility group and pMLST; reports that all 47 bla(CMY) genes were plasmid-encoded.

Results on plasmid typing: 41 isolates carried IncI1 plasmids (40 conferring only bla(CMY) resistance) and 6 carried IncA/C plasmids with additional resistance genes; pMLST shows 27 (65.8%) of IncI1 plasmids are ST12.

Further pMLST results: ST12 is the most common ST among human bla(CMY)-IncI1 plasmids, 10 plasmids belong to a new ST66 closely related to ST12, and the conclusion that spread occurred via plasmid dissemination across genetic backgrounds.

Final conclusion: the 2009 rise in ESC resistance in Salmonella Heidelberg was mainly driven by dissemination of bla(CMY) on IncI1 and IncA/C plasmids across diverse genetic backgrounds rather than clonal expansion.

Opening of the 2009 Garrod lecture on antimicrobial resistance: introduces the evolutionary adaptability of microbes and horizontal gene transfer in bacteria as the basis for their response to antibiotics.

Continuation of the introduction from the 2009 Garrod lecture: frames antibiotic resistance as a Darwinian response to antibiotics and states the paper's aim of comparing beta-lactam resistance evolution in S. aureus and P. aeruginosa over 70 years.

Closing sentence of the introduction from the 2009 Garrod lecture on antimicrobial resistance, identifying the two studied species: Staphylococcus aureus (a highly evolved human pathogen) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (an opportunistic nosocomial pathogen).

Introduction to the document on antimicrobial resistance in bacteria: lists antibiotic classes by mechanism of action (cell wall, protein synthesis, nucleic acid synthesis, metabolic pathways, membrane disruption) and notes that resistance is increasingly complicating infection treatment.
Continues the classification of antimicrobials by mechanism and introduces intrinsic versus acquired resistance, covering examples such as polymyxins and daptomycin for membrane disruption.

Describes how bacteria acquire resistance, through de novo mutation or horizontal transfer of resistance genes, and lists the resulting mechanisms: drug-destroying enzymes, efflux pumps, target modification, and bypass metabolic pathways.
Explains horizontal gene transfer routes (conjugation, transformation, transduction) and the role of transposons in assembling multiple resistance genes in the host genome or plasmids.

Covers selective pressure from antibacterial use driving resistant strain emergence and previews the three case histories: E. coli and third-generation cephalosporins, vancomycin-resistant S. aureus, and multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa.

Closing portion of the abstract naming the three case histories (E. coli cephalosporin resistance, vancomycin-resistant S. aureus, multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa) and their purpose of illustrating how resistance develops.

Introduction to antimicrobial resistance: overview of how bacteria resist antibiotics and the classes of antimicrobial agents grouped by mechanism of action (cell wall, protein synthesis, nucleic acid, metabolic pathway, membrane).

Continuation of the drug classes by mechanism, then the two routes to resistance: intrinsic resistance versus acquired resistance via de novo mutation or acquisition of resistance genes from other organisms.
Biochemical ways acquired resistance genes work: drug-destroying enzymes, efflux pumps, altered drug target sites, and bypass metabolic pathways.

Horizontal gene transfer of resistance determinants between bacteria by conjugation, transformation, or transduction, with transposons aiding incorporation of resistance genes into genome or plasmids.

Antibiotic use as selective pressure driving emergence of resistant strains, and preview of the three case histories: E. coli and third-generation cephalosporins, vancomycin-resistant S. aureus, and multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa.
Closing description of the three case histories (E. coli, vancomycin-resistant S. aureus, P. aeruginosa) that illustrate the varied ways resistant bacteria develop.

Opening summary of the document: introduces antimicrobials as valuable therapeutics undermined by resistance, and frames the debate over nontherapeutic antimicrobial (NTA) use, including growth promotion, in food animals.

Continues the summary: describes the conflicting practices and opinions on NTAs, notes European removal of NTAs under the precautionary principle, and states that the scientific evidence on NTA benefits and harms is still unclear to stakeholders. It also begins the point that animals fed NTAs show elevated antibiotic resistance.

Covers the transmission pathways of antibiotic resistance from NTA-fed animals and their food products to other animals and humans, both by direct contact and indirectly via the food chain, water, air, and manured or sludge-fertilized soils. It also notes that genetic techniques are advancing understanding of NTA ecological impact.

Explains that modeling the ecological impact of NTAs is hampered by gaps in data on microbial and antibiotic loads across the transmission chain. It argues that growing evidence of animal-to-human spread of resistant bacteria supports eliminating NTA use.

Concluding statement of the document: the expanding evidence of resistant-bacteria spread from animals to humans, including from NTA use, supports eliminating NTAs to reduce the growing environmental load of resistance genes.
Background on the burden of domestically acquired Salmonella Enteritidis (SE) foodborne illness in the US and why accurate incidence data matter for control policy.

Methods: FoodNet population-based active surveillance analysis of human SE incidence for 1996-2009, compared against passive surveillance data, chicken and egg product isolation rates, and molecular subtyping.

Methods continued and start of results: comparison with complementary surveillance and food isolate data (shell eggs not routinely tested), plus the reported 44% rise in human SE incidence since 1996-1999.
Results on trends: the 44% increase in FoodNet is mirrored nationally, with the largest increases among young children, older adults, and southern US sites; declining travel-associated cases.

Results and conclusions: rising SE isolation from chickens, shared human and chicken molecular subtypes, and the conclusion that most US SE infections are domestically acquired and chicken and eggs are likely major sources.
Final conclusion: the growing domestic SE problem points to chicken and eggs as major sources, and ongoing surveillance is needed to assess recent regulatory control measures.

Introduction and aims of a 2010 Dutch study comparing ESBL-producing bacteria contamination in organic versus conventional retail chicken meat, including prevalence, load, genes, genotypes and co-resistance.
Study design and main prevalence results: 98 raw chicken breasts (60 conventional, 38 organic) from 12 Dutch stores in 2010; ESBL prevalence 100% conventional vs 84% organic (p<0.001).
Bacterial load results (median CFU/25 g, higher in conventional samples, p=0.001) and the distribution of ESBL genes (CTX-M-1, TEM-52, SHV-12) across conventional and organic samples.
Exclusively conventional ESBL genes (CTX-M-2, SHV-2, TEM-20) and co-resistance rates to co-trimoxazole, ciprofloxacin, tobramycin and tetracycline, which were similar except for tetracycline.

Molecular typing results: MLST sequence types shared with human isolates in conventional and organic meat samples, and the conclusion that organic chicken meat was largely contaminated with ESBL E. coli similar to conventional meat.
Closing copyright notice (Elsevier B.V., 2011) at the end of the abstract.

Introduction and setup of the study: EMI survey of a broiler chicken farm guides soil sampling at a chicken-waste-impacted site versus a marginally affected site, examining how farm waste spreads antibiotic resistance genes in soil.

Site comparison results: the waste-impacted site differs from the marginally affected site in soil pH, culturable bacterial tetracycline resistance, and tet/erm gene incidence and prevalence, while the marginal site matches several pristine regional forest sites.

Gene detection over time: tet(L), tet(M), tet(O), erm(A), erm(B), and erm(C) were found while the farm operated; after waste removal, two years on, tet(L), tet(M), tet(O), and erm(C) persisted in the soil.
Quantitative PCR results: tet(L), tet(O), and erm(B) abundances normalized to 16S rRNA show tet(L) as most prevalent and tet(O) as most persistent, with all genes declining over the two-year period.

Plasmid identification: a mobilizable tet(L)-carrying plasmid was found in seven of 14 tetracycline-resistant isolates, hosted by Bhargavaea, Sporosarcina, and Bacillus species, and its mob gene was used to estimate prevalence, with the tet(L):mob ratio falling from 34:1 to 1:1.
Final summary fragment: concludes the plasmid analysis, stating the tet(L):mob ratio shift from 34:1 to 1:1 across the 2-year soil sampling period.

Introduces the study's methods: E. coli isolates from the NARMS retail meat program, covering 11,921 retail meat samples (chicken, ground turkey, ground beef, pork chop) collected 2002–2008 in four U.S. states, yielding 8,286 isolates.

Reports contamination prevalence by meat type (chicken 83.5%, turkey 82.0%, beef 68.9%, pork 44.0%) and the overall ranking of resistance to antimicrobials, led by tetracycline (50.3%) and streptomycin (34.6%).

Continues the resistance rankings (sulfamethoxazole-sulfisoxazole, ampicillin, gentamicin, kanamycin, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, cefoxitin), notes drugs with under 5% resistance, and states that all isolates were susceptible to amikacin; begins comparing poultry with beef and pork.

Compares resistance by meat source, finding poultry isolates more resistant than beef and pork to nearly all drugs (pork highest for chloramphenicol), and reports multidrug resistance (≥3 classes) highest in turkey (56%) and lowest in beef (9.3%).

Details resistance genotypes: blaCMY in all ceftriaxone- and ceftiofur-resistant isolates, cmlA, flo, and catI in chloramphenicol-resistant isolates, and gyrA and parC mutations linked to nalidixic acid resistance.

Concludes the abstract: nalidixic acid resistance is mainly due to gyrA mutations (98.5%) with few parC mutations (6.7%), and E. coli is common in retail meats with resistance profiles varying by animal origin.

Introduction motivating point-of-processing foodborne illness attribution models for Salmonella, describing their use by risk managers and policy makers and the data sources (CDC surveillance and USDA FSIS testing) that the study draws on.

Methods summary: the authors built a point-of-processing attribution model by adapting the Hald Salmonella Bayesian source attribution model, using CDC laboratory-confirmed human infection data and USDA FSIS Salmonella testing data.

Key results: estimated proportions of domestically acquired sporadic human Salmonella infections from raw meat, poultry, and egg products processed in the U.S. (1998-2003), beginning with the commodity contribution figures for chicken and ground beef.

Specific attribution findings: relative contributions by commodity (chicken 48%, ground beef 28%, turkey 17%, egg products 6%, intact beef 1%, pork under 1%) across 109 Salmonella serotypes, along with a caveat that data inputs constrain interpretation.
Conclusion: the adapted model is promising and could serve as a common cross-country framework for attributing human salmonellosis and informing food safety decisions.

Abstract of a study on reversal of fatigue in prolonged cycling exercise (70% VO2max) via carbohydrate ingestion or glucose infusion; describes baseline trial showing declining plasma glucose and respiratory exchange ratio until fatigue at about 170 min.

Abstract continuation describing the three post-rest conditions (placebo, glucose polymer ingestion at 3 g/kg, euglycemic glucose infusion) and results: placebo failed to restore glucose or respiratory exchange ratio, while carbohydrate sources raised plasma glucose to about 5 mM.

Abstract results comparing plasma glucose and respiratory exchange ratio over the second exercise bout: carbohydrate ingestion let glucose and R fall gradually, whereas glucose infusion maintained euglycemia (about 5.1 mM) and R (about 0.83).

Abstract outcome data on time to fatigue in the second exercise bout: longer for carbohydrate ingestion (26 min) and glucose infusion (43 min) than placebo (10 min), with insulin and muscle glycogen values reported as unchanged.

Abstract conclusion on metabolism: muscle glycogen and insulin stayed stable during glucose infusion, and the euglycemic glucose infusion rate (about 1.13 g/min) supplied roughly three-fourths of carbohydrate oxidation in the second bout; the abstract is truncated at 250 words.

Introduces a crossover study comparing sun-dried raisins (SDRs) with Sports Jelly Beans (SJBs) as carbohydrate fuel for endurance cyclists and triathletes, describing the trial design: a water-only acclimatization trial, then two randomized trials each with 120 minutes of glycogen depletion followed by a 10-km time trial.

Describes the experimental protocol: each trial pairs a 120-minute constant-intensity glycogen depletion period with a 10-km time trial, with isocaloric SDRs or SJBs consumed every 20 minutes, and lists the outcome measures (TT time and power, blood glucose, respiratory exchange ratio, RPE, flow, and hedonic sensory acceptance).

Reports the main endurance results: 10-km time trial time and power output were essentially identical for SDRs and SJBs, with figures given as means and standard deviations, and the chunk begins the listing of other measured outcomes.

Presents secondary findings: resting blood glucose, RPE, and flow did not differ between SDR and SJB trials, but hedonic sensory acceptance scores were significantly higher for SDRs than SJBs (50.7 vs. 44.3).

States the conclusions: SDRs and SJBs consumed during 120 minutes of intense cycling produce similar time-trial performance and similarly maintain blood glucose, so SDRs are presented as a natural, pleasant, cost-effective carbohydrate alternative for moderate- to high-intensity endurance exercise.

Final sentence of the abstract, concluding that sun-dried raisins can serve as a practical carbohydrate alternative to commercial sports jelly beans during moderate- to high-intensity endurance exercise.

Abstract opening of a study comparing raisins (moderate glycemic index) with a high-glycemic sports gel as pre-exercise carbohydrate for endurance-trained cyclists, including the study aim on metabolism and performance.

Methods section describing the design: 8 trained cyclists (4 men, 4 women), two randomized trials, 1 g/kg carbohydrate from raisins or gel 45 minutes before 70% VO2max cycling, followed by a 15-minute performance trial.

Methods and results transition: blood sampling for metabolic markers (glucose, insulin, lactate, FFAs, triglycerides, beta-hydroxybutyrate) and the start of results, reporting no performance difference between raisin (189.5 kJ) and gel (188.0 kJ) trials.

Results on pre-exercise metabolism: glucose and other fuels did not differ, but insulin was significantly higher after the gel (110.0 microU/ml) than the raisin trial (61.4 microU/ml), with post-exercise insulin values given.

Results on exercise metabolism: insulin fell to similar low levels after 45 minutes in both trials, FFAs rose significantly during the raisin trial, and the authors conclude that metabolic differences were minor and performance was unchanged.
Concluding sentence of the abstract: raisins are presented as a cost-effective pre-exercise carbohydrate alternative to sports gel for short-duration exercise bouts.

Background and aim of a randomised trial testing a daily fruit and nut snack bar's effects on weight, lipids and blood pressure in overweight adults; introduces the cardiovascular-risk rationale for fruit and nut snacks.
Methods of the trial: 94 overweight adults (BMI > 25) randomly assigned to add two fruit and nut bars (1421.9 kJ / 340 kcal) to their ad libitum diet or continue usual diet (control).

Outcome measures and design: weight as primary outcome, with waist circumference, lipid panel and blood pressure as secondary outcomes, assessed at baseline and after the 8-week treatment; start of the results section on weight change.

Results for weight and cardiometabolic outcomes: no change from baseline versus controls for weight (P = 0.44), waist circumference, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and lipid measures (total cholesterol, HDL, TC/HDL ratio, triglycerides, LDL), all non-significant.

Conclusions: two daily fruit and nut bars (340 kcal) did not cause weight gain; calls for further study of habitual snacking on nutrient-dense, satiating foods and diet quality, suggesting fibre-rich satiating snacks may aid weight stabilisation.
Closing conclusion sentences and copyright/publisher notice (2011, Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics, British Dietetic Association) for the fruit and nut bar trial article.

Introduces the study's aim: measuring glycemic indices of five date varieties in healthy people and their postprandial glucose effects in type 2 diabetes; also describes composition analysis and calculating flesh weight providing 50 g available carbohydrate.
Describes the study population: 13 healthy volunteers (mean age 40.2) and 10 type 2 diabetics on lifestyle measures and/or metformin (HbA1c 6.6%, mean age 40.8), continuing the methods section.

Details the crossover protocol: each subject tested on eight days with 50 g glucose (three times) and 50 g available carbohydrate from each date variety, plus the capillary glucose sampling schedules for healthy and diabetic groups.

Explains how glycemic index was calculated as the ratio of incremental areas under the glucose response curves (dates vs glucose), names the statistical tests used (Mann-Whitney U, repeated-measures ANOVA), and begins the Results section.
Reports mean GI values (± SEM) for the five date varieties (Fara'd, Lulu, Bo ma'an, Dabbas, Khalas) in healthy subjects and the similar values in the type 2 diabetes group.

States the key finding of no significant differences in GI between healthy and diabetic groups or among the date varieties (ANOVA F = 0.365, p = 0.83), and begins the Conclusion that date GIs are low.

Concludes that dates have low glycemic indices, do not cause significant postprandial glucose excursions in diabetics, may benefit diabetics in a balanced diet, and gives the ClinicalTrials.gov registration number NCT01307904.
Final fragment of the ClinicalTrials.gov trial registration number (NCT01307904) ending the document.

Introduction and study aim from a 2011 secondary analysis of NHANES 1999-2004 adults, examining dried fruit consumption's links to nutrient intake, diet quality (HEI-2005), and overweight/obesity measures.

Methods: adults aged 19+ (n=13,292) from NHANES 1999-2004; dried fruit consumers defined as ≥1/8 cup-equivalent per day using 24-hour recalls; diet quality assessed with the Healthy Eating Index 2005.
Statistical methods (covariate-adjusted means, SEs, prevalence, odds ratios) and key prevalence finding that about 7% of the population consumed dried fruit.

Results on nutrient differences: consumers had higher intakes of shortfall nutrients such as fiber, vitamins A, E, C, K, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, and potassium, plus improved MyPyramid food intake patterns.
Diet quality results: consumers scored higher on the solid fats/alcohol/added sugars component and total HEI-2005 (59.3 vs 49.4), and weight and BMI measures are introduced as lower in consumers.

Anthropometric results and conclusion: consumers had lower adjusted weight, BMI, and waist circumference, with the overall finding that dried fruit intake relates to better nutrient intake, diet quality, and lower adiposity; includes 2011 Elsevier copyright.
Closing copyright notice (Elsevier Inc., 2011) ending the abstract of the dried fruit and NHANES study.
Introduces the randomised cross-over trial background on chronic constipation treatment, the unmet need for natural alternatives, and the study aim to compare dried plums (prunes) with psyllium.

Describes the trial methods: an 8-week single-blind randomised cross-over design giving dried plums or psyllium (each providing 6 g/day fibre) for 3 weeks with a 1-week washout, plus a daily symptom and stool diary.

Lists the outcome assessments (complete spontaneous bowel movements, global relief, stool consistency, straining, tolerability, taste) and reports the participant demographics (40 subjects, mostly female, mean age 38) and primary results start.

Reports results: dried plums significantly improved weekly complete spontaneous bowel movements and stool consistency versus psyllium, with no significant difference in straining or global symptoms, and equal palatability and safety.

States the conclusion that dried plums are safe, palatable and more effective than psyllium for mild to moderate constipation and should be considered first-line therapy, with the 2011 Blackwell Publishing copyright notice.

Introduction of a review on date fruit (Phoenix dactylifera) as an emerging medicinal food; covers the date palm's long history, folk-medicine uses, and the historically limited scientific study of its health benefits despite its role as a staple food.
Continues the introduction by describing the recent surge of research (in vitro, animal, and phytochemical identification/quantification studies) into the health benefits of dates.

Summarizes the document's main claim that dates are nutritious and may offer health benefits, and argues that despite their sugar content, many date varieties have a low glycemic index, challenging the view that dates are like candy and cause chronic disease.

Calls for further investigation to validate dates' benefits and mechanisms, and states the review's aims: summarizing phytochemical composition, nutritional significance, and health benefits of date consumption.
Concludes the introduction by stating the review's aim to discuss dates' great potential as a medicinal food for a range of diseases affecting humans.

Introduces the study's aim: measuring glycemic indices of five date varieties in healthy people and their postprandial glucose effects in type 2 diabetes, including composition analysis and flesh weights equal to 50 g available carbohydrate.
Describes the study population: 13 healthy volunteers and 10 type 2 diabetes patients (on lifestyle measures and/or metformin, HbA1c 6.6%), with their mean ages.

Details the crossover protocol: eight test days with 50 g glucose (three times) and 50 g available carbohydrate from each date variety, plus capillary glucose sampling schedules for healthy and diabetic subjects.

Explains GI calculation as the ratio of incremental areas under the glucose response curves for dates versus glucose, names the statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U, repeated measures ANOVA), and begins the results.
Reports mean GI values (±SEM) for the five date varieties (Fara'd, Lulu, Bo ma'an, Dabbas, Khalas) in healthy subjects and the similar values in the type 2 diabetic group.

States that no significant differences existed between control and diabetic groups or among date varieties (ANOVA F = 0.365, p = 0.83), and concludes the dates have low glycemic indices with minimal glucose excursions in diabetics.
Concludes that dates may benefit diabetic individuals within a balanced diet and gives the ClinicalTrials.gov registration number NCT01307904.
Final fragment of the trial registration number NCT01307904 from the study's ClinicalTrials.gov registration.

Background and objective of the 1-year trial: rationale for studying dried apple versus dried plum in reducing cardiovascular risk factors in postmenopausal women, given the rise in CVD risk after menopause due to ovarian hormone decline.

Study objective and design setup: the 1-year clinical trial comparing dried apple and dried plum for cardiovascular risk reduction, and the start of the Design section describing recruitment of 160 postmenopausal women in Tallahassee, FL, during 2007-2009.

Methods: 160 postmenopausal women randomly assigned to dried apple (75 g/day) or dried plum (control), with fasting blood sampling at baseline, 3, 6, and 12 months, plus physical activity and 7-day dietary recalls.
Results on energy intake and body weight: neither dried fruit changed reported energy intake, and the dried apple group lost 1.5 kg, not significantly different from the dried plum group.

Results on total and LDL cholesterol between groups: dried apple gave significantly lower total cholesterol than dried plum only at 6 months, and dried plum produced small non-significant reductions in cholesterol and LDL.

Within-group cholesterol changes: dried plum lowered total cholesterol and LDL numerically at 12 months (3.5% and 8%), while dried apple significantly reduced total cholesterol and LDL by 9% and 16% at 3 months versus baseline.

Longer-term within-group apple effects: total cholesterol and LDL fell further to 13% and 24% at 6 months and then held steady, and apple improved atherogenic risk ratios while dried plum showed no lipid profile changes.
Inflammation and oxidative markers: both fruits lowered lipid hydroperoxide and C-reactive protein, with CRP significantly lower in the dried plum group than the dried apple group at 3 months.

Conclusions on between-group differences: no significant differences in atherogenic cholesterols except total cholesterol at 6 months, but within-group analysis shows 75 g dried apple (about two medium apples) lowers atherogenic cholesterol as early as 3 months.

Final conclusions on health benefits: dried apple and dried plum both show anti-inflammatory and antioxidative benefits, followed by the copyright and publisher notice (Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Elsevier, 2012).
Closing copyright and publisher attribution fragment (Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics; Elsevier Inc.; all rights reserved) ending the document.
Abstract of a crossover clinical trial on dried California Mission figs (120 g/day) and serum lipids in hyperlipidemic adults; covers background, design, and the start of the methods.
Methods and early results of the fig crossover trial: 5-week usual-diet vs. figs-added periods, six 24-hour dietary recalls, and Bonferroni-corrected null findings for LDL, HDL, and triglycerides.

Total cholesterol results from the fig crossover trial, including the sequence-specific analysis (usual-then-figs n=41 increased; figs-then-usual n=42 unchanged) and the soluble fiber intake comparison begins.
Dietary and secondary outcomes of the fig trial: soluble fiber and sugar intake differences between diets, body weight change, and the start of the conclusions on LDL and triglycerides.
Final conclusion of the dried fig lipid trial: daily figs did not lower LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides were not significantly changed despite higher sugar intake.

This chunk opens the study on herbal infusions, describing the five herbs tested (chamomile, mint, St John's wort, sage, nettle) from three producers and the mineral analysis of dried herbs and infusions for calcium, magnesium, iron, zinc and copper.

This chunk covers the methods and key findings: atomic absorption spectrometry was used, element content depended on herb type and origin, and iron showed the lowest extraction into infusions (4.4-12.4%) while copper showed the highest (26.7-50.7%).
This concluding chunk gives the study's overall conclusion that, at average consumption, herbal infusions are not an important source of calcium, magnesium, iron, zinc or copper in human nutrition.

Abstract opening of a 2011 study on Rooibos (Aspalathus linearis) and adrenal steroidogenesis, introducing adrenal steroid hormone homeostasis and its links to hypertension, metabolic syndrome, and diabetes.

Abstract continuation introducing Rooibos's phenolic compounds (aspalathin is unique) and the study's aim: testing inhibitory effects of Rooibos, aspalathin and nothofagin on adrenal steroidogenesis, with CYP17 and CYP21 activity results in COS-1 cells.

Abstract middle describing CYP17A1 (17α-hydroxylase/17,20 lyase) and CYP21 inhibition in COS-1 cells, and the development of a novel UPLC-MS/MS method quantifying 21 steroid metabolites in H295R adrenal carcinoma cells.

Abstract results on H295R cells under basal and forskolin-stimulated conditions: total steroid output decreased with Rooibos, aspalathin and nothofagin, and Rooibos cut total output 4-fold, reducing aldosterone and cortisol precursors.

Abstract specific steroid results: DHEA-sulfate unchanged, while androstenedione (A4) and 11β-hydroxyandrostenedione (11βOH-A4) were inhibited 5.5-fold and 2.3-fold, and 11βOH-A4 identified as a major steroidogenic product.

Abstract conclusion on 11βOH-A4 as the product of A4 hydroxylation by CYP11B1 (11β-hydroxylase), first confirmed here, and summary that Rooibos and its dihydrochalcones alter mineralocorticoid, glucocorticoid and androgen pathway flux.
Abstract closing statement on the possible alleviation of negative effects from elevated glucocorticoid levels, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction of a study on green tea flavonoid EGCG: states the health claims of green tea and that the double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study examines EGCG's effects on brain activity and mood, with baseline EEG and cognitive/cardiovascular measures.

Methods and first results: describes the protocol (baseline assessments, resting EEG before and 120 min after 300 mg EGCG or placebo) and reports that EGCG increased alpha, beta and theta EEG activity, most prominent in midline frontal and central regions.

Core findings: localizes the EEG effects to frontal and medial frontal gyri and reports that EGCG, relative to placebo, raised self-rated calmness and lowered self-rated stress, suggesting a relaxed but attentive state.

Interpretation and conclusion: links the results to green tea's reputation for relaxing and refreshing effects, argues for further controlled human studies on EGCG's brain effects, and carries the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
Closing fragment of the abstract containing only the tail of the Elsevier copyright statement (2011, all rights reserved), with no substantive study content.

Introduction and study design of a randomized open-label two-way crossover trial of Hibiscus sabdariffa aqueous extract (HSE) vs water in eight healthy volunteers, measuring plasma FRAP antioxidant potential and biokinetic variables.

Definition of the biokinetic endpoints: plasma AUC above pre-dose levels for FRAP, ascorbic acid and urate, and 24-hour urinary excretion of antioxidants, uric acid, malondialdehyde (oxidative stress marker) and hippuric acid (polyphenol intake marker).

Key results: HSE significantly increased plasma FRAP AUC and urinary excretion of FRAP, ascorbic acid and hippuric acid, while malondialdehyde excretion decreased; main hibiscus anthocyanins and one glucuronide conjugate were quantified in urine (0.02% of dose).

Conclusion that aqueous HSE enhanced systemic antioxidant potential and reduced oxidative stress in humans, with increased urinary hippuric acid indicating high biotransformation of HSE polyphenols, likely by colonic microbiota.
Closing statement on microbiota-driven polyphenol biotransformation after hibiscus intake, followed by the 2012 Society of Chemical Industry copyright notice.
Introduction and aim of a rat bioavailability study on a polyphenol-enriched Hibiscus sabdariffa extract, identifying metabolites in plasma and their antioxidant status.
Methods overview: HPLC-ESI-TOF-MS used for the bioavailability analysis, and the antioxidant status of plasma assessed by complementary assays (FRAP, TBARS, SOD activity).

Results summary: seventeen polyphenols and metabolites detected and quantified, eleven of them metabolites; phenolic acids found unmodified in plasma while most flavonols appear as quercetin or kaempferol glucuronides.

Mechanistic interpretation: flavonol glucuronide conjugates with longer elimination half-lives are proposed to inhibit lipid peroxidation in cell membranes, whereas phenolic acids act earlier via ferric ion reduction and superoxide scavenging.

Conclusion: flavonol-conjugated forms (quercetin and kaempferol) are proposed as the main compounds behind the observed antioxidant effects and healthy effects of the H. sabdariffa polyphenolic extract; includes the 2012 Wiley-VCH copyright notice.
Closing copyright line (2012 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim) ending the abstract of the Hibiscus sabdariffa bioavailability study.

Introduction and objective of a study on stinging nettles (Urtica dioica): it tests whether nettle spicules cause the immediate stinging and burning on skin, using electron microscopy of murine skin, and hypothesizes that the mechanism is both biochemical and mechanical.

Study design: the hypothesis that nettle action is biochemical and mechanical is tested by exposing mouse skin to nettles and examining it with electron microscopy; the methods section begins describing the source of the dermis samples (post-mortem hairless mice).

Methods detail: post-mortem hairless mouse dermis was brushed under nettle stems and leaves to mimic patient exposure, with an unexposed control group; all samples were then imaged by scanning electron microscopy. The results section begins here.

Results: unexposed control skin showed no spicules, while nettle-exposed skin showed many smooth spicules piercing the surface, some with empty-looking bases, supporting a mechanical component of the irritation.

Conclusions: nettle dermatitis appears both biochemical and mechanical, with spicule impalement accounting for mechanical irritation alongside known chemical effects, and further study of treatments is warranted.
Copyright and publication notice for the article (Wilderness Medical Society, 2011; Elsevier Inc.), closing the document.

Opening of the study abstract: purpose and design of a 6-month, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized crossover trial of Urtica dioica (stinging nettle) for LUTS from benign prostatic hyperplasia, with 620 patients and the outcome measures listed (IPSS, Qmax, PVR, PSA, testosterone, prostate size).

Continuation of the methods: the outcome measures are described, and at the 6-month mark unblinding showed placebo patients were switched to Urtica dioica, with both groups continuing treatment to 18 months.

Start of the results: retention figures (558 of 620 completed; 287/305 treated, 271/315 placebo) and the intention-to-treat finding that 81% of the Urtica dioica group versus 16% of placebo reported improved LUTS at 6 months.

Key efficacy data: the IPSS fell from 19.8 to 11.8 with Urtica dioica versus 19.2 to 17.7 with placebo (P = 0.002), and both IPSS and Qmax improved more with the drug, with peak flow gains starting in this chunk.

Further objective results: peak flow improved 8.2 mL/s with treatment versus 3.4 mL/s with placebo, postvoid residual urine fell from 73 to 36 mL in the treated group, and PSA and testosterone were unchanged in both groups.

Prostate size and safety findings: transrectal ultrasound showed a modest reduction in prostate volume from 40.1 to 36.3 cc with Urtica dioica but none with placebo, benefit at 18-month follow-up was confined to patients who continued therapy, and no side effects were reported.
Study conclusion: Urtica dioica showed beneficial effects for symptomatic BPH in this trial, but the authors call for further clinical trials to confirm the results before judging it effective.

Introduction to a case report of a 53-year-old dietitian with idiopathic Parkinson's disease (diagnosed 2000), describing the study's aim and the patient's background and early basic diet (low animal fat, fruits, vegetables, whole grains, olive oil, nuts).
Describes the patient's basic low-animal-fat diet started in 2000, which alone failed to halt PD progression, and the 2009 enhancement of the diet with dietary sources of fisetin and hexacosanol.

Reports the clinical outcome six months after starting the fisetin- and hexacosanol-enhanced diet in 2009, with the neurologist noting marked improvement in motor symptoms such as rigidity, micrographia, bradykinesia, and dystonia.

Details the resolved symptoms (rigidity, dystonia, gait changes, hypomimia, retropulsion), the effect of diet non-adherence causing worsening, minimal change in tremor or seborrhea, and the persistence of improvement to date.
Concluding claim that this is the first reported case of adjunctive diet therapy significantly reducing Parkinson's symptoms without altering or increasing medications.

Opening of the abstract describing the study design: 16 Parkinson's patients with daily levodopa response fluctuations placed on a protein redistribution diet (protein-free until evening, then unrestricted), and the result that 5 of 16 showed significant reduction in diurnal motor fluctuations.

Middle of the abstract summarizing outcomes: beyond the 5 responders with clear benefit in reducing motor fluctuations, all patients tended toward more constant levodopa response, and the authors frame the diet as a potentially useful intervention.
Concluding sentence of the abstract recommending a trial of the redistribution protein diet as a simple, worthwhile approach for Parkinson's patients who start showing oscillating levodopa responses.

Introduction and methods opening of a 6-week randomized controlled trial of caffeine in Parkinson disease, stating the rationale (epidemiologic link to lower PD risk) and the study aims on somnolence, motor severity, and nonmotor features.

Trial design and primary outcome: patients with PD and daytime somnolence (Epworth >10) receive caffeine 100 mg BID for 3 weeks then 200 mg BID for 3 weeks, or placebo; the primary outcome is the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, with secondary outcomes including motor severity, sleep, fatigue, depression, and quality of life.

Statistical methods (Bayesian hierarchical models with covariate adjustment) and enrollment/randomization numbers (61 patients: 31 placebo, 30 caffeine), plus the start of the intention-to-treat primary result showing a nonsignificant Epworth reduction.

Primary and secondary results: the nonsignificant ITT Epworth change (-1.71, 95% CI -3.57 to 0.13), the CGI-based improvement in somnolence, the significant per-protocol Epworth reduction, and the start of the motor findings on UPDRS.

Motor and other outcome results: caffeine reduced total UPDRS (-4.69) and objective motor component (-3.15); no changes in quality of life, depression, or sleep quality beyond modest global health gains; adverse events were similar between groups.

Conclusions and interpretation: caffeine gave only equivocal, borderline benefit for excessive somnolence but improved objective motor measures, supporting a larger long-term trial; the evidence classification statement begins here.
Evidence classification: the study provides Class I evidence that caffeine up to 200 mg BID for 6 weeks gave no significant benefit for excessive daytime sleepiness in PD.

Introduction to a study of seven Parkinson's patients with levodopa-induced motor fluctuations, examining how dietary protein affects their motor function, with levodopa doses and other antiparkinsonian drugs held constant.

Findings that regular and high-protein diets raise plasma large neutral amino acids (LNAAs), which compete with levodopa for blood-brain barrier transport, and that patients with elevated LNAAs had parkinsonian symptoms despite high levodopa levels.

Results showing that lowering amino acid levels relieved symptoms, and that on a low-protein diet with low LNAAs patients were dyskinetic all day, with levodopa levels slightly lower than on high-protein diets.

Conclusion describing a redistribution diet (protein-free until supper, unrestricted afterward) that patients tolerate because it allows near-normal daytime motor function by managing LNAA competition with levodopa.

Study design and population: abstract of a prospective cohort study on dietary flavonoid intake and Parkinson disease risk, describing aims, the Health Professional Follow-up Study and Nurses' Health Study cohorts, and flavonoid subclasses and food sources examined.

Methods and case count: describes flavonoid intake assessment (updated food composition database, validated food frequency questionnaire), the five major flavonoid-rich food sources, and the 805 incident PD cases (438 men, 367 women) over 20-22 years of follow-up.

Main male finding: after multivariable adjustment, men in the highest total flavonoid quintile had about 40% lower PD risk (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.43-0.83, p trend = 0.001), with the hazard ratio and trend statistics reported.

Null and subclass results: no significant association for total flavonoids in women or pooled analyses; pooled subclass analyses show anthocyanins and berries associated with lower PD risk (HR 0.76 and 0.77, p trend < 0.02).
Conclusions: intake of some flavonoids, particularly anthocyanins and berries and especially in men, may reduce PD risk, though protective effects of other plant food constituents cannot be excluded.
Introduction of a Japanese study on coffee, caffeine, and Parkinson's disease risk, noting prior research was mainly Western and motivating the Asian (Japanese) population analysis.

Study methods for the Japanese Parkinson's case-control study: 249 PD cases and 368 controls, dietary intake assessed by self-administered diet history questionnaire, and the list of adjustment covariates (demographics, smoking, BMI, glycemic index, nutrients).

Key results: coffee, black tea, and Japanese/Chinese tea intake were significantly inversely associated with PD risk, with adjusted odds ratios for highest vs. lowest quartile of 0.52, 0.58, and 0.59 and their 95% confidence intervals.

Main conclusions: a clear inverse dose-response between total caffeine intake and PD risk, confirming coffee and caffeine reduce PD risk, and the claim that this is the first study linking Japanese and Chinese tea intake inversely with PD.
Closing sentence of the abstract stating the novelty finding on Japanese and Chinese teas and PD risk, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces a 2025-era pilot study testing whether a plant-food diet (PFD) improves motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease, comparing 12 intervention patients (PDi) against 13 omnivorous-diet controls (PDc) over the study design and sample description.
