Reports the main results after 4 weeks of the plant-food diet: significant improvements in the UPDRS total score, UPDRS motor sub-score III, and modified Hoehn and Yahr stage for the PDi group versus controls, with Mann-Whitney P-values.
Concludes that the plant-food diet may help manage Parkinson's patients by improving motor performance, while noting these preliminary pilot findings require confirmation in additional studies.

Introduction and background of a study on caffeine intake and Parkinson disease risk in the CPS II Nutrition Cohort, noting the association in men and the uncertain findings in women, possibly due to hormone replacement therapy interaction; the Methods section begins here.

Methods of the CPS II Nutrition Cohort prospective study: caffeine and coffee intake assessed at baseline, 317 incident Parkinson disease cases (197 men, 120 women) confirmed by physicians and medical record review, and proportional hazards models used for relative risks.

Methods conclusion and start of Results: relative risks estimated adjusting for age, smoking and alcohol, with the main finding that high caffeine consumption is associated with reduced Parkinson disease risk.

Key quantitative results: the 5th vs 1st quintile of caffeine intake gives RR 0.43 in men and 0.61 in women; among women the protective association is stronger in never users of hormone replacement therapy (RR 0.32) than ever users (RR 0.81), and decaffeinated coffee shows no association.

Interaction p-value for hormone replacement therapy in women, the null finding for decaffeinated coffee, and the study conclusion that caffeine has a likely protective effect on Parkinson disease incidence, attenuated by hormone replacement therapy in women.

This chunk opens the study abstract on Parkinson's disease, introducing the investigation of a high insoluble fiber diet (DRIF) on motor disability and the pharmacokinetics of oral L-dopa in constipated patients, and reports its positive effect on plasma L-dopa concentration and motor function.

This chunk concludes the abstract on a diet rich in insoluble fiber for Parkinson's disease. It reports that the greatest plasma L-dopa increase occurred at 30 and 60 minutes after dosing, links constipation relief to higher L-dopa bioavailability, and suggests DRIF as a coadjuvant treatment.

Introduction of a 2007 CHE PAN conference consensus report on Parkinson's disease and environmental risk factors: states PD's prevalence rank, public interest in environmental contributors, and the June 2007 Sunnyvale expert meeting's methods.

Continuation of the methods and results framing: the expert group's aim to assess environmental contributions to PD, followed by the statement that the report presents consensus conclusions and a brief research-needs summary, and the start of the conclusions on PD complexity and multiple pathogenic pathways.

Conclusions on PD heterogeneity: multiple pathways can lead to PD, individual and population-level risk determinants differ, and rare genetic mutations cause PD in under 10% of U.S. cases, with incomplete penetrance hinting at environmental involvement.

Final conclusions on gene-environment interplay: environmental factors and genetic makeup likely interact to shape PD risk, the need to understand how risk factors interact, and the broader relevance of PD research to other neurodegenerative disorders.
Closing fragment of the final sentence of the conclusions, stating that studying PD is likely to advance understanding of other neurodegenerative diseases.

Introduction and background of a case-control study on serum organochlorine pesticide levels in Parkinson disease, stating the study objective of testing whether these pesticides are elevated in PD patients' serum.
Study design and participants (50 PD patients, 43 controls, 20 Alzheimer patients) and the start of results, showing β-HCH detection rates in PD versus controls.
Results comparing β-HCH detectability and median levels across PD, control, and Alzheimer groups, noting no notable differences for the other 15 organochlorine pesticides.
Odds ratio results showing β-HCH presence predicts PD versus controls (OR 4.39) and versus Alzheimer disease (OR 5.20), supporting the association between serum β-HCH and PD.
Conclusions that β-HCH is associated with a PD diagnosis and that further research is needed on its possible etiologic role in some PD cases.
Introduces the aim and background of a retrospective study on traumatic brain injuries (TBI) in the Asterix comic books, including the methods used to examine neurological status and risk factors.
Describes the study's methods in detail, linking clinical findings to trauma mechanism, sociocultural background, and circumstances, and begins the results with the total of 704 TBIs identified.

Reports demographic and injury characteristics from the Asterix TBI results: victims were mostly adult males, assault caused 98.8% of injuries, over half were severe (GCS 3-8), and basal skull fractures were found, with no deaths or permanent deficits.

Presents results on the nationality of victims and offenders (Romans as the largest victim group, Gauls causing nearly 90% of TBIs), helmet use and loss rates, and the share of injuries occurring under the influence of the 'magic potion'.

Gives the conclusions that over half of patients had severe initial impairment of consciousness without permanent deficit, and names the factors significantly linked to severe impairment: Roman nationality, hypoglossal paresis, lost helmet, and magic potion ingestion.
Closes the abstract by stating the statistical threshold (p ≤ 0.05) used for the significant correlations between risk factors and severe initial impairment of consciousness.

Introduces PCBs as banned but persistent environmental chemicals and their suspected role as a Parkinson's disease risk factor, setting up the study's motivation. Relevant to the background on PCB exposure and PD.
States the study objective: examining PCB levels in post-mortem brain tissue against Parkinson's diagnosis and nigral depigmentation, and whether sex stratification strengthens the association.
Describes methods: post-mortem brain samples from Emory University Brain Bank and the Nun Study, with eight prevalent PCB congeners measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry.

Reports main results: congeners 153 and 180 elevated in PD brains overall, and in females with PD total PCBs and congeners 138, 153, 180 elevated versus controls, with no significant difference in males.
Presents the Nun Study findings in cognitively unimpaired women without PD signs, where higher total PCB and congeners 138, 153, 180 appear with moderate nigral depigmentation versus mild or none.
Concludes that brain PCB levels relate to PD-related pathology and that the data support epidemiological and laboratory evidence linking PCB exposure to PD risk.
Final conclusion emphasizing the PCB-PD link and greater susceptibility in females, tying the findings back to prior epidemiological and laboratory research.

Opening excerpt of a 2004 HCUP Statistical Brief (#27) on hospital admissions for traumatic brain injury (TBI). It introduces the comparison of TBI admissions' utilization and costs against stays for all other injuries, and previews the topics covered: trends, patient characteristics, causes, and coexisting conditions.

Continuation of the brief's introductory excerpt. It previews the remaining analyses: how TBI admissions are distributed across patient characteristics, the common causes of TBI-related hospital admissions, and the coexisting conditions associated with these injuries. It also states that all reported differences are significant at the 0.05 level or better.

Final sentence of the excerpt, stating that all differences between estimates in the text are statistically significant at the 0.05 level or better. It is a methodological note on the reliability of the TBI admission statistics reported in the brief.

Abstract of a Parkinson disease study on nigral neuronal dysfunction and degeneration preceding Lewy pathology; introduces the aims and methods (TH immunoreactivity and neuron density in 63 normal, ILBD, and PD cases).

Abstract results section comparing ILBD with normal subjects: higher TH-negative cell percentages and lower nigral neuron densities at Braak PD stages 1 and 2, before Lewy pathology deposition in the nigrostriatal system.

Abstract results continuing: ILBD neuron densities fall between normal and PD cases, TH-negative percentages exceed both groups, and neuron density and dysfunction stay stable across Braak stages in ILBD.

Abstract conclusions: significant neurodegeneration and cellular dysfunction precede Lewy pathology in the substantia nigra, challenging LP's pathogenic role and the view that ILBD is always preclinical PD.

Introduction and study aim of a paper on açai (Euterpe oleracea) polyphenolics' effects on proliferation and apoptosis in HL-60 leukemia cells, including interactions between anthocyanins and non-anthocyanin polyphenolics.

Main results: açai polyphenolic fractions (0.17-10.7 microM) reduced HL-60 cell proliferation by 56-86%, likely via caspase-3-mediated apoptosis; anthocyanin and polyphenolic fractions acted nonadditively on antiproliferative activity.

Glycoside versus aglycone comparison: at equimolar concentrations, glycosidic phenolic acids and flavonoids produced larger changes in proliferation and apoptosis than their aglycones, while anthocyanin aglycones showed the opposite trend; the study concludes açai is a rich bioactive polyphenol source.
Concluding statement that whole food systems should be studied when assessing the health benefits of individual phytochemicals, as emphasized by the açai findings.

Introduces the 2010-era pilot study's background: açai (Euterpe oleracea) berry as an antioxidant functional food, with little human evidence beyond increased plasma antioxidant capacity, and the metabolic syndrome rationale.

Continues the background, noting metabolic syndrome as a cluster of cardiovascular and type-2 diabetes risk factors and the preliminary hypothesis that reducing reactive oxygen species may normalize related metabolic pathways, motivating the study.
Methods section of the açai pilot study: an open-label trial with 10 overweight adults (BMI 25-30) consuming 100 g açai pulp twice daily for one month.

Describes the outcome measures of the açai pilot study (fasting glucose, insulin, lipids, eNO, hs-CRP) and the standardized meal test of glucose, blood pressure and eNO at baseline and after the 30-day treatment.

Key results of the açai pilot study: significant reductions in fasting glucose, insulin and total cholesterol after 30 days, with borderline changes in LDL and the total/HDL cholesterol ratio (p = 0.051).
Results continued: açai blunted the postprandial plasma glucose rise (AUC, p = 0.047) but had no effect on blood pressure, hs-CRP or eNO, followed by the start of the conclusion.
Conclusion of the açai pilot study: in this uncontrolled trial, açai pulp reduced selected metabolic disease risk markers in overweight adults, and the authors call for further controlled studies.
Introduction to the study: why pomegranate juice health benefits drove pomegranate extract supplements, the key tannin compounds (punicalagins, punicalin) and ellagic acid used for standardization.

Background and study aim: ellagic acid standardization of pomegranate supplements can be undermined by adulteration with cheaper plant ellagic acid; the study sets out to compare phytochemicals and antioxidant activity of commercial supplements beyond ellagic acid.
Methods: 27 commercial pomegranate extract supplements (capsules, tablets, soft gels) analyzed for total phenolics by GAE and EAE assays, and punicalagin, punicalin, and ellagic acid by HPLC.

Methods and results: antioxidant capacity measured by TEAC assay; HPLC profiling classified supplements into 5 with typical pomegranate tannin profile, 17 dominated by ellagic acid with few or no tannins, and 5 with neither tannins nor ellagic acid.

Conclusion: ellagic acid-based standardization does not ensure authenticity of pomegranate supplements, and future research is needed on health effects of substituting ellagic acid for the full phytochemical mix.
Final sentence of the abstract restating the call for future research on the health impact of ellagic acid substitution in pomegranate extract supplements.

Introduces the open-label pilot study of an açai-based fruit and berry juice blend (MonaVie Active) on pain and range of motion in 14 participants with pain-limited ROM, including age-related osteoarthritis, and states the antioxidant rationale.

Describes the study population scope and intervention details: 120 mL daily MonaVie Active juice, mainly açai pulp (Euterpe oleracea) plus other fruit concentrates, for 12 weeks, with assessments scheduled at baseline and weeks 2, 4, 8, and 12.

Covers the outcome measures and methods: structured nurse interviews, pain and ADL questionnaires, blood sampling, a visual analogue scale for pain, and dual digital inclinometry for ROM per AMA guidelines.
Reports the main results: significant reductions in pain, improved ROM and ADLs, and serum antioxidant status (CAP-e assay) improving from week 2 onward and continuing through week 12 (P<.01).

Summarizes secondary findings: CRP reduced at 12 weeks without statistical significance, mild decrease in lipid peroxidation, and CAP-e antioxidant status correlating best with improvements in pain, ROM, and ADLs.
Concludes that the association between increased antioxidant status, better ROM, and pain reduction justifies further research, closing the abstract.
Introduction: pomegranate (Punica granatum) as a high-value crop, the health-based consumer value of pomegranate juice (PJ), and the motivation for developing an authenticity standard.
Method: the IMAS algorithm was built from existing databases and chemical characterization of 45 commercial juice samples from 23 US manufacturers.

Scope of data: non-US pomegranate juice and fruit samples (Iran, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Syria, India, China) informed the protocol, and anthocyanin/punicalagin polyphenol markers are described as the universal PJ signature.
Sugar markers: at 16 Brix, PJ should contain mannitol above 0.3 g/100 mL, with glucose:mannitol of 4-15 and glucose:fructose of 0.8-1.0, and no sucrose due to isomerase activity during processing.

Adulteration criteria: stable isotope ratio >-25 per mil excludes corn or cane sugar; sorbitol, maltose, and tartaric acid limits; proline above 25 mg/L indicates added grape; malic acid above 0.1 g/100 mL indicates other fruit juices.

Adulterant types: malic acid signals apple, pear, grape, cherry, plum, or aronia juice, and concentrated aronia, blueberry, blackberry juices or grape pigments are used to fake color, producing abnormal anthocyanin profiles.

Astringency masking: nonpomegranate sugars are added to poor-quality juice or peel extract to offset astringency, a common adulteration; the IMAS profile was derived from these analyses and literature.
Conclusion: the IMAS is validated for detecting PJ adulteration, and a survey of commercial juices found only 6 of 23 fully met all IMAS criteria.
Introduction to the study: acai (Euterpe oleraceae) is reported to have high in vitro antioxidant capacity, and the authors evaluate freeze-dried acai pulp/skin powder (OptiAcai) with several assays.
Results on specific antioxidant assays: exceptional superoxide scavenging (SOD assay) and the highest reported food activity against peroxyl radicals by ORACFL, with the assay setup described.

Quantitative findings: peroxynitrite (NORAC) and hydroxyl radical (HORAC) activity are mild, acai's SOD value is 1614 units/g, the highest among fruits and vegetables tested, and total phenolics were measured for comparison.

Further antioxidant methods: the total antioxidant (TAO) assay separates 'slow-acting' and 'fast-acting' antioxidants, and a neutrophil ROS assay shows acai antioxidants enter human cells in functional form at low doses.
Anti-inflammatory and immune bioactivities are introduced; acai is identified as a potential COX-1 and COX-2 inhibitor and weakly reduces LPS-induced nitric oxide.
Conclusion of the bioactivity findings: acai shows no effect on lymphocyte proliferation or phagocytic capacity, rounding out the immune-function results.

Introduction of the study: background on Hibiscus sabdariffa and Hibiscus anthocyanins (HAs), noting their prior antioxidant and liver-protective reports, which motivates testing HAs against human cancer cells.
Core findings: HAs induce apoptosis, strongest in HL-60 leukemia cells, shown by flow cytometry to be dose- and time-dependent across 0-4 mg/ml.

Mechanistic results: HAs increase phosphorylation of p38 and c-Jun, release cytochrome c, and upregulate tBid, Fas, and FasL, followed by the setup of kinase inhibitor experiments (SB203580, PD98059, SP600125, wortmannin).
Inhibitor experiment outcome: only the p38 inhibitor SB203580 strongly blocked HAs-induced apoptosis and related protein changes, leading to the conclusion of a p38-FasL and Bid apoptotic pathway.
Conclusion: HAs may be developed as chemopreventive agents, though further study of their specificity and mechanisms is needed.

Abstract opening of the HL-60 paper: introduces the continuous myeloid cell line and its derivation from an acute promyelocytic leukemia patient's peripheral blood, with light/electron microscopy showing promyelocyte morphology.
Describes the cultured HL-60 cells' spontaneous and chemically enhanced differentiation beyond the promyelocyte stage, comparing induction to Friend erythroleukemia cell differentiation.

Covers HL-60 immunophenotype and functional properties: lacks lymphoid markers, expresses Fc and C3 complement receptors typical of granulocytes, and shows phagocytic and chemotactic activity tied to mature cell proportion.
Reports transformation features of HL-60 cells: colony formation in soft agar, chloroma tumor formation in nude mice, and a colony-stimulating activity source boosting cloning efficiency 5–30-fold.
Describes stability of the cell line over at least 85 passages and cytogenetic findings of aneuploidy, with chromosome-count shifts from 44 to 45 or 46 during passaging.
Details the consistent karyotypic abnormalities (deletions of chromosomes 5, 8, X and added marker chromosomes) and reports absence of DNA herpesvirus or RNA retrovirus in the cells.
Concluding statement that the HL-60 cultured line serves as a continuous human source for studying molecular myeloid differentiation and effects of physiologic, pharmacologic, and virologic factors.
Introduces Açaí fruit as a supplement claimed to boost immunity, notes limited evidence on its polyphenol fraction, and sets up the prior work on γδ T cell responses to plant supplement fractions.

States the hypothesis that Açaí polyphenol and polysaccharide fractions could activate γδ T cells, reports no agonist activity from polyphenols, and finds robust γδ T cell stimulation by the polysaccharide fraction across human, mouse, and bovine PBMC cultures.
Describes the methods: fractionating the crude Açaí polysaccharide preparation and testing the fractions in human PBMC cultures, which is the start of the size-based activity analysis.

Reports results: the largest Açaí polysaccharides were most active in vitro, activating myeloid and γδ T cells; in vivo they drove myeloid cell recruitment and IL-12 production, with implications for asthma and infectious disease.
Concluding fragment completing the abstract's final sentence on implications for treating asthma and infectious disease.

Opening of a case report on rhabdomyolysis in a 22-year-old man after taking a mislabeled acai berry weight-loss supplement; introduces the case and presents his initial presentation about 2 weeks after starting the product.

Middle of the case report: the patient's history of hypertension on amlodipine, lab confirmation of rhabdomyolysis (CK 84,000 IU/L, positive urine myoglobin), exclusion of other causes, gradual recovery and discharge on hospital day 5, and the start of the Naranjo causality assessment.

Results and conclusion section: the Naranjo score of 3 indicating a possible supplement-rhabdomyolysis link, the finding that no acai berry was present on analysis despite the label, and the start of the conclusion warning clinicians about supplement variability.
Final sentence of the conclusion: clinicians should recognize that dietary supplements may vary in uniformity and contain unknown contaminants, which is the case report's main takeaway.

Introduction and hypothesis from a study on açaí and red muscadine grape polyphenolics protecting human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) against inflammation, plus the aim of testing whether endothelial-relevant microRNAs are regulated by these extracts.
Results on glucose-induced HUVEC stress: açaí and muscadine grape polyphenolics (5-20 mg GAE/L) reduce oxidative stress and inflammation, lowering IL-6 and IL-8 expression at mRNA and protein levels.

Results on LPS-induced inflammation (1 μg/L): both extracts similarly inhibit adhesion molecule gene expression and NF-κB activation, with grape more effective at reducing PECAM-1 and ICAM-1 protein, and screening identifies microRNA-126 as the modulated miRNA.
Conclusion of the findings: microRNA-126 is the mechanism by which açaí and grape polyphenolics suppress VCAM-1 gene and protein expression in endothelial cells.

This opening chunk of the document introduces an evidence-based systematic review of acai (Euterpe oleracea) by the Natural Standard Research Collaboration, describing its goal of consolidating safety and efficacy literature with a validated, reproducible grading rationale and its inclusion of clinical trial analysis and a broad list of topics (expert opinion, folkloric use, history, pharmacology, and more).

This closing chunk completes the document's description of the Natural Standard acai systematic review, listing the remaining topics covered: expert opinion, folkloric precedent, history, pharmacology, kinetics/dynamics, drug interactions, adverse effects, toxicology, and dosing for Euterpe oleracea (acai).

Introduction and background of a study on the male epidemic of ischaemic heart disease with economic development, testing whether nutritionally driven pubertal sex steroids explain sex differences, using childhood meat eating in a Chinese population.

Study design and methods: a cross-sectional analysis of 19,418 older Chinese adults (≥50 years) from the Guangzhou Biobank Cohort Study, using multivariable linear and censored regression to test associations of childhood meat eating with WHR, HDL cholesterol and fasting glucose.

Key results: childhood almost-daily meat eating versus less-than-weekly intake was linked to higher waist-to-hip ratio in men (not women) after adjusting for age, childhood hunger, life-course socioeconomic position and lifestyle; no link to fasting glucose.

Specific effect estimate for WHR in men (0.007, 95% CI 0.0003 to 0.01) and the absence of a glucose association, followed by the authors' caveats that the exposure is crude and the findings modest, so results are preliminary.

Conclusions: the findings support the idea that the male excess of premature IHD and sex divergence in IHD rates during economic development may be nutritionally driven in childhood, calling for attention to sociohistorical context and puberty in developmental origins research.
Final sentence of the conclusions, urging greater focus on sociohistorical context and the role of puberty in understanding the developmental origins of non-communicable chronic diseases.

Introduction and background of a study on serum polybrominated diphenyl ether (PBDE) flame retardants as endocrine disruptors, stating the study's objective of examining PBDE effects on age at menarche in adolescent girls using NHANES 2003–2004 data.

Continuation of the background and objectives, followed by the methods: a sample of 271 adolescent girls aged 12–19 from NHANES 2003–2004, analyzing associations of individual and total serum BDE congeners with mean age at menarche and risk of menarche before age 12.

Methods details listing the specific lipid-adjusted serum BDE congeners analyzed (BDE-28, -47, -99, -100, -153, -154), followed by the start of the results, reporting a median total serum BDE concentration of 44.7 ng/g lipid.

Main results: higher serum PBDE levels were associated with slightly earlier menarche; each natural-log unit of total BDEs corresponded to a -0.10-year change in age at menarche (95% CI -0.33 to 0.13) and a risk ratio of 1.60 (95% CI 1.12–2.28) for menarche before age 12, after confounder adjustment.
Conclusion of the study: high serum PBDE concentrations during adolescence are associated with younger age at menarche, suggesting possible endocrine disruption effects on human reproductive timing.

Introduction to a review on nutrition as a modifiable lifestyle factor in puberty timing, noting that early puberty has health risks and that childhood overweight's role in earlier menarche may be overstated.

Presents recent observational findings that dietary protein intake (vegetable protein linked to later puberty, animal protein to earlier puberty) relates to pubertal timing independently of energy balance.

Describes isoflavone intake delaying breast development and peak height velocity in girls, notes these effect sizes rival those of neuroactive steroid hormones, and states the dietary pattern implications.

Concludes that diets high in vegetable protein and isoflavones and low in animal protein may lower breast cancer and total mortality risk; includes the 2012 International Life Sciences Institute copyright notice.

Introduction of a Flemish study on internal exposure to environmental pollutants and sexual maturation in 14-15-year-old adolescents, describing the study population (1679 randomly sampled participants) and data sources.

Methods and boys' results: describes data sources (school medical files, self-assessment questionnaires) and reports that serum HCB, p,p'-DDE and PCBs (PCB138/153/180) were positively associated with pubertal staging in boys.

Boys' gynecomastia results and girls' results: higher serum HCB linked to lower gynecomastia risk, higher blood lead to higher risk; in girls, blood lead is negatively associated with pubic hair development and PCBs with delayed menarche.

Conclusion: real-world pollutant exposure levels in the Flemish population are associated with measurable effects on pubertal development, though toxic mechanisms and sensitive exposure windows need further study.
Final sentence of the abstract stating that further research on toxic mode of action and sensitive exposure windows is needed to explain the findings.

Introduction and study objective from an abstract on childhood hormones and menarche timing: links early puberty to infancy weight gain and obesity, and aims to find age-8 hormone levels linked to early menarche independent of body size, in 329 girls from a UK birth cohort.

Study population and methods: 329 girls from a UK prospective birth cohort had blood drawn at mean age 8.1 years, with menarche tracked longitudinally; the outcome measures are fasting levels of IGF-I, androstenedione, DHEAS, leptin, insulin, IGFBP-1 and SHBG.

Measurement details and first results: menarche was self-reported by questionnaire in three categories (before 12, 12-13, after 13), and earlier menarche was associated with greater weight, height and BMI at age 8 (P-trend <0.001); unadjusted hormone associations are begun.

Unadjusted hormone findings and body-size adjustment: before adjusting for body size, earlier menarche tracked with higher IGF-I, androstenedione, DHEAS, leptin and insulin and lower IGFBP-1 and SHBG; after adjusting for BMI and height, only IGF-I, androstenedione and DHEAS stayed significant.

Main conclusion: higher age-8 IGF-I and adrenal androgens (androstenedione, DHEAS) predict earlier menarche independent of body size, suggesting these hormones functionally regulate puberty timing in girls.
Final interpretation: the hormones elevated in girls with rapid infancy weight gain may reflect developmental pathways that lead to earlier sexual maturation, closing the abstract's implications.

Introduces dietary microparticles (endogenous calcium phosphate vs. exogenous ingested particles) and quantifies daily UK intake of exogenous microparticles from additives, excipients, and toothpaste.
Describes how ingested exogenous microparticles adsorb ions and molecules from the intestinal lumen, driven by entropy and ionic attraction, with calcium ions especially well adsorbed.

Explains that adsorbed calcium gives microparticles a positive surface that binds organic molecules like LPS, peptidoglycans and antigens, and identifies M-cell rich lymphoid aggregates (Peyer's patches) as the main entry route into intestinal tissue.

Notes that M-cell lymphoid aggregates are an established efficient transport route for non-biological particles, and hypothesises this pathway serves endogenous calcium phosphate microparticles with immunological benefit.
Proposes that exogenous particles such as titanium dioxide and silicates hijack this M-cell route, and states the overview's aim: their roles in gut immune tolerance, activation and inflammation.
Concludes the overview's scope, stating it addresses the role of dietary microparticles in gut immune tolerance, immune activation and gut inflammation.

Introduction/background of a single-blind, randomized, multi-centre, placebo-controlled trial on a low-microparticle diet for active Crohn's disease, stating the aim to confirm whether reducing dietary microparticles induces remission, following a prior pilot study.

Methods section describing the trial design: 83 patients with active Crohn's disease randomized in a 2x2 factorial design to a diet low or normal in microparticles and/or calcium for 16 weeks, with all patients receiving a reducing prednisolone dose.

Methods continued: outcome measures (Crohn's disease activity index, Van Hees index, quality of life, and inflammation markers including ESR, CRP, intestinal permeability, faecal calprotectin), and the design of returning to normal diet after 16 weeks followed by 36 weeks of follow-up.

Results section reporting that dietary manipulation gave no added benefit over corticosteroids on any outcome during the 16-week trial or the follow-up to one year, with example logistic regression remission (P=0.1) and clinical response (P=0.8) figures for normal versus low microparticle groups.

Conclusion: the adequately powered, carefully controlled dietary trial found no evidence that reducing microparticle intake aids remission in active Crohn's disease, along with the closing statistics of the logistic regression results.
Final chunk containing only a closing period, marking the end of the abstract's conclusion sentence on the microparticle diet trial in Crohn's disease.

Opening of the abstract for a study on micro- and nano-particle debris in human colon tissue, describing the Environmental Scanning Electron Microscope method and the 18 cancer and Crohn's disease samples examined.

Middle of the abstract reporting results: particles found in all 18 diseased colon samples, heterogeneous chemistry by X-ray microprobe but homogeneous particle size, and no debris in three healthy control cadavers.

Concluding part of the abstract stating that generally biocompatible particulate debris appears in pathological human colon specimens and suggesting a possible link between the particles and the underlying disease.
Final word of the abstract, closing the sentence about the cases analysed; a fragment with almost no standalone content, belonging to the conclusion on particles and pathology.

Introduction to dietary microparticles in Crohn's disease study: defines microparticles, endogenous (Ca/phosphate) and exogenous (TiO2, Psil) sources, and notes the unresolved question of whether intake differs in Crohn's disease.

Study aim and design: the authors state the research gap on microparticle intake in Crohn's disease, then describe comparing inactive CD patients with matched general practice controls (91 per group) using 7-day food diaries.

Methods summary: food diaries with fibre and sucrose as positive controls, and testing of foods, pharmaceuticals and toothpastes for microparticle content to compare Ca and exogenous microparticle intakes between groups.

Results: fibre and sucrose intakes differed significantly between CD cases and controls (fibre lower, sucrose higher), but Ca did not; estimated TiO2 and Psil intakes and microparticle counts are reported as similar to per capita estimates.

Key findings and conclusion: large individual variation in microparticle intake with no CD-control difference, so excess intake is ruled out as the cause of CD inflammation if microparticles are involved.
Final conclusion: identification of microparticle-containing foods enables future assessment of a low-microparticle diet as a potential intervention in Crohn's disease.

Abstract opening of a review on dietary risk factors for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD); covers background, aim, and the PubMed/Medline/Cochrane search methods, and begins the results with established non-diet risk factors.

Results section of the IBD diet review: lists non-diet risk factors (family history, smoking, appendectomy, antibiotics), notes methodological limits of retrospective case-control studies, and introduces prospective European cohort findings linking high meat and fish protein intake to higher IBD risk.

Core findings of the IBD dietary review: n-6 PUFA linoleic acid may raise ulcerative colitis risk while n-3 PUFAs may be protective, and fibre, sugar, macronutrients, energy and vitamins C, D, E, carotene and retinol showed no effect on ulcerative colitis risk.

Remaining results and conclusions of the IBD diet review: notes the lack of prospective data on fruits, vegetables and food microparticles (titanium dioxide, aluminium silicate), then concludes that high animal protein intake may raise IBD risk and relapse.

Conclusions of the IBD diet review: high protein and n-6 PUFA may increase risk, n-3 PUFA may protect, and findings need confirmation in other countries and younger subjects before dietary counselling for high-risk people is recommended.

Final fragment of the IBD diet review: closes the conclusions on dietary counselling for high-risk subjects and contains the 2011 copyright and publisher notice (Editrice Gastroenterologica Italiana / Elsevier).

Introduction and background of a Crohn's disease study: explains that ultrafine/fine microparticles act as immune adjuvants and cause inflammation, motivating a trial of a low microparticle diet as a first-ever test in Crohn's symptoms.

Methods of the double-blind randomized trial: 20 patients with active corticosteroid-treated ileal or ileo-colonic Crohn's disease receive either a low microparticle diet or control diet for 4 months, with CDAI and corticosteroid use as outcomes; start of results noting one withdrawal per group.

Results showing the trial group's CDAI falling progressively from 392 to 145 (P=0.002 vs control), with seven trial patients reaching remission, while the control group's CDAI stayed near baseline (302 to 295).

Remaining results and conclusions: no control patients were in remission, corticosteroid reduction was greater in the trial group but not statistically significant, and the authors conclude a low microparticle diet may treat ileal Crohn's disease and may explain the efficacy of elemental diets.
Final sentence of the conclusion, stating that elemental diets are similarly low in microparticles, offering a possible explanation for their therapeutic effect in Crohn's disease.
Opening of the abstract on Crohn's disease as a Western disease of transmural gut inflammation, with unknown cause, and introduces bacterial-sized microparticles as adjuvants linked to disease.

Describes TiO2 and aluminosilicate microparticles accumulating in gut-associated lymphoid tissue macrophages where early Crohn's lesions appear, and divides dietary microparticles into endogenous and exogenous origins.

Identifies endogenous microparticles as calcium phosphate (likely hydroxyapatite) precipitating in the mid-distal intestine from Ca and phosphate secretion, and exogenous ones as contaminants and food additives such as TiO2 colourant and aluminosilicate anti-caking agents.

Notes food additives alone supply about 10^12 particles per person daily and states that mechanisms by which dietary microparticles affect mucosal phagocytosis and tolerogenic or immune responses are discussed.

Reports a double-blind randomised pilot study where a low-calcium, low-exogenous-microparticle diet improved ileal Crohn's symptoms and Crohn's Disease Activity Index (P=0.002), and mentions ongoing multi-centre and cellular mechanistic work.
Final sentence stating that a multi-centre trial and further cellular-level mechanistic studies are underway to follow up the pilot diet findings.

Abstract background and objective of a study on dietary microparticles (food additive/excipient submicron particles) taken up by GI tract M cells and gut macrophages, and their possible role in inflammatory bowel disease, including Crohn's disease.

Methods section of the study: macrophages from healthy donors or active Crohn's disease patients were incubated 24 h with dietary microparticles, then assayed for cytokine production and phagocytic activity; results begin by noting microparticles alone are non-stimulatory.

Results and conclusion of the study: microparticles act as adjuvants with bacterial antigens such as LPS to induce potent cytokine responses, and high concentrations impair macrophage phagocytic capacity (not ability) for 2microM fluorescent beads.

Final conclusion of the abstract: dietary microparticles have limited effects on basic macrophage functions alone, but their adjuvant activity could aggravate inflammatory responses to bacterial antigens in the gastrointestinal tract.

Introduction stating that humans have long been exposed to dietary micro- and nanoparticles, that nanotechnology will increase this exposure, and that gastrointestinal handling of nanoparticles is poorly understood compared with respirable particles; sets up the group's motivation.

Continuation of the introduction describing the group's prior work on dietary microparticles and its extension to nanoparticles in the gut, followed by the paper's three stated aims: characterising particle-cell interactions, uptake routes via Peyer's patches, and cellular effects.

Lists the paper's three research aims in detail: (ii) mechanisms of particle uptake in the gut, especially via Peyer's patches, and (iii) cellular effects, including reactive oxygen species and inflammasome activation for nanoparticles and adjuvant/pro-inflammatory immune effects for microparticles; ends with the copyright line.

Closing fragment of the abstract's final sentence on cellular effects of nanoparticles (ROS, inflammasome activation) and microparticles (adjuvant activity, immune responsiveness), followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction to the study on titanium dioxide (TiO2) in consumer products, describing how TiO2 from food, personal care, and other products flows via sewage and WWTP effluent, biosolids, incineration, and landfill into the environment.

Study aims and key findings on titanium content: candies, sweets, and chewing gums contain the most TiO2 among foods, and toothpastes and select sunscreens contain 1% to >10% titanium by weight among personal care products.

Titanium levels in personal care and pharmaceutical products: crèmes vary, shampoos, deodorants, and shaving creams are lowest (<0.01 μg/mg), and high-consumption pharmaceuticals range from below detection limit to 0.014 μg Ti/mg.

Particle characterization and behavior of food-grade TiO2 (E171): about 36% of particles are under 100 nm in at least one dimension, and the particles disperse in water as fairly stable colloids; also notes filtration of water-solubilized products.

Filtration results showing less than 5% of titanium passes through 0.45 or 0.7 μm pores, followed by titanium levels in paints and sealants (two white paints at 110 μg Ti/mg, sealants at 25 to 40 μg Ti/mg) and the conclusion that white products do not necessarily contain titanium.

Discussion of environmental concern from widespread low-titanium product use and drain disposal to WWTPs, and the Monte Carlo dietary exposure analysis finding children have the highest exposure due to higher TiO2 in sweets.

Quantified adult dietary exposure (about 1 mg Ti per kg body weight per day for a typical US adult) and the argument that testing should prioritize food-grade TiO2 (E171) given millions of tons of titanium white pigment used annually.

Conclusion on test materials: environmental health and safety tests often use P25 TiO2, which is used in much smaller amounts in products less likely to reach the environment (e.g., catalyst supports, photocatalytic coatings), so E171 should be the focus instead.

Introduction to a study on ultrafine dietary particles and inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis), noting environmental triggers and the estimated daily ingestion of over 10^12 ultrafine particles from a Western diet.

Rationale for the study: dietary microparticles were thought to be inert, yet they adsorb intestinal luminal constituents and are taken up by intestinal lymphoid aggregates, prompting testing of titanium dioxide (TiO2) effects on gut responsiveness to LPS.

Methods: colonic biopsy specimens from 28 ulcerative colitis patients, 21 Crohn's disease patients, and 36 healthy controls, plus peripheral blood mononuclear cells, were incubated with LPS, TiO2, or LPS adsorbed to TiO2.

Methods and measurement: samples were incubated under control, LPS, TiO2, or TiO2-adsorbed LPS conditions, with IL-1 levels quantified by bioassay and ELISA; the key result begins with a 30-60-fold IL-1 increase in blood mononuclear cells from the TiO2-LPS conjugate.
Results in intestinal organ cultures: TiO2 alone or LPS up to 2,000 ng/ml did not raise IL-1 secretion, whereas the TiO2-LPS conjugate caused a significant two-to-three-fold increase.

Conclusions: ultrafine dietary particles are not immunologically inert and may help overcome normal gut hyporesponsiveness to luminal molecules, which may be especially relevant to IBD patients with abnormal intestinal permeability.
Closing copyright notice (2000, Academic Press) for the article.

This chunk opens a case report on iodine-induced overt hypothyroidism from long-term povidone-iodine gargling, introducing a 63-year-old patient who gargled for over 10 years and noting that the condition is usually mild and reversible.

This chunk continues the case report by estimating the patient's urinary iodine excretion (over 5 mg/day) against a control group of 18 normal subjects who gargled three times daily, and notes the patient became euthyroid for over 10 months after stopping gargling.
Abstract of a 2002-2003 randomized trial on gargling (water vs. povidone-iodine vs. control) to prevent upper respiratory tract infections in Japan; this chunk gives background and the study design.

Trial participants and interventions: 387 healthy adults aged 18-65 randomized to water gargling, povidone-iodine gargling, or usual care, with gargling at least three times daily and 60-day follow-up.

Outcome measures and analysis method for the gargling URTI trial: primary outcome was first URTI incidence, secondary was symptom severity, both via self-reported symptom records, analyzed intention-to-treat; also begins the results with 130 URTI cases.

Incidence results of the gargling trial: first URTI rates per 30 person-days for control, water gargling, and povidone-iodine groups, with incidence rate ratios of 0.64 (water) and 0.89 (povidone-iodine) against controls.

Statistical findings of the gargling trial: Cox regression hazard ratio of 0.60 for water gargling, a trend toward milder bronchial symptoms (p=0.055), and the start of the conclusion that water gargling is effective.

Conclusion of the gargling trial stating that simple, virtually cost-free water gargling effectively prevents upper respiratory tract infections in healthy people and could benefit the general population.

Introduction and methods of a Japanese observational study on gargling and childhood fever, describing enrollment of children from 145 nursery schools in Fukuoka City and the exposure definition (daily gargling).

Methods continued and start of results: study endpoints (daytime fever incidence and sickness absence), analysis of gargling agents, and the cohort size of 19,595 children aged 2-6 observed for 20 days.

Main results on fever onset: multivariate logistic regression shows a significantly lower overall odds ratio for gargling (OR 0.68), with age-stratified ORs significantly lower at ages 2, 4, and 5, and the start of the sickness absence results.

Sickness absence results and subgroup findings: overall OR 0.92 (not significant), age-stratified ORs significant at ages 4-6, and fever-onset ORs by gargling agent (green tea, functional water, tap water).
Final subgroup interpretation and conclusion: sickness absence ORs were not significant across gargling agents, and the authors conclude gargling might help prevent febrile diseases in children.

Introduction/background of the study: states that viral respiratory tract infection is the most common human illness, notes the lack of rigorous economic analysis of non-influenza VRTI, and lists the study's aims (updated US incidence and direct/indirect costs).

Methods, part one: describes the nationwide US household telephone survey (N = 4051, conducted Nov 2000 to Feb 2001) used to estimate self-reported incidence of non-influenza VRTI and treatment patterns, and begins listing the direct cost categories.

Methods, part two: details the direct cost components (clinician visits, OTC and prescription drugs, infectious complications) and explains that absenteeism for infected people and parents was extrapolated from National Health Interview Survey data.

Results, part one: reports that 72% of respondents had a non-influenza VRTI in the past year, averaging 2.5 episodes annually, and that these rates extrapolate to about 500 million episodes per year in the US.

Results, part two: presents the national economic estimate of about $40 billion per year, split into $17 billion direct costs and $22.5 billion indirect costs, derived by extending respondents' treatment patterns to the population.

Conclusions: argues that the high attack rate makes non-influenza VRTI a larger economic burden than many other clinical conditions, and that the forthcoming availability of effective antivirals merits greater attention to this common, costly illness.
Final fragment of the conclusions sentence, completing the word 'illness' from chunk 6; it adds no new content.

Background and rationale: gargling for preventing upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) in Japan, prior RCT evidence, and the motivation to assess cost-effectiveness from a societal rather than third-party payer perspective.

Study aim: economic evaluation alongside the gargling RCT to assess cost-effectiveness of gargling for URTI prevention from a societal perspective, noting gargling is dominant for the third-party payer since participants bear its cost.

Methods: economic analysis sample of 122 water-gargling and 130 control participants, with 60-day costs and quality-adjusted life days (QALD) compared on an intention-to-treat basis, and ICER defined.
Methods and results: ICER converted to dollars per QALY, bootstrapping used for 95% CI and probability of cost-effectiveness; results show QALD gain of 0.43 and cost difference of $37.1 at 60 days.

Main results: ICER of $31,800/QALY (95% CI $1,900–$248,100), comparable to accepted interventions like influenza vaccination, but wide CI signals substantial uncertainty; one-way sensitivity analysis highlights gargling cost and moderate URTI utility.
Limitations: the trial was conducted in winter when URTI is prevalent, and results may not generalize to off-season periods because lower incidence would raise the ICER.
Conclusion: gargling is presented as a cost-effective URTI preventive strategy acceptable to both third-party payers and society.

Opening of the study abstract: states the objective (effect of dog and cat contacts on respiratory symptoms/infections in infancy) and methods (birth cohort of 397 children followed from pregnancy, weekly diaries and a 1-year questionnaire, born in eastern/middle Finland 2002-2005).

Continuation of the methods into the results section: describes the diary and questionnaire data collection, then reports the multivariate finding that children with dogs at home had fewer respiratory symptoms or infections (aOR 1.31, 95% CI 1.13-1.52).

Specific results on otitis and antibiotic use: children with dog contact at home had less frequent otitis (aOR 0.56) and tended to need fewer antibiotic courses (aOR 0.71), and the chunk begins the univariate analysis of dog and cat contact amounts.

Univariate findings and conclusions: weekly and average yearly contact with dogs and cats were linked to lower respiratory infectious morbidity, and the authors conclude dog contact may protectively affect respiratory infections in the first year of life.

Final sentences of the conclusion: the authors argue that animal contacts during the first year of life are important, possibly building better resistance to infectious respiratory illness in childhood.

Opening chunk of an abstract on a study testing whether pet ownership improves survival after acute coronary syndrome (ACS); it describes the study's aim, the 424-patient cohort, and the 1-year follow-up of cardiac death and readmission.

Middle section of the abstract reporting results: pet owners had higher odds of death or readmission after adjusting for psychosocial and medical covariates, and cat ownership specifically was linked to greater risk when dog and cat owners were analyzed separately.

Concluding part of the abstract stating that pet ownership, especially cat ownership, was associated with higher cardiac morbidity and mortality within a year of ACS admission, contradicting earlier reports of benefit.
Final fragment of the abstract's conclusion, noting that the findings contradict previous reports claiming pets improve outcomes after acute coronary syndrome.

Opening chunk of the abstract from a South Australian diary study of 965 rural/semi-rural children aged 4–6, introducing the aim (pet ownership and gastroenteritis), data collected, and the finding that 89% of households had pets, with dogs more common than cats.

Middle section of the abstract reporting the main results: multivariable models show dog or cat ownership is associated with reduced gastroenteritis risk (adjusted ORs 0.71 for dogs and 0.70 for cats, with 95% CIs), supporting the conclusion that pets are not a major household source of gastroenteritis.

Concluding part of the abstract stating that pets are not a major source of gastroenteritis and support health benefits of pet ownership, while noting these benefits must be weighed against risks such as dog bites in young children.
Introduction of a 1990 German birth cohort study establishing reference values for how many respiratory infection episodes a normal child has, based on parental history recording.

Methods: prospective tracking of 1314 German children born in 1990 (760 followed to age 12), using parental illness diaries and yearly structured questionnaires, with age groups infancy, pre-school, and school age.
Results: mean cumulative respiratory infection episodes to age 12 (21.9) and mean annual episodes by age group (infancy 3.4, pre-school 2.3, school 1.1), plus cumulative episode duration to age 7.
Conclusions on normal ranges: using twofold SD, up to 11 episodes/year in infancy, 8 at pre-school, and 4 at school age are considered normal, including tertile persistence data for infants.
Final conclusion: episodes within the derived reference values should not prompt unwarranted concern or immunodeficiency workups or interventions.

Introduction/summary of a review on grapefruit: its popularity and the biomedical evidence of drug interactions (CYP3A4 and intestinal transporters) that have sometimes been fatal, setting up the metabolic and cardiovascular discussion.

Continuation of the summary explaining the mechanism of grapefruit-drug interactions via intestinal CYP3A4, P-glycoprotein and organic cation transporters, and noting that the clinical impact is unclear, likely because cases go unreported.

Closing part of the summary covering the unreported extent of grapefruit-drug interactions and the emerging evidence that grapefruit's flavonoids may benefit diabetes and cardiovascular disease, which the review addresses.
Final fragment of the summary, the closing sentence stating that the review covers this potentially explosive subject.

Introduction/background of a study on pet ownership and health, explaining prior research limitations (non-representative samples, small databanks, causality issues, uncontrolled confounders) and stating the study's aim to examine pet ownership against perceived health and disease while controlling for socio-demographics and exercise.

Continuation of the background's critique of prior research and statement of the study's aim: associating pet ownership with perceived health and disease indicators while adjusting for socio-demographic factors and health risk factors such as exercise, leading into the Methods section.

Methods section of the Finnish Health and Social Support (HeSSup) Study: baseline data from a 15-year study, population-based random samples from the Finnish Population Register Centre stratified by gender and four age groups (20-54 years).

Sample size and analysis plus main results of the HeSSup pet ownership study: 21,101 working-aged Finns responded in 1998, ordinal and binary logistic regression on cross-sectional data, pet ownership linked to poor perceived health, and BMI as the strongest risk factor associated with pet ownership.

Conclusions of the pet ownership and health study: pet owners, along with older individuals, had slightly higher BMI than others, and the authors call for further research on pet ownership's effects on various health dimensions across different population groups.
Final fragment of the conclusions section, ending the abstract's call for further research on effects of pet ownership on health across population groups with differing background characteristics.

Study introduction: aims and design of a cross-sectional questionnaire on 594 children aged 1-6 from 18 Helsinki day care centres, examining risk factors for acute respiratory illness (ARI) and acute otitis media (AOM).

Prevalence results and first set of risk factors: recurrent ARI rates by age group (44% of 1-3-year-olds, 23% of 4-6-year-olds) and recurrent AOM rates (15% and 2.5%), plus odds ratios for parental atopy, maternal academic education, and medium DCC attendance increasing ARI risk.

Adjusted odds ratios for recurrent ARI and AOM: furry pets and older age reduce ARI risk; recurrent ARI, maternal education, and medium DCC attendance raise AOM risk; partial breastfeeding for 6 months or more and older age reduce AOM risk.

Summary of findings that parental and environmental factors significantly affect recurrent ARI and AOM in day care children, and a call for future studies to account for these risk factors when trying to reduce DCC infections.
Final concluding sentence of the abstract: recommends that these risk factors be considered in future research aimed at reducing infections in day care centres.

Study design and population section of a pet ownership and cardiovascular risk study: community survey of 2528 adults aged 40-44 and 2551 aged 60-64 in the ACT and Queanbeyan, drawn from the Australian electoral roll in 2000-2001, with the stated objective of testing whether pet ownership reduces cardiovascular risk.

Main outcome measures and initial results from the pet ownership cardiovascular study: sociodemographic and physical health measures (BMI, alcohol, smoking, physical activity, blood pressure), and the finding that pet owners and non-owners had similar systolic blood pressure while pet owners had higher diastolic pressure.

Key results of the pet ownership cardiovascular study: pet owners had higher diastolic blood pressure, higher BMI, and were more likely to smoke, and the diastolic difference persisted after controlling for hypertensive risk factors despite pet owners doing more mild physical activity.

Conclusions of the pet ownership and cardiovascular risk study: no evidence that pet ownership itself confers cardiovascular benefits, since pet owners had higher diastolic blood pressure, likely due to other hypertensive risk factors indirectly linked to owning pets.

Final sentence of the conclusions of the pet ownership cardiovascular risk study, stating that the higher blood pressure risk is likely explained by other hypertensive risk factors only indirectly associated with pet ownership.

Introduction and methods of a Vietnam rabies molecular epidemiology study (2006-2009): intra vitam human samples (saliva, CSF) from 31 suspected patients in northern hospitals and brain samples from 176 rabid dogs nationwide, tested by RT-PCR.

Results of the Vietnam rabies study: 23 patients tested RABV-positive, and 5 positive patients had no dog or cat bite history but had butchered or eaten dog or cat meat, pointing to a non-bite transmission route.

Phylogenetic findings of the Vietnam rabies study: RABV detected in 2 of 100 slaughterhouse dogs, and 27 viral strains grouped into two clades, with Group 1 spread nationwide and similar to strains from China, Thailand, Malaysia, and the Philippines.
Group 2 rabies viruses in Vietnam: confined to northern provinces and closely related to southern Chinese strains, suggesting a recent cross-border viral influx from China into Vietnam.

Public health recommendations from the Vietnam rabies study: despite slaughterhouse-linked rabies being rarer than dog-bite transmission, control programs should monitor the health of dogs for human consumption and vaccinate slaughterhouse workers.
Concluding recommendation of the Vietnam rabies study: research on circulating RABV in dog markets is needed to identify rabies sources and curb its spread through slaughterhouses in Vietnam.

Opening of a study on molecular epidemiology of rabies in southern China: describes the rise in human rabies cases in Guizhou, Guangxi, and Hunan, and the 2005–2007 sampling of 2,887 brain specimens from apparently healthy restaurant dogs plus suspected rabid dogs and human cases.

Middle of the rabies study: states that partial nucleoprotein gene sequences were obtained from rabies-positive specimens for phylogenetic and viral distribution analysis, and begins the inference that spread of viruses from high-incidence regions may explain the epidemics.

Concluding sentence of the rabies study: proposes that long-distance movement or transprovincial translocation of dogs driven by human activities may be a cause of the recent massive human rabies epidemics in southern China.

Introduces the case report's background on vitamin D deficiency causes (diet, low sunlight in dark-skinned people at northern latitudes) and the standard treatment of vitamin D calcium supplements, which the patient rejected.

Describes the patient's self-treatment with UVB-irradiated mushrooms after independent research, reports its beneficial effect on plasma biochemical markers, and concludes that further research is needed.

Abstract opening (background and objectives) of a randomized controlled trial on vitamin D2 bioavailability from UV-B-irradiated mushrooms, introducing the ergosterol-to-vitamin D2 conversion and comparison with a supplement.

Methods section describing the mushroom UV-B irradiation dose and resulting vitamin D2 content, the 5-week single-blinded trial design, and the 26 deficient adults randomized to mushroom soup, supplement, or placebo.

Continuation of the methods (dosing of 28,000 IU vitamin D2 per group, winter intervention) and start of the results, reporting the significantly higher serum 25OHD in the mushroom group versus placebo after 2 weeks.
Results reporting the similar significant rises in serum 25OHD in the mushroom and supplement groups, with mean changes and 95% confidence intervals over the study period.
Conclusions and trial registration: the mushroom-derived vitamin D2 improved vitamin D status comparably to a supplement, and the trial is registered as DRKS00000195.

Introduction and objective of a systematic review/meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing vitamin D2 and vitamin D3 effects on serum 25(OH)D levels in humans, motivated by unclear evidence on whether they differ.

Methods: the search strategy, covering the ISI Web of Knowledge (1966 to July 2011) for adult studies directly comparing vitamin D3 with D2, and trial registries (Cochrane, ISRCTN, clinicaltrials.gov) for unpublished trials.

Main results: meta-analysis finding vitamin D3 significantly more effective than D2 at raising serum 25(OH)D (P = 0.001), plus a dosing-frequency comparison showing D3 advantage with bolus dosing (P = 0.0002) but not daily supplementation.
Results and conclusions continued: the bolus-versus-daily dosing finding and the overall conclusion that vitamin D3 is more efficacious than D2 and may be the preferred supplement.

Conclusions and limitations: D3 may be the preferred supplementation choice, but further research is needed on metabolic pathways of oral and intramuscular vitamin D administration and on effects across age, sex, and ethnicity.
Final limitation statement: the review could not verify whether the vitamin D2 versus D3 effects hold across age, sex, and ethnicity, highlighting the need for further research.

Study background and design: motivation (prior reports that vitamin D2 is less effective than D3), objective, and the randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blinded trial design in healthy adults aged 18–84 over 11 weeks at winter's end.

Study population and baseline status: the randomized trial's four arms (placebo, 1000 IU D3, 1000 IU D2, 500 IU D2 + 500 IU D3) and the finding that 60% of participants were vitamin D deficient at the start.
Main results on serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D: baseline and 11-week mean levels for the D2, D3, and combined D2+D3 groups, showing comparable increases across the 1000 IU arms.

Catabolism and dose-response findings: 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 levels were unchanged with 1000 IU D2, and neither 1000 IU D2 nor D3 raised levels in deficient subjects above 30 ng/ml; also begins the conclusion.
Overall conclusion: 1000 IU daily vitamin D2 matches 1000 IU vitamin D3 in maintaining 25-hydroxyvitamin D status without negatively affecting 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 levels.
Introduction and methods of a study measuring vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol) and sterols in retail US mushrooms, using HPLC and GC-FID/MS analysis to update the USDA Nutrient Database.

Vitamin D2 results by mushroom type: low in Agaricus bisporus and enoki, moderate in shiitake and oyster, high in morel, chanterelle, maitake and UV-treated portabella, plus the start of ergosterol findings across types.

Ergosterol ranges by mushroom type (highest in maitake and shiitake, lowest in morel and enoki, with white button composites below 10 mg/100 g) and the common and morel-specific sterols such as ergosta-5,7-dienol, ergosta-7-enol and brassicasterol.

Sterol distinctions in morel: brassicasterol and campesterol present only in morel and absence of ergosta-7,22-dienol, with the conclusion that mass spectrometry was needed to separate campesterol from ergosta-7,22-dienol.
Abstract of a Cochrane systematic review on vitamin D supplementation and adult mortality: background, objectives, and the search strategy of databases searched up to January 2011.

Continuation of the search strategy (bibliography scanning, expert and pharmaceutical company queries) and the selection criteria: randomised trials of vitamin D versus placebo or no intervention, with the start of the list of eligible vitamin D forms.

Eligible vitamin D forms (cholecalciferol, ergocalciferol, alfacalcidol, calcitriol) and the data collection and analysis methods: independent extraction by six authors, random- and fixed-effect meta-analyses, and risk ratio calculation for dichotomous outcomes.
Statistical methods in detail: risk differences and empirical continuity corrections for zero-event trials, risk of bias assessment, and trial sequential analysis to address random error.

Main results opening: 50 trials with 94,148 participants, mostly elderly women over 70, median two-year supplementation, over half at low risk of bias, and the overall mortality effect (RR 0.97) introduced.

Core mortality findings: overall RR 0.97 (CI 0.94 to 1.00), and the subgroup result that only vitamin D3 significantly reduced mortality (RR 0.94, 32 trials, 74,789 participants) versus no effect for D2, alfacalcidol, or calcitriol.
Trial sequential analysis result (161 people treated to prevent one death) and the harms: vitamin D3 with calcium raised nephrolithiasis risk, and alfacalcidol/calcitriol raised hypercalcaemia risk.

Remaining main results (quality of life and health economics inconclusive) and the start of the authors' conclusions favouring vitamin D3 for mortality reduction in elderly women in institutional or dependent care.

Authors' conclusions concluding section: vitamin D2, alfacalcidol, and calcitriol had no significant mortality effect, while D3 with calcium increased nephrolithiasis and the active forms increased hypercalcaemia.
Final fragment of the document's last sentence, completing the statement that alfacalcidol and calcitriol significantly increased hypercalcaemia.
Introduces a 6-week human trial of UV-treated white button mushrooms as a dietary vitamin D source, describing the study aim and the 38 healthy adult volunteers randomized to four treatment groups.

Details the four dosing arms: control untreated mushrooms (0.85 μg/d ergocalciferol), UV-treated mushroom groups M1 and M2 (8.8 and 17.1 μg/d), and a supplement group receiving purified ergocalciferol plus mushrooms (28.2 μg/d), with group sizes.
Reports baseline serum 25(OH)D and 25(OH)D2 levels, then the week-6 findings: 25(OH)D2 rose in all treated groups relative to control, while 25(OH)D3 fell in the M2 and S groups.
Gives the numeric changes in serum 25(OH)D2 and 25(OH)D3 (nmol/L) for each group at week 6, showing large 25(OH)D2 gains and corresponding 25(OH)D3 declines, with the control group unchanged.
Concludes that ergocalciferol was absorbed and converted to 25(OH)D2 but produced no net change in overall vitamin D status, because the decrease in 25(OH)D3 offset the increase in 25(OH)D2.
Introduction and study design of a study on coconut oil intake and lipid profiles among 1,839 Filipino women aged 35–69 in the Cebu Longitudinal Health and Nutrition Survey (Metropolitan Cebu City).
Methods and exposure measurement: coconut oil intake estimated from two 24-hour dietary recalls, plus baseline descriptive lipid measures (TC, HDL-c) from fasting plasma samples in the Cebu cohort.

Descriptive results: mean values and standard deviations for the plasma lipid outcomes (total cholesterol, HDL-c, LDL-c, triglycerides, TC/HDL ratio) and the statistical approach of linear regression.

Covariate adjustment and key finding: linear regression adjusted for energy intake, age, BMI, pregnancies, education, menopausal status, household assets and urban residency, concluding coconut oil intake is positively associated with HDL-c.

Introduction and methods of an open-label pilot study testing four weeks of virgin coconut oil in 20 obese but healthy Malay volunteers, covering weight/anthropometric/lipid efficacy measures and organ-function safety tests.
Continuation of the methods (safety assessment and paired t-test analysis) and the main results: waist circumference was the only significant reduction (2.86 cm, 0.97%, P = .02), seen only in males.

Final results and conclusion of the VCO pilot study: no lipid profile change, small drops in creatinine and alanine transferase, and the conclusion that VCO is efficacious for waist circumference reduction (especially in males) and safe for humans.

Introduction and methods of a randomised, double-blind clinical trial on coconut oil versus soybean oil supplementation in 40 women with abdominal obesity (waist circumference >88 cm), describing group sizes and the groups' daily 30 mL oil supplements.

Trial protocol details: 12-week intervention with a hypocaloric diet and 50 minutes of daily walking, measurements at T1 (1 week before) and T2 (1 week after), and dietary intake changes across both groups (lower energy and carbohydrate, higher protein and fibre, unchanged lipids).

Baseline comparability and main results at T2: no between-group differences at T1, while group C (coconut oil) had higher HDL and a lower LDL:HDL ratio than group S (soybean oil), with specific means and p-values.

Anthropometric and lipid outcomes: BMI fell in both groups, but only the coconut oil group showed a waist circumference reduction; the soybean oil group showed worsening total cholesterol, LDL, LDL:HDL ratio and decreased HDL.
Conclusion of the study: coconut oil supplementation did not induce dyslipidemia and appeared to reduce abdominal obesity, in contrast to the adverse lipid changes seen with soybean oil.
Introduction and study aim: comparing coconut oil vs. safflower oil effects on tomato carotenoid tissue accumulation in Mongolian gerbils fed a 20% fat diet.

Results part 1: coconut oil increased carotenoid levels in several tissues (serum total carotenoids, adrenal phytoene, hepatic phytofluene, testicular and prostate-seminal vesicle lycopene) relative to safflower oil, with p-values.
Results part 2: safflower oil gave higher splenic lycopene, while coconut oil raised serum cholesterol and lowered hepatic cholesterol compared to safflower oil.
Conclusion: coconut oil enhanced tomato carotenoid tissue uptake more than safflower oil, possibly via medium-chain fatty acids shifting cholesterol flux toward extrahepatic carotenoid deposition.
Final sentence of the conclusion: the proposed mechanism that medium-chain fatty acids in coconut oil shift cholesterol flux to favor extrahepatic carotenoid deposition.

Introduces a postprandial human study of inflammatory markers in healthy young women, comparing three high-fat test meals (coconut, linseed, cod liver oil) to assess how fat quality affects postprandial inflammation.

Describes the study design and test meal composition: 14 females, test days two weeks apart, blood sampled fasting and at 3 and 6 h, with three cakes enriched in coconut fat, linseed oil, or cod liver oil and their saturated fat and ALA/EPA/DHA content.

Details the cod liver oil cake's EPA, DHA, and ALA content and introduces the ex vivo PBMC experiments in eight subjects testing EPA and ALA effects on inflammatory marker release and gene expression, leading into the IL-8 results.

Reports the key result: IL-8 mRNA rose significantly at 6 h after the cod liver oil cake versus fasting and differed from linseed cake, while circulating IL-8 was unchanged; also begins noting ALA and EPA's differing effects on PBMC inflammatory markers.
Concludes the ex vivo findings, stating ALA and EPA have distinct effects on PBMC inflammatory marker release and mRNA expression, with EPA showing the strongest pro-inflammatory potential.

Study background and objective: introduces the question of whether dietary fat type (palm olein, coconut oil, virgin olive oil in high-protein Malaysian diets) affects plasma homocysteine and inflammation/CVD markers in healthy adults.

Study design: randomized crossover trial with three 5-week dietary sequences in 45 healthy subjects, comparing palmitic-rich palm olein, lauric/myristic-rich coconut oil, and oleic-rich virgin olive oil at two-thirds of 30% fat calories.

Main results part 1: no significant differences among the three diets in plasma total homocysteine, inflammatory markers (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8), hs-CRP, or interferon-γ; begins describing comparable lipid effects of palm olein and olive oil.

Main results part 2: palm olein and olive oil had comparable non-hypercholesterolemic effects, with olive oil and palm olein yielding lower lipid levels than coconut oil; coconut oil uniquely decreased postprandial lipoprotein(a). Conclusion begins.

Conclusion: saturated-fat diets (palm olein or coconut oil) and the high-oleic olive oil diet did not change postprandial or fasting homocysteine or selected inflammatory markers; trial registration NCT00941837 is noted.
Trial registration fragment: the end of the document's registration statement, identifying the trial as NCT00941837 on clinicaltrials.gov.

Introduces the AC-1202 AD study's background: reduced cerebral glucose metabolism in Alzheimer's disease, ketone bodies as brain fuel, and the trial's aim of testing whether ketosis improves cognition.

Describes the methods: a 90-day, US-based, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of daily AC-1202 in 152 mild-to-moderate AD subjects who stayed on normal diets and approved AD medications.
Names the primary endpoints (ADAS-Cog and ADCS-CGIC) and the analysis populations (ITT, per protocol, dosage compliant), and notes the predefined APOE4 stratification.
Gives the ClinicalTrials.gov registration (NCT00142805) and begins the results, reporting that AC-1202 significantly raised serum beta-hydroxybutyrate at 2 hours versus placebo.
Reports overall ADAS-Cog results at Day 45 across ITT, per protocol, and dosage compliant groups, with point differences and p-values favoring AC-1202.
Starts the APOE4-negative (E4(-)) subgroup results, stating significant Day 45 and Day 90 ADAS-Cog differences versus placebo and giving ITT figures (N=55: 4.77-point at Day 45, 3.36 at Day 90).
Gives per protocol and E4(-) subgroup figures (N=37: 5.73 points at Day 45, 4.39 at Day 90) and the ITT Day 90 p-value context.
Presents the dosage compliant E4(-) subgroup results (6.26 points at Day 45, N=38; 5.33 at Day 90, N=35) and the serum beta-hydroxybutyrate versus ADAS-Cog pharmacologic response at Day 90.
Summarizes the safety profile: adverse events were more common with AC-1202, mostly gastrointestinal, mild to moderate, and transient, and begins the conclusion on rapid ketone elevation.
Concludes that AC-1202 rapidly raised ketone bodies and improved ADAS-Cog versus placebo, with the strongest effects in dosage-compliant APOE4-negative subjects.

Introduction and objective of a study on periodontal disease, endothelial dysfunction, and systemic inflammation; begins the Methods, noting flow-mediated and nitroglycerin-mediated brachial artery dilation were assessed.

Results/methods detail: brachial artery ultrasound in 26 advanced periodontal disease subjects vs 29 controls, matched for age and sex, excluding hypercholesterolemia, diabetes, hypertension, and smoking; serum hs-CRP measurement introduced.

Key findings: flow-mediated dilation was lower in periodontal disease patients (7.8% vs 11.7%, P=0.005), nitroglycerin-mediated dilation was equivalent, and hs-CRP was elevated in the periodontitis group.

Continuation of results showing higher hs-CRP in advanced periodontitis (2.3 vs 1.0 mg/L, P=0.03), followed by the conclusion that advanced periodontal disease is linked to endothelial dysfunction and systemic inflammation.
Final sentence of the conclusion: advanced periodontal disease may place patients at increased risk for cardiovascular disease due to endothelial dysfunction and inflammation.
Introduces the Cochrane review's background and objectives: assessing whether one-to-one dietary interventions in dental care settings change dietary behaviour and oral/general health outcomes.
Continues the objectives and begins the search methods, listing the Cochrane Oral Health Group and CENTRAL registers and the MEDLINE and EMBASE databases with their search date ranges.
Lists the remaining databases searched (CINAHL, PsycINFO, Web of Science) and the conference proceedings (IADR, ORCA) searched for eligible dental dietary intervention trials.

Describes the rest of the search strategy (reference lists, theses, contacting trial authors for unpublished work) and states the selection criterion: randomised controlled trials of one-to-one dental dietary interventions.
Covers data collection methods: independent, duplicate screening and extraction by two review authors with consensus or third-author arbitration, then begins the main results.
Summarises the five included studies: two multi-intervention prevention programmes, one caries-prevention study, two general health studies, and no tooth erosion studies.
Reports that four of the five studies found significant dietary behaviour change on at least one primary outcome, and begins the authors' conclusions.

States the authors' conclusions: some evidence that dental-setting dietary interventions change behaviour, stronger for fruit/vegetable and alcohol than for sugar intake, and calls for more rigorous studies in dental practice settings.
Final conclusion calling for more studies, especially in dental practice settings, and better methodological rigour in design, statistical analysis, and reporting.

Introduction and methods of a study on the association between vasculogenic erectile dysfunction (ED) and chronic periodontitis (CP): background rationale, sample of 70 patients, and the Sexual Health Inventory and penile Doppler assessments.

Methods continued: periodontal measurements (probing depth, attachment level) and selection of five ED/CP patients for cardiac color Doppler to assess vascular integrity, leading into the results section.

Results on prevalence and correlation: mild-to-moderate vasculogenic ED was most common, CP prevalence peaked at 81.8% in severe ED, and a non-significant positive correlation between CP and vasculogenic ED was observed.

Remaining results and conclusions: two of five patients had vascular insufficiency; the authors hypothesize an ED-CP association in young males and call for larger, confounder-adjusted, longitudinal studies.
Final word of the conclusion sentence, completing the call for a large-scale study with confounder analysis and longitudinal follow-up.
Study aims and methods section of a dental study on vegetarian diet and tooth erosion/abrasion: sample of 46 vegetarians vs. 46 controls, clinical exam and questionnaire design.
Methods continued: statistical tests (Chi-square, Mann-Whitney U, logistic regression) and the start of the results on erosion prevalence in vegetarians (39.1%) vs. controls (23.9%).

Results on prevalence of tooth erosion and abrasion in vegetarians vs. controls (26.1% vs. 10.9% abrasion), reported as statistically insignificant, plus higher sour-food consumption among vegetarians.
Remaining results: similar oral hygiene in both groups and regression analysis finding no link between vegetarian diet and erosion/abrasion; the discussion begins.
