Mechanism and in vivo findings: hydroxyl radical reaction with erythritol forms erythrose and erythrulose via hydrogen abstraction; in streptozotocin-diabetic rats erythritol protects endothelium and erythrose appears in urine.
Conclusion of the abstract: erythritol acts as an antioxidant in vivo and may protect against hyperglycemia-induced vascular damage; includes the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.
Introduction to erythritol as a bulk sweetener: its industrial production, non-cariogenic nature, and rapid small-intestine absorption, with only about 10% reaching the colon.

Motivation and design of the study: prior in vitro tests showed erythritol unfermented at 12 h, so a 24 h standardised fresh human faecal fermentation was run with maltitol, lactulose and a blank as comparators.

Methods and measured parameters: fermentation patterns were tracked via total gas, hydrogen, pH, SCFA production and substrate degradation, and the results show erythritol fully resistant to bacterial attack.

Conclusion: erythritol was not fermented within 24 h, so no microbial adaptation occurred, and given that easier substrates continuously reach the colon in vivo, erythritol is very unlikely to be fermented in the human gut.

This chunk is the document's core abstract summary: it states that aspartame, a common artificial sweetener, is linked to pediatric and adolescent migraines because it is metabolized into formaldehyde, and it introduces the paper's case series linking these migraines to positive formaldehyde patch-test reactions.

Introduces the case report of two patients with aspartame-linked musculoskeletal pain; describes a 50-year-old woman with fibromyalgia whose symptoms vanished while she was abroad without aspartame and returned when she resumed it.

Continues the first patient's case: symptoms reappeared after she reintroduced aspartame and fully resolved once it was excluded. Then introduces the second patient, a 43-year-old man with three years of forearm, wrist, hand, and neck pain.

Second patient's course: a detailed history revealed three years of aspartame use, and pain fully resolved after removal without recurrence. The authors attribute both patients' chronic pain to aspartame, a widely used calorie-saving flavouring.

Weighs the benefit-risk of considering aspartame-induced chronic pain: the upside is curing a disabling disease and avoiding unnecessary tests and harmful treatments, while the downside is only a temporary dietary change.
Concludes with a clinical recommendation that practitioners ask fibromyalgia patients about aspartame intake, since this simple question may resolve a disabling chronic condition.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence, completing the statement that asking about aspartame may resolve a disabling chronic disease.
Introduction/abstract opening of a study on validating a detection method for virulent Yersinia enterocolitica and its distribution in slaughter pigs from conventional versus organic housing.

Methods section describing sample collection (tonsils, caecum, caecal lymph nodes from 60 slaughter pigs) and comparison of six culture methods against multiplex PCR for Yersinia enterocolitica detection.
Methods continuation: PCR-only screening of pigs from 6 conventional farms (210 pigs) and 3 alternative-housing farms (200 pigs), with multiplex PCR positive in 28 initial cases.
Results: culture methods were less sensitive than PCR; PCR found Y. enterocolitica in 18% of alternative-housing pigs versus 29% of conventional pigs (p<0.05), with tonsils most affected.

Results and conclusion: organ-level prevalence (tonsils, caecum, lymph nodes) by housing system, with housing identified as an important factor and conventional-system risk factors including pig suppliers, commercial feed, and transport.
Final conclusion sentence naming the main risk factors in conventional pig systems: sourcing from multiple suppliers, commercial feed use, and transportation to slaughter.

Introduction stating pigs are a major reservoir of pathogenic Y. enterocolitica and the farm-to-pork transmission route is unclear; introduces the study sampling 364 ear-tagged pigs on farm and at slaughterhouse.

Methods and key findings: pulsed-field gel electrophoresis of isolates shows matching Y. enterocolitica 4/O:3 genotypes across farm, slaughterhouse animals and carcasses, meaning carcass contamination comes from strains carried during fattening.

Findings on pluck set contamination: direct transmission from the carrier pig is the primary route, with cross-contamination having a larger effect on pluck sets than carcasses; also introduces the variable within-farm prevalence.
Farm-level results: within-farm prevalence ranged 0% to 100%, implying farm factors matter; first study of farm factors linked to high prevalence, using correlation and two-level logistic regression.

Conclusion identifying specific associated farm factors with high prevalence of pathogenic Y. enterocolitica 4/O:3: drinking from a nipple, lack of coarse feed or bedding for slaughter pigs, and no pest animal access to the pig house.

Introduction and study objectives for a 2001–2004 Ontario finisher pig Yersinia enterocolitica study: shedding prevalence, bioserotype distribution, herd-level test agreement, bioserotype clustering by farm, and spatial clustering of positive herds.

Study sample and methods: 3747 fecal samples from 100 Ontario farms (250 herd visits) in 2001, 2002, and 2004, tested by culture with positive isolates biotyped and serotyped; also reports apparent pig-level prevalence by year (1.8%, 3.2%, 12.5%).

Prevalence results: apparent versus estimated true pig-level prevalence of Y. enterocolitica by year (true prevalence 5.1%, 9.1%, 35.1%) and herd-level prevalence (16.3%, 17.9%, 37.5%), plus the start of the bioserotype distribution finding.

Bioserotype and test agreement results: bioserotype 4, O:3 was most common in all years, followed by bioserotype 2, O:5,27; kappa between pig and pooled sample herd-level status ranged 0.51–0.68, and pig samples were more sensitive for 4, O:3.

Clustering conclusions: farms repeatedly positive with the same bioserotype, but positive farms did not cluster spatially, implying no between-herd transmission or common geographic risk factor; includes the 2009 Elsevier copyright notice.
Closing fragment of the copyright statement (Elsevier B.V., 2009, all rights reserved) ending the Yersinia enterocolitica Ontario finisher pig abstract.

Opening of the abstract: introduces the study estimating US annual cost of illness and QALY loss from 14 of the 31 foodborne pathogens in Scallan et al. (2011) incidence estimates, noting these 14 cover 95% of illnesses and hospitalizations and 98% of deaths.

Abstract results: the 14 pathogens cost $14.0 billion (range $4.4–33.0 billion) and 61,000 QALYs (range 19,000–145,000) per year, with about 90% of the loss driven by five pathogens, beginning with nontyphoidal Salmonella.

Per-pathogen breakdown of the top five drivers of loss (nontyphoidal Salmonella, Campylobacter, Listeria, Toxoplasma gondii, norovirus) with their dollar costs and QALY losses, followed by mention of a companion article linking losses to food categories.

Methods overview: describes building disease outcome trees for each pathogen (symptoms, severities, durations, outcomes, likelihoods) and beginning the cost-of-illness estimation (medical costs, productivity loss, premature mortality valuation).

Methods continued: QALY loss per health state is estimated using the EuroQol 5D scale, and the detailed construction of outcome trees, outcome-specific costs, and EuroQol scoring is deferred to a second companion article.
Closing sentence: refers readers to the second companion article for detailed descriptions of disease outcome tree construction, outcome-specific cost of illness, and EuroQol 5D scoring.
Opening of the abstract: motivation for ranking microbiological hazards in the US food supply, and the study's scope of 14 pathogens across 12 food categories yielding 168 pathogen-food pairs.
Continues listing the 14 pathogens studied and introduces the health burden metrics: cost of illness and QALY losses from acute and chronic illness and mortality.
Describes the study's new food attribution method combining outbreak data and expert elicitation, with the principle that empirical outbreak data are preferred unless shown unrepresentative.

Identifies the four pathogens (Campylobacter, Toxoplasma, Cryptosporidium, Yersinia) whose outbreak-based attribution was judged unrepresentative, so expert-based attribution was used for them instead.
Notes sensitivity analyses on attribution assumptions and summarizes the concentration of burden: top 10 pathogen-food pairs account for over $8 billion and 36,000 QALYs, more than half the total.
Final result: poultry, pork, produce, and complex foods together account for nearly 60% of total cost of illness and QALY loss across all 14 pathogens.

Introduction and aims of a twin case-control study on whether Yersinia enterocolitica infection is associated with Graves' disease, including the confounding rationale for studying discordant twin pairs.

Study design and methods: a classical case-control sample (61 GD cases, 122 controls) followed by a discordant twin pair case-control study (36 pairs), measuring IgA and IgG antibodies against Yersinia outer membrane proteins (YOPs).
Results on prevalence of YOP IgA and IgG antibodies, showing higher rates in Graves' disease subjects than external controls, with p-values for the comparisons.
Results on chronic YE infection (both IgA and IgG YOP antibodies) being more frequent in cases, similar findings in discordant twin pairs, and odds ratios from the case-control analysis.
Co-twin analysis odds ratios for YE infection in the twin with GD (IgA and IgG), followed by the conclusion that the GD-YE association supports a possible aetiological role.
Final conclusion of the study noting the uncertainty of causal direction between Yersinia infection and Graves' disease and recommending future studies on the temporal relationship.

Introduction and study aim: establishes Y. enterocolitica as a food-borne pathogen in US pork production and states the goal of estimating prevalence of pathogenic strains in pig fecal samples (2,793 samples tested).

Sampling methods: describes collection of late finisher pig fecal samples from 77 production sites across 15 eastern and midwestern states over 27 weeks (Sept 2000 to March 2001) and the use of PCR and culture detection of ail-positive strains.

Results on prevalence: reports the combined mean prevalence of 13.10% (366 of 2,793 samples) and that 41 of 77 premises (53.25%) had at least one ail-positive sample, with the PCR contamination rate of 12.35% stated.

Method comparison results: contrasts PCR (345/2,793, 12.35%) with culture (114/2,793, 4.08%) detection, gives discordant counts between methods, and reports significantly higher PCR-based site positivity (46.75% vs 22.08%, P < 0.05).
Sensitivity conclusion: summarizes that the fluorogenic 5' nuclease PCR assay showed higher sensitivity than culture for detecting pathogenic Y. enterocolitica in both samples and sites.
Final conclusion: states that the findings support the hypothesis that swine serve as a reservoir for Y. enterocolitica strains potentially pathogenic to humans.

Opening chunk of a document on Yersinia enterocolitica in foods: its ubiquity in environmental and food sources, its ability to grow at refrigeration temperatures (important for food hygiene), and the invasion of HeLa cells by virulent strains.

Covers the invasion genes inv and ail, the clinical illnesses caused by pathogenic Y. enterocolitica (diarrhoea, appendicitis, post-infection arthritis), and the view that fecal-oral transmission via contaminated food is the most common route.

Discusses transmission: person-to-person spread is rare, pathogenic Y. enterocolitica has occasionally been found in vegetables and environmental water, making these potential sources, and isolation rates are low.

Attributes the low isolation rates to limited sensitivity of detection methods and calls for more extensive study of food items to identify other transmission vehicles, while noting that epidemiological factors remain unclear.
Final sentence restating that sources, transmission routes, and predominant genotypes of Y. enterocolitica remain unclear because detection methods lack sensitivity.

Introduction/background and methods of the 2010 FoodNet report on foodborne disease surveillance in the US, covering estimated national burden of contaminated-food illnesses and the surveillance design across nine pathogens.

Methods continued (incidence change periods 1996-1998 to 2010 and 2006-2008 to 2010), national burden estimates, and the start of the results: 2010 totals of 19,089 infections, 4,247 hospitalizations, and 68 deaths from FoodNet sites.

Results on 2010 pathogen burden, highlighting Salmonella as the most common infection (17.6 per 100,000) with the most hospitalizations and deaths, and no significant incidence change since 1996-1998.

Results on trends since 1996-1998: STEC O157 incidence at 0.9 per 100,000, a 23% overall decline across six key pathogens, and pathogen-specific decreases for Campylobacter, Listeria, STEC O157, Shigella, and Yersinia versus an increase for Vibrio.

Results comparing 2010 with 2006-2008 (lower STEC O157 and Shigella, higher Vibrio) and the conclusion that STEC O157 reached the 2010 national health objective target of at least 1 case per 100,000, showing that preventing foodborne illness is feasible.

Conclusion on the success of prevention and the public health implications section, which singles out Salmonella as needing targeted action because it has not declined significantly in over a decade, and notes its roughly $365 million annual direct medical cost.

Public health implications continued: applying the prevention measures that reduced STEC O157 more broadly to Salmonella and other infections, and the estimated annual medical cost of Salmonella infection.

Final recommendations from farm to table: preventing contamination during slaughter and food processing and preparation, cooking meat thoroughly, detecting and investigating outbreaks, and recalling contaminated food.

Introduces the cross-sectional study of Yersinia enterocolitica (YE) prevalence across production phases on eight U.S. swine farms, with the study objective and background on swine as the primary reservoir.

Describes methods: fecal and oral-pharyngeal swabs collected from pigs in five production phases (gestating, farrowing, suckling, nursery, finishing), a pig counted positive if either sample was positive, and cold enrichment culture on selective media.

Reports overall results: of 2,349 pigs sampled, 120 (5.1%) were YE positive and 51 of those isolates were ail positive (42.5%); notes a trend of rising prevalence as pigs mature and that suckling piglet prevalence was under 1%.

Gives phase-specific prevalence: nursery pigs 1.4% and finishing pigs 10.7% positive, with ail-positive percentages; gestating sows had the second highest prevalence at 9.1%, while farrowing sows never tested positive.
Concludes that these are the first on-farm descriptions of YE in U.S. herds and that the findings lay groundwork for future YE studies.

Introduction of the Yersinia enterocolitica review: describes it as a zoonotic gastrointestinal pathogen linked to reactive arthritis and erythema nodosum, transmitted via contaminated food, with pigs as the main carriers.

Continuation of the introduction: states the review's aim, which is to motivate further study of reservoirs, prevalence, virulence, and environmental survival of Y. enterocolitica to inform food safety measures against yersiniosis.

Closing sentence of the review's introduction: concludes that better understanding of the pathogen's reservoirs, prevalence, virulence, and environmental survival is needed to prevent or reduce disease risk.

Introduction stating the study's aims: estimating individual-animal and on-farm prevalence of Yersinia enterocolitica in hogs from NAHMS Swine 2002 tonsil samples, and linking these to fecal data to identify farm risk factors.

Sampling scope and first results: 1,218 tonsil swabs and 2,847 fecal samples from 124 farms in the top 17 pork-producing states; 10% of tonsils were PCR-positive after ITC enrichment, versus 5.6% culture-positive on CIN agar.
Comparison of detection methods and farm-level prevalence in tonsils: real-time PCR of the ail gene in ITC broth gave 32% of premises positive (32/100), while CIN agar subculture gave 19.6% (20/102).
Methods of the risk analysis: combined tonsil and fecal isolation and PCR results to estimate prevalence, then correlated these with 40 farm management practices.

Key findings: the final regression model's four risk and protective factors with odds ratios, including central-state location (OR 0.3), E. coli vaccination (OR 3.0), scours-related deaths (OR 3.5), and meat or bone meal in grower-finisher diet (OR 4.1).
Tail fragment ending the final odds ratio for meat or bone meal in the grower-finisher diet (OR = 4.1), concluding the results summary.

Abstract of a study on pathogenic Yersinia enterocolitica prevalence on pig farms: describes the survey of 788 pigs from 120 farms and the univariate screening method (random-effects logistic regression, P<0.15 cutoff) used before multivariate modeling.

Results section of the Yersinia enterocolitica pig farm study: reports protective factors, namely municipal water use against carriage and faecal shedding, and organic production and a specific feed manufacturer against total carriage.

Results and conclusion of the Yersinia enterocolitica pig farm study: lists risk factors for faecal shedding (tonsillar carriage, a different feed manufacturer, pre-transport fasting, higher farm health classification, snout contacts) and concludes management differences explain farm-level prevalence differences.
Final concluding sentence of the Yersinia enterocolitica pig farm abstract, stating that differences in farm management explain the variation in Y. enterocolitica prevalence between farms.

This chunk is the document's full summary of the study: it describes how fecal and blood samples were collected on a fattening farm to trace Yersinia enterocolitica, showing infection already present in piglets from breeding farms, spreading to all pigs after mixing, and ending with all pigs shedding the pathogen.

Introduces the study's motivation: swine confinement buildings in eastern Canada, concern that bioaerosols carry human pathogens and antimicrobial-resistant bacteria that could colonize hog producers, and the aim of analyzing bioaerosols and nasal flora.

Describes study design: culturable and non-culturable human pathogens and tet genes were investigated in bioaerosols from 18 barns, and nasal passages of 35 hog producers were sampled using calcium-alginate swabs.

Reports PCR detection targets (Campylobacter, C. perfringens, Enterococcus, E. coli, Y. enterocolitica, tet and ribosomal protection genes) and culturable airborne findings: positive facility counts of 16, 17, 11 and 6 of 18 barns for four pathogens.

Presents aerosol results: total (culturable and non-culturable) pathogens detected in 10, 6, 15, 18 and 2 barns; tet genes found in culturable pathogen isolates; tetA/tetC, tetG and ribosomal protection genes present in bioaerosols of all 18 buildings.

Summarizes nasal flora findings in workers: Campylobacter, C. perfringens, Enterococcus, E. coli and Y. enterocolitica found in 4, 9, 17, 14 and 1 workers, and tetA/tetC and tetG genes in 1 and 10 workers respectively.
Concludes that hog producers are exposed to aerosolized human pathogens and tetracycline-resistant bacteria that can contaminate their nasal flora, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.
Introduction and methods of a study on Yersinia enterocolitica infection in diarrheal patients: 2,600 stool samples tested by culture and RT-PCR, yielding 188 positives (about 7.23% incidence).
Diagnostic comparison and epidemiology: RT-PCR detects more cases than culture, incidence is higher in autumn-winter than spring-summer, and infection sources are mainly unboiled foods and pets.

Clinical manifestations of yersiniosis (gastroenteritis, pseudoappendicitis, extraintestinal complications) and age-related differences, including high morbidity in adults over 60 and children under 3 as high-risk groups.

Antimicrobial susceptibility results for 160 Yersinia isolates: most are susceptible to third-generation cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, but few to first-generation cephalosporins and penicillins.

Concluding recommendation: clinicians should focus on clinical presentation, early diagnosis, and susceptible-antibiotic treatment of yersiniosis and its complications during autumn-winter, especially in high-risk patients.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending the recommendation that clinicians target high-risk patients for yersiniosis and its complications.

Introduces ractopamine hydrochloride (RAC) in finishing pig diets, its known benefit for carcass cutting yields, the gap in knowledge about further processing, and prior reports of higher loin ultimate pH, motivating the ham study.

States the rationale that higher ham ultimate pH could improve protein interaction and textural properties, and the study's objective: whether RAC-fed pigs yield hams with greater ultimate pH and whether this improves texture and water retention.

Describes the methods: 200 hams from barrows and gilts fed RAC or control diets selected by hot carcass weight, fabricated into 5 pieces for cutting yields, 6 muscles assessed for ultimate pH, and hams processed into cured and smoked products.

Reports results for cutting yields: RAC increased whole ham, inside, outside, and knuckle yields as a percentage of chilled side weight, and begins the muscle ultimate pH results across the ham muscles.

Gives ultimate pH results by muscle (about 0.03 to 0.06 units higher in RAC pigs fed 7.4 mg/kg) and notes that cured hams from RAC-fed pigs were heavier at all production stages, with binding strength and protein fat-free comparisons beginning.

Presents the final texture and yield comparisons: no differences in binding strength (P = 0.88) or protein fat-free values (P = 0.13) between RAC and control hams, and concludes RAC boosts cutting yields, cured ham weight, and muscle pH without harming processed ham quality.
Concluding sentence of the abstract stating that feeding RAC achieves growth and cutting yield benefits without affecting further processed ham characteristics.

Introduction to metabolic modifiers in animal production: technologies that boost feed efficiency and lean deposition while reducing fat, and concerns that this focus may harm meat quality. Part of a review on dietary factors and metabolic modifiers affecting meat quality and nutritional value.

Continuation of the introduction: states the review's aim to collate literature data on how metabolic modifiers affect meat quality, and previews the meta-analysis findings on shear force and tenderness.

Meta-analysis findings: conservative use of these metabolic modifiers raises shear force by about 5-10% (0.3-0.5 kg) and reduces perceived tenderness similarly, a change comparable to that from leanness gained by nutrition or genetic selection, possibly an inherent cost of leaner meat.

Conclusion on mitigation: notes that the tenderness decline may be an inherent consequence of leaner meat, and introduces other metabolic factors and dietary additives, such as immunocastration, that could improve meat quality.
Final conclusion: immunocastration and other additives could be used alone or with somatotropin, approved β-agonists, anabolic implants and CLA to maintain or improve meat quality.

Introduction and objective of a meta-analysis of ractopamine hydrochloride (RAC, 5-10 mg/kg for up to 35 d) on carcass cutability and belly quality in finishing pigs; 10 studies for cutting yields, 8 for belly quality.
Methods scope: pooled RAC dietary concentrations (5, 7.4, 10 mg/kg, step-up programs) and feeding durations up to 35 d, compared against non-RAC control pigs.
Statistical analysis: meta-analysis using SAS mixed procedure with RAC inclusion as fixed effect and study as random effect; reports whole primal results, where only whole ham differed (P < 0.01).
Results on standardized trimmed primal yields: Boston butt, trimmed loin, and trimmed ham differed (P < 0.05), and carcass cutting yield is introduced as 74.70% RAC vs. 73.69% control.

Key cutability outcomes: RAC pigs had a 1.01% unit carcass cutting yield advantage (P = 0.02) and a 1.10% unit bone-in lean cutting yield advantage (61.43% vs. 60.33%, P = 0.03), driven by increased boneless subprimal yields in shoulder, loin, and ham.

Boneless subprimal yields by lean cut: RAC advantages of 0.32% units for boneless shoulder (Boston butt + picnic), 0.43% units for boneless loin (Canadian back + tenderloin + sirloin), and 0.51% units for boneless ham (inside + outside + knuckle).
Total boneless yield, summed from boneless shoulder, loin, and ham, was 36.28% for RAC vs. 35.20% for controls, a 1.08% unit advantage (P = 0.002).

Belly quality results: no difference in trimmed belly subprimal yield (12.18% both groups, P = 0.93); RAC pigs had narrower flop distance (15.27 cm vs. 17.08 cm, P = 0.02) and higher iodine value (73.42 vs. 71.48, P = 0.01).
Final values for belly quality comparison: control pigs had a flop distance of 17.08 cm and an iodine value of 71.48, versus RAC values of 15.27 cm and 73.42 respectively.

Introduction to a study of veterinary pharmaceuticals and steroid hormones found in lagoon wastewater and shallow groundwater at CAFOs (swine and beef cattle facilities), framing lagoons as a contamination source.

Study site selection rationale: sites were chosen as worst-case scenarios for groundwater contamination due to subsurface geology and nitrate, ammonia, and chloride monitoring indicating direct infiltration from waste lagoons.

Results on antibiotic and veterinary drug detections: specific pharmaceuticals found at cattle facilities and at swine facilities' wastewater, and the note that steroid hormones were detected less often than pharmaceuticals.
Steroid hormone results: estrone, testosterone, 4-androstenedione, and androsterone in lagoon wastewater (30 to 3600 ng/L), with only estrone and testosterone in groundwater (up to 390 ng/L).

Conclusions on contamination: co-occurrence of pharmaceuticals and steroid hormones in groundwater and correlation with downgradient groundwater shows that aquifers under some livestock lagoons are vulnerable to contamination.
Concluding statement of the groundwater susceptibility finding, followed by the 2010 Elsevier B.V. copyright notice.

Introduction of the study's motivation: aggression from social hierarchy formation on farms causes injuries, stress, and carcass losses, and factors like ractopamine feeding that affect aggression merit investigation.

Study objectives: assess effects of the swine feed additive ractopamine, along with sex and social rank, on aggressiveness and brain amine neurotransmitters in finishing pigs; begins describing the 64-pig design (32 barrows, 32 gilts).

Experimental design: barrows and gilts housed 4 per pen, fed control or ractopamine (Paylean) diets at escalating doses (5 then 10 mg/kg), with dominant and subordinate pigs identified by 36-h behavioral observation.

Methods: dominant and subordinate pigs underwent resident-intruder aggression tests (max 300 s), then at week 4 brain regions (amygdala, frontal cortex, hypothalamus, raphe nuclei) were dissected and assayed by HPLC for monoamines and metabolites.
Behavioral results: ractopamine-fed gilts showed more attacks in the first 30 s than all other subgroups; monoamine analyses are introduced as the study's neurochemical measures.

Final behavioral and neurochemical results: end-of-test attack percentages by subgroup, and gilts showing reduced norepinephrine and DOPAC in amygdala and frontal cortex, plus RAC effects on 5-HIAA and DA turnover in the amygdala.

Serotonin and mechanism results: lower frontal cortex 5-HT in gilts and lower raphe 5-HT in dominant gilts, followed by the authors' interpretation that ractopamine likely acts indirectly on central dopamine regulation of aggression.

Conclusion: the aggressive pattern, especially in gilts, is linked to a deficient serotonergic system in the raphe nuclei, amygdala, and frontal cortex and enhanced amygdala DA metabolism, regions important for aggression control.
Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that enhanced dopamine metabolism in the amygdala is relevant because that brain area is vital for regulating aggression.

Introduction to the antioxidant databank study: explains oxidative stress from reactive oxygen/nitrogen compounds and free radicals, and why knowing antioxidant content in foods matters for antioxidant therapy.

Describes the databank of antioxidant contents for 1,140 food products and beverages, and the first-time amperometric determination of fat-soluble antioxidants in dairy, fish, cacao, chocolate, and nuts alongside water-soluble ones.
Concluding fragment of the abstract specifying that the antioxidant measurements were made using an amperometric method.

This chunk explains the shared maple-like odour of fenugreek, maple syrup, and MSUD patients' urine (from sotolone), and describes the case where maternal fenugreek ingestion during labour caused newborns to smell like maple syrup, falsely suggesting MSUD.

Opening of the study's Objectives section: it defines the aim of examining screen time (TV and other screen entertainment) against all-cause mortality and clinically confirmed CVD events, plus a secondary aim of testing metabolic and inflammatory mediators (BMI, HDL and total cholesterol, C-reactive protein).

Background and start of Methods: notes that prolonged sitting is linked to CVD risk factors regardless of physical activity, but hard outcome studies are scarce, then describes the population sample of 4,512 Scottish Health Survey 2003 adults aged 35+ followed to 2007.

Methods detail: outcomes were all-cause mortality and fatal plus nonfatal CVD events; exposures were interviewer-assessed screen time categories (<2, 2 to <4, and ≥4 hours/day) and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.

Start of Results: reports 215 CVD events and 325 deaths over 19,364 person-years, and begins the covariate-adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause mortality (1.52) for ≥4 h/day versus <2 h/day screen time, with covariates listed.

Main hazard ratios: ≥4 h/day screen time versus <2 h/day gives HR 2.30 for CVD events (95% CI 1.33 to 3.96), and adjusting for physical activity only slightly attenuates the mortality and CVD estimates.

Sensitivity analyses and mediation: excluding early CVD events and prior cancer registrations left results essentially unchanged, and about 25% of the screen time–CVD association was explained by C-reactive protein, BMI and HDL cholesterol together.

Conclusions: recreational sitting measured as TV/screen viewing time is linked to higher mortality and CVD risk regardless of physical activity, and inflammatory and metabolic factors partly explain this, followed by the start of the copyright notice.
Closing copyright and publisher boilerplate (American College of Cardiology Foundation, 2011; Elsevier Inc.; all rights reserved), with no substantive study content.

Opening of the review on sleep and body weight: lists experimental findings that short-term partial sleep restriction disrupts glucose tolerance, sympathetic tone, cortisol, leptin, ghrelin, hunger and appetite.

Mechanistic explanation that short sleep impairs the hormonal recovery needed for appetite control and raises obesity risk, plus the behavioral route of more time for eating and harder healthy-lifestyle maintenance.

Continuation describing how fatigue from insufficient sleep reduces motivation to exercise, followed by the summary conclusion that short sleep is a novel, independent obesity risk factor with public health importance.

Closing summary noting the public health relevance of chronic sleep restriction and calling for future research on whether sleep extension in sleep-deprived obese people improves appetite control or reduces body fat.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the call for research on whether sleep extension reduces body fat in sleep-deprived obese individuals.

Introduces the systematic review's background on sedentary behavior and its health links, then describes the literature search methods (databases and dates) used to identify occupational sitting studies.
Continues the methods: studies were categorized by health outcome, and two independent reviewers rated methodological quality on a 15-point scale.
Reports the synthesis results: 43 included papers by design type (mostly prospective), and the number of studies per health outcome (BMI, cancer, CVD, diabetes, mortality).
Summarizes findings by outcome: median quality score of 12, mixed cross-sectional evidence for BMI, and case-control but not prospective support for a sitting-cancer link.
States the main prospective findings (higher diabetes and mortality risk with occupational sitting) and opens the conclusions that evidence is limited.
Gives the overall conclusion that evidence for occupational sitting harming health is limited and heterogeneous, followed by the journal copyright notice.
Final fragment of the copyright statement for the American Journal of Preventive Medicine article.
Introduction of a cross-sectional study on daily diet and skin ageing, setting out the aim to link fat, antioxidant micronutrient, and food group intake with biophysical skin properties in women.

Methods of the cross-sectional study: skin hydration, surface lipids, and elasticity measured in 716 Japanese women, facial crow's-foot wrinkles rated on the Daniell scale, and usual diet assessed with a validated FFQ.

Main results after adjusting for age, smoking, BMI, and lifetime sun exposure: higher total, saturated, and monounsaturated fat intake linked to greater skin elasticity, and more green and yellow vegetables linked to lower Daniell wrinkling scores.

Further findings: saturated fat remains inversely associated with wrinkling after adjusting for green and yellow vegetable intake, followed by the conclusion that more accurate methods are needed to study diet's role in skin ageing.
Final concluding sentence calling for further studies with more accurate measurement methods to clarify the role of daily diet in skin ageing.
Introduces the Gerson regimen (Max Gerson, 1930s), an alternative cancer treatment involving raw juices, salt elimination, supplements, and coffee enemas to detoxify the liver.

Describes the theoretical basis of Gerson therapy: cancer attributed to altered cell metabolism from toxins and processed food, with emphasis on raising potassium and cutting sodium to correct electrolyte imbalance and repair tissue.

Explains the believed mechanism of coffee enemas (bile duct dilation, toxin excretion) and notes that these theories lack scientific support, despite proponents' claimed 70-90% recovery rates, which NCI and NY County Medical Society reviews found unsupported.

Presents evidence against Gerson-like therapy: an NCI-sponsored study of Gonzalez therapy found patients with inoperable pancreatic cancer who received standard gemcitabine chemotherapy survived about three times longer than those who chose enzyme treatment.

Concludes the NCI pancreatic cancer comparison, stating that the enzyme treatment group (pancreatic enzymes, supplements, detoxification, organic diet) had worse survival and quality of life than the chemotherapy group.

Introduces menopausal hormone therapy's current role (short-term symptom relief, not long-term health) and defines compounded bioidentical preparations as individualized medications made per a prescriber's order.

Explains compounding as tailored individual prescriptions and begins describing how Women's Health Initiative findings and direct-to-consumer marketing drove rising popularity of compounded bioidentical hormones.
Continues on marketing of compounded bioidentical hormones as safe alternatives, the resulting surge in popularity and patient questions, and notes that evidence for superiority claims is lacking.

States that superiority claims over conventional hormone therapy are unsupported and carry risks of variable purity, potency, and unknown efficacy and safety; introduces ACOG and ASRM committees issuing guidance.
Describes the ACOG Committee on Gynecologic Practice and ASRM Practice Committee's overview of concerns and patient counseling recommendations, followed by the 2012 copyright notice.
Final fragment of the copyright and rights notice (ASRM 2012, Elsevier) closing the document.
Introduces the study's background and methods: MRI scans on 1,403 women from CEE hormone therapy placebo-controlled trials, examining brain volume links to cognitive impairment.
Describes study population and design details: women aged 65–80 free of dementia/MCI at enrollment, trials lasting 4–6 years at 14 U.S. academic medical centers, with MRI 1–4 years post-trial.
Explains the statistical method (analyses of covariance comparing treatment groups) and reports the main result that 53 women developed MCI or probable dementia during follow-up.
Reports results for the CEE group: cognitive impairment linked to smaller hippocampal (p = .0002) and total brain volumes (p = .03), seemingly independent of pretreatment cognition.

Reports placebo group results, where cognitive impairment instead tracked with greater frontal and overall ischemic lesion volumes, and states the conclusion that CEE may induce cognitive impairment via brain atrophy.
Final sentence of the conclusion, stating that brain atrophy appears to be the mechanism by which CEE-based postmenopausal hormone therapy induces cognitive impairment.
Introduction to the WHIMS study background and objectives: prior WHIMS findings on CEE plus MPA and dementia/MCI, and the aim of testing CEE alone and CEE plus MPA in older women.

Study design and population: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled WHI trials of women aged 65-79, with enrollment dates and sample sizes for the estrogen-alone and estrogen-plus-progestin trials across 39 clinical centers.
Interventions and outcomes setup: daily CEE 0.625 mg alone versus placebo, CEE plus MPA 2.5 mg versus placebo, with probable dementia and MCI as the main outcome measures.
Primary results for the estrogen-alone trial: case counts and hazard ratio (1.49, CI 0.83-2.66) for probable dementia, which was not statistically significant.
Incidence comparisons and pooled analysis: dementia rates across the two trials (45 vs 22 per 10,000 person-years, P=.11) and pooled dementia hazard ratio of 1.76 under the original WHIMS protocol.
Sensitivity analysis excluding participants with low baseline MMSE scores, plus MCI results: pooled and estrogen-alone hazard ratios for dementia, and MCI hazard ratio of 1.34 for CEE versus placebo.
Combined endpoint and conclusions setup: estrogen-alone trial showed 93 vs 69 cases of dementia or MCI combined (HR 1.38, P=.04), with the conclusion that estrogen alone did not reduce risk.

Key conclusions: estrogen therapy alone did not reduce dementia or MCI and increased combined risk; pooled data showed increased risk; hormone therapy is not recommended to prevent dementia or cognitive decline in women 65 and older.
Final sentence of the abstract's conclusions: a clinical recommendation against using hormone therapy to prevent dementia or cognitive decline in women aged 65 or older.

Opening of the abstract for the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) estrogen-plus-progestin trial: background on uncertain risk-benefit balance, the study objective, and design (randomized primary prevention trial in 16,608 postmenopausal women aged 50-79 recruited 1993-1998).

Study design and interventions: the WHI estrogen-plus-progestin trial randomized women to conjugated equine estrogens 0.625 mg/d plus medroxyprogesterone acetate 2.5 mg/d (n=8506) or placebo (n=8102).

Main outcome measures: the primary outcome was coronary heart disease, with invasive breast cancer as the primary adverse outcome, and a global index of risks and benefits combining these with stroke, PE, several cancers, hip fracture, and other-cause death.

Results begin: the trial was stopped by the data and safety monitoring board on May 31, 2002, after mean 5.2 years of follow-up, because breast cancer crossed the stopping boundary and the global index showed risks exceeding benefits.

Reported results: the stopping rationale and follow-up data cutoff (April 30, 2002), followed by the start of the estimated hazard ratios with 95% CIs for individual clinical outcomes such as CHD, breast cancer, stroke, and PE.

Individual outcome hazard ratios: CHD 1.29, breast cancer 1.26, stroke 1.41, PE 2.13, with protective effects for colorectal cancer (0.63), hip fracture (0.66), and endometrial cancer and other-cause death non-significant, including case counts.
Composite outcome hazard ratios: total cardiovascular disease 1.22, total cancer 1.03, combined fractures 0.76, total mortality 0.98, and global index 1.15, with their 95% confidence intervals.

Absolute risk estimates per 10,000 person-years: excess CHD, stroke, PE and invasive breast cancer events versus reductions in colorectal cancer and hip fracture, showing the absolute harm and benefit magnitudes behind the hazard ratios.
Conclusions: overall health risks exceeded benefits over 5.2 years of follow-up, the global index excess risk was 19 per 10,000 person-years, and all-cause mortality was unaffected.
Final conclusion: the risk-benefit profile fails the requirements for a viable primary prevention intervention, and the regimen should not be initiated or continued for primary prevention of CHD.
Closing fragment of the conclusion, restating that the combined estrogen-plus-progestin regimen should not be initiated or continued for primary prevention of coronary heart disease.

Abstract opening of a study on delusions in frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD): states the research aim and describes the retrospective case-note review of FTLD patients at a tertiary cognitive disorders clinic over three years.

Methods and early results from the FTLD delusions study: eight patients with delusions identified, all assessed with clinical, neuropsychological and MRI evaluation, pathological confirmation in two cases, and an estimated delusion prevalence of 14%, with delusions described as early and persistent.

Key findings of the FTLD delusions study: delusions were phenomenologically diverse with paranoid and somatic types most prominent, behavioural variant FTLD was the most common subtype, and atrophy was mostly bilateral or right-predominant; the chunk ends with the conclusion that delusions are a clinical issue warranting further study.
Concluding sentence of the abstract on delusions in FTLD, calling for further research into delusions as a clinical issue in this condition.

Introduces the background: US women stopped hormone therapy (especially estrogen/progestin) after the July 2002 WHI trial halted over elevated breast cancer risk, followed by reported incidence declines in 2003–2004.

States the commentary's central question of whether the 2002 HT cessation caused the 2003/2004 breast cancer incidence declines, and previews its aim to weigh the evidence and estimate the cessation's impact on US breast cancer burden.
Concluding fragment of the document's opening paragraph, specifying that the commentary will quantify the cessation's effect on the overall US breast cancer burden.

Introduction and study objective: background on nutrient gaps in vegetarian diets, the DRI panel's protein recommendation assumption that vegetarians get about 50% of protein from animal sources, and the aim of examining protein sources in young adult vegetarian women.

Study population and design: a convenience sample of 21 young adult vegetarian women who kept food logs over 4 consecutive days (3 weekdays, 1 weekend day), continuing the rationale about the DRI assumption on animal protein share.

Methods: daily percentage contributions of protein from cereals, legumes, nuts/seeds, fruits/vegetables, and dairy/egg, plus calculation of protein digestibility-corrected amino acid score (PDCAAS) of daily diets.

Results on protein quality: total dietary protein digestibility was 82% versus the DRI reference of 88%, and 4-day average PDCAAS was 80% versus the DRI reference of 100%, both significantly different (P < 0.001).

Key finding and conclusion: animal protein supplied only 21% of dietary protein, well below the expected 45-50%, leading to the suggestion that the protein DRI for such vegetarians may need raising from 0.8 to about 1.0 g/kg due to lower bioavailability.
Closing fragment of the conclusion sentence on the proposed 1.0 g/kg protein DRI adjustment, followed by the Elsevier 2011 copyright notice.

Opening of the review's abstract: it introduces the purpose (evidence that adult protein requirements are significantly underestimated) and the traditional nitrogen balance method for determining requirements, leading into the current Dietary Reference Intake figures.

Reanalysis section: critiques the Dietary Reference Intake values (0.66 and 0.8 g/kg/day), which came from single linear regression of nitrogen balance studies, and reports that two-phase linear regression yields higher mean and safe requirements (0.91 and 0.99 g/kg/day).

Methodological rationale: justifies two-phase regression as better suited to dose-response analysis, notes problems with nitrogen balance, and introduces the indicator amino acid oxidation technique as the alternative method for determining protein requirements.
Key findings: reports indicator amino acid oxidation results in adult men (0.93 and 1.2 g/kg/day), which are 41% and 50% above current Dietary Reference Intakes, and begins the summary section.

Conclusion: summarizes that both the indicator amino acid oxidation values and the nitrogen balance reanalysis exceed current recommendations, and calls for urgent reassessment of adult protein intake guidelines.

Introduction to ergothioneine: its OCTN1-mediated cellular uptake, its link to autoimmune disorders, and the stated gap in knowledge about dietary sources and physiological function, which motivates the study.

Study methods: quantifying ergothioneine in common foods by LC-MS/MS, and comparing its protective effect against oxidative stressors in OCTN1-expressing cells with glutathione using the MTT cell viability assay.

Key results: ergothioneine was found only in some foods, highest in specialty mushrooms, kidney, liver, beans, and oat bran; it protected cells only against copper(II)-induced toxicity, and was much weaker than glutathione.
Conclusion: because ergothioneine is far less potent than glutathione, the authors infer it is not part of the intracellular antioxidant thiol defense system.
Introduction to antibiotic residue monitoring in poultry: federal agencies set residue tolerances and target muscle tissue for monitoring but do not specify breast versus thigh.
Rationale and study design: if certain muscle tissues hold higher antibiotic residues, they should be chosen for monitoring, so chickens were assigned to enrofloxacin dosing groups.
Experimental methods: 33-day-old chickens were dosed with enrofloxacin (Baytril) at 25 or 50 ppm for 3 or 7 days, and breast and thigh muscle were sampled for fluoroquinolone analysis.
Key findings: enrofloxacin concentrations were significantly higher in breast than thigh muscle across all treatment groups, showing tissues differ in residue levels.
Conclusion and regulatory implications: the results suggest residue monitoring should consider which muscle tissue is tested to ensure safety tolerance levels are not exceeded.

Introduction of a Korean study on antibiotic residues: states concern about antibiotic entry into water and aims to assess how drinking water and food consumption contribute to inadvertent human antibiotic intake, naming the population (general population in Korea) and the scope of the evaluation.

Methods portion of the study describing the six target antibiotics (SMZ, SMX, STZ, TMP, EFX, RTM) and the approach of estimating daily intake by measuring antibiotics and their major metabolites in urine from 541 Korean participants.

Methods continued: describes measuring antibiotics in drinking water source and tap water, surveying participants' water consumption rates, and surveying consumption patterns of major foods suspected of containing antibiotic residues to assess dietary contribution.

Results reporting maximum urinary concentrations (pg/ml) of detected antibiotics, including SMZ-N4, TMP, EFX, CFX, and RTM, and noting that source water antibiotic levels were 10-67 ng/l, with the finding that drinking water consumption was not clearly related to estimated daily intake.

Key findings linking diet to urinary antibiotic excretion: several food groups correlated significantly with antibiotic levels, specifically beef, pork, dairy products, and raw fish associated with EFX, CFX, SMZ, and TMP intake.
Conclusion of the study: estimated daily antibiotic intakes did not exceed acceptable daily intake levels; includes the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice marking the end of the abstract.
Introduction to a pilot study of a five-day vegetarian Temple Stay program in Korea, examining whether short-term dietary change reduces exposure to antibiotics and phthalates in adults.
Study methods: 25 participants in a five-day Korean Temple Stay program gave urine samples before and after the program, and completed a questionnaire on their prior dietary patterns.

Program description and measured biomarkers: participants lived Buddhist monk routines on a vegetarian diet, and urinary antibiotics, phthalate metabolites, and the oxidative stress marker MDA were analyzed.

Key results: antibiotic and phthalate detection frequency and levels dropped during the program, and urinary MDA fell significantly (0.16 vs 0.27 mg/g creatinine), with caveats about other behavioral influences.
Conclusion and copyright notice: short-term dietary change may meaningfully reduce inadvertent antibiotic and phthalate exposure and oxidative stress, published by Elsevier in 2010.

Abstract opening of a review paper on dioxin-like contaminants (PCDDs, PCDFs, dioxin-like PCBs) in human breast milk, describing the literature search scope (2000–2009 papers on ScienceDirect) and the first study aim: levels across geographic areas and infant exposure.

Middle part of the review's stated aims: examining how maternal factors (age, deliveries, diet, smoking, childhood nutrition) and environment affect contaminant levels in breast milk, plus studying time patterns.
Final part of the abstract listing the review's fourth aim, identifying data gaps, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice for the paper on dioxins in human milk and infant intake.

Introduction of a review on PCB exposure in children versus breastfeeding benefits; sets out the health-effects overview and the question of postnatal PCB risk via breast milk, noting environmental food-chain exposure as the main source.

Continuation of the abstract: states that infant PCB exposure is mainly through breast milk, finds limited evidence of significant toxicity from this route, and concludes that breastfeeding should still be encouraged given human milk's benefits.
Final sentence of the abstract's conclusion: inconclusive evidence that lactational PCB exposure causes major harm to infant health and development, supporting continued breastfeeding.

Abstract opening of a study on pregnancy-related changes in serum levels of PCBs (CB 118, 138, 153, 156, 180), hydroxylated PCB metabolites (4-OH-CB107, 4-OH-CB146, 4-OH-CB187), and pentachlorophenol (PCP); introduces the serum lipid rise (2-fold, early vs. late pregnancy, N=10).

Findings on PCB dilution: median PCB levels in serum lipids fell 20-46% despite rising lipid content; strong intra-individual PCB correlations (Spearman r=0.61-0.99) justify using a single sample for relative body burden across pregnancy if collected in a narrow window.
Results on OH-PCB and timing: OH-PCB serum concentrations generally declined through pregnancy, though some women's levels rose near term; sets up the implication that sampling time matters.

Correlation patterns for OH-PCBs and PCP: OH-PCBs correlate positively (r=0.66-0.99) across first and second trimesters but diverge with third-trimester samples (r=-0.70 to 0.85); PCP shows no decline and no significant correlations across sampling periods.

Conclusion that OH-PCB and PCP sampling must be timed to the pregnancy period of interest; discusses how intra- and inter-individual variability may reflect lipid solubility, persistence, blood distribution, metabolic formation, and pregnancy physiology changes.
Closing discussion of factors behind differing intra- and inter-individual variability patterns across the compounds, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.
Final fragment of the Elsevier 2010 copyright statement ('All rights reserved') ending the document.

Study design: a nursery-based repeated-measures modelling and rewards intervention for preschoolers, introducing the 8 fruits and 8 vegetables organized into four food sets and the baseline procedure.
Intervention phases: the 32-day fruit intervention where rewards were given only at snacktime for fruit, followed by vegetable-targeted intervention for Food Sets 1 and 4 after Baselines 2 and 3.

Results summary: large significant increases in targeted fruit and vegetable consumption, smaller increases for non-target paired foods, within-category generalisation, and the study timeline ending with Baseline 4 and 6-month follow-up.
Generalisation and maintenance findings: increases transferred strongly to the no-rewards lunchtime context and persisted at six-month follow-up, contrary to response-decrement theory predictions.
Closing information: the six-month follow-up maintenance of fruit and vegetable consumption after reward withdrawal, plus the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.

Opening of the abstract: the objective and design of a study on how premature weaning from breast milk affects later-life chronic disease risk, using meta-analyses and Australian historical breastfeeding data since 1927.

Continues the design section (estimating exposure in Australia and the population-attributable proportion of chronic disease tied to artificial infant feeding), then begins the results: chronic disease risk is 30-200% higher in non-breastfed individuals after adjusting for confounders.
Core quantitative results: premature weaning exposure ranged 20-90% across post-WWII cohorts, and the estimated attributable proportion of chronic disease is 6-24% assuming 30% exposure.

Conclusions of the study: breastfeeding has public health significance for preventing chronic disease, with a small but consistent increase in later-life chronic disease risk from premature weaning, and substantial exposure in the Australian population.

Final conclusion: about 90% of current 35-45-year-old Australians were weaned before 6 months, and promoting longer, exclusive breastfeeding could reduce future chronic disease burden and health system costs.
Introduction to PFOS and its precursor compounds: sources in consumer products (carpets, upholstery, textiles), degradation to PFOS, and prior US human serum studies of PFOS, PFHxS, PFOA, and PFOSA.

Study design: measurement of PFOS, PFHxS, PFOA, and PFOSA in 473 human blood, serum, and plasma samples from nine countries including the United States, Colombia, Brazil, Belgium, Italy, Poland, India, Malaysia, and Korea.

Key results on country differences: PFOS is the predominant perfluorochemical in blood, with highest levels in the US and Poland, moderate levels in several countries, and lowest in India; PFOA is the next most abundant but occurs infrequently.
Further findings: PFOA results, absence of age- or gender-related differences in PFOS and PFOA serum levels, and country-dependent correlations among the four measured perfluorochemicals.

Interpretation: the country-specific correlation patterns suggest different perfluorochemical sources and exposure patterns across countries, followed by qualitative detection of additional perfluorochemicals beyond the four targets.
Additional detected compounds: qualitative detection in selected serum samples of PFDS, PFHpA, PFNA, PFDA, PFDoA, and PFUnDA, at roughly 5- to 10-fold lower concentrations than PFOS.
Conclusion: calls for future research to identify sources and exposure pathways of human perfluorochemical exposure.

Abstract opening: introduces the study measuring 10 perfluorochemicals (PFCs) in Chinese meat, meat products, eggs, and indoor dust, noting PFOA and PFOS as the most frequently detected, with food concentration ranges.

Results on contaminant levels: mean PFOA, PFHpA, and PFOS concentrations in indoor dust (ng/g dry wt), plus the start of the estimated daily intake (EDI) results from meat, meat products, and eggs, including the LOQ-handling convention.

Dietary intake results: EDI of PFOS and PFOA from meat, meat products, and eggs under the LOQ=0 and LOQ/2 substitution scenarios, and the finding that intake rises with family income; begins the dust inhalation EDI.
Dust exposure and comparison: EDI of PFOS and PFOA via dust inhalation, then the comparison of intakes from foods and dust with prior estimates from drinking water, fish, and seafood in China.

Total exposure conclusion: dietary sources make up over 99% of PFOS and 98% of PFOA total daily intake in adults, and the analyzed foods were minor contributors to PFOS exposure; begins the PFOA source finding.
Final conclusion: meat was the primary dietary contributor to PFOA exposure, while the analyzed foodstuffs were not major sources of PFOS exposure.
Introduction to the study: background on POSF-based compounds degrading to PFOS, its persistence and accumulation, and prior detection of PFCs (PFOS, PFHxS, PFOA, PFOSA) in US human sera.
Study scope: lists the ten perfluorinated compounds measured in human blood, continuing the introduction into the methods description of the study's analytes.
Sampling design: 85 whole blood samples from nine cities in eight Chinese provinces, naming each city and its province, and completing the list of measured PFCs.
Key results: PFOS is the dominant PFC, with the highest mean concentration in Shenyang (79.2 ng/mL) and lowest in Jintan (3.72 ng/mL), and PFHxS as the next most abundant compound.

Demographic and correlation findings: no age differences for major PFCs; gender differences (males higher in PFOS and PFHxS, females in PFUnDA); and inter-compound correlations (PFHxS with PFOS; PFNA, PFDA, PFUnDA with PFOA).
Conclusion: city-level differences in the percentage composition profiles of PFCs across the nine sampled cities.

Introduces the study's design: 56 seasonal snowpack samples from eight Western US national parks (2003–2005), and names the four current-use and four historic-use pesticides measured consistently across sites and years.

Reports measurement variability: mean coefficient of variation for pesticide concentrations rises from 15% (site replicates) to 41% (intra-park) to 59% (inter-annual replicates), and notes the pesticide list is continued.

Presents source-attribution findings: year-to-year pesticide profiles are consistent but distinct per park (regional source effect), historic-use pesticides correlate with cropland intensity after temperature correction, and back-trajectory analysis of upwind CUP usage explains park differences.

Quantifies regional transport: more than 75% of snowpack pesticide concentration in most parks comes from regional transport, and concludes that most contamination in the parks stems from North American pesticide use.
Concluding statement that the majority of pesticide contamination in US national parks is attributable to pesticide use within North America.

Introduces the paper's method for ranking pesticide residues and foodstuffs for national monitoring priority, combining ATMDI (agricultural uses and MRLs) and EDI (food contamination data) chronic dietary indicators across 490 substances.

Presents the main exposure results: mean ATMDI exceeds the ADI for 10% of pesticides and mean upper-bound EDI exceeds the ADI for 1.8%, and introduces the seven-level risk scale applied to substances analyzed in French food and substances not sought.

Gives the monitoring outcomes by group: of 336 analyzed substances, 70 pesticides of concern (22 priority at levels 4-5); of 154 unsought substances, 36 of concern (8 priority at level 4) should be added to monitoring programs.

Concludes that refining exposure assessment requires analytical improvements to lower detection limits for priority pesticide/commodity combinations, and notes the method could be applied at different geographic scales if developed nationally.
Contains only the publisher copyright notice (Elsevier Ltd., 2011) closing the abstract.

Introduces the USA rainfall pesticide study: 2003-2004 growing-season samples from four agricultural sites (Maryland, Indiana, Nebraska, California), analyzed for insecticides, herbicides, fungicides, and degradates; begins summary of most frequently detected pesticides, led by herbicides atrazine and metolachlor.

Lists the most frequently detected rainfall pesticides across all sites: herbicides dominate the top 10 (atrazine, metolachlor, Dacthal, acetochlor, simazine, alachlor, pendimethalin), with chlorpyrifos, carbaryl, and diazinon as the only top-10 insecticides, plus counts of rarely or never detected parent compounds.

Covers the most frequently detected degradates in rain (deethylatrazine, oxygen analogs of chlorpyrifos, diazinon, and malathion, and 1-naphthol from carbaryl) and begins noting deethylatrazine's regional detection pattern.

Describes site-specific detection patterns: deethylatrazine common in Maryland, Indiana, and Nebraska but almost absent in California, oxygen analogs mainly in California, and rare acetanilide herbicide degradates, suggesting they are not formed atmospherically or readily volatilized from soils.

Summarizes pesticide mass deposited by rainfall: herbicides made up 91-98% of deposited mass except in California in 2004 (insecticides 61%), and total rainfall deposition was estimated at under 2% of the amount applied at these agricultural areas.
Final fragment completing the conclusion, stating that rainfall deposition of pesticides was estimated at less than 2% of the total applied in these agricultural areas.

Abstract opening of a study on serum PCB congener half-lives (elimination rates) in 304 environmentally exposed children, measured at ages 8 and 12, with the study aim and method (exponential decay per child or multiple regression for the cohort).

Methods detail on handling PCB reuptake and exclusion rules (values below the limit of detection, half-lives over 30 years), followed by the start of the reported median half-life results in years for the six congeners.

Core results: median half-lives for PCB congeners 118, 138(+163), 153, 156(+171), 170 and 180, plus findings that half-lives were not systematically related to serum concentration and that reuptake percentage and congener abundance were significantly associated with half-life.
Closing sentence of the abstract on significant associations between half-life, reuptake prevalence and congener abundance, followed by the Elsevier 2010 copyright notice.

Introduces the study's purpose: measuring nine organochlorine pesticide residues in umbilical cord blood of newborns in Southern Spain and relating exposure to maternal factors, including adherence to the Mediterranean Diet.

Reports the main result that OCs were detected in 95% of cord blood samples from 318 mothers, with their mean Mediterranean Diet adherence score (56.77, SD 16.35), and explains the diet's emphasis on plant foods over meat and dairy, which are lipophilic OC sources.
Details specific dietary associations: meat, fish, and dairy intake with cord serum DDE; dairy with lindane; vegetables with lindane; and fruit with endosulfan I.

Concludes that no significant link was found between Mediterranean Diet adherence and serum OC residues, but that closer adherence may still protect against exposure by reducing meat and dairy intake; includes copyright notice.
Copyright notice (2010 Elsevier Ltd.) closing the abstract; contains no substantive content about the study.
Introduction to the study: motivation linking PBDE body burdens in the U.S. population to red meat and poultry consumption, and the goal of estimating PBDE levels in domestic meat via two surveys.
Study design: the two statistically designed surveys (2002-2003 and 2007-2008) bracket the December 2004 cessation of U.S. penta- and octa-BDE manufacturing, enabling trend analysis.
Key quantitative result: composite-sample averages of the seven most prevalent PBDEs fell more than 60%, from 1.95 to 0.72 ng/g lipid, between the two survey periods.
Species comparison and congener profile: 2008 individual samples ranked beef lowest, then hogs and chickens, then turkeys; the congener pattern resembled penta-BDE, with BDE-47 and BDE-99 dominating.
Conclusion: the survey data suggest U.S. meat and poultry PBDE levels declined after manufacturing ceased, but livestock exposure pathways remain unknown.
Study background on flame retardants in pet dogs versus pet cats and humans, introducing the hypothesis that dogs may better model human exposure to PBDEs and related contaminants.
Study methods and hypothesis: serum and food samples from 18 pet dogs were analyzed for PBDEs and emerging flame retardants, and the PBDE concentration results begin here.
Results on PBDE levels in dog serum and food (ng/g ww), with serum dominated by tetra- to hepta-BDE congeners and food by BDE-209, leading into the half-life analysis of this congener difference.

Half-life results for PBDE congeners in dog serum under a food-exposure assumption, the unreasonable residence times from dust as an added exposure source, and the other flame retardants detected (Dechlorane Plus, decabromodiphenylethane, HBCD).
Concluding clause listing the additional flame retardants (Dechlorane Plus, decabromodiphenylethane, hexabromocyclododecane) identified in the dog serum and food samples.

Abstract of a 2010 study measuring PBDE and PCB levels in breast adipose tissue from California women in a late-1990s breast cancer study, including the congener profiles observed (BDE47, BDE99, PCB153 etc.) and the analytical method.

Continuation of the abstract's findings: strong within-class but weak between-class correlations suggesting distinct exposure pathways, weak negative age associations, and PBDE levels that are among the highest reported, exceeding NHANES and consistent with California's high PBDE use.
Concluding part of the abstract: the PBDE data are framed as a possible baseline for body burdens to track changes after PBDE formulation restrictions, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.
Final fragment of the copyright statement at the end of the abstract, reading 'All rights reserved' after the Elsevier 2010 copyright notice.
Introduction and methods opening of a study on urine bisphenol-A (BPA) levels and male sexual function, describing the 427 male workers sampled in high-BPA-exposure regions and urine testing by HPLC.

Methods section describing BPA measurement in urine by high-performance liquid chromatography, assessment of male sexual dysfunction with standard inventories across 4 domains and 7 indices, and linear regression adjusting for confounders.

Results showing that higher urine BPA was linearly associated with worse sexual function on all 7 indices, specifically reduced sexual desire, erection difficulty, and ejaculation strength (all P < .001).

Results continuing with lower overall sexual satisfaction (P < .01) and a similar negative correlation in participants with only environmental (non-occupational) BPA exposure, noted as less stable due to small sample size.
Conclusion stating that urine BPA level correlates with declining male sexual function, and that this has public health implications given widespread human BPA exposure.
Closing fragment of the conclusion emphasizing the public health significance of widespread human BPA exposure.

Introduction to the BPA food study: defines bisphenol A, its uses in can linings and polycarbonate plastics, known health effects in rodents and humans, and the gap in U.S. food BPA data that motivates the study.

Study methods and initial detection results: describes measuring BPA in 105 fresh, canned, plastic-packaged, and pet food samples, and notes it was detected in 63 samples, including fresh turkey, canned green beans, and canned infant formula.

Quantitative findings: details the triplicate samples, the detected concentration range (0.23 to 65.0 ng/g ww), and the result that levels did not depend on food type or packaging but varied with pH, beginning the pH comparison.
Conclusions: pH 5 foods showed higher BPA than more acidic or alkaline foods, detected levels matched prior studies, and the authors call for larger, representative U.S. food sampling.

Introduction of the bamboo shoot pesticide study: explains why organochlorine pesticides (persistent, bioaccumulative) are a concern and motivates testing Chinese bamboo shoots, which are widely exported, for OCP residues.
Results section identifying the three organochlorine pesticides (HCH, DDT, PCNB) found in Zhejiang bamboo shoots, with detection rates of 100%, 100% and 75% respectively.
Results comparing average residue levels to China's maximum residue limit of 50 µg/kg, and reporting that 82.14% of samples were classified as safe based on residue concentrations.

Conclusion stating that all bamboo shoot samples contained organochlorine pesticides, yet most (82.14%) were considered safe for consumption, followed by the 2010 Society of Chemical Industry copyright notice.

Introduction and objective of a double-blind randomized pilot trial comparing saffron (Crocus sativus) hydro-alcoholic extract with fluoxetine for mild to moderate depression; covers prevalence of depressive disorders and saffron's traditional use in Persian medicine.

Study population and design: 40 adult outpatients meeting DSM-IV criteria for major depression (SCID-assessed) with mild to moderate severity, enrolled in a 6-week double-blind randomized trial comparing Crocus sativus with fluoxetine.
Methods and intervention: single-center, double-blind randomized allocation of patients to saffron 30 mg/day (Group 1) or fluoxetine 20 mg/day (Group 2), both given twice daily for 6 weeks.

Results: saffron at 30 mg/day was similarly effective to fluoxetine for mild to moderate depression (F = 0.13, d.f. = 1, P = 0.71), with no significant difference in observed side effects between groups.
Conclusion of the saffron vs. fluoxetine depression trial: findings indicate Crocus sativus efficacy for mild to moderate depression, and the authors state a larger-scale trial is justified.

Abstract opening of a 2010 study (Elsevier) on saffron (Crocus sativus) odor, stating the aim of examining its effects on women's menstrual symptoms (PMS, dysmenorrhea, irregular menstruation) and describing the methods: 35 women exposed to saffron odor for 20 minutes, with saliva hormone measurement (cortisol, testosterone, estradiol) and the STAI anxiety inventory.

Methods and results section of the saffron odor study: saliva hormone assays by enzyme immunoassay and the STAI psychological test, followed by results showing saffron odor significantly lowered cortisol after 20-minute exposure in both follicular and luteal menstrual phases, and raised estradiol in both phase groups.

Results and conclusions of the saffron odor study: STAI anxiety scores decreased in the saffron group in both follicular and luteal phases; the authors conclude saffron odor has physiological and psychological effects in women and may help treat PMS, dysmenorrhea, and irregular menstruation.
Closing conclusion of the saffron odor study, stating it is the first report suggesting saffron odor may be effective for menstrual distress, followed by the Elsevier GmbH 2010 copyright notice.

Introduces the double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial of saffron (Crocus sativus L.) for premenstrual syndrome (PMS), covering the study objective, design, setting (Tehran and Zanjan), and eligibility criteria (women aged 20-45 with regular cycles and 6+ months of PMS).

Describes the intervention and methods: women randomly assigned to saffron 30 mg/day (15 mg twice daily, group A) or placebo capsules over two menstrual cycles (cycles 3 and 4), with the primary outcome as the Daily Symptom Report and the secondary outcome as the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale.

Reports the trial results: saffron was effective in relieving PMS symptoms, with a significant difference between saffron and placebo in cycles 3 and 4 on Total Premenstrual Daily Symptoms and the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale.

Gives the conclusion that C. sativus L. is efficacious for PMS, noting its tolerable adverse effect profile as support for saffron as an alternative PMS treatment, and states that further investigation is warranted.
Closing sentence of the conclusion: saffron may be an alternative PMS treatment given its tolerable side-effect profile, and the results merit further research.

Opening chunk of an abstract-style review on antimutagens and anticarcinogens, introducing 'desmutagens' or 'interceptor' molecules: small biological or synthetic metabolites that bind or react with mutagenic chemicals and free radicals.

Middle chunk of the abstract describing interceptor molecules as soft and hard nucleophiles that react with major classes of direct-acting electrophilic mutagens, and noting they are a first line of defense but under-investigated.
Final chunk of the abstract, stating that interceptor molecules' spectra of activity and their relevance to prophylaxis or treatment of human disease remain under-investigated.

Introduction to a human study of aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) pharmacokinetics, summarizing prior animal and Chinese human evidence that chlorophyll and chlorophyllin reduce carcinogen exposure, and noting that AFB1 kinetics and chlorophyll effects had not been studied in humans.

Study design: an unblinded crossover trial in four human volunteers aiming to establish AFB1 pharmacokinetic parameters and test chlorophyllin or chlorophyll cotreatment in three, with protocol 1 describing a fasted 14C-AFB1 capsule dose.

Methods detail: protocol 1 dosing of 14C-AFB1 (30 ng, 5 nCi) with water and post-dose feeding, sample collection of blood and urine over 72 hours, measurement by accelerator mass spectrometry, and protocols 2 and 3 adding 150 mg purified chlorophyll or chlorophyllin to the capsules.

Results on baseline kinetics: rapid AFB1 absorption (plasma ka 5.05 h^-1, Tmax 1 hour) and near-complete urinary elimination (95% by 24 hours), plus the observation that repeated protocols were run per volunteer and that chlorophyll and chlorophyllin reduced Cmax in some subjects.

Main findings and conclusion: chlorophyll and chlorophyllin significantly impeded AFB1 absorption and lowered Cmax and plasma/urine AUCs in one or more subjects, providing first human AFB1 pharmacokinetic parameters and suggesting co-consumption may limit dietary aflatoxin bioavailability as in animal models.
Concluding sentence of the abstract, restating that chlorophyll or chlorophyllin co-consumption may limit human aflatoxin bioavailability, consistent with animal model findings.

Introduction to a review on dietary phytochemicals for cancer chemoprevention. It sets out the need for a systematic screening approach that reflects the complexity of carcinogenesis and begins presenting the molecular pathways involved.

Names oxidative stress, inflammation, and evasion of apoptosis as key mechanisms of carcinogenesis, and links them to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and pro-apoptotic activities as protective effects. Continues the review's framing of the chemoprevention rationale.

Concludes the introduction by proposing that these mechanisms can serve as a basis for screening novel phytochemicals. States the review's aim: identify molecular processes to target in routine screening and select the most promising chemopreventive candidates.
Final sentence fragment of the abstract-style introduction, restating the goal of selecting the most effective dietary phytochemical candidates for cancer chemoprevention.

Introduction of a study on dietary compounds (caffeine, theophylline, theobromine, resveratrol) and their ability to bind acridine orange, a mutagen, compared with chlorophyllin, as a possible mechanism for preventing chemical-induced mutagenesis and carcinogenesis.

Continuation of the study's aims and methods: comparing dietary xanthines and resveratrol with water-soluble chlorophyll derivative (chlorophyllin) in binding acridine orange, to identify effective binding agents for preventing chemical mutagenesis and carcinogenesis.

Key results of the study: chlorophyllin needed less than twice the concentration to bind 50% of acridine orange, resveratrol required about 20-fold higher concentration, and xanthines (caffeine, theophylline, theobromine) needed 1000- to 10,000-fold excess, showing their relative binding strength.

Introduction to a study on silkworm larvae (Bombyx mori) as an animal protein source for astronauts in bioregenerative life support during future deep space missions, fed mulberry then stem lettuce leaves.

Describes the broader terrestrial application of using inedible plant biomass to produce high-quality animal protein for people in extreme environments (polar regions, military bases, ships, submarines), and introduces the study's respiration characteristics focus.

Outlines the methods: respiration under eating vs. not-eating conditions, and nutrient analysis (protein, fat, vitamins, minerals, fatty acids) of freeze-dried silkworm powder from day 3 of the 5th instar.
Reports respiration results: higher rates in leaf-eating larvae than non-eating ones, and significant differences between mulberry- and lettuce-fed silkworms in the 4th and 5th instars (P<0.01).
Reports gas exchange findings: significant differences in exhaled CO2 and inhaled O2 between the eating and not-eating physiological states (P<0.01), with a higher respiration quotient during eating.
Summarises nutritional findings for silkworm powder: rich in protein and amino acids, containing 12 vitamins, nine minerals and twelve fatty acids, and yielding 359 kcal per 100 g dry weight.
Final fragment of the nutritional summary, stating the energy yield of 359 kcal per 100 g of silkworm powder on a dry-weight basis.

Introduces the study's background: low-grade inflammation ('metaflammation') linked to chronic disease and modern foods, and describes the randomised cross-over trial design comparing kangaroo and wagyu beef meals in healthy subjects.
