Reports the main results for postprandial plasma TAG, IL-6 and TNF-alpha at 1 and 2 h, showing significantly higher levels after wagyu beef than after kangaroo, with the corresponding P-values.

Presents the CRP results (significantly higher at 1 h, non-significant at 2 h after wagyu) and the study's conclusion that wagyu beef induces a low-grade systemic immune reaction compared with kangaroo.
Concludes the abstract by recommending future studies using isoenergetic intake and isolating the fatty acid components of meats to explain the inflammatory differences.

Introduction to a study comparing pheasants raised in captivity (aviaries) with wild pheasants, describing the natural hardships wild game birds face such as finding food, breeding, predators, and harsh weather.

Statement of the study's aim to determine the biological value of meat from captive versus wild pheasants, followed by the first result: wild males reached the highest weight (1232.4 g) with very highly significant group differences (P < 0.001).

Statistical results on group differences: very highly significant differences in overall weight, breast weight, and leg (tights with drumsticks) weight, plus significant differences in the percentage of breast and leg parts.

Results on carcass composition: wild pheasants had the heaviest breast muscles (282.6 g) and leg portions (206.2 g), and lower and lighter skin with subcutaneous fat on breasts, while females from both settings had more skin and fat on legs.

Chemical composition results: breast muscle differed significantly in calcium and phosphorus content, and wild pheasant leg muscles had higher moisture, protein, and calcium but lower fat and energy value.
Conclusion that wild-raised pheasant meat has higher biological value than aviary-raised meat, offering nutritional advantages for human consumption.
Final sentence of the conclusion restating that meat from pheasants kept in aviaries is of lower biological value, so wild-grown meat has nutritional advantages.

Introduces metaflammation (low-grade systemic inflammation) linked to chronic disease, initially thought to stem from obesity, and notes that identified lifestyle inducers include some not associated with obesity.

Explains that the most common inflammatory inducers identified are nutrition-related, so obesity may still be linked to inflammation directly or indirectly; the authors present evidence for non-nutritive inducers and restate that obesity beyond a point may be neither necessary nor sufficient to explain chronic disease.

Argues the broader cause of all inflammatory inducers is the modern post-industrial environment and its lifestyles, and begins the review's central metaphor that obesity is 'a canary in the mineshaft.'

Concludes that obesity is a warning sign of larger global, environmentally driven problems rather than a single pathway to modern chronic disease, followed by the 2010 copyright notice for Obesity Reviews.
Introduction to the paper on evolution of dietary antioxidants: oxygen's dual role, plant and human defenses against reactive oxygen species, and the opening framing of the diet-evolution hypothesis.

Continues the introduction: human antioxidant defences are imperfect, ROS-driven oxidative damage accumulates with age, and plant-based antioxidant-rich foods traditionally made up most of the human diet.

Introduces the hypothesis that plant-based dietary antioxidants support human health, justified evolutionarily by a relatively hypoxic environment, and outlines the paper's scope on diet evolution and antioxidant defence strategies.

Outlines the paper's structure: human dietary evolution, antioxidant defence strategies, dietary antioxidant evolution from plant and human perspectives, and possibilities for diet, evolution, and health.
Concludes the abstract with an evolutionary cost-benefit analysis of why humans lost the ability to synthesize ascorbic acid (vitamin C) while still requiring it dietarily.

Introduction to the paper on chemical safety of meat, framing how post-WWII consumer demand shifted from food sufficiency to quality to safe, healthy food, and why consistent standards and controls are needed.

Explains the role of chemical analysis in food safety via tracking (downstream, primary production to consumer) and tracing (upstream, consumer to primary production), as a prerequisite for ensuring safety and quality.

States the paper's scope: chemical safety of meat and meat products, covering inorganic and organic residues and contaminants, nitrite use in meat products, veterinary drug incidence, and an FMEA approach.
Describes the Failure Mode and Effect Analysis (FMEA) system used to assess and prioritize vulnerable food chain steps so that vulnerability can be reduced or eliminated.

Opening chunk of an abstract-style review on vegetarian diets and public health, introducing the idea that plant antioxidant phytochemicals may act via signaling and pro-oxidant redox effects rather than direct antioxidant action in vivo.

Middle section of the review abstract, summarizing the scope of evidence (epidemiological, biomarker, evolutionary, public health, antioxidant) and highlighting plasma ascorbic acid as a biomarker of future disease risk and basics of redox-based cell signaling.

Continuation of the abstract covering redox tone, sulfur switches, and the Antioxidant Response Element as mechanisms of phytochemical signaling, and arguing that sufficient evidence already supports public policy promoting plant-rich diets.

Concluding portion of the abstract arguing that policy need not await full mechanistic answers, and framing dietary antioxidant interplay in nonequilibrium redox systems as a research frontier for orthomolecular nutrition and aging populations.
Final fragment of the abstract ending the sentence about providing science-based evidence to advance public health in an aging population.

Introduction/abstract opening of a cross-sectional study on diet and IGF-1/IGFBP-3 in premenopausal Japanese women, setting up the breast cancer risk rationale and study population (261 women aged 20-54) and the dietary assessment aims.

Methods and main finding of the study: diet measured by semiquantitative food frequency questionnaire, and null result that soy product and soy isoflavone intake showed no significant correlation with serum IGF-1 or IGFBP-3 after adjusting for age, energy, body fat, and education.

Key results on dietary fat: total fat intake is significantly inversely correlated with serum IGFBP-3 (r = -0.13, P = 0.04), with saturated and monounsaturated fats showing borderline inverse correlations with IGFBP-3 (P = 0.06 and P = 0.07).
Final fragment of the results, completing the reported correlation coefficient and P-value for monounsaturated fat intake versus serum IGFBP-3 (r = -0.11, P = 0.07).
Abstract opening of a 2-year randomised trial on soya foods and serum IGF-1/IGFBP-3 levels in 196 premenopausal women, motivated by soya's proposed protective role against breast cancer.
Describes the trial intervention (two daily soya servings with isoflavones and protein versus controls) and the serum sampling schedule at five time points, with IGF-1/IGFBP-3 measured by ELISA.
Methods on statistical analysis using mixed models for repeated measures, plus notes on high adherence, acceptable dropout, and baseline comparability between groups.

Results: no significant intervention effect on IGF-1, IGFBP-3, or their ratio, but urinary isoflavone excretion was positively associated with IGF-1 (P=0.04) and the IGF-1:IGFBP-3 ratio (P=0.06), consistently over time.
Conclusion: adding soya foods does not appear to lower IGF-1 or IGFBP-3, and the higher soya protein intake may slightly raise IGF-1 levels.
Introduces the study's background: IGF-1 and IGFBP links to prostate cancer risk, the role of dietary protein in raising IGF-1, and the anti-proliferative effects of soy isoflavones.
Describes the study design: a Prostate Cancer Lifestyle Trial testing a very low-fat vegan diet with 58 g/day soy protein, with intervention patients reporting higher intake after one year.

Presents the main results: intervention patients had higher protein and isoflavone intake (P < 0.001), IGF-1 rose in both groups, IGFBP-1 rose only in the intervention group, and vegetable protein increases tracked with IGFBP-1 gains.

Gives the conclusions: dietary protein and isoflavones within comprehensive lifestyle changes may not significantly alter IGF-1, though the authors note literature linking high essential amino acid protein to higher IGF-1.
Closing recommendation: men with early stage prostate cancer may be prudent not to exceed dietary protein recommendations, given evidence that protein rich in essential amino acids can raise IGF-1.

Introduction and methods of a study on a low-fat diet and exercise program's effect on the IGF axis (serum IGF-I, insulin) and prostate cancer cell growth, including the design: fasting serum from 14 men after an 11-day program and 8 long-term participants.

Methods continued (ELISA measurements of insulin, IGF-I, IGFBP-1, IGFBP-3 and LNCaP cell stimulation), followed by the start of results: IGF-I fell 20% and IGFBP-1 rose 53% after 11-day diet and exercise.

Results on long-term diet and exercise participants: IGF-I 55% lower and IGFBP-1 150% higher; serum insulin down 25% after 11 days and 68% lower long-term; IGFBP-3 unchanged; LNCaP growth reduced 30% (11-day) and 44% (long-term).

Final results on apoptosis/necrosis in LNCaP cells exposed to post-diet-and-exercise serum, and the conclusion that the low-fat diet and exercise intervention alters the circulating IGF axis and reduces LNCaP prostate tumor cell growth in vitro.

Concluding phrase of the abstract summarizing that diet and exercise-induced reductions in the IGF axis are associated with reduced growth and enhanced apoptosis/necrosis of LNCaP prostate cancer cells in vitro.

Introduces the study design: a 22-year follow-up of Ecuadorian subjects with growth hormone receptor gene mutations causing GHR and IGF-I deficiency, motivated by yeast and mouse evidence that growth-signaling mutations extend lifespan and reduce cancer and insulin resistance.

Reports the main epidemiological result: GHR-deficient individuals had only one non-lethal malignancy and no diabetes, versus 17% cancer and 5% diabetes prevalence in controls, with cause-of-death surveys covering earlier deaths.

Gives the cellular mechanism for low cancer incidence: GHRD serum reduced DNA breaks and increased apoptosis in hydrogen-peroxide-treated human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs), and introduces the insulin measurements.

Presents the insulin data: GHRD subjects had markedly lower insulin (1.4 vs 4.4 μU/ml) and HOMA-IR (0.34 vs 0.96), indicating greater insulin sensitivity that may explain the absence of diabetes; also notes that GHRD serum lowered RAS, PKA and TOR expression in HMECs.

Summarizes the gene expression changes in HMECs (reduced RAS, PKA, TOR; increased SOD2) linked to cellular protection and lifespan extension in model organisms, and concludes that conserved aging pathways operate in humans and suggest a candidate drug target.
Final fragment of the abstract, completing the conclusion that the findings identify a candidate drug target for healthy life span extension.

Background and rationale of the pooled IGF1/IGFBP3 and breast cancer study: IGF1 biology and prior unclear results on consistency and effect modifiers, motivating the Endogenous Hormones and Breast Cancer Collaborative Group analysis.

Continuation of the background: uncertainty about IGF1 and IGFBP3 links to breast-cancer risk factors, and the aim of the collaborative pooled prospective-study analysis to improve precision of hormone-risk estimates.
Methods: prediagnostic IGF1 and IGFBP3 data from 17 prospective studies in 12 countries, geometric mean concentrations by risk factor in controls, and the design for estimating odds ratios.

Statistical methods: conditional logistic regression on 4790 cases and 9428 matched controls, stratified by study, baseline age and baseline date, with two-sided tests and p<0.05 as the significance threshold.

Findings on correlates of IGF1: adjusted levels rise with height and age at first pregnancy, fall with age at menarche and years since menopause, and are higher in moderately overweight women and moderate drinkers; begins the breast cancer odds ratio result.

Main result: odds ratio of 1.28 (95% CI 1.14-1.44; p<0.0001) for highest versus lowest IGF1 fifth, unchanged after adjusting for IGFBP3 and not varying significantly by menopausal status at blood collection.

Subtype and conclusion results: ORs of 1.38 for ER-positive and 0.80 for ER-negative tumours (heterogeneity p=0.007), leading to the interpretation that circulating IGF1 is positively linked to breast cancer risk, mainly for ER-positive tumours, with little modification by IGFBP3 or menopausal status.

Closing interpretation and funding: the association is not substantially modified by IGFBP3, does not differ markedly by menopausal status, appears confined to oestrogen-receptor-positive tumours, and the study was funded by Cancer Research UK.

Introduction of the review: establishes that metastatic tumours cause most cancer deaths, notes limits in preventing metastasis, and states the hypothesis that growth factors and their receptors drive metastatic development.

Scope of the review: lists the stages of metastasis examined for growth factor and receptor involvement, namely epithelial-mesenchymal transition, invasion and migration, circulation survival, distant organ seeding, and metastatic angiogenesis.
Conclusion of the abstract: states that the review discusses growth factor and receptor functions and summarizes research efforts to inform new treatment strategies for cancer metastases.
Introduction and aim of a review on why centenarians are protected from cancer, framing the question and the goal of proposing a unifying hypothesis about IGF-1, inflammation and p53.

Methods and early results of the review: it surveys literature on IGF-1, inflammation and p53 in centenarians, and reports that centenarians show low IGF-1-mediated responses and high anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10, TGF-beta).
Core findings linking the pathways: inflammation and IGF-1 both converge on the tumour suppressor p53, and genetic p53 variants are linked to longevity through reduced cancer mortality.
Conclusion of the review: well-preserved p53-mediated responses are hypothesised to be a key, though not sole, factor protecting centenarians from cancer.

Abstract opening of a 2009 review on mechanisms of breast cancer bone metastasis, introducing bone as a preferential metastatic site and previewing the multi-step process from primary tumor escape to colonization.

Closing portion of the review abstract listing the four key metastasis steps (invasion/escape, migration toward bone, adhesion/arrest in bone, establishment in bone) and noting these factors as therapeutic targets, followed by the Elsevier copyright notice.
Fragment of the copyright line (Elsevier Ireland Ltd, 2009) ending the abstract of the breast cancer bone metastasis mechanisms review.

Opening of the abstract: establishes the epidemiological and biological link between cancer and aging, and notes that an apparent drop in cancer incidence in old age stemmed from ignoring changing population size.

Middle of the abstract: discusses limits of age-specific cancer incidence and the slowing rate of increase at very advanced ages, which seems to conflict with biological data and hints at a protective mechanism.
Core claim of the paper: a mathematical model of mortality kinetics from gerontology predicts a slowing-down kinetics for cancer incidence, explaining the late-age pattern.

Conclusion of the abstract: the slowing or decline in cancer incidence in aging populations is consistent with an accelerating loss of physiological capacity, because individuals with better physiological function are selected at older ages.
Final fragment completing the last sentence about selection of individuals with better physiological function; adds no new claims beyond chunk 4.

Introduction and methods of a systematic review and meta-analysis on circulating IGF peptides, IGF-binding proteins, and prostate cancer risk; describes the biological rationale and the literature search.

Methods and study counts: random effects meta-analysis yielding summary odds ratios, with the number of studies and prostate cancer cases for each IGF peptide, binding protein, and the IGF-I:IGFBP-3 ratio.
Main results: pooled odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals per standard deviation increase for IGF-I, IGF-II, IGFBP-1, IGFBP-2, IGFBP-3 and the IGF-I:IGFBP-3 ratio.

Heterogeneity and subgroup findings: I2 above 75% for all exposures, with associations differing by study design (prospective vs retrospective) and an inverse IGFBP-3 association seen only in retrospective studies; also notes weak evidence for stronger associations in advanced disease.
Conclusions: raised circulating IGF-I is positively associated with prostate cancer risk, IGFBP-3 associations are inconsistent, and there is little evidence for a role of IGF-II, IGFBP-1 or IGFBP-2.
Final sentence of the conclusions, restating that there is little evidence linking IGF-II, IGFBP-1 or IGFBP-2 to prostate cancer risk.

Opening chunk of an abstract/review on lifestyle factors and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS); introduces age, genetics, and sex hormones as known causes and the purpose of examining modifiable lifestyle contributors.

Summarizes recent findings on lifestyle and metabolic risk factors for BPH/LUTS: obesity, diabetes, and meat/fat intake increase risk; physical activity, moderate alcohol, and vegetable intake decrease risk.
Covers factors with unclear risk (lipids, smoking) and notes that randomized trials of weight loss, exercise, and diet for BPH/LUTS prevention or treatment have not yet been done.

Summary section stating lifestyle factors offer a novel opportunity for BPH/LUTS prevention and treatment, though untested in clinical trials, and begins the recommendation to integrate healthy lifestyle advice into standard treatment algorithms.
Final sentence concluding that promoting healthy lifestyle choices alongside standard BPH/LUTS treatment algorithms is potentially beneficial.

Study design and setting for the Italian multicenter case-control study (1991–2002) of onion/garlic intake and benign prostatic hyperplasia, including sample sizes of 1369 BPH cases and 1451 hospital controls.

Continuation of the methods: trained-interviewer data collection via a validated food frequency questionnaire, and multivariate odds ratios with 95% CIs adjusted for confounders and energy intake; results begin with the comparison of nonusers.

Main results linking allium vegetable intake to lower BPH odds: highest-category ORs of 0.41 for onion and 0.72 for garlic, a combined OR of 0.65 for frequent users of both, with the inverse association consistent across age strata.
Conclusion of the onion and garlic BPH study, stating that this large European dataset shows an inverse association between allium vegetable consumption and benign prostatic hyperplasia.
Introduces the Italian case-control study (1991-2002) on dietary food groups and risk of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), describing the aims and the largely undefined dietary risk factors.
Methods detail: 1369 surgically treated BPH cases and 1451 non-neoplastic hospital controls under 75, assessed with a validated 78-item food frequency questionnaire plus an alcohol section.
Describes dietary assessment 2 years before diagnosis/admission and multivariate adjustment for energy intake and confounders, then begins the results with cereals showing a risk trend.
Results give odds ratios: increased BPH risk for cereals, bread, eggs, and poultry; inverse associations for soups, pulses, cooked vegetables, and citrus fruit.
Reports null associations for dairy, coffee/tea, pasta/rice, fish, cheese, vegetables, potatoes, fruit, and desserts, then the conclusion that diet plays a role in BPH risk.
Final sentence of the conclusion: a diet high in cereals and some meats and low in vegetables and pulses may be unfavorable for BPH risk in this Italian population.
Introduction and objectives of a pilot study testing whether a low-fat, flaxseed-supplemented diet affects prostate cancer biomarkers in men awaiting prostatectomy.

Methods: 25 prostate cancer patients awaiting prostatectomy were placed on a low-fat (20% or fewer kilocalories) diet with 30 g/day flaxseed, with baseline and follow-up PSA, testosterone, free androgen index, and cholesterol measured.
Methods continued: diet-treated patients' tumors were compared with historic matched controls for apoptosis (TUNEL) and proliferation (MIB-1) markers.
Results: diet lasted an average of 34 days, with significant drops in total cholesterol, total testosterone, and free androgen index.
Results on PSA: no significant change in the whole sample, and a non-significant decline among men with Gleason sum 6 or less (n=19).

Results on tumor biology: proliferation index was lower in diet-treated patients than historic controls (P=0.05), and apoptosis distribution differed significantly (P=0.01), with diet-treated tumors mostly scoring 1 versus 0 in controls.
Results on duration and conclusions: proliferation and apoptosis were associated with days on the diet; authors conclude the pilot data suggest the diet may affect prostate cancer biology.
Conclusion: the diet may affect prostate cancer biomarkers, and further study is needed to assess its benefit as complementary or preventive therapy.

Introduction to the document, arguing that healthy lifestyle factors matter for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) development, as they already do for cardiovascular health, and citing prospective cohort data from BPH and prostate cancer prevention trials.

Summarizes evidence that exercise and specific macronutrient and micronutrient intake from regular diet benefit prostate health, with effects comparable in size to alpha-blockers and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, and notes the large US market for prostate supplements.

Contrasts dietary micronutrients with supplements: supplements are widely used and often prescribed for prostate disease, but supplemental micronutrients and phytotherapies lack supporting evidence of efficacy.
Concluding fragment of the document's final sentence, stating that supplemental micronutrients and phytotherapies currently lack evidence of efficacy.

Abstract opening of a study on transurethral electrovaporization of the prostate (TVP) for benign prostatic hyperplasia, introducing the 32-patient cohort and the pressure-flow urodynamic methodology used before and 6 months after treatment.

Abstract results and conclusion of the TVP study: all 32 patients improved on subjective and objective obstruction measures, with few irritative symptoms and one recatheterization, concluding TVP is a promising alternative to TURP for relieving bladder outflow obstruction.
A lone period ending the abstract; it is a fragment with no standalone content and belongs to the closing sentence of the TVP study abstract's conclusion.

Introduction and purpose of a primary care review on benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and bladder outlet obstruction (BPO), covering the literature and guidelines reviewed and the introduction of the histological definition of BPH in the results.

Results section stating that BPH is a histological diagnosis causing prostate enlargement and BPO, that treatment is indicated only for troublesome symptoms, progression risk, or suspected cancer, and that effective medical and surgical treatments exist to improve quality of life.

Conclusions section on managing BPO collaboratively with the patient, preferring pharmacological and minimally invasive treatments over invasive surgery, and beginning to describe which patients primary care can manage.
Final referral guidance: patients with mild or moderate BPH/BPO symptoms can usually be managed by a primary care physician, while more complicated cases should be referred to a urologist.

Introduction and methods of an epidemiological survey of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and prostate cancer (CaP) in mainland China, covering a 1997 multi-province hospital survey and historical review of the Beijing Institute of Urology.

Results section reporting 1997 BPH (16.1%) and CaP (1.5%) hospital incidence across 187 Chinese hospitals (95,749 patients), plus historical Beijing Institute of Urology rates for 1951-1960 (BPH 7.6%, CaP 0.6%).

Remaining results comparing Beijing Institute of Urology incidence for 1991-1997 (BPH 18.5%, CaP 3.4%) and the conclusion that BPH and CaP hospital incidence is rising rapidly in China, though CaP is still uncommon.

Introduction and methods of a study on low-fat diet and exercise effects on the IGF axis and LNCaP prostate cancer cell growth, covering epidemiology of prostate cancer in Asian vs. US men and the serum collection design.

Methods and results of the study: serum from control, diet-and-exercise, and exercise-only men was used to treat LNCaP cells, with measured insulin, IGF-1, and IGFBP-1 levels showing reduced growth factors and increased apoptosis in treated groups.

Results and conclusions of the study: lower serum insulin and IGF-1, higher IGFBP-1, reduced LNCaP cell growth, and major apoptosis increase, concluding that low-fat diet and/or intensive exercise alters serum hormones to inhibit prostate tumor cells in vitro.
Final sentence of the conclusions and the copyright notice (2003 Wiley-Liss, Inc.) for the study on diet and exercise effects on LNCaP prostate tumor cell growth and apoptosis.

Introduction and objectives of the 1986-1992 Lifestyle Heart Trial: a randomized trial testing whether intensive lifestyle changes (without lipid-lowering drugs) over 5 years are feasible and can reverse coronary heart disease, building on prior 1-year regression findings.

Study design and population: randomized invitational trial of 48 patients with moderate-to-severe coronary heart disease assigned to intensive lifestyle change or usual care, with 35 completing 5-year quantitative coronary arteriography at two tertiary care university centers.

Intervention and outcome measures: the intensive lifestyle program (10% fat vegetarian whole-foods diet, aerobic exercise, stress management, smoking cessation, group psychosocial support) over 5 years, with adherence, coronary stenosis change, and cardiac events as primary measures.

Adherence results: experimental group patients sustained comprehensive lifestyle changes for 5 years (20 of 28 completed follow-up), while control group patients (15 of 20 completed) made only moderate changes.

Angiographic stenosis results in the experimental group: average percent diameter stenosis improved by 1.75 points at 1 year (4.5% relative) and 3.1 points at 5 years (7.9% relative), in contrast to the control group's progression.

Control group progression and events: controls' stenosis worsened by 2.3 points at 1 year and 11.8 points at 5 years (27.7% relative worsening, P=.001 between groups), and cardiac events were 45 in controls vs 25 in the experimental group (risk ratio 2.47).

Conclusions: the experimental group showed greater coronary atherosclerosis regression after 5 years than after 1 year, while control group atherosclerosis progressed and more than twice as many cardiac events occurred.

Final conclusion sentence: control patients' continued coronary atherosclerosis progression and more than double the cardiac events, underscoring the benefit of intensive lifestyle change over 5 years.

Study purpose and methods: a nonexperimental prospective time-series study of 2974 participants from 24 sites in an intensive cardiac rehabilitation program, measured at baseline, 12 weeks, and 1 year.
Statistical methods (paired t-tests comparing baseline, 12 weeks, and 1 year) and the start of the results, covering program retention rates.
Results after 12 weeks: 88% retention, 78.1% at 1 year, and significant improvements in BMI, lipids, HbA1c, blood pressure, depression, hostility, exercise, and functional capacity.
Results at 1 year: differences from baseline remained significant, with additional gains from 12 weeks to 1 year in BMI, HDL, functional capacity, and hostility, and recidivism in other measures.
Detailed 12-week-to-1-year changes (recidivism and p-values, with HDL unchanged from baseline), followed by the start of the conclusions about feasibility and sustainability.

Conclusions: the program was feasible and sustainable, produced subjective and objective health gains, worked across multiple clinical/community sites in four states, and benefited patients aged 65 and older.
Final sentence of the document, noting that the improvements were also seen in patients aged 65 or older.
Study design, purpose, and eligibility criteria for a 22-week worksite nutrition intervention with GEICO employees (N=113) testing weight and cardiovascular risk reduction.
Intervention details (22-week low-fat vegan diet) and the outcome measures (weight, anthropometrics, blood pressure, lipids, diet) plus the statistical analysis plan (MANOVA followed by ANOVA).
Results showing the intervention group's greater weight change versus controls (-5.1 kg vs +0.1 kg, p<.0001) and the start of the waist circumference findings.
Continued results: waist circumference change (-4.7 cm vs +0.8 cm), waist-to-hip ratio change, and the comparison of proportions achieving 5% weight loss (48.5% vs 11.1%), with the chi-square test.
Chi-square test statistic and the study's conclusion that the 22-week low-fat vegan worksite intervention effectively reduced body weight and waist circumference.

Introduces the Lifestyle Heart Trial: a 1-year randomised controlled study of comprehensive lifestyle changes (low-fat vegetarian diet, smoking cessation, stress management, moderate exercise) versus usual care, with 195 coronary lesions assessed by quantitative coronary angiography.
Reports the main angiographic results: average percentage diameter stenosis regressed slightly in the lifestyle group (40.0% to 37.8%) while progressing in the control group (42.7% to 46.1%).

Gives the subgroup analysis of severe lesions (>50% stenosis), where the lifestyle group regressed (61.1% to 55.8%) and controls progressed (61.7% to 64.4%), and notes 82% of experimental patients had regression.
Concludes that comprehensive lifestyle changes may reverse even severe coronary atherosclerosis within one year without lipid-lowering drugs.

Introduction and background of a crossover trial comparing virgin olive oil, walnuts, and almonds replacing 40% of dietary fat in hypercholesterolemic patients, focusing on cardiovascular risk markers.

Methods of the crossover design: 4-week healthy run-in, then randomized diet sequences each lasting 4 weeks with a common background diet enriched with VOO, walnuts, or almonds; outcomes were serum lipids, oxidation and inflammation markers, and plasma fatty acids for compliance.
Study population of 18 completers (9 women, mean age 56, BMI 25.7) and the key result: LDL-cholesterol reductions of 7.3% (VOO), 10.8% (walnut), and 13.4% (almond) from baseline.

Further results: total cholesterol and LDL/HDL ratio fell in parallel, LDL reductions exceeded those predicted from fatty acid and cholesterol exchanges, and no changes occurred in other lipids, oxidation, or inflammation markers.
Conclusion: nut-enriched diets confirm cholesterol-lowering effects, and phenolic-rich virgin olive oil appears to lower cholesterol independently of its fatty acid content, warranting further study.
Closing conclusion sentence and copyright notice (Elsevier B.V., 2010) for the crossover study on olive oil, walnut, and almond diets.

This chunk opens the study abstract on dried prunes as a pre-meal snack, stating the three hypotheses: greater satiety measured by ad libitum meal intake, greater VAS-rated satiety, and reduced dessert appetite versus an isoenergetic bread preload.

This chunk describes the design (45 healthy normal-weight subjects, randomised within-subject crossover) and reports that the prune preload led to less dessert eaten after lunch and lower total energy intake at the meal.

This chunk reports VAS results showing lower hunger, desire, and motivation to eat at all time points before the meal, and attributes the satiating effect of prunes, given similar macronutrients, to their high fiber content.

This chunk concludes that identifying satiating foods that do not raise overall energy intake matters, and that adding dried prunes to a snack promotes satiety while supplying valuable nutrients; it ends with the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.
This chunk is the trailing fragment of the Elsevier 2010 copyright notice ending the study abstract.

Introduction to a systematic review of over-the-counter and food-store nutraceutical weight loss supplements, framing obesity as a global health problem and herbal 'weight loss pills' as an appealing quick fix.

Concluding portion of the review's introduction, stating its purpose: to give a starting point for informed choices among nutraceutical weight loss products and advice on healthy dietary alternatives.

Study design: glycemic and insulinemic index of whole soy powder cake (SBC) in human subjects, compared with cooked paddy-rice and their combination, measuring blood glucose, insulin, and breath hydrogen in 20 subjects.

Methods and results: 20 subjects consumed SBC, cooked paddy-rice, or both in random crossover order; reported GI of SBC was 22 and insulinemic index 48, and adding 60 g SBC to rice significantly lowered the blood glucose rise.

Key findings: adding SBC to rice lowered postprandial glucose but not insulin, and breath hydrogen did not rise significantly; SBC is low GI and low II, yet it does not suppress rice-induced insulin secretion.
Conclusion: despite SBC's low glycemic and insulinemic indices, postprandial insulin response to cooked paddy-rice was not reduced by SBC.

Opening of a 2001 CHF, Inc. essay arguing that plant-based diets, not device- and risk-factor-driven treatment, are the key to addressing coronary artery disease; introduces the contrast between high-fat diets causing atherosclerosis and healthier plant-based diets in poorer nations.

Middle section critiquing the century-long device-driven, risk-factor-oriented approach to coronary heart disease as a 'rear-guard defensive' strategy that still leaves many patients progressively disabled or dead, setting up the contrast with an alternative.

Core thesis of the essay: evidence from nutrition, population, and interventional studies supports plant-based diets and aggressive lipid lowering as an 'offensive' way to arrest, prevent, and reverse heart disease; the key policy step is for US dietary guidelines to endorse plant-based eating.

Closing recommendation that an expert committee free of industrial and political influence is needed so that US dietary recommendations rest on science, followed by the copyright notice (c)2001 CHF, Inc.

Introduces the systematic review of 78 studies comparing waist-to-height ratio (WHtR), waist circumference (WC), and BMI as predictors of diabetes and cardiovascular disease, including prospective findings that WHtR and WC outperformed BMI.
Continues the review's findings: cross-sectional support in adults and children, and ROC analysis giving mean AUROC values of 0.704 for WHtR, 0.693 for WC, and 0.671 for BMI.

Reports the mean WHtR boundary value of 0.50 across diverse countries and ethnic groups, and concludes that WHtR and WC are similar, independent predictors stronger than BMI, noting a meta-analysis is needed for firmer comparison.

Concludes that WHtR may be a more useful global clinical screening tool than WC, based on AUROC analyses and a weighted mean boundary of 0.5, and states the public health message to keep waist circumference under half one's height.
Closing fragment of the public health slogan 'keep your waist circumference to less than half your height', the document's final takeaway message.

Introduction and methods summary of a systematic review on body fat distribution and morbidity/mortality in older adults, reporting the search yield (2,702 citations) and the number of studies included (25 for comorbidity, 17 for mortality).

Findings on measurement types: most included studies relied on anthropometric measures (BMI, waist circumference, waist-hip ratio) rather than direct body fat measures, and results were inconsistent about the strongest predictor of morbidity and mortality.

Key result that BMI alone is a poor predictor of morbidity and mortality in older people because it cannot detect age-related body fat redistribution, along with the BMI range (overweight to mildly obese) associated with lowest mortality in the elderly.

Conclusion that standard clinical guidelines treating overweight and obesity as major mortality and morbidity risk factors do not apply to older adults, followed by the start of the review's central message calling for new population-specific guidelines.

Closing recommendation of the review: urges government to create new guidelines for older adults based on body fat distribution measures, and to ensure these guidelines are not misapplied to other populations.
Final fragment of the review's closing sentence, ending the recommendation about not applying the new guidelines to inappropriate populations.
Abstract opening of a Belgian study on plant vs. animal protein intake and its link to overweight/obesity, using 2004 Belgian National Food Consumption Survey data (methods and sample description).
Results on the sample of about 3083 participants and protein intake levels: animal protein (47 g/d) versus plant protein (25 g/d) out of 72 g/d total, with main food sources of each protein type.
Results on protein sources by sex and legume/soya intake, plus the first regression finding that animal protein is positively associated with BMI in males.
Regression results on anthropometrics: animal protein linked to BMI and waist circumference in males, and plant protein inversely associated with BMI and waist circumference in both sexes.
Conclusion of the study: plant protein intake is lower than animal protein intake and declines with age, and plant protein may protect against overweight and obesity in Belgium.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that plant proteins may help prevent overweight and obesity in the Belgian population.

Introduction and objective of the EPIC-PANACEA study examining meat consumption (total, red, poultry, processed) and 5-year weight gain in European adults, with background on prior observational and intervention findings.
Study objective continues naming EPIC-PANACEA, and the design section begins, describing the large European cohort of 103,455 men and 270,348 women aged 25-70 recruited 1992-2000.

Design details: recruitment across 10 European countries, baseline diet assessed with country-specific validated questionnaires, a dietary calibration subsample, and baseline measured versus follow-up self-reported weight and height.

Statistical methods: linear mixed models relating energy from meat (kcal/d) to annual weight change (g/y), adjusted for age, sex, total energy, physical activity, dietary patterns and other confounders; results section starts.

Main results: total meat intake positively associated with weight gain across sex, BMI, and smoking subgroups; a 250 g/d increase in meat corresponds to about 2 kg more weight gain over 5 years (95% CI 1.5-2.7 kg).
Final results on red meat, poultry, and processed meat all showing positive associations, and the conclusion that reducing meat consumption may aid weight management.

Introduction to the satiety review: defines satiety as inhibition of eating after a meal, notes food compositional/structural factors, and frames water and gas as neglected non-nutrients for food-based weight management.
Summary of prior short-term studies on water or gas in foods: satiety generally rose, but effects on subsequent intake were inconsistent; the diverse designs and food matrices limit firm conclusions.
Key comparative findings: solids may raise satiety more than liquids, gas may match water, and gastric distension is the likely main mechanism alongside cognitive, anticipatory and sensory responses.

Timing evidence and mechanisms: limited support that water drunk before (not with) a meal reduces intake, and longer-term reasoning that increasing food volume with water or gas could aid weight management.
Conclusion and practical recommendation: use water and gas to manipulate perceived portion sizes without adding energy, as the most practical application for weight management.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the advice to manipulate perceived portion size with water or gas without increasing energy content.

Introduction of a review on whether rising winter indoor temperatures in developed countries (USA, UK) could causally contribute to rising obesity, via reduced cold exposure affecting energy expenditure.

Explains the dual mechanism by which reduced seasonal cold lowers energy expenditure: less need for thermogenesis and reduced thermogenic capacity, supported by experiments showing a graded link between mild cold and energy expenditure.
Focuses on brown adipose tissue (BAT): time in thermal comfort may reduce BAT and thermogenic capacity, and notes that cold-adiposity pathways have not yet been directly tested in humans.

Concludes that naturalistic and experimental research is needed on how changes in thermal exposure affect body weight, possibly informing new public health strategies against obesity; includes the 2011 copyright notice for Obesity Reviews.
Fragment of the copyright line from the journal Obesity Reviews (2011, International Association for the Study of Obesity).

Opening of an abstract on gut microbiota and obesity: introduces Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes as the dominant gut bacteria, and reports that Bacteroidetes proportion is lower in obese versus lean people and rises with weight loss on low-calorie diets.

Concluding sentence of the same microbial ecology abstract on human gut microbes and obesity: states that obesity has a microbial component with possible therapeutic implications, following the findings on Bacteroidetes proportions in obese, lean, and dieting individuals.

Introduces the document's central claim: lower Bacteroidetes-to-Firmicutes ratio in obesity, and contrasts probiotic intake (dairy and non-dairy, Lactobacillus) with weight gain, setting up the polyphenol discussion.

Presents polyphenol-rich foods (apples, pears, grapefruit, green tea) as weight-reducing and explains that microbial polyphenol metabolism cleaves glycosidic linkages, producing glycans that nourish gut microbiota.
Gives the two key mechanistic points: Firmicutes have fewer glycan-degrading enzymes than Bacteroidetes, and Firmicutes are more inhibited by phenolic antimicrobial effects.

Concludes the proposed mechanism: polyphenols favor Bacteroidetes, which have more glycan-degrading enzymes, explaining the weight-lowering effect; also suggests clone library, fingerprinting, dot blot and FISH methods for future studies.

Recommends future methods (clone libraries, fingerprinting, dot blot, FISH) to characterize microbiota composition and taxon abundance, and proposes high-bioavailability polyphenol supplementation for obese individuals with a high Firmicutes/Bacteroides ratio.

States the proposed regimen: high-bioavailability polyphenols combined with a probiotic-restricted diet for weight loss, with implications for dietary planning and nutraceutical or pharmaceutical preparations.

Summarizes practical recommendations: more polyphenol-rich foods and syrups and low amounts of probiotic foods (yogurt, soy yogurt, probiotic supplements), followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.
Contains only the trailing copyright line (Copyright © 2010 Elsevier Ireland Ltd. All rights reserved.), a boilerplate ending of the document with no substantive content.

Introduction of an ileostomy study on dietary polyphenols: healthy volunteers consumed polyphenol-rich apple juice or anthocyanin-rich blueberries, and effluent was analyzed by HPLC to measure polyphenols reaching the colon.

Results of the ileostomy study: most apple polyphenols are absorbed or metabolized in the small intestine, with 0-33% of the dose recovered in ileostomy bags, peaking at 2 h, while blueberry anthocyanin recovery was higher.

Key findings and implications: up to 85% of blueberry anthocyanins reached the ileostomy bags (varying by sugar moiety), implying colonic delivery, so structure-dependent bioavailability should be considered in colorectal prevention models.

Concluding fragment of the abstract, stating that polyphenol structure-related availability must be accounted for when using these compounds in model systems studying preventive effects against colorectal diseases.

Introduction of a review on butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) as immune modulators: high-fiber diets, fermentation-derived SCFAs, and their effects on immune cells and systemic inflammation linked to obesity.

Recent findings summarized: SCFAs reduce immune cell chemotaxis and adhesion in a type- and concentration-dependent way; butyrate is anti-inflammatory via NF-κB signaling and histone deacetylase inhibition, though results conflict across studies.

Summary section explaining that discrepant SCFA results may reflect differences in cell types and their proliferative/differentiation status, and that SCFAs show anti-inflammatory effects, including blocking immune cell infiltration of tissues such as adipose tissue.

Conclusion on immune mechanisms: SCFAs may inhibit T cell proliferation and activation and block antigen-presenting cell adhesion, which matters because obesity-associated inflammation may be antigen-dependent.
Closing recommendation that future studies use micromolar SCFA concentrations to better reflect physiological levels.
Introduces the document's topic: dietary fibre fermentation by colonic bacteria producing short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, acetate, propionate) and their role in colon cancer chemoprevention.

Explains the primary-prevention mechanism: butyrate activates drug-metabolising enzymes such as glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), reducing carcinogen burden and mutations, and introduces how GST activation was measured.
Reports the differential effects of butyrate on GST gene expression across colon cell types: induced GST mRNA in HT29 tumour cells, LT97 adenoma cells, and primary colon cells.
Describes post-transcriptional differences: butyrate raised GST protein levels and total enzyme activity in HT29 cells but slightly reduced them in LT97 adenoma cells.

Proposes mechanisms for GST activation by butyrate, namely histone deacetylase inhibition and MAPK/ERK signalling influence, based on increased histone acetylation and ERK phosphorylation in HT29 cells.
Covers functional consequences: butyrate and inulin fermentation supernatant increase GST activity and reduce DNA damage from carcinogens such as hydrogen peroxide and 4-HNE in colon cells.
Concludes that further animal and human studies are needed to clarify the role of dietary fibre and butyrate in inducing GST activity and reducing colon cancer risk.

Introduces propionate as a gut microbial fermentation product of dietary fiber (alongside acetate and butyrate) and its known hypophagic effects in ruminants, noting its under-explored roles in non-ruminants and humans; opening of the abstract on propionate as an anti-obesity and satiety factor.

Continues the abstract by linking propionate's hypophagic and hypocholesterolemic effects in humans to obesity prevention, and introduces short-chain fatty acids as ligands of GPR41 and GPR43, suggesting propionate and acetate may regulate adipogenesis and adipokine release.

Concludes the abstract's rationale: GPR-mediated regulation of adipogenesis and adipokine release by propionate and acetate, and states that the review summarizes evidence supporting propionate as a dietary appetite suppressant to combat the obesity epidemic.
Final sentence of the abstract stating the review's aim of combating the obesity epidemic, followed by the 2011 Elsevier Ltd. copyright notice; the closing fragment of the document.

Introduces the EPIC-Oxford cohort study design and objective: describing lifestyle and nutrient intakes across UK participants recruited via general practices or post, with a high proportion of non meat-eaters, and the four diet groups defined at baseline.
Describes the setting (United Kingdom) and study participants: 65,429 men and women aged 20-97, broken down into 33,883 meat-eaters, 10,110 fish-eaters, 18,840 lacto-ovo vegetarians and 2,596 vegans.

Reports results on diet-group differences: lifestyle and nutrient intakes differ, with meat-eaters and vegans at the extremes; fat intake is below the UK 33% energy reference, and vegans' saturated fat (about 5% of energy) is less than half that of meat-eaters (10-11%).

Summarises micronutrient patterns by diet group: vegans have the highest intakes of fibre, B1, folate, vitamin C, vitamin E, magnesium and iron, and the lowest of retinol, B12, vitamin D, calcium and zinc; conclusions begin by noting the cohort includes 31,546 non meat-eaters.

Concludes that the cohort is one of the largest vegetarian studies worldwide, that average intakes approximate current health recommendations, and that wide between-group variation in saturated fat and fibre enhances the study's power to detect diet associations.
Final sentence states that the wide range of dietary intakes should enable the EPIC-Oxford study to detect associations between diet and major cancers and causes of death.

Introduction to a review on L-arginine's anti-obesity effects, noting rising research interest over 20 years and evidence that dietary L-arginine reduces adiposity in obese rats, pigs, and humans with type 2 diabetes.

Explains that L-arginine's fat-reducing effects likely shift energy intake and expenditure toward fat loss or slowed white adipose tissue growth, with the list of species where adiposity reduction was observed continuing from chunk 1.

Describes proposed mechanisms: L-arginine may promote mitochondrial biogenesis and brown adipose tissue development via cell-signaling molecules (nitric oxide, carbon monoxide, polyamines, cGMP, cAMP) and by upregulating genes that increase whole-body energy substrate oxidation.

Concludes that L-arginine is a promising safe, cost-effective nutrient for reducing adiposity, increasing muscle mass, and improving metabolic profile in animals and humans, ending the discussion of mechanisms in chunk 3.
Introduction of a peanut trial: background on peanut/peanut butter consumption, CVD risk, and the question of whether product form and processing (roasting, flavouring) undermine health benefits.

Study aim and participant description: investigates peanut form and processing effects on fasting plasma lipids and body weight; 118 adults from Brazil, Ghana and the US with mean age 29.2 years and BMI 30.0.

Trial design and main null result: participants randomised to raw, roasted unsalted, roasted salted, honey roasted peanuts, or peanut butter for 4 weeks; no differential effect on body weight or lipids in the total sample.

Key findings: HDL-cholesterol rose at group level, and total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol and TAG fell significantly in participants with elevated fasting plasma lipids versus those with normal levels.
Conclusions and future directions: processing attributes tested do not undermine peanuts' lipid-lowering effects or harm body weight; further research on other risk factors is needed.
Introduction to nuts: their nutrient and phytochemical richness and cardiovascular benefits, versus their high fat and energy density, raising questions about weight and energy balance.

Evidence that nuts are not linked to weight gain, explained mechanistically by high satiety and low metabolizable energy (poor bioaccessibility) plus compensatory dietary responses offsetting 55-75% of their energy.
Limited data on energy dissipation from nuts via elevated resting energy expenditure and thermic effect of feeding, and trial evidence that nut-inclusive weight loss diets improve compliance.
Trial findings that permitting nuts yields better compliance and greater weight loss, and the conclusion that moderate nut intake can be included in diets without harming weight loss or maintenance.
Concluding fragment of the final sentence stating that moderate nut inclusion does not compromise weight loss or maintenance.

Study design and methods of a randomized parallel trial comparing two weeks of candy versus peanut snacking (20 kcal/kg added to usual intake) in healthy subjects, measuring basal metabolic rate and cardiovascular risk factors.

Participant numbers (11 men, 14 women) and results on energy intake, which rose similarly in both groups, plus body-weight changes: significant increase in the candy group, non-significant change in the peanut group.
Results showing waist circumference increased only in the candy group, and end-of-study LDL cholesterol and ApoB/ApoA-1 ratio were higher in candy than peanut group.

Results on basal metabolic rate, which increased only in the peanut group (candy group non-significant), followed by the start of the conclusion that peanut snacking avoids the negative metabolic effects of candy snacking.
Concluding statement that two weeks of peanut-based snacking, unlike an isocaloric candy-based diet, does not produce the same negative metabolic effects in non-obese healthy subjects.

Introduction/aim of a 2012 NHANES 1999-2004 study on out-of-hand nut consumption, its link to nutrient intake, diet quality, and cardiovascular/metabolic syndrome risk factors; describes the sample (n = 24,385, ages 2+) and 24-hour recall data.
Methods: population split into age groups (2-11, 12-18, 19+) and dichotomized into nut consumers vs. nonconsumers, with consumers defined as eating at least 1/4 oz of out-of-hand nuts per day.

Statistical methods (weighted means, SEs, covariate-adjusted ANOVA, Healthy Eating Index-2005, P < .05) and results on consumer prevalence rising with age: 2.1%, 2.6%, 6.5%, and 9.6% across age groups.

Key nutrient findings: nut consumers of all ages had higher intakes of energy, MUFA, PUFA, fiber, copper, and magnesium, and lower carbohydrate, cholesterol, and sodium intake; the 19+ groups were merged for later analyses.

Findings on diet quality and body weight: consumers had higher diet quality at all ages; children 2-11 had more overweight/obesity, while 12-18 year-old consumers had lower weight and percent overweight; adult consumers had higher HDL and folate levels.
Adult biomarker and risk findings: consumers had lower insulin, glycohemoglobin, and C-reactive protein, and a 19% lower risk of hypertension and 21% lower risk of low HDL cholesterol.

Conclusion of the study: nut consumption linked to better nutrient intake, diet quality, and fewer metabolic syndrome risk factors in adults, so health professionals should encourage nut eating as part of a healthy diet; includes 2012 Elsevier copyright notice.
Copyright footer fragment (Elsevier Inc., 2012, all rights reserved) closing the abstract; contains no substantive content beyond the copyright notice.

Introduction and study objective: this abstract's opening chunk states the background on nut and tree nut consumption and metabolic syndrome, and the aim to compare cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and MetS risk between nut consumers and nonconsumers in NHANES 1999-2004.

Study design and methods: describes the NHANES 1999-2004 sample of adults aged 19+ (n = 13,292), 24-hour recall intake assessment, the definition of nut/tree nut consumers as those eating at least 1/4 ounce per day, and the covariate-adjusted statistical analysis.

Results part one: reports nut consumer prevalence by age group (18.6% for ages 19-50, 21.0% for 51+) and shows nut consumers had lower BMI, waist circumference, and systolic blood pressure than nonconsumers.
Results part two: tree nut consumers had lower body weight, and nut consumers had lower rates of two metabolic syndrome risk factors, hypertension and low HDL-cholesterol, compared with nonconsumers.

Results part three: details tree nut consumers' lower prevalence of four metabolic syndrome risk factors (abdominal obesity, hypertension, low HDL-C, high fasting glucose), with comparison percentages, p-values, and the start of the MetS prevalence comparison.

Metabolic syndrome outcome and conclusion: tree nut consumers had lower overall MetS prevalence (21.2% vs 26.6%), and the authors conclude nut/tree nut consumption is associated with decreased prevalence of selected cardiovascular, type 2 diabetes, and MetS risk factors.
Closing fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the abstract with the reference to cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and MetS risk factors.

Abstract opening of a cross-sectional PREDIMED study on nut intake and adiposity: background on prior prospective BMI findings, population description (847 elderly high-cardiovascular-risk Mediterranean adults), and methods introduction.

Methods portion of the nut-adiposity study describing dietary assessment with a validated semi-quantitative food questionnaire, physical activity measured by the Minnesota Leisure Time Activity questionnaire, and standard anthropometric measurements; introduces the start of the quintile results on nut intake versus BMI and waist circumference.

Results of the PREDIMED cross-sectional analysis: nut intake decreases across BMI and waist circumference quintiles, with alcohol (inverse with BMI, direct with waist) and meat (direct with waist) also reported as bivariate associations.

Multivariable results from the PREDIMED adiposity study identifying independent dietary predictors: nuts and meat inversely/directly with BMI, and nuts, vegetables, and meat with waist circumference, with their P-values.

Quantitative effect estimates from the nut-adiposity study (about 0.78 kg/m2 lower BMI and 2.1 cm smaller waist per 30 g serving of nuts, similar in men and women) and the conclusion that nut consumption is inversely associated with adiposity, with a caveat about residual confounding by healthier lifestyle.

Concluding limitation and copyright statement of the PREDIMED nut-intake and adiposity paper, noting that residual confounding from a healthier lifestyle of nut eaters may partly explain the findings.

Abstract opening of an epidemiological review on nut consumption and body weight: it introduces short-term trial evidence, the review's aim of examining long-term nut intake and weight change, and the new SUN cohort analysis.

Methods and results summary: describes the literature search for studies with at least 1-year follow-up, notes inverse nut-weight change associations in the SUN and Nurses' Health Study-2 cohorts, and cites a 1-year PREDIMED trial finding on waist circumference.

Details of the new SUN cohort analysis of 11,895 participants over 6 years, reporting a borderline significant inverse trend between baseline nut intake and yearly weight gain, with adjusted mean gains by consumption level.

Specific SUN results and the paper's conclusion: adjusted yearly weight gain figures for non-consumers versus those eating over 4 servings per week, and the finding that nut consumption is not linked to higher long-term weight gain.
Closing copyright notice from the Elsevier journal publication (2010), following the conclusion that nut consumption is not associated with weight gain in long-term studies and trials.

Introduction of a review on nut consumption and body weight: explains that no single weight-loss intervention works long-term, that traditional low-fat diets often exclude nuts, and that nuts are nutritionally valuable sources of vitamins, minerals and unsaturated fats.

Findings on nuts and weight management: nuts within an energy-controlled diet sometimes aided weight loss, whereas adding nuts to an existing diet without energy control increased body weight, though less than predicted.

Evidence on type 2 diabetes and conclusion of the body-weight findings: evidence on diabetes is limited, but nuts in a healthy diet do not cause weight gain and can improve fatty acid profiles in people with diabetes.
Overall conclusion of the review: there is insufficient evidence to justify restricting nuts for weight management, and further research is needed on nuts' role in weight control.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the statement that further research is needed on nuts in weight management.

Opening of a document on phytosterol content of nuts and seeds commonly consumed in the US, describing the lipid extraction and GC-FID/GC-MS analytical methods and the Delta5-avenasterol quantification approach.

Results on phytosterol levels across nuts and seeds: sesame seed and wheat germ highest (400-413 mg/100 g), Brazil nuts lowest (95 mg/100 g), pistachio and sunflower kernel richest among snack foods, with beta-sitosterol, Delta5-avenasterol, and campesterol predominant.

Campestanol range (1.0-12.7 mg/100 g) and pumpkin seed kernel findings (only 13 mg/100 g beta-sitosterol despite 265 mg/100 g total sterols), plus the note that values exceed food composition databases, likely due to steryl glycosides.

Concluding explanation that the higher phytosterol concentrations versus existing food databases are likely because steryl glycosides, a significant share of total sterols in nuts and seeds, were included in the analysis.

Introduction/background of a crossover feeding trial testing whether intrinsic phytosterols in unmodified foods affect whole-body cholesterol metabolism, contrasted with extrinsic supplemented phytosterols.

Study design and methods: 20 of 24 subjects completed a randomized crossover metabolic-kitchen feeding trial with two 4-week diets differing in phytosterol content (126 vs 449 mg per 2000 kcal), matched for nutrients.
Methods detail on the phytosterol-poor and phytosterol-abundant diets and on measuring cholesterol absorption and excretion by GC/MS after stable isotope tracer dosing, with the start of the results.
Key results: the phytosterol-abundant diet lowered cholesterol absorption (about 54% vs 73%) and raised fecal cholesterol excretion by 79%, with confidence intervals and P-values.

Further results: plasma lathosterol/cholesterol ratio rose 82%, indicating increased cholesterol synthesis, while LDL-cholesterol was similar between diets; conclusions that intrinsic phytosterols at dietary levels are biologically active, with effects not reflected in LDL.
Concluding statement that further human research is needed on how phytosterol-mediated fecal cholesterol excretion affects coronary heart disease risk.

Introduction to the almond LDL-C study: establishes diet's role in cardiovascular disease, tree nut LDL-C reduction (3-19%), and almonds' consistent LDL-C-lowering effect across healthy and high-cholesterol/diabetic populations.

Nutrient profile of almonds: low saturated fat, rich unsaturated fat, fiber, phytosterols, plant protein, and cardioprotective nutrients (α-tocopherol, arginine, magnesium, copper, manganese, calcium, potassium) that may explain their cardiovascular benefits.

Proposed mechanisms of almond-induced LDL-C reduction: the biologically active nutrients in almonds act on primary routes, reducing cholesterol and bile acid reabsorption and increasing bile acid/cholesterol excretion.

Further mechanisms and conclusion: almond nutrients may regulate enzymes in de novo cholesterol synthesis and bile acid production, sustaining LDL-C receptor activity, and further research is needed to fully explain almonds' cardiovascular protection (ILSI 2011 copyright).

Closing fragment of the conclusion stating that further research is needed to understand all mechanisms by which almonds reduce cardiovascular disease risk, followed by the 2011 International Life Sciences Institute copyright notice.

Introduction describing how the human diet shifted over 10,000 years from Paleolithic foods (fruits, vegetables, lean meat, seafood) to processed, high-sodium, low-fiber modern foods, setting up the link to obesity and chronic disease.

Explains that these dietary changes worsened health parameters and raised obesity and chronic disease rates (CVD, diabetes, cancer), and notes that Paleolithic-pattern intervention trials showed favorable CVD and diabetes risk-factor changes.

Presents the limitations of the Paleolithic diet, which is low in vitamin D and calcium and high in fish that may contain environmental toxins, and argues for promoting ancestral foods with health benefits as functional foods instead.

Reviews functional food ingredients studied for health benefits (omega-3 fatty acids, polyphenols, fiber, plant sterols) and how these bioactive compounds may prevent or reduce chronic disease incidence.

Gives the economic argument, with estimated health cost savings of $2 to $3 billion per year from omega-3 and plant sterol case studies, and concludes that public health benefits should follow from promoting positive Paleolithic diet components as functional foods.

Introduction and stated aims of a review on the cultural and historical aspects of Mediterranean nuts, outlining the historical periods covered from prehistory through Egyptian, Greek, Phoenician, Roman and Al-Andalus civilizations.

Continues the outline of the review's scope: the spread of Mediterranean nuts through ancient civilizations and their reintroduction to Europe via Al-Andalus, with emphasis on historical nutritional and health attributes and the first global food exchange of nuts between continents.

Describes the review's remaining themes, including the symbolism of nuts in Mediterranean culture, followed by the conclusions that nuts and fruits are among humanity's earliest foods, valued for nutrition.
Concluding statements noting that past civilizations used nuts as medicinal remedies to prevent or treat diseases, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.

Background and objectives of a pooled analysis of nut consumption trials, introducing the link between nut intake and coronary heart disease and the study's aim to assess effects on blood lipids and effect modifiers.

Methods of the pooled analysis: individual data from 25 nut intervention trials across 7 countries, involving 583 normolipidemic and hypercholesterolemic participants not on lipid-lowering drugs, analyzed with mixed linear models.
Results on lipid changes at a mean intake of 67 g/day of nuts: reductions in total cholesterol, LDL-C, and LDL-C/HDL-C and total cholesterol/HDL-C ratios, with the mmol/L conversion factor.

Continuation of results: specific percentage and absolute reductions in lipid ratios and LDL-C, plus the triglyceride reduction of 20.6 mg/dL seen in participants with baseline triglycerides of at least 150 mg/dL, with its conversion factor.
Further results describing triglyceride effects limited to higher baseline levels, a dose-related response to nut consumption, and similar lipid effects across different nut types.

Effect modifiers of nut consumption on lipids: baseline LDL-C, body mass index, and diet type, with the largest benefits in high LDL-C, low BMI, and Western diet subgroups, followed by the start of the conclusion.
Conclusion that nut consumption improves blood lipids in a dose-related manner, with the greatest benefit among people with higher LDL-C or lower BMI.

Introduction and study aims from a study comparing English walnut and black walnut effects on cardiovascular health, covering blood lipids, body weight, RBC membrane fatty acids, and endothelial function.

Results on the 30-day trial of 36 participants: English walnuts improved blood lipids (sex-dependent effects for black walnuts), neither nut caused weight gain, and RBC membrane fatty acid composition improved, including greater EPA increase with English walnuts.

Findings on RBC polyunsaturated fatty acids and EPA, plus endothelial function in 6 unmedicated hypercholesterolemic participants: English walnuts preserved endothelial function after a high-saturated-fat meal, while black walnuts did not.
Overall conclusion that 1 oz of English walnuts daily may reduce cardiovascular risk, while black walnut research is insufficient to make a recommendation.
Closing statement of the walnut study abstract calling for more research on black walnuts before a recommendation can be made.

Introduction to a study of eight culinary 'healthier' oils, classifying which are rich in monounsaturated fatty acids (almond, avocado, hazelnut, macadamia) versus essential polyunsaturated fatty acids (grape seed, rice bran, toasted sesame, walnut).

Results of Rancimat oxidative stability testing at 90-120 °C, giving the ranking of oils from most to least stable (macadamia highest, walnut lowest), continuing the sentence begun in the previous chunk.

Kinetic modeling of oxidation: a linear relationship for high-MUFA oils and an exponential one for PUFA-rich oils, relating inverse induction period to total unsaturated fatty acid content (C18:2, C18:1, C18:3 weighted formula).

Shelf-life prediction using Arrhenius extrapolation and Q10 factors; predictions matched producer storage times for rice bran and hazelnut oils but were significantly lower for the other oils except macadamia, with walnut oil's figure beginning here.
Conclusion of the shelf-life comparison: walnut oil's predicted shelf-life was 15-20 times shorter than its best-before storage life, underscoring its high susceptibility to oxidation.

Opening of a study on diet composition and mood in healthy young normal-weight women on a 1,000 kcal/day weight-reducing diet over six weeks; introduces the vegetarian vs. mixed diet groups and reports better mood in the vegetarian group during the last three weeks.

Presents the key correlational results from the mood study: relative carbohydrate intake correlated negatively with global mood (r = -0.74), and the plasma tryptophan to large neutral amino acid ratio (a marker of tryptophan entry into the brain) correlated with mood (r = -0.52).

Concludes the study on weight-reducing diets and mood: group differences appear linked to carbohydrate intake, and the authors hypothesize that reduced tryptophan availability impairs central serotonergic function, worsening mood when carbohydrate intake is low.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the hypothesis that low carbohydrate intake may cause mood deterioration through reduced serotonergic function from lower tryptophan availability.

Discusses how brain tryptophan and serotonin levels respond to changes in plasma tryptophan, contrasting carbohydrate/insulin-induced rises (brain levels increase) with protein-diet-induced rises (brain levels unchanged), in a study on brain serotonin regulation by plasma neutral amino acids.

Concludes that the key determinant of brain tryptophan and serotonin is not plasma tryptophan alone but its ratio to competing large neutral amino acids (tyrosine, phenylalanine, leucine, isoleucine, valine) that share the blood-brain barrier uptake transporter; the closing conclusion of the brain serotonin regulation study.

Opening of the study abstract: design and population. It describes 19 women with severe premenstrual syndrome and 9 controls, studied as inpatients across the early follicular and late luteal menstrual phases, and introduces the mood and carbohydrate-craving measures (Hamilton Depression Scale plus an addendum).

Results on calorie and carbohydrate intake. PMS subjects significantly increased calorie intake in the late luteal phase (1892 to 2395 kcal), with carbohydrate intake rising 24% from meals and 43% from snacks.

Nutrient and mood-score results. Protein intake was unchanged, fat rose with calories, and Hamilton and addendum depression scores rose sharply in PMS subjects during the luteal phase but not in controls.

Effect of an evening test meal. In the late luteal phase, a carbohydrate-rich, protein-poor meal is described as improving depression, tension, anger, and other mood and energy scores in PMS patients, with the controls' scores unchanged.

Specificity of the meal effect and proposed mechanism. The meal had no effect in the follicular phase or in controls, and the authors suggest carbohydrate-driven brain serotonin synthesis as the reason PMS subjects may overeat carbohydrates to relieve dysphoric mood.
Concluding sentence of the abstract. It restates the serotonin hypothesis, that PMS subjects may overconsume carbohydrates to improve their dysphoric mood state.
Introduces biogenic monoamines (serotonin, tryptamine, tyramine) and their roles in animals and plants, plus their conjugation into hydroxycinnamic acid amides in plants.
Names the four hydroxycinnamic acid amides studied (CS, FS, CT, FT) and states the study's aim of measuring them in common vegetables by HPLC.
Reports detection of serotonin, tryptamine, and tyramine in all tested vegetables, with their concentration ranges in microg/g dry weight.
Identifies tomato and cherry tomato as highest in serotonin and tryptamine, paprika and green pepper as highest in tyramine, and gives the overall range for CS, FS, CT, FT.
Gives green onion as having the highest levels of CS, FT, and CT, with the specific microg/g dry weight values.
Introduces eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS), its symptoms, and its link to the 1989 L-tryptophan epidemic and FDA sale ban, which led to a rapid decline in cases.

Notes that no new EMS cases were published after the FDA ban was lifted in 2005, then states the paper's aim: reporting a new L-tryptophan-associated EMS case with clinical, histopathological, and immunogenetic findings and TGF-β and IL-4 signaling in lesional skin.
Concludes the abstract by referencing evidence of activated TGF-β and interleukin-4 signaling in the lesional skin of the new EMS case.

Introduction and background of a NHANES 1999-2004 study comparing diet quality of vegetarians, nonvegetarians, and dieters, stating the hypothesis that vegetarian diets do not compromise nutrient intake for weight management.
Study design: cross-sectional analysis of NHANES 1999-2004 data, using the USDA Healthy Eating Index 2005 to measure diet quality, and beginning the description of the participant population.

Methods: participant selection (adults 19+, N = 13,292, excluding pregnant/lactating women) and definitions of the lacto-ovo vegetarian group (no meat, poultry, or fish on survey day, n = 851) and the weight-loss dieter group (intake 500 kcal below estimated needs, n = 4,635).
Statistical methods: nutrient and BMI means adjusted for energy, sex, and ethnicity, with ANOVA comparing all vegetarians to nonvegetarians and dieting and nondieting subgroups separately.

Results: vegetarians had higher mean intakes of fiber, vitamins A, C, E, B vitamins, calcium, magnesium, and iron than nonvegetarians, with specific vitamin E, vitamin A, and magnesium values reported.

Results continued: both groups fell short of recommended intakes for some nutrients; Healthy Eating Index scores were essentially equal between all vegetarians and nonvegetarians (50.5 vs 50.1, P = 0.6), and the conclusions begin.
Conclusions that vegetarian diets are nutrient dense, consistent with dietary guidelines, and can be recommended for weight management without lowering diet quality, followed by the copyright notice.

Introduction of a review on nuts and cardiovascular health: explains that rising cardiovascular disease burden is driven by lifestyle changes (diet shifts, reduced activity) leading to obesity and diabetes, motivating dietary interventions.

Continues the introduction: states that nuts have drawn attention for cardiovascular benefits from their nutrient composition, and describes the paper as a comprehensive review of nuts' general effects, drawing on epidemiologic and clinical trial data.

Concluding part of the abstract: notes the review covers large older epidemiologic studies and recent clinical trials, and that all studies conclude nuts can be an important part of a healthy diet for minimizing cardiovascular risk and gaining health benefits.
Publication copyright and rights notice for the paper (European Federation of Internal Medicine, 2010; Elsevier B.V.), closing the document's abstract text.

Abstract of a study on metal/mineral content in heart muscle of people who died from ischemic heart disease; this chunk covers sudden-death patients versus normal controls and late-death patients, with magnesium, iron, potassium, and calcium differences.

Continuation of the abstract's findings: the late-death group showed lower manganese, copper, and probably magnesium levels than normal controls, sodium did not differ among groups, and the study introduces its discussion of ischemic heart disease.
Concluding sentence of the abstract linking the mineral findings to higher ischemic heart disease death rates in areas with soft drinking water and to possible dietary mineral salt deficiencies.
Introduction to hepcidin as the liver-derived master regulator that represses intestinal and macrophage iron release in response to systemic iron requirements.

Explains the proposed mechanism linking circulating diferric transferrin (a marker of tissue iron levels) to hepcidin expression, and introduces HFE, transferrin receptor 2 and hemojuvelin as liver mediators of this signal.
Covers the disease relevance: mutations in HFE-pathway genes or hepcidin cause hemochromatosis (systemic iron overload) because iron absorption cannot be downregulated.

Describes hepcidin's role in inflammation-associated hypoferremia, where pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 stimulate its expression, and notes open research questions on its regulation and action.
Closing sentence reiterating that hepcidin regulation and its cellular mechanism of iron release remain active research areas, followed by the journal citation (IUBMB Life, 2005).

Introduction of the review on intestinal iron absorption: establishes iron as an essential trace metal, the risks of iron imbalance, and that the body controls iron intake from diet since it cannot excrete excess iron.

Describes dietary iron forms in the review: heme iron from meat is absorbed intact, while non-heme iron bioavailability depends on dietary composition and interactions that affect its solubility and oxidation state.

Introduces the review's two main regulatory themes: nutrients that directly affect enterocyte iron transporter expression and function, and body iron status as a major systemic determinant of iron absorption.
Closing sentence of the introduction stating that the review will go on to discuss the dietary and systemic factors that regulate intestinal iron absorption.
Study background and design: a randomized crossover trial testing whether cola or diet cola, versus mineral water, alters nonheme iron bioavailability from a vegetarian pizza meal in women.
Methods and population: 16 women with serum ferritin 11-54 µg/L; the pizza meal's iron came from native iron plus a ferric chloride stable isotope label, totaling about 5.3 mg iron.
