Key results: RBC iron incorporation was similar across drinks (9.9% cola, 9.4% diet cola, 9.6% water), and serum ferritin and plasma hepcidin correlated and predicted absorption, but together explained only 30% of variation.

Interpretation: the authors note the limited understanding of how iron absorption is regulated, and conclude low-pH drinks had no effect in healthy women while raising the question of effects on other iron forms and populations.

Conclusion and future directions: low-pH drinks may still matter for fortification iron needing acid solubilization (e.g., reduced iron) and for people with low gastric acid such as older adults or those with H. pylori, which merits further study.

Opening chunk of an overview article on phytic acid (phytate) in foods and its significance for human nutrition, covering food sources, food-table data, intake levels, and the start of gastrointestinal degradation and mineral-binding mechanisms.

Middle chunk on phytate in the gut: its degradation via inositol phosphate hydrolysis, interaction with minerals and trace elements in chyme, absorption, and effects on mineral and trace element bioavailability.
Chunk covering phytate degradation during food processing and storage, and its beneficial roles such as effects on calcification, kidney stone formation, and lowering blood glucose and lipids.

Closing section of the article surveying phytic acid's antioxidative and potential anticancer activities, and the development and standardisation issues of analytical methods for phytic acid and inositol phosphates in foods.
Final fragment of the document, ending the sentence on the need for standardisation of phytic acid analysis in foods.

Introduction stating the problem: low iron and zinc bioavailability from plant foods, the need for food-based strategies against mineral deficiency, and the hypothesis drawn from sulfur-amino-acid studies in animals that sulfur-rich Allium spices may also improve mineral bioavailability.

Study objective and design: examines garlic and onion added to cereal and pulse grains to assess effects on iron and zinc bioaccessibility, using two representative cereals and pulses at two spice levels each.
Results for iron: garlic and onion enhanced iron bioaccessibility in both cereals (9.4-65.9% increase) and pulses (9.9-73.3% increase), in raw and cooked conditions.

Results for zinc: both spices similarly raised zinc bioaccessibility, by 10.4-159.4% in cereals and 9.8-49.8% in pulses, leading to the conclusion that garlic and onion promote iron and zinc bioaccessibility.
Conclusion: the findings on garlic and onion promoting trace mineral bioaccessibility may support food-based strategies to improve micronutrient bioavailability and human health.

Introduction of a critical review on DHEA supplementation in postmenopausal women, covering age-related DHEA decline, the rising popularity of supplements, and the review's goal of assessing whether DHEA has a role.

Recent findings on cardiovascular effects: DHEA levels from oral dosing match women in their 20s, observational links between low DHEA and cardiovascular risk, but interventional trials show no atherosclerosis benefit and reduced HDL cholesterol.

Recent findings on other outcomes: modest bone mineral density gains with adjuvant therapy, cognitive benefits only in mild-to-moderate impairment, and intravaginal (not oral) DHEA relieving vaginal atrophy and improving sexual function.
Summary and conclusion: current evidence supports no role for oral DHEA in healthy postmenopausal women, and long-term studies are needed to confirm the benefits seen and establish DHEA's safety.
Final sentence of the summary, calling for long-term studies to confirm the reported benefits of DHEA and verify its safety profile.
Introduction of the document: states that age-related decline in serum DHEA/DHEAS may causally contribute to aging-associated diseases, opening the case for DHEA therapy in postmenopausal women.
Continues the list of postulated consequences of low DHEA (immune, depression, well-being, cognition) and notes that the target population and dosage for DHEA therapy are not clearly defined.

Raises the open question of whether DHEA could serve as a general anti-aging therapy or as treatment for androgen deficiency syndrome, noting lack of definitive mechanistic evidence and few relevant studies.
Concluding statement: the scarcity of evidence motivates a new critical review of the literature to expose current limits and inconsistencies in DHEA therapy research for postmenopausal women.

Introduction to a 2004 review on DHEA and ageing: DHEA is the adrenal androgen whose secretion declines with age, prompting interest in it as an anti-ageing hormone, though whether this decline is actually harmful is unclear.

Mechanisms and therapeutic evidence for DHEA: it acts mainly by conversion to sex steroids, has neurosteroidal and endothelial binding actions, and shows convincing benefit in adrenal insufficiency, with possible relevance to glucocorticoid-treated patients.

Conclusion on DHEA in healthy elderly people: randomised controlled trials do not support its use, showing no major benefits and raising concern about adverse effects on sex steroid-dependent tumour growth.
Closing sentence of the DHEA and ageing abstract noting the tumour-growth risk, followed by the 2004 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction and background of a study on egg yolk cholesterol intake and carotid atherosclerosis, framing the question of whether egg consumption relates to total plaque area in Canadian vascular prevention clinic patients, with smoking as a comparison.

Methods section describing the cross-sectional design: consecutive vascular prevention clinic patients had carotid total plaque area measured by duplex ultrasound and completed lifestyle questionnaires covering smoking pack-years and egg-yolk years (eggs per week times years).

Results opening: cohort of 1262 patients (mean age 61.5 years, 47% women), with findings that carotid plaque area rises linearly with age after 40 but exponentially with smoking pack-years and egg-yolk years.

Key comparative results: mean plaque area was 125 mm2 in those eating fewer than 2 eggs weekly versus 132 mm2 in those eating 3 or more (p<0.0001 after age adjustment), and egg-yolk years stayed significant in multiple regression after adjusting for coronary risk factors.

Interpretation and conclusions: the authors suggest people at cardiovascular risk should avoid regular egg yolk consumption, while noting the need for prospective studies with better diet data and control for confounders like exercise and waist circumference.
Copyright notice from Elsevier Ireland Ltd. (2012) closing the abstract, marking publication rights and no substantive study content.

Introduction to the kiwifruit study: defines irritable bowel syndrome subtypes and states the aim of testing a 4-week kiwifruit intervention on bowel function in IBS with constipation (IBS/C) patients.

Study design and population: 54 IBS/C patients and 16 healthy adults in a 6-week, three-phase trial (1-week baseline, 4-week dietary intervention, 1-week post-intervention), with the kiwifruit group described.

Intervention and methods: two Hayward green kiwifruits daily for 4 weeks versus a placebo capsule control group of 13 IBS/C patients, with colon transit time measured before and after and daily defecation records kept.
Results: kiwifruit consumption significantly increased weekly defecation frequency and significantly reduced colon transit time (p=0.026) in the IBS/C group, as reported statistically.
Conclusion: the findings indicate that 4 weeks of kiwifruit shortens colon transit time, increases defecation frequency, and improves bowel function in adults with IBS/C.

Introduction to the document on phosphate restriction in renal diet therapy: explains why hyperphosphatemia and hyperparathyroidism in end-stage renal disease matter (bone disease, calcification, cardiovascular risk) and states that dietary protein and phosphorus restriction slows renal failure progression.

Covers how dietary phosphorus restriction is carried out (lower protein intake, avoid phosphorus-rich foods), gut absorption rates in dialysis patients (60-80%, reduced to about 40% with phosphate binders), and begins describing phosphorus removal by conventional hemodialysis.

Gives the quantitative basis for dietary phosphorus limits: conventional high-flux hemodialysis removes about 30 mmol (900 mg) phosphorus per session, so 750 mg intake is the threshold for positive phosphorus balance, corresponding to 45-50 g/day protein or 0.8 g/kg/day for a 60 kg patient.

Concludes with the target laboratory values for dialysis patients under this diet therapy: serum calcium 9.2-9.6 mg/dl, phosphorus 2.5-5.5 mg/dl, calcium-phosphorus product below 55 mg2/dl2, and intact parathyroid hormone 100-200 pg/ml.

Background and methods opening of the 2010 CDC STD Treatment Guidelines update on HPV and genital warts: April 2009 expert meeting on STD prevention/treatment and HPV, genital warts, and cervical cancer screening revisions.

Methods section describing how key questions were set with an expert panel and how PubMed English-language systematic literature reviews were conducted and incorporated into the 2010 CDC STD Treatment Guidelines.

Results opening on HPV vaccines: quadrivalent and bivalent vaccines available, routine recommendation for girls aged 11-12, and quadrivalent vaccine for boys and men aged 9-26, plus the start of the new genital wart treatment option.
Results on the new patient-applied genital wart treatment sinecatechins 15% ointment (green tea catechins) and the updated HPV, genital wart, and cervical cancer counseling messages.

Conclusions summarizing key 2010 CDC STD Treatment Guidelines additions: prophylactic HPV vaccine recommendations, patient-applied genital wart treatments, and counseling messages on HPV, warts, cervical cancer screening, and HPV tests.
Final clause of the conclusions listing counseling messages for patients on HPV, genital warts, cervical cancer screening, and HPV tests in the 2010 CDC STD Treatment Guidelines update.

Introduces a clinical study of green tea extracts (polyphenon E and EGCG) for HPV-infected cervical lesions, describing the 51 treated patients across four lesion categories versus 39 untreated controls.

Describes the treatment regimens: poly E ointment applied locally twice weekly to 27 patients, and oral 200 mg poly E or EGCG capsules daily for 8-12 weeks, with the first response results (20/27 on ointment).
Reports response rates by treatment arm: 75% for combined ointment plus capsule, 50% for poly E capsule, and 60% for EGCG capsule, leading to the overall 69% response rate (35/51).

Compares the overall 69% treatment response (35/51) against the 10% response in untreated controls (4/39, P<0.05) and concludes green tea extracts are effective and a potential therapy for HPV-related cervical lesions.
Final concluding sentence stating that green tea extracts may be a potential therapeutic regimen for patients with HPV-infected cervical lesions.

Introduction/scope of a review on green and black tea and gynecologic cancers: notes that observational data exist for ovarian and endometrial cancers but not for HPV-related cervical, vaginal, or vulvar cancers.

Methods and meta-analysis results: green tea is inversely associated with ovarian cancer (OR 0.66) and endometrial cancer (OR 0.78), while black tea shows no association with ovarian cancer and a positive association with endometrial cancer (OR 1.20).

Summary of evidence on green tea catechins: experimental data on antiviral and immunomodulatory effects, plus randomized trial results showing catechin efficacy against cervical lesions and external genital warts.

Conclusion: observational data support a protective role of green tea against ovarian and endometrial cancers, and further observational research is needed on whether green tea reduces HPV-related cancer risk.
Final sentence of the conclusion, calling for observational studies to determine whether green tea reduces risk of human papillomavirus-related cancers.
Introduces the randomised controlled trial on whether caffeinated black tea affects hydration, describing the 21 healthy male participants and the pre-test abstention and overnight fast protocol.

Describes the trial design: four counter-balanced test days with a 5-day washout, comparing 4 and 6 cups (240 ml) of black tea (168 or 252 mg caffeine) against boiled water controls, with tea prepared from tea bags with semi-skimmed milk.

Covers the controlled conditions and sampling schedule: all food and drink were controlled during the 12 h intervention, subjects rested, blood was sampled at set times, and a 24 h urine sample was collected.

Lists the blood and urine outcome measures (blood cell count, electrolytes, osmolality, urine volume and colour) and the participant characteristics, noting that only nineteen of the twenty-one men completed all conditions.

Reports the statistical analysis (factorial ANOVA in PROC MIXED) finding no significant differences between tea and water, and the conclusion that black tea hydrates similarly to water in the amounts studied.

Introduces the antimutagenic study of white tea: four white tea varieties show strong antimutagenic activity in the Salmonella assay, especially with S9, and the top variety (Exotica China) outperforms green tea.
Names the comparison green tea (Dragonwell) and lists the heterocyclic amine mutagens tested (IQ, MeIQx, 4,8-DiMeIQx, PhIP, Trp-P-2) against which the white tea was more effective.

Describes the mechanism experiments: rat liver S9 MROD assays (CYP1A2 activation marker) and Salmonella tests using the direct-acting mutagen N-hydroxy-IQ, showing white tea inhibits activation and reduces N-hydroxy-IQ mutagenicity without S9.
Reports that white tea inhibits MROD activity at low concentrations and that nine major green tea constituents, including high EGCG and other polyphenols, are also present in white tea.
Describes reconstituted 'artificial' teas built from the nine major constituents at white and green tea proportions, showing the complete tea is more antimutagenic than the artificial mix.

Concludes that white tea's greater inhibitory potency may stem from the relative levels of the nine major constituents acting synergistically with minor ones to block mutagen activation and scavenge reactive intermediates.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the mention of scavenging reactive intermediates as a proposed mechanism for white tea's antimutagenic effect.

Study design and methods for a human trial on endotoxin after a high-fat meal, introducing the 75 g fat meal and the four subject groups (nonobese control, obese, IGT, type 2 diabetic) with their demographics, in the Diabetes Care-style abstract of 'High Fat Intake Leads to Acute Postprandial Exposure to Circulating Endotoxin in Type 2 Diabetic Subjects'.

Continuation of the methods section listing the age, BMI, and sample sizes for the obese, IGT, and type 2 diabetic groups, and the blood collection timepoints (0 h baseline and 1-4 h postprandial) used to measure circulating endotoxin.

Results section reporting that baseline endotoxin was higher in type 2 diabetic and IGT subjects than nonobese controls (60.6% higher in type 2 diabetics, P < 0.05), and that a high-fat meal significantly raised endotoxin in type 2 diabetic, IGT, and obese subjects over 4 h.

Later results and start of conclusions: at 4 h postprandial, type 2 diabetic subjects had 125.4% higher circulating endotoxin than nonobese controls (P < 0.05), and the conclusion that high-fat meals raise endotoxin irrespective of metabolic state.

Conclusions of the endotoxin study: high-fat intake elevates circulating endotoxin as early as 1 h after a meal, the increase is greatest in IGT and type 2 diabetic subjects, suggesting exacerbated metabolic endotoxinemia after high-fat intake.
Final sentence of the conclusions, arguing that in type 2 diabetes a continual snacking routine would cumulatively worsen the condition faster than in others due to greater endotoxin exposure.

Introduces the anti-inflammatory effects of cocoa flavanols, covering their in vitro/ex vivo influence on cytokines, eicosanoids, platelet activation, and nitric oxide pathways in relation to atherosclerosis.

Continues the discussion by noting the limited in vivo evidence for cocoa flavanols, while citing studies linking cocoa-rich consumption to benefits for blood pressure, insulin resistance, vascular damage, and oxidative stress.
Concludes the review by calling for rigorous controlled human studies with long follow-up and sound dietary questionnaires to clarify flavanol effects on key cardiovascular health endpoints.

Introduces the Moli-sani Project cohort study and the research question: whether dark chocolate intake is associated with serum C-reactive protein (CRP), an inflammation marker, in a healthy Italian population.

Describes study sample selection from the Moli-sani Project (4849 chronic-disease-free subjects, 1317 chocolate consumers and 824 dark-chocolate-only consumers), CRP measurement by immunoturbidimetric method, and dietary assessment via the EPIC FFQ.
Reports the main adjusted result: after controlling for demographic, lifestyle, anthropometric, and dietary covariates, dark chocolate consumption was inversely associated with CRP (P = 0.038).

Gives robustness checks and univariate results: association holds after nutrient adjustment (P = 0.016), with geometric mean CRP of 1.32 mg/L in nonconsumers versus 1.10 mg/L in consumers (P < 0.0001).

States the key finding of a J-shaped dose-response, where low intake (up to one 20 g serving every 3 days) gave lower CRP than either no intake or higher intake, concluding small regular doses may reduce inflammation.
Final concluding fragment of the abstract, restating that regular consumption of small doses of dark chocolate may reduce inflammation.
Introduction and screen: fatty meals trigger low-grade inflammation; 40 food extracts screened, 7 induced TNF-α and IL-6 from human monocytes in vitro.
Methods setup: TLR2 and TLR4 stimulants quantified using HEK-293 cells transfected with each receptor, calibrated against BLP and LPS standards.

Key results: most foods lacked detectable TLR2/TLR4 stimulants, but all TNF-α-inducing foods contained them (up to 1100 ng BLP-eq/g TLR2; up to 2700 ng LPS-eq/g TLR4) in soluble and insoluble fractions.
Distribution and correlation: TLR stimulants concentrated in meat and processed foods, minimal in fresh produce; TNF-α induction correlated with TLR2 (r 0.837) and TLR4 (r 0.748) stimulant content.

Mechanism and stability: TNF-α induction fully abolished by TLR2/TLR4 inhibition; LPS and BLP resist cooking, low pH and protease treatment; conclusion that unspoiled foods can carry large TLR stimulant loads.
Concluding statement: unspoiled foodstuffs can contain large amounts of TLR2 and TLR4 stimulants that may regulate their capacity to drive inflammatory signalling.

Introduction and objectives of an E3N prospective cohort study on dietary macronutrients and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) risk in French women, noting prior reliance on recall-biased retrospective studies.

Methods describing the E3N cohort (French women aged 40-65, free of major disease at baseline), the self-administered baseline diet questionnaire, and the 24-month follow-up questionnaires on disease and lifestyle.

Methods on IBD case ascertainment (questionnaires until June 2005, then clinical and pathological validation) and the Cox proportional hazards analysis adjusted for energy intake; also begins the results with the cohort size and person-years.

Results: the study population of 67,581 participants with mean follow-up of 10.4 years, 77 validated incident IBD cases, and the start of the hazard ratio findings for total and animal protein intake.

Key findings: third-vs-first tertile hazard ratios and confidence intervals for total and animal protein (P trend values), and the finding that meat or fish, but not eggs or dairy, drives the animal protein-IBD association; concluding statement on protein intake.
Conclusion of the E3N study: high protein intake is associated with increased incident IBD risk in middle-aged French women.

Abstract opening of a cohort study (2514 adults aged ≥49) on dietary PUFAs, fish, and nuts and 15-year mortality from noncardiovascular, noncancer inflammatory diseases; states background, objective, and study design.

Study design and methods: semiquantitative food-frequency questionnaire dietary assessment, calculation of PUFA, fish, and nut intakes, and inflammatory disease death confirmation via the Australian National Death Index; also begins the results with 214 inflammatory disease deaths over 15 years.

Main results: women in the highest tertile of total n-3 PUFA intake had 44% lower inflammatory disease mortality risk (P for trend = 0.03), an association absent in men; each 1-SD increase in α-linolenic acid intake was inversely associated with mortality (HR 0.83).

Results on nuts and null findings: second and third tertiles of nut consumption showed 51% and 32% lower inflammatory disease mortality risk versus the lowest tertile; long-chain n-3 and n-6 PUFAs and fish intake showed no association.
Conclusions: the study reports a novel link between total n-3 PUFA intake and inflammatory disease mortality in older women, and a protective role for nuts but not fish.
Final concluding sentence of the abstract summarizing the protective association of nuts, but not fish, against inflammatory disease mortality.

Introduction and background of a study on how ethnicity relates to blood inflammatory markers in non-smoking church-goers, framing inflammation as a shared pathway for chronic disease shaped by sociodemographic and lifestyle factors.
Methods of the cross-sectional study: 508 adults over 35 (62% White, 38% Black) from the Biopsychosocial Religion and Health substudy of the Adventist Health Study 2.

Methods continued: covariates (socioeconomic status, exercise, diet, BMI, inflammatory conditions) analyzed by linear regression against CRP, IL-6, and TNF-α, with IL-10 also measured as an anti-inflammatory marker.
Results: Blacks had higher CRP and IL-6 than Whites; adjustment attenuated the CRP difference, while IL-6 stayed higher in Blacks (β=.118, 95% CI .014–.206, P=.025).

Results and conclusion: no ethnic differences in IL-10 or TNF-α; vegetarian diet linked to lower CRP and exercise to higher IL-10; the authors suggest higher IL-6 may explain greater inflammatory disease susceptibility in Blacks.
Final conclusion: higher IL-6 may matter for health disparities between Blacks and Whites, and vegetarian diet and exercise may counteract these disparities.

Abstract opening (background and methods) of a study comparing a legume-free calorie-restricted diet with a legume-based hypocaloric diet in 30 obese adults, focusing on metabolic and inflammatory effects of weight loss.

Methods section describing the randomized allocation of 30 obese subjects to 8-week hypocaloric diets: control legume-free (C-diet) versus legume-based (L-diet) with 4 weekly cooked legume servings, and the outcomes measured.
Methods outcomes and start of the results: the L-diet produced greater body weight loss than the C-diet (-7.8% vs -5.3%, p = 0.024), and lipid and blood pressure changes are beginning to be reported.

Results on lipid, blood pressure, and inflammatory changes: total and LDL cholesterol and systolic BP improved only with the L-diet, and CRP and complement C3 reductions were greater in the L-diet group.

Results after adjusting for weight loss: CRP and C3 reductions stayed significantly larger in the L-diet group, and CRP reduction correlated with reductions in systolic BP and total cholesterol specifically in the L-diet group.

Conclusion of the abstract: 4 weekly legume servings within a hypocaloric diet specifically reduced proinflammatory markers (CRP, C3) and improved lipid profile and blood pressure, partly independent of weight loss.
Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that legume-based hypocaloric dieting improved some metabolic features in overweight or obese subjects, in some cases independent of weight loss.

Introduction of the review: inflammation as a pathological basis of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and chronic inflammatory disease, and how dietary constituents modulate inflammatory and immune processes.

Epidemiological evidence linking dietary patterns, especially fruit, vegetable, and whole wheat intake, to lower inflammation risk, supported by human intervention studies on plant foods' anti-inflammatory potential.
Specific bioactive compounds, primarily carotenoids and flavonoids, that influence inflammatory and immunological processes, leading into the review's overall conclusion.

Conclusion that plant foods and their non-nutritive constituents modulate immune and inflammatory processes, implying a plant-based diet can reduce cardiovascular disease and cancer risk, and recommending high intake of vegetables, fruit, and whole wheat.
Final sentence of the conclusion: recommended intakes of vegetables, fruit, and whole wheat supply a broad range of bioactive compounds at health-promoting concentrations.

Introduction and single-dose acute study design: microwaved potatoes with skins vs. refined starch biscuits given to eight fasting subjects, with plasma and urine antioxidant measurements, from a study on high-antioxidant potatoes as a hypotensive agent.
Methods of the single-dose study: plasma antioxidant capacity measured by FRAP over 8 h, and 24 h urine polyphenol antioxidant capacity measured by Folin reagent with Polyclar correction.

Acute study results and the crossover trial setup: potato increased plasma and urine antioxidant capacity while refined starch acted as a pro-oxidant; 18 hypertensive subjects (BMI 29) received purple potatoes twice daily or no potatoes for 4 weeks each.
Crossover trial outcomes on metabolic measures: no significant effect of purple potatoes on fasting glucose, lipids, HbA1c, or body weight, with diastolic blood pressure beginning to show a drop.

Blood pressure findings: diastolic pressure fell 4.3% (4 mm Hg) and systolic fell 3.5% (5 mm Hg) despite 14 of 18 subjects taking antihypertensive drugs; described as the first study of potatoes and blood pressure.
Concluding statement that purple potatoes act as an effective hypotensive agent and may lower heart disease and stroke risk in hypertensive subjects without weight gain.

Introduction to a review on human immunosenescence, opening with the general role of innate immune cells (phagocytosis, killing, PRR-driven cytokine production) in initiating adaptive immunity, and noting that aging effects on innate responses are poorly understood in humans.

Continuation of the review's introduction: states the aim to survey human innate immune aging across neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, NK/NKT cells, and dendritic cells, emphasizing consequences for infection and vaccine responses in older adults.
Final clause of the abstract, specifying the review's focus on how innate immune aging affects infection and vaccination outcomes in old age.
Abstract opening of a rabbit study on dietary protein (casein vs. soy protein) and serum lipoproteins; introduces the diet switch and the early rise in LDL-cholesterol that persisted over the study.

Results continuing the casein vs. soy comparison: soy diet gives smaller LDL changes, VLDL and LDL show higher cholesterol proportion, and turnover data show reduced fractional catabolic rates (FCRs) of VLDL and LDL in casein-fed rabbits.

Mechanistic conclusion of the study: elevated LDL in casein-fed rabbits is mainly due to reduced receptor-mediated LDL-apo B catabolism, with receptor-independent removal similar between groups, linking hypercholesterolemia to cholesterol-enriched LDL.
Final summary sentence of the abstract stating the overall finding: casein-fed hypercholesterolemia is tied to cholesterol-enriched LDL and impaired receptor-dependent LDL-apo B removal.

Study design and population: introduces the comparison of soy protein versus casein diets under low (<100 mg/d) versus high (500 mg/d) dietary cholesterol, testing whether cholesterol intake changes lipoprotein responses to plant vs. animal protein in normal adults.

Methods: describes the crossover feeding protocol, with formula diets (20% calories from protein, 27% fat, 53% carbohydrate), 31-day dietary periods, and a month-long self-selected interim washout period between diets.

Results on low- vs. high-cholesterol diets: lipoprotein class concentrations were similar on soy and casein on low-cholesterol diets, while on cholesterol-enriched diets LDL-C was 16% lower on soy protein than casein.

Key quantitative findings: on cholesterol-enriched diets soy protein lowered LDL-C by 16% and raised HDL-C by 16% relative to casein, with the soy-casein differences in LDL-C and HDL-C larger on high than low cholesterol intake.
Conclusion: the level of dietary cholesterol may determine whether plant (soy) and animal (casein) proteins have similar or different effects on plasma LDL-C and HDL-C concentrations.

Introduction explaining why Salmonella microbiological criteria for raw poultry matter: foodborne salmonellosis concerns, trade-obstacle risk from poorly grounded criteria, and regulatory confusion across countries.

Describes the origin of the work: an international expert group from 16 countries convened to address scientific and technical issues in setting a Salmonella criterion for raw chicken, with concern about zero-tolerance criteria.

Explains why zero tolerance and complete absence of Salmonella were judged inappropriate: no effective elimination method or practical verification of absence exists, and stakeholders interpret the term differently.
Recommends food safety metrics based on hazard reduction rather than absence, and advises avoiding terms like 'zero tolerance' or 'absence of a microbe' unless internationally defined.
Concludes that risk assessment and health-linked performance objectives throughout the food chain are preferable to zero tolerance for defining risk and reducing public health impact.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence about reducing adverse public health effects, ending the document's recommendation on performance objectives and risk assessment.

Introduction of a 2017-style Tennessee telephone survey on public knowledge of diarrheal illness: prevalence (60% of US population yearly), survey size (2117 residents), and the reasons people would seek medical care (bloody stool, dehydration, persistent symptoms).

Findings on treatment overuse: most acute diarrhea is self-limited, yet antimicrobial overuse is common; only 4.5% thought stool cultures and 6.9% thought antibiotics are routinely needed, and over 60% identified food as the most common source.

Survey results on food safety beliefs: three-fourths thought bacteria in uncooked meat is normal, 45% thought selling such meat is legal, and the conclusion that these findings matter for medical providers, regulators, and public health.
Closing fragment of the abstract stating the implications of the diarrheal disease survey for public health management and prevention.

Introduction and methods of a 2010 study on delusional parasitosis in neurological inpatients: it reviews charts from a neuropsychiatry ward (2005–2009) and describes the syndrome's demographic, clinical and imaging features.
Methods continue and results begin: of 1598 hospitalized patients, 636 (39.80%) had neurological disease, and four of them (0.62% of the neurological sample) had delusional parasitosis.

Results detail the four delusional parasitosis cases: diagnoses were brain cysticercosis, cerebrovascular disease (two cases), and vitamin B12 deficiency dementia; all were older women with depressive features, and three had significant cognitive decline.

Continues the case description, noting that two patients had paraesthesia and pruritus from peripheral neuropathy and one had pruritus of unknown, possibly hallucinatory, origin, followed by the conclusions that the syndrome was infrequent in this sample.

Final conclusion of the study: delusional parasitosis was rare in hospitalized neurological patients, and female sex, advanced age, depression, cognitive decline, and peripheral or central pruritus/paraesthesia may contribute to it; includes the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.

Abstract opening of a study on housefly pupae peptide mixture as a food preservative for chilled pork, introducing its broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and framing the comparison against nisin and sodium dehydroacetate (DHA-S) on MAB, TVB-N, and pH.

Abstract results and conclusion: the housefly peptide mixture, nisin, and DHA-S all showed good preservation of chilled pork with no significant difference among them, suggesting the housefly peptide mixture has strong potential as a food preservative.

Abstract mechanism and practical applications: SEM and TEM findings suggest the housefly pupae peptide mixture works mainly by lysing bacterial cytoplasmic membranes and inducing membrane pores, and the peptides are low-cost and simple to extract.

Closing sentences of the abstract's practical applications section, restating that the low-cost extracted housefly peptide mixture has broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and strong potential as a food preservative based on chilled pork results.

Introduces bacteriophages and their historical use in phage therapy (PT) against bacterial infections, including early human trials in the US, Europe, and Asia, as the opening background of a review on phage biocontrol in animals and meat products.
Describes the decline of phage therapy in Western countries after antibiotics were adopted in the 1940s, and its recent revival driven by rising antibiotic resistance in human and animal pathogens.

Explains that strict human-trial regulations in the US and Europe have shifted phage use toward animal and agricultural applications, and notes FDA approval of commercial phage treatments for human food in the USA.

Acknowledges recent milestones and successful PT trials but notes persistent obstacles to widespread phage use in animals, food, and medicine, and previews the review's scope: a historical overview of PT in the West.
States the review's aim to summarize key findings of phage biocontrol studies in animals and meat products, concluding the document's introduction.

Opening portion of a pictorial essay on complications of a swallowed fish bone. Introduces that fishbone ingestion is common in seafood-heavy populations, usually passes harmlessly through the GI tract within a week, but can impact and cause complications.

Concluding sentence of the document's introduction in the pictorial essay on swallowed fish bone complications. Explains why recognizing these complications matters: patients often present with nonspecific symptoms and may not know they swallowed a fishbone.

Introduces the medical case report on ciguatera, a food poisoning from contaminated marine fish, and describes two cases where painful ejaculation in a male and dyspareunia in his female partner suggested sexual transfer of ciguatoxin (CTX).

Reports that semen immunoassays for CTX were non-diagnostic, possibly due to test sensitivity or timing, and concludes that CTX may be present in semen and cause symptoms in both males and females during intercourse.

Final fragment of the conclusion stating that ciguatoxin may cause symptoms in both males and females during sexual intercourse, the document's closing claim on possible sexual transmission of ciguatera.

Introduces the study's scope: 1280 banknotes collected from food outlets across 10 countries, with bacterial content measured; opens the document's findings on bacteria and economic indicators in the 'Dirty money' hygiene investigation.

Reports the main quantitative result: bacteria per square centimeter on banknotes correlates strongly with national economic prosperity indicators, most strongly with the 'index of economic freedom' (lower index, more bacteria).
Describes other influencing factors on banknote bacteria (note age, polymer vs. cotton material) and the pathogen screening, noting pathogens were only isolated after enrichment and are not alarming.

Presents the recommendation that food-and-money hygiene guidelines be universally adopted, based on the international findings, and begins describing the separation measures for handling food and money.
Details specific handling precautions: physically separating food and money tasks among different people, or handling food with one gloved hand and money with the other, as practical options.

Gives the fallback recommendation for food service staff: if separation or gloving is not feasible, wash hands properly after handling money and before handling food; concludes the document's practical guidance.
Opening of the HEV overview: introduces hepatitis E virus, its poor understanding and lack of vaccine, and its genotype classification (genotypes 1-2 human-restricted vs. 3-4 zoonotic).
Describes the zoonotic genotypes and how discovery of many animal HEV strains (pigs, chickens, rabbits, rats, deer, etc.) has broadened HEV's host range and diversity.
Covers cross-species infection concerns and pigs as an HEV reservoir, with pig handlers at elevated zoonotic risk, and begins the discussion of foodborne transmission.
Details foodborne cases linked to undercooked meats (pig liver, sausage, deer) and environmental pathways where manure, runoff, and feces contaminate water and produce or shellfish.
Summarizes evidence of swine HEV RNA in manure, sewage, and oysters, shellfish-linked cases, and concludes that animal HEV strains pose zoonotic, food, and environmental safety risks.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence stating animal HEV strains raise environmental safety concerns.

Case study abstract on occupational hepatitis C transmission: an HCV-infected patient's only identified risk factor was sharing a supermarket butcher's counter and ham slicer with another HCV-infected worker, with frequent hand bleeding injuries; phylogenetic analysis showed high nucleotide homology between the strains.

Closing portion of the same abstract, completing the phylogenetic finding (high nucleotide homology between the two patients' HCV strains) and giving the 2010 European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases copyright and US government works notice.

Introduction of a 2011 review on adverse effects of concentrated green tea extracts, setting out the health risks (liver damage, drug interactions, herbal combinations) that have emerged from popular high-dose green tea use.

Continuation of the review's introduction: it names the specific risks (liver damage, prescription drug interactions, harm with herbal remedies) and states the review's scope, covering documented human adverse effects and animal-study evidence on copious concentrated extract intake.
Closing part of the introduction, stating that the review does not aim to downplay green tea's established benefits and instead focuses on under-appreciated, rare adverse effects to raise awareness.
Final chunk of the document: a short closing sentence on the rare, under-appreciated risks, followed by the 2011 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA copyright notice.

Opening background of a North American study on dietary supplement marketing, covering the varying quality of evidence (solid for vitamin D and fish oil, little or none for most) and the types of supplements sold, such as goji juice and herbal products.

Background section describing common supplement health claims (antioxidants, detoxification, immune stimulation, weight loss) and sales channels, including health food stores, multilevel marketing, junk mail, spam e-mail, and websites.

Conclusions contrasting prices: well-supported supplements cost about $3-$4 per month, while heavily promoted supplements with little evidence cost $20-$60 per month. It also notes that much marketing rests on blatantly dishonest claims.
Final conclusion blaming weak US law for the problem and calling for stricter regulation and better public advice about dietary supplement marketing in North America.
Background and objectives of a Cochrane review (update of 2003 review) on interventions for nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy, covering symptom prevalence and impact on women.

Objectives and search methods of the review: assessing effectiveness and safety of interventions for nausea, vomiting and retching up to 20 weeks' gestation, with a Cochrane Trials Register search dated 28 May 2010.

Selection criteria and data-collection methods: only randomised controlled trials were included, excluding hyperemesis gravidarum trials (covered elsewhere), quasi-randomised and crossover trials; four authors in pairs assessed eligibility and risk of bias.

Main results opening: 27 trials with 4041 women met inclusion criteria, covering acupressure, acustimulation, acupuncture, ginger, vitamin B6 and antiemetics; no dietary or lifestyle intervention studies were found.

Findings on specific non-drug and herbal interventions: evidence for P6, ear acupressure and acustimulation was limited, acupuncture showed no significant benefit, and ginger's effectiveness was limited and inconsistent.

Findings on drug interventions and reporting gaps: limited evidence supports vitamin B6 and antiemetics for mild or moderate symptoms, adverse and psychosocial outcomes were poorly reported, and pooling was not possible due to heterogeneity.

Study quality and authors' conclusions: included studies were of mixed methodological quality, and health professionals need clear, evidence-based guidance given the high prevalence of nausea and vomiting, yet high-quality evidence is lacking.
Conclusion on research gaps: difficulties interpreting included studies highlight the need for specific, consistent and clearly justified outcomes and measurement approaches in future trials.
Final sentence of the review's conclusions, calling for standardised, well-justified outcome measures and measurement approaches in nausea and vomiting research.

Introduction and background of a study on health food store employees' recommendations for nausea and migraines in pregnant women, noting limited safety data on supplements and reliance on store staff advice.

Study methods: a disguised shopper phoned 155 Phoenix-area health food stores posing as an 8-week-pregnant woman asking about nausea/vomiting and migraine treatments, and responses were checked against MEDLINE literature.

Methods continued and start of results: responses were compared with MEDLINE evidence (1966 to September 2004) on whether supplements and their use in pregnancy were contraindicated; first results on store recommendation rates for nausea and migraines.

Key results: 89% of stores recommended treatments for nausea/vomiting and 82% for migraines, ginger was the top nausea recommendation, few gave correct dosage and duration, and 5% (15 of 278) of recommendations were contraindicated in pregnancy.

Conclusions begin: the willingness of health food store staff to recommend treatments during pregnancy raises concern given rising supplement use, and contraindicated products could harm mother or fetus.

Final conclusion: contraindicated supplements could cause serious harm, and the study calls for research and more stringent guidelines governing health food store recommendations to pregnant customers.

Study design and methods for a Canadian study on health food store employees' advice to simulated HIV-positive customers about natural health products, introducing the objectives and the mystery-shopper approach.

Methods continued: research assistants posing as asymptomatic HIV-positive customers asked health food store employees about product costs, side effects, drug interactions, efficacy, and CAM education, and whether staff asked about medications or referred to physicians or CAM providers.

Results begin: 32 stores were included and the breakdown of employee responses shows 25% gave no advice, 25% asked about current medications, 19% suggested a physician, and 25% suggested a CAM provider.

Results continued: 36 different products were recommended (mean 2.3 per employee) with variable evidence and cost, and employees' formal CAM education ranged from postgraduate and undergraduate degrees to college-level training or none (n=21).

Conclusion begins: advice on natural food products was highly heterogeneous, employees generally had limited formal CAM training, and recommended products had limited efficacy evidence, with some potentially harmful and costly.
Conclusion ends: the study's findings call for further examination of how best to regulate natural health products sold in stores as a growing part of the health care system.

Introduction and study setup: describes the rising popularity of alternative health practices and a survey of 32 retail health food stores in which a research assistant posed as the mother of a child with Crohn's disease to see what advice staff gave.
Survey results: 23 of 32 stores (72%) gave advice such as taking nutritional or herbal supplements, and 15 of those 23 stores (65%) based their recommendations on an information source.

Key finding on sources and conclusion: 14 of the 15 stores that used a source relied on the same reference book, which strongly shaped recommendations toward nutritional supplements; the authors conclude stores were more consistent than hypothesized but still varied in supplements recommended for the same disease.
Final conclusion sentence: retail health food stores are not as inconsistent as hypothesized, yet recommended supplement types for the same chronic disease still vary considerably.

Introduction of a case report from Cleveland Clinic describing how cancer patients often assume nutritional supplements (vitamin D, calcium, shark cartilage) are safe and may be at risk of cancer-related hypercalcemia.

Concluding part of the same case report, stating that eight Cleveland Clinic cancer patients with hypercalcemia were identified in whom vitamin D, calcium, or shark cartilage supplements may have contributed to its prevalence or severity.

Introduction and study design of a 1998 Hawaii study: a researcher posing as a breast cancer patient's daughter surveyed health food store staff about cancer product recommendations, highlighting the role of retailers on the supply side of complementary and alternative medicine.

Methods section of the study: a researcher posing as a breast cancer patient's daughter surveyed all 40 health food stores in Oahu, Hawaii (summer 1998) that sold cancer-patient products, recording recommended products, mechanisms of action, and costs.

Results of the Oahu health food store survey: staff readily gave product advice, shark cartilage was recommended most often, mechanism explanations mixed traditional, scientific, and pseudoscientific rationales, and recommended dosage costs varied widely across stores and brands.

Conclusions of the study arguing that health food store retailers act as informal sources of advice and product recommendations for breast and other cancer patients, and that understanding why patients turn to these stores can inform patient education.
Final conclusion of the study urging physicians and other providers to help cancer patients make informed decisions about health food store products, given their key position to advise patients.

Introduction and study scope: frames widespread concern about mercury (Hg) in human-consumed fish, notes canned tuna has been understudied, and states the Las Vegas purchase study examining brand, temporal, type, and packaging effects.
Brand comparison results: reports a significant brand difference (p < 0.001) with Brand 3 showing the highest mean Hg (0.777 ppm) versus Brands 1 (0.541 ppm) and 2 (0.550 ppm), with SDs.
Tuna type and other factor results: chunk white and solid white tuna have significantly higher mean Hg than chunk light tuna (0.137 ppm); no significant temporal or packaging effects were found.

Regulatory comparison: 55% of tuna exceeded the U.S. EPA safety level (0.5 ppm) and 5% exceeded the U.S. FDA action level (1.0 ppm), leading to the conclusion that stricter industry regulation is needed for sensitive groups.

Risk and exposure conclusions: applies the U.S. EPA reference dose to a 25-kg child and mean chunk white tuna Hg (0.619 ppm), calculating a 75 g meal frequency of once every 18.6 days, and states the policy implication.
Closing recommendations and citation: calls for continued industry monitoring and efforts to reduce Hg in canned tuna, followed by the journal source line and copyright notice (Environ., SETAC 2009).

Study design and population for a hair mercury study of women of reproductive age in Ontario, Canada: Motherisk callers, Japanese women in Toronto, and Canadian controls, examining fish intake and fetal safety.
Methods of the Ontario hair mercury study: hair samples analyzed by ICP-MS, seafood consumption recorded, and estimated monthly mercury intake calculated from fish types and frequency.
Key results of the Ontario hair mercury study: hair mercury correlated with monthly fish servings (Spearman r=0.73) and with estimated ingested mercury dose (Spearman r=0.81), both P<.0001.

Findings on the share of participants exceeding the 0.3 microg/g hair mercury threshold (the LOAEL from a perinatal systematic review): about two-thirds of Motherisk callers, all Japanese women, and 15% of Canadian controls.

Conclusions of the Ontario hair mercury study: wide variability means general fish serving guidelines may not protect the fetus, so pre-pregnancy hair mercury testing may be warranted for women eating over 12 oz of fish weekly.
Final sentence of the conclusions recommending dietary modification to reduce body mercury burden and ensure fetal safety, followed by the 2010 Mosby copyright notice.

Opening of the Framingham Heart Study abstract: background on conflicting dietary associations with incident atrial fibrillation, study objective (alcohol, caffeine, fiber, PUFAs), and design (4526 AF-free participants, mean age 62, followed 4 years with food-frequency questionnaires and Cox regression).

Continuation of the Framingham dietary-AF abstract methods, giving the 4-year follow-up and Cox analysis, then the results: 296 incident AF cases (177 men, 119 women) and the statement that multivariable analyses found no significant dietary associations.

Framingham dietary-AF results with hazard ratios by quartile for alcohol and caffeine, including confidence intervals and P-for-trend values, all showing no significant association with atrial fibrillation risk.

Framingham dietary-AF quartile hazard ratios for total fiber and n-3 (omega-3) PUFAs, with confidence intervals and P-for-trend values (quartile 1 as reference), none significant; fiber's second quartile is the only nominally lower estimate.

Exploratory finding in the Framingham dietary-AF abstract: eating more than 4 servings of dark fish per week was significantly associated with higher AF risk (HR 6.53, 95% CI 2.65-16.06, based on 5 cases), followed by the start of the conclusions.

Conclusions of the Framingham dietary-AF study: alcohol, caffeine, fiber, and fish-derived PUFAs showed no significant AF association, the dark fish-AF link warrants further study, and the dietary exposures carry limited attributable AF risk in the general population.
Final sentence of the Framingham dietary-AF abstract, concluding that the examined dietary exposures contribute limited attributable atrial fibrillation risk in the general population.

Opening of the abstract for a Nurses' Health Study cohort paper on dietary omega-3/omega-6 fatty acids and clinical depression in women; states the study gap and design (54,632 US women aged 50–77, depression-free at baseline, food-frequency questionnaires).
Methods and outset of results: clinical depression defined as physician-diagnosed depression plus regular antidepressant use; 10-year follow-up (1996–2006) yielding 2823 incident depression cases.

Main findings: fish-derived long-chain n−3 fatty acids showed no association with depression (RR 0.99 per 0.3 g/d), while α-linolenic acid (ALA) intake was inversely associated with depression (multivariate RR 0.82 per 0.5 g/d).

Effect modification by linoleic acid (LA): the inverse ALA–depression association was stronger in women with low LA intake (P interaction = 0.02), with significant RRs in the first three LA quintiles.

Quintile-specific results are absent in the fourth and fifth LA quintiles; conclusions that long-chain n−3 from fish is not protective, and that higher ALA and lower LA intake may reduce depression risk.
Final conclusion sentence: the hypothesized protective role of higher ALA and lower LA intake against depression is supported but requires further investigation.

Introduction and study motivation: a national US pilot study of pharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs) accumulating in fish from effluent-dominated rivers below wastewater treatment plants, including the sampling sites named.
Study design: fish sampled from five effluent-dominated rivers (Chicago, Dallas, Orlando, Phoenix, West Chester) plus the Gila River, New Mexico, used as a minimally impacted reference site.

Analytical findings for pharmaceuticals: HPLC-MS/MS detected several drugs (norfluoxetine, sertraline, diphenhydramine, diltiazem, carbamazepine) at ng/g levels in fillets from effluent-dominated sites, with fluoxetine and gemfibrozil confirmed in liver.

Concentration results: sertraline peaks of 19 ng/g in fillet and 545 ng/g in liver, and GC-MS/MS results for personal care products galaxolide and tonalide in fillets (maximums 2,100 and 290 ng/g) plus trace triclosan.
Tissue comparison: pharmaceuticals were generally found at higher concentrations and frequencies in liver than fillet, and this difference is not explained by liver lipid content.

Lipid relationships: no significant correlation between pharmaceutical concentrations and lipid content in either tissue, whereas galaxolide and tonalide accumulation was significantly related to lipid content.
Conclusion: detection of pharmaceuticals and personal care products depended on the degree of wastewater treatment applied at the discharge source.
Introduction to domoic acid: its origin in Pseudo-nitzschia diatoms, its neurotoxic glutamate-agonist mechanism, and the shellfish-consumption exposure route in the domoic acid review.
Historical account of the first recorded human domoic acid poisoning in Canada in 1987, its clinical symptoms, and the naming of amnesic shellfish poisoning (ASP) in the domoic acid review.
Effects of effective seafood monitoring, which has prevented documented ASP cases since 1987, contrasted with ongoing domoic acid poisoning of marine birds and mammals in the domoic acid review.

Growing global frequency of domoic acid-producing diatom blooms and the open concern about long-term, repetitive low-level exposure in at-risk human populations, whose effects are unknown, in the domoic acid review.

Stated scope of the domoic acid review, covering its mechanism of action, exposure routes, toxin susceptibility, and the importance of monitoring programs, with a focus on human health impacts of chronic low-level exposure.
Closing statement of the domoic acid review affirming the need to investigate long-term low-level exposure in at-risk human populations, followed by the Elsevier Ltd publication attribution.

Introduces amnesic shellfish poisoning (ASP) from domoic acid in shellfish, its hippocampal neurotoxicity, and the 1987 Canadian outbreak (150 cases, 19 hospitalisations, 4 deaths from contaminated mussels).

Describes the range of ASP symptoms from gastrointestinal upset to neurotoxic effects like hallucinations, memory loss and coma, and notes worldwide monitoring programmes that close shellfish harvesting when domoic acid exceeds regulatory limits.
States the review's scope: domoic acid chemistry, sources, metabolism and toxicology, human ASP case reports, and a proposed mechanism of toxicity.
Introduction and study objective of an EPIC-Oxford cohort study on diet and age-related cataract risk, noting the focus on vegetarian and diverse dietary groups rather than single nutrients.

Methods section describing the design: Cox proportional hazards analysis of 27,670 nondiabetic adults aged 40+ in the EPIC-Oxford cohort, with cataract cases identified via English and Scottish hospital records.
Start of the results, reporting a strong graded relation between diet group and cataract risk, ordered from high meat eaters through low meat eaters, fish eaters, vegetarians, and vegans.

Adjusted incidence rate ratios with 95% CIs for each diet group versus high-meat eaters (≥100 g meat/day), showing progressively lower cataract risk, with vegans and vegetarians having the lowest ratios.
Remaining results and the study conclusion: nutrient and food associations mirror diet group effects, and vegetarians had lower cataract risk than meat eaters in this health-conscious British cohort.
Final sentence of the conclusion restating that vegetarians had lower cataract risk than meat eaters among health-conscious British residents in the cohort.

Abstract of a hospital-based case-control study on plasma carotenoids, retinol, and tocopherols and ovarian cancer risk in Korean women; covers objective, design, setting, population (45 cases, 135 controls), and laboratory methods for measuring plasma micronutrients.

Methods and main outcome measures of the ovarian cancer case-control study: HPLC measurement of plasma micronutrients, tertile-based odds ratio estimation, and covariate adjustment for BMI, menopause, parity, oral contraceptive use, smoking, and alcohol (note the text mistakenly says endometrial cancer).

Results section of the abstract, beginning with the beta-carotene finding: highest tertile associated with substantially lower ovarian cancer risk (OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.04-0.36) compared with the lowest tertile.

Results continued: reduced ovarian cancer risk in the highest tertiles of lycopene, zeaxanthin/lutein, retinol, alpha-tocopherol, and gamma-tocopherol with their odds ratios and confidence intervals, plus note that results were consistent across socio-epidemiologic strata.

Final conclusion of the abstract: micronutrients including beta-carotene, lycopene, zeaxanthin, lutein, retinol, alpha-tocopherol, and gamma-tocopherol may help reduce ovarian cancer risk, suggesting a protective dietary role.

Introduces the study's purpose, design (cross-sectional cohort of 1,155 US women in the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures), glaucoma diagnosis method (optic nerve head photos and visual fields), and dietary assessment via Block Food Frequency Questionnaire.
Continues the methods (logistic regression analysis of fruit and vegetable intake and glaucoma) and begins the results, reporting 95 of 1,155 women (8.2%) diagnosed with glaucoma.

Presents adjusted results showing lower glaucoma odds for women eating green collards and kale at least monthly (OR 0.31), and for carrots intake is cited as the next finding, with odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals.
Reports adjusted odds ratios for higher carrot intake (OR 0.36) and for canned or dried peach intake (OR 0.53) associated with reduced glaucoma risk compared with lower-consumption groups.
Concludes that higher intake of certain fruits and vegetables may be linked to decreased glaucoma risk and that further studies are needed to confirm this relationship.

Introduction to the document's historical framing: early 18th–19th century observations (Buzzi 1782, Schulze 1866) that the macula's yellow pigment and dietary carotenoids lutein and zeaxanthin may improve human vision.

Walls and Judd (1933) hypothesis that intraocular yellow pigments (lutein/zeaxanthin) enhance visual performance by absorbing intraocular glare and atmospheric blue light, and by improving spatial contrast and reducing chromatic blur.
Closing statement of the review's scope: it evaluates evidence for the xanthophyll visual-benefit hypotheses, with particular emphasis on recent data concerning glare effects.

Introduction to a case-control study of diet quality and advanced age-related macular degeneration, covering the study objective, sample size (437 AMD cases, 259 controls), study population from North Carolina and Tennessee, and the 97-item Block food frequency questionnaire used for diet assessment.

Methods and results on diet quality measures (HEI and AHEI) and the main finding that the highest diet quality quartile had significantly reduced odds of AMD by AHEI (0.54) and non-significantly by HEI (0.75).

Results on fish intake, where the highest quartile had 51% lower odds of AMD (OR 0.49), followed by the start of the conclusions stating advanced AMD was significantly related to overall diet quality and introducing the AHEI score.
Concluding statement that the AHEI score may be a useful tool for assessing diet-related AMD risk and could be improved by adding more specific micronutrient intake information.

Abstract-style opening of a review on vegetarian and vegan diets for type 2 diabetes, introducing the benefits for prevention and management and the article's scope (efficacy, nutrition, acceptability, sustainability).

Summarizes the review's key findings: low-fat plant-based diets improve weight, glycemia, and cardiovascular risk; carefully planned vegan diets are nutritionally adequate and acceptable, with support from professional guidelines.

Concluding statement of the abstract noting professional guideline support for plant-based approaches and that vegetarian and vegan diets offer potential advantages meriting attention from patients with diabetes and their caregivers.

Introduction stating the problem: curcumin from Curcuma longa has poor bioavailability due to rapid hepatic and intestinal metabolism, and the study tests piperine (a glucuronidation inhibitor) in rats and human volunteers.

Rat pharmacokinetic results: curcumin alone (2 g/kg) gives moderate serum levels over 4 h; adding piperine 20 mg/kg briefly raises serum curcumin at 1-2 h, lengthens time to maximum, and lowers half-life and clearance.
Rat bioavailability and human baseline: piperine raises rat bioavailability by 154% with significant P-values, while in humans 2 g curcumin alone yields undetectable or very low serum levels.

Human results: adding piperine 20 mg yields much higher curcumin concentrations from 0.25 to 1 h with significant P-values, a 2000% bioavailability increase, and the conclusion that piperine enhances curcumin absorption in rats and humans without adverse effects.
Concluding fragment of the abstract restating that piperine improves curcumin serum concentration, absorption, and bioavailability in both rats and humans with no adverse effects.

Introduction to the document on lifestyle-related cancer causes and chemoprevention via dietary phytochemicals; this chunk covers cancer as a leading cause of death, the types of carcinogens, and the need for chemoprevention.
Continues the introduction, arguing that besides avoiding carcinogens, diet matters, since edible-plant phytochemicals can interfere with specific stages of carcinogenesis.

Concluding part of the introduction: anticarcinogenic mechanisms of dietary constituents, intracellular-signalling cascades as molecular targets, and the study's stated aim of describing lifestyle causes and phytochemical-based cancer prevention.
Final fragment of the introduction, restating the study's aim to cover the molecular basis of cancer prevention through phytochemicals.

Introduction to citrus limonoids: their role as secondary metabolites, the bitterness problem they cause in citrus fruit and juice, and how this drove early research into detection, origin, and removal.

Summary of citrus limonoid bioactivity and the review's scope: potential anticancer, cholesterol-lowering, and antiviral effects, and the shift of research from bitterness toward human health applications.
Concluding statement of the review's aim: tracing citrus limonoid research from its link to bitterness to its promise as a contributor to human health and well-being.
Introduction and background of a study on phytonutrient intake by US adults; sets up the objective of estimating usual intakes of nine phytonutrients in relation to fruit and vegetable consumption.

Study objective and scope: compares usual phytonutrient intakes of Americans meeting vs not meeting fruit and vegetable recommendations, and identifies food-source contributions; notes these phytonutrients are predominantly found in fruits and vegetables.

Methods (Design): NHANES 2003-2006 food consumption data combined with USDA and literature phytonutrient concentrations to estimate energy-adjusted usual intakes; Student's t tests compare meeting vs not meeting fruit and vegetable recommendations.

Methods wrap-up and start of Results: percentage contribution of each phytonutrient by food source estimated for all adults; begins reporting that energy-adjusted intakes were considerably higher among men and women meeting fruit and vegetable recommendations.

Key results: intakes of all phytonutrients except ellagic acid were higher in people meeting recommendations (ellagic acid higher only in women); for five of nine phytonutrients, a single food supplied 64% or more of total intake.

Specific food-source findings and conclusions: five named phytonutrients (α-carotene, β-cryptoxanthin, lycopene, hesperetin, ellagic acid) come mostly from one food; conclusion that carotenoid and flavonoid intakes are higher in adherents to fruit and vegetable guidance and few foods supply most intake.
Final conclusion: a limited number of foods provide most phytonutrients, and the findings serve as reference information on phytonutrient contributions of a fruit- and vegetable-rich diet.
Opening of an abstract on acne vulgaris and dairy: introduces acne as a western 'indicator disease' linked to insulinotropic diet, with milk and whey products raising postprandial insulin and IGF-I.
Explains the evolutionary rationale of milk as a growth-promoting, anabolic food, and describes whey proteins stimulating GIP from K cells and insulin secretion via amino acids.
Mechanistic core: elevated insulin/IGF-I activates PI3K/Akt, reducing nuclear FoxO1, the key nutrigenomic regulator of acne genes.

Links nuclear FoxO1 deficiency to acne pathogenesis (androgen receptor activity, comedogenesis, sebaceous lipogenesis, follicular inflammation) and calls for eliminating whey's insulinotropic effects as a research priority.
Conclusion: restricting milk or producing less insulinotropic milk could prevent acne and western diseases such as obesity, diabetes, cancer, and neurodegeneration; includes copyright notice.
Trailing fragment of the copyright line (S. Karger AG, Basel, 2011) ending the document.

Opening of a prospective cohort study on milk intake and acne in adolescent girls: introduces the sparse diet-acne evidence, prior suggestive findings, and the study population (6,094 girls aged 9-15) and dietary assessment method.

Methods and exposure-outcome measurement from the milk-acne cohort study: acne assessed by 1999 questionnaire, prevalence ratios with 95% CIs computed, and adjustment for baseline age, height, and energy intake.

Main results of the milk and adolescent acne study: adjusted prevalence ratios comparing highest (2+ servings/day) to lowest milk intake for total, whole, low-fat, and skim milk, all showing a positive association with acne.

Robustness checks and conclusion of the milk-acne cohort study: results held after excluding contraceptive users and restricting to girls under 11, and the authors conclude milk intake is positively associated with acne, supporting metabolic-effect explanations.
Final sentence of the milk-acne study abstract, concluding that milk's metabolic effects are sufficient to produce biological responses in consumers.

Introduces the study's background and methods: a Nurses' Health Study II analysis of 47,355 women, relating high school dairy intake (recalled in 1998) to physician-diagnosed severe teenage acne (in 1989).
Continues the methods and begins the results: prevalence ratios and 95% CIs for acne across intake categories, adjusted for age, age at menarche, BMI, and energy intake.

Reports the key quantitative results: adjusted prevalence ratios comparing extreme intake categories for total, whole, low-fat, and skim milk, plus positive associations for instant breakfast drink, sherbet, and cheeses.
States the conclusion that total and skim milk intake are positively associated with acne, and offers a hypothesis that hormones and bioactive molecules in milk may explain the link.

Introduction to the study on beta-casomorphin-7 in infants: it describes why casomorphins matter in the first year of life and introduces the sample of 90 infants, 37 breast-fed and 53 formula-fed with cow-milk formula.

Methods and early findings: the study measured immunoreactive human (irHCM) and bovine (irBCM) beta-casomorphin-7 in infant blood plasma, at baseline before feeding and 3 hours after feeding, with post-feeding rises seen mainly in the first 3 months.

Chromatographic characterization and key results: the irBCM material matched synthetic bovine beta-casomorphin-7 in molecular mass and polarity, and breast-fed infants with normal development had the highest basal irHCM.

Developmental associations: formula-fed infants with delayed psychomotor development and heightened muscle tone had elevated basal irBCM, and among formula-fed infants with normal development, the rate correlated directly with basal irBCM.

Conclusions: the findings suggest breast feeding benefits infant development in the first year and support the hypothesis that impaired bovine casomorphin elimination is a risk factor for psychomotor delay and conditions such as autism.
Introduction to the study: milk-derived food hormones, μ-opioid agonist/antagonist peptides crossing the gut-blood barrier, and the stated aim of testing BCM-7 and casoxin-6 effects on human PBMCs.

Study aim details: names the agonist peptides (human and bovine β-casomorphin-7) and antagonist peptide casoxin-6/D, and describes the BrdU (DNA synthesis) and WST-1 (mitochondrial dehydrogenase) assays used to measure PBMC proliferation.
Methods and early findings: ELISA measurement of IL-4, IL-8, IL-13 and IFN-γ secretion, and the WST-1 result showing no change in enzymatic activity after peptide incubation.
Key results: BrdU assay showed changes in PBMC proliferation linked to DNA incorporation, and agonists altered IL-4 and IL-13 secretion, while all peptides changed IFN-γ secretion.
Conclusions: the immunomodulatory effects of food-derived opioid peptides may be clinically relevant, particularly for allergic diseases in newborns, followed by the publisher copyright notice.
Final fragment of the document: the Elsevier copyright statement (© 2010, all rights reserved) closing the abstract.

Abstract opening of a review on beta-casomorphin and apnea in sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS), introducing SIDS as the leading infant death cause and defining beta-CM as a casein-derived opioid peptide.

Abstract middle section describing the proposed mechanism by which beta-casomorphin entering the immature infant brain may inhibit brainstem respiratory centers, causing apnea and death, and outlining the review's scope.

Abstract closing section stating the review's planned topics: beta-CM passage through the gut and blood-brain barrier, BBB peptide permeability in infants, and the casomorphin system in the brain as it relates to SIDS.

Introduces the study's aim: analyzing Mimolette (France) and Milbenkase (Germany) cheeses ripened by mites to identify the mite species, starting with literature review and morphological criteria for accurate identification.
Describes the compiled key of stored food mites (Acari, Astigmata) and the cryogenic SEM viewing of mites, and states the key finding that Mimolette is inoculated with Acarus siro L.

Lists the morphological features used to identify Acarus siro (idiosoma, setae, legs, anus and genitals, solenidia) and reports that Milbenkase is inoculated with Tyrolichus casei, identified additionally by supracoxal seta shape.

Explains the purpose of the identifications: enabling future research on chemical, physical, and microbial changes caused by mites in the two cheeses, and understanding mites' role in their distinctive characteristics.

Closing sentence of the abstract summarizing the importance of mite species identification for cheese characteristics, followed by the copyright notice (2010 American Dairy Science Association, Elsevier).

Background on creatine's role in energy metabolism (phosphocreatine as a high-energy phosphate reserve) and why muscle creatine is lower in vegetarians, introducing the study on creatine supplementation and cognition in omnivores vs. vegetarians.

Study design: young adult females (n=128) split into vegetarian and non-vegetarian groups, given a double-blind, randomized placebo or 20 g creatine supplement for 5 days, to test effects on cognitive functioning.
Results: creatine did not affect verbal fluency or vigilance, but improved memory specifically in vegetarians compared with meat-eaters.
Final result: regardless of diet, creatine supplementation reduced variability in responses on a choice reaction-time task, concluding the cognitive findings.

Opening chunk of a review on creatine monohydrate: introduces its use as a sports supplement to maintain high-energy phosphates, dosing (maintenance vs. loading), and reported benefits like muscle mass gains and neuroprotection.
Middle chunk of the creatine review covering the downsides of supplementation (e.g., muscle cramping, impurities) and the paper's stated aim to weigh positive and negative aspects.

Chunk from the creatine review's scope statement, focusing on toxicology of creatine and its metabolites, mutagenicity/carcinogenicity, genomeceutical effects, and contaminants, plus novel applications in neurology, cardiology, and diabetes.
Final fragment of the creatine review's abstract, referring to representative data on creatine for sports nutrition.
Opening of the CARDIA study abstract: objective, design, and recruitment of 5,115 young black and white adults (ages 18–30 at 1985–86 baseline) from four U.S. cities, who were followed over time.

Describes the follow-up exams (1992–93, 1995–96, 2000–01), participants' geographic spread across 48 states, and the physical activity measure: a total score in exercise units from 13 activity categories based on intensity and frequency.

Methods on exposure linkage and analysis: participants' residences were geocoded with GIS to county-level inflation-adjusted gasoline prices, and a random-effects longitudinal model with time-varying covariates was used to relate gasoline price to physical activity.

Covariates adjusted for in the model (demographics, study center, socioeconomic and county/neighborhood factors) and the main result: a 25-cent rise in gasoline price was associated with a 9.9 exercise-unit increase in total physical activity (95% CI 0.8–19.1).

Conclusion of the CARDIA gasoline price study: rising gasoline prices may unintentionally increase leisure-time physical activity, a finding relevant to the link between fuel costs and population activity levels.

Introduces the study on açaí (Euterpe oleracea) added to cigarettes and its effect on chronic smoke-induced lung damage and emphysema in mice; sets up the 60-day exposure design comparing regular cigarette smoke (CS) with CS + açaí berry stone extract (CS + A).

Describes the methods: sham-exposed control mice, sacrifice on day 60, bronchoalveolar lavage, and lung histological and biochemical analysis, followed by the first histopathology finding of enlarged alveolar spaces in CS mice versus CS + A and controls.

Reports the main results: increased leukocytes in CS mice exceeding those in CS + A mice, and reduced oxidative stress markers (antioxidant enzymes, myeloperoxidase, glutathione, 4-hydroxynonenal) in CS + A mice versus CS, with the start of the elastase finding.

Covers the reduction of macrophage and neutrophil elastase levels in CS + A mice and the conclusion that açaí in cigarettes protects against emphysema, likely by reducing oxidative and inflammatory responses, suggesting it could lessen cigarettes' harms.
Closes the abstract by stating that adding açaí extract to normal cigarettes could reduce their harmful effects, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces the study on protein oxidation (DNPH method) and its effect on colour and texture of cooked burger patties during 12-day chill storage, testing four fruit extracts (AU, CM, RC, RU) as additives.

Describes the experimental design: extracts added at 3% of patty weight, with a negative control (no extract) and a positive quercetin control (230 mg/kg), and notes the rise in protein carbonyls in control patties.

Reports results: control patties show increased protein carbonyls, redness loss and hardening, while most fruit extracts and quercetin reduce carbonyl formation and slow colour and texture deterioration.
Discusses the mechanisms by which protein oxidation drives colour and texture changes in burger patties, and concludes that RC extract is the most suitable functional ingredient for processed meats.
Final conclusion that RC extract improved oxidative stability, colour and texture of burger patties without drawbacks, followed by the copyright notice.

Abstract of a 2006 case-control study in central Japan on vegetable and fruit intake and COPD risk; covers study design, sample of 278 COPD cases and 340 controls, spirometry, and questionnaire methods.
Results on daily vegetable and fruit intake: cases consumed significantly less vegetables (155.62 g/day) and fruit (248.32 g/day) than controls (199.14 and 304.09 g/day), p<0.01.

Key findings: higher daily total vegetable intake associated with lower COPD risk (p for trend=0.037), and breathlessness odds reduced (adjusted OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.27-0.88, highest vs lowest quartile); fruit effects not significant.

Nutrient-level results: vitamin A showed the strongest association (p=0.008), with about 52% lower COPD risk at highest intake; this chunk also begins the conclusion, stating an inverse vegetable-COPD association.
Final conclusion of the study: evidence of an inverse association between vegetable consumption and COPD risk among Japanese adults.

Introduction and study design of a 3-year randomised trial on dietary shift toward antioxidant-rich foods (fruit and vegetables) and lung function in COPD patients, stating the rationale based on COPD-related oxidative stress.

Description of the randomisation of 120 COPD patients into an intervention group (increased fresh fruit and vegetable diet) versus a control group (free diet), with results showing higher antioxidant food consumption in the intervention group throughout the study.

Statistical analysis linking antioxidant food consumption to percentage predicted FEV1 using repeated-measures general linear model; overall group-by-time difference (p = 0.03) with the intervention group showing better lung function outcomes.
