Confounder analysis adjusting for sex, age, smoking status, comorbidities and exacerbations, finding no significant interactions with group or time, followed by the study's conclusion that antioxidant-rich dietary shift may improve lung function.
Final conclusion of the trial stating that dietary interventions increasing higher-antioxidant food intake may be considered as part of COPD management.

Study abstract opening: states the aim (testing whether nutritional factors, especially black tea, are inversely linked to COPD in male smokers) and begins describing the methods and the 40 COPD vs 36 healthy smoker groups.
Methods continuation: describes the adapted Arizona Food Frequency Questionnaire with 65 food items across five food groups and 25 dietary habits, and begins listing the statistical tests used.

Methods end and results start: lists the statistical tests (logistic regression, ROC, Mann-Whitney, Chi-square, etc.) and begins reporting group comparisons of black tea intake and vegetable-fruit scores.

Results section: reports significant differences between COPD and control groups for black tea intake, vegetable-fruit scores, regular breakfast habit, and salty eating, plus ROC area-under-curve values for black tea and vegetables-fruits.
Conclusion: ROC accuracy for vegetables-fruits is noted, and the authors conclude that high black tea and vegetable-fruit intake may protect male smokers from developing COPD.

Introduction and methods opening of a study developing an algorithm to estimate total antioxidant capacity (TAC) of the US diet, describing the ABTS and DPPH assays used to measure antioxidants and 50 antioxidant-rich foods.

Methods description of theoretical TAC calculation (sum of individual compound antioxidant capacities) and the results listing the top 10 TAC foods by standard serving size, led by blueberry, plum, and green tea.
Results on correlations: total phenolic and flavonoid content as major TAC contributors, and theoretical TAC versus experimental ABTS assay values for the 50 foods.
Validation results correlating theoretical TAC with DPPH assay values and USDA ORAC data (n = 44), concluding the US diet TAC database is established and validated.
Concluding sentence proposing future studies to link US diet TAC to chronic disease biomarkers.
Study introduction: aims to examine fruit and vegetable subgroups (citrus, apples, cruciferous vegetables) in relation to acute coronary syndrome risk, in the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort.
Study methods and population: 1075 incident ACS cases among 53,383 adults aged 50-64 over a median 7.7-year follow-up; diet measured by validated FFQ, with Cox model incidence rate ratios.
Main results: overall lower ACS risk with higher fruit and vegetable intake; apple intake inversely associated with ACS in men (IRR 0.97 per 25 g/d) and borderline significantly in women.

Contrasting finding and conclusion: higher fruit juice intake linked to increased ACS risk in women (IRR 1.04 per 25 g/d), and results support inverse associations of fresh fruit, especially apples, with ACS.

Opening chunk of a document on cinnamon and health: traditional spice/herbal use and the in vitro and animal evidence for anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, antioxidant, cardiovascular, and other effects, plus the start of the insulin-mimetic discussion.

Middle chunk of a document on cinnamon and health: cinnamon's possible insulin-mimetic action and strong animal hypoglycemic findings, followed by the caveat that few well-controlled human clinical trials exist.
Final chunk of a document on cinnamon and health: cinnamon as an adjunct treatment for type 2 diabetes is the most promising application, but more research is needed before firm recommendations.

Introduction to a meta-analysis on cinnamon (Cinnamomum spp.) and fasting blood glucose, establishing its traditional use and the unresolved question of its effect on FBG in type 2 diabetes and prediabetes.
Describes the meta-analysis's scope: it combined three new clinical trials with five trials from prior meta-analyses to assess cinnamon's effectiveness in lowering fasting blood glucose.

Methods section detailing the eight included studies, identified through a PubMed and Biosis literature search through May 2010 for randomized, placebo-controlled trials of cinnamon or cinnamon extract and FBG.

Statistical methods: Comprehensive Meta-Analysis software with a random-effects model computing standardized mean differences between control and cinnamon change scores, scaled by pooled post-score SD.

Key results and conclusion: cinnamon (whole or extract) significantly lowered FBG by about -0.49 mmol/L (n=8), cinnamon extract alone by -0.48 mmol/L (n=5), supporting that cinnamon improves FBG in type 2 diabetes or prediabetes.

Abstract opening (aims, methods) of a 2010 randomized, placebo-controlled trial in Diabetic Medicine on cinnamon supplementation (2 g/day for 12 weeks) in 58 multi-ethnic UK adults with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, describing the study population and design.

Results section of the cinnamon trial reporting HbA1c changes: a significant decrease in the cinnamon group (8.22% to 7.86%) versus placebo (8.55% to 8.68%), with the start of the blood pressure findings.

Results on blood pressure and anthropometrics from the cinnamon RCT: systolic and diastolic pressures fell significantly in the cinnamon group versus placebo, while fasting glucose, waist circumference and BMI changes were not significant between groups.

Remaining results and start of the conclusions of the cinnamon RCT: no significant changes in serum lipid profiles (total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL, LDL), and the conclusion that 2 g cinnamon for 12 weeks reduces HbA1c, SBP and DBP in poorly controlled type 2 diabetes.

Closing conclusion of the cinnamon RCT recommending cinnamon as an additional dietary supplement alongside conventional medications for regulating blood glucose and blood pressure in type 2 diabetes, followed by the 2010 copyright notice for Diabetic Medicine and Diabetes UK.
Final fragment of the copyright line (2010 The Authors, Diabetic Medicine, Diabetes UK) closing the cinnamon type 2 diabetes trial abstract.
Introduction to coumarin's hepatotoxic and carcinogenic properties, the EFSA 2004 dismissal of genotoxicity, and the first TDI derived from animal liver data (0.1 mg/kg bw).
Shifts to human clinical evidence: patients given coumarin as a drug revealed a subgroup more susceptible to liver toxicity than test animals, with unknown cause.
Human-data-based TDI of 0.1 mg/kg bw confirms EFSA's value; dietary exposure is mainly from cassia cinnamon used in cookies and sweets.
Christmas-season exposure survey in Germany (over 1000 randomly selected people by phone) finding heavy cassia cinnamon consumers can reach the TDI.
Concluding fragment completing the statement that heavy cassia cinnamon consumers may reach a daily coumarin intake equal to the TDI.

Introduction and method: establishes watermelon as a rich natural source of citrulline, its nitric oxide and antioxidant roles, and a GC-MS method developed to separate citrulline from co-eluting glutamic acid.
Methods and results on citrulline content by type: GC-MS analysis across watermelon varieties, showing a 3.9 to 28.5 mg/g dwt range and similar levels in seeded versus seedless types.
Results by flesh color and tissue: red-flesh watermelons had less citrulline than yellow or orange, and rind had more citrulline than flesh on a dry weight basis but less on a fresh weight basis.
Conclusion: watermelon rind, an underutilized agricultural waste, is presented as a potential natural source of citrulline.

Background and methods opening of a pilot study on watermelon (L-citrulline/L-arginine) supplementation and aortic blood pressure and arterial stiffness in prehypertensive adults, introducing the NO pathway rationale and the list of hemodynamic measures.

Methods section detailing the measured hemodynamic and arterial function variables (brachial and aortic BP, augmentation index, wave amplitudes, reflection time, pulse wave velocity) and the study population of nine prehypertensive subjects in supine position.

Methods continuation describing the randomized crossover design: 6 weeks of watermelon supplementation (2.7 g citrulline / 1.3 g arginine daily) versus placebo, separated by a 4-week washout, plus the start of the results section.

Results reporting significant watermelon-versus-placebo changes from baseline in brachial pulse pressure, aortic systolic and pulse pressure, augmentation index, AIx@75, and P2 amplitude, with their P-values.

Results showing non-significant treatment effects on brachial and aortic diastolic BP, brachial systolic BP, reflection time, P1, heart rate, and carotid-femoral PWV, followed by the conclusion that watermelon improves aortic hemodynamics by reducing reflected wave amplitude.
Final fragment ending the document's abstract, the word 'sion' completing the word 'conclusion' or 'supplementation' from the preceding chunk.

Study objectives and rationale: oral L-citrulline supplementation for erection hardness in mild erectile dysfunction, based on its bypassing presystemic metabolism and conversion to L-arginine for the nitric oxide pathway.

Study design and methods: single-blind trial in men with mild ED (hardness score 3) receiving placebo for one month, then L-citrulline 1.5 g/day for one month; outcomes were erection hardness, intercourse frequency, satisfaction, and adverse events.
Results begin: 24 patients (mean age 56.5 years) completed the study with no adverse events; hardness improvement from score 3 to 4 is introduced as the primary outcome.

Key efficacy results: hardness improved to normal in 8.3% on placebo versus 50% on L-citrulline (P < .01); intercourse frequency rose from 1.37 to 2.3 per month during treatment (P < .01) but not during placebo (P = .57).
Conclusions: L-citrulline is less effective than PDE5 inhibitors in the short term, but it is safe and well accepted; all patients who improved reported being very satisfied.
Final conclusion: L-citrulline may be an alternative for mild to moderate ED, especially for patients fearful of PDE5 inhibitors, warranting further research; includes copyright notice.
Trailing copyright line (Elsevier Inc., 2011) closing the abstract; contains no substantive study content.

Introduction and objective of an anatomical study on spinal cord blood supply, motivating the collateral network concept for preventing paraplegia after thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm (TAAA) repair.

Methods of the study: aortic cannulation and acrylic resin infusion in 12 juvenile Yorkshire pigs, followed by tissue digestion and gross, light, and electron microscopic examination of spinal cord vasculature.

Results describing vessel preservation and the anatomy of segmental arteries, including their branches to the anterior spinal artery (ASA) and an extensive paraspinous muscular network, with the ASA's diameter measured.

Quantitative results comparing the ASA and circular epidural arteries (diameters given) and the capacity of the paraspinous muscular network, which is 25-fold that of the intraspinal arterial network, plus evidence of collateralization.

Further results on collateralization between intraspinal and paraspinous networks, noting only 75% of segmental arteries supply the ASA directly, followed by the conclusion that the ASA is one part of a larger collateral network.

Concluding statement that the extensive intraspinal and paraspinous collateral network explains the physiological resilience of spinal cord perfusion when segmental arteries are sacrificed during TAAA repair.

Introduces the systematic review's objectives: how atherosclerosis blocking lumbar and middle sacral arteries that supply the lumbar spine may relate to disc degeneration and low-back pain, plus the review's data sources (Medline/PubMed search).

Continues the data sources section: the Medline/PubMed search for atherosclerosis and DD/LBP articles through October 2008, using MeSH terms and keywords such as disc degeneration, disc herniation, and back pain.
Describes the search strategy's remaining details (manual reference-list searching) and the inclusion criteria: observational studies linking atherosclerosis or its risk factors to lumbar DD/LBP.

Covers the review methods: the data extracted from studies, and the key assumptions that disc herniation counts as degeneration and cardiovascular risk factors serve as surrogates for atherosclerosis. Results begin with 179 papers identified.
Reports the results of screening: 25 papers included after exclusions, and post-mortem findings linking aortic atheromatous lesions to DD and occluded lumbar arteries to lifetime LBP.

Summarizes clinical and epidemiological findings: aortic calcification linked to LBP, lumbar artery stenosis linked to DD and LBP, and smoking and high serum cholesterol as the most consistent risk factors. Begins the conclusion.

Presents the conclusion: aortic atherosclerosis and feeding-artery stenosis are associated with DD and LBP, cardiovascular risk factors have weaker associations seen mainly in elderly or large cohorts, and more prospective studies are needed.
Final sentence calling for more prospective clinical studies to clarify the link between atherosclerosis and low-back disorders.

Introduction and aims of a study on sexual function in premenopausal women with hyperlipidemia (no cardiovascular disease) versus age-matched controls, using the FSFI; notes no prior studies exist on this relationship.
Methods: inclusion criteria for hyperlipidemia (LDL >160 mg/dL, HDL <50 mg/dL, or triglycerides >150 mg/dL), with lipid values confirmed by repeated hospital blood tests during screening.
Study sample and outcome measure: 441 premenopausal women with hyperlipidemia compared with 115 age-matched controls, with sexual function assessed using the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI).

Results: women with hyperlipidemia had lower mean global FSFI scores (22.8 vs. 29.4, P<0.001), with groups matched for age and smoking; domain analysis showed lower arousal, orgasm, lubrication, and satisfaction scores.
Prevalence of sexual dysfunction by FSFI cutoff: 51% of women with hyperlipidemia vs. 21% of controls scored 26 or less (P<0.001), with domain-level differences noted.

Conservative analysis using the lower quartile cutoff (score of 23 or less): 32% of hyperlipidemic women vs. 9% of controls; multiple regression identified age, BMI, HDL-cholesterol, and triglycerides as independent predictors of FSFI score.
Conclusions: women with hyperlipidemia have significantly lower FSFI domain scores than age-matched controls, and HDL cholesterol and triglyceride levels are independently associated with FSFI score.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence stating that HDL cholesterol and triglyceride levels are independently associated with FSFI score.

Introduces the study's premise: riding in a shopping cart beside raw meat or poultry as a Salmonella/Campylobacter risk for infants, and the survey of parents of children under 3 in FoodNet sites on this behavior.
Defines exposure and reports the survey results: 1,273 respondents, 767 (60%) whose children rode in grocery carts in the past week, and 103 (13%) of those children exposed to raw meat or poultry.

Presents the key risk finding: children riding in the cart basket had much higher odds of exposure than those in the seat (OR 17.8), followed by the multivariate model start listing riding in the basket, low income, and Hispanic ethnicity as associated factors.

Gives the adjusted odds ratios for basket riding (15.5), income under $55,000 (1.8), and Hispanic ethnicity (2.3), concludes that children can be exposed to raw meat and poultry in shopping carts, and advises parents to separate children from raw products and seat them rather than in the basket.
Closing recommendations for reducing exposure: retailer leak-proof packaging, customers bagging raw products and placing them on the lower rack, hand sanitizers and wipes, and consumer education.

Case report introduction: a rare left subclavian arterioesophageal fistula caused by chicken bone ingestion, describing a fatal upper GI hemorrhage in a 42-year-old Thai woman with mental retardation.

Postmortem findings and cause of death: the autopsy showed a chicken bone lodged in the mid-esophagus with a fistula to the left subclavian artery, following death from hypovolemic shock after laparotomy.

Introduction of the abstract: campylobacteriosis as the leading antecedent infection for Guillain-Barré and Miller Fisher syndromes, and poultry as the main C. jejuni source in industrialized countries; motivates the lack of data on neuropathy-associated strains in poultry products.
Study design: C. jejuni isolated from fresh broiler chicken products bought in Baltimore grocery stores, with LOS subtypes and genetic polymorphisms characterized by PCR and DNA sequencing.

Methods and comparison: LOS subtype proportions and cstII gene polymorphisms (cstII encodes sialyltransferases for LOS synthesis) from poultry isolates are compared with published data from GBS, MFS, and uncomplicated enteritis patients.

Key findings: poultry products carry a relatively high prevalence of neuropathy-associated C. jejuni strains; LOS class proportions resemble enteritis isolates and, in some cases, neuropathic disease isolates.
Conclusions on cstII: poultry isolates show polymorphism similarities to GBS and MFS patient isolates, followed by the copyright notice (Elsevier, 2010).
Trailing copyright fragment from the document's final sentence (Elsevier B.V., 2010, all rights reserved); contains no substantive content.
Introduction to the paper on poultry meat and egg pathogen risks: frames Salmonella and Campylobacter exposure from poultry and eggs and the need for risk management and consumer risk communication.
Discusses risk communication messages such as 'cook thoroughly' and 'wash your hands', and why knowing where risk is best mitigated matters for changing consumer food-preparation behaviour.

Explains the need to identify the relative contribution of exposure pathways to pathogen ingestion, framing the central question of whether cross-contamination or undercooking poses the greater risk in kitchens.
Describes the review of studies on internal versus external (surface) pathogen contamination of poultry meat (Salmonella, Campylobacter) and of eggs (internal Salmonella, shell contamination).
Summarises the evaluation of published risk assessments for these pathogen-commodity pairs to draw conclusions on the relative risk of internal versus external contamination of poultry and eggs.
Key conclusion: cross-contamination in the kitchen (e.g., same cutting board for chicken and salad, spread via the kitchen environment) is a greater risk than undercooking poultry or eggs.
Closing statement that risk management options are discussed in light of risk communication strategies used across different countries.

Introduces Guillain-Barré syndrome as an immune-system failure triggered by infection or rare vaccination, where cross-reactive antigens (notably Campylobacter jejuni and gangliosides) lead to attack on nerves; the active phase is short, matching primary adaptive immune response latency.

Explains the cross-reactivity mechanism between infectious and neural epitopes in motor axonal GBS, notes most people are exposed to triggers yet few develop disease, and proposes GBS reflects competing immune determinants of whether to mount a response.

Describes the proposed mechanism: in unlucky individuals, cross-reactive antigens plus danger signals activating pattern-recognition receptors override self-recognition and start a primary attack on nerve, which typically switches off quickly with rare second attacks.

Argues that the rapid shutdown of the response suggests active restoration of tolerance, aided by nerve's privileged-site properties and waning danger signals, and notes that standard immunosuppression has been ineffective in GBS.

Concludes that immunosuppression fails because tolerance is already being restored when treatment starts, so GBS outcomes may improve by protecting the attacked nerve cells and letting tolerance resume rather than using more aggressive immunosuppression.
Final sentence of the document's conclusion, stating that tolerance resumption should be allowed to proceed rather than pursuing more aggressive immunosuppressive treatments for GBS.

Introduction and background of a study on non-malignant disease mortality in the Baltimore union poultry worker cohort, explaining the rationale of high exposure to poultry-borne transmissible agents.
Methods of the Baltimore poultry cohort mortality study, comparing deaths against the US general population and a same-union comparison group using SMR, PMR, and directly standardized risk ratios.

Key results of the poultry cohort study: overall excess deaths from diabetes, anterior horn disease, and hypertensive disease, a deficit from intracerebral hemorrhage, and non-significant elevations for several other diseases including myasthenia gravis and schizophrenia.

Continuation of results showing non-significant overall but significant subgroup elevations for several diseases, followed by the conclusion that poultry workers may have excess multi-organ disease likely from widespread microbial infection.
Final conclusions of the poultry cohort study, highlighting neurologic disease findings as possible etiologic clues and noting that small death counts limit interpretation.

Introduction and background of a 2010 study on cancer mortality among poultry slaughtering and processing workers, framing zoonotic viruses that cause cancer in poultry as a possible human cancer risk and stating the study's objective.

Study objective and methods for the poultry worker cancer mortality cohort (20,132 workers), comparing observed deaths to the US general population using standardized mortality ratios, and the start of the results listing significantly elevated cancer sites.

Results listing cancer sites with significantly increased mortality among poultry workers (buccal cavity/pharynx, pancreas, lung, brain, cervix, leukemias, hemopoietic/lymphatic tumors) and sites with non-significant elevations (liver, nasopharynx, myelofibrosis, myeloma).
Remaining results noting new significantly elevated sites (cervix and penis) and the conclusion that high exposure to poultry oncogenic viruses is associated with increased cancer mortality.

Discussion of alternative explanations such as occupational carcinogens (e.g., fumes from wrapping machines), public health implications for the general population exposed to these viruses, and the call for epidemiologic studies controlling for other exposures.
Closing call for epidemiologic studies to attribute specific cancer excesses to specific occupational exposures while controlling for confounders, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.
Copyright footer of the 2010 Elsevier article on poultry worker cancer mortality, reserving all rights.
Introduction and methods opening of a study on meat/dairy consumption and lymphoma risk in the EPIC cohort, reporting cohort size, follow-up, and case counts (1,334 lymphomas).
Methods section describing dietary exposure assessment via questionnaires and Cox regression analysis, followed by the start of the overall results statement on animal-food intake and lymphoma risk.
Results summarizing that animal-origin food intake was not linked to overall NHL or HL risk, but subgroup findings emerged: processed meat raised BCLL risk and lowered follicular lymphoma risk.
Specific effect estimates (relative risks and confidence intervals) for processed meat and poultry intake across lymphoma subtypes, with the start of the conclusion.
Conclusion stating no consistent link between red/processed meat and lymphoma, poultry linked to higher B-cell lymphoma risk, and chance as a plausible explanation requiring confirmation.
Final sentence of the abstract calling for further studies to confirm the observed associations.
Introduction of a study on dioxins (PCDD/Fs) and PCBs in offal, describing the scope of the first structured survey (n=173) covering offal types and offal products.
Describes the sampled offals and products and reports the key finding that liver has the highest PCDD/F levels, with lamb liver compared to lamb kidney and heart as an example.

Summarizes that offal products tend to have lower contaminant levels, that PCDD/Fs dominate WHO-TEQ over PCBs, and that many lamb liver samples exceed the EU PCDD/F maximum limit, with deer liver generally higher.

Presents the dietary exposure conclusion that weekly intake of up to two 100g portions of lamb, ox, calf or pig liver, or one of deer liver, stays within the TDI, linking the EU limit discussion to exposure.
Concludes that more than one weekly portion of deer liver may exceed the TDI, and includes the copyright and publisher notice from Elsevier.
Final fragment of the Elsevier copyright and rights notice closing the document.

Opening chunk of an abstract on caffeine (Elsevier, 2010) introducing its objective, methods (literature review), and results, then starting the conclusion listing moderate caffeine's effects on energy, fatigue, and physical performance.
Middle chunk of the caffeine abstract's conclusion, listing effects of moderate caffeine on energy expenditure, fatigue, physical and motor performance, and alertness, continuing into reaction speed.
Later chunk of the caffeine abstract's conclusion, covering reaction speed and accuracy, concentration, short-term memory, reasoning, decision-making, and cognitive and neuromuscular function.
Final chunk of the caffeine abstract, ending the conclusion with the safety claim for otherwise healthy non-pregnant adults and the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces caffeine as a methylxanthine alkaloid and lists symptoms of severe caffeine overdose, then begins the case of a 21-year-old woman who called an ambulance after ingesting about 10,000 mg of caffeine.

Describes the ambulance scene: the patient goes into cardiac arrest on arrival, and after a 34-minute resuscitation with seven counter-shocks and 2 mg epinephrine she is stabilized enough for hospital transfer.

Covers the hospital course: the patient re-enters ventricular fibrillation and receives more shocks, epinephrine and amiodarone, and initial arterial blood gas shows acidosis (pH 6.47), high lactate (33 mmol/l) and hypokalemia (2.3 mmol/l), with no caffeine levels drawn.

Reports that myoclonus developed three days after admission and was refractory to treatment, then explains that excess caffeine can cause arrhythmias, marked hypokalemia and ventricular fibrillation, and that early amiodarone may be needed for shock-resistant VF.

Gives management advice: replace potassium early, use epinephrine and buffer solutions cautiously since they can lower potassium, and consider vasopressin as a vasopressor alternative that avoids beta-receptor effects.
Concludes the vasopressin recommendation, stating it can replace epinephrine without beta-receptor effects.
Opening of the abstract: background on soy and breast cancer prognosis, plus the aim of using WHEL study data to assess soy intake's effect on survival outcomes.

Methods continued: cohort of 3,088 early-stage breast cancer survivors from WHEL (diagnosed 1991-2000), median 7.3-year follow-up, postdiagnosis isoflavone intake via food frequency questionnaire, and semiannual self-reported events verified by records or death certificates.

Statistical methods and start of results: Cox proportional hazards (delayed entry) hazard ratios for second breast cancer event or death versus soy intake, adjusted for study group and covariates; results begin by noting death risk falls as isoflavone intake rises.

Key results and conclusion: a significant trend (P=0.02) of lower mortality with higher isoflavone intake, a nonsignificant 54% risk reduction at >16.3 mg isoflavones, and the claim that this is the third study finding no adverse soy effect on prognosis.

Impact statement: pooled evidence from three studies (two US, one China) varying in ethnicity and soy intake level/type, concluding clinicians need not advise breast cancer patients against soy; includes 2011 AACR copyright.
Final fragment of the impact statement and copyright notice (©2011 AACR), closing the abstract's clinical recommendation about soy consumption after breast cancer diagnosis.

Introduction to the review on the intestinal microbiome as a metabolic organ: the large intestine's role traditionally thought limited to water/salt resorption and waste disposal, now recognized as a microbial ecosystem functioning as a separate organ.
Microbiome as a metabolic organ exceeding liver capacity roughly 100-fold, making it central to first-pass metabolism of dietary compounds, especially botanical supplements marketed for health uses.

Polyphenols and other botanical building blocks are highly recognized by human and intestinal microbial metabolism, leading to intensive metabolism and often low circulating levels of parent compounds.

Health effects of botanicals are often due to specific active microbial metabolites produced in the body rather than the original product composition, so understanding in situ exposure is crucial for interpreting biological responses.

Recommended multidisciplinary approach: characterize food and phytochemical intake, assess gut microbiota metabolic potential, and measure exposure and response biomarkers in target tissues; polyphenol metabolism used as example.

Conclusion: incorporating microbial metabolism into evaluating botanical bioactivity increases relevance and predictive value, and knowledge of intestinal processes can inform targeted product development; includes 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.
Final copyright line (Elsevier B.V., 2010, all rights reserved) closing the abstract of the review on gut microbiome metabolism of botanicals and polyphenols.
Opening chunk of a flaxseed review introducing its industrial and food/feed/fiber value: the stem gives strong fiber, and the seed gives omega-3 oil, digestible protein, and lignans.
Continues the flaxseed overview, describing it as a rich source of alpha-linolenic acid, lignans, high-quality protein, soluble fiber, and phenolic compounds, and as a functional food ingredient.
Covers flaxseed's health relevance: lignans as anti-carcinogenic compounds, omega-3s and lignan phytoestrogens with chemo-protective potential, and the paper's stated scope as a literature review.
Closing sentence of the flaxseed review's abstract, outlining its coverage: nutritional composition, health and disease-prevention benefits, food/feed/fiber uses, and processing.
Introduction and methods of a study on alcohol intake and survival in women with invasive breast cancer, using the Swedish Mammography Cohort (3146 women) and food frequency questionnaire data.

Methods continue with Cox proportional hazards modeling; results report 385 breast cancer-specific deaths and 860 total deaths from 1987 to 2008, with no significant link between alcohol and breast cancer-specific survival.

Key result on breast cancer-specific mortality: heavier drinkers (10 g/day or more, about 0.75 to 1 drinks) had a non-significant adjusted HR of 1.36 versus non-drinkers, and the text begins describing an inverse association with non-breast cancer deaths.

Results on non-breast cancer mortality: drinkers at 3.4–9.9 g/day had a significant 33% lower risk of death from other causes (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.50–0.90), followed by the start of the conclusion on alcohol and survival.

Concluding statement: moderate alcohol intake (up to about one small drink daily) does not harm breast cancer-specific survival, and about half a drink daily is linked to lower mortality from other causes.
Introduces the study's scope: HPLC-MS/MS quantification of 24 plant lignans across cereal bran, nut, and oilseed (sesame, linseed) samples, noting 18 previously unreported lignans and 16 identified.

Describes the four extraction methods compared (alkaline, mild acid, combined alkaline/mild acid, accelerated solvent) and states that extraction method strongly affects lignan yield; also introduces 7-hydroxymatairesinol as a cereal lignan previously missed due to destructive extraction.

Reports the main findings on dominant lignans: 7-hydroxymatairesinol in many cereals and syringaresinol as the other major cereal lignan, plus cereal ranking where wheat and rye bran are highest and linseed and sesame are most lignan-rich.
Concludes the summary by stating that linseeds and sesame seeds have by far the highest lignan content among all species studied, completing the comparison of cereal and oilseed lignan levels.

Introduction to the study: background on enterolignans (enterodiol, enterolactone), their health benefits, and the gap that lariciresinol and pinoresinol are newly identified precursors lacking food composition data.
Study aim and method: the authors set out to build a lignan database covering all four major enterolignan precursors, which were quantified by LC-MS/MS across Dutch foods.

Main results for flaxseed and sesame: flaxseed is the richest lignan source, mainly secoisolariciresinol, and sesame seeds are also high, mainly pinoresinol and lariciresinol; the study covered 83 solid foods and 26 beverages.
Results for grains and vegetables/fruits: grain products have moderate lignan levels, while many vegetables and fruits show similar concentrations due to lariciresinol and pinoresinol.

Results for Brassica vegetables and beverages: Brassica vegetables have unexpectedly high lignan levels, mainly pinoresinol and lariciresinol; beverages range from none in cola to 91 µg/100 ml in red wine; only four of 109 foods lacked measurable lignans.
Conclusion: lariciresinol and pinoresinol usually outweigh secoisolariciresinol and matairesinol, so existing food databases substantially underestimate enterolignan precursor content.
Introduction stating the hypothesis that flavonoids reduce cancer risk and how incomplete flavonoid assessment in prior epidemiology studies may underestimate intake and attenuate associations.
Methods rationale: the authors built a flavonoid and lignan intake database to pair with a food-frequency questionnaire, drawing on literature and USDA data.

Methods and study population: estimated 6 flavonoid classes and lignans across 50 food items, and combined them with modified Block FFQ responses from 1,500 breast-cancer-free women on Long Island (1996-1997).
Results: food contents ranged 0-129 mg/100 g with tea, cherries, and grapefruit richest; intake ranked by class (flavan-3-ols highest, flavones lowest) with wide variation in intake levels.
Conclusion: the database is useful for quantifying flavonoid and lignan intake in other U.S. observational studies that use the Block FFQ.
Introduction and study design: a prospective cohort of women with invasive breast cancer diagnosed 1987–1999, examining post-diagnosis diet (126-item food frequency questionnaire) and survival.

Study population and outcomes: 4,441 women without recurrence at questionnaire completion; 137 died from breast cancer within 7 years; statistical methods are HRs and 95% CIs from Cox proportional hazards models for macronutrients, micronutrients, and food groups.

Covariate adjustment: models control for diagnosis-era factors (age, residence, menopause, smoking, stage, alcohol, HRT history), diagnosis-to-diet interval, and follow-up factors (energy intake, treatment, BMI, physical activity).
Key results: highest vs lowest quintile of saturated fat and trans fat intake is linked to higher all-cause mortality risk, with specific HRs, CIs, and P-trend values for each fat type.

Conclusions: breast cancer survival associations were similar but not statistically significant; the study concludes that lower saturated and trans fat intake after diagnosis is associated with better survival.
Concluding fragment of the abstract's final sentence, restating that post-diagnosis diet quality relates to survival after breast cancer diagnosis.

Introduction to heterocyclic amines (HCAs): origin of the research idea that cooking smoke from meat or fish may be carcinogenic, and the initial isolation and structure determination of more than ten HCAs formed during cooking.
Mutagenicity of HCAs: strong mutagenic activity in Salmonella typhimurium with S9 mix and in mammalian cells in vitro and in vivo, followed by chemical synthesis of HCAs for long-term animal testing.

Carcinogenicity of HCAs in animals: dietary feeding caused tumors in rodent colon, breast, and prostate and hepatomas in monkeys, with gene alterations (Apc, beta-catenin, Ha-ras) offering clues to mechanisms.

Metabolic activation and DNA damage by HCAs: cytochrome P450 oxidation to hydroxyamino derivatives, esterification by acetyltransferase and sulfotransferase, guanine N-C DNA adducts, and HCA-sensitive versus resistant rodent strains.

Human risk assessment: HCA levels in ordinary diets are too low alone to explain human cancer, but combined with other mutagens, possible genomic instability and tumor promoter sensitivity, exposure avoidance is recommended.
Practical prevention advice: using microwave ovens for cooking and dietary supplementation such as soy isoflavones, which suppressed HCA-induced breast cancers in animals, are encouraged.
Conclusion: public advice on reducing the carcinogenic load from HCAs is presented as an important contribution to cancer prevention.

Introduction and background of a review on diet and physical activity in breast, colorectal, and prostate cancer survivorship, motivated by the National Cancer Survivorship Initiative and the need to extend the WCRF survivorship review.

Methods section describing the literature search of Cochrane Library and PubMed (March 2006 to February 2010) and the inclusion/exclusion criteria restricting studies to diet, physical activity, prognostic outcomes, and breast, colorectal, or prostate cancer.
Methods detail on exclusion criteria and the 2011 update search, followed by the Results opening: 43 records included and observational evidence on low-fat, high-fibre diets and cancer recurrence.
Results on evidence strength: observational studies support a low-fat, high-fibre diet against recurrence and progression, RCT evidence is scarce, and physical activity shows a dose-response benefit.
Synthesis with WCRF RCT findings, concluding that the survival benefit of diet and activity works mainly through body weight, since excess weight is a modifiable risk factor.
Implications section: survivors want an active role in care and guidance on diet and lifestyle after diagnosis, and the challenge is integrating lifestyle support into standard aftercare models.

Introduces the study's aim and design: measuring bioavailability and kinetics of sulforaphane (from glucoraphanin hydrolysis) in eight men eating 200 g of raw or cooked broccoli in a randomized crossover trial.
Reports the key results: raw broccoli yielded higher sulforaphane bioavailability (37%) than cooked (3.4%), and absorption was faster with raw (peak ~1.6 h) than cooked (peak >6 h).

Gives the excretion half-lives, which were similar for raw and cooked broccoli, and concludes that raw broccoli produces faster absorption, higher bioavailability, and higher peak plasma sulforaphane.
Introduction on dietary sulforaphane's health value and the emerging US market for glucoraphanin-containing products, contrasting vegetable sources with crucifer seeds.

Explains why crucifer seeds are a promising glucoraphanin source (higher concentration, easier processing than vegetative parts) and states the study aims to also assess potentially harmful compounds.
States the study's analytes (glucoraphanin, 4-hydroxyglucobrassicin, other glucosinolates, erucic acid) and the sample set of 33 broccoli cultivars plus other crucifer cultivars.
Completes the sample listing: 4 cultivars each of kohlrabi, radish, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, kale, and cabbage, and 2 cultivars of raab.

Introduction to a phase I clinical study on the safety, tolerance, and pharmacokinetics of broccoli sprouts, justified by their use as delivery vehicles for glucoraphanin and sulforaphane in chemoprevention trials.

Background on the clinical trial design: a placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomized study of sprout extracts (glucosinolates or isothiocyanates) given to healthy volunteers, aimed at evaluating protection against neoplastic and other diseases.

Study population and cohort structure: healthy in-patient volunteers split into three cohorts of three treated subjects and one placebo recipient, with the extract type (glucosinolate or isothiocyanate) being administered.

Study protocol and dosing: 5-day crucifer-free acclimatization, then oral sprout extract doses every 8 hours for 7 days (21 doses), monitored for 3 days after, with doses of 25 µmol glucosinolate (A), 100 µmol glucosinolate (B), or 25 µmol isothiocyanate (C).

Pharmacokinetic results: cumulative urinary dithiocarbamate excretion as a percentage of dose, similar for glucosinolate cohorts A and B (about 18-20%) and much higher and more consistent for isothiocyanate cohort C (about 70.6%).

Safety monitoring: 32 hematology and chemistry tests before, during, and after dosing, with detailed examination of liver transaminases and thyroid function (TSH, T3, free T4), concluding no significant toxicities.
Concluding safety finding: no significant or consistent subjective or objective adverse events (toxicities) were observed with any of the broccoli sprout extract ingestions.

Introduces sulforaphane (SFR), a cruciferous-vegetable isothiocyanate with anticancer activity, and the study's aim: testing whether SFR-induced mitochondrial ROS cause DNA damage in Jurkat and HUVEC cells.

Methods and main findings: 1-3 h treatment with 10-30 microM SFR induces intracellular ROS (DHR oxidation) and DNA breakage (fast halo assay) in both Jurkat and HUVEC cells, showing no cell-type specificity.
Differential-pH fast halo assay shows SFR causes DNA single strand breaks but no double strand breaks within 3 h, and ROS originate at the mitochondrial respiratory chain.

Mechanistic evidence: rotenone (Complex I) and myxothiazol (Complex III) inhibitors block ROS, as do mitochondria-depleted Jurkat cells (MRC-/Jurkat); ROS formation is causally linked to SSB induction.
Toxicological relevance: preventing SSBs slightly but significantly reduces SFR cytotoxicity, and high-dose toxicity is proposed to involve multiple events, with GSH depletion playing a pivotal role.
Conclusion: SFR toxicity involves a novel DNA-damage mechanism, relevant because DNA damage underlies established antineoplastic drugs, suggesting SFR's therapeutic value in anticancer protocols.
Closing sentence of the conclusion about SFR's potential use in anticancer drug regimens, followed by the 2010 Elsevier B.V. copyright notice.

Introduces MIF, a proinflammatory cytokine with tautomerase activity, and isothiocyanates like sulforaphane as potent inhibitors, motivating a rapid assay for inflammation and intervention in the abstract's background section.

Describes limitations of existing spectrophotometric MIF tautomerase assays (methyl L-dopachrome conversion, 475 nm absorbance loss) and states the methods goal of improving sensitivity and efficiency.

Explains the assay improvements: lower nonenzymatic rate, pH 6.2, Bis-Tris buffer replacing catalytic phosphate, and microtiter plate format; begins the Results with the isothiocyanate structure-potency study.

Reports that sulforaphane, benzyl, n-hexyl, and phenethyl isothiocyanates are especially potent MIF tautomerase inactivators, and that the activity is measurable in ultrafiltration-concentrated human urine, with two fractions described.

Details urinary tautomerase fractions (heat-labile sulforaphane-sensitive macromolecular MIF versus heat-stable flow-through) and the in vivo finding that glucoraphanin dosing nearly abolishes urinary activity, recovering over hours.

Concludes that the simple, rapid, quantitative MIF tautomerase assay is a potential biomarker for inflammation severity and intervention effectiveness, and states the paper's impact as an improved measurement method.
Final sentence of the abstract's Impact statement, closing the summary of the improved MIF tautomerase assay and its applications.

Introduction of the study: UV sunlight as a carcinogen, prior evidence that sulforaphane (SFN) inhibits skin carcinogenesis through Nrf2, and broccoli sprout extract protection against UV-induced skin cancer in SKH-1 mice.

Background and rationale: a prior study found no difference between Nrf2 knockout and wild-type BALB/c mice after high-dose UVB, motivating the need to clarify Nrf2's role in photoprotection given its anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory functions.
Methods and early findings: Nrf2 WT and KO C57BL/6 mice received a single 300 mJ/cm2 UVB dose, and both groups showed skin inflammation at 8 h and 8 d after irradiation.
Key results: WT mice recovered to baseline inflammation more fully than KO mice, and SFN restored sunburn cell counts to baseline by 8 d only in Nrf2 WT mice, not KO mice.

Mechanistic results and conclusion: KO mice showed higher short-term IL-1β and IL-6 and more apoptotic cells than WT, concluding functional Nrf2 protects against UVB inflammation, sunburn, and SFN-mediated photoprotection.
Closing statement of the abstract with the copyright notice (Wiley-Liss, Inc., 2010), summarizing that Nrf2 confers photoprotection in the skin.
Introduction/background of an abstract on sulforaphane's anticancer and chemopreventive properties, framing carcinogenesis stages and the study's aims in human cervical cancer (HeLa) cells.
Methods section of the sulforaphane study in HeLa cells: cell viability and apoptosis assays, testing sulforaphane alone or with gemcitabine, and RT-PCR analysis of Bcl-2, COX-2 and IL-1β expression.
Results section reporting sulforaphane's dose-dependent selective cytotoxicity toward HeLa cells versus normal cells, and the start of the synergy finding with gemcitabine.

Results and early conclusion of the sulforaphane abstract: synergistic growth inhibition with gemcitabine, significant downregulation of Bcl-2, COX-2 and IL-1β, and the conclusion that anticancer effects arise from apoptosis induction and anti-inflammatory action.

Concluding statement of the sulforaphane cervical cancer study, claiming first evidence of sulforaphane-gemcitabine synergism for improving therapeutic index, followed by the start of the copyright notice (2010 Elsevier).
Final fragment of the abstract containing the end of the therapeutic-index statement on cervical cancer treatment and prevention, plus the Elsevier Ltd. 2010 copyright notice.
Abstract opening of a study on Sulforaphane (SFN) plus oxaliplatin (Ox) in Caco-2 colorectal cancer cells, describing the aim and the drug concentrations and treatment design.

Methods section of the SFN/oxaliplatin colorectal cancer study, covering the co-incubation protocol, BrdU cell growth assay, combination-index synergy analysis, ELISA, Western blot, and Annexin V/PI FACS detection.
Results portion of the abstract showing that SFN and Ox each inhibit Caco-2 growth in a dose-dependent way, with a synergistic enhancement when both agents are combined.

Abstract findings on apoptosis in co-treated Caco-2 cells, including phosphatidylserine exposure, membrane blebbing, cytoplasmic histone-associated DNA fragments, and activation of both extrinsic and intrinsic pathways.

Abstract finding that higher concentrations and longer treatment shift cell death from apoptosis to necrosis, followed by the conclusion that SFN sensitizes colon cancer cells to Ox through different modes of cell death.
Final sentence of the abstract concluding that SFN sensitizes colon cancer cells to oxaliplatin-induced growth inhibition by inducing different modes of cell death.

Introduces the study's rationale: chondrocyte death drives cartilage degeneration in osteoarthritis, and sulforaphane (SFN), a cruciferous-vegetable compound known as an anti-carcinogen, is tested for chondrocyte protection in vitro.
Reports that low micromolar SFN slows growth of C-28/I2 human chondrocyte monolayers without harming survival or inducing apoptosis, yet it reduces death under apoptosis-triggering stimuli.

Describes the apoptotic stimuli used (TNF-α plus cycloheximide, or DENSPM plus cycloheximide) and the mechanistic finding that SFN pre-treatment lowers effector and initiator caspase activity and JNK kinase activation.

Shows SFN protects against H2O2-induced death, which occurs without evident caspase activation, and that SFN prevents caspase activation in OA chondrocyte micromasses stimulated with the chemokine GROα.

Links the suppression of caspase activation in micromass cultures to reduced p38 MAPK phosphorylation, and concludes that low micromolar SFN is pro-survival and anti-apoptotic across chondrocyte lines and OA chondrocytes.
Closing summary sentence restating that SFN acts across varied chondrocyte models and death stimuli, followed by the 2010 Wiley-Liss copyright notice.

Introduces the study's premise: phenethyl isothiocyanate (PEITC), a chemopreventive compound from watercress, is tested for enhancing cisplatin-induced apoptosis in HeLa cervical cancer cells, with PEITC pretreatment strongly boosting cisplatin cytotoxicity.

Describes the mechanism: PEITC activates JNK, ERK, and p38 MAPKs, and the synergistic apoptosis is significantly blocked by MEK1/2 inhibitor U0126 but not by JNK or p38 inhibitors, implicating ERK activation.

Reports further findings: NF-κB is ruled out as a contributor, sulforaphane and benzyl isothiocyanate similarly sensitize HeLa cells to cisplatin, and the synergy is absent in normal cells, indicating cancer-selective action.

Summarizes the Noxa induction link to PEITC plus cisplatin apoptosis and concludes that PEITC sensitizes cancer cells via ERK activation, supporting its use as an adjuvant in combination chemotherapy.
Concludes the abstract by stating the translational implication that PEITC could serve as an adjuvant with cisplatin in combination therapeutic treatments.
Introductory abstract of a review on the cancer stem cell hypothesis, stating its aim to summarize core concepts, separate established facts from beliefs, and outline future challenges in the field.

Opening of the abstract introducing adult mammary gland stem cells (MaSCs), their role in puberty and pregnancy-driven gland development, and the recent progress in understanding their regulation in humans and mice.

Continuation of the abstract stating why MaSC regulation matters: MaSCs may be especially susceptible to transformation in breast cancer, and the review will cover MaSC identification, regulation, and evidence that they are breast cancer origins.

Final part of the abstract describing the review's focus: how changes in MaSC populations may explain the short-term post-pregnancy increase in aggressive ER/PR(-) breast cancer risk and the long-term reduced risk of ER/PR(+) tumors.

Study design and methods of a kale juice trial: 32 hypercholesterolemic men from a university faculty/staff health screening drink 150 mL kale juice daily for 12 weeks, with dietary, anthropometric, and blood biochemical assessments before and after.

Results on lipid outcomes: kale juice raised HDL-cholesterol by 27% and the HDL-to-LDL ratio by 52%, both highly significant (P<0.0001), following the 12-week intervention in the hypercholesterolemic men.

Further lipid and anthropometric results: LDL-cholesterol fell 10% and the atherogenic index fell 24.2%, both significant, with no change in BMI, waist/hip circumference, or nutrient intake after three months of kale juice.

Antioxidant results and subgroup finding: malondialdehyde was unchanged, but glutathione peroxidase activity and serum selenium rose significantly after kale juice, and the cardiovascular risk responses depended on smoking status.

Conclusion of the kale juice study: regular kale juice supplementation favorably improves serum lipid profiles and antioxidant systems, suggesting it may reduce coronary artery disease risk in men with hyperlipidemia.
Introduction and aim of a human study on ascorbic acid and green tea effects on urinary NDMA and NPIP excretion, building on prior nitrosoproline test findings.
Study design: 25 healthy female volunteers consume a nitrosatable amine-rich fish meal and nitrate-containing water at the ADI level for 7 days, following a low-nitrate diet.
Methods: the same protocol is used to test two doses each of ascorbic acid (250 mg, 1 g/day) and green tea (2 g, 4 g/day), with nitrate excretion rising from control levels.
Results: nitrate and fish intake significantly raise urinary NDMA excretion (871 and 640 ng/24 h vs 385 control), while NPIP is unaffected by nitrate or diet.
Results: ascorbic acid (250 mg and 1 g) and 2 g green tea significantly reduce NDMA excretion in days 4-7 but not days 1-3; NPIP findings are noted.
Results: the 4 g green tea dose unexpectedly increases NDMA excretion in days 4-7, possibly due to tea polyphenols catalyzing nitrosation or an unknown mechanism.
Conclusion: ascorbic acid and moderate green tea consumption can reduce endogenous NDMA formation in humans.

Introduction to a review on Paleolithic versus modern diets, arguing that human genetics remain adapted to the wild-game, fish, and plant diet of Stone Age humans, which sets up the discussion of pathophysiological implications.

Description of the composition of Paleolithic diets (high protein, fibre, fruit and vegetable carbohydrate, micronutrients, phytochemicals; no cereals, refined sugars, or dairy), contrasted with modern Western diets.

Statement that differences between ancestral and contemporary diets have pathophysiological consequences, followed by an outline of the review's topics: phytochemicals and cancer, calcium and bone health, dietary protein and renal acid load, and sarcopenia, adiposity, and insulin resistance.

Conclusion of the introduction stating that awareness of Paleolithic nutrition is not yet a basis for formal recommendations but should yield testable evolutionary hypotheses and challenge complacency about current nutritional beliefs.
Brief closing fragment of the introduction, ending the sentence that calls for dispelling complacency about accepted nutritional tenets.

Abstract opening of a review on vitamins C and E as inhibitors of N-nitroso compound (NNC) formation, covering chemical systems, nitrite-preserved meat, animal, and human evidence, plus dietary inhibition of carcinogenesis by preformed carcinogens.

Continues the review's summary of experimental results: vitamin C reversing transformation in vitro, carcinogenicity findings (vitamin C promoting bladder carcinogenesis), and epidemiological links between fruit and vegetable intake and reduced cancers of the stomach, esophagus, larynx, mouth, and cervix.

Concluding part of the abstract: evidence that the gastric and esophageal cancer association reflects inhibited in vivo NNC formation, the finding that vitamin C is not an effective cancer treatment, and the author's support for increasing fresh fruit and vegetable intake to reduce cancer risk.
Final fragment of the abstract's closing recommendation to increase fresh fruit and vegetable intake to lower cancer risk.
Introduction of a study on indoor cooking and ultrafine/fine particle lung dose, motivating why indoor particle exposure can exceed ambient dose and the need for a mechanistic deposition model.
Methods overview: mechanistic lung deposition model applied to 10-350 nm size distribution measurements of indoor and outdoor aerosol in a typical Athens, Greece residence, across four cases.
Key results: during a gas-fired bacon-and-egg cooking event, indoor deep-lung particle deposition was up to 10 times the outdoor equivalent for the same period.

Further findings: fine particle deposition depends on exertion level and aerosol hygroscopicity; dose is nonlinear with indoor/outdoor concentration during cooking but linear during no-activity periods. Also begins the practical implications section.
Practical implications: regional lung dose and the nonlinear concentration-dose relationship justify dosimetry models; cooking dose is compared with no-activity indoor and outdoor exposure.

Dose metrics and relevance: dose expressed as number or surface of deposited particles, which addresses dosimetry of very small particles that contribute little to PM mass but are emitted by many indoor sources.
Conclusion of the abstract: quantifies the enhancement in internal dose from cooking-generated fine and ultrafine particles relative to no indoor source and to measured outdoor aerosol.
Opening of a 1999 review on N-nitroso compounds in the diet: introduces their history (NDMA in nitrite-treated fish meal) and their status as potent, broadly acting carcinogens in animal studies.

Explains how nitrite and nitrogen oxides form N-nitroso compounds from amines, prompting worldwide food surveys that found them mainly in nitrite-containing or nitrogen-oxide-exposed foods such as cured meats.
Reports dietary NDMA levels: cured meats like bacon (especially cooked) typically near 10 µg/kg, with a 100 g portion giving about 1 µg NDMA; Japanese smoked and cured fish contain much higher NDMA.
Covers beer as an NDMA source, with German beers reaching up to 70 µg/L though typical levels are 5-10 µg/L, implying notable intake for heavy beer drinkers.
Notes that nitrosamine levels in food have declined over the past decades due to lower nitrite use in food and better control of nitrogen oxide exposure of malt in brewing.

Argues that small dietary nitrosamine amounts still matter because humans may be more sensitive than rodents, and says alkylnitrosamides (which cause brain tumors in rodents) are probably present in cured meats but evidence is limited.
Closing lines of the passage: restates the limited indirect evidence for alkylnitrosamides in nitrosated foods and gives the 1999 Elsevier copyright notice.
Study of dietary effects on urinary nitrosoproline (NPRO) excretion over 24 h; introduces the high NPRO levels seen after eating nitrite-preserved meats (intro of the meat-intake experiment).
Contrasts urinary NPRO from nitrite-preserved meat products (high, up to 78.5 µg/24 h) with non-preserved meat and fish (near zero, 0.0-0.8 µg/24 h).
Reports NPRO levels in vegetarians and lacto-vegetarians, and the roughly six-fold drop with a switch from preserved meat to a vegetarian diet, with levels still elevated for 3 days.
Shows that nitrite-trapping agents (ascorbic acid, ferulic/caffeic acid, coffee, tea) did not lower NPRO after preserved meat, though they did suppress endogenous formation from nitrate and proline.

Concludes that high NPRO after preserved meat is due to preformed NPRO rather than endogenous formation, and stresses distinguishing preformed from endogenous nitrosamines for dietary intervention design.
Final sentence of the abstract: the relative contribution of preformed versus endogenously formed nitrosamines is essential for designing dietary intervention programmes.

Introduction to a review on the tobacco carcinogen NNK (nicotine-derived nitrosamine ketone), framing its potent lung tumorigenic effects and the need to identify cofactors and biotransformation pathways involved in NNK-mediated pathogenesis.

Discussion of prior reviews, which identified NNK's carcinogenic strength and specific cellular factors and metabolic/signaling pathways behind its activation and tumor initiation, setting up the gap this review addresses.

Statement of this review's distinctive contribution: a comprehensive summary of the network of cofactors and cellular mechanisms promoting NNK-specific lung tumorigenesis, offering a fuller overview than earlier work.
Concluding aim of the review: advancing understanding of NNK's fatal consequences and identifying new avenues to break the cycle of NNK-mediated lung carcinogenesis.

Abstract opening of a study on N-nitroso compound (NOC) and NOC precursor (NOCP) analysis in foods and tobacco, describing the Walters method using HBr/HCl/HOAc/EtOAc reflux with chemiluminescence detection of NO, and the nitrite/sulfamic acid treatments used to separate NOC from NOCP.

Continuation of the abstract covering method validation: HBr dependence (no-HBr results at most 20% of HBr results), efficacy for nitrosamines but not nitrosoureas, and limits of the standard nitrosation step for NOCP, which works for readily nitrosated amines like 1-deoxy-1-fructosylvaline but not simple amines, dipeptides, or alkylureas.

Concluding abstract results giving mean NOC and NOCP levels across matrices: frankfurters, fresh meat, salted dried fish (in µmol/kg), chewing tobacco aqueous extracts, and cigarette smoke filter pad MeCN extracts (in nmol/cigarette).
Final fragment of the abstract's results sentence, reporting the cigarette smoke filter pad NOC and NOCP values (nmol per cigarette) from acetonitrile extracts.

Opening chunk of an abstract describing a study that evaluates microwave-assisted extraction and dispersive liquid-liquid microextraction with GC-MS for volatile nitrosamines in meat products, and lists the parameters optimized.

Method details: the MAE procedure (0.25 g sample in 10 mL 0.05 M NaOH, closed vessel) and the DLLME procedure (1.5 mL methanol disperser with 20 μL carbon tetrachloride extractant injected into 5 mL extract at pH 6).
Continues the DLLME procedure: cloudy-solution formation, centrifugal phase separation, 3 μL sedimented phase injected into GC-MS, and the start of the enrichment factor results (220 to 342).
Results: enrichment factors for N-nitrosodiethylamine and N-nitrosopiperidine, matrix effect evaluation supporting aqueous calibration, and detection limits in ng/mL and ng/g for meat products.
Final chunk giving the detection limit range in meat products (0.12-0.56 ng/g) and the Elsevier 2011 copyright notice.

Introduction and methods of a retrospective cohort study on esophageal carcinoma risk from long-term occupational sodium nitrite exposure at a wood screw manufacturer (1977-2000), including the setup of the exposed workers.

Describes the study and control groups: 160 exposed workers in turning and milling shops with direct sodium nitrite contact versus 255 unexposed workers from other workshops, with follow-up through 2007.
Exposure duration (16 to 23 years, mean 22.1) and the follow-up period, noting the start of case counts: 11 esophageal carcinomas and 10 other malignant tumors in the exposed group.
Specific cancer counts in the exposed group (hepatic cell carcinoma, lung cancer, breast cancer, leukemia; no cancers in controls) and the reported relative risk for esophageal carcinoma.

Statistical results (RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.08-1.46, chi-square 116.83, P < 0.001) and the study's conclusion that long-term sodium nitrite exposure markedly increases esophageal carcinoma risk, followed by copyright notice.
Final fragment of the copyright and attribution line (2010, Wiley Periodicals and the International Society for Diseases of the Esophagus) closing the abstract.

Abstract of a study on principal component analysis of dietary and lifestyle patterns and risk of esophageal and gastric cancer subtypes; this chunk covers the purpose and methods, including the case-control study setting and PCA with logistic regression.

Continuation of the abstract's methods, covering the population-based case-control study locations and the statistical approach, then transitioning into results listing the six dietary/lifestyle patterns identified by PCA.
Results section of the abstract reporting how meat/nitrite, GERD/BMI, smoking/alcohol, and fruit/vegetable pattern scores relate to risk of EA, ESCC, and GCA, and the start of the conclusions.

Conclusions of the abstract on PCA as a method for summarizing dietary and lifestyle data, and on meat/nitrite intake raising risk while fruit/vegetable intake lowers risk of several esophageal and gastric cancers.
Final sentence of the abstract's conclusions, stating that GERD/obesity are confirmed risk factors for esophageal adenocarcinoma and smoking/alcohol for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

Introduces the study's aim and design: an all-Ireland case-control study examining dietary fat and meat intake in relation to reflux esophagitis, Barrett's esophagus, and esophageal adenocarcinoma, with sample sizes and the food frequency questionnaire method.

Describes the statistical methods: unconditional multiple logistic regression across intake quartiles, reporting odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals adjusted for confounders, and begins the results on total fat intake.

Reports the main results for fat intake: highest total fat quartile raised risk of reflux esophagitis and esophageal adenocarcinoma, with saturated fat also associated with RE and EAC risk, and monounsaturated fat's odds ratios are started.

Presents the monounsaturated fat findings and the meat results: highest fresh red meat intake linked to EAC risk, highest processed meat intake linked to RE risk, and no consistent associations for Barrett's esophagus.
Concludes the abstract: no consistent fat or meat associations for Barrett's esophagus, and a call for further studies on dietary fat and its food sources to confirm the findings.
Introduction of the prostate cancer case-control study framing meat consumption, high-temperature cooking, and carcinogens (HCAs and PAHs).

Study methods: population-based case-control design with advanced and localized prostate cancer cases and controls, dietary questionnaire on meat cooking methods and doneness, and logistic regression for odds ratios.
Results for advanced prostate cancer: elevated odds ratios for hamburgers, processed meat, grilled red meat, and well-done red meat, with no localized-disease association.
Results for the heterocyclic amine PhIP showing intermediate-intake associations for advanced cancer only, plus null findings for white meat.
Concluding statement that processed meat and high-temperature-cooked red meat are linked to advanced but not localized prostate cancer.

Introduction and study objectives from the EPIC-Norfolk prospective cohort study, examining dietary N-nitroso compounds (NDMA), the endogenous NOC index, and dietary nitrite in relation to cancer incidence.

Study design: prospective EPIC-Norfolk cohort of 23,363 men and women aged 40-79 recruited 1993-1997, followed up to 2008, with diet assessed by food-frequency questionnaire; mentions 3268 incident cancers.

Main results on dietary NDMA and cancer risk: significant associations in men and women and in men alone (highest vs lowest quartile) in age- and sex-adjusted models, with hazard ratios and trend p-values; the association is not significant after multivariate adjustment.

Continuous NDMA analysis per 1-SD increase, showing increased gastrointestinal cancer risk and a particularly strong association with rectal cancer; also notes the multivariate-adjusted result for men.

Covariates adjusted for in the rectal and GI cancer models (age, sex, BMI, smoking, alcohol, energy, physical activity, education, menopausal status); endogenous NOC index and dietary nitrite showed no significant link to cancer risk; introduces the vitamin C interaction.

Key findings and conclusions: a significant interaction between plasma vitamin C and dietary NDMA on cancer incidence, and the conclusion that dietary NDMA is linked to higher gastrointestinal, particularly rectal, cancer incidence.
Final conclusion sentence: plasma vitamin C may modify the association between NDMA exposure and cancer risk in the EPIC-Norfolk cohort.

Introduces the study's aim: examining links between table salt use, processed meat intake, and cancer risk, based on mailed questionnaires from about 19,700 cancer patients and 5,039 population controls recruited 1994–1997.

Describes the methods: socioeconomic, lifestyle and diet measurement, a 69-item food frequency questionnaire covering diet two years before the study, and odds ratios with 95% CIs from unconditional logistic regression.

Reports the salt finding: frequently adding salt at the table was linked to higher stomach, lung, testicular and bladder cancer risk; processed meat was significantly associated with several cancers and leukaemia, with highest-quartile odds ratios of 1.3 to 1.7.
Concludes that the results support a possible role of high salt and processed meat consumption in the aetiology of several cancers.

Abstract opening of a study on meat intake and bladder cancer risk in the NIH-AARP cohort, introducing the biological rationale that meat-related compounds (nitrate, nitrite, HCAs, PAHs) formed during cooking and processing may drive bladder carcinogenesis.

Methods section describing the NIH-AARP prospective cohort (300,933 participants, 854 bladder cancer cases over 7 years) and how exposures were estimated: nitrate/nitrite from processed meat and HCAs/PAHs from cooked meat using measured-value databases, plus total dietary nitrate/nitrite from literature values.
Results section beginning with hazard ratios for red meat and the HCA PhIP, reporting quintile comparisons and p-trend values for borderline associations with bladder cancer risk.

Results continuing with top-quintile associations for total dietary nitrite and for nitrate plus nitrite from processed meat, including hazard ratios, confidence intervals, and p-trend values for bladder cancer.

Conclusions of the study, stating modest support for total dietary nitrite and processed-meat nitrate plus nitrite as contributors to bladder cancer, and a suggested positive link between red meat/PhIP and bladder carcinogenesis.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the abstract with the suggested positive association between red meat, PhIP, and bladder carcinogenesis.
Introduction to a case-cohort study of meat intake (total, red, processed, fish, poultry) and endometrial cancer risk, noting limited prior prospective evidence.
Methods: describes the Canadian Study of Diet, Lifestyle, and Health cohort (73,909 adults, 39,614 women, recruited 1992-1999) and the study's focus on meat exposures.
Methods continued: linkage to the Ontario Cancer Registry (1992-2007) for Ontario-resident women (n=26,024), yielding 107 incident cases and a 1,830-member age-stratified subcohort.

Results: nonsignificant increased endometrial cancer risk with red meat (HR 1.62), processed meat (HR 1.45), and total meat (HR 1.50) for high vs. low intake, with confidence intervals and P-trend values.
Results and conclusion: no clear pattern for poultry or fish; overall, relatively high meat intake may be linked to higher endometrial cancer risk, though limited by few cases.
Final sentence of the conclusion restating that high meat intake may be associated with increased endometrial cancer risk.

Background and motivation of a 2011 meta-analysis of prospective studies on red and processed meat intake and colorectal cancer risk, introducing the 2007 WCRF/AICR judgment and the aim to test for a non-linear dose-response.

Methods: literature search of PubMed through March 2011, extraction of relative risks and 95% CIs, and random-effects pooling (inverse-variance weights) for highest-vs-lowest intake and dose-response meta-analyses.

Main pooled results: highest vs. lowest intake gives a summary RR of 1.22 (95% CI 1.11-1.34), and each 100 g/day increase gives RR 1.14 (95% CI 1.04-1.24), showing increased colorectal cancer risk with meat intake.
Non-linear dose-response findings: risk rises roughly linearly up to about 140 g/day before plateauing, with similar associations for colon and rectal cancer.

Separate analyses by meat type: fresh red meat (RR 1.17 per 100 g/day) and processed meat (RR 1.18 per 50 g/day) are each linked to risk; colon cancer results mirror the overall findings, while rectal cancer showed no significant association.

Conclusions: high red and processed meat intake significantly raises risk of colorectal, colon and rectal cancer, supporting limits on consumption as a dietary recommendation for colorectal cancer prevention.
Final sentence of the conclusions, completing the recommendation to limit red and processed meat consumption as part of colorectal cancer prevention advice.

Mechanistic basis of nitrosamine toxicity (DNA damage, oxidative stress, inflammation) and how these same processes underlie aging and insulin-resistance diseases such as neurodegeneration, diabetes, and NASH, from an abstract on nitrosamine exposure and chronic disease.

Evidence from streptozotocin studies, a nitrosamine-related compound, that experimental exposure induces NASH, diabetes types 1-3, and Alzheimer-type neurodegeneration; the abstract then previews its review of mortality trends for DM, AD, and Parkinson's.

Argument that rising mortality from diabetes, Alzheimer's, and Parkinson's tracks increasing human exposure to nitrates, nitrites, and nitrosamines from processed foods, supporting a chronic-exposure rather than genetic model of the insulin-resistance disease pandemic.

Proposed remedies for nitrosamine exposure: eliminating dietary nitrites, reducing nitrates in crop fertilizer and irrigation water, and detoxifying food and water; the abstract also introduces future research needs.

Closing call for future research to better detect and monitor human nitrosamine exposure and to identify early nitrosamine-linked tissue injury and insulin resistance, concluding the abstract on nitrosamines and insulin-resistance disease.
Introduces nitrate-to-nitrite conversion in humans and its role in forming carcinogenic nitrosamines, linking dietary nitrate intake to vegetables and drinking water and to agricultural practices.
Explains how agricultural factors drive nitrate levels in water and vegetables: plants store excess nitrate in cell vacuoles when it is not metabolised, so surplus nitrate persists at harvest.

Lists factors affecting plant nitrate content (cultivar, fertiliser type and amount, harvest timing, light, temperature) and recommends meeting toxicologists' calls for a sharp cut in human nitrate intake.
Contrasts conventional farming with modern biological-organic methods, which reduce nitrate leaching and nitrate content in vegetables, setting up the point about fungicide-related nitrosamine risks.
Concludes that organic farming avoids synthetic fungicides, so the formation of carcinogenic nitroso-ethylenethiourea from their metabolites reacting with nitrites does not occur.

Introduction to the NDMA poisoning history in Norway: how sodium nitrite and formalin preservatives in fish meal, from 1953, and the 1957 mink liver disease outbreak and livestock deaths led to the discovery that NDMA forms from fish amines.

Mechanism and risk: TMAO in fish reacts with sodium nitrite or fuel-combustion nitrogen oxides to form NDMA, and mink and fox eating fish meal with enough NDMA get high rates of liver failure and tumours.

Dose-response and pathology: as little as 0.1 mg NDMA/kg b.w./day causes fibro-occlusive hepatic vessel changes in mink, cows and sheep, which progress to capillary ectasia-like lesions in cows resembling mink liver hemangiomas.
Carcinogenic progression conclusion: mink liver hemangiomas develop into hemangiosarcomas, and the capillary ectasia-like changes in NDMA-exposed cows are considered pre-cancerous lesions.

Opening of the abstract: introduces dry-cured ham as a traditional Mediterranean product with major European popularity and economic importance, and notes that health and wellbeing are growing consumer concerns.

Middle of the abstract: states the open question of ham's role in healthy nutrition, noting that origin and production methods cause compositional differences, and begins describing the review's aims.

Closing of the abstract: states the review's two goals (analyzing ham's components and their dietary role, and suggesting ways to improve its nutritional composition), followed by the 2009 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction and objective of a 2004 meta-analysis on maternal cured meat intake during pregnancy (dietary N-nitroso compounds) and childhood brain tumor risk, including the methods statement on pooling epidemiological data.

Methods section describing the variance-based meta-analytic pooling (Greenland 1986 confidence intervals), the outcome measure (summary relative risk of childhood brain tumors from maternal cured meat intake), and planned sensitivity analyses for heterogeneity.
Results opening: seven eligible observational studies identified, and heterogeneity testing (p = 0.59) showing the data could be legitimately combined.
Main quantitative findings: pooled relative risk of 1.68 (1.30-2.17) across six reports on all cured meat types, plus type-specific results where hot dog consumption raised risk by 33% (1.08-1.66).

Conclusion of the meta-analysis: sausage intake showed a similar 44% increase, and the results support a suspected causal link between dietary NOCs from cured meats in pregnancy and childhood brain tumors, though study limitations preclude definitive conclusions.
Closing remark calling for further observational and laboratory studies, followed by the copyright notice (S. Karger AG, Basel, 2004) for this abstract.

Introduction of the abstract: links processed meat intake to colorectal cancer risk, summarizing epidemiologic estimates (20-50% excess risk in highest intake group) and noting higher per-gram risk than fresh red meat.

Transition from epidemiology to mechanistic hypotheses: notes that proposed explanations are mostly drawn from red meat studies, and begins listing the experimentally tested ones, including high-fat diets (insulin resistance, fecal bile acids) and high-temperature cooking.

Continues the list of tested mechanisms: carcinogenic heterocyclic amines and PAHs from high-temperature cooking, endogenous N-nitroso compound formation, and heme iron promoting mucosal cell proliferation via lipoperoxidation or fecal water cytotoxicity.

Concluding remarks: describes nitrosation increasing heme toxicity in cured products, and argues that understanding these mechanisms could reduce cancer burden by modifying processing methods rather than banning processed meat.

Introduction and background of the Strong Heart Family Study on processed meat intake and diabetes risk among American Indians, stating the study objective of examining usual processed meat intake and incident diabetes.

Study design and methods: a prospective cohort of diabetes- and CVD-free American Indian participants from the Strong Heart Family Study with a 5-year follow-up (n = 2001), using a Block food-frequency questionnaire at baseline and generalized estimating equations.

Diabetes definition using 2003 ADA criteria and the study's main result on case count: 243 incident diabetes cases identified, with the start of the upper-versus-lower quartile comparison for intake of processed meat.
Key results: processed meat intake linked to higher incident diabetes (OR 1.63), strongest for spam (OR 2.06), with confidence intervals reported after confounder adjustment.

Unprocessed red meat showed no association with incident diabetes (OR 0.90), contrasting with processed meat, and the conclusion begins by stating that processed meat such as spam, not unprocessed red meat, raises diabetes risk in American Indians.
