Concluding statement that the processed-meat and diabetes association applies to a high-risk rural American Indian population with limited access to healthy foods.
Background and objective of a prospective cohort study on fruit and vegetable intake and coronary heart disease risk, drawing on the Nurses' Health Study and Health Professionals' Follow-Up Study.
Study setting and participants: 84,251 women (followed 14 years) and 42,148 men (followed 8 years), all free of baseline cardiovascular disease, cancer, and diabetes; outcome measurement begins.

Main outcome measured as incident nonfatal myocardial infarction or fatal coronary heart disease (1127 cases in women, 1063 in men), with diet assessed by food-frequency questionnaire; first main result on highest vs. lowest quintile risk after adjustment.

Key quantitative results: highest quintile of fruit and vegetable intake gives relative risk 0.80 for coronary heart disease, and each additional daily serving is associated with 4% lower risk (RR 0.96).

Subgroup findings: green leafy vegetables (RR 0.77 per daily serving) and vitamin C-rich fruits and vegetables (RR 0.94 per serving) contributed most to the protective effect of total fruit and vegetable intake.
Conclusion: fruit and vegetable consumption, especially green leafy vegetables and vitamin C-rich produce, appears protective against coronary heart disease.

This is the sole chunk of a short case-report style document titled 'The case of the purple colon.' It states that purple discoloration of the large bowel seen at autopsy was attributed to beetroot ingestion and post-mortem changes, i.e., a benign, non-pathological explanation for the colour.

Case report abstract describing a critically ill infant with severe multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia and bacteremia treated with garlic plus antibiotics, following in vitro disc diffusion showing altered resistance on garlic-treated Mueller Hinton agar.
Concluding claim of the case report abstract stating this is the first literature report of therapeutic garlic use in a critically ill infant, completing the sentence begun in the preceding chunk.

Abstract opening of a study using FT-IR and Raman spectroscopy to examine cell injury and inactivation of Campylobacter jejuni treated with garlic concentrate and garlic-derived compounds at different temperatures.

Abstract findings: diallyl sulfide antimicrobial activity rises with sulfur atom count, and FT-IR shows organosulfur compounds (not phenolics) drive garlic's antibacterial effect via membrane protein, lipid, and polysaccharide changes.

Abstract results on Raman microscopy (confocal, gold-particle substrate, single-cell mapping) confirming intracellular uptake of sulfur and phenolic components, and introducing SEM/TEM as imaging methods.
Abstract methods section describing electron microscopy verification of cell damage and the chemometric analyses (PCA, DFA, SIMCA) with cross-validation used to classify bacteria by degree of injury.
Abstract on PLSR modeling to quantify healthy and injured cell counts and PLSR loading plots that confirm membrane changes in C. jejuni exposed to organosulfur compounds.

Abstract conclusion stating that complementary infrared and Raman spectroscopy, with chemometrics and electron microscopy, provide an accurate chemical 'whole-organism fingerprint' of bacterial injury and inactivation.
Introduction to beeturia (pink/red urine after beetroot) and the development of an HPLC assay for betacyanin pigments to study human variability and its basis in rats.
Identification of the two major betacyanin peaks in beetroot extracts (betanin or its epimer, and its disaccharide) by UV spectra (lambda max 535 nm) and mass spectrometry.
Human study of 100 normal subjects showing 0-8 h urinary recoveries of the two betacyanins after an oral beetroot dose; distributions were skewed but not clearly bimodal.
Rat perfused jejunum and liver studies showing negligible absorption, metabolism, or biliary secretion of betacyanins, plus the four subjects with visibly red urine at the high end of recovery.

Intact anaesthetized rat i.v. studies showing betacyanin plasma clearance, high total urinary recovery (80%), and renal clearance near plasma clearance, implying no hepatic or renal deficiency causes beeturia.

Oral beetroot dosing in rats: gastric betacyanin content fell rapidly, with no visible red staining of intestines or bile duct, linking pigment instability in acid to the proposed gastric explanation.
Conclusion that variability in beetroot pigment fate, and thus beeturia, is likely governed largely by gastric pH and gastric emptying rate.

Introduction to a document on lifestyle and dietary recommendations for preventing kidney stones, noting that idiopathic calcium stones (80% of cases) are rising in wealthy industrialized countries and that diet shapes urinary risk factors.

Concluding part of the same document, describing the recommended diet (high fluids, fruits, vegetables; low salt and protein; balanced calcium, fat, carbohydrate) and other preventive measures (healthy weight, exercise, less stress), followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
Final fragment of the document consisting only of the 2011 Elsevier Inc. copyright notice that closes the abstract on kidney stone lifestyle prevention.

Introduction of a study on dietary beetroot juice (BR) and nitrate (NO3-), stating the hypothesis that BR's exercise and blood pressure effects come from its nitrate content rather than other bioactive compounds.

Study methods overview: outcomes measured (blood pressure, mitochondrial capacity Qmax, responses to walking and running) and the design comparing BR with nitrate-depleted placebo (PL) after control tests in nine healthy men.

Methods detail of the randomized, double-blind crossover design: 6 days of BR (~6.2 mmol NO3-) versus PL (~0.003 mmol NO3-), with treadmill tests on days 4-5 and 31P-MRS knee-extension tests for Qmax on day 6.
Results on plasma nitrite and blood pressure: BR raised plasma NO2- and lowered systolic blood pressure relative to PL; Qmax did not differ between conditions.
Results on oxygen cost: BR reduced the O2 cost of walking and moderate- and severe-intensity running compared with PL, with the severe-intensity values given as end-exercise O2 uptake.

Results on severe-intensity exercise and control comparison: BR increased time to exhaustion by about 15% versus PL, while PL alone did not change nitrite, blood pressure, or exercise responses relative to control.
Conclusion: the 6-day BR benefits on exercise physiology are attributed to its high nitrate content per se rather than other compounds in the juice.

Introduction on dietary nitrate as an NO synthase-independent source of nitric oxide, and its reduction to nitrite and NO, which is enhanced under hypoxia and acidosis; prior work showed reduced O2 cost of submaximal exercise.

Study rationale and methods: nine healthy nonsmoking volunteers (age 30 years, VO2max 3.72 L/min) in a randomized, double-blind crossover design, extending prior submaximal findings to maximal exercise.

Methods: 2-day supplementation with sodium nitrate (0.1 mmol/kg/day) versus NaCl placebo, a dose equal to 100-300 g of nitrate-rich vegetables like spinach or beetroot; maximal incremental arm-and-leg cranking test to exhaustion.
Results: nitrate supplementation lowered VO2max from 3.72 to 3.62 L/min (P<0.05), while time to exhaustion showed a non-significant trend upward (524 vs 563 s, P=0.13).

Results and conclusion: change in time to exhaustion correlated with change in VO2max (R2=0.47, P=0.04); moderate nitrate dose significantly reduces VO2max in large-muscle-mass maximal exercise, with a trend toward longer exhaustion time.

Discussion conclusion: the VO2max reduction and improved time to exhaustion suggest two separate mechanisms, one lowering VO2max and another improving working muscle energetic function; includes copyright notice (Elsevier 2009).
Introduction and purpose of a study on acute dietary nitrate (beetroot juice) supplementation and its effects on power output, VO2, and 4- and 16.1-km cycling time trial performance.
Methods: nine club-level male cyclists, randomized crossover design, consuming beetroot juice (high nitrate) versus nitrate-depleted placebo about 2.5 h before 4- and 16.1-km time trials.
Results begin: beetroot juice raised plasma nitrite levels and VO2 did not differ between conditions, but mean power output increased during the time trials.
Key performance results: beetroot juice increased mean power and improved 4-km (2.8%) and 16.1-km (2.7%) time trial performance versus placebo, with reported statistics.
Conclusions: 0.5 L beetroot juice improves cycling economy (higher power for the same VO2) and enhances both 4- and 16.1-km cycling time trial performance.
Introduction: background on dietary nitrate being converted to nitrite and then nitric oxide, its blood pressure effects, and the proposed role of oral bacteria in this pathway.
Study design: a cross-over trial in seven healthy volunteers testing how a chlorhexidine antibacterial mouthwash affects salivary and plasma nitrite after an oral sodium nitrate dose.

Results: after nitrate loading, saliva and plasma nitrate and nitrite rose strongly in controls, while mouthwash pre-rinse left salivary nitrate unchanged but abolished salivary nitrite formation and blunted the plasma nitrite rise.

Conclusion: the acute plasma nitrite increase after nitrate intake depends on bacterial nitrate reduction in the mouth, so removing these bacteria likely reduces nitric oxide-dependent effects of dietary nitrate.

Final implication: the closing statement that antibacterial mouthwash will very likely attenuate the NO-dependent biological effects of dietary nitrate, following from removal of oral commensal bacteria.

Introduction to a double-blind crossover trial showing dietary inorganic nitrate (converted to NO) reduces exercise oxygen cost, motivating study of its effect on basal mitochondrial function in healthy volunteers.

Results: nitrate supplementation improved skeletal muscle mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation efficiency (P/O ratio) and lowered state 4 respiration (with and without atractyloside, and without adenylates).

Key findings and mechanism: the improved P/O ratio correlated with lower exercise oxygen cost, and nitrate reduced ATP/ADP translocase expression (a proton-conductance protein), with conclusions about implications for exercise physiology and mitochondrial-dysfunction disorders.
Closing sentence and copyright notice (Elsevier, 2011) for the paper on dietary nitrate improving mitochondrial efficiency in humans.

Introduction and objective of a meta-analysis on soy protein supplementation and serum lipids: background on hypercholesterolemia as a cardiovascular risk factor and prior mixed evidence on soy's effects on cholesterol and triglycerides.

Methods, literature search and inclusion: English-language articles from MEDLINE (1966 to February 2005) and reference lists, yielding 41 randomized controlled trials where isolated soy protein was the sole intervention and serum lipid changes were reported.
Methods, data extraction and statistical analysis: standardized independent abstraction of study characteristics and outcomes, pooled with a random-effects model weighted by inverse variance.

Results, pooled effects on lipids: soy protein supplementation significantly lowered total cholesterol (-5.26 mg/dl), LDL cholesterol (-4.25 mg/dl) and triglycerides (-6.26 mg/dl), with 95% confidence intervals, and significantly raised HDL cholesterol (0.77 mg/dl).

Results, dose-response and population findings: meta-regression showed a dose-response relation between soy protein and isoflavone intake and lipid changes, and soy protein reduced serum lipids in adults with or without hypercholesterolemia.
Conclusion: replacing foods high in saturated fat, trans fat, and cholesterol with soy protein may benefit coronary risk factors.

Introduction and objective of a meta-analysis on non-soy legumes (beans, peas, seeds) and blood lipids, noting prior research focused mainly on soybeans; begins the Background and Methods sections of the abstract.

Methods section describing the literature search strategy: databases searched (MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane CENTRAL), date ranges, search terms excluding soybeans and isoflavones, and bibliography review of retrieved articles.

Study selection criteria in the Methods: from 140 relevant reports, 10 randomized controlled trials were chosen that compared a non-soy legume diet with control, lasted at least 3 weeks, and reported lipid changes.

Data extraction procedure in the Methods: two investigators independently abstracted sample size, participant characteristics, design, intervention, duration, and results using a standardized protocol; pooled data from 10 trials with 268 participants analyzed via random-effects model.

Results of the meta-analysis: pooled net changes versus control show total cholesterol reduced by 11.8 mg/dL (95% CI −16.1 to −7.5) and LDL cholesterol reduced by 8.0 mg/dL (95% CI −11.4 to −4.6) with legume diets.
Conclusion of the abstract: a diet rich in non-soy legumes decreases total and LDL cholesterol, restating the key finding from the pooled results.

Introduces the study's background: the concern that pure vegetarian/vegan diets may cause B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, and the hypothesis that a raw fruit/vegetable-based Hallelujah-style diet could avoid it naturally, along with the study's recruitment method.

Describes the study methods: 49 adherents of the Hallelujah diet (2+ years) recruited at a health ministers' reunion, serum cobalamin and urinary MMA testing, and supplementation follow-up (sublingual tablets, nutritional yeast, probiotics) for subjects with abnormal MMA.

Reports the key results: diet duration of 23-49 months, the proportion of subjects with low serum B12 (6 below 200 pg/ml; 37 or 76% below 300 pg/ml), and 47% with abnormal urinary MMA levels indicating deficiency.

Summarizes the supplementation outcomes, showing sublingual cyanocobalamin and nutritional yeast significantly lowered MMA levels while probiotics did not, and begins the conclusions that urinary MMA is effective for detecting early B12 deficiency.

Gives the study's practical recommendations: raw-food vegetarians, including Hallelujah diet followers, should regularly monitor urinary MMA, take a sublingual B12 supplement, or obtain cobalamin through fortified foods.
Introduction to a cross-sectional survey of Canadian physicians (geriatricians, hematologists, general practitioners) on oral cobalamin (vitamin B12) use, its study population, and sampling design.

Survey results on prescribing patterns: response rate of 40%, and the proportions of physicians prescribing intramuscular, oral, or both forms of cobalamin, plus awareness of the RCT evidence for oral cobalamin.

Key findings on awareness of the efficacy RCT and multivariate analysis showing that belief in oral cobalamin's effectiveness and knowing who carries oral preparations independently predicted its use, followed by the authors' statement on its efficacy, cost, and safety.
Discussion and conclusion: oral cobalamin is effective, cost-efficient, and safe yet underused by most physicians, so promotion should focus on physician education and information on where to buy it.
Final sentence of the conclusion recommending that providing physicians with prescribing and purchasing information on oral cobalamin be part of strategies to promote its use.

Introduction and methods of a study on diagnosing vitamin B12 deficiency in elderly subjects (n=700), comparing serum cobalamin, holoTC, homocysteine, MMA, and folate against red cell cobalamin <33 pmol/L as the reference.
Results showing serum holotranscobalamin has the best ROC area (0.90) for detecting B12 deficiency, significantly outperforming serum cobalamin (0.80) and methylmalonic acid (0.78).
Description of the three-zone diagnostic partition (positive, negative, indeterminate) built from holoTC, serum cobalamin, and MMA, with cutoffs set at 60% and 98% posttest probabilities.

Proportions of indeterminate results for each test (holoTC 14%, cobalamin 45%, MMA 50%), and discriminant analysis within the holoTC grey zone (20-30 pmol/L) where erythrocyte folate correctly classified 65% of cases.
Finding that renal dysfunction impairs MMA accuracy but not holoTC or serum cobalamin, and the conclusion recommending holoTC as the first-line test for vitamin B12 status.

Opening chunk of a 2008-era cohort study abstract (Nurses' Health Study and Health Professionals' Follow-up Study) introducing the background, objective, and design of the low-carbohydrate diet and mortality analysis, including the 1980/1986 start and 2006 end of follow-up.

Continues the design description: animal-based vs. vegetable-based low-carbohydrate diet scores from food frequency questionnaires, followed by the setting and study population of 85,168 women and 44,548 men free of heart disease, cancer, or diabetes.

Measurement section of the abstract reporting the death counts in women (12,555 total, including 2,458 cardiovascular and 5,780 cancer deaths) and men (8,678 total, including 2,746 cardiovascular and 2,960 cancer deaths), and the start of the Results section on the overall low-carbohydrate score.

Results on the overall low-carbohydrate score (modest, non-significant increase in all-cause mortality, HR 1.12) and the start of findings for the animal-based score, which is linked to higher all-cause mortality.

Detailed hazard ratios: animal low-carbohydrate score associated with higher all-cause, cardiovascular, and cancer mortality, contrasted with the vegetable low-carbohydrate score associated with lower all-cause (HR 0.80) and cardiovascular (HR 0.77) mortality.

Limitations section noting measurement error in diet and lifestyle data, sensitivity analyses addressing residual or unmeasured confounding, and the non-representativeness of the study sample relative to the U.S. population.

Conclusion of the abstract: animal-based low-carbohydrate diets linked to higher all-cause mortality in men and women, while vegetable-based low-carbohydrate diets linked to lower all-cause and cardiovascular mortality.
Final chunk listing the primary funding source, the NIH grants CA87969, HL60712, and CA95589, which closes the abstract of the low-carbohydrate diet mortality cohort study.
Background and rationale of a study on a plant-based low-carbohydrate (Eco-Atkins) diet versus animal-protein low-carbohydrate diets, focusing on effects on LDL cholesterol and weight loss.

Study aims and methods introduction: 47 overweight hyperlipidemic adults compared a low-carbohydrate, high-vegetable-protein diet with a high-carbohydrate, low-fat dairy and whole grain diet to assess weight loss and LDL-C.

Methods detail: macronutrient composition of the plant-based low-carbohydrate diet (26% carbs, 31% vegetable protein, 43% vegetable oil) versus the lacto-ovo vegetarian high-carbohydrate control (58% carbs, 16% protein, 25% fat), each given for 4 weeks in parallel, with food provided at 60% of calorie needs.

Results on adherence and weight: 44 of 47 subjects completed the trial, and both diets produced similar weight loss of about 4.0 kg, but LDL-C and cholesterol/apolipoprotein ratio reductions were larger on the low-carbohydrate diet.

Specific quantitative outcomes: the low-carbohydrate diet reduced LDL-C, total cholesterol-HDL-C ratio, and apoB-apoAI ratio more than the high-carbohydrate diet (roughly 8-10% with P values), and systolic and diastolic blood pressure fell modestly, with the systolic change not statistically significant.

Conclusion: the low-carbohydrate plant-based diet offers lipid-lowering and heart disease risk factor benefits over a high-carbohydrate low-fat weight-loss diet that conventional low-fat animal-product diets do not provide.

Introduction and study aim from a crossover human trial on whether a high total antioxidant capacity (TAC) diet affects gut function, specifically unabsorbed dietary antioxidants reaching the large intestine and bowel habits.

Study design details: nineteen subjects completed a 2-week crossover between high-TAC and low-TAC diets matched for energy, macronutrients, fibre and alcohol; 48 h stool output was measured, and faecal analyses (moisture, pH, ammonia, Lactobacillus/Bifidobacterium, faecal water antioxidants, genotoxicity) were run on a subset of nine.
Methods and dietary results: a 3-day weighed food record assessed diet composition, showing significant increases in TAC, vitamins E and C, and phenolic compound intake on the high-TAC diet.

Main findings: the high-TAC diet increased 48 h stool output (324 g vs 218 g on low-TAC) and raised faecal water TAC and total phenolics, with no significant differences in other measured faecal parameters.
Conclusion of the study: a diet designed to raise dietary antioxidant intake increases stool bulk and the antioxidant content of faeces.
Introduction of the study: motivation for measuring stool weight across 20 populations in 12 countries to clarify bowel cancer risk and its link to dietary nonstarch polysaccharide (fiber) intake.
Results from 220 healthy U.K. adults with careful fecal collections: median stool weight, whole-gut transit time, and sex differences, including the share of women versus men passing under 50 g/day.

Cross-population data showing stool weight varies widely and is inversely correlated with colon cancer risk, followed by a meta-analysis of 11 controlled-diet studies finding fiber intake strongly correlated with stool weight.

Conclusion linking low stool weight in Westernized populations to higher colon cancer risk, and stating that dietary NSP increases fecal output, with high-NSP diets (about 18 g/day) yielding around 150 g/day stool.
Final statement that high-NSP diets producing stool weights near 150 g/day should lower bowel cancer risk, concluding the study's recommendation.

Introduces the study's rationale: scarcely-absorbed dietary antioxidants may reach the large bowel and counter reactive oxygen species, protecting against oxidative damage-related GI disease. Aim is to measure faecal antioxidant activity in healthy subjects on free diets and relate it to nutrient and food group intake.

Describes the study design: 14 healthy subjects logged food intake three times over 2 days, collecting all faeces for 24 h after each period. Total antioxidant activity of faecal suspensions is defined in Trolox equivalents and measured by the ABTS radical cation decolorisation assay.

Reports the main faecal antioxidant measurement: mean TAA of 26.6 (SD 10.2) mmol Trolox/kg wet faeces, range 7.5-50.5. It also introduces the 24-hour total antioxidant equivalents excreted, calculated as TAA multiplied by daily faecal output.

Gives the 24-hour total excreted antioxidant equivalents, 3.24 (SD 1.51) mmol Trolox, range 0.92-5.82. This output correlated significantly with average daily intake of coffee and red wine, particularly their combined sum, and the chunk begins the conclusion.

Concludes that healthy subjects' faeces can scavenge radical cations, implying antioxidant activity in the colonic lumen. It adds that this activity is at least partly linked to dietary habits, specifically coffee and red wine intake.

Introduction of a review on assessing atherosclerosis via flow-mediated dilatation (FMD): opens by stating endothelial dysfunction is causally linked to atherogenesis and plaque destabilization, and introduces FMD as a non-invasive endothelial function measure whose variability has been reduced by technical and software improvements.

Continues the review's discussion of FMD: strict standardized protocols yield reproducible measurements, allowing the technique to move from specialized labs into population and multicentre studies, and FMD is linked to structural arterial disease.

Summarizes the validation evidence for FMD in the review: endothelial function measured by FMD is affected by cardiovascular risk factors, relates to structural arterial disease and cardiovascular outcomes, and responds to physiological and pharmacological interventions.

Concluding point of the review: FMD's value in drug development as a fast, early signal of risk or benefit, compared with slower and costlier endpoints such as structural arterial disease and cardiovascular outcomes.

Introduction of the study: background on oxidative stress and CVD, the limits of antioxidant vitamin supplementation, and the aim to test a high-antioxidant diet's effect on flow-mediated dilatation in low-risk volunteers.
Study aim and design start: the crossover trial with 24 subjects, and the Methods section introducing the high (HT) and low (LT) antioxidant diets with a wash-out period.
Methods detail: the 14-day HT and LT diets were matched for fruit, vegetable, alcohol, fibre and macronutrient intake but differed in total antioxidant capacity.
Measured outcomes and main results: the set of cardiovascular and metabolic markers assessed before and after each diet, and the significant increase in FMD during the HT diet versus LT.
Quantitative results: FMD was 2.3% higher after HT (adjusted for age, gender, diet order), with significant changes in α-tocopherol, hs-CRP and γ-glutamyltranspeptidase.
Conclusion and copyright: the authors conclude a short-term high-antioxidant diet improves endothelial function and may reduce CVD risk, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces the study's methods: ORAC(FL) assay (fluorescein probe, AAPH peroxyl radical generator) used to measure lipophilic and hydrophilic antioxidant capacity across 100+ U.S. food types, including fruits, vegetables, nuts, spices, and cereals.

Describes sampling and additional assays: foods were collected from four U.S. regions over two seasons, total phenolics were measured with Folin-Ciocalteu reagent, and it reports the hydrophilic ORAC(FL) (H-ORAC(FL)) range of 0.87 to 2641 micromol TE/g.

Reports the lipophilic ORAC(FL) (L-ORAC(FL)) range of 0.07 to 1611 micromol TE/g, notes L-ORAC is generally under 10% of H-ORAC, and explains total antioxidant capacity was computed by combining the two values.

Covers variation and processing effects: ORAC(FL) differed by season and region for some fruits and vegetables but could not be analyzed in detail due to sampling design, and cooking and peeling were tested to assess impact on ORAC(FL).

Summarizes findings on total phenolics and dietary intake: processing significantly affects ORAC(FL), TP and H-ORAC(FL) show only a very weak correlation, and estimated daily intakes are 5558 (hydrophilic) and 166 (lipophilic) micromol TE/day.

Names the data source for the intake estimates, the USDA Continuing Survey of Food Intakes by Individuals (1994-1996), used to calculate the daily hydrophilic and lipophilic antioxidant capacity intakes.

Introduction to the review on antioxidant capacity assays: it defines the two main classes, hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) and electron transfer (ET) based assays, which the rest of the document describes.

Details of HAT-based assays, which use a competitive scheme where antioxidant and substrate compete for peroxyl radicals from azo compound decomposition. Named examples include LDL autoxidation inhibition, ORAC, TRAP, and crocin bleaching.

Explains how ET-based assays work: an oxidant changes color when reduced, and the color change correlates with antioxidant concentration. Lists the total phenols (Folin-Ciocalteu) assay among the ET-based methods.

Enumerates the ET-based assays: Folin-Ciocalteu total phenols, TEAC, FRAP, the Cu(II)-complex total antioxidant potential assay, and DPPH. It also introduces assays that measure scavenging of biologically relevant oxidants.

Covers the biologically relevant oxidant scavenging assays (singlet oxygen, superoxide, peroxynitrite, hydroxyl radical) and gives the review's recommendation: Folin-Ciocalteu for reducing capacity and ORAC for peroxyl radical scavenging.
Concluding statement: beyond the two commonly accepted assays (FCR and ORAC), validated and specific assays are needed to comprehensively study the different aspects of antioxidants.

Introduces the study design: the red sap (dragon's blood) from Croton urucurana bark, tested for antidiarrhoeal activity in three models (castor oil diarrhoea in rats, cholera toxin intestinal secretion in mice, small intestinal transit in mice), with the 600 mg/kg oral dose first reported as producing marked inhibition of diarrhoea.

Reports the main results at 600 mg/kg: marked inhibition of castor oil-induced diarrhoea and cholera toxin-induced fluid accumulation, plus significant slowing of small intestinal transit that did not depend on opioid mechanisms.

Concludes the abstract: the findings suggest Croton urucurana red sap may be useful for controlling secretory diarrhoea-associated pathologies, followed by the 2001 John Wiley & Sons copyright notice.
Introduces the Croton lechleri (Dragon's blood) sap study: its folk medicine uses and the antioxidant and mutagenicity tests performed in yeast, maize, and Salmonella.

Describes the methods (Salmonella/microsome assay strains and yeast mutagenicity testing) and begins the results, reporting significant antioxidant activity against apomorphine-induced damage in yeast.

Reports the antioxidant results: protection against apomorphine damage in yeast under all conditions, hydrogen peroxide protection only in stationary-phase cells, and protection of maize plantlets from apomorphine toxicity.

Presents the mutagenicity findings: mutagenic in Salmonella TA1535 with metabolic activation and weakly mutagenic in TA98, indicating base-pair substitution and frameshift detection, plus yeast mutagenicity onset.
Concludes the mutagenicity results by naming the yeast strain XV185-14c and its specific reversion (lys1-1, his1-7) and frameshift (hom3-10) markers.

Introduces sangre de grado (SdG), a Croton tree sap used ethnomedicinally for GI ulcers, cancer, and wound healing, and states the study's aim of testing its effects on stomach (AGS) and colon (HT29, T84) cancer cells, including the dose-dependent viability decrease.
Reports SdG's anticancer effects on AGS, HT29, and T84 cells: reduced proliferation at 48 h, severely compromised cell adherence at 100 µg/ml, and induction of apoptosis at that dose.

Describes the apoptosis assays (nuclear condensation, ELISA and flow cytometry DNA fragmentation, acridine orange morphology) and compares SdG's effects to those of the reference drug Taxol, while noting microtubule architecture alteration in stomach and colon cancer cells.
Concludes that SdG induces apoptosis and microtubule damage in AGS, HT29, and T84 cells, and recommends further evaluation of sangre de grado as a potential source of anticancer agents.

Background and rationale for a study on toxic metals (lead, mercury, arsenic) in Ayurvedic medicines, including the rasa shastra practice of combining herbs with metals and minerals, and the unknown prevalence in US- vs Indian-manufactured products.

Study objectives and design framing: measuring the prevalence of lead, mercury, and arsenic in Internet-sold Ayurvedic medicines, comparing US- vs Indian-manufactured products and rasa shastra vs non-rasa shastra medicines.

Methods for sampling: an Internet search (5 engines, terms 'Ayurveda' and 'Ayurvedic medicine') identified 25 sellers and 673 products, from which 230 oral Ayurvedic medicines were randomly selected for purchase in August–October 2005.

Methods for measurement and outcomes: recording country of manufacture, rasa shastra status, and Good Manufacturing Practices claims, with metal concentrations measured by x-ray fluorescence spectroscopy and prevalence of toxic metals as the main outcome.
Key results: of 193 medicines received, 20.7% contained detectable metals overall (95% CI 15.2%–27.1%), with similar prevalence in US-manufactured (21.7%) and Indian-manufactured (19.5%) products.

Comparative results: rasa shastra medicines had significantly more metal-containing products (40.6% vs 17.1%) and higher median lead and mercury concentrations than non-rasa shastra medicines; 95% of metal-containing products came from US Web sites and 75% claimed GMP.

Final findings and conclusion: all metal-containing products exceeded at least one acceptable daily intake standard for toxic metals, and about one-fifth of both US- and Indian-manufactured Internet-purchased Ayurvedic medicines contained lead, mercury, or arsenic.
Concluding sentence restating that roughly one-fifth of Ayurvedic medicines bought online, from both US and Indian manufacturers, contain detectable lead, mercury, or arsenic.

Introduction to the study: Asian traditional herbal medicines (Ayurveda, TCM, Tibetan) can contain mercury, arsenic, or lead, which have caused intoxications worldwide; the study sets out to measure these metals in products on the Dutch market.

Study aim and sampling: researchers aimed to measure mercury, arsenic, and lead in Asian traditional herbal preparations sold in the Netherlands, collecting 292 products from Ayurvedic, Chinese, and Tibetan traditions between 2004 and 2007.

Methods and key analytical results: most samples were multi-ingredient herbal and mineral products; fewer than 20% were labeled as containing these metals, yet ICP-MS detected them in 186 of 292 products (64%).

Risk estimation method: weekly intake of each metal was calculated per product from measured concentrations and recommended dose, finding 59 products (20%) likely to exceed safety limits for these elements.

Quantitative exceedance findings: 50 of the 59 products exceeded the mercury safety limit (1.4-1747 mg/week), 26 exceeded the arsenic limit (0.53-427 mg/week), and 8 exceeded the lead limit (2.6-192 mg/week).
Conclusion: the study concludes that mercury, arsenic, and lead levels in these traditional preparations are a serious concern and call for strict regulatory control.
Final conclusion sentence: the metal contamination in Ayurvedic, Chinese, and Tibetan herbal products remains a concern and warrants strict control measures.
Introduction and abstract opening of a study on Triphala (Ayurvedic formulation) cytotoxicity in breast cancer cells, comparing p53 wild-type MCF 7 with p53-null T 47 D and MTT viability results.
Results on IC50 values (about 8 vs 26 microg/ml at 72h) and clonogenic growth inhibition in MCF 7, where pifithrin-alpha (p53 inhibitor) reversed the effect but did not alter cytotoxicity in T 47 D.

Findings that antioxidants GSH and NAC blunted Triphala's anti-proliferative effect in both cell lines, followed by the start of Annexin-V/propidium iodide apoptosis results at 2h, showing dose-dependent apoptosis.
Apoptosis magnitude comparison (higher in MCF 7 than T 47 D) and dose- and time-dependent intracellular ROS increase in both lines, leading into the summary of differential sensitivity.

Conclusions that differential Triphala sensitivity depends on p53 status, that antioxidant inhibition implicates Triphala-induced ROS in apoptosis, and the start of the closing statement on p53 as a predictor of response to prooxidant drugs.
Final sentence of the conclusion: p53 status is an important factor in predicting how cancer cells respond to prooxidant drugs such as Triphala.

Introduction and study design for a 2003 Boston-area study of heavy metal (lead, mercury, arsenic) contamination in Ayurvedic herbal medicine products from South Asia, including the stated objectives and the store-search methodology.

Methods section describing the systematic search for Boston-area stores (within 20 miles of City Hall) selling South Asian Ayurvedic herbal products, using Yellow Pages categories, Indian-related business names, and other directories and newspapers.

Continuation of the methods: store visits and purchase of all unique Ayurvedic herbal products from April to October 2003, and the outcome measures of metal concentrations by x-ray fluorescence and estimated daily ingestion compared with regulatory standards.

Outcome measures and start of the results: the daily-ingestion estimation method using manufacturer dosing and US Pharmacopeia/EPA standards, plus the headline finding that 14 of 70 products (20%, 95% CI 11%-31%) contained heavy metals.

Detailed results giving the number of products contaminated with each metal (lead, mercury, arsenic), their median concentrations and ranges, and the finding that recommended doses could exceed regulatory intake limits.

Conclusions of the study: about one in five products contains potentially harmful heavy metal levels, users may face toxicity risk, and the authors call for mandatory testing of Ayurvedic herbal products.
Final sentence of the conclusions, calling for mandatory testing of Ayurvedic herbal medicine products for toxic heavy metals.

Opening background of a review on Triphala, an Ayurvedic herbal formulation of three fruits (Phyllanthus emblica, Terminalia chebula, Terminalia belerica), describing its antioxidant properties and traditional role.

Continues the background: Triphala's common uses as a colon cleanser, digestive, diuretic, and laxative, the global need for nontoxic cancer prevention and therapy, and the start of the claim about recent experimental findings.

States the review's main findings that Triphala shows cancer-preventive, antineoplastic, radioprotective, and chemoprotective effects, and sets out the review's aim to summarize these results, possible mechanisms, and knowledge gaps.
Final sentence of the abstract's conclusions, noting that the review also discusses possible mechanisms behind Triphala's beneficial effects and gaps in current knowledge that need further research.
Introduction: rationale for testing heavy metals and pesticide residues in single herbal drugs sold in local markets, following WHO quality-assurance guidelines for herbal products.
Study scope: names the four herbs sampled (Emblica officinalis, Terminalia chebula, Terminalia belerica, Withania somnifera) and the four heavy metals targeted (arsenic, cadmium, lead, mercury).
Methods and results: pesticide classes tested (organochlorine, organophosphorus, pyrethroids) and the finding that heavy metals and pesticide residues were below detection limits in all samples.
Closing fragment: final words of the results sentence stating that all samples were below detection limits.

Abstract of a study on Triphala, an ayurvedic formulation, introducing its selective cytotoxicity against breast cancer (MCF-7) and mouse lymphoma (barcl-95) cells while sparing normal cells, with normal cell controls named.
Continuation of the abstract covering normal-cell sparing and in vitro apoptosis induction in MCF-7 and barcl-95 cells, measured by annexin-V fluorescence in a concentration-dependent manner.

Abstract passage describing DNA damage in Triphala-treated MCF-7 cells shown by single cell gel electrophoresis (comet assay), and concentration-dependent rise in intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) in cancer cells.

Abstract passage reporting that ROS increases were insignificant in normal MCF-10F, spleen and liver cells, followed by in vivo results: oral Triphala (40 mg/kg) in barcl-95-transplanted mice reduced tumor growth by volume.
Abstract passage showing higher apoptosis in excised tumor tissue from Triphala-fed mice, linking apoptosis to tumor reduction, and concluding Triphala kills tumor cells while sparing normal cells.

Abstract conclusion linking the differential normal versus tumor cell response to differential intracellular ROS generation, and citing in vitro and in vivo tumor regression as support for Triphala's anticancer potential.
Final sentence of the abstract concluding that the substantial regression of transplanted tumors in Triphala-fed mice points to its potential as a clinical anticancer drug.

This chunk opens the study on Emblica officinalis (Amla) fruit, describing its anti-hyperglycemic effects: reduced fasting and 2-hour post-prandial blood glucose in normal and type 2 diabetic volunteers after 21 days of 1-3 g daily powder.

This chunk reports the lipid-lowering results of the Amla fruit trial: significant reductions in total cholesterol and triglycerides on day 21 at 2-3 g/day, and a significant drop in total lipids in diabetic volunteers taking 3 g/day.
This chunk summarizes the Amla fruit study's effect on cholesterol fractions: at 2 or 3 g/day powder, normal and diabetic volunteers showed improved HDL-cholesterol and lowered LDL-cholesterol.
This fragment is the final word of the Amla study's LDL-cholesterol sentence, marking the end of the results on lipid profile changes in the Emblica officinalis trial.

Opening of a review on natural products as drug sources, an updated version of 1997 and 2003 reviews; defines the extended study periods (1981–2006 for all approved agents, 1950–2006 for antitumor drugs) and introduces the 'natural product mimic' (NM) subdivision.

Continues the review's methodology description and states its central conclusion that natural products remain valuable as sources of novel structures, even if they are not the final drug; begins the cancer-specific statistics.

Gives cancer-drug statistics: of 155 small molecules approved from about the 1940s to 2006, 73% are not synthetic ('S'), and 47% are natural products or directly derived from them; notes natural product influence in other therapeutic areas, especially anti-infectives.

Discusses combinatorial chemistry, which has been useful for optimizing structures of recently approved drugs, but only one de novo combinatorial compound has been approved as a drug in the 25+ year review period.
Highlights the growing recognition that many natural product drugs and leads are produced by microbes or by microbe-host interactions, and calls for a significant expansion of research in this area.
Concluding sentence of the review's abstract, recommending that research on microbially produced and host-associated natural products be substantially expanded.
Introduction to red yeast rice (RYR) as a dietary supplement for hyperlipidemia, noting its 14 monacolin compounds and the lack of standardization or label disclosure of monacolin levels.
Study methods: 12 commercial RYR products labeled 600 mg/capsule were tested for monacolins and the mycotoxin citrinin, with analyses done 2006-2008 by ConsumerLab.com using HPLC-MS-MS.
Results begin: marked variability across the 12 RYR products in total monacolins, with the reported range of total monacolin content in mg per capsule.

Key results and conclusions: ranges for monacolin K (lovastatin) and monacolin KA, four products with elevated citrinin, and the conclusion of striking monacolin content variability and citrinin in one-third of products.

Conclusion and clinical recommendation: RYR may be a lipid-lowering option, but standardization and better labeling are needed, so physicians should be cautious recommending it for hyperlipidemia and cardiovascular prevention.

Final sentence of the document, closing the clinical caution by specifying the patient populations (hyperlipidemia treatment and primary/secondary cardiovascular disease prevention) for which physicians should be cautious.

Opening of the abstract for a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies comparing rosiglitazone and pioglitazone cardiovascular risk in type 2 diabetes; states the objective, design, and that Medline and Embase were searched in September 2010.

Continuation of the study selection and data extraction methods: inclusion of observational studies directly comparing rosiglitazone and pioglitazone, and use of random effects inverse variance meta-analysis with the I2 statistic for heterogeneity.

Start of the results section: 16 observational studies (4 case-control, 12 retrospective cohort) covering about 810,000 thiazolidinedione users, selected from 189 screened citations, with the comparison of rosiglitazone versus pioglitazone beginning.

Core quantitative findings: rosiglitazone versus pioglitazone odds ratios for myocardial infarction (1.16), congestive heart failure (1.22), and death (1.14), with 95% confidence intervals, P values, study counts, and I2 heterogeneity values.

Numbers needed to treat to harm translating the risks into absolute terms per 100,000 patients: 170 excess myocardial infarctions, 649 excess heart failure cases, and 431 excess deaths, followed by the start of the conclusion.

Final conclusion of the abstract: rosiglitazone use in type 2 diabetes is associated with significantly higher odds of heart failure, myocardial infarction, and death than pioglitazone in real-world settings.
Introduction to the study of Phyllanthus emblica (Indian gooseberry) aqueous extract, stating the four anticancer tests planned: cell lines, apoptosis, mouse skin tumourigenesis, and invasiveness.
Results on cytotoxicity: PE extract at 50-100 µg/mL inhibits growth of six human cancer cell lines (A549, HepG2, HeLa, MDA-MB-231, SK-OV3, SW620) but is not toxic to normal MRC5 lung fibroblasts.

Mechanistic and in vivo findings: in HeLa cells PE induces DNA fragmentation, caspase-3/7 and caspase-8 activation (not caspase-9) and Fas upregulation, suggesting death receptor-mediated apoptosis; topical PE reduced DMBA/TPA-induced mouse skin tumour numbers and volumes by over 50%.

Invasion results and conclusion: 25 and 50 µg/mL PE inhibits MDA-MB-231 invasiveness in a Matrigel assay, and the authors conclude P. emblica has anticancer activity and merits study as a chemopreventive and antiinvasive agent.
Closing copyright notice (2010, John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.) ending the abstract of the P. emblica antitumour study.
Introduction to amla (Emblica officinalis / Phyllanthus emblica), the Indian gooseberry, a key Ayurvedic medicinal plant, and the traditional uses of its fruit.
Traditional Ayurvedic uses of amla fruit (for colds, fever, digestion, ulcers, hair, and as a diuretic/laxative/liver tonic) and the start of the preclinical pharmacological findings.

Preclinical evidence listing amla's therapeutic properties (antipyretic, cardioprotective, hepatoprotective, neuroprotective, etc.), and the transition to experimental studies on antineoplastic effects.

Experimental evidence that amla and its phytochemicals (gallic acid, ellagic acid, corilagin, geraniin, prodelphinidins, etc.) have antineoplastic effects, plus its radiomodulatory, chemopreventive, antioxidant and immunomodulatory activities relevant to cancer.
The review's stated purpose: summarizing for the first time amla's anticancer-related properties and identifying research needed to establish it as a cancer preventive and therapeutic agent.
Concluding statement that further human research is needed to establish amla's utility as a cancer preventive and therapeutic drug.

Introduction to the study: background on oxidative damage and aging, and the anti-aging potential of açai (Euterpe oleracea) pulp, which had not been studied at the whole-organism level before this Drosophila lifespan experiment.

Methods and main lifespan result: 2% açai pulp supplementation in food extended lifespan of female Drosophila melanogaster fed a high fat diet, and the study began measuring transcript changes in age-related genes.

Gene expression findings: açai mostly left transcript levels of tested age-related genes unchanged, but raised l(2)efl, gstD1 and mtnA (stress-response and detoxification genes) and lowered Pepck, the gluconeogenesis gene.

Oxidative stress and conclusion: açai extended lifespan of females with sod1 RNAi-induced oxidative stress, leading the authors to propose that açai counters the high-fat diet effect via stress response activation and suppression of Pepck.
Concluding statement: açai may counteract the harmful effects of dietary fat and reduce oxidative stress during aging, closing the abstract.
Opening chunk of the abstract for a rat study on biogenic amines, introducing the acute oral and intravenous toxicity results for tyramine, spermidine, spermine, putrescine and cadaverine.
Continues the abstract with the intravenous blood pressure effects of the amines and describes the design of the 6-week dietary studies, including dose levels for each amine in male and female rats.
Summarises the 6-week dietary study design and the finding that spermine was the most toxic amine, followed by clinical signs at the high dose such as emaciation, convulsions and hind-leg paralysis.

Describes high-dose toxic effects from the 6-week studies: reduced growth, food and water intake, slight male anaemia, plasma chemistry changes, and organ weight changes in thyroid, adrenals, spleen, heart and liver.
Details spermine-specific kidney toxicity and histopathology findings, including liver glycogen loss, reduced spermatogenesis, splenic and thymic changes, and myocardial degeneration.

Covers adverse effects in top-dose groups of the other amines, decreased body weight with reduced food intake, and haematological changes (raised packed cell volume, haemoglobin and thrombocytes) with cadaverine.
Reports clinical chemistry changes for spermidine and cadaverine and the no-observed-adverse-effect levels (NOAELs) in ppm and mg/kg/day for each amine.
Final sentence giving the spermidine and spermine NOAEL values (1000 ppm/83 mg/kg/day and 200 ppm/19 mg/kg/day), closing the abstract's toxicity summary.

Introduces the study's topic: biogenic amines formed by bacterial decarboxylation in foods, and the sample set (23 Korean Doenjang soybean paste samples) and extraction/derivatization method (perchloric acid, dansyl chloride).

Describes the analytical method (HPLC with gradient elution and UV detection at 254 nm, nine amines separated) and reports the sample pH range of 4.8 to 6.0, linking amine formation to decarboxylase activity in acidic conditions.

Reports the mean concentrations (mg%) of the nine biogenic amines measured across the 23 Doenjang samples, including tryptamine, putrescine, cadaverine, histamine, tyramine, spermidine and spermine, with spermine and tyramine highest.
Concludes that the findings improve food safety for Doenjang and other salted or fermented foods, followed by the copyright notice for the publication.
Introduction and study aim from a Swedish case-control study on indoor volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and allergic disease risk in pre-school children, including the research gap and objectives.

Methods and early results: the case-control design (198 cases with asthma/allergy, 202 controls), bedroom air sampling for eight VOC classes, and the start of the key finding on propylene glycol and glycol ethers (PGEs).
Main results: per natural-log unit of bedroom PGE concentration, adjusted odds ratios for being a case, asthma, rhinitis, and eczema, with 95% confidence intervals.

Adjustment covariates for the PGE-allergy associations (gender, secondhand smoke, parental allergies, chemical wet cleaning, building age, limonene, pet allergens, phthalates BBzP and DEHP), plus the start of the case-only IgE-sensitization analysis.
Case-only IgE-sensitization result (1.8-fold likelihood), null findings for other VOC classes, and the beginning of the conclusion proposing PGEs as a driver of allergic outcomes.
Final conclusion: the proposed hypothesis that indoor PGEs exacerbate or induce asthma, rhinitis, eczema, and IgE sensitization.

Abstract opening of a study on Polish children: motivates the rising popularity of vegetarian diets and allergy prevalence, and states the aim of examining serum lipid profiles in vegetarian children versus children with atopic disease.

Study design and methods: describes the serum lipid and fatty acid measurements (triglycerides, total, LDL and HDL cholesterol, fatty acids) and the three child groups, healthy vegetarians (n=24), children with atopic disease (n=16), and healthy omnivore controls (n=18).
Diet classification method and main results: diet was classified by questionnaire, and no group differences were found in triglycerides, LDL cholesterol, or saturated and monounsaturated fatty acids.

Results on fatty acids in vegetarian children: high intake of monounsaturated-rich vegetable oils and sunflower oil correlated with higher serum linoleic acid, and linoleic acid (n-6 PUFA) was significantly lower in the allergy group than in vegetarians (P<0.05).

Key finding on eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA, n-3) and conclusion setup: the allergy group had higher EPA than vegetarians, and the section introduces the conclusion that higher linoleic acid in vegetarians suggests a different lipid metabolism pathway.
Final conclusion: higher serum linoleic acid in vegetarian children suggests an alternative lipid metabolism pathway, and some vegetarian diet elements may protect against allergy.

Introduction and study aim: a prospective Japanese cohort (Osaka Maternal and Child Health study) examining maternal pregnancy diet, including fatty acids and selected high-fat foods, and risk of suspected atopic eczema in infants aged 3-4 months.

Study population and methods: 771 mother-child pairs; maternal diet during pregnancy assessed with a validated self-administered diet history questionnaire; suspected atopic eczema defined from maternal postpartum questionnaire at 3-4 months.

Main result: suspected atopic eczema prevalence was 8.4% (n=65); higher maternal meat intake was associated with increased risk, with multivariate OR 2.59 for highest vs lowest quartile (95% CI 1.15-6.17, p for trend 0.01).
Sensitivity analysis: restricting the outcome to physician-diagnosed atopic eczema (n=35) strengthened the meat association (OR 3.53, 95% CI 1.19-12.23, p for trend 0.02).

Null findings: no material exposure-response relationships for maternal intake of eggs, dairy, fish, total fat, various saturated, monounsaturated, n-3 and n-6 fatty acids (including EPA, DHA, ALA, linoleic and arachidonic acid), cholesterol, or the n-3 to n-6 ratio.
Conclusion: higher maternal meat intake may increase infantile atopic eczema risk, while no protective effect was found for maternal fish intake or n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids.
Publication attribution: copyright notice (2009, John Wiley & Sons A/S) closing the abstract, marking the end of the document.

Introduces the review's central hypothesis that advanced glycation end products (AGEs) and their precursors play a role in Alzheimer's disease, framing AD as converging on final inflammation and neurodegeneration pathways.

States that AGEs and methylglyoxal act as both biomarkers and causative 'gerontotoxins' in AD; notes AGEs accumulate with normal aging but faster in AD, where they appear in amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles.

Explains how AGE modification may account for AD neuropathology such as protein cross-linking, inflammation, oxidative stress and neuronal death, and proposes methylglyoxal as a major carbonyl species forming AGEs.
Proposes lowering methylglyoxal levels as a therapeutic strategy to prevent AGE formation, via reducing precursors like d-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate through the pentose phosphate pathway.
Concludes with additional strategies for reducing methylglyoxal: boosting glyoxalase system detoxification or using carbonyl scavengers, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction of the dAGE study: background on heat-processed modern diets, dietary AGEs, and their links to oxidant stress, inflammation, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, plus an overview of the report's aims.

Summary of the report's main aims and findings: expanding the dAGE database, validating testing methods, comparing cooking methods and inhibitors, and the finding that dry heat raises new dAGE formation more than 10- to 100-fold over raw food.

Food-category findings: animal-derived foods high in fat and protein are AGE-rich and form AGEs readily when cooked, whereas carbohydrate-rich foods like vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and milk stay low in AGEs even after cooking.

Strategies for reducing new dAGE formation during cooking: aminoguanidine blocks formation, and moist heat, shorter cook times, lower temperatures, and acidic ingredients such as lemon juice or vinegar significantly reduce it.
Conclusion: the new dAGE database is a useful tool for estimating dietary AGE intake and guiding food choices to lower it.

Introduction and methods of an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) risk-factor study: background on AAA mortality and screening limits, then data source (3.1M-patient retrospective cohort screened by ultrasound, 2003–2008).
Methods and early results of the AAA risk-factor study: multivariable logistic regression, followed by findings on smoking (duration, cigarettes per day, and cessation) as risk factors for AAA.

Results on additional AAA risk factors: excess weight increases risk, exercise and diets rich in nuts, vegetables, and fruits reduce it, racial/ethnic differences are noted, and established risk factors (male sex, age, family history, cardiovascular disease) are confirmed.
Development of a new AAA predictive scoring system that outperforms current criteria by including women, nonsmokers, and those under 65, followed by a national estimate of 1.1 million US AAA cases.

Conclusions of the AAA study: smoking cessation and healthy lifestyle lower AAA risk, about half of AAA patients are ineligible for current screening guidelines, and the new high-yield screening algorithm (with 569,000 estimated cases among women, nonsmokers, and under-65s) expands the screening population.
Final sentence of the AAA study's conclusions, summarizing the high-yield screening algorithm that broadens screening to at-risk individuals missed by existing criteria.
Introduction to an IOM review on Tolerable Upper Intake Levels (ULs), explaining their use in estimating population risk and why ULs were not set for trans fat, saturated fat, and cholesterol.

Explains the review's purpose: evaluating clinical trial and prospective observational data not previously used to set a UL, to test whether the current UL model fits saturated fat, trans fat, and cholesterol.
Conclusion of the review: the risk assessment model cannot set a UL for components like cholesterol that lack an intake threshold for chronic disease risk; includes the 2011 ILSI copyright notice.
Closing copyright line (2011 International Life Sciences Institute) ending the document's summary of the UL model's limitations.
Introduction framing the study question: whether statin-associated cardiovascular risk reduction can offset the risk increase from excess dietary fat, a comparison never previously made directly.

Study design: investigators compare fast-food total and trans fat-related cardiovascular risk increase against daily statin risk reduction drawn from a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (42,848 patients) in primary prevention of coronary artery disease.
Key finding: most statins (except pravastatin) reduce risk more than the daily extra fat from a Quarter Pounder with cheese and a small milkshake increases it.

Conclusion that statin therapy can neutralize harmful diet choices, followed by analogy to other risky activities (motorcycling, smoking, driving) where risk-minimizing measures like safety equipment and seatbelts are used.
Proposal that routine statin availability in fast-food outlets could be a rational means to offset cardiovascular risk, paralleling the free condiments these outlets already provide.

Argument that free statin accompaniments would counter the harm of freely available salt, sugar, and high-fat condiments, with a caveat that statins do not replace lifestyle changes such as diet, exercise, weight loss, and smoking cessation.
Closing line: complimentary statin packets would add one positive choice, at low cost, among many negative ones.

Opening passage on coronary atherosclerosis: symptoms of myocardial ischemia require large plaque buildup, nearly half of US adults reach that quantity, and the condition is rarely hereditary, mainly caused by excess fat, cholesterol, and calories.
Explains that diet-driven elevated serum total cholesterol (above 150 mg/dl) drives plaque deposition in arteries, with plaque quantity rising the further cholesterol exceeds 150 mg/dl.
Describes how keeping serum cholesterol at or below 150 mg/dl prevents plaque formation and can shrink existing plaque, noting a fruit-vegetarian-starch diet usually achieves this in most adults.

States that lipid-lowering drugs are needed for familial hypercholesterolemia and most patients with atherosclerotic events, and concludes that atherosclerosis is preventable in non-hereditary cases and arrestable by lowering total and LDL cholesterol to 150 mg/dl.
Final fragment completing the instruction to lower serum cholesterol to the 150 mg/dl level to arrest atherosclerosis.

Introduction and objectives of a GWTG study on intensive lipid-lowering therapy (statins) at discharge in patients hospitalized with acute coronary syndrome, including background on the benefit of early intensive statin therapy.

Methods describing the analysis of the Get With The Guidelines (GWTG) database of ACS hospitalizations from 2005-2009, defining intensive LLT (statin dose or combination likely to lower LDL >50%) versus less intensive LLT at discharge.

Results showing that only 38.3% of patients were discharged on intensive LLT, with higher cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides in the intensive-therapy group, and that even among patients with LDL >130 mg/dL, half or fewer received it.

Results on predictors of discharge LLT (prior LLT, hyperlipidemia, prior CAD, higher BMI, in-hospital PCI) and temporal trends: modest improvement 2005-2007 followed by a decline in 2008-2009 driven by reduced ezetimibe-statin combination use.
Conclusions that most eligible ACS patients were not discharged on lipid-lowering therapy, indicating a need for better implementation of guideline-recommended intensive statin therapy in ACS.
Closing conclusion sentence calling for better guideline-based intensive statin use in ACS patients, followed by the publisher attribution (Mosby, Inc.).

Background section of a Cochrane review on topical saline for chronic rhinosinusitis, describing the historical yogic/homeopathic origins of nasal irrigation, its growing use as an adjunct, typical dosing frequency, and the patient burden and unclear added benefit.

Continuation of the background, followed by the review's stated objective (evaluating effectiveness and safety of topical saline for chronic rhinosinusitis) and the beginning of the search strategy description.

Search strategy of the Cochrane review on saline for chronic rhinosinusitis, listing the databases searched (Cochrane ENT register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE) with coverage dates and a last-search date of November 2006, plus the start of the selection criteria.

Selection criteria and data collection methods: included randomised controlled trials comparing saline against no treatment, placebo, adjunct therapy, or other treatments, and hypertonic versus isotonic solutions; trial quality was graded using the Cochrane approach, and only certain scores were pooled.

Data analysis and main results of the saline for chronic rhinosinusitis review: pooling limited to specific symptom and radiological scores, a narrative summary of the rest, and the count of eight included trials with their comparator breakdown.

Main results detailing the eight included trials by comparator (no treatment, placebo, adjunct, intranasal steroid spray, and hypertonic vs isotonic saline) and the initial finding that saline helps chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms as sole treatment.

Key findings of the review: saline benefits symptoms as sole therapy and as an adjunct, shows no superiority over a reflexology placebo, is less effective than intranasal steroids, and hypertonic solutions improve objective measures with unclear symptom impact.

Authors' conclusions from the saline irrigation review: irrigations are well tolerated with common minor side effects that are outweighed by benefits for most patients, supporting topical saline as a treatment adjunct for chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms.
Final sentence of the authors' conclusion, recommending that topical saline could be included as an adjunctive treatment for chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms.

Introduces rhinosinusitis subtypes and the bacterial vs. viral classification of acute rhinosinusitis, noting most cases are viral (common cold), and begins describing symptomatic treatment for nonsevere cases.

Covers symptomatic treatment (analgesics, decongestants, saline irrigation) for mild cases and the indication for narrow-spectrum antibiotics (amoxicillin, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole) when symptoms persist beyond seven days or worsen.
Addresses antibiotic timing criteria, the limited evidence for intranasal corticosteroids, and advises against radiographic imaging for uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis.

Discusses when CT sinus imaging is appropriate (anatomic abnormalities, suspected complications of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis) and lists rare complications: orbital, intracranial, and bony involvement.
Gives the referral criterion: referral to an otolaryngologist if symptoms persist or progress after maximal medical therapy and CT shows sinus disease.

Study aims and design for a prospective observational study of nasal irrigation bottle contamination in recalcitrant chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) patients, including secondary goals on biofilms and sterilization methods.

Methods: 11 recalcitrant CRS patients already using nasal irrigation were sampled every 2 weeks over 6 weeks, with cultures taken from the bottle and middle meatus and a new bottle issued at each visit.

Methods continued: SEM biofilm analysis on six patients' bottles, and lab tests inoculating new bottles with Staphylococcus aureus strains, cleaning them by different methods, and culturing immediately and at 48 hours.
Results: 42 of 43 bottles (97%) showed bacterial growth, 51% of patients had concurrent sinonasal and bottle S. aureus infection, and biofilms were found on four of six bottles tested.

Results and conclusions: Milton's solution and microwaving effectively sterilized bottles both immediately and at 48 hours; patients commonly contaminate irrigation bottles, mostly with S. aureus in biofilm form.
Final conclusion: simple cleaning methods could reduce irrigation bottle contamination, closing the abstract's summary of the study's clinical implications.

Introduces the vitamin D deficiency problem (non-response to high-dose ergo/cholecalciferol) and the study's aim: testing whether taking vitamin D with the largest daily meal boosts 25(OH)D levels. Describes it as a prospective cohort study at the Cleveland Clinic Bone Clinic.

Describes the study design and population: a prospective cohort at an ambulatory tertiary-care center (Cleveland Clinic Foundation Bone Clinic) enrolling non-responding vitamin D-deficient patients, who were told to take their usual supplement with their largest meal.

Reports the main outcome measure (serum 25(OH)D after 2 to 3 months) and the demographics of the 17 analyzed patients: mean age about 64.5 years, 13 females and 4 males, with doses from 1000 to 50,000 IU daily and a baseline mean of 30.5 ng/mL.
Presents the key results: mean 25(OH)D rose from 30.5 to 47.2 ng/mL (p < .01), an average 56.7% increase, with a subgroup analysis by weekly vitamin D dose showing a similar trend.

Gives the study's conclusion: taking vitamin D with the largest meal improves absorption and yields roughly a 50% rise in 25(OH)D, with similar gains across a wide range of doses and medical conditions.
Contains only the closing copyright notice (2010, American Society for Bone and Mineral Research) that ends the abstract.

Background and methods of a community-based descriptive study on vitamin D: states the cancer-risk-associated intake range (1,100-4,000 IU/d) and serum 25(OH)D target (60-80 ng/ml), notes the gap in dose-response data above 1,000 IU/d, and introduces the cohort (n = 3,667, mean age 51.3 y).

Results section of the vitamin D dose-response study: serum 25(OH)D rises curvilinearly with self-reported supplement intake, and doses of 10,000 IU/d or lower do not push levels above the 200 ng/ml toxicity threshold.

Key quantitative findings and conclusion of the vitamin D study: unsupplemented all-source intake estimated at 3,300 IU/d, a 9,600 IU/d supplement dose gives 97.5% of the population at least 40 ng/ml, and the conclusion that intake up to 40,000 IU/day is unlikely to cause toxicity.

Concluding sentence of the vitamin D cohort study: the 9,600 IU/d dose reaching 40 ng/ml in 97.5% of participants supports the conclusion that universal vitamin D intake up to 40,000 IU per day is unlikely to cause toxicity.

Introduces how vitamin D is produced (cutaneous UVB synthesis or oral D2/D3 intake) and states that 25(OH)D serum measurement is the best way to assess vitamin D status, setting up the definition of low status.

Defines optimal 25(OH)D as about 30-32 ng/ml or higher, estimates that roughly three quarters of US adults fall below this, and notes the classic skeletal consequences (osteomalacia/rickets) of low status.
Covers newer evidence linking low vitamin D status to non-skeletal disease risk, with causality still unresolved, and gives the intake needed for optimal status (at least 1000 IU daily).

Explains that high intakes carry low toxicity risk, notes large individual variation in response to the same dose, and observes that timing of 25(OH)D monitoring is under-studied, with D3 possibly preferred over D2.
Final sentence concluding that D3 supplementation may be preferable to D2, closing the document's discussion of supplementation.

Introduction and study aim: frames vitamin D deficiency as possibly linked to chronic diseases (cardiovascular disease, cancer) and states the goal of measuring its prevalence and correlates in US adults, particularly minority groups, using NHANES 2005-2006.

Methods and key prevalence results: describes NHANES 2005-2006 data (N=4495 adults), defines deficiency as serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D ≤20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L), and begins reporting an overall deficiency rate of 41.6% with highest rates in blacks (82.1%).

Results on bivariate correlates: Hispanics had 69.2% deficiency; deficiency was significantly more common among people without college education, obese individuals, those with poor health, hypertension, low HDL cholesterol, or who did not drink milk daily (all P<.001).

Multivariate findings and summary: non-white race, lack of college education, obesity, low HDL cholesterol, poor health, and no daily milk intake were independently associated with deficiency (P<.05); concludes deficiency is common, especially among blacks and Hispanics.

Discussion and clinical implications: notes vitamin D deficiency links to risk factors for leading US causes of death, and urges health professionals to recognize this and provide dietary and other interventions, especially for minority groups.
Copyright notice: Elsevier Inc. 2011 copyright statement closing the abstract.

Opening chunk of a document on vitamin D and extraskeletal health: introduces vitamin D deficiency as the most common nutritional deficiency and argues that recommended intakes are 5- to 10-fold too low.

Middle chunk of the vitamin D extraskeletal health document: states the target 25(OH)D blood level above 30 ng/mL, that at least 1000 IU/day is needed for adults to reach it, and that increasing vitamin D intake carries no general downside for children or adults.
Final chunk of the vitamin D extraskeletal health document: concludes that increasing vitamin D intake in children or adults is generally safe, followed by the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction to a study on cranberry juice processing, stating the research gap on polyphenol changes and the aims: testing three pretreatments (grinding plus blanching, grinding only, blanching only) on anthocyanins, flavonols, and procyanidins.

Key findings on polyphenol retention: flavonols and procyanidins are retained better than anthocyanins, pressing causes the largest losses by removing seeds and skins, and heat treatment forms flavonol aglycones.

Findings on pomace drying and overall stability: drying increases extraction of flavonols and procyanidin oligomers but reduces polymeric procyanidin extraction, and cranberry polyphenols are relatively stable compared to other berries.
Concluding statement noting that, although cranberry polyphenolics are fairly stable during processing, further research is needed on their fate during juice storage.

Introduces the randomized, double-blind trial design on pomegranate juice and carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) progression, describing the eligible population (men 45-74, women 55-74, moderate coronary heart disease risk, baseline posterior wall CIMT 0.7-2.0 mm).

Describes the intervention and sample: 240 ml/day pomegranate juice (n=146) vs. control beverage (n=143) for up to 18 months, and reports the primary result of no significant difference in overall CIMT progression between groups.

Reports exploratory subgroup findings: among participants in the most adverse tertiles for lipid peroxides, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, TG/HDL and total cholesterol/HDL ratios, and apolipoprotein B-100, the pomegranate juice group showed less anterior wall and/or composite CIMT progression than controls.

States the study conclusion: pomegranate juice had no overall effect on CIMT progression at moderate coronary heart disease risk but may have slowed progression in people with increased oxidative stress and TG-rich lipoprotein/HDL disturbances.
Final sentence completing the conclusion, naming the TG-rich lipoprotein/HDL axis as the metabolic profile where pomegranate juice may have slowed carotid intima-media thickness progression.

Introduces the preclinical background on apple juice's neuroprotective and cognitive benefits, then the open-label trial design: 21 institutionalized patients with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease drinking apple juice daily.
Reports the trial's main cognitive and functional results: no change on the Dementia Rating Scale or ADCS-ADL over the one-month study, which contrasts with the later behavioral findings.

Reports the key finding of a roughly 27% (P < .01) improvement in dementia-related behavioral and psychotic symptoms on the Neuropsychiatric Inventory, especially anxiety, agitation, and delusion, and concludes that apple juice may be a useful adjunct supplement.
Concludes the pilot study by suggesting apple juice could augment pharmacological treatment to attenuate mood decline in AD progression and possibly reduce caregiver burden.

Introduces the prospective cohort study of fruit and vegetable intake and cognitive decline in aging women, covering follow-up design, food frequency questionnaires, and the telephone-administered cognitive test battery (1995-2001).

Describes the cognitive reassessment design (13,388 women, over 90% follow-up two years later), the averaging of 1984-onward dietary intake, and the use of multivariable-adjusted linear regression to estimate performance and decline differences across intake levels.

States the main findings: fruit intake showed no association with cognition, while total vegetable intake was linked to slower decline, with the highest cruciferous vegetable quintile declining more slowly on the global cognitive score (0.04 unit, CI 0.003-0.07).

Reports the green leafy vegetable result: the highest intake quintile showed slower cognitive decline than the lowest (0.05 unit, CI 0.02-0.09, p trend < 0.001), with the effect sizes compared against age differences of women.
Concludes that the observed mean differences in cognitive decline were comparable in magnitude to the difference associated with women being roughly 1 to 2 years apart in age.

Abstract opening of a Swedish Twin Registry study (HARMONY) on midlife fruit and vegetable intake and later-life dementia and Alzheimer's disease risk; introduces the objective and describes the sample of 3,779 participants who completed a diet questionnaire about 30 years before cognitive evaluation.

Methods continuation from the Swedish twin dementia study: reports 355 dementia cases, 81 discordant twin pairs (50 discordant for AD), and the analytic approach using GEE logistic regression for twin relatedness and conditional logistic regression for the co-twin control design.

Results section of the midlife fruit/vegetable and dementia twin study: medium or great fruit and vegetable intake versus none or small is linked to lower dementia and AD risk in fully adjusted models, with the effect seen among women and people with angina.

Remaining results and conclusion of the Swedish twin study on fruit and vegetable intake and dementia: co-twin control odds ratios were similar but non-significant, and the authors conclude higher midlife intake may reduce dementia risk, especially in women and those with angina pectoris.

Final fragment of the conclusion of the Swedish twin study, completing the statement that midlife fruit and vegetable consumption may reduce dementia risk, particularly among people with angina pectoris.
Introduction and study aim: a cross-sectional Hordaland Health Study examining plant food intake (fruits, vegetables) and cognitive performance in 2,031 Norwegian elderly aged 70-74.

Study population and methods: extensive cognitive test battery (Kendrick, Trail Making A, Digit Symbol, Block Design, MMSE, COWAT) plus a comprehensive validated self-reported FFQ in elderly Western Norwegians.

Main findings on group differences: subjects consuming above the 10th percentile of fruits, vegetables, grains and mushrooms performed significantly better on cognitive tests than those with very low or no intake.

Dose-response results: strongest link is for combined fruit and vegetable intake, dose-dependent up to about 500 g/day; grains and potatoes plateau at roughly 100-150 g/day, while mushrooms show a linear association.

Specific foods and conclusion: carrots, cruciferous vegetables, citrus fruits and high-fibre bread show the strongest positive cognitive associations, white bread is the only negative one, and the overall conclusion is that plant-rich diets relate to better cognition in a dose-dependent way.
Concluding summary: a diet rich in plant foods is associated with better performance across several cognitive abilities in older adults in a dose-dependent manner.

Opening of an abstract on phenolic compounds in 13 commercial UK fruit juices: introduces the Folin-Ciocalteu total phenolic assay and HPLC-PDA-MS2 compound identification, and begins the result on purple grape juice.

Results section of the phenolic juice study: purple grape juice has the most phenolic compounds and highest total phenolics, with flavan-3-ols, anthocyanins, and hydroxycinnamates making up 93%; white grape juice has the lowest total phenolics.

Antioxidant findings of the juice study: ORAC and FRAP assay results agree with total phenol content, and it introduces the Kame project's evidence linking long-term juice intake to reduced Alzheimer's risk.

Concluding recommendation of the juice phenolics study: combining diverse, phenolic-rich juices may enhance the protective effects against Alzheimer's, citing Dai et al. 2006, and naming purple grape, grapefruit, cranberry, and apple juices.

Final sentence of the abstract, completing the list of juices (purple grape, grapefruit, cranberry, apple) recommended for their diverse phenolic content in the juice-based Alzheimer's protection suggestion.
