Opening of the abstract for a study on a polyphenol-rich juice drink: its HPLC/PDA/fluorescence/MS characterization of 40 flavonoids and phenolics, listing green tea flavan-3-ols and other main constituents.

Continuation of the abstract listing the juice's main constituents (EGC, phloretin glucoside, gallic acid, hesperetin rutinoside, caffeoylquinic acid, procyanidins, trace flavonols and anthocyanins), then the human study: 10 subjects drinking 350 mL with plasma and urine sampled over 0-24 h.

Abstract results section: HPLC-MS identified 13 plasma and 20 urine metabolites after juice consumption, and glucuronide, sulfated, and methylated metabolite profiles matched earlier feeding studies with the juice's individual components.

Final sentence of the abstract naming the earlier comparison feeding studies (coffee, green tea, orange juice, apple cider) whose metabolite profiles resembled those from the polyphenol-rich juice drink.
Introduction to the study: flavanols in cocoa, their vascular and antioxidant benefits, and the aim of using BOLD fMRI to examine flavanol effects on the human brain.
Methods and main fMRI finding: 16 healthy young subjects performed a cognitive task during BOLD fMRI, and the signal increased after 5 days of 150 mg cocoa flavanols.

Interpretation and null behavioral results: the BOLD increase may reflect altered neuronal activity, vascular responsiveness, or both, while reaction times, switch cost, and heart rate were unaffected by the moderate dose.
Pilot study on cerebral blood flow: a single acute 450 mg flavanol dose increased gray matter cerebral blood flow, pointing to a possible role in vascular impairment.
Concluding implications: cocoa flavanols may help treat vascular impairment such as dementia and stroke and support cardiovascular health.

Introduction/abstract opening: motivation that flavonoid neuroprotection mechanisms are unclear due to unknown CNS entry, and the study's aim to measure naringenin and quercetin BBB permeability via in vitro (ECV304/C6) and in situ rat models.

Results on permeability: in vitro P(app) measurable and tied to lipophilicity; in situ uptake rates (K(in)) into the right cerebral hemisphere, naringenin 0.145 vs quercetin 0.019 ml/min/g, with quercetin comparable to the P-gp substrate colchicine (0.006).
Efflux transporter effects in vivo: PSC833 or GF120918 (10 mg/kg) raised colchicine K(in), but only GF120918 (also a BCRP inhibitor) altered quercetin K(in), while naringenin K(in) was unaffected.

Cell-based efflux study setup: MDCK-MDR1 and RBE4 cells used to test transporter influence; colchicine, quercetin, and naringenin all showed measurable distribution volume (Vd) accumulation in both cell types.
Cell-based inhibitor results: PSC833 or GF120918 (25 microM) significantly raised colchicine Vd in both cell lines and naringenin Vd, whereas only GF120918 significantly increased quercetin Vd.
Conclusion: flavonoids can traverse the BBB in vivo, but their permeability is shaped by lipophilicity and interactions with efflux transporters such as P-gp and BCRP.

Introduction of an study on apple juice concentrate protecting neuronal cells against amyloid-beta toxicity via oxidative stress, covering oxidative stress in aging and Alzheimer's disease and the rationale for testing apple juice.
Experimental setup: SH-SY5Y human neuroblastoma cells differentiated with retinoic acid for 7 days, treated with 20 microM amyloid-beta alongside diluted 70 degree brix apple juice concentrate (AJC).
Key results: AJC blocked Abeta-induced reactive oxygen species generation, calcium influx, and apoptosis, all partly driven by ROS, in the cultured neuronal cells.
Conclusion: the antioxidant potential of apple products can prevent amyloid-beta-induced oxidative damage in neuronal cells.

Abstract opening: introduces β-amyloid's role in Alzheimer's disease senile plaques and its neurotoxicity via oxidative/nitrosative stress, and states the study's aim of testing [6]-gingerol from ginger against Aβ(25-35)-induced cell death in SH-SY5Y cells.

Abstract results on cytoprotection: [6]-gingerol pretreatment protects SH-SY5Y cells from Aβ(25-35)-induced cytotoxicity and apoptosis, including DNA fragmentation, mitochondrial membrane potential loss, elevated Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, and caspase-3 activation.

Abstract mechanistic results: [6]-gingerol suppresses Aβ(25-35)-induced intracellular reactive oxygen/nitrogen species accumulation and restores depleted glutathione, examining the cellular antioxidant defense system.

Abstract antioxidant enzyme findings: [6]-gingerol upregulates mRNA and protein levels of GCL (γ-glutamylcysteine ligase, rate-limiting in glutathione synthesis) and HO-1 (heme oxygenase-1, heme degradation).

Abstract mechanism and conclusion: antioxidant enzyme induction is mediated via Nrf2 activation, suggesting [6]-gingerol has preventive/therapeutic potential for Alzheimer's disease by boosting antioxidant capacity; includes the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
Trailing fragment of the abstract's final sentence ('capacity') plus the 2011 Elsevier copyright statement; contains no substantive content beyond the conclusion and rights notice.
Introduction and methods of a study on MRSA contamination of retail meat: aims, sampling of pork, ground beef and chicken from Canadian retail outlets, and the testing approach.
Prevalence results of MRSA in retail meat by type (pork 9.6%, beef 5.6%, chicken 1.2%, P=0.0002) and contamination levels, with 37% below quantification threshold and mostly <100 CFU/g.
Molecular typing results: all MRSA isolates were Canadian epidemic MRSA-2 (CMRSA-2) by PFGE with two subtypes, spa type t242, plus the conclusion that meat contamination is not uncommon.

Discussion of significance: CMRSA-2 (a human epidemic clone) found in Canadian pigs, surprising absence of livestock-associated ST398, and the unclear relevance of meat contamination for food-handling exposure.
Concluding statement that the findings suggest human or animal sources of meat contamination, so those sources warrant investigation.
Introduction to the November 2009 Midwest Rural Agricultural Safety and Health Forum (MRASH) in Johnston, Iowa, where plenary talks on MRSA research on U.S. swine farms were presented.

Summary of the four plenary talks on MRSA on swine farms: prevalence on farms in swine and human workers, MRSA in air samples and barn shower facilities, and methicillin-resistant and -sensitive S. aureus in retail meats.
Concluding statement that these MRSA findings from swine farm research help define the broader picture of livestock-associated MRSA in the Midwestern United States.

Case report on xylitol-coated homeopathic globules causing chronic metabolic hyperchloremic acidosis in an infant via diarrhea-related bicarbonate loss and weight loss; this chunk opens the document's core finding that xylitol's effects go beyond laxation.

Continuation of the case report's key claim: overdosed xylitol-coated homeopathic globules in an infant can cause considerable weight loss and life-threatening enteral bicarbonate loss through diarrhea, concluding the document's main point.

Introduction of the document on non-typhoidal salmonellosis, stating two epidemiological changes in the late 20th century: multidrug-resistant S. typhimurium spreading in food animals, and S. enteritidis emerging as an egg-associated pathogen, and previewing a review of the origins of human epidemics.

Concluding sentence of the abstract-style introduction on non-typhoidal salmonellosis, noting that the article reviews available data on the origins of human epidemics caused by Salmonella enteritidis and multidrug-resistant S. typhimurium, linked to egg and food-animal sources.

Study objectives and setting: evaluates knowledge and practices of public-sector primary-care health professionals and final-year students on nutrition, physical activity and smoking cessation (lifestyle modification) in managing lifestyle-related chronic diseases in South Africa's public health sector.

Study design and sampling: comparative cross-sectional descriptive quantitative study across thirty primary health-care facilities and four tertiary institutions in Cape Town, Western Cape; health facilities selected by stratified random sampling by geographic location, students by convenience sampling.

Data collection and key result: a validated self-administered knowledge test was given to health professionals; results show differential lifestyle modification knowledge among professionals and students, with under 10% reaching the 80% benchmark score.

Main findings on practice and knowledge gaps: most health professionals promote lifestyle modification theoretically but struggle to give practical patient advice; doctors showed the best lifestyle modification knowledge among the health professionals evaluated.

Barriers and recommendations: lack of time, poor patient adherence and language barriers hinder lifestyle counselling; conclusion calls for undergraduate medical and nursing curricula to include practical training on diet, physical activity and smoking cessation.
Continuing education recommendation: the study concludes that primary health-care professionals should receive updated lifestyle modification education as part of continuing medical education.

Introduction to a U.S. national survey on nutrition education in medical schools (2008–2009), describing its purpose, the 127 accredited schools targeted, and the online survey method from the UNC Nutrition in Medicine Project.

Continues the survey methodology: data collected August 2008–July 2009 from school contacts, mostly nutrition educators, on required nutrition contact hours and whether instruction was in a dedicated course, another course, or clinical rotations.
Key results opening: 109 of 127 schools (86%) responded, and 103 of 109 required some nutrition education, with the start of the findings on course requirements.

Findings on curriculum structure and hours: only 25% of schools required a dedicated nutrition course (down from 30% in 2004), and students averaged 19.6 nutrition contact hours (range 0–70) versus 22.3 in 2004.

Benchmark compliance and conclusion: only 27% of schools met the National Academy of Sciences' 25-hour minimum (38% in 2004), leading the authors to conclude that medical students' nutrition education remains inadequate.

Opening chunk of a guide on healthy eating for women, summarizing core dietary strategies: favor unsaturated fats, whole grains, quality proteins, fruits and vegetables; limit trans and saturated fats, refined grains, and sugary drinks; and take a multivitamin with folic acid and vitamin D.

Closing chunk of the same healthy eating guide, stating that these principles remain healthy across life stages, from young adulthood through pregnancy planning, pregnancy, and old age, and completing the multivitamin recommendation.
Opening of the document, introducing the 'manufacturing uncertainty' strategy used by polluters and product makers to challenge scientific evidence behind public health and environmental regulation.

Continues the document by listing industries (asbestos, benzene, lead, plastics, etc.) that used manufactured uncertainty to avoid regulation, and notes it is central to the global warming debate and now routinely applied.

Describes how manufacturing uncertainty became a business through consulting firms offering 'product defense' or 'litigation support,' whose real aim is protecting corporations rather than generating public health knowledge.

Introduces the 'funding effect,' the documented correlation between a study funder's desired results and reported results, arguing that sponsors' financial interests should be weighed when evaluating findings.

Extends the funding-effect argument to scientists with financial conflicts and concludes that manufacturing uncertainty contradicts the public health principle of deciding on the best available evidence.
Final fragment of the document, completing the concluding sentence on using the best currently available evidence for public health decisions.
Introduction to the study: high US dietary salt intake, mostly from processed foods, and the modeling approach using the CHD Policy Model to estimate benefits of up to 3 g/day salt reduction.

Study methods and early results: subgroup analyses by age, sex, and race, comparison with other cardiovascular interventions, and cost-effectiveness versus hypertension drug treatment; begins listing projected reductions in CHD cases and strokes.
Projected annual health outcomes from a 3 g/day salt reduction (fewer CHD cases, strokes, MIs, and deaths) and how benefits differ across demographic groups by race, sex, and age.

Comparative benefits and economic impact: cardiovascular benefits rival those of tobacco, obesity, and cholesterol reduction, and a regulatory intervention would yield large QALY gains and healthcare savings.
Cost-effectiveness findings: even a modest 1 g/day gradual reduction over 2010–2019 would be cost-saving and more cost-effective than medication for all hypertensive patients.
Conclusion: modest dietary salt reduction could substantially lower cardiovascular events and medical costs, and should be adopted as a public health target.

Introduces the study's scope: genotoxicity testing of 39 food additives across six categories (dyes, color fixatives/preservatives, preservatives, antioxidants, fungicides, sweeteners) using oral dosing in male ddY mice and the comet assay.

Describes the comet assay design across eight mouse organs at 3 and 24h, and reports the main finding that dyes were the most genotoxic, with seven named dyes causing dose-related DNA damage in the stomach, colon, and/or bladder.

Details the potency of the dyes at low doses (10 or 100 mg/kg) and notes that four dyes damaged colon DNA near acceptable daily intake levels; also begins listing other additives (antioxidants, fungicides) that damaged gastrointestinal DNA.
Lists the antioxidants, fungicides, and sweeteners that induced DNA damage in gastrointestinal organs, and concludes that broader assessment of currently used food additives is needed.
Final sentence of the abstract, calling for more extensive assessment of food additives currently in use.

Introduces the study testing sorbic acid, sodium sorbate, and potassium sorbate for genotoxicity and cell transformation in Syrian hamster embryo (SHE) fibroblasts, noting that sorbic acid, potassium sorbate, and freshly prepared sodium sorbate showed no activity.

Describes the key finding that stored sodium sorbate solution, previously heated and sonicated for solubilization, gave positive genotoxic and cell-transformation results in both SHE assays, unlike freshly prepared solutions.
Concludes that oxidation products of sodium sorbate with genotoxic and cell-transforming properties form under heating, sonication, and storage conditions.

Introduction and methods of a study on whether potassium sorbate is genotoxic to human lymphocytes, listing the assays used (chromosomal aberrations, SCEs, micronucleus, comet) and the control and dose design.

Methods and results describing the controls (sterile water, MMC, H2O2) and the four PS doses (125-1000 µg/ml), with the finding of significantly increased chromosomal aberrations at the two highest doses and SCEs at several doses.
Results continuing with SCE dose-time details, the comet assay showing DNA strand breaks at all concentrations in isolated lymphocytes, and the non-significant micronucleus result.

Results on cell-cycle and proliferation indices (CBPI, RI, MI), which showed no clear cell cycle delay, followed by the start of the authors' conclusion that PS is genotoxic to human peripheral blood lymphocytes.
Concluding sentence of the abstract stating that potassium sorbate is genotoxic to human peripheral blood lymphocytes in vitro, followed by the 2009 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces the study on sorbic acid and its potassium and sodium salts, reporting that sodium sorbate induces chromosome aberrations, SCE, and 6-thioguanine-resistant mutations in cultured Chinese hamster V79 cells.

Quantifies sodium sorbate's potency: clastogenic activity under 1/100 that of MNNG, SCE induction only twice control versus 14-fold for methyl methanesulphonate, and mutagenic potency under 1/10 that of ethyl methanesulphonate at equitoxic doses.
Describes the weaker genotoxicity of sorbic acid and potassium sorbate: chromosome aberrations only at the highest doses, SCE at 1.2 times control, and no 6-thioguanine-resistant mutations induced.

Reports that sodium sorbate's cytogenetic effect is not attributable to osmotic pressure or impurity, and concludes sodium sorbate is a weak genotoxic agent while sorbic acid and potassium sorbate are less genotoxic.
Final conclusion stating that sorbic acid and potassium sorbate are less genotoxic than sodium sorbate, which is weakly genotoxic overall.

Introduces the study design: an 18-participant trial of sodium-bicarbonated mineral water's effect on cardiovascular risk in hypercholesterolemic young adults, with a control low-mineral water period followed by bicarbonated water.

Describes the intervention protocol (1 L/day bicarbonated water with specified sodium, bicarbonate, and chloride concentrations) and the list of measured outcomes and timepoints (end of control period, weeks 4 and 8).

Enumerates the measured variables: anthropometrics, blood pressure, diet, lipid panel (total, LDL, HDL cholesterol, Apo A-I, Apo B, triglycerides), glucose, insulin, adiponectin, hs-CRP, and soluble adhesion molecules sICAM and sVCAM.
Reports null and early findings: diet, weight and BMI were stable, and systolic blood pressure fell significantly by week 4 with no further change by week 8.

Presents the main lipid results: significant reductions in total cholesterol (6.3%), LDL cholesterol (10%), total/HDL and LDL/HDL ratios, and Apo B, while triglycerides, Apo A-I, adhesion molecules and hs-CRP were unchanged.

Covers glucose and insulin results (glucose trended down, P=.056; insulin unchanged) and the study's conclusion that the bicarbonated water improves lipid profile and may support dietary interventions for cardiovascular risk reduction.
Contains only the closing sentence of the conclusion and the copyright notice (Elsevier, 2010), with no new study findings.
Opening of the document: introduces the two heart-attack pandemics of the past 130 years and the beriberi case, where rice processing changes and medical beliefs about germs led to needless deaths.
Continues the beriberi history (refusal to advise rice bran or rice bran tea) and introduces myocardial infarction (MI), which struck Western nations after 1930.
Presents the hypothesis that the MI pandemic stems from post-1920 food processing by the oil seed industry, which introduced three harmful lipid substances, starting with trans-trans linoleic acid.
Explains how trans-trans linoleic acid blocked prostaglandin E1 (protective against MI) and how harmful lactones reduced blood fibrinolytic activity, raising MI risk.
Covers free radical lipid peroxides that make the myocardium vulnerable, and argues the cholesterol theory of MI is false except for familial hypercholesterolemia cases (about 1 in 500).
Concludes by comparing the cholesterol theory of MI to the false germ theory of beriberi, and states that a working knowledge exists to make MI death as rare as beriberi-induced heart attack death.
A fragment consisting of the single word 'k.', the tail end of the final sentence ('...beriberi-induced heart attack'), with no substantive content of its own.
Introduces how amino acid composition of dietary protein, especially higher non-essential amino acid content in vegan proteins like soy, may shift the glucagon/insulin balance toward glucagon.

Explains glucagon's hepatic effects (cAMP-dependent down-regulation of lipogenesis and cholesterol synthesis, up-regulation of LDL receptors and IGFBP-1) and how insulin opposes them, linking to vegan diets' insulin-sensitizing properties.
Concludes the mechanistic argument: vegan proteins and diets should lower serum lipids, promote weight loss, and reduce circulating IGF-I activity, partly via lower essential amino acid intake.
Discusses consequences of reduced IGF-I activity for cancer, inflammation, and childhood growth, and notes observed vegan traits such as low lipids, lean physique, shorter stature, and later puberty.

Reports vegan diet benefits in rheumatoid arthritis and cancer risk, particularly for insulin-resistance-linked cancers (breast, colon) and prostate cancer, and attributes Western cancer epidemics to high IGF-I from animal products.
Adds that phytochemicals may further reduce cancer risk in vegans and cites regression of coronary stenoses from low-fat vegan diets combined with exercise.

Covers additional vegan benefits, including better diabetic control and lower blood pressure, decreased risk of degenerative disorders, and a possible increased hemorrhagic stroke risk from reduced growth factor activity; it also proposes supplementing non-essential amino acids for omnivores.

Proposes that supplementing key non-essential amino acids could let omnivores gain vegan-like advantages, and warns that excess essential amino acid intake may be as serious a risk factor for Western degenerative disease as excess fat.
Final sentence restating the claim that excessive essential amino acid intake may pose a risk for Western degenerative diseases comparable to excessive fat intake.

Opening of a 2001 CHF, Inc. essay arguing that plant-based diets, not the century-old device- and risk-factor-driven approach, should guide treatment and prevention of coronary artery disease; introduces the contrast between high-fat diets causing atherosclerosis and healthier plant-based diets in poorer nations.

Continues the critique of current coronary heart disease treatment, calling the device-driven, risk-factor-oriented strategy a rear-guard defensive approach that still leaves many patients progressively disabled or dying, and introduces the evidence supporting plant-based diets and aggressive lipid lowering as an offensive alternative.

Presents the essay's proposed strategy: nutritional, population, and interventional studies supporting plant-based diets and aggressive lipid lowering to arrest, prevent, and reverse heart disease, and names the key policy step of having US dietary guidelines endorse plant-based eating.
Concludes the essay by calling for an expert committee free of industrial and political influence so US dietary recommendations rest on science, followed by the 2001 CHF, Inc. copyright notice.

Introduces the Cornell China study's design: mortality data for over 50 diseases across rural mainland China counties and villages, plus blood, urine, food, and dietary sampling of adults, with the start of the comparison of rural China diet (lower fat) against the US.

Compares rural Chinese and US diets and health markers: fat and fiber intake, animal protein intake, mean serum total cholesterol (127 vs 203 mg/dL), and coronary artery disease mortality ratios for US men and women relative to Chinese counterparts.

Reports dietary correlates of coronary artery disease mortality in rural China: inverse associations with green vegetable intake and erythrocyte monounsaturated fatty acids, and positive associations with salt/urinary sodium and plasma apolipoprotein B.

Explains how apolipoprotein B links to diet: positively associated with animal protein and meat intake, inversely with plant protein, legumes, and light-colored vegetables; also notes that other disease rates correlate with dietary factors.
Concludes the findings with the study's key takeaway: no threshold was found beyond which additional benefits stop accruing as the proportion of plant-based foods in the diet increases.

Introduces the Lifestyle Heart Trial: a 1-year randomised controlled study of comprehensive lifestyle changes (vegetarian low-fat diet, smoking cessation, stress management, exercise) versus usual care on coronary atherosclerosis, with 195 lesions assessed by quantitative coronary angiography.
Reports the main angiographic results across all lesions: average diameter stenosis regressed from 40.0% to 37.8% in the lifestyle group but progressed from 42.7% to 46.1% in the control group.

Reports results for severe lesions (>50% stenosis) and the proportion with regression: stenosis regressed from 61.1% to 55.8% in the lifestyle group versus progression from 61.7% to 64.4% in controls, with 82% of lifestyle patients showing regression.
Concludes that comprehensive lifestyle changes may reverse even severe coronary atherosclerosis within one year without lipid-lowering drugs.

Introduction to the document: motivates a systematic review of U.S. sudden cardiac death (SCD) incidence, prompted by a SCATLA Think Tank of national experts and cardiology/heart rhythm organizations, noting the need for current consistent incidence data.

Describes the methods: a MEDLINE systematic literature search using sudden death, SCD, SCA, cardiac arrest, and arrhythmic death search terms to evaluate the true magnitude of the public health problem.

Covers study selection and impact assessment: peer-reviewed primary U.S. SCD incidence studies were included, and their influence was measured by citation counts using Web of Science Cited Reference Search.

Reports key findings: six included studies estimated U.S. annual SCD incidence from 180,000 to over 450,000, with variation attributed to data sources (1980-2007), definitions, case ascertainment, and estimation methods.
Concludes the true U.S. SCA/SCD incidence is unclear because estimates vary widely and are outdated; reliable incidence data matter for risk stratification and prevention.
Final recommendation: future work should establish uniform SCA and SCD definitions and prospectively, precisely capture cases across the overall U.S. population.

Introduction and study aim: chromosomal aberration assay assessing genotoxicity of avocado (Persea americana) fruit and leaf crude extracts in cultured human peripheral lymphocytes, setting up the exposure design.
Methods and main finding: 50% methanolic fruit and leaf extracts at increasing concentrations show concentration-dependent rise in chromosomal aberrations versus control.
Quantitative results for leaf extract (58%, 72%, 78% aberrant metaphases at 100, 200, 300 mg/kg vs 6% control, p<0.0001) and the start of fruit extract results.

Fruit extract quantitative results (18%, 40%, 52% aberrant metaphases with p-values vs control), then the most common abnormalities: acrocentric associations and premature centromeric separation in both exposed groups.

Leaf extract produces a wider range of structural aberrations (breaks, fragments, dicentrics, terminal deletions, minutes, Robertsonian translocations), and leaf extract shows higher aberration frequency than fruit extract at equal concentrations.
Concluding sentence: at equal concentrations, leaf extract yields higher frequency of all aberration types than fruit extract.

Introduces the study: avocado chloroform partition D003 previously shown to selectively induce apoptosis in oral cancer but not normal oral epithelial cells; this chunk begins the description of ROS elevation in high-ROS cancer cells.
Describes the key contrast: D003 raises ROS two- to threefold in oral cancer cells and triggers apoptosis, whereas normal cells with low basal ROS show only a 1.3-fold rise and no apoptosis.

Presents mechanistic evidence: NAC antioxidant treatment confers resistance to D003-induced apoptosis and delays it in dominant-negative FADD cells, and D003 raises ROS via mitochondrial complex I of the electron transport chain.

Shows that normal oral epithelial cells transformed by HPV16 E6 or E7 have elevated basal ROS and become sensitive to D003, concluding that ROS perturbation drives selective apoptosis and chemopreventive targeting by phytochemicals.
Final fragment of the abstract, completing the concluding phrase about chemoprevention by phytochemicals.

Introduction: establishes that fruit/vegetable phytochemicals help prevent cancer and describes avocado's nutritional profile and reported anticancer effects (cell cycle arrest, growth inhibition, apoptosis) in precancerous and cancer cell lines.

Middle section: reports the authors' recent chloroform-extract findings that avocado phytochemicals hit multiple signaling pathways and raise intracellular reactive oxygen species to trigger apoptosis, and states the review's aim of surveying the phytochemicals and their molecular mechanisms and targets.
Conclusion: argues that single avocado phytochemicals or combinations could serve as an advantageous dietary approach to cancer prevention.

Introduction of a rat toxicology study on the aqueous seed extract of Persea americana (avocado), used by Nigerian herbalists for hypertension; states the aims of testing acute (LD50) and sub-acute toxicity.

Methods: acute LD50 determination and sub-acute dosing at 2.5 g/kg orally daily for 28 days, with weight and fluid intake monitored and organs and blood/serum collected at termination for toxicity markers.
Results: LD50 not reached at 10 g/kg; body and organ weights unchanged, fluid intake significantly increased (P<0.0001); begins listing hematological and biochemical findings.

Remaining results and conclusion: hematology, ALT, AST, albumin and creatinine unchanged, total protein increased in treated rats; extract judged safe sub-acutely, though extremely high doses are not advisable.
Final fragment of the conclusion, cautioning that extremely high doses of the P. americana seed extract may not be advisable.

Introduction of a probabilistic model estimating health and economic benefits to the U.S. population from reducing methyl mercury (MeHg) exposure, covering MeHg as a developmental neurotoxicant linked to fatal heart attack risk.
Reports the expected annual monetary benefit ($860 million) of a 10% reduction in U.S. MeHg exposure, with 80% attributed to fewer fatal heart attacks and the rest to IQ gains.
Gives the broad uncertainty range of benefits (5th percentile about $50 million, 95th about $3.5 billion) and identifies the largest uncertainty: whether MeHg-heart attack associations are causal.

Names the next largest uncertainties: the slope of the maternal MeHg-child IQ relationship and whether it has a threshold, and recommends further study of the possible causal link to fatal heart attacks.
Concluding recommendation that the causal relationship between MeHg and fatal heart attacks needs better characterization through more epidemiological studies and formally elicited expert judgment.

Introduction and design of a 2010 crossover, double-blind, placebo-controlled study on low-dose arachidonic acid (ARA) supplementation and blood long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid levels in 23 young Japanese women.

Methods: women took a daily capsule of triacylglycerol enriched with 80 mg ARA (about one egg's worth) for 3 weeks, with blood drawn before and after treatment to measure LCPUFA composition in blood lipid fractions.

Results and conclusion: ARA supplementation raised ARA in erythrocyte and plasma phospholipids, esterified cholesterol, and triacylglycerol without lowering n-3 LCPUFA, showing that even a very low ARA dose increases ARA across all blood lipid fractions.
Copyright footer (Elsevier Ltd., 2010) closing the abstract of the study on dietary arachidonic acid and blood LCPUFA levels.
Introduction: motivation for reducing chicken meat arachidonic acid (AA) and omega-6/omega-3 ratio for health, and the high cost of fatty acid analysis that makes optimal sample numbers a challenge.

Study objectives: (i) assess intraclass correlation of fatty acids across five 1-gram samples from the same chicken thigh, and (ii) examine individual variation in fatty acid concentrations and the omega-6/omega-3 ratio among fifteen chickens.

Methods: fifteen newly hatched broilers fed a wheat-based diet with 4% rapeseed oil and 1% linseed oil for three weeks; five mid-thigh muscle samples per chicken were analysed for fatty acid composition.
Key intraclass correlation result: 0.85-0.98 for total omega-6/omega-3 and AA/EPA ratios, implying a single 1-gram sample per animal suffices for measuring these ratios.

Conclusion on sample size: high between-chicken variation for these ratios means at least 15 animals are needed to detect significant effects of experimental factors such as feeding regimes; the meat had a favorable omega-6/omega-3 ratio.
Results on ranges: AA ranged 1.5-2.8 g/100 g total fatty acids across the fifteen broilers and AA/EPA ratio ranged 2.3-3.9; between-bird differences may reflect genetic variance usable in breeding.
Final implication: genetic variation could be exploited through breeding for lower AA content and/or a more favorable AA/EPA ratio to produce healthier chicken meat.

Introduction to the document on diet and inflammation: links chronic inflammation to degenerative diseases and describes how human studies measure habitual dietary intake (food frequency questionnaires, 24-hour recalls) against inflammatory markers such as HS-CRP, IL-6, and TNF-α.

Continues the review of diet–inflammation research: covers blood nutrient analysis and controlled intervention studies testing dietary pattern changes or single foods on inflammatory markers in defined populations.

Summarizes findings that dietary composition has a modest effect on some inflammatory markers in free-living adults, with markers varying inconsistently, and lists dietary factors with established influence: glycemic index/load, fiber, fatty acids, magnesium, and carotenoids.

Lists flavonoids as another established dietary influence on inflammation, then introduces the Mediterranean dietary pattern (high MUFA:SFA and ω-3:ω-6 ratios, abundant fruits, vegetables, legumes, grains) and its anti-inflammatory effects relative to North American and Northern European diets.

Concludes that the Mediterranean diet showed anti-inflammatory effects in most observational and interventional studies and may become the preferred diet for reducing chronic inflammation in clinical practice.
Introduction and background of a prospective EPIC-Denmark cohort study on dietary n-6 PUFA arachidonic acid (measured in adipose tissue) as a possible risk factor for ulcerative colitis.

Methods: the EPIC-Denmark cohort of 57,053 participants enrolled 1993-1997, with gluteal adipose tissue biopsies at baseline, follow-up for UC incidence, and a 2510-person random subcohort as controls.

Methods continued: arachidonic acid measured in adipose tissue, grouped into quartiles, with relative risks adjusted for smoking, aspirin/NSAID use, and n-3 PUFA levels; the start of the results describing the 34 incident UC cases.

Results: 34 incident UC cases (56% men) at median age 58.8; highest arachidonic acid quartile gave RR 4.16 (95% CI 1.56-11.04), and a per-0.1% trend gave RR 1.77 (95% CI reported across this chunk boundary).

Results and conclusions: the trend's confidence interval (1.38-2.27), the population attributable fraction of 40.3% for highest arachidonic acid levels, and the conclusion that high adipose arachidonic acid is linked to significantly greater UC risk, suggesting dietary modification may help prevent UC or ease symptoms.
Concluding sentence about dietary modification as a possible UC prevention or symptom-reduction strategy, followed by the 2010 AGA Institute / Elsevier copyright notice.

Abstract of a study on a vegetarian/fasting diet for rheumatoid arthritis (RA); introduces the comparison of 53 trial participants with 71 other RA patients on psychological parameters, finding trial participants differed significantly.

Results on psychological differences: trial participants had higher internal and lower chance scores on the Multi-dimensional Health Locus of Control Scale (MHLCS), and lower belief in ordinary medical treatment (10-cm visual analogue scale) but higher belief in 'alternative' treatments.

Within the vegetarian-diet group, MHLCS scores did not differ between diet responders and non-responders, but responders had significantly lower belief in ordinary medical treatment than non-responders.

Psychological distress during the trial, measured with the General Health Questionnaire, favoured vegetarians over omnivores and diet responders over non-responders, indicating dietary change did not increase distress.

Conclusions: trial patients were psychologically selected; MHLCS scores cannot explain clinical improvement but beliefs about ordinary and alternative treatments may have influenced it; dietary treatment reduced psychological distress.
Final concluding sentence of the abstract stating that dietary treatment decreased psychological distress.

Introduction to arachidonic acid (AA)-derived eicosanoids as lipid mediators, their production by diverse cells, and their signaling via G-protein-coupled receptors, from a review on their roles in biology and immunopathology.

Continuation of the introduction: eicosanoids' classic roles in vascular homeostasis, gastric mucosal protection and platelet aggregation, expanded to immunopathological processes including inflammation, tissue remodelling, cancer, asthma, rheumatoid arthritis and autoimmune disorders.
Closing sentence of the introduction stating the review's aim: to survey the major properties of eicosanoids and their growing roles in biology and medicine.

Opening chunk of an abstract on a clinical study of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients, introducing the background (vegetarian diet and fish oil benefits) and the study's aims: effects of a low arachidonic acid diet and fish oil on inflammation, erythrocyte fatty acids, eicosanoids, and cytokines, plus the start of the methods section describing 68 matched patients.

Methods section of the RA diet study: 34 patients per group, one on a normal western diet and one on an anti-inflammatory diet limited to under 90 mg/day arachidonic acid, then a double-blind crossover of placebo versus fish oil capsules (30 mg/kg) over 3-month periods.

Continuation of the methods (crossover design with a 2-month washout, monthly clinical and laboratory monitoring, and erythrocyte fatty acid, eicosanoid, and cytokine measurements) transitioning into the results, which report that 60 of 68 patients completed the study.

Results of the RA diet trial: in the anti-inflammatory diet group, tender and swollen joint counts fell 14% on placebo, and fish oil produced larger reductions in tender (28% vs 11%) and swollen (34% vs 22%) joints compared with the western diet group (P<0.01).

Biomarker results from the RA diet and fish oil study: anti-inflammatory diet patients showed greater eicosapentaenoic acid enrichment in erythrocyte lipids and reduced leukotriene B4, 11-dehydro-thromboxane B2, and prostaglandin metabolites relative to baseline, compared with western diet patients.

Final part of the results and the conclusion of the RA study abstract: the strongest eicosanoid effects appeared during fish oil months 6-8, and the authors conclude that a low arachidonic acid diet reduces clinical inflammation in RA and enhances the benefit of fish oil.

Introduction and methods overview of a study on vegetarian diets, plasma lipids, and platelet function in relation to coronary heart disease risk; lists the three study groups (vegans, lactovegetarians, omnivores) and the measured variables.

Methods and key findings on platelet fatty acids: vegetarians showed higher platelet linoleic acid and lower platelet arachidonic acid compared with omnivorous controls, the study's most notable results.

Results on platelet function and lipids: serum thromboxane, prostacyclin, and platelet aggregation did not differ between groups, while cholesterol was lower in both vegetarian groups and HDL/LDL lower only in vegans.
Conclusion of the study linking the observed diet-related changes in platelet fatty acids and plasma lipids to the reduced coronary heart disease and possible atherosclerosis risk in vegetarians.
Final fragment of the abstract's last sentence, ending with the word 'vegetarians' and concluding the discussion of reduced heart disease risk.

Introduction and background of a cross-sectional study on vegetarian diets and mood in Seventh Day Adventist adults, noting that vegetarian diets exclude fish, the main source of EPA and DHA omega-3 fatty acids important for brain function.

Background continues with the link between low EPA/DHA omnivorous diets and impaired mood; the Methods describe the cross-sectional study of 138 healthy Seventh Day Adventist adults in the Southwest assessing polyunsaturated fatty acid intake and mood.

Methods detail the study instruments (food frequency questionnaire, DASS, POMS) and begin the Results, reporting that vegetarians showed significantly less negative emotion than omnivores on DASS and POMS scores.

Results give specific mood score comparisons between vegetarians and omnivores (DASS and POMS means with p-values) and report vegetarians had significantly lower EPA, DHA, and arachidonic acid intake and higher ALA and linoleic acid intake.

Results describe correlations between mood scores and fatty acid intakes: DASS and POMS scores were positively related to EPA, DHA, and AA and inversely related to ALA and LA, so lower EPA/DHA/AA and higher ALA/LA associated with better mood.
Conclusion that the vegetarian diet profile does not appear to adversely affect mood despite low long-chain omega-3 (EPA and DHA) intake.

Introduction and methods of a study on human saliva fatty acid profiles as a possible biomarker of dietary fat intake, comparing mixed-diet and vegetarian adults (n=20) using a food frequency questionnaire and gas chromatography.

Study design details: 20 adults on mixed (M) or vegetarian (V) diets, dietary fat intake assessed by Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ), salivary fatty acids measured by gas chromatography, and the start of the results on alpha-linolenic acid (18:3 n-3) levels.

Key results: vegetarians had higher salivary alpha-linolenic acid than mixed-diet subjects (2.82 vs 1.65, p=0.001), while salivary arachidonic acid (20:4 n-6) was lower in vegetarians (3.93 vs 4.52, p=0.045); dietary arachidonic acid intake showed the same pattern and correlated with salivary levels in vegetarians.

Conclusion: salivary arachidonic acid, which relates to eicosanoid production involved in tumourigenesis and cardiovascular disease, is influenced by dietary fat intake, supporting saliva as an indicator of dietary fat.

Introduction of the Tonga diet study: globalization drives rising noncommunicable diseases, and the paper examines the assumption that education-based lifestyle programmes can change food preferences and consumption.
Methods: the authors state the study aim of testing the assumptions behind education-based diet policy, using a questionnaire-based survey of food issues in Tonga.

Findings: survey data link food preferences, perceived nutritional value, and consumption frequency for traditional and imported foods; consumption of unhealthy imported foods is unrelated to preferences or nutrition perceptions, implying education may not work.

Policy implications: because trade liberalization and WTO rules may limit tariffs or import bans, controlling diet-related disease through alternative measures is difficult, posing challenges for health policymakers in economically marginal populations.
Conclusion: some population health problems cannot be addressed without understanding how global trade shapes food consumption.

This chunk opens the document on fibre and bowel transit times, introducing a study comparing vegetarians and non-vegetarians and linking bowel transit time to dietary fibre intake and diverticular disease, with vegetarians showing less disease and faster transit.

This chunk continues the findings on fibre and transit times: subjects eating over 30 g/day of fibre all had transit under 75 h, while 38% of lower-fibre eaters exceeded 75 h (up to 124 h), and people with diverticular disease had faster transit than those without.
This final chunk gives the concluding point of the study: a fibre-depleted diet may make the colon either hyperactive, favouring diverticular disease, or hypoactive, causing constipation.

Introduces the study design: a Netherlands Cohort Study on Diet and Cancer analysis of men (n=58,279) examining bowel movement and constipation frequency in relation to colorectal cancer, with dietary fiber as a possible effect modifier, and the follow-up period and case-cohort sample sizes.

Reports the main positive finding: men having 1-2 bowel movements per day, versus once daily, had significantly higher hazard ratios for overall colorectal cancer and rectal cancer, with the specific HRs, CIs, and trend p-values.

Reports the protective finding: constipation sometimes or more often, versus never, was associated with significantly lower hazard ratios for overall colorectal cancer and rectal cancer, with the specific HRs, CIs, and trend p-values.

Summarizes null results for proximal and distal colon cancer and non-significant fiber interactions, then states the overall conclusion that frequent bowel movements relate to higher rectal cancer risk and constipation to lower risk.
Concludes the abstract by restating that frequent bowel movements are linked to increased rectal cancer risk in men while constipation is linked to decreased risk.

Introduction of the study: motivation linking low fecal weight and slow transit to bowel cancer risk, and the aim of measuring stool weight across 20 populations in 12 countries and quantifying its relationship with dietary fiber (NSP) intake.

Results from healthy U.K. adults: median stool weight of 106 g/day and whole-gut transit time of 60 hours, with sex differences, and the much higher share of women than men passing under 50 g of stool per day.

Wider evidence: stool weight worldwide ranges from 72 to 470 g/day and is inversely related to colon cancer risk, plus a meta-analysis of 11 controlled-diet studies (n=206) showing a strong positive correlation between fiber intake and daily stool weight.

Implications for diet: Westernized populations have low stool weights (80-120 g/day) linked to higher colon cancer risk, fecal output rises with dietary NSP, and high-NSP diets (about 18 g/day) yield roughly 150 g/day stool.
Conclusion: the high-fiber diet's association with stool weights of about 150 g/day, and the recommendation that such diets should reduce bowel cancer risk.
Opening background of a PASSCLAIM paper on gut health and immunity, introducing the integrated gut-immune system and the difficulty of interpreting normal variation in function.

Continues the background: sets out why standards for optimal gut and immune function are needed for consumers, industry, and public health, and notes the large market for gut-functional foods and frequent functional claims about the digestive tract.
States the paper's aim (defining normal gut and immune function and methods to measure it) and begins the results, covering normal bowel habit, transit time, and their role as disease risk factors.

Results on gut microbiota and motility: defines healthy gut flora by dominant genera and metabolism, lists measurement methods, and notes difficulty setting boundaries for optimal gastric emptying, motility, absorption, and liver, gallbladder, and pancreas function.

Discusses gastrointestinal well-being as a subjective, ill-defined state where sensations shade from acceptable to unacceptable, and flags it as an important area for future work and method development.

Explains that immune function is harder to quantify than gut function, that clinical problems arise only when it is defective (an uncommon state), and introduces the innate and adaptive immune systems.
Describes how the innate and adaptive immune arms work synergistically, with redundancy providing robust defence, and notes that new immune functions are regularly discovered.

Covers limits of immune measurement: it is unclear whether immunity can be 'improved', no single test defines immune status or capacity, and human sampling is restricted to blood or secretions such as saliva.
Notes that only about 2% of lymphocytes circulate at a time, limiting data interpretation, and recommends assessing immune capacity via ex vivo cell function tests and in vivo challenge responses.

Concludes the recommendations for assessing immune function: measuring antibody or antigen responses in vivo and tracking infection incidence and severity in target populations during natural episodes or with attenuated pathogens.

This chunk opens the study abstract: it introduces a cohort of 1481 white women examined for epithelial dysplasia in nipple aspirate breast fluid, and reports a significant association with severe constipation (two or fewer bowel movements weekly), with risk ratio 4.5.

This chunk gives the contrast with frequent bowel movers (no association above one movement daily), notes raised risk ratios for once-daily or every-other-day frequency, and proposes that breast epithelial cytological abnormalities linked to severe constipation may matter for diet and breast disease research.
This chunk closes the abstract with the proposed mechanism: intestinal flora metabolize liver-secreted bile salts and oestrogens in the gut, a process that severe constipation may enhance.

Introduces the study question: whether diet, via fiber and enterohepatic estrogen circulation, relates to breast cancer risk. Describes the design: 31 postmenopausal women across omnivore, vegetarian, and BC omnivore groups, with dietary and hormone measurements.

Reports the main vegetarian-versus-BC results: vegetarians had a lower fat/fiber ratio, higher fiber intake, and significantly lower estrone-sulfate, estradiol, free estradiol, free testosterone, and ring D oxygenated estrogens, plus higher SHBG than BC subjects.

Covers omnivore comparisons: omnivores ate slightly more fiber than BC subjects and had lower testosterone and estrone-sulfate with higher SHBG than BC subjects. No urinary 16-oxygenated estrogen difference was found.

Highlights the 2-MeO-E1/2-OH-E1 catechol estrogen ratio, which was lower in omnivores than BC subjects and tracks positively with fat/fiber ratio. Concludes testosterone may alter catechol and 16-oxygenated estrogen levels.
Final conclusion: the fat/fiber ratio is a useful marker for evaluating dietary effects on estrogen metabolism, closing the abstract's summary of diet, sex hormones, and breast cancer.

Opening of the study abstract on a California Seventh-day Adventist women cohort: sample size, 1976 lifestyle questionnaire, follow-up length, case count, and the postmenopausal age profile of breast cancer cases.

Continues the abstract with established breast cancer risk factors (age at first birth, maternal history, menopause age, education, obesity) that were significantly associated with risk, contrasting with the dietary findings that follow.

Presents the dietary null findings: high-fat animal product intake was inconsistently linked to risk, childhood/teenage vegetarian vs. nonvegetarian habits were unrelated, and adult percent of calories from animal fat was not significantly associated with risk.
Concludes the abstract by noting the dietary results held after simultaneous control for confounders using Cox proportional hazards regression models.

This chunk opens the study on estrogen excretion in vegetarian versus omnivorous premenopausal women, describing the 10-vs-10 design, the measurement of estrogens in plasma, urine, and feces, and the dietary differences (lower fat and higher fiber in vegetarians).

This chunk reports the fiber-related findings: vegetarians had higher fecal weight and fecal estrogen excretion (positive correlation in both groups), and lower urinary estriol excretion, within the study of vegetarian versus omnivorous women's estrogen levels.

This chunk presents the plasma and bacterial findings: estrone and estradiol plasma levels were negatively correlated with fecal estrogen excretion, and fecal bacterial beta-glucuronidase activity was reduced in vegetarians, leading into the study's conclusion.

This final chunk states the study's conclusion that vegetarian women's increased fecal output raises fecal estrogen excretion and lowers plasma estrogen concentration, summarizing the estrogen excretion study.
Introduction and methods of a case-control study on vitamin and mineral supplement use and prostate cancer risk, using 1,706 cases and 2,404 controls from the US Case-Control Surveillance Study.
Methods continued: conditional logistic regression estimating odds ratios and 95% CIs, followed by the start of the results on multivitamin use without zinc and prostate cancer risk.

Results: multivitamins without zinc showed no clear trend in prostate cancer risk by duration, while men using zinc for 10+ years had about a 2-fold increased risk (OR 1.9); vitamin E, beta-carotene, folate and selenium showed no significant association.

Results continued for vitamin E, beta-carotene, folate and selenium, followed by the conclusion that long-term zinc intake doubles prostate cancer risk, supporting an unfavorable role of zinc in carcinogenesis.
Final concluding sentence stating that the zinc-prostate cancer association adds to growing evidence that zinc has an unfavorable effect on prostate carcinogenesis.

Abstract opening of a Nurses' Health Study II study on adolescent fiber intake and proliferative benign breast disease (BBD), a marker of breast cancer risk, describing the cohort of 29,480 women and 682 confirmed cases.

Results section showing that the highest quintile of adolescent fiber intake was associated with a 25% lower risk of proliferative BBD (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.59-0.96, p-trend 0.01) versus the lowest quintile, using multivariate Cox regression.

Results continuing with high school intake of nuts and apples linked to reduced BBD risk, specifically women eating at least 2 servings of nuts weekly having a 36% lower risk (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.48-0.85) than those eating under 1 serving monthly.

Sensitivity analysis restricted to 142 prospective cases diagnosed after the high school diet questionnaire, which yielded essentially the same results, followed by the conclusion that adolescent fiber and nut intake may influence later breast disease risk and aid breast cancer prevention.
Final sentence of the conclusions, stating that adolescent diet may offer a viable means for breast cancer prevention.

Introduction and study design of a prospective cohort study (Multiethnic Cohort, Hawaii and California, 1993-1996, n=182,099) examining whether multivitamin/mineral supplement use is linked to mortality and cancer risk.

Study results: about 11 years of follow-up with 28,851 deaths; Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for tobacco and other confounders show no association between multivitamin use and all-cause mortality, with hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals reported separately for men and women.

Continuation of the results: no association with cardiovascular or cancer mortality, and subgroup analyses by ethnicity, age, BMI, preexisting illness, single supplement use, hormone replacement therapy, and smoking status show consistent findings.

Cancer incidence findings: no evidence that multivitamin use affects overall cancer risk or risk at major sites (lung, colorectum, prostate, breast), followed by the study's overall conclusion of no clear decrease or increase in mortality or morbidity.
Final conclusion of the multivitamin study: no clear benefit or harm of multivitamin supplement use on all-cause, cardiovascular, or cancer mortality, or on overall or major cancer morbidity.

Opening of the aromatase structural biology paper: introduces aromatase (CYP19) as the vertebrate enzyme converting androgens to oestrogens, and its clinical relevance as a target of breast cancer therapy.

Describes the three-step aromatase reaction (androstenedione, testosterone, 16α-hydroxytestosterone to oestrone, oestradiol, oestriol), noting the two C19-methyl hydroxylations and the unique A-ring aromatization, and the androgen selectivity that distinguishes it from other P450s.

States the problem that the aromatase structure, an endoplasmic reticulum membrane P450, was unknown for decades, and announces the crystal structure of human placental aromatase as the first full-length natural mammalian hormone-pathway P450 solved.

Explains that the aromatase active site is an androgen-specific cleft that snugly binds androstenedione, with hydrophobic and polar residues complementing the steroid, in contrast to the drug-metabolizing microsomal P450s.

Summarizes mechanistic findings: locations of catalytic residues, and how the hydrophobic N-terminal membrane anchor and the cleft opening explain why membrane anchoring is needed for lipophilic substrate access.
Concluding sentence: the structural basis of androgen specificity and the catalytic mechanism can guide design of next-generation aromatase inhibitors.

Introduces aromatase (CYP19) as the rate-limiting enzyme converting androgens to estrogens, and its inhibition as the standard adjuvant treatment for hormone-dependent breast cancer in postmenopausal women.
Notes that natural compounds have broad biological activities (antioxidant, anti-tumor, anti-viral) and that many studies have examined aromatase inhibition by plant extracts and phytochemicals.

Explains the motivation: natural aromatase inhibitors could serve chemopreventive purposes and inform new aromatase-inhibiting drug development, and previews that the review covers whole food extracts and phytochemical classes.
States the review's scope: it will examine reported aromatase inhibition, kinetic data, and structural features of phytochemicals that enhance or reduce their interaction with the aromatase enzyme.

Introduction and background of a study testing whether the sharp 2002-2003 drop in breast cancer incidence among non-Hispanic white women continued after 2003, with stated aims covering black and Hispanic women and postmenopausal hormone use.

Study aims and methods overview: breast cancer incidence trends for NH black and Hispanic women and hormone use are also presented, with the methods introduced as incidence calculated by race/ethnicity, age, and ER status.

Data sources and methods: SEER 12 registry data (2000-2007) for incidence, National Health Interview Survey data (2000, 2005, 2008) for postmenopausal hormone use, and the start of the results showing no significant change in overall NH white incidence 2003-2007.

Key results: no significant change in NH white incidence in any age group, but ER+ incidence rose 2.7% per year at ages 40-49 while ER- incidence fell at ages 40-49 and 60-69; black and Hispanic overall incidence was also stable.

Hormone use results and conclusions: hormone use kept falling 2005-2008 in all groups but more slowly than 2000-2005, and the sharp 2002-2003 decline among NH white women did not persist through 2007.
Closing impact statement calling for further studies on recent breast cancer trends, followed by the 2011 AACR copyright notice.

Opening definition of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS): breast epithelial cells that are abnormally proliferating but remain confined to ducts and lobules, from the document's introduction on DCIS terminology and natural history.

Continuation of the introduction explaining why DCIS is considered nonlethal yet clinically important as the immediate precursor of potentially lethal invasive breast cancer, and previewing the article's sections on history, classification, current perspective, and future goals.
Final fragment of the introduction's roadmap, listing the article's coverage of DCIS classification methods, current perspective, and future goals.
Introduction/background of a NHANES 2003–2004 study on dietary intake and phthalate body burden, stating the study objective of assessing how different food types contribute to phthalate exposure.
Background on phthalate toxicity and food contamination, followed by the Methods section describing an exploratory analysis of 2003–2004 NHANES data.

Methods detail: 24-hr dietary recall food categories (meat, poultry, fish, fruit, vegetable, dairy) analyzed against urinary phthalate metabolites via multiple linear regression, then the start of the Results.
Key results: DEHP and high-molecular-weight phthalate metabolites linked to poultry consumption; monoethyl phthalate (DEP metabolite) linked to tomato and potato (vegetable) consumption.
Discussion concluding diet is an important phthalate exposure route and calling for research on food contamination sources and levels in a representative U.S. sample.
Final sentence of the conclusion, calling for research on contamination levels in U.S. food using a large, representative U.S. sample.

Introduces the study's hypothesis that sexual selection shapes primate genital anatomy, testing whether multi-male mating systems (where sexual selection is enhanced) correlate with more spinous penises.

Explains taxonomic constraints: most prosimians but few anthropoids have penile spines, and their predominant mating systems differ, so this is accounted for; states that sexual selection does not act on penile spines like it does on other genital traits, since spinosity is not highest in multi-male taxa.

Proposes that penile spines may stimulate reproductive readiness and synchrony in dispersed social systems and during 'stolen' extra-pair copulations, where the sexes lack other ways to signal reproductive state.

Concludes that the spine hypotheses (reproductive stimulation and scent marking) have problems, so penile spines may serve several functions or their evolution in primates and other orders remains unexplained.
Final word fragment of the conclusion, completing 'remains to be explained' about the unresolved function of penile spinosity.
Introduction and methods of a cross-sectional study on urinary phthalate exposure and ADHD symptoms in school-age children (Korean cohort, ages 8-11, n=261).
Results section defining the urinary phthalate metabolites measured: MEHP and MEOP (from DEHP) and MNBP (from DBP), in a study of phthalates and ADHD in children.
Reported mean urinary concentrations of MEHP, MEOP, and MNBP, and adjusted findings linking teacher-rated ADHD scores to DEHP metabolites but not DBP metabolites.
Results on DBP metabolites and continuous performance test (CPT) omission and commission errors, followed by the start of the conclusion on phthalate-ADHD association.
Conclusion of the phthalates and ADHD study stating a strong positive association between urinary phthalate metabolites and ADHD symptoms in school-age children.

Introduction of a human study on prenatal phthalate exposure and male genital development, reporting anogenital distance (AGD) measurements in 134 boys and their correlations with penile volume and incomplete testicular descent.
Defines the anogenital index (AGI = AGD/weight) and age-adjusted AGI, and describes the study's approach of testing nine phthalate monoester metabolites from prenatal urine as predictors of AGI.

Methods and sample description: analysis of nine phthalate metabolites in prenatal urine from 85 participants, using regression and categorical analyses, with four metabolites (MEP, MBP, MBzP, MiBP) identified as inversely related to AGI.
Regression p-values after age adjustment and odds ratios for shorter-than-expected AGI, highlighting MBP with an odds ratio of 10.2 comparing highest and lowest quartiles.
Odds ratios for MEP, MBzP, and MiBP, plus a summary phthalate score for joint exposure showing a significant decline in age-adjusted AGI with increasing score.
Interpretation linking findings to incomplete virilization syndrome seen in prenatally exposed rodents, and comparison framing of exposure levels.

Comparison of metabolite concentrations associated with short AGI and incomplete testicular descent against US female population levels, concluding that environmental phthalate exposure may harm male reproductive development.
Final concluding sentence of the abstract restating that prenatal phthalate exposure at environmental levels can adversely affect male reproductive development in humans.

Introduces the study's background: nutrients and antioxidants (carotenoids) affect skin, and the pharmacokinetics of systemically applied carotenoids in skin were poorly understood. Describes the design: oral kale extract vs. placebo oil given to 22 volunteers for 4 weeks.

Describes the methods: carotenoid bioaccessibility measured non-invasively by resonance Raman spectroscopy on palm and forehead skin, with blood serum analyzed by standard HPLC. Continues the kale extract vs. placebo oil supplementation study in healthy volunteers.

Presents the main results: blood and skin carotenoid levels rose significantly, but skin increases lagged behind serum and varied by dermal site and carotenoid. Lycopene rose more in skin than blood, suggesting the natural extract mixture stabilizes the skin's antioxidant network.

Reports post-supplementation findings: carotenoids fell much faster in blood than in skin, which may reflect a peripheral buffer role of skin for carotenoids. Ends with the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.

Contains only the trailing copyright notice (Copyright 2010 Elsevier B.V.) closing the abstract of the study on carotenoid bioavailability in human skin versus blood after kale extract supplementation.

Introduction of the study: prior research on skin condition (texture, color) and perceived health, age, and attractiveness in faces, and the aim to test overall skin color using color-calibrated face photos.

Method and key result: participants manipulated skin color in CIELab space (a*, b*, L*) on face photos, and increased redness (a*) to make faces look healthier, consistent with skin blood color findings.
Main findings on yellowness (b*) and lightness (L*), linked to carotenoid and low melanin coloration, plus the conclusion that these preferences match red and yellow health cues in nonhuman animals.
Final fragment of the conclusion: the color preferences parallel red and yellow health signals seen across many nonhuman animal species.

Introduction of the study: motivation (iodine-induced thyroid dysfunction risk from popular dietary seaweeds) and description of sample sourcing from US commercial products and harvester samples from Canada, Tasmania, and Namibia.
Main results: iodine content across 12 seaweed species, ranging from low in nori (Porphyra tenera) to extremely high in Laminaria digitata kelp granules used as a salt substitute.
Preharvest variation study on two Namibian kelps (Laminaria pallida and Ecklonia maxima), showing iodine content is lowest in sun-bleached blades and highest in freshly cut juvenile blades.
Conclusions: iodine is lost in cooking and storage, making prepared-food estimates hard, and some Asian seaweed dishes may exceed the 1100 microg/day tolerable upper intake level.

Introduction of a 2011 Journal of Paediatrics and Child Health case report on iodine excess causing neonatal hypothyroidism from maternal seaweed consumption in Australia and New Zealand, contrasting with the known problem of mild iodine deficiency.

Conclusion of the same article: it notes that attention has focused on iodine inadequacy in Australian diets, cautions that iodine excess (from seaweed soup eaten to boost breast milk) must not be overlooked, and ends with the message that neither feast nor famine is desirable, followed by the journal copyright line.
Final fragment of the 2011 Journal of Paediatrics and Child Health article's copyright attribution, naming the Royal Australasian College of Physicians and its Paediatrics and Child Health Division.

Introduction to exogenous hyperthyroidism from thyroid-contaminated food, describing the case of a 77-year-old man with hyperthyroidism caused by sausage consumption, in a Dutch case report on hyperthyroidism causes.

Clinical presentation and workup of a 77-year-old man with hyperthyroidism: normal physical exam, undetectable TSH receptor antibodies, and low 123I thyroid uptake (under 1%), leading to a provisional diagnosis of silent thyroiditis.

Diagnostic course in the case report: silent thyroiditis was diagnosed and observed without improvement, low thyroglobulin was found, and anamnesis revealed excessive daily sausage consumption containing detectable thyroid hormones.
Outcome and conclusion of the case: after the patient stopped eating the contaminated sausages he became and stayed euthyroid, highlighting the importance of a thorough anamnesis in hyperthyroidism.

Context: The document is a case report on iodine toxicity from seaweed-containing foods. This chunk introduces the cases: adult thyroid dysfunction from a kombu (seaweed) soy milk brand, a neonatal hypothyroidism case from a mother drinking that milk, and two more neonatal cases from maternal seaweed soup, all linked to high iodine content.

Context: This chunk concludes the document's summary, noting the high iodine levels in the implicated products and the broader point that iodine toxicity from sources like seaweed is under-recognised despite awareness of iodine deficiency.

Introduction on why iodine matters in pregnancy (fetal neurodevelopment) and the decline in U.S. urinary iodine concentrations since the 1970s, setting up the NHANES 2001-2006 study of women of reproductive age.

Study methods: NHANES 2001-2006 urine iodine spot-test data for pregnant, lactating, and nonpregnant nonlactating women aged 15-44, with WHO criteria used to define iodine sufficiency thresholds for each group.

Results: median urinary iodine concentrations by group, with pregnant women borderline sufficient (153 µg/L) and lactating and nonpregnant nonlactating women iodine sufficient, including 95% confidence intervals.

Key finding that dairy product consumption strongly influences iodine status in pregnant and nonpregnant nonlactating women, so non-dairy consumers may be at risk of iodine deficiency; notes that larger samples are needed to confirm.
Conclusion calling for monitoring of U.S. women's iodine levels, especially at-risk subgroups such as pregnant women and women of reproductive age who avoid dairy.
Introduction and objective of a study on iodine status and thyroid function in U.S. vegetarians and vegans, including the hypothesized effects of perchlorate and thiocyanate exposure.

Study objective definitions of vegetarian and vegan diets, plus the design: a cross-sectional assessment of urinary iodine, perchlorate, thiocyanate, and serum thyroid function in Boston-area participants.
Study subjects (141 recruited, 78 vegetarians and 63 vegans, one vegan excluded) and the start of results: vegans had lower median urinary iodine than vegetarians.

Results comparing urinary iodine ranges and medians between vegans and vegetarians, and adjusted urinary thiocyanate levels, which were higher in vegans (smoking and thiocyanate-rich food consumption adjusted).
Results showing no between-group differences in urinary perchlorate, TSH, or free T4, and no association of urinary iodine, perchlorate, or thiocyanate with thyroid function measures.

Study conclusions: vegetarians are iodine sufficient, vegans may be at risk for low iodine, and vegan women of child-bearing age should take 150 μg iodine daily; the environmental exposures were not linked to thyroid dysfunction.
Final sentence of the conclusions stating that perchlorate and thiocyanate exposures are not associated with thyroid dysfunction in the vegetarian and vegan groups studied.

Abstract opening of a Norwegian dairy study (178 herds) on Staphylococcus aureus isolated about one week after calving, and its links to milk yield, somatic cell count, clinical mastitis, and culling; introduces the mixed-model and survival-analysis methods.

Results on somatic cell count: cows with S. aureus had higher SCC than culture-negative cows, with mean SCC by number of infected quarters shown separately for cows without post-milking teat disinfection (PMTD).

Continues the SCC results with iodine PMTD means by number of infected quarters, then begins the milk yield findings for primiparous cows, which matched culture-negative cows except when S. aureus was in more than 2 quarters.

Milk yield losses in multiparous cows infected with S. aureus, by parity and number of infected quarters, over a 305-day lactation, with primiparous cows losing 229 kg when infected in more than 2 quarters.

Hazard ratios for clinical mastitis (2.0) and culling (1.7) in cows with S. aureus in at least one quarter compared with culture-negative cows, plus evidence that iodine PMTD lowered SCC and clinical mastitis risk in culture-negative cows.

Conclusion on iodine PMTD: it appears to have a preventive effect in healthy cows, but in cows with S. aureus in more than 2 quarters at calving it had a negative effect on clinical mastitis risk and SCC over the remaining lactation.

Opening of a passage on endemic cretinism: defines its two syndromes (neurological form with deaf mutism and spastic paresis, and hypothyroid form with growth retardation) and states both are caused by dietary iodine deficiency and preventable before pregnancy.

Continues the discussion by placing endemic cretinism within the 'iodine deficiency disorders (IDDs)' spectrum, which includes milder cognitive defects also preventable by correcting iodine deficiency, and begins noting WHO recognition of iodine deficiency as a leading preventable cause of brain damage.

Gives global scale of iodine deficiency: WHO calls it the most common preventable cause of brain damage, with over 2 billion people at risk in 130 countries, and reports UN prevention progress, with household iodised salt use rising to 68% by 2000 from under 20% before 1990.
Final fragment containing the end of the UN iodised salt statistic (under 20% before 1990 rising to 68% by 2000) and the copyright notice (Elsevier, 2009), closing the document.

Abstract opening of a 22-week randomized double-blind trial of saffron (Crocus sativus) for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease; states rationale and objective, and introduces the study population of 54 Persian-speaking community-dwelling adults aged 55+.

Methods section of the saffron vs. donepezil Alzheimer's trial: describes the 22-week double-blind parallel-group design and the primary efficacy outcomes (ADAS-cog and CDR-SB change from baseline), with systematic adverse event recording.

Methods and results of the saffron Alzheimer's trial: participants randomized to saffron 30 mg/day or donepezil 10 mg/day, followed by the key result that saffron at this dose was similarly effective to donepezil after 22 weeks.

Adverse event and conclusion portion of the saffron Alzheimer's trial abstract: AEs were similar between saffron and donepezil except vomiting, which was more frequent with donepezil; concludes the phase II study gives preliminary evidence of a possible therapeutic effect of saffron extract.
Closing trial registration statement for the saffron Alzheimer's study, identifying it as registered with the Iranian Clinical Trials Registry under ID IRCT138711051556N1.

Introduction and background of a 2010 randomized placebo-controlled trial of saffron (Crocus sativus) for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease; states the rationale (amyloid β aggregation inhibition) and the study objective.

Methods section describing the design: 46 probable AD patients screened for a 16-week double-blind parallel-group study, with cognitive outcome measures ADAS-cog and clinical dementia rating sum of boxes.
Methods continued: random assignment to saffron 30 mg/day (15 mg twice daily) versus placebo capsules over 16 weeks, followed by the start of the results section on cognitive outcomes.

Results and conclusion: saffron outperformed placebo on cognitive function at 16 weeks (ADAS-cog and CDR, P=0.04), with no significant difference in adverse events, and the 'what is new' statement that saffron appears safe and effective short-term.
Concluding statement of the saffron Alzheimer's trial calling for larger confirmatory randomized trials, followed by the copyright notice (2010, JCPT/Blackwell Publishing).

Introduction of the study: 1991 neurocysticercosis cases in an Orthodox Jewish community linked to infected immigrant housekeepers, and the seroprevalence survey (9% of households) that begins reporting results (23 of 1,789 seropositive).

Survey results: 1.3% seropositivity among 1,789 persons from 612 families, all asymptomatic with no intracerebral lesions on brain imaging, and risk factors including female sex and hiring domestic child-care workers.

Risk factor findings and conclusions: seropositivity linked to employing Central American employees (RR 2.70), with the authors concluding T. solium exposure is unexpectedly high due to widespread hiring of domestic workers from endemic regions and high employee turnover.
Final sentence of the abstract concluding that employment of domestic workers from endemic regions and high employee turnover contribute to exposure risk for Taenia solium cysticercosis.

Opening of the abstract: the study's objective and design. It aims to assess knowledge and practices of public-sector primary-care health professionals and final-year students on nutrition, physical activity and smoking cessation (lifestyle modification) in managing chronic lifestyle diseases in South Africa's public health sector.

Study design and setting: a comparative cross-sectional descriptive quantitative study in 30 primary health-care facilities and 4 tertiary institutions with medical/nursing programmes in Cape Town, Western Cape. Health facilities were chosen by stratified random sampling by geographic location; students by convenience sampling.

Methods and key results: a validated self-administered knowledge test was used with health professionals. Results show differential lifestyle modification knowledge among professionals and students, with under 10% reaching the 80% or higher target score.

Main findings: most health professionals promote lifestyle modification theory but struggle to give practical patient advice. Doctors showed the best lifestyle modification knowledge among the health professionals evaluated.

Barriers and conclusions: lack of time, poor patient adherence and language barriers were the main obstacles to lifestyle counselling. Conclusions recommend stronger undergraduate medical and nursing training on practical diet, physical activity and smoking cessation advice.
Closing recommendation: primary health-care professionals should receive continuing medical education on lifestyle modification to keep their knowledge current and practical.

Introduction to a U.S. national survey on nutrition education in medical schools: its purpose (quantifying required nutrition hours and course types, and comparing with prior surveys) and the method of distributing an online survey to all 127 accredited U.S. medical schools.

Survey methodology continued: a two-page online survey from the UNC Chapel Hill Nutrition in Medicine Project, administered August 2008 to July 2009 to school contacts (mostly nutrition educators), asking about required nutrition contact hours and whether instruction was in a dedicated course, another course, or clinical rotations.
Initial results of the nutrition education survey of U.S. medical schools: 109 schools (86%) responded, and most (103 of 109) required some form of nutrition education.
