Continuation describing how IGF-1 may be absorbed from or stimulated by milk, and how milk's 5α-pregnanedione (5α-P) acts as a precursor to dihydrotestosterone in prostate cancer and induces estrogen receptors in breast cancer cells.

Concluding part of the document's discussion of 5α-P's estrogen-receptor effects in breast cancer cells, followed by the general hypothesis that exogenous hormones and growth factors threaten tissues lacking feedback inhibition, promoting hyperplasia or neoplasia.

Final sentence of the document, summarizing the proposed threat: exogenous hormones and growth factors directly stimulate organ systems lacking defensive feedback inhibition, leading to hyperplasia or neoplasia.

Background and rationale: introduces concern that modern dairy cows lactate during pregnancy, so commercial milk contains estrogens and progesterone, and states the study's aim of measuring serum and urine sex hormones after cow milk intake.

Study methods for men and children: describes the subjects (seven men, six prepubertal children, five women), the milk dose of 600 mL/m² for men and children, and the urine sampling schedule around milk intake.

Remaining methods: serum sampling times in men (before and up to 120 min after intake), the 21-day nightly 500 mL milk regimen for women starting on the second menstruation, and ovulation tracking across three cycles with an ovulation checker.

Results part one: men showed rising serum estrone and progesterone and falling LH, FSH and testosterone after milk intake; urinary E1, estradiol, estriol and pregnanediol rose in all adults and children.

Results part two and conclusions start: four of five women ovulated during milk intake with consistent timing across cycles; authors conclude estrogens in milk were absorbed and gonadotropin secretion was suppressed, lowering testosterone.
Final conclusion: suppression of gonadotropins and testosterone implies that ordinary cow milk intake could affect sexual maturation in prepubertal children.

Abstract opening (Objective, Design, start of Results) of a 2010 Elsevier review critically assessing whether soy isoflavone supplements or soy foods feminize men, based on a Medline literature review; introduces the rodent-vs-clinical evidence contrast.

Abstract Results on hormones: a recent meta-analysis and later studies show isoflavones do not change total or free testosterone, and the nine identified clinical studies show essentially no effect on circulating estrogen in men.

Abstract Results on reproductive outcomes: isoflavones show no effect on sperm or semen parameters, based on only three short (under 3 months) intervention studies; also dismisses rodent erectile dysfunction findings as inapplicable to humans due to metabolism differences and excessive animal doses.
Abstract Conclusion start: intervention data indicate isoflavones do not feminize men at intakes equal to or considerably above typical Asian male intake levels.
Final sentence of the conclusion (feminizing effects at intake levels typical for Asian males) plus the copyright line: Copyright 2010, Published by Elsevier Inc.

Introduction and objectives of a cross-sectional study on animal product consumption and postmenopausal circulating steroid hormones and SHBG, motivated by steroid hormones' link to breast cancer risk.

Methods: plasma from 766 naturally postmenopausal women, steroid hormone and SHBG measurement, dietary intake estimated via a 121-item food frequency questionnaire, and regression of log-transformed hormones on quartiles of meat, dairy, fat, protein, and cholesterol intake.
Results begin: total and fresh red meat intake is inversely associated with SHBG (P for trend 0.04 and <0.01), with SHBG about 8% and 13% lower in the highest vs lowest quartile.

Results continue: dairy product intake is positively associated with total and free estradiol (P for trend 0.02 and 0.03), with the highest quartile showing estradiol levels higher than the lowest quartile.

Results conclude with the dairy-estradiol magnitudes (15% total, 14% free higher in highest quartile) and the null findings for processed meat, chicken, fish, eggs, cholesterol, fats, and protein, followed by the start of the conclusions.
Conclusions: greater red and fresh red meat intake may lower SHBG and greater dairy intake may raise estradiol in postmenopausal women; the authors call for confirmation and further research.

Introduces the cross-sectional study comparing sex hormone and metabolic profiles of omnivores and vegetarians, describing the sample of 41 omnivorous and 21 vegetarian pre- and post-menopausal women and the measures collected (plasma hormones, fasting insulin, NEFA, apolipoproteins, BMI, diet, activity, faecal and urinary excretion).

Continues the list of measured variables (fasting insulin, NEFA, apo-A and apo-B, BMI, 3-day dietary records, physical activity, 72-hour faecal and urinary excretion) and begins reporting that vegetarians had higher SHBG, apo-A, faecal excretion and fibre intake.

Reports the group differences: vegetarians had lower apo-B, free oestradiol, free testosterone, DHEA-s and BMI, and after adjusting for BMI most differences persisted except apo-B; also states that fibre intake explained 15.2% of SHBG variation in stepwise regression.

Summarises the main conclusion that pre- and post-menopausal vegetarians have higher SHBG concentrations, partly explained by higher fibre intake, and begins linking this to a possible lower risk of type 2 diabetes.
Final sentence of the abstract, stating that the higher SHBG and fibre intake in vegetarians may partly explain their lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes.

Abstract opening (Aim and Methods) of a 2008 Adventist Health Studies prospective cohort on meat intake and incident diabetes, describing the 8,401 non-diabetic adult participants and 17-year follow-up.

Results section of the meat and diabetes study: odds ratios for weekly all-meat consumers (OR 1.29) and processed meat consumers such as salted fish and frankfurters (OR 1.38), with 543 incident diabetes cases identified.
Results continued: long-term adherence to a weekly-meat diet versus vegetarian diet (OR 1.74), and the note that part of the diabetes risk may be explained by obesity and weight gain.

Discussion of the meat-diabetes findings: obesity and weight gain as strong risk factors, and weekly meat intake remaining a significant risk (OR 1.38) after adjusting for weight and weight change, with a correction note.
Conclusion of the Adventist cohort study (Karger, Basel, 2008) stating that meat intake, especially processed meat, may be a dietary risk factor for diabetes.

Introduction of a review on SHBG, estradiol and breast cancer: SHBG regulates bioavailable estradiol and its polymorphisms are linked to breast cancer risk; the chunk begins the summary of SHBG's role in breast cancer pathophysiology.

Middle of the abstract describing SHBG's direct action in breast cancer cells: it interacts with the cells, triggers an intracellular pathway that cross-talks with estradiol signaling, and inhibits several estradiol effects.

Concluding section of the abstract: SHBG's regulation of free estrogen and inhibition of estradiol-induced breast cancer cell growth and proliferation are associated with reduced breast cancer risk after estrogen exposure.
Final fragment of the abstract containing the copyright notice (2009 Elsevier Ireland Ltd. All rights reserved), ending the summary of SHBG's protective role against estradiol-related breast cancer.

Introduction to the gut microbiome: its size (about 100 trillion microbes, 100-fold more genes than the human genome) and its role in host homeostasis and energy extraction, setting up the article's review of microbiome effects on metabolism and obesity.

Summary of key evidence linking gut flora to obesity: metagenomic studies showing certain microbiota mixes protect or predispose to obesity, and germ-free mouse transplant studies showing obese-type flora's efficient energy-extraction traits are transmissible.

Proposed mechanisms by which the microbiome may drive obesity (increased dietary energy harvest, fat deposition, systemic inflammation) and the conclusion that future obesity treatments may modulate gut microbiota with probiotics or prebiotics.
Brief closing fragment of the conclusion, referring to modulating gut microbiota with probiotics or prebiotics as a possible future obesity treatment.

Study design and methods of a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of probiotics (L. acidophilus NCFM, with or without B. animalis Bi-07) in 326 healthy 3-5 year old children during winter to prevent colds and influenza-like illness.

Randomized groups and dosing details (twice daily for 6 months) followed by primary results on reduced fever, coughing, and rhinorrhea incidence with single and combination probiotic strains versus placebo, including percentage reductions and P values.

Results on symptom duration (fever, cough, rhinorrhea) and antibiotic use reductions in children receiving single-strain or combination probiotics compared with placebo, with percentage reductions and P values.

Results showing fewer days absent from group child care for children taking single or combination probiotics versus placebo, plus the start of the conclusion that daily probiotic supplementation is safe and effective.

Conclusion of the trial: 6 months of daily dietary probiotic supplementation safely reduced fever, rhinorrhea, cough incidence and duration, antibiotic prescriptions, and missed school days due to illness in children aged 3 to 5.
Final fragment of the conclusion specifying the target population of children aged 3 to 5 years for the probiotic supplementation benefits.
Introduces the obesity epidemic and prior findings that obesity is linked to shifts in the Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes gut microbiota in mice and humans.

States the study's main approach: metagenomic and biochemical analyses showing these microbiota changes alter the mouse gut microbiome's metabolic potential, with an increased capacity to harvest dietary energy.

Reports the transmissibility result: germ-free mice colonized with an obese microbiota gained significantly more body fat than those given a lean microbiota, implicating the microbiota in obesity pathophysiology.
Concludes that the gut microbiota is an additional contributing factor to the pathophysiology of obesity.
Introduction and study design of a gut microbiota study in pregnant women: aims, and grouping of 50 women by BMI into normal-weight and overweight groups.

Methods and main microbiota findings: qPCR analysis of faecal microbiota at 24 weeks of pregnancy, showing lower Bifidobacterium and Bacteroides and higher Staphylococcus, Enterobacteriaceae and E. coli in overweight women.

Findings on weight gain and the whole-population results: E. coli higher with excessive gestational weight gain, Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila trending opposite, and total bacteria and Staphylococcus linked to plasma cholesterol.

Associations between gut bacterial groups and plasma biochemical markers: Bacteroides with HDL-cholesterol, folic acid and TAG; Bifidobacterium with folic acid; Enterobacteriaceae and E. coli with ferritin and transferrin.

Conclusion of the abstract: Enterobacteriaceae/E. coli and Bifidobacterium show opposite relations to ferritin and transferrin, and gut microbiota is concluded to relate to body weight, weight gain and metabolic biomarkers in pregnancy, with implications for maternal and infant health.
Final sentence fragment of the abstract's conclusion, stating the relevance of gut microbiota management for the health of women and infants.
Introduction and objective of a cohort study on dietary intake of 21 food groups and 5-year changes in waist circumference (abdominal obesity), motivated by inconsistent prior macronutrient findings.

Methods: cohort of 22,570 women and 20,126 men aged 50-64 at baseline, using a 192-item food frequency questionnaire, adjusting for BMI and confounders such as smoking, sport, and alcohol, analyzed with multiple linear regression.

Results for women: waist circumference change was inversely linked to red meat, vegetables, fruit, butter, and high-fat dairy, and positively linked to potatoes, processed meat, poultry, and snack foods.

Results for men: red meat and fruit were inversely associated and snack foods positively associated with 5-year waist change; sex differences were found for vegetables, high-fat dairy, and processed meat.

Conclusions: a diet low in fruit and red meat and high in snack foods predicted larger waist gains in both sexes; in women, low vegetables, butter, and high-fat dairy plus high poultry, potatoes, and processed meat were likely determinants.
Final sentence of the conclusions, summarizing that processed meat, poultry, and potatoes intake in women were likely determinants of subsequent waist gain.

Introduction of the review on viral obesity: states obesity is multifactorial, is usually attributed to lifestyle, and notes recent evidence linking obesity to viral infections, with animal findings on adenovirus-36 (insulin sensitivity, glucose uptake, leptin changes).

Continues the animal-model evidence: lists other viruses linked to increased obesity in animals (canine distemper, Rous-associated virus 7, scrapie, Borna disease virus, SMAM-1, other adenoviruses) and states the review's aims of testing viral infection as a cause and discussing mechanisms.

States the review's purpose (whether viral infection may cause obesity) and mechanisms by which viruses could produce obesity, then begins the conclusion that a link between obesity and viral infection is supported.
Conclusion: a viral-obesity link cannot be ruled out, but epidemiologic studies are needed to establish causality and assess implications for obesity management and prevention.
Introduction and study background: prior chicken research on avian adenovirus SMAM-1 and the screening of 52 obese humans in Bombay for SMAM-1 antibodies via AGPT.
Methods and grouping: AGPT antibody screening results, splitting subjects into SMAM-1-positive (P-AGPT, n=10) and negative (N-AGPT, n=42) groups for comparison.
Results on anthropometrics: P-AGPT subjects had higher bodyweight and BMI than N-AGPT subjects, with reported means and p-values, and lower serum cholesterol and triglycerides begin.
Results on blood lipids and antigen evidence: P-AGPT cholesterol and triglyceride values versus N-AGPT values, and cross-reactivity between two positive subjects' sera suggesting shared antigens.
Chicken embryo inoculation experiments: sera from the two positive subjects produced SMAM-1-compatible lesions, unlike N-AGPT sera, and the study's concluding summary of evidence begins.
Conclusion: the combined findings of obesity, SMAM-1 antibodies, lower blood lipids, and embryo-infecting viremia suggest SMAM-1 or a similar human virus may contribute to human obesity.

Introduction to infectobesity: motivates studying infectious etiology of obesity amid rising obesity and health care costs, noting infection as an unusual causative factor; the chapter overview begins here.

Reports that about 10 adipogenic pathogens (viruses, scrapie agents, bacteria, gut microflora) were identified in the past two decades, some linked to human obesity without established causation; previews the chapter's coverage of hosts, symptoms, and pathogenesis.

States the chapter's scope (natural hosts, signs and symptoms, pathogenesis of adipogenic microbes) and argues that infectobesity, if relevant to humans, would be a novel and significant concept warranting new research.
Concluding aim: a new infectious-etiology perspective could drive research into unknown pathogens contributing to human obesity and into preventing or treating obesity of infectious origin.
Abstract of a study on adenovirus infection in chickens, describing experimentally verified excess fat accumulation (adiposity) despite lower weight gain, not explained by food intake differences.

Continuation of the abstract on adenovirus-infected chickens: naturally infected birds showed similar adiposity, and serum cholesterol and triglycerides were significantly lower than controls, marking a first-reported link between adenovirus infection and adiposity relevant to obesity research.
Concluding sentence of the abstract stating that the adenovirus-adiposity association may aid understanding of obesity, completing the claim of a first-time demonstration in chickens.

Introduction of a study on human liver DHFR activity: it frames the wide use of folic acid in clinical trials against the fact that only tetrahydrofolate and its derivatives carry out folate functions, and notes folic acid must first be reduced by DHFR.

Core finding: the study's sensitive assay shows human liver DHFR reduces folic acid at well under 2% of the rate seen in rat liver at physiological pH, with human samples from donors or surgery (n = 6).

Key result on variability: human liver DHFR activity differs almost 5-fold across samples, unlike rats, and the limited conversion of synthetic folic acid raises concerns for high-dose clinical trials.

Implication and conclusion: saturation of DHFR will likely limit benefits of high-dose folic acid, especially in people with below-average enzyme activity, consistent with reports of unmetabolized folic acid in plasma and urine.
Final fragment of the abstract's conclusion, ending the sentence that links the low conversion rate to reports of unmetabolized folic acid in plasma and urine.

Opening evidence list from a document arguing that non-anaemic pregnant women should not take iron supplements; covers iron-deficiency anaemia risks and an iron-supplementation trial linking supplementation to low birth weight and maternal hypertension.

Middle of the same document's evidence list on iron supplementation in pregnancy; covers a trial of supplemented women showing high haemoglobin at 28 weeks linked to preterm birth and low birth weight, and a link between high maternal haemoglobin and low birth weight.

Final part of the document's evidence list on iron supplementation in pregnancy; ends with the practical recommendation that pregnant women with haemoglobin above trimester-specific thresholds (11 g/100 ml in the 1st and 3rd trimesters, 10.5 g/100 ml in the 2nd) should not take iron supplements.

Abstract-style excerpt on maternal iron absorption in early pregnancy, citing a murine teratogenicity finding and iron's oxidative (hydroxyl radical) properties, and proposing study of first-trimester iron supplementation and miscarriage or fetal abnormalities.
Concluding sentence of the same passage, stating the research need: whether first-trimester iron supplementation is associated with miscarriage or fetal abnormalities.

Opening of an article on caffeine during pregnancy: introduces caffeine as the most widely ingested active substance (in coffee, tea, soft drinks, cocoa/chocolate, medications) and why its health effects are of public and scientific interest.

Middle of the article on caffeine in pregnancy: explains that the scientific community is concerned about caffeine's possible adverse health effects, identifies pregnant and reproductive-aged women as at-risk groups needing advice on moderating caffeine, and states the article's aims.

Closing of the introduction to the article on caffeine in pregnancy: the article will review the latest evidence on caffeine intake in pregnancy and give practical recommendations for obstetrician-gynecologists providing peripartum care.

Abstract of a Japanese prospective cohort study (Shizuoka elderly cohort) on green tea consumption and mortality; this chunk covers the purpose and the methods, describing the 14,001 randomly selected elderly participants aged 65-84 and their questionnaires.

Methods and early results of the Shizuoka elderly green tea cohort: follow-up from December 1999 to March 2006, 12,251 subjects analyzed, 64,002 person-years, 1,224 deaths, and a 71.6% follow-up rate.

Main results of the Shizuoka green tea cohort: multivariate hazard ratios for CVD mortality comparing 7+ cups/day with under 1 cup/day, overall and by sex (men and women), with 95% confidence intervals.

Findings and conclusions of the Shizuoka green tea study: no inverse association with overall cancer mortality, but an inverse dose-response link with colorectal cancer mortality; green tea is linked to lower all-cause and CVD mortality.
Final conclusion of the Shizuoka elderly green tea cohort abstract, suggesting green tea may have protective effects against colorectal cancer.
Introduction of a review on tea (Camellia sinensis) and tea polyphenols for obesity prevention; sets out the obesity burden (>20% of US adults) and the case for dietary prevention agents.
Continues the introduction: laboratory studies show green/black tea may prevent obesity, but mechanisms are unclear, human intervention results are mixed, and caffeine's role is unestablished.
Introduction passage noting emerging evidence of adverse effects from high-dose tea polyphenols, and why toxicity matters given their translation into dietary supplements.
States the review's aims: critically evaluate evidence for tea in obesity prevention, assess proposed mechanisms against polyphenol bioavailability, and review toxicity of high-dose tea polyphenols.
Closing statement of the introduction, hoping the review will identify gaps for further study and spur research on tea and obesity as a public health issue.
Introduction to green tea as a diet-based cancer prevention strategy, its anti-carcinogenic and anti-mutagenic activity, and its main polyphenol components (EGCG and related catechins).

Continuation of the introduction: green tea's anti-carcinogenic and anti-mutagenic effects and the polyphenols (EGCG, epicatechin, epicatechin-3-gallate, epigallocatechin) responsible for its pharmacological actions.

Green tea's antioxidant effects against oxidative stress, its immune-enhancing role on humoral and cell-mediated immunity, its potential in inflammatory disorders, and the start of the discussion on EGCG's chemopreventive mechanisms.

Mechanisms of EGCG's cancer chemopreventive action: inducing apoptosis and growth arrest, altering cell cycle regulators, activating killer caspases, suppressing NF-kB, and promoting IL-23-dependent DNA repair and cytotoxic T cell activity.

EGCG blocking carcinogenesis by modulating signal transduction pathways tied to proliferation, transformation, inflammation and metastasis, and the review's stated aims covering green tea chemistry, antioxidant and immunopotentiating properties.

Review's scope: the chemistry, antioxidant potential, immunopotentiating properties and anticancer mode of action of green tea, showing its chemopreventive potential against colon, skin, lung, prostate, and breast cancers.

Abstract opening of a study on tea (Camellia sinensis) methanolic leaf extract testing inhibition of hydrolytic venom enzymes from Naja naja kaouthia and Calloselasma rhodostoma snakes, linked to local tissue damage.

Continuation of the abstract summarizing the extract's inhibition of phospholipase A2, proteases, hyaluronidase, and L-amino acid oxidase in vitro, plus reduced hemorrhagic and dermonecrotic effects in vivo.

Concluding sentence of the abstract proposing that the extract's protective effect against snake venom local tissue damage stems from complexation and chelation between venom proteins and the extract's phenolic compounds.
Introduction and background of a meta-analysis on tea consumption and type 2 diabetes risk, stating the study's objective and noting that prior epidemiologic findings were inconsistent.

Methods section describing the systematic literature search (PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane through November 2008), English-language restriction, exclusion of type 1 diabetes and animal studies, and random-effects pooling of nine cohort studies.
Results overview: nine cohort studies with 324,141 participants and 11,400 incident type 2 diabetes cases, follow-up 5 to 18 years, and the start of the summary adjusted relative risk finding.

Key findings: the overall pooled RR of 0.96 (95% CI 0.92-1.01) showed no significant protective association, while stratified analysis found tea intake of 4 or more cups per day associated with RR 0.8 (95% CI 0.7-0.93).
Stratified results for sex and follow-up duration showed no significant associations, and the conclusion that drinking 4 or more cups of tea daily may lower type 2 diabetes risk.
Final fragment of the document's text ending with the phrase 'type 2 diabetes.', closing the meta-analysis conclusion sentence.

Study design and population: cross-sectional Ohsaki Cohort 2006 analysis of 25,078 Japanese adults aged 40-64 on green tea intake and tooth loss, with methods using multivariate logistic regression and tooth-count cut-offs (10, 20, 25).
Main results begin: consuming at least 1 cup/day of green tea is linked to lower odds of tooth loss, following a threshold pattern; this chunk introduces the men's analysis.

Male-specific adjusted odds ratios for tooth loss (cut-off <20 teeth) by green tea frequency, with the reference at under 1 cup/day and ORs of 0.82, 0.82, and 0.77 for higher intakes, each with 95% CIs.
Women's and other cut-off results were similar to men's; conclusion that green tea consumption is associated with decreased odds of tooth loss.
Copyright footer of the 2010 Elsevier Inc. article (all rights reserved).
Introduces the survey of US-marketed chocolate and cocoa products, its aim to analyze procyanidin flavan-3-ol monomers, oligomers, and polymers, and the six product categories sampled.

Describes the composite samples and the analytical measures used: % fat, % nonfat cocoa solids, ORAC antioxidant level, total polyphenols, epicatechin, catechin, total monomers, and procyanidin oligomers/polymers.
Reports the gram-basis ranking of epicatechin and catechin across product categories and the two types of monomer/oligomer profiles found within categories.
Presents the correlation results, with epicatechin strongly correlated to % nonfat cocoa solids (R²=0.834) and N=2-5 oligomers also well correlated.

Gives weaker catechin-to-% NFCS correlation (R²=0.680) and similar correlations of epicatechin and oligomers with total polyphenols, plus the start of the calculated percent cacao correlation discussion.
Covers the lesser but still good correlation with calculated percent cacao and introduces the principal component analysis that separates products into five classes.
Describes PCA groupings of antioxidant activity, total polyphenols, and flavanol measures, noting catechin and % fat separate, and motivates the epicatechin-to-catechin ratio analysis.
Reports the >5-fold variation in epicatechin:catechin ratio and begins the procyanidin per-serving results, ranging from cocoa powder to chocolate syrup.

Gives the per-serving procyanidin range (227.34 mg for cocoa powder down to 25.75 mg for chocolate syrup) and states the discussion scope: comparison to other studies, flavanol bioavailability, and processing effects on catechin.
Final fragment completing the discussion sentence about how processing may affect catechin levels in commercial products.

Introduction and methods opening of a case-control study on soy intake and breast cancer risk in Asian American women (Chinese, Japanese, Filipino descent), motivated by higher U.S. breast cancer rates and migration effects.

Study methods detailing the population-based case-control design across San Francisco-Oakland, Los Angeles, and Oahu, with participant numbers and response rates for cases and controls interviewed about diet and cultural practices.

Methods continued: maternal interviews about daughters' childhood exposures for subset with U.S.-resident mothers, plus the proportion of premenopausal participants at diagnosis, followed by the start of the results.

Main results giving multivariate relative risks and trend p-values for highest vs. lowest tertiles of childhood, adolescent, and adult soy intake, with the childhood association's consistency across races, sites, and birthplaces.

Results on westernization adjustment, which weakened adolescent and adult soy associations but not the childhood effect, followed by the start of the discussion summarizing soy's link to lower breast cancer risk.
Discussion conclusion stating that childhood soy intake shows the strongest protective effect and proposes soy as a hormonally related, early-life exposure affecting breast cancer incidence.

Introduction and rationale of the LACE study on soy isoflavone intake and breast cancer recurrence risk among breast cancer survivors, stating the hypothesized hormonal and non-hormonal mechanisms and the aim to examine effects by hormone receptor status, menopausal status, and tamoxifen use.
Methods of the LACE cohort study: 1954 female breast cancer survivors diagnosed 1997–2000, prospectively followed for 6.31 years with 282 recurrences ascertained.

Methods for exposure and analysis in the LACE study: soy isoflavone intake measured with modified Block and soy food frequency questionnaires about 23 months post-diagnosis, and recurrence risk estimated by multivariable delayed-entry Cox proportional hazards models yielding hazard ratios and 95% CIs.

Results of the LACE study showing suggestive trends toward reduced recurrence with higher daidzein and glycetin intake quintiles among postmenopausal women and tamoxifen users, with P-for-trend values around .05–.10.
Key result of the LACE study: postmenopausal women on tamoxifen with the highest daidzein intake had about a 60% lower recurrence risk versus the lowest intake (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.21–0.79, P = .008).

Conclusion of the LACE soy isoflavone study: intake at levels comparable to Asian populations may reduce recurrence risk in tamoxifen-treated women without impairing tamoxifen efficacy, though larger prospective confirmation is needed before dietary recommendations.
Final sentence of the LACE study conclusion stating that further large prospective studies are required before soy intake recommendations can be given to breast cancer survivors.

Opening of the abstract on soy food and breast cancer: introduces isoflavones as phytoestrogens and states the aim of studying adolescent and adult soy intake in 73,223 Chinese women from the Shanghai Women's Health Study.

Methods and early results from the Shanghai Women's Health Study: a validated food-frequency questionnaire assessed adult and adolescent diet, 592 incident breast cancer cases over 7.4 years of follow-up were analyzed with Cox regression, and adult soy consumption begins to be linked to lower risk.

Main result on adult soy intake and premenopausal breast cancer: inverse association by soy protein or isoflavone intake (P for trend < 0.001), with adjusted relative risks for the highest versus lowest quintile of 0.41 for soy protein and 0.44 for isoflavones.

Results on adolescent soy intake and breast cancer: high adolescent soy consumption is linked to reduced premenopausal breast cancer risk (RR 0.57), and women with consistently high soy intake across adolescence and adulthood show substantially lower breast cancer risk.

Null postmenopausal finding and conclusion of the soy-breast cancer abstract: no significant association for postmenopausal breast cancer, and the large prospective cohort provides strong evidence of a protective effect against premenopausal breast cancer.
Final fragment of the abstract's conclusion, completing the statement that soy food intake protects against premenopausal breast cancer.

Introduction and study design of the NIH-AARP cohort analysis examining physical activity intensity and life-period timing in relation to postmenopausal breast cancer risk, including the 118,899-woman sample.

Methods detail: exposure definitions for light and moderate-to-vigorous activity across historical life periods (ages 15-18, 19-29, 35-39) and the recent past 10 years, self-reported at baseline, with 4287 incident cases over 6.6 years of follow-up.

Main results: Cox regression findings showing that more than 7 hours/week of recent moderate-to-vigorous activity is linked to a 16% lower postmenopausal breast cancer risk (RR 0.84), with the association persisting after BMI adjustment.

Secondary results and conclusion start: null associations for historical moderate-to-vigorous activity and for light activity at any life period, no variation by tumor characteristics, and the opening of the conclusion about recent but not historical activity.

Final conclusion: high recent moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, but not historical activity, is associated with lower postmenopausal breast cancer risk, with more precise recall of recent activity offered as a possible explanation.

Study overview: six-month randomized controlled trial of aerobic exercise in older adults with amnestic mild cognitive impairment at a VA Puget Sound clinical unit, with objectives on cognition, Alzheimer-related biomarkers, and sex as a predictor of response.
Participant and intervention details: 33 adults (17 women) aged 55-85 with amnestic MCI, randomized to high-intensity aerobic exercise or a stretching control group.

Intervention protocol: supervised aerobic exercise at 75-85% heart rate reserve for 45-60 min/day, 4 days/week for 6 months, versus stretching controls kept at or below 50% heart rate reserve; baseline and post-study glucometabolic, treadmill, and DXA fat assessments.

Measurement schedule and outcomes: blood collection and cognitive testing at baseline, month 3, and month 6; main outcomes include executive and memory test batteries and fasting plasma insulin, cortisol, BDNF, IGF-I, and beta-amyloids 40 and 42.

Main results summary: six months of high-intensity aerobic exercise produced sex-specific effects on cognition, glucose metabolism, and HPA axis and trophic activity despite comparable fitness gains and body fat reduction.

Results by sex: in women, exercise improved executive function tests, increased glucose disposal during the metabolic clamp, and lowered fasting insulin, cortisol, and BDNF; in men, exercise raised IGF-I and improved only Trails B.
Conclusions: rigorous controlled evidence that aerobic exercise is a potent nonpharmacologic intervention improving executive control in older women at high risk of cognitive decline.
Interpretation: the sex-based cognitive response difference may be explained by sex-based differences in glucometabolic and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis responses to aerobic exercise.

Opening of a short review arguing that copper toxicity is the main cause of the rising epidemic of mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease in aging populations, written for a Journal of the American College of Nutrition special issue honoring Stanley Wallach and Pearl Small.

Describes the epidemic's recent emergence (over the last 50-60 years), its near absence a century ago, and its restriction to developed countries using copper plumbing, which the author links to environmental exposure to copper.

Explains the proposed mechanism: dietary organic copper is handled safely by the liver, whereas inorganic copper from drinking water (copper pipes) and copper supplements bypasses the liver and enters the blood's free copper pool.

States that this free blood copper may cross the blood-brain barrier, and previews the review's assembly of animal and human evidence linking copper toxicity to Alzheimer's disease and cognitive loss.
A lone period closing the final sentence of the document's abstract-style summary of the copper toxicity hypothesis; carries no independent content.

Opening of a document arguing that farmed fish consumption, recommended for omega-3 benefits, could transmit prions from BSE-infected cows to humans and cause variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Introduces the health rationale and the safety concern about aquaculture.

Continuation and conclusion of the document's concern that farmed fish may transmit infectious prions from BSE-infected cows to humans, causing variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Completes the sentence begun in the first chunk and states the hypothesized risk.
Introduces TSEs and the central pathogenic event: accumulation of abnormal PrPSc from host cellular PrPC, which must be expressed for prion propagation; notes little is known about TSEs in fish.
States the study's aim: gilthead sea bream orally challenged with brain homogenates from BSE-infected cow or scrapie-infected sheep, with prior fish TSE research being scarce.

Reports that challenged fish showed no clinical disease at two years, but brains had neurodegeneration and PrP-positive deposits detected with sea bream PrP antibodies; uninfected controls were normal.
Compares the two inocula: deposits formed faster and more extensively with BSE than scrapie, with many deposits proteinase K-resistant.

Describes the plaque-like aggregates as congophilic and birefringent (amyloid-like), and raises public health concerns about prion-challenged fish, especially with BSE, given aquaculture's role as a protein source.
Concludes that contamination of farmed fish with mammalian PrPSc or development of prion disease in farmed fish is alarming and needs further evaluation.

Introduction to CA-MRSA: its global concern (especially in the USA), the need for epidemiological definitions distinguishing CA-MRSA, healthcare-associated community MRSA, and HA-MRSA, and the role of Panton-Valentine leukocidin.

Discussion of PVL prevalence in CA-MRSA isolates from North America and Europe, the debated role of PVL in pathogenesis, and how most CA-MRSA lineages differ from HA-MRSA, with some lineages (ST1, ST5, ST8, ST22) shared by both.

Specific lineages: CA-MRSA ST8 (USA300) prevalent in the USA and reported in Europe, and CA-MRSA ST80 widespread in Europe, whose oxacillin heteroresistance means cefoxitin-based assays are recommended for detection.
Epidemiological conclusion: CA-MRSA infections appear much less frequent in Europe than in the USA, with patients having particular predispositions and low social status at greatest risk in the USA.

Opening portion of a short abstract reporting a study of 41 children with gastrointestinal complaints who were found to have community-associated Clostridium difficile infection via routine screening over 3 years, and who responded to metronidazole treatment.
Concluding sentences of a short abstract arguing that community-associated C. difficile is on the rise, can present with atypical disease, and may therefore be misdiagnosed.

Introduces C. difficile as a major hospital-associated human pathogen and lists three reasons for concern about it as a foodborne threat: community-associated infection, detection in food animals and food, and isolate similarity across animals, food, and humans.

States that C. difficile is widely found in food animals and food, including key human-infection strains (ribotype 027/NAP1/toxinotype III and ribotype 078/toxinotype V), but that it is unclear whether eating contaminated food causes colonization or infection.
Lists open questions about C. difficile in community-associated diarrhoea: the source when it contaminates food, the infective dose, and whether ingesting contaminated food is linked to disease.

Concludes that the pathogen's importance in human disease and emergence in the community call for careful evaluation of all exposure sources including food, though establishing food's role in infection is difficult.
Final sentence restating that determining food's potential role in C. difficile infection may be difficult.

Introduces the study's aims and scope: a 2006 survey of Clostridium difficile prevalence across swine age and production groups in a Texas integrated operation, based on 131 isolates from 1008 samples (13% overall prevalence).

Reports prevalence of C. difficile by production group, showing suckling piglets had the highest rate (50.0%), followed by lactating sows and farrowing barn effluent (23.8%), with lower rates in nursery, pork products, grower-finisher, and breeding stock.
Describes molecular characterization of the 131 isolates: toxin A/B gene PCR positivity, the 39 bp tcdC deletion, toxinotype V classification, and universal presence of the binary toxin gene cdtB.

Summarizes antimicrobial susceptibility results: all isolates resistant to cefoxitin, ciprofloxacin, and imipenem, sensitive to metronidazole, vancomycin and related agents, with mixed patterns for clindamycin, ampicillin, tetracycline, and chloramphenicol.
Concludes with a seasonal finding: significantly more isolates were recovered from September to February than from March to August.

Abstract opening of a review on the efficacy of environmental and hand cleaning products in preventing Clostridium difficile–associated diarrhea (CDAD); describes the literature search (MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane) and rates the evidence as level II.

Main message section arguing that reducing CDAD in geriatric rehabilitation units supports patient function and community discharge, and that environmental control of C difficile spores by staff and visitors is a key secondary prevention strategy.

Conclusion stating that chlorine-releasing agents outperform detergents at killing C difficile spores, with no level I evidence yet showing they reduce CDAD rates; introduces hand-washing as the recommended transmission-reduction strategy.

Remaining conclusion on hand hygiene: alcohol gels do not inactivate C difficile spores, yet increased alcohol hand gel use has not been linked to higher CDAD rates; then the start of the French abstract (Résumé) with its objective.

French résumé (translation of the abstract) covering the objective of assessing cleaning products for environmental and hand hygiene against C difficile diarrhea (DDCD) and the search methods and level II evidence rating.

French translation of the main message: reducing DDCD in geriatric rehabilitation units is essential for patient function and community reintegration, and environmental control of C difficile spores by staff and visitors is a secondary prevention priority.
French translation of the conclusion: chlorine-releasing agents are more effective than detergents against C difficile spores, with no level I evidence that they affect DDCD rates.
French translation of the hand hygiene conclusion: hand-washing is the recommended strategy, alcohol gels do not inactivate spores, and greater alcohol gel use has not increased DDCD rates.
Final fragment of the French résumé, concluding that increased alcohol gel use was not associated with a rise in DDCD rates; the end of the document.

This chunk is the complete abstract of a 2007 US study on Clostridium difficile in retail meat, reporting that 42% of cooked and uncooked meat sampled in Tucson, Arizona carried toxigenic strains (ribotype 078/toxinotype V and 027/toxinotype III), and suggesting food may contribute to interspecies C. difficile transmission.
Study of Clostridium difficile prevalence in retail chicken from Ontario, Canada; introduces the aims and the sampling methods (legs, thighs, wings bought from retail outlets, selective culture).
Reports the results: C. difficile isolated from 12.8% of chicken samples (thighs, wings, legs compared, P = 0.19), all isolates ribotype 078, and all positives found only by enrichment culture.
Conclusions and significance: C. difficile is relatively common in retail chicken at low levels, the first report of C. difficile in chicken meat, raising concern about food as a source of infection.

Closing implications: contamination with human-infection-associated strains raises food-source concerns; the relevance is unclear, but food should be investigated as a possible source of C. difficile infection.

Opening of the document on MRSA in food production animals: introduces the MRSA CC398 clone, reported since 2005 colonizing pigs, veal calves, broiler chickens and infecting dairy cows, and notes unclear prevalence in pigs.

Middle section on MRSA CC398 in livestock and food: covers unclear colonization and reservoir status in other livestock, uncertain risk from contaminated meat, and the main concern that the clone can spread to humans.

Concluding discussion of MRSA CC398 implications: its spread to humans may complicate human healthcare MRSA control, infections are less reported than carriage so pathogenic potential needs study, and the clone's origin and evolution are unknown.
Final fragment of the document, completing the last sentence stating that the origin and evolution of the MRSA CC398 clone remain unknown.

Introduction and methods of a U.S. pilot study on MRSA carriage in swine and swine workers, describing prior Netherlands/Canada research and the sampling design (nares swabs from 299 pigs and 20 workers across Iowa and Illinois farms).

Methods continued: laboratory typing approaches for MRSA isolates (PFGE with SmaI and EagI, MLST, SCCmec and pvl PCR), followed by the start of the results on overall MRSA prevalence in swine (49%) and workers (45%).

Results detailing MRSA prevalence by age in production system A's swine (36% in adults to 100% in 9- and 12-week-old animals), worker prevalence on that system (64%), and the absence of MRSA on production system B.

Typing results: PFGE with SmaI was non-typeable, EagI showed clonal isolates unrelated to common Iowa human USA types (USA100/300/400), and MLST identified the isolates as ST398; the conclusions begin by noting high swine colonization on one midwestern system.

Conclusions of the study: swine MRSA colonization was very common on one midwestern production system, suggesting livestock may be an important MRSA reservoir, with ST398 as the only strain found on that farm and further multi-farm studies underway.
Closing sentence of the document noting that ongoing studies are examining MRSA carriage rates on additional farms.

This chunk opens the study's abstract, describing a survey of 120 retail meat samples from 30 Baton Rouge, LA grocery stores. It reports S. aureus and MRSA prevalence by meat type (pork vs. beef) and the count of MRSA-positive samples.

This chunk completes the abstract's findings on MRSA from Louisiana retail meats. It describes the six MRSA isolates as two clonal strain types: one carrying Panton-Valentine leucocidin and typed as PFGE USA300, the other typed as USA100.

Introduces the study on alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) efficacy against Clostridium difficile spores, noting alcohol's ineffectiveness and the aim to measure spore retention on hands and transfer by physical contact.

Methods: nontoxigenic C. difficile spores applied to palms of 10 volunteers; compares three ABHRs and chlorhexidine soap-and-water against plain water rubbing, with plate stamping cultures and a handshake transfer test.

Results baseline: plain water rubbing reduced palmar C. difficile spore counts by 1.57 log10 CFU/cm2, which was set as the zero reference point for comparing other products; also describes the handshake transfer test setup.

Comparative results: chlorhexidine soap washing reduced spores by 0.89 log10 CFU/cm2 relative to water, and the ABHRs Isagel, Endure, and Purell showed small reductions with their respective P values.

Statistical comparisons: no significant differences among ABHRs, only Endure differed from water rubbing (P = .040); after ABHR use, handshaking transferred about 30% of residual spores to recipients.
Conclusions: soap and water removes C. difficile spores significantly better than ABHRs, and residual spores are readily transferred by handshaking after ABHR use.
Final fragment of the conclusion, stating that residual spores are readily transferred by a handshake after alcohol-based hand rub use.

Introduction and study aim: describes rising concern about colibacillosis in caged layer flocks, the lack of prior risk-factor research, and the design comparing 20 outbreak flocks with 20 healthy control flocks on non-infectious factors.

Methods and setup: data on management, biosecurity and housing were collected from 20 affected and 20 control layer flocks, analysed with multiple logistic regression, with the first key finding on distance to the nearest poultry farm (OR=0.16).

Key results: greater distance to the nearest poultry farm (per km) and larger cage volume per hen (per litre) were each associated with reduced odds of colibacillosis outbreaks (ORs 0.16 and 0.75), leading to the conclusion.
Conclusion: the final sentence states that inter-farm distance and hen density in cages are important non-infectious risk factors for colibacillosis outbreaks in layer hen flocks.

Opening of the abstract introducing E. coli as a well-known, frequently isolated bacterium and listing underappreciated aspects of its role as an extraintestinal pathogen, starting with the variety of infections it causes.

Continuation of the list of underappreciated features: the high incidence, morbidity, mortality and costs of extraintestinal E. coli syndromes, intestinal versus extraintestinal pathogenic potential of strain groups, and rising antimicrobial resistance.

Framing of E. coli extraintestinal infections as an underappreciated endemic problem amid sensationalized health news, followed by the scale of burden: billions in health care costs, millions of work days, and hundreds of thousands of deaths yearly.
Conclusion of the abstract stating the annual toll of E. coli extraintestinal infections and calling for new treatments and prevention measures to improve outcomes and reduce disease burden.

Introduces the study's aim and methods: screening of 7,258 NARMS retail meat E. coli isolates (2002–2007) for Shiga toxin genes, plus virulence-gene testing of 1,275 isolates from 2006 for other diarrheagenic E. coli.
Reports the main STEC results: 17 stx-positive isolates (16 from ground beef, 1 from pork chop) and their stx1/stx2 gene distribution, with the serotype list beginning the description.
Describes characterization of the 17 STEC isolates: the 10 serotypes, absence of eae, presence of EHEC hlyA in seven, Vero cell cytotoxicity, and starting stx2 sequence findings.
Details further findings: Stx2d variant identified in five isolates, PFGE subtyping yielding 14 distinct patterns, and 2006 results showing 11 atypical EPEC and 3 STEC isolates.
Concludes that retail meat, mainly ground beef, harbors diverse STEC strains and that atypical EPEC in retail meat is a potential human health concern.

Introduction and methods of a 2001-2003 Minneapolis-St. Paul retail food survey of 1648 items testing for antimicrobial-resistant and extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC), using selective culture, disk diffusion, PCR, and O serotyping.
Methods continuation (assays used to isolate resistant E. coli and define ExPEC traits) and the first result: E. coli prevalence rising from miscellaneous foods (9%) across food categories.

Key results showing prevalence gradients by food type (miscellaneous foods, beef or pork, poultry) for E. coli contamination, antimicrobial resistance, and ExPEC contamination, all statistically significant (P<.001).

Multivariate findings that natural-food store beef, pork, and poultry had lower risks of contamination and resistance, indirect evidence of on-farm resistance selection, and four food ExPEC isolates matching human clinical isolates by O antigen and genomic profile.
Conclusion that retail foods may spread antimicrobial-resistant E. coli and ExPEC community-wide, positioning ExPEC as a newly recognized group of medically significant foodborne pathogens.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending with the phrase 'foodborne pathogens' describing ExPEC's potential medical significance.

Introduction and study design of a food reservoir study for E. coli causing urinary tract infections, describing the three isolate sources (UTI patients, retail meat, restaurant/ready-to-eat foods) collected 2005–2007.

Methods and sample sizes: E. coli isolates from women with UTI, retail meat, and restaurant foods are characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility, O:H serotype, and four genotyping methods, yielding 17 clonal groups shared across sources.

Key findings and conclusion: E. coli from retail chicken (O25:H4-ST131, O114:H4-ST117) and honeydew melon (O2:H7-ST95) match or closely resemble human UTI isolates, supporting foodborne transmission of community-acquired UTIs.
Final sentence of the abstract, concluding that food reservoirs or foodborne transmission contribute to spread of E. coli causing common community-acquired UTIs.

Study of bowel function (transit time, stool frequency, stool form) in 51 subjects on omnivorous, vegetarian, or vegan diets, showing vegans had more frequent defecation and softer stools despite similar transit times.

Findings on how dietary fibre relates to bowel function measures (shorter transit, more frequent and softer stools with higher fibre), plus sex differences (men passed softer, larger faeces) and menstrual cycle effects in women.

Concluding findings: during the luteal phase women had harder stools and longer transit times, and mean transit time correlated most strongly with faecal form, a result suggested to be practically important.
Introduces keriorrhea, the oily anal leakage caused by eating deep-sea fish like escolar and oilfish that store indigestible wax esters, as an opening to the document on fish-induced keriorrhea.

Defines keriorrhea as oily, water-free rectal discharge (called 'oily diarrhea' or 'orange oily leakage' in media) and notes that outbreaks have been reported across continents, following the description of wax ester accumulation.

Lists additional symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea) attributed likely to anxiety or panic, and reports that escolar and oilfish are banned from import and sale in Italy, Japan, and South Korea, with a call for rapid detection.
Concludes the document by stressing that rapid detection of escolar and oilfish is needed for proper labeling and public safety before and after keriorrhea outbreaks.

Opening of a document on hepatitis E epidemiology: introduces HEV as a zoonosis and anthroponosis, names pigs, boars, deer as reservoirs, and meat, offal, and shellfish as transmission vehicles, with dietary/culinary practices affecting inactivation before ingestion.

Continues the hepatitis E epidemiology discussion: covers how cooking and food preparation affect HEV inactivation, the environmental route of infection from enteric shedding by humans and animals, and the conclusion that zoonotic HEV spreads via both foodborne and environmental routes.
Final sentence of the hepatitis E epidemiology passage, summarizing that zoonotic HEV transmission can occur through both foodborne and environmental routes.

Introduces Hepatitis E virus as a zoonotic pathogen with pigs as reservoirs, and describes the study's screening of 127 commercial pig liver packages from US grocery stores using a universal RT-PCR assay.

Reports the screening results: 14 of 127 livers were HEV RNA-positive, all genotype 3 by sequence and phylogenetic analysis, and introduces the follow-up pig infection study testing whether these PCR-positive livers contained infectious virus.

Presents the animal infectivity results: two of three PCR-positive liver homogenates infected pigs, shown by faecal shedding, viraemia and seroconversion, concluding that grocery pig livers are HEV-contaminated with infectious virus and pose a food-borne public-health risk.
Closing sentence of the abstract stating the public-health concern about food-borne HEV infection from contaminated commercial pig livers.

Introduction and aims of the study: it revisits a 1985 finding linking national pig-meat consumption to chronic liver disease mortality, proposes hepatitis E via pig meat as a possible mechanism, and sets out to test the association with 1990s data.

Methods section: describes the regression approach and data sources, including WHO data on CLD mortality, alcohol use, and HBV/HCV seroprevalence for 18 developed countries (1990-2000), and UN data on pig-meat and beef consumption.
Univariate results: alcohol and pig-meat consumption are associated with CLD mortality, while beef consumption and HBV/HCV seroprevalence are not.

Effect sizes: each 1 litre per capita rise in alcohol adds over 1.6 CLD deaths per 100,000, and each 10 kg rise in per capita pork consumption adds roughly 4-5 deaths per 100,000; multivariate results show alcohol, pig meat, and HBV (but not HCV) are independently associated.

Conclusion: pig-meat consumption stays independently associated with CLD mortality in developed countries in 1990-2000, but the underlying mechanism, such as hepatitis E transmission, still needs further study.
Introduces HEV in swine: background on its rarity in North America, worldwide ubiquity in pigs, and zoonotic transmission risk via raw or undercooked meat; sets up the slaughterhouse study.
Covers Canadian context (no documented HEV outbreak, genotype 3 found in swine) and states the study objective: measure HEV viral load across 9 pig sample types from 43 slaughtered pigs.
Describes methods: feline calicivirus used as process/inhibition/amplification control in the FCV/HEV multiplex TaqMan RT-qPCR, and the overall detection result of 14 of 43 animals positive.

Reports per-tissue HEV detection counts (lymph node 11/43, bladder 10/43, liver 9/43, bile 8/43, faeces 6/43, tonsil 3/43, plasma 1/43), no positive loin, and viral loads of 10^3 to 10^7 copies/g in liver and bile.
Closing fragment of the results: the viral load range (10^3 to 10^7 copies/g) for positive liver and bile samples, followed by the publication copyright (Crown Copyright 2010, Elsevier B.V.).

Abstract-style excerpt comparing thermal stability of hepatitis E virus (HEV) and hepatitis A virus (HAV) in heated fecal suspensions (45–70 °C), noting HEV is less heat-stable than HAV and may survive rare-cooked meat temperatures.
Concluding fragment of the same study on hepatitis E virus heat stability, stating that some HEV would likely survive the internal temperatures of rare-cooked meat, a food safety implication.

Study of sporadic hepatitis E in Hokkaido, Japan: patient exposure history to pig liver (9 of 10 cases) and the initial RT-PCR survey of 363 retail raw pig liver packages, 7 positive for HEV RNA (1.9%).

Molecular characterization of swine HEV isolates from retail pig liver packages: genotype III/IV classification, and sequence identity (100% for swJL145; 98.5-100% for swJL234 and swJL325) to HEV isolates from Hokkaido patients HE-JA18 and HE-JA4.
Conclusion of the Hokkaido hepatitis E study linking swine HEV in pig liver to human infections, supporting the finding that inadequately cooked pig liver may transmit hepatitis E virus to humans.

This opening chunk introduces the document's topic: clinical and ecological evidence linking HPV-related tumors to dietary factors, and presents a case report of a 19-year-old man whose urethral condyloma regressed after abstaining from high fried pork intake while on interferon gamma.

This closing chunk summarizes the ecological evidence and conclusion: international correlations link higher pork intake with cervical cancer incidence, and the authors suggest pork meat or pork-associated dietary factors may contribute to HPV-related diseases.

Introduces the Baltimore union poultry cohort study: an earlier mortality follow-up to 1989 of 2,639 union members exposed to poultry-borne oncogenic viruses, here updated to 2003 for 2,580 exclusive poultry workers, with the comparison method (proportional mortality and SMRs vs. US population).
Describes the statistical comparison of cancer mortality in poultry workers against the US general population, by race/sex group and whole cohort, and begins listing the cancer sites found in excess.

Lists the cancers found in excess among poultry workers (oral cavity, pharynx, nasal/sinus, esophagus, rectosigmoid/rectum/anus, liver and biliary, myelofibrosis, lymphoid leukemia, multiple myeloma) and introduces the viral and fume etiologic hypothesis.

States the proposed etiologic explanation that oncogenic poultry viruses and fume exposure may account for some excess cancers in poultry workers, and calls for larger studies controlling for confounders.
Closing fragment stating that larger studies are needed to determine the significance of the findings.

Abstract opening of a prospective cohort study on cancer incidence in British vegetarians: describes the study population (61,566 men and women split into meat eaters, fish eaters, and vegetarians), average follow-up of 12.2 years, and total incident cancer counts by diet group.

Abstract Methods and start of Results: explains that relative risks were estimated with Cox regression, stratified by sex and recruitment protocol, and adjusted for age, smoking, alcohol, BMI, physical activity, and (in women) parity and oral contraceptive use; then introduces the finding of significant between-group heterogeneity in cancer risk.

Core Results of the vegetarian cancer incidence study, giving relative risks versus meat eaters for stomach cancer and ovarian cancer in fish eaters and vegetarians, with 95% confidence intervals and heterogeneity P values.

Continuation of the Results: relative risks compared with meat eaters for bladder cancer and for lymphatic and haematopoietic cancers in fish eaters and vegetarians, plus the overall all-cancer relative risks beginning in fish eaters.

Final Results and Conclusion of the abstract: overall all-malignant-neoplasm relative risks for fish eaters and vegetarians, and the conclusion that incidence of some cancers may be lower in fish eaters and vegetarians than in meat eaters.

Introduces the NIH–AARP Diet and Health Study cohort (491,163 participants, 1995–2003) and its 338 incident acute myeloid leukemia cases, analyzed with Cox models; begins reporting smoking hazard ratios versus never smokers.
Continues the smoking results: hazard ratios by former and current smoking status and cigarettes per day (≤1 vs >1 pack/day), then begins the meat intake finding.

Reports that higher meat intake (fifth vs first quintile) raised AML risk, with a borderline trend p-value, and that meat cooking method and doneness showed no clear effects; also starts the coffee drinking finding.
Summarizes the remaining dietary findings: non-coffee drinkers had higher AML risk, fruit and vegetable intake were unrelated, and the study concludes smoking and meat intake are AML risk factors.
Final fragment of the abstract's last sentence, completing the conclusion that smoking and meat intake are risk factors for acute myeloid leukemia.

Opening chunk of an abstract from a population-based pancreatic cancer case–control study (532 cases, 1,701 controls). It states the study aims on sweets, sweetened/unsweetened beverages, and sugars, and notes that results are reported for men, women, and combined because associations differed by sex.

Continues the Methods/Results. Reports that among men, total and specific sweets were linked to higher pancreatic cancer risk, with odds ratios and 95% CIs for total sweets, sweet condiments, chocolate candy, and other mixed candy bars at 1+ servings/day versus none/rarely.

Covers the beverage and sex-specific findings. Sweets showed no consistent link among women, and sweetened beverages were not associated with risk. Low-calorie soft drinks were associated with risk in men only, while other low/non-caloric drinks such as coffee, tea, and water showed no association.

Summarizes the sugar analysis and the conclusion start. Among lactose, fructose, and sucrose, only lactose was associated with pancreatic cancer risk (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.5–2.7, extreme quartiles). The conclusion begins by saying the results offer limited support for the sugar/sweets hypothesis.
Final sentence of the abstract's conclusion. The authors say the findings give only limited support to the hypothesis that sweets or sugars increase pancreatic cancer risk.

Introduction and methods of the NIH-AARP cohort study on dietary fat and exocrine pancreatic cancer, describing the population (308,736 men, 216,737 women), the 124-item food frequency questionnaire, and Cox regression adjustments.

Methods continued: hazard ratio and confidence interval calculation via Cox models with covariate adjustment for energy, smoking, BMI, and diabetes, followed by the start of the results describing average follow-up of 6.3 years.

Results opening: case counts of exocrine pancreatic cancer in men (865) and women (472), with incidence rates per 100,000 person-years, and the start of the highest-vs-lowest quintile total fat comparison.

Results on fat subtypes: multivariable hazard ratios for total, saturated, and monounsaturated fat intake and pancreatic cancer risk, with incidence rates and trend p-values; polyunsaturated fat showed no association.

Results on fat food sources: saturated fat from animal sources had the strongest association with pancreatic cancer risk, and red meat and dairy product intakes were each significantly associated with increased risk.

Specific hazard ratios for red meat (1.27) and dairy (1.19), followed by the conclusion that animal-origin dietary fat is associated with higher pancreatic cancer risk in this large prospective cohort.

Opening of a Japanese nationwide study on chronic pancreatitis (CP) and pancreatic cancer (PC) epidemiology: 2002 patient counts for CP and PC deaths, plus alcoholic pancreatitis as the most common CP type.
Middle section on risk factors: smoking as an independent CP risk factor, cancer risk rising during CP, and alcohol versus smoking as contributors to PC via CP.
Discussion of diet and lifestyle: rising PC incidence linked to animal fat intake, shared lifestyle between CP and PC patients, and gene-environment interaction.
Concluding recommendation that improving drinking, smoking, and nutrition habits may reduce the risk of both chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer.

Opening of an abstract-style review of pancreatic cancer epidemiology: states the disease burden and prognosis, the review's aim of assessing risk and protective exposures, and the Medline literature search up to April 2007.

Summarizes the review's findings on established and suggestive risk factors: consistent evidence for family history and smoking, and positive associations with diabetes and chronic pancreatitis, with other exposures having inconsistent or limited evidence.

Lists the weaker or inconsistent associations found in the review, including positive links to red meat, sugar, fat, BMI, gallstones, and H. pylori, protective effects of parity, folate, aspirin, and statins, and no evidence for alcohol or coffee.

Concludes that many exposure associations need clarification through better epidemiologic studies with precise exposure measurement, confounder adjustment, and detailed dietary food preparation and consumption data, to help reduce this fatal disease.
Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that such research is important for reducing the incidence of pancreatic cancer, which is a fatal disease.

Abstract opening of a 2009 Italian hospital-based case-control study on macronutrients, fatty acids, cholesterol and pancreatic cancer risk, describing the study design and sample size (326 cases, 652 controls).

Continuation of the methods description: control selection (frequency-matched by sex, age, study centre) and the multiple logistic regression models (conditioned on age, sex, centre) used to estimate odds ratios and confidence intervals.

Main results from the abstract: positive association for animal protein (OR=1.85, highest vs lowest quintile, p for trend=0.039) and negative association for sugars (OR=0.52, p for trend=0.003), with adjustment covariates listed.

Remaining results and conclusion: non-significant inverse associations for vegetable proteins and polyunsaturated fatty acids, and the conclusion that a diet low in animal proteins and rich in fruit-derived sugars may protect against pancreatic cancer.
Trailing copyright notice (Elsevier Ltd., 2009) at the end of the abstract, a fragment of the final chunk with no substantive content.
Introduction and background of a study on serum cholesterol and prostate cancer risk, motivated by prior statin and cholesterol findings, setting up the PCPT analysis.
Methods section describing the PCPT cohort: 5,586 placebo-arm men aged 55+, enrolled 1993-1996, enzymatic serum cholesterol at entry, 1,251 confirmed cancer cases.
Methods on logistic regression odds ratios comparing low (<200 mg/dL) versus high (≥200 mg/dL) cholesterol across total cancer and Gleason grade groups, transitioning into the results.
Results: men with low cholesterol had reduced odds of Gleason 8-10 cancer (OR=0.41), with no association for overall cancer, Gleason 2-6, or Gleason 7; begins the conclusion.
Conclusion: prospective findings support lower high-grade prostate cancer risk with low cholesterol, and call for further investigation of cholesterol metabolism in prostate cancer etiology.

Introduction and methods of a study on statin-associated myopathy: vastus lateralis biopsies from 83 patients (44 with myopathy, 19 statin users without myopathy, 20 never-users), including groups by current versus discontinued statin therapy.
Methods continued: definition of muscle injury as 2% or more damaged muscle fibres on biopsy, RT-PCR gene expression analysis of candidate myocyte injury genes, and description of the control groups.

Results summary: muscle injury found in 25 of 44 myopathy patients and 1 non-myopathy patient, and a note that only one structurally injured patient had markedly elevated creatine phosphokinase (above 1950 U/L).

Key findings and interpretation: ryanodine receptor 3 expression significantly upregulated in biopsy-confirmed structural damage (1.7, SEM 0.3), and persistent statin myopathy reflects structural muscle damage.
Conclusions: normal circulating creatine phosphokinase does not exclude structural muscle injury, and ryanodine receptor 3 upregulation suggests an intracellular calcium leak.

Introduction and study design of a prospective population-based cohort of 774 community-dwelling older adults examining statin use, muscle mass, muscle function and falls risk (background, aim, design, methods start).

Study population and measures: 774 older adults examined at baseline and follow-up, with outcomes %appendicular lean mass, leg strength, leg muscle quality (specific force) and falls risk; also reports statin user prevalence at baseline (19%) and follow-up (23%).

Longitudinal results: baseline statin use predicted increased falls risk over 2.6 years and a non-significant trend toward higher %ALM; statin users at both time points showed the start of the reduced leg strength finding.

Cross-sectional and persistent-use comparisons: statin users at both time points had lower leg strength and leg muscle quality and a trend toward higher falls risk versus controls, and users at both baseline and follow-up had reduced strength and quality versus those who stopped statins.
Conclusion: statin use may worsen age-related declines in muscle performance and increase falls risk without reducing muscle mass, and these effects may be reversible after stopping statins.
Final fragment of the conclusion stating that the effect of statin use on muscle performance and falls risk may be reversible with cessation.

Introduction to statin-associated muscle symptoms: myalgia and weakness in patients on HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, with normal or marginally raised creatine kinase and no reported structural muscle defects, motivating the study of the mechanism of statin-induced muscle damage.

Study methods and key claim: skeletal muscle biopsies from statin-treated and non-statin-treated patients were examined by electron microscopy and biochemical methods, showing clear muscle damage in statin-treated patients who were asymptomatic.

Description of the damage pattern in statin-treated patients: slight overall damage with a characteristic pattern of T-tubular system breakdown and subsarcolemmal rupture, and reproduction of these abnormalities by in vitro cholesterol extraction from muscle fibres.

Conclusions of the study: findings support the idea that statin-induced cholesterol lowering itself contributes to myocyte damage, and that the specific lipid/protein organization of skeletal muscle cells makes them particularly vulnerable; includes the 2006 Pathological Society copyright notice.
Publication copyright and attribution footer for the article (2006, Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland, published by John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.).

Introduction to the review: establishes dyslipidemia as a cardiovascular risk factor, notes diet as first-line therapy, and motivates examining plant-based diets given prospective evidence on ischemic heart disease mortality.

Review purpose and scope: states the investigators' aim of assessing how plant-based diets (especially vegetarian and vegan) modify plasma lipid concentrations, and that the review covers the published literature.

Key findings on diet types and results: 27 trials were included; combination diets (vegetarian/vegan plus nuts, soy, or fiber) produced the largest LDL cholesterol reductions (up to 35%), followed by vegan and ovolactovegetarian diets.

Comparative results and conclusion: diets allowing small amounts of lean meat gave smaller reductions in total and LDL cholesterol, and the authors conclude that plant-based interventions effectively lower plasma cholesterol.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, completing the statement that plant-based dietary interventions lower plasma cholesterol concentrations.

Introduction and study aim: kiwifruit intervention on lipids, antioxidants, and lipid peroxidation in hyperlipidemic adults in Taiwan, motivated by CVD being a leading health problem and fruit/vegetable protective effects.
Study design and participants: 43 hyperlipidemic adults (13 men, 30 women) consumed two kiwifruit daily for 8 weeks, with anthropometric measurements and the intervention's timeline.

Methods and measured outcomes: fasting blood sampling before, at 4, and at 8 weeks for lipid panel (total cholesterol, triacylglycerol, LDL-C, HDL-C), plus vitamins C and E, MDA+4-HNE, and LDL oxidation lag time, with the start of results on lipid changes.

Lipid results: no significant change in triacylglycerol, total cholesterol, or LDL-C over 8 weeks, but HDL-C significantly increased and LDL-C/HDL-C and total cholesterol/HDL-C ratios significantly decreased.

Antioxidant and oxidation results: vitamin C and vitamin E rose significantly; LDL oxidation lag time and MDA+4-HNE changed significantly at 4 and 8 weeks, with the study's conclusion that kiwifruit may benefit antioxidant status and CVD risk factors.
Concluding statement: regular kiwifruit consumption may benefit antioxidative status and cardiovascular disease risk factors in hyperlipidemic subjects.
Introduction and study objective: testing whether adding strawberries (antioxidant source) to a cholesterol-lowering dietary portfolio improves its antioxidant effect in 28 hyperlipidemic subjects.

Study design: 28 hyperlipidemic subjects on the soy/viscous fiber/plant sterol/nut portfolio were randomized in a 1-month crossover trial (2-week washout) to strawberry supplements (454 g/d) or oat bran bread (65 g/d, ~2 g beta-glucan) as control.
Key result on oxidative damage: strawberry supplementation produced a greater reduction in LDL oxidative damage, measured as TBARS in the LDL fraction (P = .014).

Lipid outcomes and palatability: LDL cholesterol and total/HDL cholesterol ratio reductions were maintained at the end of the strawberry period (-13.4% and -15.2%, P < .001), similar to oat bran values, and strawberries improved diet palatability.

Conclusion: strawberries reduced LDL oxidative damage while preserving blood lipid reductions and enhancing palatability, suggesting added fruit can improve diets aimed at lowering coronary heart disease risk.
Introduction of the Oslo Health Study cola/soft drink study: rationale (sucrose from soft drinks may affect lipids), study design, and sample size of 14,188 subjects with soft drink intake data.

Study population details (both sexes, three age groups) and the main finding that cola intake frequency is linked to higher HDL decrease and TG increase in both sexes, with no sugar-related differences noted.
Results contrasting colas with non-cola soft drinks: significant cola associations with serum lipids, no consistent non-cola associations, and no differences by sugar presence or absence.

Multivariable regression methods: cola-lipid associations remained significant (p < 0.001) after adjusting for 13 confounders, listing covariates such as demographics, lifestyle, diet, and medication.
Conclusion of the Oslo Health Study: self-reported cola intake frequency, unlike other soft drinks, is negatively associated with HDL and positively associated with TG and LDL.

Abstract opening of a randomized controlled trial on whole-grain ready-to-eat oat cereal (viscous beta-glucan fiber) combined with a weight-loss diet, examining effects on LDL cholesterol and cardiovascular risk markers versus diet alone; includes objective and study design.
Continuation of the abstract's design and subjects section: a randomized parallel-arm trial in 204 overweight/obese adults with LDL 130-200 mg/dL, with 144 included in the per-protocol main analysis.

Intervention details: participants received two daily portions of oat cereal (3 g/day oat beta-glucan) or energy-matched low-fiber control foods within a ~500 kcal/day reduced-energy diet program with portion control and physical activity.

Main outcome measures (lipids, waist circumference, skinfold thickness, body weight at baseline through week 12) and the start of the results, reporting the larger LDL cholesterol reduction with oat cereal versus control.
Results on secondary lipids: total and non-HDL cholesterol decreased significantly more with oat cereal, while HDL and triglyceride changes did not differ between the two groups.

Results on body weight and waist size: weight loss did not differ between groups, but waist circumference fell more with oat cereal, and LDL, total, and non-HDL reductions appeared as early as week 4.
Conclusions that whole-grain RTE oat cereal within a weight-loss program favorably affected fasting lipid levels and waist circumference, followed by the start of the copyright statement.
Copyright and publisher notice (2010 American Dietetic Association, Elsevier Inc.) closing the abstract.

Introduction and aims of a Nepal study (Kathmandu Medical College) on gallstone disease: background on cholelithiasis as a common surgical disorder, with the objective of determining the prevalence of gallstone types and correlating them with clinical findings.

Methods section describing the sample: gallstones from 80 patients who underwent cholecystectomy, collected January 2005 to May 2006 at the Pathology Department of Kathmandu Medical College Teaching Hospital, with detailed patient history taken.

Results and conclusion on demographics and risk factors: most affected age group is 30-39 years (32.5%), female predominance (M:F = 1:3.2), and higher prevalence among non-vegetarians (vegetarian:non-vegetarian ratio 1:9); the stone analysis method is also indicated at the start of this chunk.
Final results on stone composition: mixed stones are most common (78.75%), followed by cholesterol stones (12.5%), brown pigment stones (7.5%), and black pigment stones (1.25%).
