Opening of an abstract on cholesterol gallstone disease: epidemiology (10-15% prevalence in Western adults, a leading cause of hospital admission) and the need for coordinated hepatobiliary and GI function to prevent biliary cholesterol crystallisation.

Continuation of the abstract's introduction: identifying metabolic and transcriptional pathways regulating biliary lipid secretion, and the review's focus on gene regulation of cholesterol absorption, synthesis, catabolism and secretion in gallstone pathogenesis.

Middle of the abstract summarising the review's scope: physical-chemical mechanisms of gallstone formation in bile, the roles of gallbladder and intestine, and remaining knowledge gaps and gene-targeted therapy potential.
Final sentence of the abstract, closing on gene targeting as a potential therapeutic approach for cholesterol gallstone disease.

Case report of a 62-year-old woman with a migrated fish bone causing an acute left upper neck lump; initial rigid esophagoscopy was negative and CT revealed the foreign body in the subcutaneous layer.

Management and outcome of the migrating fish bone case: CT showed penetration through the left sternocleidomastoid with neck emphysema, removal via a 1-cm neck incision under general anesthesia, and discharge on hospital day 5 without complications.
Discussion comparing this case with the literature: migrating fish bones usually cause neck lumps weeks to months after ingestion with stable conditions, unlike this rare presentation.
Key distinguishing feature of the case: the neck lump appeared only 1 day after fish ingestion and was accompanied by acute toxic symptoms, contrasting with typical delayed, stable presentations.

This chunk opens the document's abstract, describing the objective (evaluating evidence on homeopathy's effectiveness), the data source (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews searched January 2010), and the study selection criteria yielding six included reviews.

This chunk, from the abstract's data extraction section of a review of Cochrane homeopathy reviews, lists what was extracted from the six reviews and begins enumerating the conditions they covered (cancer, ADHD, asthma, dementia).

This chunk, from the abstract's later sections, completes the list of conditions covered by the six Cochrane homeopathy reviews, notes that narrative synthesis was used due to heterogeneity precluding meta-analysis, and states the main conclusion.
This final chunk is the concluding sentence of the abstract, stating that the available Cochrane reviews of homeopathy show no effects of homeopathic medicines beyond placebo.

This chunk opens the study on recurrent aphthous ulcers (RAU): its objective of measuring serum antibodies to gliadin and cow's milk proteins (CMP) by ELISA, and the design of 50 RAU patients versus 50 healthy controls.

This chunk gives the methods (ELISA for serum IgA/IgG to gliadin and IgA/IgG/IgE to CMP) and the first results: antigliadin IgA and IgG were not significantly higher in RAU patients than controls, with P values reported.

This chunk reports the main positive finding: anti-CMP IgA, IgG and IgE were significantly higher in RAU patients than controls (P < 0.005, < 0.002, < 0.001), plus counts of patients with raised IgA or IgG and combined immunoreactivity to CMP.

This chunk finishes the patient counts (16 of 50 with IgA, IgG and IgE reactivity to CMP) and gives the conclusion that high serum anti-CMP IgA, IgG and IgE levels are strongly associated with clinical RAU manifestations.

Introduces a 2009 randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial testing antioxidant-rich purslane against placebo for oral lichen planus (OLP), describing the 37 biopsy-proven patients (20 purslane, 17 placebo) and the 3-month treatment and assessment schedule.

Describes the outcome measures (visual analog scale and clinical lesion type/size assessments) and the clinical response rates: about 83% of purslane patients showed partial to complete improvement, versus 17% partial improvement, 73% no response, and 10% worsening in the placebo group.

Reports the VAS-based results: all purslane-treated patients showed partial to complete response, while controls had 71% partial response, 15% no response, and 14% worsening, with a significant VAS decrease at study end (p < 0.001).

Concludes that purslane is clinically effective for OLP, with no serious side effects in either group, suggesting it may be a favorable alternative treatment; includes the 2009 John Wiley & Sons copyright notice.
Final fragment of the document containing the closing phrase on purslane as a favorable alternative OLP treatment and the 2009 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd. copyright line.

Introduces the earlier report that fasting followed by a one-year vegetarian diet improved rheumatoid arthritis, and states this study's aim: measuring how biochemical and immunological laboratory variables changed during that clinical trial.

Reports the main lab results after one month: the vegetarian group showed significant drops in platelets, leukocytes, calprotectin, IgG, IgM RF, C3-activation products, C3 and C4, while omnivores showed no significant change.

Compares groups: 14 of 15 variables favored vegetarians, but only leukocyte count, IgM RF, C3 and C4 differed significantly; laboratory markers fell markedly in vegetarians whose clinical symptoms improved, indicating reduced inflammation.

Argues the leukocyte decline occurred in all vegetarians regardless of clinical response, so it likely reflects the diet itself rather than lower disease activity; begins stating agreement with the clinical trial findings.
Concludes that the laboratory findings match the clinical trial: dietary treatment can reduce disease activity in some rheumatoid arthritis patients.

Introduction to the document: defines rheumatoid arthritis as synovial joint inflammation, previews a review of dietary components linked to it, and describes an ecological study comparing female RA prevalence across countries with national dietary supply data.

Key quantitative findings: fat from meat and offal (two years before prevalence data) showed the strongest association with female RA prevalence across eight countries (r² 0.877, P<0.001), with meat and offal correlations nearly as high as fat.

Temporal evidence: between 1968 and 1978, as meat was added to European national diets, RA effect indices changed in parallel, with correlations stronger for meat than for fat; this leads to the hypothesis that meat and offal drive RA inflammation.

Conclusion and scope: the author states that meat and offal may be a major contributor to RA inflammation and says the short review will examine data linking meat consumption to RA and candidate mechanisms such as fat, iron (Fe) and nitrite.

Opening of a randomised controlled trial abstract on fasting plus a one-year vegetarian diet for rheumatoid arthritis, describing the health-farm intervention group (27 patients) and its initial 7-10 day subtotal fast.
Describes the diet protocol after the fast (gluten-free vegan for 3.5 months, then lactovegetarian) and introduces the control group of 26 patients on an ordinary diet at a convalescent home.

Reports the four-week outcomes in the fasting/diet group, listing significant improvements in joint measures, pain, morning stiffness, grip strength, inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, WBC), and HAQ score, and notes the control group's pain-score change.

States that only pain score improved in the control group, that diet-group benefits persisted at one year, and that the whole-course evaluation favored the diet group across all indices, concluding it may supplement conventional RA treatment.
Final sentence of the abstract concluding that the vegetarian dietary regimen is a useful supplement to conventional medical treatment for rheumatoid arthritis.

Abstract opening of a study on a strict uncooked vegan diet in rheumatoid arthritis patients: describes the randomized design (vegan group n=16 vs omnivorous control n=13) and the initial finding that serum total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, and phospholipids decreased.

Results on serum sterols: cholestanol and lathosterol levels fell but their ratios to total cholesterol were unchanged, and plant sterols diverged, with campesterol decreasing while sitosterol increased.

Key quantitative finding: the vegan group had a markedly higher sitosterol:campesterol ratio than controls (1.48 vs 0.72, P<0.001), and the chunk notes that campesterol exceeding sitosterol is normal in omnivores, explained by lower sitosterol absorption and esterification.
Concluding interpretation: the authors suggest the strict uncooked vegan diet alters the relative intestinal absorption rates of campesterol and sitosterol and/or their biliary clearance.

Introduces the review's motivation: clinical interest in fasting followed by a vegetarian diet for rheumatoid arthritis, and the search methods (MEDLINE and reference checking) used to find fasting studies in RA.

Describes the review's inclusion criteria and findings: controlled studies with at least three months of post-fasting follow-up were pooled; 31 RA fasting reports were found, but only four controlled studies met the long-term criterion.

States the main result and conclusion: pooled long-term data showed a statistically and clinically significant benefit, suggesting fasting plus vegetarian diet may help RA, while calling for more randomised long-term trials.
Final fragment of the conclusion, calling for more methodologically convincing randomised long-term studies to confirm the benefit of fasting followed by vegetarian diet in RA.

Introduces the earlier one-year trial in which rheumatoid arthritis patients received fasting followed by an individualized vegetarian diet, and defines the diet responder and nonresponder groups; this is the opening of the two-year follow-up study.

Describes the follow-up design: after the trial, patients could change diet or medication, were re-examined about a year later, and change from baseline was compared among diet responders, diet nonresponders, and omnivorous controls.

Reports the clinical outcomes that favored diet responders (pain, morning stiffness, HAQ index, tender and swollen joints, Ritchie index, ESR, platelets) and notes significant between-group differences for all clinical variables except grip strength.
States that laboratory and anthropometric variables did not differ significantly between groups, and that at follow-up all responders but only half of nonresponders still followed the diet.
Concludes that a subgroup of rheumatoid arthritis patients benefits from dietary manipulation and that the improvement is sustained over a two-year period.

Study design: introduces a randomized trial of an uncooked, lactobacilli-rich vegan diet versus control in rheumatoid arthritis patients, covering subjective symptom relief, worsening after returning to an omnivorous diet, and adverse effects that led half the patients to drop out.

Objective outcomes: notes that the intervention's subjective benefit was not reflected in standard disease activity measures (HAQ, morning stiffness, pain scores), and that adverse effects like nausea and diarrhoea caused early withdrawal.

Composite and regression results: a composite index showed more intervention patients with 3-5 improved measures, and stepwise regression linked lower DAS disease activity to lactobacilli- and chlorophyll-rich drinks, higher fibre intake, and no need for gold, methotrexate, or steroids (R2=0.48, P=0.02).

Conclusions: summarizes that the uncooked vegan, lactobacilli-rich diet reduced subjective rheumatoid arthritis symptoms and suggests daily living lactobacilli may also benefit objective disease measures.

Final concluding sentence: suggests that large daily amounts of living lactobacilli may positively affect objective measures of rheumatoid arthritis, a tentative claim beyond the trial's main findings.

Introduction to the living food (LF) uncooked vegan diet study on antioxidants and rheumatic/inflammatory disorders, opening with plant-based antioxidant sources and the rationale for examining rheumatoid disease.

Describes what the LF diet consists of (berries, fruits, vegetables, roots, nuts, sprouts) and reports serum increases in carotenoids (beta and alpha carotene, lycopene, lutein) and vitamins C and E in LF subjects.

Reports that LF subjects had roughly 3-fold higher berry intake and correspondingly greater intake of polyphenols (quercetin, myricetin, kaempferol) than omnivorous controls, and notes the diet's high fibre content.

Covers urinary excretion of lignan-derived polyphenols (enterodiol, enterolactone, secoisolariciresinol) rising on LF, and clinical results in fibromyalgia patients who shifted to LF, with reduced joint stiffness and pain.

Summarizes rheumatoid arthritis patients' positive responses on the LF diet, supported by objective measures, and the correlation between RA improvement and day-to-day fluctuations in subjective symptoms.
Concludes that rheumatoid patients subjectively benefited from the antioxidant-, lactobacilli-, and fibre-rich vegan diet, with the benefit also seen in objective measures.
Introduces the RA dietary trial design: fasting 7-10 days, then a gluten-free vegan diet, then a lactovegetarian diet, in a controlled single-blind study of RA patients.
Reports the trial's main result: fasting/vegetarian group (27 patients) improved significantly on clinical and most lab measures versus the omnivorous control group (26 patients).

Describes the one-year follow-up reexamination, where diet responders showed significantly greater improvement than nonresponders and omnivores, and rules out psychological factors as the explanation.

Covers the mechanistic findings: the benefit was not explained by antibodies to food antigens or prostaglandin/leukotriene changes, but fecal flora differed between high- and low-improvement time points.
Concludes that some RA patients benefit from fasting followed by a vegetarian diet, suggesting dietary treatment may be a useful adjunct to standard RA therapy.

Abstract of a study on rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients: introduces the suspected dietary link to RA and states the primary aim (self-reported adverse food reactions) and secondary aim (relating dairy/wheat reactions to rectal challenge mucosal reactivity).

Methods section: a questionnaire on self-reported food reactions sent to 347 RA patients, rectal challenge with cow's milk protein and wheat gluten in 27 patients and 18 healthy controls, and the setup of the mucosal patch technique.

Methods and early results: the 15-hour challenge measures mucosal nitric oxide, myeloperoxidase, and eosinophil cationic protein; results begin with 27% of RA patients reporting food intolerance, especially to milk, meat, and gluten.

Results on mucosal reactivity: strong reactivity to cow's milk in 11% of patients, moderate reactivity to milk and gluten in 22% and 33%, and no relationship between self-reported reactions and mucosal reactivity.

Conclusions: perceived food intolerance is common in RA patients at rates similar to the general population, while mucosal reactivity to milk and gluten is rare and unrelated to perceived intolerance.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending the statement that mucosal reactivity to milk protein and gluten is unrelated to perceived intolerance to these proteins.

Introduces the study's objective, design (single-blind dietary intervention), and population: 24 free-living adults with rheumatoid arthritis on a 4-week very low-fat (~10%) vegan diet, with the methods for outcome assessment.

Describes outcome measurement methods: a blinded rheumatologist assessed RA symptoms before and after the study, biochemical measures and 4-day diet records were collected, and subjects had weekly diet instruction and compliance checks.

Reports the main results: significant drops in fat (69%), protein (24%), energy (22%), and rise in carbohydrate (55%), plus significant improvement in most RA symptom measures (except morning stiffness duration) and weight loss.

Gives the inflammatory marker results at 4 weeks, where CRP (16%) and RA factor (10%) decreases were not statistically significant and ESR was unchanged, followed by the conclusion that a vegan low-fat diet can significantly reduce RA symptoms in moderate-to-severe patients.
A final fragment completing the conclusion sentence, stating that switching to a very low-fat vegan diet can produce significant reductions in RA symptoms.

Introduces the rheumatoid arthritis trial background: clinical improvement after fasting and sustained improvement on vegan and lactovegetarian diets, plus the rationale that dietary fatty acids can modulate RA inflammation.

States the study's aim: analysing how switching to a vegetarian diet changes plasma phospholipid fatty acid profiles and relating those changes to RA disease activity; begins reporting reductions in 20:3n-6 and 20:4n-6 after the vegan diet.

Reports results: 20:3n-6 and 20:4n-6 fell after the vegan diet but returned to baseline on the lactovegetarian diet, and 20:5n-3 decreased after both vegan and lactovegetarian diets, with reported P values.

Concludes that fatty acid concentrations did not differ between diet responders and non-responders, so the fatty acid changes cannot explain the clinical improvement in RA patients on vegetarian diets.

Introduces the meta-analysis of RCTs on Rosa canina (rosehip) hip powder for symptomatic osteoarthritis treatment, stating the objective of estimating its pain-reducing efficacy and the inclusion criteria for trials (OA patients randomized to rosehip or placebo).

Describes the statistical methods: pain reduction as the primary outcome measured by standardized mean difference (effect size), responder analysis as odds ratios and number needed to treat, and REML mixed-effects meta-analysis models.

Reports the results of the three included studies (287 patients, median 3-month duration, all manufacturer-supported by Hyben-Vital International), comparing pain score reduction in rosehip powder (145 patients) versus placebo (142 patients).

Presents the pooled effect size (ES 0.37, 95% CI 0.13-0.60, P=0.002), homogeneity results (I²=0%) supporting a consistent effect across trials, and the responder odds ratio (OR=2.19) indicating roughly twice the likelihood of response with rosehip.

Gives the responder OR of 2.19 (P=0.0009) and corresponding number needed to treat of six (95% CI 4-13), then the conclusion that rosehip powder reduces pain, caveated by sparse data and suggesting possible use as a nutraceutical.
Concludes that rosehip's efficacy and safety require further evaluation and independent replication in larger, longer-term trials before firm recommendations can be made.

Abstract of a double-blind placebo-controlled RCT on standardised rose-hip (Rosa canina) powder for rheumatoid arthritis: study objective, design, randomisation to 5g/day rose-hip vs placebo for 6 months at Berlin and Copenhagen clinics, and outcome measures (HAQ primary; DAS-28, RAQoL, SF-12 secondary).

Continuation of the abstract's methods, naming the primary outcome (HAQ at 6 months) and secondary outcomes (DAS-28, physician global evaluation, RAQoL, SF-12, pain medication), then opening the results with the study population: 89 patients, 90% female, mean age and disease duration.

Abstract results on the primary outcome: HAQ-DI improved in the rose-hip group (0.105) versus worsened in placebo (0.039), adjusted p=0.032, plus the HAQ pain scale showing no significant group difference and a trend on the HAQ Patient Global Scale favouring rose-hip.

Abstract results on secondary outcomes: DAS-28 improvement in rose-hip versus placebo (p=0.056, moderate clinical relevance), physician global assessment significantly better with rose-hip (p=0.012), and the start of the RAQoL and SF-12 physical score findings.

Abstract remaining results and conclusion: RAQoL and SF-12 physical scores improved significantly with rose-hip, SF-12 mental score unchanged, pain medication intake equal across groups, per-protocol analysis confirmed findings, and the conclusion that RA patients may benefit from rose hip powder.
Final sentence of the conclusion (rose hip powder as additional RA treatment) and the publisher copyright notice (Elsevier GmbH, 2009), closing the abstract.

Introduction of the benzene-in-infant-carrot-juice study (DONALD, 2009): describes benzene as a heat-induced contaminant, its possible precursors in carrot juice (beta-carotene, phenylalanine, terpenes), and the motivation for a quantitative risk assessment given links to childhood leukaemia.

Methods summary of the benzene in infant carrot juice study: a quantitative risk assessment combining DONALD study food consumption data with survey data on benzene levels across juice categories, focused on infants.

Results and conclusions of the benzene in infant carrot juice study: infant exposures (3-12 months) of about 1-10 ng/kg bw/day, margin of exposure above 100,000, judged unlikely to pose a health risk, with recommendation to reduce carcinogens as low as reasonably achievable.

Concluding recommendation and copyright notice of the benzene in infant carrot juice study: improving sterilization conditions is the priority for reducing benzene contamination, followed by the Elsevier 2009 copyright statement.
Introduction/background of a 2009 Karger study on whether plasma beta-carotene validly reflects fruit and vegetable intake, motivating comparison of women on different long-term plant-food diets.

Methods section describing the study groups: women on an average Western diet (n=172), wholesome nutrition (n=238), or a raw food diet (n=104), with dietary and plasma beta-carotene compared across these groups.

Key results: mean dietary beta-carotene intake (5.5, 9.3, 14.7 mg/day) and multivariate-adjusted plasma beta-carotene (1.07, 1.65, 1.16 micromol/l) across Western, wholesome, and raw food diet groups, all p<0.001.

Results showing that for equal dietary beta-carotene intake, women on raw food or Western diets had lower plasma beta-carotene than those on wholesome nutrition (p<0.001 up to 20 mg/day), and fruit/vegetable intake did not predict plasma levels in raw food dieters.

Conclusions: plasma beta-carotene differed by diet group, highest with wholesome nutrition, and plasma beta-carotene may not reflect beta-carotene intake or fruit and vegetable consumption, so it is a poor biomarker in this population.
Final citation fragment with the publication year and publisher, 2009 S. Karger AG, Basel, closing the abstract.
Introduction and processing stage of a blueberry jam study: fresh berries made into sugar and sugar-free jams, with polyphenol and ORAC losses from processing, flavonols retained.
Storage effects on blueberry jams over 6 months: marked losses of anthocyanins and procyanidins with rising polymeric color, chlorogenic acid decline, flavonols and ORAC stable.

Storage temperature and sugar content effects on blueberry jams: 4 °C storage retains more anthocyanins, procyanidins and ORAC with lower polymeric color than 25 °C; sugar-free jams retain more anthocyanins late in storage; refrigeration recommended.
Concluding recommendation of the blueberry jam study: refrigerate blueberry jams to better retain polyphenolics and antioxidant capacity (continuation of the final sentence).
Introduction of a blueberry memory study: dementia prevalence rising, blueberry anthocyanins' antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuronal/glucose benefits motivating the research.
Study design: daily wild blueberry juice in nine older adults with early memory changes, with anthocyanin rationale for neuronal signaling and glucose disposal.
Results at 12 weeks: improved paired associate learning (p=0.009) and word list recall (p=0.04), plus trends for reduced depression (p=0.08) and lower glucose (p=0.10).

Placebo comparison with a demographically matched berry-placebo group from a companion trial showing comparable paired associate learning, and the conclusion that moderate-term blueberry supplementation may benefit cognition and warrants larger trials.
Closing conclusion calling for more comprehensive human trials to examine blueberries' preventive potential and neuronal mechanisms.
Introduction and background of an EPIC cohort study on fruit and vegetable intake and overall cancer risk, including methods aims (1992-2000 prospective analysis).
Methods section describing the EPIC cohort prospective analysis, dietary and lifestyle data collection, cancer incidence and mortality ascertainment, and Cox regression approach.
Methods continued: Cox regression HR and CI estimation, stratified analyses for tobacco- and alcohol-related cancers, then start of results with cohort size (142,605 men, 335,873 women).
Results: number of incident cancer cases (9604 men, 21,000 women) over median 8.7 years follow-up, crude incidence rates, and initial association findings for fruit and vegetable intake.
Main results with hazard ratios: fruit and vegetable combined (HR 0.97 per 200 g/d), total vegetables (HR 0.98 per 100 g/d), and weaker association for total fruits (HR 0.99 per 100 g/d).
Subgroup results: inverse vegetable association restricted to women, stronger risk reduction in heavy drinkers confined to smoking- and alcohol-related cancers, and start of conclusions.
Conclusion: a very small inverse association between total fruit and vegetable intake and cancer risk, with caution warranted given the small effect magnitude.

Introduction and aims of the apple skin antioxidant study: motivation (lipid oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids in foods) and the evaluation of phenolic composition and antioxidant properties of 21 apple genotypes.

Methods and phenolic results: lipid stabilizing ability tested in an aqueous methyl linolenate emulsion, and total phenolic concentrations (150-700 mg/100 g DW) measured by HPLC-MS/MS of methanolic skin extracts.
Antioxidant capacity results across the apple genotypes: Folin-Ciocalteu, FRAP, ORAC values and percent inhibition of methyl linolenate oxidation (73.8%-97.2%), showing variation among genotypes.

Conclusion of the apple skin study: crab apple varieties such as 'Dolgo' were the most effective inhibitors of polyunsaturated fatty acid oxidation, supporting apple skin as a natural food antioxidant source.
Introduces a study of antioxidant activities and phenolic profiles across 11 lentil cultivars grown in the northern US, including HPLC quantification and the CAA and PRSC assay methods.

Reports that cultivar Morton had the highest flavan-3-ols (catechin, epicatechin), total flavonoids, and antioxidant activity (PRSC and CAA), and begins listing the phenolic acids detected across lentils.
Lists the benzoic-type and cinnamic-type phenolic acids detected in all lentil cultivars, and names flavan-3-ols and luteolin as compounds found in every cultivar.
Identifies sinapic acid as the predominant phenolic acid and catechin and epicatechin as the predominant flavonoids, concluding that cultivars vary considerably in phenolic and antioxidant profiles.
Reports correlations: caffeic acid, catechin, epicatechin, and total flavonoids correlate with the peroxyl radical scavenging assay, and the cellular antioxidant assay correlates with ORAC.
Concludes that the findings may guide lentil breeding programs to develop lentils as functional foods.
Abstract opening of a study on V79-4 cells: H2O2 (1 mM) cytotoxicity, LDH release, ROS and superoxide scavenging tests of herbal tea extracts and flavonoids such as catechin and EGCG.
Results on cell viability after H2O2 treatment, protection of cells by catechin and EGCG against LDH release, and total catechin content of green tea versus other herbal teas.
Findings on the relative ranking of the four major tea catechins (EGCG > EGC > EC > C) and superoxide radical scavenging IC50 comparison showing green tea as the strongest antioxidant.
Concluding ranking of herbal teas by superoxide radical scavenging activity, listing black tea, dandelion, hawthorn, rose hip, and chamomile after green tea.

Abstract opening: background on yerba mate's antioxidant benefits versus reported genotoxicity and cancer risk, stating the study's aim to assess cyto- and genotoxicity of mate in human peripheral lymphocytes in vitro.

Abstract results: yerba mate extract causes concentration-dependent increases in apoptotic and necrotic cells and decreased nuclear division index; exposed lymphocytes show reduced rDNA transcription and more micronuclei.

Abstract findings on mechanism: FISH detected acrocentric signals in mate-induced micronuclei, suggesting aneugenic activity; this leads into the rationale for testing caffeine, a major mate constituent, separately.
Abstract conclusion: caffeine alone at the same concentrations was more potently cyto- and genotoxic, possibly explaining part of the adverse effects of yerba mate extract.

Introduction: background on LDL oxidation theory of atherogenesis, popularity of vitamin E antioxidant supplementation, and disappointing RCT and meta-analysis findings linking high-dose vitamin E to increased mortality.
Criticism of meta-analyses that found vitamin E harmful, and the authors' recent Markov-model study designed to avoid meta-analysis limitations.

Key result of the Markov-model study: vitamin E-supplemented individuals had 0.30 QALY (95% CI 0.21-0.39) less than untreated people, supporting that indiscriminate high-dose supplementation should not be recommended to the public.
Outline of the review's aims: examining recent studies showing vitamin E harms, proposed mechanisms for those harms, and studies of patient subgroups that benefited from supplementation.

Argument that although high-dose vitamin E is not beneficial on average, specific populations may benefit, creating the challenge of defining selection criteria for who should receive it, based on oxidative stress or specific diseases.
Conclusion: vitamin E is a 'double-edged sword' that should not be consumed until criteria predicting beneficiaries of high-dose supplementation are established; includes 2009 IUBMB copyright notice.
Closing copyright line (2009 International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Inc.) ending the document's abstract/summary text.

Introduction to a toxicology study of stevioside (sweetener from Stevia rebaudiana, used in Japan) and its aglycone steviol, listing the seven mutagenicity test types used (bacterial, mammalian cell, and mouse micronucleus assays).

Results summary: stevioside was non-mutagenic in all assays, while steviol gave dose-related positives in the Salmonella TM677 forward mutation assay and in CHL chromosomal aberration and gene mutation tests.

Details on metabolic activation: S9 liver fraction from PCB- or phenobarbital/5,6-benzoflavone-pretreated rats was required for steviol's mutagenicity and clastogenicity, and steviol was weakly positive in the umu test.

Negative results for steviol: reverse mutation assays across multiple Salmonella strains (TA97 through TA1537) and E. coli WP2 uvrA/pKM101, plus the Bacillus subtilis rec-assay, even with S9 activation.
Conclusion of the study: steviol was negative in the mouse micronucleus test, and the paper closes by discussing the genotoxic risk of steviol to humans.
Opening of a Stevia review abstract: notes its historical use as sweetener and medicine, and a systematic literature review of papers up to 2007 covering Stevia's functional and sensory properties.

Continuation of the Stevia review abstract: states that Stevia leaves have superior functional and sensory properties to other high-potency sweeteners, likely making it a major natural sweetener source, and identifies groups that benefit most (diabetics, calorie-conscious people, children).

Middle of the Stevia review abstract: describes Stevia as a small perennial shrub used for centuries as a bio-sweetener and to lower blood sugar, and begins describing the sweetening compound stevioside.
Closing of the Stevia review abstract: stevioside is a zero-calorie natural herbal sweetener that is 100-300 times sweeter than table sugar.

Opening of a Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee report on food additive safety, introducing the purpose (ADIs and identity/purity specifications) and the general principles for toxicological evaluation of flavouring agents and additives.

Continues the report's introduction and begins listing the specific food additives evaluated (asparaginase, calcium lignosulfonate, ethyl lauroyl arginate, paprika extract, and others), including dietary exposure assessments.

Lists the remaining named additives (phospholipase C, phytosterols, polydimethylsiloxane, steviol glycosides, sulfites) and begins enumerating the 10 groups of related flavouring agents, such as aliphatic branched-chain alcohols, aldehydes and acids.

Enumerates further flavouring agent groups, including aliphatic linear alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehydes, aliphatic secondary alcohols and ketones, alkoxy-substituted allylbenzenes, and esters of aliphatic primary alcohols.

Continues the list of flavouring agent groups, covering furan-substituted aliphatic compounds, miscellaneous nitrogen-containing substances, and monocyclic and bicyclic secondary alcohols and ketones, and starts hydroxy- and alkoxy-substituted benzyl derivatives.

Finishes the flavouring group list (benzyl derivatives and menthol-related substances) and begins the summary of specification revisions for additives such as canthaxanthin, carob bean gum, chlorophyllin copper complexes, and guar gum.

Lists more revised specifications (Fast Green FCF, iron oxides, isomalt, Patent Blue V, Sunset Yellow FCF, trisodium diphosphate) and notes re-evaluations of flavourings 2-isopropyl-N,2,3-trimethylbutyramide and L-monomenthyl glutarate based on poundage data.
Closing sentence of the introductory summary, noting that annexed tables give the Committee's recommended intakes and toxicological evaluations for the additives considered.
Introduction of the study: background on anatoxin-a, a neurotoxin from cyanobacteria, and concerns about marketed cyanobacteria-containing dietary supplements (Spirulina/Arthrospira, Aphanizomenon).

Continuation of the background on supplement genera and the exposure risk from lack of quality control, followed by the study's aim: screening commercial cyanobacteria supplements for anatoxin-a using HPLC with fluorescence detection.
Methods and sample scope: confirmation of derivatized anatoxin-a by GC-MS, the total of 39 supplement samples analysed, and the start of the results statement.

Key findings and conclusion: 3 of 39 samples (7.7%) contained anatoxin-a at 2.50 to 33 µg/g, with the authors concluding that quality control of cyanobacterial supplements is needed to protect human and animal health.

Opening of the document introducing monosodium glutamate (MSG) as a food additive and the history of reported symptoms ('Chinese restaurant syndrome', 1968), based on anecdotal and small clinical studies.

Continues the background on MSG-attributed symptoms and states that MSG has been suggested as an aetiologic factor for asthma, urticaria, angio-oedema, and rhinitis; the review's stated scope begins here.

States the review's scope: critically assessing literature on MSG's role in 'Chinese restaurant syndrome', asthmatic bronchospasm, urticaria, angio-oedema, and rhinitis, and notes that decades of research found no clear, consistent link.
Concluding sentence of the abstract: despite early concerns, research has not shown a clear and consistent relationship between MSG ingestion and these conditions.
Abstract's objective and data sources section of a 2009-era systematic review on vitamin safety, adverse effects, and drug interactions, including the databases searched and literature date range.

Continues the data sources description (four online databases and reference-list searching, 1966 to October 2009) and begins the study selection criteria, emphasizing randomized controlled trials and clinically important adverse event and interaction data.

Data synthesis from the vitamin safety review: vitamin use prevalence in North America, documented toxicities and drug interactions, and the start of the contrast between minor vitamins and those with serious effects.

Data synthesis findings distinguishing vitamins with minor, reversible adverse effects (B vitamins, biotin, vitamin K) from fat-soluble vitamins A, E, D and water-soluble folic acid and niacin with serious toxicities, leading into the conclusions.

Conclusions of the vitamin review recommending that vitamins A, E, D, folic acid, and niacin be categorized as over-the-counter medications, with labeling requirements for toxicity, dosing, and upper intake limits, and the start of the recommendation on vitamin A.

Final conclusion sentence of the review stating that vitamin A should be excluded from multivitamin supplements and food fortificants, completing the regulatory recommendations on vitamin safety labeling.

Introduction and case presentation of a rare hypervitaminosis A case: intrahepatic cholestasis from 12 years of Herbalife shakes and multivitamins exceeding the recommended daily vitamin A intake, with deranged liver tests noted.

Diagnostic workup and outcome of the vitamin A toxicity case: cholestatic liver tests, a liver biopsy showing vitamin A toxicity features without fibrosis, and complete normalization of jaundice and alkaline phosphatase after stopping the supplements.

Concluding takeaway of the case report, stressing that clinicians should document non-prescribed dietary supplements and consider them in the cause of cholestatic liver disease, followed by the 2009 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces a food poisoning outbreak in three patients after eating liver of a large lutjanid fish, with symptoms like headache, nausea, and later skin peeling, and identifies the implicated species as Etelis carbunculus via genetic methods.

Describes the species identification methods (cytochrome b sequencing, PCR-RFLP) confirming Etelis carbunculus, and states that specimens of varying body weight were then collected to measure vitamin A in muscle and liver by HPLC.

Reports the vitamin A results: about 12 IU/g in muscle and roughly 9,844 IU/g in liver, and concludes from regression models that larger body and liver weight are associated with higher liver vitamin A.
Brief closing fragment completing the final sentence on regression findings linking body and liver weight to higher liver vitamin A levels in E. carbunculus.

Opening of the review's abstract: frames gastrointestinal symptoms and introduces the review's focus on gluten sensitivity as a possible cause of functional bowel disorder-like symptoms in some patients.

Continues the abstract with the review's proposed model for gluten-induced GI symptoms in functional bowel disorders and organic disease, and the hypothesis that gluten can cause FBD-like symptoms even without full celiac disease.
Middle of the abstract: discusses gluten sensitivity and post-infectious IBS as two triggers explaining part of the IBS spectrum, linking mucosal responses to luminal factors in FBDs.

Closing part of the abstract: proposes the HLA-DQ8 mouse model of gluten sensitivity for studying pre-inflammatory mucosal changes, and states the goal of clarifying host genotype, diet, and microbiota interactions in IBS-like symptoms.

Final sentence of the abstract: concludes that understanding how gluten causes symptoms in sensitive individuals will clarify gene-diet-microbiota interactions behind one of the most common GI conditions.

Abstract opening (Objective) of a 2009 study screening Alzheimer's, ALS, Huntington's, and control postmortem brain tissue for the cyanobacterial neurotoxin BMAA, noting cyanobacteria's freshwater, marine, and terrestrial habitats.

Background section explaining prior evidence for broad human BMAA exposure: earlier detection in Guam ALS/Parkinsonism-dementia patients and later in North American AD patients, motivating testing outside Guam.
Methods section describing the cohort (13 ALS, 12 AD, 8 HD, 12 age-matched controls, neuropathologically confirmed) and the validated fluorescent HPLC quantification method used for BMAA.
Results section reporting BMAA detected in US patients with sporadic AD and ALS but not HD, confirmed by tandem mass spectrometry, with incidental detections in control regions.

Results detail on concentrations: levels were below those reported in Guam ALS/PDC patients, showed a twofold range across diseases and brain regions, and were confirmed by triple quadrupole LC-MS/MS.

Conclusions suggesting BMAA in North American ALS and AD patients may reflect a gene-environment interaction in which BMAA triggers neurodegeneration in vulnerable individuals, followed by journal copyright line (2009).
Final copyright and publisher attribution line (2009 The Authors; Blackwell Munksgaard) closing the abstract.

Background on telomeres and telomerase: introduces telomere shortening as a prognostic marker in several cancers and the enzyme telomerase that counteracts it. Sets up the study's rationale for the pilot lifestyle trial.

Rationale for the study: lifestyle factors linked to cancer and cardiovascular disease may impair telomerase function, but no prior work tested whether improved nutrition and lifestyle raise telomerase activity. States the study aim.

Methods: 30 men with low-risk prostate cancer adopted comprehensive lifestyle changes for 3 months; primary endpoint was telomerase enzymatic activity per viable cell in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) at baseline and follow-up.
Findings begin: 24 of 30 patients had enough PBMCs for longitudinal analysis; trial registered as NCT00739791. Log-transformed PBMC telomerase activity rose from 2.00 to 2.22 (p=0.031).

Detailed results: raw telomerase values rose from 8.05 to 10.38 arbitrary units. Increases correlated with reduced LDL cholesterol (r=-0.36, p=0.041) and reduced psychological distress (r=-0.35, p=0.047).

Interpretation: the authors conclude comprehensive lifestyle change significantly increases telomerase activity and telomere maintenance capacity in immune cells, while framing results as associations given the pilot design.
Closing caveat: because causation cannot be inferred from this pilot, the authors call for larger randomised controlled trials to confirm the findings.
Introduction and objective of a cross-sectional study in 840 white, black, and Hispanic adults from MESA examining diet and leukocyte telomere length, a marker of biological aging.
Study design: leukocyte telomere length measured by quantitative PCR as the T/S ratio, and dietary exposures (food groups and beverages) assessed via a baseline 120-item food-frequency questionnaire.

Dietary exposure list (whole grains, fruit and vegetables, dairy, nuts, fish, coffee, refined grains, fried foods, red and processed meat, sugar-sweetened soda) and computation of two empirical dietary pattern scores.
Main results: after adjustment, only processed meat intake was associated with telomere length, with each daily serving linked to a 0.07 smaller T/S ratio (beta -0.07, P = 0.006).

Categorical results: weekly processed meat consumption of at least one serving was associated with 0.017 smaller T/S ratios than nonconsumption; other foods and both dietary patterns showed no association; conclusion that only processed meat showed the expected inverse link.
Concluding statement that processed meat showed the expected inverse association with telomere length while other dietary features did not show their expected associations.

Introduces the study's method: estimating age from DNA by measuring telomere length (terminal restriction fragment length via Southern blot) in peripheral blood and blood stains stored at room temperature for 5 months, noting average TRF shortens with aging.

Describes the age-estimation formula built on the correlation between average TRF length and subject age, notes estimates depend on environmental and genetic factors, and states the method is feasible for rough age estimates of forensic samples when DNA is well preserved.
Concludes that the telomere-based method can give a rough age estimate for forensic samples lacking morphological information, followed by the 2002 Elsevier Science Ireland copyright notice.

Abstract of a 2009 rat study (S. Karger AG) on whether a very-low-carbohydrate, horsemeat-based (Atkins-like) diet and 70% restricted feeding affect serum cholesterol, triglycerides, glucose, ketone bodies and insulin; this chunk gives the background aims and begins the Methods (experiment 1 design).

Methods section of the rat diet study: experiment 1 is a 2x2 factorial of high-carb AIN-93G vs. 53% horsemeat low-carb diet, each with ad libitum or restricted feeding; experiment 2 compares AIN-93G control with 53% beef or horsemeat low-carb diets.

Results section of the rat study on serum lipids: restricted feeding and the low-carb diet lowered serum triacylglycerol (p<0.01) versus ad libitum and AIN-93G respectively, while total, HDL and LDL cholesterol effects were inconsistent, with restricted feeding raising LDL cholesterol.

Remaining results and conclusion of the rat diet study: low-carb diet raised serum ketone bodies versus AIN-93G in experiment 2, and the authors conclude that restricted feeding and low-carb diet are beneficial for cardiovascular risk factors, with additive effects and restricted feeding more pronounced.
Final sentence of the conclusion and the copyright line (S. Karger AG, Basel, 2009) for the abstract on low-carb and restricted-feeding effects on cardiovascular risk factors in rats.

Introduction and methods summary of a study on microbial transglutaminase (MTGase) effects on lizardfish (Saurida undosquamis) mince gel properties, covering MTGase levels, setting temperatures, and the resulting breaking force and deformation.
Results on how MTGase amount and prior setting conditions (40 °C for 30 min vs 25 °C for 2 h) affect gel breaking force, plus SDS-PAGE evidence that myosin heavy chain polymerizes more with MTGase.
Microstructure findings showing MTGase gels have finer structure and smaller voids regardless of setting, and the conclusion that setting temperature influences MTGase-treated gel properties.
Effect of fish freshness: gels from lizardfish stored on ice for 0 to 10 days, with and without MTGase at 0.6 units/g, showing declining gel strength with storage time.
Conclusion that MTGase raises breaking force and deformation across all storage times, and that both fish freshness and MTGase addition directly determine lizardfish mince gel properties.

Methods and results of a randomized trial (38 infants with cow's milk allergy, aged 2-24 months, 14 days) comparing chicken-based formula with soy-based formula, starting with the soy group's intolerance rate of 12 of 18.

Results continuation: 12 of 18 soy-formula infants were intolerant versus 4 of 20 chicken-formula infants, with 16 chicken-formula infants tolerating it successfully, and the intolerance difference reported as significant.

Statistical result (p = 0.009) comparing intolerance between chicken and soy formula groups, followed by the study's conclusion that chicken-based formula can be used more effectively than soy-based formula for infants with cow milk allergy.

This chunk is the document's abstract, describing a review of the art of the musical anus (a flatulence-based performance art, as the title "Flatufonia" indicates), covering its notable performers and the anorectal physiology involved in producing these sounds.

Introduction to an MRI study of tomato fruit structure: describes the 0.2-T scanner setup on cv. Tradiro tomatoes, spin-echo macrostructure imaging, and gradient-echo susceptibility methods for air bubble content.

Continuation of the methods: microstructure characterized via T2 and T1 relaxation time distributions, with NMR relaxometry, macro vision imaging, and chemical analysis used as complementary methods to support the MRI results.
Results summary: air bubble content varies between tomato tissues, gas presence confirmed by macro vision images, and T2/T1 quantitative maps distinguish structural differences between tissues.
Conclusion: cell size and chemical composition are identified as contributors to the MRI relaxation mechanism in tomato tissues.
Introduction and methods opening of a randomized controlled trial on flaxseed and low-fat diets in men with prostate cancer, describing background rationale and trial design.

Trial methods continued: 161 prostate cancer patients randomized before prostatectomy into four diet arms (control, flaxseed 30 g/day, low-fat diet under 20% energy, and combined flaxseed plus low-fat).
Trial methods continued: blood biomarkers measured (PSA, hormones, IGF-1, CRP, cholesterol), and tumors assessed for Ki-67 proliferation (primary endpoint) and apoptosis.
Results begin: men stayed on protocol about 30 days, flaxseed arms showed significantly lower proliferation (P<0.002), with median Ki-67 ratios reported for flaxseed and low-fat arms.

Results and conclusion: Ki-67 values for control and low-fat arms, no differences in side effects, apoptosis or most serology, low-fat diet significantly lowered serum cholesterol, and flaxseed judged safe and potentially protective.
Final conclusion: flaxseed appears safe and linked to biologic changes that may protect against prostate cancer, and low-fat diets support cholesterol management.

Study background and aim: introduces the Prostate Cancer Lifestyle Trial's prior 1-year findings (lower PSA, LNCaP growth inhibition, fewer clinical events) and states this report examines clinical events over 2 years.

Methods setup: describes the 1-year randomized trial of 93 early-stage prostate cancer patients on active surveillance (Gleason <7, PSA 4-10 ng/mL) and begins describing the experimental lifestyle intervention (low-fat, plant-based diet).

Intervention details and primary results: experimental arm also got exercise, stress management, and group support, while controls got usual care; reports that 27% of controls vs 5% of experimental patients underwent conventional treatment by 2 years (P < .05).

Secondary outcomes: no group differences in other clinical events such as cardiac events, no deaths, and PSA findings among treated patients, where treated controls had higher PSA levels (>=10 ng/mL) than treated experimental patients.

Untreated-patient and conclusion details: no significant PSA change or velocity differences between untreated groups at 2 years; conclusion begins that early-stage patients on active surveillance may avoid or delay conventional treatment.
Final conclusion: patients with early-stage prostate cancer on active surveillance may avoid or delay conventional treatment for at least 2 years through diet and lifestyle changes.

Introduces the study's aim: examining how intensive lifestyle modification affects angina pectoris, coronary risk factors, quality of life, and lifestyle behaviors in stable coronary artery disease patients in the multisite cardiac lifestyle intervention program.

Describes the program's design and participants: a health-insurance-covered intervention at 22 US sites, enrolling nonsmoking CAD patients (mean age 61) asked to adopt a low-fat plant-based diet, 3 hours/week of moderate exercise, and daily stress management.
Reports baseline angina prevalence (108 with mild, 174 with limiting angina) and the 12-week outcome: 74% became angina free and an additional 9% improved from limiting to mild angina.

States that the angina improvement was significant regardless of gender (p<0.01), alongside broader gains in risk factors, quality of life, and lifestyle, with the greatest gains in exercise capacity, depression, and health-related quality of life among those becoming angina free.
Concludes that the angina improvements from intensive lifestyle change (p<0.05 for the secondary outcomes) could substantially reduce the need for revascularization procedures.

Introduction and background: links comprehensive lifestyle changes to prostate cancer progression, notes unknown molecular mechanisms, and introduces the pilot study of low-risk prostate cancer patients under surveillance.

Study population and intervention: men with low-risk prostate cancer who declined surgery, hormonal therapy, or radiation, enrolled in an intensive nutrition and lifestyle program with careful tumor surveillance; begins describing clinical outcomes such as weight and blood pressure improvements.

Clinical results and methods: reports significant improvements in weight, abdominal obesity, blood pressure, and lipids, confirms surveillance safety, and describes gene expression profiling of paired pre- and 3-month post-intervention prostate biopsies from 30 participants.

Gene expression analysis: describes qRT-PCR validation of array results and significance analysis of microarrays showing 48 up-regulated and 453 down-regulated transcripts after the intervention, followed by pathway analysis.

Key findings and conclusions: pathway analysis shows modulation of tumorigenesis-related processes (protein metabolism and modification, protein traffic, phosphorylation), concluding that intensive nutrition and lifestyle changes may modulate prostate gene expression.

Closing implications: argues that understanding the prostate molecular response to lifestyle change could inform prevention and treatment, and calls for larger clinical trials to confirm this pilot study's results.
Introduction and hypothesis of a study on diet/exercise, serum insulin, and growth of prostate epithelial cells in relation to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
Methods: serum from overweight men before and after a 2-week Pritikin diet/exercise intervention and from long-term lifestyle followers used to stimulate cultured primary prostate epithelial cells.

Results on cell growth at 48 and 96 h and apoptosis: no difference at 48 h; growth reduced at 96 h by 13% (2-week) and 14% (long-term) versus Pre; apoptosis unchanged; fasting insulin begins to be reported.

Results on fasting insulin (down 30% at 2 weeks, 52% long-term) and unchanged testosterone at 2 weeks, plus the conclusion that the diet and exercise lower insulin and reduce prostate epithelial cell growth.
Concluding implications: lifestyle may influence BPH development or progression, and future prospective trials should examine effects on BPH symptoms and progression.

Opening of an epidemiology review on sudden cardiac death: gives US annual incidence estimate (180–250,000) and notes a declining trend in the second half of the 20th century tied to falling coronary artery disease mortality, with obesity/diabetes rises threatening that trend.

Continues the argument that rising obesity and diabetes in the 2000s will likely reverse the favorable SCD trend, with coronary artery disease and heart failure resurging, making sudden cardiac death a worldwide public health problem.

Argues that developing meaningful risk stratification and prevention methods requires prospective community-wide studies using large biobanks of DNA, serum, and tissue linked to well-phenotyped databases.
States the review's purpose: summarize current knowledge of sudden cardiac death epidemiology, cover the value of community-wide studies, and summarize recent findings from such studies.
Closing of the introduction: says the review will highlight potential predictors worth further study as determinants of sudden cardiac death in the general population.

Introduction and objective of a prospective cohort study on egg consumption and type 2 diabetes risk, noting no prior research had examined this link (only inconsistent findings on fasting glucose and dietary cholesterol).

Research design and methods: data from the Physicians' Health Study I (20,703 men, 1982–2007) and the Women's Health Study (36,295 women, 1992–2007), with egg intake from questionnaires and Cox proportional hazards models for relative risk.

Results opening: follow-up of 20.0 years in men and 11.7 years in women, with 1,921 men and 2,112 women developing type 2 diabetes, and the start of the multivariable hazard ratios by weekly egg intake category for men.

Detailed hazard ratios with 95% CIs for type 2 diabetes by weekly egg intake for men (rising to 1.58 at ≥7 eggs/week, P trend <0.0001) and women (1.77 at ≥7 eggs/week, P trend <0.0001), showing higher risk at high intake levels.
Conclusions: daily-level high egg consumption is associated with increased type 2 diabetes risk in both men and women, and the authors call for confirmation in other populations.

Introduces the ARIC study's objective: examining links between incident heart failure and intake of seven food categories (whole grains, fruits/vegetables, fish, nuts, high-fat dairy, eggs, red meat) among 14,153 African-American and white adults aged 45-64 from four US communities.

Describes the methods: dietary intake measured via a 66-item food frequency questionnaire at baseline (1987-1989), later averaged with Exam 3 (1993-1995) responses, with hazard ratios computed per 1-daily-serving difference in food group intake.

Reports the main results: over a mean of 13 years, 1,140 HF hospitalizations occurred, and multivariable models adjusted for energy intake, demographics, lifestyle, prevalent CVD, diabetes and hypertension were applied.

Gives the key findings: whole-grain intake was linked to lower HF risk (HR 0.93), while egg (HR 1.23) and high-fat dairy (HR 1.08) intake were linked to higher risk, with the other four food categories showing no association.

Concludes that in this large population-based sample, whole grains are protective against heart failure, whereas eggs and high-fat dairy are associated with increased risk after adjusting for confounders.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, completing the statement that eggs and high-fat dairy intake are tied to greater HF risk after adjusting for several confounders.

Abstract and introduction of a cross-sectional study on veganism, bone mineral density, and body composition in postmenopausal women, comparing Buddhist nuns (vegan) with omnivorous women in Ho Chi Minh City.
Study population and methods: 105 Mahayana Buddhist vegan nuns versus 105 omnivorous women (average age 62) sampled from monasteries in Ho Chi Minh City.

Methods detail: DXA measurements (Hologic QDR 4500) of lumbar spine, femoral neck, and whole-body BMD plus body composition, and dietary calcium and protein estimated via a validated food frequency questionnaire.
Results begin: vegans and omnivores show no significant difference in lumbar spine, femoral neck, and whole-body BMD values, with reported means, SDs, and P values.

Results continued: no significant differences in lean mass or fat mass, and osteoporosis prevalence at the femoral neck (17.1% vegans vs 14.3% omnivores, P = 0.57); vegans had significantly lower median dietary calcium intake.

Results on calcium and protein: vegans' calcium intake was markedly lower, yet calcium did not correlate with BMD; whole-body BMD was positively correlated with the animal-to-vegetable protein ratio, but not lumbar spine or femoral neck BMD.
Conclusion: despite much lower calcium and protein intake, veganism showed no adverse effect on bone mineral density and no alteration of body composition in these postmenopausal women.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence restating that veganism does not alter body composition.
Opening background section of the acne vulgaris study: prevalence of acne in westernized adolescents and adults, and the premise that acne is much rarer in nonwesternized societies.

Introduces the study's aim: reporting acne prevalence in two nonwesternized populations (Kitavan Islanders and Aché hunter-gatherers) and examining environmental influences, followed by the start of the observations.
Observational results: no acne cases among 1200 Kitavan subjects (300 aged 15-25) and 115 Aché subjects (15 aged 15-25) over 843 days, with the start of the conclusions.

Conclusion: the large gap in acne rates between nonwesternized and modernized societies is unlikely to be due to genetics alone and likely reflects environmental factors, which could inform Western acne treatment.
Final sentence of the conclusions, stating that identifying these environmental factors may help treat acne in Western populations.

Introduces how cow's milk consumption alters the insulin/growth hormone/IGF-1 hormonal axis, raising IGF-1 levels across life stages and especially during puberty. Part of a document arguing milk is a promoter of Western chronic diseases.

Explains IGF-1's role as a potent mitogen that drives cell proliferation and blocks apoptosis, stimulating keratinocytes, sebocytes, and androgen-producing adrenal and gonadal tissue. Continues the document's argument linking milk-driven IGF-1 to acne and chronic disease.

Links the epidemic of adolescent acne in milk-consuming Western societies to milk-induced insulin and IGF-1 stimulation of sebaceous glands, presenting acne as a model for chronic diseases with excess IGF-1 signaling.

Notes that many other organs (thymus, bones, glands, vascular smooth muscle, neurons) are similarly over-stimulated, and lists conditions the milk-induced IGF-1 change may contribute to, including macrosomia, atopy, atherosclerosis, carcinogenesis, and neurodegeneration.
Concludes that molecular biology findings and epidemiologic data together identify milk consumption as a promoter of chronic diseases in Western societies, closing the document's central argument.

Opening of the EPIC study abstract: describes the cohort (142,251 men in EPIC), the Cox regression methods stratified by centre and adjusted for covariates, and introduces the exposures of animal foods, protein and calcium in relation to prostate cancer risk.

Reports follow-up results from the EPIC prostate cancer analysis: 8.7 years average follow-up, 2727 incident cases (1131 localised, 541 advanced), and the main finding that top vs bottom fifth of dairy protein intake gives HR 1.22 (95% CI 1.07–1.41, Ptrend=0.02).

Presents the calibrated, measurement-error-corrected estimate: each 35 g/day increase in dairy protein is associated with a 32% higher prostate cancer risk (95% CI 1–72%, Ptrend=0.04), and notes that dairy calcium, but not calcium from other foods, is positively associated with risk.
Concluding sentence of the abstract: the findings support the hypothesis that high intake of protein, or calcium from dairy products, may increase prostate cancer risk.
Introduces the LC-MS/MS study measuring free and total estrogen metabolites (EM), linked to reproductive cancers, in commercial milks as a possible dietary source.

Reports results: milk products contain considerable EM, skim milk has lower free EM than whole, 2%, and buttermilk; whole milk has the lowest total EM and buttermilk the highest; soy milk lacks mammalian EM.
Concludes that catechol estrogens are high in milk products, supporting milk as a dietary EM source that may influence breast and reproductive cancer risk.

Opening of the review abstract: states its purpose (summarizing berry effects on aging brain function) and reports that berry supplementation reverses age-related cognitive decline in animal studies, introducing the mechanism discussion that follows.

Mid-abstract on mechanisms: reports animal-model evidence that berry polyphenols are bioavailable and accumulate in the brain with long-term intake, and that berries influence cell-signaling cascades, continuing the discussion of how berries act on the central nervous system.

Concluding part of the recent-findings section: cell-signaling evidence in vivo and in culture supports the theory that berries and antioxidant-rich foods act beyond simple oxygen radical neutralization, leading into the summary.

Summary of the review's conclusion: dietary antioxidant-rich berries improve learning and memory in aged animals, attributed to direct polyphenol interaction with aging neurons that reduces stress signaling and supports neuronal function.
Final fragment of the summary sentence completing the proposed mechanism: berry polyphenols boost neurons' capacity to maintain proper functioning during aging.

Study overview of blackberry juice (BJ) consumption in humans, comparing water-based (BJW) and defatted milk-based (BJM) preparations, focusing on plasma antioxidant capacity and enzymatic/nonenzymatic antioxidants; reports a significant rise in plasma ascorbic acid after both juices.

Results on plasma urate, alpha-tocopherol, and ORAC antioxidant capacity after blackberry juice intake, including a non-significant ORAC increase only with BJW and correlations of plasma antioxidant capacity with ascorbic acid (positive, r = 0.93) and urate (negative, r = -0.79).

Findings that plasma antioxidant capacity was unrelated to total cyanidin or ellagic acid, that plasma catalase rose after juice intake while plasma and erythrocyte CAT and glutathione peroxidase activities were unchanged, and that urinary antioxidant capacity significantly decreased between 1 and 4 h.

Correlation results linking total antioxidant capacity with urate and total cyanidin, and the conclusion that anthocyanin levels associate with CAT activity and antioxidant capacity with ascorbic acid in human plasma after blackberry juice intake.
Concluding statement that follow-up studies are needed to confirm the antioxidant properties and health benefits of blackberry polyphenols, as the study's results are preliminary.
Introduction and aims of a human and rat study on whether adding milk to tea blocks tea's vascular protective effects, including methods planned (human FMD, rat aortic rings, HPLC).
Methods of the study: 16 healthy female volunteers drank black tea, black tea with 10% skimmed milk, or water, with flow-mediated dilation measured by vascular ultrasound before and 2 h after.

Results: black tea improved FMD in humans versus water, but milk blunted this effect; rat aortic ring and endothelial cell experiments showed tea induced vasorelaxation and eNOS phosphorylation, both abolished by milk.
Mechanistic findings: all tea effects were inhibited by milk, and caseins (not other milk proteins) were responsible, likely by forming complexes with tea catechins.
Conclusion: milk counteracts tea's favourable vascular health effects, so researchers studying nutritional flavonoids need to account for milk addition in study interpretation and design.

Opening of the blueberry-milk study abstract: background on phenolics binding proteins, and the design of an 11-volunteer crossover trial comparing blueberries with water versus blueberries with whole milk.

Middle of the abstract describing the crossover protocol (200 g blueberries with 200 ml water or whole milk), plasma sampling timepoints at baseline, 1, 2, and 5 h, and the finding that blueberries raised plasma reducing and chain-breaking antioxidant capacity and caffeic and ferulic acid levels.

Results section of the abstract: milk co-ingestion eliminated the rise in plasma antioxidant capacity and reduced peak caffeic and ferulic acid concentrations (-49.7% and -19.8%), with a reduced caffeic acid AUC.
Concluding sentence of the abstract stating that consuming blueberries with milk impairs their in vivo antioxidant properties and reduces caffeic acid absorption.

Introduction and study aim: background on black rice pigment fraction's anti-atherogenic effects in animal models, motivating a human trial in coronary heart disease patients (abstract of a CHD dietary supplementation study).

Study design and population: 60 CHD patients aged 45-75 from Sun Yat-Sen University's Second Affiliated Hospital in Guangzhou, randomized to test (10 g black rice pigment fraction) or placebo (10 g white rice pigment fraction) groups.
Baseline comparability and main intervention outcome setup: groups had similar baseline antioxidant and inflammatory markers; after 6 months, BRF supplementation was compared against WRF placebo.
Key results: BRF raised plasma total antioxidant capacity (p=0.003) and lowered sVCAM-1 (p=0.03), sCD40L (p=0.002), and hs-CRP (p=0.002) relative to the WRF placebo group.

Null findings and conclusion: no significant change in T-SOD activity, lipid levels, or carotid IMT; authors conclude BRF may be cardioprotective via improved antioxidant status and reduced inflammation.
Concluding fragment completing the final sentence of the abstract, stating the proposed mechanism that BRF inhibits inflammatory factors.

Abstract opening of a study on antiallergic effects of pigmented black rice bran ethanol-water extracts, comparing them with a nonpigmented cultivar in suppressing histamine and beta-hexosaminidase release from RBL-2H3 basophilic cells.

Continues the abstract: histamine and beta-hexosaminidase release is stimulated by A23187 and IgE-antigen complexes in RBL-2H3 cells; the same suppression appears in rat peritoneal mast cells, linked to calcium ion influx.
Abstract section on cytokine modulation: pigmented brans reduce TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-4, and IL-6 mRNA expression, measured by RT-PCR, confirming inhibition of the immune process.

Abstract section on protein-level confirmation: ELISA shows reduced TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6 release from cell line and peritoneal cells; the LK1-3-6-12-1-1 cultivar is the most effective inhibitor.
Concluding sentence of the abstract: the LK1-3-6-12-1-1 rice variety warrants further human dietary evaluation for protection against allergic diseases such as hay fever and asthma.
Introduction to a study on black rice anthocyanins (peonidin 3-glucoside and cyanidin 3-glucoside) as anti-metastatic agents, framing tumor metastasis as the leading cause of cancer death.
Describes the main findings: these black rice anthocyanins inhibit invasion and motility of SKHep-1 cells, linked to reduced MMP-9 and u-PA expression.
Covers mechanistic and broader findings: reduced AP-1 DNA binding and nuclear translocation, plus inhibited invasion of SCC-4, Huh-7, and HeLa cancer cells.
Concluding finding that anthocyanins from O. sativa L. indica (OAs) inhibit SKHep-1 tumor growth in vivo.

Introduction to the review on aluminium (Al) and lead (Pb) toxicity: both metals are known toxicants that accumulate throughout the body, with the central nervous system being a primary target, and Al is linked to neurodegeneration risk.

Background on public health relevance: Al may be implicated in neurodegenerative disease etiology in at-risk populations, Pb is a widespread environmental neurotoxic hazard, and the underlying neurotoxic mechanisms remain incompletely understood despite extensive research.

Scope statement of the review, which focuses on four mechanistic themes in Al and Pb neurotoxicity: oxidative stress, membrane biophysics alterations, deregulated cell signaling, and impaired neurotransmission.
Closing fragment of the review's scope sentence, ending the abstract's description of Al and Pb neurotoxicity as the topic.

Introduces the study's aim: testing whether oral aluminum bioavailability from drinking water is much greater than from foods, using rat experiments with basic [26Al]-sodium aluminum phosphate (basic SALP).

Reports the main experimental results: cheese containing 1.5% or 3% basic SALP gave oral Al bioavailability of about 0.1% and 0.3%, with peak serum 26Al at 8-9 h, placed between prior drinking water and biscuit (acidic SALP) values.

Compares bioavailability across sources (drinking water ~0.3%, acidic SALP in biscuit ~0.1%) and argues that because food supplies about 95% of daily Al intake versus 1.5% from water, food likely contributes far more absorbed Al.
Concludes that the findings do not support the hypothesis that drinking water disproportionately contributes to total gastrointestinal Al absorption.

Introduces arsenic exposure as a major preventable disease burden (cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular disease), noting natural groundwater contamination as the main source, and sets up the anthropogenic source discussed next.

Identifies the anthropogenic arsenic source: widespread arsenical drug use in food-animal production (US, China, others), causing residual contamination of food and environmental contamination from animal waste disposal.

Describes exposure pathways from animal waste: land disposal contaminating surface and groundwater, and fertilizer pellets and waste incinerators increasing exposure opportunities; frames arsenical feed additives as a preventable exposure source.

Notes that poultry use of arsenical drugs has received media and limited research attention, while swine production and the fast-growing foreign animal production industry remain largely uncharacterized.
Concludes that the continued expansion of arsenical drug use will likely increase global human arsenic exposure and risk.
Opening chunk of the document: introduces that rice contains more arsenic than other grains and that rice bran carries inorganic arsenic at roughly 1 mg/kg, about 10-20 times bulk grain levels.
Middle chunk describing rice bran solubles, marketed as a superfood and as a supplement for malnourished children in aid programs, and noting the document's concern about these products.
Chunk reporting test results for five rice bran solubles products (0.61-1.9 mg/kg inorganic arsenic) and the intake calculation from the recommended 20 g daily serving (0.012-0.038 mg).
Chunk on regulatory context: no food maximum concentration levels exist for arsenic, while EU and US water limits of 0.01 mg/L assume 1 L/day, a 0.01 mg daily benchmark.

Final chunk concluding that recommended rice bran solubles intake exceeds the 0.01 mg/day water-based benchmark, noting the target population of malnourished children and that risk depends on body-weight-normalized intake.

Introduces potato glycoalkaloids (alpha-solanine, alpha-chaconine): typical tuber content, maximum levels, health hazards, and the critical effect dose (CED) of 1-3 mg/kg b.w. used as the toxicity benchmark.

Describes the methodology: probabilistic modelling of acute and chronic glycoalkaloid exposure in the Czech Republic, Sweden and The Netherlands, using national food consumption databases, 439 Czech and Swedish tuber GA concentration results, and processing factors.

Presents the key acute exposure findings: current European potatoes may give acute intakes above 1 mg GAs/kg b.w./day for the top 0.01% of consumers in all three countries, and a proposed limit of 50 mg GAs/kg raw unpeeled tubers protects 99.99% of the population from exceeding the CED.

Reports chronic (usual) intake estimates of 0.25, 0.29 and 0.56 mg/kg b.w./day (97.5% upper confidence limit) for the three countries, and raises the open question of whether GA poisoning is underreported or the assumptions are worst-case for sensitive people.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence on uncertainty, stating that the assumptions may reflect worst-case scenarios for extremely sensitive individuals.

Introduction to a review on potato glycoalkaloids (GAs), explaining that potatoes are a globally important staple and that their tubers contain toxic GAs linked to human poisoning outbreaks and livestock deaths.

Conclusion of the article's introduction, outlining its scope (GA toxic effects, risk factors, detection methods, and biotechnological potato breeding) and posing the central question of whether potato GAs are dangerous to humans and animals, and to what extent.

Opening of the abstract: introduces a human dietary risk assessment built on tuber glycoalkaloid levels in potato plants defoliated by Colorado potato beetles versus undefoliated controls, which were significantly higher in both skin and inner tissue.

Continues the abstract's methods and main result: dietary risk to human subgroups is estimated at US national consumption percentiles (50th, 95th, 99.9th) against a 1.0 mg/kg body weight toxic threshold, and beetle defoliation raises dietary risk by about 48%.

Closing finding of the abstract: inner-tube glycoalkaloid levels, including controls, exceed the toxic threshold for all subgroups at the sub-99.9th percentile exposure but not at the 95th percentile.

Introduction to the study: identification and quantification of agaritine (a phenylhydrazine marker) by HPLC in cultivated Agaricus mushrooms, with initial levels in fresh A. bitorquis versus supermarket samples.
Agaritine concentrations across 28 supermarket samples (range 165-457 mg/kg, mean 272), plus distribution within the mushroom: highest in cap skin and gills, lowest in the stem.

Comparison of the two species showing no significant difference, followed by reductions in agaritine during refrigerated or frozen storage and drying, with the extent depending on storage length and conditions.
Effects of storage and drying: 20-75% reduction typical, no loss from freeze-drying; introduction to household cooking effects, beginning with boiling and its extraction of agaritine into the broth.
Boiling results: about 50% transferred to cooking broth within 5 minutes, 20-25% degraded, and prolonged boiling for sauce leaving only about 10% after 2 hours; dry baking reduces it by about 25%.

Cooking method comparison: frying in oil, butter, or deep frying causes 35-70% reduction, microwave leaves one-third of the original level, concluding that processed mushrooms yield much lower agaritine exposure than raw.

Conclusion and caveat: processed mushrooms give substantially less agaritine exposure than raw, but whether agaritine and related phenylhydrazines convert into other bioactive compounds during cooking remains unknown.
Final fragment completing the last sentence of the conclusion about cooking-related degradation of agaritine and other phenylhydrazine derivatives.

This chunk opens the document's abstract, stating the review's aims and methods (recent meta-analyses and clinical trials on soy and menopausal hot flashes) and reporting the main finding that isoflavone supplementation cut hot flashes by 34%, with efficacy rising with baseline flash frequency and dose.

This chunk continues the abstract's main results, describing a second review that attributes symptom reduction to at least 15 mg of genistein rather than total isoflavones, notes that randomized trials largely support both reviews, and begins the conclusions on the 30 mg/day soy isoflavone dose.

This chunk gives the abstract's conclusions: 30 mg/day of soy isoflavones (or at least 15 mg genistein) reduces hot flashes by up to 50%, including the placebo effect, with the greatest benefit when doses are divided and taken by women with at least four hot flashes per day.

This is a short fragment ending the abstract's conclusion, specifying that the greatest benefit of isoflavone intake in divided doses applies to subjects experiencing at least four hot flashes per day.

Introduction and study design of a study on undiagnosed celiac disease (CD): the Warren Air Force Base cohort (1948–1954 sera, 9,133 young adults) and recent Olmsted County, Minnesota comparison cohorts, with the study's aims on long-term outcome and prevalence trends over 50 years.

Methods describing serologic testing (tissue transglutaminase, then endomysial antibodies if abnormal) across the Air Force and recent Olmsted County cohorts (matched by birth year or age at sampling), and the 45-year survival follow-up of the Air Force cohort.
