Initial results: 14 of 9,133 Air Force cohort members (0.2%) had undiagnosed CD, and the start of the mortality finding showing higher all-cause death rates in undiagnosed CD versus seronegative persons over 45 years of follow-up.

Key quantitative findings: all-cause mortality hazard ratio of 3.9 (95% CI 2.0–7.5, P<.001) for undiagnosed CD, and prevalence comparisons showing 0.9% and 0.8% undiagnosed CD in the recent cohorts, 4- to 4.5-fold higher than the Air Force cohort.
Conclusions: undiagnosed CD is linked to nearly 4-fold increased mortality risk over 45 years, and its prevalence in the United States appears to have risen dramatically over the past 50 years.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence stating the rise in undiagnosed celiac disease prevalence in the United States over the past 50 years.

Opening of a 10-year follow-up study on mass screening for childhood celiac disease: states the objective (whether screening improves long-term health and quality of life) and methods (32 children aged 2-4 identified by screening, split into gluten-free vs. normal-diet groups).
Study methods continued: lists follow-up assessments (general health, symptoms, antibodies, quality of life) and begins the results, noting 81% adherence to a gluten-free diet at 10 years.

Main results: health status improved in 66% of treated children (41% via early treatment, 25% via preventing later gluten-dependent symptoms), while 19% had no symptoms at screening and stayed symptom-free on gluten, so treatment would not have helped them.
Quality-of-life results: children with symptoms improved significantly after one year of gluten-free diet, and at 10 years their quality of life matched the reference population.

Conclusion: mass screening led to health improvement in 66% of children without worsening generic quality of life, with good compliance; it also notes that delaying treatment for asymptomatic children may be an option in research settings.

Final conclusion: delaying treatment for asymptomatic children after a positive screen may be reasonable in research, and long-term studies are needed to assess complications in untreated, non-symptomatic celiac disease.
Introduces celiac disease and the study's aim: measuring its prevalence among at-risk and not-at-risk groups in the United States, where large epidemiologic data were previously lacking.
Describes the study methods: antibody screening (antigliadin, anti-endomysial), follow-up tTG-IgA and HLA DQ2/DQ8 typing in EMA-positive subjects, and biopsy where possible.
Gives the study population of 13,145 subjects, broken into first-degree relatives, second-degree relatives, symptomatic patients, and not-at-risk individuals, and begins the results section.

Reports the main prevalence findings: 1:22 in first-degree relatives, 1:39 in second-degree relatives, 1:56 in symptomatic patients, 1:133 in not-at-risk groups, and biopsy confirmation in all EMA-positive subjects tested.

States the conclusions that celiac disease is common beyond symptomatic patients, including in relatives and in people with common associated disorders without GI symptoms, with prevalence comparable to Europe.
Final conclusion that celiac disease is more common yet under-recognized in the United States than generally thought.

Introduction of a randomized trial on mild-enteropathy celiac disease: rationale that endomysial antibodies predict villous atrophy and hypothesis that a gluten-free diet helps patients with only mild (Marsh I-II) enteropathy.

Methods of the trial: 70 adults with positive endomysial antibodies underwent small-bowel endoscopy; 23 with only mild enteropathy (Marsh I-II) were randomized to gluten-containing diet or gluten-free diet.
Study design continued: 1-year follow-up with clinical, serologic, and histologic re-evaluation; 47 participants with Marsh III lesions served as disease controls.

Results comparing groups: on a gluten-containing diet, mild-enteropathy villi worsened and symptoms and antibodies persisted, whereas the gluten-free diet group improved, with inflammation diminishing to the level of Marsh III controls.
Conclusions: endomysial-antibody-positive patients benefit from a gluten-free diet regardless of enteropathy severity, and celiac diagnostic criteria need re-evaluation given the trial findings.
Final conclusion: endomysial antibody positivity without villous atrophy is part of the genetic gluten intolerance spectrum and warrants dietary treatment with a gluten-free diet.

Opening of a paper on the 'glyconutrient sham': introduces glycobiology's legitimate peer-reviewed research and notes how its discoveries are being co-opted to market plant-extract 'glyconutrient' products, including the industry's scale of sales staff and revenue.

Continuation of the same opening passage: gives the glyconutrient industry's annual sales (nearly half a billion USD) and states the paper's aim to examine the relationship between glyconutrients and glycobiology and the public and disciplinary impact of their claims.

Introduces the VITAL cohort study (Washington State, ages 50–76) and the research question of whether high-dose β-carotene linked to lung cancer risk in trials applies to the general population, examining supplements including β-carotene, retinol, vitamin A, lutein, and lycopene.

Describes the study methods: the 2000–2002 baseline of 77,126 participants, the 24-page questionnaire capturing 10-year supplement use (duration, frequency, dose), and the cohort's sources of exposure data.

Reports the outcome ascertainment (521 incident lung cancers through December 2005 via SEER registry linkage) and the key finding that longer duration of individual β-carotene, retinol, and lutein use, not total average dose, was linked to higher lung cancer risk by cell type.

Provides specific hazard ratio results: lutein with total lung cancer (HR 2.02) and β-carotene with small-cell lung cancer after more than 4 years of use (HR 3.22), each versus no use, with confidence intervals.

Summarizes that effect modification by gender or smoking status was minimal, and concludes that long-term individual β-carotene, retinol, and lutein supplement use should not be recommended for lung cancer prevention, especially in smokers.
Introduction and objective of a WHI cohort study on multivitamin use and risk of cancer, cardiovascular disease, and mortality in postmenopausal women, describing the population and motivation.
Study design and participants: 161,808 WHI women across Clinical Trials and Observational Study arms, enrollment 1993–1998, with follow-up durations (median 8.0 and 7.9 years).
Follow-up period through 2005 and the specific outcome measures: cancers of several sites, cardiovascular disease subtypes (MI, stroke, venous thrombosis), and total mortality.
Results overview: 41.5% multivitamin use and event counts for cancer (9,619), CVD (8,751), and deaths (9,865) over median follow-up.

Multivariate-adjusted hazard ratios showing no association of multivitamin use with site-specific cancers (breast, colorectal, endometrial, lung, ovarian) or with CVD outcomes (MI, stroke, VT), with 95% confidence intervals.
Mortality hazard ratio (HR 1.02) and the study conclusion that multivitamin use has little or no influence on common cancers, cardiovascular disease, or total mortality in postmenopausal women.
Final conclusion sentence and clinical trial registration identifier NCT00000611 on clinicaltrials.gov.

Introduction of a review on brain iron and neurodegeneration in the elderly: states its purpose (iron physiology in healthy adult brain and links to age-related neurodegenerative diseases) and begins describing iron's essential roles in normal CNS metabolism.

Explains the double-edged role of iron in the brain: essential for normal metabolism, but excess iron promotes neurotoxicity via free radicals, lipid peroxidation, and cell death, and notes iron increases with aging per imaging and pathology studies.

Lists neurological diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, stroke) where brain iron deposition is elevated, then the summary stating that imaging and experimental work clarify the iron-neurodegeneration link.
Concluding statement of the review: proposes that therapies removing excess brain iron could become part of clinical treatment to reduce the burden of neurodegenerative diseases in the elderly.

Abstract background and methods opening of a randomized trial on vitamins C and E and beta carotene supplementation and cancer risk in the Women's Antioxidant Cardiovascular Study, introducing the trial design and population of 8171 women.

Methods detail describing the double-blind, placebo-controlled 2x2x2 factorial trial doses (vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 600 IU every other day, beta carotene 50 mg every other day) and the 7627 cancer-free women analyzed.

Methods on outcome ascertainment (hospital reports and National Death Index) and statistical analysis (Cox proportional hazards models, subgroup analyses by duration of use, two-sided tests) in the antioxidant cancer trial.
Results opening reporting the average 9.4-year follow-up, with 624 incident invasive cancers and 176 cancer deaths, and noting no significant effects on total cancer incidence.
Results giving relative risks and 95% confidence intervals for total cancer incidence in the vitamin C, vitamin E, and beta carotene groups versus placebo, all non-significant.
Results on cancer mortality relative risks and 95% confidence intervals for vitamin C, vitamin E, and beta carotene versus placebo, showing no significant effect on cancer death.

Final results on duration and combined antioxidant use showing no effect, and the conclusion that vitamin C, vitamin E, or beta carotene supplementation gives no overall primary prevention benefit for total cancer incidence or mortality.

Background and objective of the Physicians' Health Study II trial testing whether long-term vitamin E or vitamin C supplementation reduces major cardiovascular events in men, noting prior gaps for low-risk men and vitamin C alone.

Design and setting of PHS II: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled factorial trial of vitamins E and C, begun in 1997 and completed August 31, 2007, enrolling U.S. male physicians aged 50 or older.

Participant characteristics and interventions: 14,641 male physicians including 754 with prevalent CVD, given 400 IU vitamin E every other day or 500 mg vitamin C daily; the main composite outcome is nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, and CVD death.

Primary results for vitamin E: over a mean 8.0-year follow-up with 1,245 major cardiovascular events, vitamin E showed no effect on major events (HR 1.01) or on MI, stroke, or cardiovascular mortality.

Primary results for vitamin C: no significant effect on major cardiovascular events (HR 0.99) or on total MI, total stroke, or cardiovascular mortality, with event rates per 1,000 person-years reported.
Mortality and safety results: neither vitamin E nor vitamin C significantly changed total mortality, and vitamin E was associated with a higher risk of hemorrhagic stroke (HR 1.74, P=0.036).
Conclusions of the trial: neither vitamin E nor vitamin C reduced major cardiovascular events in this large, long-term study of male physicians.
Final clinical implication: the findings provide no support for using vitamin E or C supplements to prevent cardiovascular disease in middle-aged and older men.
Introduction of a case report on liver damage (cirrhosis) from habitual daily intake of an over-the-counter vitamin A supplement (13,000 µg), framing concern about OTC vitamin toxicity.

Conclusion of the same case report: the vitamin A supplement's liver damage was reversed after discontinuation, underscoring the risk of long-term OTC vitamin use and the need for medical supervision.

Opening of the review on aquaculture and human health: introduces the rapid growth of global aquaculture production (tripled in 15 years, projected 39% of seafood by weight by 2015) and its welcome role in addressing nutrition-related disease burden.

Continues the introduction by noting that expanding aquaculture increasingly depends on formulated feeds, antibiotics, antifungals, and agrochemicals, and states the review's aim of summarizing chemical, biological, and emerging agents used in aquaculture and their public health impacts.

Presents the review's key findings: current aquaculture practices elevate levels of antibiotic residues, antibiotic-resistant bacteria, persistent organic pollutants, metals, parasites, and viruses in farmed finfish and shellfish, and identifies populations at risk of exposure.

Identifies the at-risk groups (aquaculture workers, nearby residents, and consumers) and calls for further research comparing health risks of farmed versus wild-caught fish and developing interventions to reduce those risks.

Concludes with a call for coordination among researchers, policymakers, governments, and industry to exchange information and develop targeted policies that address aquaculture's health impacts at local, national, and global levels.
Final sentence of the conclusion, stating that the collaborative policies must be practical, effective, and enforceable.

Introduction of a PBDE study on farmed and wild salmon in the Northeastern US, extending earlier PCB and chlorinated pesticide analysis; reports sample origins and initial total PBDE concentration ranges (ng/g wet weight).

Comparison of total PBDE levels between farmed salmon and wild Alaskan Chinook, finding no significant difference among regions, but significant intra-regional variation in total PBDEs and BDE-47 in Canadian farmed salmon (p<0.01).

Congener profile results (BDE-47 dominant, then BDE-99 and -100), comparison showing Canadian PBDE levels declined from two years earlier, and the finding that skin removal did not reduce PBDE concentrations and sometimes increased them.

Lipid correlation findings: PBDEs correlated with lipids only in skinned samples, implying greater PBDE accumulation and retention in muscle lipids than skin fat; also begins reporting modest PBDE-PCB correlations in skin-on samples.
Final results on skin-on samples showing modest correlations of PBDEs with total PCBs (R2=0.47) and mono-ortho PCBs (R2=0.50), but no correlation with non-ortho PCBs.

Abstract opening of a study on atmospherically deposited organic contaminants (PBDEs, pesticides, PCBs, PAHs) in fish from 14 remote high-elevation lakes in western US National Parks, 2003–2005, including the analytical method setup.

Abstract passage on analytical method performance (detection limit, recovery, reproducibility, accuracy) and comparison of western US park fish contaminant levels to mountain fish from Europe, Canada, and Asia.
Abstract passage comparing dieldrin and PBDE levels to other mountain fish and Pacific salmon, and stating that most contaminants fall well below recreational fishing human health thresholds.

Abstract passage on health risk findings: subsistence fishing cancer screening values exceeded in 8 of 14 lakes, and wildlife thresholds exceeded for piscivorous mammals (5 lakes) and piscivorous birds (all lakes).
Concluding abstract sentence stating that atmospherically deposited organic contaminants accumulate in high-elevation fish at concentrations relevant to human and wildlife health.

Abstract opening of a study on polychlorinated naphthalenes (PCNs) in human adipose tissue, introducing PCNs as persistent, bioaccumulative toxins and reporting the first US data from New York City samples (2003-2005), with male and female concentration ranges.

Abstract results on PCN concentrations in human fat: male and female ranges, predominant congeners 52/60 and 66/67 accounting for 66% of total PCNs, and PCNs being 2-3 orders of magnitude below PCB and PBDE levels.
Abstract conclusions on PCNs in human adipose tissue: no correlation with PCB levels, and PCNs contributing under 1% of dioxin-like TEQs compared with PCDD/F-TEQs.
Final clause of the abstract stating that PCNs contribute less than 1% of the PCDD/F-TEQ dioxin-like toxic equivalents in human adipose tissue, concluding the study on New York human fat PCN levels.

Introduction and study design of a 2-week randomized trial in 32 adults comparing DHA bioavailability from algal-oil capsules versus cooked salmon, motivating the question of whether supplement nutrients equal food-derived ones.

Methods: the 2-week study giving 600 mg DHA/day from algal-oil capsules or assayed cooked salmon, with plasma phospholipid and erythrocyte DHA change from baseline analyzed by Student's t tests and post-hoc bioequivalence analysis planned.
Results: post-hoc bioequivalence analysis of least-squares mean ratios; DHA rose about 80% in plasma phospholipids and about 25% in erythrocytes in both groups, with similar changes between groups.
Conclusions: fish and algal-oil capsules were equivalent in delivering DHA to plasma and red blood cells, and both regimens were generally well tolerated, indicating bioequivalence.
Final conclusion: algal-oil DHA capsules are presented as a safe, convenient source of non-fish-derived DHA, closing the abstract's bioequivalence claim.
Introduction establishing that Antarctic pollution was documented from the late 1960s and that persistent organic pollutants (POPs) reach remote Antarctica via global transport, motivating the study.

Describes the study's scope: measuring PBDEs, PCBs, PCDDs and PCDFs in tissues of two Antarctic fish species (Chionodraco hamatus and Trematomus bernacchii) and calculating 2,3,7,8-TCDD toxic equivalents (TEQs) for risk assessment.

Summarizes key findings: POP levels were generally higher in T. bernacchii than C. hamatus, peaked in liver tissue of both species, and gives the PBDE concentration range (160.5 to 789.9 pg/g wet wt).
Reports PCB concentrations (0.3 to 15.1 ng/g wet wt, the dominant organochlorines, exceeding PBDEs) and states that TEQs were higher in C. hamatus and driven mainly by PCDDs.
Concluding statement that detection of PBDEs and organochlorine pollutants in Antarctic fish tissues confirms their global transport and distribution to remote regions.

Study design and objective: a cell culture study testing four PCB congeners (PCB-77, -105, -153, -180) on TGF-β1, VEGF, and type I collagen expression in human peritoneal and adhesion fibroblasts from three patients.
Methods: fibroblasts were treated with each PCB at 20 ppm for 24 hours, RNA was extracted, and mRNA levels of type I collagen, VEGF, and TGF-β1 were measured by real-time RT/PCR.

Results on controls and viability: PCB exposure left β-actin housekeeping gene mRNA and cell viability (trypan blue) unchanged, validating the assay, and normal peritoneal fibroblasts were shown to express collagen I, VEGF, and TGF-β1.
Key findings: PCBs produced no significant change in TGF-β1 or VEGF mRNA, but markedly increased type I collagen mRNA in both normal and adhesion fibroblasts after 24 hours (P<0.0001).

Conclusion: PCB-induced collagen I upregulation is presented as the first evidence linking organochlorines to tissue fibrosis, suggesting organochlorine exposure may be an etiologic factor in diverse fibrotic diseases.
Closing statement of the conclusion: organochlorine exposure may contribute to a wide range of previously unlinked human conditions characterized by fibrosis.

Introduction of the dieldrin/Parkinson's disease review: frames PD as strongly linked to environmental chemical exposures, with environmental risk possibly outweighing genetic factors, while noting alpha-synuclein and parkin gene mutations.

Continues the introduction: describes the need to understand gene-environment interplay in PD and states that pesticides and metals are the most common environmental chemicals promoting dopaminergic degeneration.
Introduces dieldrin, an organochlorine pesticide found in postmortem PD brain tissue, suggesting it may promote nigral cell death, and notes ongoing human exposure despite its ban.

States the review's scope: summarizes cell culture and animal model neurotoxicity studies of dieldrin and links them to nigral dopaminergic degeneration, including exposure via contaminated dairy and meat.
Closing clause of the abstract listing the pathological mechanisms examined in relation to dieldrin: oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, protein aggregation, and apoptosis.

Introduces the study's background on dioxin effects on infant growth and neurodevelopment, and describes the design: 42 breast milk samples collected from Japanese mothers on postpartum days 5-8 to assess maternal dioxin exposure against newborn head circumference.

Describes the methods: seven dioxins and 10 furan isomers were measured in each milk sample by HR-GC/MS, and each isomer's concentration was then analyzed against newborn size, including head circumference, after adjusting for confounders.

Presents the main finding: maternal breast milk TCDD, the most toxic dioxin isomer, was negatively correlated with newborn head circumference even after adjusting for gestational age, infant sex, parity and other confounders.

Reports the null results for other dioxin and furan isomers versus height, weight and chest circumference, and concludes that maternal environmental TCDD exposure may influence fetal brain development.
Final fragment of the abstract, completing the last word of the concluding sentence about maternal TCDD exposure from the environment.

Introduction/abstract of a paper on dioxin and environmental toxicant exposure as a possible trigger of endometriosis, proposing that disruption of the endometrial endocrine-immune interface links toxicant exposure to disease development.

Capsule summary at the end of the abstract, stating that environmental toxicant exposure induces an inflammatory-like endometrial response that may promote endometriosis; it restates the chunk 1 theme as the paper's key takeaway.
Introduces the NHANES 1999-2002 study of 11 PCBs and hypertension, noting sample sizes and that all PCBs showed unadjusted associations with hypertension.

Reports that after covariate adjustment (age, gender, race, smoking, BMI, exercise, cholesterol, family history), seven specific PCBs (126, 74, 118, 99, 138/158, 170, 187) remained significantly associated with hypertension, with dioxin-like PCBs 126 and 118 strongest.

Gives the adjusted odds ratios for the strongest findings: high PCB 126 (OR 2.45) and high PCB 118 (OR 2.30) versus low reference levels, with 95% confidence intervals, and begins the result on having one or more elevated PCBs.

Presents the combined exposure result (one or more elevated PCBs, adjusted OR 1.84 versus none), estimates the population prevalence (22.76%, about 32 million US adults), and states the hypothesis that elevated PCBs are a hypertension risk factor.
Concludes that the seven-PCB association suggests PCBs may be a hypertension risk factor, and notes that clinical application is limited without wider availability of the required laboratory testing.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending the sentence about patient testing; it is part of the discussion on clinical implications of the PCB-hypertension findings.
Introduction to a study of persistent organic pollutants (PCBs and organochlorine insecticides) detected in 30 fish and seal oil dietary supplements sold in Vancouver, Canada, collected 2005-2007.
Reports the highest and lowest residue levels: shark oil had the peak SigmaPCB (10400 ng/g) and SigmaDDT (3310 ng/g), while mixed anchovy, mackerel and sardine oils had the lowest.

Gives mean SigmaPCB concentrations by supplement type (unidentified fish, mixed fish with and without salmon, salmon, vegetable with mixed fish, shark, menhaden, seal), with shark highest at 5260 ng/g.

Notes that seal oil had the highest levels of other organochlorines, that hexachlorinated PCBs dominated SigmaPCB, and that SigmaDDT was the main organochlorine contributor; also introduces intake estimates based on label maximum dosages.
Concludes with the calculated average daily intakes of SigmaPCB (736 +/- 2840 ng/d) and SigmaDDT (304 +/- 948 ng/d), whose wide variability reflects the large range in residue concentrations.

Context: From a discussion of methylmercury (MeHg) exposure from fish consumption. This chunk contrasts wild fish, where MeHg and omega-3 fatty acids can be balanced by species choice, with farmed fish fed fish meal, which can bioconcentrate MeHg in muscle and organohalogen pollutants in fat. It opens with a citation to Dorea (2006) on fish meal in animal feed.

Context: Continues the Dorea (2006) citation on fish meal in animal feed and persistent pollutants. It concludes that fish-meal-fed farm animals may deliver both saturated fat with organohalogen pollutants and MeHg, and calls for addressing dietary Hg sources from fish-meal-raised animals that may raise tissue Hg levels.

Context: Final sentence of the document's argument, calling for attention to dietary mercury from animals raised on fish meal, which may increase tissue Hg concentrations. It summarizes the concern about fish-meal-fed farmed animals as a mercury exposure source.

Introduction and study design: a 1990s-era cross-sectional field study comparing 22 adult male tuna-eating subjects with 22 controls on mercury exposure and early neurotoxic effects (neurobehavioral, tremor, serum prolactin measures).

Biomarker measures and sample availability: urinary mercury (U-Hg) and serum prolactin were measured in all subjects, while blood organic mercury (O-Hg) was available only for a subset (10 exposed, 6 controls); U-Hg is introduced as significantly higher in exposed subjects.

Exposure results: U-Hg medians and ranges for exposed vs. control subjects, O-Hg medians for tuna eaters vs. controls, and correlations of both mercury measures with weekly fish consumption; serum prolactin differences begin here.

Prolactin and neurobehavioral findings: exposed subjects had higher serum prolactin, sPRL correlated with both mercury measures, and tuna eaters performed worse on color word reaction time, digit symbol reaction time, and finger tapping speed.

Regression conclusion: after adjusting for education and other covariates, stepwise regression identified O-Hg concentration as the strongest predictor of neurobehavioral test performance, explaining about 65% of variance in scores.
Concluding fragment of the regression finding: O-Hg accounts for roughly 65% of variance in test scores, completing the sentence from the final chunk of the study's results.

Introduces the study's aim of linking Hong Kong male subfertility to fish consumption, and reports hair mercury levels in 159 Hong Kong males (ages 25-72), which rise with age and exceed European and Finnish levels.
Compares hair mercury between 117 subfertile and 42 fertile Hong Kong males, finding subfertile men had about 40% more (4.5 ppm vs 3.9 ppm, P < 0.05).

Reports that the 35 women had significantly lower hair mercury than similarly aged men (men about 60% higher overall), and introduces 16 long-term Hong Kong vegans who avoided fish, shellfish, and meat.
Gives the result for the 16 vegetarians: very low hair mercury, with a mean of 0.38 ppm, the lowest group in the study and consistent with fish being the main mercury source.

Introduction of the study: background on high mercury deposition along the Florida Gulf Coast, the state's fish consumption advisories, and the lack of systematic human mercury exposure data near Pensacola.

Continues the background: explains why coastal populations near Pensacola in the Florida Panhandle may face elevated mercury exposure due to high seafood consumption, and notes that advisory efficacy has rarely been assessed.
Describes the study design: hair mercury measurements and surveys of fish consumption and advisory awareness among women aged 16-49 who lived near Pensacola for at least a year.

Reports the main findings: higher hair mercury among women who ate fish in the prior 30 days and among those unaware of the advisory (both p<0.05), and only 31% knew of the advisory, with pregnant women less aware.
Concludes that education and fish advisories have not reached most at-risk women in counties surrounding Pensacola, who are most exposed to mercury from fish.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending the sentence about mercury levels in at-risk women.

Introduction to the document: establishes methyl mercury as a developmental neurotoxicant, its main exposure route (seafood eaten by pregnant women), its anthropogenic vs. natural sources, and the EPA's 1990s progress on power plant emissions.

Motivation for the study: notes the EPA's recent proposal to slow mercury emission reductions due to abatement costs, and introduces the aim of estimating economic costs of methyl mercury toxicity attributable to American power plants.

Methods: describes the environmentally attributable fraction model limited to neurodevelopmental effects (loss of IQ), and reports CDC blood mercury data showing 316,588 to 637,233 children per year with cord blood mercury above 5.8 μg/L.

Key findings on cost: explains that IQ loss from elevated cord blood mercury causes lifetime productivity losses, which are the major cost of methyl mercury toxicity, totaling $8.7 billion annually (range $2.2–43.8 billion, 2000 US$).

Power plant attribution and conclusion: states that $1.3 billion annually (range $0.1–6.5 billion) of the total is attributable to American power plant mercury emissions, and argues this toll should inform mercury pollution control debates.
Concluding sentence: argues that the economic toll threatens US economic health and security and should be weighed in debates over mercury pollution controls.

Opening of the abstract: introduces the US pubertal timing controversy, noting that the old precocious puberty cutoffs (breast budding before 8 in girls) no longer fit, while menarche timing has stayed stable, and begins linking early maturation to later obesity.
Middle of the abstract: covers obesity and weight at puberty onset by race and sex, and links premature pubarche to hyperinsulinaemia and to functional ovarian and adrenal hyperandrogenism in girls.

Core hypothesis of the paper: early menarche is preceded by prepubertal hyperinsulinaemia, and insulin and insulin resistance are proposed to influence pubertal onset (though not necessarily its tempo).

Conclusion: if the insulin hypothesis holds, insulin resistance may be more common in US children than previously thought; puberty timing advances have not been reported elsewhere but may spread as other countries adopt American lifestyles and diets.
Final fragment of the closing sentence, restating that the early puberty trend may spread to other countries as they adopt American lifestyle and diet.

Study abstract opening: states the objective (testing environmental estrogens PCBs and phthalate esters as hazards to semen quality in unexplained male infertility), the randomized controlled design, the clinic/research setting, and the start of the patient description.

Study population and sampling: 21 infertile men meeting low sperm count, motility, or morphology thresholds with no obvious cause, versus 32 fertile control men with normal semen analyses and documented conception; semen and blood were collected during the treatment protocol.

Outcome measures and first results: lists the semen parameters evaluated (volume, count, motility, morphology, vitality, osmoregulation, chromatin stability, DNA integrity) and reports PCBs found only in infertile men's seminal plasma and higher phthalate ester levels in infertile men.

Results on semen quality and exposure patterns: infertile men show lower ejaculate volume, sperm count, progressive motility, normal morphology, and fertilizing capacity than controls, and PCB/PE levels rank highest in urban fish eaters, then rural fish eaters, urban vegetarians, and rural vegetarians.

Key quantitative finding and conclusion: total motile sperm counts in infertile men fall inversely with xenoestrogen concentration and are significantly below controls, leading to the conclusion that PCBs and PEs may contribute to declining semen quality.
Final conclusion sentence: the study suggests PCBs and phthalate esters may play a causal role in deteriorating semen quality in infertile men with no identifiable etiology.

Introduction and study aim from a cross-sectional study of zinc and selenium nutritional status in vegetarians in São Paulo, including inclusion criteria (age ≥18, no food or pharmaceutical supplements).
Study population description (30 vegetarians, mean age 27, 4.5 years of vegetarianism, mean BMI 21.5) and reported zinc plasma and erythrocyte concentrations by sex.
Reported selenium plasma and erythrocyte concentrations by sex, and the conclusion that selenium blood levels are adequate while erythrocyte zinc is deficient in this vegetarian population.
Concluding recommendation that vegetarians be regularly assessed and given nutritional support to counter inadequate zinc status.

Study objective and design: an eight-year prospective cohort of 18,555 married women without prior infertility, examining dietary animal and vegetable protein intake in relation to incident ovulatory infertility.

Main results: 438 cases of ovulatory infertility; multivariate relative risks for highest vs. lowest quintile of animal protein (RR 1.39, 95% CI 1.01-1.90) and vegetable protein (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.54-1.12), with trend P values.

Substitution finding and conclusion: replacing 5% of energy from animal protein with vegetable protein linked to over 50% lower ovulatory infertility risk (P = 0.007), leading to the conclusion that swapping animal for vegetable protein may reduce risk.
Concluding sentence of the abstract: the suggestion that replacing animal protein sources with vegetable protein may lower the risk of ovulatory infertility.

Introduction and methods of a study of US men's semen quality (387 partners of pregnant women, five US cities, 1999-2005), examining links to their mothers' self-reported beef consumption during pregnancy, motivated by concern about anabolic steroids and xenobiotics in beef.

Methods continued (regression analysis, maternal beef intake vs. son's semen parameters and subfertility history) and start of results: sperm concentration inversely related to mothers' beef meals per week (P = 0.041).

Key results for 'high beef consumers' (>7 beef meals/week): sperm concentration 24.3% lower, three times more men below 20 x 10^6/ml (17.7% vs 5.7%), and more frequent previous subfertility history among these sons.

Specificity findings and conclusion: no significant link between sperm concentration and mothers' other meat or sons' meat intake; authors suggest maternal beef consumption, possibly via xenobiotics, may alter testicular development in utero and reduce reproductive capacity.

Final fragment of the conclusion, restating that maternal beef consumption and possibly xenobiotics in beef may alter a man's in-utero testicular development and adversely affect his reproductive capacity.

Opening of the document's introduction: the rise of research into infectious agents as a cause of schizophrenia, and the list of reasons Toxoplasma gondii is a prime candidate, starting with higher antibody prevalence in schizophrenia patients.

Middle portion of the Toxoplasma-schizophrenia discussion listing further evidence: toxoplasmosis-induced psychosis, epidemiological similarities, antipsychotics inhibiting T. gondii, and parasite-induced dopamine elevation.

Continuation of the evidence list in the Toxoplasma-schizophrenia passage, covering elevated dopamine in infected animals and greater childhood exposure to cats among schizophrenia patients, followed by the open research questions.

Summary of unresolved questions about Toxoplasma's role in schizophrenia (strain variation, timing and source of infection, host genetic susceptibility), and the value of establishing a firm causal link for treatment and prevention.
Closing sentence of the document stating that a confirmed Toxoplasma–schizophrenia association would be a major breakthrough enabling new treatment and prevention methods.
Introduction and methods start of a study on viable Toxoplasma gondii in lamb hearts from USA slaughterhouses: sample size (383 lambs) and sampling location (Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia).

Serology step of the methods: blood from each lamb heart tested by modified agglutination test (MAT) at several dilutions, and the overall seroprevalence result (104 of 383 lambs, 27.1%) that determined which hearts went to bioassay.
Bioassay methods for isolating viable T. gondii from the 68 seropositive lamb hearts, describing feeding myocardium to cats (oocyst shedding in feces) and acid pepsin digest inoculation into mice.
Results of isolation and genotyping: 53 T. gondii isolates obtained from 68 seropositive lambs, and the PCR-RFLP genotyping panel of 10 markers that identified 57 strains and 15 genotypes.
Genotyping results by lineage: 57 strains including lambs with mixed infections, with proportions of clonal Type II (45.6%) and Type III (15.7%) strains, and the remaining strains as atypical.

Conclusions: the remaining 22 strains fell into 11 atypical genotypes, indicating high T. gondii prevalence and genetic diversity in lambs with public health implications, and claim of the first in-depth genetic analysis of sheep isolates in the USA.
Final sentence of the abstract restating the claim that this is the first in-depth genetic analysis of T. gondii isolates from sheep in the USA.

Introduction of the Sarcocystis beef study: parasite transmission via undercooked meat, the pathogenic difference between S. hominis and S. cruzi, and the aim to measure regional prevalence using histology and PCR.

Results on PCR screening: 60 of 110 retail beef samples amplified Sarcocystis rRNA, all 41 sequenced were S. cruzi, and a parallel histology vs. PCR comparison on 48 samples gave 16 histology-positive and 26 PCR-positive, with 5 histology-positive samples PCR-negative.

Comparison of detection methods: 15 PCR-positive samples lacked sarcocysts on first histologic sections, but additional sections found sarcocysts in 12 more samples; combined histology and PCR yielded 31 positives out of 48.

Conclusions: no S. hominis (human pathogen) found, S. cruzi (cattle parasite) is highly prevalent in the regional beef sample, and PCR may improve sensitivity and diagnostic precision for Sarcocystis detection.

Introduction to biogenic amines in fish: definition (decarboxylation of amino acids) and identification of histamine, cadaverine, and putrescine as the key amines for fish safety and quality, including the histamine–scombroid poisoning link.

Role of putrescine and cadaverine in potentiating histamine toxicity, and cadaverine as the only useful spoilage index for early fish decomposition, with spoilage relationships tied to trimethylamine and sensory evaluation.

Bacterial load and regulatory threshold: a mesophilic count of log 6-7 cfu/g corresponds to about 5 mg histamine/100 g, the FDA maximum allowable level, and spoilage relationships depend on bacterial composition and free amino acids.
Nitrosamine formation: in vitro evidence linking cadaverine to NPIP and putrescine to NPYR, plus factors that promote (impure salt, high temperature, low pH) or inhibit (pure NaCl) their formation.
Conclusion on implications: understanding biogenic amine–nitrosamine relationships may explain the mechanism of scombroid poisoning and help ensure the safety of fish products.
Introduces tetrodotoxin as a puffer fish neurotoxin and describes the 2007 Chicago poisoning incident where two people fell ill after eating home-cooked puffer fish bought from a retailer.

Covers the supplier's and retailer's denials that they sold puffer fish, their claim that the product was monkfish, and the genetic and visual evidence plus high tetrodotoxin levels showing the fish were Tetraodontidae.
Describes the regulatory response: a voluntary monkfish recall across three states and the supplier's placement on the FDA Import Alert for species misbranding.

Draws the public health lessons from the case: stricter FDA regulation of puffer fish imports, public education on puffer fish dangers, and medical provider awareness and reporting of foodborne toxin cases.
Concludes the document by stating the final call for reporting foodborne toxin ingestions to public health agencies.

Opening case report describing scombroid (histamine) fish poisoning in an elderly patient who collapsed with hypotension after eating mackerel, diagnosed via food history and exclusion and resolved with antihistamines.

Introduces the topic of illness from contaminated fish: a case report describing two patients with muscle weakness and rhabdomyolysis after eating salmon, and noting that fresh-water fish rhabdomyolysis is rare in the US but common in the Baltic region.

Names the syndrome Haff disease, notes its unknown etiology (believed to be a toxin), and points to palytoxin from marine fish as a possible model for the suspected toxin in freshwater fish-associated rhabdomyolysis.
Gives public health guidance: if Haff disease is suspected, contact the CDC and collect any uneaten fish for laboratory analysis.

Background and study aim from a retrospective study of necrotizing soft-tissue infections and sepsis caused by Vibrio vulnificus and V. cholerae non-O1, describing risk groups (hepatic disease, diabetes) and seafood/seawater exposure.

Study population and methods: 30 retrospectively reviewed patients with Vibrio necrotizing fasciitis or sepsis, with seawater or raw seafood exposure history and counts of hepatic disease and diabetes cases.

Patient characteristics and microbiology: counts of patients with hepatic disease, diabetes, and combined hepatic dysfunction plus diabetes, and culture confirmation of 23 V. vulnificus and 7 V. cholerae non-O1 cases.
Results on treatment and mortality: surgical debridement or amputation in all necrotizing cases, 11 of 30 deaths (37%), and higher mortality for V. cholerae non-O1 (57%) than V. vulnificus (30%).

Mortality predictors: significantly higher death rates with initial systolic BP of 90 mm Hg or lower, leukopenia, decreased platelet counts, and combined hepatic dysfunction with diabetes; also the conclusion that Vibrio infection should be suspected given exposure history.

Conclusions on clinical management: V. cholerae non-O1 causes bacteremia more often than V. vulnificus in cirrhosis patients, and early fasciotomy plus culture-directed antibiotics are recommended for shock, leukopenia, high band forms, low platelets, and hypoalbuminemia.

Final list of high-risk outcome indicators for early fasciotomy and culture-directed therapy: hypotensive shock, leukopenia, high band cell forms, decreased platelets, severe hypoalbuminemia, and chronic illness such as hepatic dysfunction and diabetes.

Opening of the review on fishborne and foodborne parasitic zoonoses in Asia; introduces the risk of anisakiasis from sushi and sashimi tied to the global spread of Japanese cuisine, and freshwater/brackish fish dishes in Japan.

Continues the introduction: notes that wild animal meats and freshwater fish served raw in rural Japan, and similar traditional dishes across Asia, sustain endemic parasitic zoonoses, and that travelers are increasing exposure.

Concludes the introduction by pointing out that travelers and infectious disease specialists underestimate the infection risk from exotic ethnic dishes, and states the review's aim: to give practical background on representative endemic zoonoses in Asia.
Final fragment of the introduction, closing the sentence that describes the endemic parasitic zoonoses in Asian countries covered by the review.

Introduces the study's scope and baseline microbial counts (aerobic mesophiles, psychrotrophs, coliforms) for 272 aquacultured catfish, salmon, tilapia, and trout fillets from local and Internet retail markets.

Reports that market type and fish species mostly showed no significant microbial differences, with the exception of higher aerobic mesophiles in Internet trout, and gives E. coli prevalence in trout, salmon, and tilapia, none exceeding 1.0 log MPN/g.
Covers E. coli in catfish (13.2%, mean 1.7 log MPN/g) and Listeria prevalence, noting about 27% of fillets contained Listeria spp. and its correlation with L. monocytogenes.

Compares Listeria and L. monocytogenes prevalence between Internet and local fillets, gives L. monocytogenes rates by species (highest in catfish at 23.5%), and notes Salmonella and E. coli O157 were absent.
Concludes with a follow-up catfish processing study showing that gut waste exposed during evisceration is a potential source of coliforms and Listeria spp. contamination.
Introduces ciguatera fish poisoning: its definition, global case estimates, endemic regions, and U.S. incidence rates per 10,000 persons.
Describes the typical gastrointestinal and neurologic symptoms of CFP, including nausea, vomiting, fatigue, tingling, and the characteristic reversal of hot and cold sensation.
Summarizes the June 2007 North Carolina cluster of nine CFP cases, including symptom patterns and persistence of symptoms beyond six months in some patients.
Reports that most sexually active patients in the cluster had painful intercourse, then highlights the risks of contaminated ocean fish and the need for physician training.
Concludes that health departments should train emergency and urgent care physicians to recognize CFP, since symptoms may last months to years.

Opening of the abstract: introduces the 2003-2007 cluster of severe diarrhea cases from V. cholerae O75 carrying the cholera toxin gene in southeastern US states (Georgia, Alabama, South Carolina), the first US illness reports, and an initial 2004 Louisiana pond water isolate.

Describes the Louisiana isolates: the 2004 pond water sample, plus three previously O141-designated Louisiana isolates (two patient isolates from 2000, one water isolate from 1978) reclassified as serogroup O75, starting the Results section.

Results on patient demographics and isolate characteristics: all 8 infected patients were adults who ate seafood, two after eating raw Gulf Coast oysters; all 10 isolates carried the cholera toxin gene and were antimicrobial susceptible; PFGE pattern matches between clinical and water isolates.

Conclusions begin: the multi-year case occurrence and concurrent detection of O75 in Gulf Coast state water suggest the strains can persist for long periods in that environment, supporting an environmental reservoir interpretation.

Public health implications: exposure histories link infection to consuming raw Gulf Coast oysters, and clinicians and health authorities are urged to watch for emerging toxigenic V. cholerae serogroups that can cause severe diarrhea.
Final fragment of the closing recommendation, a short tail of the conclusion stating that the new toxigenic V. cholerae serogroups can cause severe diarrhea and need surveillance.

Introduces the overall topic: Vibrio species are common in seafood, and specific pathogenic strains (cholera toxin-producing V. cholerae, TDH-producing V. parahaemolyticus, and V. vulnificus causing sepsis) cause human disease.

Explains transmission routes: epidemic V. cholerae spreads from environmental reservoirs via seafood or contaminated water/food, while nonepidemic Vibrio strains are mainly acquired by eating seafood such as raw oysters.

Describes clinical outcomes: nonepidemic V. cholerae, V. parahaemolyticus, and V. vulnificus usually cause gastroenteritis, and can cause wound infections or septicemia, especially in people with liver disease or weakened immunity.
Concludes the at-risk population point: septicemia from Vibrio infection, notably V. vulnificus, is most serious in persons with liver disease or who are immunocompromised.

Introduction and rationale: improperly washed hands spread pathogens to food, and prior studies on food service hand washing lacked frequency analysis by sector and benchmarks; this chunk introduces the study design (five 3-hour observation periods).

Study scope and sample: 240 hours of direct observation of 80 employees across 16 retail food service operations, four each from assisted living, childcare, restaurants, and schools, covering menu production, service, and cleaning phases.
Methods: a validated observation form based on 2005 Food Code guidelines, used by two trained researchers to record when hands should be washed, when they were washed, and how.
Key results: overall Food Code frequency compliance ranged from 5% (restaurants) to 33% (assisted living), with procedural compliance also low; this introduces the proposed hand washing benchmarks.

Proposed benchmarks of hand washing per employee per hour by sector: seven for assisted living, nine for childcare, 29 for restaurants, and 11 for schools; the authors note these are high, especially for restaurants.

Conclusions and implications: benchmarks risk lost productivity and dermatitis, so managers need active control over work assignments; the benchmarks can guide training and employee hand washing behavior.
Introduces heterocyclic amines (HCAs) formed in high-temperature meat cooking and their unclear safety threshold, motivating the study of commercially cooked restaurant foods.

Notes the gap in HCA measurement (lab and home cooking, little commercial food data) and the need to account for restaurant dining; describes the survey of 7 California chain restaurants with at least 9 locations each.
Describes the methods: collecting one or two grilled chicken entrees per location from seven chains and analyzing them for PhIP by HPLC-MS/MS.
Reports results: PhIP detected in all 100 samples at 0.08 to 43.2 ng/g, with absolute amounts exceeding 1,000 ng per entree when weight is factored in.
Concludes with exposure-reduction advice: avoid meats cooked by methods known to form PhIP.
Introduction to urinary OH-PAH biomarkers and their use by NHANES for US population reference ranges and benchmarks.
Study scope: 22 OH-PAH metabolites measured in 2748 NHANES participants (2001-2002), with detection frequencies varying by parent compound.
Detection rates by parent PAH and the geometric mean concentration of 1-hydroxypyrene (1-PYR), the standard PAH exposure biomarker, in ng/L and ng/g creatinine.
Age-group differences in 1-PYR levels (children highest, then adolescents and adults) with model-adjusted geometric means, plus inter-metabolite correlations.
Conclusion that correlations between 1-PYR and other OH-PAHs (r = 0.17-0.63) support using 1-PYR as a surrogate for overall PAH exposure.

Introduces the importance of roasting in coffee production and notes that it can form undesirable polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs); leads into the paper's described analytical method for PAHs in coffee brew.
Describes the analytical method: saponification and liquid-liquid extraction with small hexane volumes, no further purification, and GC-MS analysis in single ion monitoring (SIM) mode.

Reports the results: total PAH (28 compounds, SigmaPAH) concentrations in coffee brew of 0.52 to 1.8 µg/l and carcinogenic PAHs (B[a]P-equivalent) of 0.008 to 0.060 µg/l, and begins discussing isomeric ratios.
Concludes that coffee contributes very insignificantly to daily human intake of carcinogenic PAHs, and that isomeric ratios indicate most PAHs in the samples come from high-temperature processes.

Background and aims of a cross-sectional study on serum polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) exposure in low-income children, including asthmatic and non-asthmatic groups and environmental exposure pathways.
Study population and methods: 75 Saudi children aged 15 and under (61 asthmatic, 14 non-asthmatic) completed a dietary questionnaire, and serum PAH levels were measured by HPLC with UV detection.

Results comparing serum PAH levels by asthma status: naphthalene and pyrene were elevated in asthmatic children, while acenaphthylene, fluorene and 1,2-benzanthracene were higher in non-asthmatic children, with reported p-values.

Results on household smoking: presence of a smoker in the family correlated with serum carbazole, pyrene, 1,2-benzanthracene and benzo(c)phenanthrene levels, with correlation coefficients and p-values; also begins describing correlations with daily meat intake.

Results on dietary exposure: daily meat intake correlated with serum acenaphthylene, benzo(a)pyrene and 1,2-benzanthracene; followed by the conclusion that serum PAH relate to meat intake and household smokers.
Public health conclusion: parents should be educated to prevent indoor smoking and reduce children's intake of grilled and smoked meat to lower exposure to carcinogenic PAH.

Introduces the study's design: airborne fumes from frying hamburgers (beef), bacon (pork) and tempeh burgers (soy) were collected and tested for mutagenicity, with pork and beef fumes mutagenic and tempeh fumes not.

Compares mutagenic potency: well-done non-charred bacon fumes were 8x more mutagenic than hamburger fumes and about 350x more than tempeh burger fumes in the TA98 with S-9 Ames test; also begins noting bacon's higher mass of the compound measured versus beef.
Reports heterocyclic amine (HCA) findings in well-done, non-charred food: bacon had about 15-fold more HCA mass than beef, tempeh had none, and PhIP, MeIQx and DiMeIQx were the main HCAs detected.
Notes A-alpha-C was absent from the fried foods but present in airborne products, and gives total HCA levels in smoke condensates: bacon 3 ng/g, beef 0.37 ng/g, soy-based food 0.177 ng/g.

Concludes that cooks are potentially exposed to high levels of airborne mutagens and carcinogens, and recommends long-term sampling in restaurants and kitchens to assess the risk of prolonged exposure.

Introduction to the ET study: defines harmane as a tremor-producing neurotoxin, notes elevated blood harmane in essential tremor patients, and states the hypothesis that meat intake and doneness are higher in cases.

Methods and early results: names the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory Meat Questionnaire and reports current meat consumption by sex, showing a significant difference in men with ET but none in women.
Adjusted regression results for males: meat consumption linked to ET odds (OR 1.006 per g/day, about 6% per 10 g/day), plus quartile comparison showing higher odds in the top consumption quartile.

Quartile findings and conclusion: men with ET had much higher odds in the top meat-consumption quartile (adjusted OR 21.36), meat doneness did not differ, and the authors call for further study of the dietary difference.
Publication copyright line: attribution of the article to S. Karger AG, Basel, with a 2008 copyright notice closing the abstract.

Introduction of a human PhIP biomonitoring study: eleven volunteers ate cooked chicken containing PhIP and 4'-OH-PhIP, and urine was collected over 16 hours to compare human and rodent metabolism for dietary risk assessment.

Methods and findings on urinary analysis: hydrazine hydrate and hydrolytic enzymes reduced the many PhIP metabolites to three measured compounds, 4'-OH-PhIP (detoxification biomarker), PhIP, and 5-OH-PhIP (activation biomarker), with large 4'-OH-PhIP excretion reported.

Quantitative metabolite results: most urinary 4'-OH-PhIP came from the chicken itself, implying only 11% of PhIP was metabolized to 4'-OH-PhIP; 38% was recovered as unchanged PhIP and 51% as 5-OH-PhIP, indicating extensive activation in humans.

Conclusion and cross-species comparison: humans convert much PhIP to reactive 5-OH-PhIP, whereas rats eliminate less than 1% as 5-OH-PhIP, suggesting human cancer risk from PhIP is considerably higher than rodent-bioassay extrapolations predict.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence stating that rodent-bioassay-based risk estimates underestimate human cancer risk from dietary PhIP exposure.

Introduces the study's goal: testing fluorescence imaging to detect diluted feces from colon, ceca, small intestine, and duodenum on poultry carcasses, and notes the challenge of low fluorescence yield being masked by ambient light.

Describes the laser-induced fluorescence imaging system (LIFIS) used to capture fluorescence from feces-contaminated carcasses in ambient light, with 415-nm excitation and 630-nm emission imaging, and mentions threshold and erosion image processing.

Reports the detection results: fecal spots undiluted and diluted up to 1:5 were detected with 100% accuracy regardless of feces type, and processing identified spots diluted up to 1:10 by weight in double distilled water.

Summarizes the findings: 96.6% detection accuracy for fecal matter diluted up to 1:10, concluding that the LIFIS shows good potential for detecting diluted poultry feces, which can harbor pathogens, on carcasses.

Introduces the 12-month in vivo study of 10 healthy volunteers measuring skin levels of beta-carotene and lycopene via resonance Raman spectroscopy, with daily lifestyle questionnaires on supplements and stress.
Reports that carotenoid skin levels varied individually and strongly correlated with lifestyle, specifically carotenoid supplement intake and stress factors.
Describes the effects: carotenoid-rich diet (lots of fruit and vegetables) raises skin carotenoids, while fatigue, illness, smoking, and alcohol lower them.
Gives the timing of changes (decreases within a day, increases lasting up to 3 days) and the seasonal pattern, with summer/autumn increases and an average seasonal increase of 1.26-fold.
Fragment completing the seasonal increase figure: the average seasonal increase in skin carotenoid content was 1.26-fold.

Abstract opening of a 2013-era prospective cohort study (NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study) on meat intake and mortality; covers the background, objective, and study population of about half a million adults aged 50-71.

Methods section describing meat intake assessment via baseline food frequency questionnaire, Cox proportional hazards regression for hazard ratios within meat intake quintiles, and the list of adjustment covariates such as age, smoking, BMI, and diet.

Continuation of the covariate list in the methods, then the outcome measures (total, cancer, CVD, accident, and other-cause mortality) and the start of results: 47,976 male and 23,276 female deaths over 10 years of follow-up.
Results on total mortality: hazard ratios comparing highest versus lowest quintiles of red and processed meat intake for men and women, showing elevated overall mortality risk.
Results on cancer-specific mortality: elevated hazard ratios for red and processed meat intake in men and women, and the start of the CVD mortality findings.
Results on CVD mortality for red and processed meat, followed by the white meat findings, which show an inverse association with total, cancer, and other deaths.
Final part of the results on white meat, and the study conclusion that red and processed meat intake is associated with modest increases in total, cancer, and CVD mortality.

Introduces the benefits of vegetarian and vegan diets for diabetes, covering lower diabetes incidence in observational studies and superior glycemic control from low-fat vegan diets in type 2 diabetes trials versus conventional diets.

Explains the mechanisms behind plant-based diets' glycemic effects: mainly weight loss, plus reduced saturated fat and high-glycemic-index foods, more fiber and vegetable protein, lower intramyocellular lipids, and decreased iron stores.

Summarizes further benefits of vegetarian and vegan diets for type 2 diabetes: improved plasma lipids, reversal of atherosclerosis progression, and acceptability comparable to other therapies in clinical studies.
Concludes that the current literature indicates vegetarian and vegan diets offer potential advantages for managing type 2 diabetes.

Opening of the abstract for a 74-week randomized trial comparing a low-fat vegan diet with conventional diabetes diet guidelines in adults with type 2 diabetes; covers background rationale and study design and sample sizes.

Continues the design section (randomization, group sizes, 2003 ADA guideline comparator, 74-week duration, measurement schedule for HbA1c and lipids) and begins the results, noting weight loss within each group.

Results on weight change (-4.4 kg vegan vs -3.0 kg conventional, not significantly different) and its correlation with HbA1c change, plus the primary HbA1c changes at 74 weeks or last available value, which were not significantly different.

Secondary HbA1c results when adjusting for medication changes (-0.40 vegan vs 0.01 conventional, P=0.03), followed by lipid results before lipid-lowering medication changes, starting with total cholesterol.

Lipid outcomes (total and LDL cholesterol reductions, both significantly greater on vegan diet) and the conclusions that both diets sustained weight and lipid reductions, with the vegan diet improving glycemia and lipids more after controlling for medication changes.

Concluding interpretation that the vegan diet appeared superior for glycemia and lipids after controlling for medication, caveat that clinical benefit for macro- or microvascular complications is unproven, and the start of the trial registration statement.
Final sentence of the abstract's caveat about unestablished clinical complication benefits, followed by the clinicaltrials.gov registration number NCT00276939.

Introduction and background of a systematic review on rosiglitazone (a thiazolidinedione) safety in type 2 diabetes; states cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in this population and that the drug was approved based on glucose-lowering and surrogate cardiovascular markers, then lists the review's objective of assessing cardiovascular, skeletal and hematologic safety.

Methods and conclusion of the rosiglitazone safety review: evidence was synthesized from recent trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, regulatory documents and manufacturer trial registries, concluding that rosiglitazone increases the risk of heart failure, myocardial infarction and fractures (in women) in type 2 diabetes.
Final fragment of the conclusion of the rosiglitazone safety review, specifying that the increased fracture risk applies to women with type 2 diabetes.

Study design and methods from the Adventist Health Study-2 (2002–2006) examining type 2 diabetes prevalence across vegetarian diet types versus nonvegetarians, including sample size and data collection.

Methods continued: self-reported data from Seventh-Day Adventist church members in North America, diet categories from a food-frequency questionnaire, and multivariate-adjusted logistic regression for odds ratios; begins the results with mean BMI by diet group.

Results showing BMI rising from vegans (23.6) to nonvegetarians (28.8), and type 2 diabetes prevalence rising from 2.9% in vegans to 7.6% in nonvegetarians, with intermediate prevalence for lacto-ovo, pesco, and semi-vegetarian diets.

Adjusted odds ratios for type 2 diabetes after controlling for demographics, lifestyle factors, and BMI, showing vegans, lacto-ovo, pesco-, and semi-vegetarians all had lower risk than nonvegetarians, with confidence intervals.

Conclusions: the 5-unit BMI gap between vegans and nonvegetarians suggests vegetarianism may protect against obesity, and greater adherence to vegetarian diets was associated with lower type 2 diabetes risk after accounting for lifestyle and BMI.
Final conclusion sentence: pesco- and semi-vegetarian diets offered intermediate protection against type 2 diabetes, placing them between vegan/lacto-ovo diets and nonvegetarian diets.

Introduction and background of a retrospective chart review of a high nutrient density (HND) vegetable-based diet for weight loss in a family practice, with patients prescribed the diet during extended counseling.

Methods section describing the convenience sample of 56 family practice patients seeking weight-loss dietary counseling over 3 years, with no identifying data recorded and initial one-hour counseling sessions.

Methods continued: patients received a sample HND meal plan, recipes, and verbal/written rationale; chart data (weight, blood pressure, cholesterol panel, cholesterol:HDL ratio) were recorded at 6-month intervals for up to 2 years.
Methods on statistical analysis and survey: Friedman rank order exact test for related samples was used, and a follow-up survey on adherence and medication use was completed by 38 patients.

Results on weight and lipid outcomes: mean weight loss of 31 lbs at 1 year (n=33) and 53 lbs at 2 years (n=19), with cholesterol, LDL, triglycerides reductions and cardiac risk ratio falling from 4.5 to 3.8.

Results on blood pressure and adherence: systolic and diastolic blood pressure changes were highly significant at all intervals, and adherence correlated significantly with degree of weight loss (P = .011); conclusions begin noting sustained weight loss and attrition.

Conclusions: weight loss was sustained and greater with good adherence among returning patients, many were lost to follow-up, lipid and blood pressure benefits were noted, and HND diet may offer sustainable long-term weight loss and reduced cardiac risk for motivated patients with extended counseling.

Conclusions and recommendations: extended one-on-one counseling and follow-up are emphasized, patient retention tools need study, and randomized clinical trials with long-term follow-up are called for to test the diet's therapeutic potential and adherence issues.
Final concluding statement that the HND diet, as shown in this group, may be the most health-favorable and effective weight-loss approach for appropriately motivated patients, ending the abstract.

Study setup and methods from the Adventist Health Study-2 (2002–2006) examining type 2 diabetes prevalence across vegetarian diet types versus nonvegetarians, including sample size of over 60,000 participants and logistic regression approach.

Methods continued: data collection from Seventh-Day Adventist church members in North America, diet classification via food-frequency questionnaire, and multivariate-adjusted logistic regression yielding odds ratios with 95% CIs; begins the results with mean BMI by diet group.

Results on BMI and diabetes prevalence: mean BMI rises from vegans (23.6) to nonvegetarians (28.8), and type 2 diabetes prevalence rises from 2.9% in vegans to 7.6% in nonvegetarians, with intermediate values for lacto-ovo, pesco, and semi-vegetarian diets.

Adjusted risk results: after controlling for demographics, lifestyle factors, and BMI, all vegetarian groups had lower odds of type 2 diabetes than nonvegetarians, with specific odds ratios and confidence intervals for vegans, lacto-ovo, pesco-, and semi-vegetarians.

Conclusions: the 5-unit BMI gap between vegans and nonvegetarians suggests vegetarianism may protect against obesity, and greater adherence to vegetarian diets is associated with lower type 2 diabetes risk after accounting for lifestyle and BMI.
Final conclusion sentence: pesco-vegetarian and semi-vegetarian diets provide intermediate protection against type 2 diabetes, closing the study's summary of diet type and diabetes risk.
Introduction and background of an NHANES 1999-2002 study on bean consumption, legumes, cardiovascular disease, and obesity, stating the study objective of examining beans as a separate food variable.
Methods of the NHANES 1999-2002 secondary analysis: 24-hour dietary recall data used to identify three groups of bean consumers (N = 1,475) and compare them with non-consumers.

Statistical methods (least square means, standard errors, ANOVA with survey sample weights, adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, and energy) and the start of results: bean consumers had higher intakes of fiber, potassium, magnesium, iron, and copper.

Key results on health outcomes: bean consumers had lower body weight and smaller waist size, a 23% reduced risk of increased waist size, a 22% reduced risk of obesity, and baked bean consumption was linked to lower systolic blood pressure.
Conclusions of the study: bean consumers had better overall nutrient intake, body weight, waist circumference, and systolic blood pressure than non-consumers, supporting benefits of bean consumption.
Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that the findings support bean consumption for improving nutrient intake and health parameters.

Introduces the study's scope: measuring bisphenol A and bisphenol B in peeled canned tomatoes from Italian supermarkets, covering can lacquer types and the start of the sample-preparation method (SPE on C-18 and Florisil cartridges).
Describes the analytical method (RP-HPLC with UV and fluorescence detection) and the main results: BPA found in 22 of 42 tomato samples (52.4%) and BPB in 9 samples (21.4%).
Reports that BPA and BPB co-occurred in 8 samples and concludes that BPA levels are far below the EU migration limit of 3 mg/kg food and the EFSA daily intake limit of 0.05 mg/kg body weight.
Final fragment completing the EFSA reference (European Food Safety Authority) from the regulatory safety-limit comparison in the conclusion.

Abstract of a randomized crossover trial on low-salt vs usual-salt diet effects on brachial artery flow-mediated dilatation (FMD) in overweight/obese normotensive adults; covers background, objective, and study design.

Study design details: 29 normotensive overweight/obese participants, 2-week low-salt and usual-salt diets matched for potassium and saturated fat and weight stability; outcomes measured were FMD, pulse wave velocity, augmentation index, and blood pressure.
Key results: FMD, systolic blood pressure, and 24-h urinary sodium excretion values under low-salt versus usual-salt diets, with corresponding P-values showing significant differences.

Further results and conclusion: no correlation between changes in FMD and sodium excretion or blood pressure, no change in augmentation index or pulse wave velocity, and the conclusion that salt reduction improves endothelial vasodilation independent of blood pressure.
Interpretation of findings as suggesting cardioprotective effects of salt reduction beyond blood pressure lowering, followed by the start of the trial registration information (ANZCTR registry).
Final part of the trial registration citation: the Australian and New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry identifier ANZCTR12607000381482 and its registry URL.

Introduces the study's background on moderate alcohol and cardioprotection, and states the aims: examining alcohol intake and myocardial infarction over 17 years in 9655 people, and testing whether benefit varies by other health behaviours.

Continues the aims text, describing the population (9655 men and women without prevalent disease) and the health-behaviour categories (healthy, moderately healthy, unhealthy), then begins the Method: a longitudinal British civil service cohort with 1985-8 baseline.

Covers the Method's cohort design and the main Results: moderate drinking was beneficial versus abstinence or heavy drinking among those with poor health behaviours, while the healthiest group showed no added alcohol benefit.

Defines the healthiest behaviour profile (3+ hours of vigorous exercise weekly, daily fruit or vegetable intake, non-smoking) and gives the Conclusion that alcohol's cardioprotective benefit varies across drinkers and should be emphasised in public health messaging.
Final fragment of the Conclusion, completing the closing sentence about emphasising variability in public health messages.

Introduction of the paper on salicylic acid (SA) as an endogenous compound in humans and animals, not only a plant defense molecule or aspirin metabolite; covers SA and salicyluric acid levels in vegetarians versus low-dose aspirin patients and SA's presence in animal blood.

Evidence that plasma SA persists during fasting (even after total proctocolectomy) and a 13C6 benzoic acid tracer study in volunteers showing about 33.9% labeling of urinary salicyluric acid, pointing to benzoic acid as a possible source of SA.
Conclusion of the paper: benzoic acid's contribution to circulating SA turnover needs more study, and SA's partly endogenous origin calls for reassessing its role in human and animal pathophysiology.

Study design and population: introduces the caloric restriction vs. unsaturated fatty acid vs. control trial in 50 healthy elderly adults (mean age 60.5, mean BMI 28), motivated by animal studies on diet and cognition.

Intervention arms and methods: describes the three groups (30% caloric restriction, 20% increased UFA intake with unchanged total fat, control) and the 3-month memory assessment before and after the intervention.
Key results: reports a 20% rise in verbal memory after caloric restriction (P < 0.001), correlated with lower fasting insulin and hs-CRP, strongest in best-adherent subjects; BDNF unchanged.
Conclusions: states that caloric restriction benefits memory in healthy elderly and no memory changes occurred in the UFA or control groups.

Proposed mechanisms and implications: suggests improved insulin sensitivity and reduced inflammation may enhance synaptic plasticity, and frames the findings as informing prevention strategies for cognitive decline in aging.
Introduction to curcumin's anti-obesity and anticancer potential, and the study's aim of identifying AMPK downstream targets in adipocyte differentiation and cancer cell proliferation inhibition.
Results showing curcumin-activated AMPK down-regulates PPAR-gamma in 3T3-L1 adipocytes and reduces COX-2 in MCF-7 cells, with a synthetic AMPK activator supporting AMPK as upstream of PPAR-gamma.
In cancer cells AMPK regulates ERK1/2, p38 MAPK, and COX-2; the conclusion that curcumin's regulation of AMPK and its targets (PPAR-gamma, MAPKs, COX-2) controls adipocytes and cancer cells.
Final fragment closing the abstract's concluding sentence about curcumin controlling adipocytes and cancerous cells via AMPK and its downstream targets.
Introduction to a study on curcumin and related turmeric curcuminoids (DMC, BDMC) and their antimetastatic activity in human fibrosarcoma cells, framing the role of MMPs and uPA in ECM degradation.
Continuation of the background: rationale for comparing Cur, DMC and BDMC effects on uPA, MMP-2, MMP-9, MT1-MMP and TIMP-2 expression and in vitro invasiveness of fibrosarcoma cells.

Key results: BDMC and DMC are at least as potent as curcumin in inhibiting cancer cell invasion without affecting migration, and zymography shows reduced uPA, active MMP-2 and MMP-9 secretion in a dose-dependent manner.

Mechanistic findings: reduced active MMP-2 correlates with lower MT1-MMP and TIMP-2 protein levels involved in pro-MMP-2 activation; BDMC and DMC are more potent than curcumin, which is a key comparative result.

Specific protein and activity findings at 10 microM: BDMC and DMC lower both MT1-MMP and TIMP-2, while curcumin only slightly lowers MT1-MMP; all three curcuminoids inhibit collagenase, MMP-2 and MMP-9 activity but not uPA activity. Ends with the conclusion.
Concluding statement: DMC and BDMC have greater antimetastatic potency than curcumin through differential downregulation of ECM-degrading enzymes.
Background and objectives of a study on cinnamon and turmeric supplements, focusing on urinary oxalate excretion as a hyperoxaluria and kidney stone risk, plus fasting glucose and lipid changes.

Study design: an 8-week randomized crossover trial in 11 healthy young adults, with 4-week supplement periods delivering 55 mg oxalate/day, and oxalate load tests plus fasting glucose and lipid measurements at each time point.

Methods detail on the 63-mg oxalate load test using the test spices and water-only control, followed by the start of results comparing urinary oxalate excretion across cinnamon, turmeric, and control treatments.

Results showing turmeric produced significantly higher urinary oxalate excretion than cinnamon and control, with no significant changes in fasting plasma glucose or lipids from either spice; conclusions begin with oxalate water solubility differences (cinnamon 6%, turmeric 91%).

Conclusion that the much higher water solubility of turmeric oxalate (91% vs 6% for cinnamon) likely explains its greater urinary oxalate excretion and absorption, so turmeric supplements, but not cinnamon, may raise kidney stone risk.
Final sentence of the conclusion: supplemental turmeric may increase kidney stone formation risk in susceptible individuals.
Abstract opening of a study on curcumin as a lead compound against hormone-independent, multidrug-resistant breast cancer, introducing the MCF-7R MDR cell line and its lack of aromatase and ERalpha.

Continuation of the abstract describing MCF-7R overexpression of ABCB1 and survival genes (c-IAP-1, NAIP, survivin, COX-2), and that curcumin retains substantial antitumor activity in both MCF-7 and MCF-7R cells.
Abstract passage on chemical modification of curcumin's diketone system, where benzyloxime, isoxazole, and pyrazole analogues increased antitumor potency in parental and MDR MCF-7 cells.

Abstract passage reporting that curcumin and especially the isoxazole analogue early reduced diverse gene transcripts (Bcl-2, Bcl-X(L) in MCF-7; IAPs and COX-2 in MCF-7R), showing cell-line-specific molecular activity.
Abstract discussion of curcumin's proposed mechanisms: ER-dependent and ER-independent antitumor effects, and acting as a drug-transporter-mediated MDR reversal agent.
Concluding sentence of the abstract stating that curcumin's structure may serve as a basis for developing new anticancer agents for hormone-independent MDR breast cancer.

Introduction and background of a study on tofu and tempe soy intake and memory in elderly Indonesians; introduces phytoestrogen cell-culture findings and the paradoxical Honolulu Asia Aging Study tofu result.

Methods of the cross-sectional study of 719 elderly Javanese and Sundanese adults at rural (Borobudur, Sumedang) and urban (Jakarta) sites, measuring memory with a dementia-sensitive word learning test and soy intake via food frequency questionnaire; begins results on tofu and memory.
Key results: high tofu intake linked to worse memory (beta = -0.18), while tempe intake linked to better memory (beta = 0.12), especially over age 68; fruit intake also positively associated.
Covariate adjustment and conclusion linking the tofu-memory finding to Honolulu Asia Aging Study data, with the open question of whether harm stems from toxins or phytoestrogen levels.

Discussion of possible mechanisms: phytoestrogen receptor effects, estrogen and dementia risk in older women, and tempe's high phytoestrogen and fermentation-derived folate content as a possible protective factor.
Closing call for future studies to validate findings and explore mechanisms, followed by the 2008 S. Karger AG, Basel copyright notice.
Abstract opening of a study on genistein (soy isoflavone and phytoestrogen) and its effects on adipogenesis and estrogen receptor expression in primary human preadipocytes.
Abstract results on genistein's dose-dependent inhibition of lipid accumulation and its biphasic effect on cell viability (increase at 3.25 microM, decrease at 25 and 50 microM).
Abstract continuation describing Oil Red O confirmation of lipid accumulation effects and the link to reduced glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase activity and adipocyte-specific gene downregulation.
Abstract listing the specific adipogenic marker genes (PPARgamma, C/EBPalpha, GPDH, aP2, FAS, SREBP1, perilipin, leptin, LPL, HSL) suppressed by genistein during differentiation.
