Abstract conclusion linking genistein's antiadipogenic effects to downregulation of ERalpha and ERbeta, and its contribution to understanding phytoestrogen mechanisms against adipogenesis.

Introduction and study design of a 5-year longitudinal weight-gain study in UK meat-eaters, fish-eaters, vegetarians and vegans (EPIC-Oxford), describing background, objectives, and baseline/follow-up data collection.
Study design details and subject population: 21,966 EPIC-Oxford participants aged 20-69 at baseline, baseline (1994-1999) and follow-up (2000-2003) timing, median follow-up of 5.3 years.

Main results on mean annual weight gain (about 389 g in men, 398 g in women) and BMI differences between diet groups at follow-up, which mirrored baseline patterns, plus initial multivariable findings for vegans.

Diet-group comparisons of adjusted weight gain: vegans and women fish-eaters gained less than meat-eaters, and participants who shifted toward more plant-based diets (meat-eater to vegan) had the smallest annual gains (242 g men, 301 g women).

Conclusions: average weight gain was about 400 g per year in this health-conscious UK cohort, differences between diet groups were small, and the lowest gain occurred in those who moved to diets with fewer animal foods.
Final conclusion sentence: lowest weight gain was observed in participants who switched during follow-up to a diet containing fewer animal foods.

Study design and methods: a community-based study of 368 Hong Kong pre-school children aged 3-5, comparing constipated (Rome criteria) and non-constipated children, with diet assessed via a 3-day food record for vegetables, fruits, whole-grain cereals and fluids.

Results on prevalence and fibre intake: 28.8% of children had constipation, and constipated children had significantly lower median dietary fibre intake (3.4 vs 3.8 g/d, P = 0.044) than non-constipated peers.

Micronutrient and plant food differences: constipated children had lower vitamin C, folate and magnesium intakes, and lower fruit and total plant food intake (61 vs 78 g/d; 142.5 vs 161.1 g/d), with the fibre intake reported as about 40% of the reference level.

Fluid and milk findings: total fluid intake did not differ between constipated and non-constipated children, while milk intake was marginally higher in the constipated group (P = 0.055), not reaching significance.

Conclusion on fibre and plant foods: insufficient fibre intake is common in Hong Kong pre-schoolers, and constipation is linked to lower fibre and micronutrient intake, attributed to under-consumption of plant foods, with milk intake marginally higher.
Recommendations: the study concludes that public education for parents is needed to build healthy dietary and bowel habits early in life and prevent childhood constipation.

Introduces the study's methods: projecting future US obesity prevalence and BMI distribution from NHANES survey data (1970s–2004), and estimating adult obesity-related health-care costs using Census projections and per capita excess cost estimates.

States the study's objective of illustrating the future burden of obesity and overweight in the US if current trends continue, and notes steady prevalence increases across all US population groups with differing annual rates.
Reports faster annual increases in adult overweight/obesity than in children and in women than men, then gives 2030 projections: 86.3% of adults overweight or obese and 51.1% obese.

Identifies the most affected groups (Black women at 96.9%, Mexican-American men at 91.1%), projects all adults overweight or obese by 2048 (Black women by 2034), and forecasts childhood overweight nearly doubling to about 30% by 2030.

Projects obesity-attributable health-care costs doubling each decade to $860.7–956.9 billion by 2030 (16–18% of total costs), notes the US is moving away from Healthy People 2010 goals, and calls for urgent corrective policies.
Concludes that timely, effective programs and policies are needed to avoid the health and societal consequences implied by the projections.

Abstract opening of a study on plasma adiponectin, lifestyle factors, and female twins: introduces adiponectin as a link between obesity, type 2 diabetes, and CVD, and describes the cross-sectional TwinsUK co-twin design with 877 female twin pairs.

Methods and key results: within-pair co-twin analyses adjusting for confounding, reporting log-transformed percent change in adiponectin per SD of dietary/body composition variables, with significant positive links for nonstarch polysaccharides and magnesium intake.

Specific dietary results from the twin study: nonstarch polysaccharide and magnesium intake show modest positive associations with adiponectin (with CIs and P values), and fruit and vegetable intake shows a trend toward association (P = 0.08), not explained by shared lifestyle confounding.

Additional dietary findings: adiponectin is associated with three derived dietary patterns (fruit and vegetable, dieting, traditional English), plus carbohydrate, protein, trans fat, and alcohol intake; also begins reporting strong inverse BMI association with adiponectin.

Body composition results: strong inverse associations between adiponectin and BMI, total fat mass, and central fat mass, significant both between individual twins and within twin pairs, suggesting a direct effect; also a summary sentence on modest dietary associations.

Conclusion of the abstract: dietary associations with adiponectin are modest and independent of adiposity, while body composition shows strong inverse links; the authors recommend weight maintenance and plant-rich diets to prevent CVD and type 2 diabetes.
Final fragment of the abstract's conclusion sentence, recommending diets rich in plant-based foods to prevent cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.

Introduction to a paper on bariatric surgery in pediatrics: it frames rising childhood and adolescent morbid obesity, notes that lifestyle changes have failed for many patients, and argues surgery should be considered in special cases.

Continuation of the introduction: acknowledges that bariatric surgery has high, potentially severe short- and long-term complications, yet may be the only option that restores a more normal metabolic state and achieves significant weight loss.
Closing of the introduction: states that the paper reviews the main surgical approaches for morbid obesity and weighs the pros and cons of each.

Introduction and methods of a meta-analysis of RCTs on avocado-soybean unsaponifiables (ASU) for hip/knee osteoarthritis, describing the inclusion criteria and the co-primary pain and Lequesne index outcomes measured as standardized mean differences.
Statistical methods (restricted maximum likelihood, mixed effects models, odds ratios for responders) and the start of the results, noting that all four included trials were manufacturer-supported.

Results describing the pooled population of 664 OA patients (hip 41.4%, knee 58.6%) randomized to 300 mg ASU or placebo, average trial duration, and the pooled pain reduction effect size with high heterogeneity (I² = 83.5%) favoring ASU.
Remaining key findings: the Lequesne index effect size favoring ASU, the secondary responder analysis (OR = 2.19, number needed to treat of six), and the beginning of the conclusions.
Conclusions of the meta-analysis: patients may be advised to try ASU for about 3 months, and the evidence suggests better treatment success in knee OA than hip OA.

Introduction to avocado fruit's cancer-preventive potential: phytochemicals' role in fruit-based cancer prevention, avocado's nutritional profile, and evidence that avocado extracts induce cell cycle arrest, growth inhibition, and apoptosis in precancerous and cancer cells.

Presents the authors' recent findings that chloroform-extracted avocado phytochemicals act on multiple signaling pathways and raise intracellular reactive oxygen species to trigger apoptosis, and announces the review's aim of summarizing avocado phytochemicals and their molecular mechanisms and targets.
Concludes that individual avocado phytochemicals and their combinations may serve as an advantageous dietary strategy for cancer prevention.
Introduction of the study on AV119, a patented avocado-derived sugar blend that induces human beta-defensin-2 in keratinocytes, and its effect on Malassezia furfur, a commensal skin yeast.
Results on AV119's effects: microbiological assays show it causes yeast aggregation and inhibits M. furfur invasiveness without affecting growth; cytokine modulation in keratinocytes is introduced.
Real-time PCR findings: AV119 modulates the HBD-2 response in keratinocytes, peaking at 48 hours, and restores a proinflammatory response; the authors link aggregation to reduced yeast penetration.
Conclusion proposing AV119 as an ingredient in cosmetics or pharmaceuticals to limit skin colonization by pathogenic M. furfur strains.

Introduces the coconut flakes cholesterol study: design (21 subjects, double-blind randomized crossover, 14 weeks with four 2-week periods and washouts) and baseline serum cholesterol range of 259-283 mg/dL.

Describes the test foods (corn flakes control, oat bran flakes reference, corn flakes with 15% and 25% coconut flake fiber) and begins the results on significant percent reductions in total and LDL cholesterol.
Reports the percent reductions in serum total and LDL cholesterol for oat bran, 15% coconut, and 25% coconut flakes, and begins the triglyceride findings.
Gives serum triglyceride percent reductions for corn, oat bran, and both coconut flake groups, and notes only 60% of subjects had triglycerides above 170 mg/dL and were included in that analysis.
States the conclusion that 15% and 25% coconut flakes lowered total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides, and attributes the effect to soluble and insoluble fiber from coconut flour.

Claims this is the first study linking fiber from a coconut by-product to a lipid biomarker and argues the results support coconut flakes/flour as a functional food and increased coconut by-product production.
Final fragment of the discussion, ending the sentence on justifying increased production of coconut and coconut by-products.

Introduction of a study on high-fat meals and endothelial function: background on endothelial dysfunction in coronary artery disease, brachial artery flow-mediated dilation by Doppler ultrasound, and the aim to assess high-fat intake in a local population.

Study design describing the test meals: the local high-fat dish nasi-lemak (coconut milk, saturated fat), a Western high-fat McDonald's meal, and a low-fat control meal, all used to study endothelial function.

Methods: 10 healthy non-smoking young males with normal BMI, fasting glucose and lipids; nitric oxide-dependent flow-mediated dilation and GTN-induced independent dilation measured by brachial Doppler before and 4 hours after each meal, by blinded sonographers.

Results begin: baseline brachial artery size, baseline flow and post-cuff-deflation flow increase were similar across the six arterial studies; endothelium-dependent dilation after reactive hyperaemia differed significantly between meals.

Key findings: endothelium-dependent dilation dropped markedly after the Western high-fat meal (8.6% vs -0.8% for low-fat, P<0.006) and after the local high-fat meal (7.7% vs -0.8% for low-fat, P<0.001), showing meal-induced endothelial impairment.

Further results: the two high-fat meals did not differ significantly from each other (P=0.678), and GTN-induced endothelium-independent dilation did not differ significantly across low-fat, Western and local high-fat conditions (P=0.094).

Conclusion: high-fat intake impairs endothelial function, a possible atherosclerosis mechanism beyond lipid effects, seen with both local and Western high-fat meals; the study concludes the technique may serve as a non-invasive screening tool for dietary effects on atherosclerosis.

Closing conclusion sentence: the brachial flow-mediated dilation technique may be a useful non-invasive screening tool for studying other high-fat diets and educating people about how dietary choices influence atherosclerosis.

Introduction of a study on coconut-consuming Minangkabau in West Sumatra: it frames saturated fat, serum cholesterol and CHD risk, and notes low hyperlipidaemia and heart disease despite coconut (a saturated-fat source) consumption.
Study aim and design: a case-control study among high coconut-consuming Minangkabau comparing food patterns and CHD risk between gender- and age-matched CHD cases and healthy controls.
Recruitment details: CHD cases were identified via five hospitals in Padang and Bukittinggi, West Sumatra, yielding 93 cases (62 men, 31 women) and 189 controls (113 men, 76 women).

Dietary assessment and food intake results: a semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire covering the prior 12 months showed cases ate more meats, eggs, sugar, tea, coffee and fruits, and less soy, rice and cereals than controls.

Nutrient results: coconut (flesh or milk) intake did not differ between groups, cases had higher protein and cholesterol and lower carbohydrate intake, and saturated and unsaturated fatty acid intakes were similar.

Main conclusion: total or saturated fat, including coconut-derived fat, was not a CHD predictor in this food culture, whereas animal foods, total protein, dietary cholesterol and less plant-derived carbohydrate were predictors of CHD.
Isolated period fragment closing the document's final sentence; contains no substantive content beyond the end of the conclusion on dietary predictors of CHD.

Introduction of the paper: motivates the report by noting that resource shortages in remote regions limit standard intravenous hydration and resuscitation, and previews the coconut water case in a Solomon Islands patient.

Closing summary of the paper's scope: lists the three components of the report (the clinical case using coconut water as IV fluid, lab analysis of local coconuts, and review of prior intravenous coconut use), completing the abstract's introduction.

Abstract of a dietary intervention study (objective, design, and subjects) comparing plasma lathosterol, lipids, lipoproteins and apolipoproteins during butter, coconut fat, and safflower oil diets in Pacific Islander Polynesians living in New Zealand.

Study subjects and interventions section of the abstract: 41 healthy Pacific island Polynesians in New Zealand received test-fat foods and regular dietary advice, and the results section begins, reporting lathosterol and LDL/apoB differences across diets.

Results section of the abstract reporting significant diet differences: plasma lathosterol, lathosterol/cholesterol ratio, LDL cholesterol and apoB were lower on coconut and safflower oil diets than on butter, with p-values given.

Remaining results and conclusions of the abstract: total, HDL cholesterol and apoA-I differed among diets (no significant difference between butter and coconut), and the authors conclude cholesterol synthesis and apoB-lipoprotein production are lower on coconut and safflower oil diets.
Final sentence of the abstract's conclusion, stating that lower cholesterol synthesis on coconut fat and safflower oil diets may be linked to reduced production rates of apoB-containing lipoproteins.

Background and methods of a retrospective cross-sectional study on betel-nut chewing and chronic kidney disease (CKD) in 3264 men from a hospital health-check screening programme (2003-2006), with CKD defined by eGFR under 60 using the MDRD formula.

Methods continued: CKD defined as eGFR below 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 via MDRD; risk factors considered include diabetes, hypertension, BMI, smoking, alcohol use and age. Start of results on CKD prevalence in the cohort.

Results: 677 men (20.7%) had CKD and 427 (13.1%) reported betel-nut use. CKD prevalence was 24.8% in betel-nut users versus 11.3% in non-users (P = 0.026). Multivariate logistic regression adjusted for age, hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidaemia begins.

Key statistical results: betel-nut use was independently associated with CKD (P < 0.001), adjusted odds ratio 2.572 (95% CI 1.917-3.451). Conclusions state betel-nut use is associated with CKD in men, independent of age, BMI, smoking, alcohol, hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidaemia.
Final conclusion of the study: the association between betel-nut use and CKD in men holds independently of age, BMI, smoking, alcohol consumption, hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidaemia.

Introduction and key recent findings of an AAP review on early nutrition and atopic disease, covering maternal diet restriction during pregnancy and lactation and the protective effect of exclusive breastfeeding in high-risk infants.

Findings on supplementing breastfeeding with hydrolyzed formula to protect against atopic dermatitis, and the lack of evidence that delaying complementary foods beyond 4 to 6 months protects against allergy.
Conclusion that dietary interventions beyond 4 to 6 months of age lack sufficient data for protection against atopic disease, followed by the start of the summary section on high-risk infants.

Summary of evidence that exclusive breastfeeding for at least 4 months, delayed complementary foods, and hydrolyzed formula supplementation may prevent allergy in high-risk infants, with the summary's statement on maternal diet beginning.

Final conclusion that there is no convincing evidence that maternal diet manipulation during pregnancy or lactation, soy product use, or infant dietary restrictions beyond 4 to 6 months affect atopic disease development.
Opening of the review on cancer chemopreventive potential of apples; introduces apple (Malus sp.) phytochemical classes such as polyphenols, procyanidins, flavonols, and anthocyanins.

Continues the introduction by noting apples' broad biological activities linked to health benefits (cardiovascular, asthma, diabetes, obesity, cancer), citing Boyer and Liu 2004, and sets up the review's scope.

States the review's aim: summarizing evidence on cancer-preventive effects of apples, apple juice, and apple extracts (termed apple products), and highlights in vitro findings for oligomeric procyanidins.
Lists the in vitro cancer-prevention mechanisms of apple components, including antimutagenic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antiproliferative, apoptotic, epigenetic, and innate immunity effects.
Summarizes animal and epidemiological evidence: apple products prevent skin, mammary, and colon carcinogenesis in animals, and eating one or more apples daily may lower lung and colon cancer risk.

Abstract opening of a study on Red Delicious apple peel phytochemicals: bioactivity-guided fractionation, isolation of 29 compounds (triterpenoids, flavonoids, organic acids, sterols) via column chromatography and preparative HPLC, and structure elucidation by HR-MS and NMR.

Methods and early results: the isolation techniques (Diaion HP-20, silica gel, ODS columns) and structure identification are described, then antiproliferative testing against HepG2 liver and MCF-7 breast cancer cells, and the start of the flavonoid yield ranking (compounds 18-23).

Flavonoid yield results from apple peel isolation: quercetin-3-O-glucopyranoside (compound 20, 82.6%) is the dominant flavonoid, followed by the galactoside (19, 17.1%), with trace amounts of quercetin (18), catechin (22), epicatechin (23), and the arabinofuranoside (21).

Antiproliferative results: quercetin (18) and quercetin-3-O-glucopyranoside (20) are the most potent compounds, with EC50 values against HepG2 liver cancer cells and MCF-7 breast cancer cells, and the antioxidant findings begin with six flavonoids (18-23).

Antioxidant results: six flavonoids (18-23) and three phenolics (10, 11, 14) are potent antioxidants; caffeic acid (10), quercetin (18), and the arabinofuranoside (21) have EC50 below 10 microM, with the arabinofuranoside named as the beta-D-arabinofuranoside in the text.

Conclusion: most tested flavonoids and phenolics outperform ascorbic acid in antioxidant activity and likely explain apple antioxidant effects, supporting the overall finding that apple peel phytochemicals have potent antioxidant and antiproliferative activity.

Introduction to a study of star fruit-induced acute renal failure: prior finding of oliguric acute renal failure from star fruit, and the aim to probe mechanisms of acute oxalate nephropathy using cell and animal models, including renal function, kidney histopathology, and TUNEL apoptosis assays.

Experimental design: four rat groups (control on tap water; star fruit juice group with about 0.2M oxalate; oxalate solution groups at 0.2M and 0.4M), plus flow cytometry on MDCK kidney cells treated with star fruit juice or oxalate.

Results: mean creatinine clearance was significantly reduced in the star fruit and both oxalate groups; TUNEL showed dose-dependent apoptosis, and flow cytometry of MDCK cells showed dose- and time-dependent effects.

Conclusion: star fruit juice causes acute renal injury via calcium oxalate crystal obstruction and also via oxalate-linked apoptosis of renal epithelial cells, the latter likely driven by the fruit's oxalate content.
Closing fragment of the conclusion sentence, noting that the apoptosis may be caused by oxalate levels in the star fruit.

Introductory case-report abstract describing severe lactic acidosis linked to mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana) juice sold as a dietary supplement in the US, noting its traditional Southeast Asian use and marketed health claims.

Introduction to the case report: first described green algal (unicellular Chlorophyta) infection in a human, in a 30-year-old woman with a persistent infected surgical wound on the right foot after possible river-water exposure while canoeing.

Histopathology of the infected tissue: mixed suppurative and granulomatous inflammation with endosporulating 6-9 micron round-to-oval organisms that stain PAS-, Gomori methenamine-silver-, and Gridley-positive in cytoplasmic granules.

Diagnostic findings distinguishing the organism: no staining with antibodies to the two pathogenic Prototheca species, and electron microscopy showing degenerated chloroplast remnants, supporting a green algal diagnosis.
Concluding sentence of the case report stating that the combined findings are consistent with a green algal infection.

Case report of a dog with ataxia and a lingual mass (earlier diagnosed as protothecosis) found at necropsy to have disseminated green algal infection; describes gross green discoloration of tongue, lungs, lymph nodes, liver, and meninges.

Histopathology and special stains of disseminated algal infection in a dog: pyogranulomatous inflammation in multiple tissues, PAS-positive algal cell walls with cytoplasmic granules, and ultrastructural features (grana, thylakoids, starch-like dense bodies) leading toward identification as Chlorella.

Conclusion of the canine case report identifying the algae as Chlorella by histochemical and electron microscopic methods, and claiming it is the first reported disseminated Chlorella infection and the first in a companion animal.

Methods section of a study on microcystin detection in Spirulina products: compares gel filtration, ultrafiltration, and silica gel SPE clean-up after a reversed-phase ODS cartridge, for LC-MS/MS analysis.

Optimized extraction protocol details: specific wash and elution solvent conditions (water, 20% and 90% methanol on the ODS cartridge, then 80% methanol on silica gel), and introduction of the 36-sample survey of Chinese retail Spirulina health foods.

Results of the survey: microcystins found in 34 of 36 Chinese Spirulina health food samples (94%), at 2 to 163 ng/g (mean 14 ± 27 ng/g), lower than levels reported previously for blue-green algae products.

Congener distribution and risk note: MC-RR was most prevalent (94.4% of samples), followed by MC-LR (30.6%) and MC-YR (27.8%), with a warning that chronic exposure risks remain despite low concentrations.

Conclusion: emphasizes that chronic exposure risk from microcystin-contaminated Spirulina food should not be dismissed despite low levels, and presents the method as suitable for detecting microcystins in commercial Spirulina samples.

Study background and objective: introduces the hypothesis that fruit, vegetable, and dark fish intake may protect against sudden cardiac death and arrhythmias, and states the aim to test links with heart rate variability (HRV) in older men from the Veterans Administration Normative Aging Study.

Study design and methods: describes the Normative Aging Study cohort (586 older men, 928 observations, 2000-2007), HRV measurement, and dietary assessment using a self-administered semiquantitative food-frequency questionnaire grouped into quartiles.

Main result on green leafy vegetables: after adjusting for confounders, greater green leafy vegetable intake was linked to higher normalized high-frequency HRV power and lower normalized low-frequency power (P for trend < 0.05), and these links held after adjusting for lifestyle factors like physical activity and multivitamin use.

Null and modifier findings: no significant HRV association for other fruits and vegetables, vitamin C, carotenoids, tuna and dark fish, or omega-3 fatty acids; effect modification by obesity (noncitrus fruit) and cigarette smoking (total and cruciferous vegetables) was observed and flagged for further study.
Conclusion: higher green leafy vegetable intake may lower cardiovascular disease risk by improving cardiac autonomic function, as reflected in favorable HRV changes.
Introduction and design of a hospital-based case-control study on diet and ischemic heart disease (IHD) risk in India, covering New Delhi and Bangalore, with 350 acute MI cases and matched controls.

Study methods: 350 acute myocardial infarction cases and 700 age-, sex-, and hospital-matched controls from 8 hospitals; long-term diet measured with region-specific food-frequency questionnaires; conditional logistic regression used.
Main results begin: a significant dose-dependent inverse association between vegetable intake and IHD risk, strongest for green leafy vegetables, with the multivariate analysis introduced.

Key quantitative findings: median 3.5 servings/wk of vegetables linked to 67% lower relative risk (RR 0.33) versus 0.5 servings/wk; robustness to dietary covariates; cereal intake linked to lower risk; mustard oil (alpha-linolenic acid) introduced versus sunflower oil.
Mustard oil results (cooking RR 0.49, frying RR 0.29 versus sunflower oil) and the conclusion that vegetable-rich diets and mustard oil use may contribute to lower IHD risk among Indians.
Final fragment of the abstract's conclusion sentence stating that these diet patterns may lower IHD risk among Indians.

Introduces the case-control study of diet and renal cell carcinoma (2003-2006), describing the design and how the case and control participants (n=335 cases, n=337 controls) were recruited and matched.

Methods detail: diet was assessed with the 70-item Block food frequency questionnaire, and the statistical approach used logistic regression with ORs, 95% CIs, and trend tests, adjusted for age, sex, race, income, BMI, and smoking pack-years.
Results begin: vegetable consumption is associated with decreased renal cell carcinoma risk in all subjects and men (ORs 0.56 and 0.49), while fruit consumption shows no such association.

Results continue: tomato consumption is linked to decreased risk in the total population and men, while red meat consumption is linked to increased risk among all subjects and women (e.g., OR 4.43 overall).

Results and conclusions: white bread and total dairy consumption increase risk among women only (ORs 3.05 and 2.36), and the conclusions state that the protective role of vegetables and the harmful role of meat are supported, but not for fruit.
Conclusions and novel findings: increased risk with white bread and white potato consumption and decreased risk with tomato consumption are highlighted as new contributions of the study.
Final fragment of the novel findings sentence, completing the reference to decreased renal cell carcinoma risk associated with tomato consumption.

Study design and setting for a coconut-derived emulsion (CDE) head lice shampoo trial: a UK school trial (Bristol, Weston-super-Mare) with treatment on days 0 and 7 and checks on days 8 and 15, plus a family trial in Northern Somerset with follow-up at days 14 and 70.

Setting and results of the coconut-derived emulsion head lice study: UK schools and Somerset families, the main outcome of children free from infestation, and school trial cure rates at day 8 comparing permethrin (14%, n=7) with CDE shampoo (61%, n=37).

Family trial results for the coconut-derived emulsion head lice shampoo: a 96% cure rate (n=28) when all family members were treated, and only 1 of 12 children re-infested after 10 weeks when used as a cosmetic shampoo.

Conclusion of the coconut-derived emulsion head lice shampoo study: CDE shampoo is an effective novel treatment for head lice, and using it as a cosmetic shampoo after treatment can help reduce re-infestation.

Opening chunk of the JACC study abstract (Ikehara et al., SLEEP 2009): states the objectives, cohort design, community setting, and participant numbers (98,634 Japanese adults aged 40–79, enrolled 1988–1990, followed to 2003), then begins the Measurements and Results section on follow-up.

Results section of the JACC sleep-duration abstract: median 14.3-year follow-up and sex-specific death counts for stroke, coronary heart disease, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and all causes among Japanese men and women.

Middle of the results: compares sleep of 4 hours or less with 7 hours, linking it to higher coronary heart disease mortality in women and noncardiovascular/noncancer and all-cause mortality in both sexes, and starts listing the hazard ratios with confidence intervals.

Continues the hazard ratios for short sleep (noncardiovascular/noncancer and all-cause mortality in men and women) and introduces long sleep of 10 hours or more, which was linked to roughly 1.5- to 2-fold higher stroke, cardiovascular, noncardiovascular/noncancer, and all-cause mortality.

Covers the remaining findings: long sleep's associations, no link between sleep duration and cancer mortality in either sex, and the start of the Conclusions, which report increased cardiovascular, noncardiovascular/noncancer, and all-cause mortality at both extremes of sleep.

Conclusion and citation: short and long sleep both raise mortality, giving a U-shaped curve for total mortality with its lowest point at 7 hours; also gives the full citation (Ikehara S, Iso H, et al., SLEEP 2009;32(3)) and begins the author list.
Final fragment of the citation: the end of the JACC Study title and the journal reference, SLEEP 2009;32(3):259–301, for the Japanese sleep duration and mortality paper.

Introduction and methods of a study on sleep habits and common cold susceptibility: 153 adults aged 21–55 logged sleep duration, sleep efficiency, and feeling rested over a 14-day baseline before rhinovirus exposure.

Methods continued: sleep variables (duration, efficiency as percent of time in bed asleep, feeling rested) were averaged over 14 days, then participants received nasal rhinovirus drops and were quarantined and monitored for clinical colds.
Results on sleep duration: a graded association where under 7 hours of sleep carried 2.94 times the odds of developing a cold compared with 8 or more hours (95% CI 1.18–7.30).

Results on sleep efficiency: a graded association where efficiency below 92% carried 5.50 times the risk of a cold versus 98% or higher (95% CI 2.08–14.48), with confounders such as antibodies, demographics, season, and health practices ruled out as explanations.

Final results and conclusions: feeling rested was not linked to colds, and shorter sleep duration and poorer sleep efficiency before rhinovirus exposure were associated with lower resistance to illness.
Concluding fragment of the study's conclusion stating that poorer sleep before rhinovirus exposure was associated with reduced resistance to illness.

Introduction of a case-control study on childhood leukemia (Los Angeles County, 1980-1987) examining dietary N-nitroso compound (NOC) precursors and inhibitors, including how cases and controls were recruited.

Study methods continued: control recruitment via friends and random-digit dialing, interview sample sizes (232 cases and 232 controls), and the specific food groups of interest, such as breakfast meats, luncheon meats, hot dogs, and citrus.
Additional dietary items surveyed (apples, charcoal-broiled meats, milk, coffee, cola) and the assessment of parental and child consumption frequencies, leading into the key adjusted findings.

Main results: after adjustment, children's and fathers' hot dog intake were the only persistent significant risk associations with leukemia (with odds ratios and confidence intervals), and fruit showed no protective effect.
Conclusion: the hot dog findings are consistent with animal studies and the NOC-leukemia hypothesis, but potential data biases mean more focused epidemiologic research is needed.
Final fragment of the conclusion calling for further comprehensive epidemiologic studies of the NOC hypothesis.

Opening of the document: introduces cancer as largely preventable, citing expected US and worldwide diagnoses, and states that 90-95% of cases stem from environment and lifestyle rather than genetics. Lists the first lifestyle factors (smoking, diet).

Lists the full set of lifestyle risk factors (smoking, diet, alcohol, sun, pollutants, infections, stress, obesity, inactivity) and gives the estimated shares of cancer deaths attributed to tobacco, diet, and infections.
Concludes the statistics on cancer deaths and draws the prevention implication: lists the recommended measures such as smoking cessation, diet changes, exercise, sun avoidance, and vaccination.
States the review's thesis: inflammation links cancer-causing agents with cancer-preventing agents, and that cancer is preventable and requires major lifestyle changes.
Fragment closing the document's final sentence, restating that cancer is a preventable disease requiring major lifestyle changes.
Study abstract opening: describes the cohort design, meat exposure groups assessed, and sample sizes (234 cancer cases including ALL and brain tumor cases, versus controls) in Denver, Colorado.
Results on maternal hot-dog consumption and childhood brain tumors, with the odds ratio and confidence interval, plus the case-control comparison setup in Denver.
Child-level results: hamburger consumption linked to acute lymphocytic leukemia and hot-dog consumption linked to brain tumors, each with odds ratios and confidence intervals.
Interaction finding that lacking vitamin use combined with meat eating raises risk of ALL and brain cancer more than either factor alone, and the authors' link to the earlier hot-dog study.
Concluding interpretation: the hot-dog and brain tumor replication and the vitamin-meat synergism suggest a possible harmful role of dietary nitrites and nitrosamines.

Introduces a Canadian case-control study of meat and fish intake and cancer risk, describing the cancer sites studied, sample sizes (19,732 cases, 5,039 controls), and data collection period (1994-1997) across 8 provinces.

Describes study methods: socioeconomic, lifestyle, and diet measurement, a 69-item food frequency questionnaire covering diet 2 years before data collection, and unconditional logistic regression for odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals.

Reports main findings that total and processed meat were linked to risk of many cancers (stomach, colon, rectum, pancreas, lung, breast, prostate, testis, kidney, bladder, leukemia), red meat specifically to colon, lung, and bladder cancer, and no association for ovary, brain, or NHL.

Summarizes that fish and poultry showed no consistent excess cancer risk and were inversely related to several cancers, concluding red and processed meat are unfavorable dietary factors while fish and poultry are favorable.
Final concluding sentence stating that fish and poultry are favorable dietary indicators in the context of cancer risk from the Canadian meat and fish intake study.

Opening of an abstract for a meta-analysis of case-control studies on long-term mobile phone use and brain tumour risk; introduces the glioma pooled odds ratio and latency and laterality (ipsilateral vs contralateral) subgroup results.

Middle section of the abstract reporting mobile phone use and brain tumour meta-analysis results: ipsilateral and contralateral odds ratios for glioma and the acoustic neuroma pooled and latency-stratified estimates.
Continuation of the abstract's results on acoustic neuroma laterality and meningioma: the overall meningioma odds ratio and its latency-stratified and ipsilateral/contralateral estimates.

Final results and conclusion of the meta-analysis abstract on mobile phone use and brain tumours, summarising the meningioma subgroup findings and concluding an ipsilateral association with glioma and acoustic neuroma at 10+ years latency.
Fragment ending the abstract's conclusion, completing the phrase about the ≥10-year latency period in the consistent association finding for mobile phone use and brain tumours.

Introduction to a study of carob (Ceratonia siliqua) extract and its main phenolic compound gallic acid, examining chemopreventive gene-expression effects in human colon cell lines LT97 (adenoma) and HT29 (carcinoma).

Results on stress-response genes: catalase (CAT) and SOD2 were induced by carob extract and gallic acid in LT97 adenoma cells but not HT29 carcinoma cells, and 24 h pretreatment reduced H2O2-induced DNA damage despite no change in protein or enzyme activity.
Conclusion stating that carob extract and gallic acid modulate gene expression and protect colon adenoma cells from H2O2-induced genotoxicity, which is the study's main takeaway.
Final sentence of the abstract noting that the upregulation of stress-response genes did not translate into demonstrated functional consequences.

Opening chunk of a summary paper introducing cocoa polyphenols' biological activities and the nutritional and pharmacological interest in cocoa and chocolate consumption, framing the review of health effects presented at a 2007 Milan conference.

Closing chunk of the same introductory paragraph, completing the description of the paper's aim: summarizing new findings on cocoa and chocolate's effects on human health, as presented at the 'Chocolate, Lifestyle, and Health' conference in Milan on March 2, 2007.

Introduction of a review on cocoa and cardiovascular health: opens with epidemiological evidence that plant-food intake lowers coronary heart disease and stroke risk, and proposes cocoa as a possible key mediator, citing benefits for blood pressure, insulin resistance, and vascular and platelet function.

Continuation of the review's introduction on cocoa and cardiovascular health: notes that the mechanisms are still debated and lists proposed pathways (nitric oxide activation, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects), then previews the review's aims covering cardiovascular effects, mechanisms, and clinical implications.

Closing sentence of the review's introduction on cocoa and cardiovascular health, stating the review's scope: summarizing cardiovascular effects of cocoa, outlining its mechanisms, and highlighting clinical implications of consumption.

Abstract opening of a randomized crossover trial on acute dark chocolate and cocoa effects on endothelial function and blood pressure in 45 overweight adults, including study design and participant characteristics.
Study design details: phase 1 assigns subjects to dark chocolate bar (22 g cocoa) or cocoa-free placebo bar; phase 2 assigns sugar-free cocoa, sugared cocoa (both 22 g cocoa), or placebo.
Results on endothelial function measured as flow-mediated dilatation, showing dark chocolate and sugar-free and sugared cocoa improved FMD versus placebo, with mean percentage changes and P values.
Blood pressure results: systolic and diastolic blood pressure decreased after dark chocolate and sugar-free cocoa compared with placebo, with mean mm Hg changes and P values.
Blood pressure results continued for sugar-free cocoa, plus comparison showing endothelial function improved significantly more with sugar-free than regular (sugared) cocoa.

Conclusions: acute intake of solid dark chocolate and liquid cocoa improves endothelial function and lowers blood pressure in overweight adults; sugar may attenuate effects while sugar-free preparations may enhance them.

Introduction of the Panama study: flavonoid-rich diets and cardiovascular disease/cancer prevention, and the Kuna of San Blas who drink flavanol-rich cocoa (>900 mg/day), likely the highest-flavonoid diet studied.

Study methods: death-certificate diagnoses used to compare cause-specific death rates (2000-2004) between mainland Panama and the San Blas islands inhabited only by Kuna, with the hypothesis that flavanol-driven nitric oxide activation would lower rates of NO-sensitive diseases.

Results for mainland Panama deaths (77,375 total; 558 in San Blas), where cardiovascular disease led (83.4 per 100,000 age-adjusted) and cancer ranked second (68.4), providing the baseline for comparison with the Kuna.
Comparative mortality results: Kuna in San Blas had much lower age-adjusted rates for cardiovascular disease (9.2), cancer (4.4), and diabetes mellitus (6.6 vs 24.1 on the mainland).

Interpretation and conclusion: the lower disease burden among the Kuna may reflect very high flavanol intake and sustained nitric oxide synthesis, but as an observational study with many confounding risk factors it cannot give definitive evidence.
Final sentence of the abstract's conclusion, cautioning that the observational design cannot provide definitive evidence of a causal flavanol effect.

Introduces the Kuna Indians of Panama's Caribbean archipelago, whose low blood pressure, longevity, and reduced rates of heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and cancer are noted, alongside their high dietary intake of flavanol-rich cocoa.

States the mechanistic link that cocoa flavonoids activate nitric oxide synthesis in healthy humans, and argues that the Kuna's high flavanol intake may protect against hypertension, ischemic heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and cancer.
Concludes that this possibility is important enough to justify large, randomized controlled clinical trials to test the protective effects of flavanols.
Abstract opening of a study on Hibiscus sabdariffa L. extracts, introducing the aim to test phenolic compounds' effects on 1-nitropyrene mutagenicity and antiproliferative activity in HeLa cells.
Results on phenolic content of the extracts: hot aqueous extract contains 22.27 mg protocatechuic acid per gram, similar to cold aqueous and chloroform extracts, with ethyl acetate extract lowest.
Main findings on bioactivity: extracts inhibit 1-NP mutagenicity dose-dependently, hot aqueous extract reduces HeLa cell proliferation dose-dependently without inducing DNA fragmentation.
Concluding statement that H. sabdariffa extracts show antimutagenic activity against 1-NP and reduce HeLa cell proliferation, likely due to their phenolic acid composition.

Abstract of a study on Ocimum sanctum (holy basil) extract's anti-genotoxic effect against cyproterone acetate-induced DNA damage in human lymphocytes; this chunk introduces the methods and the ~30 microM cyproterone acetate treatment with the plant infusion.

Continuation of the abstract giving the three O. sanctum infusion dosages (g/ml of culture medium) and the main result: a clear dose-dependent reduction in cyproterone acetate genotoxicity, suggesting a modulating role for the plant infusion.
Concluding sentence of the abstract stating the plant infusion alone is not genotoxic but can modulate cyproterone acetate's genotoxicity in human lymphocytes in vitro.

Introduction and background of a study on food phytochemicals suppressing CD74 expression in NCI-N87 gastric carcinoma cells, establishing CD74 as high in these cancer cells relative to fetal gastric cells, as a possible H. pylori urease adhesion target.
Methods portion describing the discovery of a novel cell-based ELISA for screening CD74 suppressants and treatment of NCI-N87 cells with 25 food phytochemicals at 4–100 µM for 48 h.

Results of the screen identifying bergamottin as the top CD74 suppressant (LC50/IC50 >7.1), followed by luteolin, nobiletin, and quercetin, with the concluding implication that these compounds could prevent H. pylori adhesion and infection.
Concluding sentence of the abstract stating that the CD74-suppressing compounds are unique candidates for preventing H. pylori adhesion and infection, with plausible mechanisms of action.

Introduction and study objective: background on tea catechins' chronic disease benefits, poorly understood digestive stability, and the aim to test food additives on catechin recovery in green tea beverages with specified EC, EGC, EGCG, and ECG levels.

Methods: formulation details, listing the catechin doses per 100 mL and the commercial additives tested (citric acid, BHT, EDTA, ascorbic acid, milks, and citrus juices) added to finished tea beverages at incremental dosages.

Methods and initial results: in vitro gastric and small intestinal digestion with HPLC catechin profiling, and the finding that green tea catechin stability is poor, with under 20% remaining after digestion and EGC and EGCG most sensitive.

Results on recovery: milk-containing teas (bovine, soy, rice) raised total catechin recovery to 52, 55, and 69%, and 30 mg ascorbic acid per 250 mL significantly increased recovery of each catechin (EGC 74%, EGCG 54%, EC 82%, ECG 45%).

Results on juice and conclusions: citrus juice formulations gave the highest recovery for all catechins (EGC 81-98%, EGCG 56-76%, EC 86-95%, ECG 30-55%), and the authors conclude that consumption practices and formulation affect digestive catechin recovery and physiological outcomes.
Concluding sentence of the abstract: formulation factors and tea consumption practices likely influence catechin digestive recovery and may produce diverse physiological profiles.

Introduces the study's aim (link between habitual green tea intake and blood glucose/glucose metabolism biomarkers) and its design: a cross-sectional study of 35 Japanese men aged 23–63 from Shizuoka Prefecture.

Describes the data collected (biochemical measures, health/lifestyle/nutrition questionnaire, green tea consumption frequency and 1%/2%/3% concentrations) and the key result that 3% green tea drinkers had lower fasting blood glucose and fructosamine than 1% drinkers.

Reports the statistical findings: fasting blood glucose significantly associated with green tea concentration (β = −0.14, p = 0.03), no significant differences by consumption frequency for glucose, fructosamine, or HbA1c, and the overall conclusion that high-concentration green tea may lower blood glucose.
Final concluding sentence of the abstract, restating that high-concentration green tea consumption may have the potential to reduce blood glucose levels.
Introduction to a HepG2 cell study of green tea and EGCG against ethanol toxicity, setting up the question of active compounds and mechanism, with GGT chosen as the toxicity marker.
Results on ethanol-induced toxicity in HepG2 cells: dose-dependent rise in GGT activity and loss of viability, and green tea extract pretreatment significantly attenuating these changes.

Comparison of green tea constituents: EGCG effectively attenuates ethanol cytotoxicity while L-theanine and caffeine do not, and cytotoxicity is also blocked by an ADH inhibitor, a GGT inhibitor, and thiol modulators.
Mechanistic conclusion: EGCG does not prevent ethanol-induced intracellular glutathione loss but is a strong GGT inhibitor, so green tea's cytoprotection is attributed to GGT inhibition by EGCG.
Closing implication of the study: GGT inhibitors, including EGCG, may be a novel strategy for attenuating ethanol-induced liver damage.

Abstract opening (Objective and Methods) of a clinical study on soy (kinako) and green tea, alone or combined, for hypolipidemic and antioxidant effects in 100 dyslipidemic adults across four groups, including the soy, green tea, combination, and control diet arms.

Methods continuation describing the daily green tea and combined soy/green tea dosing, the control group on a hypocholesterolemic diet, the 0/45/90-day evaluation timepoints, and lipid measurements, including LDL calculated by the Friedewald equation.

Methods end describing LDL isolation by ultracentrifugation, chemiluminescence assays for total plasma antioxidant capacity and lipid hydroperoxides, statistical reporting as medians with 25th-75th percentiles at a 5% significance level, and the start of the Results section.

Results describing lipid outcomes: no significant group differences in LDL, HDL, or triacylglycerols, but a significant total cholesterol reduction in the soy/green tea combination group at 45 and 90 days.

Results and conclusion on oxidative markers: no significant change in lipid hydroperoxides (total or LDL-linked), increased total plasma antioxidant potential in all soy and/or green tea groups, and the summary that both agents raised antioxidant capacity in hypercholesterolemic patients.

Final conclusion sentence stating that only the soy plus green tea combination lowered total cholesterol, while either agent alone or combined raised total antioxidant potential in hypercholesterolemic patients.
Introduction to L-theanine, an amino acid found in tea, and its prior EEG evidence of a direct effect on human brain function; sets up the study's motivation.

Explains that L-theanine increases alpha-band EEG activity (relaxation without drowsiness), but this was only shown at higher doses than a cup of black tea (~20mg), so the study aims to test realistic dietary levels.
Methods of the study: EEG measured in healthy young participants before and at multiple time points after 50mg L-theanine versus placebo, with participants resting with eyes closed.

Results: alpha activity increased more over time in the L-theanine group than placebo, a second study replicated this in passive activity, and the authors conclude L-theanine at dietary levels affects mental alertness/arousal.
Conclusion and future directions: since alpha activity is linked to attention, the authors plan further research on L-theanine's effects on attentional processes.

Opening of a literature review on green tea and health: states the review's aim (clinical evidence on green tea, its extracts, and EGCG for chemoprevention and cardiovascular protection) and begins describing the search methods.

Methods continuation and start of Results: names the databases searched (PubMed 1966-2009, Cochrane Library 2008) and summarizes observational findings that green tea's cancer-prevention benefit is inconclusive, with trends for breast and prostate cancer.

Results on interventional and observational studies: reports reduced colorectal adenoma relapse after resection and higher survival in ovarian cancer, plus observational hints that green tea protects against hypertension and stroke.
Results end and Conclusion begins: overall evidence is inconclusive, but green tea may offer some chemoprevention for prostate and breast cancer, and may attenuate atherosclerosis risk factors.
Final sentence of the conclusion: green tea may lower the incidence of cardiovascular events and stroke by attenuating atherosclerosis risk factors.

Abstract opening for a case-control study on artificial sweetener use and urinary tract tumors (UTT) in Córdoba, Argentina, stating the objective, design, and the 197 cases and 397 controls recruited from 1999 to 2006.

Methods and results continuation: all subjects were interviewed about artificial sweetener and other UTT risk-factor exposure, and the results report that 26% of cases and 22% of controls used artificial sweeteners, with increased risk noted for long-term users.

Key quantitative findings: adjusted odds ratios show long-term (10+ years) artificial sweetener users had OR 2.18 (1.22-3.89) versus 1.10 (0.61-2.00) for short-term users, after adjusting for age, gender, BMI, social status, and tobacco years; the conclusion links 10+ years of regular use to UTT.
Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that regular artificial sweetener use for 10 years or more was positively associated with urinary tract tumors.

Introduction to the document on the potential toxicity and safety controversy of artificial sweeteners, covering their role as sugar substitutes amid obesity concerns and their beneficial use for diabetics.

Discusses scientific disagreement over links between artificial sweeteners and a list of diseases (cancers, chronic fatigue syndrome, neurological disorders, autism, lupus), plus recent attention to their effects on glucose regulation.

States the article's purpose for occupational health nurses who counsel individuals on sweetener use, and previews the article's scope: types, history, chemistry, biological fate, physiological effects, studies, and regulations.
Final part of the article's outline, listing the remaining topics covered: physiological effects, published animal and human studies, and current standards and regulations for artificial sweeteners.

Introduces stevia leaf extracts as sweeteners and identifies steviol glycosides (stevioside, rebaudiosides A and C) as the sweet compounds; begins the genetic toxicology review of stevioside and steviol.

Summarizes the overall genotoxicity findings: most tests are negative, and neither stevioside nor steviol binds DNA or shows relevant genotoxic damage; notes the mutagenicity seen in strain TM677 for steviol and derivatives.

Covers the specific contrary evidence: the TM677 mutagenicity was not reproduced in bacteria with normal DNA repair, and a single positive in vivo rat study on DNA strand breaks was not confirmed in mice and likely reflects non-DNA-damage processes.
Reports the in vivo clastogenicity results (none even at very high doses) and the Weight-of-Evidence conclusion that stevioside and steviol pose no genetic damage risk to humans from consumption.
Concludes the final sentence of the review, restating that the substances do not pose a risk of genetic damage following human consumption.
Introduction and background of a study on the antioxidant content of refined sugar alternatives, covering oxidative damage links to disease and the list of alternative sweeteners.

Continues the background by listing alternative sweeteners (raw cane sugar, plant syrups, molasses, honey, date sugar) and the hypothesis that unrefined sweeteners have more antioxidants, plus the study objective.
Covers the study design: FRAP assay used to measure total antioxidant capacity, with major US retail brands of 12 sweetener types plus refined white sugar and corn syrup sampled.
Presents the first results: refined sugar, corn syrup, and agave nectar had minimal antioxidant activity, raw cane sugar was higher, and dark and blackstrap molasses had the highest FRAP values.
Gives the remaining results for maple syrup, brown sugar, and honey (intermediate values), and the estimated 2.6 mmol/day antioxidant intake increase from substituting alternative sweeteners.
Concludes the abstract, comparing the 2.6 mmol/day gain to berries or nuts and stating that many readily available refined-sugar alternatives offer antioxidant benefits.

Introduction to high fructose corn syrup (HFCS): its rising use in food over the past 40 years and concern that it promotes obesity and other health problems more than other caloric sweeteners; describes HFCS-42/HFCS-55 composition relative to sucrose.

Compositional comparison of HFCS and sucrose: both contain roughly equal fructose and glucose, with HFCS having free monosaccharides while sucrose is a disaccharide that is cleaved in the small intestine, so both are absorbed as free sugars.

Food-industry rationale for HFCS (flavor, stability, freshness, texture, color, pourability, consistency) and the conclusion that HFCS's near-identical absorption to sucrose makes it unlikely to contribute more to obesity than sucrose.
Research gaps: few studies have examined differential effects of sweeteners on long-developing conditions like obesity, leaving the comparative question insufficiently tested.

Recommended research needs (better nutrient databases, stronger experimental designs on mechanisms and fructose dose-response) and the finding that current evidence is insufficient to ban, restrict, or label HFCS-containing products.
Concluding policy and dietary recommendation: no regulatory restriction or warning labels are currently justified, but limiting intake of all added caloric sweeteners, including HFCS, is advised.
Opening chunk of a review on sucrose and behavioral problems; introduces food intolerance as the first proposed mechanism by which sucrose might affect behavior.

Continuation discussing hypoglycemia as a second mechanism: sub-clinical low blood glucose linked to irritability and violence, though sucrose is not the main driver of glucose swings; introduces micronutrient status as a third mechanism.

Covers the micronutrient mechanism: supplementation reduced antisocial behavior, but micronutrient intake tracks total energy rather than sucrose, so sucrose rarely causes deficiency; cites meta-analysis findings.
Concluding sentence of the document: a meta-analysis of well-designed studies on sucrose and children's behavior found no evidence of an adverse effect.

Opening chunk of the FAO/WHO JECFA 71st report on food additives: introduces the Committee's purpose of recommending ADIs and identity/purity specifications, and the general toxicological principles section.

Continues the report introduction, moving from general principles into the summary list of food additives evaluated, beginning with branching glycosyltransferase, cassia gum, cyclamic acid, and cyclotetraglucose.

Middle of the report's list of evaluated additives, covering ferrous ammonium phosphate, glycerol esters of rosins, lycopene, mineral oils, octenyl succinic acid modified gum arabic, sodium hydrogen sulfate, and sucrose oligoesters.

Transitions from the list of evaluated additives to the list of food additives whose specifications were revised, including diacetyltartaric acid esters, ethyl lauroyl arginate, nisin, nitrous oxide, pectins, and titanium dioxide.

Closing chunk of the report summary: ends the revised-specifications list with starch sodium octenyl succinate, tannic acid, titanium dioxide and triethyl citrate, and notes the annexed tables of intake recommendations and toxicological evaluations.

Introduces the abstract of a San Francisco Bay Area population-based case-control study of animal exposures and non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL), covering the study population (1,591 cases, 2,515 controls), methods, and the start of the results on pet ownership.

Reports the main pet-ownership findings: pet owners had lower odds of NHL and of diffuse large-cell/immunoblastic large-cell lymphoma (DLCL), and dog and/or cat ownership was linked to reduced NHL and DLCL risk.

Presents dose-response and species-specific pet results: longer cat, dog, and dog/cat ownership was inversely associated with NHL (p-trend values), and ownership of other pets was associated with reduced NHL and DLCL risk.

Gives the farm-animal exposure results: cattle exposure for 5 or more years and pig exposure were associated with increased NHL and DLCL risk, followed by the conclusion that animal exposure and NHL warrant pooled analyses.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending the abstract with the recommendation for further investigation of animal exposure and NHL in pooled analyses.

Introduces BLV as an oncogenic cattle retrovirus and the earlier, insensitive serological studies (immunodiffusion, complement fixation) that found no human antibodies, leading to the view that BLV posed no public health risk.
Explains the motivation for reexamining human exposure to BLV using more sensitive immunological methods, and describes the immunoblotting study design applied to 257 human sera.

Reports the main result: immunoblotting detected BLV-reactive antibodies (IgG1, IgM, IgA, IgG4 against capsid p24) in 74% of sera, with specificity supported by competition assays and exclusion of cross-reacting antibodies to other chronic viruses.
Interprets the findings: anti-BLV capsid antibodies may be a biomarker of widespread exposure, but do not prove infection, since the antibodies could stem from heat-denatured BLV antigens in food.
Concludes that, despite the caveats, the findings justify further research into human exposure to BLV.

Introduces the randomised, double-blinded, placebo-controlled crossover trial design and study population (153 3-year-olds, 144 8/9-year-olds) testing artificial food colours and additives (AFCA) with sodium benzoate, and defines the primary outcome, the global hyperactivity aggregate (GHA).

Describes the outcome measures (GHA from z-scores of observed behaviour and teacher/parent ratings, plus a computerised attention test for 8/9-year-olds), the trial registration number ISRCTN74481308, and the per-protocol analysis approach.

Reports findings on attrition (16 and 14 children dropped out for reasons unrelated to behaviour) and the main result that AFCA mix A significantly worsened GHA versus placebo in 3-year-olds (effect size 0.20, p=0.044), while mix B showed no effect.

Presents sensitivity results: the 3-year-old mix A effect persisted among children consuming over 85% of juice with no missing data, and 8/9-year-olds showed significant adverse effects from both mix A and mix B under the same compliance restriction.

Gives the document's interpretation that artificial colours and/or the sodium benzoate preservative increase hyperactivity in 3-year-old and 8/9-year-old children in the general population, concluding the findings from the restricted analyses.
Closing fragment of the interpretation sentence, completing the conclusion that the effects apply to children in the general population.

This chunk is the document's single conclusion/recommendation on food additives and hyperactivity: the evidence supports a trial elimination period for artificial colourings and preservatives in the diet, relevant to children's behaviour and hyperactivity symptoms.
Intro and aim of the Brussels sprout intervention trial (300 g/day, n=8): comet assay measuring lymphocyte DNA migration, showing reduced PhIP-induced DNA damage but no effect for Trp-P-2.
Key finding that sprout consumption reduced PhIP-induced DNA damage (97%), possibly via inhibition of sulfotransferase 1A1 that activates PhIP, contrasted with no effect on Trp-P-2.

Results on endogenous oxidized bases and hydrogen peroxide-induced DNA damage (39% lower after intervention); antioxidant enzyme induction (glutathione peroxidase, superoxide dismutase) ruled out as explanation, with in vitro evidence of direct ROS scavenging by sprout compounds.
Serum vitamin C rose 37% after sprout intake, but individual vitamin changes did not correlate with DNA damage prevention; in vitro scavenging evidence noted.
Concluding statement that sprout consumption is the first demonstration of sulfotransferase inhibition in humans and protects against PhIP and oxidative DNA damage.

Introduction and study setup: anthocyanins from Concord grape extract (CGE) and delphinidin are tested for inhibiting benzo[a]pyrene-DNA adduct formation in noncancerous MCF-10F human breast epithelial cells.
Main results on carcinogen-DNA adducts: CGE at 10 and 20 µg/mL and delphinidin at 0.6 µM significantly inhibit benzo[a]pyrene (BP)-DNA adduct formation in MCF-10F breast cells.

Mechanistic findings: the inhibition is linked to increased phase II detoxification enzymes (glutathione S-transferase, NAD(P)H:quinone reductase 1), reduced ROS formation, and no induction of antioxidant response element transcription.

Conclusion: CGE and delphinidin show breast cancer chemopreventive potential by blocking carcinogen-DNA adducts, modulating carcinogen-metabolizing enzymes, and suppressing ROS in noncancerous breast cells.
Final sentence of the conclusion, closing the abstract by specifying that the protective effects were observed in noncancerous human breast cells.

Background and objective of a randomized trial testing whether a very high vegetable, fruit, and fiber, low-fat diet reduces breast cancer recurrence and all-cause mortality in early-stage breast cancer survivors.

Study design and participants: a multi-institutional randomized controlled trial of 3088 women treated for early-stage breast cancer, aged 18-70 at diagnosis, enrolled 1995-2000 and followed through June 2006.

Intervention arm details: telephone counseling with cooking classes and newsletters targeting 5 vegetable servings plus 16 oz vegetable juice, 3 fruit servings, 30 g fiber, and 15-20% energy from fat, versus the comparison group.
Comparison group receiving 5-A-Day print materials, plus the start of the results section describing dietary differences between groups at baseline.

Dietary results: the intervention group sustained significant differences through 4 years (vegetables +65%, fruit +25%, fiber +30%, fat energy -13%), validated by plasma carotenoids, with similar clinical care in both groups.
Primary outcome results over a mean 7.3-year follow-up: invasive breast cancer events occurred in 16.7% of intervention vs 16.9% of comparison women (adjusted HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.80-1.14, P=.63).

Mortality results (155 vs 160 deaths; adjusted HR 0.91, P=.43) and subgroup analysis showing no significant interactions by demographics, tumor characteristics, baseline diet, or treatment, leading into the conclusion.

Conclusion: among early-stage breast cancer survivors, a very high vegetable, fruit, and fiber, low-fat diet did not reduce additional breast cancer events or mortality over 7.3 years; includes trial registration NCT00003787.
Trial registration identifier NCT00003787 on clinicaltrials.gov, the final fragment of the trial registration statement.

Introduction to the document, which argues that health benefits of fruits and vegetables come from complex mixtures of interacting plant chemicals rather than single compounds, and that these components accumulate together in plants for defense.

Continues the introduction by describing the lab's approach to studying natural chemical cooperation in pigmented, flavonoid-rich functional foods, using both whole fruits and plant cell culture systems.

Describes the lab's methodology: successive gentle, rapid, large-volume fractionations of plant material linked to bioassays of mixtures and semi-purified compounds, using anthocyanin- and proanthocyanidin-rich sources.

Explains the purpose of the strategy, which is to identify additive or synergistic interactions among related compounds, and notes that same-class phytochemical interactions boost flavonoid-rich fruits' efficacy against multiple diseases.
Concludes the passage by listing the disease conditions targeted by these flavonoid-rich fruits, namely cardiovascular disease (CVD), cancer, metabolic syndrome, and others.

Introduction to a study of antiproliferative effects of polyphenol-rich berry extracts on HeLa cervical cancer cells, comparing which berry extracts are effective versus less effective, with the strongest extracts ranked and their EC50 values given.

Continues the berry extract study: ranks the most effective extracts (strawberry, arctic bramble, cloudberry, lingonberry) by EC50 values, then reports their effects on CaCo-2 colon cancer cells, which are more sensitive at low and less sensitive at high concentrations.

Explains that strawberry, cloudberry, arctic bramble, and raspberry extracts share ellagitannins as known antiproliferative constituents, while the active components of lingonberry extracts remain unidentified and motivate further investigation.

Describes the fractionation of lingonberry extract on Sephadex LH-20 into anthocyanin-rich and tannin-rich fractions, finding that antiproliferative activity is largely lost in the anthocyanin fraction and retained in the tannin fraction.

Reports LC-MS analysis of lingonberry polyphenols, which matched prior reports, and states that the tannin fraction consists almost entirely of A- and B-type procyanidins, concluding that procyanidins mainly cause lingonberry's antiproliferative activity.
Final sentence of the lingonberry study conclusion, stating that the antiproliferative activity of lingonberry is predominantly due to procyanidins.
Introduction and rationale: explains why anthocyanin absorption and tissue deposition (liver, eye, brain) are studied in a pig model of human digestion, following the blueberry-fed pig study.
Methods: pigs fed 0-4% w/w blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum 'Jersey') diets for 4 weeks, fasted 18-21 h before euthanasia, with plasma and urine sampling for anthocyanins.

Results and conclusion: intact anthocyanins were found in all sampled tissues, with LC-MS/MS quantification of 11 anthocyanins in liver, eye, cortex, and cerebellum, suggesting accumulation beyond the blood-brain barrier.
Concluding fragment: the final words of the conclusion sentence about anthocyanin accumulation in tissues beyond the blood-brain barrier.

Introduction and study design of a lycopene asthma trial: background on antioxidant-rich diets and asthma prevalence, the stated objective, and the methods (32 asthmatic adults on a 10-day low-antioxidant diet, then a randomized crossover with placebo, tomato extract, and tomato juice arms, each providing 45 mg lycopene/day).

Study methods and early results: the randomized crossover design with three 7-day treatment arms, followed by findings that the low-antioxidant diet lowered plasma carotenoids, worsened Asthma Control Score, reduced %FEV1 and %FVC, and increased %sputum neutrophils.

Main results and conclusions on treatment effects: tomato juice and tomato extract both reduced airway neutrophil influx, tomato extract additionally lowered sputum neutrophil elastase activity, and the authors conclude dietary antioxidants modify asthma outcomes.

Concluding statements of the lycopene asthma study: the authors suggest changing dietary antioxidant intake may contribute to rising asthma prevalence and recommend further investigation of lycopene-rich supplements as a therapeutic intervention.

Abstract of a study on almond skin polyphenols and antioxidant activity across industrial processing methods (blanching/freeze-drying, blanching plus drying, roasting), introducing the 31 phenolic compounds identified.

Continues the abstract's breakdown of the phenolic compound classes found in almond skins from three varieties, with each class's percentage share of total phenolics (flavan-3-ols, flavonol glycosides, hydroxybenzoic acids, flavonols, flavanones, etc.).

Reports how total phenolic content varied by processing method: roasted almond skins had about twice the phenolics of freeze-dried blanched skins, and oven drying of blanched skins modestly increased phenolics, with significance only for some samples.
Presents antioxidant capacity results (ORAC, mmol Trolox/g) ranked by processing type, with roasted samples highest, followed by blanching plus drying, then blanched freeze-dried samples.
Concludes the abstract by stating that roasting is the most suitable industrial processing method for obtaining almond skin extracts with the greatest antioxidant capacity.

Introduction to a study on how microwave cooking conditions affect health-promoting compounds (glucosinolates, phenolics, minerals, vitamin C) in broccoli, a Brassica vegetable, noting conflicting literature results.
States the study's aim: to examine how microwave cooking time, power, and added water influence the bioactive compounds of broccoli, and previews that compounds generally decrease.

Key findings: most compounds decline while minerals stay stable; vitamin C has the greatest losses from degradation and leaching, while phenolics and glucosinolates are lost mainly by leaching into water.
Conclusion and practical recommendation: avoid long microwave cooking times and large volumes of cooking water to minimize nutrient losses in broccoli.

Introduces sulforaphane's cancer-protective role in brassica vegetables and how it forms from glucoraphanin via myrosinase or gut microbiota; sets up the designed human study on meal composition and broccoli cooking time.

Describes the volunteer study design (n=12): meals with or without beef, paired with lightly or fully cooked broccoli or seed extract, plus 3 g mustard providing pre-formed allyl isothiocyanate; names the urinary biomarkers AMA and SFMA.

Reports key results: sulforaphane yield about 3-fold higher from lightly cooked than fully cooked broccoli, measured via 24-hour urinary mercapturic acid excretion; begins the finding on AITC absorption.
Gives the AITC absorption result (about 1.3-fold higher with the meat meal) and states the meal matrix did not significantly affect glucoraphanin hydrolysis or SFMA excretion from broccoli.

Concludes that pre-formed isothiocyanates may interact more with the meal matrix than those produced in vivo, and that cooking method, not meal matrix, mainly determines in vivo isothiocyanate production.
Final fragment completing the conclusion, stating that cooking method matters more than the meal matrix for isothiocyanate production.
Introduces the study's aim: comparing boiling, steaming, and frying effects on phytochemicals, antioxidant capacity (TEAC, TRAP, FRAP) and physicochemical traits of carrots, courgettes, and broccoli.
Reports that water-based cooking best preserved antioxidant compounds, especially carotenoids, across vegetables and ascorbic acid in carrots and courgettes.

Describes texture and colour outcomes: steaming kept texture better than boiling, boiling limited discoloration, and frying caused the least softening but lower antioxidant retention; cooked vegetables showed higher TEAC, FRAP, and TRAP values.

Explains the rise in antioxidant assay values as likely due to matrix softening, better compound extractability, and conversion into more antioxidant species, and concludes processed vegetables are not necessarily less nutritious.
Concludes that the best cooking method depends on the vegetable, chosen to preserve its nutritional and physicochemical qualities.

Introduction and study setup: motivation for concern over bottled water quality amid rising US consumption, and sampling of 35 bottled water brands (three bottles each) from Houston-area grocery stores.

Breakdown of the 35 sampled brands by type (16 spring, 11 purified/fortified tap, 5 carbonated, 3 distilled) and the list of properties tested, including pH, conductivity, bacteria counts, anions, trace and heavy metals, and volatile organics.
Analytical methods used: ICP-MS for elemental analysis, GC-ECD and GC-MS for volatile organics, and ion chromatography with ion-selective electrodes for anions.
Bacterial identification via Biolog software, and the reference standards used for comparison: IBWA, US FDA, US EPA, and WHO drinking water guidelines.

Main chemical results: most analyzed chemicals fell below the maximum admissible concentration (MAC) limits of the drinking water standards, and volatile organic chemicals were below detection limits.
Key microbial finding and conclusion: four of the 35 bottled water brands were contaminated with bacteria.

Introduces the study design: solid fermentation of steamed black soybeans with five GRAS filamentous fungi (Aspergillus and Rhizopus strains), and the start of the mutagenicity/antimutagenicity assessment of methanol extracts.

Describes the assay setup: methanol extracts tested against the direct mutagen 4-NQO and the indirect mutagen B[a]P in Salmonella Typhimurium TA100 and TA98, and reports that neither unfermented nor fermented extracts were mutagenic at the doses tested.

Summarizes the main antimutagenic findings: extracts inhibited mutagenesis from both mutagens in both strains, fermentation enhanced antimutagenic effect, and the effect depended on starter organism, mutagen, and bacterial strain.
Highlights A. awamori-fermented extract as the most antimutagenic, with TA100 inhibition at 5.0 mg/plate of 92% (4-NQO) and 89% (B[a]P), compared with 41% and 63% for unfermented extract.

Gives TA98 inhibition figures (94% and 81% for fermented extract versus 58% and 44% for unfermented) and begins describing the optimization of A. awamori fermentation conditions across temperature and time.

Concludes the fermentation optimization: among 25, 30 and 35 degrees C and 1-5 day fermentations, the extract from beans fermented at 30 degrees C for 3 days gave the greatest inhibition of 4-NQO and B[a]P mutagenicity.

Study design and methods for a trial of pinto beans, black-eyed peas, and carrot placebo on heart disease and diabetes risk factors in mildly insulin-resistant adults over 8 weeks, including the crossover design and blood sample measures.

Methods continued: participant demographics, washout periods, and the list of fasting blood markers measured (cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides, CRP, insulin, glucose, HbA1c), followed by the start of the results on treatment-by-time effects.

Results on the statistical significance of the treatment-by-time effect on serum total cholesterol and LDL after eight weeks, paired t-test findings attributing the effect to pinto beans, and mean TC changes by treatment group.

Mean serum LDL-C changes by treatment group (pinto bean, black-eyed pea, placebo), the significant pinto bean versus placebo difference, null findings for other blood markers, and the start of the conclusions.
Conclusion that pinto bean intake should be encouraged to lower serum total cholesterol and LDL-C, thereby reducing coronary heart disease risk.

Introduction to a study on black bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) seed coat phytochemicals, covering bioactivity-guided isolation of 24 compounds (triterpenoids, flavonoids, others) and their antiproliferative and antioxidant activities.

Methods overview: structure identification of isolated black bean seed coat compounds by MS, NMR, and X-ray diffraction, and evaluation of antiproliferative activity against Caco-2, HepG2, and MCF-7 cancer cell lines.
Results on HepG2 liver cancer cell proliferation inhibition: listed compounds (1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 13-16, 19, 20) with their EC50 values in microM.
Results on Caco-2 colon cancer cell antiproliferative activity: listed compounds (1-3, 5-11, 14, 15, 19, 20) with their EC50 values in microM.

Results on MCF-7 breast cancer cell antiproliferative activity in a dose-dependent manner: listed compounds (5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 19, 20) with EC50 values in microM, and the start of the HepG2 and Caco-2 comparison.
Conclusion of the results: flavonoids 14-19 showed potent antioxidant activity, and black bean seed coat extracts overall have potent antioxidant and antiproliferative activities.
Final fragment of the abstract's concluding sentence stating the black bean seed coat extracts' antiproliferative activity.

Study background and aims: introduces raisins (fiber and polyphenols) and walking as possible CVD-risk-reducing interventions, and states the goal of testing their effects on blood pressure, lipids, glucose, insulin, and inflammatory cytokines.
