Study design and population: 34 men and postmenopausal women, matched for weight and gender, randomized to RAISIN (1 cup raisins/day), WALK (more daily steps), or RAISINS + WALK combined.

Main results on blood pressure and cholesterol: systolic blood pressure fell for all subjects (P = 0.008); total cholesterol dropped 9.4%, driven by a 13.7% LDL-C reduction (P < 0.001). The 2-week run-in preceded the 6-week intervention.

Results on triglycerides, inflammation and adhesion markers: TG fell 19.5% in the WALK group; TNF-α dropped from 3.5 to 2.1 ng/L in RAISIN; sICAM-1 decreased in all subjects (P < 0.01). Conclusion begins, stating simple lifestyle changes have benefits.
Overall conclusion: adding raisins to the diet or increasing walking steps each produce distinct beneficial effects on cardiovascular disease risk.

Introduction to a study on apple waste phenolics and colon carcinogenesis: covers colorectal cancer prevalence, diet as a risk factor, and apple phenolics' known antioxidant activity, noting limited knowledge of their anti-cancer effects.

Study methods: describes using HT29, HT115 and CaCo-2 colon cell lines as in vitro models, treated with 0.01-0.1% apple phenolic extract, and the assays used for DNA damage, barrier function, and cell cycle progression, with invasion mentioned.

Key results: the crude apple phenolic extract protected against DNA damage, improved colonic barrier function, and inhibited invasion (p<0.05), with the Matrigel invasion assay and TER and cell-cycle assays named.

Conclusion: the anti-invasive effect was enhanced by 24-hour cell pretreatment, and the study concludes that a crude phenolic extract from apple waste beneficially affects key stages of colon carcinogenesis in vitro.

Introduction stating that plant-based diets lower chronic disease risk, questioning whether antioxidants drive this benefit given null supplement trials, and motivating measurement of total electron-donating antioxidant content in foods.

Rationale for measuring total reductant antioxidant concentration in individual dietary plants, and the scope of the study: a systematic survey of fruits, berries, vegetables, cereals, nuts and pulses worldwide.
Methods: sampling design (three or more samples from three regions where possible) and the FRAP assay, which measures reduction of Fe(3+) to Fe(2+) by reductants with potentials above Fe(3+)/Fe(2+).
Key results: the FRAP values reflect electron-donating antioxidant concentration, and total antioxidant content varies more than 1000-fold across dietary plants.
Plant families with the highest antioxidant content, including Rosaceae berries and fruits, crowberry, blueberry, black currant, walnut, sunflower seed, pomegranate and ginger.

Contribution of food groups to antioxidant intake in a Norwegian diet (fruits 43.6%, berries 27.1%, cereals 11.7%, vegetables 8.9%) and the study's conclusion that the analysis will support research on the combined nutritional effects of dietary antioxidants.
Final sentence of the abstract concluding that the systematic analysis will support research into the nutritional role of combined dietary plant antioxidants.

Introduces the study's main finding: a survey of antioxidant content in culinary and medicinal herbs, showing over 1000-fold variation, and names the high-antioxidant herbs (oregano, sage, peppermint, thyme, clove, cinnamon, etc.) and Chinese herbs.
Continues the list of high-antioxidant herbs (>75 mmol/100 g) and argues that herbs may be a better dietary antioxidant source than fruits, berries, cereals and vegetables.

Notes that the glycyrrhizin herbal drug Stronger Neo-Minophagen C, used for chronic hepatitis, boosts total antioxidant intake, and speculates that the herbs' effects stem from their antioxidant activity.
Concluding sentence of the abstract, suggesting that several health effects of these herbs may be mediated by their antioxidant activities.

Introduces the study's scope: the seven adhesion factors examined for NaCl on potato chips (frying-to-coating delay, surface oil, temperature, oil type, salt size and shape, electrostatic coating), plus the chip types and coating timing design.

Describes the experimental design: coating timing (immediate, 1 day, 1 month), five NaCl particle sizes from 24.7 to 388 microns coated electrostatically and nonelectrostatically, and the cubic, dendritic, and flake crystal shapes tested, with chips coated at varied temperatures.

Reports the main findings on surface oil and temperature: high surface oil gives the highest salt adhesion and is the dominant factor, lower temperature reduces oil and adhesion, and delay before coating only hurts low-oil chips.

Summarizes further results: oil composition has no effect, larger salt size reduces adhesion (especially on low-oil chips), cubic crystals adhere best then flake then dendritic, and electrostatic effects vary by surface oil level.

Concludes the electrostatic coating findings: no change for small crystals on high and low oil chips, reduced adhesion for large salt on those chips, and improved small-crystal adhesion but no change for large crystals on no-oil chips.

Introduction and methods opening of a cohort study on dietary acrylamide and endometrial, ovarian, and breast cancer risk in Dutch women, stating the study aim and background on acrylamide as a carcinogen.

Methods continuation describing the Netherlands Cohort Study population (62,573 women aged 55-69), the case-cohort design with a 2,589-woman random subcohort, and how acrylamide intake was assessed via food frequency questionnaire and Dutch food chemical analysis; also introduces never-smoker subgroup analysis.

Results opening reporting 11.3 years of follow-up with case counts for endometrial (327), ovarian (300), and breast (1,835) cancers, and beginning the comparison of highest versus lowest acrylamide intake quintiles.

Main quintile hazard ratio findings: highest versus lowest acrylamide intake quintile (8.9 vs 40.2 mug/day) for endometrial (HR 1.29), ovarian (HR 1.78, significant), and breast (HR 0.93) cancer, with 95% CIs and P-trend values.

Never-smoker subgroup hazard ratios for endometrial (1.99), ovarian (2.22), and breast (1.10) cancer, followed by the conclusion that increased endometrial and ovarian cancer risk is seen with higher acrylamide intake, especially in never-smokers.
Final conclusion sentence stating that breast cancer risk was not associated with dietary acrylamide intake, closing the abstract of the prospective Netherlands cohort study.

Introduction and study aim: opens the abstract by describing acrylamide as a probable carcinogen formed in foods during high-temperature cooking, notes prior epidemiology found no link, and states the nested case-control design within a cohort to test acrylamide exposure and breast cancer using biomarkers.

Methods: describes the biomarker measurement, N-terminal hemoglobin adducts of acrylamide and its metabolite glycidamide in red blood cells (LC/MS/MS), and the study population of 374 breast cancer cases and 374 matched controls from a cohort of postmenopausal women.

Descriptive and unadjusted results: reports that adduct levels were similar between cases and controls, that smokers had roughly threefold higher levels, and that no association with breast cancer appeared before or after adjusting for HRT duration, parity, BMI, alcohol and education.

Key finding: after adjusting for smoking, acrylamide-hemoglobin levels were positively associated with estrogen receptor positive breast cancer, with an incidence rate ratio of 2.7 (95% CI 1.1-6.6) per 10-fold increase in level.

Glycidamide results and conclusion: a weak glycidamide-hemoglobin association with ER-positive breast cancer disappeared after mutual adjustment with acrylamide levels; ends with the copyright line (c) 2008 Wiley-Liss, Inc.

Opening of a review on acrylamide mitigation in fried potato products; introduces high acrylamide levels (sometimes above 1 mg/L) and states that many reduction strategies exist, with the review's stated criterion being preservation of product quality.
Continuation of the review's framing sentence: the key requirement for any acrylamide-reduction strategy is maintaining the final product's overall organoleptic (sensory) and nutritional qualities.

Introduces the Netherlands Cohort Study abstract: background on acrylamide as a probable carcinogen in heat-treated carbohydrate foods, prior epidemiology, and the aim to prospectively study dietary acrylamide and renal cell, bladder, and prostate cancer.

Describes the study design: the Netherlands Cohort Study (120,852 adults aged 55-69, baseline 1986), a 5000-person random subcohort analyzed with Cox proportional hazards, and acrylamide intake estimated from a food-frequency questionnaire using chemical analysis of Dutch foods.

Reports the main results after 13.3 years of follow-up: case counts for renal cell (339), bladder (1210), and prostate (2246) cancer, and the setup of comparing the lowest and highest acrylamide intake quintiles.

Gives the key hazard ratios: highest vs lowest quintile (about 40.8 vs 9.5 microg/d) yielded HR 1.59 for renal cell cancer (significant trend), and null results for bladder (0.91) and prostate (1.06) cancer, plus a nonsignificant inverse trend for advanced prostate cancer in never smokers.
States the conclusions: a possible positive association between dietary acrylamide and renal cell cancer risk, with no positive associations found for bladder or prostate cancer.

Introduction to the Adventist Health Study: the objective and methods of a cross-sectional study linking meat and food consumption to degenerative arthritis and soft tissue disorders, using logistic regression adjusted for age, smoking, alcohol, BMI, sex hormones, and parity.

Results begin: the overall prevalence of degenerative arthritis and soft tissue disorders (22.60%), higher rates in women and with age, and factors associated with higher prevalence (smoking, BMI, no oral contraceptive use, current hormone replacement therapy).
Key odds ratios for meat consumption (<1/week and >=1/week vs. no meat) by sex, showing increased odds in women (1.31 and 1.49) and men (1.19 and 1.43), with 95% confidence intervals.

Remaining results on other foods (weak risk associations with dairy fat and fruit, protective associations with nuts and salad), followed by the conclusion that greater meat intake and hormone replacement therapy in women are linked to higher prevalence in both sexes.

Final conclusion sentence restating that hormone replacement therapy in women is associated with higher prevalence of these disorders, closing the abstract of the Adventist Health Study meat consumption and arthritis analysis.

Abstract opening of a randomized trial on maternal DHA (docosahexaenoic acid) supplementation in pregnancy: background, objective of testing whether DHA deficiency in pregnant women impairs infant development, and study design framing.

Study design rationale: no defined cutoffs for DHA deficiency exist, so the trial aims to establish a developmental score distribution from infants of women given DHA above requirements, to compare with infants of women on usual diets.

Methods: women received 400 mg/d DHA (n=67) or placebo (n=68) from 16 weeks gestation to delivery; outcomes measured were maternal red blood cell phospholipid fatty acids, dietary intakes at 16 and 36 weeks, and infant visual acuity at 60 days.

Results on multivariate analyses: infant visual acuity associated with infant sex and maternal DHA intervention (beta, SE, and odds ratio reported), plus an approach to identify DHA deficiency when biochemical and functional markers are unknown.

Key findings: more placebo-group girls than DHA-group girls had below-average visual acuity (P=0.048); maternal red blood cell DPA (docosapentaenoic/docosatetraenoic acid) was inversely correlated with visual acuity in boys and girls.
Conclusion of the abstract: the findings suggest some pregnant women in the study population were DHA-deficient, linking maternal DHA status to infant visual acuity maturation.
Background and aim of a 4-year follow-up study on DHA and ARA supplemented infant formula, stating the gap in long-term randomized trial data on visual and cognitive outcomes.

Methods of the study: 52 of 79 term infants from a double-blind randomized DHA/ARA formula trial were followed up at 4 years, with 32 breast-fed infants as a gold standard; outcomes were visual acuity and the WPPSI-R.
Results at 4 years: control formula group had poorer visual acuity than breast-fed infants, while DHA and DHA+ARA groups did not differ significantly from breast-fed infants.

Verbal IQ results and conclusion: control and DHA-supplemented groups had poorer Verbal IQ than breast-fed infants, and DHA+ARA formula supports visual acuity and IQ development similar to breast-fed infants.
Background and objective of a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial on maternal DHA intake during pregnancy and infant problem-solving and recognition memory, noting prior gaps in research.

Study design: pregnant women received DHA-containing or placebo functional food from gestation week 24 until delivery, with the hypothesis that DHA-exposed infants would show better problem-solving and recognition memory.

Methods: group sizes and bar details (300 mg DHA per 92-kcal bar, about 5 bars/week), and infant testing at 9 months using the Infant Planning Test and Fagan Test of Infant Intelligence, including the problem-solving trial structure.

Scoring method for the problem-solving task (support and search steps, intention score, total intentional solutions) based on cumulative performance over 5 trials, and the start of the results section.

Results: DHA treatment significantly improved problem-solving measures (total intention score, total intentional solutions, and intentional solutions on cloth and cover steps), with no group differences on the Fagan recognition memory test.
Conclusion: maternal DHA functional food during pregnancy benefits 9-month infant problem solving but not recognition memory.

Opening of a case report on Diphyllobothrium nihonkaiense, a tapeworm first documented in a human infection in North America; identifies the species via 18S rRNA and COI gene sequencing of expelled proglottids.
Continuation of the case report: the infected patient is a Czech tourist who ate raw Pacific sockeye salmon (Oncorhynchus nerka) caught in British Columbia, Canada, the probable source of infection.
Introduction and study background on DHA omega-3 importance and the lack of bioavailability data for algal (vegetarian) DHA oils versus fish oils, setting up the bioequivalence study design.

Study design: a 28-day randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial comparing two algal DHA capsule oils (DHASCO-T, DHASCO-S) at 200, 600, and 1,000 mg/day against an algal DHA-fortified food, with n=12 per group.

Outcome measures and key findings: bioequivalence judged by plasma phospholipid and erythrocyte DHA changes, with secondary effects on ARA, DPAn-6, and EPA; both DHASCO capsule oils gave equivalent DHA levels.

Dose-response results: DHA response was dose-dependent and linear, with plasma phospholipid DHA rising 1.17, 2.28, and 3.03 g/100 g fatty acid at 200, 600, and 1,000 mg; DHASCO-S fortified snack bars matched capsule DHA delivery, and adverse event monitoring was reported.
Conclusion: the study's overall finding that the two algal oil capsules and the algal oil-fortified food are bioequivalent and safe DHA sources, with an excellent safety and tolerability profile.

Study design and aims: an observational study of fat intake and n-3/n-6 fatty acid status in erythrocyte sphingolipids and phospholipids (PC, PS, PE) across omnivores, vegetarians, vegans, and semi-omnivores.

Methods: the sample of 98 Austrian adults grouped by diet (23 omnivores, 25 vegetarians, 37 vegans, 13 semi-omnivores), with anthropometry, 24-hour dietary recall for fat intake, and gas chromatography of phospholipid fatty acids.

Results: unbalanced n-6/n-3 ratio and scarce dietary EPA and DHA in vegans and vegetarians lowered C20:5n-3, C22:5n-3, C22:6n-3 and total n-3 in SPL, PC, PS and PE versus omnivores and semi-omnivores.
Results and conclusion: total PUFA, MUFA and SFA were unchanged across groups, and the vegetarian diet (n-6/n-3 ratio about 10/1) was concluded to promote biochemical n-3 tissue decline.

Conclusion and recommendations: vegetarians should lower the n-6/n-3 ratio and take direct EPA and DHA sources for physical, mental and neurological health, regardless of age or gender; includes the 2008 S. Karger AG copyright notice.

Review abstract introducing the purpose: summarizes recent evidence linking early-life mercury exposure (maternal fish intake in pregnancy, thimerosal in vaccines, dental amalgam) to child neurodevelopment, and begins noting prior evidence of mild prenatal methylmercury neurocognitive harm.
Recent findings section: new studies show prenatal fish consumption has benefits, while advising avoidance of high-mercury fish, based on the methylmercury evidence built on earlier work.

Recent findings continued: calls for future research weighing methylmercury against fish's docosahexaenoic acid to refine maternal and child recommendations, then reports recent studies supporting the safety of thimerosal vaccines and dental amalgam for children; the Summary begins by stating mercury may harm child development.

Summary section: argues that interventions to reduce low-level early-life mercury exposure must be weighed against harms from behavior changes, such as lower DHA intake from less seafood, fewer childhood vaccinations, and poorer dental care.
Closing clause of the summary, listing the last of the unintended harms of mercury-reduction interventions: suboptimal dental care.
Introduction to a QALY-based risk-benefit analysis of French fish consumption, framing why methylmercury risks and omega-3 benefits from fish must be evaluated together rather than separately.

Describes the study's method: a common QALY metric is used to model a shift from medium to high n-3 PUFA intake, assessing cardiovascular outcomes (CHD and stroke mortality/morbidity) and fetal neurodevelopment (IQ change).

Explains the study's purpose as a sensitivity analysis of the model, testing how changing cardiovascular dose-response relationships affects results, and summarizes the finding that increased fish intake appears beneficial.

Presents the key caveat: the confidence interval for the overall estimate has a negative lower bound, so higher fish intake could harm health due to MeHg contamination; also introduces the first limits of the QALY approach.

Concludes the discussion of QALY limitations (dose-response determination, economic and individual-preference foundations) and recommends that future models include more beneficial and risk components beyond the single pair studied.
Introduction to the fish consumption dilemma: nutritional benefits for brain development versus methyl mercury (MeHg) neurotoxicity, with prenatal exposure as the main concern.
States the open question of the prenatal MeHg level linked to neurodevelopmental risk and outlines the review of brain-relevant fish nutrients and MeHg risk evidence.
Introduces the Seychelles Child Development Study, a prospective cohort of daily fish consumers whose MeHg levels resemble ocean fish in industrialized countries, making them a sentinel population.
Summarizes Seychelles findings: no consistent adverse associations between prenatal MeHg exposure and child outcomes through age 9, and the shift toward studying fish nutrients.
Names the fish nutrients studied in Seychelles (long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids, iodine, iron, choline) and the preliminary conclusion that fish nutrients may offset MeHg harm.
Brief closing fragment completing the final sentence on MeHg's effects on the developing nervous system.

Introduction to the document on public health guidance about fish consumption: it frames historical concerns about contaminants like methylmercury and PCBs, the emerging recognition of PUFA benefits from fish oil, and why guidance must weigh both since they affect the same outcomes in opposite directions.

Continues the introduction by noting that PUFAs and methylmercury co-occur in fish and act oppositely on health outcomes, requiring careful public health guidance. It introduces Mozaffarian and Rimm (JAMA 2006), who strongly support PUFA benefits for coronary heart disease.

Critique of Mozaffarian and Rimm (JAMA 2006): they downplayed methylmercury's coronary heart disease risks and concluded that fish benefits exceed risks for adults. The author argues this conclusion rests on an inaccurate and insufficiently critical literature analysis.

Closing of the introduction, stating the document will re-examine the literature behind Mozaffarian and Rimm's conclusions and consider the available and appropriate public health options for fish consumption guidance.

Opening passage of a document on nutrient and contaminant tradeoffs when choosing meat, poultry, or seafood as dietary protein; introduces the dilemma between health benefits and toxin exposure, and the intake analysis for young children and women of child-bearing age.

Continuation of the document's conclusion comparing seafood, chicken, and beef (similar protein, differing key nutrients and contaminant levels); recommends varying meat, poultry, and seafood choices within dietary guideline and advisory amounts to meet nutritional needs and reduce exposure to any single contaminant.
Final fragment of the document's concluding sentence, completing the recommendation to reduce exposure to any single type of contaminant by diversifying protein sources.

Introduces the study on dietary exposure to dioxins, PCDFs and dioxin-like PCBs from seafood, motivated by the health benefits of LC n-3 PUFAs versus seafood contamination, and states the aim of a Monte Carlo intake assessment relative to Belgian Federal Health Council recommendations.

Describes the study design, with two LC n-3 PUFA intake scenarios (0.3 E% and 0.46 E%) based on the Belgian recommendation, and begins reporting total dioxin and dioxin-like exposure estimates for the 0.3 E% scenario.
Reports the percentile exposure results (5th, 50th, 95th) in pg TEQ/kg bw/day for both the 0.3 E% and 0.46 E% LC n-3 PUFA scenarios, showing exposure rises with higher fish-based intake.

Concludes that if fish is the only extra source for the recommended LC n-3 PUFA intake, most of the study population would exceed the proposed health-based guidance values for dioxins and dioxin-like substances.

Introduction of a study on brominated flame retardants in US food and human milk, noting PBDE congener measurements and the extremely high PBDE levels found in US women's milk compared with Europe and worldwide.

Continues the findings: US milk PBDE levels are the highest reported worldwide, and the paper's market basket comparison of PBDE levels in meat, fish, and dairy shows US food studies running somewhat higher than elsewhere.

Food-specific PBDE results: fish is the most contaminated food by median, followed by meat and dairy; dietary PBDE intake in the US comes mostly from meat rather than fish as in some European countries, and broiling reduces PBDEs per serving.
Concludes with HBCD, another brominated flame retardant, measured in human milk at lower levels (0.16-1.2 ng/g) similar to European levels, contrasting with the much higher US PBDE levels.

Introduction of a 1995 study on dioxins, PCBs, and DDE in U.S. fast food; establishes that food is the main dioxin exposure route and fast food data is scarce, motivating the expanded study beyond a prior pilot.
Study scope: extends the earlier pilot (dioxins and dibenzofurans only) by adding dioxin-like PCBs and the DDT metabolite DDE, tested across four popular U.S. fast food items.
Names the four tested foods (Big Mac, Pizza Hut Personal Pan Pizza, KFC chicken, Häagen-Dazs ice cream) and reports the dioxin plus dibenzofuran TEQ ranges in pg/g for each.
Reports estimated daily dioxin TEQ intake per kg body weight from one serving for adults (65 kg) and children (20 kg), with the range of values across the fast foods.
Summarizes total PCDD/F levels (0.58 to 9.31 pg/g), DDE levels (180 to 3170 pg/g), and the start of mono-ortho PCB results, including the KFC maximum.
Final findings on di-ortho PCBs (highest in pizza) and total PCB values, with the chicken sample giving the highest total PCB TEQ of 1.29 pg/g.

Abstract opening of a prospective cohort study on dietary dairy intake and teenaged acne in boys, introducing the objective, sample of 4273 boys, and food frequency questionnaire methods from 1996-1998 with acne assessed in 1999.
Results section reporting adjusted prevalence ratios and 95% CIs for acne comparing highest versus lowest milk intake categories in 1996, adjusted for baseline age, height, and energy intake.

Specific prevalence ratios and trend P values for total, whole/2%, low-fat, and skim milk intake with acne, plus the Limitations section noting non-response, self-reported acne, and lack of adjustment for steroid use.

Remaining limitations (no exclusion of underlying disorders, no adjustment for other lifestyle factors) and the Conclusion linking skim milk intake to acne, suggesting hormonal constituents in milk as a possible explanation.
Final sentence of the conclusion proposing that skim milk contains hormones or hormone-influencing factors in amounts large enough to produce biological effects in consumers.

This chunk is the sole section of a short abstract on diet and acne. It explains that acne is driven by dihydrotestosterone (from endogenous and exogenous precursors) acting synergistically with IGF-1, and proposes a mechanism plus dietary changes to limit these hormones.

Introduction of a study quantitatively evaluating HTST pasteurization and homogenization for inactivating Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (MAP) in raw milk contaminated with cow feces, including the rationale for using fecal contamination.

Experimental setup: raw milk contaminated with fecal material from cows with Johne's disease at MAP concentrations of 10^2 to 3.5×10^5 cells/ml, with pilot-scale simulation of 22 time-temperature HTST combinations (60–90°C, 6–15 s holding times).
Results: no viable MAP recovered after 72°C for 6 s, or 70°C for 10 and 15 s and more stringent conditions, giving >4.2- to >7.1-log... fold reductions depending on initial inoculum.

Kinetic modeling of 69 quantitative data points giving Ea, lnk0, D-value (1.2 s at 72°C) and Z-value (7.7°C) for MAP heat inactivation; homogenization had no significant effect, with a concluding statement on pasteurization requirements.
Conclusion: HTST pasteurization at 15 s at ≥72°C yields a more-than-sevenfold reduction of Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis in milk.
Introduction and objective of a study on Prato cheese made from raw milk with low versus high somatic cell counts, including the milk groups and vat setup.
Methods: milk quality testing of pasteurized milk, cheese composition assessed at 2 days, and the sampling schedule for microbiological counts during storage.

Methods continued: pathogen testing schedule (Salmonella, Listeria, coagulase-positive Staphylococcus), the 2x5 factorial design with 4 replications, and sensory evaluation timing with a 9-point hedonic scale.
Results on composition: somatic cell levels did not affect protein or salt:moisture, but high-SCC cheeses had higher pH and moisture and longer clotting time.
Results on microbiology: pathogens absent in both cheeses, staphylococci low throughout, and lactic acid bacteria declined faster in high-SCC cheese.
Results on other microbial groups and sensory outcomes: high-SCC cheese had fewer psychrotrophs and more yeasts/molds, and low-SCC cheese was preferred by consumers.
Conclusion: lower acceptance of high-SCC cheese is attributed to texture and flavor defects likely linked to greater proteolysis.
Introduction and study purpose: evaluating whether hotdog package labels accurately reflect meat and water content across eight brands, with background on US hotdog consumption and sales.

Methods: eight hotdog brands assessed for water content by weight, using surgical pathology techniques (light microscopy with H&E, special stains, immunohistochemistry, electron microscopy) to identify meat and other components.

Results on labeling and composition: labels listed meat as the top ingredient in all brands, with water or another meat second; water was 44-69% by weight and microscopic meat content was 2.9-21.2%, with cost per hotdog roughly tracking meat content.

Results on non-muscle tissues: besides skeletal muscle, hotdogs contained bone, collagen, blood vessels, plant material, peripheral nerve, adipose, cartilage, and skin in varying numbers of brands; GFAP immunostaining was negative in all samples.

Results on lipid and ultrastructure, plus conclusions: oil red O staining showed moderate or marked lipid content, electron microscopy showed degenerated skeletal muscle, and the authors conclude labels are misleading since most brands are over 50% water.

Conclusions: meat (skeletal muscle) was under 10% of cross-sectional area in most brands, pricier brands contained more meat, all samples contained non-muscle tissues such as bone and cartilage, and no brain tissue was found.
Final sentence of the conclusions, stating that brain tissue was absent from the hotdogs examined.
Introduces the Southern France breast cancer case-control study (437 cases, 922 controls, 2002-2004) and the two dietary analysis methods, classical and spline, used to compute adjusted odds ratios.

Reports null findings for total fruit and vegetable intake and nonsignificant trends for cooked vegetables, legumes and fish, contrasting the spline method's lack of association with the classical method's results.

Presents the classical method's significant findings: lower raw vegetable intake (OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.43-0.93) and dairy intake (OR 1.57, 95% CI 1.06-2.32) associated with breast cancer risk, with the spline method showing no association.
Notes the overall results were inconsistent and that the spline method found significant associations for cereal, meat and olive oil, which the classical method did not.

Summarizes the spline-method results: cereal and olive oil inversely associated with risk, meat raising risk by 56% per additional 100 g/day, and calls for novel methods to confirm dietary thresholds.
Concluding statement that future research should analyze dietary patterns rather than individual foods.

Opening of the abstract for a Shanghai Women's Health Study paper: it states the hypothesis that legume-rich diets may prevent type 2 diabetes, notes limited prior evidence, and sets the study aim of examining legume and soy food intake against self-reported type 2 diabetes.

Study design section: a prospective cohort of 64,227 middle-aged Chinese women free of diabetes, cancer, and cardiovascular disease at recruitment, followed for an average of 4.6 years, with in-person interviews on risk factors.

Methods details: covers the collection of diabetes risk factors, adult diet and physical activity, and anthropometric measurements, plus dietary assessment via a validated food-frequency questionnaire at baseline and at a follow-up 2-3 years later. It then begins the Results section.

Main findings: an inverse association between legume intake quintiles (total, peanuts, soybeans, other legumes) and type 2 diabetes incidence, with multivariate relative risks of 0.62 for total legumes and 0.53 for soybeans comparing upper to lower quintile.

Null and concluding findings: soy products (excluding soy milk) and soy protein showed no significant association with type 2 diabetes, and the conclusion states that legume consumption, especially soybeans, is inversely associated with type 2 diabetes risk.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that legume, particularly soybean, consumption is inversely associated with type 2 diabetes risk.
Study design and methods of a trial comparing a soy-based low-calorie diet with a traditional low-calorie diet in 30 obese adults over 8 weeks, including the protein sources used in each group.
Methods continued: 1200 kcal/d diet protocol for 8 weeks, daily diet records, food intake analysis, weekly anthropometric measurements, and pre/post biochemical comparisons.

Results on weight and body composition: body weight, BMI, body fat percentage, and waist circumference fell in both groups, with a larger body fat percentage reduction in the soy group (2.2%) than the traditional group (1.4%).

Results on blood lipids and liver function: total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and liver function parameters decreased significantly in the soy group versus the traditional group, while triacylglycerol, HDL cholesterol, and fasting glucose showed no significant change.
Conclusion stating soy-based low-calorie diets lowered total and LDL cholesterol and reduced body fat percentage more than traditional low-calorie diets.
Final conclusion that soy-based diets offer health benefits for weight reduction and blood lipid control, closing the abstract.

Introduction to the review's methodology: it explains that early soy-breast cancer studies were weakly designed, and that this review restricts itself to studies with thorough dietary soy assessment and adequate confounder control.

Meta-analysis results for high-soy Asian populations: 8 studies (1 cohort, 7 case-control) show a significant decreasing risk trend with rising soy food intake, with the lowest intake (≤5 mg isoflavones/day) as reference.

Quantified dose-response findings: the odds ratios for modest (~10 mg/day) and high (≥20 mg/day) isoflavone intake in Asian studies, contrasted with null results from 11 low-soy Western populations (intake roughly 0.15–0.8 mg/day).
Concluding summary: Western low-intake data show no association, so the evidence, mostly from case-control studies, suggests Asian-level soy food consumption may protect against breast cancer.
Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that soy food at Asian consumption levels may be protective against breast cancer.
Introduction: outlines reported health benefits of soy phytoestrogens and raises concerns about genotoxicity, noting in vitro effects often occur at doses far above dietary levels.

Background on in vitro genotoxic findings for phytoestrogens, stating that effective concentrations were typically much higher than physiologically relevant intake; introduces the review's focus on genistein.

Scope of the review: centers on genistein, the most abundant soy phytoestrogen, and defines in vitro concentrations above 5 microM as non-physiological 'high' doses based on dietary uptake and bioavailability.

Consequence of the dose definition: apoptosis, growth inhibition, and topoisomerase inhibition appear less prominent, while recent cellular, epigenetic, and microarray studies examine effects at low, dietarily relevant concentrations.
Conclusion: applies the principle 'the dose defines the poison' to distinguish genotoxic from potentially beneficial in vitro effects of genistein and similar dietary products.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence, naming genistein as an example of a natural dietary product.

Introduction and background of a population-based Long Island study on dietary flavonoid intake before breast cancer diagnosis and subsequent survival, noting prior evidence on reduced breast cancer risk but unknown effects on survival.

Methods: study population of 1,210 women aged 25-98 diagnosed with first primary invasive breast cancer in 1996-1997, followed for vital status through 2002; dietary intake assessed by FFQ at case-control interview.
Methods continued: mortality outcomes (173 all-cause deaths, 113 breast cancer-specific deaths) ascertained via the National Death Index; start of results section.

Results: age- and energy-adjusted hazard ratios showing reduced all-cause mortality for highest vs. lowest quintile of flavones, isoflavones, and anthocyanidins among premenopausal and postmenopausal women, with confidence intervals.

Results and conclusion: no significant trends in risk, similar findings for breast cancer-specific mortality, and conclusion that high flavone and isoflavone intake may reduce mortality in postmenopausal U.S. breast cancer patients, with larger studies needed.
Final sentence of the conclusion calling for larger studies to confirm the findings on flavonoid intake and breast cancer mortality.

Introduction and objective of a Japanese nested case-control study on plasma isoflavones (genistein, daidzein) as biomarkers for breast cancer risk, from the Japan Public Health Center-based prospective cohort.
Study population and design: 24,226 Japanese women aged 40-69 in the JPHC cohort, blood drawn 1990-1995, follow-up to 2002 (mean 10.6 years), 144 breast cancer cases matched 1:2 to controls.

Methods for exposure assessment: plasma and food frequency questionnaire isoflavone measures, with conditional logistic regression used to estimate breast cancer odds ratios; results begin with a significant inverse genistein association.

Key quantitative results: adjusted odds ratios comparing highest vs lowest plasma quartile, showing genistein OR 0.34 (significant, P trend .02) versus daidzein OR 0.71 (not significant, P trend .54).

Supporting details: median control plasma genistein levels by quartile (31.9 vs 353.9 ng/mL), nonsignificant dietary isoflavone associations, and the conclusion of an inverse plasma genistein-breast cancer association in Japan.
Final sentence of the abstract's conclusion restating the inverse association between plasma genistein and breast cancer risk in Japanese women.

This chunk opens the trial abstract, stating the objective (comparing two soy milks against low-fat dairy milk on lipids, insulin, and glucose), the randomized cross-over design, and the eligibility criteria for the 28 hypercholesterolemic adults.

This chunk describes the intervention protocol: participants consumed milk supplying 25 g protein/day from each source, across three 4-week treatment phases separated by washout periods of at least 4 weeks.

This chunk reports the primary LDL-cholesterol results: end-of-phase means for whole bean soy milk, soy protein isolate milk, and dairy milk, with p-values showing no difference between soy milks but significance versus dairy.

This chunk gives the null secondary outcomes (HDL-cholesterol, triacylglycerols, insulin, glucose show no milk-type differences) and begins the conclusion about a 25 g daily soy protein dose modestly lowering LDL-C by about 5%.
This chunk completes the conclusion, stating that the LDL-C effect did not differ between soy milk types and that neither soy milk significantly affected other lipids, insulin, or glucose.

Introduces human gammadeltaT lymphocytes and how they are primed by bisphosphonates and short-chain alkylamines to proliferate and secrete cytokines against microbes and tumor cells; the document is about L-theanine enhancing gammadeltaT lymphocyte function.

Identifies L-theanine, a tea-specific amino acid and the largest dietary source of alkylamines (catabolized to ethylamine), and reports that L-theanine plus catechin supplementation reduced cold and flu incidence while enhancing gammadeltaT cell function.
Concludes the study's finding that L-theanine and catechin supplementation decreased cold and flu symptom incidence while enhancing gammadeltaT cell function.

Opening of an abstract on the anticancer effects of chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla) extracts, stating that its anticancer activity was previously unknown and that aqueous and methanolic extracts were tested on human cancer cell lines.

Results from the chamomile abstract: extracts showed minimal growth inhibition in normal cells but significant loss of viability in cancer cells, with differential apoptosis, and HPLC identified apigenin 7-O-glucoside as the main constituent.

Findings on chamomile's active compounds: apigenin glucosides inhibit cancer cell growth less than the aglycone apigenin, and ex vivo work suggests glycosides are deconjugated to aglycone in vivo, particularly in the small intestine.

Conclusion of the chamomile anticancer study: it is the first report of chamomile's anticancer effects, and further mechanistic research is recommended to assess its potential use in cancer patient management.
Final fragment of the concluding sentence of the chamomile abstract, ending with the phrase 'cancer patients'.

Abstract opening of a study on polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) exposure from yerba mate drinking, introducing the cancer associations and the aim to test whether benzo[a]pyrene and other carcinogenic PAHs reach harmful levels.

Methods section describing how 21 PAHs were measured in eight yerba mate brands and in hot (80°C) and cold (5°C) infusions via GC/MS with deuterated surrogates, and the repeated 12-cycle infusion procedure.
Methods end and results begin: describes the repeated infusion process and reports total PAH concentrations (536–2,906 ng/g) and benzo[a]pyrene levels (8.03–53.3 ng/g) across yerba mate brands.

Results on PAH transfer into infusions, e.g., brand 1 hot-water infusions releasing 37% of total PAHs and 50% of benzo[a]pyrene, followed by the start of the conclusion that carcinogenic PAHs are very high in leaves and infusions.
Final conclusion: very high levels of carcinogenic PAHs in yerba mate leaves and in both hot and cold infusions, supporting the idea that mate's carcinogenicity may stem from its PAH content.

Introduction of a paper on evidence standards for public dietary advice, contrasting clinical guideline evidence (RCT meta-analyses) with epidemiological evidence used for public health nutrition guidelines, using tea and coffee as the case study.

Explains why RCT meta-analyses are often unrealistic or unethical for public health nutrition, so epidemiological studies dominate nutrition guideline evidence; introduces tea and coffee as a case study since they are widely consumed yet receive little dietary advice.

Summarises the evidence on coffee and tea and disease: mainly epidemiological, supplemented by animal and in vitro work, indicating both beverages are safe, with tea possibly beneficial for preventing certain cancers and cardiovascular disease.

Concludes that tea is the healthier choice given possible roles in preventing cancers and CVD, though the evidence is not strong; argues the public will keep drinking both and asking nutritionists for guidance.
Final argument that dietary advice should be based on the best available data rather than waiting for complete evidence, since delay could have serious public health consequences.

Introduction and objectives of the Physicians' Health Study egg consumption paper: background on dietary cholesterol reduction for cardiovascular disease prevention, and the stated aim of examining eggs' link to CVD and mortality.

Methods and early results of the Physicians' Health Study I cohort (21,327 male physicians): study design, egg intake assessed by an abbreviated food questionnaire, Cox regression, and event counts for MI and stroke after about 20 years of follow-up.

Main results: egg consumption showed no association with incident MI or stroke, and the mortality hazard ratios by weekly egg intake category (<1 to 7+ per week) with p for trend, showing a graded increase at high intake.

Subgroup findings on mortality: the egg-mortality association was stronger in diabetic participants (HR 1.22 for highest versus lowest category, p for interaction 0.09), with the start of the conclusions.
Conclusions: infrequent egg consumption does not affect CVD risk, but egg intake is positively related to total mortality, more strongly among diabetic men in this selected physician population.
Final sentence of the conclusions, restating that the egg-mortality relationship was stronger among diabetic subjects in this selective population of male physicians.

Abstract opening of a study on whole-grain intake and inflammation-related mortality: states the background on oxidative stress, infection, and inflammation, the objective, and the design (postmenopausal women aged 55-69 at 1986 baseline, followed 17 years).

Continuation of the study design: exclusions for cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes, colitis, and cirrhosis leave 27,312 participants, 5,552 of whom died over 17 years; Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for age, smoking, adiposity, education, physical activity, and diet. Transitions into the RESULTS section.

Main results: inflammation-related death was inversely associated with whole-grain intake. Hazard ratios versus women who rarely or never ate whole grains are given for 4-7, 7.5-10.5, and 11-18.5 servings/week, with 95% confidence intervals.

Remaining results and conclusion start: the highest intake group (>=19 servings/week) has HR 0.66; trend P = 0.01; inverse associations with total and coronary heart disease mortality persisted at 17 years; inflammatory mortality reduction exceeded that reported for coronary heart disease and diabetes.

Discussion of mechanism: whole grains contain phytochemicals that may directly or indirectly inhibit oxidative stress, and oxidative stress is an inevitable consequence of inflammation, leading to the suggestion that oxidative stress reduction is a likely mechanism.

Concluding sentence of the abstract: the authors propose that reduction of oxidative stress by whole-grain constituents is a likely mechanism for the protective effect against inflammation-related death.

Introduction and background on food safety risks of fresh green sprouts, stating that proper sanitation and industry/regulatory guidelines can make sprout production very low risk, while contamination occurs when guidelines are not followed.

Continuation of the background on sprout safety guidelines, followed by the Methods section describing a one-year microbial hold-and-release testing program with strict seed and facility cleaning across 13 U.S. broccoli sprout growers.

Methods and early Results: the scope of the study, with 6839 drums (about 5 million consumer packages) tested, and the finding that 24 of 3191 samples (0.75%) initially tested positive for E. coli O157:H7 or Salmonella.

Results and Conclusion: re-testing found 3 drums still positive, composite pooling of up to 7 drums was as sensitive as single-drum testing, and the 'test-and-re-test' protocol helped growers minimize crop destruction.
Conclusion on cost and safety outcomes: drum pooling reduced testing costs, a major expense in sprout growing, and the test-and-hold scheme caught contaminated batches before packaging and shipping.
Final conclusion: the contamination events were isolated and only safe sprouts reached the food supply.

Introduces UV radiation as a complete carcinogen with multiple harmful effects (DNA damage, oxidative lipid damage, inflammation, immune suppression) and motivates the need for skin protection strategies given rising nonmelanoma skin cancer rates.

Explains that rising skin cancer incidence stems from aging populations' greater UV exposure, argues for cellular strategies to protect skin, and states the study's claim that UV-induced erythema is a noninvasive biomarker for quantifying UV damage in humans.

Summarizes the key findings: topical sulforaphane-rich broccoli sprout extracts raised phase 2 enzymes in mouse and human skin, reduced UV-induced inflammation and edema in mice, and lessened erythema from 311-nm narrow-band UVR in humans.

Reports the human trial results: in six subjects (3 male, 3 female, aged 28–53), sulforaphane reduced UV-induced erythema by a mean of 37.7% (range 8.37–78.1%, P = 0.025) across six UV doses, concluding the protection is catalytic and long lasting.
Concludes the study's claim that sulforaphane's protection against UV carcinogenesis in humans is catalytic and long lasting, completing the sentence begun in the prior chunk.
Introduction and objective of a 1993-2003 Oxford longitudinal cohort study on vitamin B-12, folate, homocysteine, and cognitive decline in older adults.
Study design: Mini-Mental State Examination cognitive testing over 10 years, linear mixed models, and 1648 participants with blood samples from 1995 measuring B-12, holoTC, tHcy, MMA, and folate.
Results begin: cognitive decline patterns vary across participants, and multivariate analyses show holoTC, tHcy, and MMA predict decline while folate does not.
Quantitative effect sizes: doubling holoTC linked to ~30% slower cognitive decline, while doubling tHcy or MMA linked to >50% faster decline, with specific slope values.
Robustness and conclusion: holoTC and MMA stay significant after adjusting for all vitamin markers, and low B-12 status is associated with faster cognitive decline; trials are needed.
Final conclusion: randomized trials are required to test whether vitamin B-12 supplementation can prevent dementia.

Introduction and methods from a 2007 Karger study on vitamin B12 levels in a high-income clinic population in Southern Israel; states the hypothesis that falling B12 is driven by reduced animal product consumption.

Methods and results: 512 patient medical histories reviewed, with 192 patients (37.5%) having B12 below 250 pg/ml; conclusion begins by attributing reduced meat, especially beef, intake to media linking meat and cholesterol to cardiovascular disease.

Conclusion discussing causes of declining animal product consumption: lifestyle changes among high-socioeconomic groups and poverty in others, leading to lower B12 levels and more B12 deficiency pathology.
Concluding recommendation that vitamin B12 fortification be seriously considered and discussed to prevent future deficiency-related health problems, followed by the 2007 S. Karger AG copyright line.
Final fragment of the document: the end of the recommendation for vitamin B12 fortification and the 2007 S. Karger AG, Basel copyright notice.

Case report opening: introduces cobalamin (B12) deficiency as usually causing hematologic and neuropsychiatric signs, notes psychiatric symptoms are rarely the main presentation, and describes a young vegetarian man with a cobalamin-induced psychotic episode lacking prior neurologic or hematologic symptoms.

Case report conclusion: the young vegetarian patient with cobalamin-induced psychosis recovered with a short antipsychotic course plus oral B12 supplementation, and at 1-year follow-up he remained symptom-free and functionally independent.
Introduction to vitamin B12 dietary sources (animal foods) and how bioavailability falls as the per-meal dose rises, due to intrinsic factor absorption saturation at about 1.5-2.0 µg per meal.

Species-specific bioavailability figures for vitamin B12 from fish, sheep, and chicken meat, plus poor egg absorption (<9%), and the 50% absorption assumption used in US and Japanese Dietary Reference Intakes.

Plant and algal sources of vitamin B12: nori (dried laver) contains substantial B12 while most other edible algae have none or only traces, and it introduces cyanobacteria with the transition to their unsuitability.

Why edible cyanobacteria are unsuitable B12 sources because they mainly contain inactive pseudovitamin B12, especially for vegans, and fortified breakfast cereals as a valuable B12 source for vegans and elderly people.
Closing note on emerging alternatives: efforts to develop vitamin B12-enriched vegetables as an additional plant-based source.

Case report abstract introducing vitamin B12 deficiency as a possible cause of depressive disorder, noting that psychiatric symptoms can precede hematological anemia and that little literature exists on B12's role in depression; it presents a patient with recurrent depressive episodes attributed to B12 deficiency.
Case report opening: a 7-month-old girl with acute anemia, hypotonia, and failure to thrive, found to have cobalamin (B12) deficiency caused by her mother's vegan diet.

Clinical teaching points: the floppy baby triad with megaloblastic anemia and failure to thrive indicates infantile B12 deficiency; neurological damage is often irreversible and may show delayed myelination on MRI; normal maternal B12 or absent anemia does not rule out subclinical deficiency.

Recommendation: in suspected deficiency (e.g., vegan pregnant women), measure urinary methylmalonic acid and plasma homocysteine and start B12 supplementation early to prevent irreversible fetal harm.

Introduction and overarching recommendation from an ESPGHAN position paper on complementary feeding for healthy European infants: breastfeeding for about 6 months as the goal, and the timing window for introducing solid foods (17 to 26 weeks).
Guidance on allergen introduction: no convincing evidence that avoiding or delaying potentially allergenic foods such as fish and eggs prevents allergy, in either high-risk or general infants.

Iron guidance during complementary feeding: complementary foods must supply over 90% of a breastfed infant's iron needs with bioavailable iron, and cow's milk is a poor iron source and should not be the main drink before 12 months.

Gluten introduction timing: avoid introducing gluten before 4 months or after 7 months, and introduce it gradually during breastfeeding, which may lower risk of celiac disease, type 1 diabetes, and wheat allergy.

Dietary recommendations for special diets and closing conclusions: vegetarian infants need about 500 mL of breast milk, formula, or dairy daily, and vegan diets should not be fed to infants or young children.
Final fragment of the document, consisting only of a closing period from the vegan diet recommendation at the end of the position paper.

Introduction of a case report on West syndrome caused by vitamin B12 deficiency in a 10-month-old infant, summarizing typical neurological and haematological signs of B12 deficiency and the diagnostic difficulty when macrocytic anaemia is absent.

Case presentation begins: a 10-month-old girl with West syndrome due to B12 deficiency without macrocytic anaemia, attributed to maternal nutritional inadequacy; normal development until age 9 months, then sudden flexion spasms of head, trunk, arms and legs.

Clinical workup of the infant: exclusively breast-fed with no vitamin supplementation, EEG showing modified hypsarrhythmia leading to a West syndrome diagnosis, and treatment with synthetic ACTH, which stopped the spasms but left her apathetic and unable to sit unaided.

Diagnosis and outcome: after B12 deficiency was identified, parenteral vitamin B12 was given, resolving symptoms and normalizing EEG; the infant had an age-appropriate developmental and neurological profile by 20 months.

Conclusion of the case report: the 20-month follow-up showing normal development, and the authors' claim that this is the first report of West syndrome as a presenting symptom of vitamin B12 deficiency.

Introduction and objective of a systematic review/meta-analysis (searches through October 2005) on whether antioxidant supplements (beta carotene, vitamin A, C, E, selenium) affect all-cause mortality in primary and secondary prevention randomized trials.

Methods: eligibility criteria for included adult randomized trials (antioxidants vs placebo or no intervention), bias markers (randomization, blinding, follow-up), and the random-effects analysis of all-cause mortality reported as relative risks with 95% CIs.
Methods continued: meta-regression for covariates, and data extraction yielding 68 randomized trials with 232,606 participants from 385 publications.
Results: pooling all trials shows no significant mortality effect (RR 1.02); multivariate meta-regression finds low-bias risk status and selenium significantly associated with mortality.

Results: restricted to 47 low-bias trials (180,938 participants), antioxidants significantly increase mortality (RR 1.05); excluding selenium, beta carotene, vitamin A, and vitamin E each significantly raise mortality.
Results and conclusions: vitamin C and selenium show no significant mortality effect; beta carotene, vitamin A, and vitamin E may increase mortality, while vitamin C and selenium need further study.
Final conclusion sentence: the potential roles of vitamin C and selenium on mortality require further study, closing the abstract of the antioxidant mortality meta-analysis.

Introduction to black pepper (Piper nigrum): its widespread use as a spice, preservative, medicinal agent, and in perfumery, and the piperine alkaloid responsible for its pungency and many reported physiological effects.

Piperine's effects on digestion: stimulating pancreatic digestive enzymes to improve digestive capacity and shorten gastrointestinal food transit time, with in vitro evidence of free radical and reactive oxygen species scavenging.

Antioxidant effects of black pepper and piperine: in vivo reductions in lipid peroxidation and improved thiol status, antioxidant molecules, and antioxidant enzymes under oxidative stress, leading into piperine's influence on liver drug metabolism.

Piperine's most far-reaching property: inhibition of hepatic and intestinal drug-metabolizing enzymes (aryl hydrocarbon hydroxylase, UDP-glucuronyl transferase), which enhances the bioavailability of therapeutic drugs and phytochemicals.

Mechanisms and safety of piperine's bioavailability enhancement: partly via altered intestinal brush border ultrastructure and increased absorption, plus a transition to the history of controversial food-additive safety reports.
Safety and anticancer profile of piperine: later animal studies established its safety despite earlier controversy, and piperine is non-genotoxic while showing anti-mutagenic and anti-tumor effects.
Closing fragment of the document's final sentence, stating piperine's anti-mutagenic and anti-tumor influences.

Opening of the 2010s-era Hohenheim consensus update on monosodium glutamate (MSG): states the objective (updating the 1997 consensus on physiology and safety), the expert-panel design, the setting at University of Hohenheim, and the method of reaching consensus.

Conclusion section giving estimated European dietary glutamate intake of 5-12 g/day, broken down into free glutamate (~1 g), protein-bound (~10 g), and added flavor (~0.4 g), and noting that L-glutamate from all sources is mainly used as an energy fuel in enterocytes.

Core safety conclusions: a maximum intake of 6000 mg/kg body weight is considered safe, glutamate salts used as food additives are deemed harmless for the general population, and even very high doses of glutamate do not cross into fetal circulation.

Remaining research gaps and practical recommendations: further study is needed on high bolus doses when the blood-brain barrier is impaired, and low-dose MSG can improve palatability for people with decreased appetite, such as elderly persons.
Final fragment of the recommendation sentence, completing the statement that low-dose monosodium-L-glutamate use can improve palatability in situations of decreased appetite.

Opening section of a document arguing that FDA should reassess aspartame's safety, citing animal bioassay evidence of cancer risk and noting that aspartame is produced in China, Japan, France, and the United States.

Closing section of the same document, noting that no long-term occupational health studies of aspartame workers exist and recommending that FDA sponsor a prospective epidemiologic study of those workers. It continues the production-location discussion from chunk 1.

Introduction to a study on red meat diet and axillary body odor: states that body odor is individually specific, influenced by genetics and eating habits, and that the effect of dietary components on body odor is poorly understood.

Methods of the within-subject study: 17 male odor donors ate a 'meat' or 'nonmeat' diet for 2 weeks, with axillary pads collecting odor over the final 24 hours, and odor samples were rated for pleasantness, attractiveness, masculinity, and intensity by women.

Procedure and analysis: the study was repeated a month later with donors switched to the opposite diet, and repeated measures ANOVA results are introduced, showing nonmeat-diet odor was judged more attractive.
Conclusion of the study: nonmeat-diet body odor was rated more attractive, pleasant, and less intense, suggesting red meat consumption negatively affects perceived body odor hedonicity.
Introduces the study's objective, design, and participants: a 1970 British birth cohort study of 8170 people aged 30, linking childhood IQ at age 10 to adult self-reported vegetarianism.

Reports the prevalence of vegetarianism in the cohort (366, 4.5%) and that many self-described vegetarians (33.6%) ate fish or chicken, plus the demographic profile of vegetarians: more often female, higher social class, and higher qualifications.
Presents the main result: higher childhood IQ at age 10 was associated with greater odds of adult vegetarianism (OR 1.38 per SD, 95% CI 1.24-1.53).

Reports that the IQ association stayed significant after adjusting for social class, qualifications, and sex (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.06-1.36), and that excluding fish/chicon-eating vegetarians had little effect.
States the study's conclusion that higher childhood IQ is associated with a greater likelihood of being vegetarian as an adult.

Case report opening: introduces an irreversible subacute sclerotic combined degeneration of the spinal cord in a 57-year-old Western vegan man (13 years in a vegan group), listing his neurological symptoms: paraplegia, hyperreflexia, sensory loss, and neurogenic bladder/bowel.

Imaging and diagnosis: cervical and dorsal spine MRI shows T2 hyperintensity in the posterior and lateral columns, leading to a diagnosis of subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord and initiation of cobalamin (vitamin B12) treatment.

Clinical course: despite rehabilitation, the patient developed spastic hypertonia with only mild paresthesia improvement; at six months B12 levels and blood tests were normal, and at one year spastic paraplegia persisted with inability to walk despite MRI improvement.
Conclusion: the case report concludes that irreversible subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, though rare, is a possible consequence of a strict vegetarian diet.

Abstract of a study on the methanol extract of the edible seaweed Gloiopeltis furcata (MEGF) in human hepatocarcinoma HepG2 cells; this chunk introduces the prior cancer cell growth findings and the study's aims on cell growth and cyclooxygenase (COX) expression.
Abstract of the MEGF study on HepG2 liver cancer cells; this chunk reports the results on cell viability, G2/M cell cycle arrest, and the cell cycle regulators cyclin A, p21 (WAF1/CIP1), and Cdc25C.

Conclusion of the MEGF HepG2 abstract; this chunk describes decreased COX-2 mRNA and protein without changes in COX-1, the drop in prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) synthesis, and the suggested therapeutic potential for hepatoma patients.
Final word fragment of the MEGF HepG2 abstract, completing the phrase 'hepatoma cancer patients' from the concluding sentence about therapeutic potential.

Introduces the study's aim and methods: measuring total and inorganic arsenic in 31 retail dried seaweed samples (five varieties) from London and online sellers, to inform dietary exposure estimates and consumer advice.

Describes the sample preparation and analysis: for four of the five seaweed varieties soaking is recommended, so arsenic was measured before and after the prescribed preparation, including in the soaking water.

Reports the main results: arsenic was found in all samples (total 18-124 mg/kg), inorganic arsenic (a liver cancer risk) was found only in the nine hijiki samples at 67-96 mg/kg, and other seaweeds had under 0.3 mg/kg.

Explains the significance of the findings: hijiki's high inorganic arsenic could substantially raise dietary exposure, which led the UK Food Standards Agency to advise consumers to avoid eating hijiki.
Concludes the FSA advice, a short fragment completing the sentence that tells consumers to avoid eating hijiki seaweed.

Opening of the EPIC-Oxford abstract: states the objective (comparing fracture rates across meat eaters, fish eaters, vegetarians, and vegans), the prospective cohort design, the UK setting, and the study population of about 34,000 adults aged 20-89.

Continues the subjects and methods (recruitment, Cox regression) and begins the results: about 5.2 years of follow-up with 343 men and 1555 women reporting fractures, and the start of the age- and sex-adjusted fracture incidence rate ratios comparing diet groups with meat eaters.

Core results: fracture incidence rate ratios for fish eaters (1.01), vegetarians (1.00), and vegans (1.30, CI 1.02-1.66) versus meat eaters, then vegans after adjustment for energy and calcium intake (1.15, CI 0.89-1.49).

Calcium-stratified analysis among those consuming at least 525 mg/day calcium (fish eaters 1.05, vegetarians 1.02, vegans 1.00, all with no elevated risk), followed by the start of the conclusions on similar fracture risk across meat eaters, fish eaters, and vegetarians.

Conclusions and interpretation: the higher vegan fracture risk appears due to lower mean calcium intake, emphasizing adequate calcium for bone health regardless of diet, plus the EPIC-Oxford funding sponsorship by the Medical Research Council and Cancer Research UK.
Final sentence of the sponsorship statement naming the Medical Research Council and Cancer Research UK as funders of the EPIC-Oxford study.

Introduction and study aims for a cocoa powder trial: polyphenols (catechins, procyanidins) in cocoa are linked to inhibition of oxidized LDL and atherogenesis; the study tests LDL and oxidized LDL responses to 13, 19.5, and 26 g/d cocoa in normo- and mildly hypercholesterolemic adults.

Study design: a comparative, double-blind trial of 160 subjects randomized to a placebo cocoa (low-polyphenol) group or low, middle, and high cocoa groups (13, 19.5, 26 g/d high-polyphenol) for 4 weeks.
Methods and primary results: cocoa was consumed as a hot-water beverage twice daily, with blood drawn at baseline and week 4; plasma oxidized LDL decreased in all cocoa groups relative to baseline.

Stratified subgroup analysis of 131 subjects with baseline LDL cholesterol of at least 3.23 mmol/L, reporting decreases in LDL cholesterol, oxidized LDL, and apo B and an increase in HDL cholesterol across the cocoa groups.
Conclusion: polyphenolic substances in cocoa powder may lower LDL cholesterol, raise HDL cholesterol, and suppress oxidized LDL, supporting a cardioprotective effect.

Introduction and study aim: examines how cocoa flavanols and procyanidins affect innate immune responses in vitro, using PBMCs from healthy volunteers, within a broader context of nutrition and immunity research.

Methods: describes isolation of PBMCs, monocytes, and CD4/CD8 T cells from healthy volunteers and their culture with two cocoa flavanol fractions differing by polymerization degree: SCFF (monomers to pentamers) and LCFF (hexamers to decamers).

Methods continued: cells are challenged with LPS and activation is measured via CD69/CD83 expression; parallel experiments test purified flavanol monomers and procyanidin dimers, with cytokine readouts described.

Results: lists the measured cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-10, GM-CSF) and reports that flavanol chain length significantly affects cytokine release from unstimulated and LPS-stimulated PBMCs.

Key findings: LCFF markedly boosts LPS-induced IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-10 and TNF-alpha; LCFF and SCFF alone induce GM-CSF and increase CD69 and CD83 expression, with differential responses across mononuclear cell populations.
Conclusion: the cocoa procyanidin oligomers are potent stimulators of innate immunity and early adaptive immune events, concluding the abstract.

Background and rationale of a trial on cocoa and blood pressure: observational links to lower cardiovascular mortality, prior short-term high-dose cocoa studies, and the unclear effect of low habitual cocoa intake on BP.

Study objective and design of the cocoa/dark chocolate trial: randomized, investigator-blinded, parallel-group, 44 older German adults (56-73 years) with untreated prehypertension or stage 1 hypertension, conducted in a primary care clinic 2005-2006.
Intervention details: 18 weeks of 6.3 g/day (30 kcal) polyphenol-rich dark chocolate (30 mg polyphenols) versus matching polyphenol-free white chocolate control.

Outcome measures of the trial: primary outcome is change in blood pressure at 18 weeks; secondary outcomes are plasma S-nitrosoglutathione (nitric oxide marker), 8-isoprostane (oxidative stress), and cocoa polyphenol bioavailability.
Results: dark chocolate reduced systolic BP by 2.9 mm Hg and diastolic BP by 1.9 mm Hg without changes in weight, lipids, glucose, or 8-isoprostane; hypertension prevalence fell from 86% to 68%.

Mechanistic and control-group results: the BP decrease coincided with a sustained rise in S-nitrosoglutathione of 0.23 nmol/L and appearance of cocoa phenols in plasma, while white chocolate produced no BP or biomarker changes; conclusions on efficient BP reduction and nitric oxide formation in a small sample.
Conclusion and trial registration: small amounts of dark chocolate in a usual diet reduced BP and improved vasodilative nitric oxide formation; registered at clinicaltrials.gov as NCT00421499.
Trial registration identifier NCT00421499 at clinicaltrials.gov, the final identifier line of the abstract.

Background and design of a 12-week randomized trial of cocoa powder polyphenols (catechins, procyanidins) vs. sugar control on plasma lipids and LDL oxidation in normocholesterolemic and mildly hypercholesterolemic adults.

Trial design details (25 subjects, 12 g sugar/day control vs. 26 g cocoa powder plus sugar for 12 weeks, baseline and 12-week sampling) and the outcomes measured: plasma lipids, LDL oxidative susceptibility, and urinary oxidative stress markers, with the start of the results on LDL oxidation lag time.
Results for LDL oxidation lag time (9% prolongation in cocoa group vs. -13% in control) and plasma HDL cholesterol (24% increase in cocoa group vs. 5% in control) at 12 weeks.
Further results: negative correlation between HDL cholesterol and oxidized LDL, and the 24% dityrosine (urinary oxidative stress marker) reduction in the cocoa group vs. -1% in control.
Conclusion of the cocoa powder study: HDL cholesterol increases may contribute to suppressing LDL oxidation, and cocoa polyphenols may raise HDL cholesterol.
Introduction and study design: acute single-dose and 7-day chronic high-flavanol cocoa effects on flow-mediated dilation (FMD) in smokers with endothelial dysfunction.

Methods and chronic results: 7-day daily flavanol-rich cocoa drink (3 x 306 mg flavanols/day, n=6) raised baseline fasted FMD and sustained FMD at 2 hours post-ingestion; nitrite and nitrate were measured.
Chronic time-course results: fasted FMD rose from 3.7% on day 1 to 6.6% by day 8 and returned to 3.3% after a cocoa-free washout week (day 15).

Nitrite findings and acute dose-response: nitrite tracked FMD gains (not nitrate); single doses of 28 to 918 mg flavanols dose-dependently raised FMD, peaking at 2 hours, with a half-maximal dose of 616 mg.

Safety biomarkers and conclusion: oxidative stress and antioxidant markers (MDA, TEAC, ascorbate, urate) were unchanged, supporting that daily high-flavanol cocoa can sustainably, dose-dependently reverse endothelial dysfunction.
Final sentence of the conclusion: summarizes that daily flavanol-rich cocoa has potential to reverse endothelial dysfunction in a sustained and dose-dependent manner.

Introduction/opening of the review on flavonoid-rich cocoa and chocolate; states that cocoa and chocolate are plant-derived sources of antioxidant flavonoids and lists their cardiovascular benefits (antioxidant activity, vasodilation/blood pressure reduction, platelet inhibition, reduced inflammation).
Concluding statement of the document's abstract; summarizes growing experimental and clinical evidence that high-flavanol cocoa and chocolate products protect the heart and vascular system.

Introduction and objectives of a study on aging and vascular responses to flavanol-rich cocoa: tests whether vascular responsiveness to cocoa increases with age, building on prior evidence of NO-dependent endothelial improvement.

Methods and start of results: blood pressure and peripheral arterial responses measured in 15 young (<50) and 19 older (>50) healthy subjects after several days of cocoa; introduces L-NAME (NOS inhibitor) pressor response findings.

Results on L-NAME-induced blood pressure increases after cocoa, seen only in older subjects (SBP +13 mmHg, DBP +6 mmHg, with significance values), plus higher SBP in older subjects and onset of flow-mediated vasodilation findings by finger tonometry.

Results on flow-mediated vasodilation, enhanced by cocoa more in older subjects (P = 0.01), and pulse wave amplitude (PWA) changes: basal PWA rose over 4-6 days of cocoa in both groups, with an acute-dose timeline on the final day.

Results on peak vasodilation and PWA after acute cocoa on the final day, with a more robust response in older subjects, plus the finding that L-NAME reversed dilation in both groups; begins the conclusions.

Conclusions: flavanol-rich cocoa improved several endothelial function measures more in older than younger healthy adults, suggesting NO-dependent vascular effects are greater in older people with more disturbed endothelial function.

Study background and objectives: comparing effects of adding walnuts vs. olive oil to a high-fat meal on postprandial endothelial function, lipoproteins, oxidation, endothelial activation, and ADMA, motivated by prior walnut-diet findings in hypercholesterolemic patients.

Study design: randomized crossover trial of 12 healthy and 12 hypercholesterolemic subjects receiving high-fat meals with 25 g olive oil or 40 g walnuts, with the hypothesis that walnuts would reverse postprandial endothelial dysfunction.
Methods detail: both test meals had 80 g fat and 35% saturated fat, were separated by one week, and brachial artery FMD ultrasound plus venipuncture were done fasting and 4 hours after the meal.

Key results on FMD: flow-mediated dilation was worse after the olive oil meal than the walnut meal (p = 0.006); fasting triglycerides, not postprandial, inversely correlated with FMD (r = -0.324, p = 0.024).

Other results: flow-independent dilation and ADMA were unchanged, oxidized LDL decreased after either meal, and inflammatory cytokines and adhesion molecules fell regardless of meal type, with E-selectin dropping more after walnuts (p = 0.033).

Conclusions: adding walnuts to a high-fat meal acutely improves FMD independently of oxidation, inflammation, or ADMA changes, and both walnuts and olive oil preserve the protective endothelial phenotype.
Abstract opening: study objective, cross-sectional design, sample of 159 college students (mean age 19.9) at a large state university, and methods for measuring grain intake and BMI.
Methods and results: food-record measures and BMI categorization with ANOVA, then findings that cereal grain intake averaged 5.4 servings/day, with only 0.7 servings/day being whole grains.

Results and conclusions: whole-grain intake was significantly higher in normal-weight than overweight/obese students, and the low intake motivates interventions toward the recommended 3 servings/day minimum.
Implications: students concerned about weight may be motivated to eat more whole grains, but intake depends on availability in campus dining halls and other campus locations.
Final sentence of the abstract, noting that whole-grain availability in campus dining halls and surrounding campus locations shapes students' intake.

Trial objective, design, and setup of a randomized double-blind study of soy protein vs. isocaloric casein placebo on body composition and insulin metabolism in 15 non-diabetic postmenopausal women; lists interventions (CT at L4/L5, DXA, hyperglycemic clamps).

Outcome measures listed (total, abdominal, visceral, subcutaneous fat, insulin secretion) and the first results: DXA-measured weight change did not differ between placebo and soy groups (+1.38 vs +0.756 kg, p=0.48).

Key result: total and subcutaneous abdominal fat increased significantly more in the placebo group than the soy group (total abdominal fat p=0.005; subcutaneous abdominal fat p=0.013), with the start of the note on insulin secretion.

Remaining results: insulin secretion, visceral fat, total body fat, and lean mass showed no between-group differences; isoflavone levels rose more in the soy group. Conclusion that soy protein prevents the rise in subcutaneous and total abdominal fat versus casein.
Final fragment of the conclusion, ending the statement that soy protein prevents abdominal fat gain compared with an isocaloric casein placebo in postmenopausal women.
Introduction to tea leaves' natural defense compounds (catechins and methylxanthine alkaloids) against pathogens, establishing the document's antimicrobial focus on tea flavonoids and teas.

Explains how postharvest processing differs: enzyme inactivation preserves green tea catechins, while fermentation oxidizes catechins into theaflavins and thearubigins that give black and oolong teas their color and phenolic profile.
States the rationale for the review: a need to better understand polyphenolic tea compounds in food and medical microbiology, and outlines the scope of pathogens and toxins surveyed.

Lists the scope of the overview's coverage, including foodborne bacteria, bacterial toxins, bacteriophages, viruses, and fungi, plus synergy, mechanism, and bioavailability, and suggests future research directions.
Concludes that the antimicrobial findings matter both for basic science and for practical applications in nutrition, food safety, and animal and human health.

Abstract opening (Background/Methods) of a case series on toxic hepatitis and severe liver injury linked to Herbalife herbal supplements, describing the Swiss hospital questionnaire study and CIOMS causality assessment.

Results section of the Herbalife hepatotoxicity case series: 12 Swiss cases of toxic hepatitis (1998-2004), 10 analyzed, with patient demographics (median age 51) and latency to onset (median 5 months).

Results continuing the Herbalife case series: liver biopsy findings (necrosis, lymphocytic/eosinophilic infiltration, cholestasis), a fulminant liver failure patient who received transplant with giant cell hepatitis, a sinusoidal obstruction syndrome case, and hepatocellular or mixed injury in patients without biopsy.

Results and conclusions of the Herbalife hepatotoxicity study: causality ratings (certain, probable, possible) for the adverse drug reactions and the concluding statement that herbal supplement liver toxicity can be severe.
Final conclusion of the Herbalife supplement hepatotoxicity case series, calling for fuller ingredient disclosure and more proactive regulatory agency oversight of herbal products.

Introduction and methods of a study on acute liver injury (hepatitis) linked to Herbalife nutritional supplements, describing the 2004 Israeli Ministry of Health investigation that followed four index cases and included twelve patients.
