Results describing the patient cohort: mostly female (eleven of twelve), mean age about 49.5 years, two patients with pre-existing liver conditions (stage I primary biliary cirrhosis and hepatitis B), and a latency of roughly 11.9 months from starting Herbalife to diagnosis of liver injury.

Clinical and histologic findings: liver biopsies showing active hepatitis with eosinophil-rich portal inflammation, ductular reaction, and peri-central parenchymal inflammation, plus severity data including one sub-fulminant and two fulminant hepatic failure episodes.

Outcomes and rechallenge evidence: hepatitis resolved in eleven patients, one died after liver transplantation, and three patients who resumed Herbalife had a recurrence of hepatitis, supporting a causal link; the conclusions state an association between Herbalife intake and acute hepatitis in Israel.

Conclusion and recommendations: the authors call for prospective evaluation of Herbalife products for hepatotoxicity and advise consumers, especially those with underlying liver disease, to exercise caution until more evidence is available.

Opening of the cannabis-and-lung-cancer case-control study: states the aim, and describes the New Zealand study design, case identification, and control selection from the electoral roll with frequency matching.

Methods and start of results from the New Zealand cannabis and lung cancer case-control study: covers interviewer-administered questionnaires, logistic regression for relative risk, and the sample of 79 cases and 324 controls.
Main results of the cannabis and lung cancer study: risk rises 8% per joint-year of cannabis smoking and 7% per pack-year of cigarette smoking, each adjusted for the other exposure.

Key findings of the cannabis and lung cancer study: highest-tertile cannabis use gives RR=5.7 (95% CI 1.5-21.6) after adjusting for cigarette smoking, and the conclusion that long-term cannabis use raises lung cancer risk in young adults.
Final word of the conclusion of the cannabis and lung cancer study, which states that long-term cannabis use increases lung cancer risk in young adults.

Introduces pine needles (Pinus densiflora) as a Korean traditional medicinal food and describes the study's aim of testing their antioxidant, antimutagenic, and antitumor activities, plus initial antioxidant results for the ethanol extract (PNE).

Reports PNE's in vitro results: antimutagenic effects in Ames tests against 2-anthramine, 2-nitrofluorene, and sodium azide in Salmonella strains, and growth inhibition of cancer cell lines (MCF-7, SNU-638, HL-60) versus normal HDF cells in an MTT assay.

Describes the in vivo antitumor design: a 5% freeze-dried pine needle powder diet fed to Sarcoma-180 tumor-bearing mice and to rats given the mammary carcinogen DMBA (50 mg/kg), with the finding that tumorigenesis was suppressed.

Presents the in vivo safety and biochemical findings: lower blood urea nitrogen and aspartate aminotransferase levels in pine needle-fed DMBA rats, and the overall conclusion that pine needles show antioxidant, antimutagenic, and antiproliferative effects supporting their potential in cancer prevention.

Concludes the abstract by summarizing that pine needles have strong antioxidant, antimutagenic, antiproliferative, and in vivo antitumor effects, pointing to their potential usefulness in cancer prevention.

Introduces the Nurses' Health Study investigation of dietary flavonols and flavones (flavonoid subgroups) and their prospective link to nonfatal myocardial infarction and fatal coronary heart disease, using 1990-1998 food frequency questionnaire data.

Describes the methods (cumulative average intakes, Cox regression with time-varying variables) and the cohort results: 12 years of follow-up (1990-2002) with 938 nonfatal MIs and 324 CHD deaths among 66,360 women, finding no overall association.
Reports the null overall findings for flavonols and flavones, then notes a weak protective association with CHD death for higher kaempferol intake, a flavonol found mainly in broccoli and tea.

Gives the kaempferol result: highest versus lowest quintile multivariate relative risk of 0.66 (95% CI 0.48-0.93, p for trend 0.04), attributed probably to broccoli consumption, and concludes the prospective data do not support an inverse flavonol/flavone-CHD association.
Concluding sentence stating that the prospective data do not support an inverse association between flavonol or flavone intake and coronary heart disease risk.
Introduction to a study of broccoli flower head's antimutagenic effect, using crude ethanol extract tested in the Ames Salmonella reverse mutation assay against chemical mutagens.

Methods: three Salmonella tester strains (TA98, TA102, TA1535) challenged with their mutagens and broccoli flower head ethanol extract at 23 and 46 mg/plate, incubated 72 h, revertant colonies counted.
Results: the crude extract was not promutagenic, and at 46 mg/plate it suppressed mutagenicity induced by the positive mutagens in all three tester strains.
Cytotoxicity and conclusion: the extract alone was non-cytotoxic even at 46 mg/plate, and the 46 mg/plate ethanol extract shows diverse antimutagenic potential against the mutagens tested.
Publisher copyright line (John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.) closing the abstract of the broccoli antimutagenicity Ames assay study.

Case report opening: a 24-year-old woman with mild transaminase and bilirubin elevation who had received interferon beta-1a for multiple sclerosis; viral hepatitis was excluded and the drug was stopped for suspected drug-induced hepatitis.

Clinical progression: one week after interferon withdrawal, the patient returned with severe icterus, marked transaminase and bilirubin rise, reduced prothrombin time, and transfer to a specialist unit for suspected fulminant hepatitis and early acute liver failure.

Diagnostic workup: alternative causes (hepatotropic viruses, alcoholic hepatitis, Budd-Chiari, hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease) were excluded; high liver-kidney microsomal type 1 autoantibody titers were present with normal gamma globulin, and fine-needle liver biopsy ruled out autoimmune hepatitis.

Key finding: biopsy showed drug-induced toxicity, and the patient disclosed 4 weeks of Noni juice (Morinda citrifolia, a Polynesian herbal remedy) use for 'immune stimulation', identifying it as a likely hepatotoxic cause.
Outcome and source: transaminases normalized within a month after stopping Noni juice, supporting it as the cause; the chunk ends with the 2006 S. Karger AG, Basel copyright line.

Introduction: background on dietary putrescine benefiting neonatal animals under nutritional stress, and the high turkey poult mortality hypothesized to stem from poor feeding behavior and underdeveloped intestines, motivating the study's aim.
Methods (start): 160 one-day-old turkey poults assigned to a corn-soybean starter diet with 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, or 0.3 g/100 g purified putrescine, with 8 birds per pen and 5 pens per diet.

Methods (continued): at 14 days of age half the birds were infected with about 43,000 sporulated oocysts; the 24-day trial included fecal total collection on days 3-5 postinfection and bird sampling on days 6 and 10.

Results: the coccidial infection significantly depressed growth and feed intake and damaged small intestine morphology without mortality; in challenged poults, 0.3 g/100 g putrescine improved weight gain, jejunal protein, and duodenal, jejunal, and ileal morphometry versus controls.
Conclusion: dietary putrescine supplementation may benefit poult growth, small intestinal mucosal development, and recovery from subclinical coccidiosis.
Introduction and background: states the rationale that watermelon citrulline converts to arginine, and notes no prior long-term human studies on arginine response to plant-derived citrulline.
Study aim and methods begin: the research question on whether watermelon juice raises fasting plasma arginine, ornithine, and citrulline in healthy adults, plus the subject count and design.

Methods detail: crossover design with control, 780 g, and 1560 g daily watermelon juice for 3 weeks, providing 1 and 2 g citrulline per day, with 2-4 week washouts; results open with the lower-dose arginine increase.
Results: arginine rose 12% on lower dose and 22% on higher dose, ornithine rose 18% on higher dose, and citrulline did not rise relative to control.
Conclusion: rising arginine and ornithine with stable citrulline indicates plant-derived citrulline is effectively converted to arginine, supporting watermelon as an arginine source.
Final sentence of the conclusion, restating that consuming citrulline from watermelon can raise plasma arginine concentration.

Introduces the review's main claim: cranberry and blueberry (Vaccinium spp.) flavonoid-rich fruits may limit certain cancers, atherosclerosis, ischemic stroke, and neurodegenerative diseases of aging, based on tissue, animal, and clinical evidence.

Lists the candidate bioactive phytochemicals in cranberry and blueberry (anthocyanins, flavonols, proanthocyanidins, cinnamic acids, stilbenes, ursolic acid and esters) that could drive the protective effects.

Describes proposed mechanisms of action (counteracting oxidative stress, reducing inflammation, modulating macromolecular interactions and gene expression) and concludes that dietary berries may help prevent cancer and vascular disease, calling for research on bioavailability and metabolism.
Closing clause of the conclusion: calls for further research on how berry phytonutrient bioavailability and metabolism affect their activity in vivo.
Introduction/objectives of a mouse study on genistein (soy phytoestrogen), vinclozolin (fungicide), and hypospadias risk from in utero exposure.
Background on the UK maternal diet study linking nonorganic vegetarian diets to hypospadias, motivating concern about pesticide residues like vinclozolin alongside genistein.
Study rationale and methods start: pregnant mice on soy-free diet, with the objective of testing realistic daily exposure doses of genistein and vinclozolin.
Methods detail: oral gavage dosing (GD13-17) of genistein, vinclozolin, or both in corn oil, with controls, and fetal examination at GD19 for hypospadias.
Results and conclusions: hypospadias incidence was 0% in controls, 25% with genistein, 42% with vinclozolin, and 41% with combined exposure, supporting gestational exposure as a contributor.
Final fragment of the conclusion stating that gestational exposure to these compounds could contribute to hypospadias development.
Opening of the abstract: study objective and methods on maternal diet (vegetarianism, phytoestrogens) as a possible cause of rising hypospadias, using prospective questionnaires in the ALSPAC cohort.

Methods continued: prospective questionnaire data on lifestyle and diet, examination of environmental and parental factors with a focus on the hormonal hypothesis, and multivariate logistic regression; start of the results describing the 7928 boys in ALSPAC.

Results: 51 hypospadias cases among 7928 boys, with no significant link to smoking, alcohol, or previous reproductive history such as pregnancies, miscarriages, contraceptive pill use, time to conception, or age at menarche.
Results on diet: vegetarianism and first-half-of-pregnancy iron supplementation were the significant dietary factors, and the adjusted OR for vegetarian mothers (4.99) begins here.

Key odds ratios: vegetarian mothers OR 4.99 (95% CI 2.10-11.88) versus omnivores not taking iron; omnivores taking iron OR 2.07 (95% CI 1.00-4.32); influenza in the first trimester is the only other significant association (OR 3.19).
Final results on influenza (adjusted OR 3.19, 95% CI 1.50-6.78) and the conclusion that vegetarians' higher phytoestrogen exposure supports a possible harmful effect on male reproductive development.
Closing sentence of the conclusion: phytoestrogens may have a deleterious effect on the developing male reproductive system.

Study design: a 30-week monitoring of 14 household kitchen and bathroom sites for faecal coliform, total coliform and heterotrophic plate count bacteria, covering a 10-week control period followed by hypochlorite cleaning phases.

Continuation of the study: the final 10-week strict hypochlorite cleaning regimen, then findings on relative contamination (kitchen higher than bathroom, toilet seat lowest) and where the highest bacterial concentrations occurred (moist or frequently touched sites).

Key results: the most contaminated sites (sponge/dishcloth, kitchen and bath sink drain areas, kitchen faucet handles) and the conclusion that a hypochlorite cleaning regimen significantly reduced all three bacterial classes at these and other household sites.
Concluding fragment of the abstract stating that the hypochlorite cleaning regimen significantly reduced all three bacterial classes at the four highlighted sites and other household sites.
Introduction of a study on microbiological quality of sushi: background on raw fish sushi and health risks from pathogenic bacteria/parasites, plus the study's sample size (250 sushi samples).

Study methods and results comparing frozen supermarket sushi with fresh sushi bar sushi, focusing on aerobic mesophilic bacteria counts (2.7 vs 6.3 log CFU/g) and higher E. coli and S. aureus prevalence in fresh samples.

Pathogen findings and conclusion: Salmonella in 4 (1.6%) and Listeria monocytogenes in 3 (1.2%) sushi samples, with the conclusion that industrially processed sushi has higher microbiological quality than freshly prepared sushi.
Closing conclusion of the sushi microbiology study: freshly prepared sushi quality depends on the variable skills and hygiene habits of the cooks preparing it.

Introduces the study's objective and methods: prevalence of EHEC, E. coli O157, Salmonella, and L. monocytogenes in 2,050 retail food samples (ground beef, mushrooms, sprouts) from Seattle over 12 months, tested by PCR and culture confirmation.
Reports ground beef results from the 1,750-sample set: EHEC in 61 (3.5%), of which 20 (1.1%) were E. coli O157, and Salmonella in 67 (3.8%); methods description continues from chunk 1.
Gives L. monocytogenes in 18 (3.5%) of 512 ground beef samples, then sprout results: EHEC in 12 (6.0%) with 3 (1.5%) O157, Salmonella in 14 (7.0%), no L. monocytogenes; begins mushroom results.
Summarizes mushroom results from the 100-sample set: EHEC in 4 (4.0%) with none O157, Salmonella in 5 (5.0%), and L. monocytogenes in 1 (1.0%); concludes the findings.
Introduction to a double-blind study on spirulina for allergic rhinitis: background on rising prevalence, inadequate control by current drugs, and motivation to seek an alternative therapy.

Continues the introduction by noting prior research on spirulina, Tinospora cordifolia, and butterbur for allergic rhinitis, then describes spirulina as a blue-green alga sold as a dietary supplement for immune modulation.

Describes the study design: a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluating spirulina's effectiveness and tolerability in allergic rhinitis patients, and reports its significant symptom improvement versus placebo.

Concludes the abstract: spirulina is clinically effective for allergic rhinitis compared with placebo, specifically for nasal discharge, sneezing, congestion, and itching, and further mechanistic studies are needed.

This chunk is the document's opening passage: it introduces rhabdomyolysis as a potentially life-threatening condition and reports the first documented case of acute rhabdomyolysis caused by ingesting Spirulina (Arthrospira platensis), a blue-green alga sold as a dietary supplement.

Introduction to a cross-sectional EPIC-Oxford study of nutrition and lifestyle factors in relation to bowel movement frequency, including the design and the definition of 'daily' (7+ per week) versus 'less than daily' bowel movements.

Methods continuation: logistic regression odds ratios with mutual adjustment for factors, the EPIC-Oxford UK setting, and participant characteristics (20,630 adults aged 22-97, about 30% vegetarian or vegan).

Results opening: women have fewer and less frequent daily bowel movements than men, and mean bowel movement frequency is higher in vegetarians and vegans (figures for men and women) than in meat-eaters.

Results continuation: specific mean bowel movement figures by diet group for men and women, plus significant positive associations of bowel movement frequency with BMI, dietary fibre, and non-alcoholic fluid intake.
Remaining results on vigorous exercise (positive in women, unclear in men) and alcohol intake (positive in men only), followed by the start of the conclusion on vegetarian and vegan diets.
Conclusion: vegetarian and especially vegan diets are strongly linked to more frequent bowel movements, as are high fibre and fluid intake and high BMI.

Introduces the flaxseed lignan extract study: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 87 BPH patients testing 0, 300, or 600 mg/day SDG over 4 months for lower urinary tract symptom relief.
Reports trial results on the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) by SDG dose group, with completion counts (78 of 87) and changes from baseline and placebo comparisons.
Presents Quality of Life (QOL) score changes by dose group and the number of subjects whose LUTS grade improved from moderate/severe to mild, with associated P values.
Describes non-significant changes in maximum urinary flow rate and postvoiding urine volume across the placebo and SDG dose groups.

States that plasma levels of secoisolariciresinol, enterodiol, and enterolactone rose significantly after supplementation, and that symptom score decreases correlated with plasma lignan concentrations.
Concludes that flaxseed lignan extract meaningfully improves LUTS in BPH, with efficacy comparable to alpha1A-adrenoceptor blockers and 5alpha-reductase inhibitors.
Final fragment completing the conclusion sentence naming the comparator drug classes (alpha1A-adrenoceptor blockers and 5alpha-reductase inhibitors).

Introduces a 2005 phase 2 pilot study of flaxseed for hot flashes in women declining estrogen therapy, describing eligibility, the baseline week, and the 40 g daily crushed flaxseed regimen over 6 weeks.

Continues the flaxseed hot flash pilot study methods: weekly toxicity and quality-of-life reporting, the daily hot flash diary as primary endpoint, and enrollment of 30 women between June and November 2005.

Reports the main efficacy results of the flaxseed pilot study: mean hot flash score decrease of 57%, mean daily frequency reduction of 50% (7.3 to 3.6), and the abdominal distention rate in participants.

Summarizes the flaxseed study's adverse events (diarrhea, flatulence, withdrawals due to toxicity) and concludes that dietary flaxseed reduces hot flashes in non-estrogen users, beyond expected placebo effect.
Final sentence of the flaxseed hot flash study abstract, stating that the observed reduction in hot flashes exceeds what would be expected with placebo.

Introduction and study design: an 8-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of flaxseed lignan extract (SDG at 0, 300, or 600 mg/d) in 55 hypercholesterolaemic subjects, aimed at effects on plasma lipids and fasting glucose.

Main results on significance: flaxseed SDG produced significant reductions (P < 0.05 to < 0.001) in total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol and glucose, both absolute and as percentage change from baseline.

Dose-specific lipid results: at weeks 6 and 8 the 600 mg SDG group showed significant TC and LDL-C decreases versus placebo, while the 300 mg group showed only within-group changes from baseline for TC and LDL-C.

Glucose results: the 600 mg SDG group had substantial fasting glucose reductions at weeks 6 and 8, strongest in subjects with baseline glucose at or above 5.83 mmol/l, with significant differences versus placebo. Also reports rises in plasma SECO, ED and enterolactone.

Mechanistic correlation and conclusion: cholesterol-lowering effects correlated with plasma SECO and ED levels (r 0.128-0.302), and the authors conclude flaxseed lignan extract lowers plasma cholesterol and glucose in a dose-dependent manner.
Final fragment: the closing conclusion sentence stating that dietary flaxseed lignan extract reduced plasma cholesterol and glucose concentrations in a dose-dependent manner.

Abstract opening: background on alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) as precursor of n-3 fatty acids and its possible cardiovascular benefit; states study aim of examining ALA intake effect on blood pressure in flaxseed oil dyslipidaemia trial.

Study design and subjects: prospective two-group parallel-arm 12-week trial in middle-aged dyslipidaemic men (n=59), flaxseed oil (8 g/day ALA) versus safflower oil control (11 g/day linoleic acid, n=28), with blood pressure measured at baseline and end.
Control group and measurement details, then the start of Results: ALA supplementation compared with linoleic acid control, reporting significantly lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure.

Results statistics and conclusion: ANOVA for repeated measures gave P=0.016 (systolic) and P=0.011 (diastolic); authors conclude ALA has a hypotensive effect that may partly explain its cardioprotective action.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, stating that the hypotensive effect of this n-3 fatty acid may partly account for its apparent cardioprotective effect.
Introduction and study aim of a cluster-analysis case-control study on dietary patterns and colorectal adenomas, including whether energy adjustment before clustering changes results.
Methods describing the case-control population of 725 colonoscopy patients (203 cases with adenomas, 522 controls), FFQ dietary assessment, and standardization of 18 food groups into Z-scores.
Methods detail on energy adjustment per 1000 kcal before clustering, and the result that no association appeared without energy adjustment because clusters reflected energy intake.

Results identifying three dietary clusters after energy adjustment (high fruit-low meat, high vegetable-moderate meat, high meat) and the adjusted odds ratios for adenoma risk of the two other clusters.

Adjusted odds ratios showing higher adenoma odds for the high vegetable-moderate meat and high meat clusters versus the high fruit-low meat cluster, and the conclusion that a high-fruit, low-meat diet is protective.
Final fragment of the conclusion comparing the protective high-fruit, low-meat pattern against the vegetable-and-meat-heavy dietary pattern.

Abstract of the UK Women's Cohort Study (UKWCS) dietary fibre and breast cancer paper: background on inconsistent prior findings, and methods describing the 350 post- and 257 pre-menopausal invasive breast cancer cases among 35,792 women.
Methods continued: the UKWCS cohort's wide range of total dietary fibre intake (quintiles from <20 g/day to >30 g/day), and the analytic approach of Cox regression adjusted for measurement error.

Results start: separate analyses for pre- and post-menopausal women, finding a significant inverse total fibre–breast cancer relationship only in pre-menopausal women (P for trend = 0.01), and the top-quintile hazard ratio of 0.48 (95% CI 0.24–0.96) versus the lowest quintile.

Results on fibre subtypes: pre-menopausal inverse associations for cereal fibre (P for trend = 0.05) and a borderline inverse association for fruit fibre (P for trend = 0.09), plus the effect of adding dietary folate to the model.

Results conclusion and study conclusions: adding dietary folate strengthened the pre-menopausal total fibre association, and the authors conclude total fibre, especially cereal and possibly fruit fibre, is protective against breast cancer in pre-menopausal women.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that fibre from cereals and possibly fruit is particularly protective against pre-menopausal breast cancer.

Introduction and study design of a prospective California Teachers Study cohort analysis examining whether dietary phytochemicals (isoflavones, isothiocyanates) and other nutrients relate to ovarian cancer risk, as this had not been studied prospectively before.

Study population and methods: 97,275 women in the California Teachers Study who completed the 1995–1996 baseline diet assessment, 280 incident invasive or borderline ovarian cancer cases through 2003, analyzed with multivariable Cox regression using age as the timescale.
Main result on isoflavones: higher intake (>3 mg/day vs <1 mg/day) was associated with a reduced ovarian cancer relative risk of 0.56 (95% CI 0.33–0.96).

Null findings for other dietary components: isothiocyanates, macronutrients, antioxidant vitamins, and other micronutrients showed no association with ovarian cancer risk, followed by the authors' conclusion that isoflavones may be protective while most diet factors play little role.
Final concluding sentence of the abstract stating that most dietary factors are unlikely to be major contributors to ovarian cancer development, despite the isoflavone association.

This chunk is the opening of the abstract from a breast cancer case-control study on dietary lignan intake, reporting that premenopausal women in the highest lignan quartile had reduced ER-negative breast cancer risk.
This chunk completes the abstract's conclusion, stating that the inverse association of lignans with breast cancer may be confined to estrogen receptor negative (ER-) tumors, not ER-positive ones.

Introduction and methods opening of the Nambour Skin Cancer Cohort study on dietary food intake and incident squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the skin in an Australian sub-tropical community of 1,056 adults.

Methods detail: measurement-error corrected intake for 15 food groups from a validated 1992 food frequency questionnaire, and Poisson and negative binomial regression of histologically confirmed SCC cases over 1992-2002.

Results: no food group was significantly associated with SCC after adjustment; stratified analysis in people with prior skin cancer shows lower SCC risk with green leafy vegetables and higher risk with unmodified dairy.

Specific stratified results (relative risks and confidence intervals) for green leafy vegetables and unmodified dairy in prior skin cancer patients, plus no association among those without skin cancer history.

Conclusions: green leafy vegetables may help prevent subsequent SCC in people with prior skin cancer, while unmodified dairy products (whole milk, cheese, yoghurt) may raise risk in susceptible individuals; copyright notice.

Introduces the population-based case-control study of endometrial cancer in Shanghai (1,204 cases, 1,212 controls), describing dietary assessment via a validated food frequency questionnaire and the logistic regression method used.

Describes the energy density method used in the analysis and reports the main finding that higher energy intake raises endometrial cancer risk, attributed to animal-source energy and high protein and fat proportions.

Gives odds ratios for highest vs. lowest quintiles: elevated risk for animal protein (OR 2.0) and fat (OR 1.5), and reduced risk for plant-source protein (OR 0.7) and fat (OR 0.6), with confidence intervals.

Reports fatty acid subtype results (saturated and monounsaturated fat linked to higher risk, polyunsaturated fat unrelated) and lists nutrients inversely associated with risk, including retinol, beta-carotene, vitamins C and E, fiber, and supplements, plus null findings for vitamins B1 and B2.

Summarizes the study's conclusion that the source of macronutrients (animal vs. plant origin) determines their association with endometrial cancer risk, and begins the closing statement on protective nutrients.
Concludes that dietary fiber, retinol, beta-carotene, vitamin C, vitamin E, and vitamin supplementation may lower endometrial cancer risk.
Background on known nitrosamine bladder carcinogens in meat (highest in bacon) and the scarcity of prior cohort studies on meat intake and bladder cancer, motivating the study of specific meat types.

Study objective and design: analysis of 808 incident bladder cancer cases from two large prospective cohorts with up to 22 years of follow-up, using repeated food-frequency questionnaires to measure meat intake.

Methods and initial results: Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for confounders including detailed smoking history, and the first finding that high bacon intake (>=5 servings/wk) is linked to elevated bladder cancer risk.

Bacon results: RR 1.59 for high bacon intake, not statistically significant overall for trend, but the association is described as stronger after excluding people who greatly changed red meat or bacon intake in the 10 years before baseline.

Sensitivity analysis result: after excluding those with major diet changes, bacon RR rises to 2.10 and becomes significant (P for trend 0.006); chicken without skin shows a positive association, while chicken with skin and other meats, including processed meats, hot dogs, and hamburgers, do not.
Conclusions: combined across both cohorts, frequent bacon consumption is associated with higher bladder cancer risk, and further studies on specific meat items are needed to confirm these findings.

Introduction of a case-control study on adolescent dairy, milk fat, and galactose intake and risk of testicular germ cell cancer, describing the study population and the dairy-testicular cancer hypothesis.

Methods on how diet was measured (food frequency questionnaires for cases and their mothers, including diet at age 17) and the conditional logistic regression approach adjusted for social status and height.
Main results: overall testicular cancer risk per 20 extra monthly milk servings in adolescence, with the elevated risk concentrated in seminoma (RR 1.66).

Results for milk fat and galactose: seminoma risk rises per additional 200 g of each per month in adolescence, leading to the conclusion that milk fat and/or galactose may explain the milk-seminoma association.
Concluding sentence of the abstract restating that milk fat and/or galactose may explain the association between dairy consumption and seminomatous testicular cancer.

Introduces the hospital-based case-control study at MD Anderson Cancer Center (2002-2006) examining dietary food mutagen exposure and pancreatic cancer risk, describing the 626 cases and 530 controls matched on race, sex, and age, with exposure gathered by meat preparation questionnaire.

Reports dietary findings: cases more often preferred well-done pork, bacon, and grilled or pan-fried chicken (not hamburger or steak) and had higher daily intake of food mutagens and mutagenic activity per gram of meat than controls.

Presents the predictor results: after adjusting for confounders, daily intakes of DiMeIQx and benzo(a)pyrene (BaP) and mutagenic activity were significant predictors of pancreatic cancer (P = 0.008, 0.031, 0.029).

Describes dose-response and subgroup findings: a significant rising trend in cancer risk with DiMeIQx intake across quintiles (Ptrend = 0.024), and about a 2-fold risk increase with high mutagen intake only among people without a family history of cancer.

Reports a possible synergistic interaction between smoking and high exposure (top 10%) to PhIP and BaP on pancreatic cancer risk (P-interaction = 0.09 and 0.099), and states the study's conclusion that mutagen exposure alone and with other factors contributes to pancreatic cancer.
Concludes the abstract by restating that the data support the hypothesis that dietary mutagen exposure, alone and interacting with other factors, contributes to the development of pancreatic cancer.

Introduces the Shanghai population-based case–control study of animal food intake and cooking methods in relation to endometrial cancer risk, describing the sample of 1204 cases and 1212 controls and the food frequency questionnaire and logistic regression methods.

Reports the main finding that high meat and fish intake is associated with increased endometrial cancer risk, giving adjusted odds ratios for highest versus lowest quartiles (1.7 and 2.4) with 95% confidence intervals.

States that the elevated risk applies to all types of meat and fish, that eggs and milk showed no link, and that cooking methods and doneness levels neither affected risk nor modified the meat and fish association.
Concludes that animal food consumption likely plays an important role in endometrial cancer etiology among Chinese women, while cooking methods have minimal influence on risk.

Introduces the study's hypothesis linking high calcium and dairy intake to prostate cancer risk, noting inconsistent prior prospective evidence, and describes the ATBC cohort of 29,133 male smokers aged 50-69 from Finland.

Describes the methods: baseline dietary assessment with a validated 276-item food questionnaire, Cox proportional hazards adjustment for risk factors, and 17 years of follow-up yielding 1,267 incident prostate cancer cases in the ATBC cohort.

Reports the main calcium result: intake of 2,000 mg/day or more versus under 1,000 mg/day gave a multivariate RR of 1.63 (95% CI 1.27-2.10, p trend <0.0001), and begins the total dairy intake finding.

Gives the dairy results: comparing extreme quintiles, total dairy intake had RR 1.26 (95% CI 1.04-1.51, p trend 0.03), but the association disappeared after adjusting for calcium (p trend 0.17), and findings were similar by stage and grade.
Concludes that calcium, or a related component in dairy foods, is associated with increased prostate cancer risk, based on this large prospective study.

Abstract opening (Background, Objective, Design) of a Nurses' Health Study paper on plasma and erythrocyte dairy fat biomarkers (15:0, trans 16:1n-7) and ischemic heart disease risk in US women; describes the 1989-1990 blood-sample cohort of 32,826 participants, 166 IHD cases, and 327 matched controls.

Design details and start of Results from the dairy fat biomarker and ischemic heart disease study: case-control matching (age, smoking, fasting status, blood draw date) and the beginning of correlations between 1986-1990 dairy fat intake and biomarker levels among controls.

Results showing correlation coefficients between average dairy fat intake and plasma/erythrocyte 15:0 and trans 16:1n-7 (r = 0.36, 0.30 plasma; 0.30, 0.32 erythrocytes), plus the finding that higher plasma 15:0 was significantly linked to IHD risk after multivariate adjustment.

Key multivariate results from the Nurses' Health Study dairy biomarker study: relative risks of IHD across plasma 15:0 tertiles (1.0, 2.18, 2.36; P for trend = 0.03), note that other biomarkers were not significant, and the start of the conclusion that 15:0 and trans 16:1n-7 serve as dairy fat intake biomarkers.

Concluding statement of the dairy fat biomarker and ischemic heart disease study: plasma and erythrocyte 15:0 and trans 16:1n-7 are valid biomarkers of dairy fat intake, and high dairy fat intake is associated with greater IHD risk in US women.
Introduction and objective of the Boyd Orr cohort study on childhood dairy intake and later cancer risk, outlining the rationale that adult dairy links are studied but childhood exposure is not.

Study design: about 4,999 British children (England and Scotland) from 1937-1939 had family food consumption measured via 7-day household inventories; cancer registrations and deaths were traced through NHS registers 1948-2005 among 4,383 cohort members.

Exposure measurement and key results: household per capita dairy and calcium intake served as proxies for individual intake, and 770 cancer registrations or deaths were recorded, with high childhood total dairy intake linked to colorectal cancer risk.

Main colorectal cancer finding: high childhood total dairy intake gave a multivariate odds ratio of 2.90 (95% CI 1.26-6.65, P for trend 0.005), independent of meat, fruit, vegetable and socioeconomic factors; milk intake showed a similar association.

Secondary cancer outcomes: milk was weakly inversely associated with prostate cancer, dairy showed no link to breast or stomach cancer, and a lung cancer association was explained by adult smoking; the conclusion stresses a dairy-rich childhood diet and greater adult colorectal cancer risk.
Closing conclusion: the study calls for confirmation of the biological mechanisms that could explain the link between childhood dairy consumption and adult colorectal cancer.

Introduces the study design: a survival analysis of meat consumption and meat type versus breast cancer risk in the UK Women's Cohort Study, covering the 1995–1998 recruitment of 35,372 women and the Cox regression methods used.

Reports the hazard ratios for premenopausal and postmenopausal women by meat type, noting that high total and non-processed meat intake showed the premenopausal HRs and that postmenopausal women showed larger effects across meat types.

Summarizes the main findings: postmenopausal associations for total, processed and red meat, with processed meat giving the strongest hazard ratio (HR=1.64), and the overall conclusion that high meat consumers have the highest breast cancer risk.
Concluding fragment restating that women who consumed the most meat, both pre- and postmenopausal, had the highest breast cancer risk.

Introduces the prospective cohort study of dairy intake and Parkinson's disease risk, covering 57,689 men and 73,175 women from the ACS Cancer Prevention Study II Nutrition Cohort with follow-up 1992–2001, and begins reporting the positive association.

Reports the main cohort result: compared with the lowest dairy intake quintile, relative risks for quintiles 2–5 were 1.4–1.6 (95% CI 1.1–2.2; p for trend=0.05), with a higher risk in both sexes but a non-linear pattern in women.

Presents the meta-analysis of prospective studies showing a moderately elevated Parkinson's risk with high dairy intake, with pooled RRs of 1.6 for men and women combined, 1.8 for men, and 1.3 for women, the latter with a CI that includes 1.
Concludes that dairy consumption may increase Parkinson's disease risk, especially in men, and calls for further studies to confirm the findings and explore underlying mechanisms.
Final fragment consisting only of a trailing period, the end of the abstract's last sentence with no added content.

Opening of the study abstract: background on PAHs and HCAs as carcinogens formed in well-done, high-temperature cooked meat, and the methods introduction for a Long Island case-control breast cancer study (1996-1997).

Methods continuation: lifetime grilled/barbecued/smoked meat intake from interviews, PAH and HCA intake from a food frequency questionnaire one year before reference date, and unconditional logistic regression for adjusted odds ratios.

Main results: modest increased breast cancer risk among postmenopausal but not premenopausal women with highest lifetime intake of grilled, barbecued, or smoked meats (OR 1.47), and the odds ratio comparing highest with lowest tertile.

Results on effect modification: postmenopausal women with low fruit and vegetable intake and high lifetime grilled/smoked meat intake had OR 1.74, and no associations were found for FFQ-derived PAH and HCA intake except a possible benzo(alpha)pyrene effect in ER/PR-positive tumors.

Benzo(alpha)pyrene result in ER- and PR-positive postmenopausal tumors (OR 1.47, CI 0.99-2.19, borderline non-significant), followed by the conclusion that carcinogen-forming cooking methods may raise postmenopausal breast cancer risk.
Final sentence of the conclusions, restating that consuming meats cooked by carcinogen-promoting methods may increase risk of postmenopausal breast cancer.

Opening of a study on why colorectal cancer incidence is far higher in African Americans than Native Africans, introducing the diet-by-colonic-bacteria hypothesis and the three comparison groups (AAs, NAs, CAs).

Study methods: 50-65 year old healthy participants in three groups; diet assessed by 3-day recall, colonic metabolism by lactulose breath tests, fecal bacterial cultures, and colonoscopic biopsies for proliferation.

Results comparing African Americans with Native Africans: higher protein, fat, meat, saturated fat and cholesterol intake in AAs, higher calcium, vitamin A and C, equal fiber, and higher breath hydrogen.
Further results: AAs show higher 7-alpha dehydroxylating bacteria, fewer Lactobacilli, and markedly higher colonic crypt cell proliferation rates than NAs.
Conclusion linking higher CRC risk in AAs to dietary animal products and bacteria producing hydrogen and secondary bile salts, supporting the idea that diet-bacteria interactions determine CRC risk.
Final sentence of the conclusion restating that CRC risk depends on interactions between the external (dietary) and internal (bacterial) environments.

Introduction to a study of egg protein assimilation in healthy humans: notes prior methods (ileostomy, intubation) and introduces a noninvasive stable isotope tracer approach to measure protein escaping small-intestine digestion.

Study design and key result: 10 healthy volunteers ate 25 g of 13C/15N/2H-labeled egg protein either cooked or raw; about 5.73% of cooked vs 35.10% of raw meal escaped digestion/absorption in the small intestine (P < 0.005).

Fate of malabsorbed protein and conclusions: more of the unabsorbed raw egg protein was recovered in urine as colonic fermentation metabolites, confirming substantial easily digestible protein can escape assimilation.
Final conclusion: the results support the hypothesis that colonic protein metabolism depends on how much protein reaches the colon.
Introduces the study design: an uncooked extreme vegan diet trial measuring fecal hydrolytic enzymes, with 18 randomized subjects split into test and control groups over two months.

Reports the main fecal enzyme results: within one week of starting the vegan diet, urease fell 66%, cholylglycine hydrolase 55%, beta-glucuronidase 33%, and beta-glucosidase 40%, and phenol and p-cresol measures were also tracked.

Describes the reversal and toxin findings: enzyme levels stayed low on the vegan diet, phenol and p-cresol in serum and urine declined, and fecal enzymes returned to normal within two weeks of resuming a conventional diet, with toxins normalizing after one month.
Summarizes the control group showing no changes and concludes that the uncooked extreme vegan diet lowers bacterial enzymes and toxic products linked to colon cancer risk.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that the diet's reduction in toxic products is implicated in colon cancer risk.

Introduction of a study on diet, colonic microbiota, and colon cancer risk: the hypothesis that the gut milieu interior regulates mucosal proliferation, and the plan to compare colonic contents across high- and low-risk populations.

Study population details: healthy 50- to 65-year-olds from low-risk Native Africans, high-risk African Americans, and Caucasian Americans, with cancer incidence rates and sample sizes, plus contrasting dietary patterns (American high animal protein/fat vs. African maize-based resistant starch diet).

Methods and first key result: overnight fasting, rapid colonic evacuation with polyethylene glycol, analysis of evacuants for SCFA, vitamins, nitrogen, and minerals, and the finding that total SCFA and butyrate were higher in Native Africans than in both American groups.

Results on vitamins and minerals: colonic folate and biotin exceeded normal dietary intake (assayed by Lactobacillus bioassays), and calcium and iron were higher in Caucasian Americans while zinc was higher in African Americans, relative to Africans.

Remaining results and conclusion: nitrogen content did not differ among the three groups, and the authors conclude that microbiota mediate diet's effect on colon cancer risk through production of butyrate, folate, and biotin.
Final sentence of the conclusion stating that butyrate, folate, and biotin are known regulators of epithelial proliferation, linking microbial metabolites to colon cancer risk.

Abstract/summary opening of a chemistry paper on GHB (γ-hydroxybutyric acid), a date-rape drug, introducing its newly discovered major metabolite (GHB glucuronide 2) as a potential way to extend the forensic detection window.

Abstract continuation describing the synthetic approach: a Koenigs–Knorr glucuronidation route to prepare GHB glucuronide 2 and its deuterium-labelled analogue d4-2 for analytical use, plus a stability study at urine-relevant pH.

Closing part of the abstract reporting the NMR-based finding that GHB glucuronide 2 is highly stable to aqueous hydrolysis across the urine pH range, even at elevated temperature, relevant to new analytical method development.

Explains how dietary fiber is fermented by colonic microbes, which use ammonia from urea and nitrogenous substances to synthesize protein, and how fatty acids from fermentation lower free ammonia by reducing pH.
Describes how fiber's bulk, water content, and shortened transit time reduce the mucosa's exposure to free ammonia, the most toxic and readily absorbed form of nitrogen.

Lists harmful effects of ammonia at lower-bowel concentrations typical of Western diets, including cell destruction, altered nucleic acid synthesis, mucosal cell mass increase, viral infections, and favoring cancerous cell growth.
States that bowel ammonia rises with protein intake and summarizes epidemiological comparisons of low-fiber, high-protein/fat/refined-carbohydrate diets that implicate ammonia in carcinogenesis.
Concludes that the attributes of ammonia and epidemiological evidence implicate it in carcinogenesis and other disease processes.

Introduction to the review on protein fermentation and gut health: contrasts beneficial carbohydrate fermentation (short chain fatty acids) with protein fermentation in the distal colon, which yields potentially toxic metabolites like ammonia, amines, phenols and sulfides.

Context on the limited evidence for protein fermentation toxicity (mostly in vitro) and its link to the distal colon, where colorectal cancer and ulcerative colitis commonly occur, motivating the review.

Epidemiological rationale linking meat-rich Western diets to colorectal cancer risk, noting that meat intake raises protein fermentation as well as fat, heme and heterocyclic amine intake, which may contribute to CRC development.

Summary of the research gap: the relationship between gut health and protein fermentation is not thoroughly investigated, and the review aims to summarize in vitro, animal and human evidence on its potential toxicity.
Closing copyright notice for the review (© 2012 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim), identifying the publisher of the document.

Abstract opening of a population-based colorectal cancer case-control study (989 cases, 1,033 controls) examining meat-related compounds, using a food frequency questionnaire and logistic regression to explore mechanisms.

Methods and results from the same colorectal cancer study: regression approaches (multivariable and polytomous logistic) and the list of significant positive associations for heterocyclic amines (DiMeIQx, MeIQx, PhIP), nitrites/nitrates, and benzo[a]pyrene with colorectal subsites.

Continuation of the results listing significant compound-subsite associations (DiMeIQx, MeIQx, nitrites/nitrates, PhIP, benzo[a]pyrene), then introducing the analyses by meat type, cooking method, and doneness preference.

Results on meat type, cooking method, and doneness: positive links for processed and pan-fried red meat, followed by inverse associations for poultry (unprocessed, grilled, well-done) with colorectal subsites.
Closing conclusions: HCAs, PAHs, nitrites, and nitrates may be involved in colorectal cancer etiology, and the unexpected inverse poultry associations warrant further investigation.
Final sentence of the abstract, calling for further examination of the unexpected inverse associations between poultry and colorectal cancer.

Introduction to UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs): describes glucuronidation as a detoxification/excretion pathway for xenobiotic and endogenous compounds, encoded by a multigene family, and introduces the review by Tephly and Burchell.

Conclusion of the UGT introduction: recent biochemical and molecular advances have clarified UGT function and structure, noting these enzymes are structurally similar yet able to conjugate a wide variety of chemicals.
Human volunteer study comparing fecal bacterial beta-glucuronidase activity under a high-meat Western diet versus a nonmeat diet; reports the enzyme is significantly higher on the high-meat diet.
Concludes that the high-meat diet's greater glucuronidase-hydrolyzing flora may increase carcinogens and other substances within the colonic lumen, linking diet to colon cancer risk.

Introduction and objective of a study on why colon cancer is rare in black South Africans, covering the research question, the study population sampling from rural and urban regions, and the methods used for dietary assessment and colonic fermentation.

Methods continued: dietary assessment techniques (home visits, food frequency questionnaires, 72-hour recall, blood sampling), breath hydrogen and methane tests after a traditional meal and lactulose, and cancer risk estimated via Ki-67 and BrdU proliferation indices in rectal biopsies.

Results begin: rectal epithelial proliferation is lower in black than white South Africans, and black diets are low in animal products and high in boiled maize meal, versus white diets rich in fresh animal products, cheese, and wheat.

Results on nutrient intake: blacks fall below RDA for fiber, vitamins A, C, folic acid, and calcium, while whites exceed RDA for animal protein and fat; also reports breath methane production two to three times higher in blacks.

Conclusions: dietary protective factors such as fiber, calcium, and vitamins A, C, and folic acid do not explain the low colon cancer rate, which may instead relate to the absence of aggressive factors like excess animal protein and fat and to colonic fermentation differences.
Final conclusion sentence: the low colon cancer prevalence in black Africans may be attributed to the lack of excess animal protein and fat and to differences in colonic bacterial fermentation.
Case report opening: a 5-year-old autistic boy presenting with dry eye, xerophthalmia, and undetectable serum vitamin A, traced to a two-year diet of only fried potatoes and rice balls.

Concluding part of the case report: notes that children with autism who develop dietary vitamin A deficiency have typically eaten excess fried potatoes, and advises checking for vitamin A deficiency whenever fried potatoes are the sole food.

Introduction and methods opening of a 2008 study of eye disease and xerophthalmia in malnourished children at Bushulo Health Center, rural south Ethiopia, describing its aims and retrospective cross-sectional design.

Methods continuation describing the study population (children aged 6 months to 14 years treated for malnutrition, June-July 2008) and data collection via caretaker interviews, pediatric ophthalmologist eye exams, and anthropometry.
Results giving the sample of 173 malnourished children (mean age 2.9 years, sex split) with malnutrition severity breakdown and prevalence of trachoma, blepharitis, and xerophthalmia (20.8%).

Key findings linking severe malnutrition to higher xerophthalmia risk (p < 0.0001), weight percentile as the only anthropometric measure significantly associated with xerophthalmia (p = 0.008), and the conclusion on xerophthalmia as a global pediatric blindness cause.
Concluding sentence of the abstract calling for continued efforts to improve nutrition and outcomes for these patients.

Study design and aims: a hospital-based cross-sectional study of 111 older adults testing whether plasma osmolality (hydration status) differs between dry eye and non-dry eye individuals, with methods for DE assessment and hydration measurement introduced.

Study population and measures: 111 participants (56 male, 55 female, mean age 77) assessed on admission using tear osmolarity, DEQ-5 questionnaire, VAS eye dryness rating, and NITBUT; hydration measured by freezing-point depression osmometry of plasma osmolality.

Main results: plasma osmolality was higher in dry eye than controls using the 316 mOsm/L tear osmolarity cutoff (about +11 mOsm/kg, P=0.004, d=0.83), with effect sizes reported including the stricter Tosm >324 vs <308 mOsm/L classification.

Results continued: stricter tear osmolarity classification gave about +12 mOsm/kg (P=0.006, d=0.94), and higher plasma osmolality in dry eye persisted across composite definitions combining Tosm with DEQ-5 or NITBUT and VAS with DEQ-5.
Conclusions: first published evidence that dry eye individuals have higher plasma osmolality, indicating suboptimal hydration, so whole-body hydration should be considered in dry eye management.

Study purpose and methods for a prospective case series on punctal occlusion using a high heat-energy cautery device (Optemp II V) in severe dry eye patients with recurrent punctal plug extrusion; sample of 70 puncta from 44 eyes of 28 patients.

Methods continued: all patients had recurrent punctal plug extrusion history; outcome measures compared pre-surgery and 3 months post-surgery, including symptom scores, BCVA, fluorescein and rose bengal staining, tear break-up time, Schirmer test, and punctal recanalization rate.

Results for the cautery procedure at 3 months: symptom score fell from 3.9 to 0.56 (P<.0001) and logMAR best-corrected visual acuity improved from 0.11 to 0.013 (P=.003), with the start of the recanalization finding.

Remaining results and conclusion start: staining scores, tear break-up time and Schirmer values improved significantly; only 1 of 70 puncta recanalized (1.4%); the conclusion begins by stating the cautery device's low recanalization rate.

Study conclusions and copyright notice: the high heat-energy cautery punctal occlusion gave a low recanalization rate along with better ocular surface wetness and visual acuity; Elsevier Inc. 2011 copyright.

Introduction of the systematic review on dry eye disease (DED) clinical trials: it frames the rising complexity of DED treatment, the new agents, and the problem of heterogeneous outcome definitions and few comparative studies that limit efficacy evaluation.

Methods of the systematic review: clinical trial reports were gathered from eight databases plus free public trial registries, and the data were assessed by endpoints such as symptoms, Schirmer test, ocular surface staining, patient recruitment, drug type and efficacy, and study design and site.

Results summary: 49 clinical trials covering 5,189 DED patients were evaluated. Study design heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis, so a descriptive analysis was done; artificial tears were the most common drug category, followed by anti-inflammatories and secretagogues.
Trial registry and publication findings: of 116 completed trials in the registry, only 17 (15.5%) were published; of 185 registered DED trials, 72% were conducted in the USA.

Concluding findings: the pharmaceutical industry sponsored 78% of the registered DED trials, and progress in identifying effective treatments is hindered by the absence of accepted definitive criteria for grading disease severity. Includes the copyright notice.

Introduction to the 2007 International Dry Eye WorkShop Epidemiology Subcommittee report: summarizes prevalence and incidence of dry eye disease and calls for broader geographic, multi-ethnic studies and consensus diagnostic criteria.

Covers the report's methodological recommendations (questionnaire characteristics for epidemiological studies and randomized trials) and its identification of dry eye risk factors, morbidity, and quality-of-life and visual function impacts.
Concludes the Epidemiology Subcommittee report by outlining impacts on quality of life and visual function and recommending prospective research to improve eye and general public health.

Introduction of a review on lacrimal occlusion complications: opens by describing punctal and canalicular plugs used to treat dry eye, noting their proven symptom benefit but the lack of any general review of their complications beyond single-device case series.

Continuation of the introduction stating the review's aims: examine the track record of various plugs in current use, review complication management, and propose strategies for prevention and treatment of complications.
Final fragment of the aims sentence from the document's introduction, ending with the review's goal of proposing prevention and treatment strategies for plug-related complications.
Opening of the paper: introduces vitamin A deficiency (VAD) as a public-health problem in South Asian developing countries and lists its causes (economic, sociocultural, dietary, absorption).

Continues the discussion of VAD risk factors (lack of education, poor sanitation, weak food laws and surveillance) and notes higher morbidity and mortality among children and women of childbearing age.
Describes xerophthalmia and its ocular stages as the leading cause of preventable childhood blindness, and explains why children need extra vitamin A from their diet.

Presents the three strategies for improving vitamin A status (supplementation, fortification, dietary diversification) and why they have fallen short in South Asia due to weak government support and supervision.
Methods section: describes the literature review, including the PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar searches and the article selection process.
Concluding statement: high VAD prevalence drives morbidity and mortality in infants, children, and pregnant women, calling for urgent action in South Asian lower- and middle-income countries.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the call for action on VAD in lower- and middle-income South Asian countries.

Introduction and stated purpose: motivates tear fluid osmolarity as a noninvasive hydration marker, contrasting it with invasive plasma osmolality and noting urine specific gravity as another noninvasive comparator.

Study design and methods: 14 healthy volunteers underwent fluid restriction (to 1-3% body mass loss, plus overnight restriction) versus fluid intake trials in heat, with tear osmolarity measured via the TearLab system.

Early results: plasma osmolality and urine specific gravity rise with progressive dehydration; tear osmolarity rises significantly from 293 to 305 mOsm/L at 3% body mass loss and stays elevated overnight.

Remaining results: tear and plasma osmolality fall during exercise with fluid intake and recover by morning; rehydration returns all markers to preexercise levels; tear osmolarity correlates strongly with plasma osmolality (r = 0.93) versus urine specific gravity (r = 0.72).

Conclusions: tear osmolarity increases with dehydration, tracks plasma osmolality as well as urine specific gravity does, and may serve as a practical, rapid hydration assessment for sports medicine and clinical use.
Closing sentence of the conclusions: restates that TearLab-measured tear osmolarity offers practitioners, clinicians, and researchers a practical, rapid hydration assessment technique.

Introduces the role of diet in tear function, citing malnutrition-induced xerophthalmia as a clear example and noting that dietary habits in well-nourished North American society may contribute to some tear dysfunction. Also summarizes nutrients (protein, vitamins A, B6, C, potassium, zinc) considered necessary for normal tear function.

Continues the discussion of diet and tear function: lists dietary excesses (fats, salt, cholesterol, alcohol, protein, sucrose) linked to tear dysfunction, and concludes that no clear evidence connects diet to remission of dry eye in well-nourished people.

Opening chunk of an abstract introducing dry eye disease: its prevalence, symptoms, and limits of current treatments (P2Y2 agonists, cyclosporine), noting no therapy restores normal lacrimal function.
Continues the abstract's motivation: the lack of fundamental dry eye treatments, and the proposal that advances in aging research open a new approach, since dry eye is accelerated by aging.

Presents the review's central premise: because aging accelerates dry eye, targeting the aging process may prevent or treat it, citing calorie restriction's life-extending effects across animal species as a proven anti-aging intervention.

Introduces the two aging theories the review examines, calorie restriction and the free radical theory, and states they suggest aging can be managed by controlling calories or reactive oxygen species.
Closing statement of the abstract: the review examines calorie restriction and free radical aging theories and discusses applying them to preventing and treating dry eye.

Abstract opening: states the study's aim (estimating direct and indirect annual costs of dry eye disease in the US from societal and payer perspectives) and introduces the decision analytic model and its cost categories.

Abstract methods continued: lists the direct cost components (lubricants, cyclosporine, punctal plugs, physician visits, supplements), defines indirect costs as productivity loss from absenteeism and presenteeism, and describes model data sourced from online-recruited dry eye patient surveys.

Abstract methods and start of results: covers sensitivity analyses, conversion of costs to 2008 US dollars, and the survey sample of 2171 respondents with DED, then begins the average annual per-patient cost finding.

Abstract results with key cost figures: payer-perspective average of $783 per patient (range $757-$809), nationwide payer burden of $3.84 billion, and societal per-patient cost of $11,302 totaling $55.4 billion for US society.
Abstract conclusions: summarizes that DED imposes a substantial economic burden on payers and society, and notes the findings can inform health plan and employer budget estimation.

Introduction of a case report on xerophthalmia and keratomalacia from multiple vitamin and protein deficiencies, describing a 27-year-old woman's bizarre restricted diet and its resulting nyctalopia, xerophthalmia, and keratomalacia with bilateral corneal perforation.

Case outcome and ocular pathology findings: the patient remained comatose and died after admission despite therapy; pathology showed bilateral corneal melting with intraocular prolapse, conjunctival epidermidalization, goblet cell atrophy, and retinal outer nuclear layer thinning.
Concluding comparison noting that experimental pure vitamin A deficiency in animals causes epithelial atrophy followed by keratinization, linking the observed ocular changes to avitaminosis A.

Introduction and methods of a review on medications and herbal products that can worsen dry eye symptoms after blepharoplasty, describing the MEDLINE/PubMed search strategy and keywords used (1991-2011).

Continuation of the methods section listing additional search terms (e.g., herbal supplements, drugs and dry eye, tear film) and describing reference-list and manual citation searches for dry eye and drug/herbal risk factors.

Results section reporting article screening: 232 papers found, 196 excluded for not discussing medications or herbal products as dry eye risk factors, leaving 36 articles on dry eye pathophysiology and risk factors.

Results continued: nine books reviewed for medication and herbal associations with dry eye, agents grouped by mechanism and use, and a list of implicated drug classes such as antihistamines, decongestants, antidepressants, antipsychotics, beta-blockers, and hormone replacement therapy.

Key findings: niacin, echinacea, and kava identified as the three main herbal contributors to dry eye, a strong link between anticholinergic alkaloids and dry eye, and the conclusion that these agents matter for blepharoplasty patients with dryness symptoms.
Concluding statement that the review identifies medications and herbal products to consider when a blepharoplasty patient reports dry eye symptoms, closing the abstract.

Introduction to post-LASIK tear dysfunction: states that dry eye symptoms occur in nearly all LASIK patients, mostly resolve, and are a heterogeneous, non-uniform condition rather than a single disease, with the umbrella term post-LASIK tear dysfunction syndrome introduced.

Defines post-LASIK tear dysfunction syndrome/dry eye as a spectrum covering neurotrophic disease, tear instability, aqueous tear deficiency, and neuropathic pain, and notes corneal neural changes and neuropathic mechanisms may contribute to symptoms.

Prognosis and management: most early post-LASIK dry eye resolves with ocular surface optimization before and after surgery, but severe symptoms or those lasting beyond 9 months rarely respond to standard treatments and need aggressive care.
Scope of the review: outlines that the document covers theories, pathophysiology, risk factors, and management options across the post-LASIK tear dysfunction and neuropathic pain spectrum.

Introduces dry-eye syndrome as a multifactorial disease and lists contributing factors (age, hormones, genetics, immune status, etc.) that disrupt the ocular surface, setting up the document's discussion of cyclosporine for dry eye.

Describes the vicious cycle of desiccation, epithelial damage, and chronic inflammation in dry eye, then notes that lubricants and steroids were used as prior treatments before cyclosporine A became an option.

States that cyclosporine A has become an increasingly useful dry-eye treatment, is the only FDA-approved prescription drug for dry eye in the United States, and has safety and efficacy supported by numerous studies.
Concludes the document's summary by stating that the safety and efficacy of cyclosporine have been shown in numerous studies, tying off the discussion of cyclosporine as a dry-eye therapy.

Abstract opening (Aims and Methods) of a 2010-era RCT comparing a calorie-restricted vegetarian diet with a conventional diabetic diet, with and without exercise, for insulin resistance, visceral fat and oxidative stress in Type 2 diabetes; introduces the 24-week randomized design and the 74 participants.

Methods section detailing the randomization of 74 Type 2 diabetes patients into vegetarian (n=37) and conventional diabetic diet (n=37) groups, both isocaloric at -500 kcal/day with all meals provided, and aerobic exercise added in the second 12 weeks.

Methods continued: study timepoints (baseline, 12 and 24 weeks), primary outcomes (hyperinsulinaemic clamp insulin sensitivity, MRI visceral and subcutaneous fat, thiobarbituric acid reactive substances for oxidative stress), and intention-to-treat analysis.
Results opening: medication reduction (43% vs 5%, P<0.001) and greater body weight loss in the vegetarian diet group (-6.2 kg vs -3.2 kg) with confidence intervals and group x time interaction.
Results on insulin sensitivity (30% vs 20% increase, P=0.04) and greater visceral and subcutaneous fat reduction in the vegetarian group (P=0.007 and P=0.02).
Results on adipokines and antioxidants: adiponectin up and leptin down in the vegetarian group, plus increases in vitamin C, superoxide dismutase and reduced glutathione with their P values.

Results summary noting larger between-group differences after adding exercise and correlations between insulin sensitivity/enzymatic oxidative stress changes and visceral fat change, followed by the start of the Conclusions on greater insulin sensitivity improvement with the vegetarian diet over 24 weeks.

Conclusions: the greater visceral fat loss and improved adipokine and oxidative stress markers with the vegetarian diet may explain reduced insulin resistance, and exercise further augmented outcomes.
Final sentence of the conclusions stating that adding exercise training further enhanced the improved outcomes seen with the vegetarian diet.

Abstract opening of a study comparing estrogen and androgen excretion (fecal, urinary, plasma) in pre- and postmenopausal vegetarian versus omnivorous women, including dietary differences in animal protein and fat intake and the higher fecal output in vegetarians.

Middle of the abstract reporting preliminary findings: vegetarians excrete 2-3 times more fecal estrogens, omnivores have roughly 50% higher plasma unconjugated estrone and estradiol, and urinary estriol-3-glucuronide (a marker of intestinal reabsorption of estriol) is lower in vegetarians.

Concluding part of the abstract interpreting the results: vegetarians appear to lose more biliary estrogens to feces rather than reabsorbing them, and this altered estrogen metabolism is proposed as a possible explanation for vegetarians' lower breast cancer incidence.
Final fragment of the abstract's last sentence, linking vegetarian estrogen metabolism to lower breast cancer incidence in vegetarian women.

Introduces type 2 diabetes as an inflammatory disease rooted in adipose tissue of obese subjects, and attributes the chronic adipose inflammation to rising obesity from Western diet overeating and inactivity.

Explains mechanisms of obesity-driven adipose inflammation: overnutrition makes adipocytes secrete chemokines that recruit immune cells, and saturated fatty acids may directly trigger the inflammatory cascade.

Describes hypoxia in obese adipose tissue and its effect on gene expression in adipocytes and neighboring cells as central to the inflammatory response, then pivots to natural foods and beverages with curative health effects.

Names specific anti-inflammatory phytochemicals, spices curcumin, capsaicin, and gingerol and plant metabolites catechin, resveratrol, genistein, and quercetin, reported to improve health, particularly for diabetes.

States the review's aim: to overview these phytochemicals, their interference with inflammatory cascades in adipose tissue, and their potential against inflammatory diseases like diabetes as shown in vivo.
Closing copyright notice (Elsevier Inc., 2012) ending the abstract.

Introduction of the paper on meat consumption as a type 2 diabetes risk factor: explains why epidemiological risk factors matter for clinicians, policymakers, and individuals, and notes that such evidence mostly comes from cross-sectional and prospective studies rather than randomized trials.

Continues the introduction: argues that eating habits, unlike non-modifiable risks, can be changed through individual action and policy, and notes that meat consumption is frequently studied in relation to diabetes but has not yet been established as a diabetes risk factor.

States the article's aim: to evaluate whether meat consumption is a clinically useful risk factor for type 2 diabetes, by reviewing studies that assess meat intake as a categorical, scalar, or dietary-pattern exposure.
Specifies the three ways meat consumption is analyzed in the reviewed studies: categorical (meat vs. no meat), scalar (graded amounts), and as part of a broader dietary pattern.

Introduction and study objective: introduces the hypothesis that dietary composition affects insulin secretion and CVD risk, and describes the aim of comparing fiber with other macronutrients (CARDIA study setting begins).

Study design and participants: describes the CARDIA multicenter cohort (four US cities, 1985-1996 follow-up) and the 2909 healthy black and white young adults aged 18-30 enrolled, plus main outcome measures.
Results begin: after confounder adjustment, dietary fiber shows linear associations with lower body weight across quintiles of intake, for both white and black participants.

Quantitative results on weight, waist-to-hip ratio, and fasting insulin: fiber quintile trends with body weight, waist-to-hip ratio, and BMI-adjusted fasting insulin, reported with P values for whites and blacks.

Results on postglucose insulin and other risk factors: 2-hour postglucose insulin trends by fiber intake, plus fiber's associations with blood pressure, lipids, and fibrinogen, which were attenuated after adjusting for fasting insulin.

Comparison with other nutrients and early conclusions: fat, carbohydrate, and protein showed weak or inconsistent associations with CVD risk factors, while the conclusion statement begins that fiber predicted insulin, weight gain, and CVD risk factors.

Final conclusions: fiber predicted insulin levels, weight gain, and CVD risk factors more strongly than total or saturated fat, suggesting high-fiber diets may protect against obesity and CVD by lowering insulin.

Introduction of a review on plant-based foods as sources of lipotropes; opens by linking plant product intake to lower chronic disease and naming the main studied effects (antioxidant, anticarcinogenic, hypolipidemic, hypoglycemic), then introduces lipotropic compounds.

Defines lipotropic action in animals (reducing hepatic fat via phospholipid synthesis through transmethylation, lipoprotein export, and fatty acid β-oxidation and gene regulation), continuing the review's introduction of lipotropic effects.

Names the main plant lipotropes (choline, betaine, myo-inositol, methionine, carnitine) and the indirect supporting nutrients (magnesium, niacin, pantothenate, folates), and begins describing the review of rat studies on phytochemicals and hepatic lipid metabolism.

Summarizes rat study review findings: a list of candidate lipotropic phytochemicals including fatty acids, acetic acid, melatonin, phytic acid, fibers, oligofructose, resistant starch, phenolic acids, flavonoids, lignans, stilbenes, curcumin, saponins, coumarin, plant extracts and solid foods.

Concludes that the lipotropic effects of these phytochemicals still need confirmation in humans, since intervention studies are nearly absent, and notes supplemental material is available from the journal, Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition.
Final fragment of the document's closing sentence, pointing readers to the publisher's online edition of Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition for the free supplemental file.
Introduction to insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes and the open question of whether diverse insults share a common mechanism; sets up the genomic study of TNF-alpha and dexamethasone cell models.
Genomic study of two cellular insulin-resistance models (TNF-alpha and dexamethasone); gene expression suggests elevated reactive oxygen species, confirmed by cellular redox measures.

Background that ROS were proposed in insulin resistance without strong causal evidence; cell-culture tests using six ROS-altering treatments (two small molecules, four transgenes) that all ameliorated insulin resistance.
Results extend to an in vivo test: one ROS-altering treatment improved insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis in obese, insulin-resistant mice; concludes ROS are a key trigger across settings.
Concluding sentence of the abstract: increased ROS levels are an important trigger for insulin resistance in numerous settings.

Introduces the core claim that elevated plasma free fatty acids in obesity cause insulin resistance in muscle, liver, and endothelium, leading to T2DM, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and NAFLD; this chunk begins describing the intracellular mechanism (lipid accumulation).

Continues the mechanism of FFA-induced insulin resistance: intramyocellular and intrahepatocellular triglyceride and diacylglycerol buildup, serine/threonine kinase activation, reduced IRS-1/2 tyrosine phosphorylation, and impaired IRS/PI3-kinase insulin signaling.

Describes FFA-driven low-grade inflammation in muscle and liver via NF-kappaB and proinflammatory cytokine release, then summarizes the overall conclusion that high FFA (from obesity or high-fat feeding) causes muscle/liver insulin resistance (T2DM) and inflammation (atherosclerosis, NAFLD).
Final concluding clause linking FFA-induced low-grade inflammation to atherosclerotic vascular disease and NAFLD, completing the document's summary of the inflammation-related consequences.
Study introduction: dietary AGEs in diabetic subjects, defining the high-AGE (H-AGE) vs low-AGE (L-AGE) diets and the study sizes (2-week crossover, n=11; 6-week study, n=13).
Two-week crossover results: serum AGEs rose on H-AGE and fell on L-AGE, along with TNF-α/β-actin mRNA ratios and serum VCAM-1 levels by diet.
Six-week study results: monocyte TNF-α, C-reactive protein, and VCAM-1 changes by diet, with the H-AGE diet increasing inflammatory markers and the L-AGE diet decreasing them.
Six-week results for serum AGEs and AGE-LDL, showing increases on H-AGE and reductions on L-AGE, followed by the paper's overall conclusion that dietary AGEs promote inflammation in diabetes.
Concluding statement: dietary AGEs promote inflammatory mediators and tissue injury in diabetes, and restricting dietary AGEs suppresses these effects.

Introduces the review on meat consumption and diabetes, establishing prospective evidence linking meat intake (especially processed meat) to type 2 diabetes, plus CHD and stroke, and the scope covering T1DM, T2DM and their complications.

Describes the review's scope and methods, including a new T2DM meta-analysis (publications through October 2012), notes that T1DM evidence is limited, and says the evidence is strongest for T2DM, CHD and stroke.

Gives the core quantitative findings: pooled relative risks for T2DM per 100 g of total, unprocessed red, and poultry meat, and per 50 g of processed meat (RR 1.32), concluding processed red meat shows the strongest T2DM association.

Compares associations across outcomes: processed meat shows the strongest link to T2DM and a similar pattern to CHD, while stroke shows moderately elevated risk for both processed and fresh meat; microvascular complication evidence is sparse and mostly inferred from hyperglycemia and hypertension.

Discusses the biological mechanisms, listing meat constituents thought to drive risk: saturated and trans fats, cholesterol, protein, heme-iron, sodium, nitrites/nitrosamines, and advanced glycation end products.
Concludes with public health recommendations: a diet moderate to low in red meat, favoring unprocessed, lean meat prepared at moderate temperatures, as the best choice.

Introduction and study aims for the EPIC-InterAct meat and type 2 diabetes study: background hypothesis that meat-rich diets raise diabetes risk, and the design as a case-cohort study nested within EPIC.

Methods of the EPIC-InterAct study: 11.7 years of follow-up, 12,403 incident type 2 diabetes cases among 340,234 adults from eight European countries, centre-stratified random subsample of 16,835 for the case-cohort design, and Prentice-weighted Cox regression.
Main results beginning with multivariate hazard ratios per 50 g increment for total meat (HR 1.08), red meat (HR 1.08) and processed meat (HR 1.12) and incident type 2 diabetes.

Results on effect modification: borderline association with meat iron, sex-specific findings where men confirmed the overall results, and in women attenuated total/red meat associations plus an emerging poultry association, with BMI class modifying effects.

Final results showing the poultry association in women (HR 1.20), the absence of associations among obese participants, and the conclusion that high total and red meat intake is positively associated with incident type 2 diabetes in European adults.
Closing fragment of the conclusion sentence stating the study's finding of a positive link between high meat intake and type 2 diabetes in a large European adult cohort.
