Opening preface of a review on mTOR signaling. It introduces the TOR pathway as coupling energy, nutrient, stress, and growth-factor signals to cell growth and division, and names mTORC1 and mTORC2 as the complexes that act through kinases like S6K and Akt.

Closing part of the preface to the mTOR review. It finishes the description of mTORC1/mTORC2 regulating S6K and Akt, then states that recent advances show mTOR's critical role in diabetes, cancer, and ageing, previewing the review's themes.
Opening of the review: introduces the rising global prevalence of diabetes and obesity, questions lifestyle explanations, and motivates looking at environmental risk factors.

Continues the rationale: after the industrial revolution, many chemicals entered the environment as pollutants, leading to interest in persistent organic pollutants (POPs) as possible diabetes contributors.
States the review's aim: to summarise and critically appraise epidemiological evidence linking POPs to diabetes and identify gaps and flaws, followed by the copyright notice.
Final chunk containing only the copyright line (Elsevier Masson SAS, 2013), marking the end of the abstract.
Introduction of a review arguing that dairy and meat (leucine-rich) consumption drives type 2 diabetes and obesity via leucine over-activation of mTORC1.
Background on mTORC1 as a nutrient-sensitive kinase, and on dairy and meat raising insulin/IGF-1 signaling and leucine, an independent mTORC1 activator.
Mechanism: the mTORC1 downstream kinase S6K1 causes insulin resistance by phosphorylating IRS-1 (raising beta-cell burden), and leucine-mTORC1-S6K1 signaling promotes adipogenesis and obesity.
Consequences of high leucine-rich protein intake: exaggerated mTORC1-driven insulin secretion, beta-cell growth and proliferation, leading to early replicative beta-cell senescence and apoptosis.

Hallmarks of T2D (beta-cell mass dysregulation and insulin resistance) linked to mTORC1 hyperactivation; metformin antagonizes leucine-mTORC1 signaling, and plant polyphenols/flavonoids act as natural mTORC1 inhibitors.

Bariatric surgery lowers elevated leucine and branched-chain amino acids; proposes limiting daily leucine-rich animal and dairy protein intake to attenuate mTORC1 signaling and prevent T2D and obesity.
Conclusion extending the implications: curbing mTORC1 signaling may also help prevent cancer and neurodegenerative diseases, which are often associated with T2D.
Final punctuation fragment closing the document's concluding sentence; no standalone content, belongs to the conclusion on mTORC1 and prevention of disease.

Introduction/background of a study on dietary advanced glycation endproducts (AGEs) and glycotoxins, stating the diabetic kidney disease context and the study's aim of examining oral absorption and renal clearance of food AGEs.

Study design: 38 diabetics with or without kidney disease and 5 healthy subjects ate a single egg-white meal cooked with fructose (AGE-diet) or without it (CL-diet), with serum and urine monitored for AGE immunoreactivity and crosslinking activity.

Results on serum AGE levels: only the AGE-rich diet raised serum AGEs in proportion to the amount ingested, and the serum area under the curve was tied to kidney disease severity, with the correlation coefficient and significance reported.

Renal excretion findings: dietary AGE excretion was incomplete (about 30% of absorbed), correlated inversely with albuminuria and directly with creatinine clearance, and fell below 5% in patients with renal failure.

Crosslinking activity and conclusions: post-meal serum showed elevated AGE-crosslinking activity that aminoguanidine inhibited, and the authors conclude that renal excretion of dietary AGEs is suppressed in diabetic nephropathy, dietary AGEs may add renal-vascular risk, and AGE restriction may help.

Concluding statements of the paper: renal excretion of orally absorbed AGEs is suppressed in diabetic nephropathy, dietary glycotoxins may add chronic risk for vascular and renal injury, and restricting dietary AGEs could reduce AGE burden and improve prognosis.
Final sentence of the conclusions, ending the abstract with the suggestion that reducing dietary AGE intake may improve prognosis in diabetic patients.

Opening of the meta-analysis abstract and introduction: summarizes findings that coffee shows no clear link to hip fracture risk and tea shows a nonlinear association, and begins the background on prior inconsistent cohort and case-control studies.

Introduction conclusion and methods start: notes inconsistent prior evidence on coffee and tea with hip fracture, states the aim, and describes systematic searches of MEDLINE, EMBASE, and OVID up to February 20, 2013.

Methods details: random-effects models for pooled relative risks with 95% CIs, and the categorical, dose-response, heterogeneity, publication bias, and subgroup analyses; begins results describing the study population.

Results on the pooled sample: 195,992 individuals, 9,958 hip fracture cases, 14 studies (six cohort, eight case-control), and pooled RRs for highest vs. lowest coffee (0.94) and tea (0.84) consumption, both non-significant.
Dose-response results: evidence of a nonlinear tea-hip fracture association (p nonlinearity < 0.01), with reduced risks for 1-2, 2-3, and 3-4 cups of tea per day versus none (RRs 0.72, 0.63, 0.79).

Conclusions: no significant coffee-hip fracture association; nonlinear tea association with lower risk for 1-4 cups daily compared with no tea, and the start of the statement that 5 or more daily cups needs further study.
Final conclusion sentences: 1-4 daily cups of tea linked to lower hip fracture risk than no tea, and a recommendation to investigate the association for 5 or more daily cups of tea.
Introduction and methods of a study on caffeine intake and urinary incontinence in US men, using NHANES 2005-2008 data; background notes that prior evidence is mostly in women.

Methods detail: NHANES 2005-2008 male participants, urinary incontinence defined by Incontinence Severity Index score of 3 or greater (moderate to severe), and caffeine, water, and dietary moisture measured by structured dietary recall.

Statistical methods: stepwise multivariable logistic regression assessing caffeine intake at the 75th and 90th percentiles against moderate-to-severe incontinence, adjusting for confounders, risk factors, and prostate conditions in men aged 40 and older.
Results on the study population: 3,960 of 5,297 men included, with 12.9% prevalence of any urinary incontinence, 4.4% moderate-to-severe, and mean caffeine intake of 169 mg per day.

Key findings: caffeine at or above the 75th percentile (234 mg/day) and 90th percentile (392 mg/day) was significantly associated with moderate-to-severe incontinence (OR 1.72 and 2.08), and the association persisted after adjusting for prostate conditions.

Conclusions: caffeine intake equal to about two cups of coffee (250 mg/day) is significantly associated with moderate-to-severe urinary incontinence in US men, supporting further study of caffeine modification as a treatment approach.
Closing copyright and publisher notice (American Urological Association Education and Research, Inc., published by Elsevier Inc., 2013) for the study on caffeine and urinary incontinence in men.

Abstract opening of a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis (2014) on coffee consumption and fracture risk; covers the rationale (inconclusive prior data) and the database search methods (MEDLINE, EMBASE, etc., through February 2013) with exposure and outcome keywords.

Methods section of the coffee-fracture meta-analysis describing the search keywords (coffee, caffeine, drink, beverage as exposures; fracture as outcome) and the statistical approach: pooled relative risks comparing highest versus lowest coffee intake plus a dose-response analysis.

Results section of the coffee and fracture meta-analysis reporting the study pool (253,514 participants, 12,939 fracture cases from 9 cohort and 6 case-control studies) and the pooled relative risk at highest coffee intake: 1.14 in women versus 0.76 in men, with heterogeneity statistics.

Remaining results and conclusion of the coffee-fracture meta-analysis: dose-response estimates in women at 2 and 8 cups per day (RR 1.02 and 1.54), and the conclusion that coffee is linked to higher fracture risk in women but lower risk in men, pending confirmatory studies.
Final sentence of the conclusions and the copyright notice (Elsevier, 2014) closing the abstract of the coffee consumption and fracture risk systematic review and meta-analysis.

Introduces coffee as the most widely consumed US beverage and main adult caffeine source, noting its many bioactive compounds beyond caffeine and wide-ranging chronic health effects; opens the cardiovascular/metabolic review of coffee consumption.

Covers coffee's cardiovascular-related effects: possible reduced risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, obesity and depression, but possible adverse lipid effects depending on preparation method; also notes growing evidence that habitual intake is neutral to beneficial for CV outcomes.

Summarizes evidence that habitual coffee drinking is neutral to beneficial for coronary heart disease, heart failure, arrhythmias and stroke, and that regular drinkers have lower cardiovascular and all-cause mortality in large epidemiological studies.

Lists other potential benefits (neurodegenerative disease protection, asthma control, lower risk of some GI diseases) and states that about 2 to 3 cups daily appears safe with neutral to beneficial effects for most outcomes studied.

Caveats that most coffee health evidence is observational with few randomized trials and association does not prove causation; introduces the need to weigh benefits against risks, mainly from caffeine.

Details caffeine-related risks such as anxiety, insomnia, tremulousness, palpitations, bone loss and possibly fractures, and includes the 2013 American College of Cardiology Foundation copyright and Elsevier publication notice.
Final fragment of the copyright line (Elsevier Inc. all rights reserved) closing the document; contains no substantive health content.
Background and aims of a study on gastro-oesophageal reflux from coffee and tea, including decaffeination and caffeine comparisons, introducing the ambulatory pH-metry design.

Methods detail: three-hour ambulatory pH-metry in 16 healthy volunteers given 300 ml of coffee, tea, or water variants (regular, decaffeinated, caffeine-adjusted, caffeine-free/containing water) with a standardized breakfast.

Results part 1: regular coffee raised reflux versus tap water and normal tea (which did not differ), and decaffeinating coffee reduced reflux, while decaffeinated tea or caffeine in water had no effect.
Results part 2 and conclusions: caffeine-adjusted coffee increased reflux; coffee, unlike tea, increases reflux, less so when decaffeinated, suggesting caffeine is not the cause.
Final conclusion: caffeine is not responsible for coffee-induced gastro-oesophageal reflux, which must be attributed to other coffee components.

Introduction and methods opening of a meta-analysis on caffeine's effect on intraocular pressure (IOP), covering the study aim, background on conflicting prior data, and the Cochrane-methodology literature search of CENTRAL, PubMed and EMBASE for RCTs.

Methods continuation describing the systematic review and meta-analysis design, with IOP at 0.5, 1 and 1.5 hours after caffeine ingestion defined as the primary outcome, leading into the start of the results.

Results describing the six included RCTs (two parallel, four crossover) with 144 participants, uncertain risk of bias, and the split of 103 normal individuals versus 41 patients with glaucoma or ocular hypertension.

Core quantitative findings: in normal individuals caffeine did not alter IOP, with non-significant weighted mean differences at each time point, whereas in glaucoma/OHT patients IOP rose at every measurement point, with the WMD and 95% CI values given.
Reports that no publication bias was found by Begg's or Egger's tests, and begins the conclusion by stating caffeine affects IOP differently across population groups.

Conclusion stating that caffeine does not change IOP in normal individuals but significantly increases it in glaucoma or OHT patients, calling for more high-quality RCTs and further study of mechanisms and clinical significance.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence noting that the underlying mechanisms and clinical significance of the caffeine-IOP effect remain to be explored.

Study introduction and methods: a prospective cohort of ~121,000 US women and men aged 40+ followed for POAG (primary open-angle glaucoma) incidence, examining caffeine's effect on intraocular pressure and disease risk.

Methods continued and start of results: 1,011 confirmed incident POAG cases via medical record review; pooled multivariable rate ratios computed, with the reference group being daily caffeine intake under 150 mg.

Main pooled results by caffeine dose: no significant association across 150 mg to 600+ mg per day (RRs about 1.05 to 1.19, CIs spanning 1), with no trend. Heavy coffee intake (5+ cups daily) shows a borderline elevated RR of 1.61.

Results on beverage type and family history: tea and cola show no association, while greater caffeine intake is linked to higher POAG risk in people with a family history of glaucoma, especially high-tension (elevated IOP) POAG, with a significant trend and interaction.

Conclusion: overall caffeine intake is not associated with increased POAG risk. Secondary analyses suggest higher risk of high-tension POAG among those with a family history, possibly due to chance and needing further study.

Introduces the case topic: substance-induced atrial fibrillation, specifically the methylxanthines in chocolate (caffeine, theobromine) and their adenosine-antagonist mechanism, noting that normal caffeine intake was not linked to AF or flutter.

Describes caffeine overdose cardiac toxicity, where catecholamine-mediated sympathomimetic effects cause tachyarrhythmias including atrial fibrillation, and begins discussing salbutamol's cardiac safety profile.

Summarizes evidence that commonly used inhaled salbutamol doses caused no acute ischaemia or arrhythmia in stable asthma/COPD patients with coronary disease, and that two-week treatment increases sympathetic responsiveness and mild beta2 tolerance.
Presents the case report of a 19-year-old Italian woman with atrial fibrillation linked to chocolate abuse and chronic salbutamol inhaler abuse, framing the study's focus.
Concludes that chocolate abuse combined with chronic salbutamol abuse may be the substrate for atrial fibrillation, with the 2008 Elsevier copyright notice.
Opening of a review on coffee's health benefits and risks, introducing its global trade size and the ongoing debate over cardiovascular and cancer concerns.

Continues the review by attributing coffee's health-promoting effects to its phytochemicals (caffeine, chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid, HHQ) and epidemiological links to lower rates of diabetes, cancers, Parkinson's and Alzheimer's.
Describes mechanisms by which coffee reduces oxidative stress via Nrf2-ARE pathway activation and how caffeine and its metabolites support cognitive function.
Discusses coffee lipids cafestol and kahweol, which may protect against malignant cells, but can raise serum cholesterol and threaten coronary health, including infarction and insomnia.
Covers caffeine's action on adenosine receptors, withdrawal effects such as muscle fatigue, and advice that pregnant or postmenopausal women limit coffee due to interactions with hormones.

Concludes the review's stated aim of disseminating general information, health claims, and risk factors of coffee consumption to scientists, stakeholders, and readers, followed by the publisher copyright notice.
Final fragment of the review's closing sentence and the Taylor and Francis Group, LLC copyright line.

Introduction/background of a meta-analysis of prospective studies on coffee consumption and mortality (all-cause, cancer, CVD, CHD/IHD, stroke), motivating pooled estimates because individual studies were underpowered.
Methods: describes the literature search of PubMed and Embase (updated to January 2013) for prospective observational studies reporting mortality outcomes in relation to coffee consumption.

Methods and first key results: systematic review using random-effects models to estimate pooled relative risks, reporting all-cause mortality RR of 0.88 (0.84-0.93) across 23 studies, comparing highest vs low (≤1 cup/day) coffee intake.
Results on smoking-adjusted all-cause mortality (0.87, 19 studies) and cardiovascular disease mortality RRs for highest vs low intake (0.89) and per 1 cup/day increment (0.98).
Results for CHD/IHD (0.95), stroke (0.95) and all cancers (1.03) comparing highest with low coffee intake, with confidence intervals and study counts, followed by the start of the conclusion.
Concluding statement of the meta-analysis: coffee intake is inversely associated with all-cause mortality and probably with CVD mortality.

Case report opening: introduces the rare link between dietary habits and seizure frequency, describing a man with partial symptomatic epilepsy whose heavy daily coffee drinking increased his seizures.

Concluding part of the case report: describes the dramatic seizure reduction after the patient stopped coffee, and proposes that caffeine, as a global stimulant, may be reduced to help treat epilepsy.

Introduction and methods of a systematic review/meta-analysis on caffeine and atrial fibrillation risk: background, objective, design, and data sources (PubMed, CENTRAL, ISI, LILACS through Dec 2012).

Study selection and data synthesis methods: two independent reviewers, random-effects meta-analysis pooling ORs with 95% CIs, I(2) heterogeneity testing, and subgroup analyses by caffeine dose and coffee source.
Results opening: seven observational studies (six cohort, one case-control) covering 115,993 individuals were included in the meta-analysis of caffeine and AF.
Main quantitative findings: overall pooled OR 0.92 showing no increased AF risk, high-quality studies showing OR 0.87 with lower heterogeneity, and low-dose caffeine showing OR 0.85 with I(2)=0%.
Subgroup results and conclusions: no AF risk from coffee-only caffeine or other dose strata, concluding caffeine is not associated with increased AF risk and low-dose caffeine may be protective.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that low-dose caffeine may have a protective effect against atrial fibrillation.

Introduction and methods of a dose–response meta-analysis on tea consumption and fracture risk, covering the rationale, literature search sources (PubMed, Embase), and STATA-based analysis of observational studies.
Methods continuation and start of results: inclusion criteria for observational studies on tea drinking and fracture incidence, and the total of 9 studies with 147,950 participants.
Main pooled result: random-effects meta-analysis yielding a pooled OR of 0.89 (95% CI 0.78–1.04) for tea consumption and fracture risk, and the beginning of the subgroup analyses.
Subgroup and dose–response findings: no significant association in cohort studies (OR 0.97) or case–control studies (OR 0.91), and no significant dose–response effect, leading into the conclusions.
Conclusion that tea consumption may not be linked to fracture risk, a call for larger well-designed studies, and a virtual slide link provided as article metadata.
Opening of the caffeine and urinary incontinence study in US women: states the aim (link caffeine intake to UI severity), the hypothesis, and begins the Methods describing NHANES 2005–2008 data.

Methods continued: NHANES cross-sectional survey, UI classified via Incontinence Severity Index as 'any' or 'moderate/severe' and by type (stress, urge, mixed, other), with food-diary water, moisture, and caffeine intake grouped into quartiles.

Methods conclusion and start of Results: describes the stepwise logistic regression covariates (sociodemographics, chronic disease, BMI, health, depression, alcohol, dietary water, reproductive factors) and the sample of 4309 non-pregnant women.

Results on prevalence: any UI 41.0%, moderate/severe UI 16.5%, stress UI most common (36.6%), mean caffeine intake 126.7 mg/day, and the start of the adjusted caffeine findings for the highest quartile.

Key adjusted findings: caffeine ≥204 mg/day linked to any UI (POR 1.47, 95% CI 1.07–2.01) but not moderate/severe UI (POR 1.42, 95% CI 0.98–2.07); UI type not associated with caffeine; start of Conclusions.
Final conclusion sentence: caffeine intake ≥204 mg/day is associated with any urinary incontinence but not moderate/severe UI among US women.

Opening of the abstract for a 2014 meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies on habitual caffeine/coffee intake and incident atrial fibrillation; covers background, aim, and the literature search methods (PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane through November 2013).

Continues the methods (eligibility: prospective cohorts reporting RR/HR and 95% CIs for AF by caffeine intake) and begins the results, reporting six cohort studies with 228,465 participants and the weak inverse association in the primary pooled analysis.

Presents the primary pooled estimate (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.81-1.01, I² 73%) and subgroup results for studies adjusted for confounders, showing risk reductions of 11% for low doses and 16% for high doses of caffeine.

Reports the dose-response meta-analysis findings: an inverse relation between habitual caffeine intake and AF risk (trend P = 0.015, nonlinearity P = 0.27), with about a 6% lower AF incidence per 300 mg/day increment.

Gives the conclusions: caffeine consumption is unlikely to cause or contribute to AF and habitual intake might reduce AF risk, followed by the 2014 Canadian Cardiovascular Society / Elsevier copyright statement.
Final fragment of the copyright line (Elsevier Inc., all rights reserved) closing the abstract of the caffeine and atrial fibrillation meta-analysis.

Opening of the abstract: introduces the study's aim to assess coffee consumption's effect on four acid-related diseases (GU, DU, RE, NERD), noting the weak prior evidence behind assumed negative effects.
Study design and diagnosis methods: 9,517 healthy adults, with GU, DU, and RE confirmed by endoscopy and NERD defined by heartburn/regurgitation without esophageal erosion; lists covariates examined.

Methods continued: covariates adjusted for (age, gender, BMI, H. pylori, pepsinogen I/II ratio, smoking, alcohol), a random-effects meta-analysis planned, and the analytic sample of 8,013 subjects (5,451 coffee drinkers vs 2,562 non-drinkers).
Results: univariate associations of age, BMI, pepsinogen ratio, smoking, and alcohol with coffee consumption, and the start of the multiple logistic regression findings for GU.
Multivariate regression results for each disease (GU, DU, RE, NERD) listing correlated factors, plus meta-analysis finding no association of coffee with GU or DU.
Conclusion: coffee consumption shows no significant relationship with the four major acid-related upper gastrointestinal disorders.
Introduction and objective of a literature review on tea consumption and cardiovascular disease risk, examining observational studies and meta-analyses on tea and tea flavonoids.

Study design: searches of three databases for meta-analyses, comparison with their subsumed studies, and an additional search for later studies to check whether conclusions remain consistent; begins the results on the epidemiologic evidence.

Results summary: five meta-analyses cover tea or flavonoid intake and cardiovascular disease or stroke; heterogeneity appears for all-cardiovascular outcomes, and a dose-response pattern emerges for stroke.

Quantitative stroke findings: tea and flavonoid intake show consistent dose-response associations with stroke incidence and mortality, with pooled RRs of 0.80 (flavonoids) and 0.79 (tea) for high vs. low intake or each additional 3 cups/day.
Conclusion: the evidence supports the hypothesis that tea consumption may reduce stroke risk.

Introduction/abstract opening of a prospective cohort study (NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study) on coffee drinking and mortality, describing the study population of 229,119 men and 173,141 women aged 50-71 at baseline.

Methods and results continuation: cancer, heart disease, and stroke exclusions, single baseline coffee assessment, follow-up of 5,148,760 person-years, and 33,731 male and 18,784 female deaths; notes that age-adjusted models showed increased mortality among coffee drinkers.

Results describing confounding: coffee drinkers were more likely to smoke, and after adjusting for smoking and other confounders, coffee consumption showed a significant inverse association with mortality.
Adjusted hazard ratios for death among men by daily coffee intake (less than 1 cup through 6+ cups), with 95% confidence intervals and a P<0.001 trend, showing lowest risk around 4-5 cups per day.

Adjusted hazard ratios for women by daily coffee intake with confidence intervals and trend P-value, plus cause-specific findings: inverse associations for heart disease, respiratory disease, stroke, injuries, diabetes, and infections, but not cancer.

Subgroup robustness findings (never-smokers, self-rated very good to excellent health) and the start of the conclusions stating coffee consumption was inversely associated with total and cause-specific mortality.
Study conclusion noting that causality versus association cannot be determined from the data, followed by the funding statement from the NIH Intramural Research Program and National Cancer Institute.
Closing fragment of the funding acknowledgment, the end of the NIH National Cancer Institute, Division of Cancer Epidemiology and Genetics attribution for the coffee-mortality study.

Opening of the abstract: study objective and data source (Aerobics Center Longitudinal Study, 43,727 participants, 699,632 person-years) for the coffee consumption and all-cause/CVD mortality cohort analysis.

Continuation of the methods: baseline assessment (questionnaires, medical exam incl. fasting blood tests, ECG, graded exercise test, 1971–2002) and the Cox regression approach for coffee and mortality.
Results opening: 17-year median follow-up, 2512 deaths (32% CVD), and the multivariate finding that coffee intake was positively linked to all-cause mortality in men, with HR 1.21 for >28 cups/week.

Age-stratified results: after stratifying by age (<55), younger men and women with >28 cups/week coffee showed significant all-cause mortality associations, with adjusted HRs of 1.56 (men) and 2.13 (women).

Conclusion of the abstract: the positive coffee–all-cause mortality association in men and in men and women under 55, followed by the start of the recommendation that younger people avoid heavy coffee intake.
Closing of the conclusion: the practical advice to younger people to avoid heavy coffee use (>4 cups/day) and the call for replication in future studies from other populations.

Abstract opening of a study on virgin olive oil phenolics and endothelial function: states the aim, background on postprandial impairment of endothelial vasodilatation linked to oxidative stress, and the methods design (21 hypercholesterolemic volunteers, randomized crossover breakfasts).

Methods section describing the crossover breakfast protocol, where the same olive oil was given with phenolic acid content reduced from 400 to 80 ppm, the laser-Doppler measurement of ischemic reactive hyperemia at baseline, 2 h and 4 h, and the plasma biomarkers sampled (lipids, lipoperoxides, 8-epi PGF2alpha, NOx).

Start of the results: the polyphenol-rich breakfast improved endothelial function and produced a greater rise in nitrates/nitrites (NOx) with a smaller rise in lipoperoxides and 8-epi prostaglandin-F2alpha compared with the low-polyphenol fat meal.

Specific statistical findings: group comparisons with p-values for NOx, LPO and 8-epi PGF2alpha, a positive correlation between NOx and improved endothelial function at 2 h (r = 0.669), and the start of the negative correlation between IRH and LPO.

Remaining results on negative correlations of IRH with LPO (r = -0.203) and 8-epi PGF2alpha (r = -0.440), followed by the conclusions that high-phenolic virgin olive oil improves postprandial ischemic reactive hyperemia.
Final conclusion sentence proposing the mechanism: the endothelial benefit may be mediated by reduced oxidative stress and increased nitric oxide metabolites, closing the abstract.

Abstract opening (objective and design) of a study on acute effects of MUFA vs SAFA meals on endothelial function (flow-mediated dilatation) in type 2 diabetes, with 33 participants given isocaloric olive oil or butter meals.
Methods and results from the same type 2 diabetes study: FMD was unchanged after the olive oil (MUFA) meal but declined after the butter (SAFA) meal, measured as incremental AUC.

Quantitative results and conclusions: FMD rose 5.2% after the MUFA meal and fell 16.7% after the SAFA meal (difference -11.5%, P=0.008), concluding SAFA meals harm endothelium while MUFA meals do not.
Final fragment of the abstract's sentence, ending the phrase 'in subjects with type 2 diabetes' from the conclusions of the MUFA vs SAFA endothelial function study.

Abstract opening (Context, Objective, and start of Design) of a randomized trial on a Mediterranean-style diet's effect on endothelial dysfunction and vascular inflammation in metabolic syndrome patients, Italy 2001-2004.

Design, setting, and patients: single-blind randomized trial at an Italian university hospital with 180 metabolic syndrome patients (ATP III criteria), followed by the start of the interventions description.

Interventions: Mediterranean-style diet group (n=90) advised to increase whole grains, fruits, vegetables, nuts, and olive oil versus control group (n=90) on a prudent diet with macronutrient targets; also lists the main outcome measures start.

Main outcome measures include nutrient intake, endothelial function score (blood pressure and platelet response to l-arginine), lipids, glucose, insulin sensitivity, and inflammatory markers hs-CRP, IL-6, IL-7, IL-18; results section begins with dietary intake changes.

Results on dietary change after 2 years: intervention group ate more monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fat and fiber foods, lower omega-6:omega-3 ratio, and higher fruit, vegetable, nut, whole grain, and olive oil intake (P<.001).

Results on physical activity (similar increase in both groups, no difference) and body weight, which fell significantly more in the intervention group (-4.0 kg vs -1.2 kg, P<.001); begins comparison of inflammatory markers.

Results on inflammation and insulin resistance: intervention diet significantly reduced hs-CRP, IL-6, IL-7, IL-18 and insulin resistance versus control; endothelial function score rose in intervention group (+1.9) but was stable in controls (+0.2).

Endothelial function outcome and metabolic syndrome prevalence: after 2 years 40 intervention patients still had metabolic syndrome versus 78 controls (P<.001); conclusion begins that the Mediterranean diet may reduce metabolic syndrome prevalence and cardiovascular risk.

Final fragment of the results (metabolic syndrome prevalence difference, P<.001) and the concluding statement that a Mediterranean-style diet might effectively reduce metabolic syndrome prevalence and its associated cardiovascular risk.

Abstract opening of a study on postprandial effects of extra virgin olive oil: introduces the link between high post-meal lipids, oxidative stress, atherosclerosis, and the Mediterranean diet, and states the study's aims.

Continues the abstract's methods: measured inflammatory and oxidative stress markers in 12 healthy normolipemic subjects given a fat-rich meal, using a Latin square crossover design comparing EVOO, olive oil, and corn oil.
Describes the crossover protocol details (three oils with potatoes, 2-week washouts, blood draws at baseline and 1, 2, 6h) and the key result: decreased TXB2 and LTB4 after EVOO but not other oils.

Concludes the abstract's results and interpretation: EVOO raised serum antioxidant capacity and lowered inflammatory markers, supporting the protective role of Mediterranean diet phenolics in coronary heart disease.
Final fragment of the abstract's concluding sentence, completing the claim that phenolic components of extra virgin olive oil protect against coronary heart disease.

Introduction and objective of a randomized crossover study on how a high-fat meal versus a high-carbohydrate meal affects endothelial function (vasomotor, antiplatelet, hemostatic) in healthy subjects, opening with the background on coronary heart disease mortality and dietary guidelines.

Study design details: observer-blinded randomized crossover trial with 25 healthy subjects receiving three test meals (high-fat 760 kcal, isoenergetic high-carbohydrate, high-fat with vegetable antioxidants 865 kcal) at weekly intervals, with endothelial function assessed via responses to L-arginine, the nitric oxide precursor.

Results on plasma triacylglycerol and hemostasis: the high-fat meal raised triacylglycerol unlike the high-carbohydrate meal, both meals activated hemostasis, and the high-carbohydrate meal left blood pressure unchanged.

Key quantitative results on blood pressure and platelet aggregation after L-arginine: the high-carbohydrate meal lowered blood pressure by about -7.1 mm Hg and platelet aggregation by -8.5%, while the high-fat meal blunted the blood pressure drop to about -1 mm Hg.

Platelet aggregation paradoxically rose after the high-fat meal (+4.1%, P < 0.01 versus high-carbohydrate), and adding dietary antioxidants partially restored the vascular response to L-arginine; this sets up the conclusion about an atherogenic endothelial profile.

Concluding statement: a high-fat meal shifts endothelial function toward a more atherogenic profile compared with a high-carbohydrate meal, and this effect is partially prevented by dietary antioxidants from vegetables.

Introduction and rationale from a study of simvastatin's effect on endothelium-dependent flow-mediated brachial artery vasoactivity in healthy middle-aged men whose cholesterol already meets NCEP desirable targets.
Methods: noninvasive 7.5 MHz ultrasound measurement of flow-mediated brachial artery diameter change in 7 healthy men during simvastatin 10 mg/day cholesterol lowering.
Results: flow-mediated vasoactivity increased from about 5% at baseline to 10.5%, 13.3%, and 15.7% at 2, 4, and 12 weeks as cholesterol fell to roughly 153-169 mg/dl.
Reversibility and correlation: vasoactivity and cholesterol returned to baseline after simvastatin was stopped, and vasoactivity correlated inversely with cholesterol (r = -0.47, p = 0.004).
Conclusion: flow-mediated vasoactivity responds rapidly to cholesterol changes, suggesting endothelial function improves when cholesterol is lowered below current guideline targets.

Study background and objective: comparing a saturated fat-rich diet against the NCEP-1 low-fat diet and a Mediterranean monounsaturated-fat diet on endothelial function in hypercholesterolemic men, from the Mediterranean and low-fat diets endothelial function trial.

Study design and setting: a randomized crossover dietary intervention with a baseline phase, conducted at Hospital Universitario Reina Sofía in Córdoba, Spain, comparing NCEP-1 and Mediterranean diet periods.

Patients and intervention: 22 hypercholesterolemic men followed a saturated fat-high diet, then were crossover-assigned to the NCEP-1 or Mediterranean diet, with each 28-day dietary period outcomes measured via P-selectin, lipids, and endothelial function.

Key results: flow-mediated dilatation improved only on the Mediterranean diet versus the saturated fat diet, while cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B, and P-selectin decreased on both the NCEP-1 and Mediterranean diets.
Conclusion: low-fat (especially low saturated fat) and monounsaturated fat-rich Mediterranean diets both improve endothelial function in hypercholesterolemic men.

Introduction and study design of an EPIC-Spain cohort analysis of olive oil intake and incident coronary heart disease (CHD), including sample size (40,142 participants) and rationale based on olive oil's cardioprotective reputation and limited epidemiological evidence.

Methods of the EPIC-Spain olive oil and CHD study: recruitment from five centres (1992-1996), follow-up to 2004, baseline interview-based diet and lifestyle data, and Cox proportional hazards models for validated incident CHD events.

Main results of the olive oil and CHD study: 10.4-year follow-up with 587 CHD events (79% male), and the initial finding of an inverse association between olive oil intake and CHD risk after excluding dietary mis-reporters, with hazard ratios reported.

Quantitative hazard ratios from the EPIC-Spain olive oil and CHD study: HR 0.93 per 10 g/d increment and HR 0.78 for upper vs lower quartile after excluding mis-reporters, plus start of subgroup analysis by smoking status.

Subgroup findings and conclusion of the EPIC-Spain olive oil and CHD study: stronger inverse associations in never smokers, never/low alcohol drinkers, and virgin olive oil consumers, concluding olive oil is linked to reduced CHD risk and supporting traditional Mediterranean diet use.

Final concluding sentence of the EPIC-Spain olive oil and CHD study, recommending preservation of traditional culinary olive oil use within the Mediterranean diet to reduce the coronary heart disease burden.
Introduction and background of a human study on Colombian vegetable oil intake via deep-fried foods, motivating an investigation of how deep-frying affects oils' effects on endothelial function.

Study objective and setup description: evaluating acute effects of olive, soybean and palm oils (fresh and deep-fried at two levels) on glucose, lipid profiles and endothelial function, with the methods beginning in ten healthy volunteers.

Methods: ten healthy young volunteers receive a randomly assigned potato soup meal containing 60 mL of olive, soybean, or palm oil, fresh or deep-fried, after baseline cardiovascular risk assessment and fasting blood sampling.
Outcome measurement methods: flow-mediated vasodilation (FMD) assessed fasting and 3 hours after the oil-rich meal, with blood samples taken for lipid profiles and plasma glucose at the same stages.

Key results: all meals caused similar acute endothelial impairment (FMD decrease of 32.1%) and postprandial triglyceride increase (27.03%), with no significant differences by oil type or deep-fry level, and no correlation between the two effects.
Conclusions: no difference in acute adverse endothelial effect among vegetable oils, and all oils, fresh or deep-fried, raised plasma triglycerides in healthy subjects.

Final conclusion sentence: all vegetable oils, fresh and deep-fried, increased triglyceride levels in healthy subjects, supporting the study's overall finding of similar acute effects across oil types.

Abstract opening of a study on type 2 diabetes, introducing the aim of testing an oleic-acid-rich diet's effect on insulin resistance and endothelium-dependent vasoreactivity in 11 patients switched from a linoleic-acid-rich diet.

Methods section describing the 2-month dietary intervention and measurements: insulin-mediated glucose transport in isolated adipocytes, adipocyte membrane fatty acid composition by gas-liquid chromatography, and flow-mediated vasodilatation in the superficial femoral artery.

Results on fatty acid changes and metabolic control: oleic acid rose and linoleic acid fell on the oleic-acid diet (p<0.0001), with no difference in diabetic control but a small significant drop in fasting glucose/insulin.

Key quantitative results: insulin-stimulated glucose transport was higher on the oleic-acid diet (0.56 vs 0.29 nmol/10^5 cells/3 min, p<0.0001), and flow-mediated dilatation (FMD) improved (3.90% vs 6.12%, p<0.0001).

Correlation findings: adipocyte membrane oleic/linoleic ratio correlated with insulin-mediated glucose transport (p<0.001), but insulin-stimulated transport showed no relationship with change in FMD; the ratio correlated positively with FMD (r=0.61, p<0.001).

Conclusion: switching from polyunsaturated to monounsaturated fat reduced insulin resistance and restored endothelium-dependent vasodilatation in type 2 diabetes, offering a possible explanation for the anti-atherogenic benefits of a Mediterranean-type diet.

Introduction and background of a study on how Mediterranean diet components affect postprandial endothelial function (flow-mediated dilation), citing the Lyon Diet Heart Study and the cardiovascular benefits of the diet.

Background on the Lyon Diet Heart Study (canola oil substitution) followed by the study's methods: a meal-feeding protocol with 10 normolipidemic subjects testing olive oil, canola oil, salmon, and antioxidant-enriched olive oil meals.

Methods detail on the five test meals (fat sources and antioxidant vitamins or vinegar/salad add-ons) and how serum lipids, glucose, and brachial artery FMD were measured before and 3 hours after each meal, leading into the results.

Results showing all meals raised postprandial triglycerides, the olive oil meal significantly reduced FMD by 31% (14.3% to 9.9%, p=0.008), and triglyceride change inversely correlated with FMD (r=-0.47), while the other meals did not significantly reduce FMD.

Conclusions that the beneficial components for postprandial endothelial function are antioxidant-rich foods (vegetables, fruits, vinegar) and omega-3-rich fish and canola oils, summarizing the study's findings relative to the Mediterranean and Lyon diets.
Final sentence of the conclusions listing the beneficial dietary components: derivatives such as vinegar and omega-3-rich fish and canola oils, closing the abstract.

Introduction and study design summary for a randomised cross-over trial of 20 healthy men comparing three 4-week diets (Western, Mediterranean, low-fat ALA) on postprandial endothelial function and inflammatory biomarkers.
Description of the three dietary interventions and their fatty acid compositions (SFA, MUFA, and alpha-linolenic acid percentages of energy), within the randomised cross-over design of the study.
Methods section describing the postprandial study performed after each diet period and the measured outcomes (lipids, sICAM-1, sVCAM-1, NOx, laser Doppler endothelial function) at 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 h.

Key results on postprandial timepoints: greater endothelium-dependent vasodilation at 4 h after the MUFA-rich diet, lower 4 h sVCAM-1 versus the ALA low-fat diet, and higher NOx bioavailability after the MUFA diet.
Remaining results (no differences in other parameters) and the study's main conclusion that a Mediterranean diet avoids the postprandial endothelial deterioration seen with Westernised diets.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that Mediterranean diet intake avoids postprandial endothelial deterioration associated with Westernised diets in healthy individuals.

Introduction and methods of a study on how phenolic compounds from extra virgin olive oil affect inflammatory mediator production in LPS-stimulated diluted human whole blood cultures, including the list of phenolics tested and concentration range.

Continuation of the methods: the phenolics tested (vanillic, p-coumaric, syringic, homovanillic, caffeic acids, kaempferol, oleuropein glycoside, tyrosol) at 10^-7 to 10^-4 M, and the cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6) and prostaglandin E2 measured by ELISA.

Key results showing that oleuropein glycoside and caffeic acid reduce interleukin-1beta, with oleuropein inhibiting it by 80% and caffeic acid by 40% at 10^-4 M, and the start of the finding that kaempferol lowers prostaglandin E2.
Results continued: kaempferol inhibits prostaglandin E2 by 95% at 10^-4 M; no effects on IL-6 or TNF-alpha and no effects from the other phenolics; the start of the conclusions.

Conclusion that only some extra virgin olive oil phenolics reduce inflammatory mediator production in human whole blood cultures, suggesting a possible contribution to olive oil's antiatherogenic and cardiovascular protective effects.

Abstract opening (Background and Methods) of a study on polyphenol-rich olive oil and blood pressure/endothelial function in young women with high-normal BP or stage 1 hypertension; describes the double-blind, randomized, crossover design.

Methods section of the olive oil polyphenol study: the 4-month run-in baseline, the two diets (about 30 mg/day polyphenol-rich vs polyphenol-free olive oil), 2-month dietary periods, 4-week washout, and the outcomes measured (BP, endothelial, oxidative stress, inflammation, forearm hyperemia).

Results section start: compared with baseline, only the polyphenol-rich olive oil diet significantly lowered systolic (7.91 mm Hg) and diastolic (6.65 mm Hg) blood pressure, with the start of biomarker findings including ADMA.

Results of the olive oil polyphenol trial on biomarkers: significant decreases in ADMA, ox-LDL and CRP, plus increases in plasma nitrites/nitrates and post-ischemia hyperemic area with the polyphenol-rich diet.

End of results and conclusion of the olive oil polyphenol study: nitrite/nitrate and hyperemia increases, and the conclusion that a polyphenol-rich olive oil diet lowers blood pressure and improves endothelial function in young women with high-normal BP or stage 1 hypertension.
Final fragment of the conclusion of the olive oil polyphenol study, ending the sentence on young women with high-normal BP or stage 1 essential hypertension.

Introduction and background of a study on postprandial angina, stating the study's aim to investigate its mechanism, the long history of the condition, and the proposed role of coronary blood flow redistribution.

Study methods: 20 healthy young controls and 20 patients with significant LAD or left main stenosis had distal LAD coronary blood flow measured by transthoracic Doppler echocardiography at fixed intervals after eating.

Methods continued: the measured Doppler indices (diastolic flow time velocity integral and its product with heart rate), and the repeat measurements in six patients after successful coronary intervention.

Results in healthy controls: Dtvi and Dtvi x HR rose after food with a peak at 15 minutes, showing a postprandial surge in coronary blood flow, with fasting versus peak values reported as significantly different.
Results in patients: despite a rise in double product after eating, Dtvi and Dtvi x HR fell after food intake, reaching a nadir at 45 minutes, with fasting and nadir values significantly different.

Post-intervention results and conclusion: in six patients, the normal postprandial coronary flow surge returned after successful intervention, and the authors conclude that a 'steal phenomenon' may contribute to postprandial angina.
Concluding statement of the abstract: the study's findings suggest that a coronary steal phenomenon may play a role in the mechanism of postprandial angina.

Background section of a study on olestra vs. high-fat meals and coronary artery endothelial dysfunction measured by Rb-82 PET; introduces endothelial dysfunction as a precursor to plaque, its clinical consequences, and its reversibility with risk-factor modification and low-fat diets.

Continues the background on reversibility of coronary endothelial dysfunction via cholesterol-lowering and low-fat diet studies, then states the study's purpose: comparing myocardial perfusion and post-prandial serum triglycerides after low- versus high-TG meals.

Methods section describing the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design with 19 patients (10 with endothelial dysfunction, 9 normal), Rb-82 PET at rest and adenosine stress, and the olestra meal versus high-fat meal protocol.

Meal composition details (olestra meal with 2.7g TG and 44g olestra; high-fat meal with 46.7g TG, matched for carbohydrate, protein, and cholesterol) and the results showing 11-12% higher myocardial perfusion after the olestra meal in patients with endothelial dysfunction.

Results on serum triglycerides over 6 hours: significant rise in the non-olestra group (median to 170.0 mg/dl, p<0.01) versus 21.5 mg/dl in the olestra group, followed by the conclusion that a single olestra meal reduces post-prandial TG and improves perfusion in endothelial disease.

Final sentence of the study's conclusions, restating that a single olestra meal reduces post-prandial serum triglyceride levels and improves myocardial perfusion in patients with endothelial dysfunction.

This chunk is the document's summary of findings on dietary effects on vascular health: a meal high in monounsaturated fat acutely impaired endothelial function compared with a carbohydrate-rich meal, suggesting a divergent vascular response relevant to health and disease.

Introduces endothelial dysfunction as an early marker of atherosclerosis, measurable noninvasively with brachial artery ultrasound, and begins listing lipoprotein factors (LDL forms, postprandial chylomicron remnants) that impair endothelial function.

Continues the list of impairing factors (fasting triglyceride-rich particles, free fatty acids), notes the adverse effect of high-fat diet, and states that interventions improving endothelial function also reduce cardiovascular events, suggesting endothelial measurement as a risk index.
Concludes that measuring endothelial function may eventually serve as a useful index for predicting an individual's risk of coronary artery disease.

Study design and methods: the abstract's opening section describing the population (50 normocholesterolemic CAD patients and 25 controls) and the ultrasound measurement of brachial artery flow-mediated vasodilatation before and after a high-fat meal.

Meal protocol and main results: details the high-fat meal (800 kcal, 50 g fat), the rise in serum triglycerides at 2-7 h, and the significant impairment of flow-mediated vasodilatation across 75 subjects (4.22% to 2.75%).

Correlation and group comparison results: the positive correlation between the 2-hour triglyceride increase and the postprandial drop in flow-mediated dilatation (r = 0.459), plus higher postprandial triglycerides in CAD patients versus controls and CAD-specific vasodilatation values.

Group-specific impairment and conclusion: flow-mediated dilatation falls in both CAD patients (44.41% impairment) and controls (25.99%), with the more severe CAD impairment, and the authors' conclusion that postprandial endothelial dysfunction was severe in normocholesterolemic subjects.

Final interpretation: the closing conclusion that disordered postprandial metabolism of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins may play an atherogenic role by inducing endothelial dysfunction after a single high-fat meal.

Intro and background of a study on triglyceridemia and endothelial function: hypertriglyceridemia as a coronary heart disease risk factor, with impaired endothelial function as an atherogenesis marker; methods begin with brachial artery ultrasound dilatation in healthy young men.

Methods section describing the study design: high-resolution ultrasound measurement of brachial artery flow- and nitroglycerin-induced dilatation in seven young healthy men, and induction of transient triglyceridemia with the Intralipid emulsion infusion.

Key results: Intralipid raised free fatty acids about twofold and triglycerides fourfold; flow-induced vasodilatation fell from 7.1% to 1.6% and nitroglycerin-induced vasodilatation fell from 20.5% to 11.5% after 1 hour of infusion, with p-values reported.
Conclusion: transient triglyceridemia reduces vascular reactivity, likely through both endothelium-dependent and endothelium-independent mechanisms.

Opening of an abstract-style review on the vascular endothelium; introduces endothelial cells' role in keeping capillaries patent and functional, and lists diseases (peripheral vascular disease, stroke, heart disease, diabetes, etc.) where endothelial alterations contribute to pathogenesis.

Continues the list of endothelium-linked diseases (chronic kidney failure, tumor growth, metastasis, venous thrombosis, severe viral infections) and states that endothelial dysfunction is a hallmark of human disease; ends by naming the review's focus: cancer, diabetes mellitus, atherosclerosis, and viral infections.
Final sentence of the abstract stating that the review addresses the main endothelial abnormalities in cancer, diabetes mellitus, atherosclerosis, and viral infections.

Introduction and objectives of a study on postprandial angina pectoris, including background on the syndrome and the study's aim to assess coronary artery disease severity, plus the start of the methods (408 patients surveyed).

Methods continuation: the study population split into Group A (35 patients with postprandial angina, 8.6%) and Group B (373 control patients with nonpostprandial angina), all of whom underwent coronary angiography.

Results on demographics and angiographic findings: postprandial angina was more common in men and linked to higher rates of rest angina, left main disease, and three-vessel coronary artery disease compared with controls.

Remaining results showing lower ejection fraction in postprandial angina patients and timing of symptoms (at rest and on exertion, most often after dinner), followed by the conclusion that postprandial angina marks severe coronary disease and warrants angiography.
Final sentence of the conclusion restating that postprandial angina should be considered an indication for coronary angiography.

Opening chunk of a review on chocolate/cocoa and human health. It covers historical views of chocolate as harmful (fat content, links to acne, obesity, heart disease, diabetes) and why physicians warned against it.

Middle section of the review on chocolate and health. It describes how discovery of bioactive cocoa phenolics shifted views toward research on ageing, oxidative stress, blood pressure, and atherosclerosis, and how chocolate became praised for antioxidant potential.

Closing part of the introduction. It notes that contradictory results and methodological concerns make chocolate's health effects hard to assess, and states the review's aim: to interpret the last decade's research on chocolate's benefits and risks.
Final sentence of the abstract-style introduction, stating the review's purpose: interpreting research from the past decade on the benefits and risks of chocolate consumption.
Abstract opening (Objective and Methods) of a study on habitual chocolate intake and body weight, introducing the prospective ARIC cohort analysis that tests earlier cross-sectional findings.

Methods section detailing the ARIC cohort dietary assessment, how chocolate intake was measured as servings per frequency, body weight/height measurement, multiple imputation for missing data, and linear mixed-effects modeling.

Results opening reporting sample sizes (15,732 and 12,830 participants) and the main finding that more frequent chocolate consumption predicted significantly greater prospective weight gain in a dose-response pattern.

Specific quantitative prospective results: BMI increases over six years for participants eating chocolate 1–4 times monthly versus weekly or more, with 95% confidence intervals, plus the start of the cross-sectional inverse association.

Cross-sectional findings showing chocolate intake was inversely related to body weight, attenuated after excluding people with obesity-related illness, and how ill participants differed in BMI, chocolate, calorie, and fruit/vegetable intake.

Reverse-causation explanation that diet changes followed illness, plus the Conclusions stating chocolate habit predicts long-term weight gain dose-dependently and the cross-sectional inverse link does not hold without serious illness.
Final sentence of the conclusions: the cross-sectional finding linking chocolate intake to lower body weight does not apply to participants without preexisting serious illness.
Introduction of the cocoa paper: frames high blood pressure as a major cardiovascular risk factor and introduces cocoa flavanols/polyphenols as a possible protective dietary component.

Describes proposed mechanisms by which cocoa and its flavanols may act: improved endothelial vasodilation via nitric oxide synthase, l-arginine availability, reduced NO degradation, plus antioxidant, antiplatelet, lipid and insulin-resistance effects.

Summarizes the reported benefits: blood pressure lowering and a trend toward fewer cardiovascular events and strokes, notes prior meta-analyses on cocoa-rich foods, and states the need for long-term trials on chronic blood pressure effects.

Calls for long-term clinical trials to test whether daily cocoa intake chronically lowers blood pressure and reduces cardiovascular events, and cites the estimate that a 3 mmHg systolic reduction lowers cardiovascular and all-cause mortality risk.
Closing statement of the paper's aim: summarizing new findings on cocoa's effects on blood pressure and cardiovascular health, with focus on mechanisms of action and nutraceutical perspectives.

Introduction to the document on dark chocolate and obesity: states obesity as a growing public health problem, notes diet and exercise advice gives conflicting results, and introduces polyphenols as possible complementary agents for obesity management.

Explains why dark chocolate, rich in polyphenols especially flavanols, is studied for obesity, citing possible effects on fat and carbohydrate metabolism and satiety, continuing from the discussion of polyphenols as complementary obesity agents.

Describes the evidence base: the research on dark chocolate and obesity has used animal models, cell cultures, and a few human observational and clinical studies, and reports promising results so far.

Summarizes the proposed mechanisms by which cocoa/dark chocolate may modulate obesity and body weight (reduced fatty acid synthesis gene expression, reduced fat and carbohydrate digestion/absorption, increased satiety), followed by the 2013 John Wiley & Sons copyright notice.

Introduction and study aims of a NHANES 1999-2004 analysis of adult candy consumption (total, chocolate, sugar) and its links to energy intake, weight, cardiovascular risk factors, metabolic syndrome, and diet quality, with n = 15,023 adults aged 19+.

Methods section: 24-hour dietary recall for intake, covariate-adjusted means and prevalence by candy consumption group, and odds ratios to assess cardiovascular risk factor and metabolic syndrome likelihood in the NHANES adult sample.
Results on candy consumption prevalence (21.8% total, 12.9% chocolate, 10.9% sugar candy) and daily per capita and consumer-only intake amounts in grams for each candy type.
Results comparing candy consumers with nonconsumers: higher energy, saturated fatty acid, and added sugar intake, per the reported means, SEs, and P values.
Results comparing candy consumers with nonconsumers: lower body mass index, waist circumference, and C-reactive protein, plus reduced odds of elevated diastolic blood pressure among candy consumers.

Conclusion of the candy consumption NHANES study: chocolate consumers showed lower risk of low HDL cholesterol and metabolic syndrome, and current candy consumption was not associated with health risks; includes copyright notice.

Introduces the study's aims: whether background music genre (classical, jazz, hip-hop, rock; single vs. multiple performers) alters food perception and acceptance, varying by emotional (milk chocolate) vs. non-emotional (bell peppers) food.

Describes the method: music edited into four genres by single or multiple performers, then participants rated sensory perception and impression after eating emotional (milk chocolate) or non-emotional (bell peppers) food while listening, with an initial result that jazz produced higher liking than hip-hop.

Reports key findings: jazz led to significantly higher food liking than hip-hop; music's effect on overall impression appeared for emotional food but not non-emotional food; and genre differences in flavor pleasantness and overall impression emerged only for single-performer music, not multiple-performer music.

Concludes that music genre alters flavor pleasantness and overall impression of food, and that this influence depends on food type (emotional vs. non-emotional) and performer source (single vs. multiple); includes the publisher credit (Elsevier Ltd.).
Final fragment of the abstract: states that the effect of music genre on food acceptance varies by served food type and performer source, followed by the Elsevier Ltd. publication credit.

Abstract background and methods of a 2-arm randomized trial comparing 6 g/day vs 25 g/day flavanol-rich dark chocolate on 24-hour blood pressure in 102 high-risk patients with prehypertension or stage 1 hypertension over 3 months.

Methods continuation: participants with prehypertension/stage 1 hypertension plus cardiovascular end-organ damage or diabetes were randomized to 6 or 25 g/day dark chocolate for 3 months; primary outcome was between-group difference in 24-h mean blood pressure.

Results on ambulatory 24-hour blood pressure: significant within-group reductions for 6 g/day (-2.3 mm Hg) and 25 g/day (-1.9 mm Hg), with no significant difference in BP change between the two dose groups.
Results on body weight and conclusions: the higher-dose (25 g/day) group gained a slight 0.8 kg, and the authors state the findings are consistent with dark chocolate reducing blood pressure.

Closing conclusion caveat: the absence of a control group means confounding is possible, so the blood pressure findings from this dark chocolate dose-comparison trial should be interpreted cautiously.

Opening of the abstract: states the objective (whether trial-observed blood pressure reductions from dietary salt reduction match population-based predictions, and the resulting estimated impact on stroke and ischaemic heart disease mortality) and begins the design description of 68 crossover and 10 randomised trials.

Continues the design and main outcome measure (observed vs. predicted systolic blood pressure reductions from between-population analysis) and begins the results, noting that the 45 trials of four weeks or less showed smaller observed reductions than predicted.

Results on trial duration: short trials (four weeks or less) showed observed reductions below predictions, with the gap largest in the shortest trials; the 33 trials of five weeks or longer matched predictions across a wide range of observed reductions.

Results showing the longer-trial agreement holds across all age groups and across normal and high blood pressure, then estimates the effect of a 50 mmol (about 3 g salt) daily sodium reduction in people aged 50-59: about 5 mm Hg systolic drop overall and 7 mm Hg in those with high blood pressure.

Quantified effects: diastolic reduction about half the systolic, and population-level projections of a 22% fall in stroke incidence and 16% fall in ischaemic heart disease from a whole-population Western salt reduction (corrected figures noted).

Conclusions: trial results support the observational estimates in the companion papers, and universal moderate salt reduction would substantially lower stroke and ischaemic heart disease mortality, more than fully implementing drug treatment policy for high blood pressure.

Final conclusion: reducing salt added to processed foods would lower blood pressure at least twice as much as moderate dietary reduction and could prevent about 75,000 deaths a year in Britain, plus substantial disability (corrected figure noted).
Single-word fragment completing the final sentence, 'disability.', ending the conclusions of the abstract on reduced disability from salt reduction in Britain.

Opening of the document: introduces the long-standing research on salt and blood pressure and notes that a growing debate questions the benefits of salt restriction based on some observational studies.

Presents the core quantitative claim that cutting daily salt from 9-12 g to under 5-6 g yields major cardiovascular and healthcare cost benefits, and begins citing the WHO's recommendation to reduce salt intake.

Describes WHO policy: salt reduction is a top priority against non-communicable diseases and hypertension, stroke, and CVD deaths. Also introduces the counterargument that very low salt intake may raise CVD risk.
Discusses the remaining uncertainty about low-salt risks, calls for future research to set optimal sodium targets, and urges consensus on the benefits of salt reduction for CVD prevention.
Concluding statement: salt reduction strategies should stay at the top of the public health agenda.

Introduction to the Yanomamo Indians, an unacculturated Amazon rainforest tribe that uses no dietary salt, framing the study of sodium hormonal regulation and blood pressure in lifelong low-sodium conditions.
Blood pressure trends across the lifespan in Yanomamo adults, plus 24-hour urinary sodium excretion measurements (about 1 mEq) showing extreme sodium restriction in adult male Indians.
Hormonal findings: plasma renin activity is elevated, comparable to civilized subjects on 10 mEq sodium diets, and aldosterone excretion matches acculturated subjects on low-sodium diets.

Interpretation that life-long low sodium intake produces hormonal adjustments similar to acute sodium restriction, and that elevated renin and aldosterone may be the ancestral human norm, with civilized control values depressed by excess modern salt intake.
Concluding fragment stating that civilized control hormone values are depressed by excessive salt intake in contemporary diets.

Introduction/background of the GBD 2010 comparative risk assessment: motivation for quantifying disease burden from risk factors, noting no complete global revision since the 2000 assessment and no prior analysis of changes over time.
Methods overview: estimation of deaths and DALYs (YLD plus YLL) attributable to 67 risk factors and risk clusters across 21 regions for 1990 and 2010.

Methods detail: exposure distributions by year, region, sex and age, and relative risks obtained from systematic review of published and unpublished data, combined with GBD 2010 cause-specific burden estimates.

Methods on attributable burden calculation relative to the theoretical-minimum-risk exposure, plus incorporation of uncertainty; then the start of the Findings: leading global risks in 2010, led by high blood pressure.

Findings on global rankings: 2010 leaders were high blood pressure, tobacco smoking, and alcohol use; 1990 leaders were childhood underweight, household air pollution from solid fuels, and tobacco, with percentages of global DALYs and uncertainty intervals.
Findings on diet and activity: dietary risks and physical inactivity together accounted for 10.0% of global DALYs in 2010, with low fruit and high sodium diets most prominent.

Findings on childhood risks: unimproved water and sanitation and childhood micronutrient deficiencies declined in rank from 1990 to 2010; in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia, childhood underweight, household air pollution, and breastfeeding practices remained leading risks.

Findings on regional patterns: alcohol use led in Eastern Europe, most of Latin America and southern sub-Saharan Africa; high blood pressure led in much of Asia, North Africa/Middle East and central Europe.

Findings on smoking and body weight: smoking remained the top risk in high-income North America and western Europe, while high body-mass index rose and leads in Australasia and southern Latin America.

Interpretation: global shift in risk burden from childhood communicable diseases toward adult non-communicable diseases, attributed to ageing, lower child mortality, changing causes of death and risk exposures.

Interpretation on new evidence: revised magnitudes for unimproved water and sanitation, vitamin A and zinc deficiencies, and ambient particulate matter, and the regional variation in the epidemiological transition.

Conclusion: the epidemiological shift and leading risks vary widely by region, with sub-Saharan Africa still dominated by poverty-related and child-affecting risks; also includes the funding source (Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation).
Final fragment of the funding acknowledgement, naming the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation as the study's funder.
Opening of a study on serum lipid profiles of 62 adult Yanomamo Indians in the Amazonian rain forest, introducing sample size, measurements taken, and age/sex demographics.
Reports mean serum cholesterol and triglyceride levels for Yanomamo men and women, comparing them with Western and U.S. samples, and notes significant sex differences in total cholesterol and BMI.

Presents remaining sex differences in HDL and LDL cholesterol, multivariate regression results showing age as an independent correlate of cholesterol and BMI as borderline, and begins the conclusion about very low lipid levels.
Concluding statement attributing the very low serum lipid levels in this isolated population to a largely vegetarian, low-fat, high-fiber diet and high physical activity linked to low BMI.

Background and rationale of a study on dietary salt, plasma sodium, and blood pressure, introducing the unclear mechanism of salt-related blood pressure elevation and the aim to test a single salted meal.

Study design: a randomized crossover trial in 10 normotensive volunteers comparing soup with and without 6 g added salt, measuring the resulting rise in plasma sodium concentration (3.13 mmol/l) and blood pressure.

Key results: salted soup raised plasma sodium and systolic blood pressure, with a significant positive correlation and a regression estimate of 1.91 mm Hg systolic rise per 1 mmol/l plasma sodium increase.
Conclusion: each salty meal alters plasma sodium, suggesting that this change is a potential mechanism linking dietary salt intake to blood pressure increases.
Introduces the Yanomami Indians' participation in the INTERSALT study of blood pressure and salt intake across 52 populations, including the study objectives and sample design.

Describes the INTERSALT study scope (10,079 participants aged 20-59 in 52 populations across 32 countries) and the variables measured, such as 24-hour urinary sodium and potassium, BP, BMI, and alcohol intake.
Reports the Yanomami results: very low urinary sodium, mean systolic and diastolic BP values, absence of hypertension and obesity, no alcohol knowledge, and BP not rising with age.

Gives the key finding that urinary sodium correlates positively and urinary potassium negatively with systolic BP in Yanomami, independent of age and BMI, and states the study conclusion on salt intake and blood pressure.
Concludes that the positive salt-BP relation held across diverse INTERSALT populations including the Yanomami, and notes that qualitative observation of their lifestyle added information.

Introduces the study design: 19 patients with mild-to-moderate essential hypertension, baseline BP 156/98 mm Hg, advised to stop adding salt and avoid sodium-rich foods, then entering an 8-week double-blind randomised crossover trial of 'Slow Sodium' versus placebo.

Reports the crossover results: supine BP was 7.1 mm Hg (6.1%) lower during the placebo phase than during Slow Sodium (p<0.001), and urinary sodium excretion was about 162 mmol/24h on Slow Sodium versus 86 mmol/24h on placebo (p<0.001).

Concludes that potassium excretion did not differ between arms and that moderate sodium restriction (no added salt, avoiding sodium-laden foods) should be incorporated into essential hypertension management.
Closing fragment of the conclusion, ending the sentence on management of essential hypertension.

Opening section of a document on reducing dietary salt: covers high blood pressure as a cardiovascular risk factor, the evidence linking high salt intake to hypertension and related diseases (stroke, kidney disease, stomach cancer, etc.), and the benefits of salt reduction.

Middle section arguing that salt reduction lowers blood pressure and cardiovascular disease with no harmful effects and high cost-effectiveness, then introduces national salt intake recommendations, starting with France's targets.

Section on France's specific daily salt targets by sex and age, the finding that 80% of salt comes from manufactured foods (so the food industry must take part), and the role of consumer education in reducing intake.
Closing section noting that salt intake in France has already fallen but must keep decreasing, followed by the 2013 Elsevier Masson copyright notice.

Opening of the 2005 US study abstract: aims to estimate mortality effects of 12 modifiable dietary, lifestyle, and metabolic risk factors using consistent methods, beginning with high blood glucose, LDL cholesterol, and blood pressure.

Abstract continuation listing the 12 risk factors (overweight-obesity, trans fats, salt, polyunsaturated fats, omega-3, fruits and vegetables, physical inactivity, alcohol, smoking) and the start of the Methods and Findings section describing data sources.

Methods of the abstract: risk factor exposure data from US national health surveys and NCHS mortality statistics, plus effect estimates from systematic reviews and meta-analyses adjusted for confounders and regression dilution bias.

Methods conclusion (estimating deaths attributable to non-optimal exposure by age and sex) and the start of the key results: 2005 smoking and high blood pressure death estimates with confidence intervals.

Main quantitative results of the study: deaths attributed to smoking (467,000) and high blood pressure (395,000), plus overweight-obesity, physical inactivity, and the leading dietary risks of salt, omega-3, and trans fats.
Dietary risk results and alcohol findings: salt, omega-3, and trans fat death estimates, then the net effect of alcohol, with 26,000 deaths averted versus 90,000 deaths caused.
Abstract conclusions: smoking and high blood pressure cause the most US deaths and have effective interventions, while other dietary, lifestyle, and metabolic risks also contribute substantially.
Start of the Editors' Summary, introducing modifiable factors behind premature deaths and the effect of overweight/obesity and smoking on life expectancy.

Editors' Summary explanation of the three groups of modifiable risk factors: lifestyle (smoking, inactivity, alcohol), with alcohol's protective effects noted, and dietary risks such as salt and low fruit/vegetable intake.
Editors' Summary on dietary risk factors and definition of metabolic risk factors, which raise cardiovascular disease and diabetes risk.

Editors' Summary listing metabolic risk factors (high blood pressure, cholesterol, obesity) and the 'Why Was This Study Done?' section introducing the premise that changing modifiable risks can reduce preventable deaths.
Why the study was done: policies and regulations can reduce risk exposures, and knowing how many deaths each risk causes is needed before setting health priorities.
Gaps in prior research that motivated the study: inconsistent methods for attributing deaths to risk factors, and little attention to dietary and metabolic risks.
Description of this study's approach: estimating deaths from 12 modifiable risks in the US using comparative risk assessment, which models deaths prevented by shifting exposures to optimal levels.
Explanation of comparative risk assessment and the start of 'What Did the Researchers Do and Find?': data sources of national health surveys and NCHS 2005 death statistics.
Methods summary: published studies quantify how each risk raises disease mortality, and a mathematical formula converts this into deaths; also begins the 2.5 million US deaths in 2005 figure.

Key findings in plain language: nearly half a million deaths linked to smoking and about 400,000 to high blood pressure, each roughly one in five US adult deaths; overweight-obesity and inactivity each near one in ten.

Plain-language findings on diet and alcohol: high salt intake caused about 4% of adult deaths, and alcohol prevented 26,000 deaths while causing 90,000 other deaths including road accidents and violence.
What the findings mean: smoking and high blood pressure are the leading preventable causes of US death, and several other modifiable risks also contribute many deaths.
Interpretation and limits: estimate accuracy depends on data quality, targeting a few risk factors could greatly reduce premature US mortality, and findings may partly generalize to other countries.

Implications: effective individual and population interventions already exist for smoking and high blood pressure, and combined regulation, pricing, and education could reduce exposure to other risks.
Closing of the Editors' Summary on policy implications for other risk factors, followed by the 'Additional Information' pointer to the online version of the summary.
Final reference: the DOI link (journal.pmed.1000058) to the online version of the summary, ending the document.

Introduces the first of four evidence sources for the claim that eliminating dietary salt can prevent hypertension: epidemiological data from unacculturated peoples showing hypertension prevalence falls as salt intake falls.

Continues the list of four evidence sources, covering hemodynamic studies that treat chronic experimental hypertension as a homeostatic response to sustained extracellular fluid volume expansion, and the ECF comparison between salt eaters and no-salt eaters.

Gives the fourth evidence source (blood pressure falls track ECF reduction under strict salt restriction or diuretics) and the document's conclusion that restricting salt below 2 g/day would likely prevent essential hypertension, though the underlying mechanism remains unclear.
Final sentence of the passage, concluding that preventing essential hypertension through salt reduction would eliminate it as a major public health problem.

Introduction to the study: the US diet is high in salt, mostly from processed foods, and the paper uses the CHD Policy Model to assess methods for estimating cardiovascular benefits of reducing dietary salt by up to 3 g/day.

Continuation of the methods, describing analyses of cardiovascular disease rates and costs across age, sex, and race subgroups, comparison with other cardiovascular risk interventions, and cost-effectiveness versus drug treatment of hypertension; it then begins the results with projected reductions in CHD cases and strokes.

Main results of a 3 g/day salt reduction: projected annual reductions in CHD cases, strokes, MIs, and all-cause deaths, plus how benefits differ across subgroups (blacks, women, older and younger adults).

Comparative and economic results: salt reduction's cardiovascular benefits rival those of reducing tobacco, obesity, or cholesterol, and a regulatory intervention would yield substantial quality-adjusted life-year gains and healthcare cost savings annually.

Cost-effectiveness findings: even a modest 1 g/day reduction phased in over 2010–2019 would be cost-saving and more cost-effective than medication treatment of all hypertensive individuals; the conclusions section begins here.
Concluding statement that modest dietary salt reduction could substantially lower cardiovascular events and medical costs and should be adopted as a public health target.
