Introduces the rising hypertension burden in Nigeria (prevalence up from 11% two decades ago to about 30%) within the wider global context of cardiovascular disease deaths in low- and middle-income countries, framing the review's motivation.

States the review's aim: examining population-wide dietary salt reduction as a way to lower hypertension burden in Nigeria, covering the supporting evidence, approaches used in other countries, and recommendations for the Nigerian context.

Concludes the abstract by suggesting that effective population-wide salt reduction could match the mortality and morbidity gains historically achieved by 19th-century provision of drains and safe water, with the 2013 Royal Society for Public Health copyright notice.
Final fragment of the abstract containing the end of the 19th-century drains and safe water comparison and the 2013 Royal Society for Public Health copyright line.
Introduction and objectives of the study: measuring US disease, injury, and risk-factor burden from 1990-2010 and comparing with OECD countries, motivated by national health policy needs.

Study design: the Global Burden of Disease 2010 analysis covering 291 diseases and injuries, 1160 sequelae, and 67 risk factors across 187 countries, used to compare US outcomes with 34 OECD countries.
Methods definition of YLLs: years of life lost from premature mortality, computed by multiplying deaths at each age by a reference life expectancy at that age.

Methods definitions of YLDs and DALYs: years lived with disability calculated from prevalence times disability weight, with DALYs defined as the sum of YLDs and YLLs, and disability meaning any short- or long-term health loss.

Methods for risk-factor attributable burden and HALE: risk-related deaths and DALYs come from systematic reviews and relative risks, and healthy life expectancy summarizes length of life and ill health; results begin with US life expectancy trends.

Results on life expectancy and leading causes of years lost: US life expectancy rose from 75.2 to 78.2 years and HALE from 65.8 to 68.1 years (1990-2010), with ischemic heart disease, lung cancer, stroke, COPD, and road injury causing the most YLLs in 2010.

Results on trends and disability: age-standardized YLL rates rose for Alzheimer disease, drug use disorders, chronic kidney disease, kidney cancer, and falls; low back pain, depression, musculoskeletal disorders, neck pain, and anxiety led YLDs, which grew as a share of DALYs with population aging.

Results on risk factors and international ranking: dietary risks, smoking, high BMI, high blood pressure, high glucose, physical inactivity, and alcohol use were leading risk factors, and the US rank among 34 OECD countries declined on death rate, YLLs, life expectancy, and HALE.

Detailed OECD rank changes for the US from 1990 to 2010 (death rate 18th to 27th, YLL rate 23rd to 28th, YLD rate 5th to 6th, life expectancy 20th to 27th, HALE 14th to 26th), followed by the start of the conclusions.

Conclusions: the US made substantial health progress, with rising life expectancy and HALE and falling all-cause death rates, but chronic morbidity and disability now make up nearly half the burden and US gains lag other wealthy nations.
Final conclusion sentence: US population health improvements from 1990 to 2010 have not kept pace with advances in other wealthy nations.

Opening of the review: introduces brown adipose tissue (BAT) and its role in fatty acid and glucose oxidation, and states the review's aim of showing L-arginine regulates BAT growth to reduce obesity.
Recent findings: L-arginine reduces white adipose tissue in obese rats, pregnant sheep, and humans with type II diabetes, and enhances BAT growth in fetuses and postnatal animals.

Molecular and whole-body effects of L-arginine: upregulates PGC-1α, nitric oxide synthase, heme oxygenase, and AMPK; increases blood flow, lipolysis, and substrate catabolism while inhibiting fatty acid synthesis and oxidative stress.
Summary of mechanisms: L-arginine increases BAT growth via gene expression, nitric oxide signaling, and protein synthesis, boosting energy substrate oxidation and reducing white fat accretion.
Conclusion: L-arginine is promising for preventing and treating obesity in humans.

Introduction to a study on spiced food and metabolic rate: background on the thermic effect of food (also called specific dynamic action or diet-induced thermogenesis), first noted since Lavoisier, and its early focus on macronutrients.

Review of prior research on the thermic effect: early work centered on macronutrients, and later studies showed minor dietary constituents such as caffeine and methylxanthines in tea and coffee also strongly affect metabolic rate.

Literature context showing alcohol also raises metabolic rate, and stating the paper's aim: to examine another minor dietary constituent, spices, whose effect on metabolic rate has received little study despite rising use.
Study scope: estimates that about 40 spices are used in modern diets, and identifies the two spices tested in this communication, chilli (capsicum annuum) and mustard (Brassica juncea).

Introduction to the document on brown adipose tissue (BAT) anatomy: it raises why BAT sits where it does in humans, proposing that its distribution protects vital organs from hypothermia via adaptive thermogenesis, and notes relevance to obesity and type 2 diabetes therapy.

Continues the introduction: argues that anti-obesity and anti-diabetes interventions must act on BAT function in people at thermoneutrality, and that differing responsiveness across BAT depots suggests subtle, previously overlooked functions and regulatory mechanisms.
Concluding sentence of the introduction: predicts that BAT's depot-specific differences in responsiveness will reveal more subtle, previously unrecognized functions and control mechanisms.
Introduction and aims of a study on capsaicin (CAPS) and energy expenditure, substrate oxidation, and blood pressure during a 25% negative energy balance, including the study design overview.
Methods describing the four 36-hour respiration chamber sessions (100%CAPS, 100%Control, 75%CAPS, 75%Control) and the capsaicin dose of 2.56 mg per meal from red chili pepper (39,050 SHU).
Results opening: the 25% induced deficit was effectively 20.5% due to adaptation, and diet-induced thermogenesis and resting energy expenditure comparisons across the conditions, with p-values.
Results on sleeping metabolic rate and fat oxidation across conditions versus 100%Control, with p-values for SMR and fat oxidation differences.

Results on respiratory quotient changes under CAPS versus Control at 75% intake, the lack of blood pressure difference, and the start of the conclusion on capsaicin counteracting reduced energy expenditure.
Conclusion stating that 2.56 mg capsaicin per meal supports negative energy balance, promotes fat oxidation, and does not significantly raise blood pressure.
Trial registration information for the study, listing the Nederlands Trial Register number NTR2944.

Opening of the document: introduces dinitrophenol's early 1930s popularity as a weight-loss drug, promoted by Stanford clinical pharmacologist Maurice Tainter, and begins describing its narrow safety margin leading to harm.

Continuation of the document's discussion of dinitrophenol: physicians eventually abandoned the drug after thousands were irreversibly harmed, and the 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act was needed before regulators could stop patent medicine sellers from marketing it.
Final fragment of the document: closes the sentence describing the misleading promise of a drug that would safely melt away fat, which patent medicine sellers used to lure Americans.

Introduction of a review on capsaicin and capsinoids as food ingredients that raise energy expenditure and reduce body fat, framed around the role of brown adipose tissue (BAT) in humans and the possibility of other antiobesity foods.

Key recent finding: a single oral dose of capsinoids raises energy expenditure only in people with metabolically active BAT, showing capsinoids work by activating BAT and explaining inconsistent results in earlier studies; also notes human BAT may consist largely of inducible beige adipocytes.

Evidence for the beige-adipocyte nature of human BAT: its gene expression resembles murine beige cells, and supraclavicular preadipocytes can differentiate into brown-like adipocytes in vitro, indicating inducible brown adipogenesis in adults.

Summary and conclusion: because human BAT is inducible, prolonged capsinoid intake could recruit active BAT to raise energy expenditure and lower body fat, and many other food ingredients may likewise activate BAT for obesity prevention.
Closing statement that beyond capsinoids, numerous dietary ingredients are expected to activate BAT and could help prevent obesity in everyday life.

Introduction stating the clinical problem: supraclavicular lymph node metastasis imaging on 18F-FDG PET, and the commonly cited but questioned 'muscle uptake' explanation, motivating PET/CT correlation.
Methods section describing the retrospective review of the first 359 whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT studies (347 patients) and how supraclavicular abnormal uptake was evaluated against CT.

Methods definition of the three uptake patterns: pattern A (USA-fat, fat-localized uptake without node or muscle correlate), pattern B (muscle uptake), and pattern C (lymph node or soft-tissue mass uptake).

Results start: prevalence of abnormal supraclavicular uptake (49 of 347 patients, 14.1%), demographics, and counts for muscle uptake (group B, 20 patients) and definite lymph nodes (group C, 15 patients).
Results on the USA-fat group: 14 patients (4.0%) with fat-localized uptake and very low Hounsfield foci, confirmed on 68Ge and non-attenuation-corrected images.

Results describing USA-fat uptake pattern (bilateral, symmetric, intense, multifocal) and statistical comparisons of age and SUV measures between groups, showing SUVs could not separate USA-fat from nodal uptake.
Results on SUV values showing muscle uptake (group B) had significantly lower SUVs, plus the conclusion that so-called muscle uptake may often be the unrelated USA-fat process.
Conclusion interpreting USA-fat as a likely nonpathologic process, hypothesized to reflect brown fat, and advising that it not be mistaken for metastasis or muscle uptake.
Final sentence of the conclusion warning clinicians not to misread intense supraclavicular fat uptake as malignant metastasis or muscle uptake.

Introduction/abstract of a review on brown adipose tissue (BAT) and body weight management; explains that BAT's many mitochondria and UCP1 make it inefficient at ATP production but efficient at heat generation, supporting thermoregulation.

Continues the introduction: BAT's energy-wasting heat production enables body temperature regulation; debate over whether this thermogenesis affects body weight; recent rediscovery of BAT in adults motivates anti-obesity research.

Concludes the rationale: obese individuals have less BAT mass/activity than lean people, motivating new obesity treatments; states the review's aim to examine BAT's thermogenic relevance and its usefulness for human weight control.
Final sentence of the review's introduction stating its scope: the physiological relevance of brown adipose tissue to thermogenesis and its potential for body weight control in humans.

Abstract of a study on measuring human brown adipose tissue (BAT) with MRI; introduces an MRI protocol exploiting BAT's higher water-to-fat ratio and contrast under water-saturation in fast spin echo and T2-weighted images, versus prior 18F-FDG PET/CT methods.

Abstract continuation of the human brown adipose tissue MRI study: reports higher water-to-fat ratio in BAT via Dixon water/fat images, MRI-derived BAT volume and location matching PET/CT in the same subjects, and introduces the cold-challenge fMRI result.
Final sentence of the abstract on human brown adipose tissue MRI: cold challenge at 14 °C produces significant fMRI BOLD signal increases in BAT, showing functional MRI can assess BAT activity.

Introduces 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), a weight-loss agent sold online that causes uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation and is linked to serious toxicity; this chunk begins describing the classic toxic symptom complex of phenol-based products.

Continues the symptom description (hyperthermia, tachycardia, diaphoresis, tachypnoea, leading to death), notes fatalities since the early 1900s, cites 62 published deaths in the literature, and states the review's aims.
Concludes the document's stated aims: the review will describe the pattern and pathophysiology of DNP toxicity and summarise previously reported DNP-associated fatalities.
Introduction and background of a study on brown adipose tissue (BAT) in adult humans, covering obesity, UCP1-mediated thermogenesis, and methods for analyzing 18F-FDG PET-CT scans.

Methods section describing the analysis of 3640 consecutive 18F-FDG PET-CT scans from 1972 patients and the criteria used to define substantial depots of putative brown adipose tissue (size, CT density, SUV threshold).

Continuation of methods: definition of BAT depots by CT density and FDG uptake, comparison of clinical indexes with date-matched controls, and UCP1 immunostaining of neck and supraclavicular biopsy specimens.

Results section: PET-CT identification of substantial BAT depots from anterior neck to thorax, histological confirmation of UCP1-positive multilocular adipocytes, and the start of sex-based detection rates.

Results on sex differences and predictors: BAT detected in 7.5% of women versus 3.1% of men (female:male ratio above 2:1), greater BAT mass and FDG uptake in women, and inverse associations with age and outdoor temperature.

Further predictors of BAT detection (beta-blocker use, body-mass index in older patients) and the start of the conclusions, stating that functionally active BAT exists in adults and is noninvasively quantifiable by PET-CT.
Concluding statement that BAT amount is inversely correlated with body-mass index, especially in older people, suggesting a potential role of BAT in adult human metabolism and obesity.
Introduces the study design: FDG-PET identification of brown adipose tissue (BAT) in 13 healthy young men after 2-hour cold exposure at 19 °C.

Splits subjects into BAT-positive (6, marked supraclavicular/paraspinal FDG uptake) and BAT-negative (7, none) groups, with similar BMI and body fat, and begins reporting warm-condition energy expenditure.

Reports energy expenditure results: warm baseline is similar between groups, cold exposure raises it markedly in BAT-positive subjects (+410 kcal/day) but only slightly in BAT-negative subjects (+42 kcal/day, not significant).

Links cold-induced energy expenditure rise positively to FDG-quantified BAT activity, and reports supraclavicular skin temperature changes, which dropped less near BAT deposits in the BAT-positive group (0.14 °C vs 0.60 °C).

Notes skin temperature changes in non-BAT regions were similar between groups, and concludes that BAT contributes to cold-induced whole-body energy expenditure and to control of body temperature and adiposity in adult humans.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that BAT helps regulate body temperature and adiposity in adult humans.

Introduction and objectives of a human study on capsinoids (nonpungent capsaicin analogs), examining their acute effect on energy expenditure and its relation to brown adipose tissue (BAT) activity measured by FDG-PET.

Study design: 18 healthy young men underwent FDG-PET after cold exposure, then energy expenditure and skin temperature were measured for 2 h under warm conditions after oral capsinoids (9 mg) or placebo, in a single-blind, randomized, crossover design.
Results grouping: 10 subjects were BAT-positive (marked FDG uptake in supraclavicular and paraspinal fat) and 8 were BAT-negative, which sets up the comparison of capsinoid effects between groups.

Key quantitative results: resting energy expenditure did not differ between BAT-positive and BAT-negative groups, but capsinoids raised EE by about 15.2 kJ/h in BAT-positive subjects versus 1.7 kJ/h in BAT-negative subjects (P < 0.01).

Conclusion and registration: placebo had no effect and capsinoids did not change skin temperature near BAT, leading to the conclusion that capsinoids increase energy expenditure via BAT activation in humans; trial registered as UMIN 000006073.
Trial registration identifier: the study was registered at the UMIN Clinical Trials Registry under number UMIN 000006073, the final fragment of the abstract.
Introduction of the USA-Fat study: defines supraclavicular fat FDG uptake on PET/CT, its suspected link to brown adipose tissue, and the hypothesis that it varies with ambient temperature.
Study aim and methods: evaluates USA-Fat frequency versus outdoor temperature, using 1,017 consecutive clinical whole-body PET/CT scans with 18F-FDG from July 2001 to June 2002.
Results: USA-Fat found in 68 scans from 62 patients, with incidence 13.7% in January-March (cold season) versus 4.1% the rest of the year.
Conclusion: USA-Fat is more frequent in cooler months, suggesting cold stimulation of brown adipose tissue as its underlying cause.

Introduction of the study: explains brown adipose tissue's role in heat production and fat burning, prior FDG-PET/CT findings that BAT declines with age and contributes to fat accumulation, and motivates BAT recruitment for fat reduction.

Study design and acute findings: capsinoids and repeated cold are tested in healthy low-BAT subjects; a 2-hour 19°C cold exposure raises energy expenditure, and cold-induced EE increase correlates strongly with BAT activity independent of age and fat-free mass.

Chronic intervention results: 6 weeks of daily 2-hour 17°C cold exposure increases BAT activity and cold-induced thermogenesis while reducing body fat, with inverse correlation between BAT change and fat mass change; daily capsinoid intake also raises cold-induced thermogenesis.
Conclusion: the study shows human BAT can be recruited even when its activity is low, through cold exposure or capsinoids, contributing to body fat reduction.

This chunk opens the abstract of a 2009 Karger study on faecal bacteria in vegetarians vs. omnivores, stating the aims (qPCR and DGGE-based changes in bacteria, Bacteroides, Bifidobacterium, Clostridium cluster IV) and the methods (15 vegetarians, 14 omnivores, qPCR, PCR-DGGE, PCA, Shannon index).

This chunk continues the abstract's results: vegetarians showed 12% higher bacterial DNA, a non-significant trend toward less Clostridium cluster IV and more Bacteroides, with the differences attributed to high interindividual variation.

This chunk reports the PCA grouping of bacteria with Clostridium cluster IV and two DGGE bands significantly more frequent in omnivores, one identified as Faecalibacterium sp. and one 97.9% similar to an uncultured gut bacterium (DQ793301).

This chunk gives the study's conclusions: a vegetarian diet alters the gut microbiota, notably reducing and changing the diversity of Clostridium cluster IV, with effects on host metabolism and disease risk still unknown, followed by the copyright line.
This final chunk is a fragment of the conclusion sentence about host metabolism and disease risks, plus the 2009 Copyright S. Karger AG, Basel notice that ends the abstract.

Introduction and overview of a 2011 Obesity Reviews review on endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) and human obesity, noting effects vary by chemical type, dose, timing, and gender, with DDE showing the most consistent association with increased body size.

Summarizes chemical-specific findings: nearly all DDE studies link exposure to larger body size, PCB results depend on dose, timing, and gender, and hexachlorobenzene, polybrominated biphenyls, beta-hexachlorocyclohexane, oxychlordane, and phthalates are generally associated with increased body size.

Covers dioxin and furan findings (polychlorinated dibenzodioxins and dibenzofurans linked to weight gain or waist circumference increase or showing no association) and the single bisphenol A study, which found no association with obesity.

Reports that prenatal (in utero) EDC exposure may cause permanent physiological changes predisposing to later weight gain, and concludes that some endocrine disruptors may contribute to the obesity epidemic alongside commonly recognized factors.

Final concluding sentence stating EDCs may be a contributor to the obesity epidemic beyond conventional causes, followed by the 2011 copyright and publisher attribution (Obesity Reviews / International Association for the Study of Obesity).

Introduction and study rationale: links high-fat diet to obesity and its health risks, notes lack of research on high-fat diet effects on lung function, and states the aim to test whether a high-fat meal increases airway inflammation and reduces pulmonary function in healthy subjects.

Study aim restated with methods: pulmonary function tests (FEV1, FVC, FEF25-75) and exhaled nitric oxide (eNO, a marker of airway inflammation) measured in 20 healthy inactive subjects before and 2 h after a high-fat meal.

Methods continued: meal size (1 g fat per kg body weight, about 74 g fat), venous blood collection for total cholesterol, triglycerides, and CRP (systemic inflammation) pre and post meal, and body composition measured by DXA.
Key results: high-fat meal raised triglycerides by 93% and total cholesterol by 4%, and increased eNO by 19% (17.2 to 20.6 ppb, p<0.05); eNO correlated with triglycerides at baseline and post-meal.

Conclusion of results: despite eNO rising, pulmonary function and CRP were unchanged; the authors conclude that the triglyceride-driven rise in exhaled NO suggests high-fat diets may promote chronic airway and lung inflammatory disease.
Final sentence of the discussion/conclusion: a high-fat diet may contribute to chronic inflammatory diseases of the airway and lung.
Introduction/objective of an AHS-2 study on blood pressure in white vegetarians and omnivores, motivating the work by noting lower BMI and higher fruit and vegetable intake as possible explanations.

Design and setting: a calibration sub-study of AHS-2 participants who attended church-based clinics across the USA and Canada and completed validated FFQs, with dietary patterns (vegan, lacto-ovo, partial, omnivore) defined by criteria.

Study subjects (500 white AHS-2 participants) and main results: covariate-adjusted regressions show vegans and lacto-ovo vegetarians have lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure than omnivores, with specific beta coefficients and p-values.

Results on medication and hypertension: vegetarians, mainly vegans, are less likely to take antihypertensive drugs, and hypertension is defined by BP thresholds or medication use, with odds ratios versus omnivores for vegans, lacto-ovo and partial vegetarians.
Hypertension odds ratios with confidence intervals for each dietary group, noting that the effects shrink after adjusting for BMI, followed by the start of the conclusions.
Conclusion: vegetarians, especially vegans, have lower systolic and diastolic BP and less hypertension than omnivores, but this advantage is only partly explained by their lower body mass.

Opening of a document on red meat, processed meat, and colorectal cancer risk: introduces the controversy, meta-analysis findings of a modest 20-30% increased risk, WCRF-AICR intake guidelines, and the authors' rat studies on beef and cured pork.

Mechanistic middle section explaining that heme iron is the main promoter of colon carcinogenesis in meat (via N-nitrosation or fat peroxidation) and that dietary additives can suppress heme iron's toxic effects, continuing the cured-meat rat study.

Concluding section reporting that dietary calcium and alpha-tocopherol suppressed colon carcinogenesis in rats fed cooked, nitrite-treated, oxidized high-heme cured meat, that a volunteer study supported these protective effects in humans, and that such additives could prevent colorectal cancer; ends with the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
Standalone copyright line (Copyright 2011 Elsevier B.V.) that closes the document on red meat, heme iron, and colorectal cancer prevention; contains no substantive content beyond the notice.

Abstract opening of a study on Western Australian Raine Cohort adolescents (age 14), introducing the objective of examining dietary patterns and mental health and the CBCL behaviour measure used in the methods.

Methods continuing from the CBCL description: identification of Western and Healthy dietary patterns via factor analysis of a 212-item food frequency questionnaire, and the general linear modelling approach.

Methods covering the confounder adjustment list (energy intake, BMI, physical activity, screen use, family factors, income, gender, maternal education), followed by the start of the Results with CBCL total and internalizing coefficients for the Western pattern.

Results reporting the association of the Western dietary pattern (takeaway foods, confectionery, red meat) with higher externalizing and internalizing problem scores, and the link between better behaviour scores and leafy greens and fresh fruit from the Healthy pattern.

Conclusion of the abstract: the Western dietary pattern is implicated in poorer behavioural outcomes, while higher fresh fruit and leafy green vegetable intake is linked to better behaviour in adolescents.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, restating that fresh fruit and leafy green vegetables are associated with better behavioural outcomes.

Introduction and methods of a study on vegetarian diets and diabetes incidence in the Adventist Health Study-2, describing the cohort of 15,200 men and 26,187 women (17.3% Black) free of diabetes at baseline and the dietary groups used.

Methods and early results: diet groups (vegan, lacto-ovo, pesco, semi-vegetarian, non-vegetarian reference), the two-year follow-up questionnaire, and the raw percentage of diabetes cases in each diet group (0.54% vegan up to 2.12% non-vegetarian).

Results on ethnicity and adjusted risk: Black participants had higher odds of diabetes (OR 1.364) than non-Blacks, and multiple logistic regression begins reporting lower odds for vegans relative to non-vegetarians after covariate adjustment.

Adjusted multivariable results: vegans, lacto-ovo and semi-vegetarians had significantly lower diabetes odds than non-vegetarians, with stratified estimates for non-Black and Black participants showing which diets were protective in each group.

Stratified findings and sensitivity analysis: protective associations among Blacks (vegan and lacto-ovo) and non-Blacks, noting that associations strengthened when BMI was removed from the models, followed by the start of the conclusion.

Conclusion of the study: vegetarian diets (vegan, lacto-ovo, semi-vegetarian) are independently linked to substantially lower diabetes incidence, with the protective effect in Blacks comparable in size to the excess risk associated with Black ethnicity.

Abstract of a 1990s-era clinical study (Ornish-style lifestyle program) on a 12-day strictly vegetarian, very low-fat diet with exercise and stress management; this chunk covers the objective, study population (500 participants in a hospital-based live-in program), and the start of the results.

Results section of the study abstract reporting short-term improvements: about 11% reduction in total serum cholesterol and 6% drop in blood pressure (both p < 0.001), weight loss of 2.5 kg for men and 1 kg for women, and mention of triglyceride behavior in subgroups.

Continuation of the results and the conclusion of the abstract: triglyceride exceptions in specific female subgroups, a 19% decrease in HDL cholesterol measured in 66 subjects, and the opening of the conclusion about the strict vegetarian diet.

Final conclusion sentence of the abstract stating that a strict, very low-fat, animal-product-free vegetarian diet combined with exercise and weight loss effectively lowers serum cholesterol and blood pressure.

Introduction and rationale: high-fat meal triglyceride-rich lipoproteins as a possible atherogenic factor beyond serum cholesterol, study aim to test their direct effect on endothelial function in healthy volunteers.
Study design: 10 healthy normocholesterolemic volunteers given isocaloric 900-calorie high-fat (50 g) or low-fat (0 g) meals, with flow-mediated vasoactivity monitored for 6 hours.

Methods and early results: brachial artery flow-mediated vasoactivity measured by 7.5-MHz ultrasound after arterial occlusion, serum lipids and glucose sampled; triglycerides rose from 94 to 147 mg/dl at 2 hours after the high-fat meal.
Key results: after the high-fat meal, flow-dependent vasoactivity fell from 21% to about 10-11% at 2, 3, and 4 hours (p<0.05 vs low-fat), with no changes after the low-fat meal.

Correlation findings: fasting LDL cholesterol inversely correlated with preprandial flow-mediated vasoactivity (r = -0.47), and the postprandial vasoactivity change correlated with the 2-hour triglyceride change (r = -0.51).
Conclusions: a single high-fat meal transiently impairs endothelial function, suggesting a mechanism by which high-fat diets may promote atherosclerosis independently of cholesterol changes.
Fragment ending the correlation sentence: the reported correlation coefficient r = -0.51 between postprandial vasoactivity change and 2-hour triglyceride change, a continuation of chunk 6's sentence.

Opening of the Finnish North Karelia Project paper: introduces the global NCD burden rising in developing countries due to lifestyle and dietary changes, framing diet and nutrition as a major public health challenge.

Background on Finland's rapid post-WWII health transition with very high cardiovascular mortality, and the launch of the North Karelia Project in 1972 as a community-based, later national, diet and lifestyle programme for CVD prevention.

Description of the North Karelia Project's approach: a strong theoretical base, comprehensive strategies, and broad community organisation with strong public participation as key elements for lifestyle and CVD prevention.

Reported outcomes of the project: changes in diet especially fat consumption, reductions in population serum cholesterol and blood pressure, and a 73% (North Karelia) and 65% (nationwide) decline in working-age ischaemic heart disease mortality from 1971 to 1995.

Context on North Karelia as a rural, low socio-economic region with social problems in the 1970s-1980s, and the project's low-cost approach relying on people's participation and community organisations.

Expansion of the project into national activities (expert guidelines, media, industry collaboration, policy), and the argument that similar nutrition intervention principles could be adapted for developing countries.
Concluding statement of the paper: it reviews North Karelia Project experiences in light of the needs of less-industrialised countries and offers general recommendations.

Introduction and study aim: links gut microbial butyrate production to colonic health, immunity and epigenetics, and introduces the butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase gene and Clostridium clusters IV and XIVa as markers, with faecal samples from young omnivores, vegetarians and elderly omnivores.

Study population and methods: describes the three cohorts (young omnivores, vegetarians, elderly omnivores, with their mean ages) and the questionnaire-based diet and lifestyle assessment, then reports that elderly participants had significantly fewer butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase gene copies than young omnivores (P=0.014).

Gene copy and variant results: vegetarians had the highest butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase gene copy numbers (P=0.048), and melting-curve variability of the Roseburia/Eubacterium rectale gene variant was greater in vegetarians than in the elderly; begins describing Clostridium cluster XIVa abundance.

Clostridium cluster XIVa abundance and conclusions: cluster XIVa was more abundant in vegetarians (P=0.049) and omnivores (P<0.01) than in the elderly, leading to the conclusion that elderly gut microbiota has reduced butyrate production capacity, implying higher risk of degenerative disease.

Final conclusion and publication notice: the authors propose the butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase gene as a valuable marker of gastrointestinal microbiota function, followed by the 2011 FEMS / Blackwell Publishing copyright statement.

Abstract opening of a 2008 study on vegetarian diet effects on fat/carbohydrate metabolism and collagen synthesis; introduces the aim and the oral mucosa gene expression comparison between omnivores and vegetarians.

Methods and early results from the study: qRT-PCR measurement of OCTN2, CPT1A, CPT1B and collagen (COL2A1) mRNA in oral mucosa, and the finding that vegetarians consumed 22% more carbohydrates than omnivores.

Core results and conclusion: vegetarians showed CPT1A (+50%) and OCTN2 (+10%) upregulation with collagen synthesis lowered by 10%, interpreted as a link between altered fat metabolism, reduced collagen synthesis, and aging.
Final sentence of the conclusion noting a possible role in aging, followed by the copyright line (S. Karger AG, Basel, 2008) closing the abstract.

Introduction to a pilot study on protein-source tryptophan (deoiled gourd seed) plus glucose as a treatment for social anxiety disorder, explaining why intact protein was previously dismissed due to competing LNAAs at the blood-brain barrier.

Explains the mechanism that glucose lowers competing LNAA serum levels, enabling gourd seed tryptophan to produce effects like pharmaceutical tryptophan, and introduces the anxiety measures and double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design for social phobia.

Describes the methods of the double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study: 1-week washout and random assignment of subjects to start with either gourd seed tryptophan plus carbohydrate or carbohydrate alone.

Covers the crossover sequence in which subjects received the opposite treatment at follow-up one week later, notes all 7 participants completed the 2-week protocol, and reports the key result that tryptophan with carbohydrate, but not carbohydrate alone, improved an objective anxiety measure.
Concludes the study by stating that protein-source tryptophan combined with a high glycemic carbohydrate is a potential anxiolytic for people with social phobia.

Introduces the question of whether a vegan diet reduces Parkinson's disease risk, citing case-control studies linking animal fat and cholesterol to higher PD risk and plant fat to no increase, plus comparison of PD prevalence across regions.

Continues the epidemiological comparison: vegan or quasi-vegan populations (sub-Saharan Africans, rural Chinese, Japanese) have lower PD rates, and since African-American rates match whites, environmental factors are likely the cause.

Summarizes that vegan diets may be notably protective against PD, but notes the evidence cannot separate which dietary component of animal products (saturated fat, animal protein, related compounds, or combined effects) drives the risk.

Proposes a mechanism: caloric restriction protects dopaminergic neurons in mice via heat-shock proteins, so vegan diets may protect similarly, and raises the possibility of vegan diets slowing PD progression.

Concludes that vegan diets might slow loss of dopaminergic neurons and help PD patients through vascular health and improved blood-brain barrier transport of L-dopa, warranting further study; includes the 2001 copyright line.
Contains only the copyright notice (Copyright 2001 Harcourt Publishers Ltd.) that closes the article on vegan diets and Parkinson's disease.

Introduction and stated purpose of a study on comprehensive diet and lifestyle changes in men with early, biopsy-proven prostate cancer, examining effects on PSA, treatment trends, and LNCaP cell growth after one year.

Methods: recruitment of men who declined conventional treatment, creating a nonintervention randomized control group, and the random assignment of 93 volunteers (PSA 4-10 ng/ml, Gleason score under 7) to lifestyle-change or usual-care groups.
Results begin: no experimental-group patients required conventional treatment versus 6 controls, which was due to rising PSA or MRI-detected disease progression.

Key results: PSA fell 4% in the experimental group and rose 6% in controls (p=0.016), and serum from the experimental group inhibited LNCaP prostate cancer cell growth far more than control serum (70% vs 9%).

Further results and conclusion: changes in PSA and LNCaP cell growth correlated with degree of diet and lifestyle change, suggesting intensive lifestyle changes may affect progression of early, low-grade prostate cancer.
Closing statement calling for further studies and longer-term followup to confirm the effects of lifestyle changes on early prostate cancer progression.

Background and rationale: explains that advanced CKD patients have positive phosphorus balance maintained by FGF23 and PTH-driven phosphaturia, underpinning the 800 mg/d dietary phosphate restriction, and raises the question of whether the protein source of phosphate matters.

Study design: a crossover trial in nine CKD patients (mean eGFR 32 ml/min) comparing vegetarian and meat diets with equivalent nutrients, with the methods describing inpatient monitoring during the final 24 hours of each 7-day diet period.
Key results: one week of a vegetarian diet lowered serum phosphorus and decreased FGF23 levels, and inpatient monitoring tracked blood and urine measurements across the diet periods.

Detailed findings: both diets showed similar diurnal variation in phosphorus, calcium, PTH, and fractional excretion of phosphorus, but differed significantly; 24-hour fractional excretion of phosphorus correlated strongly with a 2-hour fasting urine sample only on the vegetarian diet.
Conclusions and clinical implication: protein source significantly affects phosphorus homeostasis in CKD, so dietary counseling should address the protein source of phosphate as well as the amount.
Final sentence of the conclusion restating that dietary counseling for CKD patients should cover the protein source from which phosphate comes, not just the phosphate quantity.

Introduction to a study testing whether E. coli causing urinary tract infections (UTI) is linked to meat and production animals, stating the aim of finding a clonal link among animal, meat, and UTI isolates and describing the 22 matched B2 E. coli sources.

Methods section: the 22 B2 E. coli isolates from UTI patients, community humans, broiler meat, pork and broiler chickens were typed by microarray virulence profiling and PFGE clonal analysis, and nine selected isolates were tested for virulence in a mouse ascending UTI model.

Results of the study: UTI and community human strains were clonally related to meat strains, all nine tested isolates were virulent in the mouse UTI model, and isolates sharing a gene profile produced similar bacterial counts in urine, bladder and kidneys.

Conclusion of the study: the clonal link between meat and human E. coli is presented as solid evidence that UTI is a zoonosis, and the close human-UTI relationship suggests a point source such as contaminated meat.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the statement that a point source spread, such as through contaminated meat, may explain the close relationship between community and UTI isolates.

Introduces a study of renal function in Thai vegans versus non-vegetarians, noting that vegetarian diets reduce health risk factors and that their effects on the kidneys (nephrological system) are poorly understood.

Reports the study's results: among 25 Thai vegans and 25 non-vegetarian controls, urine protein was the only renal parameter significantly different (p < 0.05), with vegans showing lower urine protein levels.

Introduces the study's aim: testing how a diet and exercise intervention affects breast cancer risk factors (estrogen, obesity, insulin, IGF-I) in overweight/obese postmenopausal women, and sets up the in vitro serum experiments on estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer cell lines.

Describes the intervention design (low-fat, high-fiber diet plus daily exercise for 2 weeks) and reports the hormonal results: serum estradiol fell in both hormone-treated and non-hormone-treated women, and insulin and IGF-I dropped.
Reports the endocrine and in vitro findings: IGF binding protein-1 rose, and serum from the intervention reduced growth of MCF-7, ZR-75-1, and T-47D breast cancer cells (6.6%, 9.9%, 18.5%).

Summarizes the apoptosis results (20% to 30% increases across the three cell lines, n = 12) and concludes that the very-low-fat, high-fiber diet with daily exercise substantially lowers breast cancer risk factors even without weight loss, with serum changes slowing growth and inducing apoptosis in vitro.
Closing fragment of the conclusion, stating that the in vivo serum changes induced apoptosis in serum-stimulated breast cancer cell lines in vitro.

Introduction and background of a cross-sectional study on vegetarian diets and mood in Seventh Day Adventist adults, explaining that fish-free vegetarian diets lack EPA and DHA, key brain-related fatty acids.

Study methods: a cross-sectional design with 138 healthy Seventh Day Adventist adults in the Southwest, assessing polyunsaturated fatty acid intake via food frequency questionnaire and mood via DASS and POMS.

Study population and measures, followed by initial results showing vegetarians reported less negative emotion than omnivores on DASS and POMS mood scores, with group sizes of 60 vegetarians and 78 omnivores.

Detailed results with DASS and POMS mood score comparisons between vegetarians and omnivores, plus group differences in fatty acid intakes: vegetarians had lower EPA, DHA, and arachidonic acid and higher ALA and linoleic acid.
Correlation results linking mood scores to fatty acid intakes: better mood was positively related to EPA, DHA, and AA and inversely related to ALA and linoleic acid intake.
Conclusion that the vegetarian diet profile does not appear to harm mood despite low long-chain omega-3 intake, summarizing the study's main finding.
Opening of the document's abstract on internists-in-training (housestaff) and how they cope with medical mistakes, introducing in-group coping practices after patient harm.
Continues the abstract by naming the three coping mechanisms housestaff used to define and defend mishaps (denial, discounting, distancing) and begins describing denial.

Details the three components of denial (negating error as 'art' with gray areas, repressing mistakes, redefining mistakes as non-mistakes) and introduces discounting as externalizing blame to uncontrollable circumstances.

Lists the forms of discounting (blaming the bureaucracy, superiors/subordinates, disease, patient) and notes that distancing was used when a mistake's magnitude could no longer be denied or discounted.
Reports that despite these defenses, doubts and guilt persisted for many housestaff, with unresolved questions of culpability and oscillation between self- and other-blame.

States that for many 'the case was never closed' even after training ended, and that the 3-year graduate program offered little help processing vulnerability and ambiguity, making the defenses maladaptive.
Describes accountability during residency as variable and contradictory, with housestaff seeing themselves as the sole arbiter of their mistakes.
Explains that housestaff feel no one can judge them, discount internal accountability bodies (department, faculty, peers), and have built an ideology protecting their guarded autonomy.
Final fragment of the abstract, noting that it is truncated at 400 words.

Introduction and aims of the INTERHEART-based study: CHD is a leading killer, women develop it ~10 years later than men, and the study examines whether risk factor distributions by sex and age explain the later acute MI onset in women.

Methods and sample: INTERHEART global case-control study (27,098 participants, 52 countries, 6,787 women), reporting median age at first acute MI (65 years for women vs. 56 for men) and the nine modifiable risk factors associated with MI.

Results on sex differences in risk factor strength: hypertension, diabetes, physical inactivity and moderate alcohol use show stronger associations with MI in women than men, with odds ratios and confidence intervals given.

Results on remaining risk factors and attributable risk: abnormal lipids, smoking, abdominal obesity, diet and psychosocial stress have similar associations in both sexes, associations are stronger in younger people, and the population attributable risk of the nine factors exceeds 94% (96% women vs. 93% men).
Results on age-specific MI and adjustment: men are much more likely than women to have MI before age 60, but adjusting for risk factor levels reduces this sex difference in early MI by over 80%.

Conclusion: women's first MI occurs on average 9 years later than men's; the nine modifiable risk factors explain over 90% of attributable risk and largely account for the age gap, due to higher risk factor levels in younger men.
Final sentence of the conclusion: the age difference at first MI is mainly explained by men having higher risk factor levels at younger ages than women.

Opening of the document reflecting on the five-year anniversary of the IOM's To Err Is Human report: progress on patient safety has been slow, but the report shifted focus to systems change, engaged stakeholders, and prompted hospitals to adopt safe practices, with change expected to accelerate.

Continues the discussion of expected acceleration in patient safety, citing electronic health records, diffusion of safe practices, team training, and disclosure to injured patients, and noting pay for performance as an incentive if aimed at hospitals with high safety levels; then transitions to the need for national goals to achieve the IOM's envisioned improvement.

Concludes the argument that large-scale safety improvement requires strict, ambitious, quantitative, well-tracked national goals, and recommends that AHRQ convene all stakeholders, including payers, to set explicit ambitious patient safety goals for 2010.
Final fragment of the document's closing sentence, specifying that the explicit and ambitious patient safety goals should be reached by 2010.

Opening of an AOA critical-issues commentary on resident duty-hour restrictions, arguing that medical training must cultivate professionalism and selflessness, and that clock-based work-hour limits may discourage the professional behavior desired in future physicians.

Middle portion of the same commentary, asserting that a competency-based model of resident education is needed regardless of duty-hour or fitness-for-duty issues, and noting the lack of evidence that duty-hour limits reduce medical errors or improve patient safety.

Concluding argument of the commentary: until competency-based resident education is established and duty-hour limits are shown to improve safety, overzealous limits on work hours should not erode the professionalism physicians and patients expect.

Final fragment of the commentary's closing sentence, ending with the phrase 'ct of a physician' (completing 'expect of a physician'), which concludes the argument about professionalism and duty-hour restrictions.
Introduction/background on how resident-physician and nurse work hours affect sleep, performance, and patient safety, including the nurse risk for shifts over 12.5 hours.
Continues the background with the elevated risks for physicians-in-training on traditional 24-plus-hour on-call shifts: sharps injuries, drowsy-driving crashes, and serious or fatal medical errors.
Presents quantitative findings comparing 24-hour and 16-hour on-call residents: twice the attentional failures overnight, 36% more serious medical errors, and 300% more fatigue-related fatal errors.
Conclusion stating that extended shifts significantly increase fatigue and impair performance and safety, and that U.S. health care provider hours are unsafe for providers and patients.
Final policy recommendation that the United States must establish and enforce safe work-hour limits to reduce preventable fatigue-related medical errors and injuries among health care workers.

Introduction to the document on rye bran, lignans, and human health: covers the bioactive compounds in the dietary fibre complex and enterolactone as a biomarker of lignan intake, and notes insufficient human evidence that rye, whole grains, or phyto-oestrogens protect against cancer.

Continues the discussion of rye, whole grains, and cancer: some studies suggest protection, particularly for upper digestive tract cancers, while prospective studies clearly link wholegrain cereals to lower risk of myocardial infarction.

Concluding part of the document on rye and whole grains: wholegrain cereals are also associated with protection against diabetes and ischaemic stroke, and these effects are likely tied to components of the dietary fibre complex.
Study introduction: objective, design, and methods of the AGES-Reykjavik cohort analysis of whole-grain and rye bread intake across life stages and prostate cancer risk.

Methods continued: dietary assessment via validated food frequency questionnaire, cancer and mortality registry linkage through 2009, and regression models (ORs/HRs) adjusted for fish, fish liver oil, meat, and milk intake.
Results opening: case counts (347 PCa, 63 advanced) and the key finding that daily adolescent rye bread consumption was linked to lower PCa diagnosis risk (OR 0.76).
Results detail: advanced PCa association for adolescent rye bread (OR 0.47), and null findings for adolescent high oatmeal intake (OR 0.99 overall, 0.67 advanced).

Null life-stage findings and conclusion: mid- and late-life intake of rye, oatmeal, or whole-wheat bread was unrelated to PCa, suggesting adolescent rye bread may reduce risk, particularly advanced disease.

Introduction and methods of a randomised controlled pilot study on rye bran bread in prostate cancer patients: 10 men on rye bran bread vs 8 men on wheat bread control for three weeks, with blood, prostate biopsy, and urine sampling.

Results of the rye bran bread prostate cancer pilot trial: rye group showed increased plasma enterolactone and a significant rise in prostate tumour apoptotic index (2.1% to 5.9%, TUNEL-measured), with weight loss in both groups.

Secondary results and conclusion of the rye bran bread prostate cancer trial: only small changes in PSA, sex hormones, oestrogens, IGF-I, and fibrinolytic markers, with the study suggesting high rye bran bread intake increases prostate tumour apoptosis.
Final concluding sentence of the rye bran bread prostate cancer study, stating that high rye bran bread intake is suggested to increase apoptosis in prostate tumours.
Introduction of a Finnish case-control study on serum enterolactone (a lignan phytoestrogen) and breast cancer risk, within the Kuopio Breast Cancer Study, stating the study's purpose.

Study population and methods: 194 breast cancer cases (68 premenopausal, 126 postmenopausal) and 208 community controls from the Kuopio Breast Cancer Study, with diet assessed by food frequency questionnaire and prediagnostic serum samples.
Laboratory and statistical methods (time-resolved fluoroimmunoassay, logistic regression) and the main result that mean serum enterolactone was lower in cases (20 nmol/l) than controls (26 nmol/l).

Key quantitative findings: enterolactone quintile ranges and an adjusted odds ratio of 0.38 (95% CI 0.18-0.77, P for trend 0.03) for the highest quintile, showing an inverse association with breast cancer.

Results by menopausal status showing the inverse association in both premenopausal and postmenopausal women, plus dietary correlates of high enterolactone (rye, tea, fiber, vitamin E) and the overall conclusion of a significant inverse association.
Concluding sentence of the abstract restating that serum enterolactone level is significantly inversely associated with breast cancer risk.

Introduces the study's aim: examining whole grain intake and breast cancer risk, stratified by ER/PR receptor status and ductal/lobular histology, and whether HRT use modifies the association, in postmenopausal women.

Describes the study population and design: 25,278 postmenopausal Danish women from the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort (1993-1997), with 9.6 years mean follow-up yielding 978 breast cancer cases, and Cox regression methods.
Reports the main result: higher whole grain intake was not associated with lower breast cancer risk; per 50 g/day increment the adjusted incidence rate ratio was 1.01 (95% CI 0.96-1.07).
Gives specific findings: rye bread, oatmeal and whole grain bread showed no link to breast cancer, and no association with ER+/ER-, PR+/PR-, combined ER/PR status, or ductal/lobular subtypes.

Reports no interaction between whole grain intake and HRT use, and concludes that whole grain products were not associated with breast cancer risk in Danish postmenopausal women; includes the 2008 Wiley-Liss copyright notice.
Fragment of the copyright line (Wiley-Liss, Inc.) at the end of the abstract; contains no substantive content beyond publisher attribution.

Introduces the study design: a nationwide Swedish Family-Cancer Database analysis of cancer risk (SIRs with 95% CIs across 17 sites) in Sweden-born descendants of European and North American immigrants, using native Swedes as the reference.

Reports the main SIR findings: overall cancer slightly below Swedish levels, with decreased risks for breast cancer (Norwegian descent), melanoma (Hungarian fathers), and ovarian and bladder cancer (Finnish mothers), consistent with origin-country incidence differences.

Describes elevated risks: cervical cancer in daughters of Danish men, and thyroid cancer and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma in offspring of Yugoslav and Asian parents, with results compared against higher incidence rates in the parents' countries.

Discusses interpretation: results mostly match parental-country incidence patterns, except non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, which may reflect immune dysfunction; also compares first- and second-generation immigrants, highlighting the first two decades of life as critical for later cancer patterns.

Gives the study's central conclusion: Sweden-born individuals follow the Swedish cancer incidence pattern regardless of ancestry, while migrating to Sweden in one's 20s is too late to alter the early-life environmentally programmed cancer risk.
Contains only the copyright notice (Wiley-Liss, Inc., 2002) that closes the abstract, with no substantive content.

Introduces the review's topic: the health effects of lignan-rich foods, focusing on how intestinal microflora convert plant lignans into enterolactone and enterodiol (enterolignans) and their protective role in chronic Western diseases.

Identifies the main protective foods (fiber- and lignan-rich whole grains, beans, berries, nuts, seeds) and lists non-dietary factors such as gut microflora, smoking, antibiotics, and obesity that influence circulating lignan levels.

Summarizes evidence that lifelong lignan-rich diets may be beneficial, citing animal studies showing anticarcinogenic effects of flaxseed and pure lignans, and explaining why epidemiological findings on enterolactone are inconsistent across countries.
Concludes that the lignan source matters because other food components contribute to protection, and that while results are promising, further research is needed.
Study abstract opening: background on whole-grain intake and prostate cancer, stating the aim and describing the Danish Diet, Cancer and Health cohort of 26,691 men aged 50-64 years.

Methods section of the abstract: cohort size, dietary data collection, median 12.4-year follow-up yielding 1,081 prostate cancer cases, and Cox regression analysis of whole-grain intake and incidence.

Main results of the abstract: no overall association between total whole-grain intake and prostate cancer risk (adjusted IRR 1.00 per 50 g/day, 95% CI 0.96-1.05), and no association for rye bread, whole-grain bread, or oatmeal.

Remaining results and conclusions: risk estimates did not differ by cancer stage or grade, and the study concludes higher whole-grain intake is not associated with prostate cancer risk in Danish middle-aged men.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, specifying that the null finding applies to a population of Danish middle-aged men.

Introduces the study's background: rye whole grain and bran showed anti-prostate-cancer effects in animal models (lower tumor take, smaller tumors, reduced PSA), and a human pilot found increased apoptosis; this study examines rye intake and PSA in men with prostate cancer.

Describes the methods: 17 men received either 485 g/day of rye whole grain and bran products (RP) or refined wheat with added cellulose (WP), about 50% of daily energy, in a randomized crossover trial.
Outlines sampling and the main PSA result: fasting blood drawn at 2, 4, and 6 weeks and 24-h urine collected; plasma total PSA was lower after RP than WP, a mean treatment effect of -14% (P = 0.04).
Reports secondary results: fasting plasma insulin and 24-h urinary C-peptide were lower after RP (P < 0.01 and P = 0.01), and urinary excretion of five lignans was higher after RP (P < 0.001).

Gives the conclusion: rye whole grain and bran lowered plasma PSA versus cellulose-supplemented refined wheat in prostate cancer patients, possibly via reduced insulin exposure inhibiting cancer progression.
Final fragment of the conclusion, restating that the proposed mechanism of reduced insulin exposure is indicated by plasma insulin and urinary C-peptide excretion.

Introduces the document's review of rye, a bread cereal richer in fibre and bioactive compounds than others, as a possible protective factor against breast cancer, setting the objective and Nordic-based short-review design.
Continues the Design and Results sections, beginning the mechanistic argument that fibre fermentation esterifies bile acids (lowering free bile acid toxicity) and produces anticancer butyrate.

Covers the middle mechanisms: fibre reducing enterohepatic oestrogen recirculation to lower plasma oestrogen, and rye's lignans and alkylresorcinols as antioxidative, potentially anticarcinogenic compounds.
Concludes the review: vitamins, minerals and phytic acid may add protection, and the overall conclusion that wholegrain rye flour products are likely to reduce breast cancer risk.

Introduces the study's rationale: alkylresorcinols as biomarkers of rye and whole-grain wheat intake, motivating their use to examine breast cancer risk via cereal fiber effects on estrogen enterohepatic circulation in Finnish women.

Describes the cross-sectional pilot design and participant groups (20 omnivores, 20 vegetarians, 16 breast cancer patients) sampled twice six months apart, plus the methods: 5-day dietary records and plasma/urinary AR metabolites DHBA and DHPPA.

Reports the main results: plasma and urinary DHBA and DHPPA, along with cereal fiber intake, were significantly lower in the breast cancer group than in vegetarian and omnivore groups, with the reported P values.
Summarizes the conclusion that whole-grain rye and wheat fiber intake is low in breast cancer patients, so urinary and plasma AR metabolites may serve as potential breast cancer risk biomarkers.
Closes with implications: the approach may aid studies of rye and wheat fiber intake and other diseases, and the findings need confirmation in larger populations.

Study design and cohort: Icelandic population-based cohort of 8,894 men born 1907–1935, followed for prostate cancer diagnosis and mortality via registry linkage from 1967–1987 entry through 2009, examining early-life residency and milk intake.

Milk intake assessment and outcomes: 2,268 subgroup participants reported milk intake in 2002–2006; mean follow-up 24.3 years, 1,123 prostate cancer diagnoses, 371 advanced cases (stage 3+ or prostate cancer death).

Main residency findings: rural early-life residency (first 20 years) vs. capital area showed a marginal association with advanced prostate cancer (HR 1.29, 95% CI 0.97–1.73), strongest among men born before 1920 (HR 1.64).

Milk consumption findings: daily milk intake in adolescence (vs. less than daily), but not in midlife or currently, associated with a 3.2-fold risk of advanced prostate cancer (95% CI 1.25–8.28); conclusion that frequent adolescent milk intake increases risk.
Closing fragment of the abstract's final sentence, restating the conclusion that frequent milk intake in adolescence increases risk of advanced prostate cancer.
Introduction and study rationale for a cross-sectional study of depression and dietary antioxidant, fruit, and vegetable intake in older adults, noting prior research gaps.

Study methods: sample of 278 elderly participants (144 depressed, 134 non-depressed) aged 60+, with intake measured by a Block 1998 food frequency questionnaire administered 1999-2007; begins the reporting of key results on vitamin C, lutein, and cryptoxanthin.

Key results: lower vitamin C, lutein, and cryptoxanthin intakes and lower fruit and vegetable consumption in depressed individuals, plus multivariable findings after adjusting for demographic, health, and dietary covariates.

Further findings: vitamin C, cryptoxanthin, fruits and vegetables stay significant in adjusted models; supplement-derived antioxidants show no link to depression; overall conclusion that antioxidant and produce intake is lower in late-life depression.
Conclusion and implications: the dietary differences may partly explain higher cardiovascular disease risk in depressed older adults, supporting whole food antioxidant sources over supplements.

Trial design and objective: the study compares EPA-enriched versus DHA-enriched omega-3 monotherapy against placebo for major depressive disorder, with eligibility criteria (DSM-IV MDD, HDRS-17 ≥ 15) and the 2-site randomized double-blind design.

Methods continued: the randomization period (2006–2011), the 8-week double-blind dosing of 1000 mg/d EPA-enriched n-3, DHA-enriched n-3, or placebo, and the completion count (154 subjects) and modified intent-to-treat sample (n = 177) with MMRM analysis.

Primary efficacy results: all three arms improved significantly on HDRS-17 (primary outcome), QIDS-SR-16, and CGI-S, with mITT demographics and the MMRM analysis, but the statistical comparison lists the efficacy measures used in the trial.

Comparative efficacy and safety results: neither omega-3 preparation separated from placebo, response rates were about 40%–50% and remission about 30% with no between-group differences, and one EPA discontinuation for worsening depression is reported.

Conclusions and registration: neither EPA- nor DHA-enriched n-3 was superior to placebo for MDD, a placebo discontinuation for an unspecified 'negative reaction' is noted, and the trial is registered as NCT00517036 with a 2015 copyright line.
Trial registration and copyright footer: the ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT00517036 and the 2015 Physicians Postgraduate Press copyright notice closing the abstract.
Background and objective of a systematic review and meta-analysis of dietary patterns (overall diet, not single nutrients) and depression in community-dwelling adults.

Methods section describing the search of six electronic databases through August 2013 for studies on total diet and depression in adults, restricted to methodologically rigorous studies, with two independent reviewers.
Methods and results overview: random-effects pooling of effect sizes, presentation of non-pooled studies, and the count of 21 identified studies, with 13 observational studies pooled.

Key results of the meta-analysis: a healthy dietary pattern linked to reduced odds of depression (OR 0.84), and a non-significant association for the Western diet (OR 1.17, P = 0.094) based on few studies.
Conclusions: high intake of fruit, vegetables, fish and whole grains may reduce depression risk, with a caveat about the Western diet estimate and the need for more high-quality evidence.
Closing conclusion calling for more high-quality randomized controlled trials and cohort studies to confirm the association and establish its temporal sequence.

Abstract opening (Objective and Methods) of a Japanese cross-sectional study on dietary patterns and depressive symptoms: 521 municipal employees aged 21-67, recruited from a periodic health checkup survey.

Methods continuation: depressive symptoms measured with the CES-D scale; dietary patterns derived by principal component analysis of 52 food and beverage items from a validated brief diet history questionnaire.

Methods end and Results start: logistic regression with confounder adjustment defines depression as CES-D >=16; three dietary patterns identified, with the healthy Japanese pattern (vegetables, fruit, mushrooms, soy) linked to fewer symptoms.
Key results: multivariate-adjusted odds ratios across tertiles of the healthy Japanese dietary pattern score (1.00, 0.99, 0.44), with a significant trend test (P=0.006).
Closing results and conclusions: other dietary patterns showed no appreciable association, and the healthy Japanese dietary pattern may be linked to lower prevalence of depressive status.
Introduction/objective of a JPHC cohort study on fish, EPA, and DHA intake and suicide risk among Japanese adults, motivated by high fish consumption and suicide rates in Japan.

Methods of the JPHC cohort study: 47,351 men and 54,156 women aged 40-69, food frequency questionnaire in 1995-1999, follow-up through December 2005, and Cox proportional hazards models by intake quintile.
Results opening: 213 male and 85 female suicide deaths over 403,019 and 473,351 person-years, with finding that higher fish, EPA, or DHA intake was not associated with lower suicide risk.

Key quantitative results: multivariate hazard ratios for highest vs lowest fish quintile (men 0.95, women 1.20, both non-significant), plus elevated suicide risk among women with very low fish intake.
Conclusions of the study: findings do not support a protective role of higher fish, EPA, or DHA intake against suicide in Japanese men and women, followed by copyright notice.
Final fragment of the copyright statement (Elsevier B.V., 2010) closing the abstract of the JPHC fish/EPA/DHA suicide study.

Introduces the review's premise: depression's multifactorial aetiology and the proposed role of oxidative stress in its pathogenesis, as the opening of the paper 'Antioxidants as antidepressants: fact or fiction?'.

Explains the mechanistic link between reactive oxygen/nitrogen species and key depression neurotransmitters (noradrenaline, serotonin, dopamine, glutamate), and notes lowered endogenous antioxidant levels in major depression.

Summarizes reduced antioxidants (vitamin E, zinc, coenzyme Q10, glutathione peroxidase) and impaired total antioxidant status in depression, framing antioxidants as new therapeutic targets and stating the review's focus.

Describes the review's aim to evaluate antioxidants as co-adjuvant therapy with conventional antidepressants, citing N-acetylcysteine's benefit on depressive symptoms in a randomized placebo-controlled trial.

Discusses curcumin's antidepressant potential in animal models via redox homeostasis modulation and monoamine oxidase inhibition, and argues for better-tolerated treatments amid the need for new options.
Concludes the document by stating that antioxidant treatments appear promising for depressive disorders and merit further study.

Introduction and objective of a prospective SUN cohort study on Mediterranean diet adherence and incident clinical depression, including the diet's hypothesized anti-inflammatory, vascular, and metabolic mechanisms and the design using a validated 136-item food frequency questionnaire.

Methods detail on how the Mediterranean dietary pattern score was built: positive weights for vegetables, fruit and nuts, cereals, legumes, fish, monounsaturated-to-saturated fat ratio, and moderate alcohol; negative weights for meat products and whole-fat dairy. Also introduces the SUN university-graduate cohort setting.
Study population and setting: 10,094 initially healthy Spanish participants in the SUN Project (University of Navarra graduate cohort), recruited starting December 21, 1999, with recruitment ongoing.

Outcome definition for incident depression (free of depression and antidepressants at baseline; later physician-diagnosed depression or antidepressant use) and the start of results: median follow-up of 4.4 years yielding 480 new depression cases.

Main results: multiply adjusted hazard ratios with 95% CIs for depression across four upper adherence categories versus lowest adherence (0.74, 0.66, 0.49, 0.58), with a significant P for trend below .001.

Dose-response findings showing inverse associations for fruit and nuts, the monounsaturated-to-saturated fatty acid ratio, and legumes, followed by the conclusion that the Mediterranean diet may protect against depression and that longitudinal studies and trials are needed to confirm this.
Final sentence of the conclusions calling for additional longitudinal studies and trials to confirm the protective association between the Mediterranean dietary pattern and depressive disorders.

Abstract-style opening of an InCHIANTI Study analysis (Tuscany, Italy) of 958 older adults aged 65+, introducing the aims, population, and the plasma carotenoids and CES-D depressive symptoms measures.
Methods continued: baseline plasma total carotenoids, CES-D depressive symptom assessment at baseline and 3- and 6-year follow-up, with depressed mood defined as CES-D≥20; results begin.

Key results: baseline higher carotenoids linked to lower odds of depressed mood (OR=0.82), and after excluding baseline depression and antidepressant users, lower risk of incident depressed mood at 6 years (OR=0.72), adjusted for confounders and baseline CES-D.

Mediation finding that the inflammatory marker interleukin-1 receptor antagonist partially mediates the carotenoid–depression association, followed by the Discussion's conclusion that low carotenoid levels relate to and predict depressive symptoms in older persons.
Final concluding sentences of the discussion: the mechanism behind the carotenoid–depression link may reveal targets for prevention and treatment of depression in older adults.

Introduction and methods opening of a prospective cohort study of suicide mortality in relation to dietary n-3/n-6 PUFA and fish intake, describing the three US cohorts (HPFS, NHS, NHS II) and their enrollment periods.

Methods section detailing cohort sizes and follow-up years, the every-4-years validated food-frequency questionnaire used to assess fish and PUFA intake, and blinded physician review of death certificates and records to ascertain suicide deaths.

Statistical methods for the suicide mortality study: multivariable Cox proportional hazards models for adjusted relative risks, pooled across cohorts with random-effects meta-analysis, and the start of the results on highest versus lowest intake quartiles.

Results and conclusion of the suicide and PUFA study: pooled relative risks for highest vs lowest quartile of n-3 (1.08-1.46) and n-6 (0.68-1.19) PUFA intake with trend p-values, concluding no evidence that n-3 PUFAs or fish lowered completed suicide risk.
Final sentence of the conclusion of the suicide mortality cohort study, stating that n-3 PUFA or fish intake was not shown to reduce the risk of completed suicide.
Introduction and methods opening of the EUROSAVE study on suicide and self-inflicted injury mortality trends in the 15 EU countries, motivated by roughly one million suicides worldwide per year.
Methods detail: data sources (WHO, EUROSTAT, national statistical agencies) covering 1984-1998 for EU countries, plus a secondary group of 'undetermined' or 'other violence' deaths.
Methods conclusion and results start: age-standardized rates and time trends, with Finland highest and Greece lowest suicide rates in 1997, and Mediterranean countries generally lowest.

Results on trends: most countries show downward suicide trends, Ireland and Spain show upward trends, and Portugal and Greece have the highest and lowest undetermined-death rates in 1984 and 1998 or 1997.
Results on undetermined deaths: five countries including Ireland and Spain show downward trends, while Belgium and Germany show borderline upward trends, followed by the start of the conclusions.

Conclusions: suicide rates appear to be falling, but data validity is uncertain; misclassification may contribute to variation but does not explain it, and better cross-EU recording comparisons are needed.
Final conclusion: without adequate EU-wide suicide data, effective prevention will likely remain difficult to achieve.

Introduction and background of a prospective SUN cohort study on long-chain omega-3 (w-3 PUFA) intake and fish consumption as possible protective factors against mental disorders, stating the aim and noting the scarcity of large cohorts.

Methods section describing the study population of 7,903 participants, dietary exposure assessed with a validated semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire, and the three outcomes measured after 2 years: incident mental disorder, depression, and anxiety.

Statistical methods (logistic regression and generalized additive models, ORs with 95% CIs) followed by the start of results, reporting case counts of depression (173), anxiety (335), and stress (4) over 2-year follow-up.

Results giving odds ratios by successive energy-adjusted quintiles of w-3 PUFA intake for mental disorder (reference 1, then 0.72, 0.79, 0.65, 1.04), and beginning the fish consumption findings with quintile median intakes.

Fish consumption findings showing a relative risk reduction above 30% for moderate intake (third and fourth quintiles, medians 83.3 and 112 g/day), and the conclusion that w-3 PUFA intake may benefit total mental disorders though no linear trend was apparent.

Abstract opening of a systematic review and meta-analysis on omega-3 fatty acids for major depressive disorder, describing the search of PubMed (1965-2010) for placebo-controlled RCTs and the primary outcome of standardized mean difference in depression severity.

Continuation of the methods section listing the stratified meta-analysis moderators: trial duration, methodological quality, baseline depression severity, diagnosis, EPA/DHA dose, and monotherapy versus augmentation use.

Main results of the omega-3 depression meta-analysis: 13 trials with 731 participants showing no significant benefit over placebo (SMD=0.11, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.26), with significant heterogeneity and publication bias noted.

Publication bias findings: after trim-and-fill adjustment, nearly all apparent omega-3 benefit disappears (SMD=0.01, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.15), followed by the start of secondary analyses on moderators of efficacy.

Secondary analysis results suggesting larger omega-3 effects in lower-quality trials, shorter trials, trials analyzing completers rather than intention-to-treat, and participants with greater baseline depression, with the conclusion of a small non-significant published benefit.

Concluding statement of the omega-3 depression meta-analysis: current published trials show only a small, non-significant benefit, and most of the apparent treatment efficacy may be due to publication bias.
Introduces dysmenorrhea (painful menses): its epidemiology, risk factors, and the initial empiric diagnostic approach, with NSAIDs as first-line therapy.

Covers the medical treatment ladder for dysmenorrhea: NSAIDs first, then hormonal options such as oral contraceptives, depo-medroxyprogesterone, and prolonged-cycle or intravaginal OCP use when pain relief is insufficient.

Lists non-hormonal alternatives for women who avoid hormonal contraception (heat, herbal remedy, supplements, diet, acupressure) and the next step of pelvic ultrasound and laparoscopy referral to rule out secondary causes.

Addresses severe refractory primary dysmenorrhea in women who want to conceive, naming safe alternatives such as TENS, acupuncture, nifedipine, and terbutaline, and begins discussing the escalation options.
Concludes the escalation options for refractory dysmenorrhea: danazol or leuprolide, rare hysterectomy, and the unproven effectiveness of surgical pelvic nerve interruption.
Introduction of a retrospective Cardiff study on surgery for severe treatment-resistant mastalgia (breast pain), stating its aims: auditing surgical efficacy and patient satisfaction.
Study methods: retrospective review of mastalgia clinic records at University Hospital of Wales, Cardiff since 1973, with a postal questionnaire sent to surgically treated patients.
Results: of 1054 clinic patients, 12 (1.2%) had surgery, mainly subcutaneous mastectomies with implants, plus bilateral simple mastectomy and quadrantectomies; median symptom duration was 6.5 years.
Outcomes: 50% of surgical patients became pain free; complications included 3 capsular contractures and 2 wound infections with dehiscence; pain persisted after both quadrantectomies.
Conclusion: surgery for mastalgia should be reserved for a minority of patients, who must be warned about reconstructive complications and that half will not have pain relief.

Introduction of a review on ginger (Zingiber officinale) for preventing nausea and vomiting; opens by describing these symptoms as protective physiological processes and noting the limits of existing antiemetic drugs.

Continues the review's introduction: notes shortcomings of current antiemetics (ineffective against some stimuli, costly, side effects) and presents ginger's long traditional use as a broad-spectrum antiemetic, with herbal medicines as effective antiemetics.

Summarizes the evidence base for ginger: preclinical and clinical studies show antiemetic effects against various emetogenic stimuli, but conflicting reports, especially for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting and motion sickness, prevent firm conclusions.

Closing statement of the review's introduction: states this is the first review to summarize the results, aims to address gaps in published studies, and highlights areas needing further research before clinical use of ginger.

Introduction and methods of a systematic review on ginger for pregnancy-induced nausea and vomiting (PNV): background on ginger's traditional use and rising Western popularity, stated objectives, and the search sources (CINAHL, Cochrane, MEDLINE, TRIP) for RCTs.

Methods and results of a systematic review of ginger for pregnancy-induced nausea and vomiting: quality appraisal of RCTs with the CASP tool, the four included trials, and their finding that oral ginger outperformed placebo in reducing vomiting frequency and nausea intensity.

Results and conclusion of a systematic review on ginger for pregnancy-induced nausea and vomiting: mild, infrequent adverse events, and the conclusion that ginger appears safe and effective for PNV, with uncertainty about maximum dose and treatment duration.
