Introduction and objective of a Korean case-control study examining soy intake and breast cancer risk, stratified by menopausal and hormone receptor status; sets up the inconsistent prior evidence from Asian populations.

Methods and descriptive results: 358 breast cancer cases and 360 age-matched controls, dietary soy assessed via a 103-item food frequency questionnaire, with mean daily soy (76.5 g) and isoflavone (15.0 mg) intakes.

Main finding: multivariate logistic regression shows a significant inverse, dose-response association between soy intake and breast cancer risk (highest vs lowest quartile OR 0.36), and the protective effect appears in postmenopausal women (OR 0.08).

Subgroup results: the protective effect of soy is seen only among postmenopausal women, with no difference by ER/PR status overall, while isoflavone intake was inversely associated only in postmenopausal women with ER+/PR+ tumors.
Conclusions of the study: high soy consumption may be linked to lower breast cancer risk, and the effect of soy may depend on several factors such as menopausal and hormone receptor status.
Final sentence of the conclusions, noting that the effect of soy intake on breast cancer risk may vary depending on several factors.

Introduction and study aim: establishes that thallium uptake by green cabbage cultivars and its tissue distribution are poorly understood, and describes the Tl-spiked pot-culture experiment with five cultivars.

Main results on tissue distribution: Tl concentrates mainly in leaves (101-192 mg/kg DW) rather than roots or stems, with no significant cultivar differences (p = 0.455), and begins describing the leaf subcellular fractionation pattern.

Subcellular fractionation findings: Tl in leaves is ranked cytosol and vacuole >> cell wall > organelles, with about 88% in cytosol/vacuole, which is also the main storage site for Ca and Mg; this is linked to protecting organelles.

Conclusion: the subcellular storage pattern is suggested to help cabbage tolerate and detoxify Tl, and all five cultivars are concluded to have good potential for phytoremediation of Tl-contaminated soils.
Opening of a double-blind trial abstract on boric acid vs. nystatin capsules for vulvovaginal candidiasis, introducing the dosing regimen and the study design.

Results of the boric acid vs. nystatin trial: cure rates at 7-10 days and 30 days, similar symptom relief speed, no side effects or cervical cytology changes, and in vitro findings that boric acid is fungistatic and pH-independent.

Pharmacokinetic findings (little vaginal absorption, under 12-hour half-life) and conclusion that boric acid capsules are better accepted than vaginal creams and far cheaper than commonly prescribed medication.
Final sentence of the abstract restating the cost comparison: self-made boric acid capsules cost 31 cents for fourteen versus costly standard prescriptions.

Abstract of a study of 92 women with chronic mycotic (yeast) vaginitis, introducing a microscopic cytologic finding of vaginal discharge as a diagnostic tool during prolonged antifungal and boric acid therapy.

Continuation of the abstract: the microscopy method detects symptomatic and subclinical yeast infection and predicts relapse, attributes chronic infections mainly to conventional antifungal failure, and reports boric acid curing 98% of antifungal-refractory patients.

Final sentence of the abstract concluding that boric acid, which cured 98% of patients who failed common antifungals, is the treatment of choice for prophylaxis against chronic mycotic vaginal infections.

Introduces HDAC (histone deacetylase) function and HDAC inhibitors as epigenetic cancer drugs, then notes prior work linking valproic acid and trichostatin A to histone hyperacetylation and axial skeleton malformations in mouse embryos.

States the study's aim: testing whether boric acid, which causes teratogenic malformations similar to valproic acid and trichostatin A, works through the same HDAC inhibition and histone hyperacetylation mechanism.

Methods: pregnant mice receive a teratogenic intraperitoneal dose of boric acid on gestation day 8; embryos are analyzed by Western blot and immunostaining for hyperacetylated H4, which shows hyperacetylation in somites.
Results: embryonic nuclear extract HDAC assays show significant, mixed-type partial inhibition by boric acid, with kinetic constants alpha=0.51 (substrate affinity) and beta=0.70 (maximum velocity).
Conclusion: the work provides the first evidence that boric acid inhibits HDAC, proposing this as a molecular mechanism for boric acid-related malformations.
Introduction and objectives of an in vitro study on boric acid as a treatment for recurrent yeast (Candida) vaginitis, stating the knowledge gap about its antifungal spectrum and mechanism.

Methods and start of results: agar dilution testing of yeast and bacterial isolates for boric acid's intrinsic activity, plus physiology methods on Candida albicans, including activity against fluconazole-resistant strains at intravaginal concentrations.

Quantitative results: broth dilution MICs (1563-6250 mg/L), fungistatic effect shown by reduced CO2 generation, fungicidal effect at 50,000 mg/L, and comparison with organic acids and sodium borate, which had lower pH but were less inhibitory.

Results on conditions and cell damage: cold or anaerobic incubation protected yeast at high concentrations; cell integrity held for 6 h at 37 C, with propidium iodide uptake after 24 h, and loss of plate count viability preceding vital stain uptake.

Results on molecular and virulence effects: sub-MIC exposure reduced ergosterol, CDR1 efflux pump expression was abrogated so it gave no protection, and boric acid inhibited biofilm formation and hyphal transition; also begins the conclusions on concentration- and temperature-dependent fungistatic/fungicidal activity.

Final conclusions: boric acid is fungistatic or fungicidal depending on concentration and temperature; inhibition of oxidative metabolism is the key antifungal mechanism, and virulence inhibition likely contributes to in vivo efficacy.

Opening of the abstract for a large US prospective cohort study (492,186 participants) on meat intake, meat-related mutagens, and renal cell carcinoma (RCC), including clear cell and papillary subtypes.

Study design section of the RCC abstract: dietary assessment linked to a database of heme iron, heterocyclic amines, PAHs, nitrate and nitrite in cooked and processed meats, with 1814 RCC cases over about 9 years of follow-up.

Methods and early results from the RCC meat-intake abstract: case counts by subtype (498 clear cell, 115 papillary), Cox regression within quintiles, and the red meat intake comparison with an overall HR of 1.19 (P-trend = 0.06).

Key findings from the RCC abstract: papillary RCC risk roughly doubled with red meat intake, and benzo(a)pyrene (a PAH marker) and PhIP (an HCA) were each linked to 20–30% higher RCC risk and about 2-fold higher papillary RCC risk.
Conclusions of the RCC abstract: red meat may raise RCC risk via cooking compounds BaP and PhIP, RCC associations are driven by papillary subtype, and no associations were seen for clear cell RCC.
Closing sentence of the RCC meat-intake abstract noting that the study is registered at clinicaltrials.gov under NCT00340015.

Introduction and aims of a meta-analysis on folate intake and MTHFR polymorphisms in relation to esophageal, gastric, and pancreatic cancer risk, with the literature search scope described in the background.
Methods section describing the MEDLINE literature search through March 2006 and random-effects inverse-variance pooling, followed by the start of the results on relative risks.

Results reporting summary relative risks for highest versus lowest dietary folate intake for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, esophageal adenocarcinoma, and pancreatic cancer, with study counts and 95% confidence intervals.

Results continuing with heterogeneity findings and inconsistent gastric cancer folate results, then describing the MTHFR 677TT variant genotype's association with increased risk of esophageal, gastric, and pancreatic cancers.
Summary of MTHFR 677TT odds ratios across cancer sites (22 estimates, 13 significant) and the limited, inconsistent evidence for the A1298C polymorphism, leading into the conclusions.
Conclusion of the meta-analysis stating that findings support a role for folate in carcinogenesis of the esophagus, stomach, and pancreas.
Introduces Barrett's oesophagus: definition, its cause (chronic GORD), its 40-fold increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, and the gap in understanding its cell of origin.

Covers research limitations in Barrett's oesophagus, notably the lack of a universally accepted animal model, and lists the major open clinical questions (surveillance validity, optimal treatment, and cancer-preventing agents without unacceptable side effects).
Names the main chemopreventive candidates for Barrett's oesophagus, aspirin and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), and mentions other suggested agents such as green tea, berries, antioxidants and diet.

States that the review discusses the evidence for dietary and other suggested chemoprevention strategies, and calls for better clinical trial infrastructure to test new pharmacological and endoscopic interventions; includes the copyright notice.
Contains only the tail of the copyright notice (Elsevier Ltd., 2011, all rights reserved), with no substantive content about Barrett's oesophagus.
Introduction and methods of an Italian case-control study (1992-1997) on dietary fiber and oral, pharyngeal, and esophageal cancer, describing the case and hospital control populations.

Continues the methods: hospital controls with acute nonneoplastic diseases, validated food frequency questionnaire interviews, and odds ratio adjustment for age, sex, alcohol, tobacco, and energy intake.
Main results: odds ratios for highest vs. lowest fiber intake quintile across combined cancers, showing protective ORs for total, soluble, cellulose, insoluble, and lignin fiber fractions.

Results by fiber source (vegetable, fruit, grain) and by subgroup, noting stronger inverse associations for oral and pharyngeal than esophageal cancer and consistency across sex, age, education, and lifestyle strata.
Conclusion of the study: fiber intake may have a protective role against oral, pharyngeal, and esophageal cancers.

Study introduction and methods: objective of presenting a child with gastric ulcers after hydrogen peroxide 3% ingestion, and a retrospective chart review of Long Island Regional Poison Control Center cases (1992-1995) describing the data collected.

Methods continued and start of results: data fields extracted, then the total of 670 hydrogen peroxide 3% exposures out of 81,126 reported over 40 months, with the oral route and pediatric age predominating.

Core results and conclusion lead-in: most exposures were asymptomatic and benign, but one child with bloody emesis developed multiple gastric ulcers and duodenal erosions after a 2-4 oz ingestion, prompting the conclusion that severe gastric injury is possible.

Study conclusions and clinical recommendations: hydrogen peroxide 3% exposure is usually benign, but small ingestions can cause severe gastric injury in children, so persistent vomiting or bloody emesis warrants medical evaluation and consideration of endoscopy.

Introduction and case report opening: defines cerebral air gas embolism (CAGE) from small-volume concentrated hydrogen peroxide ingestion, states HBOT is standard of care, and introduces a 48-year-old male case of 33% hydrogen peroxide ingestion treated with HBOT.

Case report presentation: after swallowing two sips of 33% hydrogen peroxide, the patient develops hematemesis, left hemiplegia, confusion, and left homonymous hemianopsia; initial labs, chest x-ray, and CT are normal, while MRI shows diffusion restriction and T2 hyperintensities in multiple vascular territories from CAGE.

Treatment and outcome: 18 hours after arrival the patient receives HBOT (3 ATA for 30 minutes, then 2.5 ATA for 60 minutes) with clinical improvement, and six-month follow-up MRI shows resolution of the hyperintensities.

Discussion of the literature: a MEDLINE search (1950 to present) finds only two prior CAGE cases from concentrated hydrogen peroxide ingestion treated with HBOT, both with full symptom resolution, versus seven untreated cases where only one reported symptom resolution.
Conclusion: even small ingestions of concentrated hydrogen peroxide can cause CAGE, and HBOT may reverse symptoms and prevent permanent neurological impairment.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, ending with the phrase 'permanent neurological impairment' regarding HBOT's potential benefit in CAGE from hydrogen peroxide ingestion.
Introduction to hydrogen peroxide: its common household, industrial (paper/pulp bleaching) and medicinal uses, which set up the exposure sources discussed in the poisoning document.
Mechanisms of hydrogen peroxide toxicity (corrosive damage, oxygen gas formation, lipid peroxidation) and its historical medicinal use in wound irrigation and instrument sterilisation.
Caustic local tissue damage from concentrated peroxide and gas embolism risk from oxygen generated after ingesting concentrated (>35%) solutions, including the proposed mechanism of CNS injury.

Consequences of rapid oxygen generation: mechanical distension and rupture of hollow viscera, and intravascular foaming that impairs right ventricular output and can cause complete loss of cardiac output.
Direct cytotoxicity via lipid peroxidation and the gastrointestinal effects of ingestion (nausea, vomiting, haematemesis, foaming that can obstruct the airway or cause aspiration).

Gastric effects of ingestion: painful distension and belching from oxygen liberation, mucosal blistering and oropharyngeal burns with concentrated solutions, and reported laryngospasm and haemorrhagic gastritis.

Systemic clinical features after ingestion, such as tachycardia, neurological depression, convulsions, airway obstruction signs, cardiorespiratory arrest, and cerebral infarction from oxygen embolism.
Inhalation toxicity: usually mild coughing and dyspnoea, but concentrated solutions cause mucosal inflammation, shock, coma, convulsions and delayed pulmonary oedema up to 24-72 hours.
Severe toxicity from wound irrigation within closed body cavities or under pressure causing gas embolism, plus dermal injury and ocular effects of 3% solutions.
Eye injury from more concentrated solutions (>10%) causing corneal ulceration or perforation, and the rationale for not performing gut decontamination because catalase rapidly breaks peroxide down.
Management: release of painful gastric distension with a gastric tube, early aggressive airway management as the key to survival, and indications for endoscopy.
Further treatment: corticosteroids (unproven value) for laryngeal and pulmonary oedema, intubation or rarely tracheostomy for life-threatening laryngeal oedema, and skin decontamination with water.
Skin lesions managed as thermal burns with surgery for deep burns, and immediate prolonged eye irrigation with water or 0.9% saline, with local anaesthetic to aid decontamination.
Closing sentence on local anaesthetic instillation during eye irrigation to reduce discomfort and improve decontamination.

Introduces the research question: inconsistent prior findings on dietary alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) intake and prostate cancer risk, and the meta-analysis method (systematic search through December 2008, inverse-variance weighting of log relative risks).
Reports the main pooled result: across five prospective studies, the highest vs. lowest ALA intake category gave a pooled RR of 0.97 (95% CI 0.86-1.10), with heterogeneity between studies.
Gives the threshold analysis based on case and non-case counts: intake above 1.5 g/day vs. below was associated with a significantly lower prostate cancer risk (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.91-0.99).

Discusses sources of divergent results (sample size, adjustment, limits of dietary ALA assessment) and concludes that the evidence suggests a weak protective association, though more research is needed.
Closing fragment of the conclusion stating that further research is required before drawing firm conclusions about ALA and prostate cancer risk.

Introduction and study background: motivation for irradiating fruits and vegetables and the knowledge gap on vitamin effects, plus the baby-leaf spinach cultivars ('Lazio' and 'Samish') and their sanitization/growing methods.
Experimental design: baby-leaf spinach packaged under air or N2 and exposed to cesium-137 gamma radiation at 0.0 to 2.0 kGy, followed by assays of vitamins and carotenoids.

Results overview: packaging atmosphere had little consistent effect, though N2 was linked to higher dihydroascorbic acid; the list of analytes assayed (vitamins C, E, K, B9 and carotenoids) is introduced.

Key findings: B9, E, K vitamins and neoxanthin were stable across doses, while total and free ascorbic acid, lutein/zeaxanthin, violaxanthin and beta-carotene declined significantly at 2.0 kGy and at lower doses depending on cultivar.
Conclusion on oxidative stress: dihydroascorbic acid was the most affected compound, serving as a stress indicator from irradiation-generated oxidative radicals, rising at doses above 0.5 kGy.

Introduction to microgreens as a culinary trend and the motivation for the study: no prior scientific nutritional data exist for microgreens, so the study aims to measure their vitamin and carotenoid content.

Study aim and scope: measures ascorbic acid, carotenoids, phylloquinone, and tocopherols across 25 commercially available microgreens, and notes large variation in vitamin and carotenoid levels among them.

Reported quantitative ranges of nutrients across the 25 microgreens: ascorbic acid (20.4-147.0 mg/100 g FW), β-carotene, lutein/zeaxanthin, violaxanthin, phylloquinone (0.6-4.1 μg/g FW), and α- and γ-tocopherol concentrations.

Key comparative findings: red cabbage had the highest ascorbic acid, cilantro the highest carotenoids, garnet amaranth the highest phylloquinone, and green daikon radish the highest tocopherols; also begins comparison with mature leaf values from the USDA database.

Conclusion that microgreen cotyledon leaves have higher nutrient density than mature leaves per USDA data, and that the results can support food composition databases and health and consumer recommendations.
Final concluding statement that the data can serve as a reference for health agencies' recommendations and consumers' choices of fresh vegetables.

Introduction and methods of a case-control study of whole-blood fatty acids and dietary fat intake in relation to prostate cancer risk among men in Jamaica (209 cases, 226 controls from urology clinics).

Results on whole-blood fatty acid tertiles: higher oleic acid and moderate palmitic acid were associated with lower prostate cancer odds, while the table of odds ratios and confidence intervals is reported for each tertile.

Findings that high linolenic acid increased prostate cancer odds, that myristic, stearic and palmitoleic acids showed no association, and that higher dietary MUFA intake was inversely related to prostate cancer risk.

Source of dietary MUFA identified as avocado, other dietary fats showed no association, and conclusions that whole-blood and dietary MUFA may reduce prostate cancer risk, possibly via avocado, while high blood linolenic acid is linked to higher risk.
Closing sentence of the abstract stating that the observed associations of blood linolenic acid and MUFA with prostate cancer warrant further investigation.

Introduction of a study on vitamin D status: explains UVB skin synthesis as the main vitamin D source and introduces traditional East African populations as an evolutionary reference for optimal 25(OH)D levels.
Study methods: describes the sample of Maasai pastoralists and Hadzabe hunter-gatherers in Tanzania, with their ages and sex distribution, and the goal of measuring serum 25(OH)D.
Population characteristics and measurement: notes skin type VI, clothing and outdoor habits, LC-MS/MS assay, and begins reporting mean serum 25(OH)D for Maasai (119 nmol/l) and Hadzabe.
Results: gives Hadzabe mean 25(OH)D (109 nmol/l) and ranges, reports no link to age, sex or BMI, and states the pooled mean of about 115 nmol/l in traditionally living people.

Conclusion: argues it is uncertain whether the traditional 115 nmol/l level is optimal for Western lifestyles, and suggests investigating it alongside other calcium homeostasis factors changed since the agricultural revolution.
Case report on a penetrating eye injury caused by a falling durian fruit during harvesting, recommending facial and eye protection in durian harvesting season.

Introduces the document's topic: hepatotoxicity of Ganoderma lucidum (Lingzhi) mushroom powder, first reported in a Hong Kong patient in 2004, and a 2005 fatal fulminant hepatitis case; notes patients previously tolerated boiled Lingzhi and other drugs before switching to powder.

Concludes the case report: after 1-2 months of switching to Lingzhi powder, hepatotoxicity occurred in both patients, so the toxic role of the powder, especially combined with other drugs, needs close future monitoring.
Introduction to the bitter melon prostate cancer study: background on prostate cancer mortality, limits of advanced-disease treatment, and the rationale for dietary prevention.
Background continued: dietary prevention of prostate cancer and the traditional Ayurvedic use of bitter melon (Momordica charantia), followed by the study's in vitro design using PC3 and LNCaP cells.
Mechanistic in vitro findings: bitter melon extract (BME) causes S-phase cell cycle accumulation in prostate cancer cells and modulates cyclin D1, cyclin E, and p21 expression.
Apoptosis and in vivo findings: BME increases Bax, induces PARP cleavage, and oral BME gavage delays progression to high-grade PIN in TRAMP mice (31%).

Conclusion of the abstract: BME-fed mice show about 51% reduced PCNA, and the authors conclude oral BME slows prostate cancer progression in TRAMP mice by disrupting cell cycle progression and proliferation.

Introduction to a review of bitter melon (Momordica charantia), covering its pharmacology, clinical efficacy, adverse effects, drug interactions, and therapeutic role, with emphasis on its use as an alternative therapy for lowering blood glucose in diabetes and its insulin-like structural components.

Summarizes the evidence base: in vitro antiviral and antineoplastic findings, and four small, non-randomized, non-double-blind clinical trials showing a moderate hypoglycemic effect of bitter melon juice, fruit, and dried powder, followed by the start of the list of reported adverse effects.

Lists the reported adverse effects of bitter melon (hypoglycemic coma and convulsions in children, reduced fertility in mice, favism-like syndrome, liver enzyme elevations in animals, headaches) and notes additive interaction risk with other glucose-lowering agents, leading into the call for adequately powered randomized placebo-controlled trials.

Concludes the review: rigorous randomized, placebo-controlled trials are needed before routine recommendation, and current data are insufficient to support bitter melon use for hypoglycemia without careful supervision and monitoring.

Opening of the trial abstract for a study of Momordica charantia (Ampalaya) capsules in type 2 diabetes, stating the background rationale and the primary objective of lowering HbA1c in poorly controlled diabetic patients.

Study design and setting: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at the Philippine General Hospital outpatient clinics (April to September 2004) enrolling 40 adult type 2 diabetics with HbA1c between 7% and 9%.
Intervention details: patients on standard therapy were randomized to M. charantia capsules (two capsules three times daily after meals for 3 months) or placebo at the same dose.

Endpoint definitions: the primary endpoint was change in HbA1c, secondary endpoints were fasting blood sugar, cholesterol, and weight, and safety endpoints included creatinine, liver enzymes (ALT, AST), sodium, potassium, and adverse events.
Main results: baseline characteristics were similar, and the between-group difference in HbA1c change was 0.22% favoring M. charantia (95% CI -0.40 to 0.84, P=0.4825), not statistically significant.

Remaining results and conclusion opening: no significant effect on fasting glucose, cholesterol, weight, or safety labs; adverse events were few and mild; the study is described as the first RCT on the hypoglycemic effect of M. charantia.

Power analysis and interpretation: the trial targeted a 1% HbA1c decline with 88% power but achieved only 11% power for the observed 0.24% decline, so no definite conclusion on effectiveness can be drawn.
Final conclusion: the study's results can be used to estimate sample size for larger future trials of M. charantia in diabetes.

Introduction to the study: rare, poorly prognosed adrenocortical carcinoma, dietary cancer prevention, bitter melon background, and the use of human and mouse adrenocortical cancer cell lines to test bitter melon extract (BME) as an anticancer agent.

Methods and first results: BME protein concentrations were measured, BME dose-dependently reduced adrenocortical cancer cell proliferation, and blueberry, zucchini, and acorn squash extracts showed no antiproliferative effect.
Apoptosis findings: BME-induced apoptosis in adrenocortical cancer cells with increased caspase-3 activation and PARP cleavage, plus BME raising p53, p21, and ATF3 levels.
Cell cycle and survival mechanisms: BME suppressed G1/S cyclins D1, D2, and D3 and MAPK8 (JNK) expression, suggesting regulation of cell cycle and cell survival pathways.
Steroidogenesis and CDK7 findings: BME decreased key steroidogenesis proteins and reduced phosphorylation of CDK7, which is needed in part for steroidogenic factor 1 (SF-1) activation.

IGF-1 receptor signaling: BME significantly reduced IGF-1 receptor levels and downstream signaling, shown by lower phosphorylated AKT, with concluding summary of bitter melon's multi-mechanism inhibition of adrenocortical cancer proliferation.
Concluding sentence summarizing that bitter melon inhibits adrenocortical cancer cell proliferation through modulation of diverse mechanisms.

Introduction of a study on Yerba Mate tea and bone health: background on its popularity in South America and the lack of prior research, then the study design selecting postmenopausal women who drank at least 1 L daily for 4+ years (n=146) and matching them to non-drinkers by age and time since menopause.

Study methods continuing from the cohort description: bone mineral density was measured by DXA at the lumbar spine and femoral neck, and the passage begins reporting results, with Yerba Mate drinkers showing higher lumbar spine BMD (0.952 vs 0.858 g/cm2).

Key results of the study: Yerba Mate drinkers had 9.7% higher lumbar spine BMD and 6.2% higher femoral neck BMD versus controls, with p-values, and multiple regression identified Yerba Mate drinking as a factor positively correlated with BMD apart from body mass index.

Conclusion of the abstract: regression findings for femoral neck BMD, the authors' interpretation that chronic Yerba Mate consumption has a protective effect on bone, and the copyright notice from Elsevier (2011).

Introduction to Ilex paraguariensis (yerba mate): its traditional preparation as a brewed tea, its origins with the Guarani, its social role in South America, and its use as a caffeine source and therapeutic agent.
Context on the research gap: biomedical study of yerba mate has lagged behind green tea and coffee, but literature on its properties has grown several-fold over the past 15 years.

Summary of the range of effects studied in the past 15 years: antioxidant, vasodilating, lipid-reducing, antimutagenic, anti-glycation, weight-reduction effects, and a controversial link to oropharyngeal cancer.

Statement of the review's aim: a concise summary of the last three years of research, emphasizing translational studies, inflammation and lipid metabolism, with mention of promising human intervention results.

Key human findings: mate lowers LDL-cholesterol in dyslipoproteinemia with effects synergistic with statins, and it improves plasma antioxidant capacity and antioxidant enzyme expression; also introduces the inconclusive cancer evidence.

Discussion of cancer risk: evidence linking heavy mate consumption to neoplasias is inconclusive, though contamination with alkylating agents during leaf drying should be avoided; also begins the review of antimutagenic findings.

Antimutagenic and weight-reduction evidence: protection against DNA double-strand breaks in cell and mouse studies, weight loss in mice and rats, and mechanisms including pancreatic lipase inhibition, AMPK activation and uncoupling of electron transport.
Anti-inflammatory evidence from animal studies, notably protection against cigarette-induced lung inflammation via effects on macrophage migration and inactivation of matrix metalloproteinases.

Overall conclusions: confirmed antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimutagenic and lipid-lowering activities, with support for benefits in chronic inflammatory diseases and lipid disorders, while noting the lack of double-blind randomized clinical trials.
Closing copyright notice (Elsevier Ireland Ltd, 2010) for the minireview.
Introduction to the study: dental amalgam's mercury content (50% Hg) and how Hg vapour from amalgam fillings accumulates in body fluids, organs, and maternal-foetal tissues and breast milk.

Continuation on maternal amalgam transfer to foetal and breast-milk compartments, followed by US population statistics: 181.1 million Americans with 1.46 billion restored teeth, including young children, mostly restored with amalgam.
Methods overview: using US body weight and restored-surface frequency data plus urinary Hg increment research to estimate amalgam-related Hg exposure across five US age groups.
Exposure modelling: three scenarios progressively reduce the number of amalgam-restored tooth surfaces, with the least conservative scenario giving the basis for the exposure estimates.
Key results: 67.2 million Americans exceed the US EPA reference exposure level (0.3 μg/m³) and 122.3 million exceed the California EPA REL (0.03 μg/m³) under the least conservative scenario.

Concluding findings: estimates match Health Canada's 1995 figures, giving 0.2–0.4 μg/day per amalgam surface or 0.5–1 μg/day per amalgam-filled tooth depending on age; includes the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
Final fragment of the document: the tail of the copyright notice (Elsevier B.V., 2011, all rights reserved).

Background and aims of a study on vanillin's effects on the HT-29 colorectal cancer cell line, introducing vanillin as a flavoring agent with known anti-mutagenic properties and its unexplored role in cancer.

Methods section listing the experimental assays used to test vanillin's cytolytic and cytostatic effects on HT-29 cells, including viability, AO-EB staining, cell cycle, annexin V-PI apoptosis, and BrdU proliferation assays.

Results showing vanillin induces apoptosis in HT-29 cells, with IC50 values of 400 µg/ml for cancer cells versus 1000 µg/ml for normal NIH/3T3 cells, and concentration-dependent cell cycle arrest at different checkpoints.

Specific cell cycle findings: G0/G1 arrest at lower vanillin concentration (200 µg/ml) by BrdU assay, and G2/M arrest at higher concentration (1000 µg/ml) by flow cytometry, followed by the conclusion that vanillin may be a colorectal cancer preventive agent.

Closing conclusion noting vanillin's potential as a colorectal cancer preventive agent based on its cytolytic and cytostatic effects, and calling for future in vivo animal studies to confirm these effects.
Abstract of a study on vanillin sensitizing TRAIL-resistant HeLa cervical cancer cells; introduces TRAIL as an anticancer agent and vanillin's prior antimetastatic and antiangiogenic effects.

Methods section of the vanillin/TRAIL HeLa study: WST-1 viability assay, caspase-3 activation and PARP cleavage by immunoblot, and TRAIL pathway and NF-kappaB assessment via immunoblot and luciferase reporter.
Results section of the vanillin/TRAIL HeLa abstract: vanillin pretreatment enhances TRAIL-induced apoptotic cell death and begins describing inhibition of TRAIL-induced NF-kappaB pathway activation.

Results and conclusion of the vanillin/TRAIL HeLa abstract: vanillin blocks TRAIL-induced p65 phosphorylation and NF-kappaB transcriptional activity, concluding vanillin sensitizes cells to TRAIL apoptosis via NF-kappaB inhibition.

Abstract of a study on vanilla extract as a bacterial quorum sensing inhibitor, introducing the aim and the methods: 75% aqueous methanol extraction of vanilla beans tested on Chromobacterium violaceum CV026.

Methods and results of the vanilla study: violacein production in C. violaceum CV026 measured spectrophotometrically, showing concentration-dependent reduction by vanilla extract, followed by the conclusion that vanilla inhibits quorum sensing.

Conclusions and significance section of the vanilla quorum sensing study, suggesting vanilla-containing food may promote human health by inhibiting bacterial quorum sensing and pathogenesis, and calling for isolation of the active substances.
Final sentence of the vanilla study's significance section, calling for further work to isolate the specific compounds in vanilla extract that act as quorum sensing inhibitors.

Introduction and methods opening of a case-control study on Mediterranean diet adherence, antioxidant intake, and spontaneous conversion of atrial fibrillation; sets up 800 subjects, 400 with first-detected AF.

Methods continuation describing dietary assessment: a validated food frequency questionnaire plus a 7-day diet recall, with adherence scored by the Mediterranean Score and antioxidant intake calculated from food.
Results comparing Mediterranean Scores between AF patients and controls (lower in AF, p<0.001, with mean and median values) and showing lower estimated total antioxidant intake in AF patients.

Results on conversion outcomes: highest-quartile Mediterranean Score associated with higher odds of spontaneous AF conversion (OR 1.9), and high antioxidant intake also linked to higher conversion odds (OR 1.8).

Statistical detail on the antioxidant association (OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.56-2.99, P<0.01) followed by the conclusions: AF patients had lower MedD adherence and antioxidant intake, and higher Med Scores predicted spontaneous conversion.
Final conclusion sentence restating that higher Mediterranean Score predicts spontaneous AF conversion, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.

Background and methods of a study on energy drinks and platelet/endothelial function: introduces the link between energy drinks, myocardial infarction, and the hypothesis, then describes the 50 healthy volunteers enrolled.

Methods continued: testing protocol before and 1 hour after drinking a sugar-free energy drink, with platelet aggregation measured by ADP-induced optical aggregometry and endothelial function measured by peripheral arterial tonometry as the reactive hyperemia index.
Results begin: reports the significant rise in ADP-induced platelet aggregation after energy drink consumption compared with the control condition, with the specific percentage values and P value.

Results continued: reports the decline in reactive hyperemia index (endothelial function) after energy drink use versus control, the significant rise in mean arterial pressure, and that heart rate was unchanged, followed by the start of the conclusion.
Conclusion and copyright: summarizes that energy drinks acutely increase platelet aggregation and reduce endothelial function in healthy young adults, and carries the 2010 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduction and objective of a study on acute effects of coffee on endothelial function, measured by brachial artery flow-mediated dilation (FMD), in healthy subjects; background on caffeine and antioxidants in coffee.

Study methods: 20 healthy non-obese subjects (10 men, 10 women) in a double-blind crossover design, ingesting one cup of caffeinated or decaffeinated Italian espresso in random order at 5-7 day intervals.
Results for FMD: after caffeinated coffee, FMD declined significantly over 60 minutes (7.7% to 6.0%), while decaffeinated coffee produced no significant increase (6.9% to 8.5%, P=0.115).

Further results: caffeinated coffee significantly raised systolic and diastolic blood pressure (not seen with decaf); blood glucose was unchanged, while insulin and C-peptide decreased significantly only after caffeinated coffee.
Conclusions: caffeinated coffee acutely produced unfavorable cardiovascular effects, especially on endothelial function, and likely reduced insulin secretion in the fasting state.
Closing conclusion: future studies are needed to determine whether caffeinated coffee has clinically relevant detrimental effects, particularly in unhealthy subjects.

Introduction to a study on caffeine and vascular function: background on caffeine's widespread use, its unclear cardiovascular/hypertension effects, and the stated aim of testing its effect on endothelial function in humans.

Study design and methods: a double-blind, randomized placebo-controlled trial in healthy young men measuring forearm blood flow responses to acetylcholine (endothelium-dependent) and sodium nitroprusside (endothelium-independent) before and after oral caffeine or placebo.

Methods and initial results: caffeine 300 mg vs. placebo groups (n=10 each), FBF measured by strain-gauge plethysmography; caffeine raised systolic and diastolic blood pressure but did not change heart rate or baseline blood flow.

Key results: caffeine enhanced forearm blood flow response to acetylcholine, while nitroprusside-induced vasodilation was unchanged; L-NMMA (nitric oxide synthase inhibitor) infusion abolished the caffeine-induced enhancement.

Placebo comparison and conclusion: placebo group showed no change in vasodilation responses over time; the authors conclude acute caffeine augments endothelium-dependent vasodilation in healthy young men via increased nitric oxide production.
Final conclusion sentence: the study's finding that acute caffeine improves endothelium-dependent vasodilation through increased nitric oxide production in healthy young men.

Introduces the study on how cooking methods affect oxalate content in vegetables, covering kidney stone (calcium oxalate) background, the enzymatic analysis of nine vegetables, and the finding that boiling strongly reduces soluble oxalate.

Compares cooking methods: boiling reduces soluble oxalate more than steaming, baking shows no loss for potatoes, cooking water recovers nearly all leached oxalate, and insoluble oxalate losses vary widely (0-74%).
Concludes that soluble oxalate is better absorbed than insoluble oxalate, so cooking methods that cut soluble oxalate may help reduce oxaluria and kidney stone risk in predisposed individuals.
Final fragment completing the document's last sentence on preventing kidney stone development through cooking methods that reduce soluble oxalate.

Study setup: methods section of a human trial comparing oxalate bioavailability from sugar beet fibre, spinach, and sodium oxalate solution in nine women using a Latin square design with breakfast dosing and 24-hour urine collection.

Study protocol and timing: the 2-day control period followed by three test periods (test day then control day), daily 24-hour urinary oxalate analysis, and the result that sugar beet fibre did not significantly raise oxalate excretion.

Key results: urinary oxalate excretion was significantly higher for spinach and sodium oxalate than for sugar beet fibre and control, and the estimated oxalate bioavailability values (0.7% for sugar beet fibre, 4.5% spinach, 6.2% oxalate solution).

Conclusion and explanation: the low oxalate bioavailability from sugar beet fibre is attributed to its high mineral (calcium and magnesium) to oxalate ratio, its complex fibre matrix, or loss of soluble oxalate during sugar beet processing.
Closing fragment of the discussion: completes the sentence on processing-related loss of soluble oxalate from sugar beets as a possible reason for low bioavailability.

Background and rationale of a study comparing hempseed oil and flaxseed oil as sources of the essential fatty acids linoleic acid (n-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (n-3), and their possible metabolic competition.
Study aim and stated knowledge gap: comparing hempseed and flaxseed oil effects on serum lipids, lipoprotein lipids, plasma glucose, insulin, and haemostatic factors in healthy humans.
Methods of the randomised, double-blind crossover trial: 14 healthy volunteers consumed 30 ml/day of hempseed or flaxseed oil for 4 weeks each, separated by a 4-week washout.

Key results on fatty acid profiles: hempseed oil raised linoleic and gamma-linolenic acid levels in serum cholesteryl esters and triglycerides, while flaxseed oil raised alpha-linolenic acid, with arachidonic acid differences in cholesteryl esters.
Remaining results: the hempseed period gave a lower total-to-HDL cholesterol ratio (trend), and no significant differences between periods in fasting lipids, glucose, insulin, or haemostatic factors.

Conclusions: hempseed and flaxseed oils differ significantly in their effects on serum lipid fatty acid profiles, but have only minor effects on total and lipoprotein lipids, glucose, insulin, and haemostatic factors.
Final fragment of the conclusions sentence noting no significant changes in haemostatic factors.
Introduction and aims of a study on how simulated commercial storage affects colored-flesh potato polyphenols, antioxidant activity, and anticancer effects on HCT-116 and HT-29 colon cancer cells.
Study design: seven potato clones (white, yellow, purple flesh) analyzed fresh and after 90 days of storage; antioxidant activity rose with storage across all clones.

Results on phenolics and anthocyanins: total phenolics increased with storage only in purple-fleshed clones, and advanced selection CO97227-2P/PW outperformed Purple Majesty; purple potatoes were most antiproliferative and pro-apoptotic against colon cancer cells.

Anticancer findings: extracts (10-30 μg/mL) from fresh and stored potatoes suppressed colon cancer cell proliferation and induced apoptosis versus solvent control, with stronger effects in fresh potatoes.

Conclusion on storage effects: storage duration correlated positively with antioxidant activity and viable cancer cell percentage and negatively with apoptosis, indicating antioxidant gains coincide with suppressed anticancer activity.

Final takeaway: farm-to-fork processing can raise antioxidant content while lowering health-relevant bioactivity, so quantitative chemistry must be paired with in vitro and/or in vivo biological assays.
Closing fragment of the final sentence recommending combined analytical and biological assays for evaluating post-harvest effects on plant food health benefits.

Study design and methods: 3T3-L1 adipocytes treated with purple sweet potato (PSP) extract at 1,000-3,000 μg/mL for 24 h, measuring adipocyte size, leptin secretion, and lipogenic/inflammatory/lipolytic gene and protein expression, as part of an anti-obesity and anti-inflammatory in vitro study.

Key results on adipogenesis and inflammation: PSP extract reduced leptin secretion (suggesting suppressed fat droplet growth), suppressed mRNA of lipogenic and inflammatory factors, and promoted lipolysis in 3T3-L1 adipocytes.

Antioxidant assessment: the PSP extract's antioxidative activity was measured by three in vitro assays (DPPH radical scavenging, ferric reducing ability potential, and transition metal ion chelating), introducing the concluding summary of the study.

Conclusion: the PSP extract shows antilipogenic, anti-inflammatory, and lipolytic effects on adipocytes, along with radical scavenging and reducing activity, summarizing the purple sweet potato study's findings.

Introduces the Harbin, China case-control study of diet and colorectal cancer, describing the 336 histologically confirmed incident cases (111 colon, 225 rectal) and matched non-neoplastic disease controls interviewed in hospital wards, and the methods of data collection.

Describes the dietary history questionnaire used to measure food consumption frequency and amounts, the statistical methods (odds ratios, confidence limits, multiple regression), and the main finding that vegetables, especially green vegetables, chives and celery, are strongly protective against colorectal cancer.

Summarizes the remaining dietary findings: lower intake of meat, eggs, bean products and grain raised rectal cancer risk, and alcohol intake was an important risk factor for colon cancer and male rectal cancer.
Introduces the study's validated SPE-derivatization-GC-MS method for measuring bisphenol A in canned foods, applied to 78 products, and states all levels fall below the EU 0.6 mg/kg migration limit.
Reports BPA levels by food type, with canned tuna showing the highest concentrations (mean 137 ng/g, max 534 ng/g) and noting that all products remain under the EU migration limit.

Compares BPA in soups: condensed soups contain much higher levels (mean 105, max 189 ng/g) than ready-to-serve soups (mean 15, max 34 ng/g), and notes that most canned vegetables are low (about 60% under 10 ng/g).
Compares tomato products, finding tomato paste has lower BPA (mean 1.1, max 2.1 ng/g) than pure tomato products (mean 9.3, max 23 ng/g).
Final fragment closing the sentence on pure tomato products, the last part of the tomato comparison within the canned food BPA study.

Introduction and objective of a study on dietary sodium and coronary flow reserve (CFR) in middle-aged male twins, stating the hypothesis that higher sodium intake is linked to lower microvascular function.
Study design: 286 male middle-aged twins had habitual sodium intake estimated via the Willett food-frequency questionnaire, and CFR was to be measured by PET with N13-ammonia.
Methods and key result: CFR was quantified at rest and under adenosine stress using mixed-effects regression, and each 1000 mg/d rise in sodium was associated with a 10.0% lower CFR after adjustment.
Quintile and within-pair results: CFR declined across sodium quintiles (P-trend = 0.03), with the highest quintile showing 20% lower CFR than the lowest, and the association held between brothers.

Within-pair finding and conclusions: a 1000 mg/d difference between brothers corresponded to a 10.3% CFR difference, and the authors conclude sodium is inversely linked to CFR independent of familial and genetic factors.
Closing conclusion and registration: the authors propose a novel mechanism for sodium's cardiovascular effects, and the trial is registered at clinicaltrials.gov as NCT00017836.

Background and aim of the C. zeylanicum (Ceylon cinnamon) vs. C. cassia glucose study: prior healthy-subject findings on C. cassia, and coumarin liver-risk rationale for studying the coumarin-free Ceylon variety in impaired glucose tolerance.

Study design: ten subjects with impaired glucose tolerance in a crossover trial, a standard 75 g OGTT given with placebo or C. zeylanicum capsules, and the outcomes measured (plasma glucose, insulin, GI, GII).

Methods detail: sampling protocol with finger-prick capillary glucose and venous insulin measured at baseline and 15 to 180 minutes after the OGTT start, followed by the main result that 6 g C. zeylanicum had no significant effect on glucose, insulin, GI or GII.

Conclusion and regulatory context: C. zeylanicum does not affect postprandial glucose or insulin, and the European Food Safety authority (EFSA) suggestion to replace C. cassia with Ceylon cinnamon or aqueous extracts to reduce coumarin exposure, with the caveat about losing C. cassia's glycaemic benefits.

Closing implication: the trade-off concluding the paper, where switching from C. cassia to lower-coumarin alternatives to limit coumarin exposure would forfeit the positive glycaemic effects seen with C. cassia in people with poor glycaemic control.

Opening chunk of a study on asthma exacerbations triggered by orange drinks: 272 asthma patients, 30 reporting reactions, and provocation tests with sulphur dioxide, sodium benzoate, and tartrazine in 14 patients.

Middle section of the asthma-and-food-additive study reporting which agent caused FEV1 drops (8 sulphur dioxide, 4 benzoate, 1 tartrazine), overlap between benzoate and sulphur dioxide sensitivity, and patient profiles (young extrinsic vs. middle-aged intrinsic asthma).

Concluding findings of the orange drink asthma study: cromoglycate pre-treatment inhibited reactions, sulphur dioxide as a food preservative had not previously been linked to asthma, and its widespread use in acidic foods and drinks.
Final sentence of the study recommending that sulphur dioxide be considered a possible cause in cryptogenic asthma and asthma apparently due to food allergy.

Study introduction: methods for measuring how polyphenol-containing beverages (coffee, herb teas, black tea, cocoa) affect non-haem iron absorption from a bread meal in adults, using radio-iron erythrocyte incorporation.

Beverage classification by polyphenol type (phenolic acids, monomeric flavonoids in herb teas, complex polymerized polyphenols in black tea and cocoa) and the main finding that all beverages inhibit iron absorption in a dose-dependent manner.

Quantitative results: inhibition of iron absorption relative to a water control, with 20-50 mg polyphenols/serving giving 50-70% reduction and 100-400 mg giving 60-90%, plus the specific inhibition figures for black tea and peppermint tea.

Comparative findings per beverage: black tea and peppermint tea inhibit most, pennyroyal, cocoa, vervain, lime flower and camomile progressively less; at equal polyphenol content black tea outperforms cocoa and several herb teas, equal to peppermint tea.

Conclusions: milk addition has little effect on coffee or tea inhibition; herb teas, black tea, coffee and cocoa are potent iron absorption inhibitors, with implications for dietary advice on iron nutrition.
Final fragment of the conclusion sentence, stating that this property should be considered when giving dietary advice on iron nutrition.
Opening of an abstract for a UK review on tea drinking and iron status: states the review's aims and describes the literature search method (35 black-tea iron studies).
Continues the abstract's Method and Results: study quality assessment, and the core finding that tea clearly limits nonheme iron absorption, but few studies examine actual iron status indicators.
Results section noting the evidence gap: no intervention studies, with conclusions drawn from 12 mostly non-UK observational studies showing negative associations between tea and iron status.
Results continue: observational studies linked tea drinking to lower blood iron indicators and more anemia, and multiple dietary and non-dietary factors complicate iron status.
Conclusion of the abstract: no restriction on tea for healthy people without iron deficiency risk; at-risk groups should drink tea between meals and wait at least 1 hour after eating.
Final fragment of the conclusion, completing the advice that at-risk groups should wait at least 1 hour after eating before drinking tea.

Introduces Heiner syndrome, a milk-caused food hypersensitivity pulmonary disease in infants, and the case series of eight patients: their age at diagnosis, early cow's milk feeding, and onset of respiratory symptoms.
Lists the clinical symptoms in the eight Heiner syndrome cases, including cough, wheezing, hemoptysis, recurrent otitis media, fever, gastrointestinal complaints, and failure to thrive.

Reports the diagnostic findings: radiologic pulmonary infiltrates in all cases, high precipitating antibody titers to milk proteins, milk-specific IgE results, and pulmonary hemosiderosis confirmed by iron-laden macrophages in one patient.

Describes additional lab findings (eosinophilia, anemia, elevated immunoglobulins) and the response to milk elimination, with rapid symptom improvement and clearing of infiltrates; also begins the milk challenge results.

Covers milk challenge outcomes: the three challenged patients relapsed, and one patient who tolerated milk briefly after two years of avoidance developed recurrent symptoms, precipitins, infiltrates and iron-laden macrophages; begins the clinical recommendations.

Gives the clinical takeaways: suspect Heiner syndrome in young children with unexplained chronic lung disease, support diagnosis with positive milk precipitins and response to milk elimination, and suspect pulmonary hemosiderosis with anemia or hemoptysis, confirmed by iron-laden macrophages.
Final sentence restating that pulmonary hemosiderosis in severe Heiner syndrome cases is confirmed by demonstrating iron-laden macrophages.

Introduces the retrospective study of cow's milk allergy (CMA) in Thai children at King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital (1998–2007), including the diagnostic criteria (symptom improvement on elimination, recurrence on reintroduction).

Describes the study population: 382 children with CMA (168 girls, 214 boys), average age at diagnosis 14.8 months (range 7 days–13 years), average symptom duration before diagnosis 9.2 months, and a 64.2% family history of atopic disease.

Reports maternal and clinical findings: all mothers increased cow's milk intake during pregnancy, and the most common presenting symptoms were respiratory (43.2%), gastrointestinal (22.5%), and skin (20.1%), with failure to thrive (10.9%) and anemia (2.8%) among less common ones.

Gives further symptom prevalence (delayed speech from chronic serous otitis media and anaphylactic shock, each 0.2%), prick skin test positivity (61.4%), exclusive breastfeeding rate (13.2%), and begins the list of treatment outcomes by formula type.

Details successful dietary treatments: soy formula (42.5%), partial hydrolysate formula (35.7%), extensive hydrolysate formula (14.2%), amino acid formula (1.7%), and continued breastfeeding with maternal cow's milk restriction (5.9%); concludes that CMA presents with varied manifestations, especially respiratory symptoms.
Concluding statement that CMA in Thai children shows a wide range of clinical manifestations, with respiratory symptoms being especially important and often overlooked.

Introduction of an allergy cohort study linking infant cow's milk allergy (CMA) to recurrent otitis media (ROM) and chronic ear infections in 56 milk-allergic vs 204 control schoolchildren, with the ROM result begins here.

Results comparing ROM (at least 15 acute otitis media episodes by age 10) and adenoidectomy/tympanostomy rates between CMA and control children, showing the difference applies only to children who developed respiratory atopy.

Findings on which atopic manifestations (asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis) predict ROM or secretory otitis media, plus the association of positive food versus inhalant skin prick tests with ear problems.
Concluding statement that children with infant CMA, even when properly treated, had significantly more ROM, with the risk linked to concomitant respiratory atopy development.

Introduces the study's aim: assessing in vitro cytotoxicity of Moringa stenopetala plant extracts in HEPG2 liver cells, using LDH leakage and viability as measures, with ATP and glutathione as functional markers.

Reports LDH leakage and viability results: ethanol leaf and seed extracts raised LDH leakage in a dose- and time-dependent way, while water leaf and ethanol root extracts did not; the highest concentration of ethanol leaf and seed extracts strongly reduced cell viability.
Describes ATP level changes: at 500 µg/mL the water leaf extract increased ATP and the ethanol leaf extract decreased it, while root and seed extracts had no significant effect on ATP.
Details glutathione (GSH) depletion by ethanol leaf and seed extracts and concludes the water leaf extract appears non-toxic, consistent with its use as a vegetable.

Concludes that ethanol leaf and seed extracts contain toxic substances extractable with organic solvents or formed during extraction, and notes ATP and GSH depletion only occurred at concentrations that also caused LDH leakage.
Recommends further identification of the toxic constituents and their in vivo and in vitro effects, and highlights cell culture as a useful screening method for plant extract toxicity.
Copyright notice for the article (Copyright 2005 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.), closing the document.

Introduction and aims of a study on Moringa oleifera leaf extract (MLE) antiproliferative and apoptotic effects on KB human tumor cells, framing medicinal plants and apoptosis as anticancer strategies.

Methods and first results: KB cells treated with MLE for 48 h, viability measured by MTT assay, showing dose-dependent inhibition of proliferation and introducing apoptosis and DNA fragmentation findings.

Mechanistic assays describing apoptosis evidence: DAPI and propidium iodide nuclear morphology staining, agarose gel electrophoresis of DNA fragmentation, and MLE-induced ROS production suggesting redox-sensitive mechanisms.
Phytochemical and conclusion section: HPTLC identifies phenolics quercetin and kaempferol in MLE, and the authors conclude the extract has strong antiproliferative and apoptosis-inducing activity.
Final concluding statement that M. oleifera leaf extract has potential for cancer chemoprevention and as a therapeutic target, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.
Introduction of a systematic review and meta-analysis on pasteurization's effects on milk vitamins and raw milk health claims (allergies, cancer, lactose intolerance), setting up the study's purpose.
Describes the review's scope: 40 studies on pasteurization and vitamin levels, with qualitative findings that B12 and E decreased and A increased after pasteurization.
Presents random-effects meta-analysis results for vitamin B6 (not significant) and reports SMD and confidence intervals for vitamin B1 decreases, beginning the list of significant vitamin reductions.
Reports significant meta-analytic decreases for vitamins B2, C, and folate after pasteurization, and concludes the nutritive impact is minimal because these vitamins occur at low natural levels.

Notes that milk is an important source of vitamin B2 so heat treatment matters, and summarizes raw milk's possible protective link to allergy (six studies), flagged as potentially confounded by farming factors.

Concludes that raw milk showed no association with cancer (two studies) or lactose intolerance (one study), and cautions that findings are limited by poor methodological quality across included studies.

Introduction and background of the study on Hibiscus sabdariffa: its traditional Mexican uses for hypertension and related conditions, and prior evidence that its blood-pressure effect is mediated by ACE inhibition.
Study aim and methods overview: the goal of isolating the ACE-inhibiting constituents of the aqueous Hibiscus sabdariffa extract, using bioassay-guided fractionation of dried calyces.

Methodology details and initial results: preparative reversed-phase HPLC with an in vitro ACE inhibition assay as the activity monitor, spectroscopic characterization, and identification of the anthocyanin delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside (1) and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside (2).

Key quantitative and mechanistic results: IC50 values of about 84.5 and 68.4 µg/mL for compounds 1 and 2, comparable to related flavonoid glycosides, and kinetic evidence of competitive inhibition at the enzyme's active site.

Conclusions: the competitive ACE inhibitory activity of anthocyanins 1 and 2 is reported for the first time, consistent with the folk antihypertensive use of Hibiscus sabdariffa calyces; includes the 2009 Elsevier copyright notice.
Final fragment of the copyright statement (Elsevier Ireland Ltd., 2009) closing the abstract.

Case report introduction: annatto dye (from Bixa orellana seeds) as a food colorant, prior reports of urticaria/angioedema, and this patient's anaphylaxis (urticaria, angioedema, hypotension) after milk and Fiber One cereal containing annatto.

Case report diagnostic workup: negative skin tests to milk, wheat, and corn; strong positive skin test to annatto dye versus no response in controls; SDS-PAGE of the nondialyzable annatto fraction showing two ~50 kD protein bands.

Mechanism findings and conclusion of the annatto anaphylaxis case: immunoblot shows patient-specific IgE binding to one ~50 kD band, suggesting contaminating or residual seed proteins cause IgE hypersensitivity, making annatto a rare cause of anaphylaxis.
Final concluding sentence of the annatto dye case report, stating that annatto dye is a potential rare cause of anaphylaxis.

Introduction/background of the INTERSTROKE case-control study (22 countries) on risk factors for ischaemic and intracerebral haemorrhagic stroke, stating aims: association of risk factors with stroke subtypes, their population burden, and differences from myocardial infarction.
Methods section describing the standardised multinational case-control design (2007-2010): acute first-stroke cases within 5 days of onset, and age- and sex-matched controls without stroke history.

Methods continued: data collection via structured questionnaire, physical examination, and blood/urine samples, and the analytic approach of computing odds ratios and population-attributable risks for stroke subtypes.

Findings section opening with the sample of the first 3000 cases (78% ischaemic, 22% intracerebral haemorrhagic) and 3000 controls, and the first significant risk factors for all stroke: hypertension, smoking, waist-to-hip ratio, diet, with their ORs and PARs.
Findings continued with ORs and PARs for all stroke: physical activity (protective), diabetes, and alcohol intake, showing effect sizes and confidence intervals for each risk factor.
Findings continued with ORs and PARs for psychosocial stress, depression, cardiac causes, and the apolipoprotein B to A1 ratio as risk factors for all stroke.

Key combined results: the ten risk factors together account for 88.1% of population-attributable risk for all stroke, rising to 90.3% under an alternate hypertension definition, and all significant for ischaemic stroke.

Subtype results for intracerebral haemorrhage (hypertension, smoking, waist-to-hip ratio, diet, alcohol) and the interpretation that ten risk factors account for about 90% of stroke risk, with implications for interventions.

Conclusion recommending targeted interventions on blood pressure, smoking, physical activity, and healthy diet to reduce stroke burden, followed by the funding sources (CIHR, Heart and Stroke Foundation, Pfizer, Merck, AstraZeneca, Boehringer Ingelheim).
Closing copyright notice (Elsevier Ltd., 2010) ending the abstract of the INTERSTROKE study.

Opening chunk of the abstract on ascorbic acid degradation kinetics in amla (Phyllanthus emblica) and pure ascorbic acid solutions, studied at 50-120 °C, establishing first-order kinetics and the temperature range.

Continuation of the abstract covering Arrhenius modeling of temperature dependence and the reported activation energies (4.09 kcal/mole for amla, 4.49 kcal/mole for pure vitamin solution), plus the start of the cooking-method comparison.

Abstract section describing evaluation of ascorbic acid loss in open pan cooking, pressure cooking, and the patented EcoCooker (unsteady-state heating), and a mathematical model built from steady-state kinetic parameters to predict losses from time-temperature data.
Concluding sentence of the abstract stating that ascorbic acid degradation is of a similar order of magnitude across all cooking methods tested.

Opening of the abstract on garlic (Allium sativum) antiplatelet activity: introduces raw garlic's antiplatelet effects and the study's setup of heating crushed vs. uncrushed cloves and monitoring allicin and pyruvate.

Results on cooking effects: oven-heating at 200 °C or boiling for 3 min or less left antiaggregatory activity intact, and the paragraph begins describing the 6-minute heating effect on uncrushed vs. crushed samples.

Findings on heating duration and microwaving: 6-minute heating abolished activity in uncrushed but not crushed garlic, prolonged incubation (over 10 min) fully suppressed it, and microwaved garlic showed no effect alone.

Findings on microwaved garlic and juice supplementation: dose-response effect seen only in crushed microwaved samples, and adding raw garlic juice to uncrushed microwaved garlic restored full antiplatelet activity.

Conclusions: allicin and thiosulfinates appear responsible for the antiplatelet effect, crushing before moderate cooking limits activity loss, and the reduced effect of crushed-cooked garlic may be offset by consuming more.
Final conclusion sentence: the partial loss of antithrombotic effect in crushed-then-cooked garlic may be compensated by eating a larger amount.

Introduces Naegleria fowleri as a free-living amoeba found in warm freshwater, defines it as the cause of fatal primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), and notes rising case counts. Opening background of the review on Naegleria fowleri infections in recreational waters.

Explains why PAM is hard to diagnose (symptoms mimic bacterial meningitis), so physician awareness and clinical suspicion are key. Continues the document's background on PAM's rising incidence and diagnostic challenges.

States the review's purpose: to raise awareness among travel medicine practitioners and the tourism industry, covering PAM's presenting features, prevention, and treatment. Closing statement of scope, followed by the copyright notice.

Introduces the clinical trial on prunes (Prunus domestica) and liver function, describing the 166 healthy volunteers randomized into three groups and the low (3 prunes) and high (6 prunes) soaking doses.

Describes the trial protocol: test groups drank prune juice and ate the whole fruit daily for 8 weeks while controls drank water, with blood drawn at weeks 0 and 8 for chemical analysis, and reports the first significant result, the reduction in serum alanine transaminase.

Reports the trial's key liver-function results: significant drops in alanine transaminase (p 0.048) and alkaline phosphatase (p 0.017) with the lower prune dose, no change in aspartate transaminase or bilirubin, and the authors' conclusion that prunes may benefit hepatic disease.
Final sentence of the report concluding that prunes might prove beneficial in hepatic disease, closing the summary of the liver-function trial.

Introduction of a 2011 literature review on the safety assessment of genetically modified (GM) plants, opening with concern about GM food safety and calls from consumers and NGOs for long-term animal feeding studies before approval.

Background on the authors' earlier reviews of GM food/plant toxicological and health-risk literature in 2000 and 2006, which found very few such studies, and statement of the review's main goal: assessing the current state of GM plant safety for human consumption.

Describes the growth in published citations on GM plant safety in PubMed and Scopus since 2006, notes that no new studies were found for crops such as potatoes, cucumber, peas, or tomatoes, and introduces the crops covered: maize, rice, and soybeans.

Summarizes the research landscape: studies are evenly split between those finding GM maize and soybean varieties as safe and nutritious as conventional counterparts and those raising serious safety concerns.

Notes a caveat that most safety studies were run by biotechnology companies that commercialize the GM plants, and frames the findings as a notable advance over the scarcity of company-published studies in recent years.
Concluding sentence stating that the recent literature is critically reviewed, followed by the 2011 Elsevier copyright notice.

Introduces Chinese wild rice's long history of consumption and its unestablished food safety, then summarizes its nutritional profile (higher protein, ash, fibre) and low levels of arsenic, cadmium and lead, plus a human eating-pattern study of elderly people showing no ill-effects.

Reports animal safety testing of Chinese wild rice: acute toxicity in mice fed 21.5 g/kg diet showed no abnormal reactions or deaths, and bone marrow micronucleus, sperm abnormality and Salmonella mutagenicity tests were all negative.
Concludes the investigation, stating that Chinese wild rice is safe for human consumption.
Introduction and rationale for a 1997–1998 study of heavy metals in wild rice from north-central Wisconsin, motivated by known contamination elsewhere and the lack of prior Wisconsin data.
Study design: wild rice collection sites in six northern Wisconsin counties (Sept 1997 and 1998), with plants divided into roots, stems, leaves and seeds for elemental analysis.

Sample size and methods: 194 samples from 51 plants, averaging 49 per plant part, cleaned, wet digested and analyzed by ICP for ten elements (Ag, As, Cd, Cr, Cu, Hg, Mg, Pb, Se, Zn); begins listing where metals concentrate, with roots highest for several elements.

Results on tissue distribution: roots had the highest Ag, As, Cd, Cr, Hg, Pb and Se; Cu peaked in roots and seeds, Zn in seeds, Mg in leaves; seed baseline ranges set from 95% confidence intervals of medians.

Key findings and health implications: seed levels of nutritional elements Cu, Mg and Zn were normal, Ag, Cd, Hg, Cr and Se were low or normal, but As and Pb were elevated, posing possible human health risk.
Conclusion on source: the likely pathway for As, Hg and Pb uptake into the plants is atmospheric deposition.

Introduces the phenolic and vitamin C profile of Scottish-grown red raspberries, naming the key anthocyanins and ellagitannins (sanguiin H-6, lambertianin C), as the opening of a study on freezing and storage effects on raspberry phytochemicals.

Reports that freezing did not change antioxidant capacity, vitamin C, or phenolic levels, then describes a simulated supply-chain storage test (4 °C for 3 days, then 18 °C for 24 h) where anthocyanins held steady, vitamin C fell, and ellagitannins rose.

Summarizes that overall antioxidant capacity was unchanged after storage, and concludes that fresh-picked, fresh commercial, and frozen raspberries contain similar phytochemical and antioxidant levels per serving.
Closing fragment of the conclusion stating that freshly picked, commercial, and frozen raspberries provide similar amounts of phytochemicals and antioxidants per serving.

Introduces the study's background: fructose malabsorption causes GI intolerance, glucose enhances fructose absorption, and the hypothesis that paracellular erythritol absorption might similarly enhance fructose absorption in healthy adults.

Describes the design: a randomized, double-masked, controlled crossover study of 37 nondiabetic healthy adults, with the proposed glucose-enhancement pathway as the mechanistic rationale for testing erythritol.

Details the methods: after an overnight fast, participants drank one of three beverages (fructose+glucose, fructose+equimolar erythritol, or fructose alone), with breath hydrogen measured over 8 hours and GI symptoms and stool data over 24 hours.

Reports the key breath hydrogen results: the fructose+erythritol AUC was 2 times that of fructose alone and 8.75 times that of fructose+glucose (P < .001), indicating greater malabsorption with erythritol.

Summarizes the symptom outcomes and conclusion: fructose+erythritol increased watery stools and worsened GI tolerance versus the other beverages (P < .05), suggesting equimolar coingestion increases carbohydrate malabsorption; includes copyright notice.
Trailing fragment of the copyright line (Elsevier Inc., 2011, all rights reserved) from the end of the abstract; contains no substantive study content.

Opening of the Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline on vitamin D deficiency: states the guideline's objective (evaluation, treatment, prevention, focus on at-risk patients) and describes the Task Force composition and absence of corporate funding.

Describes the consensus process behind the guideline: systematic evidence reviews, conference calls, and successive review by Endocrine Society subcommittees, cosponsoring associations, and member review on the society website.

Continues the methods description of stakeholder review with written comments and revisions, then begins the conclusions by noting that vitamin D deficiency is very common and few foods contain vitamin D, motivating supplementation recommendations.

Core recommendations: supplementation at suggested daily intake and tolerable upper limit levels by age and clinical circumstances, serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D measurement by a reliable assay as the initial diagnostic test for at-risk patients, and treatment with vitamin D2 or D3 for deficiency.
Final guideline limitations: insufficient evidence to recommend screening people not at risk for deficiency, or prescribing vitamin D for noncalcemic cardiovascular benefit.
Concluding fragment of the sentence on noncalcemic cardiovascular protection, ending the document's statement that evidence does not yet support vitamin D for cardiovascular benefit.

Abstract opening of a review on vitamin D as an adjunct treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis, covering its pre-antibiotic-era use and renewed interest driven by 1alpha,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D's immunomodulatory effects.

Abstract closing of a review on vitamin D in pulmonary tuberculosis, stating its aims to discuss host-response mechanisms against Mycobacterium tuberculosis and to review three clinical trials and ten case series using vitamin D in treatment.

Opening of the document: introduces tuberculosis as a major cause of mortality (1.68 million deaths in 2009), the high prevalence of latent M. tuberculosis infection, and the need for new agents due to drug-resistant strains.

Covers the historical and mechanistic background of vitamin D in TB: its use in the pre-antibiotic era, the immune-enhancing role of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D against mycobacteria, and the common vitamin D deficiency seen in active TB patients, leading into adjunctive treatment trials.

Discusses the conflicting results of clinical trials on adjunctive vitamin D treatment for active TB, attributing the inconsistency to differences in baseline vitamin D status, dosing, and outcomes, and notes high vitamin D deficiency among people with latent TB infection.

Summarises observational evidence linking vitamin D deficiency with increased reactivation risk in latent TB across high- and low-burden settings, and states that randomised controlled trials of vitamin D for preventing active TB have not yet been done.
Concludes that trials of vitamin D supplementation for TB prevention are a research priority, citing its safety, low cost, and the potentially large public health impact if results are positive.
Abstract-style introduction of a study on vegetarian diets and nutrient status (B12, folate, vitamins A/E/D, homocysteine, antioxidant status, iron) in Polish children.
Methods section: the study population of 50 children aged 5-11 (32 vegetarian, 18 omnivore) recruited from the Institute of Mother and Child, with age details for each group.
Methods section describing dietary analysis software (Dietetyk2) and the laboratory assays used for folate, B12, homocysteine, and TAS (total antioxidant status).
Methods section on HPLC for vitamins A and E, ELISA for vitamin D, and iron-marker kits; also the start of the results, reporting dietary intake of vitamin B12 in vegetarian children.
Results on dietary intakes of B12, folate, vitamins A, E and D versus reference allowances, and serum levels of B12, folate, vitamins A and E and D in vegetarian children.
Results comparing vegetarian and omnivorous children: homocysteine and vitamin A were similar, while vitamin E was lower; also the start of the TAS comparison.
Results reporting lower TAS and vitamin E in vegetarians (p<0.05 and p<0.0001), normal iron markers, and the start of the conclusion on B12, folic acid, homocysteine and iron.
Conclusion discussing the adequacy of B12 and folate intake, minor effects of high vitamin A and low vitamin E, and the link between lower vitamin E and lower total antioxidant status.
Final conclusion: insufficient vitamin D intake and low serum levels need monitoring in vegetarian children, and age-appropriate supplementation should be considered to prevent deficiency.

Introduction and setup of a study on dexamethasone (glucocorticoid) effects on lipid metabolism in broiler chicken skeletal muscle, including animal details (35-day-old male Arbor Acres chickens, 3-day treatment) and the main finding that dexamethasone slows growth while increasing lipid accumulation.
Gene expression results in the glycolytic M. pectoralis major (PM) muscle under dexamethasone: increased GR, FATP1, H-FABP and LCAD mRNA, and decreased L-CPT1, AMPKα2 and LPL mRNA.

Further findings: decreased LPL activity in PM, increased GR, FATP1 and L-CPT1 mRNA in the oxidative M. biceps femoris (BF), reduced AMPK Thr172 phosphorylation and CPT1 activity in muscle, and the start of results for fed chickens (VLDLR and AMPK activity).

Results in fed chickens: dexamethasone raised VLDLR and muscle AMPK activity, impaired LPL and L-CPT1 mRNA and LPL activity in PM, boosted GR, LPL, H-FABP, L-CPT1, LCAD and AMPKα2 mRNA in BF, left ATGL protein unchanged, and begins the conclusion about fasting-state fatty acid utilisation.

Conclusions: in the fasting state, dexamethasone-retarded fatty acid utilisation may drive intramyocellular lipid accumulation in both PM and BF; in the fed state, it boosts transcription of genes for lipid uptake and oxidation.
Final concluding sentence: unmatched lipid uptake and utilisation are proposed as the mechanism behind augmented intramyocellular lipid accumulation after dexamethasone treatment in chicken muscle.

Introduction of a case report on severe metabolic alkalosis from baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) overdose, describing home use for indigestion and the risks of metabolic derangements and clinical signs such as seizures, dysrhythmias, and cardiopulmonary arrest.

Conclusion of the case report on baking soda overdose, presenting two patients with severe metabolic alkalosis from unsuspected antacid overdose and stating that the pathophysiology and presentation of antacid-related metabolic alkalosis are reviewed.

Case report opening: a six-week-old infant with life-threatening sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) poisoning after a mother gave it as a home remedy to help the baby burp, introducing the paper's literature review on baking soda misuse.

Closing of the paper's abstract: calls for warning labels on baking soda antacid products and urges clinicians to consider poisoning in the differential for altered mental status or status epilepticus at any age.

Case report opening: introduces a severe metabolic alkalosis caused by sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) ingestion, describing the emergency department presentation with a stable, alert patient showing only carpopedal spasm before sudden cardiopulmonary arrest.
